ADR-011: Serviceability consistency levels

Context. Serviceability is read ~10⁶ times per write. Stale answers at checkout cause paid, undeliverable orders (incident, 1,900 orders). The DB must not be a hard dependency for browsing.

Decision. (1) Browse is served from a per-pod in-memory snapshot, refreshed by events (~1–2 s) and a 30 s full reload, so staleness is ≤ 60 s including one missed reload. (2) Checkout does a fresh primary-key read with an 80 ms budget. (3) When a fresh check is unavailable, checkout fails closed with a retryable 503. (4) Rollout is SHADOW for one week, then ENFORCE.

Consequences. (+) Browse survives DB and Kafka outages. (+) Checkout correctness no longer depends on cache freshness. (−) Checkout availability now includes serviceability + its DB (99.95 % × 99.95 % ≈ 99.9 % for this step), accepted because a failed checkout is retryable and an undeliverable order is not. (−) One more Kafka topic and an outbox relay to operate.

Revisit when: serviceability moves from pincode to geofence polygons (dataset grows ~1000×), or checkout volume grows past what PK reads can serve.

docs.title: What changed from L1 to L4
docs.text:
Concern L1 L2 L3 L4 Storage HashMap PostgreSQL PostgreSQL + per-pod snapshot + outbox + Kafka Latency (browse) ~100 ns 1–3 ms + pool ~100 ns + HTTP same Survives DB outage n/a ❌ ✅ browse (stale) ✅ browse (stale) Staleness none none ≤ 30 s, measured ~1–2 s typical, ≤ 60 s worst, measured Checkout correctness n/a exact (if used) exact (fresh endpoint) exact and enforced, fail closed Multi-pod agreement n/a yes (shared DB) eventual, ≤ 30 s eventual, ~seconds Operability none ops can edit rows age metric, readiness + audit via version, shadow rollout Moving parts 1 2 2 4 (DB, relay, Kafka, listener) Right for learning internal tool single-region prod multi-team platform

Would you stop at L3?

Often, yes. If the business accepts ≤ 30 s browse staleness and checkout uses the fresh endpoint, L3 already fixes the incident with two fewer moving parts. L4's event path is worth it when many services need to react to serviceability changes (search index, slot-service, marketing) because then the event has several consumers. That judgement is exactly what B4 questions test.

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Detection signal Blast radius Mitigation DB down snapshot.reload.failures ↑, snapshot.age.seconds climbing, fresh 503s Browse: none (stale). Checkout: blocked (retryable). Stale-serving for browse; fail-closed checkout; DB HA (Ch 10, 27) Kafka down / relay stuck Outbox unpublished-row count ↑; consumer lag Browse staleness grows to ≤ 30 s Full reload safety net; alert on outbox backlog > 60 s Pod starts with no DB Readiness DOWN None: pod gets no traffic Readiness includes serviceabilitySnapshot Bad bulk change (ops disables a whole city) lookup{outcome=not_serviceable} rate spike All customers in the city Admin guardrail: changes affecting > 50 pincodes require two-person approval; version-based rollback Snapshot version goes backwards snapshot.version gauge decreases Serves older data getAndAccumulate never-go-backwards rule Serviceability slow → checkout slow checkout p99 ↑, serviceability.lookup{consistency=fresh} p99 ↑ Checkout latency 80 ms read timeout; latency budget in ADR Event storm (bulk import of 5K rows) Reload rate ↑ CPU on read pods reloadIfOlderThan coalescing; bulk imports publish one summary event

docs.title: 6.2 Observability
docs.text:
Signal Type Alert serviceability.snapshot.age.seconds Gauge per pod > 90 s for 2 min → page serviceability.snapshot.version Gauge per pod max − min across pods > 0 for > 2 min → ticket serviceability.snapshot.reload.failures Counter rate > 0 for 5 min → ticket serviceability.lookup{consistency,outcome} Timer fresh p99 > 50 ms (SLO burn) → page checkout.serviceability.decision{decision,mode} Counter UNKNOWN > 0.5 % of checkouts → page Outbox backlog (count(*) where published_at is null) Gauge > 100 rows or oldest > 60 s → page

Log fields: correlationId, pincode, consistency, snapshotVersion, outcome. Trace spans: serviceability.lookup (attr: consistency), db.select serviceable_area.

SLOs:

  • Browse availability 99.95 %, p99 ≤ 10 ms in-service.
  • Fresh availability 99.9 %, p99 ≤ 50 ms.
  • Staleness SLO: 99 % of minutes have max pod snapshot age ≤ 60 s.

Staleness is an SLO too

Teams write latency and availability SLOs and forget freshness. If a guarantee isn't measured, it isn't being kept.

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• The public endpoint only offers browse consistency, so external callers can't force DB reads. That closes a cheap DoS vector.
  • /internal/** is blocked at the gateway and by a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. Service identity via mTLS comes in Ch 23.
  • The admin API requires an ops role. Every change records updated_by and flows to audit-service.
  • Pincode is not PII on its own, but combined with a user ID it's location data. Keep it out of public logs keyed by user.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance & tuning knobs
docs.text: Knob Default Guidance full-reload-interval 30 s Lower bound on worst-case staleness when events fail; 30 s × 3 pods = 0.1 reload/s, negligible jakarta.persistence.query.timeout 80 ms Must be below the checkout client's read timeout, or the client gives up before the server does Hikari maximum-pool-size 10 Fresh ≈ 350/s × 2 ms ≈ 0.7 concurrent (Little's Law). 10 is plenty. connection-timeout 250 ms Fail fast; queueing behind a sick DB turns latency into an outage Virtual threads on I/O-light service; removes thread-pool sizing as a concern (Ch 19)

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text: Three pods × 0.5 vCPU / 512 MB handle 6 K req/s. The Kafka topic is 1 partition with a few KB per day. The cost is dominated by the fixed platform overhead per service (CI, dashboards, on-call), not by compute. That's a real argument in the B4 question "should this be its own service?" (Q15).

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. The unstated NFR. Symptom: Behaviour determined by a constant someone picked (TTL = 6h). Cause: Requirements captured as features only. Fix: Every cache, timeout, and retry value traces back to a written NFR.

// ❌ before
@Cacheable(value = "serviceability")          // TTL configured somewhere as 6h "for performance"
public boolean isServiceable(String pincode) { ... }

// ✅ after: staleness is a named, configured, measured property tied to NFR-3
@Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${serviceability.snapshot.full-reload-interval:PT30S}")
public void reload() { ... }   // + snapshot.age.seconds gauge + alert

2. One consistency level for the whole system. Symptom: Either everything is slow (all strong) or correctness bugs appear (all cached). Fix: Assign consistency per use case (browse vs checkout).

3. Designing for scale you don't have, and skipping estimation. Symptom: Redis cluster plus sharding for a 2.4 MB dataset. Fix: Do the estimate first. The numbers in §4 showed memory beats every distributed option here.

4. Averages instead of percentiles. Symptom: "Average 40 ms," while the p99 is 1.2 s and checkout conversion drops. Fix: SLOs on p99/p999. Dashboards show percentiles and never average them across pods.

5. Silent fail-open on a correctness check.

// ❌ before: dependency failure silently means "yes"
try { return client.isServiceable(pin); } catch (Exception e) { return true; }

// ✅ after: explicit tri-state + explicit policy (ADR), measured
Decision d = client.checkFresh(pin);            // SERVICEABLE | NOT_SERVICEABLE | UNKNOWN
if (d == Decision.UNKNOWN) throw new DependencyUnavailableException("serviceability"); // fail closed

Fail-open vs fail-closed is a business decision. Make it deliberately, per check. Fail open for recommendations. Fail closed for payments and deliverability.

6. Dual write.

// ❌ before: DB commit succeeds, Kafka send fails → pods never learn about the change
repository.save(area);
kafkaTemplate.send("serviceability.area.changed.v1", event);

// ✅ after: outbox row in the same transaction; relay publishes at-least-once (L4)

7. Serving before ready. Symptom: Right after a deploy, new pods answer "not serviceable" for everything because the snapshot is empty. Fix: Readiness depends on the first successful load. Never default an empty dataset to a business answer.

8. Microservices by default. Symptom: A 5-person team runs 26 services, and every feature touches six repos. Fix: Draw bounded contexts first. Deploy them as a modular monolith until team or scaling needs justify a split (§2.8, Q15).

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What is system design, and how is HLD different from LLD?

30-second answer: System design is deciding how a software system's parts fit together so that it meets both its functional requirements and its quality requirements (scale, availability, latency, cost) under real-world failures. HLD covers the parts and their interactions: services, datastores, APIs, and data flow. LLD covers how each part is built inside: classes, schemas, algorithms, concurrency.

Deep answer: HLD for serviceability says "a service with an in-memory snapshot, PostgreSQL as the source of truth, and Kafka for change events." LLD says "an immutable record in an AtomicReference, reloaded in a repeatable-read transaction." The two meet where a low-level parameter encodes a high-level requirement, like a cache TTL.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Time spent on HLD is cheaper than time spent fixing wrong boundaries later. LLD is where correctness bugs live.

Follow-ups the interviewer will ask: 1. Give an example of an LLD decision with HLD impact. → Cache TTL on serviceability determined business correctness. 2. Who owns each? → HLD: architect/tech lead with stakeholders. LLD: implementing team.

Red flags: Saying "HLD is diagrams, LLD is code." Saying design is only about scale.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Mentions that design means making decisions explicit and reviewable, and names the one-way-door decisions in HLD.

Q2 [B1] ⭐ What's the difference between functional and non-functional requirements? Give examples.

30-second answer: Functional requirements say what the system does ("reject orders to non-serviceable pincodes"). Non-functional requirements say how well it does it, as measurable targets ("p99 ≤ 50 ms", "99.95 % availability", "changes effective within 10 s").

Deep answer: NFRs drive architecture far more than FRs do. The same FR, a pincode lookup, is a HashMap at 10 req/s and a replicated snapshot with event refresh at 6 K req/s with a freshness requirement. Every NFR needs metric, percentile, threshold, scope, and window.

Trade-offs I'd call out: NFRs conflict (latency vs freshness), so they need priorities.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you get NFRs when stakeholders say "fast"? → Ask about percentiles, scope, cost of violation, and propose numbers. 2. Which NFR is most often missed? → Freshness/staleness and operability.

Red flags: NFRs without numbers. Listing only performance.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Treats freshness, operability, and cost as NFRs, and ties each to a metric and an alert.

Q3 [B1] What is scalability? Vertical vs horizontal?

30-second answer: Scalability is handling more load by adding resources, ideally proportionally. Vertical means a bigger machine: simple, but it has a ceiling and is a single point of failure. Horizontal means more machines: no hard ceiling and built-in redundancy, but it needs stateless services or partitioned state, plus load balancing.

Deep answer: Scalability is always along a dimension: users, data, write rate, tenants. The serviceability service scales horizontally for reads trivially because each pod holds the full 2.4 MB dataset. If the dataset were 200 GB, we'd need partitioning (Ch 11).

Trade-offs: Horizontal adds coordination and consistency issues, such as pods disagreeing on snapshot version.

Follow-ups: 1. When is vertical scaling the right answer? → Early stage, or databases before sharding. It's often cheaper than the engineering cost of horizontal. 2. What makes a service hard to scale horizontally? → Local state, sticky sessions, singletons, DB write bottlenecks.

Red flags: "Just add more servers" without addressing state.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Names the dimension and the bottleneck, and knows that vertical scaling is a legitimate, often underrated choice.

Q4 [B1] What's the difference between latency and throughput?

30-second answer: Latency is how long one request takes. Throughput is how many requests are completed per unit time. They're linked by Little's Law: concurrency = throughput × latency.

Deep answer: At 5,000 req/s and 40 ms latency, 200 requests are in flight at once, which sizes threads, connections, and memory. You can raise throughput with batching while making latency worse, or lower latency with caching without changing throughput capacity. Always discuss latency as percentiles.

Trade-offs: Batching and queueing trade latency for throughput.

Follow-ups: 1. Why p99 and not average? → Averages hide tail pain. Fan-out amplifies tails. 2. What happens to latency as utilization nears 100 %? → It rises sharply (queueing). Keep headroom (Ch 25).

Red flags: Using the terms interchangeably.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Uses Little's Law to size a real pool on the spot.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ Walk me through how you approach a system design problem in 45 minutes.

30-second answer: Clarify requirements and non-goals (5 min), estimate load and data (5), define APIs (5), data model and storage choice (5), draw the simplest working HLD (10), deep-dive the 2–3 hardest parts (10–15), then cover failure modes and trade-offs (5).

Deep answer: I state assumptions out loud and pick numbers. I start simple and evolve the design when the estimate or a failure forces it, rather than front-loading Kafka and sharding. I let the interviewer steer the deep dives, and I name the trade-off at each decision.

Trade-offs: Breadth vs depth. Most candidates fail by staying shallow everywhere.

Follow-ups: 1. What if the interviewer skips requirements? → Take 2 minutes anyway and state assumptions. 2. How do you pick deep dives? → The parts where the NFRs are hardest, such as contention, consistency, or hot keys.

Red flags: Drawing boxes immediately. Having no numbers. Never mentioning failure.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Keeps time, calls out one-way-door decisions, and ends with "what I'd build first and what I'd defer."

Q6 [B2] ⭐ Checkout synchronously calls 5 services, each 99.9 % available. What's checkout's availability, and how would you improve it?

30-second answer: About 0.999⁵ ≈ 99.5 %, roughly 3.6 hours down per month, assuming independent failures. Improve it by removing synchronous dependencies from the critical path (cache, async, precompute), adding redundancy, degrading instead of failing for non-critical calls, and reducing MTTR.

Deep answer: Classify each dependency as must-be-correct (inventory reservation, payment) or nice-to-have (recommendations, loyalty points). Nice-to-have calls get timeouts and fallbacks. Some calls can become async (invoice, notifications). Parallel redundancy only helps if failures are independent, meaning no shared DB, zone, or deploy.

Trade-offs: Fallbacks add complexity and can hide problems, so meter them.

Follow-ups: 1. Two replicas at 99.9 %? → 1 − 0.001² = 99.9999 % if independent, which in practice they rarely are. 2. Is 99.99 % worth it? → Compare cost per extra nine against the revenue at risk.

Red flags: Adding availabilities. Ignoring correlated failures.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Talks about MTTR, correlated failure (shared config push), and the business cost per nine.

Q7 [B2] Give a grocery example where you'd choose strong consistency and one where you'd accept eventual consistency.

30-second answer: Strong for stock reservation and payment status, where a wrong answer means overselling or double charging. Eventual (bounded) for product ratings, recommendations, and serviceability during browsing, where brief staleness costs little.

Deep answer: The unit of decision is the use case, not the dataset. Serviceability is the same data with two consistency levels: browse ≤ 60 s stale from memory, checkout fresh from the DB. Always bound "eventual" with a number and measure it.

Trade-offs: Strong consistency costs latency and availability under partitions (CAP/PACELC, Ch 06).

Follow-ups: 1. How do you enforce the bound? → Refresh interval plus event push, plus an age metric and alert. 2. What's read-your-writes? → A user sees their own update immediately (address change).

Red flags: "We use eventual consistency" with no bound.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Splits one dataset into two consistency paths and prices the cost of staleness.

Q8 [B2] ⭐ Why aren't microservices always better than a monolith?

30-second answer: Microservices trade in-process calls and local transactions for network calls, partial failures, distributed data consistency, and much higher operational cost. They pay off for team autonomy and independent scaling at organizational scale. They cost more than they return for small teams or unclear domains.

Deep answer: A distributed monolith (services that must deploy together and share a DB) gets the costs of both styles. A modular monolith with strict boundaries (Spring Modulith) gives most of the design benefits, and lets you extract services along proven seams later.

Trade-offs: Speed of change per team vs system-wide complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. When would you split a module out? → Different scaling profile, different change cadence, different team, or fault isolation needs. 2. Signs of a distributed monolith? → Lockstep deploys, shared schemas, chatty sync call chains.

Red flags: "Microservices scale better," full stop.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Frames it around Conway's law and operating cost, and has an extraction path.

Q9 [B2] A product manager says 'the app must be fast.' How do you turn that into a requirement?

30-second answer: Ask fast for which journey, measured where, at what percentile, under what load, and what a slow experience costs. Then propose numbers: "Home page API p99 ≤ 300 ms at the gateway at 3× current peak."

Deep answer: Separate perceived speed (client rendering, skeleton screens) from server latency. Set budgets per hop: gateway 20 ms, service 150 ms, DB 30 ms. Make them SLOs with error budgets so they drive decisions.

Trade-offs: Tighter latency targets cost money (more cache, more replicas) and can reduce freshness.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you pick the percentile? → p99 for user-facing, p999 for fan-out-heavy paths. 2. What if the target isn't achievable? → Show the cost curve and negotiate.

Red flags: Accepting "fast" as-is. Using averages.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Latency budgets per hop, tied to business metrics like conversion.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ Our service meets its p99 SLO, but users say the app is slow. What's going on?

30-second answer: Likely causes: the SLO is measured in the wrong place (service, not user), the percentile is too low for a fan-out page, averaging across pods hides hot pods, client-side or network time is excluded, or specific segments (a city, low-end devices, one API) are slow while the aggregate looks fine.

Deep answer: A page calling 20 services each with a good p99 is slow about 18 % of the time. Check real-user monitoring and gateway-level percentiles per journey. Break down by region, device, and endpoint. Look at p999 and at retries, which hide as success but double latency. Check whether timeouts plus retries are inflating tails.

Trade-offs: More granular SLOs mean more alerting noise, so target journeys, not endpoints.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you fix fan-out tails? → Parallelize, hedge requests, cache, precompute, cut dependencies. 2. Can you average p99s across pods? → No. Aggregate histograms.

Red flags: "The SLO is met, so the users are wrong."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Redefines the SLO around the user journey and fixes measurement before tuning.

Q11 [B3] Which quality attributes typically conflict, and how do you resolve the conflict in practice?

30-second answer: Latency vs consistency (caching), availability vs consistency (partitions), durability vs write latency (sync replication), scalability vs operability and cost (more components), security vs UX. I resolve them by splitting use cases, bounding the trade-off with numbers, pricing the failure, and preferring reversible choices.

Deep answer: Serviceability is the example. Browse wants latency and availability, checkout wants correctness, so they get two paths. Bound staleness at 60 s and measure it. Price the incident (1,900 orders) against the cost of a fresher design. Record the decision in an ADR with a "revisit when" clause.

Trade-offs: More paths mean more code, so only split when the costs differ materially.

Follow-ups: 1. What if stakeholders insist on both? → Show the cost of each option. There's usually a cheap split. 2. How do you document it? → ADR (Ch 31).

Red flags: Claiming a design achieves everything.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Uses money and the incident history to decide, and writes down when to revisit.

Q12 [B3] Explain durability vs availability with an example where you have one but not the other.

30-second answer: Durability means acknowledged data isn't lost. Availability means the system responds correctly when asked. An in-memory cache is available but not durable. A database whose primary is down while its data is safe on disk and replicas is durable but temporarily unavailable.

Deep answer: Durability is set by replication (sync vs async), fsync policy, backups, and RPO. Availability is set by redundancy, failover time, and dependencies (RTO, MTTR). Async replication improves write latency but risks losing the last seconds of writes on failover. That's acceptable for the analytics clickstream but not for orders.

Trade-offs: Sync replication costs write latency and can reduce availability if replicas lag.

Follow-ups: 1. RPO vs RTO? → Data loss tolerated vs time to recover. 2. Where does serviceability need durability? → Source of truth (DB), not the snapshot.

Red flags: Treating the terms as synonyms.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Assigns RPO/RTO per data class and mentions tested restores ("an untested backup isn't a backup").

Q13 [B3] How do you design for operability?

30-second answer: Make the system observable (metrics for its key guarantees, not just CPU), safe to change (feature flags, canaries, fast rollback), safe to operate (admin controls with guardrails and audit), and quick to recover (runbooks, readiness and liveness done right, stale-serving modes).

Deep answer: For serviceability that means a snapshot-age metric with an alert, readiness tied to the first load, SHADOW → ENFORCE rollout, version-based rollback of ops changes, and two-person approval for bulk changes. Ask "what will on-call see and do at 3 am?" during design review, not after the first incident.

Trade-offs: Operability features take engineering time that doesn't ship user features. Budget it explicitly.

Follow-ups: 1. Liveness vs readiness? → Liveness says restart me. Readiness says don't route to me yet. 2. What's a good alert? → Symptom-based, tied to SLO burn, and actionable.

Red flags: "We'll add monitoring later."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Designs metrics for the business guarantee (freshness, deliverability) and treats MTTR as an availability lever.

Q14 [B3] ⭐ A cached serviceability answer caused 1,900 undeliverable orders. Walk me through your fix.

30-second answer: Immediately, shorten the refresh and make checkout re-validate against the source of truth. Structurally, split consistency by use case (browse from snapshot with bounded staleness, checkout fresh and fail-closed), add event-driven refresh via outbox, make staleness a measured SLO, and roll out in shadow mode first.

Deep answer: Run a blameless postmortem. The root cause is an unstated freshness requirement, not "the TTL." Write NFRs (browse ≤ 60 s, checkout exact), an ADR choosing fail-closed, metrics (snapshot.age), and alerts. Add an ops guardrail so closing a store triggers the change and confirms propagation. Remediate: refunds and proactive customer communication.

Trade-offs: Checkout now depends on the serviceability DB, costing about 0.05 % availability, accepted because failed checkouts are retryable.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not just a 30 s TTL everywhere? → Still wrong at checkout for 30 s, and staleness is unmeasured. 2. Fail-open or fail-closed? → Closed. An undeliverable paid order costs more than a retry.

Red flags: "Reduce the TTL" as the whole answer.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Fixes the process (NFRs, ADRs, freshness SLOs) as well as the code, and quantifies the availability cost of the fix.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ A team proposes 26 microservices for an MVP with 8 engineers. What's your response in the design review?

30-second answer: Keep the 26 bounded contexts as the domain model, but deploy them as a modular monolith (or 3–4 deployables) until team count, scaling needs, or change-rate differences justify splitting. Enforce module boundaries in code so extraction stays cheap.

Deep answer: 26 services for 8 people means more than 3 services per engineer. Each needs a CI pipeline, dashboards, on-call, versioning, and deployment, and distributed transactions appear on day one (checkout saga). Candidates to split early: things with a genuinely different profile, such as tracking-service (high-volume location writes), search (a different datastore), and payment (a PCI scope boundary). Everything else waits. Define the extraction trigger up front: "when team X exceeds N people or component Y needs independent scaling."

Trade-offs: A monolith risks eroding boundaries, so mitigate with Spring Modulith verification tests and architecture fitness functions.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you prevent a big ball of mud? → Module APIs, no cross-module table access, automated architecture tests. 2. What would make you agree to 26? → Multiple teams already exist, with independent roadmaps and a mature platform.

Red flags: Dogmatic answers either way.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Separates the logical architecture (contexts) from the physical one (deployables), and gives objective split criteria.

Q16 [B4] You're starting a new platform. How do you decide which NFRs matter most?

30-second answer: Start from business risk and value. What failure is most expensive (money, trust, regulation)? What quality differentiates the product? Rank NFRs by those, set targets per user journey, and accept weaker targets elsewhere to fund the strong ones.

Deep answer: For quick-commerce grocery: correctness of money and deliverability (payments, stock, serviceability), availability during peak windows (7–10 pm, sales), and browse latency (conversion) come first. Compliance (RBI localization, DPDP, GST) is non-negotiable. Analytics freshness, recommendation quality, and admin tooling latency can be weaker. Use a utility tree (ATAM, Ch 31) to make priorities explicit, and revisit quarterly.

Trade-offs: Everything "high priority" means nothing is. Force ranking.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you validate targets? → Load tests, game days, and business data such as conversion vs latency. 2. Who signs off? → Product plus engineering plus SRE. Compliance signs off on its own items.

Red flags: A generic list with no ranking.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Links NFRs to revenue and regulatory exposure, and makes them explicit trade-offs with owners.

Q17 [B4] How do you treat cost as an architectural attribute?

30-second answer: Define unit economics (₹ infra per order or per active user), estimate them in the design doc, attribute costs to services and teams, and review them like latency. Architecture decisions such as service count, replication factor, cross-AZ traffic, and retention dominate spend.

Deep answer: Examples: 26 services × 3 replicas × 3 environments is a fixed cost before any traffic. Chatty cross-AZ calls cost egress. Log volume can exceed compute cost. Over-provisioning for a 20× sale peak all year is waste, so use autoscaling plus pre-scaling for known events. Tag resources and show teams their cost per request.

Trade-offs: Cost optimization can cut availability headroom. Make that explicit.

Follow-ups: 1. Where have you cut cost significantly? → Give a real story with numbers. 2. How do you avoid penny-pinching? → Optimize only the top cost drivers.

Red flags: "Cost is finance's problem."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Has a number (₹ per order) and a mechanism (tagging, showback, review cadence).

Q18 [B4] ⭐ What are reversible vs irreversible decisions? Give examples, and how you handle each.

30-second answer: Reversible (two-way door) decisions are cheap to undo: cache TTLs, library choices inside a service, instance sizes. Irreversible (one-way door) decisions are expensive to undo: service and data boundaries, public APIs, event schemas, partition keys, primary database, tenancy model, data residency. Decide reversible ones fast and measure. Give irreversible ones design docs, alternatives, reviews, and ADRs.

Deep answer: An architect's leverage is turning one-way doors into two-way doors: versioned APIs and events, anti-corruption layers, feature flags, strangler migrations, abstractions over vendors where the switching risk is real. Also watch for hidden one-way doors, such as a sync dependency other teams build latency budgets around.

Trade-offs: Excess abstraction to keep options open costs complexity now. Only pay it where switching is plausible.

Follow-ups: 1. Example of a one-way door you got wrong? → Tell a real story: what it cost and how you migrated. 2. How do you speed up one-way decisions? → Timebox, prototypes, spikes.

Red flags: Treating all decisions with the same process.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Names hidden one-way doors and describes converting them.

Q19 [B4] How do you evaluate a design document you didn't write?

30-second answer: Check that requirements and NFRs are explicit and numeric. Check that the estimate supports the chosen design. Look for real alternatives, failure modes with detection and mitigation, operability, security, migration and rollback plans, cost, and one-way-door decisions called out. Then probe the riskiest assumption.

Deep answer: My questions: "What happens when X is down?", "How stale can this be, and how would we know?", "What's the rollback?", "What does this cost per order?", "Who's on call for this?", "What would make us revisit this?" I separate blocking concerns from suggestions, and review the decision, not the author.

Trade-offs: Heavy reviews slow teams. Scale rigour to reversibility and blast radius.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you handle disagreement with a senior author? → Data, prototypes, disagree and commit with a revisit trigger. 2. What do most docs miss? → Failure modes and rollout.

Red flags: Reviewing only diagrams, or nitpicking style.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: A consistent checklist, proportional rigour, and focus on the riskiest assumption.

Q20 [B4] Trace the evolution from monolith to SOA to microservices. What's next, and what did each era teach us?

30-second answer: Monoliths were simple but coupled. SOA added service contracts but centralized logic in ESBs. Microservices gave team autonomy via small, independently deployed services with their own data, but brought distributed-systems cost. The current correction is right-sized services, modular monoliths, platform engineering, and cell-based architectures for blast-radius control at huge scale.

Deep answer: Lessons: boundaries matter more than deployment units (DDD). Smart endpoints and dumb pipes beat central ESBs. Independent data ownership is the real decoupling. Operational maturity (CI/CD, observability, platform) is a prerequisite, not a follow-up. Each era overcorrected. Today's best practice is choosing per context: a modular monolith for most, services where autonomy and scaling justify it, cells for massive scale.

Trade-offs: Every style trades simplicity against autonomy and isolation.

Follow-ups: 1. What is cell-based architecture? → Independent full-stack copies serving subsets of users, limiting blast radius (Ch 34). 2. Where does serverless fit? → Spiky, event-driven workloads. Watch cold starts and cost at steady load.

Red flags: Presenting microservices as the end state.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Has lived through the transitions and can describe a real migration: the drivers, the costs, and what went wrong.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. System design means making important decisions explicitly: requirements, qualities, failure behaviour, and cost.
  2. HLD decides parts and interactions. LLD decides internals. A low-level parameter can encode a high-level requirement.
  3. NFRs need metric + percentile + threshold + scope + window. "Fast" is not a requirement.
  4. The eight core attributes are scalability, availability, latency, consistency, durability, cost, operability, and security/compliance. Freshness is part of consistency, and it needs an SLO too.
  5. Serial dependencies multiply unavailability. Redundancy helps only when failures are independent.
  6. Choose consistency per use case, not per system. Bound "eventual" with a number.
  7. Resolve conflicts by splitting use cases, bounding trade-offs, pricing failures, and preferring reversible choices.
  8. Follow the process: requirements → estimate → API → data → HLD → deep dives → failures → trade-offs.
  9. Spot one-way doors, and convert them to two-way doors where you can.
  10. Choose monolith vs microservices by team autonomy and change rates, not fashion.

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: If… Then consider… Dataset is small and read-mostly Full in-memory replica per instance + refresh Correctness matters on a low-volume path Read source of truth; fail closed High-volume path tolerates staleness Cache/snapshot with measured, bounded staleness Many consumers must react to a change Outbox + event topic Dependency is nice-to-have Timeout + fallback (fail open), metered Decision is hard to undo Design doc + ADR + review Small team, new domain Modular monolith with bounded contexts

docs.title: 02. Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation ⭐
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 01 · What you will build: A capacity estimator, taken from a plain-Java calculator (L1) to a planner that reads real production metrics and generates Kubernetes pre-scaling config for a festival sale (L4) · Reading time: 80 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: the sale that autoscaling couldn't save
docs.text:
A grocery platform announced a Diwali sale starting at 8:00 pm sharp: ₹1 onions, 60 % off dry fruits. Engineering was confident. Every service had a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) at 60 % CPU, and "the cloud scales."

At 8:00:00 pm, gateway traffic went from 9 K req/s to 170 K req/s in 40 seconds.

  • 8:00:15. Prometheus scraped the first high CPU samples.
  • 8:00:30. The HPA decided to scale catalog-service from 12 to 60 pods.
  • 8:00:30–8:02:30. The cluster had no spare nodes. The node autoscaler requested 30 machines, which took about 3 minutes to join.
  • 8:03:40. New JVMs finished starting and warming up.

For roughly four minutes, the existing pods were overloaded. Latency rose, clients timed out and retried, which multiplied load by 2–3×. Liveness checks failed, Kubernetes restarted "unhealthy" pods, and capacity dropped further. The first 10 minutes of the sale, the most valuable 10 minutes of the quarter, returned errors to most customers.

Nobody had done the arithmetic: peak ÷ per-pod capacity = pods needed before 8:00 pm. A ten-minute estimate on a whiteboard would have shown that reactive autoscaling could not react in time. The fix was trivial: pre-scale at 7:30 pm.

The thesis of this chapter

Estimation isn't about getting the right number. It's about finding which part of the design the numbers break, and doing that before production does.

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text: Band After this chapter you can… B1 Convert daily volumes to QPS, recall the key latency numbers, and estimate storage B2 Derive peak factors, apply Little's Law to pools, and estimate bandwidth, memory and servers B3 Produce a full festival-sale estimate, find hot spots and connection-budget limits, and size for zone failure B4 Run capacity planning as a process, present estimates with uncertainty, and tie capacity to cost and risk

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: packing for a trip B1
docs.text:
You don't weigh every shirt before a trip. You think: "5 days, 1 shirt per day, plus 2 spare, so 7 shirts. That fits in a cabin bag." That's back-of-the-envelope estimation: rough numbers, simple arithmetic, a decision.

The goal is being right within a factor of 2–3, not within 1 %. A factor-of-10 error changes the design. A factor-of-2 error usually changes only the instance count.

docs.title: 2.2 The toolkit: numbers you must know by heart B1
2.2.1 Powers of two and ten
docs.text: Power Exact Approx Name 2¹⁰ 1,024 10³ 1 KB 2²⁰ 1,048,576 10⁶ 1 MB 2³⁰ ~1.07 × 10⁹ 10⁹ 1 GB 2⁴⁰ ~1.1 × 10¹² 10¹² 1 TB 2⁵⁰ ~1.13 × 10¹⁵ 10¹⁵ 1 PB Handy constant Value Use Seconds per day 86,400 ≈ 10⁵ Per-day → per-second: divide by 10⁵ Seconds per month ~2.6 × 10⁶ Seconds per year ~3.15 × 10⁷ ≈ π × 10⁷ 1 M/day ≈ 12 per second Memorize this one 1 B/day ≈ 12 K per second Java object header 12–16 bytes Memory estimates UUID 16 bytes binary, 36 as text Index size long / Instant 8 / ~24 bytes (object)

docs.title: 2.2.2 Latency numbers (order of magnitude, 2026 hardware)
docs.text:
Operation Approx. time Relative to a RAM read L1 cache reference ~1 ns 0.01× Branch mispredict ~3–5 ns L2 cache reference ~4 ns Mutex lock/unlock (uncontended) ~20 ns Main memory reference ~100 ns 1× Compress 1 KB (Snappy/LZ4) ~1–2 µs 10–20× Send 1 KB over a 10 Gbps network ~1 µs Read 1 MB sequentially from memory ~10 µs NVMe SSD random read (4 KB) ~20–100 µs ~500× Read 1 MB sequentially from NVMe ~150–300 µs Round trip within the same AZ ~0.1–0.5 ms ~2,000–5,000× Round trip across AZs (same region) ~0.5–2 ms Simple PostgreSQL PK query (incl. network) ~0.5–2 ms Redis GET (incl. network) ~0.2–1 ms HDD seek ~5–10 ms Mumbai ↔ Hyderabad ~15–25 ms Mumbai ↔ Singapore ~55–70 ms Mumbai ↔ US East ~180–220 ms TLS 1.3 handshake on a new connection +1 RTT Spring Boot pod: schedule → start → warm ~20–90 s Plan for it in scaling New Kubernetes node joins the cluster ~1–4 min The hidden cost of "autoscaling"

Three ratios to remember

  • Memory is ~1,000× faster than a network hop.
  • A same-region network hop is ~100× faster than a cross-continent one.
  • Anything that needs a new JVM or a new node takes tens of seconds to minutes, which is an eternity during a spike.

docs.title: 2.2.3 Throughput priors (planning defaults, replace with measurements)
docs.text:
These are starting assumptions for estimates, not facts. Every real design replaces them with load-test data (§5 L3/L4).

Component Planning prior Notes Spring Boot endpoint, in-memory work only 2–5 K req/s per vCPU JSON serialization dominates Spring Boot endpoint, 1–2 DB calls 300–1,000 req/s per vCPU Depends on query cost PostgreSQL (8 vCPU), simple PK reads 20–50 K/s From buffer cache; drops sharply when disk-bound PostgreSQL (8 vCPU), simple writes 3–10 K TPS fsync, WAL and indexes matter Redis, single shard ~100 K ops/s Single-threaded command execution Kafka partition ~5–10 MB/s write (conservative) Consumer processing is usually the real limit One hot DB row, locked updates ~200–1,000 updates/s Serialized by the row lock, ~1–5 ms each CDN edge Effectively unlimited You pay per GB

docs.title: 2.3 From users to QPS ⭐ B1 B2
docs.text:
The core chain:

\[ \text{Avg QPS} = \frac{\text{DAU} \times \text{actions per user per day}}{86{,}400} \qquad \text{Peak QPS} = \text{Avg QPS} \times \text{peak factor} \]

Example (normal day). 2 M DAU × 40 API calls per user per day = 80 M calls/day → 80 M ÷ 10⁵ ≈ 800 req/s average at the gateway. With the evening peak factor of 5, that's 4,000 req/s.

docs.title: Deriving the peak factor B2
docs.text:
Peak factors aren't magic constants. They come from traffic shape:

Source of peak Typical factor over the daily average How to know Daily curve (evening dinner rush) 2–5× Hour-of-day histogram from last month Weekly (Sunday mornings) 1.2–1.5× on top Day-of-week histogram Marketing push notification to 5 M users 5–15× for 2–5 minutes Past campaign dashboards Scheduled sale start ("8 pm sharp") 15–40× for the first 1–3 minutes Past sales; this is the dangerous one Retry storm after an incident 2–3× on top of whatever caused it Retry policy × failure rate

Peaks are measured over the wrong window

A dashboard with 5-minute averages hides a 30-second spike that is 3× higher. Size for the per-second peak your autoscaler can't absorb. That's the rise time from §1.1.

docs.title: 2.4 Read/write ratio B2
docs.text:
Classify every workload by its ratio, because the ratio decides the architecture:

Ratio Example Architecture implication 10⁶ : 1 Serviceability, GST rate tables Full replica in memory; push invalidation 100 : 1 Catalog, product page Cache + CDN; read replicas 10 : 1 Cart Cache-friendly, but writes matter; Redis 1 : 1 Inventory reservations during a sale Contention; per-row throughput matters 1 : 10+ Rider location pings, clickstream Write-optimized store, batching, time-series/LSM, async

docs.title: 2.5 Storage estimation ⭐ B1 B2
docs.text:
\[ \text{Storage} = \text{records/day} \times \text{bytes/record} \times \text{retention days} \times \text{overhead} \]

The overhead multiplier covers indexes (×1.5–3), replication (×2–3) and headroom (×1.3).

Worked example: orders.

Item Estimate Order header row ~1 KB (IDs, amounts, address snapshot, status, timestamps) Line items 8 items × ~250 B = 2 KB Status history 6 transitions × ~150 B ≈ 1 KB Raw per order ~4 KB Orders/day (year-round average incl. festivals) ~500 K Raw per day 500 K × 4 KB = 2 GB/day Per year ~730 GB raw × indexes (2) × copies (3 = primary + 2 replicas) ~4.4 TB/year provisioned GST record retention (multi-year, confirm with finance) Hot data 1 year in OLTP, older in a cheap archive

What the estimate tells us

A few TB/year in PostgreSQL is fine for one well-provisioned cluster. There's no need to shard orders on day one. But plan partitioning by month so old data moves to archive cheaply (Ch 05, 28). The estimate turned "should we shard?" into "not yet, and here's the trigger."

Other storage in the platform (rough):

Data Volume Store GST invoice PDFs 500 K/day × 60 KB = 30 GB/day → ~11 TB/yr Object storage + lifecycle to a cold tier Rider location pings 40 K riders × 1 ping/4 s = 10 K writes/s × 100 B ≈ 86 GB/day Redis (latest) + time-series (7-day retention) Product images 250 K SKUs × 6 images × 4 sizes × 60 KB ≈ 360 GB Object storage + CDN Application logs 26 services × ~3 KB/request × 80 M requests ≈ 240 GB/day Often the largest cost line; sample and set retention

docs.title: 2.6 Bandwidth estimation B2
docs.text:
\[ \text{Bandwidth} = \text{QPS} \times \text{response size} \]

Sale start, catalog API: 110 K req/s × 20 KB JSON ≈ 2.2 GB/s ≈ 18 Gbps uncompressed. With gzip or Brotli (~5–8× on JSON), that's ~2–3.5 Gbps. Images go to the CDN, so they aren't your origin's problem, but they are your bill: 6 M DAU × 40 images × 40 KB ≈ 9.6 TB/day of CDN egress.

Bandwidth estimates catch a class of bugs early

A product-list API returning full product objects (80 KB) instead of list DTOs (8 KB) is a 10× bandwidth and serialization-CPU bug. Estimating response sizes during API design (Ch 04) prevents it.

docs.title: 2.7 Memory estimation B2
docs.text:
Can it fit in memory? That question decides between an in-process cache, Redis, and "must go to disk."

\[ \text{Memory} = \text{entries} \times (\text{key} + \text{value} + \text{per-entry overhead}) \] Structure Rough per-entry overhead Java HashMap entry (node + refs) ~32–48 B + key and value objects Java String (short, compact strings) ~40 B + 1 B/char (Latin-1) Redis small key-value ~50–90 B overhead

Example: carts in Redis. 1.5 M active carts at peak × (8 items × 60 B + 200 B overhead) ≈ 1.5 M × 680 B ≈ 1 GB. That fits comfortably in a single Redis shard (with a replica), so memory doesn't force clustering. The deciding factor is ops/s (§4).

docs.title: 2.8 Server count and Little's Law ⭐ B2 B3
CPU-based sizing
docs.text:
\[ \text{cores needed} = \frac{\text{peak QPS} \times \text{CPU ms per request}}{1000 \times \text{target utilization}} \]

Checkout at 850 req/s × 6 ms CPU/request ÷ (1000 × 0.5) ≈ 10.2 cores → 6 pods × 2 vCPU.

Why target 50–60 % utilization, not 90 %?

Queueing theory (M/M/1 intuition): waiting time grows as ρ / (1 − ρ). At 50 % utilization the multiplier is 1×. At 80 % it's 4×. At 95 % it's 19×. Tail latency explodes long before CPU hits 100 % (Ch 25).

docs.title: Little's Law: in-flight work
docs.text:
\[ L = \lambda \times W \quad\text{(in-flight = arrival rate × time in system)} \] Use Calculation Result Concurrent checkout requests 850 req/s × 0.15 s ~128 in flight DB connections checkout needs 850 req/s × 20 ms of DB time per request ~17 connections busy Threads (platform threads) 128 in flight + headroom ~200 (virtual threads remove this limit) Kafka consumer parallelism 1,000 events/s × 30 ms processing ≥ 30 partitions/consumers

The connection budget

PostgreSQL connections are expensive (several MB each, with contention above a few hundred). If 26 services × 6 pods × a pool of 20 all point at shared clusters, that's 3,120 potential connections. Little's Law says you need far fewer busy connections. Size pools from Little's Law, not from defaults, and add PgBouncer as pod counts grow (Ch 05).

docs.title: 2.9 Worked example: the festival-sale checkout estimate ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Given: a festival day with 1.5 M orders. The sale starts at 8:00 pm. 20 % of the day's orders happen in the first hour, and minute one runs at 5× that hour's average.

Step Calculation Result Orders in the first hour 1.5 M × 0.2 300 K Average orders/s in that hour 300 K ÷ 3,600 ~83/s Peak-minute orders/s 83 × 5 ~420 orders/s Checkout attempts (payment failures, retries, drop-offs: ×2) 420 × 2 ~850 checkout req/s Concurrent users at 8:00 pm 6 M DAU × ~13 % online ~800 K Gateway requests (1 request per 4 s per user) 800 K ÷ 4 ~200 K req/s …of which catalog/search/product reads ~55 % ~110 K req/s Reservations for the "₹1 onion" SKU (in 30 % of orders, spread over ~50 busy stores) 850 × 0.3 ÷ 50 ~5/s per store-SKU row …if one metro store gets 20 % of that demand 850 × 0.3 × 0.2 ~50/s on one row: fine for a row lock (~500/s max) Order DB statements (order + items + outbox) 420 × ~12 ~5 K statements/s on the orders primary Payment webhook callbacks ~420/s + retries Idempotent handler required (Ch 20, 45) Kafka order.order.placed.v1 420/s × 2 KB ~0.8 MB/s: tiny for Kafka; partitions sized by consumer time

What this estimate tells us (the real value)

  1. Checkout compute is not the problem. ~850 req/s needs ~6 pods.
  2. Read traffic is the problem. ~110 K req/s of catalog needs CDN plus multi-layer caching, and pre-scaling (Ch 07, 21).
  3. Contention is a watch item, not a crisis. The hot SKU row sits at ~10 % of lock capacity. We'd re-estimate if the sale became a single national flash deal (Ch 46).
  4. Rise time kills. From 9 K to 200 K req/s in about 40 s is faster than any reactive autoscaler. Pre-scale.

docs.title: 2.10 Estimation in interviews vs at work B2 B4
docs.text:
Interview At work Time 3–5 minutes Hours to days Inputs Assumed, stated aloud Measured (metrics, load tests, business forecasts) Precision Order of magnitude Ranges with confidence (P50 / P90 forecasts) Output Which parts of the design matter Capacity plan, budget, pre-scale schedule, risk register Failure mode Precision theatre (computing 83.33/s) Estimating once and never validating

Interview script:

"Let me assume 2 M DAU and about 40 API calls each, so 80 M a day, which is about 1 K per second average. Evening peak is maybe 5×, so 5 K/s. Sale starts are much spikier, maybe 20–40× in the first minute. The read:write ratio is around 100:1, so reads dominate and caching is the main lever. Storage is about 4 KB per order and 500 K orders a day, so 2 GB a day and under 1 TB a year raw. That fits one Postgres cluster, so no sharding yet, and I'll partition by month."

docs.title: 2.11 Uncertainty, ranges and presenting estimates B4
docs.text:
Senior estimates are ranges with drivers, not single numbers:

Scenario Orders on sale day Peak checkout req/s Catalog req/s Catalog pods (before AZ headroom) P50 (last year × 1.4 growth) 1.5 M 850 165 K 55 P90 (marketing overperforms, × 1.15) 1.75 M 980 190 K 64 Stress (P90 × 1.5 safety) 2.6 M 1,470 285 K 95
  • Plan capacity at P90 plus zone-failure headroom.
  • Load test at the stress scenario.
  • Protect beyond stress with load shedding (Ch 18): serve 429 to a slice of low-priority traffic rather than fail everyone.
  • Tell executives the drivers: "Every extra 1 M users notified in the 7:55 pm push adds ~35 K req/s at 8:00."

docs.title: 2.12 Zone-failure headroom B3 B4
docs.text:
If you run in 3 availability zones and must survive losing one at peak:

\[ \text{pods provisioned} = \left\lceil \text{pods needed} \times \frac{\text{zones}}{\text{zones} - 1} \right\rceil \]

64 pods needed → 96 provisioned (32 per zone). That's the real cost of the availability NFR from Ch 01. Put it in the design doc so finance sees it as a decision, not waste.

docs.title: 3.3 Sequence: failure path, reactive-only autoscaling at sale start
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as 800K users
    participant GW as api-gateway
    participant Cat as catalog-service (12 pods)
    participant Prom as Prometheus
    participant HPA as HPA
    participant CA as Node autoscaler
    U->>GW: 20:00:00 traffic 9K → 170K req/s in 40 s
    GW->>Cat: forward
    Note over Cat: CPU 100 %, queueing, p99 250 ms → 6 s
    Cat-->>GW: timeouts
    GW-->>U: 504
    U->>GW: client retries ×2-3 (load amplification)
    Prom->>Prom: scrape at 20:00:15
    HPA->>Prom: sync at 20:00:30
    HPA->>CA: need 48 more pods, no room on nodes
    CA->>CA: provision nodes (2-4 min)
    Note over Cat: liveness probes time out → restarts → capacity DROPS
    CA-->>HPA: nodes ready 20:02:40
    HPA->>Cat: pods scheduled, JVM start + warm-up ~60 s
    Note over U,Cat: ~4 minutes of heavy errors during the most valuable minutes
    alt with gateway load shedding (Ch 18)
        GW-->>U: 429 + Retry-After for 30 % of low-priority traffic
        Note over GW,Cat: remaining traffic served within SLO
    end

What the system guarantees after this failure path

Without pre-scaling, nothing: a correct design can still fail on arithmetic alone. With pre-scaling as the primary defence and gateway load shedding as the backstop, the platform degrades a controlled slice of traffic instead of failing everyone. Liveness probes must not depend on request latency, or overload turns into a restart storm.

docs.title: 3.4 State: the lifecycle of a capacity plan
docs.text:
An estimate is only useful if it becomes a plan that is checked against reality after the event. The same states apply to every sale or launch.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Estimated: requirements plus back-of-envelope numbers
    Estimated --> Reviewed: assumptions written down and challenged
    Reviewed --> Estimated: an assumption is wrong or missing
    Reviewed --> LoadTested: per-pod capacity measured
    LoadTested --> Estimated: measured capacity below estimate
    LoadTested --> Scheduled: cron floors and headroom committed
    Scheduled --> Live: sale starts with capacity in place
    Live --> Shedding: demand above plan, gateway sheds low-priority traffic
    Shedding --> Live: demand falls back within capacity
    Live --> Retrospective: event over
    Retrospective --> [*]: actuals recorded as next year's inputs

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Diwali 2026 Capacity Plan
docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers Platform capacity owner / SRE, Checkout, Catalog, Finance Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-014 Pre-scale for scheduled events

1. Context & Problem. Last year's sale start caused ~4 minutes of errors due to reactive autoscaling lag (§1.1). This year's marketing plan is 1.4× bigger.

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: meet SLOs at P90 demand, including loss of one AZ. Degrade gracefully up to the stress scenario.
  • Non-goals: redesigning inventory contention (tracked in Ch 46 work); multi-region (Ch 27).

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement NFR-1 Gateway availability ≥ 99.9 % during 19:45–22:00 IST NFR-2 Catalog p99 ≤ 300 ms, checkout p99 ≤ 800 ms at P90 load NFR-3 Survive loss of 1 of 3 AZs at P90 without breaching NFR-2 NFR-4 Beyond stress load, shed low-priority traffic (recommendations, non-cart browsing) first NFR-5 Infra spend for the event ≤ ₹18 lakh

4. Capacity estimates.

Service Last year peak × growth 1.4 P90 (× 1.15 on top) Per-pod capacity at SLO (load test) Pods needed × AZ headroom 1.5 Provision catalog 118 K/s 165 K/s 190 K/s 3,000 req/s 64 96 96 search 22 K/s 31 K/s 35 K/s 800 req/s 44 66 66 cart 9 K/s 12.6 K/s 14.5 K/s 2,500 req/s 6 9 9 checkout 610/s 850/s 980/s 180 req/s 6 9 9 (+1 deploy surge) inventory 2.1 K/s 2.9 K/s 3.4 K/s 900 req/s 4 6 6

Data-tier checks.

  • Orders PostgreSQL: ~5 K statements/s at P50, ~6 K at P90. The load test showed 14 K/s at 60 % CPU. OK.
  • Connection budget (orders DB): checkout 10 pods × 10 + order 8 × 10 + outbox relay 2 × 2 = 184 ≤ 300 via PgBouncer. OK.
  • Redis carts: 14.5 K req/s × ~3 ops = 44 K ops/s on one shard (limit ~100 K). OK at 44 %. Watch item.
  • Kafka: order.order.placed.v1 has 24 partitions; consumers at 30 ms/event → capacity ~800 events/s vs ~560/s at P90. OK.

7. Alternatives considered.

Option Pros Cons Verdict Reactive HPA only Cheapest Fails on rise time (proven last year) Rejected Permanently over-provision Simple ~₹60 lakh/quarter of idle capacity Rejected Scheduled pre-scale (KEDA cron) + reactive above floor + load shedding Capacity ready before the spike; still elastic; bounded failure Needs a forecast; cost for a 3.5 h window Chosen Staggered sale start by city Smooths the spike ~4× Marketing objection Proposed for 2027

8. Failure modes. Forecast too low → reactive scaling above the cron floor, plus load shedding. Node capacity unavailable in the region → reserve capacity with the cloud provider 7 days before. A deploy during the event → change freeze 18:00–23:00.

10. Observability. A dedicated event dashboard showing actual vs forecast req/s per service, headroom % (capacity ÷ load), connection-pool saturation, and Kafka consumer lag. A "headroom < 25 %" alert pages the event war room.

11. Rollout. A full-scale load test at stress level on D-5 (shadow environment); a pre-scale dress rehearsal on D-2 (scale up, verify nodes, scale down); on the day, the cron trigger fires at 19:30.

12. Cost. 3.5 h × ~200 extra pods (~300 vCPU), plus reserved node capacity, plus CDN egress ≈ ₹11 lakh, within budget.

14. Decision (ADR-014 summary). For any scheduled event with a forecast peak above 3× normal, pre-scale with a cron-based floor sized at P90 × AZ headroom, starting 30 minutes before the event. Reactive autoscaling stays active above the floor. Gateway load shedding is mandatory beyond the stress scenario.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
We build a capacity estimator four times. Each level answers a harder question:

Level Question it answers L1 "What are the rough numbers?" (a calculator you can run in 10 seconds) L2 "Can the team share, save and compare scenarios?" (a Spring service) L3 "How many pods do we actually provision, including zone failure, and what breaks first?" (a measured, policy-driven planner with warnings) L4 "Generate the sale-day plan from last year's real traffic and ship it as GitOps config." (Prometheus + KEDA)

docs.title: L1 — Concept (plain Java) B1
docs.text:
// CapacityEstimatorL1.java — run with: java CapacityEstimatorL1.java
import java.util.Locale;

public class CapacityEstimatorL1 {

    static final double SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86_400;

    record Traffic(long dau, double actionsPerUserPerDay, double peakFactor) {
        double avgQps()  { return dau * actionsPerUserPerDay / SECONDS_PER_DAY; }
        double peakQps() { return avgQps() * peakFactor; }
    }

    record Storage(long recordsPerDay, long bytesPerRecord, int retentionDays, double overhead) {
        double totalBytes() { return (double) recordsPerDay * bytesPerRecord * retentionDays * overhead; }
    }

    /** Little's Law: items in the system = arrival rate × time in system. */
    static double inFlight(double arrivalsPerSecond, double secondsInSystem) {
        return arrivalsPerSecond * secondsInSystem;
    }

    static double coresNeeded(double qps, double cpuMsPerRequest, double targetUtilization) {
        return qps * cpuMsPerRequest / (1000.0 * targetUtilization);
    }

    static String human(double bytes) {
        String[] units = {"B", "KB", "MB", "GB", "TB", "PB"};
        int i = 0;
        while (bytes >= 1024 && i < units.length - 1) { bytes /= 1024; i++; }
        return String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%.1f %s", bytes, units[i]);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Normal day at the gateway
        var normal = new Traffic(2_000_000, 40, 5);
        System.out.printf(Locale.ROOT, "Gateway avg %.0f req/s, evening peak %.0f req/s%n",
                normal.avgQps(), normal.peakQps());

        // 2. Festival checkout: 1.5M orders, 20% in first hour, minute-one = 5x hour avg, attempts = 2x orders
        double ordersPerSecPeak = 1_500_000 * 0.20 / 3_600 * 5;
        double checkoutQps = ordersPerSecPeak * 2;
        System.out.printf(Locale.ROOT, "Festival peak: %.0f orders/s, %.0f checkout req/s%n",
                ordersPerSecPeak, checkoutQps);

        // 3. Pods for checkout: 6 ms CPU per request, 50% target utilization, 2 vCPU pods
        double cores = coresNeeded(checkoutQps, 6, 0.5);
        System.out.printf(Locale.ROOT, "Checkout needs %.1f cores → %d pods of 2 vCPU%n",
                cores, (int) Math.ceil(cores / 2));

        // 4. DB connections actually busy (20 ms DB time per checkout)
        System.out.printf(Locale.ROOT, "Busy DB connections ≈ %.0f%n", inFlight(checkoutQps, 0.020));

        // 5. Order storage for one year: 500K/day, 4 KB, indexes x2, 3 copies
        var orders = new Storage(500_000, 4 * 1024, 365, 2 * 3);
        System.out.println("Order storage / year (provisioned): " + human(orders.totalBytes()));

        // 6. Catalog bandwidth at sale start: 110K req/s x 20 KB
        System.out.println("Catalog egress (uncompressed): " + human(110_000 * 20 * 1024.0) + "/s");
    }
}

Output:

Gateway avg 926 req/s, evening peak 4630 req/s
Festival peak: 417 orders/s, 833 checkout req/s
Checkout needs 10.0 cores → 5 pods of 2 vCPU
Busy DB connections ≈ 17
Order storage / year (provisioned): 4.1 TB
Catalog egress (uncompressed): 2.1 GB/s

What L1 gets right: every formula from §2 in one place, with named inputs.

What L1 can't do:

Gap Why it matters Inputs are hard-coded guesses Nobody can review or reuse them No per-pod capacity from load tests "6 ms CPU" is a guess; real limits are often I/O, GC or locks No zone-failure headroom Plan fails exactly when an AZ fails at peak No cross-service checks (DB connections, Kafka) Local answers can be globally impossible

A small capacity-planner service where teams save named scenarios and compare them.

package com.grocery.capacity.domain;

/** Pure functions. No Spring, no I/O — trivially testable and reusable in L3/L4. */
public final class CapacityMath {

    public static final double SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86_400;

    private CapacityMath() { }

    public static double avgQps(long dau, double actionsPerUserPerDay) {
        return dau * actionsPerUserPerDay / SECONDS_PER_DAY;
    }

    public static double coresNeeded(double qps, double cpuMsPerRequest, double targetUtilization) {
        if (targetUtilization <= 0 || targetUtilization >= 1) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("targetUtilization must be in (0,1)");
        }
        return qps * cpuMsPerRequest / (1000.0 * targetUtilization);
    }

    public static double inFlight(double qps, double latencyMs) {
        return qps * latencyMs / 1000.0;
    }

    public static int podsFor(double cores, int vcpuPerPod) {
        return Math.max(1, (int) Math.ceil(cores / vcpuPerPod));
    }
}

@Service
public class EstimateService {

    private final CapacityScenarioRepository repository;
    private final Clock clock;

    public EstimateService(CapacityScenarioRepository repository, Clock clock) {
        this.repository = repository;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    @Transactional
    public EstimateResponse estimateAndSave(EstimateRequest r) {
        double avg   = CapacityMath.avgQps(r.dau(), r.actionsPerUserPerDay());
        double peak  = avg * r.peakFactor();
        double cores = CapacityMath.coresNeeded(peak, r.cpuMsPerRequest(), r.targetUtilization());
        int pods     = CapacityMath.podsFor(cores, r.vcpuPerPod());
        double egressMb = peak * r.responseBytes() / 1_000_000.0;
        double inFlight = CapacityMath.inFlight(peak, r.latencyMs());

        var id = UUID.randomUUID();
        repository.save(new CapacityScenario(id, r.name(), r.dau(), r.actionsPerUserPerDay(),
                r.peakFactor(), peak, cores, pods, clock.instant()));
        return new EstimateResponse(id, r.name(), avg, peak, egressMb, cores, pods, inFlight);
    }
}

What L2 fixed: shared, reviewable, validated scenarios, and math isolated in pure functions.

What L2 still assumes: CPU is the bottleneck, "6 ms CPU per request" is true, and each service can be sized in isolation. Real systems hit connection limits, zone failures and measured per-pod ceilings first.

L3 replaces guesses with measured per-pod capacity from load tests. It applies an explicit policy (growth, P90 factor, zone headroom) and runs cross-service checks that produce warnings. It refuses to plan a service it has no measurements for.

    LI["Data-store limits<br/>max connections"] --> PL
    PL --> OUT["CapacityPlan<br/>pods per service + warnings"]

public record PlanPolicy(double growthFactor, double p90Factor, int zones, int minPodsPerZone) {
    public PlanPolicy {

        if (growthFactor <= 0 || p90Factor < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid factors");

package com.grocery.capacity.plan;

import java.util.List;

public record ServicePlan(String service, double forecastQps, int podsNeeded,
                          int podsProvisioned, double headroomPercent) { }

public record PlanWarning(Severity severity, String subject, String message) {
    public enum Severity { INFO, WARN, BLOCKER }
}

public record CapacityPlan(List<ServicePlan> services, List<PlanWarning> warnings) {
    public boolean hasBlockers() {
        return warnings.stream().anyMatch(w -> w.severity() == PlanWarning.Severity.BLOCKER);
    }

Note

In a real module, PlanWarning and CapacityPlan each go in their own file. They're shown together here for brevity.

package com.grocery.capacity.plan;

import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class CapacityPlanner {

    public CapacityPlan plan(List<ServiceDemand> demands,
                             Map<String, ServiceProfile> profiles,
                             Map<String, Integer> dbMaxConnections,
                             PlanPolicy policy) {

        List<ServicePlan> plans = new ArrayList<>();
        List<PlanWarning> warnings = new ArrayList<>();
        Map<String, Integer> connectionsByDb = new HashMap<>();

        for (ServiceDemand d : demands) {
            ServiceProfile p = profiles.get(d.service());
            if (p == null) {
                // Never guess capacity for an unmeasured service.
                warnings.add(new PlanWarning(PlanWarning.Severity.BLOCKER, d.service(),
                        "no load-test profile; run a load test before planning"));
                continue;
            }

            double forecast = d.peakQps() * policy.growthFactor() * policy.p90Factor();
            int needed = (int) Math.ceil(forecast / p.perPodQpsAtSlo());

            // Survive loss of one zone at forecast load, then round UP to a multiple of zones
            double withHeadroom = needed * (double) policy.zones() / (policy.zones() - 1);
            int perZone = Math.max(policy.minPodsPerZone(),
                                   (int) Math.ceil(withHeadroom / policy.zones()));
            int provisioned = perZone * policy.zones();

            if (provisioned > p.maxPods()) {
                warnings.add(new PlanWarning(PlanWarning.Severity.BLOCKER, d.service(),
                        "needs %d pods but maxPods is %d: raise the limit or change the design (cache, shed, async)"
                                .formatted(provisioned, p.maxPods())));
            }

            double capacity = provisioned * p.perPodQpsAtSlo();
            double headroom = (capacity - forecast) / capacity * 100.0;
            plans.add(new ServicePlan(d.service(), forecast, needed, provisioned, headroom));

            if (p.database() != null) {
                connectionsByDb.merge(p.database(), provisioned * p.dbPoolPerPod(), Integer::sum);
            }
        }

        // Cross-service check: the sum of pools must fit each database's connection limit
        connectionsByDb.forEach((db, total) -> {
            Integer max = dbMaxConnections.get(db);
            if (max == null) {
                warnings.add(new PlanWarning(PlanWarning.Severity.WARN, db, "unknown max connections"));
            } else if (total > max) {
                warnings.add(new PlanWarning(PlanWarning.Severity.BLOCKER, db,
                        "pools total %d connections > limit %d: shrink pools (Little's Law) or add PgBouncer"
                                .formatted(total, max)));
            } else if (total > max * 0.8) {
                warnings.add(new PlanWarning(PlanWarning.Severity.WARN, db,
                        "pools at %d%% of connection limit".formatted(total * 100 / max)));
            }
        });

        plans.sort(Comparator.comparing(ServicePlan::service));
        return new CapacityPlan(List.copyOf(plans), List.copyOf(warnings));
    }
}

package com.grocery.capacity.plan;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.*;

class CapacityPlannerTest {

    private final CapacityPlanner planner = new CapacityPlanner();
    private final PlanPolicy policy = new PlanPolicy(1.4, 1.15, 3, 1);

    @Test
    void sizesCatalogForP90AndZoneLoss() {
        var plan = planner.plan(
                List.of(new ServiceDemand("catalog-service", 118_000)),
                Map.of("catalog-service", new ServiceProfile("catalog-service", 3000, 5, "catalog-db", 150)),
                Map.of("catalog-db", 1000), policy);

        ServicePlan p = plan.services().getFirst();
        assertThat(p.forecastQps()).isCloseTo(189_980, within(1.0));
        assertThat(p.podsNeeded()).isEqualTo(64);
        assertThat(p.podsProvisioned()).isEqualTo(96);          // 64 × 3/2, multiple of 3 zones
        assertThat(p.podsProvisioned() % 3).isZero();
        assertThat(plan.hasBlockers()).isFalse();
    }

    @Test
    void losingOneZoneStillLeavesEnoughPods() {
        var plan = planner.plan(List.of(new ServiceDemand("checkout-service", 610)),
                Map.of("checkout-service", new ServiceProfile("checkout-service", 180, 10, "orders-db", 40)),
                Map.of("orders-db", 300), policy);
        ServicePlan p = plan.services().getFirst();
        int survivingPods = p.podsProvisioned() * 2 / 3;
        assertThat(survivingPods).isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(p.podsNeeded());
    }

    @Test
    void blocksWhenConnectionBudgetExceeded() {
        var plan = planner.plan(
                List.of(new ServiceDemand("checkout-service", 610), new ServiceDemand("order-service", 2_000)),
                Map.of("checkout-service", new ServiceProfile("checkout-service", 180, 20, "orders-db", 40),
                       "order-service",    new ServiceProfile("order-service", 400, 20, "orders-db", 40)),
                Map.of("orders-db", 300), policy);

        assertThat(plan.hasBlockers()).isTrue();
        assertThat(plan.warnings()).anySatisfy(w -> assertThat(w.subject()).isEqualTo("orders-db"));
    }

    @Test
    void refusesToGuessUnmeasuredService() {
        var plan = planner.plan(List.of(new ServiceDemand("new-service", 500)), Map.of(), Map.of(), policy);
        assertThat(plan.services()).isEmpty();
        assertThat(plan.hasBlockers()).isTrue();
    }
}

Why no Testcontainers here?

L3's planner is pure logic, so plain unit tests are the right tool. The Testcontainers rule applies when infrastructure is involved. That starts in L4, where the planner talks to Prometheus (tested with a mock HTTP server).

What L3 still lacks: the demand input is typed in by hand, and the output is a report someone must turn into Kubernetes config. Both steps are error-prone on sale day.

docs.title: L4 — Enterprise: Plan from Real Traffic, Ship as GitOps B4
docs.text:
L4 closes the loop:

  1. Demand comes from Prometheus: last event's peak rate per service.
  2. Output is KEDA ScaledObject YAML with a cron floor for the event window plus a Prometheus trigger so reactive scaling still works above the floor.
  3. The YAML is committed to the GitOps repo and reviewed like code.

package com.grocery.capacity.prometheus;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/** Minimal mapping of the Prometheus HTTP API instant-query response. */
public record PromResponse(String status, Data data) {
    public record Data(String resultType, List<Series> result) { }
    public record Series(Map<String, String> metric, List<Object> value) { }
}

package com.grocery.capacity.prometheus;

import com.grocery.capacity.plan.ServiceDemand;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;

public class PrometheusDemandSource {

    @ConfigurationProperties("capacity.prometheus")   // registered via @ConfigurationPropertiesScan
    public record Props(String baseUrl, String serviceLabel, Duration timeout) { }

    private final RestClient client;
    private final Props props;

    /** The RestClient is built (with timeouts) in PrometheusConfig, so tests can inject a mocked one. */
    public PrometheusDemandSource(RestClient prometheusRestClient, Props props) {
        this.client = prometheusRestClient;
        this.props = props;
    }

    /**
     * Peak 1-minute request rate per service within [windowEnd - window, windowEnd].
     * Uses a subquery so the peak is the max of per-minute rates, not a long average.
     */
    public List<ServiceDemand> peakDemand(Instant windowEnd, Duration window) {
        String label = props.serviceLabel();   // e.g. "application" (Micrometer common tag)
        String query = "max_over_time((sum by (%s) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[1m])))[%dm:1m])"
                .formatted(label, window.toMinutes());

        PromResponse response = client.get()
                .uri(u -> u.path("/api/v1/query")
                           .queryParam("query", "{q}")
                           .queryParam("time", windowEnd.getEpochSecond())
                           .build(query))
                .retrieve()
                .body(PromResponse.class);

        if (response == null || !"success".equals(response.status())) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Prometheus query failed");
        }
        return response.data().result().stream()
                .map(s -> new ServiceDemand(s.metric().get(label),
                                            Double.parseDouble(String.valueOf(s.value().get(1)))))
                .toList();
    }
}

package com.grocery.capacity.prometheus;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.http.client.JdkClientHttpRequestFactory;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.time.Duration;

@Configuration
public class PrometheusConfig {

    @Bean
    RestClient prometheusRestClient(RestClient.Builder builder, PrometheusDemandSource.Props props) {
        var factory = new JdkClientHttpRequestFactory(
                HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).build());
        factory.setReadTimeout(props.timeout());
        return builder.baseUrl(props.baseUrl()).requestFactory(factory).build();
    }

    @Bean
    PrometheusDemandSource prometheusDemandSource(RestClient prometheusRestClient,
                                                  PrometheusDemandSource.Props props) {
        return new PrometheusDemandSource(prometheusRestClient, props);
    }
}

package com.grocery.capacity.keda;

import com.grocery.capacity.plan.ServicePlan;
import com.grocery.capacity.plan.ServiceProfile;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;

/** Generates a KEDA ScaledObject: cron floor for the event window + reactive Prometheus trigger. */
public class KedaScaledObjectGenerator {

    public record EventWindow(String eventId, LocalDateTime startIst, LocalDateTime endIst) { }

    public String generate(ServicePlan plan, ServiceProfile profile, EventWindow window,
                           int normalMinReplicas, String prometheusUrl, double targetUtilization) {

        long perPodTarget = Math.round(profile.perPodQpsAtSlo() * targetUtilization);
        return """
            apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
            kind: ScaledObject
            metadata:
              name: %1$s-%2$s
              labels:
                capacity.grocery.com/event: %2$s
            spec:
              scaleTargetRef:
                name: %1$s
              minReplicaCount: %3$d
              maxReplicaCount: %4$d
              triggers:
                # Floor during the event window (pre-scale 30 min before start)
                - type: cron
                  metadata:
                    timezone: Asia/Kolkata
                    start: "%5$s"
                    end: "%6$s"
                    desiredReplicas: "%7$d"
                # Reactive scaling above the floor
                - type: prometheus
                  metadata:
                    serverAddress: %8$s
                    query: sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="%1$s"}[1m]))
                    threshold: "%9$d"
            """.formatted(
                plan.service(), window.eventId(), normalMinReplicas, profile.maxPods(),
                cron(window.startIst().minusMinutes(30)), cron(window.endIst()),
                plan.podsProvisioned(), prometheusUrl, perPodTarget);
    }

    /** minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week */
    static String cron(LocalDateTime t) {
        return "%d %d %d %d *".formatted(t.getMinute(), t.getHour(), t.getDayOfMonth(), t.getMonthValue());
    }
}
