Cron without a year

Cron expressions have no year field. The generated window recurs every year on that date. Label the objects with the event and delete them after the event (§6.1). A stale ScaledObject that pre-scales on the wrong date is just wasted money, but that's still money.

package com.grocery.capacity.service;

import com.grocery.capacity.config.CapacityProperties;
import com.grocery.capacity.keda.KedaScaledObjectGenerator;
import com.grocery.capacity.keda.KedaScaledObjectGenerator.EventWindow;
import com.grocery.capacity.plan.*;
import com.grocery.capacity.prometheus.PrometheusDemandSource;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import java.time.*;
import java.util.*;

@Service
public class EventPlanService {

    public record EventPlanResult(CapacityPlan plan, Map<String, String> manifests) { }

    private static final ZoneId IST = ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata");

    private final PrometheusDemandSource demandSource;
    private final CapacityProperties props;
    private final CapacityPlanner planner = new CapacityPlanner();
    private final KedaScaledObjectGenerator generator = new KedaScaledObjectGenerator();

    public EventPlanService(PrometheusDemandSource demandSource, CapacityProperties props) {
        this.demandSource = demandSource;
        this.props = props;
    }

    public EventPlanResult planEvent(EventWindow thisYear, LocalDateTime lastYearEndIst,
                                     Duration lastYearWindow, String prometheusUrl) {
        List<ServiceDemand> demand = demandSource.peakDemand(
                lastYearEndIst.atZone(IST).toInstant(), lastYearWindow);

        CapacityPlan plan = planner.plan(demand, props.profilesByService(),
                props.databaseMaxConnections(), props.policy());

        // Never emit manifests for a plan with blockers — humans must resolve them first
        if (plan.hasBlockers()) return new EventPlanResult(plan, Map.of());

        Map<String, String> manifests = new TreeMap<>();
        for (ServicePlan sp : plan.services()) {
            ServiceProfile profile = props.profilesByService().get(sp.service());
            manifests.put(sp.service() + ".yaml",
                    generator.generate(sp, profile, thisYear, 3, prometheusUrl, 0.6));
        }
        return new EventPlanResult(plan, manifests);
    }
}

package com.grocery.capacity.prometheus;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.test.web.client.MockRestServiceServer;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;
import java.time.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.springframework.test.web.client.match.MockRestRequestMatchers.requestTo;
import static org.springframework.test.web.client.response.MockRestResponseCreators.withSuccess;
import static org.hamcrest.Matchers.startsWith;

class PrometheusDemandSourceTest {

    @Test
    void parsesPeakDemandPerService() {
        RestClient.Builder builder = RestClient.builder().baseUrl("http://prom");
        MockRestServiceServer server = MockRestServiceServer.bindTo(builder).build();
        server.expect(requestTo(startsWith("http://prom/api/v1/query")))
              .andRespond(withSuccess("""
                  {"status":"success","data":{"resultType":"vector","result":[
                    {"metric":{"application":"catalog-service"},"value":[1730000000,"118000"]},
                    {"metric":{"application":"checkout-service"},"value":[1730000000,"610.5"]}]}}
                  """, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON));

        var source = new PrometheusDemandSource(builder.build(),
                new PrometheusDemandSource.Props("http://prom", "application", Duration.ofSeconds(5)));

        var demand = source.peakDemand(Instant.parse("2025-10-20T17:30:00Z"), Duration.ofHours(3));

        assertThat(demand).extracting("service").containsExactlyInAnyOrder("catalog-service", "checkout-service");
        assertThat(demand).anySatisfy(d -> assertThat(d.peakQps()).isEqualTo(610.5));
        server.verify();
    }
}

package com.grocery.capacity.keda;

import com.grocery.capacity.plan.*;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class KedaScaledObjectGeneratorTest {

    @Test
    void cronFloorStartsThirtyMinutesEarlyWithPlannedReplicas() {
        var gen = new KedaScaledObjectGenerator();
        var yaml = gen.generate(
                new ServicePlan("checkout-service", 980, 6, 9, 50),
                new ServiceProfile("checkout-service", 180, 10, "orders-db", 40),
                new KedaScaledObjectGenerator.EventWindow("diwali-2026",
                        LocalDateTime.of(2026, 11, 8, 20, 0), LocalDateTime.of(2026, 11, 8, 23, 0)),
                3, "http://prometheus.monitoring:9090", 0.6);

        assertThat(yaml).contains("start: \"30 19 8 11 *\"")
                        .contains("end: \"0 23 8 11 *\"")
                        .contains("desiredReplicas: \"9\"")
                        .contains("threshold: \"108\"");      // 180 × 0.6
    }
}

ADR-014: Pre-scale for scheduled events

Context. Scheduled sale starts rise 15–40× within about a minute. Reactive scaling needs 2–5 minutes (scrape + HPA sync + node provisioning + JVM warm-up). The incident in §1.1 cost ~4 minutes of errors at peak.

Decision. For events forecast above 3× normal peak: (1) generate the plan from the last comparable event's measured peak × growth × P90; (2) size with measured per-pod capacity and one-zone-loss headroom; (3) apply a KEDA cron floor from T−30 min to event end; (4) keep a Prometheus trigger for reactive scaling above the floor; (5) block manifest generation while the plan has blockers; (6) gateway load shedding is mandatory as the backstop.

Consequences. (+) Capacity is in place before the spike. (+) The plan is reviewable in Git. (−) We pay for idle capacity for ~30 minutes before the event and during low-demand parts of the window (~₹11 lakh per major event). (−) The forecast can still be wrong, which is why the reactive trigger and load shedding remain.

Revisit when: start-time staggering is accepted by marketing, or warm-up drops below ~30 s (for example with CRaC/AOT-cached JVMs), making reactive scaling viable for part of the spike.

docs.title: What changed from L1 to L4
docs.text:
Concern L1 L2 L3 L4 Inputs Hard-coded guesses Saved scenarios Measured per-pod capacity + policy Real past traffic + measured capacity Bottleneck model CPU CPU Measured SLO capacity + DB connections + max pods Same, per service Zone failure ❌ ❌ ✅ (zone headroom, zone multiples) ✅ Cross-service checks ❌ ❌ ✅ connection budgets ✅ Refuses to guess ❌ ❌ ✅ blockers ✅ no manifests with blockers Output Console JSON Plan + warnings Plan + GitOps KEDA manifests Right for Interview, whiteboard Team discussions Quarterly capacity reviews Sale-day operations

Would you build L4?

Only if you run several large scheduled events a year. For one Diwali sale, L3 plus a hand-written ScaledObject reviewed in a PR is enough. The process (forecast → measured capacity → zone headroom → pre-scale → shed) matters more than the tool.

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes of capacity planning itself
docs.text: Failure Detection signal Blast radius Mitigation Forecast too low Actual/forecast ratio > 1.2 on the event dashboard Services above their floor rely on reactive scaling Reactive trigger above floor; load shedding; P90 not P50 Per-pod capacity stale (code got slower since the load test) Per-pod req/s at SLO drifts in production metrics Every plan built on it is wrong Re-run load tests after major releases; track "capacity per pod" as a metric Node capacity unavailable in region Pending pods; node autoscaler errors Pre-scale silently fails Reserve capacity ahead; dress rehearsal on D-2 Cron window in the wrong timezone Pre-scale happens 5.5 h off Idle cost, or no capacity at start timezone: Asia/Kolkata explicit; test the generated cron Stale ScaledObject repeats next year Unexpected scale-up on a random date Cost Label objects by event; post-event cleanup job Connection budget exceeded on scale-up too many connections errors; Hikari timeouts Scaling up makes things worse Planner blocker; PgBouncer; pools sized by Little's Law Retry amplification during overload Request rate rises while success rate falls Overload feeds itself Retry budgets, jittered backoff, Retry-After honored by clients (Ch 18) Liveness probe tied to latency Restart storms during overload Capacity collapses Liveness = process health only; readiness for traffic

docs.title: 6.2 Observability for capacity
docs.text:
Signal Type Why http_server_requests_seconds_count rate per service Counter → rate Demand input for L4 Per-pod throughput at SLO Derived (rate ÷ ready pods, when p99 within SLO) Validates load-test capacity in production Headroom % = (pods × per-pod capacity − load) ÷ capacity Recording rule The single most useful event-day number Hikari hikaricp_connections_active / _pending Gauge Little's Law in practice; pending > 0 means pool saturation Kafka consumer lag Gauge Consumers under-provisioned Pending pods, node provisioning time Gauge Scaling mechanics health Actual vs forecast Dashboard panel Calibrates next year's estimate

Example Prometheus recording rule for headroom (catalog, 3,000 req/s per pod):

groups:
  - name: capacity
    rules:
      - record: capacity:headroom_ratio:catalog
        expr: |
          1 - (
            sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="catalog-service"}[1m]))
            /
            (count(up{application="catalog-service"} == 1) * 3000)
          )
      - alert: CatalogHeadroomLow
        expr: capacity:headroom_ratio:catalog < 0.25
        for: 2m
        labels: { severity: page }
        annotations:
          summary: "catalog-service headroom below 25 %: scale up or start shedding"

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Capacity plans reveal business forecasts (order volumes, growth). Treat planner output as confidential and keep it in a restricted repo.
  • The planner's Prometheus access should be read-only, through a service account.
  • Load tests must not hit real payment gateways or send real SMS. Use sandbox endpoints (Razorpay test mode) and stub providers.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance & tuning knobs
docs.text: Knob Typical value Guidance Target utilization 50–60 % CPU Lower for latency-critical paths; queueing grows as ρ/(1−ρ) P90 factor 1.15–1.5 Derive from forecast error history Pre-scale lead time 30 min ≥ node provisioning + JVM warm-up + safety Zone headroom zones ÷ (zones − 1) 1.5 for 3 AZs; 2.0 for 2 AZs (expensive) Hikari pool size Little's Law × 1.5–2 Not the default of 10 for every service KEDA Prometheus threshold per-pod capacity × target utilization So reactive scaling starts before saturation

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
A capacity plan is a cost plan. For the Diwali example:

Item Estimate Extra pods (~200 × 1.5 vCPU × 3.5 h) ~1,050 vCPU-hours Reserved node capacity (a day's reservation) Largest line item CDN egress (~9.6 TB extra) Per-GB pricing, negotiate committed-use Load-test environment (D-5, 4 h at stress) ~equal to one event hour

Show finance the cost of the alternative: last year's four minutes of errors at ~420 orders/s is ~100 K lost or delayed orders. At an average basket of ₹700, that's ~₹7 crore of GMV at risk against ~₹11 lakh of capacity.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Precision theatre. Symptom: "83.333 orders per second" in an interview, while the peak factor is a guess. Fix: Round aggressively (10⁵ seconds/day) and spend the time on what the numbers imply.

2. Sizing on averages. Symptom: "We do 1 K req/s, 10 pods is plenty," then the evening peak is 5× and a sale start is 30×. Fix: Always carry a peak factor, justified by traffic shape (§2.3).

3. Trusting reactive autoscaling for step changes.

# ❌ before: only reactive; nothing is ready at 20:00:00
spec:
  minReplicas: 12
  metrics: [{ type: Resource, resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 } } }]

# ✅ after: cron floor for the event window + reactive above it (L4)
triggers:
  - type: cron
    metadata: { timezone: Asia/Kolkata, start: "30 19 8 11 *", end: "0 23 8 11 *", desiredReplicas: "96" }
  - type: prometheus
    metadata: { query: "...", threshold: "1800" }

4. Guessing per-pod capacity. Symptom: "A pod can do 2,000 req/s" from a blog post. The real endpoint does 3 DB calls and manages 180. Fix: Load test each critical service to the point where p99 breaks its SLO, and use that number.

5. Default pool sizes everywhere.

# ❌ before: every service, every pod — adds up to thousands of connections
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size: 50

# ✅ after: sized from Little's Law (850 req/s × 20 ms ≈ 17 busy across the fleet), per pod
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size: 10     # 10 pods × 10 = 100 ≥ 2 × 17 with headroom

6. Ignoring zone failure. Symptom: Capacity is exactly enough at peak. One AZ outage at peak becomes a total outage. Fix: zones ÷ (zones − 1) headroom for tier-1 services, and write down which services are tier-1.

7. Forgetting the data tier. Symptom: The app tier scales to 96 pods, and the database falls over from connections, CPU or hot rows. Fix: Every capacity plan has a data-tier check section (§4).

8. Estimating once. Symptom: The plan from two years ago still drives min replicas. Fix: Compare actual vs forecast after every event, and recalibrate the peak factors and per-pod capacity.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ Why do back-of-the-envelope estimates in a system design interview at all?

30-second answer: To find out which parts of the design matter. Estimates tell you whether data fits in memory, whether you need caching, sharding or async processing, and where the bottleneck will be. Without numbers, every design choice is a guess.

Deep answer: A 2.4 MB dataset means an in-memory replica; 4 TB/year means one DB with partitioning; 110 K read req/s means CDN plus cache. The estimate also shows the interviewer you can reason quantitatively, which is a core senior signal.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Time spent estimating is time not spent on the design. Keep it to 3–5 minutes.

Follow-ups: 1. How precise should it be? → Order of magnitude. Round freely. 2. What if the interviewer gives no numbers? → State assumptions and carry on.

Red flags: Skipping estimates, or spending 15 minutes on arithmetic.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Ends every number with "…which means we should/shouldn't do X."

Q2 [B1] ⭐ Convert 10 million requests per day into requests per second, and give the peak.

30-second answer: 10 M ÷ 10⁵ ≈ 100 req/s average (116 exactly). Peak depends on traffic shape. With a typical 3–5× daily peak, that's 300–500 req/s. A scheduled event can reach 20–40×.

Deep answer: Use 1 M/day ≈ 12/s as the anchor. State the peak factor and why: "Food and grocery peak around dinner, so 5×."

Trade-offs: Designing for the extreme peak all day is expensive, which is where pre-scaling and elasticity come in.

Follow-ups: 1. How would you find the real peak factor? → Hour-of-day histograms and past campaigns. 2. What about per-second spikes? → Minute averages hide them. Measure at 1 s or 10 s resolution.

Red flags: No peak factor at all.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Distinguishes daily peak, campaign peak and retry amplification.

Q3 [B1] Which latency numbers should every engineer know, and why do they matter?

30-second answer: Memory ~100 ns, SSD random read ~20–100 µs, same-AZ round trip ~0.1–0.5 ms, cross-region ~50–200 ms, and new pod/JVM start in tens of seconds. They tell you what a design can achieve: memory is ~1,000× faster than a network call.

Deep answer: A page with 10 sequential service calls at 1 ms each can't be under 10 ms. Cross-region synchronous replication adds ~60 ms to every write. Scaling that needs new JVMs can't absorb a 40-second spike.

Trade-offs: Faster tiers are smaller and costlier (memory vs disk).

Follow-ups: 1. Why is a sequence of calls worse than parallel? → Latencies add in sequence; in parallel you pay roughly the max. 2. Where does JSON serialization fit? → Often the dominant CPU cost for in-memory endpoints.

Red flags: Not knowing the orders of magnitude.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Includes operational latencies (JVM warm-up, node provisioning, DNS TTLs), not just hardware ones.

Q4 [B1] Estimate storage for 1 million orders per day for one year.

30-second answer: Around 4 KB per order (header, ~8 items, status history) × 1 M/day ≈ 4 GB/day ≈ 1.5 TB/year raw. With indexes (×2) and 3 copies, ~9 TB provisioned. That fits a single well-provisioned relational cluster with monthly partitions.

Deep answer: Mention what's not in the orders table: invoice PDFs go to object storage (~60 KB each, so a much bigger total), events go to Kafka with retention, and analytics goes to a warehouse. Retention rules (GST) decide archive strategy.

Trade-offs: Hot vs cold storage cost. Partitioning makes archiving cheap.

Follow-ups: 1. When would you shard? → When write throughput or working set exceeds one primary, not on storage size alone. 2. How do you shrink it? → Drop redundant snapshots, compress, archive.

Red flags: Forgetting indexes, replicas, or the blobs.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Separates OLTP, object storage and archive, and ties retention to regulation.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do you derive a peak factor instead of just picking one?

30-second answer: From traffic shape: hour-of-day and day-of-week histograms, past campaigns and sale starts, and retry behaviour during incidents. Take the per-second or 10-second maximum over the relevant window, divided by the daily average.

Deep answer: Different peaks need different responses. Daily peaks are handled by autoscaling. Push-notification bursts are handled by pre-scaling or rate-limited sends. Sale starts are handled by pre-scaling, queues and shedding. Retry storms are handled by retry budgets. The factor is only useful alongside its rise time.

Trade-offs: Higher factors mean more idle cost, so pair them with scheduled scaling.

Follow-ups: 1. What if there's no history? → Use analogous products or events, then run a canary launch. 2. Why does the measurement window matter? → Averaging hides spikes.

Red flags: "Peak is 2× average" for every system.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Talks about rise time, and about shaping the peak (staggered notifications, virtual queues).

Q6 [B2] ⭐ Use Little's Law to size a database connection pool.

30-second answer: Busy connections = request rate × time each request holds a connection. At 850 req/s × 20 ms = 17 busy connections across the fleet. Give 1.5–2× headroom and split across pods: with 10 pods, ~4 per pod minimum, so 10 per pod is generous.

Deep answer: The common mistake is multiplying default pools (10–50) by pod count and exceeding max_connections. Also, a connection held during a remote HTTP call inside a transaction inflates W dramatically. Keep transactions short, and use PgBouncer when fleets grow.

Trade-offs: Too small a pool means requests wait on the pool. Too large means DB contention and memory use.

Follow-ups: 1. What does hikaricp_connections_pending > 0 mean? → Pool saturation. Check W first, not the pool size. 2. Do virtual threads change this? → No. They remove the thread limit, which makes pool limits more important.

Red flags: "Set the pool to 100 to be safe."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Reasons about the sum across services per database, and about transaction scope inflating W.

Q7 [B2] Why does the read/write ratio matter for design?

30-second answer: It tells you where to optimize. Read-heavy workloads (100:1) want caches, replicas and CDNs. Write-heavy workloads want append-friendly stores, batching and partitioning. 1:1 contended workloads need attention to locking and hot keys.

Deep answer: Serviceability (10⁶:1) is a full in-memory replica. Catalog (100:1) is cache plus CDN. Rider pings (write-heavy) go to Redis and a time-series store with batching. Inventory at sale time (1:1 on hot rows) needs reservation design (Ch 46).

Trade-offs: Caching read-heavy data introduces staleness, so bound it (Ch 01).

Follow-ups: 1. How does the ratio change during a sale? → Inventory flips from read-heavy to contended. 2. What store for write-heavy time series? → LSM-based or a time-series DB.

Red flags: Treating all data the same way.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Notes that the ratio changes with time and events.

Q8 [B2] Estimate bandwidth for the product listing API at peak and how to reduce it.

30-second answer: 110 K req/s × 20 KB ≈ 2.2 GB/s (~18 Gbps) uncompressed. Reduce it with compression (5–8× on JSON), list DTOs instead of full objects, pagination limits, sparse fields, HTTP caching or CDN for anonymous listings, and images served only via CDN.

Deep answer: Serialization CPU scales with payload size, so shrinking responses cuts both bandwidth and compute. Cache listing pages per store and pincode cluster at the edge where personalization allows.

Trade-offs: Compression costs CPU; CDN caching limits personalization.

Follow-ups: 1. Brotli vs gzip? → Brotli compresses better; watch CPU at origin (pre-compress static assets). 2. What about mobile networks? → Smaller payloads matter even more for p99 on 4G.

Red flags: Ignoring payload size.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Connects payload size to CPU, cost and mobile UX.

Q9 [B2] How many servers do you need for 20 K req/s?

30-second answer: It depends on per-request cost. If a pod sustains 1,000 req/s at SLO (from a load test), that's 20 pods at 100 % utilization. At a 60 % target, ~34. With 3-AZ headroom, ~51, rounded to a multiple of 3.

Deep answer: Without a load test, estimate from CPU ms per request (profiling) or a prior, and say so. Check that dependencies scale too: DB connections, cache ops, downstream rate limits.

Trade-offs: Bigger pods mean fewer JVMs to warm but a coarser scaling granularity.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not 90 % utilization? → Queueing blows up tail latency. 2. What limits scaling besides CPU? → Locks, connections, GC, downstream limits.

Red flags: A number without its assumptions.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Includes zone headroom and dependency checks unprompted.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ Walk me through a capacity estimate for checkout during a festival sale.

30-second answer: 1.5 M orders that day, 20 % in the first hour, first minute at 5× → ~420 orders/s, ~850 checkout attempts/s. That's ~6 pods for checkout. The real risks are ~110 K req/s of catalog reads, hot inventory rows, DB connection budgets, and the 40-second rise time, so pre-scale.

Deep answer: Go through the fan-out: each checkout calls serviceability, pricing, promotion, inventory reserve, slot, order and payment. Compute per-dependency rates, then data-tier checks: orders DB ~5 K statements/s, Redis cart ops, Kafka partitions from consumer time. Identify hot keys (₹1 SKU in one metro store ~50 reservations/s, under row-lock capacity). Close with the plan: pre-scale, shed, and dashboards.

Trade-offs: Pre-scaling cost vs outage risk. Staggering the sale start vs marketing impact.

Follow-ups: 1. What if the hot SKU is one national deal? → ~250/s on one row approaches lock limits, so split stock into buckets or use a reservation queue (Ch 46). 2. How do you validate? → Load test at stress; dress rehearsal.

Red flags: Sizing only checkout pods.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Finds that the bottleneck is reads and rise time, not checkout compute.

Q11 [B3] ⭐ We have autoscaling. Why did the sale still fail in the first minutes?

30-second answer: Reactive scaling has latency: metrics scrape (~15 s), HPA sync (~15 s), node provisioning (1–4 min), JVM start and warm-up (20–90 s). A spike rising in 40 s outruns all of it. Meanwhile, overload, retries and latency-based liveness probes reduce capacity further.

Deep answer: Fixes: scheduled pre-scaling (cron floor), reserved node capacity, probes that don't restart overloaded pods, gateway load shedding and admission control, client retry budgets, and faster starts (CDS/AOT, CRaC) to shorten the gap.

Trade-offs: Pre-scaled idle capacity costs money; it's cheaper than lost GMV.

Follow-ups: 1. What's a virtual waiting room? → Queue users at the edge and admit at a controlled rate. 2. Liveness vs readiness under overload? → Readiness can go false to shed load; liveness should stay true.

Red flags: "Set min replicas higher" without a rationale or a time window.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Quantifies each delay and treats probes and retries as part of the capacity system.

Q12 [B3] How do you manage the database connection budget across 26 services?

30-second answer: Treat connections per database as a budget. Size each service's pool from Little's Law, sum pods × pool per database including peak scale-out, and keep the total under a safe limit. Use PgBouncer (transaction pooling) when the fleet is large, and enforce this in the capacity plan.

Deep answer: Scale-out multiplies pools: 96 catalog pods × 5 = 480. That's why the L3 planner blocks on budgets. Also separate read replicas for read-heavy services, keep transactions short, and don't hold connections across remote calls.

Trade-offs: PgBouncer transaction pooling breaks session features (session-level prepared statements, advisory locks). Know what you rely on.

Follow-ups: 1. Symptoms when exceeded? → too many connections, pool timeouts, DB CPU in context switching. 2. Who owns the budget? → The DB-owning team, with limits per consumer.

Red flags: Only thinking per service.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Plans connections at peak scale-out and knows PgBouncer's trade-offs.

Q13 [B3] How would an estimate reveal a hot key problem before production?

30-second answer: Estimate per-key load, not just total load. Multiply total rate × fraction touching the key × concentration (one store, one SKU), and compare with single-key capacity (row lock ~200–1,000 updates/s, Redis key on one shard ~100 K ops/s shared).

Deep answer: 850 checkouts/s × 30 % containing the ₹1 onion × 20 % in one metro store ≈ 50/s on one row: fine. Make it a national single-SKU flash deal and it's ~250/s on one row: risky. Mitigations: split stock into N buckets, reserve in batches, or queue reservations (Ch 46).

Trade-offs: Bucketing complicates "is it in stock" reads and can strand stock in empty buckets.

Follow-ups: 1. Hot keys in caches? → Replicate hot keys or add an L1 local cache. 2. How to detect in prod? → Per-key metrics sampling, Redis --hotkeys / LFU stats.

Red flags: Only aggregate QPS.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Computes skew explicitly and has mitigations ready.

Q14 [B3] Your estimate was 3× off in production. What went wrong and how do you catch it earlier?

30-second answer: Usual causes: a wrong peak factor or window, per-pod capacity taken from a guess or stale load test, missing fan-out or retries, a new feature adding calls per page, or a marketing change nobody told engineering about. Catch it with actual-vs-forecast dashboards, early canary traffic, load tests after major releases, and a forecast process that includes marketing.

Deep answer: Do a post-event review. Decompose the error into demand error (users, actions) and supply error (per-pod capacity). Recalibrate both, and add the missing driver (for example, "push notification size → req/s") to the model.

Trade-offs: More modelling effort vs over-provisioning to compensate.

Follow-ups: 1. Which is more common, demand or supply error? → Supply is often underestimated because code slows down over releases. 2. How do you make the forecast robust? → Ranges (P50/P90), stress test beyond P90.

Red flags: Blaming "unexpected traffic" without analysis.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Separates demand and supply error and fixes the process.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ How would you set up capacity planning as an ongoing process for a 26-service platform?

30-second answer: Assign ownership (a capacity owner per tier-1 service and a platform owner overall). Keep measured per-pod capacity profiles current through regular load tests. Forecast quarterly and per event with business input. Plan with policy (P90, zone headroom). Check data tiers. Ship plans as GitOps config. Review actual vs forecast after each event.

Deep answer: Put capacity into the release process ("perf regression > 10 % blocks release") and into the business calendar (marketing events trigger plans automatically). Report headroom and unit cost to leadership monthly. Tooling (the L3/L4 planner) supports the process but doesn't replace it.

Trade-offs: Process overhead vs incidents. Scale rigour to tier and event size.

Follow-ups: 1. Who pays for headroom? → It should be an explicit, approved line in the budget. 2. How do you handle new services? → No profile, no plan; block launch until a load test exists.

Red flags: "The cloud scales automatically."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Ties capacity to release gates, the business calendar and finance.

Q16 [B4] How do you estimate the infrastructure cost of a new feature per order?

30-second answer: Estimate added requests per order (fan-out), CPU per request, storage and egress per order, and third-party costs (SMS, maps API). Convert to ₹ with unit prices, then divide by orders. Compare with the feature's revenue or retention impact.

Deep answer: For example, live rider tracking adds 1 ping/4 s × 25-minute delivery ≈ 375 writes per order, plus WebSocket connections, plus maps API calls. Once per-order infra and third-party costs are estimated, they can be checked against the delivery margin. The estimate may also push the design toward sampling (1 ping/10 s) or server-side interpolation.

Trade-offs: Cost vs UX fidelity.

Follow-ups: 1. What dominates such costs? → Often third-party APIs and logs, not compute. 2. How do you track it after launch? → Cost allocation tags and showback.

Red flags: Not knowing unit economics.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Uses the estimate to change the design before building.

Q17 [B4] ⭐ The business expects 10× growth in 2 years. What breaks first and how do you plan?

30-second answer: Estimate each component at 10×. Usually the first to break are single-writer databases (write throughput, connections), hot keys, shared infra (Kafka cluster, Redis shard), cost lines like logs and CDN, and org or operational load, before stateless compute. Plan changes in order of "time to break × lead time to fix."

Deep answer: Orders DB at 10× ≈ 50–60 K statements/s at peak, beyond one primary, so plan partitioning or sharding by region with a 6–9 month lead time. Carts at 10× exceed one Redis shard's ops, so cluster. Catalog scales horizontally, so it just costs money. Build a timeline: each component's break date vs the migration's lead time.

Trade-offs: Premature scaling work vs a late emergency migration.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you prioritize? → Lead time to fix × likelihood × impact. 2. What's a scalability runway? → Months until a component hits its limit on the current growth curve.

Red flags: "Add more pods."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Uses a runway-vs-lead-time chart and includes org and cost limits.

Q18 [B4] How do you present capacity estimates and their uncertainty to executives?

30-second answer: Give scenarios (P50/P90/stress) with their drivers, what each costs, and what happens if we're wrong (degradation, not outage). Lead with the decision you need: "Approve ₹11 lakh to protect ~₹7 crore of GMV at risk in the first hour."

Deep answer: Show a small table, one chart of last event's actual vs forecast, and the top three risks with owners. Avoid false precision. Make the trade-off theirs to make, with numbers.

Trade-offs: Simplicity vs completeness. Put details in an appendix.

Follow-ups: 1. What if they reject the budget? → Offer degraded options (smaller window, stagger, shedding) with explicit risk. 2. How do you build trust? → Track forecast accuracy over time.

Red flags: Technical detail without a decision.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Frames capacity as a business risk decision.

Q19 [B4] How do you estimate when there's no historical data (a new city launch or a new product)?

30-second answer: Use analogues (a similar city scaled by population or penetration), top-down market sizing checked against bottom-up (store capacity × riders × slots), wide ranges, and a staged launch (invite-only, one pincode cluster) that produces real data quickly. Then design for elasticity plus hard limits (admission control, slot caps).

Deep answer: Physical capacity often caps demand. A dark store can pick maybe N orders/hour, so a digital system sized for 5× the physical cap is enough. Use that as a sanity bound.

Trade-offs: Under-provisioning a launch hurts the first impression. Over-provisioning wastes money on uncertainty.

Follow-ups: 1. What's the fastest way to reduce uncertainty? → Launch small and measure. 2. Which bound do you trust most? → Physical capacity limits.

Red flags: A single confident number.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Bounds digital demand with physical operations capacity.

Q20 [B4] Is N+1 or zone-failure headroom worth the cost? How do you decide?

30-second answer: Decide per tier. Tier-1 paths (checkout, payment, catalog during events) get zones ÷ (zones − 1) headroom because an AZ loss at peak is a total outage otherwise. Tier-2/3 services accept degradation or shed load. Weigh the headroom cost against the probability of an AZ event × revenue at risk × duration.

Deep answer: With 3 AZs, headroom is +50 % for tier-1 compute. You can reduce it by shedding tier-3 traffic during a zone loss (freeing capacity), by using spot instances for non-critical headroom, or by accepting degraded SLOs for a bounded time. Document it as a decision (ADR) with finance.

Trade-offs: Cost vs availability, which is the Ch 01 trade-off in money terms.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not 2 AZs? → Headroom becomes +100 %, and it's weaker against a correlated failure. 2. Does headroom help regional outages? → No. That's multi-region (Ch 27).

Red flags: Always yes or always no.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Tiers services and uses shedding to reduce headroom cost.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Estimation finds which part of the design breaks, not a precise number.
  2. Anchors: 1 M/day ≈ 12/s, a day ≈ 10⁵ s, memory ~100 ns, same-AZ hop ~0.5 ms, new JVM or node = tens of seconds to minutes.
  3. Peak factors come from traffic shape and rise time. Scheduled sale starts are the dangerous case.
  4. The read/write ratio decides the architecture: memory replica, cache/CDN, write-optimized store, or contention design.
  5. Storage = records × size × retention × overhead (indexes, replicas). Separate OLTP, blobs and archive.
  6. Little's Law sizes pools, threads and partitions. Size connection pools from it, never from defaults.
  7. Target 50–60 % utilization. Queueing makes tails explode near saturation.
  8. Add zone-failure headroom for tier-1 services: zones ÷ (zones − 1).
  9. Reactive autoscaling can't absorb step changes. Pre-scale, and keep load shedding as the backstop.
  10. Present ranges with drivers and cost, and recalibrate after every event.

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: If the estimate shows… Then… Dataset < a few hundred MB, read-mostly In-memory replica per instance Read:write ≥ 100:1 Cache + CDN + read replicas Write-heavy time series LSM / time-series store, batching Per-key rate near single-key limits Split keys, bucket, queue (Ch 46) Σ pools > DB connection limit Little's Law sizing, PgBouncer Spike rise time < scaling time Pre-scale (cron floor) + shedding Growth breaks a component before a migration could finish Start the migration now (runway vs lead time)

docs.title: 03. Networking Essentials
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 01, Ch 02 · What you will build: Live order-tracking updates, taken from polling vs a raw SSE stream (L1) to a multi-pod SSE service with heartbeats, resume-after-disconnect, Redis fan-out and graceful drain (L4) · Reading time: 90 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: the tracking screen that went quiet after 60 seconds
docs.text:
The grocery app launched live order tracking: Packed → Rider assigned → Out for delivery → Arriving. It worked perfectly on office Wi-Fi. In production, a pattern emerged in support tickets: "The app stopped updating. I reopened it and my order was already delivered."

The team spent a week on the application code. It was fine. The problem was the network path between the phone and the server:

  1. The cloud load balancer had a 60-second idle timeout. Between "Rider assigned" and "Out for delivery" there are often 5–10 minutes with no data, so the load balancer silently closed the connection.
  2. The mobile carrier's NAT (carrier-grade NAT on Indian 4G networks) dropped idle TCP mappings even sooner on some networks.
  3. The app's WebSocket client didn't notice the connection was dead. TCP doesn't tell you a peer vanished unless you send something.
  4. When a rider's phone switched from Wi-Fi to 4G, the client's IP address changed, and every TCP connection it had was gone.

The fix was about 40 lines: a heartbeat every 15 seconds, a reconnect with Last-Event-ID so missed updates are replayed, and aligning timeouts along the whole path.

The thesis of this chapter

Every request crosses a chain of networks, proxies and timeouts you don't own. Good system design treats the network as unreliable, stateful and full of middleboxes, and makes every long-lived interaction survive a dropped connection.

docs.title: 1.2 Where this lives in the grocery platform
docs.text: Interaction Networking concern App → api-gateway TLS 1.3, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, CDN edge, mobile network variability Live order tracking Long-lived connections, idle timeouts, NAT, reconnects (this chapter's code) Rider app location pings Connection migration on network switch (QUIC), battery, batching Service → service Keep-alive, connection pools, mTLS, DNS-based discovery, timeouts payment-service → Razorpay Outbound TLS, egress NAT, IP allow-listing, DNS TTLs Kafka, PostgreSQL, Redis Long-lived TCP, private subnets, security groups Webhooks from Razorpay Public ingress, signature verification, firewall rules

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text: Band After this chapter you can… B1 Explain the layers, TCP vs UDP, what DNS and TLS do, and polling vs SSE vs WebSockets B2 Reason about handshake costs, keep-alive and pooling, HTTP/1.1 vs 2 vs 3, and choose a real-time transport B3 Diagnose idle timeouts, NAT and port exhaustion, DNS caching, TLS failures, and design reconnect-safe streams B4 Design network topology (VPC, subnets, egress, zero trust), set org-wide timeout and TLS policy, and choose transports across a platform

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: sending a parcel across India B1
docs.text:
Sending an HTTP request is like sending a parcel from Bengaluru to Delhi:

  • The address (DNS) turns "Mehta Sweets, Chandni Chowk" into a precise PIN and street, just as DNS turns api.grocery.in into an IP address.
  • The courier's tracking and signatures (TCP) make sure every box arrives, in order, and is re-sent if lost.
  • The sealed, tamper-proof box (TLS) means nobody on the way can read or change the contents.
  • The language of the letter inside (HTTP) is what the recipient actually reads.
  • Checkpoints and warehouses on the way (proxies, load balancers, NAT) each have their own rules, such as "we throw away parcels that sit here too long."

Most production networking bugs happen at those checkpoints.

docs.title: 2.2 The layers: OSI vs TCP/IP ⭐ B1
docs.text:
OSI layer TCP/IP layer Examples What a backend engineer controls 7 Application Application HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket, DNS, Kafka protocol Almost everything: APIs, timeouts, retries 6 Presentation (Application) TLS, encoding (JSON, Protobuf), compression TLS config, serialization 5 Session (Application) Connection/session semantics Keep-alive, reconnection logic 4 Transport Transport TCP, UDP, QUIC (over UDP) Socket options, pools, timeouts 3 Network Internet IP, ICMP, routing VPC CIDRs, routes (via IaC) 2 Data link Link Ethernet, Wi-Fi, ARP Rarely 1 Physical Link Fibre, radio Never (but it's why cross-region is 60 ms)

Why load balancers are called L4 or L7

An L4 load balancer sees TCP/UDP connections (IP + port) and forwards bytes without understanding HTTP. An L7 load balancer terminates HTTP, so it can route by path or header, retry, and add headers. It also owns HTTP-level timeouts that affect your long-lived streams (Ch 08).

docs.title: 2.3 TCP vs UDP ⭐ B1 B2
docs.text: TCP UDP Connection Yes (3-way handshake) No Delivery Reliable, retransmits lost segments Best effort Ordering In order (a byte stream) No ordering (datagrams) Flow/congestion control Built in None (the app must do it) Head-of-line blocking Yes: one lost segment stalls everything after it No Typical use HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, databases, Kafka DNS, video/voice, gaming, QUIC (HTTP/3)

docs.title: The cost of a new connection B2
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client (Bengaluru, 4G)
    participant D as DNS resolver
    participant S as Server (Mumbai)
    C->>D: A? api.grocery.in
    D-->>C: 203.0.113.10 (TTL 60 s)
    Note over C,S: TCP: 1 RTT (~30-60 ms on 4G)
    C->>S: SYN
    S-->>C: SYN-ACK
    C->>S: ACK
    Note over C,S: TLS 1.3: +1 RTT
    C->>S: ClientHello (+ key share)
    S-->>C: ServerHello, cert, Finished
    C->>S: Finished + HTTP request (GET /orders/42)
    S-->>C: HTTP response
    Note over C,S: New connection ≈ DNS + 2 RTT before the first byte of data. A reused connection ≈ 0.5-1 RTT.

On a 50 ms mobile RTT, a fresh connection costs ~100–150 ms before your server does any work. That's why connection reuse (keep-alive, pooling, HTTP/2 multiplexing) is one of the highest-leverage performance settings you have.

TCP slow start. A new connection begins with a small congestion window (~10 segments ≈ 14 KB) and grows as ACKs arrive. A new connection can't send a 200 KB response at full speed immediately. Warm connections can. That's another reason to reuse connections.

docs.title: Connection teardown and TIME_WAIT B3
docs.text: The side that closes first keeps the socket in TIME_WAIT for 2×MSL (often ~60 s on Linux) so that late packets aren't misread. A service that opens and closes thousands of outbound connections per second (no pooling) exhausts ephemeral ports: ~28 K by default on Linux, per destination IP and port. The symptom is intermittent Cannot assign requested address or connect timeouts. The fix is connection pooling and keep-alive, not kernel tweaks.

docs.title: Nagle, delayed ACK and small messages B3
docs.text: Nagle's algorithm batches small writes, and delayed ACK holds acknowledgements briefly. Together they can add tens of milliseconds to request/response patterns with small writes. Most HTTP stacks set TCP_NODELAY, but check it for custom protocols and for SSE, where you want each small event sent immediately (flush after each event).

docs.title: 2.4 Keep-alive, connection pools and head-of-line blocking ⭐ B2
docs.text:
Keep-alive keeps a TCP (+TLS) connection open after a response so the next request can reuse it. A connection pool is a set of kept-alive connections a client reuses.

Setting Where Typical value Why Client connect timeout Every HTTP client 0.5–2 s internal, 3–5 s external Fail fast when the destination is unreachable Client read/response timeout Every HTTP client From the latency budget (Ch 01: 80 ms fresh check) Never wait forever Pool max connections per route Client Little's Law × 1.5 (Ch 02) Enough in-flight capacity, not a DoS on the server Idle connection TTL in pool Client Below the server's/LB's idle timeout Avoid reusing a connection the other side already closed Server keep-alive timeout Server (Tomcat/Jetty/Netty) 60–75 s Free resources held by idle clients LB idle timeout Cloud LB 60 s default on many LBs; configurable Silently kills idle long-lived connections

The stale pooled connection bug

If a client pool keeps idle connections longer than the server or load balancer does, the client sometimes sends a request on a connection the other side has already closed. The result is an intermittent Connection reset on the first request after a quiet period. The rule: client idle TTL < server keep-alive < LB idle timeout, and retry idempotent requests once on a reset.

Head-of-line (HOL) blocking happens when one slow item blocks everything behind it:

Protocol Where HOL blocking happens HTTP/1.1 At the HTTP level: one request at a time per connection, so a slow response blocks the next. Browsers open ~6 connections per host to compensate. HTTP/2 Solved at HTTP level (multiplexed streams), but still at TCP level: one lost packet stalls all streams on that connection HTTP/3 (QUIC) Solved at transport level: streams are independent over UDP. A lost packet stalls only its own stream

docs.title: 2.5 HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 ⭐ B2
docs.text:
Feature HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 HTTP/3 Transport TCP TCP QUIC over UDP Framing Text Binary frames Binary frames Requests per connection 1 at a time (pipelining unused in practice) Many concurrent streams Many concurrent streams Header compression None HPACK QPACK TLS Optional Effectively required by browsers Built in (TLS 1.3 in QUIC) Handshake to first byte TCP + TLS (2 RTT) TCP + TLS (2 RTT) 1 RTT, or 0-RTT on resumption Connection migration (IP change) No No Yes: the connection ID survives Wi-Fi ↔ 4G HOL blocking HTTP + TCP TCP only None across streams Where it shines Simple internal calls, legacy Service mesh, gRPC, browsers Mobile clients on lossy networks

Grocery platform choices:

  • Edge (CDN/LB → apps): HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 enabled. Mobile users on flaky 4G benefit most from HTTP/3's migration and loss handling.
  • Edge → origin and service-to-service: HTTP/2 (gRPC) or HTTP/1.1 with keep-alive pools. Internal networks are low-loss, so HTTP/3's benefits are smaller.
  • Long-lived streams (SSE): HTTP/2 lets a browser open many SSE streams over one connection. HTTP/1.1 browsers limit ~6 connections per host, which SSE can exhaust.

0-RTT has a price

TLS 1.3 / QUIC 0-RTT early data can be replayed by an attacker. Only allow it for idempotent, safe requests (GET the catalog), never for POST /checkout. Most CDNs let you restrict 0-RTT to safe methods.

docs.title: 2.6 DNS: resolution, TTLs and caching ⭐ B1 → B3
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App as JVM (payment-service)
    participant OS as OS / node-local cache
    participant R as Recursive resolver (VPC / CoreDNS)
    participant Root as Root
    participant TLD as .com TLD
    participant Auth as Authoritative (razorpay.com)
    App->>OS: resolve api.razorpay.com
    OS->>R: cache miss
    R->>Root: where is .com?
    Root-->>R: TLD servers
    R->>TLD: where is razorpay.com?
    TLD-->>R: authoritative NS
    R->>Auth: A api.razorpay.com?
    Auth-->>R: A records, TTL 60 s
    R-->>OS: answer (cached for TTL)
    OS-->>App: answer (the JVM caches too)
Concept What it means for your design TTL How long resolvers may cache an answer. Low TTL (30–60 s) enables fast failover but means more lookups. High TTL (hours) is cheap but slow to change. JVM DNS cache networkaddress.cache.ttl (security property). Default is ~30 s when no security manager is installed. Negative lookups are cached ~10 s. Never set it to "forever" in cloud environments where IPs change. Connection pools ignore DNS changes A pooled connection stays on the old IP until it's closed. Cap connection lifetime (e.g. 5–10 min) so traffic follows DNS failover. Kubernetes DNS service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local resolves to a ClusterIP. ndots:5 causes several search-path lookups for external names, so use FQDNs with a trailing dot or tune ndots for hot external calls. DNS as a dependency DNS outages look like "everything is down." Cache sensibly, run node-local DNS caches, and alert on resolver errors. DNS load balancing / GeoDNS Returns different IPs by location or health. Coarse-grained, and clients cache beyond TTLs. Good for region selection, not for fine load balancing (Ch 08). 
# $JAVA_HOME/conf/security/java.security (or -Dsun.net.inetaddr.ttl for older setups)
networkaddress.cache.ttl=30
networkaddress.cache.negative.ttl=5

docs.title: 2.7 TLS 1.3 and mTLS ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
TLS provides confidentiality (encryption), integrity (tamper detection) and server authentication (certificate chain to a trusted CA, and hostname match).

Topic Key point TLS 1.3 handshake 1 RTT (vs 2 in TLS 1.2); forward secrecy mandatory; fewer, safer cipher suites Session resumption / 0-RTT Faster reconnects; 0-RTT early data is replayable (restrict to idempotent requests) SNI Client sends the hostname in the handshake so one IP can serve many certificates Certificate chain Server sends leaf + intermediates. A missing intermediate causes errors on some clients only (a classic Android issue) Certificate expiry A top cause of self-inflicted outages. Automate renewal (ACME, cert-manager) and alert at 30/14/7 days Where TLS terminates At the CDN/LB (common), then re-encrypted to the origin; or end-to-end. Every hop that decrypts is a trust boundary mTLS Both sides present certificates, so the server authenticates the client. Used service-to-service (service mesh, Ch 17, 23) and for some partner APIs Pinning Mobile apps pinning certificates must plan rotation (pin the public key or CA, ship backup pins) or a cert rotation bricks the app

In the grocery platform

Customers reach the CDN on TLS 1.3 (HTTP/2 + HTTP/3). The CDN talks to the regional LB over TLS. Inside the cluster, services use mTLS via the mesh, so payment-service accepts calls only from workloads with the checkout-service identity. Outbound calls to Razorpay use TLS with the platform's trust store, and go out through a fixed egress IP that Razorpay can allow-list.

docs.title: 2.8 Real-time delivery: polling, long polling, SSE, WebSockets ⭐ B1 → B3
docs.text:
Short polling Long polling Server-Sent Events (SSE) WebSocket Direction Client pulls Client pulls, server holds until data Server → client Bidirectional Transport Repeated HTTP requests Repeated HTTP requests (held open) One long HTTP response (text/event-stream) HTTP upgrade → WebSocket frames Latency of an update Up to the poll interval ~Immediate ~Immediate ~Immediate Wasted requests Most Few None None Auto-reconnect + resume App-built App-built Built into browsers (EventSource, Last-Event-ID) App-built Works through proxies/CDNs Always Mostly Mostly (disable buffering) Needs upgrade support; some corporate proxies block it HTTP/2 multiplexing Yes Yes Yes Only with RFC 8441 (limited support) Server cost Request per poll Held request Held connection Held connection + frame handling Grocery use Fallback, low-frequency checks Legacy clients Order tracking, rider location to customer Customer ↔ rider chat, rider app two-way ops (Ch 41)

The L1 program in §5 measures the difference on a compressed 2-second order lifecycle:

Polling (100 ms): 18 requests for 6 status changes (67% wasted)
SSE: 1 request for 6 status changes

Over a real 35-minute delivery with a 10-second poll, that's ~210 requests for ~8 changes (96 % wasted), and each update is up to 10 seconds late.

Choosing between SSE and WebSockets

If the client mostly listens, use SSE: it's plain HTTP, reconnects and resumes automatically, and multiplexes over HTTP/2. If the client talks back frequently and with low latency (chat, collaborative editing, games), use WebSockets. For mobile apps, both need app-level heartbeats and reconnect logic, because OS network changes kill connections regardless.

docs.title: 2.9 NAT, firewalls and VPC basics B2 → B4
NAT (Network Address Translation)
docs.text:
NAT rewrites private addresses to a shared public address, and keeps a mapping table with idle timeouts.

Where Effect on your design Mobile carrier CGNAT (most Indian 4G/5G users) Idle mappings can expire in minutes, silently killing idle long-lived connections. Heartbeat every 15–30 s. Many users share one public IP, so IP-based rate limits hit innocent users. Cloud NAT gateway (private subnet → internet) Has its own idle timeout (minutes) and a limit on concurrent connections per destination. Heavy outbound calls to one partner API can exhaust NAT ports. Pool connections. Kubernetes SNAT (pod → outside) Pod IPs are translated to the node's IP. Conntrack table limits apply per node.

docs.title: Firewalls, security groups and network policies
docs.text: Control Scope Stateful? Use Security group (cloud) Instance / ENI Stateful "Only the LB may reach app nodes on 8080" Network ACL (cloud) Subnet Stateless Coarse deny rules, compliance boundaries Kubernetes NetworkPolicy Pod labels Stateful (CNI-dependent) "Only checkout pods may call payment on 8080" WAF (at CDN/LB) HTTP requests L7 OWASP rules, bot mitigation, rate limits (Ch 23) Service mesh authorization Workload identity (mTLS) L7 Identity-based rules that survive IP changes

flowchart TB

        subgraph Pub["Public subnets (3 AZs)"]

        end

Principle Why Data stores in private subnets with no internet route They can't be reached from outside, even if misconfigured Egress through NAT with fixed IPs Partners can allow-list; you can audit outbound traffic Private endpoints for cloud services (object storage, KMS) Traffic doesn't cross the internet; no NAT cost Three AZs for every tier Zone-failure tolerance (Ch 02 headroom) Non-overlapping CIDRs across VPCs/regions Future peering and multi-region (Ch 27) won't need renumbering Identity-based rules (mTLS) on top of IP rules IPs change constantly in Kubernetes; identities don't

docs.title: 2.10 Timeouts across a path: the timeout ladder B3 B4
docs.text:
Every hop has its own timeouts. They must be ordered, or the wrong layer gives up first, which causes retries, duplicate work and confusing errors.

flowchart LR
    A["Mobile app<br/>request timeout 10 s<br/>SSE heartbeat check 45 s"] --> B["CDN<br/>origin read 30 s<br/>idle 120 s"]
    B --> C["L7 LB<br/>idle 120 s"]
    C --> D["api-gateway<br/>route timeout 8 s<br/>stream routes: no timeout, idle 110 s"]
    D --> E["Service<br/>server timeout 7 s<br/>SSE emitter 100 s"]
    E --> F["DB / downstream<br/>query 80 ms - 2 s"]

The rules:

  1. Request/response calls: each inner timeout is shorter than the outer one. A downstream call times out before the service does, the service before the gateway, and the gateway before the client. Otherwise the outer layer gives up and retries while the inner one is still working.
  2. Long-lived streams: heartbeat interval < the smallest idle timeout on the path (NAT, LB, CDN). Server stream lifetime < LB idle timeout, so the server closes cleanly and the client reconnects, rather than a middlebox silently killing it.
  3. Pools: client idle TTL < server keep-alive < LB idle timeout (§2.4).
  4. Write the ladder in the design doc. It's an NFR, not a config detail.

docs.title: 3.1 Component view: live order tracking
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Producers
        OR["order-service"] -->|"order.order.status-changed.v1"| K[["Kafka"]]
        TR["tracking-service"] -->|"tracking.location.updated.v1"| K
    end
    K --> RT["tracking-router<br/>(consumer group)"]
    RT -->|"XADD trk:order:{id}<br/>replay buffer, TTL 3 h"| RS[("Redis Streams")]

    CDN --> GW["api-gateway"] --> S1

docs.title: 3.2 Sequence: happy path, subscribe and receive updates
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App as Customer app
    participant GW as api-gateway
    participant S as tracking-stream pod 2
    participant R as Redis
    participant RT as tracking-router
    participant K as Kafka
    App->>GW: GET /api/v1/orders/42/events (Accept: text/event-stream, JWT)
    GW->>S: forward (stream route, no response timeout)
    S->>S: verify order 42 belongs to user
    S->>R: SUBSCRIBE trk:live:42 (first local subscriber for order 42)
    S->>R: XREVRANGE trk:order:42 + - COUNT 1 (current state)
    S-->>App: 200 text/event-stream, id: 1727..-0, event: status, data: PACKED
    K--)RT: order.order.status-changed.v1 {42, RIDER_ASSIGNED}
    RT->>R: XADD trk:order:42 * status RIDER_ASSIGNED
    RT->>R: PUBLISH trk:live:42 {id, RIDER_ASSIGNED}
    R--)S: message on trk:live:42
    S-->>App: id: 1727..-1, event: status, data: RIDER_ASSIGNED
    loop every 15 s with no events
        S-->>App: ": heartbeat" (SSE comment line)
    end

docs.title: 3.3 Sequence: failure path, network switch mid-delivery and resume
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App as Customer app
    participant NAT as Carrier NAT
    participant S2 as tracking-stream pod 2
    participant S3 as tracking-stream pod 3
    participant R as Redis
    Note over App: Stream open on pod 2, last event id 1727..-1 (RIDER_ASSIGNED)
    App->>App: phone moves Wi-Fi → 4G (new IP)
    Note over App,S2: Old TCP connection is dead. Nobody tells either side.
    R--)S2: PUBLISH OUT_FOR_DELIVERY (id 1727..-2)
    S2-xApp: write fails on next event or heartbeat → emitter completed, unsubscribe
    App->>App: no event or heartbeat for 45 s? No: OS reports network change → reconnect now
    App->>NAT: new connection
    NAT->>S3: GET /orders/42/events, Last-Event-ID: 1727..-1 (LB picks pod 3)
    S3->>R: XRANGE trk:order:42 (1727..-1 +   → events after the last seen id
    R-->>S3: [1727..-2 OUT_FOR_DELIVERY]
    S3-->>App: replay: id 1727..-2 OUT_FOR_DELIVERY
    S3->>R: SUBSCRIBE trk:live:42
    Note over App,S3: No update lost, no duplicate: the client ignores ids ≤ the last seen id

What the system guarantees after this failure path

Every status change is delivered at least once to a client that reconnects within the replay window (3 hours). Duplicates are removed on the client by event id. A missed heartbeat is detected within 45 s at most, and an OS-reported network change triggers an immediate reconnect. No pod stickiness is needed: any pod can serve any order.

docs.title: 3.4 State: client stream lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CONNECTING
    CONNECTING --> OPEN: 200 + first event
    CONNECTING --> BACKOFF: error / 5xx / timeout
    OPEN --> OPEN: event or heartbeat (reset 45 s watchdog)
    OPEN --> BACKOFF: watchdog expired / network change / server closed (retry hint)
    BACKOFF --> CONNECTING: after jittered backoff (1 s → 30 s max)
    OPEN --> CLOSED: terminal event (DELIVERED / CANCELLED) or user leaves screen
    BACKOFF --> CLOSED: user leaves screen
    CLOSED --> [*]

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Live Order Tracking Stream
docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers Fulfilment platform / Mobile, SRE, Security Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-017 SSE for customer tracking; WebSockets reserved for chat

1. Context & Problem. Tracking updates were delivered over a WebSocket without heartbeats or resume. Middleboxes silently closed idle connections, and users saw frozen screens (§1.1).

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: push status and rider-location updates within 2 s p95; survive disconnects without losing updates; work through CDN, LB and carrier NAT; no sticky sessions.
  • Non-goals: customer ↔ rider chat (WebSocket, Ch 41); rider app telemetry ingestion (Ch 47).

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement FR-1 Stream order status changes and rider location (every ~4 s while out for delivery) to the order's owner FR-2 A reconnecting client receives all events missed within the last 3 hours NFR-1 Event delivery latency (Kafka publish → client) p95 ≤ 2 s NFR-2 Detect a dead connection within 45 s NFR-3 Support 150 K concurrent streams at festival peak NFR-4 Only the order's owner (or support staff with a role) can subscribe NFR-5 Pod deploys must not drop updates

4. Capacity estimates.

Item Calculation Result Orders in flight, normal evening peak ~48 K orders/h × 35 min lifecycle ~28 K Orders in flight, festival peak Ch 02: first hour ≈ 300 K orders ≈ 83 orders/s sustained × 35 min ~175 K Concurrent streams ~85 % of in-flight orders have the tracking screen open at the busiest moment ~150 K (sizing target) Messages to clients 150 K × (location every 4 s during ~40 % of lifecycle) + status changes ~15 K msgs/s + heartbeats 10 K/s Memory per stream (servlet async + buffers + emitter) ~30–60 KB 150 K × 60 KB ≈ 9 GB across the fleet Pods (≈ 15 K streams per 2 vCPU / 2 GB pod, to be load-tested) 150 K ÷ 15 K × AZ headroom 1.5 15 pods Redis Pub/Sub channels One per watched order ~150 K channels, well within Redis capacity; ~25 K publishes/s Replay buffer 150 K streams × ~60 entries × ~150 B ~1.4 GB in Redis, TTL 3 h

What the estimate tells us

Connections, not CPU, are the resource to plan: memory per stream, LB and NAT connection limits, and file descriptors (ulimit -n ≥ 65 K per pod). Location updates dominate message volume. Throttling them to 1 per 4 s, and only while out for delivery, is the biggest lever.

5. Proposed design. SSE over HTTP/2 (HTTP/3 at the edge). tracking-router consumes Kafka, appends to a per-order Redis Stream (replay buffer), and publishes to a per-order Pub/Sub channel. tracking-stream pods hold SSE connections, subscribe to per-order channels only while they have at least one local subscriber, send heartbeats every 15 s, close streams after 100 s with a retry hint (below the 120 s LB idle timeout), and replay from the Redis Stream on Last-Event-ID.

5.2 API.

GET /api/v1/orders/{orderId}/events
Accept: text/event-stream
Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
Last-Event-ID: <optional, redis stream id>

200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream
Cache-Control: no-cache
X-Accel-Buffering: no

retry: 3000

id: 1727340000000-0
event: status
data: {"orderId":"42","status":"PACKED","at":"2026-09-26T14:40:00Z"}

: heartbeat

id: 1727340004000-0
event: location
data: {"orderId":"42","lat":12.9116,"lng":77.6389,"etaMinutes":9}

5.5 Timeout ladder (NFR).

Hop Setting Value Carrier NAT Idle mapping timeout (not ours) Assume ≥ 60 s Server heartbeat SSE comment interval 15 s Client watchdog No bytes received → reconnect 45 s Server stream lifetime Close with retry hint 100 s ± 10 s jitter Gateway stream route Response timeout disabled, idle timeout 110 s LB / CDN idle timeout 120 s Client reconnect backoff Jittered exponential 1 s → 30 s max

7. Alternatives considered.

Option Pros Cons Verdict Short polling every 10 s Trivial, cache-friendly 96 % wasted requests; up to 10 s late Fallback only WebSocket Bidirectional We don't need client → server; no built-in resume; proxy issues Chat only SSE + Redis replay + Pub/Sub HTTP-native, resume built in, HTTP/2 multiplexing, any pod serves any order Server → client only; per-connection memory Chosen Mobile push notifications only No connection held Not real-time for map; delivery not guaranteed Complementary (status changes when app backgrounded)

8. Failure modes. Redis down → streams stay open with heartbeats; new events aren't delivered until recovery, the client screen shows "updates delayed", and push notifications still arrive. Kafka lag → the router's lag alert fires, and the UI shows the last known ETA with its timestamp. A pod killed → clients reconnect to other pods and replay.

9. Security. JWT validated at the gateway, order ownership checked at the pod, no PII in event payloads beyond coarse rider location near the destination, and location updates stop at delivery.

10. Observability. Gauges tracking.streams.active, tracking.subscriptions.channels; counters tracking.events.sent{type}, tracking.replays, tracking.stream.closed{reason}; timer tracking.delivery.lag (event time → sent).

11. Rollout. Behind the flag tracking.transport=SSE|POLL, rolled out by app version and city. Polling stays as a fallback for 2 releases.

14. Decision (ADR-017 summary). Customer tracking uses SSE. Every long-lived connection on the platform must have a heartbeat below the smallest idle timeout on its path, a bounded server-side lifetime, and resume by event id. WebSockets are reserved for bidirectional use cases.

docs.text:
We build live order-tracking updates four times:

Level New requirement that forces the step L1 "Show that pushing beats polling." (plain JDK server + client, measured) L2 "Push real order events to the right customer from a Spring service." L3 "Survive idle timeouts, disconnects and deploys on one pod: heartbeats, resume, limits, metrics." L4 "Run many pods with no stickiness, deliver events from Kafka, replay from Redis, drain safely."

docs.title: L1 — Concept (plain JDK) B1
docs.text:
One JDK HttpServer offers a polling endpoint and an SSE stream for a simulated order moving through six statuses (compressed to 400 ms per step). A JDK HttpClient consumes both and counts the requests.

// OrderUpdatesL1.java — run with: java OrderUpdatesL1.java
// Plain JDK only: a tiny HTTP server offering (1) a polling endpoint and (2) an SSE stream,
// and a client that measures how many requests/connections each approach costs.
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.OutputStream;
import java.net.InetSocketAddress;
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class OrderUpdatesL1 {

    static final List<String> LIFECYCLE =
            List.of("PLACED", "CONFIRMED", "PACKED", "RIDER_ASSIGNED", "OUT_FOR_DELIVERY", "DELIVERED");
    static final long STEP_MILLIS = 400;          // compressed time: one status change every 400 ms
    static final AtomicInteger requestsServed = new AtomicInteger();

    /** Current status of the (single, simulated) order, derived from elapsed time. */
    static volatile long orderStart;
    static String currentStatus() {
        int idx = (int) Math.min((System.currentTimeMillis() - orderStart) / STEP_MILLIS, LIFECYCLE.size() - 1);
        return LIFECYCLE.get(idx);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("127.0.0.1", 0), 0);
        server.setExecutor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor());

        // (1) Polling: client asks "what's the status now?" repeatedly
        server.createContext("/orders/42/status", ex -> {
            requestsServed.incrementAndGet();
            byte[] body = currentStatus().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            ex.sendResponseHeaders(200, body.length);
            try (OutputStream os = ex.getResponseBody()) { os.write(body); }
        });

        // (2) Server-Sent Events: one long-lived response, server pushes when status changes
        server.createContext("/orders/42/events", ex -> {
            requestsServed.incrementAndGet();
            ex.getResponseHeaders().add("Content-Type", "text/event-stream");
            ex.getResponseHeaders().add("Cache-Control", "no-cache");
            ex.sendResponseHeaders(200, 0);              // 0 = chunked, length unknown
            try (OutputStream os = ex.getResponseBody()) {
                String last = null;
                int id = 0;
                while (true) {
                    String now = currentStatus();
                    if (!now.equals(last)) {
                        String frame = "id: " + (++id) + "\nevent: status\ndata: " + now + "\n\n";
                        os.write(frame.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
                        os.flush();                      // push immediately — don't wait for a buffer to fill
                        last = now;
                        if (now.equals("DELIVERED")) break;
                    }
                    Thread.sleep(20);                    // L1 shortcut: real servers are event-driven, not sleeping
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            } catch (IOException clientWentAway) {
                // client disconnected — normal for streams
            }
        });

        server.start();
        String base = "http://127.0.0.1:" + server.getAddress().getPort();
        HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient();

        // --- Polling every 100 ms until DELIVERED ---
        orderStart = System.currentTimeMillis();
        requestsServed.set(0);
        String seen = "";
        int changes = 0;
        while (!seen.equals("DELIVERED")) {
            String s = client.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(base + "/orders/42/status")).build(),
                                   HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body();
            if (!s.equals(seen)) { changes++; seen = s; }
            Thread.sleep(100);
        }
        System.out.printf("Polling (100 ms): %d requests for %d status changes (%.0f%% wasted)%n",
                requestsServed.get(), changes, 100.0 * (requestsServed.get() - changes) / requestsServed.get());

        // --- SSE: one request, events pushed as they happen ---
        orderStart = System.currentTimeMillis();
        requestsServed.set(0);
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        HttpResponse<java.util.stream.Stream<String>> resp = client.send(
                HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(base + "/orders/42/events"))
                           .header("Accept", "text/event-stream").build(),
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofLines());
        resp.body().filter(line -> line.startsWith("data: "))
                   .forEach(line -> System.out.printf("  SSE +%4d ms  %s%n",
                           (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, line.substring(6)));
        System.out.printf("SSE: %d request for %d status changes%n", requestsServed.get(), LIFECYCLE.size());

        server.stop(0);
    }
}

Actual output from running it:

Polling (100 ms): 18 requests for 6 status changes (67% wasted)
  SSE +  10 ms  PLACED
  SSE + 410 ms  CONFIRMED
  SSE + 816 ms  PACKED
  SSE +1203 ms  RIDER_ASSIGNED
  SSE +1608 ms  OUT_FOR_DELIVERY
  SSE +2013 ms  DELIVERED
SSE: 1 request for 6 status changes

What L1 shows: the SSE wire format (id:, event:, data:, blank line), why you flush() per event, chunked responses (sendResponseHeaders(200, 0)), and virtual threads making "one thread per held connection" affordable.

What L1 can't do:

Gap Networking consequence Loops with sleep instead of reacting to events Wastes CPU; latency depends on the sleep No heartbeat Idle LBs and NATs silently kill the stream No resume A disconnect loses every event sent while the client was away No authorization Anyone can watch anyone's order One process Can't scale or deploy without dropping everyone

package com.grocery.tracking.domain;

import java.time.Instant;

public record OrderStatusChanged(String orderId, String status, Instant at) { }

package com.grocery.tracking.domain;

public record OrderSummary(String orderId, String customerId, String status) { }

package com.grocery.tracking.repository;

import com.grocery.tracking.domain.OrderSummary;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;
import java.util.Optional;

/** Read model of orders (a projection owned by tracking; populated from order events — Ch 15). */
@Repository
public class OrderSummaryRepository {

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;

    public OrderSummaryRepository(JdbcClient jdbc) { this.jdbc = jdbc; }

    public Optional<OrderSummary> find(String orderId) {
        return jdbc.sql("SELECT order_id, customer_id, status FROM order_summary WHERE order_id = ?")
                   .param(orderId)
                   .query((rs, n) -> new OrderSummary(rs.getString(1), rs.getString(2), rs.getString(3)))
                   .optional();
    }
}

package com.grocery.tracking.service;

import com.grocery.tracking.domain.OrderStatusChanged;
import org.springframework.context.event.EventListener;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation.SseEmitter;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArraySet;

@Service
public class OrderStreamService {

    /** orderId -> emitters currently watching it on THIS instance. */
    private final Map<String, Set<SseEmitter>> watchers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public SseEmitter open(String orderId, String currentStatus) {
        SseEmitter emitter = new SseEmitter(0L);   // L2: no timeout (fixed in L3)
        watchers.computeIfAbsent(orderId, k -> new CopyOnWriteArraySet<>()).add(emitter);
        Runnable remove = () -> watchers.computeIfPresent(orderId, (k, set) -> {
            set.remove(emitter);
            return set.isEmpty() ? null : set;
        });
        emitter.onCompletion(remove);
        emitter.onTimeout(remove);
        emitter.onError(e -> remove.run());
        send(emitter, "status", currentStatus);    // initial state, so the screen isn't blank
        return emitter;
    }

    @EventListener
    public void onStatusChanged(OrderStatusChanged event) {
        for (SseEmitter emitter : watchers.getOrDefault(event.orderId(), Set.of())) {
            send(emitter, "status", event.status());
        }
    }

    int watcherCount(String orderId) {
        return watchers.getOrDefault(orderId, Set.of()).size();
    }

    private void send(SseEmitter emitter, String name, String data) {
        try {
            emitter.send(SseEmitter.event().name(name).data(data));
        } catch (IOException | IllegalStateException e) {
            emitter.completeWithError(e);          // client went away; callbacks remove it
        }
    }
}

package com.grocery.tracking.delegate;

import com.grocery.tracking.repository.OrderSummaryRepository;
import com.grocery.tracking.service.OrderStreamService;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.server.ResponseStatusException;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation.SseEmitter;

@Component
public class OrderStreamDelegate {

    private final OrderSummaryRepository orders;
    private final OrderStreamService streams;

    public OrderStreamDelegate(OrderSummaryRepository orders, OrderStreamService streams) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.streams = streams;
    }

    public SseEmitter open(String orderId, String userId) {
        var order = orders.find(orderId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND));
        if (!order.customerId().equals(userId)) {
            // 404, not 403: don't reveal that someone else's order id exists
            throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);
        }
        return streams.open(orderId, order.status());
    }
}

package com.grocery.tracking.controller;

import com.grocery.tracking.delegate.OrderStreamDelegate;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation.SseEmitter;

@RestController
public class OrderStreamController {

    private final OrderStreamDelegate delegate;

    public OrderStreamController(OrderStreamDelegate delegate) { this.delegate = delegate; }

    @GetMapping(path = "/api/v1/orders/{orderId}/events", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
    public SseEmitter stream(@PathVariable String orderId, @RequestHeader("X-User-Id") String userId) {
        return delegate.open(orderId, userId);
    }
}

package com.grocery.tracking.service;

import com.grocery.tracking.domain.OrderStatusChanged;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation.SseEmitter;
import java.time.Instant;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class OrderStreamServiceTest {

    @Test
    void deliversOnlyToWatchersOfThatOrderAndCleansUp() {
        var service = new OrderStreamService();
        SseEmitter a = service.open("42", "PACKED");
        service.open("43", "PLACED");

        // Before the servlet container attaches a handler, SseEmitter buffers sends — safe to call here.
        service.onStatusChanged(new OrderStatusChanged("42", "RIDER_ASSIGNED", Instant.now()));
        assertThat(service.watcherCount("42")).isEqualTo(1);
        assertThat(service.watcherCount("43")).isEqualTo(1);

        a.complete();
        // VERIFY: completion callbacks fire once the async request completes; in a pure unit test
        // they may not run. The L3 integration test covers cleanup end-to-end over real HTTP.
    }
}

What L2 fixed: real events, authorization by order ownership, and cleanup callbacks.

What L2 exposes: new SseEmitter(0L) means "never time out", so connections live until a middlebox kills them silently (§1.1). There's no heartbeat, no resume, no connection limit, no metrics, and a deploy drops everyone without telling them to reconnect.

docs.title: L3 — Production-Grade (one pod) B3
docs.text:
This level applies the §4 timeout ladder in code:

  • Heartbeat every 15 s (an SSE comment line: invisible to EventSource, but it keeps NATs and LBs from closing the connection).
  • Bounded lifetime of 100 s ± 10 s jitter. The server closes the stream with a retry hint before the LB's 120 s idle timeout, and the jitter prevents synchronized reconnect waves.
  • Resume from an in-memory replay buffer by Last-Event-ID (a per-order sequence). This is correct on one pod. L4 moves it to Redis.
  • Limits: at most 5 streams per user; the pod-wide cap comes from load testing.
  • Headers that stop proxy buffering and caching.
  • Graceful drain on shutdown: tell every client to reconnect, then close.
  • Metrics: active streams, events sent, replays, close reasons.

dependencies {
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-actuator")
    implementation("io.micrometer:micrometer-registry-prometheus")
    testRuntimeOnly("com.h2database:h2")   // embedded DB so the test context starts; the repository is mocked
}
