docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Least privilege per service: the app role has DML on its own tables only. Migrations use a separate owner role. No superuser in apps.
  • One database (or schema) per service. No cross-service table access. Share data via APIs or events (Ch 16).
  • Parameterized SQL only (JdbcClient params, JPA bind parameters). Never concatenate user input, including sort fields, which need an allow-list (Ch 04).
  • Encryption: TLS to the DB (sslmode=verify-full), encryption at rest via the platform, and column-level encryption or tokenization for sensitive fields (Ch 23).
  • Secrets: DB credentials from a vault, rotated. Consider short-lived IAM-based auth where the platform supports it.
  • Row-level security for multi-tenant tables (seller data), as defense in depth (Ch 30).
  • Auditing: DDL and privileged access logged (pgaudit), with retention per compliance needs (Ch 36).
  • Backups encrypted and tested by restore drills (Ch 27).

docs.title: 6.4 Performance & tuning knobs
docs.text: Knob Typical starting point Guidance shared_buffers ~25 % of RAM The OS page cache handles the rest effective_cache_size ~50–75 % of RAM A planner hint only work_mem 8–64 MB Per sort/hash operation per query. Raise per role or session for reports, not globally max_connections Low hundreds Use PgBouncer rather than raising it into the thousands random_page_cost 1.1 on SSD/NVMe Default 4.0 assumes spinning disks checkpoint_timeout / max_wal_size 15 min / several GB Smooth checkpoints for write-heavy loads synchronous_commit on (orders, payments) off only for tolerably lossy data Table fillfactor 80–90 for hot-update tables Enables HOT updates Autovacuum per table Scale factors ~0.01–0.05 on hot tables Keep dead tuples low statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout 2 s / 1 s / 10 s for OLTP roles Server-side guards Hibernate jdbc.batch_size, order_inserts, order_updates 50, true, true With SEQUENCE ids default_batch_fetch_size 16–64 Blunt but effective N+1 mitigation

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• RAM is the lever. A working set that fits in memory turns disk reads into cache hits. Size instances by working set, not by total data.
  • Indexes cost storage, RAM and write I/O. Drop unused ones.
  • Read replicas are cheaper than a bigger primary for read-heavy loads, and each adds a cross-AZ replication traffic cost.
  • Partitioning plus archiving moves cold data to object storage at a fraction of the price.
  • Managed services (RDS/Aurora, Cloud SQL, Azure) trade higher unit cost for less operational toil (patching, backups, failover). For most teams, that's the right trade.
  • The expensive database is usually a query problem: one missing index or an N+1 can cost more CPU than the rest of the workload combined. Review pg_stat_statements before scaling hardware.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Read-modify-write in application code.

// ❌ before: two transactions read 12, both write 11
Stock s = repo.findById(key).orElseThrow();
s.setAvailable(s.getAvailable() - qty);
repo.save(s);

// ✅ after: the database does the arithmetic and the check atomically
int updated = jdbc.sql("UPDATE stock SET available = available - :q WHERE store_id=:s AND sku=:k AND available >= :q")
                  .param("q", qty).param("s", store).param("k", sku).update();

2. Believing @Transactional means "serialized". Symptom: "It's in a transaction, so it can't race." Fix: Know your isolation level. READ COMMITTED allows lost updates in app-level read-modify-write and write skew.

3. Remote calls inside transactions.

// ❌ before: holds a DB connection + row locks while waiting on Razorpay (seconds)
@Transactional
public void placeOrder(...) { reserveStock(); paymentClient.createPayment(); saveOrder(); }

// ✅ after: short DB transactions; remote call outside; outbox/saga for coordination (Ch 13)
public void placeOrder(...) { tx.execute(s -> reserveStock()); var p = paymentClient.createPayment(); tx.execute(s -> saveOrder(p)); }

4. N+1 queries hidden by lazy loading. Symptom: The endpoint does 200 queries, and nobody notices until the peak. Fix: Batch or fetch explicitly, disable open-in-view, and use query-count tests.

5. Indexing everything (or nothing). Symptom: Slow writes and bloated storage, or sequential scans on hot paths. Fix: Design indexes from access patterns, verify with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), and drop unused ones.

6. Offset pagination on large tables. See Ch 04. Use keyset.

7. Unbounded queries and no timeouts. Symptom: One report query holds locks and connections for 10 minutes. Fix: statement_timeout per role, LIMIT on every OLTP query, and analytics on replicas or a warehouse.

8. Blocking schema changes in a deploy.

-- ❌ before: blocks writes on a 3M-row hot table for the whole build
CREATE INDEX idx_stock_updated ON stock (updated_at);

-- ✅ after
SET lock_timeout = '5s';
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_stock_updated ON stock (updated_at);

9. Pool size = "big number." Symptom: 50 × 30 pods = 1,500 connections, and the database spends its time context-switching. Fix: Size from Little's Law and the DB core count, and add PgBouncer.

10. Random UUIDv4 primary keys on huge insert-heavy tables (especially InnoDB). Symptom: Page splits, index bloat, and poor cache locality. Fix: Time-ordered ids (UUIDv7, ULID, sequences) (Ch 20).

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ Explain ACID with an example from an e-commerce order.

30-second answer: Atomicity: order, items, stock reservation and outbox commit together or not at all. Consistency: declared constraints (unique order id, available >= 0, foreign keys) hold after commit. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work, to the degree of the isolation level. Durability: once committed, the order survives a crash (WAL fsync).

Deep answer: The "C" only covers constraints you declare, so business rules must be encoded as constraints or enforced by atomic statements. Isolation is configurable, and the default (READ COMMITTED) does not prevent lost updates in read-modify-write code.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Stronger isolation costs throughput and causes retries. Durability costs commit latency.

Follow-ups: 1. Does ACID span two databases? → No. That needs 2PC or sagas (Ch 13). 2. How does the database achieve durability? → WAL flushed at commit, plus replication for disk loss.

Red flags: "Consistency means replicas agree" (that's the CAP C, a different thing).

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Points out which guarantees are not given by default.

Q2 [B1] ⭐ What is an index, and when does it not help?

30-second answer: A sorted structure (a B+ tree) mapping key values to row locations, so lookups and ranges avoid full scans. It doesn't help when the query doesn't use the index's leftmost prefix, when a filter matches a large fraction of rows (a scan is cheaper), when functions are applied to the column without an expression index, or on tiny tables.

Deep answer: Composite order matters (equality first, then range or sort). Covering indexes avoid heap lookups. Partial indexes target hot subsets. Every index slows writes.

Trade-offs: Read speed vs write cost and storage.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you check index use? → EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). 2. Why is WHERE lower(email) = ? slow? → The index is on email, not on lower(email).

Red flags: "Add an index on every column."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Designs indexes from access patterns and measures them.

Q3 [B1] Normalization vs denormalization: when do you denormalize?

30-second answer: Normalize writes so each fact lives in one place. Denormalize deliberately for read performance or for historical truth: snapshotting price, tax and address on an order is correct because they must not change later. Read models built from events are denormalized copies with a clear owner.

Deep answer: Ask "should this value change when the source changes?" If not, snapshot it. If yes, reference it, or keep a derived copy updated by events with a known staleness.

Trade-offs: Faster reads vs update anomalies and sync logic.

Follow-ups: 1. Example of a harmful denormalization? → Copying the customer phone into orders and then failing to update it for delivery calls. 2. Where do read models live? → Often in a different store or service (Ch 15).

Red flags: Treating denormalization as always bad or always good.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: The snapshot vs reference question.

Q4 [B1] What is a transaction isolation level?

30-second answer: It defines which concurrency anomalies a transaction can observe: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates, write skew. The levels are READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED (the PostgreSQL default), REPEATABLE READ (snapshot isolation in PostgreSQL) and SERIALIZABLE.

Deep answer: Higher levels prevent more anomalies but cause more waits or aborts. In PostgreSQL, SERIALIZABLE uses SSI and can fail with 40001, so apps must retry.

Trade-offs: Correctness vs throughput and complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. Default in MySQL? → REPEATABLE READ (with gap locks). 2. Which prevents write skew? → Only SERIALIZABLE (or explicit locking).

Red flags: Not knowing your database's default.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Knows implementation differences across databases.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do you prevent overselling inventory under high concurrency?

30-second answer: Use a single atomic conditional update, UPDATE stock SET available = available - :q WHERE … AND available >= :q, and treat 0 rows as sold out. Add CHECK (available >= 0). For multi-item orders, do it in one transaction with lines locked in sorted order, and roll back if any line fails.

Deep answer: Alternatives: optimistic locking (retry storms on hot rows), SELECT … FOR UPDATE (longer locks), SERIALIZABLE (aborts). For extreme hot SKUs, split stock into buckets or queue the reservations (Ch 46). Add reservation expiry so abandoned checkouts return stock.

Trade-offs: Hot-row throughput ceiling (~hundreds to a thousand per second per row).

Follow-ups: 1. Why does the conditional UPDATE work at READ COMMITTED? → The row lock plus re-evaluation of the WHERE clause on the latest committed version. 2. What about Redis DECR? → Fast, but not transactional with the order and outbox. Use it as a gate at most.

Red flags: "Wrap it in @Transactional."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Covers all-or-nothing, lock ordering, expiry, and the hot-row ceiling.

Q6 [B2] ⭐ Optimistic vs pessimistic locking: when do you use each?

30-second answer: Optimistic (a version column, 0 rows = conflict) suits low-contention edits and user-facing concurrency (ETags). Pessimistic (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) suits high-contention or multi-step logic that can't be one statement, at the cost of holding locks. For counters, an atomic conditional update beats both.

Deep answer: Optimistic under contention causes retry storms and wasted work. Pessimistic needs consistent lock order and short transactions. SKIP LOCKED is for queues, and NOWAIT is for fail-fast UX.

Trade-offs: Wasted work vs lock waits.

Follow-ups: 1. How does JPA @Version work? → UPDATE … WHERE id = ? AND version = ?, and 0 rows throws OptimisticLockException. 2. What is lock escalation? → Row → page/table (SQL Server). PostgreSQL doesn't escalate row locks.

Red flags: Using optimistic locking for hot counters.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Chooses per contention profile and mentions the conditional-update option.

Q7 [B2] ⭐ What is the N+1 problem, and how do you fix it in JPA?

30-second answer: Loading N parents, then lazily loading each parent's association, issues 1 + N queries. Fix it with fetch joins or @EntityGraph for single queries, batch fetching (@BatchSize or default_batch_fetch_size) for collections, DTO projections for read APIs, and a two-query pattern (page parents, then fetch children by IN list) when paginating.

Deep answer: Turn off open-in-view so lazy loads can't hide in serialization. Assert query counts in tests (Hibernate statistics). Avoid fetch-joining collections with pagination, because Hibernate paginates in memory.

Trade-offs: Fetch joins can multiply rows (cartesian products with multiple collections).

Follow-ups: 1. Two collections to fetch? → Separate queries or batch fetching, not one join. 2. How do you detect it in prod? → pg_stat_statements shows a small query with huge call counts.

Red flags: "Make everything EAGER."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Guards against regressions with query-count tests.

Q8 [B2] ⭐ How do you size a HikariCP pool?

30-second answer: From Little's Law: busy connections = request rate × DB time per request, plus headroom. Split across pods, and check that Σ pods × pool fits the database's connection budget, which should stay near a small multiple of DB cores. Keep connection-timeout short, and use a fixed-size pool.

Deep answer: More connections than the DB can run in parallel just adds contention. Long transactions and remote calls inside transactions inflate the DB time and the pool need, so fix those rather than growing the pool. Use PgBouncer when fleets grow.

Trade-offs: Too small means queueing. Too large means DB thrashing.

Follow-ups: 1. Symptom of undersizing? → pending > 0 and acquire-time spikes. 2. With virtual threads? → The pool becomes the DB concurrency limiter, which is good if sized deliberately.

Red flags: "Set it to 100."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Both constraints (app and DB side), plus the transaction-scope fix.

Q9 [B2] Explain MVCC and why long-running transactions are dangerous.

30-second answer: MVCC keeps multiple row versions so readers see a snapshot without blocking writers. Old versions are removed by vacuum once no snapshot needs them. A long-running (or idle-in-transaction) session keeps an old snapshot alive, so vacuum can't clean anything newer, and tables and indexes bloat across the whole database.

Deep answer: The symptoms are growing dead tuples, slower queries, and replica conflicts. Prevent it with idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, no remote calls inside transactions, analytics off the primary, and monitoring of the oldest transaction age.

Trade-offs: Snapshot consistency for long reports vs vacuum health. Use a replica or warehouse.

Follow-ups: 1. What are HOT updates? → Updates that don't touch indexed columns and fit on the same page, which avoids index updates. 2. What's wraparound? → The transaction ID counter limit. Vacuum must freeze old tuples in time.

Red flags: Not knowing vacuum exists.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Connects app behaviour (transaction scope) to database health.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ You're seeing deadlocks during peak. How do you diagnose and fix them?

30-second answer: Read the deadlock report in the PostgreSQL logs (the processes, the waiting locks and the statements). Typical causes are multi-row updates in inconsistent orders, or foreign-key checks and triggers taking locks. Fix by locking in a deterministic order (sort by key), keeping transactions short, avoiding lock upgrades (read then update the same row, which should be a single UPDATE), and adding bounded retries for 40P01.

Deep answer: For MySQL, gap and next-key locks on range predicates are a common hidden cause, so use precise index predicates. Verify the fix with a concurrency test that shuffles orders.

Trade-offs: Retries hide symptoms. Fix the ordering first.

Follow-ups: 1. Why do FKs cause locks? → Inserting a child takes a FOR KEY SHARE lock on the parent row. 2. What's deadlock_timeout? → The time before the deadlock detector runs (1 s default).

Red flags: Just raising timeouts.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Designs lock order into the code and proves it with a test.

Q11 [B3] ⭐ What is write skew, and how do you prevent it? Give a real example.

30-second answer: Two transactions each read a condition, then write different rows, and together they violate an invariant. For example, each rider checks "at least one other rider is on shift at this store" and both go off shift. REPEATABLE READ (snapshot isolation) doesn't prevent it. Prevent it with SERIALIZABLE (and retries), by locking a common row (SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the store's shift record), or by materializing the invariant as a constraint or counter updated atomically.

Deep answer: Counter materialization is often cleanest: UPDATE store_shift SET riders_on = riders_on - 1 WHERE store_id = ? AND riders_on > 1. Serializable is general but needs retry loops and has abort rates under contention.

Trade-offs: Generality vs contention and complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. Why doesn't snapshot isolation catch it? → The writes don't conflict on the same rows. 2. How does SSI detect it? → It tracks read/write dependencies and aborts dangerous structures.

Red flags: Confusing write skew with lost updates.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Offers the "materialize the conflict" technique.

Q12 [B3] Walk me through reading an EXPLAIN plan for a slow query.

30-second answer: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Find the node with the most actual time. Compare estimated vs actual rows (big gaps mean statistics problems), look for Seq Scans with large "Rows Removed by Filter" (a missing index), nested loops over large outer sets, sorts spilling to disk, and high buffer reads (cache misses).

Deep answer: Fixes include a composite or covering index, rewriting the predicate to be index-friendly, ANALYZE or extended statistics, raising work_mem for that query, and keyset pagination. Validate on production-like data, since plans depend on distributions.

Trade-offs: New indexes cost writes. Query hints are a last resort (and not native to PostgreSQL).

Follow-ups: 1. What is an index-only scan? → Served from the index plus the visibility map, with no heap visit. 2. Why is the estimate wrong? → Correlated columns, stale statistics, parameter sniffing effects.

Red flags: Only reading cost=.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Estimate-vs-actual reasoning and production-like data.

Q13 [B3] How do you change the schema of a hot, large table without downtime?

30-second answer: Expand → migrate → contract across releases. Add nullable columns first. Backfill in batches. Add constraints as NOT VALID and then validate. Create indexes CONCURRENTLY. Set lock_timeout so migrations fail fast instead of queuing traffic. Only drop or rename after no running code uses the old shape.

Deep answer: Watch for table rewrites (type changes, some defaults), long transactions blocking DDL locks, and replication lag from big backfills (throttle them). Use tooling (Flyway with non-transactional scripts for CONCURRENTLY) and rehearse on a production-size copy.

Trade-offs: Multi-release changes take longer but avoid outages.

Follow-ups: 1. Why can a tiny ALTER cause an outage? → It waits for an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock behind a long query, and everything queues behind it. 2. How do you rename a column safely? → Add the new one, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop the old one.

Red flags: "Run the migration during low traffic."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Lock queue awareness and lock_timeout.

Q14 [B3] ⭐ When and how do you use read replicas safely?

30-second answer: Route read-only, staleness-tolerant queries to replicas (browsing, history, dashboards). Keep decision reads and anything right after a user's write on the primary, or verify the replica has replayed the write's LSN (read-your-writes). Monitor lag, and never run analytics on OLTP replicas.

Deep answer: Use LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy with a read-only DataSource keyed on @Transactional(readOnly), plus a consistency token (LSN) from writes echoed by clients. Handle replica query cancellations (max_standby_streaming_delay, hot_standby_feedback trade-offs).

Trade-offs: Offloaded reads vs complexity and staleness.

Follow-ups: 1. What is hot_standby_feedback? → It prevents cancellations but can cause bloat on the primary. 2. Can replicas take writes? → Not in streaming replication. Multi-primary is a different world.

Red flags: "Just send all GETs to the replica."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Read-your-writes via LSN tokens.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ The orders database is growing 2 TB a year and writes are rising. What's your plan?

30-second answer: First, measure (top queries, write mix, working set). Then, in order: fix queries and indexes; partition orders by month (pruning, cheap retention); archive cold partitions to object storage or a warehouse; move reads to replicas and read models; reduce write amplification (fewer indexes, batching). Only when a single primary's write capacity is on a runway shorter than the migration lead time, plan sharding (by customer or region) or a distributed SQL database.

Deep answer: Compute the runway (months to the limit on the current growth curve) against the lead time (the migration takes 6–9 months). Choose a shard key that matches access patterns (customer id for history, but store-level views then need fan-out or read models). Keep cross-shard transactions out of the design.

Trade-offs: Sharding complexity vs vertical scaling cost.

Follow-ups: 1. What breaks with sharding? → Cross-shard joins, global uniqueness, transactions, rebalancing. 2. Distributed SQL? → Simpler app code, but latency and cost trade-offs.

Red flags: Jumping straight to sharding.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Runway vs lead time, and a sequence of cheaper steps.

Q16 [B4] How do you choose isolation levels and locking strategies as a platform standard?

30-second answer: Default to READ COMMITTED with atomic statements for counters and invariants, optimistic versions for user edits, pessimistic locks with deterministic order where logic can't be one statement, and SERIALIZABLE only for complex cross-row invariants (ledgers) with mandatory retry wrappers. Declare invariants as constraints. Encode the rules in shared libraries, review checklists and architecture tests.

Deep answer: Provide a @RetryOnConcurrencyFailure wrapper (bounded, jittered), lint rules against entity read-modify-write for counters, and concurrency tests as part of the definition of done for money and stock paths.

Trade-offs: A uniform stronger isolation level is simpler to reason about but costs throughput.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not SERIALIZABLE everywhere? → Abort rates under contention, and every path needs retries. 2. How do you enforce the standard? → ArchUnit rules, code review, tests.

Red flags: No standard; each team guesses.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Standard plus tooling plus tests.

Q17 [B4] Should each microservice have its own database? What about reporting across them?

30-second answer: Yes: database-per-service (or schema-per-service with enforced ownership) keeps services independently deployable and prevents hidden coupling. Cross-service reporting goes through events or CDC into a warehouse or lakehouse (Ch 21), not cross-database joins. Share data via APIs and events.

Deep answer: Physical consolidation (several services' schemas on one PostgreSQL cluster) is fine for cost, as long as ownership and permissions are enforced. Watch shared-resource contention and plan to split hot services out.

Trade-offs: Independence vs duplicated data and eventual consistency.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you handle a query needing data from three services? → A read model built from events, or API composition in a BFF. 2. What about foreign keys across services? → Not possible. Use ids plus eventual validation.

Red flags: A shared database with cross-service joins.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Separates logical ownership from physical consolidation.

Q18 [B4] Managed PostgreSQL vs self-managed on Kubernetes: how do you decide?

30-second answer: Managed services (RDS/Aurora, Cloud SQL) give automated backups, patching, failover and monitoring, which is the right default for most teams. Self-managed (operators like CloudNativePG on Kubernetes) gives control, portability and possibly lower cost at scale, but needs real DBA and SRE expertise for backups, upgrades, failover testing and storage performance.

Deep answer: Decide on team capability, compliance (data residency, audit), required extensions and versions, cost at the target scale, and multi-cloud needs. Whatever you pick, test restores and failovers regularly.

Trade-offs: Control vs operational burden.

Follow-ups: 1. What's the hidden cost of self-managed? → On-call expertise and incident risk. 2. Aurora vs RDS? → Storage architecture, failover speed and pricing model differences. Evaluate for your workload.

Red flags: Self-hosting "because it's cheaper" without staffing.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: A capability- and risk-based decision, with restore drills.

Q19 [B4] How do you design a ledger (wallet) in a relational database?

30-second answer: Use append-only double-entry records: every transfer inserts balanced debit and credit entries in one transaction (the sum is zero), and entries are never updated. Balances are either derived (sum of entries) or kept as a cached balance row updated atomically with a CHECK (balance >= 0) in the same transaction. Use idempotency keys for every movement, and reconcile daily with external sources (Razorpay settlements).

Deep answer: For invariants across accounts, use SERIALIZABLE or ordered row locks on the account balance rows. Partition entries by time, and snapshot balances periodically for fast reads. Store amounts as integers in minor units.

Trade-offs: Derived balances are always correct but slower. Cached balances are fast but must be kept consistent.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you fix a wrong entry? → A compensating (reversal) entry, never an update. 2. How do you prove correctness? → Invariant checks (sum of entries = 0) and reconciliation jobs.

Red flags: An updatable balance column with no history.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Immutability, idempotency and reconciliation (Ch 45).

Q20 [B4] When would you move a workload off PostgreSQL entirely?

30-second answer: When the access pattern fits another model much better, and the relational benefits (transactions, joins, constraints) aren't needed for that workload. Examples: very high write rates of time-series or events (a time-series or LSM store), full-text relevance search (a search engine), large key-value session state (Redis or DynamoDB), graph traversals, or analytical scans over TBs (a columnar warehouse). Keep the system of record relational where correctness matters.

Deep answer: Prefer adding a specialized store fed from the relational source of truth (CDC, events) over replacing it. Evaluate operational cost, consistency needs and team skills (Ch 06).

Trade-offs: Specialized performance vs another system to run and keep in sync.

Follow-ups: 1. What stays in PostgreSQL in this platform? → Orders, payments, inventory, ledgers. 2. What moves? → Search, rider location history, analytics, caches.

Red flags: Replacing the database because "NoSQL scales."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Polyglot persistence with a clear system of record.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. ACID gives you only what you declare and choose: constraints for consistency, isolation levels for concurrency.
  2. At READ COMMITTED, app-level read-modify-write loses updates. Use atomic conditional updates for counters, and back invariants with CHECK constraints.
  3. MVCC lets readers and writers coexist, but long transactions block vacuum and cause bloat everywhere.
  4. Indexes are sorted B+ trees. Design composite, covering and partial indexes from access patterns, and verify with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).
  5. Lock in a deterministic order to prevent deadlocks, keep transactions short, and never make remote calls inside them.
  6. Write skew needs SERIALIZABLE, a common lock, or a materialized counter. Snapshot isolation isn't enough.
  7. JPA pitfalls: N+1, open-in-view, IDENTITY disabling batching, collection fetch + pagination. Assert query counts in tests.
  8. Pool size is set by Little's Law and the database's capacity, not by guesswork. Use server-side statement, lock and idle timeouts.
  9. Replicas need read-your-writes handling (LSN tokens) and lag monitoring.
  10. Grow with partitioning, archiving and online migrations before considering sharding.

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: Situation Choose Counter with an invariant (stock, slots, coupons) UPDATE … SET x = x - n WHERE … AND x >= n + CHECK User editing a record Optimistic version / ETag (Ch 04) Multi-row logic that can't be one statement SELECT … FOR UPDATE in sorted order, short tx Cross-row invariant (write skew risk) SERIALIZABLE + retry, or a materialized counter Work queue in the DB FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED Filter + sort list Composite index matching WHERE equality + ORDER BY + keyset Only a small subset is queried Partial index Huge time-ordered table Range partitioning by time (+ BRIN for some cases) Read-heavy, staleness-tolerant Replica + read-your-writes tokens

docs.title: 06. NoSQL & Polyglot Persistence ⭐
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 02, Ch 05 · What you will build: Rider location storage, taken from a hand-written LSM tree (L1) to a polyglot pipeline where Kafka feeds Redis (latest position + geo search), Cassandra (7-day history) and an analytics sink, each sized, modeled per access pattern and independently recoverable (L4) · Reading time: 100 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: the PostgreSQL table that ate the orders database
docs.text:
When the delivery fleet reached 30,000 riders, the team stored location pings the familiar way, as rows in PostgreSQL next to the orders:

INSERT INTO rider_location(rider_id, lat, lng, recorded_at) VALUES (...);   -- every 4 seconds per rider

At 7,500 inserts/s, with two indexes and 90 days of retention, the table reached 2 billion rows in three months. Autovacuum couldn't keep up. The WAL volume from location inserts saturated replication, so order-history replicas lagged by minutes. A nightly DELETE … WHERE recorded_at < now() - interval '90 days' locked up I/O for hours. During one festival evening, checkout latency tripled because orders and locations shared a disk, a WAL stream and a buffer cache.

The data wasn't relational at all. Nobody joined locations with anything. Every read was either "where is rider X now?", "which riders are near store Y?", or "rider X's path today." Those are three access patterns, and each fits a different storage model better than a B-tree table on the orders primary:

Access pattern Better fit Latest position of a rider In-memory key-value (Redis HASH) Riders within 3 km of a store Geo index (Redis GEO, or geohash/H3 keys) A rider's path for a day, for 7 days Wide-column, LSM-based, TTL-expiring (Cassandra/ScyllaDB) Fleet analytics over months Columnar store / warehouse (Ch 21)

The thesis of this chapter

There's no "best database," only the best fit for an access pattern at a scale with a consistency requirement. Start from the queries, not the data. Keep one system of record per fact, and feed specialized stores from it.

docs.title: 1.2 Where this lives in the grocery platform
docs.text: Data Store Why Orders, payments, inventory, ledgers PostgreSQL Transactions, constraints, joins (Ch 05) Carts, sessions, OTP attempts, rate-limit counters Redis Low latency, TTLs, atomic counters Rider latest location + geo Redis GEO/HASH 20 K writes/s, radius queries Rider location history Cassandra/ScyllaDB Write-heavy, time-partitioned, TTL Product search, autocomplete OpenSearch Inverted index, relevance (Ch 22) Catalog read model for app screens Document store (or PostgreSQL JSONB) Denormalized product documents "Frequently bought together" Graph (or precomputed in batch) Relationship traversal Metrics, pings for analytics Time-series DB / columnar warehouse Aggregations over time

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text: Band After this chapter you can… B1 Name the NoSQL families, their data models, and a use case for each B2 Model data for key-value, document and wide-column stores from access patterns, and explain CAP B3 Explain LSM trees, compaction, tunable consistency, hot partitions and tombstones, and size a cluster B4 Apply PACELC to real choices, design polyglot persistence with a single system of record, and use a decision matrix to defend store choices

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: different cupboards for different things B1
docs.text:
A kitchen doesn't keep everything in one cupboard:

  • The fridge (key-value in memory) holds what you grab constantly and can afford to lose if the power goes out (you'd restock).
  • The recipe binder (a document store) keeps each recipe as one self-contained page.
  • The spice rack sorted by name, with a shelf per month (wide-column) lets you add jars constantly and find "all spices bought in September" fast.
  • The family tree on the wall (a graph) is for "who's related to whom."
  • The cookbook index (a search engine) finds "every recipe mentioning paneer."
  • The accounts ledger (relational) is where money is recorded, carefully.

Putting the spice rack inside the ledger (§1.1) makes both worse.

docs.title: 2.2 The NoSQL families ⭐ B1 B2
docs.text:
Family Data model Strengths Weaknesses Examples Grocery use Key-value key → value (opaque, or typed structures in Redis) Sub-ms reads/writes, TTLs, atomic ops, simple scaling No queries by value; memory cost (Redis) Redis, Memcached, DynamoDB (also document-ish) Carts, sessions, OTP, rate limits, latest rider location Document JSON-like documents in collections, secondary indexes Flexible schema, aggregates read in one fetch, rich queries Cross-document transactions are limited or costly; joins are weak MongoDB, Couchbase, Firestore, PostgreSQL JSONB Product catalog read model, seller onboarding forms Wide-column Partition key → sorted rows (clustering columns) Massive write throughput, linear scale-out, TTLs, multi-DC Query only by partition key (+ clustering range); no joins; modeling discipline Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, Bigtable Location history, event logs, notification history Graph Nodes + edges with properties Multi-hop relationship queries Harder to scale writes; niche skills Neo4j, Neptune, JanusGraph Recommendations, fraud rings Time-series (series, timestamp) → value, downsampling, retention Compression, time-window aggregation Not general purpose Prometheus, TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, VictoriaMetrics Metrics, telemetry Search engine Inverted index over documents Full-text relevance, facets, fuzzy, geo Not a system of record; eventual indexing; ops heavy OpenSearch, Elasticsearch, Solr Product search (Ch 22) Columnar / analytical Column-oriented storage Scans and aggregations over billions of rows Poor at point writes and updates ClickHouse, BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake Fleet analytics, BI (Ch 21)

\"NoSQL\" is not one thing

The word says what these systems aren't, not what they are. Compare specific properties: data model, consistency model, query capability, scaling model, and operational cost.

docs.title: 2.3 Key-value in depth: Redis data structures B2
docs.text:
Structure Commands Grocery use STRING GET/SET EX, INCR, SET NX PX OTP code with TTL, idempotency marker, simple lock (Ch 20) HASH HSET/HGETALL Cart (sku → qty), rider latest state SORTED SET ZADD/ZRANGEBYSCORE/ZREM Leaderboards, "last seen" timestamps, delayed jobs GEO (sorted set of geohashes) GEOADD, GEOSEARCH … BYRADIUS … ASC COUNT Nearest available riders to a store LIST / STREAM LPUSH/BRPOP, XADD/XREADGROUP Simple queues; the tracking replay buffer (Ch 03) HyperLogLog PFADD/PFCOUNT Approximate unique visitors Bloom (module) BF.ADD/BF.EXISTS "Have we seen this coupon code?" pre-check

Persistence and durability: Redis is in-memory, with optional RDB snapshots and an AOF log (appendfsync everysec can lose ~1 s of writes). Treat it as a cache or ephemeral store unless you've deliberately configured and tested durability, and even then prefer it for data you can rebuild.

Scaling: Redis Cluster shards keys across 16,384 hash slots. Multi-key operations need the keys in the same slot (use hash tags: {BLR}:riders:geo, {BLR}:riders:lastseen).

docs.title: 2.4 Document stores: embedding vs referencing B2
docs.text:
{
  "_id": "sku_AASHIRVAAD_ATTA_5KG",
  "name": "Aashirvaad Whole Wheat Atta 5 kg",
  "brand": "Aashirvaad",
  "category": ["staples", "atta-flours"],
  "gstRate": 5,
  "variants": [
    { "packSize": "5 kg", "mrpPaise": 29900 },
    { "packSize": "10 kg", "mrpPaise": 57500 }
  ],
  "nutrition": { "per100g": { "energyKcal": 340, "proteinG": 12.1 } },
  "images": ["https://cdn.grocery.in/p/atta5/1.webp"],
  "updatedAt": "2026-09-20T08:00:00Z"
}
Rule Embed when… Reference when… Ownership The child only exists with the parent (variants, nutrition) The child is shared (a brand used by 400 products) Access Always read together Read independently or rarely Size Bounded (a handful of variants) Unbounded (reviews, order history) → separate collection Change rate Changes with the parent Changes independently and often (price, stock) → keep out of the catalog document

Unbounded arrays are the document-model N+1

Embedding all 20,000 reviews in the product document creates huge documents, slow updates and 16 MB limits (in MongoDB). Put reviews in their own collection keyed by product, and embed only a summary (ratingAvg, ratingCount).

PostgreSQL JSONB is often enough. A product_document JSONB column with a GIN index gives flexible attributes inside your existing relational database, with transactions. Reach for a dedicated document database when you need its scale-out, operational model, or developer ergonomics across many teams.

docs.title: 2.5 Wide-column (Cassandra) data modeling ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
In Cassandra-style stores you design one table per query. Denormalization is the normal case.

-- Query: "rider X's path on day D, newest first"
CREATE TABLE rider_location_by_day (
    rider_id     text,
    day          date,              -- bucket: bounds partition size
    recorded_at  timestamp,
    lat          double,
    lng          double,
    speed_kmph   float,
    order_id     text,
    PRIMARY KEY ((rider_id, day), recorded_at)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (recorded_at DESC)
  AND default_time_to_live = 604800            -- 7 days
  AND compaction = {'class': 'TimeWindowCompactionStrategy',
                    'compaction_window_unit': 'HOURS', 'compaction_window_size': 6};
Concept Meaning Design rule Partition key (rider_id, day) Decides which nodes own the data (hashed on the token ring) Must appear in every query with =. It spreads load: no hot partitions Clustering column recorded_at DESC Sort order within a partition, on disk Range queries and ordering only within a partition Partition size All rows sharing a partition key Keep it bounded, ideally < ~10 MB (guidance: well under 100 MB). Bucket by time for time series No joins, limited secondary indexes — Duplicate data into another table for another query (rider_location_by_order) TTL Per-row expiry The natural retention mechanism; pair with TWCS so whole SSTables expire Tombstones Deletes and expired TTLs are markers until compaction Many tombstones in a read path slow queries or fail them (tombstone_failure_threshold). Avoid delete-heavy patterns and queue-like tables

Partition-size check for our table: one ping every 4 s during a 12-hour shift is ~10,800 rows × ~100 B ≈ 1 MB per partition. That's comfortable. Without the day bucket, 90 days of retention would be ~100 MB per rider partition: too big.

docs.title: 2.6 LSM trees and compaction ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Most write-optimized stores (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, RocksDB, HBase, LevelDB, and the storage behind many time-series DBs) use a Log-Structured Merge tree:

flowchart LR
    W["Write"] --> CL["Commit log<br/>(sequential append, durability)"]
    W --> MT["Memtable<br/>(sorted, in memory)"]
    MT -->|"full → flush"| S1["SSTable (newest)<br/>immutable, sorted, Bloom filter"]
    S1 --> S2["SSTable"] --> S3["SSTable (oldest)"]
    S1 & S2 & S3 -->|"compaction: merge, keep newest version,<br/>drop tombstones past gc_grace"| C["Merged SSTable"]
    R["Read"] --> MT
    R -->|"newest → oldest, skip via Bloom filter"| S1

L1 (§5) implements exactly this. Its real output shows the trade-offs:

After 200,000 writes: 41 SSTables holding 39,725 entries for 1,000 live keys (space amplification ~40x)
1 read of a missing key  : 1 table probes, 40 tables skipped by Bloom filters
After compaction: 1 SSTable, 999 entries (38,726 stale versions and tombstones dropped)
B+ tree (PostgreSQL, InnoDB) LSM tree (Cassandra, RocksDB) Write path Update pages in place (random I/O) + WAL Append + sorted flush (sequential I/O) Write throughput Good Excellent Read path One tree traversal Memtable + possibly several SSTables (Bloom filters help) Read amplification Low Higher, until compaction catches up Space amplification Low (dead tuples until vacuum) Higher (old versions until compaction) Write amplification Moderate Compaction rewrites data repeatedly Background work Vacuum Compaction (can compete with foreground I/O) Compaction strategy How Best for Size-tiered (STCS) Merge similar-sized SSTables Write-heavy, general Leveled (LCS) Levels with non-overlapping key ranges Read-heavy, update-heavy; lower read/space amplification, more write amplification Time-window (TWCS) One bucket per time window; old windows never re-merged Time series with TTL: whole SSTables expire and drop cheaply

docs.title: 2.7 CAP and PACELC ⭐ B2 → B4
docs.text:
CAP: during a network partition (P), a distributed system must choose between Consistency (every read sees the latest write, or errors) and Availability (every request gets a non-error response, possibly stale).

  • CAP's "C" is linearizability, not ACID's "C."
  • Partitions are not optional in real networks, so the real choice is C or A when partitioned.
  • It's per operation, not per product. Many databases let you choose per query.

PACELC adds the everyday case: if Partitioned, choose A or C; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency.

System (typical configuration) If partitioned Else Notes PostgreSQL primary + async replicas C (writes go to the primary only; lagging replicas can serve stale reads) C for primary reads / L for replica reads Failover can lose the last async writes Cassandra / ScyllaDB A (with CL=ONE) … C-ish (with QUORUM on both sides) L (tunable) Tunable per query: R + W > RF for read-your-writes on that key DynamoDB A (eventually consistent reads) or C (strongly consistent reads) L / C per read Strong reads cost more and are single-region MongoDB (replica set, majority) C (the minority side can't elect a primary) C with majority read/write concern / L with local reads Configurable concerns Redis (single primary + replicas) Mostly A-leaning, can lose acknowledged writes on failover L Don't use it as a source of truth for money Spanner, CockroachDB C C (pays latency) Consensus per range; cross-region latency

Tunable consistency (Cassandra-style): with replication factor RF, write consistency W and read consistency R:

\[ R + W > RF \;\Rightarrow\; \text{a read overlaps at least one replica that saw the write} \]

With RF=3 and LOCAL_QUORUM (2) for both reads and writes, 2 + 2 > 3, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write in that datacenter. With ONE/ONE you get the lowest latency and the highest availability, with possibly stale reads.

Choosing per access pattern for rider locations

  • Latest position (Redis): availability and latency first. A 4-second-old position is fine, and the next ping repairs it.
  • History writes (Cassandra): LOCAL_ONE is acceptable. The data is valuable, but a few lost pings don't matter, and throughput is king. We still use LOCAL_QUORUM by default for predictable reads (L3), and measure before relaxing it.
  • Delivery proof for disputes ("the rider was at the door at 8:42 pm"): write the delivery event to the order system of record (PostgreSQL), not only to the location store.

docs.title: 2.8 Data modeling per access pattern: the method ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
1. List the queries with their frequency, latency and consistency needs.
  2. Estimate the volume per query and the growth (Ch 02).
  3. Choose keys so that each frequent query hits one partition or key, and load spreads evenly.
  4. Bound partition and document size (bucketing, separate collections).
  5. Duplicate for reads (a table or index per query), and decide who keeps the copies in sync (dual write is forbidden: use events or CDC).
  6. Plan retention (TTL, time buckets, partitions).
  7. Plan the failure and rebuild story. Can this store be rebuilt from the system of record or a log?
Query (rider domain) Frequency Latency Consistency Store / key Q1 latest position of rider ~20 K/s (tracking stream, dispatch) < 5 ms Seconds-stale OK Redis HASH {city}:rider:<id> Q2 available riders within 3 km of store ~2 K/s (dispatch, Ch 47) < 10 ms Seconds-stale OK Redis GEO {city}:riders:geo + last-seen prune Q3 rider path for day ~50/s (support, disputes) < 100 ms Complete within minutes Cassandra (rider_id, day) Q4 path for one order ~200/s (customer "delivered" map) < 100 ms Complete within minutes Cassandra rider_location_by_order (order_id) Q5 fleet speed/idle analytics Batch Minutes Hours-stale OK Columnar warehouse

docs.title: 2.9 Graph, time-series and search: when they're the right tool B2
docs.text:
Graph. A good fit when the question is a multi-hop traversal:

// "Customers who bought X also bought" — 2-hop traversal
MATCH (p:Product {sku: 'AMUL_BUTTER_500G'})<-[:CONTAINS]-(:Order)-[:CONTAINS]->(other:Product)
WHERE other <> p
RETURN other.sku, count(*) AS together ORDER BY together DESC LIMIT 10;

For many platforms, the same answer comes cheaper from a nightly batch over the warehouse that writes the top-N per SKU into Redis. Use a graph database when traversals are interactive, deep, or ad hoc (fraud rings, social networks).

Time-series. Metrics and telemetry with downsampling and retention (Ch 24, 52). Rider pings can live in a TSDB, but per-rider path queries fit wide-column partitioning better.

Search engines. An inverted index plus relevance scoring, fed from the system of record. Never the source of truth (Ch 22).

docs.title: 2.10 Polyglot persistence and the system of record B3 B4
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph SoR["Systems of record"]
        PG[("PostgreSQL<br/>orders, inventory")]
        LOG[["Kafka topic<br/>tracking.location.updated.v1<br/>(retained 3 days)"]]
    end
    PG -->|"CDC / outbox"| K2[["Kafka"]]
    K2 --> OS[("OpenSearch<br/>product search")]
    K2 --> DOC[("Catalog documents")]
    LOG --> RD[("Redis<br/>latest + geo")]
    LOG --> CS[("Cassandra<br/>7-day history")]
    LOG --> WH[("Warehouse<br/>analytics")]
Principle Why One system of record per fact Everything else is a derived, rebuildable view No dual writes from the application A crash between writes leaves stores inconsistent forever. Write once (DB + outbox, or the log), and fan out Each derived store has its own consumer One slow sink doesn't stall the others. Each can replay independently Idempotent sink writes At-least-once delivery means duplicates. Upserts keyed by natural ids A rebuild path is part of the design Retain the log long enough, or re-snapshot from the SoR (Ch 13, 15) Operate what you add Every new store adds on-call load, backups, upgrades, security reviews and skills. That's the real cost

docs.title: 2.11 Choosing a database: the decision matrix ⭐ B4
docs.text:
Question If the answer is… Lean toward Do you need multi-row/multi-entity transactions and constraints? Yes Relational (PostgreSQL) Is the data model a self-contained aggregate read as a whole? Yes, with a flexible schema Document (or JSONB) Is access by key only, needing sub-ms and TTLs, and is the data rebuildable? Yes Redis / key-value Are writes massive (≫10 K/s), append-mostly, time-bucketed, and read by key + range? Yes Wide-column (Cassandra/ScyllaDB) Are queries multi-hop over relationships? Yes, interactive Graph Is it full-text relevance, facets, fuzzy matching? Yes Search engine (derived) Is it aggregations over months or billions of rows? Yes Columnar warehouse / OLAP Is it metrics with downsampling and retention? Yes TSDB Does the team already operate it well? No Pay heavily for this in the decision: prefer managed services or existing stores

Scoring template used in design reviews:

Criterion (weight) PostgreSQL Cassandra Redis DynamoDB Fits access pattern (×3) Consistency needs met (×3) Scale headroom 3 years (×2) Operability for our team (×2) Cost at target scale (×2) Ecosystem / Spring support (×1)

§4 fills this in for rider locations.

docs.title: 3.1 Component view: the location pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    RA["Rider app<br/>ping every 4 s (batched 2-3 per request)"] --> GW["api-gateway"]
    GW --> TI["tracking-ingest<br/>validate, stamp, publish"]
    TI --> K[["Kafka tracking.location.updated.v1<br/>key = riderId, 48 partitions, 3-day retention"]]
    K -->|"group: loc-latest"| LW["latest-writer"] --> RD[("Redis Cluster<br/>HASH {city}:rider:id<br/>GEO {city}:riders:geo<br/>ZSET {city}:riders:lastseen")]
    K -->|"group: loc-history"| HW["history-writer"] --> CS[("Cassandra RF=3<br/>rider_location_by_day<br/>rider_location_by_order")]
    K -->|"group: loc-analytics"| AW["analytics sink"] --> WH[("Warehouse")]
    DS["dispatch-service"] -->|"GEOSEARCH nearest"| RD
    TS["tracking-stream (Ch 03)"] -->|"latest"| RD
    SUP["support tools"] -->|"path by day / order"| CS

docs.title: 3.2 Sequence: happy path, one ping to all stores
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant R as Rider app
    participant TI as tracking-ingest
    participant K as Kafka
    participant LW as latest-writer
    participant RD as Redis
    participant HW as history-writer
    participant CS as Cassandra
    R->>TI: POST /pings [{lat,lng,ts,seq}] (batched)
    TI->>TI: validate (bounds, speed sanity), server timestamp
    TI->>K: produce key=riderId (acks=all)
    TI-->>R: 202
    par independent consumer groups
        K--)LW: batch of 500 pings
        LW->>RD: one Lua call per batch: HSET if newer seq, GEOADD, ZADD lastseen
        LW->>K: commit offsets
    and
        K--)HW: batch of 500 pings
        HW->>CS: async INSERTs (idempotent: same PK = same row), LOCAL_QUORUM
        HW->>K: commit offsets after all acks
    end

docs.title: 3.3 Sequence: failure path, Cassandra degraded, Redis unaffected
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant K as Kafka
    participant LW as latest-writer
    participant RD as Redis
    participant HW as history-writer
    participant CS as Cassandra (1 of 3 nodes down, then slow)
    K--)LW: pings
    LW->>RD: writes OK (dispatch + tracking unaffected)
    K--)HW: pings
    HW->>CS: INSERT LOCAL_QUORUM → 2 of 3 replicas ack → OK
    Note over CS: second node slows (compaction backlog)
    HW->>CS: INSERT → WriteTimeout
    HW->>HW: retry with backoff (idempotent), do NOT commit offsets
    Note over K,HW: consumer lag grows for loc-history only
    alt lag < retention (3 days)
        CS-->>HW: recovers
        HW->>CS: catch up from Kafka at max throughput
    else outage > retention
        HW->>HW: accept gap, alert, history missing for that window
    end

What the system guarantees after this failure path

A degraded history store never affects latest-position or dispatch, because each sink has its own consumer group. History is eventually complete as long as the outage is shorter than Kafka retention (3 days), since the writer only commits offsets after writes are acknowledged, and duplicate writes on retry are harmless (same primary key → same row). Delivery evidence for disputes lives in PostgreSQL, not in the history store.

stateDiagram-v2

    ABSENT --> ONLINE: ping (GEOADD + lastseen)
    ONLINE --> ONLINE: ping every ~4 s
    ONLINE --> STALE: no ping for 60 s
    STALE --> ONLINE: ping arrives
    STALE --> ABSENT: pruner removes from GEO + lastseen

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Rider Location Storage
docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers Fulfilment platform / Dispatch, Tracking, SRE, Data platform Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-027 Move rider locations out of PostgreSQL into Redis + Cassandra fed by Kafka

1. Context & Problem. Location pings in the orders PostgreSQL caused vacuum debt, WAL-driven replica lag and I/O contention with checkout (§1.1).

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: 20 K pings/s at festival peak with headroom; latest position and radius queries < 10 ms p99; 7-day path history; complete isolation from the orders database; rebuildable stores.
  • Non-goals: dispatch algorithms (Ch 47); long-term analytics modeling (Ch 21).

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement FR-1 Latest position per rider; nearest riders within radius of a point FR-2 Rider path by day and by order, for 7 days NFR-1 Ingest 20 K pings/s sustained, 40 K/s burst NFR-2 Q1/Q2 p99 < 10 ms; Q3/Q4 p99 < 100 ms NFR-3 Stale riders (no ping for 60 s) excluded from radius results NFR-4 A store outage must not affect other stores' consumers or the orders DB NFR-5 Any derived store rebuildable from Kafka (3-day retention) within 2 hours

4. Capacity estimates.

Item Calculation Result Peak pings 80 K riders ÷ 4 s 20 K/s (normal peak 10 K/s) Kafka ingress 20 K/s × ~150 B ~3 MB/s; 48 partitions give consumer parallelism headroom Redis memory 80 K riders × (~150 B hash + ~60 B geo + ~40 B lastseen) ~20 MB: trivial Redis ops 20 K pings/s × 3 ops (pipelined) ~60 K ops/s: a single shard can do it, cluster of 3 shards for headroom and HA Cassandra writes 20 K/s × 2 tables 40 K rows/s at peak Cassandra storage ~10 K/s avg × 86,400 × 2 tables × ~100 B × RF 3 × 7 days ~3.6 TB raw → ~1.2 TB with compression Cassandra nodes ~15–20 K writes/s per node comfortably (to be load-tested) 6 nodes (RF 3) with headroom Partition size 10,800 pings/shift × 100 B ~1 MB per (rider, day)

7. Alternatives considered (decision matrix).

Criterion (weight) PostgreSQL (partitioned, separate cluster) Cassandra/ScyllaDB Redis only DynamoDB Fits access pattern (×3) 2 3 (history) 3 latest / 1 history 3 Consistency needs met (×3) 3 3 2 3 Scale headroom 3 yrs (×2) 1 3 1 (memory for history) 3 Operability for our team (×2) 3 2 (managed service; 1 if self-run) 3 3 (managed) Cost at target scale (×2) 2 2 1 1 (per-write pricing at 40 K writes/s) Spring/Java support (×1) 3 3 3 2 Weighted total 30 35 22 (history) 34

Hash tags concentrate load

A city-level hash tag puts a whole city on one shard. At ~20 K Bengaluru riders × 1 ping/4 s ≈ 5 K pings/s (batched into ~50 Lua calls/s), one shard is comfortable. For a mega-city beyond one shard's capacity, split the tag by zone ({BLR-south}) and search the neighbouring zones.

Decision: Redis for latest and geo (clear winner). For history, a managed Cassandra-compatible service (35) narrowly beats DynamoDB (34). Self-run Cassandra would score 33 and lose, which shows how much operability matters. The deciding factor was sustained write cost at 40 K writes/s. DynamoDB wins if the platform standardizes on AWS or write volume drops. A near-tie in the matrix is a signal to name the deciding factor explicitly in the ADR, not to trust the arithmetic.

5.3 Data model. Cassandra tables as in §2.5, plus:

CREATE TABLE rider_location_by_order (
    order_id     text,
    recorded_at  timestamp,
    rider_id     text,
    lat          double,
    lng          double,
    PRIMARY KEY ((order_id), recorded_at)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (recorded_at ASC)
  AND default_time_to_live = 604800
  AND compaction = {'class': 'TimeWindowCompactionStrategy', 'compaction_window_unit': 'HOURS', 'compaction_window_size': 6};

Redis keys. The {BLR} hash tag puts all of a city's keys in one cluster slot, so one Lua script can update them atomically (keys in different slots fail with CROSSSLOT):

Key Type Content {BLR}:rider:<riderId> HASH lat, lng, ts, seq, with TTL 1 h {BLR}:riders:geo GEO member = riderId {BLR}:riders:lastseen ZSET member = riderId, score = epoch seconds

8. Failure modes. Redis node failure → replica promotion (a few seconds of lost pings are healed by the next ping). Cassandra node loss → LOCAL_QUORUM continues with 2 of 3. Two replicas lost → writes fail, the history writer lags, and Kafka retains the data. Kafka unavailable → ingest returns 503, and the rider app buffers pings locally (bounded) and resends.

10. Observability. Consumer lag per group, Redis ops/s and latency, Cassandra write latency p99, timeouts, pending compactions, tombstones per read, partition size histogram (nodetool tablehistograms), and a stale-rider count.

14. Decision (ADR-027 summary). Rider locations leave PostgreSQL. Kafka is the log of record for pings (3-day retention). Redis holds the latest position and geo membership with a 60 s staleness prune. Cassandra holds 7-day history in day-bucketed partitions with TTL and TWCS. Each sink is an independent, idempotent consumer group. Delivery-critical events (arrived, delivered, OTP verified) are written to the order system of record, not inferred from pings.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
We build rider location storage four times:

Level New requirement that forces the step L1 "Understand why write-heavy stores use LSM trees." (a working mini LSM engine) L2 "Store latest positions and find nearby riders from a Spring service." (Redis) L3 "20 K pings/s: atomic out-of-order protection, one round trip per batch, stale-rider pruning, 7-day history in Cassandra with bounded partitions." L4 "Kafka as the log: independent sinks, at-least-once with idempotent writes, poison-message handling, and rebuilds by replay."

docs.title: L1 — Concept: a mini LSM tree (plain Java) B1
docs.text:
// MiniLsmL1.java — run with: java MiniLsmL1.java
// A tiny Log-Structured Merge tree: the storage engine behind Cassandra, RocksDB, ScyllaDB, HBase...
//   write → in-memory sorted memtable → flushed as immutable sorted "SSTables" → merged by compaction
//   read  → memtable, then SSTables newest-first (Bloom filters skip tables that can't contain the key)
import java.util.*;

public class MiniLsmL1 {

    static final String TOMBSTONE = "\u0000DELETED";

    /** Minimal Bloom filter: k hash probes into a bitset. False positives possible, false negatives never. */
    static final class Bloom {
        private final BitSet bits; private final int size, k;
        Bloom(int expected) { size = Math.max(64, expected * 10); k = 4; bits = new BitSet(size); }
        private int h(String key, int i) { return Math.floorMod(key.hashCode() * 31 + i * 0x9E3779B9 + (key.hashCode() >>> 16) * i, size); }
        void add(String key) { for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) bits.set(h(key, i)); }
        boolean mightContain(String key) { for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) if (!bits.get(h(key, i))) return false; return true; }
    }

    /** Immutable, sorted run of key → value (an SSTable). */
    record SSTable(int id, TreeMap<String, String> data, Bloom bloom) {
        static SSTable of(int id, SortedMap<String, String> entries) {
            var b = new Bloom(entries.size());
            entries.keySet().forEach(b::add);
            return new SSTable(id, new TreeMap<>(entries), b);
        }
    }

    static final class Lsm {
        private final int memtableLimit;
        private TreeMap<String, String> memtable = new TreeMap<>();
        private int writesSinceFlush = 0;                           // real engines flush by memtable BYTES, incl. overwrites
        private final Deque<SSTable> tables = new ArrayDeque<>();   // newest first
        private int nextId = 1;
        long bytesWrittenToDisk = 0, logicalBytesWritten = 0;       // for write amplification
        long tableProbes = 0, bloomSkips = 0;

        Lsm(int memtableLimit) { this.memtableLimit = memtableLimit; }

        void put(String key, String value) {
            logicalBytesWritten += key.length() + value.length();
            memtable.put(key, value);                               // (real engines also append to a commit log / WAL)
            if (++writesSinceFlush >= memtableLimit) flush();
        }

        void delete(String key) { put(key, TOMBSTONE); }

        String get(String key) {
            String v = memtable.get(key);
            if (v != null) return v.equals(TOMBSTONE) ? null : v;
            for (SSTable t : tables) {                              // newest → oldest: first hit wins
                if (!t.bloom().mightContain(key)) { bloomSkips++; continue; }
                tableProbes++;
                v = t.data().get(key);
                if (v != null) return v.equals(TOMBSTONE) ? null : v;
            }
            return null;
        }

        void flush() {
            if (memtable.isEmpty()) return;
            var t = SSTable.of(nextId++, memtable);
            bytesWrittenToDisk += size(t.data());
            tables.addFirst(t);
            memtable = new TreeMap<>();
            writesSinceFlush = 0;
        }

        /** Full compaction: merge all tables, keep only the newest version, drop tombstones. */
        void compact() {
            TreeMap<String, String> merged = new TreeMap<>();
            Iterator<SSTable> oldestFirst = tables.descendingIterator();
            while (oldestFirst.hasNext()) merged.putAll(oldestFirst.next().data());   // newer overwrite older
            merged.values().removeIf(TOMBSTONE::equals);
            tables.clear();
            var t = SSTable.of(nextId++, merged);
            bytesWrittenToDisk += size(t.data());                  // compaction rewrites data: write amplification
            tables.addFirst(t);
        }

        int tableCount() { return tables.size(); }
        long storedEntries() { return tables.stream().mapToLong(t -> t.data().size()).sum(); }
        private static long size(Map<String, String> m) {
            return m.entrySet().stream().mapToLong(e -> e.getKey().length() + e.getValue().length()).sum();
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var lsm = new Lsm(5_000);   // flush every 5,000 writes
        var rnd = new Random(7);

        // 200,000 location pings from 1,000 riders: every write is an append, overwrites are cheap
        for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) {
            String rider = "rider-%04d".formatted(rnd.nextInt(1_000));
            lsm.put(rider, "%.5f,%.5f@%d".formatted(12.90 + rnd.nextDouble() / 10, 77.60 + rnd.nextDouble() / 10, i));
        }
        lsm.delete("rider-0007");                                    // rider logs off → tombstone
        lsm.flush();

        System.out.printf("After 200,000 writes: %d SSTables holding %,d entries for 1,000 live keys (space amplification ~%.0fx)%n",
                lsm.tableCount(), lsm.storedEntries(), lsm.storedEntries() / 1_000.0);

        lsm.tableProbes = lsm.bloomSkips = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) lsm.get("rider-%04d".formatted(i));
        System.out.printf("1,000 reads of live keys : %,d table probes (newest table usually has the key)%n", lsm.tableProbes);

        lsm.tableProbes = lsm.bloomSkips = 0;
        lsm.get("rider-9999");                                        // a key that doesn't exist
        System.out.printf("1 read of a missing key  : %d table probes, %d tables skipped by Bloom filters%n",
                lsm.tableProbes, lsm.bloomSkips);
        System.out.println("rider-0007 after delete  → " + lsm.get("rider-0007") + " (tombstone shadows older versions)");

        long flushedBytes = lsm.bytesWrittenToDisk;
        long before = lsm.storedEntries();
        lsm.compact();
        System.out.printf("After compaction: %d SSTable, %,d entries (%,d stale versions and tombstones dropped)%n",
                lsm.tableCount(), lsm.storedEntries(), before - lsm.storedEntries());
        System.out.printf("Bytes: app wrote %,d; flushes wrote %,d (memtable absorbed overwrites); compaction rewrote %,d more%n",
                lsm.logicalBytesWritten, flushedBytes, lsm.bytesWrittenToDisk - flushedBytes);
    }
}

Actual output from running it:

After 200,000 writes: 41 SSTables holding 39,725 entries for 1,000 live keys (space amplification ~40x)
1,000 reads of live keys : 1,009 table probes (newest table usually has the key)
1 read of a missing key  : 1 table probes, 40 tables skipped by Bloom filters
rider-0007 after delete  → null (tombstone shadows older versions)
After compaction: 1 SSTable, 999 entries (38,726 stale versions and tombstones dropped)
Bytes: app wrote 6,688,908; flushes wrote 1,328,779 (memtable absorbed overwrites); compaction rewrote 33,966 more

What L1 shows:

  • Writes are cheap appends into a sorted memtable, which absorbs overwrites (6.7 MB written by the app, 1.3 MB flushed).
  • Unmerged SSTables cause space amplification (~40× here) and potentially more read probes.
  • Bloom filters let a missing-key read skip 40 of 41 tables. The single probe was a false positive, which is expected.
  • Tombstones hide deleted keys until compaction removes them.
  • Compaction restores compactness at the cost of rewriting data.

What L1 can't do: there's no durability (commit log), no concurrency, and no distribution or replication. That's what Cassandra and ScyllaDB add.

import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

@Repository
public class RiderLocationRepositoryL2 {

    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;

    public RiderLocationRepositoryL2(StringRedisTemplate redis) { this.redis = redis; }

    /** ⚠️ L2: three separate round trips, no ordering check, no pruning. */
    public void save(String city, String riderId, double lat, double lng, long ts, long seq) {
        redis.opsForHash().putAll("{" + city + "}:rider:" + riderId,
                Map.of("lat", Double.toString(lat), "lng", Double.toString(lng),
                       "ts", Long.toString(ts), "seq", Long.toString(seq)));
        redis.opsForGeo().add("{" + city + "}:riders:geo", new Point(lng, lat), riderId);   // Point(x=lng, y=lat)!
        redis.opsForZSet().add("{" + city + "}:riders:lastseen", riderId, ts);
    }

    public List<NearbyRider> nearby(String city, double lat, double lng, double radiusKm, int limit) {
        var args = RedisGeoCommands.GeoSearchCommandArgs.newGeoSearchArgs()
                .includeDistance().sortAscending().limit(limit);
        GeoResults<RedisGeoCommands.GeoLocation<String>> results = redis.opsForGeo().search(
                "{" + city + "}:riders:geo",
                GeoReference.fromCoordinate(new Point(lng, lat)),
                new Distance(radiusKm, Metrics.KILOMETERS), args);
        if (results == null) return List.of();
        return results.getContent().stream()
                .map(r -> new NearbyRider(r.getContent().getName(), r.getDistance().getValue()))
                .toList();
    }
}

What L2 still gets wrong:

Problem Consequence 3 round trips per ping, no batching 60 K round trips/s at peak Out-of-order pings overwrite newer ones (mobile retries, batch resends) A rider "jumps back" on the map; dispatch picks stale positions Riders who go offline stay in the geo set forever Dispatch offers orders to riders who switched off their phones Writes aren't atomic across the three keys A crash between writes leaves the hash and geo disagreeing No history Support can't answer "where was the rider at 8:42?"

package com.grocery.tracking.latest;

import org.springframework.data.redis.core.StringRedisTemplate;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.script.DefaultRedisScript;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;
import java.util.*;

/**
 * All keys share the {city} hash tag → same Redis Cluster slot → one Lua script can update them atomically.
 * One EVALSHA per batch (up to ~100 pings) instead of 3 round trips per ping.
 */
@Repository
public class LatestLocationStore {

    public record Ping(String riderId, double lat, double lng, long ts, long seq) { }

    /** Applies a ping only if its seq is newer than the stored one (out-of-order protection). */
    private static final DefaultRedisScript<Long> APPLY_BATCH = new DefaultRedisScript<>("""
            -- KEYS[1]=geo  KEYS[2]=lastseen  KEYS[3..]=rider hashes
            -- ARGV[1]=ttlSeconds, then 5 args per ping: riderId, lng, lat, ts, seq
            local ttl = ARGV[1]
            local applied = 0
            for i = 3, #KEYS do
              local b = 2 + (i - 3) * 5
              local id, lng, lat, ts, seq = ARGV[b], ARGV[b+1], ARGV[b+2], ARGV[b+3], ARGV[b+4]
              local cur = redis.call('HGET', KEYS[i], 'seq')
              if (not cur) or tonumber(cur) < tonumber(seq) then
                redis.call('HSET', KEYS[i], 'lat', lat, 'lng', lng, 'ts', ts, 'seq', seq)
                redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[i], ttl)
                redis.call('GEOADD', KEYS[1], lng, lat, id)
                redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[2], ts, id)
                applied = applied + 1
              end
            end
            return applied
            """, Long.class);

    /** Removes riders not seen since cutoff from BOTH the geo set and lastseen, atomically. */
    private static final DefaultRedisScript<Long> PRUNE = new DefaultRedisScript<>("""
            local stale = redis.call('ZRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[2], '-inf', ARGV[1], 'LIMIT', 0, ARGV[2])
            if #stale > 0 then
              redis.call('ZREM', KEYS[2], unpack(stale))
              redis.call('ZREM', KEYS[1], unpack(stale))   -- GEO is a sorted set: ZREM removes members
            end
            return #stale
            """, Long.class);

    static final long HASH_TTL_SECONDS = 3600;

    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;

    public LatestLocationStore(StringRedisTemplate redis) { this.redis = redis; }

    public long applyBatch(String city, List<Ping> pings) {
        if (pings.isEmpty()) return 0;
        List<String> keys = new ArrayList<>(pings.size() + 2);
        keys.add(geoKey(city));
        keys.add(lastSeenKey(city));
        List<String> args = new ArrayList<>(1 + pings.size() * 5);
        args.add(Long.toString(HASH_TTL_SECONDS));
        for (Ping p : pings) {
            keys.add("{" + city + "}:rider:" + p.riderId());
            args.addAll(List.of(p.riderId(), Double.toString(p.lng()), Double.toString(p.lat()),
                    Long.toString(p.ts()), Long.toString(p.seq())));
        }
        Long applied = redis.execute(APPLY_BATCH, keys, args.toArray());
        return applied == null ? 0 : applied;
    }

    public long pruneStale(String city, long cutoffEpochSeconds, int max) {
        Long n = redis.execute(PRUNE, List.of(geoKey(city), lastSeenKey(city)),
                Long.toString(cutoffEpochSeconds), Integer.toString(max));
        return n == null ? 0 : n;
    }

    public Optional<Ping> latest(String city, String riderId) {
        Map<Object, Object> h = redis.opsForHash().entries("{" + city + "}:rider:" + riderId);
        if (h.isEmpty()) return Optional.empty();
        return Optional.of(new Ping(riderId, Double.parseDouble((String) h.get("lat")),
                Double.parseDouble((String) h.get("lng")), Long.parseLong((String) h.get("ts")),
                Long.parseLong((String) h.get("seq"))));
    }

    static String geoKey(String city) { return "{" + city + "}:riders:geo"; }
    static String lastSeenKey(String city) { return "{" + city + "}:riders:lastseen"; }
}

package com.grocery.tracking.latest;

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.scheduling.annotation.Scheduled;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import java.time.Clock;
import java.util.List;

/** Keeps the geo index honest: riders silent for 60 s disappear from nearby searches. */
@Component
public class StaleRiderPruner {

    private final LatestLocationStore store;
    private final List<String> cities;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final MeterRegistry metrics;

    public StaleRiderPruner(LatestLocationStore store, @Value("${tracking.cities}") List<String> cities,
                            Clock clock, MeterRegistry metrics) {
        this.store = store; this.cities = cities; this.clock = clock; this.metrics = metrics;
    }

    @Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "PT5S")
    public void prune() {
        long cutoff = clock.instant().getEpochSecond() - 60;
        for (String city : cities) {
            long removed;
            do {
                removed = store.pruneStale(city, cutoff, 500);   // bounded work per script call
                metrics.counter("tracking.riders.pruned", "city", city).increment(removed);
            } while (removed == 500);
        }
    }
}

Idempotent by design

Running the pruner on every pod is safe: removal is idempotent, and each Lua call is atomic. Keep scripts short (bounded LIMIT), because a long Lua script blocks the whole Redis shard.
