package com.grocery.tracking.history;

import com.datastax.oss.driver.api.core.CqlSession;
import com.datastax.oss.driver.api.core.DefaultConsistencyLevel;
import com.datastax.oss.driver.api.core.cql.*;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;
import java.time.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

@Repository
public class LocationHistoryStore {

    public record Point(String riderId, String orderId, double lat, double lng, float speedKmph, Instant recordedAt) { }

    private static final ZoneId IST = ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata");   // "day" bucket follows the operating day
    private final CqlSession session;
    private final PreparedStatement insertByDay, insertByOrder, selectDay, selectOrder;
    private final Semaphore inFlight = new Semaphore(256);         // bound concurrent async writes per pod

    public LocationHistoryStore(CqlSession session) {
        this.session = session;
        this.insertByDay = session.prepare("""
                INSERT INTO tracking.rider_location_by_day
                  (rider_id, day, recorded_at, lat, lng, speed_kmph, order_id) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)""");
        this.insertByOrder = session.prepare("""
                INSERT INTO tracking.rider_location_by_order
                  (order_id, recorded_at, rider_id, lat, lng) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)""");
        this.selectDay = session.prepare("""
                SELECT recorded_at, lat, lng, speed_kmph, order_id FROM tracking.rider_location_by_day
                WHERE rider_id = ? AND day = ? LIMIT ?""");
        this.selectOrder = session.prepare("""
                SELECT recorded_at, rider_id, lat, lng FROM tracking.rider_location_by_order
                WHERE order_id = ?""");
    }

    /**
     * Individual async INSERTs, NOT a multi-partition BATCH (which would funnel through one coordinator).
     * Idempotent: the same (rider, day, recorded_at) primary key overwrites itself on retry.
     */
    public void writeAll(List<Point> points, Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException, TimeoutException {
        List<CompletableFuture<?>> futures = new ArrayList<>(points.size() * 2);
        for (Point p : points) {
            futures.add(submit(insertByDay.bind(p.riderId(), LocalDate.ofInstant(p.recordedAt(), IST),
                    p.recordedAt(), p.lat(), p.lng(), p.speedKmph(), p.orderId())));
            if (p.orderId() != null) {
                futures.add(submit(insertByOrder.bind(p.orderId(), p.recordedAt(), p.riderId(), p.lat(), p.lng())));
            }
        }
        try {
            CompletableFuture.allOf(futures.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).get(timeout.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            throw new HistoryWriteException(e.getCause());           // caller retries the whole batch (idempotent)
        }
    }

    private CompletableFuture<?> submit(BoundStatement stmt) throws InterruptedException {
        inFlight.acquire();
        return session.executeAsync(stmt.setConsistencyLevel(DefaultConsistencyLevel.LOCAL_QUORUM)
                                        .setIdempotent(true))           // allows driver speculative retries
                .toCompletableFuture()
                .whenComplete((r, e) -> inFlight.release());
    }

    public List<Point> pathForDay(String riderId, LocalDate day, int limit) {
        List<Point> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Row r : session.execute(selectDay.bind(riderId, day, limit)
                .setConsistencyLevel(DefaultConsistencyLevel.LOCAL_QUORUM))) {
            out.add(new Point(riderId, r.getString("order_id"), r.getDouble("lat"), r.getDouble("lng"),
                    r.getFloat("speed_kmph"), r.getInstant("recorded_at")));
        }
        return out;                                                  // newest first (clustering order DESC)
    }

    public List<Point> pathForOrder(String orderId) {
        List<Point> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Row r : session.execute(selectOrder.bind(orderId))) {
            out.add(new Point(r.getString("rider_id"), orderId, r.getDouble("lat"), r.getDouble("lng"),
                    0f, r.getInstant("recorded_at")));
        }
        return out;
    }

    public static class HistoryWriteException extends RuntimeException {
        public HistoryWriteException(Throwable cause) { super(cause); }
    }
}

package com.grocery.tracking.service;

import com.grocery.tracking.dto.PingBatch;
import com.grocery.tracking.history.LocationHistoryStore;
import com.grocery.tracking.latest.LatestLocationStore;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import java.time.*;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;

/** L3: synchronous dual sink (L4 moves both behind Kafka consumers). */
@Service
public class LocationService {

    private final LatestLocationStore latest;
    private final LocationHistoryStore history;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final MeterRegistry metrics;

    public LocationService(LatestLocationStore latest, LocationHistoryStore history, Clock clock, MeterRegistry metrics) {
        this.latest = latest; this.history = history; this.clock = clock; this.metrics = metrics;
    }

    public void record(PingBatch batch) throws Exception {
        long now = clock.instant().getEpochSecond();
        // Sanity: reject device clocks far in the future; keep order by seq
        List<PingBatch.Ping> sane = batch.pings().stream()
                .filter(p -> p.ts() <= now + 30)
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(PingBatch.Ping::seq))
                .toList();

        long applied = latest.applyBatch(batch.city(), sane.stream()
                .map(p -> new LatestLocationStore.Ping(batch.riderId(), p.lat(), p.lng(), p.ts(), p.seq()))
                .toList());
        metrics.counter("tracking.pings.applied").increment(applied);
        metrics.counter("tracking.pings.ignored_out_of_order").increment(sane.size() - applied);

        history.writeAll(sane.stream().map(p -> new LocationHistoryStore.Point(batch.riderId(), null,
                p.lat(), p.lng(), 0f, Instant.ofEpochSecond(p.ts()))).toList(), Duration.ofSeconds(2));
    }
}

L3 is still a dual write

record() writes Redis, then Cassandra. If Cassandra fails, Redis already moved on. For locations that's tolerable (the next ping repairs everything), but the pattern doesn't generalize. L4 removes it by making Kafka the single write, with each store consuming independently.

package com.grocery.tracking;

import com.grocery.tracking.history.LocationHistoryStore;
import com.grocery.tracking.latest.LatestLocationStore;
import com.grocery.tracking.latest.LatestLocationStore.Ping;
import com.datastax.oss.driver.api.core.CqlSession;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.testcontainers.cassandra.CassandraContainer;       // VERIFY: package/class in your Testcontainers version
import org.testcontainers.containers.GenericContainer;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.*;
import java.time.*;
import java.util.List;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest(properties = {"spring.cassandra.local-datacenter=datacenter1", "tracking.cities=BLR"})
@Testcontainers
class LocationStoresIT {

    @Container @ServiceConnection(name = "redis")
    static GenericContainer<?> redis = new GenericContainer<>("redis:7-alpine").withExposedPorts(6379);

    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static CassandraContainer cassandra = new CassandraContainer("cassandra:5");

    @Autowired LatestLocationStore latest;
    @Autowired LocationHistoryStore history;
    @Autowired CqlSession session;

    @BeforeAll
    static void schema(@Autowired CqlSession session) {
        session.execute("CREATE KEYSPACE IF NOT EXISTS tracking WITH replication = {'class':'SimpleStrategy','replication_factor':1}");
        session.execute("""
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tracking.rider_location_by_day (rider_id text, day date, recorded_at timestamp,
              lat double, lng double, speed_kmph float, order_id text,
              PRIMARY KEY ((rider_id, day), recorded_at)) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (recorded_at DESC)""");
        session.execute("""
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tracking.rider_location_by_order (order_id text, recorded_at timestamp,
              rider_id text, lat double, lng double, PRIMARY KEY ((order_id), recorded_at))""");
    }

    @Test
    void outOfOrderPingIsIgnored() {
        latest.applyBatch("BLR", List.of(new Ping("r1", 12.91, 77.63, 1_000, 10)));
        long applied = latest.applyBatch("BLR", List.of(new Ping("r1", 12.80, 77.50, 990, 9)));   // late retry of older ping
        assertThat(applied).isZero();
        assertThat(latest.latest("BLR", "r1")).get().extracting(Ping::seq).isEqualTo(10L);
    }

    @Test
    void staleRidersArePrunedFromGeoAndLastSeen() {
        latest.applyBatch("BLR", List.of(new Ping("r-old", 12.91, 77.63, 100, 1), new Ping("r-new", 12.91, 77.63, 10_000, 1)));
        long removed = latest.pruneStale("BLR", 5_000, 500);
        assertThat(removed).isEqualTo(1);
    }

    @Test
    void historyIsNewestFirstAndIdempotentOnRetry() throws Exception {
        Instant t0 = Instant.parse("2026-09-26T14:30:00Z");
        var points = List.of(
                new LocationHistoryStore.Point("r9", "ord_1", 12.91, 77.63, 18f, t0),
                new LocationHistoryStore.Point("r9", "ord_1", 12.92, 77.64, 20f, t0.plusSeconds(4)));
        history.writeAll(points, Duration.ofSeconds(5));
        history.writeAll(points, Duration.ofSeconds(5));                  // retry: same PKs, no duplicates

        var path = history.pathForDay("r9", LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 26), 100);
        assertThat(path).hasSize(2);
        assertThat(path.getFirst().recordedAt()).isEqualTo(t0.plusSeconds(4));
        assertThat(history.pathForOrder("ord_1")).hasSize(2);
    }
}

What L3 guarantees: one atomic Redis round trip per batch, out-of-order pings can't regress positions, silent riders drop out of nearby searches within ~65 s, and history is stored in bounded, TTL-expiring partitions with idempotent retries.

What L3 still lacks: the request thread writes to both stores synchronously (a dual write, and ingest latency depends on Cassandra). There's no replay if a store was down, and no way to add a third sink (analytics) without touching the ingest path.

docs.title: L4 — Enterprise: Kafka as the log, independent idempotent sinks B4
What changed from L1 to L4
docs.text: Concern L1 L2 L3 L4 Storage Mini LSM in memory Redis HASH + GEO + ZSET Redis (Lua, hash-tagged) + Cassandra (bucketed, TTL) same, fed by Kafka Round trips per ping — 3 ~1/100 (batched Lua) + async Cassandra same, off the request path Out-of-order safety — ❌ ✅ seq guard ✅ also during replays Stale riders — Stay forever Pruned after 60 s (atomic) same History — ❌ 7 days, idempotent same Coupling — — Dual write on the request thread Single write to the log; independent sinks Recovery — — Manual Offset reset, rebuild, DLT for poison

docs.title: 6.2 Observability
docs.text: Store Key metrics Redis ops/s, latency (p99 via LATENCY/client metrics), memory, evictions, keyspace hits/misses, replication offset/lag, SLOWLOG, connected clients Cassandra/ScyllaDB read/write latency p99 per table, timeouts, unavailable errors, pending compactions, SSTables per read, tombstones per read, partition size histograms, disk usage, dropped messages, repair status Document DB (MongoDB) op latencies, query targeting (scanned/returned), replication lag, WiredTiger cache, slow query log Pipeline consumer lag per group, DLT rate, end-to-end freshness (event ts → visible in store) Business stale-rider count, pings.ignored_out_of_order, nearby query result sizes per store

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Network isolation: data stores in private subnets. Redis should never be internet-exposed. Use AUTH/ACLs even internally (Redis 6+ ACL users per service with command restrictions, and no FLUSHALL/KEYS in app users).
  • TLS in transit for Redis, Cassandra and MongoDB clients.
  • Authentication and least privilege: Cassandra roles per service with keyspace-level grants. MongoDB users per database.
  • Injection: document stores have injection risks too (MongoDB operator injection via $where/$ne in user input). Build queries with typed APIs, never string concatenation. The same goes for Lua scripts: pass data as ARGV, never interpolate it into script text.
  • PII and location privacy: rider location is personal data. Set retention (TTL 7 days), restrict access (support tools audited), and exclude it from analytics exports unless aggregated (DPDP, Ch 36).
  • Backups and encryption at rest according to data class. Derived stores can rely on rebuild, but the log (Kafka) and SoR need backups.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance & tuning knobs
docs.text: Knob Value Guidance Cassandra consistency LOCAL_QUORUM default LOCAL_ONE for tolerant writes after measuring; never cross-DC QUORUM on hot paths Compaction strategy TWCS for TTL time series; LCS read-heavy; STCS general Wrong strategy is the most common Cassandra performance issue Partition size target < 10 MB typical, well below 100 MB Bucket by time or hash suffix Driver Prepared statements, token-aware routing, setIdempotent(true), bounded in-flight Speculative execution only for idempotent queries Redis pipelining / Lua batching 50–200 ops per round trip Latency and CPU savings Redis maxmemory-policy Caches: allkeys-lru/volatile-lfu; state: noeviction Decide per instance, not per key Redis persistence Caches: none/RDB; state: AOF everysec Durability vs latency Kafka consumer max.poll.records 500 Batch size vs processing time within max.poll.interval.ms GEO search COUNT Small (20) Bounded work per query

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text: Driver Note Redis memory ~20 MB for latest locations is trivial; carts and sessions dominate Redis costs. Managed Redis is priced per GB-hour of memory Cassandra storage × RF 3× replication plus compaction headroom (disk ≤ 50–60 % used) → provision ~2× the data size Write-priced managed stores (DynamoDB, Keyspaces) At 40 K sustained writes/s, per-request pricing can exceed a provisioned cluster. Model it (Ch 02) Kafka retention 3 days × 3 MB/s × RF 3 ≈ 2.3 TB. It buys the ability to rebuild stores Operational cost Every new database: on-call runbooks, upgrades, backups, security reviews, skills. Often the biggest cost; count it in the decision matrix

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Choosing NoSQL "because it scales" without access patterns. Symptom: A document database for relational, transactional data, followed by app-level joins and consistency bugs. Fix: List the queries and consistency needs first (§2.8). The system of record for money stays relational.

2. Modeling Cassandra like a relational database.

-- ❌ before: normalized tables + ALLOW FILTERING queries = full-cluster scans
SELECT * FROM rider_location WHERE recorded_at > '2026-09-26' ALLOW FILTERING;

-- ✅ after: a table per query, partition key always in WHERE
SELECT * FROM rider_location_by_day WHERE rider_id = 'r9' AND day = '2026-09-26';

3. Unbounded partitions. Symptom: PRIMARY KEY (rider_id, recorded_at) produces multi-GB partitions for veteran riders. Fix: Add a time bucket: ((rider_id, day), recorded_at).

4. Using Cassandra (or any LSM store) as a queue. Symptom: Insert-then-delete per message produces tombstones, and reads slow down until they fail. Fix: Use Kafka or a queue for queues. Use TTL-based expiry with TWCS for time series.

5. Multi-partition BATCH for "performance".

// ❌ before: one coordinator handles 500 partitions → slower, and one hot node
BatchStatement batch = BatchStatement.newInstance(DefaultBatchType.UNLOGGED); /* 500 inserts for different riders */

// ✅ after: individual async, token-aware, bounded in-flight writes (L3)
futures.add(session.executeAsync(insert.bind(...).setIdempotent(true)).toCompletableFuture());

6. Redis as a durable database without a rebuild story. Symptom: A failover loses the last seconds of writes, and it's discovered that it held the only copy of wallet balances. Fix: Keep only rebuildable or loss-tolerant data in Redis, or data backed by a SoR.

7. KEYS * (and friends) in production. Symptom: The whole Redis shard freezes while it iterates millions of keys. Fix: SCAN with COUNT, secondary structures (sets/zsets) for lookups, and ACLs that forbid KEYS for app users.

8. Dual writes to several stores from the app. Symptom: The search index and database disagree forever after a crash. Fix: One write (DB + outbox, or the log), and independent consumers (§2.10, L4).

9. Locale-dependent machine formats.

// ❌ before: on a JVM with a comma-decimal default locale → "12,911600" → unparseable JSON
"{\"lat\":%.6f}".formatted(lat);

// ✅ after
String.format(Locale.ROOT, "{\"lat\":%.6f}", lat);   // or a real JSON serializer

10. Embedding unbounded arrays in documents. Reviews, events and history belong in their own collection or table.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ SQL vs NoSQL: how do you choose?

30-second answer: Start from access patterns and consistency needs, not labels. Relational databases give transactions, constraints, joins and flexible queries, which suit the system of record for orders and money. NoSQL families trade some of that for a specific strength: key-value for sub-ms access, document for self-contained aggregates, wide-column for massive writes by key, graph for traversals, search for relevance.

Deep answer: Most platforms are polyglot: PostgreSQL for the core, plus Redis, a search engine and maybe a wide-column store, fed from the SoR via events or CDC. Operability (can we run it well?) is often the deciding factor.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Specialization vs operational complexity and consistency across stores.

Follow-ups: 1. Can PostgreSQL do document workloads? → Often yes, with JSONB + GIN. 2. Does NoSQL mean no schema? → The schema lives in the application instead. You still need versioning.

Red flags: "NoSQL is faster" or "NoSQL scales, SQL doesn't."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Talks about system of record, derived stores and operability.

Q2 [B1] What is Redis good for, and what should you not use it for?

30-second answer: Good for caches, sessions, carts, rate limits, counters, leaderboards, OTPs with TTLs, geo lookups, and lightweight queues or streams: anything needing sub-ms access and rich data structures. Not good as the sole store for data you can't lose (acknowledged writes can be lost on failover), or for datasets much larger than memory, or for complex queries.

Deep answer: Configure the eviction policy per purpose, use TTLs, design hash tags for cluster multi-key operations, keep Lua short, and have a rebuild path from the SoR.

Trade-offs: Speed vs durability and cost per GB.

Follow-ups: 1. RDB vs AOF? → Snapshots vs append log (everysec can lose ~1 s). 2. Why is KEYS * dangerous? → It's O(N) and blocks the single-threaded server.

Red flags: Storing wallet balances only in Redis.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Failover data-loss awareness and a rebuild story.

Q3 [B1] In a document database, when do you embed vs reference?

30-second answer: Embed data that's owned by, bounded with, and read together with the parent (product variants, nutrition). Reference data that's shared, unbounded, independently accessed, or frequently changing (brands, reviews, price, stock).

Deep answer: Unbounded arrays hurt performance and hit document size limits. Keep summaries embedded (rating average) and details separate. Frequently changing fields in a big document cause write amplification.

Trade-offs: Fewer reads vs duplication and update fan-out.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you keep embedded copies in sync? → Events, and accept brief staleness. 2. Transactions across documents? → Supported in some stores, but costly. Design to avoid them.

Red flags: Embedding everything.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Adds change-rate and boundedness as criteria.

Q4 [B1] ⭐ Explain the CAP theorem in practical terms.

30-second answer: When a network partition splits a distributed system, each side must choose between returning possibly stale or divergent answers (availability) and refusing requests to stay consistent (consistency). Partitions happen, so the choice is really C vs A during partitions, and it can be made per operation.

Deep answer: CAP's C is linearizability. PACELC adds that without partitions you trade latency against consistency. For example, Cassandra with QUORUM favours consistency at some latency, while ONE favours latency and availability.

Trade-offs: Consistency vs availability and latency.

Follow-ups: 1. Is a single-node PostgreSQL "CA"? → It's not distributed, so CAP doesn't really apply. With replicas you choose. 2. Can you pick "CA"? → Not in a distributed system that must tolerate partitions.

Red flags: "MongoDB is CP, Cassandra is AP" with no nuance.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Per-operation choices and PACELC.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ Model rider location history in Cassandra.

30-second answer: One table per query. For "a rider's path for a day": PRIMARY KEY ((rider_id, day), recorded_at) with recorded_at DESC clustering, a 7-day TTL, and TWCS compaction. For "path for an order": a second table keyed by order_id. Bucketing by day bounds partitions (~1 MB per rider per day).

Deep answer: Write with prepared, async, idempotent inserts at LOCAL_QUORUM, and avoid multi-partition batches. Keep delivery-critical events in the order SoR. Size nodes from write rate and storage × RF with compaction headroom.

Trade-offs: Duplicate tables for each query vs flexible queries.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not partition by rider_id alone? → Unbounded partitions. 2. Why TWCS? → TTL'd data expires in whole SSTables, which avoids tombstone-heavy compactions.

Red flags: ALLOW FILTERING or secondary indexes for main queries.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Partition sizing math plus compaction strategy.

Q6 [B2] ⭐ What is tunable consistency, and what does R + W > RF mean?

30-second answer: In Dynamo-style stores you choose per operation how many replicas must acknowledge a write (W) and answer a read (R). If R + W > RF, every read overlaps at least one replica that has the latest acknowledged write, giving read-your-writes for that key (absent concurrent writes and failures during repair).

Deep answer: RF=3 with QUORUM/QUORUM is the common default. ONE/ONE is fastest and most available. LOCAL_ variants keep quorums within a datacenter to avoid cross-region latency. Read repair and anti-entropy repair converge the replicas.

Trade-offs: Latency and availability vs staleness.

Follow-ups: 1. Does QUORUM give linearizability? → Not fully. Use lightweight transactions (Paxos) for compare-and-set. 2. What if a node is down? → QUORUM still works with 2 of 3.

Red flags: Assuming eventual consistency means "no guarantees at all."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Mentions LWT/CAS and repair.

Q7 [B2] LSM tree vs B+ tree: trade-offs?

30-second answer: A B+ tree updates in place: cheap reads, moderate writes. An LSM tree appends to a memtable, flushes sorted immutable SSTables, and merges them by compaction: very fast writes, but reads may check several files (mitigated by Bloom filters), with space and write amplification from compaction.

Deep answer: Choose LSM for write-heavy, append-mostly workloads (time series, events), and B+ trees for read-heavy, update-heavy OLTP with rich queries. The compaction strategy tunes the read/space/write amplification trade.

Trade-offs: Write throughput vs read latency and background I/O.

Follow-ups: 1. What are Bloom filters for? → Skipping SSTables that can't contain the key. 2. What's write amplification? → Bytes written to disk ÷ bytes written by the app.

Red flags: "LSM is always faster."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Relates compaction strategies to workloads.

Q8 [B2] ⭐ How would you find the nearest available riders to a dark store?

30-second answer: Keep the latest positions in a geo index (Redis GEO) per city. GEOSEARCH by radius ascending with a small count, then filter by availability. Prune riders not seen for 60 s, and guard updates with sequence numbers so out-of-order pings don't regress positions.

Deep answer: Hash-tag keys per city so a Lua script can update hash, geo and last-seen atomically. For road distance and ETA, re-rank the top candidates with a routing service. At larger scale use H3/geohash cells with sharded indexes (Ch 47).

Trade-offs: Straight-line distance vs road ETA; freshness vs write load.

Follow-ups: 1. How accurate is Redis GEO? → Geohash-based, with small errors at centimetre–metre scale; fine for dispatch. 2. What about riders crossing city boundaries? → Search the adjacent zones.

Red flags: SQL distance calculations over all riders per request.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Staleness pruning, out-of-order protection and re-ranking.

Q9 [B2] When is PostgreSQL JSONB enough, and when would you pick MongoDB?

30-second answer: JSONB is enough when document data sits alongside relational data, needs transactions with it, and fits one primary's scale. Choose MongoDB (or similar) when the workload is primarily document-shaped at a scale needing native sharding, when teams benefit from its tooling and developer model, or when flexible schemas across many teams dominate.

Deep answer: Consider indexes (GIN for JSONB), query ergonomics, operational skills and cost. Avoid picking a new database just for flexible attributes.

Trade-offs: One system to operate vs a better fit at scale.

Follow-ups: 1. JSONB pitfalls? → Large documents rewritten on update (TOAST), and weaker planner statistics. 2. MongoDB transactions? → Available. Design aggregates so you rarely need them.

Red flags: Choosing by popularity.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Counts operability and team skills.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ How do you detect and fix a hot partition?

30-second answer: Detect it with uneven node metrics, nodetool toppartitions, per-partition latency, or cloud "hot key" metrics. Fix it by changing the partition key to spread load (add a bucket such as time or a hash suffix), splitting hot keys into N sub-keys and merging on read, caching hot reads, or rate-limiting abusive producers.

Deep answer: Prevent it at design time: estimate per-key rates (Ch 02) and plan buckets. For counters, use sharded counters. For celebrity-style reads, use replication or caching. Changing a partition key means a data migration (dual write via the log, then backfill).

Trade-offs: Read fan-out across sub-keys vs write spreading.

Follow-ups: 1. Hot key in Redis Cluster? → Client-side caching, replicas for reads, or splitting keys. 2. How do you migrate the key? → A new table fed by the log, a backfill, then switching reads.

Red flags: "Add more nodes." That doesn't help one partition.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Estimation-driven prevention and a migration plan.

Q11 [B3] What are tombstones, and why do they cause outages?

30-second answer: Deletes (and expired TTLs) in LSM stores write tombstone markers that shadow older data until compaction removes them after gc_grace_seconds. Reads over ranges full of tombstones must scan them all, which slows or fails queries (tombstone thresholds). Queue-like or delete-heavy patterns are the usual cause.

Deep answer: Use TTL with TWCS for time series, avoid deleting individual rows in wide partitions, don't model queues in Cassandra, run repairs within gc_grace (or deleted data can resurrect), and monitor tombstones per read.

Trade-offs: Shorter gc_grace reduces tombstones but raises resurrection risk without repairs.

Follow-ups: 1. Why wait gc_grace at all? → So all replicas learn about the delete. 2. How do nulls relate? → Inserting nulls creates tombstones too. Use unset values.

Red flags: Using Cassandra as a job queue.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Links repairs, gc_grace and resurrection.

Q12 [B3] How do you do atomic multi-key operations in Redis Cluster?

30-second answer: Multi-key commands and Lua scripts require all keys in one hash slot. Use hash tags ({BLR}:…) to co-locate related keys, then use MULTI/EXEC or Lua for atomicity. Otherwise you get CROSSSLOT errors.

Deep answer: Hash tags concentrate load, so choose tag granularity (city vs zone) by capacity. Keep scripts short and bounded, pass data via ARGV, and use EVALSHA with script caching.

Trade-offs: Atomicity vs load distribution.

Follow-ups: 1. Does MULTI give isolation? → Commands run sequentially without interleaving, but with no rollback on errors. 2. WATCH? → Optimistic check-and-set.

Red flags: Discovering CROSSSLOT in production.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Designs tags for both atomicity and load.

Q13 [B3] ⭐ How do you keep multiple stores (DB, cache, search, Cassandra) consistent?

30-second answer: Don't dual-write from the app. Write once to the system of record (DB + transactional outbox, or an event log), then feed each derived store from that log with its own consumer, using idempotent writes and replay for recovery. Accept and measure eventual consistency.

Deep answer: Use CDC (Debezium) or outbox, one consumer group per sink, per-key ordering via partition keys, and version or sequence guards against out-of-order updates. Run reconciliation jobs for critical projections, and rebuild from the log or a SoR snapshot.

Trade-offs: Complexity and lag vs correctness.

Follow-ups: 1. What if you need read-your-writes on a derived store? → Read from the SoR for that user briefly, or wait for a version. 2. Why per-sink groups? → Isolation and independent replay.

Red flags: "We write to both in the same method."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Idempotency, ordering guards and rebuild paths.

Q14 [B3] Migrate rider locations from PostgreSQL to Cassandra with zero downtime.

30-second answer: Introduce the log first: ingest publishes to Kafka while still writing PostgreSQL (or CDC from PostgreSQL). Stand up Cassandra consumers from the log and backfill recent history from PostgreSQL. Verify with shadow reads comparing results. Switch reads behind a flag, stop the PostgreSQL writes, then drop the table (after a retention period).

Deep answer: Throttle the backfill to protect the source, make it idempotent (same PKs), compare counts and sample paths, keep rollback possible until verified, and communicate the retention change.

Trade-offs: Duration of dual paths vs risk.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you verify? → Shadow reads with diff metrics. 2. What about downtime for readers? → None: they switch via a flag.

Red flags: A big-bang cutover over a weekend.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Log-first, shadow reads and a reversible switch.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ A team wants a new database for a feature. How do you run the decision?

30-second answer: Require a short design doc: access patterns with volumes and SLOs, consistency needs, growth, the system of record, rebuild story, and a weighted decision matrix (fit, consistency, scale, operability, cost, ecosystem) including "use an existing store." Prefer existing or managed stores unless the gap is large, and record the deciding factor in an ADR.

Deep answer: Maintain a platform "paved road" of supported stores with runbooks, monitoring and backups. New stores need an owner, on-call readiness, security review and exit criteria. Near-ties in the matrix should favour operability.

Trade-offs: Team autonomy vs platform sprawl.

Follow-ups: 1. What if the matrix is a tie? → Name the deciding factor explicitly (cost at scale, lock-in, skills). 2. How do you avoid sprawl? → A paved road plus a review for anything off it.

Red flags: Letting each team pick freely with no operability plan.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Operability weighting and a paved road.

Q16 [B4] Managed vs self-hosted NoSQL: how do you decide?

30-second answer: Managed services remove patching, backups, failover and scaling toil at higher unit cost and with some feature or version limits. Self-hosting gives control and possibly lower cost at large scale, but requires deep expertise (repairs, compaction tuning, upgrades) and 24×7 on-call. For most teams, managed wins until scale economics and in-house expertise justify otherwise.

Deep answer: Model the total cost: infra plus people plus incident risk. Check compatibility gaps (for example, API-compatible services that differ from open-source behaviour), data residency, and exit strategy.

Trade-offs: Control and cost vs toil and risk.

Follow-ups: 1. What's a hidden managed-service risk? → Behavioural differences and limits discovered late. 2. When is self-hosting worth it? → Very large clusters with a dedicated team.

Red flags: Deciding on the infra bill alone.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Total cost of ownership, including people.

Q17 [B4] How do you set consistency expectations per data class across the platform?

30-second answer: Classify the data. Money and inventory: strong consistency in the SoR (PostgreSQL), with idempotent, auditable writes. User-visible state after own writes: read-your-writes (primary reads or tokens). Browsing and search: bounded staleness (seconds–minutes), measured. Analytics: hours. Locations: seconds-stale, loss-tolerant. Document it and give each class SLOs.

Deep answer: Map each class to allowed stores and patterns (for example, no Redis-only money data), freshness SLOs with monitoring, and the conflict resolution approach. Review new features against the classes.

Trade-offs: Uniform strong consistency is simpler but costly. Per-class rules need governance.

Follow-ups: 1. Example of a class violation? → Showing "in stock" from the search index at checkout. 2. How do you enforce it? → Design reviews, architecture tests, freshness alerts.

Red flags: "Everything is eventually consistent."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Data classes with freshness SLOs and allowed stores.

Q18 [B4] What is DynamoDB single-table design, and when is it a good idea?

30-second answer: Storing multiple entity types in one table with overloaded partition and sort keys (PK=CUSTOMER#123, SK=ORDER#2026-09-26#ord_9) and GSIs, so that each access pattern is one query. It's good when access patterns are known and stable and very high scale with predictable latency matters. It's painful when access patterns change often or ad hoc queries are needed.

Deep answer: It needs careful key design, GSI projection planning, hot-key avoidance and migrations for new patterns. Many teams do better with a few purpose-specific tables.

Trade-offs: Performance and cost efficiency vs flexibility and readability.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you add a new query? → A new GSI or a backfill into new key shapes. 2. Transactions? → TransactWriteItems with limits and cost.

Red flags: Single-table design for an evolving MVP.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Ties it to access-pattern stability.

Q19 [B4] Your Redis cluster lost all data. Walk through recovery and what the design should have guaranteed.

30-second answer: Immediately: the platform should degrade, not fail. Carts fall back to the SoR snapshot, rate limits fail open with conservative defaults, and sessions force re-login. Rebuild derived state from the SoR or the log: replay loc-latest from Kafka offsets a few minutes back, and warm caches gradually to avoid stampedes. After recovery, audit which data had no rebuild path.

Deep answer: Design guarantees: every Redis dataset is classified (cache / rebuildable state / critical), with a rebuild runbook, a tested replay, and fallback behaviour. Critical state isn't Redis-only.

Trade-offs: Recovery speed vs complexity of fallbacks.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you avoid a cache stampede on warm-up? → Request coalescing and staggered TTLs (Ch 07). 2. Which fallbacks fail open vs closed? → Fraud and limits carefully, UX features open.

Red flags: No answer beyond "restore from backup."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Data classification plus tested rebuilds.

Q20 [B4] How many databases is too many?

30-second answer: When the operational load (expertise, on-call, upgrades, security, backups) exceeds the team's capacity, or when new stores are added for marginal gains. A healthy platform has a small paved road: a relational SoR, a cache or key-value store, a search engine, a log (Kafka), and perhaps one analytical or wide-column store, each with owners and runbooks.

Deep answer: Track the store inventory with owners, SLOs and costs. Consolidate where one store serves several needs acceptably (PostgreSQL JSONB instead of a document DB). Require exit plans for experiments.

Trade-offs: Best fit per workload vs total cost of ownership.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you retire a store? → Migrate consumers via the log, then decommission with a verification period. 2. Who owns the paved road? → The platform team, with input from the architecture guild.

Red flags: A different database per microservice "for autonomy."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Treats persistence choices as a platform portfolio.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Choose stores by access pattern, scale and consistency, not by label. Keep a single system of record per fact.
  2. Key-value (Redis) gives sub-ms structures with TTLs, but treat it as rebuildable. Hash-tag keys for cluster atomicity.
  3. Documents: embed what's owned, bounded and read together, and reference the rest. JSONB is often enough.
  4. Wide-column: one table per query, the partition key in every query, bounded partitions (time buckets), TTL + TWCS for time series.
  5. LSM trees make writes cheap with memtables, SSTables and compaction, at the cost of read, space and write amplification. Bloom filters and compaction strategy are the tuning levers.
  6. CAP is about partitions, and PACELC adds latency vs consistency the rest of the time. Consistency is tunable per operation (R + W > RF).
  7. No dual writes. One write to the log or SoR, and independent, idempotent consumers per derived store.
  8. Out-of-order updates need sequence or version guards, especially during replays.
  9. The decision matrix must weight operability. Near-ties call for naming the deciding factor.
  10. Every store needs a failure and rebuild story before it goes to production.

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Store Money, inventory, orders PostgreSQL (SoR) Latest state, sessions, counters, geo radius Redis Massive append-only time series by key Cassandra/ScyllaDB (TWCS + TTL) Self-contained aggregates, flexible attributes Document DB or PostgreSQL JSONB Full-text relevance, facets OpenSearch (derived) Multi-hop relationships, interactive Graph DB (or batch-precompute) Aggregations over billions of rows Columnar warehouse Metrics with downsampling TSDB Fan-out to several stores Kafka log + per-sink consumer groups

docs.title: 07. Caching ⭐
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 02, Ch 05, Ch 06 · What you will build: The product-card cache, taken from LRU + single-flight + XFetch in plain Java (L1) to a two-level Caffeine + Redis cache with race-free versioned writes, event-driven invalidation across pods, hot-key protection, CDN surrogate keys and pre-sale warming (L4) · Reading time: 100 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: "flush the cache so the sale prices show up"
docs.text:
At 7:59 pm on sale day, the pricing team loaded the festival prices. To make them "show up immediately," someone ran FLUSHALL on the catalog Redis cluster at 8:00:00, the exact second the sale opened.

  1. Stampede. 110 K req/s that had been served ~98 % from cache now all missed at once. Every miss ran the same 8 ms product-card query. The catalog PostgreSQL went from 2 K to 60 K queries/s and hit 100 % CPU in seconds. Queries slowed to 2 s, and the cache couldn't refill because every loader was stuck waiting on the database.
  2. Stale prices anyway. Each catalog pod also had an in-process cache (Caffeine, 10-minute TTL) that FLUSHALL didn't touch. For ten minutes, customers saw old prices on some requests and new prices on others, depending on which pod served them. The cart re-priced at checkout, and customers saw "price changed" errors.
  3. One stale price forever. A price update raced with a cache fill: a reader loaded the old price, the writer updated the DB and deleted the key, and then the reader wrote the old price back. It stayed until the Redis TTL expired six hours later.

Every one of these is a caching design failure, not a database failure: no stampede protection, no invalidation across cache layers, and no protection against the read/write race.

The thesis of this chapter

A cache is a copy of data with a lifetime and a staleness contract. Caching is easy to add and hard to get right. The hard parts are what happens on a miss storm, how copies are invalidated, and what staleness each reader is allowed to see.

docs.title: 1.2 Where this lives in the grocery platform
docs.text: Layer What's cached Staleness allowed Mobile app / browser Category trees, images, config Minutes to hours (versioned URLs for images) CDN Product images, static assets, anonymous category listings Minutes; purge on change API gateway / BFF Rarely: some anonymous GETs Seconds Service in-process (L1, Caffeine) Hot product cards, GST rates, serviceability snapshot (Ch 01) Seconds Distributed cache (L2, Redis) Product cards, store prices, cart, sessions Seconds to minutes, invalidated on change Database Buffer cache, query plans n/a (always consistent)

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text: Band After this chapter you can… B1 Explain cache hits and misses, TTLs, LRU/LFU, and where caches sit B2 Choose cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind or refresh-ahead, and use Spring Cache with Redis B3 Prevent stampedes, fix the cache-aside race, handle hot keys, design multi-level caches, and measure hit ratios B4 Design invalidation across layers (L1, L2, CDN), cache warming, per-data staleness contracts, and caching's cost and availability trade-offs

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: the shopkeeper's counter B1
docs.text:
A kirana shopkeeper keeps the ten most-asked-for items on the counter (cache) and everything else in the storeroom (database).

  • Most customers are served from the counter: a hit.
  • For something rare, the shopkeeper walks to the storeroom: a miss. He may then keep it on the counter.
  • The counter is small, so when it's full he removes what nobody asked for recently: eviction (LRU).
  • If the price of sugar changes, the price tag on the counter must change too, or customers pay the wrong price: invalidation.
  • If 50 customers ask for sugar at once and the counter is empty, he shouldn't make 50 trips to the storeroom: stampede protection.

docs.title: 2.2 The numbers that make caching worth it B1 B2
docs.text:
\[ \text{Effective latency} = h \times t_{cache} + (1-h) \times t_{origin} \qquad \text{Origin load} = (1-h) \times \text{request rate} \] Hit ratio h Origin load at 110 K req/s Effective latency (cache 1 ms, origin 10 ms) 0 % 110 K/s 10 ms 90 % 11 K/s 1.9 ms 98 % 2.2 K/s 1.18 ms 99.5 % 550/s 1.05 ms

Your database is sized for the misses, not the hits

At 98 % hits, the database sees 2.2 K/s. If the cache disappears, it sees 110 K/s, 50× its normal load. The cache has become a load-bearing part of availability. Design for cache loss: stampede protection, gradual warming, and load shedding.

    CDN --> GW["Gateway / BFF<br/>(rare, anonymous GETs)"]

docs.title: 2.4 Caching patterns ⭐ B2
docs.text:
Pattern Read path Write path Pros Cons Grocery use Cache-aside (lazy loading) App checks the cache, and on a miss loads from the DB and populates the cache App writes the DB, then deletes the cache key Simple; cache only holds what's read; cache failure doesn't block reads First read is slow; race conditions (§2.8); stampedes Product cards, store prices Read-through Cache library loads on a miss (loader function) As cache-aside Cleaner code; enables single-flight Same staleness issues Caffeine LoadingCache L1 Write-through Cache is always populated Write to cache and DB synchronously Reads always hit after writes Write latency; caches data nobody reads; still inconsistent if one write fails Rarely: config values Write-behind (write-back) Reads from the cache Write to the cache; flush to the DB asynchronously Very fast writes; batching Data loss on cache failure; ordering and consistency complexity Counters for analytics (view counts), never money Refresh-ahead Serve from the cache; refresh before expiry — Hot keys never miss Refreshes data that may not be read again Hot SKUs during sales; GST rate tables

Delete, don't update, on writes (cache-aside)

After a DB write, delete the cache key rather than writing the new value. Two concurrent writers updating the cache can leave the older value last (their DB order and cache order differ). Deleting means the next reader loads the current value. That's not the whole story, though: see the read/write race in §2.8.

docs.title: 2.5 Eviction policies B1 B2
docs.text:
Policy Evicts Good for Weakness LRU Least recently used Recency-heavy workloads A one-off scan (bulk export) flushes hot items LFU Least frequently used Stable popularity (top SKUs) Slow to adapt; old popular items linger (use aging) W-TinyLFU (Caffeine) Admission by frequency sketch + windowed LRU Mixed workloads; near-optimal hit rates — (the best default for JVM L1 caches) TTL / TTI Expired entries (time-to-live / time-to-idle) Bounding staleness Not a memory policy by itself Random Random entry Very cheap Unpredictable

Redis maxmemory-policy: allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu for pure caches, volatile-* when only keys with TTLs may be evicted, and noeviction for stateful data (writes fail instead of silently losing data).

docs.title: 2.6 TTLs and the staleness contract B2 B3
docs.text:
Every cached item has a staleness contract: the maximum time a reader may see an old value. The TTL is the safety net that bounds it even when invalidation fails. It isn't the primary freshness mechanism for data that changes.

Data Changes Invalidation TTL (safety net) Contract Product content (name, images, description) Rarely Event-driven delete 6 h ± jitter ≤ ~5 s after change (event), ≤ 6 h worst case Store price Several times/day; bursts before sales Event-driven delete + versioned writes 10 min ± jitter ≤ ~5 s; checkout re-prices from the SoR Stock availability badge Constantly Not cached, or 5–10 s TTL 10 s "In stock" is a hint; reservation is exact (Ch 05) GST rate table Rarely (government notification) Event + refresh-ahead 1 h ≤ 1 min Serviceability Rarely Snapshot (Ch 01) Full reload 30 s Browse ≤ 60 s; checkout fresh

Add jitter to TTLs

If 250 K keys are warmed at 7:30 pm with TTL = 30 min, they all expire at 8:00 pm, at the sale start. Use TTL × (1 ± 10 %) so expiries spread out.

docs.title: 2.7 Cache stampede (thundering herd) ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
A stampede happens when many requests miss the same key at the same time (the key expired, was deleted, or the cache was cold) and all of them hit the origin.

L1 (§5) measures it: 1,000 concurrent requests → 1,000 DB calls naively, 1 with single-flight.

Technique How Scope Single-flight / request coalescing Concurrent misses for a key share one in-flight load Per process (Caffeine does this for get(key, loader)) Distributed lock on miss SET lock:key NX PX 3000: the winner loads, others wait or serve stale Across pods (costlier; deadline needed) Stale-while-revalidate Keep serving the expired value while one caller refreshes Needs a "soft TTL" plus a "hard TTL" Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch) Each reader refreshes early with a probability that rises near expiry Across pods, with no coordination Refresh-ahead for known hot keys Background refresh before expiry Hot SKUs, config TTL jitter Avoid synchronized expiry Everywhere Warming Pre-populate before known peaks Sales, deploys, cache node replacement Load shedding / circuit breaker at origin Protect the DB if misses spike anyway Last line (Ch 18)

XFetch (Vattani et al., VLDB 2015) refreshes early when:

\[ \text{now} - \delta \cdot \beta \cdot \ln(\text{rand}()) \ge \text{expiry} \]

where δ is the recompute time and β ≥ 1 is aggressiveness. From L1's run, with 10,000 req/s on one key, a 300 s TTL and δ = 0.2 s:

   at t=298.0s:     1 of 10,000 callers would refresh early
   at t=299.0s:    64 of 10,000 callers would refresh early
   at t=299.8s: 3,667 of 10,000 callers would refresh early

In practice the first early refresh (~2 s before expiry) repopulates the key, so the key never actually expires under load. Combined with single-flight, only one caller per pod does the work.

docs.title: 2.8 The cache-aside race and versioned writes ⭐ B3
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant R as Reader (pod A)
    participant C as Redis
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant W as Writer (pricing)
    R->>C: GET price:BLR-HSR-01:ONION → miss
    R->>DB: SELECT price → ₹40 (v7)
    Note over R: reader is slow (GC pause, network)
    W->>DB: UPDATE price = ₹1 (v8), COMMIT
    W->>C: DEL price:BLR-HSR-01:ONION
    R->>C: SET price... = ₹40 (v7)   ← stale value written AFTER the delete
    Note over C: ₹40 stays until TTL (hours) — the §1.1 bug
Fix How Trade-off Versioned conditional set Store {version, value} and only SET if the incoming version ≥ the cached version (Lua); the delete writes a tombstone with the new version Needs a monotonic version from the SoR (row version column); a small Lua script Short TTL Bounds the staleness window Only reduces the damage Delayed double delete Delete, then delete again after ~1 s Heuristic; timing-dependent Lease tokens (Facebook memcache) A miss returns a lease; the set is accepted only with a valid lease, and a delete invalidates leases Needs cache support Update the cache from the change stream only (CDC) Only the CDC consumer writes the cache, in commit order More infrastructure; the app never writes the cache

L3 implements versioned conditional sets with version tombstones, which is simple and robust with Redis Lua.

docs.title: 2.9 Invalidation across layers B3 B4
docs.text:
"There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things." — Phil Karlton

Layer Invalidation mechanism Latency L2 Redis Writer (or CDC consumer) deletes or versions the key ms L1 per pod Broadcast event (Kafka, per-pod group; or Redis Pub/Sub) → each pod evicts locally; plus a short TTL ~1 s CDN Purge by URL or surrogate key (tag all pages containing SKU X, then purge the tag) seconds Browser/app Cache-Control + ETags; versioned URLs for immutable assets Next request (or never, if immutable)

The order matters: invalidate from the inside out (L2 → L1 → CDN). Otherwise an outer layer can re-fill from an inner layer that still holds the old value.

docs.title: 2.10 Hot keys B3
docs.text:
A single key receiving a large share of traffic ("₹1 onions" product card during the sale) concentrates load on one Redis shard (Ch 06).

Technique How L1 in-process cache Each pod absorbs repeated reads; Redis sees ~1 read per pod per L1 TTL Key replication Write card:ONION#0..#7 and read a random replica, spreading across shards Client-side caching (Redis 6+ tracking) The server notifies clients when keys they cached change Pre-computation Build the sale landing page once and serve it from the CDN

docs.title: 2.11 Spring Cache abstraction B2
docs.text:
Annotation Meaning @EnableCaching Turns on cache proxies @Cacheable(cacheNames = "productCard", key = "#sku", sync = true) Cache-aside read. sync = true makes concurrent misses in the same JVM wait for one loader (single-flight per JVM, if the cache provider supports it) @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "productCard", key = "#sku") Delete on write @CachePut Always execute and put the result (write-through style) @Caching Combine several

Pitfalls:

  • Proxies don't intercept self-invocation.
  • @CacheEvict runs before the transaction commits, unless you defer it to after commit, which opens a stale-read window.
  • There's no versioning, so the §2.8 race remains.
  • Default Java serialization is fragile. Use JSON with explicit types.
  • Null values get cached (or don't) depending on disableCachingNullValues.
  • Keys need explicit namespaces and versions (v2::productCard::SKU) for schema changes.

docs.title: 2.12 Caching and consistency: what must never be cached B3 B4
docs.text:
Never serve from a cache for… Why Instead Stock decisions at reservation Oversell (Ch 05) Atomic DB update Payment status for fulfilment decisions Money SoR / payment provider Final price at checkout Price contracts Re-price from the SoR at checkout (show "price updated" if it changed) Authorization decisions with revocation needs Security Short TTLs plus revocation events, or direct checks Idempotency records Correctness Same DB as the business write (Ch 04)

The pattern: use caches for displaying, and the system of record for deciding.

docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App as App
    participant Pod as catalog pod
    participant L1 as Caffeine L1
    participant L2 as Redis L2
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant K as Kafka
    App->>Pod: GET /stores/BLR-HSR-01/products/ONION-1KG
    Pod->>L1: get(card, price)
    L1-->>Pod: miss
    Pod->>L2: MGET card:ONION-1KG, price:BLR-HSR-01:ONION-1KG

    App->>Pod: GET again
    Pod->>L2: price → tombstone v9 → treat as miss

docs.title: 3.3 Sequence: failure path, a slow reader racing a price update (fixed)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant R as Reader (pod A)
    participant L2 as Redis (Lua: set-if-newer)
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant INV as Invalidator
    R->>L2: GET price key → miss
    R->>DB: SELECT → ₹40, version 8
    Note over R: long GC pause
    DB->>DB: price updated → ₹1, version 9 (committed)
    INV->>L2: tombstone {version 9}
    R->>L2: SET-IF-NEWER {version 8, ₹40}
    L2-->>R: rejected (8 < 9)
    Note over L2: next reader misses, loads v9 ₹1 and caches it

What the system guarantees after this failure path

A stale value can never overwrite a newer one, and a delete can't be undone by a slow reader, because every write to L2 carries the SoR version and the Lua script accepts only versions ≥ the stored one (including tombstones). The worst case is a transient extra miss. L1 staleness is bounded by its 5 s TTL even if a broadcast is missed. Checkout always re-prices from the SoR.

docs.title: 3.4 State: a cache entry with soft and hard TTLs
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ABSENT
    ABSENT --> LOADING: miss (single-flight winner)
    LOADING --> FRESH: loaded (version v)
    LOADING --> ABSENT: load failed
    FRESH --> FRESH: hit
    FRESH --> REFRESHING: XFetch early-refresh chosen / soft TTL passed
    REFRESHING --> FRESH: refreshed (serve old value meanwhile)
    FRESH --> TOMBSTONE: invalidation (version v+1)
    TOMBSTONE --> LOADING: next read
    FRESH --> ABSENT: hard TTL expired / evicted

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Product Card & Price Caching for Sales
docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers Catalog team / Pricing, SRE, Mobile, Web Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-029 Versioned cache writes and version tombstones; ADR-030 No cache flushes: invalidate by event, warm before events

1. Context & Problem. A cache flush at sale start caused a stampede that took down the catalog database, L1 caches served stale prices across pods, and a read/write race pinned a stale price for hours (§1.1).

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: ≥ 98 % hit ratio at 110 K req/s; price changes visible within 5 s p99; no stale-forever values; survive a cold or lost Redis without taking down PostgreSQL.
  • Non-goals: stock availability caching (a hint only, 10 s TTL); search results (Ch 22).

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement FR-1 Serve product card (content) + store price for (store, SKU) NFR-1 p99 ≤ 15 ms in-service at 110 K req/s (P90 190 K/s, Ch 02) NFR-2 Price change visible to readers ≤ 5 s p99 (L1 + L2) NFR-3 A newer value can never be overwritten by an older one in L2 NFR-4 With Redis unavailable, the DB sees ≤ 10 K req/s (single-flight per pod + L1 + shedding) NFR-5 Checkout prices always come from the pricing SoR

4. Capacity estimates.

Item Calculation Result Card requests at sale start (P90) Ch 02 ~190 K/s Distinct SKUs requested in the first 10 min Sale concentrates demand ~20 K; the top 500 = 60 % of traffic L2 dataset: cards 250 K SKUs × ~2 KB ~500 MB L2 dataset: prices 500 stores × 6 K SKUs × ~80 B ~240 MB L1 per pod 10 K hottest cards × 2 KB + prices ~25 MB heap L1 hit ratio (5 s TTL, hot-skewed) Hot keys re-read many times per 5 s per pod ~80 % Redis load 190 K × 20 % L1 misses × 2 keys (MGET = 1 op) ~38 K ops/s → 3 shards DB load at 98 % overall hit ratio 190 K × 2 % ~3.8 K/s (DB sized for 10 K/s) Redis cold (worst case) 96 pods × ~20 K distinct keys ÷ 60 s warm-up, single-flight per pod ~32 K/s for the first minute → too high: needs warming + L2 lock on miss for top keys + shedding

What the estimate tells us

Steady state is easy. The dangerous moments are cold starts and invalidation storms. That's why warming, cross-pod stampede control for the hottest keys, and the ban on flushes are requirements, not optimizations.

5. Proposed design.

  • L1 Caffeine: 5 s TTL, W-TinyLFU, ~10 K entries, get(key, loader) single-flight, and eviction by per-pod Kafka broadcast.
  • L2 Redis: values stored as {version, payload} with a set-if-newer Lua script, invalidation via version tombstones written by an invalidator consuming outbox events, XFetch early refresh, TTL with jitter (cards 6 h, prices 10 min), and hot keys replicated ×8.
  • CDN: product images with immutable versioned URLs; anonymous category listings with s-maxage=30, stale-while-revalidate=60, tagged by surrogate keys (sku-{id}, category-{id}) and purged on change.
  • Warming: at T−30 min, a job loads the sale SKU list × stores into L2 (throttled).
  • Flushing is prohibited. Price reloads publish change events instead.

5.3 Cache key and value format.

key:   v1:card:{sku}                       value: {"v":12,"d":{...card json...}}      TTL 6h ± 10%
key:   v1:price:{store}:{sku}              value: {"v":9,"d":{"paise":100}}           TTL 10m ± 10%
tomb:  v1:price:{store}:{sku}              value: {"v":10,"t":1}                       TTL 60s (only blocks older writes)
hot:   v1:card:{sku}#0 .. #7               replicas for the top-500 SKUs during sales

The v1: prefix is the cache schema version: changing the payload format means bumping it to v2:, with no flush and no deserialization errors during a rolling deploy.

7. Alternatives considered.

Option Pros Cons Verdict Spring @Cacheable + @CacheEvict only Minimal code Race (§2.8), no L1 invalidation, stampedes across pods Rejected for prices; fine for low-risk data Write-through prices to Redis Always warm Still races between writers; caches all 3 M prices Rejected CDC-only cache writes (app never writes the cache) Commit-ordered Every miss must wait for CDC; complex Considered for 2027 Cache-aside + versioned set-if-newer + tombstones + L1 broadcast + XFetch + warming Race-free, bounded staleness, stampede-resistant Lua scripts, events, more moving parts Chosen No L1 Simpler invalidation Hot keys hammer single Redis shards Rejected (hot keys)

8. Failure modes. Redis down: L1 continues (5 s TTL, then per-pod single-flight to the DB), a concurrency limiter caps DB loads per pod at 16, and excess requests get 503 with Retry-After for low-priority traffic. Kafka lag on invalidation: L1 staleness bounded at 5 s by TTL. L2 bounded by TTL, but checkout re-prices. Invalidator bug: TTLs bound the damage, and a version tombstone replay tool exists.

10. Observability. Hit ratio per layer and cache name, load latency, loads/s to the DB, single-flight waiters, XFetch refreshes, rejected stale sets (Lua result), invalidation lag (event time → tombstone), Redis ops/s per shard (hot-shard detection), and evictions.

14. Decision (ADR-029/030 summary). All L2 writes carry the SoR version and go through set-if-newer. Invalidations write version tombstones. L1 caches have TTLs ≤ 5 s for mutable data and subscribe to change events. Caches are never flushed wholesale. Change events drive invalidation, and known peaks are pre-warmed. Displays may use caches. Decisions (checkout price, stock, payment) use the system of record.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
We build the product card + store price cache four times:

Level New requirement that forces the step L1 "Show LRU, the stampede, and early refresh working." (plain Java) L2 "Cache reads in Redis with Spring's @Cacheable, and evict on writes." L3 "Two levels (Caffeine + Redis), no stale-forever race, stampede-proof, DB protected when Redis is cold." L4 "Invalidate every layer (L1 on all pods, L2, CDN) from change events, survive hot keys, and pre-warm before the sale."

docs.title: L1 — Concept (plain Java) B1
docs.text:
// CachingL1.java — run with: java CachingL1.java
// Three caching ideas in plain Java:
//   A. LRU eviction with LinkedHashMap
//   B. Cache stampede: 1,000 concurrent misses on one hot key — naive vs single-flight (request coalescing)
//   C. Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch): refresh BEFORE expiry, spread across callers
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class CachingL1 {

    // ---------- A. LRU ----------
    static final class LruCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
        private final int capacity;
        LruCache(int capacity) { super(16, 0.75f, true); this.capacity = capacity; }   // accessOrder = true
        @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > capacity; }
    }

    // ---------- B. Stampede ----------
    static final AtomicInteger dbCalls = new AtomicInteger();

    static String loadFromDb(String sku) {
        dbCalls.incrementAndGet();
        try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }   // slow query
        return "card:" + sku;
    }

    /** Naive cache-aside: every concurrent miss goes to the database. */
    static final class NaiveCache {
        final ConcurrentHashMap<String, String> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        String get(String sku) {
            String v = map.get(sku);
            if (v == null) { v = loadFromDb(sku); map.put(sku, v); }
            return v;
        }
    }

    /** Single-flight: concurrent misses for the same key share ONE in-flight load. */
    static final class SingleFlightCache {
        final ConcurrentHashMap<String, String> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>> inFlight = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        String get(String sku) {
            String v = map.get(sku);
            if (v != null) return v;
            CompletableFuture<String> mine = new CompletableFuture<>();
            CompletableFuture<String> existing = inFlight.putIfAbsent(sku, mine);
            if (existing != null) return existing.join();          // someone else is loading: wait for it
            try {
                String loaded = loadFromDb(sku);
                map.put(sku, loaded);
                mine.complete(loaded);
                return loaded;
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                mine.completeExceptionally(e);
                throw e;
            } finally {
                inFlight.remove(sku, mine);
            }
        }
    }

    static int stampede(java.util.function.Function<String, String> cacheGet) throws Exception {
        dbCalls.set(0);
        CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1);
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) pool.submit(() -> { go.await(); return cacheGet.apply("ONION-1KG"); });
            go.countDown();
        }
        return dbCalls.get();
    }

    // ---------- C. XFetch ----------
    /**
     * Returns true if this caller should refresh early. delta = how long a recompute takes, beta >= 1 (aggressiveness).
     * Probability rises as expiry approaches; slower recomputes start refreshing earlier.
     * Vattani, Chierichetti, Lowenstein — "Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention" (VLDB 2015)
     */
    static boolean shouldRefreshEarly(double nowSec, double expirySec, double deltaSec, double beta, Random rnd) {
        return nowSec - deltaSec * beta * Math.log(rnd.nextDouble()) >= expirySec;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("A. LRU with capacity 3");
        var lru = new LruCache<String, String>(3);
        lru.put("atta", "A"); lru.put("milk", "M"); lru.put("rice", "R");
        lru.get("atta");                                  // touch → most recently used
        lru.put("eggs", "E");                             // evicts least recently used: milk
        System.out.println("   keys after access(atta) + put(eggs): " + lru.keySet());

        System.out.println("B. 1,000 concurrent requests for a cold hot key (50 ms DB query)");
        System.out.println("   naive cache-aside : " + stampede(new NaiveCache()::get) + " DB calls");
        System.out.println("   single-flight     : " + stampede(new SingleFlightCache()::get) + " DB call(s)");

        System.out.println("C. XFetch: 10,000 requests/s during the last 10 s of a 300 s TTL (recompute takes 0.2 s)");
        Random rnd = new Random(1);
        double expiry = 300;
        for (double t : new double[]{290, 295, 298, 299, 299.8}) {
            int early = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) if (shouldRefreshEarly(t, expiry, 0.2, 1.0, rnd)) early++;
            System.out.printf("   at t=%5.1fs: %,5d of 10,000 callers would refresh early%n", t, early);
        }
    }
}

Actual output from running it:

A. LRU with capacity 3
   keys after access(atta) + put(eggs): [rice, atta, eggs]
B. 1,000 concurrent requests for a cold hot key (50 ms DB query)
   naive cache-aside : 1000 DB calls
   single-flight     : 1 DB call(s)
C. XFetch: 10,000 requests/s during the last 10 s of a 300 s TTL (recompute takes 0.2 s)
   at t=290.0s:     0 of 10,000 callers would refresh early
   at t=295.0s:     0 of 10,000 callers would refresh early
   at t=298.0s:     1 of 10,000 callers would refresh early
   at t=299.0s:    64 of 10,000 callers would refresh early
   at t=299.8s: 3,667 of 10,000 callers would refresh early

What L1 shows: LinkedHashMap(accessOrder=true) is a correct LRU in 5 lines. 1,000 concurrent misses mean 1,000 DB calls, unless loads are coalesced (1 call). XFetch makes an early refresh likely just before expiry, and rare before that.

What L1 can't do: it runs in one process, has no invalidation, no versions (so the §2.8 race is possible), and no memory bounds on the single-flight maps under key churn.

package com.grocery.catalog.service;

import com.grocery.catalog.domain.StorePrice;
import com.grocery.catalog.repository.PriceRepository;
import org.springframework.cache.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class PriceServiceL2 {

    private final PriceRepository repo;

    public PriceServiceL2(PriceRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }

    /** sync = true: concurrent misses for the same key IN THIS JVM share one load. Other pods still stampede. */
    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "storePrice", key = "#storeId + ':' + #sku", sync = true)
    public StorePrice price(String storeId, String sku) {
        return repo.find(storeId, sku).orElseThrow(() -> new PriceNotFoundException(storeId, sku));
    }

    /**
     * ⚠️ Two problems:
     *  1. @CacheEvict runs at method exit, which is INSIDE the transaction proxy here → it may evict before COMMIT;
     *     a reader can re-cache the OLD value in between.
     *  2. Even after commit, the §2.8 race (slow reader writes an old value after the delete) remains.
     */
    @Transactional
    @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "storePrice", key = "#storeId + ':' + #sku")
    public void updatePrice(String storeId, String sku, long paise) {
        if (repo.update(storeId, sku, paise) != 1) throw new PriceNotFoundException(storeId, sku);
    }
}

What L2 fixed: 90 % of the benefit with a few annotations: TTL per cache, JSON values, versioned key prefix, and per-JVM single-flight (sync = true).

What L2 still gets wrong:

Problem Consequence at sale scale Stampede across pods 96 pods × 1 load each per hot key on expiry or cold start Evict before commit, and the read/write race Stale prices for up to the TTL (§1.1 bug 3) No L1 Hot keys hammer one Redis shard Writes that bypass the service (bulk SQL, other services) never evict Stale until TTL No protection for the DB when Redis is cold §1.1 bug 1

package com.grocery.catalog.cache;

import org.springframework.data.redis.core.StringRedisTemplate;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.script.DefaultRedisScript;
import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;

/**
 * L2 entries are Redis HASHes: v (SoR version), d (payload) | t=1 (tombstone), e (soft expiry ms), c (compute ms).
 * Writes go through SET_IF_NEWER, so an older version can never overwrite a newer value or tombstone.
 */
public class VersionedRedisCache {

    public record Entry(long version, String payload, boolean tombstone, long softExpiryMs, long computeMs) {
        public boolean isData() { return !tombstone && payload != null; }
    }

    static final DefaultRedisScript<Long> SET_IF_NEWER = new DefaultRedisScript<>("""
            -- KEYS[1]=key  ARGV: 1=version 2=payload 3=ttlMs 4=isTombstone(0/1) 5=softExpiryMs 6=computeMs
            local cur = redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'v')
            if cur then
              local c = tonumber(cur)
              local n = tonumber(ARGV[1])
              if n < c then return 0 end
              if n == c then
                local curTomb = redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 't') == '1'
                -- same version: only real data may replace a tombstone; everything else is a no-op
                if ARGV[4] == '1' or not curTomb then return 0 end
              end
            end
            redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1])
            if ARGV[4] == '1' then
              redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'v', ARGV[1], 't', '1')
            else
              redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'v', ARGV[1], 'd', ARGV[2], 'e', ARGV[5], 'c', ARGV[6])
            end
            redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[3])
            return 1
            """, Long.class);

    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;
    private final Clock clock;

    public VersionedRedisCache(StringRedisTemplate redis, Clock clock) { this.redis = redis; this.clock = clock; }

    public Optional<Entry> get(String key) {
        List<Object> f = redis.opsForHash().multiGet(key, List.of("v", "d", "t", "e", "c"));
        if (f.get(0) == null) return Optional.empty();
        return Optional.of(new Entry(Long.parseLong((String) f.get(0)), (String) f.get(1), "1".equals(f.get(2)),
                f.get(3) == null ? 0 : Long.parseLong((String) f.get(3)),
                f.get(4) == null ? 0 : Long.parseLong((String) f.get(4))));
    }

    /** @return true if stored; false if a newer version (or same-version data) is already there */
    public boolean setIfNewer(String key, long version, String payload, Duration ttl, long computeMs) {
        long jittered = (long) (ttl.toMillis() * (0.9 + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextDouble() * 0.2));
        long softExpiry = clock.millis() + jittered;
        Long r = redis.execute(SET_IF_NEWER, List.of(key), Long.toString(version), payload,
                Long.toString(jittered + 60_000),        // hard TTL a bit longer than soft: allows serve-stale
                "0", Long.toString(softExpiry), Long.toString(computeMs));
        return r != null && r == 1L;
    }

    /** Invalidation: a tombstone at the NEW version blocks slow readers holding older versions. */
    public boolean tombstone(String key, long newVersion) {
        Long r = redis.execute(SET_IF_NEWER, List.of(key), Long.toString(newVersion), "",
                "60000", "1", "0", "0");
        return r != null && r == 1L;
    }
}

package com.grocery.catalog.cache;

import com.github.benmanes.caffeine.cache.*;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.function.Function;

/**
 * get(key):
 *   L1 (Caffeine, per pod, 5 s)  →  L2 (versioned Redis)  →  loader (DB) guarded by a per-pod semaphore.
 * Caffeine.get(key, fn) is atomic per key → single-flight within the pod.
 * XFetch on L2 soft expiry → one early refresh before the key actually expires.
 */
public class TwoLevelCache {

    public record Versioned(long version, String payload) { }

    private final Cache<String, Versioned> l1;
    private final VersionedRedisCache l2;
    private final Semaphore dbPermits;
    private final Duration l2Ttl;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final MeterRegistry metrics;
    private final String name;

    public TwoLevelCache(String name, VersionedRedisCache l2, Duration l1Ttl, long l1MaxEntries, Duration l2Ttl,
                         int maxConcurrentDbLoads, Clock clock, MeterRegistry metrics) {
        this.name = name; this.l2 = l2; this.l2Ttl = l2Ttl; this.clock = clock; this.metrics = metrics;
        this.dbPermits = new Semaphore(maxConcurrentDbLoads);
        this.l1 = Caffeine.newBuilder()
                .expireAfterWrite(l1Ttl)
                .maximumSize(l1MaxEntries)              // W-TinyLFU admission/eviction
                .recordStats()
                .build();
        // VERIFY: CaffeineCacheMetrics.monitor(metrics, l1, name) binds hit/miss/eviction metrics
    }

    public Versioned get(String key, Function<String, Optional<Versioned>> dbLoader) {
        return l1.get(key, k -> fromL2OrDb(k, dbLoader));        // single-flight per pod
    }

    public void invalidateLocal(String key) { l1.invalidate(key); }

    private Versioned fromL2OrDb(String key, Function<String, Optional<Versioned>> dbLoader) {
        Optional<VersionedRedisCache.Entry> e = safeL2Get(key);
        if (e.isPresent() && e.get().isData()) {
            var entry = e.get();
            if (!shouldRefreshEarly(entry)) {
                metrics.counter("cache.l2", "cache", name, "result", "hit").increment();
                return new Versioned(entry.version(), entry.payload());
            }
            metrics.counter("cache.l2", "cache", name, "result", "early_refresh").increment();
            // Unlucky caller refreshes; on failure, serve the still-valid value (stale-while-revalidate)
            try { return loadAndStore(key, dbLoader); }
            catch (RuntimeException ex) { return new Versioned(entry.version(), entry.payload()); }
        }
        metrics.counter("cache.l2", "cache", name, "result", e.isPresent() ? "tombstone" : "miss").increment();
        return loadAndStore(key, dbLoader);
    }

    private Versioned loadAndStore(String key, Function<String, Optional<Versioned>> dbLoader) {
        boolean acquired;
        try { acquired = dbPermits.tryAcquire(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); }
        catch (InterruptedException ie) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw new CacheLoadRejectedException(name); }
        if (!acquired) {                                          // DB guard: shed instead of piling on
            metrics.counter("cache.load.rejected", "cache", name).increment();
            throw new CacheLoadRejectedException(name);
        }
        try {
            long t0 = clock.millis();
            Versioned v = dbLoader.apply(key).orElseThrow(() -> new CacheMissNotFoundException(key));
            long computeMs = Math.max(1, clock.millis() - t0);
            boolean stored = safeL2Set(key, v, computeMs);
            if (!stored) metrics.counter("cache.l2.set_rejected_stale", "cache", name).increment();
            return v;
        } finally {
            dbPermits.release();
        }
    }

    /** XFetch: now - δ·β·ln(rand) ≥ expiry, with δ = last compute time, β = 1. */
    boolean shouldRefreshEarly(VersionedRedisCache.Entry e) {
        if (e.softExpiryMs() == 0) return false;
        double r = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextDouble();
        return clock.millis() - e.computeMs() * Math.log(r) >= e.softExpiryMs();
    }

    private Optional<VersionedRedisCache.Entry> safeL2Get(String key) {
        try { return l2.get(key); }
        catch (RuntimeException redisDown) {                     // Redis outage → behave as a miss (guarded by the semaphore)
            metrics.counter("cache.l2.errors", "cache", name).increment();
            return Optional.empty();
        }
    }

    private boolean safeL2Set(String key, Versioned v, long computeMs) {
        try { return l2.setIfNewer(key, v.version(), v.payload(), l2Ttl, computeMs); }
        catch (RuntimeException redisDown) { metrics.counter("cache.l2.errors", "cache", name).increment(); return false; }
    }

    public static class CacheLoadRejectedException extends RuntimeException {
        public CacheLoadRejectedException(String cache) { super("load shed for cache " + cache, null, false, false); }
    }
    public static class CacheMissNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
        public CacheMissNotFoundException(String key) { super("not found: " + key); }
    }
}

Why computeMs goes into the entry

XFetch refreshes slower-to-compute keys earlier. Storing the last compute time with the value lets every pod make the same probabilistic decision with no coordination.

package com.grocery.catalog.service;

import com.grocery.catalog.cache.TwoLevelCache;

@Service
public class PriceService {

    private final TwoLevelCache cache;
    private final PriceRepository repo;

    public PriceService(TwoLevelCache priceCache, PriceRepository repo) { this.cache = priceCache; this.repo = repo; }

    /** Display price (cached). Checkout must call PricingClient for the authoritative price (Ch 01 principle). */
    public long displayPricePaise(String storeId, String sku) {
        Versioned v = cache.get(key(storeId, sku), k -> repo.find(storeId, sku)
                .map(p -> new Versioned(p.version(), Long.toString(p.paise()))));
        return Long.parseLong(v.payload());
    }

    static String key(String storeId, String sku) { return "v1:price:" + storeId + ":" + sku; }
}
