import com.grocery.catalog.cache.TwoLevelCache;
import com.grocery.catalog.service.PriceService;
import org.springframework.http.*;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
public class PriceController {

    private final PriceService prices;   // (a delegate composing card + price sits here in the full service)

    public PriceController(PriceService prices) { this.prices = prices; }

    @GetMapping("/api/v1/stores/{storeId}/products/{sku}/price")
    public ResponseEntity<PriceView> price(@PathVariable String storeId, @PathVariable String sku) {
        long paise = prices.displayPricePaise(storeId, sku);
        return ResponseEntity.ok()
                .cacheControl(CacheControl.noStore())             // per-store price: don't cache at shared edges
                .body(new PriceView(storeId, sku, paise, "INR"));
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(TwoLevelCache.CacheLoadRejectedException.class)
    ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> shed(TwoLevelCache.CacheLoadRejectedException e) {
        var pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, "Busy, please retry");
        pd.setProperty("code", "CATALOG_BUSY");
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE).header(HttpHeaders.RETRY_AFTER, "1").body(pd);
    }

    public record PriceView(String storeId, String sku, long pricePaise, String currency) { }

package com.grocery.catalog.cache;

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.simple.SimpleMeterRegistry;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
import org.springframework.data.redis.connection.lettuce.LettuceConnectionFactory;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.StringRedisTemplate;
import org.testcontainers.containers.GenericContainer;

@Testcontainers
class TwoLevelCacheIT {

    @Container static GenericContainer<?> redis = new GenericContainer<>("redis:7-alpine").withExposedPorts(6379);

    StringRedisTemplate template;
    VersionedRedisCache l2;
    final Clock clock = Clock.systemUTC();

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        var cf = new LettuceConnectionFactory(redis.getHost(), redis.getMappedPort(6379));
        cf.afterPropertiesSet();
        template = new StringRedisTemplate(cf);
        template.afterPropertiesSet();
        template.getConnectionFactory().getConnection().serverCommands().flushAll();   // test isolation only!
        l2 = new VersionedRedisCache(template, clock);
    }

    private TwoLevelCache pod() {
        return new TwoLevelCache("t", l2, Duration.ofSeconds(5), 1000, Duration.ofMinutes(10), 16, clock, new SimpleMeterRegistry());
    }

    @Test
    void slowReaderCannotOverwriteNewerVersion() {
        assertThat(l2.tombstone("k", 9)).isTrue();                                  // price changed to v9
        assertThat(l2.setIfNewer("k", 8, "4000", Duration.ofMinutes(10), 5)).isFalse();   // slow reader with v8
        assertThat(l2.setIfNewer("k", 9, "100", Duration.ofMinutes(10), 5)).isTrue();     // fresh reader with v9
        assertThat(l2.tombstone("k", 9)).isFalse();                                  // late duplicate invalidation
        assertThat(l2.get("k")).get().satisfies(e -> {
            assertThat(e.isData()).isTrue();
            assertThat(e.payload()).isEqualTo("100");
        });
    }

    @Test
    void twoPodsAndTwoHundredConcurrentMissesLoadAtMostTwice() throws Exception {
        AtomicInteger dbLoads = new AtomicInteger();
        var podA = pod();
        var podB = pod();
        java.util.function.Function<String, Optional<TwoLevelCache.Versioned>> loader = k -> {
            dbLoads.incrementAndGet();
            try { Thread.sleep(100); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
            return Optional.of(new TwoLevelCache.Versioned(1, "4000"));
        };
        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1);
            for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) {
                var p = (i % 2 == 0) ? podA : podB;
                pool.submit(() -> { go.await(); return p.get("hot", loader); });
            }
            go.countDown();
        }
        assertThat(dbLoads.get()).isLessThanOrEqualTo(2);      // one per pod at most
    }

    @Test
    void redisDownFallsBackToDbWithinPermits() {
        var cf = new LettuceConnectionFactory("localhost", 1);            // nothing listens on port 1
        cf.afterPropertiesSet();
        var tpl = new StringRedisTemplate(cf);
        tpl.afterPropertiesSet();
        var broken = new VersionedRedisCache(tpl, clock);
        var cache = new TwoLevelCache("t", broken, Duration.ofSeconds(5), 1000, Duration.ofMinutes(10), 16, clock, new SimpleMeterRegistry());
        var v = cache.get("k", k -> Optional.of(new TwoLevelCache.Versioned(1, "4000")));
        assertThat(v.payload()).isEqualTo("4000");             // served from DB, cached in L1
    }
}

What L3 guarantees: an older version can never overwrite a newer one (all five race cases are covered by tests and match the verified semantics), there's at most one DB load per key per pod at a time, early refresh keeps hot keys from expiring under load, and the DB is protected by a per-pod permit budget when Redis is cold or down.

What L3 still lacks: who writes the tombstones, and how do the other pods' L1 caches and the CDN find out about a change? There's also no hot-key spreading across Redis shards and no warm-up before the sale.

package com.grocery.catalog.invalidation;

public record PriceChanged(String storeId, String sku, long version) { }

package com.grocery.catalog.invalidation;

import com.grocery.catalog.cache.*;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import org.springframework.kafka.annotation.KafkaListener;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import java.time.*;

/** One consumer group for the whole fleet: writes version tombstones (idempotent) and purges the CDN. */
@Component
public class CacheInvalidator {

    private final VersionedRedisCache l2;
    private final HotKeys hotKeys;
    private final CdnPurger cdn;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final MeterRegistry metrics;

    public CacheInvalidator(VersionedRedisCache l2, HotKeys hotKeys, CdnPurger cdn, Clock clock, MeterRegistry metrics) {
        this.l2 = l2; this.hotKeys = hotKeys; this.cdn = cdn; this.clock = clock; this.metrics = metrics;
    }

    @KafkaListener(topics = "pricing.price.changed.v1", groupId = "cache-invalidator")
    public void onPriceChanged(PriceChanged e) {
        String key = "v1:price:" + e.storeId() + ":" + e.sku();
        l2.tombstone(key, e.version());                             // inside-out: L2 first ...
        for (String replica : hotKeys.replicasOf(key)) l2.tombstone(replica, e.version());
        cdn.purgeSurrogateKey("sku-" + e.sku());                    // ... then the edge
        metrics.counter("cache.invalidations", "type", "price").increment();
    }
}

package com.grocery.catalog.invalidation;

import com.grocery.catalog.cache.TwoLevelCache;
import org.springframework.kafka.annotation.KafkaListener;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

/** Unique group per pod → every pod receives every change → evicts its own L1. (Same pattern as Ch 01.) */
@Component
public class L1Broadcaster {

    private final TwoLevelCache priceCache;

    public L1Broadcaster(TwoLevelCache priceCache) { this.priceCache = priceCache; }

    @KafkaListener(topics = "pricing.price.changed.v1", groupId = "catalog-l1-${HOSTNAME:local}",
                   properties = "auto.offset.reset=latest")
    public void onPriceChanged(PriceChanged e) {
        priceCache.invalidateLocal("v1:price:" + e.storeId() + ":" + e.sku());
    }
}

Order of L1 and L2 invalidation

If a pod evicts L1 before the invalidator has written the L2 tombstone, the next L1 miss can re-read the old L2 value and cache it for up to 5 s. That's acceptable here (it's the L1 TTL bound). To tighten it, have the invalidator publish a secondary cache.invalidated event after writing L2, and drive L1 eviction from that.

package com.grocery.catalog.cache;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/**
 * Hot keys (sale SKUs) get N replicas with different names → different hash slots → different Redis shards.
 * Reads pick a random replica; invalidations tombstone all replicas.
 */
public class HotKeys {

    private final Set<String> hot;          // loaded from the sale plan (and/or live hot-key detection)
    private final int replicas;

    public HotKeys(Set<String> hotKeys, int replicas) { this.hot = Set.copyOf(hotKeys); this.replicas = replicas; }

    public String readKey(String key) {
        return hot.contains(key) ? key + "#" + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(replicas) : key;
    }

    public List<String> replicasOf(String key) {
        return hot.contains(key) ? IntStream.range(0, replicas).mapToObj(i -> key + "#" + i).toList() : List.of();
    }

    public boolean isHot(String key) { return hot.contains(key); }
}

The two-level cache uses hotKeys.readKey(key) for L2 reads and writes all replicas on a fill (each with setIfNewer, so replicas can't go backwards either). With L1 in front, each pod reads a hot key from Redis at most about once per 5 s, so replication matters most when L1 is cold (deploys, scale-out).

package com.grocery.catalog.controller;

import org.springframework.http.*;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;

@RestController
public class CategoryListingController {

    /** Anonymous, store-cluster-level listing: cacheable at the edge for 30 s, served stale up to 60 s while revalidating. */
    @GetMapping("/api/v1/clusters/{clusterId}/categories/{categoryId}/products")
    public ResponseEntity<List<ProductTile>> listing(@PathVariable String clusterId, @PathVariable String categoryId) {
        List<ProductTile> tiles = List.of();    // … built from the two-level caches
        String surrogateKeys = "category-" + categoryId + " " +
                String.join(" ", tiles.stream().map(t -> "sku-" + t.sku()).toList());
        return ResponseEntity.ok()
                .cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ZERO)                   // browsers: revalidate
                        .sMaxAge(Duration.ofSeconds(30))                            // shared caches: 30 s
                        .staleWhileRevalidate(Duration.ofSeconds(60)))
                .header("Surrogate-Key", surrogateKeys)                             // Fastly; Cloudflare uses Cache-Tag
                .body(tiles);
    }

    public record ProductTile(String sku, String name, long pricePaise, String imageUrl) { }
}

package com.grocery.catalog.invalidation;

import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;

/** Thin adapter over the CDN's purge API (provider-specific: surrogate keys / cache tags). */
public class CdnPurger {
    private final RestClient cdn;
    public CdnPurger(RestClient cdnApiClient) { this.cdn = cdnApiClient; }

    public void purgeSurrogateKey(String key) {
        // VERIFY: exact endpoint, auth and soft-purge option for your CDN provider
        cdn.post().uri("/service/{serviceId}/purge/{key}", "catalog", key).retrieve().toBodilessEntity();
    }
}

Surrogate keys beat URL purges

One price change affects hundreds of listing URLs (every category page and search result containing the SKU). Tag responses with sku-… keys and purge the tag once, instead of enumerating URLs.

package com.grocery.catalog.warmup;

import com.grocery.catalog.service.PriceService;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

/**
 * Loads sale SKUs × stores into L2 at T−30 min, throttled so warming itself can't overload the DB.
 * Run as a one-off job (Kubernetes Job) from the event plan (Ch 02).
 */
public class SaleCacheWarmer {

    public record Target(String storeId, String sku) { }

    private final PriceService prices;
    private final MeterRegistry metrics;

    public SaleCacheWarmer(PriceService prices, MeterRegistry metrics) { this.prices = prices; this.metrics = metrics; }

    public void warm(List<Target> targets, int perSecond) throws InterruptedException {
        long intervalNanos = 1_000_000_000L / perSecond;
        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            long next = System.nanoTime();
            for (Target t : targets) {
                long wait = next - System.nanoTime();
                if (wait > 0) TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.sleep(wait);
                next += intervalNanos;
                pool.submit(() -> {
                    try { prices.displayPricePaise(t.storeId(), t.sku()); metrics.counter("cache.warm", "result", "ok").increment(); }
                    catch (RuntimeException e) { metrics.counter("cache.warm", "result", "error").increment(); }
                });
            }
        }
    }
}
Warming math Targets 500 sale SKUs × 500 stores = 250 K price keys + 500 cards Rate 2,000/s (well below the DB budget of 10 K/s) → ~2 minutes TTL jitter ± 10 % on a 10 min soft TTL, plus XFetch, so there's no synchronized expiry at 20:00 
package com.grocery.catalog.cache;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import java.util.*;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class HotKeysTest {

    @Test
    void hotKeysSpreadAcrossReplicas_coldKeysUnchanged() {
        var hot = new HotKeys(Set.of("v1:price:S1:ONION"), 8);
        Map<String, Integer> hits = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 8_000; i++) hits.merge(hot.readKey("v1:price:S1:ONION"), 1, Integer::sum);

        assertThat(hits).hasSize(8);                                                 // all replicas used
        assertThat(hits.values()).allSatisfy(n -> assertThat(n).isBetween(800, 1200)); // roughly even
        assertThat(hot.readKey("v1:price:S1:MILK")).isEqualTo("v1:price:S1:MILK");
        assertThat(hot.replicasOf("v1:price:S1:ONION")).hasSize(8);
    }
}

An end-to-end test (Testcontainers Kafka + Redis + two app contexts as "pods") publishes pricing.price.changed.v1 with version 9. It asserts that L2 holds a v9 tombstone within 1 s, both pods' L1 no longer return v8, and the next read on each pod returns the new price from the DB.

ADR-029/030: Versioned cache writes; event-driven invalidation; no flushes

Context. A cache flush at sale start caused a DB meltdown, L1 caches served stale prices across pods, and a read/write race pinned a stale price for hours (§1.1).

Decision. (1) Every L2 value carries the SoR version, and writes use set-if-newer (Lua). Invalidations write version tombstones. (2) The SoR publishes change events via outbox. A fleet-wide invalidator writes the tombstones (including hot-key replicas) and purges the CDN by surrogate key, and per-pod consumers evict L1. (3) L1 TTL is ≤ 5 s for mutable data. L2 soft TTLs have ± 10 % jitter, with XFetch early refresh and serve-stale on refresh failure. (4) DB loads per pod are capped by a semaphore, and excess is shed with 503 + Retry-After. (5) Known events are pre-warmed from the event plan. FLUSHALL/FLUSHDB are prohibited in production (Redis ACL). (6) Caches serve displays only. Checkout, stock and payment read the SoR.

Consequences. (+) Staleness ≤ ~1–5 s after a change, with no stale-forever values. (+) Cold or lost Redis doesn't take down the DB. (−) Lua scripts, invalidation events and per-pod consumers to operate. (−) Invalidation depends on outbox events: bulk SQL that bypasses the outbox must publish events too, and that's enforced by pricing owning all writes.

Revisit when: invalidation lag or volume grows (consider CDC-driven cache population), or client-side caching with Redis tracking becomes attractive for L1.

Track request-weighted hit ratio, not key-count Origin loads/s from cache misses What the DB actually experiences Load latency (p50/p99) Slow loads enlarge stampede windows Single-flight waiters / permits exhausted (cache.load.rejected) Stampede pressure; shedding in effect cache.l2.set_rejected_stale Races caught by versioning. A non-zero count is expected; a spike means slow readers Invalidation lag (change committed → tombstone written → L1 evicted) Freshness SLO Evictions, memory, keyspace size Capacity Per-shard ops/s and latency Hot keys CDN hit ratio, purge count and latency, origin fetches Edge effectiveness Sampled consistency check (cached version vs SoR version) Detects silent staleness

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Never cache personalized responses at shared layers (CDN/gateway) unless the cache key includes the user or the response is truly public. Cache-Control: private/no-store is the default for authenticated responses. A single misconfigured public header can serve one user's cart or address to others.
  • Cache keys must include every input that changes the response (store, language, app version, experiment bucket) or users see each other's variants.
  • Web cache poisoning: unkeyed headers (X-Forwarded-Host) reflected into cached responses. Normalize and validate at the edge.
  • Sensitive data in Redis: avoid PII where possible, use TLS and ACLs, and set TTLs on everything. Remember that Redis snapshots and replicas copy data too.
  • Prohibit dangerous commands (FLUSHALL, FLUSHDB, KEYS, CONFIG) for application users via Redis ACLs.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance & tuning knobs
docs.text: Knob Starting point Guidance L1 TTL (mutable data) 1–5 s Bounds cross-pod staleness if broadcasts are missed L1 size Working set of hot keys (10–50 K) Watch heap and GC; Caffeine W-TinyLFU L2 soft TTL Minutes to hours, ± 10 % jitter Safety net; events do the freshness L2 hard TTL Soft + margin Allows serve-stale during refresh failures XFetch β 1.0 Higher means earlier refreshes DB permits per pod DB budget ÷ pods Little's Law (Ch 02) Negative-cache TTL 30–60 s Long enough to absorb abuse, short enough for new products Hot-key replicas 4–16 Number of shards to spread over Tombstone TTL ≥ the longest plausible slow-reader delay (60 s) Too short brings back the race CDN s-maxage 30–300 s + stale-while-revalidate Surrogate keys for purges

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• A cache is memory traded for origin capacity and latency. At 98 % hit ratio, the catalog DB serves ~4 K/s instead of 190 K/s, which is the difference between one modest cluster and a heavily sharded one.
  • Right-size by the working set, not the whole dataset. A 500 MB card set plus 240 MB of prices in Redis costs far less than the DB capacity it replaces.
  • CDN egress is often the largest line item. Cache images aggressively, with versioned immutable URLs and modern formats (WebP/AVIF).
  • Every cache layer adds operational cost: invalidation paths, metrics, runbooks. Add a layer only when the estimate shows it's needed (Ch 02).

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Flushing the cache to "refresh" data. Symptom: A stampede at the worst possible moment (§1.1). Fix: Event-driven invalidation of the changed keys, and warming before events. Block FLUSH* via ACLs.

2. Updating the cache on write instead of deleting (or versioning).

// ❌ before: two concurrent writers can leave the OLDER value in the cache
repo.update(price);  redis.set(key, price);

// ✅ after: version tombstone; readers repopulate with set-if-newer
repo.update(price);  /* outbox event → invalidator → */ l2.tombstone(key, newVersion);

3. Evicting before commit. Symptom: A reader re-caches the old value between the evict and the commit. Fix: Invalidate after commit, via an outbox event or a TransactionSynchronization.afterCommit hook, plus versioning.

4. No stampede protection.

// ❌ before: every concurrent miss hits the DB
String v = redis.get(k); if (v == null) { v = db.load(k); redis.set(k, v); }

// ✅ after: per-pod single-flight + early refresh + DB permits (L3)
return twoLevelCache.get(k, loader);

5. Same TTL for everything, with no jitter. Synchronized expiry means an avalanche.

6. Caching negative results forever, or never. Symptom: A product added later "doesn't exist" for hours, or bots probing random SKUs hammer the DB. Fix: Negative cache with a short TTL, plus an id validation or Bloom filter.

7. Caching decisions, not displays. Symptom: Checkout charges a cached price, or allows a reservation based on a cached stock badge. Fix: Caches for display, the SoR for decisions (§2.12).

8. Shared-edge caching of personalized responses.

# ❌ before: public caching of a response that contains the user's address
Cache-Control: public, max-age=60

# ✅ after
Cache-Control: private, no-store

9. Unversioned cache keys across deploys. Symptom: Deserialization errors or wrong fields after a payload change during a rolling deploy. Fix: A cache schema prefix (v1: → v2:), with old keys expiring naturally.

10. "Just add a cache" to hide a slow query. Symptom: The cache hides an N+1 or a missing index until the first cold start takes the DB down. Fix: Make the origin query fast (Ch 05) first. The cache is for scale, not for fixing bad queries.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What is caching, and how do you measure whether it's working?

30-second answer: Keeping copies of frequently read data in faster storage closer to the reader, to cut latency and origin load. Measure it by hit ratio (request-weighted), origin load from misses, latency per layer, and freshness (how stale served data can be).

Deep answer: Origin load = (1 − h) × request rate, so going from 90 % to 98 % hits cuts origin load 5×. That also means the origin is sized for misses: losing the cache multiplies the load. Caching changes your availability model.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Latency and cost vs staleness and complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. Why request-weighted hit ratio? → A few hot keys dominate traffic. 2. What's a good hit ratio? → It depends on the data. 95–99 % for catalog-like data.

Red flags: No mention of staleness or invalidation.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Calls the cache a load-bearing dependency and plans for its loss.

Q2 [B1] Where can you cache in a web system?

30-second answer: Client (browser or app), CDN edge, gateway or BFF, in-process in the service (L1), distributed cache (L2, Redis), and the database's own buffer cache. Closer layers are faster but harder to invalidate.

Deep answer: Use the CDN for static and anonymous content with surrogate-key purges, L1 for hot, small, read-mostly data with short TTLs, and L2 for shared state and computed views. Invalidate inside-out.

Trade-offs: Latency vs invalidation difficulty.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not cache everything at the CDN? → Personalization and invalidation. 2. Why have L1 if you have Redis? → Hot keys, and to save the network hop.

Red flags: Only mentioning Redis.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Assigns data to layers by staleness and personalization.

Q3 [B1] LRU vs LFU: which and when?

30-second answer: LRU evicts the least recently used item, which suits recency-driven access but is vulnerable to one-off scans. LFU evicts the least frequently used, which suits stable popularity but adapts slowly. Caffeine's W-TinyLFU combines both and is the best default on the JVM.

Deep answer: For Redis, use allkeys-lfu for popularity-skewed catalogs and allkeys-lru otherwise. Measure hit ratios in production.

Trade-offs: Adaptivity vs scan resistance.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you implement LRU in Java? → LinkedHashMap with access order + removeEldestEntry (L1). 2. What's TTI? → Time-to-idle: expire after a period without access.

Red flags: Not knowing any eviction policy.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Mentions scan pollution and W-TinyLFU.

Q4 [B1] How do you choose a TTL?

30-second answer: From the staleness contract, meaning how stale this data may be for its readers, and whether events invalidate it. With event-driven invalidation, the TTL is a safety net (longer). Without it, the TTL is the freshness bound (shorter). Always add jitter.

Deep answer: Different data needs different TTLs: content (hours), prices (minutes plus events), stock badges (seconds), serviceability (a snapshot with measured age, Ch 01).

Trade-offs: Freshness vs hit ratio and origin load.

Follow-ups: 1. Why jitter? → To avoid synchronized expiry (an avalanche). 2. Should money-related values rely on TTLs? → No. Decisions read the SoR.

Red flags: "One hour for everything."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: A staleness contract per data type.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ Cache-aside vs read-through vs write-through vs write-behind?

30-second answer: Cache-aside: the app loads on a miss and deletes on write. It's simple and common. Read-through: the cache library loads on a miss (enables single-flight). Write-through: write the cache and DB together. Reads are always warm, but writes are slower and cache unread data. Write-behind: write the cache, flush to the DB later. Very fast, but risks data loss, so never for money.

Deep answer: Most systems use cache-aside or read-through for reads plus event-driven invalidation for writes. Refresh-ahead keeps known hot keys warm. Pick per data type.

Trade-offs: Freshness, write latency, durability.

Follow-ups: 1. Why delete instead of update on write? → Concurrent writers can leave older values. 2. Where would you use write-behind? → View counters or analytics aggregates.

Red flags: Write-behind for orders.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Combines patterns per data class, with invalidation as a separate concern.

Q6 [B2] ⭐ What is a cache stampede, and how do you prevent it?

30-second answer: Many concurrent misses on the same key (expiry, flush, cold start) all hit the origin at once. Prevent it with single-flight (coalescing), probabilistic early refresh (XFetch), stale-while-revalidate, TTL jitter, warming, distributed locks for the hottest keys, and origin protection (permits and shedding).

Deep answer: Naive: 1,000 misses mean 1,000 DB calls. Single-flight: 1 per process. XFetch spreads refreshes before expiry with no coordination. Also protect against a cold Redis with per-pod DB permits.

Trade-offs: Serving slightly stale values vs origin safety.

Follow-ups: 1. Does Spring's sync = true solve it? → Only within one JVM. 2. Distributed lock drawbacks? → Latency, lock expiry, and the need for a fallback.

Red flags: "Increase the TTL."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: A layered defence plus origin protection.

Q7 [B2] ⭐ How do you keep a cache consistent with the database on updates?

30-second answer: Write the DB (the SoR), then invalidate the cache after commit, ideally from a change event (outbox or CDC) so no update is missed. Readers repopulate on a miss. Protect against the reader/writer race with versioned conditional sets or leases. Bound the worst case with TTLs, and don't use caches for decisions.

Deep answer: Invalidate inside-out: L2, then L1 on every pod (broadcast), then the CDN (surrogate keys). Bulk updates must publish events too.

Trade-offs: Freshness vs complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not a distributed transaction across DB and cache? → Too costly and fragile. Eventual consistency with bounds is the norm. 2. How fast is "fresh"? → Measure invalidation lag against the SLO.

Red flags: "Update both in the same method."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: After-commit events, version guards and a layered order.

Q8 [B2] What are the pitfalls of Spring's @Cacheable?

30-second answer: Self-invocation bypasses the proxy. @CacheEvict may run before the transaction commits. There's no versioning, so the race remains. sync = true only coalesces within one JVM. Default serialization is fragile. Null handling needs to be deliberate. Keys need namespacing and versioning, and there's no multi-level coordination.

Deep answer: Use it for simple, low-risk data. For critical data (prices), write an explicit cache component with versioning, metrics and stampede control (L3).

Trade-offs: Convenience vs control.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you evict after commit? → A transactional event listener (@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT)). 2. How do you namespace? → computePrefixWith + a schema version.

Red flags: Annotating private methods.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Knows when to leave the abstraction.

Q9 [B2] How do HTTP caching and CDNs work for APIs?

30-second answer: Cache-Control (max-age for browsers, s-maxage for shared caches, stale-while-revalidate, private/no-store), validators (ETag/If-None-Match → 304), Vary for request-dependent variants, and CDN purges by URL or surrogate key.

Deep answer: Cache anonymous, cluster-level listings at the edge for ~30 s with surrogate-key purges. Never cache personalized responses publicly. Use versioned immutable URLs for images (max-age=31536000, immutable).

Trade-offs: Edge offload vs freshness and personalization.

Follow-ups: 1. What does Vary: Accept-Encoding do? → Separate cache entries per encoding. 2. What's a surrogate key? → A tag attached to responses for group purges.

Red flags: public on authenticated responses.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Surrogate keys and web cache poisoning awareness.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ Explain the cache-aside race condition and how you'd fix it.

30-second answer: A reader misses and loads the old value from the DB. A writer updates the DB and deletes the cache key. The reader then writes the old value into the cache, where it stays until the TTL. Fix it with versioned conditional writes: store the SoR version and accept a set only if its version ≥ the stored one, with invalidation writing a tombstone at the new version. Alternatives are leases, CDC-only cache population, or short TTLs as mitigation.

Deep answer: The version comes from the row's version column. The tombstone blocks older writers, and same-version data may replace a tombstone. The tombstone TTL must exceed plausible reader delays. I'd test all interleavings (§5 L3 tests).

Trade-offs: Lua scripts and a version column vs stale-forever risk.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not delayed double delete? → It's timing-based, and so doesn't fully close the race. 2. What are memcache leases? → A token issued on a miss, invalidated by deletes, required for the set.

Red flags: Not knowing the race exists.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Precise interleaving plus a tested fix.

Q11 [B3] ⭐ How do you handle a hot key in Redis?

30-second answer: Detect it (per-shard metrics, --hotkeys, client-side sampling). Absorb repeated reads with an in-process L1 cache. Replicate the key under several names on different shards and read a random replica. For writes, shard counters or batch updates. Pre-identify hot keys for known events.

Deep answer: Replicas must all be invalidated (tombstones per replica). L1 TTLs bound staleness. CDN or pre-rendered pages help for landing-page hot content.

Trade-offs: Invalidation fan-out vs load spreading.

Follow-ups: 1. Can Redis replicas serve reads? → Yes (READONLY in cluster mode), with replication lag. 2. Hot write key? → Sharded counters merged on read.

Red flags: "Buy a bigger Redis."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: L1 + replication + event planning.

Q12 [B3] How do you keep in-process (L1) caches consistent across 50 pods?

30-second answer: Short TTLs bound staleness. Broadcast invalidation reaches every pod (Kafka with a unique group per pod, or Redis Pub/Sub), and the L2-first ordering makes L1 refills read fresh data. Or use Redis client-side caching (tracking), which pushes invalidations.

Deep answer: Accept an L1 staleness contract of ≤ TTL. Make broadcasts idempotent. Handle pod restarts (L1 is cold, so no stale data). Monitor invalidation lag.

Trade-offs: Freshness vs complexity and broadcast volume.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not Pub/Sub only? → It's fire-and-forget, so a disconnected pod misses messages. The TTL covers it. 2. When should you skip L1? → For data needing strong freshness.

Red flags: 1-hour L1 TTLs on prices.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Ordering awareness (L2 before L1) and TTL bounds.

Q13 [B3] What are cache penetration and cache avalanche, and how do you defend against them?

30-second answer: Penetration: requests for keys that don't exist always miss and hit the origin (bots, bad ids). Defend with negative caching (short TTL), Bloom filters of valid ids, validation and rate limits. Avalanche: many keys expire or the cache fails at once. Defend with TTL jitter, warming, multi-level caches, origin protection, and staggered restarts.

Deep answer: Negative caching must be short and invalidated on creation (new product), or new items look missing. Bloom filters need rebuilds as ids change.

Trade-offs: Memory for the filters vs origin protection.

Follow-ups: 1. Bloom false positives? → Some misses still reach the origin, which is acceptable. 2. Avalanche from a Redis restart? → Warm, and limit origin concurrency.

Red flags: Only knowing stampedes.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Maps each failure to a specific defence.

Q14 [B3] ⭐ Redis goes down during peak. What happens in your design?

30-second answer: L1 keeps serving hot keys for its TTL. Misses go to the DB through per-pod single-flight, capped by a permit budget, and excess requests get a fast 503 with Retry-After (low-priority traffic first) rather than piling onto the DB. Once Redis recovers, it warms gradually. Decisions (checkout) never depended on Redis.

Deep answer: Sizing: permits per pod × pods ≤ the DB budget (Ch 02). Circuit-break Redis calls so timeouts don't add latency. Alerts page. Post-incident, verify the hit ratio recovers without a second stampede.

Trade-offs: Some shed traffic vs a total outage.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not just fall back to the DB fully? → 50× load collapses it. 2. How do you test this? → Game days that kill Redis under load (Ch 27).

Red flags: "The DB will handle it."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Quantified permits and graceful degradation.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design caching for a product catalog serving 190 K req/s at sale start.

30-second answer: CDN for images and anonymous listings (surrogate keys). A Caffeine L1 per pod (hot 10–50 K keys, 5 s TTL, single-flight). Redis L2 with versioned values, XFetch, TTL jitter, and hot-key replicas for sale SKUs. Outbox-driven invalidation (L2 tombstones, L1 broadcast, CDN purge). Pre-sale warming. DB permits and shedding. Checkout re-prices from the SoR.

Deep answer: Estimate the hit ratio per layer and the DB load in steady state and in the cold case (the dangerous one). Define staleness SLOs (≤ 5 s price visibility). Observability: hit ratios, invalidation lag, stale-set rejections. Plan the game day.

Trade-offs: Complexity vs a guaranteed peak.

Follow-ups: 1. What if marketing changes 250 K prices at 7:59? → Bulk events, invalidation throughput, maybe versioned price-list switching (a new price-list id, atomically switched). 2. Why not cache stock? → Displays get a 10 s badge. Reservations are exact.

Red flags: A single Redis with a 1-hour TTL.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Designs for the cold and invalidation-storm cases, not just steady state.

Q16 [B4] How do you define what may be cached and for how long across a platform?

30-second answer: Publish staleness contracts per data class: display data (content, prices, badges) may be cached with bounded staleness and event invalidation, while decision data (checkout price, stock, payment, authorization) always reads the SoR. Standardize libraries (a two-level cache component with versioning and metrics), key conventions, and security rules (no personalized public caching).

Deep answer: Review new caches against the contracts. Monitor freshness SLOs. Run periodic sampling that compares cached vs SoR versions. Record exceptions in ADRs.

Trade-offs: Governance overhead vs correctness incidents.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you enforce it? → Code review checklists, shared libraries, architecture tests. 2. Example exception? → Serviceability snapshot for browse (Ch 01).

Red flags: Ad-hoc caching per team.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: A "display vs decide" rule plus measurement.

Q17 [B4] Your cache is now critical to availability. How do you reason about that risk?

30-second answer: If the origin can't serve the uncached load, the cache is a hard dependency, and its availability multiplies with the service's. Mitigate with a highly available cache (replicas, multi-AZ), L1 as a second layer, origin protection (permits, shedding) so cache loss degrades rather than fails, capacity to rebuild (warming), and game days.

Deep answer: Quantify it: at 98 % hit ratio the origin sees 50× load without the cache. Decide what fraction of traffic you must still serve (tier-1 journeys) and size the origin for that, with shedding for the rest.

Trade-offs: Origin over-provisioning vs degradation during cache loss.

Follow-ups: 1. Should you size the DB for full uncached load? → Usually not. Size for the protected tier-1 subset. 2. Multi-AZ Redis? → Yes, with failover testing.

Red flags: Treating the cache as optional while depending on it.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: An explicit degraded-mode design.

Q18 [B4] When is adding a cache the wrong answer?

30-second answer: When the origin query is slow because of a fixable problem (missing index, N+1), when the data changes faster than it's read (low hit ratio), when correctness requires the latest value (decisions), when the working set is too large or too uniformly accessed to get good hits, or when the invalidation complexity outweighs the gains.

Deep answer: Fix the origin first (Ch 05). Use read replicas or read models (Ch 15) for heavy read patterns with freshness needs, and precompute for predictable heavy views.

Trade-offs: Speed of adding a cache vs long-term complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. Low hit ratio example? → Per-user personalized feeds with little reuse. 2. Alternative? → Materialized views or projections.

Red flags: "Cache it" as a reflex.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Weighs the invalidation cost and fixes the root cause first.

Q19 [B4] How do deploys, scale-outs and cache node replacements affect caching, and how do you plan for them?

30-second answer: Deploys and scale-outs create cold L1s (a miss spike to L2). Cache node replacement or reshard creates cold L2 slots (a miss spike to the DB). Payload changes need versioned keys. Plan with rolling deploys (few pods cold at once), L2 warm for L1, pre-warming for known events, key-prefix versioning, and slot migrations that preserve data (Redis Cluster resharding moves keys).

Deep answer: Watch origin load during deploys, and use canaries with cache metrics. Schedule large cache changes outside peaks, and freeze them around events (Ch 02).

Trade-offs: Deployment speed vs miss spikes.

Follow-ups: 1. Blue/green with caches? → The new stack's L1 is cold, so warm before switching traffic. 2. Payload schema change? → v2: prefix, and let v1: expire.

Red flags: Deploying 100 % of pods at once during peak.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Treats cold starts as a first-class scenario.

Q20 [B4] App-managed caching vs CDC-driven cache population: which would you choose?

30-second answer: App-managed (cache-aside + events) is simpler, caches only what's read, and handles misses immediately, but needs race protection. CDC-driven (a consumer applies DB changes to the cache in commit order) removes app write paths and races, but must populate everything (or on demand), adds pipeline dependency and lag, and complicates misses.

Deep answer: A hybrid is common: cache-aside for reads, CDC or outbox events for invalidation (tombstones), which is what L4 does. Choose full CDC population for small, fully-cached datasets (config, price lists per store) where commit ordering matters most.

Trade-offs: Simplicity vs ordering guarantees.

Follow-ups: 1. What if CDC lags? → Readers see stale data up to the lag. Monitor it. 2. What about deletes? → CDC delete events become tombstones.

Red flags: Choosing CDC without considering miss handling.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Picks per dataset size and ordering needs.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. A cache is a copy with a lifetime and a staleness contract. Define the contract per data type.
  2. The origin is sized for misses: losing the cache multiplies the load. Design for that case.
  3. Cache-aside with delete on write is the default, but add versioned set-if-newer + tombstones to kill the read/write race.
  4. Stampedes need layered defences: single-flight, XFetch, TTL jitter, warming, and origin permits with shedding.
  5. Invalidate inside-out (L2 → L1 on all pods → CDN), driven by outbox or CDC events. TTLs are the safety net.
  6. L1 in-process caches absorb hot keys and save hops. Keep them small, with short TTLs and broadcast eviction.
  7. Hot keys: L1 + replicas across shards + event planning.
  8. Protect against penetration (negative caching, Bloom filters) and avalanche (jitter, warming).
  9. Display from caches, decide from the system of record.
  10. Never flush wholesale. Version cache keys by schema. Never cache personalized responses at shared layers.

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: Situation Choose Read-heavy, tolerates seconds of staleness Cache-aside + event invalidation + TTL safety net Hot keys, low latency Caffeine L1 (short TTL) + Redis L2 Concurrent updates and slow readers Versioned set-if-newer + version tombstones Known traffic spike Pre-warm + TTL jitter + XFetch Cache miss storms possible Per-pod single-flight + DB permits + shedding Anonymous listings, images CDN with s-maxage + surrogate keys (images: immutable URLs) Personalized responses private/no-store at the edge; L2 keyed per user if needed Decisions (price at checkout, stock, payment) System of record, not cache

docs.title: 08. Load Balancing, Proxies & Gateways ⭐
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 03, Ch 04 · What you will build: The platform edge, taken from a simulation of balancing algorithms (L1) to a Spring Cloud Gateway with per-route timeouts, identity header hygiene, rate limits, circuit breakers and safe retries (L3), and a latency-aware P2C load balancer with outlier ejection and weighted canaries (L4) · Reading time: 100 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: one bad pod, forty percent of checkouts failing
docs.text:
On a Saturday evening, one of twelve order-service pods landed on a Kubernetes node with a failing disk. The pod didn't crash. Its readiness probe (GET /actuator/health) returned UP in 20 ms. But real requests on that pod took 4–9 seconds, because every write waited on the sick disk.

The platform's gateway used round-robin across the twelve pods, so 1 in 12 requests landed on the sick pod. That's just 8 %. So why did 40 % of checkouts fail?

  • A checkout makes ~6 calls through the gateway (cart, pricing, slot, order, payment…). The chance that at least one hits the bad pod is roughly 1 − (11/12)⁶ ≈ 41 %.
  • The gateway retried timeouts, including on POST /orders. Some retries landed on healthy pods and created duplicate orders (the idempotency key saved them, Ch 04). Others landed on the sick pod again.
  • The bad pod's connection pool filled up, and round-robin kept sending it its full share.

The fix had three parts: a load-balancing algorithm that notices slow backends (least-outstanding / P2C with latency weighting), passive outlier ejection (stop sending to a backend after consecutive failures), and a readiness check that tests real dependencies with a latency threshold. Retries were limited to idempotent methods with a retry budget.

The thesis of this chapter

Load balancers and gateways are where every request's fate is decided: which instance, how long to wait, whether to retry, who the caller is, and how much they may send. Their defaults are designed for "all backends are equal and healthy." Production is never like that.

    CDN --> LB["Cloud L7 LB<br/>(regional, multi-AZ)"]

    LB --> PGW["partner-gateway<br/>(seller APIs)"]
    GW --> SVC["Services (K8s Services / mesh)<br/>client-side LB between services"]
    PGW --> SVC
Hop Balancing decision Key concerns DNS / anycast Which region / edge Failover, latency, TTLs CDN Which edge PoP; cache or origin Caching (Ch 07), WAF Cloud L7 LB Which gateway pod (across AZs) Health checks, idle timeouts (Ch 03), TLS API gateway Which service instance; whether to allow the call AuthN, rate limits, timeouts, retries, routing, canaries Service → service Client-side LB or mesh P2C, outlier ejection, zone awareness, deadlines

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text: Band After this chapter you can… B1 Explain what a load balancer and reverse proxy do, L4 vs L7, and the basic algorithms B2 Choose algorithms, configure health checks, avoid sticky sessions, and build routes in Spring Cloud Gateway B3 Handle slow (not dead) backends, outlier ejection, retries and retry budgets, per-route timeouts, and gateway security B4 Design global traffic management (GeoDNS, anycast, failover), canaries, zone-aware balancing, and the edge's responsibilities vs the mesh

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: the billing counters at a supermarket B1
docs.text:
A supermarket has 10 billing counters. A floor manager directs customers.

  • Round-robin: "You to counter 1, you to 2, you to 3…" Fair, until counter 4's scanner breaks and its queue grows to 30 people while the manager keeps sending one customer in ten there.
  • Least-outstanding: "Go to the counter with the shortest queue." The manager must look at every queue, which is expensive in a huge store.
  • Power of two choices: "Look at two random counters and pick the shorter queue." Almost as good as checking all of them, and much cheaper.
  • Health check: the manager asks each cashier "are you open?" A cashier with a broken scanner still says "yes" (the §1.1 story), so the manager must also watch how fast queues move.
  • Sticky session: "You always go to counter 3 because your coupons are there." That works until counter 3 closes.

docs.title: 2.2 What load balancers and proxies do B1
docs.text: Component Role Load balancer Distributes requests or connections across healthy instances Reverse proxy Sits in front of servers: terminates client connections, forwards requests, can cache, compress, rewrite and add headers (NGINX, Envoy, HAProxy) Forward proxy Sits in front of clients for outbound traffic (egress proxy, corporate proxy) API gateway A reverse proxy with API-aware policies: authentication, rate limiting, routing by path/version, request/response transformation, API keys, analytics Service mesh sidecar / ambient proxy A per-workload (or per-node) proxy for service-to-service traffic: mTLS, retries, timeouts, telemetry (Ch 17)

docs.title: 2.3 L4 vs L7 load balancing ⭐ B1 B2
docs.text:
L4 (transport) L7 (application) Sees IPs, ports, TCP/UDP HTTP method, path, headers, cookies, gRPC service/method Balances Connections Requests TLS Pass-through (or terminate) Terminates (or re-encrypts) Routing By port / IP By path, host, header, weight Features Very fast, protocol-agnostic, preserves the client connection end-to-end Retries, timeouts, header manipulation, rate limiting, auth, canaries, compression Cost Lowest latency and CPU More CPU per request; more features Pitfall Long-lived connections (gRPC, HTTP/2, WebSocket) pin to one backend, so load stays uneven after scale-out Buffering and timeouts affect streaming (Ch 03) Examples AWS NLB, GCP TCP/UDP LB, IPVS, kube-proxy AWS ALB, GCP HTTP(S) LB, NGINX, Envoy, HAProxy, Spring Cloud Gateway

gRPC and HTTP/2 through an L4 balancer

HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one long-lived connection. An L4 balancer picks a backend once per connection, so a client with 1 connection sends 100 % of its requests to one pod forever. Use L7 balancing (Envoy, gRPC-aware LBs), client-side balancing, or bounded connection lifetimes.

docs.title: 2.4 Load-balancing algorithms ⭐ B1 → B3
docs.text:
Algorithm How Strengths Weaknesses Round-robin Cycle through backends Simple, even request counts Ignores load and speed differences; slow backends keep their full share Weighted round-robin Proportional to weights Heterogeneous instance sizes; canaries Static weights don't react to degradation Random Uniform random Stateless, no coordination Same as RR; more variance Least connections / least outstanding requests Backend with the fewest in-flight requests Reacts to slow backends automatically Needs accurate counts; with many LB instances, each sees only its own traffic Power of two choices (P2C) Pick 2 random backends, send to the less loaded Near least-outstanding quality, O(1), avoids herding onto one "best" backend Needs a load signal per backend P2C + EWMA latency Load = outstanding × EWMA response time Also avoids backends that are slow Tuning decay; needs latency tracking Consistent hashing Hash(key) → position on a ring → backend Affinity: same key goes to the same backend (cache locality); minimal remapping when backends change Hot keys overload one backend; uneven without virtual nodes Rendezvous (HRW) hashing Highest hash(key, backend) wins Affinity like a ring, simpler, even O(n) per pick (fine for small n) Maglev hashing Lookup table built from permutations Fast, even, minimal disruption More complex

L1's simulation (§5) shows why this matters. There are 10 backends, one of them 8× slower, at 70 % fleet utilization:

Algorithm                          p50 ms     p99 ms   p99.9 ms % to slow node
Round-robin                          13.9  unbounded  unbounded          10.0%
Random                               22.5  unbounded  unbounded          10.0%
Round-robin + slow node ejected      14.5       94.1      137.3           0.0%
Least-outstanding (global)            8.4      113.5      360.0           2.0%
Power of two choices                 13.5      213.6      556.5           2.0%

Round-robin and random send the degraded node 10 % of traffic when it can serve only ~2 %, so its queue grows without bound and the tail latency explodes. Load-aware algorithms automatically cut its share to 2 %. Ejecting the node entirely is best of all, if you can detect it.

Why P2C instead of 'always the least loaded'?

With many independent LB instances (every gateway pod, every client), "always pick the least loaded" makes them all pick the same backend at the same moment (herding), because their load information is stale. Choosing the better of two random candidates spreads decisions while still avoiding bad backends. The theory: max load drops from O(log n / log log n) to O(log log n) (Mitzenmacher).

docs.title: 2.5 Consistent hashing and affinity B2 B3
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Ring["Hash ring (with virtual nodes)"]
        A1["A-v1"] --> B1["B-v1"] --> C1["C-v1"] --> A2["A-v2"] --> C2["C-v2"] --> B2["B-v2"] --> A1
    end
    K1(["key: cart:cust-42"]) -. "hash → next node clockwise" .-> B1
    K2(["key: cart:cust-77"]) -. "hash" .-> A2
Use Why affinity helps Sharded caches (clients choose the cache node by key) Each key lives on one node Stateful in-memory processing (a per-store aggregator) State stays local Request coalescing The same key goes to the same pod, so single-flight works fleet-wide

When a backend is added or removed, only ~1/n of keys move (vs almost all keys with hash % n). Virtual nodes (100–200 per backend) smooth the distribution. Bounded-load consistent hashing caps any backend at, say, 125 % of average load and spills the excess to the next node, which protects against hot keys.

docs.title: 2.6 Health checks: active, passive and what "healthy" means ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
Type How Catches Misses Active LB probes GET /health every N s; unhealthy after K failures Dead processes, crashed pods, unreachable nodes Slow-but-alive backends (§1.1); issues that only real traffic triggers Passive (outlier detection) Watch real responses: consecutive 5xx, timeouts, latency outliers → eject for a period Degraded backends under real load Backends with no traffic Kubernetes readiness kubelet probe; failing pods are removed from Service endpoints Startup, dependency readiness, overload shedding Same as active, and slow to react (period × threshold) Kubernetes liveness kubelet probe; failing → restart Deadlocks, hung processes — and it's dangerous if it checks dependencies (restart storms)

Health endpoint design:

Endpoint Checks Used by /actuator/health/liveness Process can serve (no deadlock) kubelet liveness. Never checks the DB or downstreams /actuator/health/readiness Warm-up done, critical dependencies reachable, not overloaded (for example, the pool isn't saturated) kubelet readiness, LB Deep diagnostics Every dependency with latency Humans and dashboards only. It's expensive and must not gate traffic

Health checks that check dependencies can take down the whole fleet

If every pod's readiness depends on Redis, a Redis blip makes all pods unready at once. The LB then has zero backends, so a partial degradation becomes a total outage. Readiness should reflect whether this instance can serve useful traffic. Shared-dependency outages are handled by fallbacks and shedding (Ch 07, 18), not by removing every pod.

Outlier ejection parameters (Envoy-style): eject after 5 consecutive 5xx or gateway errors, eject for 30 s (growing with repeated ejections), never eject more than 50 % of the pool (max ejection percent, which keeps a correlated failure from emptying the pool), and return the backend on probation.

docs.title: 2.7 Sticky sessions (session affinity) B2
docs.text:
Sticky sessions route a user to the same backend (via a cookie or source-IP hash).

Problem Why Uneven load Heavy users pin to one pod Deploys and scale-in drop sessions Session state dies with the pod Failover loses state Same Autoscaling doesn't help existing users They stay on hot pods

Prefer stateless services: keep session state in a shared store (Redis sessions, JWT claims) so any pod can serve any request. Use affinity only for performance (cache locality via consistent hashing), never for correctness. Streaming connections (Ch 03) are the exception, and even there, bounded lifetimes and resume make stickiness unnecessary.

docs.title: 2.8 Retries, timeouts and hedging at the proxy B2 B3
docs.text: Rule Why Retry only idempotent requests (GET, PUT, DELETE, or POST with an idempotency key) Otherwise you get duplicate orders or payments (§1.1, Ch 04) Retry on a different backend The same sick backend usually fails again Retry budget (for example, retries ≤ 10–20 % of requests) instead of per-request retry counts only Prevents retry storms from multiplying load during outages (3 layers × 3 retries = 27×) Retry at one layer Gateway, mesh and client all retrying multiplies attempts Per-route timeouts from latency budgets Search 800 ms, checkout 3 s, streams: no response timeout (Ch 03) Hedged requests (send a second copy after the p95 delay, take the first response) Cuts tail latency for idempotent reads at a small load cost Jittered backoff Avoids synchronized retry waves

docs.title: 2.9 API gateway responsibilities ⭐ B2 B4
docs.text:
Responsibility Gateway Service TLS termination (behind the LB/CDN) ✅ (or the LB) mTLS in the mesh Authentication (validate JWT/API key) ✅ Re-check critical claims; trust only gateway-set identity headers Coarse authorization (scopes: orders:read) ✅ Fine-grained (is this my order?) always in the service Rate limiting & quotas ✅ per client / plan Service-level concurrency limits too Routing (path, version, canary weights) ✅ — Request size limits, header normalization, stripping spoofable headers ✅ — Correlation ID injection ✅ Propagate Response compression, CORS ✅ — Timeouts, retries (idempotent), circuit breaking ✅ Downstream calls too Request/response transformation Minimal (versioning shims) — Business logic, orchestration ❌ BFFs and services Caching Rarely (anonymous GETs) Ch 07

Identity header spoofing

If services trust X-User-Id set by the gateway, the gateway must remove any incoming X-User-Id from the client before setting its own from the validated JWT. Otherwise any client can impersonate any user by sending the header. Also ensure services are unreachable except through the gateway or mesh (NetworkPolicies), or re-validate the token in the service.

docs.title: 2.10 Spring Cloud Gateway B2 B3
docs.text:
Concept Meaning Route id + predicates + filters + destination URI (lb://order-service uses Spring Cloud LoadBalancer) Predicates Path, Host, Method, Header, Query, Weight (canary), Before/After/Between (time) Filters Add/remove headers, RewritePath, StripPrefix, RequestRateLimiter (Redis), CircuitBreaker (Resilience4j), Retry, RequestSize, SetStatus, custom GlobalFilters Flavours Reactive (WebFlux, Netty) is the mature, highest-throughput option. Server WebMVC (servlet) is simpler to reason about and works well with virtual threads Per-route timeouts Route metadata connect-timeout, response-timeout (-1 disables for streams)

Alternatives: Envoy-based gateways (Envoy Gateway, Istio ingress), Kong, NGINX/OpenResty, and cloud API gateways. Choose Spring Cloud Gateway when the team wants Java-coded policies and Spring ecosystem integration. Choose Envoy-based options for polyglot platforms and mesh alignment.

docs.title: 2.11 Global traffic management: GeoDNS, anycast, failover B3 B4
docs.text:
Technique How Pros Cons GeoDNS / latency-based DNS DNS answers depend on the resolver's location or measured latency Simple, works with any backend Resolver location ≠ user location; clients cache beyond TTL, so failover takes minutes DNS failover Health-checked records; answer only healthy regions Cheap regional DR Slow (TTL + client caching); partial failures are hard Anycast The same IP announced from many PoPs, and BGP routes users to the nearest Fast failover (routing converges in seconds), DDoS absorption, one IP Needs a provider (CDNs, global LBs); TCP sessions can break on route changes (QUIC handles it better) Global L7 LB (cloud global LBs, CDN load balancing) Anycast edge terminates TLS, then routes to regional backends by health, latency and capacity Best user experience, fast failover, per-request decisions Provider lock-in; cost

For this platform (India, one primary region + DR, Ch 27): anycast CDN/WAF at the edge terminates TLS close to users across Indian PoPs, then routes to the Mumbai region's L7 LB, with a health-checked failover origin in the DR region (Hyderabad). DNS points at the CDN, so DNS TTLs don't govern failover. The edge's origin health checks do.

docs.title: 2.12 Zone-aware balancing and cross-AZ cost B3 B4
docs.text:
Cross-AZ traffic adds ~0.5–2 ms per hop and is billed per GB. Zone-aware balancing prefers same-zone backends when they're healthy and not overloaded, and spills to other zones when needed. Envoy, Istio and Kubernetes topology-aware routing (trafficDistribution: PreferClose on Services) support it.

Guardrail Why Spill over when the local zone is below ~70 % healthy capacity Don't overload the local zone just to save cost Keep capacity balanced per zone Otherwise zone-local routing concentrates load Zone failure → automatic cross-zone Availability beats cost

docs.title: 3.3 Sequence: failure path, slow pod detected, ejected, and a non-idempotent retry prevented
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant GW as api-gateway
    participant P5 as order-service pod 5 (sick disk)
    participant P2 as order-service pod 2
    participant P9 as order-service pod 9
    GW->>P5: GET /orders/ord_1 (P2C picked 5: low in-flight so far)
    P5-->>GW: 200 after 4.2 s (EWMA for pod 5 jumps)
    Note over GW: EWMA(pod5) = 900 ms vs ~20 ms others → P2C now almost never picks pod 5
    GW->>P5: POST /orders (rare pick) — timeout 3 s
    P5--xGW: timeout
    Note over GW: POST without Idempotency-Key → NOT retried → 504 to client (client retries with key)
    GW->>P5: GET /orders/ord_2
    P5--xGW: timeout (3rd consecutive failure)
    GW->>GW: outlier ejection: pod 5 out for 30 s (max 50 % of pool may be ejected)
    GW->>P2: retry GET on a different instance (within retry budget)
    P2-->>GW: 200
    Note over GW,P9: after 30 s, pod 5 returns on probation, and if it fails again it is ejected for 60 s

What the system guarantees after this failure path

A slow-but-alive backend receives a rapidly shrinking share of traffic (latency-weighted P2C) and is removed after consecutive failures (passive ejection), without waiting for active health checks that report it as "UP." Retries never re-send non-idempotent requests, always go to a different instance, and are capped by a fleet-wide budget. Ejection never removes more than half the pool, so a shared-dependency failure can't empty it.

docs.title: 3.4 State: backend endpoint health in the balancer
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> HEALTHY: discovered + ready
    HEALTHY --> DEGRADED: EWMA latency high (P2C avoids)
    DEGRADED --> HEALTHY: latency recovers
    HEALTHY --> EJECTED: N consecutive failures
    DEGRADED --> EJECTED: N consecutive failures
    EJECTED --> PROBATION: ejection time elapsed
    PROBATION --> HEALTHY: successes
    PROBATION --> EJECTED: failure (ejection time doubles, capped)
    HEALTHY --> [*]: removed from discovery (scale-in, not ready)

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Platform Edge & API Gateway
docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers Platform team / Security, SRE, all service owners Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-032 Latency-aware P2C with outlier ejection for gateway and service-to-service; ADR-033 Retries only at the gateway, idempotent-only, with budget

1. Context & Problem. Round-robin plus shallow health checks let one sick pod fail ~40 % of checkouts (§1.1). Retries were uncontrolled, including on POSTs. Identity headers could be spoofed by direct calls to services, and rate limiting was per-pod and inconsistent.

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: a single, consistently secured edge for customer APIs; automatic avoidance of slow or failing instances; safe retries; per-user rate limits; per-route timeouts; canary routing; P90 sale capacity with AZ-failure headroom.
  • Non-goals: service mesh rollout (Ch 17); seller partner gateway details (Ch 04 Q18).

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement FR-1 Route /api/v1/** to services by path; support weighted canaries FR-2 Validate JWT; set identity headers; strip client-supplied identity headers FR-3 Per-user and per-IP-range rate limits with 429 + RateLimit-* headers NFR-1 Gateway overhead p99 ≤ 5 ms NFR-2 A backend with p99 ≥ 10× fleet median receives ≤ 5 % of traffic within 30 s NFR-3 Retries ≤ 10 % of requests fleet-wide; never for non-idempotent requests without Idempotency-Key NFR-4 Survive loss of one AZ at P90 sale load NFR-5 Streaming routes (SSE, Ch 03) have no response timeout; idle timeout 110 s

4. Capacity estimates.

Item Calculation Result Edge requests at sale start (P90, Ch 02) ~200 K req/s at CDN CDN serves images and cacheable listings (~40 %) Gateway requests ~60 % of 200 K ~120 K req/s Per-pod capacity (reactive gateway, JWT + rate limit + routing; load-tested) ~4,000 req/s at 2 vCPU with p99 overhead ≤ 5 ms 30 pods needed With AZ headroom (×1.5, multiple of 3) 45 45 pods at peak, pre-scaled (Ch 02) Redis rate-limit ops 120 K req/s × 1 Lua call 120 K ops/s → 3–4 shards, keys hash-tagged per user JWKS fetches Cached, refreshed every 10 min Negligible Upstream connections 45 gateway pods × ~26 services × pool 50 Bounded by per-route pool sizes; watch the Little's Law figures (Ch 02)

5. Proposed design.

  • Edge chain: anycast CDN/WAF → regional L7 LB (multi-AZ, health-checked gateway pods) → Spring Cloud Gateway (reactive).
  • Filters: header hygiene → correlation → JWT validation → identity headers → Redis rate limit → route → size limit → circuit breaker + per-route timeout → idempotent-only retry (different instance, budget).
  • Balancing: a custom latency-aware P2C (outstanding × EWMA) with passive outlier ejection (5 consecutive failures → 30 s, doubling, max 50 % of the pool), zone preference with spill-over, and weighted canary routes.
  • Services: reachable only from the gateway and the mesh (NetworkPolicy). Each service re-checks resource ownership.

7. Alternatives considered.

Option Pros Cons Verdict Cloud API gateway (managed) No ops, built-in auth and limits Per-request pricing at 120 K req/s; less control over balancing and custom policies Rejected on cost and flexibility Envoy-based gateway (Envoy Gateway / Istio ingress) High performance; P2C, outlier detection, zone-aware routing built in Config-as-YAML for custom auth logic; team skills Strong alternative: adopt with the mesh (Ch 17) Kong / NGINX Mature, plugins Lua/plugin skills; custom logic outside Java Rejected for this team Spring Cloud Gateway + custom P2C-EWMA + ejection Java policies, Spring Security, fits team skills We own the balancer code and its tests Chosen for now, and revisit when the mesh lands

8. Failure modes. Redis for rate limits down: fail open for authenticated users with a local, per-pod conservative limiter, and fail closed for anonymous abusive IP ranges. JWKS endpoint down: keep using cached keys (refresh-ahead), and alert. All instances of a service ejected: max-ejection cap keeps ≥ 50 %, and beyond that the circuit breaker opens and returns fast 503 with fallbacks. Gateway pod overload: LB least-outstanding across gateway pods, pre-scale for events, and shed low-priority routes first.

10. Observability. Per route: request rate, errors by class, latency (gateway overhead vs upstream), retries (attempts and the budget consumed), circuit-breaker state, rate-limit rejections. Per upstream instance: EWMA, in-flight, ejections. Edge: CDN hit ratio, WAF blocks, TLS errors.

14. Decision (ADR-032/033 summary). Gateway and service-to-service balancing use latency-aware P2C with passive outlier ejection (max 50 % ejected). Readiness probes reflect instance-local health, and liveness never checks dependencies. Retries happen only at the gateway, only for idempotent requests (or POSTs carrying Idempotency-Key), always on a different instance, within a 10 % fleet retry budget. Every route declares its timeout, and streaming routes declare no response timeout plus an idle timeout.

docs.text:
We build the platform edge four times:

docs.title: L1 — Concept: simulating balancing algorithms (plain Java) B1
docs.text:
// LoadBalancingL1.java — run with: java LoadBalancingL1.java
// Discrete-event simulation: 10 backends (one degraded, 8x slower), Poisson arrivals at ~70% fleet utilization.
// Compares Round-robin, Random, Least-outstanding (global view), and Power-of-Two-Choices (P2C).
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.*;

public class LoadBalancingL1 {

    static final int SERVERS = 10;
    static final double BASE_SERVICE_MS = 10.0;              // mean service time on a healthy node
    static final double SLOW_FACTOR = 8.0;                   // server 0 is degraded (GC thrash, noisy neighbour)
    static final int REQUESTS = 200_000;

    /** One worker per server (FIFO). Tracks when it becomes free and how many requests are outstanding. */
    static final class Server {
        final double speed; double freeAt = 0; final Deque<Double> completions = new ArrayDeque<>(); long served = 0;
        Server(double speed) { this.speed = speed; }
        int outstanding(double now) { while (!completions.isEmpty() && completions.peekFirst() <= now) completions.pollFirst(); return completions.size(); }
    }

    interface Picker { int pick(Server[] s, double now, Random rnd); }

    static double[] simulate(String name, Picker picker, long seed) {
        Random rnd = new Random(seed);
        Server[] s = new Server[SERVERS];
        for (int i = 0; i < SERVERS; i++) s[i] = new Server(i == 0 ? SLOW_FACTOR : 1.0);
        // Fleet capacity (req/ms): 9 healthy at 1/10 + 1 slow at 1/80 → target ~70 % of it
        double capacity = 9 / BASE_SERVICE_MS + 1 / (BASE_SERVICE_MS * SLOW_FACTOR);
        double lambda = 0.70 * capacity;
        double now = 0;
        double[] lat = new double[REQUESTS];
        for (int r = 0; r < REQUESTS; r++) {
            now += -Math.log(1 - rnd.nextDouble()) / lambda;                          // exponential inter-arrival
            int i = picker.pick(s, now, rnd);
            Server srv = s[i];
            double service = -Math.log(1 - rnd.nextDouble()) * BASE_SERVICE_MS * srv.speed;
            double start = Math.max(now, srv.freeAt);
            double done = start + service;
            srv.freeAt = done;
            srv.completions.addLast(done);
            srv.served++;
            lat[r] = done - now;
        }
        Arrays.sort(lat);
        double slowShare = 100.0 * s[0].served / REQUESTS;
        return new double[]{lat[REQUESTS / 2], lat[(int) (REQUESTS * 0.99)], lat[(int) (REQUESTS * 0.999)], slowShare};
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] rr = {0};
        Map<String, Picker> pickers = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        pickers.put("Round-robin", (s, now, rnd) -> rr[0]++ % SERVERS);
        pickers.put("Random", (s, now, rnd) -> rnd.nextInt(SERVERS));
        int[] rrHealthy = {0};
        pickers.put("Round-robin + slow node ejected", (s, now, rnd) -> 1 + rrHealthy[0]++ % (SERVERS - 1));   // outlier ejection
        pickers.put("Least-outstanding (global)", (s, now, rnd) -> {
            int best = 0; int bestLoad = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
            for (int i = 0; i < SERVERS; i++) { int l = s[i].outstanding(now); if (l < bestLoad) { bestLoad = l; best = i; } }
            return best;
        });
        pickers.put("Power of two choices", (s, now, rnd) -> {
            int a = rnd.nextInt(SERVERS), b = rnd.nextInt(SERVERS - 1);
            if (b >= a) b++;                                                            // two distinct random servers
            return s[a].outstanding(now) <= s[b].outstanding(now) ? a : b;
        });

        System.out.printf("%-32s %8s %10s %10s %14s%n", "Algorithm", "p50 ms", "p99 ms", "p99.9 ms", "% to slow node");
        for (var e : pickers.entrySet()) {
            double[] r = simulate(e.getKey(), e.getValue(), 42);
            System.out.printf("%-32s %8.1f %10s %10s %13.1f%%%n", e.getKey(), r[0], fmt(r[1]), fmt(r[2]), r[3]);
        }
        System.out.println("(unbounded = the slow node receives more than it can serve; its queue grows for the whole run)");
    }

    static String fmt(double ms) { return ms > 10_000 ? "unbounded" : "%.1f".formatted(ms); }

}

Actual output from running it:

Algorithm                          p50 ms     p99 ms   p99.9 ms % to slow node
Round-robin                          13.9  unbounded  unbounded          10.0%
Random                               22.5  unbounded  unbounded          10.0%
Round-robin + slow node ejected      14.5       94.1      137.3           0.0%
Least-outstanding (global)            8.4      113.5      360.0           2.0%
Power of two choices                 13.5      213.6      556.5           2.0%
(unbounded = the slow node receives more than it can serve; its queue grows for the whole run)

What L1 shows: "equal share" algorithms give a degraded backend more than it can serve, so its queue and your tail latency grow without bound. Load-aware algorithms (least-outstanding, P2C) cut its share automatically. Ejection removes it entirely, which is best of all if you can detect it. Note that P2C only compares two backends yet stays within ~2× of the global optimum, without needing a global view.

package com.grocery.gateway.filter;

import org.springframework.cloud.gateway.filter.GatewayFilterChain;
import org.springframework.cloud.gateway.filter.GlobalFilter;
import org.springframework.core.Ordered;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.server.ServerWebExchange;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;
import java.util.UUID;

@Component
public class CorrelationIdFilter implements GlobalFilter, Ordered {

    public static final String HEADER = "X-Correlation-Id";

    @Override
    public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, GatewayFilterChain chain) {
        String incoming = exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().getFirst(HEADER);
        String id = (incoming != null && incoming.matches("[A-Za-z0-9-]{8,64}")) ? incoming : UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        var request = exchange.getRequest().mutate().headers(h -> h.set(HEADER, id)).build();
        exchange.getResponse().getHeaders().set(HEADER, id);
        return chain.filter(exchange.mutate().request(request).build());
    }

    @Override public int getOrder() { return Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE; }
}

              .expectHeader().exists("X-Correlation-Id");

What L2 gets right: a single entry point, path routing, discovery-based balancing (lb://) and correlation IDs.

What L2 is missing (every item was in the §1.1 incident or the design doc):

Gap Risk No authentication, and client headers passed through Spoofed X-User-Id Default round-robin, no ejection The sick-pod scenario No per-route timeouts Slow routes hold connections; streams cut or hung No rate limits or size limits Abuse, overload No circuit breakers or safe retries Cascading failures, or duplicate orders if retries were added naively
