package com.grocery.gateway.filter;

import org.springframework.cloud.gateway.filter.GatewayFilterChain;
import org.springframework.cloud.gateway.filter.GlobalFilter;
import org.springframework.core.Ordered;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.resource.authentication.JwtAuthenticationToken;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.server.ServerWebExchange;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * 1. ALWAYS strip identity/internal headers sent by clients (spoofing protection).
 * 2. If authenticated, set X-User-Id / X-User-Scopes from the VALIDATED token.
 * Services trust these headers only because NetworkPolicy makes them unreachable except via gateway/mesh.
 */
@Component
public class IdentityHeadersFilter implements GlobalFilter, Ordered {

    static final List<String> STRIP = List.of("X-User-Id", "X-User-Scopes", "X-Internal-Caller", "X-Forwarded-User");

    @Override
    public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, GatewayFilterChain chain) {
        var cleaned = exchange.getRequest().mutate().headers(h -> STRIP.forEach(h::remove)).build();
        var cleanedExchange = exchange.mutate().request(cleaned).build();
        return cleanedExchange.getPrincipal()
                .filter(JwtAuthenticationToken.class::isInstance)
                .cast(JwtAuthenticationToken.class)
                .map(auth -> cleanedExchange.mutate().request(cleaned.mutate().headers(h -> {
                    h.set("X-User-Id", auth.getToken().getSubject());
                    h.set("X-User-Scopes", String.join(" ", auth.getToken().getClaimAsStringList("scope") == null
                            ? List.of() : auth.getToken().getClaimAsStringList("scope")));
                }).build()).build())
                .defaultIfEmpty(cleanedExchange)
                .flatMap(chain::filter);
    }

    @Override public int getOrder() { return Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 10; }
}

package com.grocery.gateway.config;

import org.springframework.cloud.gateway.filter.ratelimit.*;
import org.springframework.cloud.gateway.route.RouteLocator;
import org.springframework.cloud.gateway.route.builder.RouteLocatorBuilder;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.util.unit.DataSize;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;
import java.time.Duration;
import static org.springframework.cloud.gateway.support.RouteMetadataUtils.*;

@Configuration
public class RoutesL3 {

    /** Per-user key; anonymous callers keyed by client IP (the CDN's verified client-IP header, not raw XFF). */
    @Bean
    KeyResolver userKeyResolver() {
        return exchange -> Mono.justOrEmpty(exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().getFirst("X-User-Id"))
                .switchIfEmpty(Mono.justOrEmpty(exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().getFirst("True-Client-IP"))
                        .map(ip -> "ip:" + ip))
                .defaultIfEmpty("anonymous");
    }

    @Bean RedisRateLimiter standardLimiter() { return new RedisRateLimiter(10, 20, 1); }    // 10/s, burst 20
    @Bean RedisRateLimiter checkoutLimiter() { return new RedisRateLimiter(1, 5, 1); }     // 1/s, burst 5

    @Bean
    RouteLocator routes(RouteLocatorBuilder b, KeyResolver userKeyResolver) {
        return b.routes()
                // Reads: short timeout, retry once on a different instance for GET only
                .route("orders-read", r -> r.path("/api/v1/orders/**").and().method(HttpMethod.GET)
                        .filters(f -> f
                                .requestRateLimiter(c -> c.setRateLimiter(standardLimiter()).setKeyResolver(userKeyResolver))
                                .circuitBreaker(c -> c.setName("orders").setFallbackUri("forward:/fallback/unavailable"))
                                .retry(c -> c.setRetries(1).setMethods(HttpMethod.GET)
                                        .setStatuses(HttpStatus.BAD_GATEWAY, HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE)
                                        .setBackoff(Duration.ofMillis(20), Duration.ofMillis(100), 2, true)))
                        .metadata(CONNECT_TIMEOUT_ATTR, 500)
                        .metadata(RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_ATTR, 2000)
                        .uri("lb://order-service"))
                // Writes: NO gateway retry (clients retry with Idempotency-Key, Ch 04); stricter limit; small bodies
                .route("orders-write", r -> r.path("/api/v1/orders/**").and().method(HttpMethod.POST, HttpMethod.PATCH)
                        .filters(f -> f
                                .requestRateLimiter(c -> c.setRateLimiter(checkoutLimiter()).setKeyResolver(userKeyResolver))
                                .setRequestSize(DataSize.ofKilobytes(64))
                                .circuitBreaker(c -> c.setName("orders-write").setFallbackUri("forward:/fallback/unavailable")))
                        .metadata(CONNECT_TIMEOUT_ATTR, 500)
                        .metadata(RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_ATTR, 3000)
                        .uri("lb://order-service"))
                // SSE tracking stream (Ch 03): no response timeout; idle handled by server lifetime + LB
                .route("tracking-stream", r -> r.order(-1).path("/api/v1/orders/*/events")   // BEFORE orders-read
                        .metadata(RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_ATTR, -1)
                        .uri("lb://tracking-stream"))
                .route("catalog", r -> r.path("/api/v1/stores/**", "/api/v1/clusters/**")
                        .filters(f -> f.requestRateLimiter(c -> c.setRateLimiter(standardLimiter()).setKeyResolver(userKeyResolver)))
                        .metadata(RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_ATTR, 800)
                        .uri("lb://catalog-service"))
                .build();
    }
}

Route order matters

/api/v1/orders/*/events also matches /api/v1/orders/**. The stream route has r.order(-1), so it's matched first. Without that, the SSE request inherits the 2 s response timeout and every stream dies after 2 s.

package com.grocery.gateway.controller;

import org.springframework.http.*;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;

@RestController
public class FallbackController {

    /** Circuit open or upstream failing: fast, explicit, retryable Problem Details (Ch 04). */
    @RequestMapping("/fallback/unavailable")
    public Mono<ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail>> unavailable() {
        var pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, "Service temporarily unavailable");
        pd.setProperty("code", "UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE");
        pd.setProperty("retryable", true);
        return Mono.just(ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE)
                .header(HttpHeaders.RETRY_AFTER, "2").body(pd));
    }
}

package com.grocery.gateway;

import okhttp3.mockwebserver.*;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.context.ApplicationContext;
import org.springframework.test.context.*;
import org.springframework.test.web.reactive.server.WebTestClient;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.springframework.security.test.web.reactive.server.SecurityMockServerConfigurers.*;

@SpringBootTest(properties = "spring.cloud.gateway.redis-rate-limiter.include-headers=true")
class GatewayPoliciesTest {

    static MockWebServer orders = new MockWebServer();

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void props(DynamicPropertyRegistry r) throws Exception {
        orders.start();
        r.add("spring.cloud.discovery.client.simple.instances.order-service[0].uri", () -> orders.url("/").toString());
        // Rate limiter needs Redis: point at a Testcontainers Redis in the full suite; here the limiter bean is replaced
    }

    @Autowired ApplicationContext ctx;
    WebTestClient client;

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        client = WebTestClient.bindToApplicationContext(ctx).apply(springSecurity()).configureClient().build();
    }

    @Test
    void spoofedIdentityHeaderIsReplacedFromToken() throws Exception {
        orders.enqueue(new MockResponse().setBody("[]"));
        client.mutateWith(mockJwt().jwt(j -> j.subject("cust-42")))
              .get().uri("/api/v1/orders").header("X-User-Id", "cust-999-victim")
              .exchange().expectStatus().isOk();
        assertThat(orders.takeRequest().getHeader("X-User-Id")).isEqualTo("cust-42");
    }

    @Test
    void unauthenticatedOrdersCallIsRejected() {
        client.get().uri("/api/v1/orders").exchange().expectStatus().isUnauthorized();
    }

    @Test
    void getIsRetriedOnceOn503_postIsNeverRetried() throws Exception {
        int before = orders.getRequestCount();
        orders.enqueue(new MockResponse().setResponseCode(503));
        orders.enqueue(new MockResponse().setBody("[]"));
        client.mutateWith(mockJwt()).get().uri("/api/v1/orders").exchange().expectStatus().isOk();
        assertThat(orders.getRequestCount() - before).isEqualTo(2);

        before = orders.getRequestCount();
        orders.enqueue(new MockResponse().setResponseCode(503));
        client.mutateWith(mockJwt()).post().uri("/api/v1/orders")
              .header("Idempotency-Key", "7f3c2a4e-0b8d-4c1e-9f6b-2d5a1e8c9b10").bodyValue("{}")
              .exchange().expectStatus().is5xxServerError();
        assertThat(orders.getRequestCount() - before).isEqualTo(1);        // exactly one attempt
    }

    @AfterAll static void stop() throws Exception { orders.shutdown(); }
}

What L3 guarantees: client identity headers can never reach services, only validated identities can. Per-user limits are consistent across all gateway pods (Redis). Each route has its own timeout, and streams aren't cut. Writes are never retried by the gateway. Reads retry once on 502/503 with jittered backoff. Open circuits fail fast with retryable Problem Details.

What L3 still lacks: the balancer is still round-robin, so the §1.1 sick-pod scenario remains. The built-in retry can't express "a POST with Idempotency-Key may be retried." There are no canaries and no zone awareness.

docs.title: L4 — Enterprise: latency-aware P2C, outlier ejection, zones, canaries B4
What changed from L1 to L4
docs.text: Concern L1 L2 L3 L4 Algorithm Simulated: RR, random, least-outstanding, P2C, ejection Round-robin via lb:// Round-robin P2C × peak-EWMA, verified by simulation Slow backend handling Measured ❌ Circuit breaker per route only Traffic share < 1 % in seconds Failing backend — ❌ Circuit breaker Passive ejection, 50 % cap, probation Identity — Pass-through Strip + set from validated JWT + strip canary headers Retries — ❌ GET only, once, jittered + budget; POSTs only client-side with key Timeouts — Global Per route; streams exempt same Rate limits — ❌ Redis token bucket per user/IP same Zones & canaries — — — Load-aware zone preference; weighted and tester canaries

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Detection signal Blast radius Mitigation Slow-but-healthy backend Per-instance latency outlier; EWMA divergence Share of requests × calls per journey (§1.1) Latency-aware P2C, passive ejection, deeper readiness All backends ejected / unready due to a shared dependency Ejection count spikes, empty endpoints Total outage of the route Max-ejection cap; readiness excludes shared dependencies; fallbacks Retry storm Upstream RPS ≫ client RPS; retry budget exhausted Amplifies any incident Retry budgets, one retrying layer, jitter, circuit breakers Non-idempotent retries Duplicate orders/payments Money Retry only idempotent requests or those with idempotency keys Wrong route precedence Streams cut at 2 s; wrong service gets traffic One route Explicit route order; route tests L4 connection pinning (gRPC/HTTP/2) One pod hot after scale-out Uneven load L7 balancing, client-side LB, max connection age Gateway overload Gateway CPU / event-loop lag; LB 5xx Everything Pre-scaling (Ch 02), shedding low-priority routes, efficient filters JWKS / auth provider outage Token validation errors All authenticated routes Cache keys with refresh-ahead; long-enough key overlap on rotation Rate-limit Redis outage Limiter errors Unprotected upstreams or blocked users Fail open with a local limiter; alert Health check thundering Health endpoints dominate traffic (hundreds of LBs × fast intervals) Backend CPU Reasonable intervals; cheap endpoints; passive checks Header spoofing Unexpected identities in service logs Account takeover Strip at the gateway; NetworkPolicy; services verify ownership DNS / anycast misrouting Region traffic imbalance; latency by geography Regional users Health-checked origins; monitoring by PoP

docs.title: 6.2 Observability
docs.text: Signal Why Per-route RPS, errors (4xx/5xx by upstream vs gateway), latency split into gateway overhead and upstream Know who's slow Per-upstream-instance: in-flight, EWMA, success rate, ejections Detect sick pods before users do Retry attempts, retry budget utilization Early warning of storms Circuit breaker state transitions Dependency health Rate-limit decisions by key class (user, IP range, plan) Abuse vs legitimate spikes LB: healthy host count per AZ, surge queue / rejected connections Capacity at the LB tier Edge: CDN hit ratio, WAF actions, TLS handshake failures by client Edge health Canary vs stable SLO comparison Promotion decisions (Ch 26)

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Single ingress path: services accept traffic only from the gateway or the mesh (NetworkPolicies, security groups). This is what makes gateway-set identity headers trustworthy.
  • Strip, then set identity and internal headers. Never let clients choose X-User-Id, X-Canary, X-Internal-*.
  • Trust client-IP headers only from your CDN/LB (use the provider's verified header or the PROXY protocol). Raw X-Forwarded-For is client-controlled.
  • WAF at the edge (OWASP rules, bot management), request size limits, header size limits, slow-loris protection (read timeouts).
  • TLS policies: TLS 1.2+ (1.3 preferred) at the edge and mTLS internally (Ch 23).
  • Admin endpoints (actuator, gateway route management) are never exposed publicly.
  • Rate limits keyed by identity (not only IP, because of CGNAT, Ch 03), with separate, stricter limits on auth/OTP endpoints.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance & tuning knobs
docs.text: Knob Value Guidance P2C EWMA decay ~10 s Faster reacts quicker but is noisier Ejection 5 consecutive failures, 30 s → 5 min, max 50 % Tune per service criticality Zone preference ≥ 70 % local healthy, local load ≤ 1.25 × fleet Watch the cross-zone traffic cost Per-route timeouts From the latency budget; streams: none Inner < outer (Ch 03 ladder) Retry 1 retry, GET/idempotent, 20–100 ms jittered, budget 10 % Only at the gateway Upstream connection pools Little's Law per route Separate pools per upstream to isolate Health checks 5–10 s interval, 2–3 failures Plus passive ejection Gateway pods Pre-scaled for events; target 50–60 % CPU Event-loop latency is the key metric (reactive) Max connection age (HTTP/2, gRPC) 5–10 min Rebalances long-lived connections

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• Managed LBs and gateways charge per hour, per new connection, per active connection and per GB processed. At 120 K req/s, managed per-request API gateway pricing can exceed the cost of running your own gateway pods by a large factor. Model it (Ch 02).
  • Cross-AZ traffic between LB, gateway and services is billed per GB. Zone-aware routing reduces it, but only with the load checks from §2.12.
  • CDN offload (Ch 07) reduces origin LB and gateway capacity directly.
  • WAF and bot management are priced per request. Filter the worst traffic at the edge before it costs gateway CPU.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Round-robin with shallow health checks. Symptom: A slow pod keeps its full share, and multi-call journeys fail disproportionately (§1.1). Fix: Latency-aware P2C plus passive ejection plus meaningful readiness.

2. Readiness or liveness checking shared dependencies.

# ❌ before: Redis blip → every pod unready (or restarted) at once → zero backends
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include: readinessState,db,redis,kafka

# ✅ after: instance-local readiness; shared deps handled by fallbacks/breakers
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include: readinessState,snapshotLoaded,poolNotSaturated
management.endpoint.health.group.liveness.include: livenessState

3. Retrying non-idempotent requests at the proxy. Symptom: Duplicate orders during slowdowns. Fix: GET/idempotent-only retries. Writes are retried by clients with Idempotency-Key.

4. Retries at every layer. Symptom: Client 3 × gateway 3 × mesh 3 × SDK 3 = 81 attempts per click during an outage. Fix: One retrying layer, budgets and circuit breakers.

5. Sticky sessions for state. Symptom: Uneven load, and lost carts on deploys. Fix: Stateless services with a shared session store.

6. Trusting client identity or IP headers.

// ❌ before: the service trusts whatever X-User-Id arrives (reachable directly, or not stripped at gateway)
String user = request.getHeader("X-User-Id");

// ✅ after: gateway strips + sets from validated JWT; NetworkPolicy blocks direct access; service checks ownership

7. One timeout for all routes. Symptom: SSE streams die at 30 s, while checkout waits 30 s on a dead dependency. Fix: Per-route timeouts from latency budgets, with streams exempted.

8. Zone affinity without load awareness. Symptom: All traffic from one zone's callers piles onto that zone's pods. The first L4 simulation reproduced this: p50 > 150 s. Fix: Spill over when the local zone is busier than the fleet, or when too few local pods are healthy.

9. Business logic in the gateway. Symptom: The gateway becomes a deploy bottleneck and a distributed monolith. Fix: Gateway for cross-cutting policy only. Composition goes in BFFs, and domain rules in services.

10. gRPC behind an L4 load balancer. Symptom: New pods get no traffic after scale-out. Fix: An L7 or gRPC-aware balancer, client-side LB, and max connection age.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What's the difference between a load balancer, a reverse proxy and an API gateway?

30-second answer: A load balancer distributes traffic across instances. A reverse proxy fronts servers, terminating client connections and forwarding requests (and can balance, cache, compress). An API gateway is a reverse proxy with API-specific policies: authentication, rate limiting, routing by path and version, quotas and transformations.

Deep answer: In practice they overlap: NGINX and Envoy do all three. Architecturally, keep the gateway for cross-cutting API policy, keep business logic out, and use BFFs for client-specific composition.

Trade-offs I'd call out: More features at the edge means more CPU and more coupling.

Follow-ups: 1. Is a service mesh a load balancer? → Yes, a distributed one for east-west traffic, plus mTLS and telemetry. 2. Where does TLS terminate? → At the CDN/LB, then re-encrypted, with mTLS internally.

Red flags: Putting domain logic in the gateway.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Separates north-south (gateway) from east-west (mesh) concerns.

Q2 [B1] ⭐ L4 vs L7 load balancing?

30-second answer: L4 balances connections based on IP and port, with no HTTP awareness. It's fast and protocol-agnostic. L7 understands HTTP/gRPC and balances individual requests, enabling path routing, retries, header manipulation and auth, at more CPU cost.

Deep answer: Long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connections through L4 pin to one backend, so use L7 or client-side balancing. L7 LBs impose timeouts and buffering that affect streams (Ch 03).

Trade-offs: Performance vs features.

Follow-ups: 1. Which for WebSockets? → Either, but configure idle timeouts and consider connection rebalancing. 2. Why NLB + ALB together? → Static IPs or PrivateLink from NLB, HTTP features from ALB.

Red flags: Not knowing about connection pinning.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: The connection vs request distinction and its consequences.

Q3 [B1] Name load-balancing algorithms and when each fits.

30-second answer: Round-robin and weighted round-robin (equal or proportional capacity), random, least connections / least outstanding (variable request cost), power of two choices (load-aware and scalable), P2C with latency EWMA (also avoids slow nodes), and consistent/rendezvous hashing (affinity for caches or state).

Deep answer: In a simulation with one 8× slower node, round-robin's tail latency grows without bound, while load-aware algorithms cut the slow node's share from 10 % to 2 %, and ejection removes it.

Trade-offs: Simplicity vs adaptivity. Affinity vs balance.

Follow-ups: 1. Why do weights matter for canaries? → Controlled traffic percentages. 2. What's bounded-load consistent hashing? → A cap on each node's load, with spill-over.

Red flags: Only knowing round-robin.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Ties algorithm choice to failure modes (slow nodes).

Q4 [B1] Liveness vs readiness probes: what should each check?

30-second answer: Liveness answers "is the process stuck? Restart me." It should check only internal health, never dependencies. Readiness answers "should I receive traffic now?" It checks warm-up and instance-local ability to serve, possibly including overload. Shared dependencies shouldn't flip readiness for all pods at once.

Deep answer: Also use startup probes for slow JVM starts. Combine with passive outlier detection, because probes miss slow-but-alive pods.

Trade-offs: Deeper checks catch more but risk fleet-wide flapping.

Follow-ups: 1. What happens if liveness checks the DB? → The DB blips, and every pod restarts: a restart storm. 2. Can readiness shed load? → Yes, briefly, but cap it so you don't empty the pool.

Red flags: One /health endpoint for everything.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Explains fleet-wide correlated failure.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ Why avoid sticky sessions, and when are they acceptable?

30-second answer: They create uneven load, lose state on deploys, scale-in or failures, and stop autoscaling from helping existing users. Make services stateless with shared session stores. Affinity is acceptable for performance (cache locality via consistent hashing) when losing it is harmless.

Deep answer: For streams, use bounded lifetimes and resume instead of stickiness (Ch 03). For in-memory aggregations, use consistent hashing with rebalancing and state handoff.

Trade-offs: Locality vs resilience and balance.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you store sessions? → Redis with TTL, or stateless JWTs with revocation lists. 2. What about the WebSocket affinity? → It's inherent per connection; plan for reconnects.

Red flags: Sticky sessions required for correctness.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Distinguishes performance affinity from correctness affinity.

Q6 [B2] ⭐ Explain consistent hashing and why virtual nodes are needed.

30-second answer: Keys and servers hash onto a ring, and each key goes to the next server clockwise. Adding or removing a server moves only ~1/n of keys, unlike hash % n, which moves almost all of them. Virtual nodes (many ring points per server) smooth the distribution and let you weight servers.

Deep answer: Hot keys still overload one node, so use bounded-load variants or replicate hot keys. Rendezvous hashing is a simpler alternative, and Maglev is a fast, stable lookup table.

Trade-offs: Affinity vs even load.

Follow-ups: 1. Where is it used? → Caches, sharded stores (Ch 11), Envoy ring-hash/Maglev. 2. What happens on node failure? → Its keys move to the successors, whose caches are cold.

Red flags: Using hash % n for sharding caches.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Mentions hot keys and bounded load.

Q7 [B2] ⭐ How do you configure retries at a gateway safely?

30-second answer: Only for idempotent requests (GET, PUT, DELETE, or POST with an idempotency key), on a different instance, at most once or twice with jittered backoff, within a fleet-wide retry budget, at a single layer, and never beyond the caller's deadline. Pair with circuit breakers.

Deep answer: Retry on connection failures and 502/503. Be careful with 504 and timeouts, because the request may have executed. Track retry rates and alert when the budget is exhausted.

Trade-offs: Higher success rates for transient failures vs load amplification.

Follow-ups: 1. What's a retry budget? → Retries allowed ≤ X % of requests over a window. 2. What are hedged requests? → Parallel duplicates for tail latency, for idempotent reads only.

Red flags: Retrying POSTs automatically.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Budgets, single layer, idempotency.

Q8 [B2] What belongs in the API gateway vs in the services?

30-second answer: Gateway: TLS termination (or the LB), authentication, coarse authorization (scopes), rate limits and quotas, routing and versioning, size limits, header hygiene, correlation IDs, CORS, compression, timeouts, idempotent retries, circuit breaking. Services: fine-grained authorization (ownership), business rules, data access, orchestration (or BFFs).

Deep answer: Services must still validate critical assumptions (defence in depth) and must be unreachable except via the gateway or mesh. Keep transformations minimal to avoid a smart-gateway monolith.

Trade-offs: Centralized policy vs a bottleneck and coupling.

Follow-ups: 1. Should the gateway call multiple services per request? → That's a BFF's job. 2. Who owns gateway config? → The platform team, with self-service routes via GitOps.

Red flags: Authorization only at the gateway.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Defence in depth plus clear ownership.

Q9 [B2] How do you load balance gRPC services?

30-second answer: gRPC uses long-lived HTTP/2 connections, so L4 balancing pins traffic. Use L7 (Envoy or mesh) per-request balancing, or client-side balancing (gRPC name resolution + a round_robin or custom policy, look-aside LB / xDS), plus max connection age so clients reconnect and rebalance.

Deep answer: Kubernetes ClusterIP is L4. Use headless services with client-side LB, or a mesh. Also propagate deadlines and apply outlier detection.

Trade-offs: Client complexity vs proxy hops.

Follow-ups: 1. What's xDS? → Envoy's dynamic configuration APIs, also usable by gRPC clients (proxyless mesh). 2. Why max connection age? → It forces periodic rebalancing.

Red flags: "Kubernetes Service handles it."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Knows the headless service / xDS options.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ One of twelve pods is slow but passes health checks, and 40 % of checkouts fail. Explain and fix it.

30-second answer: Each checkout makes ~6 calls, so P(at least one hits the bad pod) ≈ 1 − (11/12)⁶ ≈ 41 %. Round-robin keeps sending it 1/12 of traffic, and shallow health checks don't notice. Fix it with latency-aware balancing (P2C with EWMA), passive outlier ejection, readiness reflecting real capacity, idempotent-only retries on different instances, and per-instance latency alerts.

Deep answer: Also find the root cause (a node disk problem → node-level health/taint automation). The simulation evidence: a slow node's share drops from 10 % to < 1 %, and p99 goes from unbounded to 75 ms.

Trade-offs: Balancer complexity vs tail reliability.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not just a tighter health check? → It checks the probe endpoint, not the real workload. 2. Why doesn't least-connections alone suffice? → It helps, but latency weighting reacts to slowness faster.

Red flags: "Restart the pod."

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Fan-out probability math plus a systemic fix.

Q11 [B3] Why P2C instead of always choosing the least-loaded backend?

30-second answer: With many independent balancers and slightly stale load data, "always least loaded" makes every balancer pick the same backend simultaneously (herding), which then overloads. P2C compares only two random candidates. That's almost as good at avoiding bad backends, spreads choices, is O(1), and is robust to stale information.

Deep answer: Theory: max load improves exponentially over random choice (O(log log n)). In practice, Envoy's least-request and Finagle/Linkerd use P2C variants, often with EWMA latency.

Trade-offs: A tiny loss vs the global optimum, in exchange for robustness.

Follow-ups: 1. What load signal? → In-flight requests, possibly × EWMA latency. 2. Why peak-EWMA? → It reacts immediately to slowness and recovers gradually.

Red flags: Unaware of herding.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Explains stale information and herd behaviour.

Q12 [B3] Design outlier ejection. What can go wrong?

30-second answer: Watch real responses per instance. Eject after N consecutive errors or when latency or success rate deviates from peers. Eject for a period that grows on repeated ejection, return on probation, and cap the ejected fraction (for example 50 %).

Deep answer: What can go wrong: a shared-dependency failure makes every instance fail, and without a cap you'd eject the whole pool. Low-traffic instances need minimum request volumes before statistical ejection. Ejection hides problems, so alert on ejections. Also coordinate with the circuit breaker (per route) vs ejection (per instance).

Trade-offs: Fast isolation vs over-ejection.

Follow-ups: 1. Success-rate ejection? → Compare with the fleet mean minus a standard-deviation multiple. 2. Circuit breaker vs outlier detection? → Per dependency vs per instance.

Red flags: No max-ejection cap.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: The correlated-failure cap and alerting.

Q13 [B3] ⭐ How do you prevent identity spoofing between the gateway and services?

30-second answer: The gateway strips client-supplied identity and internal headers, validates the token, and sets identity headers itself. Services are unreachable except through the gateway or mesh (NetworkPolicy + mTLS identities). Services still check resource ownership. Alternatively, forward the original JWT and have services validate it.

Deep answer: With a mesh, use workload identity (mTLS) to verify the caller is the gateway, then trust its headers. For zero trust, propagate a signed internal token (short-lived) rather than plain headers.

Trade-offs: Validating everywhere costs CPU but is stronger.

Follow-ups: 1. What if an internal service is compromised? → Signed tokens limit forged identities, and authorization checks limit damage. 2. What about service-to-service user context? → Token exchange (RFC 8693) or propagated JWT.

Red flags: Services directly exposed with trusted headers.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Network plus identity plus authorization layers.

Q14 [B3] Implement distributed rate limiting at the gateway: design choices?

30-second answer: A token bucket per key (user, API key, IP range) in Redis via an atomic Lua script (Spring Cloud Gateway's RedisRateLimiter), with limits per route class. Return 429 with Retry-After and RateLimit-* headers. Fail open with a local fallback if Redis fails, and fail closed for abusive classes. Hash-tag keys to spread load.

Deep answer: Cost: one Redis call per request, so at 120 K req/s you need multiple shards. Alternatives: local limiters with approximate global limits (divide the limit by pod count), or sliding-window counters (Ch 39). Protect OTP endpoints with stricter, identity-based limits.

Trade-offs: Accuracy vs latency and dependency.

Follow-ups: 1. Token bucket vs sliding window? → Bursts vs smoothness (Ch 18, 39). 2. Why not IP-only limits? → CGNAT (Ch 03).

Red flags: Per-pod in-memory limits presented as global.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Failure behaviour of the limiter itself.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design global traffic management for an India-focused platform with DR.

30-second answer: Anycast CDN/WAF with Indian PoPs terminates TLS near users and routes to the primary region's L7 LB (Mumbai) based on health, with a health-checked failover origin (Hyderabad) for DR. DNS points at the CDN, so failover doesn't depend on DNS TTLs. Regional stacks are three-AZ.

Deep answer: Define RTO/RPO (Ch 27), keep the DR region warm (scaled down with data replication), rehearse failovers, handle sticky data concerns (sessions, idempotency keys, data residency), and monitor per-PoP latency. Multi-region active-active only if the business case justifies the data-consistency complexity.

Trade-offs: Cost and complexity vs RTO.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not GeoDNS only? → Slow failover due to caching; the resolver's location isn't the user's. 2. Anycast TCP issues? → Route changes can break connections; QUIC is resilient.

Red flags: Relying on 1-hour DNS TTLs for failover.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Edge-controlled failover with rehearsals.

Q16 [B4] API gateway vs service mesh: how do you divide responsibilities?

30-second answer: Gateway (north-south): client-facing auth, API keys, rate limits, quotas, API versioning, WAF integration and public routing. Mesh (east-west): mTLS workload identity, service-to-service authorization, retries and timeouts (one layer!), outlier detection, telemetry and traffic shifting for internal canaries.

Deep answer: Avoid duplicate retries and timeouts across both. Mesh ingress can serve as the gateway in an Envoy-based stack. Policy ownership: the platform team owns both, with self-service configs per team.

Trade-offs: Two systems vs a unified control plane.

Follow-ups: 1. Do you need both? → Small platforms: gateway + libraries. Larger: both. 2. What about ambient mesh? → Lower overhead, still maturing (Ch 17).

Red flags: Retries configured in both layers.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Clear boundary plus a single-retry-layer rule.

Q17 [B4] How do you run progressive delivery at the edge?

30-second answer: Deploy a canary version beside stable. Route internal testers by header, then a small weighted slice (1–5 %), ideally by user hash for consistency. Compare canary vs stable SLOs (errors, latency, business metrics) automatically, and promote in steps or roll back instantly by weight. Feature flags separate deploy from release.

Deep answer: Tools: Argo Rollouts / Flagger with mesh or gateway weights. Guard against data-migration incompatibility (expand/contract, Ch 28). Keep canaries long enough to see the daily traffic shape.

Trade-offs: Speed vs safety.

Follow-ups: 1. Why user-hash routing? → Consistent experience, and cleaner metrics. 2. How do you prevent outsiders opting in? → Strip canary headers at the edge.

Red flags: Manual canaries without metrics comparison.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Automated analysis and consistency of assignment.

Q18 [B4] Zone-aware routing: when does it help, and when does it hurt?

30-second answer: It helps by cutting latency and cross-AZ cost when callers and capacity are balanced across zones. It hurts when callers are skewed (all traffic in one zone overloads it), when a zone is partially degraded, or when autoscaling is uneven. Always include health and load spill-over.

Deep answer: The L4 simulation reproduced the failure: with all callers in one zone and no load check, p50 exceeded 150 s. With a load-ratio spill-over it's healthy. Keep per-zone capacity balanced (topology spread constraints), and measure cross-zone bytes.

Trade-offs: Cost and latency vs resilience.

Follow-ups: 1. Kubernetes support? → Topology-aware routing / trafficDistribution: PreferClose, which has its own safeguards. 2. What about zonal outages? → Spill to healthy zones automatically.

Red flags: Hard zone pinning.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Evidence-based spill-over rules.

Q19 [B4] The gateway is a single point of failure. How do you make it not one?

30-second answer: Run many stateless pods across AZs behind a redundant cloud LB. Keep gateway state external (Redis for limits, with fallbacks) and config in GitOps with validation and canaries. Pre-scale for events, shed load by route priority, avoid heavy synchronous dependencies (auth keys cached), and have a break-glass bypass for critical internal traffic.

Deep answer: Protect against bad config pushes (the most common gateway outage): staged rollout, route tests, instant rollback. Separate gateways per trust zone (public, partner, internal) to limit blast radius, or cells for very large scale (Ch 34).

Trade-offs: More gateways mean more to operate.

Follow-ups: 1. Largest gateway risk? → A config change affecting all routes. 2. How do you test gateway config? → Route unit tests (like L3) in CI.

Red flags: Hand-edited production gateway config.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: Config-change safety and blast-radius segmentation.

Q20 [B4] Spring Cloud Gateway vs Envoy-based gateway vs a managed cloud gateway: how do you choose?

30-second answer: Spring Cloud Gateway: Java-coded policies, Spring Security, fits Java teams, and you own scaling. Envoy-based: high performance, rich balancing (P2C, outlier detection, zone-aware) built in, a polyglot platform, and mesh alignment, but config and extension (Wasm/Lua) skills are needed. Managed: least ops, but per-request cost at scale, feature limits, and lock-in.

Deep answer: Decide with a matrix (fit, operability, cost at 120 K req/s, latency overhead, security features, team skills, mesh roadmap). For this platform: Spring Cloud Gateway now with a custom balancer, and re-evaluate an Envoy gateway when the mesh arrives (ADR-032 revisit clause).

Trade-offs: Control vs operational burden vs cost.

Follow-ups: 1. When is managed clearly better? → Low-volume APIs and small teams. 2. What's the migration path? → Run both behind the LB and move routes gradually.

Red flags: Choosing on familiarity alone, ignoring cost at scale.

What distinguishes a 15-year answer: A revisit trigger tied to the mesh roadmap.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. The edge chain (DNS/anycast → CDN/WAF → L7 LB → gateway → services) decides where every request goes, how long it waits, and whether it's retried or allowed.
  2. L4 balances connections, L7 balances requests. Long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connections need L7 or client-side balancing.
  3. Equal-share algorithms (round-robin, random) break on slow-but-healthy backends. Use P2C with latency (peak-EWMA) and passive outlier ejection capped at 50 %.
  4. Liveness never checks dependencies. Readiness is instance-local. Probes alone miss slow pods.
  5. Avoid sticky sessions for state. Use consistent hashing only for performance affinity.
  6. Retries: idempotent only, a different instance, one layer, jittered, within a budget. Writes are retried by clients with idempotency keys.
  7. The gateway strips then sets identity headers from validated tokens. Services must be reachable only through the gateway or mesh, and they still check ownership.
  8. Per-route timeouts from latency budgets, and streams exempted by explicit, ordered routes.
  9. Zone-aware routing needs load-aware spill-over, or skewed callers overload a zone.
  10. Global failover belongs at an anycast edge with health-checked origins, not in DNS TTLs.

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Choose Balance HTTP requests across pods with varied performance P2C × peak-EWMA + outlier ejection Cache or state affinity Consistent / rendezvous hashing (bounded load) gRPC / HTTP/2 L7 or client-side LB + max connection age Canary release Weighted routes (user-hash for UI changes) + tester header Protect upstreams from abuse Redis token bucket per identity at the gateway Stream routes No response timeout; explicit route order; idle timeouts (Ch 03) Regional failover Anycast CDN/global LB with health-checked origins East-west traffic policy Service mesh (Ch 17) or shared client libraries

docs.title: 09. Scalability Fundamentals ⭐
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 02, Ch 05, Ch 07, Ch 08 · What you will build: The cart service, taken from an Amdahl/USL model fitted to load-test data (L1) to stateless pods with externalized sessions (L2), first-class Redis carts with atomic guest-to-customer merge and scale-safe jobs (L3), and city-level Z-axis partitioning with online shard moves (L4) · Reading time: 100 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: we added pods and it got slower
docs.text:
The grocery platform had grown 10× in a year. For the festival sale, the cart team did what had always worked: they raised the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler's maximum from 20 to 80 pods for cart-service.

At 8:00 pm the HPA did its job and scaled from 20 to 64 pods. Cart throughput dropped from ~17,000 to ~13,000 requests/s, and p99 latency tripled. Three hidden costs grew faster than the pod count:

  1. Contention. Every "add to cart" took a Redis lock on a global cart:config key to read the per-customer item limit. More pods meant more waiters on the same key.
  2. Coherency. Each pod held an in-memory promotion cache and broadcast an invalidation to every other pod whenever a promotion changed. With N pods that's N × (N − 1) messages per change. At 64 pods, promotion churn during the sale alone generated millions of messages per minute.
  3. Connection limits. 64 pods × a PostgreSQL pool of 20 = 1,280 connections against a max_connections of 500 (behind PgBouncer, which was now queueing). Cart snapshots to PostgreSQL waited seconds for a connection.

Scaling back to 40 pods improved throughput. Afterwards, a 30-minute load test at 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 24 pods, fitted with the Universal Scalability Law, would have predicted this: peak capacity at about 43 pods, then decline.

The thesis of this chapter

Horizontal scaling is a property you design in, not a knob you turn. A system scales only as far as its shared parts allow: the locks everyone waits on, the coordination everyone does, and the connections everyone holds. Find those, remove or partition them, and measure before you buy capacity.

docs.title: 1.2 Where this lives in the grocery platform
docs.text: Service What limits its scaling Scaling move catalog-service, search-service Read QPS X-axis clones + caches (Ch 07) cart-service Session state, per-customer atomicity, connection budgets Stateless pods + Redis carts + Z-axis by city inventory-service Hot rows (Ch 05), single-writer per store/SKU Short transactions, then Z-axis by store order-service Write throughput on one primary Partition by time, then Z-axis by region (Ch 11) tracking-service Write-heavy pings (Ch 06) Kafka partitions + independent sinks notification-service Third-party provider rate limits (SMS, WhatsApp) Queues with rate-limited consumers Scheduled jobs (abandoned-cart reminders, slot release) "Runs on every pod" duplication Leader election / distributed job locks

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text: Band After this chapter you can… B1 Explain vertical vs horizontal scaling, why stateless services scale, and where session state should live B2 Externalize sessions, find hidden state, use read replicas, and apply the X/Y/Z scale cube B3 Use Amdahl and the USL to explain and predict scaling limits, budget connections, and make jobs scale-safe B4 Plan a platform's 1 → 1M-user journey, choose partition keys and cells, and defend when not to scale out

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: billing counters and the manager's approval B1
docs.text:
A supermarket adds billing counters for the festival. Throughput rises, until two things happen:

  • Every bill over ₹5,000 needs the floor manager's signature. One manager, many counters: queues form at the manager, not at the counters. That's contention (σ).
  • Every counter must tell every other counter whenever a price changes. With 5 counters that's 20 messages. With 40 counters it's 1,560, and cashiers spend their time on messages instead of customers. That's coherency (κ).

Adding counters helps while counters are the bottleneck. Past a point, it makes the queue at the manager longer and the chatter louder. The fix isn't more counters. It's more managers (partition the approval) and fewer broadcasts (publish price changes to a board everyone reads).

docs.title: 2.2 What scalability means B1 B2
docs.text:
Term Meaning Grocery example Performance How fast one request is Cart add p99 = 40 ms Scalability How capacity grows as you add resources 2× pods → ~1.9× throughput Elasticity How quickly capacity follows demand, up and down Pre-scale at 7:30 pm, scale in at 11 pm (Ch 02) Efficiency Capacity per rupee ₹ per 1,000 cart operations

Scalability always has a dimension:

Dimension Question Typical limit Load (req/s) Can we serve 10× traffic? Shared locks, databases, connection budgets Data volume Can we hold 10× data? Single-primary storage, index size, backup/restore time Geography Can we serve new cities or regions? Latency, data residency, per-region ops Tenants / sellers Can we onboard 10× sellers? Noisy neighbours, per-tenant config (Ch 30) Organization Can 10× engineers work in parallel? Shared codebase and deploys (Ch 16, 37)

docs.title: 2.3 Vertical vs horizontal scaling ⭐ B1 B2
docs.text:
Vertical (scale up) Horizontal (scale out) How Bigger machine: more vCPU, RAM, faster disk More machines or pods Code changes None Needs stateless design or partitioned state Ceiling The largest instance you can buy Set by shared components (USL) Failure isolation One big failure domain Many small ones Cost curve Superlinear at the top end Roughly linear, plus coordination overhead Time to add Minutes to hours (often a restart) Seconds to minutes (Ch 02 warm-up) Best for Databases before sharding, stateful systems, early stage Stateless services, read paths, anything behind a load balancer

Vertical scaling is underrated

A modern 64-vCPU, 512 GB database server handles a surprising amount of load. Moving the orders database from 16 to 32 vCPU buys a year of growth in an afternoon. Sharding it costs two quarters of engineering and permanent complexity (Ch 11). Scale up the stateful parts while it's cheap, and scale out the stateless parts from day one.

docs.title: 2.4 Amdahl's law and the Universal Scalability Law ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Amdahl's law. If a fraction s of the work is serial, speed-up with N workers is capped at 1/s:

\[ S(N) = \frac{N}{1 + s(N-1)} \qquad \lim_{N\to\infty} S(N) = \frac{1}{s} \]

Universal Scalability Law (Gunther). It adds a coherency term for the cost of keeping workers consistent with each other, which grows with the number of pairs:

\[ C(N) = \frac{N}{1 + \sigma(N-1) + \kappa N(N-1)} \] Parameter Meaning Effect σ (contention) Fraction of time waiting on a shared resource Throughput plateaus (Amdahl) κ (coherency / crosstalk) Cost of pairwise coordination Throughput peaks, then declines (retrograde) N* = √((1 − σ) / κ) Pod count at peak capacity Adding pods beyond it makes things worse

L1 (§5) computes both and fits σ and κ from load-test measurements. The real output:

B. USL: σ = 0.03 (contention), κ = 0.0005 (coherency)
     8 pods →   6.5x capacity
    32 pods →  13.2x capacity
    44 pods →  13.6x capacity   ← peak: N* = √((1−σ)/κ)
    96 pods →  11.4x capacity
   fitted σ = 0.0303, κ = 0.000523 → peak at ~43 pods, max ≈ 19,634 req/s
   halving κ (e.g. stop broadcasting to every pod) → peak at ~60 pods, max ≈ 23,733 req/s

Where σ and κ come from in real systems:

Source σ or κ Example Fix Global lock / single hot key σ cart:config lock (§1.1), a hot DB row (Ch 05) Remove the lock, read immutable config, partition the key Single-writer database σ All pods writing one primary Batch, partition, move writes off the hot path Serialized sections in code σ synchronized around a shared map Lock-free structures, per-key locks Broadcast invalidation to all pods κ N × (N − 1) messages (§1.1) Publish to a log everyone reads (one write, N reads) Cluster membership / gossip κ Embedded caches that replicate to every member External cache, or smaller clusters Distributed locks and consensus κ Every request coordinating through a lock service Avoid per-request coordination (Ch 20) Cross-shard queries κ Scatter-gather to every partition Route by partition key; read models Connection pools to one DB σ + κ Pods × pool > the DB's useful concurrency Pool budgets, PgBouncer (Ch 05)

Fitting the USL needs real measurements

Measure throughput at several pod counts (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, …) with the same workload mix, with each run saturated (enough load to keep the pods busy) and long enough to be stable. Fit σ and κ, then predict. Treat the prediction as a warning light, not a guarantee: the model assumes the bottlenecks don't change shape between measurements.

docs.title: 2.5 Stateless services ⭐ B1 B2
docs.text:
A service is stateless when any instance can serve any request, and losing an instance loses nothing but in-flight work. State still exists; it just lives in a store designed to hold it.

Hidden state Why it breaks scaling Where it should live In-memory HTTP sessions Sticky sessions required; a pod loss logs users out Redis (Spring Session) or signed tokens Carts in pod memory Lost on scale-in or deploy Redis (+ DB snapshot) Uploaded files on local disk Only one pod has them Object storage (S3-compatible) In-process caches without invalidation Pods disagree (Ch 07) Short TTL + broadcast, or an external cache Scheduled jobs running on every pod Duplicate reminders, double processing Leader election or a job lock (§2.7) Per-pod rate limits Limit multiplies with pod count Central limiter (Ch 08) Local counters and sequences Duplicate ids DB sequences, UUIDv7/Snowflake (Ch 20) WebSocket/SSE connections Inherent per connection Resumable streams, no stickiness (Ch 03)

The 12-factor rules that matter most for scaling: processes are stateless and share nothing (factor VI), config comes from the environment (III), backing services are attached resources (IV), and processes are disposable, meaning fast startup and graceful shutdown (IX).

docs.title: 2.6 Session externalization ⭐ B2
docs.text:
Option How Pros Cons Use Sticky sessions LB pins a user to a pod No code change Uneven load; lost on pod loss or deploy (Ch 08) Avoid Replicated in-memory sessions App servers copy sessions to peers No external store κ grows with cluster size; memory × N Avoid at scale External session store Spring Session with Redis (or JDBC) Any pod serves any request; survives restarts A Redis round trip per request; session blob size Web apps with server sessions Client-side tokens (JWT) Signed claims travel with each request Zero server session lookups Revocation is harder; size limits; claims must be small APIs and mobile apps (Ch 08, 23)

For the grocery platform: identity is a JWT validated at the gateway (Ch 08), so there's no server-side login session. The cart is not session data. It's first-class state keyed by customer (or by a device-issued guest cart id) in Redis, with a periodic snapshot to PostgreSQL. That distinction matters: a session blob is rewritten whole on every change and can't be updated atomically from two tabs.

Guest cart → customer cart merge is the classic correctness problem of externalized state:

  • A guest adds items on the web, then logs in with OTP. The customer already has a cart from the app last week.
  • Both carts must merge exactly once, atomically, even if two pods receive "login" and "add item" at the same moment.
  • L3 implements it as a single Redis Lua script with a merge marker for idempotency.

docs.title: 2.7 Scheduled jobs and singletons in a horizontal world B2 B3
docs.text:
With 40 pods, @Scheduled runs 40 times.

Approach How When Job lock (ShedLock, Redis SET NX PX, DB row lock) Each run acquires a named lock with a lease; others skip Periodic jobs that must run once per interval Leader election (Kubernetes Lease, ZooKeeper/etcd) One pod is leader and runs singletons Long-running singleton processes Partitioned work (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, Kafka partitions) Every pod takes a disjoint slice Large batches that should use all pods External scheduler (Kubernetes CronJob) Runs a separate job pod Batch jobs that don't belong in the service

Whatever the mechanism, make jobs idempotent. Leases expire, and a slow or paused pod can still be running when another acquires the lock (fencing, Ch 20).

docs.title: 2.8 Scaling reads and writes B2 B3
docs.text:
To scale… In order of cost Reads Fix queries → cache (Ch 07) → CDN → read replicas (Ch 05) → read models / CQRS (Ch 15) → search engine (Ch 22) Writes Fix queries and indexes → batch and coalesce → move non-critical writes async (queue) → vertical scale → functional split (a DB per service) → partition / shard (Ch 11)

Reads are easy to scale because copies are cheap. Writes are hard because every copy must agree. Most scaling work is moving writes off shared hot paths.

docs.title: 2.9 Connection limits: the hidden ceiling ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Adding pods multiplies every per-pod resource that points at something shared:

Resource Limit What happens at scale-out Guard DB connections max_connections, and far lower useful concurrency (Ch 05) Pods × pool exceeds budget; queueing, context switching Pool from Little's Law; PgBouncer; budget checks (Ch 02) Redis connections maxclients (10 K default), per-shard CPU Connection storms on deploy Shared multiplexed clients (Lettuce), limits Kafka consumers Consumers per group ≤ partitions Pods beyond the partition count sit idle Partitions sized for max consumers (Ch 14) Third-party APIs Razorpay, SMS/WhatsApp providers' rate limits More pods = more 429s, not more throughput Central rate-limited queue NAT gateway ports Connections per destination (Ch 03) Outbound failures to one partner Pooling, more egress IPs File descriptors ulimit -n Streaming or pooled services hit FD limits Raise limits, load test LB / gateway Connections, new connections per second Rejected connections during reconnect storms Pre-scaling, jitter (Ch 03)

The fastest way to take down a database is to autoscale its clients

An HPA with maxReplicas: 100 and a pool of 20 is a promise of up to 2,000 connections. Set maxReplicas from the connection budget and the USL peak, not from hope.

docs.title: 2.10 The scale cube (X, Y, Z) ⭐ B2 B4
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    O["One monolith,<br/>one DB"] -->|"X-axis: clone"| X["N identical stateless copies<br/>behind a load balancer"]
    O -->|"Y-axis: split by function"| Y["cart, catalog, order, payment...<br/>each with its own data"]
    O -->|"Z-axis: split by data"| Z["Same code, each copy owns a<br/>slice of data (city, customer, store)"]
    X & Y & Z --> ALL["Real platforms combine all three:<br/>Y-split services, X-scaled pods,<br/>Z-partitioned hot data"]
Axis How Scales Costs Grocery example X (horizontal duplication) Clone stateless instances Request volume Shared data stays a bottleneck 40 catalog-service pods Y (functional decomposition) Split by capability or bounded context Team autonomy, independent scaling, fault isolation Distributed transactions, network calls (Ch 13, 16) cart, order, payment as separate services Z (data partitioning) Each copy owns a subset of data, routed by a key Data volume, writes, blast radius Routing, rebalancing, cross-partition queries (Ch 11) Carts and inventory partitioned by city; cells per region (Ch 34)

Choosing a Z-axis key for the grocery platform: city (or zone within a mega-city) is natural because orders, stores, riders and inventory rarely cross cities. It keeps most queries partition-local and limits a failure to one city. The risk is skew (Bengaluru is far bigger than Mysuru), handled by giving big cities their own partitions and packing small cities together.

docs.title: 2.11 Elasticity: scaling on the right signal B2 B3
docs.text:
Signal Good for Pitfall CPU CPU-bound services I/O-bound services saturate on connections or latency at low CPU In-flight requests / concurrency Most request-response services Needs a custom metric Requests per second per pod Predictable per-request cost Doesn't reflect slow dependencies Queue depth / consumer lag (KEDA) Workers and consumers Consumers beyond the partition count do nothing Schedule (cron) Known events (Ch 02) Needs a forecast

Autoscaling has reaction time (metric scrape, HPA sync, node provisioning, JVM warm-up), so it handles gradual growth and not step changes. Always pair it with a maxReplicas derived from connection budgets and the USL peak, and with admission control or load shedding for what can't be scaled in time (Ch 18).

docs.title: 2.12 The 1 → 1 M users journey ⭐ B2 → B4
docs.text:
Each stage is triggered by a measured limit, not by fashion. The numbers use the Ch 00 assumptions (~20 API calls per user per day on average; peak 5× average).

Stage Users (DAU) Peak req/s What breaks Move 0. One box 100 < 1 Nothing yet; a single point of failure App + PostgreSQL on one VM; daily backups 1. Separate the database 1 K ~1 App deploys restart the DB; resource fights Managed PostgreSQL; app on its own VM 2. Stateless app behind a LB 10 K ~10 One app instance = downtime on deploy; sessions in memory 2+ app instances, LB, sessions/carts in Redis, uploads in object storage 3. Cache and CDN 50 K ~60 Catalog reads dominate DB CPU CDN for images; Redis cache (Ch 07); fix slow queries 4. Async work and read replicas 200 K ~250 Invoices, SMS and emails block requests; report queries slow the primary Queue + workers (Kafka/RabbitMQ); read replica for reports/history 5. Split hot capabilities (Y-axis) 500 K ~600 One deployable for 6 teams; search needs a different datastore; tracking writes swamp the DB (Ch 06) Modular monolith → extract search, tracking, payments; DB per service 6. Multi-AZ, pre-scaling, data partitioning (Z-axis) 1 M ~1.2 K (sale starts 20–40×) AZ outage = platform outage; sale spikes; single-primary writes for carts and inventory 3-AZ everything, cron pre-scaling (Ch 02), city partitioning for carts and inventory 7. Cells and regions 5 M+ 6 K+ Blast radius of a bad deploy or noisy city; DR region Cell-based architecture per region or city group (Ch 34); DR region (Ch 27) 
flowchart TB
    subgraph S2["Stage 2: stateless behind a LB"]
        LB2["LB"] --> A1["app"] & A2["app"]
        A1 & A2 --> R2[("Redis<br/>sessions, carts")]
        A1 & A2 --> P2[("PostgreSQL")]
    end
    subgraph S6["Stage 6: Y-split, X-scaled, Z-partitioned"]
        GW6["gateway (Ch 08)"] --> C6["cart pods"] & O6["order pods"] & CAT6["catalog pods"]
        C6 --> RB[("Redis: BLR")] & RM[("Redis: MUM")] & RS[("Redis: small cities")]
        O6 --> OP[("orders DB")]
        CAT6 --> CC[("cache + catalog DB")]
    end

The journey isn't a ladder you must climb

Many profitable businesses stay at stage 3–4 forever. Each stage adds permanent operating cost. Move up only when a measured limit (Ch 02 estimates, load tests, USL fits) says the current stage can't meet the next year's forecast.

docs.title: 3.1 Component view: a stateless, partitioned cart service
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    APP["App / web<br/>(JWT, or signed guest cart id)"] --> GW["api-gateway<br/>X-User-Id, X-City"]
    GW --> P1["cart pod"] & P2["cart pod"] & PN["cart pod ... N"]
    P1 & P2 & PN --> RT["CityShardRouter<br/>(shard map v7)"]
    RT --> RB[("Redis shard: blr")]
    RT --> RM[("Redis shard: mum")]
    RT --> RX[("Redis shard: small-cities")]
    P1 & P2 & PN -. "snapshot every 5 min (bounded pool)" .-> PG[("PostgreSQL<br/>cart_snapshot")]
    JOB["abandoned-cart job<br/>(runs once: Redis job lock)"] --> RT

docs.title: 3.2 Sequence: happy path, guest adds items, logs in on a different pod, carts merge once
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant W as Web (guest)
    participant P1 as cart pod 1
    participant P2 as cart pod 7
    participant R as Redis (blr shard)
    W->>P1: PUT /carts/guest/items/ATTA-5KG qty 1 (guest cart id g-91, signed)
    P1->>R: EVALSHA set_qty(cart:g-91, ATTA-5KG, 1)
    R-->>P1: ok (1 line)
    W->>W: OTP login → JWT for cust-42
    W->>P2: POST /carts/merge {guestCartId: g-91}
    P2->>R: EVALSHA merge(cart:cust-42, cart:g-91, marker merged:g-91)
    R-->>P2: merged 1 line (customer cart now 3 lines), guest cart deleted
    P2-->>W: 200 cart (3 lines)
    Note over P1,P2: No sticky sessions: any pod can serve any step

docs.title: 3.3 Sequence: failure path, retry of a merge and a pod dying mid-request
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant W as Web
    participant P2 as cart pod 7
    participant P3 as cart pod 3
    participant R as Redis
    W->>P2: POST /carts/merge {g-91}
    P2->>R: EVALSHA merge(...) → committed atomically
    P2--xW: pod killed (scale-in) before responding
    W->>P3: retry POST /carts/merge {g-91}
    P3->>R: EVALSHA merge(...)
    R-->>P3: marker merged:g-91 exists → 0 lines merged (no double quantities)
    P3-->>W: 200 cart (same 3 lines)

What the system guarantees after this failure path

The merge happens exactly once, because the Lua script checks and sets the merge marker in the same atomic step as the merge itself. A retry on any pod returns the same cart without doubling quantities. Scale-in or a crash loses only the in-flight response, never cart state.

docs.title: 3.4 State: cart lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> GUEST: first item (signed guest cart id)
    [*] --> ACTIVE: first item (logged in)
    GUEST --> ACTIVE: login → merge (exactly once)
    GUEST --> EXPIRED: 7 days idle (TTL)
    ACTIVE --> ACTIVE: add / update / remove (TTL refreshed)
    ACTIVE --> CHECKED_OUT: order placed (Ch 04)
    ACTIVE --> ABANDONED: 2 h idle (reminder job, once)
    ABANDONED --> ACTIVE: customer returns
    ABANDONED --> EXPIRED: 30 days idle
    CHECKED_OUT --> [*]
    EXPIRED --> [*]

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Cart Service Scaling to 10×
docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers Cart team / Platform, SRE, Checkout Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-035 Carts as first-class Redis state, partitioned by city; ADR-036 maxReplicas from connection budget and USL fit

1. Context & Problem. Scaling cart-service from 20 to 64 pods reduced throughput (§1.1): a global config lock (σ), all-pod broadcast invalidation (κ), and a connection budget overrun. Carts lived in server sessions, requiring sticky routing for guests.

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: 10× cart throughput headroom over last festival; no scaling cliff below the planned max replicas; any pod serves any request; exactly-once guest merge; carts survive pod loss.
  • Non-goals: checkout pricing (the SoR re-prices, Ch 07); cross-city carts (a customer's cart belongs to the delivery city).

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement FR-1 Add, update, remove cart lines; view cart; merge guest into customer cart on login NFR-1 60 K cart ops/s at P90 sale peak, p99 ≤ 30 ms in-service NFR-2 USL-fitted peak N* ≥ 2 × planned max replicas NFR-3 Σ (pods × pool) ≤ connection budget for every shared store NFR-4 Merge is idempotent and atomic under concurrent requests NFR-5 Losing any pod or zone loses no cart state; losing a Redis shard affects one partition only

4. Capacity estimates and scaling analysis.

Item Calculation Result Cart ops at P90 sale peak Ch 02: ~14.5 K cart req/s × ~4 Redis ops per request ~60 K Redis ops/s Carts in Redis 1.5 M active × ~1 KB ~1.5 GB (+ replicas) Load test (pods → req/s) 1 → 1,470 … 24 → 17,800 σ ≈ 0.030, κ ≈ 0.00052, N ≈ 43* (L1 fit) Planned peak pods (Ch 02 method) 14.5 K req/s ÷ ~1.2 K per pod × 1.5 AZ headroom ~18–24 pods NFR-2 check before fixes N* 43 ≥ 2 × 24? Fails (43 < 48) After removing the config lock (σ → ~0.01) and broadcasts (κ → ~0.0001) re-test Target N* ≥ 90 (verified by load test) DB connection budget (snapshots) Snapshot writes ~100/s × 20 ms ≈ 2 busy Pool of 2 per pod → 48 at 24 pods Redis connections Lettuce: 1 multiplexed connection per shard per pod 24 pods × 3 shards = 72

What the analysis tells us

The fleet was never short of pods. It was short of independence. Fixing σ and κ roughly doubles the useful pod count and raises the throughput ceiling, while adding pods to the old design would have lowered it.

5. Proposed design.

  1. Stateless pods. Identity from the gateway JWT. Guest carts are identified by a server-issued, HMAC-signed guest cart id (no server session). No sticky sessions.
  2. Carts are first-class Redis state. One HASH per cart (sku → qty), with atomic Lua scripts for set-quantity (with max lines and max quantity per line) and merge (with an idempotency marker). TTL refreshed on write. A snapshot job writes changed carts to PostgreSQL every 5 minutes.
  3. Remove σ and κ sources. Cart limits come from immutable config loaded at startup and refreshed through a versioned snapshot (the Ch 01 pattern), with no per-request lock. Promotion changes are published once to a Kafka topic, and pods read it (one write, N reads) instead of pod-to-pod broadcasts.
  4. Z-axis by city. A CityShardRouter maps city to Redis shard via a versioned shard map. Bengaluru and Mumbai get dedicated shards, and small cities share one. A city can move between shards online (lazy copy-on-read, L4).
  5. Scale-safe jobs. The abandoned-cart reminder runs once per interval under a Redis job lock with a lease, and it's idempotent (a reminder marker per cart).
  6. Elasticity guardrails. HPA on in-flight requests per pod. maxReplicas = min(connection-budget limit, N*/2).

7. Alternatives considered.

Option Pros Cons Verdict Keep carts in server sessions, add sticky sessions No code change Uneven load; carts lost on deploy; session blob contention Rejected Spring Session (Redis) with cart in the session Stateless pods quickly Whole-session rewrites; last-write-wins across tabs; no atomic merge Interim step (L2), rejected as the end state Carts in PostgreSQL only One store, transactional 60 K ops/s of small writes on the orders cluster Rejected (snapshot only) Carts as Redis HASHes + Lua + city partitioning + DB snapshots Atomic ops, fast, partitionable, survives pod loss Redis is a critical store: needs replicas, a snapshot for recovery Chosen Just raise maxReplicas Instant Retrograde scaling (§1.1) Rejected

8. Failure modes. A Redis shard failover: a few seconds of errors for that city only. Carts are replicated, and in the worst case they're restored from the last 5-minute snapshot. Shard map misconfiguration: the router refuses unknown cities and uses the last good map version. A job lock lease expires mid-run: the job's per-cart idempotency markers prevent duplicate reminders.

10. Observability. Throughput per pod vs pod count (a live USL view), lock wait time, broadcast or message rates per pod, connection counts per store vs budget, Redis ops per shard, merge outcomes (merged, already_merged, empty), job lock acquisitions.

14. Decision (ADR-035/036 summary). Carts are first-class Redis state, partitioned by city, mutated only through atomic scripts, with DB snapshots for recovery. Every horizontally scaled service publishes a USL fit from its latest load test, and its maxReplicas is the lower of the connection-budget limit and half the fitted peak. Per-request global locks and all-pod broadcasts are prohibited on hot paths.

We build the cart service's scalability four times:

Level New requirement that forces the step L1 "How far can adding pods take us, and why does it stop?" (Amdahl, USL, fitting a load test) L2 "Any pod must serve any request." (externalized sessions with Spring Session + Redis) L3 "Carts are real state: atomic line updates from any pod, exactly-once guest merge, limits, jobs that run once." L4 "Partition carts by city (Z-axis) and move a city between shards online, with stale pods and no lost lines."

docs.title: L1 — Concept: Amdahl, USL and fitting a load test (plain Java) B1 B3
docs.text:
// ScalabilityL1.java — run with: java ScalabilityL1.java
// Why "just add pods" stops working:
//   A. Amdahl's law: a serial fraction caps speed-up
//   B. Universal Scalability Law (USL): contention (σ) + coherency (κ) → throughput PEAKS, then falls
//   C. Fit σ and κ from load-test measurements and predict the peak BEFORE you buy the pods
import java.util.*;

public class ScalabilityL1 {

    /** Amdahl: speed-up with N workers when a fraction s of the work is serial. */
    static double amdahl(int n, double s) { return n / (1 + s * (n - 1)); }

    /** USL relative capacity C(N) = N / (1 + σ(N−1) + κ·N(N−1)). */
    static double usl(int n, double sigma, double kappa) {
        return n / (1 + sigma * (n - 1) + kappa * n * (n - 1.0));
    }

    /**
     * Fit σ, κ from measured throughput X(N). With C(N) = X(N)/X(1) and x = N−1:
     *   N/C(N) − 1 = (σ+κ)·x + κ·x²      → least squares through the origin for a·x + b·x²
     */
    static double[] fitUsl(int[] n, double[] throughput) {
        double x1 = throughput[0];                               // requires a measurement at N = 1
        double sxx = 0, sx3 = 0, sx4 = 0, sxy = 0, sx2y = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n.length; i++) {
            double x = n[i] - 1, y = n[i] / (throughput[i] / x1) - 1;
            sxx += x * x; sx3 += x * x * x; sx4 += x * x * x * x; sxy += x * y; sx2y += x * x * y;
        }
        double det = sxx * sx4 - sx3 * sx3;
        double a = (sxy * sx4 - sx2y * sx3) / det;               // a = σ + κ
        double b = (sxx * sx2y - sx3 * sxy) / det;               // b = κ
        return new double[]{a - b, b};
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("A. Amdahl: speed-up with 5% serial work");
        for (int n : new int[]{1, 4, 16, 64, 256})
            System.out.printf("   %3d workers → %5.1fx (ceiling 1/s = 20x)%n", n, amdahl(n, 0.05));

        System.out.println("B. USL: σ = 0.03 (contention), κ = 0.0005 (coherency)");
        for (int n : new int[]{1, 8, 16, 32, 44, 64, 96, 128})
            System.out.printf("   %3d pods → %5.1fx capacity%s%n", n, usl(n, 0.03, 0.0005),
                    n == 44 ? "   ← peak: N* = √((1−σ)/κ)" : "");

        System.out.println("C. Fit from a load test of cart-service (req/s per pod count)");
        // Synthetic measurements generated from σ=0.03, κ=0.0005 with ±3 % noise — replace with your results
        int[] pods = {1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24};
        double[] measured = new double[pods.length];
        Random rnd = new Random(9);
        for (int i = 0; i < pods.length; i++)
            measured[i] = 1_450 * usl(pods[i], 0.03, 0.0005) * (1 + (rnd.nextDouble() - 0.5) * 0.06);
        for (int i = 0; i < pods.length; i++) System.out.printf("   %2d pods: %,8.0f req/s%n", pods[i], measured[i]);

        double[] fit = fitUsl(pods, measured);
        double sigma = fit[0], kappa = fit[1];
        int peak = (int) Math.floor(Math.sqrt((1 - sigma) / kappa));
        System.out.printf("   fitted σ = %.4f, κ = %.6f → peak at ~%d pods, max ≈ %,.0f req/s%n",
                sigma, kappa, peak, measured[0] * usl(peak, sigma, kappa));
        System.out.printf("   prediction: 64 pods → %,.0f req/s (fewer than at %d pods)%n",
                measured[0] * usl(64, sigma, kappa), peak);
        System.out.printf("   halving κ (e.g. stop broadcasting to every pod) → peak at ~%d pods, max ≈ %,.0f req/s%n",
                (int) Math.floor(Math.sqrt((1 - sigma) / (kappa / 2))),
                measured[0] * usl((int) Math.floor(Math.sqrt((1 - sigma) / (kappa / 2))), sigma, kappa / 2));
    }
}

Actual output from running it:

A. Amdahl: speed-up with 5% serial work
     1 workers →   1.0x (ceiling 1/s = 20x)
     4 workers →   3.5x (ceiling 1/s = 20x)
    16 workers →   9.1x (ceiling 1/s = 20x)
    64 workers →  15.4x (ceiling 1/s = 20x)
   256 workers →  18.6x (ceiling 1/s = 20x)
B. USL: σ = 0.03 (contention), κ = 0.0005 (coherency)
     1 pods →   1.0x capacity
     8 pods →   6.5x capacity
    16 pods →  10.2x capacity
    32 pods →  13.2x capacity
    44 pods →  13.6x capacity   ← peak: N* = √((1−σ)/κ)
    64 pods →  13.0x capacity
    96 pods →  11.4x capacity
   128 pods →   9.9x capacity
C. Fit from a load test of cart-service (req/s per pod count)
    1 pods:    1,470 req/s
    2 pods:    2,858 req/s
    4 pods:    5,378 req/s
    8 pods:    9,421 req/s
   12 pods:   12,785 req/s
   16 pods:   14,679 req/s
   24 pods:   17,798 req/s
   fitted σ = 0.0303, κ = 0.000523 → peak at ~43 pods, max ≈ 19,634 req/s
   prediction: 64 pods → 18,735 req/s (fewer than at 43 pods)
   halving κ (e.g. stop broadcasting to every pod) → peak at ~60 pods, max ≈ 23,733 req/s

What L1 shows: a 5 % serial fraction caps you at 20× no matter how many workers you add. Any coherency cost (κ > 0) creates a peak, and past it more pods mean less throughput. Seven load-test points are enough to recover σ and κ within a few percent and predict the peak, before an HPA finds it for you in production. Reducing κ (removing all-pod broadcasts) moves the peak further than any amount of hardware.

What L1 can't do: it only models the system. The next levels remove the actual σ and κ sources.

The quickest way to stop needing sticky sessions: keep the HttpSession but store it in Redis.

Repository, Service, Delegate, ControllerConfigurationTest: two pods, one session 
package com.grocery.cart.repository;

import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpSession;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** L2: the cart lives INSIDE the HTTP session, which Spring Session stores in Redis. */
@Repository
public class SessionCartRepository {

    static final String ATTR = "cart";

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public Map<String, Integer> load(HttpSession session) {
        Object c = session.getAttribute(ATTR);
        return c == null ? new LinkedHashMap<>() : new LinkedHashMap<>((Map<String, Integer>) c);
    }

    /** Writes the WHOLE cart back: Spring Session saves the changed attribute to Redis. */
    public void save(HttpSession session, Map<String, Integer> cart) {
        session.setAttribute(ATTR, new LinkedHashMap<>(cart));
    }
}

package com.grocery.cart.service;

import com.grocery.cart.repository.SessionCartRepository;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpSession;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import java.util.Map;

@Service
public class SessionCartService {

    private final SessionCartRepository repo;

    public SessionCartService(SessionCartRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }

    /** ⚠️ Read-modify-write of a session attribute: two tabs → last write wins (Ch 05, same lost-update shape). */
    public Map<String, Integer> setQty(HttpSession session, String sku, int qty) {
        Map<String, Integer> cart = repo.load(session);
        if (qty <= 0) cart.remove(sku); else cart.put(sku, qty);
        repo.save(session, cart);
        return cart;
    }

    public Map<String, Integer> view(HttpSession session) { return repo.load(session); }
}

package com.grocery.cart.delegate;

import com.grocery.cart.service.SessionCartService;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpSession;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import java.util.Map;

@Component
public class SessionCartDelegate {
    private final SessionCartService service;
    public SessionCartDelegate(SessionCartService service) { this.service = service; }
    public Map<String, Integer> setQty(HttpSession s, String sku, int qty) { return service.setQty(s, sku, qty); }
    public Map<String, Integer> view(HttpSession s) { return service.view(s); }
}

package com.grocery.cart.controller;

import com.grocery.cart.delegate.SessionCartDelegate;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpSession;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.*;
import org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.util.Map;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/session-cart")
@Validated
public class SessionCartController {

    private final SessionCartDelegate delegate;

    public SessionCartController(SessionCartDelegate delegate) { this.delegate = delegate; }

    @PutMapping("/items/{sku}")
    public Map<String, Integer> setQty(HttpSession session, @PathVariable String sku,
                                       @RequestParam @Min(0) @Max(10) int qty) {
        return delegate.setQty(session, sku, qty);
    }

    @GetMapping
    public Map<String, Integer> view(HttpSession session) { return delegate.view(session); }
}
