docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Detection signal Blast radius Mitigation Writes lost during a move (no fence) Reconciliation finds rows only on the old shard; "missing order" tickets Silent data loss (L4 naive: 88 writes) Fence + final delta + checksum before flip; delete only after a grace period Stale shard map in a pod BUCKET_MOVED / MOVED rate; map version skew across pods Retries; errors if the client doesn't refresh Refresh on refusal, poll with a version, versions only increase Checksum mismatch at flip Mover alert One bucket's writes blocked while fenced Keep fence, don't flip, page; runbook to diff and repair Hot shard Per-shard CPU/latency skew; top-N buckets by QPS Everyone on that shard (~1/N of customers) Move hot buckets; salt hot keys; cache One shard down Health checks; errors on 1/N of buckets ~1/N of customers, not all Each shard is a replicated cluster (Ch 10); degrade per shard; don't let one shard's timeouts exhaust shared pools (bulkheads, Ch 18) Scatter-gather tail latency Fan-out p99 ≫ single-shard p99 Admin/support endpoints; pool exhaustion if on a hot path Deadlines, per-shard limits, partial results, move to a read model Cross-shard write needed Code review; "transaction spans two shards" Inconsistency on partial failure Co-locate by key; saga/outbox for the rest (Ch 13) Bucket function changed by accident Golden-value test fails; routing to wrong shards Every key misrouted: "data missing" everywhere Pin with golden tests; function lives in one versioned library Duplicate ids across partitions Constraint can't catch it (PK includes partition key) Wrong order shown/updated Globally unique id generator (Ch 20); id carries bucket Redis CROSSSLOT in production Errors after moving to Cluster Multi-key ops fail Hash tags for keys used together; no multi-key ops across entities Read model lag Consumer lag Stale store dashboard Show "as of"; alert on lag; replay from Kafka

docs.title: 6.2 Observability
docs.text:
• Per shard: QPS, p50/p99 latency, CPU, disk, connections, replication lag (each shard is a Ch 10 cluster).
  • Skew: max/avg across shards for QPS and storage, alert when > 1.5x. Top-N buckets and keys by QPS (sampled), which is how hot keys are found before they're incidents.
  • Routing: shard map version per pod (a gauge), BUCKET_MOVED/MOVED/ASK rates, retries after refusal.
  • Moves: buckets in flight, bytes copied, catch-up rounds, final delta size, freeze time per bucket (histogram), checksum results, grace-period deletes pending.
  • Fan-out: shards touched per request (a histogram, tagged by endpoint). A new endpoint that fans out to every shard shows up here before it shows up in latency.
  • Read models: consumer lag in seconds per partition.

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Shards are a tenant isolation tool too: a big B2B customer or a regulated region can get dedicated buckets on a dedicated shard (data residency, Ch 36).
  • Each shard has its own credentials. The mover's account needs read on source, write on target and bucket_fence — nothing more. Application pods never get DDL.
  • Order ids that carry a bucket leak a little structure. Keep a random suffix (as OrderIds does) so ids can't be guessed, and always check ownership (customer_id from the token) after routing.
  • Scatter-gather admin endpoints are a data-exfiltration path: authorize, rate-limit, and audit them.
  • Backups and PITR are per shard: a restore must be coordinated with the shard map version at that time.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance & tuning knobs
docs.text: Knob Default here Effect Number of buckets 1,024 ≥ 10× max shards; more buckets = finer moves, bigger map Buckets moved in parallel 1 per shard pair More = faster rebalance, more I/O on live shards Catch-up threshold 20 rows (sim) / ~1 MB (prod) Smaller = shorter freeze, more rounds Grace period before delete 24 h Longer = safer rollback, more disk Map poll interval 5 s Shorter = fewer refusals, more config reads Scatter-gather deadline 300 ms Shorter = more partial results PostgreSQL partitions per table 8–64 Too many = slower planning; too few = big partitions Hot-key salts 4–8 for listed keys More = flatter load, wider reads Connection pools One per shard, sized per shard Total connections = pods × shards × pool size: watch the database's max_connections, use PgBouncer

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• Shards multiply everything: 4 shards × (primary + 2 standbys) = 12 database servers, plus monitoring, backups and on-call surface. Sharding too early is one of the most expensive mistakes in this handbook.
  • Connections: pods × shards × pool size grows fast. A pooler (PgBouncer) per shard is usually needed past a few shards.
  • Read models double storage for the data they copy and add a consumer, but they are much cheaper than making every store query a fan-out.
  • Rebalancing costs I/O on live shards. Schedule moves off-peak and rate-limit them.
  • Engineering: the router, mover, tooling, cross-shard reporting, per-shard migrations (schema changes must run on every shard, and be backwards-compatible while they roll).

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. hash(key) % number_of_shards. Symptom: Adding a shard moves ~80 % of the data (L1), for days, with lost writes (§1.1).

// ❌ before: the shard count is part of the key's address
String shard = "shard-" + Math.floorMod(customerId.hashCode(), shardCount);

// ✅ after: the address is a fixed bucket; only the small map changes
int bucket = Buckets.of(customerId);                 // CRC32C mod 1024, never changes
String shard = shardMap.shardForBucket(bucket);      // versioned, moved one bucket at a time

2. Moving data without a fence. Symptom: Writes that arrive between the copy and the map flip go to the old copy and vanish. No errors are raised (L4 naive: 88 lost). Fix: Copy, catch up, fence the source, copy the final delta, verify, flip, delete later.

3. Sharding by a low-cardinality or skewed key. Symptom: A few shards run hot forever, and adding shards makes it worse (L1 C: 1.11x → 3.90x). Fix: Pick a high-cardinality key (customer). Give store-level queries their own read model, and salt the hot keys (4.11x → 1.68x).

4. Using an unstable hash.

// ❌ before: Object.hashCode() of a record/entity, or a language whose string hash is randomized per process
int bucket = Math.floorMod(Objects.hash(order.customer()), 1024);   // changes with the class's fields or the runtime

// ✅ after: a named hash over bytes, pinned by a golden test
int bucket = Buckets.of(customerId);
assertEquals(532, Buckets.of("cust-42"));   // this test must never be "updated"

5. A primary key that doesn't include the partition key, "fixed" by dropping the constraint. Symptom: PostgreSQL refuses a PK on id alone (lab A). Someone drops the constraint, and duplicate ids appear on different partitions. Fix: PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, id) and a globally unique id generator (Ch 20).

6. Scatter-gather on a hot path. Symptom: The store dashboard fans out to every shard every 10 seconds per open dashboard. p99 tracks the slowest shard, and load grows with the shard count. Fix: An event-fed read model partitioned by the query's key. Keep scatter-gather for rare, bounded, deadline-limited admin queries.

7. Cross-shard transactions by accident. Symptom: "Transfer wallet credit from customer A to B" opens two connections and commits both, and one commit fails. Fix: Co-locate data that's written together. For truly cross-key operations, use a saga with an outbox (Ch 13), not two commits.

8. Sharding before it's needed. Symptom: 12 database servers, a routing library and a mover for 200 GB that one primary could handle. Fix: Ch 09's order: indexes and queries, caching, read replicas, partitioning inside one server, a bigger machine. Shard when writes or storage truly exceed one primary, with numbers (§4).

9. Range-partitioning across servers by time or sequence. Symptom: Every insert goes to the newest shard (L1 D), so one shard does all the writes. Fix: Hash (or bucket) across servers. Range-partition by time inside each shard for retention.

10. Redis multi-key commands without hash tags.

❌ MGET cust:42:name cust:77:name        → CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot
✅ MGET {cust-42}:orders {cust-42}:cart  → 3 2     (same slot 3330, lab C)

Don't overuse hash tags either: {global}:* puts every key in one slot on one node.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What's the difference between partitioning, sharding and replication?

30-second answer: Partitioning splits a dataset into disjoint pieces. Sharding is partitioning across servers, so each server holds and writes only part of the data. Replication copies the same data to several servers. Replication scales reads and survives failures, and only partitioning scales writes and storage. Real systems do both: each shard is replicated.

Deep answer: PostgreSQL declarative partitioning splits a table on one server (pruning, retention, maintenance), which is partitioning without sharding. A sharded system has shard clusters, each with a primary and replicas (Ch 10).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Sharding adds routing, cross-shard queries, rebalancing and operational cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Does adding read replicas help a write-bound database? → No. Every replica applies every write. 2. What's a shard key? → The column(s) that decide which shard a row lives on.

Red flags: Using "replication" and "sharding" interchangeably.

Q2 [B1] ⭐ Range vs hash partitioning?

30-second answer: Range partitioning keeps contiguous key ranges together, so range scans are cheap and old ranges drop easily, but monotonic keys (time) send all writes to one partition. Hash partitioning spreads keys evenly, including monotonic ones, but any range query or query without the key touches every partition.

Deep answer: L1 D: by month, all 10,000 of today's writes went to one partition. By hash, ~2,500 per shard. Common combination: hash across servers, range by month inside each server for retention.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Scan locality vs write spread.

Follow-ups: 1. Who uses range partitioning across servers? → Bigtable/HBase, Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, with automatic splitting of hot or big ranges. 2. How do they avoid the hot newest range? → Split it, or prefix keys with a hash.

Red flags: "Hash partitioning has no downside."

Q3 [B1] Why does a query without the partition key get slower as you add partitions?

30-second answer: The router can't tell which partition holds matching rows, so it must ask all of them and merge (scatter-gather). The work grows with the partition count, and the response is as slow as the slowest partition.

Deep answer: Lab A: by customer, one partition, 0.138 ms. By store, eight partitions, 2.818 ms. Across servers there's also network fan-out and tail latency: with many shards, the chance that one of them is slow is high.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Keep such queries rare and bounded, or build a copy partitioned by that other key.

Follow-ups: 1. What's partition pruning? → The planner skipping partitions that can't match the WHERE clause. 2. How to make "orders by store" fast? → A read model partitioned by store.

Red flags: Expecting secondary indexes alone to fix it.

Q4 [B1] What's a hot partition, and how can it happen with a good hash?

30-second answer: A partition that gets far more load than the others. A hash spreads keys evenly, but if one key (a mega store, a viral product) gets a large share of traffic, its partition is hot no matter how good the hash is.

Deep answer: L1 C: one store with 5 % of orders made the busiest shard 1.11x the average at 4 shards and 3.90x at 64. Fixes: salt/split the key, cache, move the bucket to a dedicated shard.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Salting spreads writes but turns reads of that key into a fan-out over its salts.

Follow-ups: 1. Does adding shards help? → Not for one hot key. It makes the imbalance ratio worse. 2. How do you find hot keys? → Per-key sampling, top-N metrics.

Red flags: "Just add more shards."

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do you choose a shard key?

30-second answer: From access patterns. List queries and transactions by volume and latency need, and choose the key that keeps the most important ones on one shard, with high cardinality, low skew and spread-out writes. Then plan explicitly for every query that doesn't use it.

Deep answer: Orders: customer_id keeps order history, checkout (order + items + payment co-located) and by-id reads (bucket in the id) on one shard. Store queries get a read model keyed by salted store_id. Analytics go to the warehouse. Rejected: store_id (skewed), created_at (hot newest shard), order_id alone (customer history becomes a scatter).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Every key makes some queries cheap and others expensive, and changing the key later means moving all the data.

Follow-ups: 1. Multi-tenant SaaS? → Usually tenant_id, with big tenants moved to their own shards. 2. Composite keys? → Partition key + clustering key (Cassandra), or (customer_id, id) in PostgreSQL.

Red flags: Picking the key from the data model instead of the queries.

Q6 [B2] ⭐ Why is hash mod N a bad sharding function?

30-second answer: Changing N remaps almost every key: a key stays only if h mod N == h mod (N+1). L1 measured 80.1 % of keys moving from 4 to 5 shards. Consistent hashing or fixed buckets move only ~1/N.

Deep answer: The root problem is that the shard count is part of each key's address. Fixed buckets separate the two: key → bucket never changes, and bucket → shard is a small, versioned map. The exception is doubling N, which moves exactly half the keys and lets each shard split into two, but still moves half the data.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Buckets need a map, which is small and worth it.

Follow-ups: 1. How much should move when adding the (N+1)th shard? → 1/(N+1) of the data. 2. Why does Redis use 16,384 slots? → Fixed slots + a gossiped slot map, and it fits in the cluster bus heartbeat bitmap.

Red flags: Not knowing how much data a reshard moves.

Q7 [B2] Explain consistent hashing and why virtual nodes matter.

30-second answer: Keys and nodes are hashed onto a ring, and a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves only the keys between it and its neighbour, ~1/N. With one point per node, arcs are uneven and a new node takes load from just one neighbour. Virtual nodes (many points per node) even out the load and spread the moves across all nodes.

Deep answer: L1: one point per shard was 1.80x max/avg with 17.2 % moved. 150 vnodes: 1.02x, 20.3 % moved. Vnodes also let bigger machines take more points. Used in Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak and client-side cache sharding.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Less control over exactly what moves than an explicit bucket map. Ring membership must be agreed on.

Follow-ups: 1. Consistent hashing vs rendezvous (HRW) hashing? → HRW: pick the node with the highest hash(key, node). No ring, O(N) per lookup, also ~1/N movement. 2. Jump consistent hash? → Minimal memory and even, but nodes can only be added or removed at the end.

Red flags: Consistent hashing without vnodes for uneven clusters.

Q8 [B2] Why must a unique constraint on a partitioned table include the partition key?

30-second answer: Each partition enforces uniqueness with its own local index. Without the partition key in the constraint, two rows with the same id could sit in different partitions, and no single index would see both. PostgreSQL refuses to create it (lab A shows the error).

Deep answer: Use PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, id), and get global uniqueness of id from the generator (UUIDv7, Snowflake-style, or bucket-carrying ids, Ch 20). A global unique index across shards needs a separate index store and cross-shard writes, which is what distributed SQL databases provide at a latency cost.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Constraint simplicity vs partition independence.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you look up an order by id alone? → The id carries the bucket, or a lookup table. 2. Does Citus have the same rule? → Yes, for distributed tables the distribution column must be part of unique constraints.

Red flags: Dropping the constraint to make the migration pass.

Q9 [B2] Local vs global secondary indexes?

30-second answer: A local index covers one partition's rows, so writes stay local but reads by the indexed column scatter to all partitions. A global index is partitioned by the indexed value, so reads hit one partition but writes touch another partition, usually asynchronously (eventual consistency) or with a distributed transaction.

Deep answer: DynamoDB GSIs are global and eventually consistent. Elasticsearch and PostgreSQL partitioned indexes are local. Our orders_by_store is a hand-built global index fed by events, with version guards for ordering and idempotency.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Read fan-out vs write amplification and staleness.

Follow-ups: 1. How stale is the read model? → Consumer lag, shown in the UI. 2. What if an event is lost? → Outbox guarantees delivery, and a periodic reconciliation compares counts.

Red flags: Assuming a global index is transactionally consistent for free.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ Design sharding for an orders database that must grow from 4 to 16 shards.

30-second answer: Hash customer_id into 1,024 fixed buckets, keep a versioned bucket → shard map, co-locate orders/items/payments by bucket, put the bucket in order ids, and build an online mover (copy, catch up, fence, verify, flip, delete later). Store queries use an event-fed read model. Each shard is a replicated cluster.

Deep answer: Numbers: ~17 TB → ~17 GB per bucket, 64–256 buckets per shard. Going 4 → 5 moves ~205 buckets (~20 %). Routing: client-side, with the map cached, polled and refreshed on BUCKET_MOVED. Admin scatter-gather with deadlines and partial results. Schema changes run on every shard, backwards compatible.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Build vs Vitess/Citus/distributed SQL: control and any engine vs time to build and own the tooling.

Follow-ups: 1. Why 1,024 and not 16? → Fine-grained moves, even distribution, room for 64+ shards. 2. How do you handle a customer who outgrows a bucket? → Rare for consumers. For tenants, move the tenant to its own shard or sub-shard it.

Red flags: A design without an answer for resharding.

Q11 [B3] ⭐ How do you route a request that only has an order id?

30-second answer: Encode the bucket in the id at creation (ord_214_… → bucket 532), so any service can compute the shard without a lookup. Alternatives are a global id → key lookup table (another store to keep consistent and highly available) or a scatter-gather (expensive).

Deep answer: The id format includes a version so the layout can evolve. Validate it (the harness rejects ord_42), and after routing, check ownership against the caller. Instagram embedded a logical shard id in its 64-bit ids for the same reason.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Ids expose a little structure. A random suffix keeps them unguessable.

Follow-ups: 1. What about legacy ids without a bucket? → A lookup table for the legacy range only, which shrinks over time. 2. What if the bucket function ever changes? → It must not. The bucket stored in the id and the row is the source of truth.

Red flags: A global lookup table on every read without discussing its availability.

Q12 [B3] How do you run a query across all shards safely?

30-second answer: Fan out in parallel with a deadline, push down filters and a per-shard limit (top-K), merge with a heap, and return partial results flagged as incomplete if a shard is slow or down. Keep it off hot paths, rate-limit it, and track fan-out per endpoint.

Deep answer: The harness: shard-c took 500 ms against a 200 ms deadline, and the result was the top 4 from the other shards with complete=false. Pagination across shards needs a merge cursor (last seen sort key per shard), not OFFSET. Aggregations push down partial aggregates (count/sum per shard) and combine them.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Completeness vs latency, and a UI that can say "partial".

Follow-ups: 1. Global ORDER BY … LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000? → Every shard must return 10,020 rows. Use keyset cursors. 2. When does scatter-gather become unacceptable? → When it's on a user-facing hot path or its QPS × shard count dominates load.

Red flags: Unbounded fan-out with no deadline.

Q13 [B3] ⭐ How do you handle a hot key like a mega store or a flash-sale product?

30-second answer: First identify it (per-key metrics). For write-heavy keys, split it into N salted sub-keys and read all salts. For read-heavy keys, cache and replicate it. For a hot bucket, move it to a dedicated shard. For counters, use sharded counters.

Deep answer: Salting the mega store into 4 keys took the busiest shard from 4.11x to 1.68x, and more salts barely helped because the rest is normal variance. Salt only listed keys, and never shrink the salt count without a rebuild. Flash-sale reads: cache with request coalescing (Ch 07), and inventory reservations in Redis with Lua (Ch 09).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Write spread vs read fan-out and complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. How do DynamoDB/Bigtable handle hot keys? → Adaptive capacity and split-for-heat, which still can't split a single key. 2. What's a sharded counter? → N sub-counters incremented at random and summed on read.

Red flags: Salting every key "just in case".

Q14 [B3] How does Redis Cluster route keys, and what are MOVED and ASK?

30-second answer: Keys map to one of 16,384 slots via CRC16 mod 16384, and each master owns ranges of slots. A node that doesn't own a slot replies MOVED <slot> <node>, and the client updates its slot map. During migration, the source replies ASK <slot> <node> for keys already moved. The client sends ASKING plus the command to the target, once, without updating its map.

Deep answer: Lab C showed all of it: MOVED 4133 127.0.0.1:7001, ASK 4133 127.0.0.1:7002 for a moved key while an unmoved key is still served by the source, the target refusing without ASKING, and MOVED after SETSLOT NODE. Multi-key commands need all keys in one slot (CROSSSLOT otherwise), which hash tags {…} provide. Adding a fourth node moved 25 % of keys.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Smart clients vs proxies. Hash tags vs hot slots.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not update the map on ASK? → The slot still belongs to the source until migration finishes. 2. Can you run Lua on keys from different slots? → No, all keys must hash to one slot.

Red flags: Using {} with one constant tag for everything.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ How do you move a bucket to a new shard without losing writes?

30-second answer: Bulk copy while writable. Catch up deltas until they're small. Fence the source for the bucket so writes there are refused. Copy the final delta, verify with count + checksum, flip the versioned map, and delete from the source after a grace period. Stale writers get BUCKET_MOVED, reload the map and retry.

Deep answer: The simulation with 8 concurrent writers lost 88 acknowledged writes with naive copy → flip → delete, and 0 with the fenced protocol. Only 2 rows needed copying under the fence across 512 buckets, and the max freeze was 36 ms. The fence must be atomic with the write (a trigger or a check in the same transaction), not a flag the app reads earlier. A mismatch keeps the fence and pages.

Trade-offs I'd call out: A short unavailability per bucket vs correctness. Retries vs complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you capture deltas in PostgreSQL? → A change-sequence column, or logical replication with a row filter. 2. What about deletes? → Tombstones, because a delta can't see a missing row.

Red flags: "We'll copy and switch over at night."

Q16 [B4] How do sharding and replication interact during failures?

30-second answer: Each shard is its own replicated cluster, so a primary failure affects only that shard's buckets (~1/N), with the Ch 10 guarantees (quorum sync, fenced failover). The shard map points at the shard's writer endpoint, not at node IPs, so failover doesn't change the map.

Deep answer: Watch for moves during failovers. Pause the mover when either side is failing over, because a fence written on an old primary might be lost with it. Backups and PITR are per shard, so a consistent restore across shards needs a common timestamp or accepted per-shard skew. Timeouts to one bad shard must not exhaust shared thread pools (bulkheads).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Blast radius shrinks with more shards, but the number of things that can fail grows.

Follow-ups: 1. Cross-shard consistent snapshot? → Hard. A logical timestamp or a pause, or accept per-shard skew for analytics. 2. Shard down: fail everything or just its buckets? → Just its buckets, degrade gracefully.

Red flags: A shard map with node IPs in it.

Q17 [B4] When would you choose Vitess, Citus or a distributed SQL database over app-level sharding?

30-second answer: When you'd rather operate a system than build one. Vitess (MySQL) and Citus (PostgreSQL) give routing, resharding and some cross-shard queries on familiar engines. Distributed SQL (Spanner, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, TiDB) gives automatic range splitting, rebalancing, distributed transactions and global indexes. App-level sharding fits when there's one clear key and the team wants full control.

Deep answer: Criteria: engine compatibility, need for cross-shard transactions or global indexes, multi-region, managed-service availability, team skills, migration cost, latency budgets (consensus writes cost cross-zone round trips). Many companies started app-level and migrated to Vitess (e.g. Slack, publicly documented), or started on distributed SQL for multi-region.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Control vs time to build. Latency and cost vs features.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you migrate from app sharding to Vitess? → Mirror the bucket → shard mapping in Vitess's keyspace/vindex, move shard by shard. 2. Hidden cost of distributed SQL? → Transactions across ranges, hot ranges, and operational expertise.

Red flags: Choosing by popularity instead of access patterns.

Q18 [B4] How do you run schema changes on 16 shards?

30-second answer: Every change is expand/contract and backwards-compatible, rolled to one canary shard first, then the rest, with a migration tool that tracks the version per shard. The application must work with any mix of old and new schema while the rollout is in progress.

Deep answer: Add nullable columns, backfill in batches per shard, deploy code that writes both, switch reads, then drop. Online DDL tools (gh-ost/pt-osc for MySQL; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, lock timeouts for PostgreSQL). The mover must copy using an explicit column list so shards at different schema versions don't break a move.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Rollout time vs risk.

Follow-ups: 1. What if one shard fails the migration? → Stop, fix, retry. The app still works because of compatibility. 2. Where's the version recorded? → Per shard (Flyway history), exported as a metric.

Red flags: "Run the migration on all shards in a loop."

Q19 [B4] Your busiest shard is at 90 % CPU during the evening peak. Walk me through it.

30-second answer: Confirm it's one shard (skew metric). Find whether it's a few hot buckets or keys (top-N) or an expensive query pattern (fan-out, missing index). Short term: cache or rate-limit the offender, move hot buckets to cooler shards. Long term: salt the hot key, move the query to a read model, or add a shard.

Deep answer: Check the query mix first. A scatter-gather endpoint loads every shard, but the shard holding a hot key suffers most. Check replicas: move read-only traffic to replicas with session guarantees (Ch 10). A move adds I/O on the hot shard, so move the other buckets off it first. Record what happened and add an alert for skew.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Fast relief (cache, throttle) vs structural fixes.

Follow-ups: 1. What if one customer is the hot key? → A tenant-level limit, or a dedicated shard. 2. Why not just scale the machine vertically? → A valid short-term fix, but it doesn't solve skew.

Red flags: Adding shards without knowing what's hot.

Q20 [B4] What are the long-term costs of sharding, and how do you keep them in check?

30-second answer: More infrastructure, more on-call, cross-shard queries, per-shard migrations and backups, a routing library in every service, rebalancing tooling, and analytics that can't just query "the database". Keep them in check by delaying sharding, choosing a key that makes the main paths single-shard, pushing everything else to read models and a warehouse, and automating moves and migrations.

Deep answer: Budget per shard (servers × 3 for HA, monitoring, backups). Connection counts grow with pods × shards. Staff costs: the mover, map service and tooling need owners. Measure fan-out per endpoint to stop cross-shard creep. Reassess build vs buy (Vitess, Citus, distributed SQL) as the team and product change.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Capacity and blast radius vs complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. Can you un-shard? → Yes, if machines grow faster than the data: move buckets back. 2. How do analytics work? → CDC from every shard into a warehouse or lake (Ch 21).

Red flags: Treating sharding as a one-time project.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Replication scales reads and survives failures. Partitioning scales writes and storage. Real systems do both.
  2. Range keeps scans local but concentrates monotonic writes. Hash spreads writes but scatters range and non-key queries.
  3. Never let the shard count be part of a key's address. mod N moved 80 %. Fixed buckets + a versioned map move ~1/N (19.7 %), one verifiable bucket at a time.
  4. Choose the key from the dominant queries and transactions, co-locate what's written together, and plan every other query explicitly.
  5. Put the bucket in the id so by-id reads route with no lookup.
  6. Unique constraints include the partition key. Global uniqueness comes from the id generator.
  7. Scatter-gather is bounded: deadlines, per-shard limits, partial results, off hot paths. Use read models for frequent non-key queries.
  8. Hashing doesn't fix a hot key. Salt it (4.11x → 1.68x), cache it, or isolate it.
  9. Moves need a fence: copy while writable, catch up, fence, final delta, verify, flip, delete later. Naive moves lost 88 writes. Fenced moves lost 0.
  10. Stale routing must fail safe and self-heal: MOVED, ASK, BUCKET_MOVED, map versions that only increase.

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Choose Big table, one server is enough Declarative partitioning (hash or range) + indexes Retention of time-series data Range partitions by month, DROP old ones Writes beyond one primary Hash-based sharding with fixed buckets + versioned map Nodes join/leave automatically (caches) Consistent hashing with vnodes Frequent queries on a non-shard key Event-fed read model (global index) Rare admin queries on a non-shard key Bounded scatter-gather By-id lookup without the shard key Bucket encoded in the id One very hot key Salting (writes), caching (reads), dedicated shard Adding a shard online Copy → catch up → fence → final delta → verify → flip → delete later Want it built for you Vitess (MySQL), Citus (PostgreSQL), distributed SQL

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: Band Exercise Hint B1 Run L1 with 8 → 9 shards. How much does each scheme move? ~89 % for mod N, ~11 % otherwise B1 Run lab A with partition by range (created_at) and query by customer No pruning without the key B2 Add rendezvous (HRW) hashing to L1 and compare balance and movement max over nodes of hash(key + node) B2 Add a created_at range sub-partition under each hash partition in lab A Multi-level partitioning B3 Add keyset pagination to ScatterGather (a cursor per shard) Last seen (created_at, id) per shard B3 In lab B, move buckets with the L4 protocol (copy while writable, fence last) and compare freeze times Change sequence column B4 Break the mover on purpose: skip the final delta. Does the checksum catch it? It should: keep the fence, don't flip B4 Design the migration from one orders primary to 4 shards with zero downtime Dual-write or CDC, backfill, verify, cut over per bucket

docs.title: 12. Consistency, Time & Consensus ⭐
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 05, Ch 10, Ch 11 · What you will build: Coordination and ordering for the grocery platform. L1 compares clocks: wall clocks with skew, Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks, and monotonic vs wall-clock timeouts. L2 checks histories of a replicated register for linearizability. L3 is a Raft simulator with fault injection and safety checks, including two deliberately broken rules and the paper's Figure 8 scenario. L4 builds leader election with leases and fencing tokens, and linearizable reads (ReadIndex vs leases under clock drift). Two real labs: PostgreSQL 16 shows a paused leader corrupting a settlement without a fencing token, and being rejected with one. A 3-member etcd 3.5 cluster shows lease-based election with revision tokens, leader failover, a minority member serving a stale serializable read, CAS on mod_revision, and watches vs compaction. · Reading time: 130 min + code + labs

docs.title: 1.1 A story: 214 dark stores paid twice
docs.text:
The nightly store-settlement job computes each dark store's payout (sales minus refunds, commission and GST) and writes it for the bank file. It must run on exactly one pod, so the team used a Redis lock with a 10-second TTL: SET settle-lock pod-A NX PX 10000. Whoever got the lock was "the leader".

One Diwali night, pod A took the lock and loaded the day's sales. Then it stopped for 14 seconds: a full GC on a heap swollen by the sale-day data, while its VM was also being live-migrated. The lock expired. Pod B took it, recomputed every payout (now including 3,100 late refunds) and wrote them. Pod A woke up. From its point of view no time had passed. It still "held the lock", so it wrote its payouts over B's, and the bank-file step, triggered by both, picked up both batches. 214 stores were paid twice, ₹38 lakh in total. Recovering it took three weeks of calls.

The same week, support was confused by order timelines that showed "Packing" before "Paid". Events from different services were sorted by their wall-clock timestamps, and the order-service host's clock had drifted 90 ms behind after an NTP misconfiguration.

Neither was a bug in one service. Both came from assumptions about time and agreement that don't hold in a distributed system:

  • A lock with a TTL doesn't stop a paused process. The process doesn't know it paused. The fix is a fencing token: a number that increases with every new lease, sent with every write, and checked by the resource (update … where fence <= :token). The lab shows both outcomes on real PostgreSQL.
  • "Who is the leader" must be decided by a consensus system (etcd, ZooKeeper, a Kubernetes Lease backed by etcd, or a database acting as the single linearizable store), not by a cache that can lose writes on failover (Ch 10).
  • Wall-clock timestamps from different machines don't order events. Causally related events need a logical or hybrid logical clock. Timeouts need a monotonic clock.

The thesis of this chapter

In a distributed system there is no global "now" and no reliable way to know whether another process is dead or just slow. Consistency models say exactly which orderings a reader may observe. Clocks give you orderings that are either causal (logical) or approximate (physical). Consensus lets a majority agree anyway. Anything else that claims "exactly one leader" or "latest value" is relying on timing assumptions, so make those assumptions explicit and put a fence behind them.

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text: Band After this chapter you can… B1 Explain strong vs eventual consistency, why wall clocks on different machines disagree, and what "consensus" is for B2 Describe the consistency-model ladder, use Lamport, vector and hybrid clocks correctly, and use monotonic clocks for timeouts B3 Explain Raft (elections, log replication, the commit rule), CAP/PACELC precisely, and how to check a history for linearizability B4 Design leader election with leases and fencing tokens, choose between ReadIndex and lease reads, reason about TrueTime/HLC-based databases, and know when not to use consensus

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: a family WhatsApp group deciding dinner B1
docs.text:
Five family members decide on dinner over WhatsApp.

  • Messages arrive late and out of order. Your phone shows "Sure, pizza!" before "Pizza or biryani?" because the first message was stuck on a slow network. Each phone's clock also differs by a few seconds, so timestamps don't settle who said what first.
  • Someone goes quiet. Is Uncle offline, asleep, or just typing slowly? You can't tell. That's the core problem of distributed systems: a slow process looks exactly like a dead one.
  • The decision rule: "whatever a majority (3 of 5) agrees to is final." Two majorities always share at least one person, so the family can never "decide" both pizza and biryani. If only 2 people are online, no decision is made (the system is unavailable), but it's never inconsistent. That's consensus.
  • The rule for the delivery app: only the person holding the family's payment card orders. If Mom hands the card to Dad while she's stuck in a lift, and then she comes out of the lift and orders anyway, you get two dinners. Unless the restaurant only accepts orders from the latest card holder: that's a fencing token.

docs.title: 2.2 What "consistency" means (it's used for three different things) B1
docs.text:
Word Meaning Where C in ACID Transactions keep invariants (constraints, business rules) Ch 05 C in CAP / consistency models What values reads may return when data is replicated/distributed: linearizable, causal, eventual… This chapter Isolation (often called consistency) How concurrent transactions interleave: read committed, snapshot, serializable Ch 05

"Strongly consistent" usually means linearizable: the system behaves as if there's one copy of the data, and every operation takes effect at a single instant between its start and its end. "Eventually consistent" means replicas converge if writes stop, with no promise about what you read before that.

docs.title: 2.3 The consistency-model ladder ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
From strongest to weakest (for single objects, plus the transactional versions):

Model Guarantee Cost Example Strict serializable (linearizable + serializable) Transactions appear in one order that respects real time Coordination on every transaction, cross-region latency Spanner, CockroachDB (mostly), FoundationDB, single-node PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE Linearizable Single-object ops appear atomic at one instant within their real-time interval; once any read sees a value, all later reads do A leader or a quorum round per op etcd (default reads), ZooKeeper writes, a PostgreSQL primary Sequential All clients see the same order of ops, and each client's ops stay in program order, but not necessarily real-time order Cheaper than linearizable ZooKeeper reads (without sync) Causal Operations that are causally related are seen in the same order by all; concurrent ones may differ No global coordination; needs dependency tracking COPS, MongoDB causal sessions, many CRDT systems Session guarantees Read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads, per client Session tokens (Ch 10 L2) Our replica reads Eventual Replicas converge when writes stop Cheapest, always available DNS, Cassandra ONE, caches

Linearizability vs serializability: serializability is about transactions (multi-object) appearing in some serial order, which need not match real time. Linearizability is about single objects respecting real time. Snapshot isolation is neither. A read-only replica in a serializable database can still serve stale reads, which is serializable but not linearizable.

Why the distinction matters in practice. Linearizability is what makes these work:

  • Leader election and locks: "the lock is mine" must be the same answer for everyone right now.
  • Uniqueness constraints: "is this username taken?" must see the latest write.
  • Cross-channel ordering: a service writes an image and then sends "resize image X" through Kafka. If the resizer reads a stale replica, it doesn't find the image.

L2 checks histories: an async follower read was non-linearizable in 61.67 % of histories. A quorum read with R + W > N, which people often assume is enough, was still non-linearizable in 0.06 %: one client read 2 and a later client read 1. Only a read that writes back what it read (ABD) got to 0.

docs.title: 2.4 CAP and PACELC, precisely ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
CAP (Brewer, proven by Gilbert & Lynch): during a network partition, a system that stores replicated data must choose between linearizability (C) and availability (A: every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response). Common misreadings:

  • "Pick two of three" is wrong. Partitions aren't optional, so the choice is C or A when partitioned.
  • The C is linearizability only, and the A is a very strict availability (every node answers). A "CP" system is usually still highly available when a majority is reachable. It just refuses on the minority side.
  • Most systems are neither fully C nor fully A. They make per-operation choices (Cassandra consistency levels, etcd serializable vs linearizable reads).

PACELC (Abadi) adds the everyday trade-off: if Partition, choose A or C; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. Without any partition, strong consistency still costs round trips to a leader or quorum.

System P: A or C E: L or C etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul (default) C (minority refuses) C PostgreSQL with async replicas, reads on replicas A (replicas answer) L PostgreSQL quorum sync (Ch 10), reads on primary C C Cassandra / DynamoDB (tunable) A by default L by default Spanner, CockroachDB C C Redis Cluster A-ish (async replication, can lose writes) L

docs.title: 2.5 Physical time: why clocks lie ⭐ B1 → B3
docs.text:
Each machine has a quartz oscillator that drifts (roughly 10–100 parts per million, up to ~8.6 s a day at 100 ppm), and temperature changes the rate. NTP synchronizes clocks over the network to within about 1–10 ms on a good LAN and tens of ms across the internet, and much worse if the time server is unreachable or wrong. Cloud time services (AWS Time Sync, Google's) with PTP or local hardware references get to microseconds, but offsets are never zero and never guaranteed.

Clocks also jump:

  • NTP step: if the offset is large, ntpd/chrony may step the clock (possibly backwards) instead of slewing it.
  • Leap seconds: some hosts step, repeat a second or smear it (Google, AWS spread it over hours).
  • VM pauses and live migration: the guest's clock catches up in one jump.
  • Manual changes by operators, containers inheriting a bad host clock.

Two different clocks in every OS and in Java:

Clock Java API Use for Never use for Wall clock (time of day) Instant.now(), System.currentTimeMillis(), InstantSource/Clock Timestamps shown to humans, "created at", expiry dates stored in a DB Measuring durations, timeouts, ordering events across machines Monotonic clock System.nanoTime() Durations, timeouts, rate limits, lease checks inside one process Comparing across machines or restarts (arbitrary origin)

L1 E: a 2 s timeout measured with the wall clock while NTP steps it back 5 s reports −3,800 ms elapsed and fires 5.8 s late. With the monotonic clock it fires on time.

Clock skew breaks things silently: last-write-wins picks the wrong write (Ch 10 L1: a 90 s skew kept the older edit), TTL-based locks expire early or late, events sort in the wrong order (L1 A: the effect was timestamped 87 ms before its cause), and certificate validation fails (Ch 23).

docs.title: 2.6 Logical clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
Happened-before (→): a → b if a and b are on the same process in that order, or a is the send of a message and b its receipt, or transitively. If neither a → b nor b → a, they're concurrent.

Lamport clock. Each process keeps a counter: increment on every event, send it with messages, on receipt set max(local, received) + 1.

  • Guarantee: a → b ⇒ L(a) < L(b). Ties are broken by process id, which gives a total order consistent with causality.
  • Limitation: L(a) < L(b) doesn't mean a → b. L1 B: an unrelated refund quote got L=2 < 6 even though it didn't cause the packing event. You can't detect concurrency.

Vector clock. Each process keeps a vector of counters, one per process. Compare component-wise: ≤ in every component means happened-before, and neither ≤ means concurrent. L1 C: phone and web edits of the same cart are CONCURRENT, so the system keeps both and merges (Ch 10 OR-Set). Cost: vector size grows with the number of writers (use per-replica version vectors, and prune).

Hybrid logical clock (HLC) (Kulkarni et al., 2014). A timestamp (wall, logical): wall tracks the max physical time seen, and logical breaks ties and preserves causality when clocks are behind.

  • a → b ⇒ HLC(a) < HLC(b), like Lamport.
  • wall stays within the clock-skew bound of real physical time, so timestamps are meaningful to humans and usable for time-range queries.
  • Fits in 64 bits (48-bit ms + 16-bit counter).
  • L1 D: with the same 90 ms skew, PAYMENT_CAPTURED 1000.0 < ORDER_PACKING 1000.1.

Used by CockroachDB, YugabyteDB and MongoDB (cluster time). We put an HLC in every domain event's envelope (Ch 14) for ordering timelines and audit logs.

docs.title: 2.7 TrueTime, commit wait and uncertainty intervals B4
docs.text:
Spanner doesn't pretend clocks are exact. TrueTime returns an interval [earliest, latest] guaranteed to contain real time, with ε typically a few ms thanks to GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every data centre. A transaction gets commit timestamp s = TT.now().latest, then waits until TT.now().earliest > s before making the commit visible (commit wait, ~2ε). Any transaction that starts after this one finishes gets a larger timestamp, so timestamp order = real-time order. That's external consistency (strict serializability) from clocks, at a cost of a few ms per write.

CockroachDB uses HLC without atomic clocks and a configured max clock offset (500 ms by default). A read that sees a value with a timestamp inside its uncertainty window can't tell whether it's before or after, so it restarts at a higher timestamp. Nodes whose clock offset exceeds the bound shut themselves down, because correctness depends on it.

The lesson for everyone else: if correctness depends on clocks, the bound must be explicit, monitored and enforced.

docs.title: 2.8 The consensus problem ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
Several nodes must agree on a value (or on a sequence of values, which is a replicated log) such that:

  • Agreement: no two nodes decide differently.
  • Validity: the decided value was proposed by someone.
  • Termination: every non-failed node eventually decides.

FLP impossibility (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985): in a fully asynchronous system where even one process may crash, no deterministic algorithm guarantees all three. Practical algorithms (Paxos, Raft) keep safety always (never two decisions) and get liveness only when the network behaves "well enough for long enough" (partial synchrony), using timeouts and randomization.

Majorities: with 2f + 1 nodes, the system tolerates f failures, because any two majorities intersect.

Cluster size Majority Failures tolerated Note 1 1 0 No fault tolerance 3 2 1 The common choice, spread over 3 AZs 4 3 1 No better than 3, and more to replicate 5 3 2 Survives a failure during maintenance 7 4 3 Rarely worth the write latency

What consensus gives you: a replicated state machine. If every node applies the same log of commands in the same order, all nodes have the same state. That's the foundation of etcd, ZooKeeper (Zab), Consul, Kafka KRaft, CockroachDB/TiKV ranges (Raft per range), Spanner (Paxos per split) and Chubby.

Consensus ≈ linearizable CAS ≈ atomic broadcast ≈ leader election with a fence. They're equivalent problems. If you have one, you can build the others.

docs.title: 2.9 Raft in depth ⭐ B3 B4
docs.text:
Raft (Ongaro & Ousterhout, 2014) splits consensus into understandable parts.

Terms. Time is divided into numbered terms, each with at most one leader. A node that sees a higher term immediately adopts it and becomes a follower. Terms are the fencing tokens inside Raft.

Leader election.

  1. A follower that hears nothing from a leader for a randomized election timeout (e.g. 150–300 ms) becomes a candidate, increments its term, votes for itself and sends RequestVote(term, lastLogIndex, lastLogTerm).
  2. A node grants at most one vote per term, and only if the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as its own: a higher last term, or the same last term and an index at least as long.
  3. With votes from a majority, the candidate becomes leader and sends heartbeats. Randomized timeouts make split votes rare.

Log replication.

  1. The leader appends a client command to its log and sends AppendEntries(term, prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm, entries, leaderCommit).
  2. A follower accepts only if its log has an entry at prevLogIndex with prevLogTerm. Otherwise it rejects, and the leader backs up and retries. Conflicting follower entries are overwritten by the leader's.
  3. That consistency check gives the Log Matching property: if two logs have an entry with the same index and term, the logs are identical up to that entry.

Commit rule. An entry is committed when the leader has replicated it to a majority and it's from the leader's current term. Earlier-term entries are committed only indirectly, when a current-term entry after them commits. That's why a new leader immediately appends a no-op entry. L3 runs the paper's Figure 8 scenario: with the rule broken (committing an old-term entry just because it's on a majority), a later leader overwrites a "committed" entry. With the correct rule, the entry was never declared committed.

Safety properties (all checked continuously in L3):

Property Meaning L3 check Election Safety At most one leader per term leaderOfTerm map Log Matching Same index + term ⇒ same prefix Implied by the append check Leader Completeness A committed entry is in every later leader's log Checked at every election State Machine Safety No two nodes apply different commands at the same index Checked at every apply

L3 ran 300 randomized runs per variant (5 nodes, 20 s each, 5 % message loss, partitions, crash/restarts). The correct Raft had 0 violations over 23,845 elections and 416,335 committed entries. Removing the up-to-date vote check broke safety in 294/300 runs. The broken commit rule showed 0/300 in random runs and failed only in the targeted Figure 8 script. That's a lesson in itself: random testing misses rare interleavings, so write the known-dangerous scenarios as explicit tests (Jepsen does both).

Beyond the core:

  • Membership changes: add or remove one server at a time, or use joint consensus, so two disjoint majorities can never exist during a change.
  • Log compaction: snapshots of the state machine plus InstallSnapshot for lagging followers.
  • PreVote and check-quorum: a node first asks "would you vote for me?" without bumping terms, so a flapping node can't disrupt a healthy leader. A leader that can't reach a majority steps down.
  • Client interaction: commands carry a client id and sequence number, so a retried command after a leader change is applied once (idempotency, Ch 20).

docs.title: 2.10 Paxos, Zab and friends B3 B4
docs.text:
Algorithm Idea Used by Paxos (Lamport) Two phases per value: prepare/promise with a ballot number, then accept/accepted by a majority. Proposers adopt the highest-ballot accepted value they learn about Chubby, Spanner (per split), many databases Multi-Paxos A stable leader skips phase 1 for a sequence of values: in effect the same shape as Raft Most "Paxos" systems in practice Zab Primary-backup atomic broadcast with epochs, built for ZooKeeper ZooKeeper Viewstamped Replication View changes with a primary. It predates Paxos's publication and is very close to Raft Academic, some storage systems EPaxos / leaderless Any replica can lead a command, and only conflicting commands need extra rounds Research, some geo-distributed systems Byzantine (PBFT, HotStuff, Tendermint) Tolerate lying nodes, 3f + 1 nodes Blockchains; not needed inside one company's trust boundary

For interviews: know Raft well, know that Multi-Paxos and Raft are structurally similar (a leader, terms/ballots, majority acceptance), and know why Byzantine tolerance isn't used for internal systems.

docs.title: 2.11 Reading from a consensus system ⭐ B4
docs.text:
Writes go through the log. Reads are the subtle part: a leader can't simply answer from its own state, because it may have been deposed without knowing it (partitioned away, or paused). L4's read experiment, on top of the correct Raft from L3:

Read method How Stale reads in the simulation Cost Leader answers from local state Nothing extra 66,224 of 509,784 Free, but wrong ReadIndex Record the commit index, confirm leadership with a heartbeat round acked by a majority, wait until applied ≥ that index, then answer 0 of 321,661 One round trip per read (batched) Log read Put the read through the log like a write 0 A full write per read Lease read After a majority acks a heartbeat, the leader answers locally until sentAt + lease (lease < minimum election timeout), measured on its own clock 0 with accurate clocks and 10 % drift; 298 when the leader's clock ran 50 % slow No round trip, but depends on bounded clock drift Follower read A follower asks the leader for the ReadIndex, then serves locally 0 Spreads load

Bug found while building ReadIndex: the first version answered a pending read as soon as the node had applied up to the read index, before the majority confirmation came back. It produced 355 stale reads, and the fix was to answer only rounds that a majority had confirmed. That's exactly the kind of bug that passes code review. The safety checks caught it.

In etcd, Get is linearizable by default (ReadIndex). With WithSerializable() (etcdctl get --consistency=s) a member answers from local state, which is fast but possibly stale. Lab 2 shows a member cut off from its peers refusing the linearizable read and answering the serializable one with a value that was already overwritten. ZooKeeper reads are local (sequential consistency), and sync() before a read makes it linearizable.

Lease reads also need leader stickiness: a follower that heard from the leader recently must refuse to vote for anyone else, otherwise a new leader could be elected while the old lease is still valid. The simulation's fault model (symmetric partitions, message loss, crashes) didn't produce that case: 0 stale reads without stickiness. Asymmetric partitions (A hears B, B doesn't hear A) do, which is why etcd and TiKV pair lease reads with check-quorum/PreVote.

docs.title: 2.12 Coordination services: etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul ⭐ B3
docs.text:
etcd ZooKeeper Consul Consensus Raft Zab Raft Data model Flat keys, MVCC revisions Hierarchical znodes, versions KV + service catalog Liveness primitive Leases (TTL, keep-alive), keys attached to leases Sessions + ephemeral znodes Sessions Change notification Watches from a revision (no missed events if the revision is still retained) One-shot watches (re-register), persistent watches (3.6+) Blocking queries Conditional writes Transactions: If(modRevision == x).Then(put).Else(…) setData(path, data, expectedVersion) CAS with ModifyIndex Typical users Kubernetes, Patroni, CoreDNS, our shard map Kafka (pre-KRaft), HBase, Solr Service mesh/discovery

Recipes built on these: leader election, distributed locks (with fencing), configuration with atomic updates and watches, service discovery, barriers, and membership.

Limits: these are small, strongly consistent metadata stores. etcd recommends keeping the database to a few GB (default quota 2 GB) and requests small (1.5 MiB max). Write throughput is thousands to tens of thousands per second, bounded by fsync and majority round trips. Don't put orders or carts in etcd.

docs.title: 2.13 Leases and fencing tokens ⭐ B3 B4
docs.text:
A lease is a lock with an expiry: whoever holds it may act until it expires, so a crashed holder doesn't block others forever. But leases rest on timing assumptions:

  • The holder can pause (GC, VM migration, swap, a blocked syscall) past the expiry without noticing. After waking it checks nothing, or checks a stale local timer.
  • Its clock may run slow, so it thinks the lease has time left.
  • Network delay means a write it sent while it held the lease can arrive after the lease expired.

So a lease guarantees "at most one holder at any instant according to the lease store". It doesn't guarantee "at most one process acting". The fix (Kleppmann's fencing tokens, and Chubby's sequencers):

  1. The lease store hands out a monotonically increasing token with every grant: an epoch, a Raft term, an etcd revision, a ZooKeeper zxid.
  2. The holder sends the token with every write to the protected resource.
  3. The resource rejects any write with a token lower than the highest it has seen: update … set fence = :t where … and fence <= :t.

The lab shows it on real PostgreSQL: without the check, a pod that paused for 6 s overwrote its successor's payout (41250.00 written_by pod-A). With the check, the stale write updated 0 rows and the correct payout stayed (39980.00 written_by pod-B fence 2).

The resource must participate. If the resource can't check tokens (an external email API, a bank file drop), make the operation idempotent with a key derived from the business action (Ch 20). Or have the leader write its intent to a fenced table, and let a single dispatcher perform the side effect.

Redlock (Redis locks across 5 independent masters) doesn't provide fencing tokens and relies on timing assumptions. It's fine for efficiency locks (avoid duplicate work) and not for correctness locks (Kleppmann vs Sanfilippo, 2016). The §1.1 incident used a single Redis lock, which is worse again: a failover to an async replica can lose the lock key (Ch 10).

docs.title: 2.14 When not to use consensus B4
docs.text:
Consensus costs a majority round trip per write (cross-AZ: ~1–3 ms, cross-region: 50–200 ms), limits throughput, needs 3+ nodes, and becomes unavailable without a majority. Avoid it when:

  • One authority already exists: a single PostgreSQL primary per shard is already linearizable for its data. Use its row locks, SELECT … FOR UPDATE, unique constraints or advisory locks.
  • Conflicts can be merged: carts, likes, counters, presence → CRDTs or LWW with care (Ch 10).
  • Duplicates are harmless or preventable: idempotent consumers are simpler than exactly-one executors.
  • Coordination can be avoided by design: partition the work so each partition has one owner (Kafka consumer groups, Ch 14), or make the operation commutative.

The principle behind this is coordination avoidance (Bailis et al.; the CALM theorem): coordinate only for invariants that truly need it, such as money, uniqueness and leadership.

docs.title: 3.3 Sequence: failure path, the leader pauses, loses its lease and wakes up
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as pod-A
    participant E as etcd
    participant B as pod-B
    participant DB as settlement DB
    A->>E: leader with revision 88412
    Note over A: full GC and VM migration, 14 s pause
    E->>E: lease 7a1 expires after 10 s, leader key deleted
    E-->>B: B elected, revision 88519
    B->>DB: write payouts with fence 88519
    DB-->>B: rows updated
    Note over A: wakes up, local state still says leader
    A->>DB: write stale payouts with fence 88412
    DB-->>A: 0 rows, fence 88519 is newer
    A->>A: treat as lost leadership, abort, re-campaign
    A->>E: keep-alive 7a1
    E-->>A: lease not found

Without the fence check that produces step 7, A's stale write in step 6 would have overwritten B's payouts from step 4: the §1.1 incident, and the lab's first run.

docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers Platform team / Payments, Finance, Orders, SRE Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-044 etcd as the coordination store; ADR-045 Fencing tokens on all leader-only writes; ADR-046 HLC timestamps in event envelopes; ADR-047 Clock policy

1. Context & Problem. A Redis-lock "leader" paused past its TTL and overwrote its successor's settlement: 214 stores were paid twice (§1.1). Order timelines sorted by wall-clock timestamps from different hosts showed effects before causes. Several jobs (settlement, reconciliation, bucket mover, report exporters) each had their own ad-hoc locking.

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: one standard for "exactly one active runner"; no write from a deposed leader can take effect; a linearizable store for shard maps and critical config; causal ordering of events across services; clock offsets measured and alerted.
  • Non-goals: strict serializability across order shards (Ch 13 covers sagas); multi-region consensus (Ch 27).

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement NFR-1 At most one leader per job as seen by the resource: stale-token writes are rejected (0 accepted in tests) NFR-2 Leader failover ≤ 15 s (lease TTL 10 s + campaign) NFR-3 Coordination store survives one AZ loss; p99 write ≤ 20 ms in-region NFR-4 Shard map reads linearizable on change; watches deliver every revision NFR-5 Events carry an HLC; cause < effect for every causal pair NFR-6 Host clock offset > 50 ms alerts; > 250 ms removes the host from leader candidacy

4. Capacity & latency estimates.

Item Calculation Result etcd data Shard map (1,024 keys) + ~200 flags + ~20 election keys + Patroni < 10 MB (quota 2 GB) etcd writes Keep-alives: 30 candidates / 3 s + Patroni + map changes ~20 writes/s (trivial) etcd write latency Majority round trip cross-AZ ~1–2 ms + fsync ~1–5 ms p99 ~10 ms Watches ~600 pods × 2 watches ~1.2 K watches (fine for 3 nodes) Failover time TTL 10 s, keep-alive every 3 s, campaign ~50 ms ≤ ~11 s HLC size 48-bit ms + 16-bit logical 8 bytes per event

5. Proposed design.

  1. etcd, 3 members in 3 AZs (5 in a later phase if maintenance windows show a need), on dedicated SSD-backed VMs, TLS + client certificates, per-job RBAC prefixes, defragmented and snapshotted on a schedule. Shared with Patroni (separate prefix), monitored as tier-0.
  2. Leader election library (FencedLeadership): lease TTL 10 s, keep-alive 3 s, campaign on a job-specific election name. Fencing token = the leader key's create revision, which is cluster-wide monotonic. The leader loop checks leadership before each batch and passes the token into every write.
  3. Resources enforce the fence: tables written by leader-only jobs have a fence bigint column, and every write is … where fence <= :token. A zero-row result means "lost leadership": abort and re-campaign. External side effects go through an idempotent outbox, never straight from the leader.
  4. Shard map and flags in etcd, updated only with transactions (If(modRevision == expected)), and read through watches starting at the revision last seen.
  5. HLC in the event envelope (hlc: "<ms>.<logical>"), sent on every outgoing call and message, merged on receipt. Timelines sort by HLC, then event id.
  6. Clock policy: chrony against the cloud time service, makestep only at boot, offset exported as a metric, and every timeout and duration uses System.nanoTime (a lint rule bans currentTimeMillis differences).

7. Alternatives considered.

Option Pros Cons Verdict Redis SET NX PX lock (status quo) Simple, fast No fencing; async replication can lose the lock (Ch 10) Rejected for correctness Redlock Tolerates master loss Timing assumptions, no fencing token Rejected etcd election + fencing tokens Linearizable, monotonic revisions, leases, watches A tier-0 cluster to run Chosen ZooKeeper Mature, ephemeral nodes, zxid tokens JVM ops, heavier; Kafka no longer needs it Rejected (no existing footprint) Kubernetes Lease objects No new infrastructure, etcd-backed Coupled to the cluster API server; no token in the API (use leaseTransitions or resourceVersion) Accepted for in-cluster, non-money jobs PostgreSQL lease table + epoch (the lab) Uses the DB that holds the data; fence in the same DB Load on the primary; failover semantics (Ch 10) Accepted where job and data share one DB

8. Failure modes. etcd minority loss: keeps working. Majority loss: no elections or map changes, current leaders keep going only until their lease can't be renewed, and fenced resources refuse stale tokens. Leader pause: fenced (lab). Clock skew on a candidate: over 250 ms it withdraws from campaigning. etcd slow disk: leader elections flap, so alert on fsync latency. Watch compaction: re-list from the current revision, then watch.

10. Observability. Leader identity and token per job, leadership changes per hour, fenced-write rejections (a nonzero value means a pause or partition happened, which is worth a look), lease keep-alive failures, etcd raft proposals committed/failed, fsync and backend commit durations, DB size vs quota, watch count, host clock offset, HLC logical-counter growth (a large counter means a clock far behind).

14. Decision (ADR-044–047 summary). Leader-only work uses etcd elections with leases, and the leader key revision is the fencing token enforced by every resource. Shard maps and flags live in etcd with revision-checked transactions and watches. Events carry HLC timestamps. Durations use monotonic clocks, and host offsets are monitored with hard limits for leadership candidates.
