docs.title: 6.2 Observability
docs.text:
• Consumer lag per group and partition, in records and seconds (the age of the oldest unconsumed record). This is the single most important streaming SLI.
  • Rebalances per hour and time spent rebalancing. Commit latency and failures.
  • Broker: under-replicated partitions, under-min-ISR partitions, offline partitions (page on all three), ISR shrink/expand rate, request latency p99 (produce/fetch), disk usage vs retention.
  • Producer: record error rate, retries, record-queue-time-avg, batch size, compression ratio.
  • DLT/retry topics: rates, age of the oldest message, by exception class.
  • End-to-end latency: event occurred_at (HLC) → consumer effect timestamp, as a histogram per consumer. It catches problems lag alone misses (slow producers, outbox backlog, Ch 13).
  • Tracing: propagate W3C trace context in headers, with producer and consumer spans linked (Ch 24).

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• TLS everywhere (client-broker and inter-broker). Authenticate with SASL/SCRAM, mTLS or OAUTHBEARER, and ACLs per topic and group (a service writes only its own domain's topics).
  • Events are data: minimize PII, and encrypt sensitive fields at the application level (the broker and its backups can be read by operators). Apply retention and deletion policies for DPDP compliance (Ch 36), keeping in mind compacted topics keep the latest value forever unless tombstoned.
  • The schema registry and Connect REST APIs are admin surfaces: authenticate and restrict them.
  • DLT replay is a privileged operation: audit who replayed what.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance & tuning knobs
docs.text: Knob Default here Effect acks / enable.idempotence all / true Durability and dedup vs a few ms of latency linger.ms / batch.size 5 ms / 64 KB Throughput vs latency compression.type zstd CPU vs network/disk min.insync.replicas 2 (RF 3) Refuse writes vs risk loss Partitions Sized for consumer parallelism × 2 Parallelism vs overhead; can't shrink max.poll.records / max.poll.interval.ms 100 / 5 min Batch efficiency vs rebalance risk fetch.min.bytes / fetch.max.wait.ms 1 KB / 100 ms Consumer throughput vs latency Retention / tiered storage 7 days hot Replay window vs disk max_ack_pending / prefetch (NATS/RabbitMQ) Sized to consumer capacity Backpressure (lab: 5)

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• Storage = bytes/s × retention × RF: RF 3 triples the disk. Tiered storage cuts hot-disk cost for long retention.
  • Cross-AZ traffic is often the biggest line item for Kafka in the cloud: replication (RF − 1 copies) plus consumers reading from leaders in other AZs. Use rack-aware follower fetching (KIP-392), so consumers read from a replica in their own AZ.
  • Partitions have a per-unit cost (memory, controller load, managed-service pricing). Don't create thousands "just in case".
  • Managed Kafka (MSK, Confluent Cloud, Aiven) trades money for operations. At this platform's scale (a few MB/s), a small managed cluster is usually cheaper than a team's time.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Producing without a key when order matters.

// ❌ before: sticky/round-robin partitioning; an order's events land on different partitions
kafka.send("order.order.status-changed.v1", event);

// ✅ after: key = aggregate id → one partition → per-order order
kafka.send("order.order.status-changed.v1", event.orderId(), event);

2. acks=1 (or acks=all with min.insync.replicas=1) for business events. Symptom: Acked events vanish after a broker failure (L3: 1,160; case B: 1,000). Fix: acks=all, idempotence, RF 3, min.insync.replicas=2, no unclean election.

3. Auto-commit with slow or failing processing. Symptom: Records skipped after a crash (L4: 8,413). Fix: Manual commit after processing, with idempotent effects.

4. Infinite in-place retries. Symptom: One bad record stops a partition for hours (§1.1). Fix: Bounded retries → retry topic → DLT, with a classifier.

5. More consumers than partitions, or scaling consumers to fix a hot key. Symptom: Idle pods, no throughput gain. Fix: Partitions ≥ peak consumers. Fix the key skew.

6. Increasing partitions on a keyed topic in place. Symptom: Out-of-order processing right after the change (L2: 50 % of keys move). Fix: Create a new topic with the right count, dual-write, then migrate consumers.

7. Long processing inside the poll loop. Symptom: max.poll.interval.ms exceeded → member kicked → rebalance → the same batch is reprocessed. Fix: Smaller max.poll.records, faster processing, or pause/resume with async work and careful commits.

8. Treating the broker as a database. Symptom: Services query topics for current state, or keep infinite retention without compaction. Fix: Build a read model (Ch 15). Use compacted topics only for latest-value feeds.

9. Breaking schema changes on an existing topic.

// ❌ before: renaming a field in place breaks every existing consumer and every replay
{"name": "amount", "type": "long"}  →  {"name": "amountPaise", "type": "long"}

// ✅ after: add a new optional field with a default; deprecate the old one; breaking changes → order.order.placed.v2
{"name": "amountPaise", "type": ["null", "long"], "default": null}

10. Retention shorter than the worst plausible consumer outage. Symptom: A consumer is down over a long weekend, and events are deleted before it's back (Redis lab: ~2,000 events never delivered). Fix: Retention ≫ lag alert threshold, tiered storage, and a replay-from-source path (CDC re-snapshot, Ch 13).

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ Queue vs pub/sub log: what's the difference?

30-second answer: In a queue, each message is processed by one consumer and removed when acknowledged. Consumers compete, and there's no history. In a log such as Kafka, messages are appended and kept for a retention period. Each consumer group tracks its own offset, so many independent consumers can read the same events at their own pace and replay them.

Deep answer: L1: a late subscriber to the queue got nothing, while a new log consumer group replayed from offset 0 (until retention removed records). Parallelism in a log is bounded by partitions per group. In a queue it's bounded by consumers. The lines blur: Kafka share groups, RabbitMQ streams, and JetStream work-queue vs limits retention.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Per-message ack and routing (queue) vs replay, ordering and fan-out (log).

Follow-ups: 1. Which for sending SMS jobs? → Queue semantics, with per-message retry and DLQ. 2. Which for order events? → A log: many consumers and replay.

Red flags: "Kafka is just a faster RabbitMQ."

Q2 [B1] ⭐ What do at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once mean?

30-second answer: At-most-once: a message is processed zero or one time (can be lost). At-least-once: one or more times (can be duplicated). Exactly-once: once in effect. Where you commit or acknowledge decides it: before processing gives at-most-once, after processing gives at-least-once, and at-least-once plus an idempotent effect gives effectively-once.

Deep answer: L4: committing before processing skipped 8,413 of 1 M records after crashes, committing after processing duplicated 9,362, and storing the offset with the effect in one DB transaction gave 0 and 0. Kafka's transactions give exactly-once only within Kafka.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Simplicity vs correctness guarantees.

Follow-ups: 1. Which default do most systems use? → At-least-once + idempotent consumers. 2. Is exactly-once delivery possible over a network? → Not in general. Exactly-once effect is.

Red flags: Believing a broker setting alone guarantees exactly-once to a database.

Q3 [B1] Why would you put a message broker between services?

30-second answer: To decouple them in time (the producer doesn't wait, and the consumer can be down), to fan out one event to many consumers, to absorb bursts (load leveling), and to let new consumers replay history. The cost is eventual consistency, duplicates, ordering concerns, lag, and another system to operate.

Deep answer: Use messaging for facts and deferrable work. Use synchronous calls when the caller needs an answer (price, payment result). Combine the two with outboxes (Ch 13).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Resilience and scalability vs complexity and latency.

Follow-ups: 1. When not to use one? → Request/response needing an immediate answer, or tiny systems. 2. What's load leveling? → The queue absorbs peaks, and consumers work at a steady rate.

Red flags: Messaging for everything, including queries.

Q4 [B1] What is a consumer group?

30-second answer: A set of consumers that share the work of reading a topic: each partition is assigned to exactly one member. Different groups read the same topic independently, each with its own offsets. That's how one topic serves picking, notifications and analytics.

Deep answer: More members than partitions leaves some idle. Membership changes trigger rebalancing. Offsets are committed per group and partition in __consumer_offsets.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Parallelism is capped by partitions.

Follow-ups: 1. What happens if a member dies? → Its partitions are reassigned after the session timeout. 2. How do you get queue-like per-message parallelism? → Share groups (Kafka 4.x) or a queue broker.

Red flags: Thinking every consumer in a group gets every message.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How does Kafka guarantee ordering, and how can you break it?

30-second answer: Order is guaranteed within a partition, and the key picks the partition (murmur2 mod N). So all events for one key are ordered if you key by the entity. You break it with no or wrong keys, by changing the partition count (keys remap), with non-idempotent retries with several in-flight requests, with retry topics, and with parallel processing inside a partition.

Deep answer: L2 using the real client: 12 → 24 partitions moves 50.1 % of keys. L4: a retry topic applied one event after later ones for the same order. Defence in depth: version-guarded consumers that ignore older versions.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Parallelism (more partitions, parallel processing) vs ordering.

Follow-ups: 1. Global ordering? → One partition, which means no parallelism. It's rarely needed. 2. Idempotence and ordering? → Idempotent producers keep order with up to 5 in-flight requests.

Red flags: "Kafka guarantees order" without "per partition".

Q6 [B2] ⭐ How many partitions should a topic have?

30-second answer: Enough for peak consumer parallelism (and producer throughput) with headroom for 2–3 years, because you can't shrink partitions and growing them remaps keys. Compute it from the slowest consumer's per-record time and the peak rate, then multiply by about 2.

Deep answer: Orders: 420 events/s at peak; the slowest consumer does ~40/s per instance, so 11 consumers, ×2 = 24 partitions. Too many partitions costs memory, file handles, longer failovers and managed-service fees. A hot key doesn't benefit from more partitions (L2: 1.87x skew).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Parallelism vs overhead and ordering stability.

Follow-ups: 1. What if we need more later? → A new topic with a migration, or accept temporary reordering with version guards. 2. Is throughput usually the limit? → Rarely for business events. Consumer processing is.

Red flags: "1,000 partitions to be safe."

Q7 [B2] Retention vs compaction?

30-second answer: Retention deletes old segments by time or size: the topic is a window of history. Compaction keeps at least the latest record per key and removes older ones (and deleted keys via tombstones): the topic becomes a changelog of current state, good for "latest stock per SKU" and for rebuilding caches or state stores.

Deep answer: They can be combined (compact,delete). Compaction runs in the background, so consumers may still see intermediate values (min.compaction.lag.ms). The JetStream lab showed the same idea with max-msgs-per-subject=1: three statuses became one. Beware of PII: compacted keys stay until tombstoned.

Trade-offs I'd call out: History vs size.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you delete a key? → Produce a null value (tombstone). 2. Is an order events topic compacted? → No, we need the full history. A latest-status topic could be.

Red flags: Compacting an event topic whose history consumers need.

Q8 [B2] Where should a consumer commit offsets?

30-second answer: After the effect is durable, making the effect idempotent (at-least-once + dedup). Or atomically with the effect by storing offsets in the same DB transaction. Never before processing, unless losing messages is acceptable.

Deep answer: L4 over 1 M records with crashes: commit-first lost 8,413, commit-after duplicated 9,362, in-DB offsets gave 0/0. With Spring Kafka: enable-auto-commit=false, AckMode.RECORD or BATCH, and an inbox in the same transaction. Commit on partition revocation to reduce duplicates during rebalances.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Commit frequency (throughput) vs the amount of reprocessing after a crash.

Follow-ups: 1. Auto-commit? → It commits on poll intervals, so it's effectively at-most-once when processing is slow. 2. Batch commits? → A larger replay window after a crash.

Red flags: Enabling auto-commit and processing asynchronously.

Q9 [B2] What causes consumer-group rebalances, and how do you reduce their impact?

30-second answer: Members joining or leaving, crashes (missed heartbeats and session timeout), and a member exceeding max.poll.interval.ms because processing is slow. To reduce them: use the cooperative-sticky assignor (or KIP-848), static membership for rolling restarts, keep poll batches short, and commit on revoke.

Deep answer: L2 with the real assignors: when a 4th consumer joined, eager range and roundrobin revoked all partitions (moving 6 or 9), while cooperative-sticky revoked only 3 and handed them over in a second round, with the others never stopping.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Faster failure detection (short timeouts) vs false rebalances.

Follow-ups: 1. What's static membership? → group.instance.id, so a restart within the session timeout keeps the assignment. 2. What does KIP-848 change? → The broker computes assignments incrementally, and there are no client-side sync barriers.

Red flags: Scaling consumers during an incident without understanding the rebalances it triggers.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ Explain ISR, high watermark, acks and min.insync.replicas together.

30-second answer: Followers fetch from the leader. Those caught up within replica.lag.time.max.ms form the ISR. The high watermark is the highest offset all ISR members have, and consumers read only up to it. acks=all waits for the current ISR. min.insync.replicas makes the leader refuse writes when the ISR is too small, so acks=all can't silently degrade to one copy.

Deep answer: L3: acks=1 lost 1,160 acked records on leader failures. acks=all with min.insync=1 is safe until the leader is the only ISR member and its disk dies (case B: 1,000 lost). min.insync=2 refused those writes instead (0 lost). Unclean election brings the partition back sooner but lost 15,566.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Availability of writes vs durability.

Follow-ups: 1. What does the producer do on NotEnoughReplicas? → Retry until the delivery timeout, then fail to the caller or outbox. 2. RF 3 with min ISR 3? → Any single broker outage blocks writes.

Red flags: "acks=all means all replicas."

Q11 [B3] ⭐ How do you handle poison messages in Kafka?

30-second answer: Classify failures. Non-retryable ones (bad data, deserialization) go to a DLT immediately. Retryable ones get bounded retries, either in place for strictly ordered consumers (with a small budget) or through delayed retry topics so the partition keeps flowing, then the DLT. Every DLT has an owner, an alert and a replay tool.

Deep answer: L4: blocking retries kept order but put 5 s of lag on every record behind the poison message (hours in §1.1). A retry topic kept lag at 2 ms but reordered one event for its order. Keep the original coordinates and error in headers. The NATS lab showed a native equivalent: max_deliver plus an advisory for the dead-letter handler.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Ordering vs availability of the partition.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you replay from the DLT safely? → An idempotent consumer, replaying to the original topic or a replay topic, rate-limited. 2. A deserialization error? → Use ErrorHandlingDeserializer, then route to the DLT.

Red flags: An infinite retry loop, or a DLT nobody monitors.

Q12 [B3] Does Kafka's exactly-once solve duplicate side effects?

30-second answer: Only inside Kafka. The idempotent producer removes duplicates from retries (L3: 30 → 0), and transactions atomically write outputs and consumer offsets for Kafka-to-Kafka processing (read_committed consumers). Side effects in databases, emails or APIs still need idempotency or offsets stored with the effect.

Deep answer: Kafka Streams exactly_once_v2 is the clean case. With a DB sink: an inbox table in the same transaction (Ch 13), or Kafka Connect sinks with upserts keyed by primary key. The transaction coordinator adds latency and needs transactional.id management.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Throughput and complexity vs duplicate handling in consumers.

Follow-ups: 1. What does read_committed hide? → Records from aborted transactions, and records beyond the last stable offset. 2. Is idempotence on by default? → Yes, since Kafka 3.0.

Red flags: "EOS means the SMS is sent once."

Q13 [B3] How do you evolve event schemas without breaking consumers?

30-second answer: Use a schema registry with a compatibility mode (backward or full, transitive), and only make compatible changes: add optional fields with defaults, never reuse or retype fields. For breaking changes, create a versioned topic and dual-publish during migration. Enforce this in CI with contract tests.

Deep answer: Avro and Protobuf give compact encoding plus evolution rules, and JSON needs discipline or JSON Schema. Consumers must tolerate unknown fields. Events are long-lived because of replay, so old consumers and old data must keep working. The event envelope carries the schema version and event type.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed of change vs consumer safety.

Follow-ups: 1. Backward vs forward? → New readers read old data, vs old readers read new data. 2. How do you remove a field? → Deprecate it, stop reading it everywhere, then remove it (with a default).

Red flags: Renaming fields in place.

Q14 [B3] ⭐ Consumer lag is growing. What do you do?

30-second answer: Measure lag in time per partition to see whether it's all partitions (capacity) or one (hot key or poison message). For one partition: check for a stuck record or DLT flow, or a hot key. For all partitions: scale consumers up to the partition count, speed up processing (batching, async I/O, a slow dependency?), and shed non-critical work. Watch retention: lag must never reach it.

Deep answer: Check rebalance churn (it looks like lag), consumer error rates, and downstream latency (DB, APIs). A slow DB behind a consumer is the most common cause. The Redis lab showed retention silently trimming what lagging groups hadn't read.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Throughput vs ordering (parallel processing within a partition).

Follow-ups: 1. Can you add consumers beyond the partition count? → Not in one group. Add partitions via migration, or process in parallel within a partition by key. 2. Which alert? → Age of the oldest unconsumed record, against the SLO and against retention.

Red flags: Only alerting on lag in records.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Kafka, RabbitMQ, Pulsar, NATS, SQS: how do you choose?

30-second answer: From the model you need and the operations you can afford. Kafka for a durable, replayable event backbone with a big ecosystem. RabbitMQ for work queues with rich routing and per-message ack. Pulsar for multi-tenant, geo-replicated streaming with tiered storage. NATS JetStream for lightweight low-latency streams with Raft replication. SQS/SNS for zero-ops cloud queues without replay.

Deep answer: Criteria: replay/retention, ordering scope, per-message semantics, routing, throughput, multi-region, ecosystem (Connect, Debezium, Streams), team skills, managed availability and cost. Many platforms run two: a log for events and a queue for jobs. The labs showed JetStream (R3 failover, dedup, max_deliver) and Redis Streams (consumer groups, PEL, trimming) doing similar jobs with different operational profiles.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Capability vs operational cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Could Redis Streams replace Kafka? → For small, ephemeral streams. Its replication is async and memory-bound. 2. Kafka for jobs? → Share groups (4.x) help, but per-message delay and priority are still awkward.

Red flags: Choosing by popularity.

Q16 [B4] Design the event backbone for the grocery platform.

30-second answer: Kafka (managed) with RF 3 across AZs and min ISR 2. Topics per event type named <domain>.<entity>.<event>.v<N>, keyed by aggregate id and sized for consumer parallelism. Producers go through outboxes with idempotence and acks=all. Consumers use cooperative-sticky assignment, static membership, commit-after with inboxes, retry topics and owned DLTs. Avro with a registry. Lag-in-time SLOs.

Deep answer: Plus compacted topics for latest-state feeds, CDC for analytics, rack-aware fetching to cut cross-AZ cost, ACLs per domain, PII minimization, tiered storage for replay, and a DR plan (MirrorMaker 2 / cluster linking, Ch 27). Estimates: ~1.3 MB/s, 2.8 TB at 7-day retention, 24 partitions for the order topic.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Managed cost vs ops; event granularity vs topic count.

Follow-ups: 1. Multi-region? → An active cluster per region plus replication of selected topics; keys must stay region-affine. 2. Who owns topics? → The producing domain team, with the platform team owning the cluster.

Red flags: One giant events topic for everything.

Q17 [B4] How do you make a consumer both ordered and fast?

30-second answer: Partition by the ordering key and parallelize across partitions. Within a partition, process in parallel by key (a key-ordered executor, e.g. Confluent's Parallel Consumer), and commit only the contiguous processed prefix. Batch I/O, and keep per-record work short.

Deep answer: Throughput per partition becomes (distinct keys in flight) × (per-key rate). Offsets must track completion gaps, and a hot key still caps throughput. Alternatively, split the ordered part (the state machine) from the unordered part (side effects), and emit a second event for the slow part.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Complexity of offset tracking vs throughput.

Follow-ups: 1. What's the commit risk? → Committing past an unprocessed record loses it on a crash. 2. When does this beat adding partitions? → When you can't repartition, or the keys are many and fine-grained.

Red flags: A thread pool per partition without key ordering.

Q18 [B4] How would you migrate a keyed topic from 12 to 48 partitions without breaking consumers?

30-second answer: Create …v1 with 48 partitions as a new topic (or a new version), and dual-publish from the producers (via the outbox relay) to both. Start consumers on the new topic from a point where they can dedup (inbox/versions). Switch readers, then stop the old publish and retire the old topic after retention.

Deep answer: In-place growth would remap ~75 % of keys (for 12 → 48, a key stays only if its hash mod 48 < 12). Idempotent, version-guarded consumers make the overlap safe. Cut over per consumer group, and monitor lag on both.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Migration effort vs ordering safety.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you decide the new count? → Parallelism × headroom, plus hot-key analysis. 2. Can you avoid dual publishing? → A mirror job that re-keys from old to new, with the same caveats.

Red flags: kafka-topics --alter --partitions 48 on a keyed topic during peak.

Q19 [B4] Your DLT for payments events has 3,000 messages after a deploy. Walk me through it.

30-second answer: Stop the bleeding (roll back or disable the failing path), group the DLT by exception and schema version to find the root cause (a schema change? a new validation? a downstream failure?), fix it, then replay from the DLT with an idempotent consumer at a controlled rate, verifying with reconciliation (Ch 45). Postmortem on why the contract test or canary didn't catch it.

Deep answer: Check whether any messages were non-retryable because of data (they need correction before replay). Communicate the delay to Finance. Make sure replays keep per-key order where it matters, for example by replaying per key in offset order.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed of recovery vs risk of repeating side effects.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you prevent it? → Registry compatibility checks, contract tests, a canary consumer. 2. What if some messages are no longer valid? → Compensate, and record the decision.

Red flags: Bulk-replaying the DLT before understanding the failure.

Q20 [B4] What are the hidden costs of an event-driven architecture?

30-second answer: Eventual consistency everywhere, duplicate and out-of-order handling in every consumer, schema governance, DLT operations, lag monitoring, harder debugging (flows are implicit), data duplication across read models, PII spread, and a platform to run, plus cross-AZ network costs.

Deep answer: Mitigations: an event catalog with owners, tracing across async boundaries, standard consumer libraries (inbox, retries, DLT, metrics), contract tests, and reconciliation jobs. Use events for facts and decoupling, and keep synchronous calls where an immediate answer is required.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Autonomy and resilience vs cognitive and operational load.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you debug a lost order event? → Trace id, outbox row, broker offsets, consumer inbox. 2. When is EDA the wrong choice? → Small teams, simple CRUD, strong consistency needs.

Red flags: "Events decouple everything for free."

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Queue or log is the first choice: removal on ack vs retained history with per-group offsets and replay.
  2. Order is per partition. Key by the aggregate id, and never grow a keyed topic in place (L2: 50 % of keys move).
  3. Size partitions for peak consumer parallelism with headroom, and watch for hot keys (1.87x).
  4. Durability = RF 3 + acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2 + no unclean election + an idempotent producer. L3 quantified each piece.
  5. The commit point decides the semantics. Commit after processing with idempotent effects (L4: 8,413 lost vs 9,362 duplicated vs 0/0).
  6. Kafka exactly-once is Kafka-to-Kafka. Databases and APIs need Ch 13's patterns.
  7. Poison messages: classify, bound retries, use retry topics, and give every DLT an owner.
  8. Rebalances hurt: use cooperative-sticky / KIP-848, static membership and short polls (3 vs 6–9 partitions moved).
  9. Lag in time is the key SLI, and retention is the hard deadline for lag.
  10. Schemas are contracts: use a registry, backward-compatible changes, and versioned topics for breaking ones.

docs.title: 15. Event-Driven Architecture, CQRS & Event Sourcing
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B2 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 05, Ch 13, Ch 14 · What you will build: The store-credit wallet as an event-sourced aggregate, and order tracking as CQRS read models.

  • L1 compares event notification, event-carried state transfer and event sourcing (plain Java).
  • L2 is a PostgreSQL event store with optimistic concurrency. A negative control without the version check lets the wallet go overdrawn.
  • L3 runs projectors tailing the store while writers append. The naive "max position seen" checkpoint misses 2,954 of 12,000 events. A transaction-id-aware checkpoint misses none, and a rebuild repairs the broken model.
  • L4 loads a 200,437-event aggregate with and without snapshots (180 ms vs 3.4 ms), and upcasts legacy rupee amounts to paise, where a double-based upcaster silently loses ₹57.40.

L2–L4 run as real Java (JDBC) against real PostgreSQL 16. · Reading time: 100 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: "Your order is being packed", for three days
docs.text:
The team rebuilt order tracking with CQRS:

  • Commands wrote events to an event store table in PostgreSQL.
  • A projector polled select * from events where id > :last_id order by id, updated an order_tracking read model, and saved last_id.
  • The app read only from order_tracking.

It was fast, and load tests passed.

In production, about 1 in 40 orders got stuck in their tracking view: delivered orders still showed "Packing". Nothing had failed. The events were in the store and the projector had no errors. The cause took two weeks to find:

  • id was a bigserial, so the id was assigned when the row was inserted, but it became visible when the transaction committed.
  • Under concurrency, event 1,041 could commit after event 1,042. The projector read 1,042, saved last_id = 1042, and never looked back. Event 1,041 was skipped forever.

L3 reproduces it: 2,954 of 12,000 events missed with 8 concurrent writers.

The same quarter, a different team event-sourced the shopping cart. Every "add 1 banana, remove 1 banana" was an event. A year later, carts had up to 40,000 events, loading a cart took seconds, and nobody had ever asked for cart history. They also needed to change the event format, which meant writing upcasters for four historical versions of ItemAdded.

Both teams used good patterns in the wrong way:

  • A projector must checkpoint by what is safe to read, not by the highest number it has seen. In PostgreSQL, use the transaction id and the snapshot's xmin. Or use a log that assigns positions at commit (Kafka, EventStoreDB).
  • Event sourcing is for aggregates whose history is the business, like wallets, ledgers, orders and bookings. It's not for carts or profiles. Where it is used, it needs snapshots, versioned events and upcasters from day one.

The thesis of this chapter

Events can play three roles: notifications, carriers of state, or the source of truth. CQRS separates the model you write from the models you read, and those read models are disposable and rebuildable. Event sourcing makes the log the source of truth, which gives you history, audit and time travel. In return you must handle concurrency per stream, checkpoints that don't skip events, snapshots, schema versions and rebuilds. Use each pattern where its benefit is the requirement.

docs.text: Area Pattern Why Store credit / wallet Event sourcing (Opened, Credited, Debited, Expired) Balance must be explainable; RBI/finance audit; disputes need exact history Order lifecycle State in tables + events via outbox (Ch 13) Current state is what matters; events for others Order tracking, order history, store dashboard CQRS read models built from order events Query shapes differ from the write model; scale reads independently Search, recommendations Read models in OpenSearch / feature stores Specialized stores fed by events (Ch 22) Catalog updates to other services Event-carried state transfer (ProductUpdated with full product) Consumers keep local copies; no callbacks "Order shipped" notifications Event notification + small payload Consumers need only the fact Cart Plain table (+ events for analytics) No business need for history (§1.1) Delivery slot bookings Event-sourced aggregate per slot (Ch 48) Contention + audit of who took which slot

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text: Band After this chapter you can… B2 Distinguish event notification, event-carried state transfer and event sourcing, and explain CQRS and read models B3 Build an event store with optimistic concurrency, projectors with safe checkpoints, idempotent projection and rebuilds, and snapshots B4 Version events and write upcasters, handle GDPR/DPDP erasure in immutable logs, choose where ES/CQRS fit and where they don't, and operate projections in production

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: the bank passbook B2
docs.text:
An old-style bank passbook doesn't store "your balance". It stores every deposit and withdrawal, and the balance printed on each line is derived from them.

  • The passbook lines are events. They're facts in the past tense ("Deposited ₹500 on 3 March"), and they're never erased. A mistake is corrected with a new line ("Reversal of entry 41").
  • The balance is a projection of those lines. So is "total spent this month" and "all cheques above ₹10,000". Each is a different view of the same lines.
  • The branch keeps the passbook, but the head office builds its own reports from copies of the entries. That's CQRS: writes happen in one place, and reads use models shaped for each question.
  • After 20 years, the clerk doesn't re-add every line to answer "what's the balance?". They start from last year's closing balance. That's a snapshot.
  • When the bank changed from "Rs." to "₹" and from annas to paise, old pages weren't rewritten. Staff learned to read the old format. That's upcasting.

docs.title: 2.2 Three things called "event-driven" ⭐ B2
docs.text:
Martin Fowler's distinction, which L1 measures:

Style Event carries Consumer does L1 result (order-service down) Event notification The fact + ids (AddressChanged{orderId}) Calls the producer back for details 10,000 callbacks, all failed. Tight runtime coupling, and load on the producer Event-carried state transfer (ECST) The new state (AddressChangedWithState{orderId, address}) Keeps a local copy 0 callbacks; the local copy equals the source Event sourcing Each change as the durable record (AddressSet{…, version}) State = fold(events) Same current state, plus the full history (5 versions of ord-985)
  • Event-driven architecture usually means the first two between services.
  • Event sourcing is an internal persistence choice of one service or aggregate, and it doesn't require the others.
  • CQRS is orthogonal to both, and it's common with either.

Choose per event:

  • Notification when consumers need only the fact, or the data is large or sensitive (fetch with authorization).
  • ECST when consumers need the data and must keep working when the producer is down.
  • Never use "events as RPC" (PleaseSendSms as an event): that's a command. Send it to a queue with an owner (Ch 14).

docs.title: 2.3 Domain events vs integration events B2 B3
docs.text:
• Domain events live inside a bounded context (WalletDebited). They can be fine-grained and change with the model.
  • Integration events are the context's public contract (order.order.placed.v1). They're stable, versioned and carry what consumers need, and they're usually mapped from domain events in the outbox (Ch 13) or by a translator.
  • Don't publish internal event-sourcing events directly as integration events. That couples consumers to your aggregate's internals, and every internal refactor becomes a breaking change (Ch 14 §2.10).

docs.title: 2.4 CQRS ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
Command Query Responsibility Segregation (Greg Young, building on Meyer's CQS):

  • The command side validates intentions against an aggregate and records changes.
  • The query side serves reads from read models (projections) optimized for each query.
command → aggregate (write model) → events / changes ─┬→ projector → order_tracking (PostgreSQL)
                                                      ├→ projector → store_dashboard (PostgreSQL, per store)
                                                      └→ projector → order_search (OpenSearch)
query ───────────────────────────────────────────────────→ read model
Benefit Cost Read models shaped per query (no 7-table joins at read time) Eventual consistency between write and read (lag) Read and write scale independently (Ch 11 orders_by_store) More moving parts: projectors, checkpoints, rebuilds Different stores per read (search, cache, graph) Duplicate data; schema changes touch several models Read models are disposable: drop and rebuild (L3: 12,000 events in 549 ms) Rebuild time grows with history, so plan for it

CQRS doesn't need event sourcing: the write side can be ordinary tables plus an outbox (Ch 13). Nor does it need separate databases. A second table updated by a projector is CQRS.

Read-your-writes on a CQRS system:

  • Return the new state from the command (the command side knows it).
  • Or return a version/position, and have the query wait until the read model has reached it (like the Ch 10 LSN token).
  • Or read from the write model for the user's own freshly changed entity.

docs.title: 2.5 Event sourcing ⭐ B3
docs.text:
The aggregate's state isn't stored. Its events are, and the state is rebuilt by folding them:

Wallet w = new Wallet();
for (WalletEvent e : store.read("wallet-cust-42")) w.apply(e);   // state = fold(apply, events)
List<WalletEvent> decided = w.debit(100, "ord-77");               // decide from current state
store.append("wallet-cust-42", w.version, decided);              // expected version = what we decided on

What you gain:

  • A complete audit trail by construction. L2's running balance at any version: v52 → ₹50.00, v101 → ₹1.00.
  • Time travel: "what did the wallet look like on 31 March?"
  • New read models from old history (replay into a new projection).
  • Debugging by replaying a production stream.
  • Natural integration events.

What you pay:

  • Every read of current state needs a projection or a replay, so snapshots are needed for long streams (L4).
  • Event schemas are forever: versioning and upcasting (L4 B).
  • You need concurrency control per stream (L2).
  • Projections must be correct under concurrency (L3).
  • Erasure of personal data in an immutable log (§2.10).
  • The team must think in events, and queries across aggregates need projections.

docs.title: 2.6 The event store and optimistic concurrency ⭐ B3
docs.text:
An event store needs:

  1. Append with an expected version, failing if the stream moved on.
  2. Read a stream in order.
  3. Read all events in a global order for projectors, with a position that is safe to checkpoint (§2.7).
  4. Optionally, subscriptions/notifications, snapshots and metadata (correlation/causation ids, user, HLC timestamp).

In PostgreSQL, primary key (stream_id, version) makes the database enforce (1): a concurrent writer that decided on the same version gets a unique violation (23505), reloads and decides again.

L2 ran 16 threads × 20 debits of ₹1 against a ₹100 wallet:

Store Debits accepted Final balance Events sharing a version No expected-version check 111 −₹11.00 (overdrawn) 56 Expected version (PK on stream, version) 100 ₹0.00 0, after 649 retried conflicts
  • The invariant balance ≥ 0 is enforced only because every decision was made against the exact version it appended after.
  • The 649 conflicts show the cost of contention on one stream. A hot stream needs a design fix: smaller aggregates, or commands that commute. Retrying harder doesn't help.

Stream = aggregate = consistency boundary. One transaction appends to one stream. Invariants across streams (e.g. "a customer's total credit ≤ ₹10,000 across wallets") need a different aggregate design or a saga (Ch 13).

docs.title: 2.7 Projections and the checkpoint problem ⭐ B3 B4
docs.text:
A projector:

  1. Reads events after its checkpoint.
  2. Applies them to a read model.
  3. Stores the new checkpoint in the same transaction as the read-model change, which makes it exactly-once in effect.

Correctness hinges on what "after the checkpoint" means.

Why "max position seen" is wrong on a database: sequences hand out numbers at insert, and transactions commit in a different order. When the projector sees position 1,042 committed and 1,041 still in flight, it advances past 1,041 forever. L3: 2,954 of 12,000 events missed, and 417 orders show a stale status, with no error anywhere.

Fixes:

Approach How Trade-off Transaction-id bound (PostgreSQL) Store pg_current_xact_id() with each event. Read where (tx_id, position) > checkpoint and tx_id < pg_snapshot_xmin(pg_current_snapshot()), ordered by (tx_id, position) Waits for the oldest open transaction; long transactions add lag. L3: 0 missed Single writer / serialize appends Take an advisory lock per append, so commit order = position order Throughput cap Commit-ordered log Kafka offsets, EventStoreDB/KurrentDB, Axon Server, or CDC from the WAL (commit order, Ch 13) Another system, but the log order is the commit order Gap detection with a wait Treat a missing position as "maybe in flight" and wait up to T before skipping it Complex; the timeout is a guess

Idempotent projections:

  • Projectors are at-least-once (crashes between apply and checkpoint if they aren't in one transaction, or replays).
  • Use upserts keyed by entity, where last_version < :v guards, or the inbox pattern (Ch 13).
  • Side effects (emails) don't belong in projectors that get rebuilt, or every rebuild re-sends them. Put them in separate process managers/reactors with their own dedup.

Rebuilds:

  • A read model is derived data. Drop it, reset its checkpoint and replay. L3 rebuilt the broken model in 549 ms.
  • For big histories, build the new version alongside the old (order_tracking_v2), then switch reads when it catches up (blue/green projections).

docs.title: 2.8 Snapshots ⭐ B3
docs.text:
A snapshot stores an aggregate's state at version N. Loading = latest snapshot + the events after it.

  • L4: 200,437 events, full replay 179.8 ms vs snapshot + 437 events 3.4 ms, same state.
  • Take a snapshot every N events, or when load time exceeds a threshold. Write it asynchronously; snapshots are caches, not truth.
  • Version the snapshot format. On a mismatch, discard it and replay (snapshots are disposable, events aren't).
  • Long streams are often a modelling smell. Close accounting periods ("book closing": a PeriodClosed event carrying balances, then a new stream per period), or split the aggregate, before reaching for snapshots.

docs.title: 2.9 Event versioning and upcasting ⭐ B3 B4
docs.text:
Events are immutable, but understanding improves. Techniques, from the least to the most invasive:

  1. Additive change: add an optional field with a default, and old events still deserialize.
  2. Weak schema: readers ignore unknown fields and default missing ones.
  3. Upcasting: on read, a chain of pure functions converts v1 → v2 → v3 into the shape the code knows. Stored events are untouched. Upcasters must be exact and deterministic: L4's double-based rupees-to-paise upcaster turned "19.99" into 1,998 paise and was wrong on 5,740 of 100,000 legacy events, ₹57.40 in total. The BigDecimal version was exact.
  4. New event type (WalletDebitedV2), with both handled in apply.
  5. Copy-and-transform migration: rewrite streams into a new store (the last resort, with an audit trail of the migration itself).

Record schema_version (or the event type version) in every stored event, and test upcasters against real samples from production history.

docs.title: 2.10 Personal data in immutable logs B4
docs.text:
DPDP (India) and GDPR give people a right to erasure, and logs don't forget. Options:

  • Keep PII out of events. Reference a customer id, and store details in a mutable profile service.
  • Crypto-shredding: encrypt PII fields with a per-customer key kept in a key store. To erase, delete the key, and the events stay but the PII is unreadable. Projections must handle "unreadable" gracefully.
  • Tombstones and compaction for Kafka-compacted topics (Ch 14). Don't forget read models, backups and the data warehouse.
  • Keep an erasure log of what was erased and when, without the data itself (Ch 36).

docs.title: 2.11 Process managers and event-driven workflows B3
docs.text: A process manager (or reactor) reacts to events by issuing commands: "when PaymentCaptured and StockReserved both arrived for an order, send ConfirmOrder". It keeps its own state, keyed by correlation id, and is essentially an orchestration saga driven by events (Ch 13). Separate reactors that cause side effects from projectors that build read models: projectors must be safe to replay, and reactors must not re-send on replay (dedup by event id, or skip on replay).

docs.title: 2.12 When to use ES and CQRS, and when not ⭐ B4
docs.text:
Use event sourcing when… Don't, when… History is the business: ledgers, wallets, bookings, claims, compliance Current state is all anyone needs (carts, profiles, settings) Audit/dispute resolution needs exact "who, what, when" A simple audit table or CDC to a history table would do Many future read models are likely (analytics, ML features) The team is new to it and the domain is CRUD Temporal queries ("as of") are frequent Aggregates would have very long, very hot streams without natural closing periods Natural concurrency boundaries (per account/booking) Cross-aggregate invariants dominate Use CQRS when… Don't, when… Read shapes differ a lot from write shapes, or reads ≫ writes One table + indexes serves reads fine Different read stores are needed (search, cache, analytics) Users can't tolerate any read lag and the command can't return state Read and write scaling differ (Ch 11 orders_by_store) Small team, small system

Most of the grocery platform is CRUD + outbox events + a few read models. Event sourcing is used for the wallet and slot bookings only.

docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Building: new projection version created
    Building --> CatchingUp: replaying history from position 0
    CatchingUp --> Live: lag below threshold

Reads switch from vN to vN+1 only when vN+1 is Live. Rebuilding never takes the old model offline.

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Event-Sourced Wallet and CQRS Order Tracking
docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers Payments & Orders teams / Finance, SRE, Security Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-058 Event-source the wallet; ADR-059 PostgreSQL event store with xid-safe projections; ADR-060 Snapshots and period closing; ADR-061 Event versioning and upcasters; ADR-062 Order tracking as rebuildable read models

1. Context & Problem. Wallet balances were a single mutable column, and disputes ("why is my credit ₹0?") needed log archaeology. Order tracking projections skipped events under concurrency (§1.1), and the cart was event-sourced without a need.

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: every wallet balance is explainable event by event; no overdraft under concurrency; projections never skip events; read models rebuildable without downtime; event formats can evolve safely; PII erasable.
  • Non-goals: event-sourcing orders or carts (tables + outbox suffice); a global event store for all services.

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement NFR-1 Wallet invariant balance ≥ 0 holds under any concurrency (0 violations in tests) NFR-2 Wallet load p99 ≤ 20 ms regardless of history length NFR-3 Projection completeness: 0 missed events (checked by a nightly count/sum reconciliation against the store) NFR-4 Projection lag p99 ≤ 2 s; read-your-writes available via min-version queries NFR-5 A full rebuild of order tracking completes in ≤ 1 h and switches over with no read downtime NFR-6 Every stored event carries type, schema version, correlation/causation ids and an HLC timestamp

4. Capacity & latency estimates.

Item Calculation Result Wallet events ~120 K debits/credits per day at P90 ~44 M/year, ~1 KB each → ~44 GB/year Longest streams B2B wallets: ~300 events/day ~110 K/year → snapshots + yearly period closing Load time L4: 200 K events 180 ms full vs 3.4 ms with snapshot Snapshot every 1,000 events Order tracking rebuild ~1.3 K events/s peak, ~40 M events/month kept 3 months; L3 rate ~22 K events/s single-threaded ~1.5 h single projector → partition by order hash, 4 workers → ~25 min Contention One wallet: at most a few concurrent debits (checkout + refund) Retry on conflict is fine (L2 showed the worst case with 16 threads)

5. Proposed design.

  1. Event store in PostgreSQL:
    • events(global_position bigserial, tx_id xid8 default pg_current_xact_id(), stream_id, version, type, schema_version, payload jsonb, metadata jsonb, recorded_at).
    • primary key (stream_id, version), plus indexes on (tx_id, global_position).
    • Append-only: UPDATE/DELETE revoked from application roles.
  2. Wallet aggregate: stream per customer wallet, expected-version appends, and idempotency by (stream, command id) in metadata. A saga step (Ch 13) retries with the same command id.
  3. Projections: a projector framework with a (tx_id, position) checkpoint below pg_snapshot_xmin, read-model update + checkpoint in one transaction, upserts with version guards, and blue/green rebuilds.
  4. Integration events: mapped from domain events through the outbox to Kafka (Ch 13/14). Consumers never read the event store directly.
  5. Snapshots every 1,000 events (async, versioned), and period closing each financial year: PeriodClosed{balance} starts a new stream wallet-cust-42-2027.
  6. Versioning: schema_version per event, an upcaster chain per type with golden tests from production samples, and exact decimal arithmetic only.
  7. PII: events carry customer_id only. Where free text could contain PII (a support note), encrypt it with a per-customer key (crypto-shredding).

7. Alternatives considered.

Option Pros Cons Verdict Mutable balance + audit table Simple Audit can drift from the balance; no replay Rejected for the wallet Event sourcing on PostgreSQL One database the team knows; transactional with outbox Must solve global ordering for projectors (xid approach) Chosen EventStoreDB/KurrentDB Purpose-built: commit-ordered $all, subscriptions New system to operate Revisit if more services adopt ES Axon Framework + Server Aggregates, sagas, upcasters built in Framework lock-in Rejected Kafka as the event store Commit-ordered log, replay No per-stream expected-version append; stream reads are expensive Rejected as the source of truth; used for integration

8. Failure modes. Concurrent debits: conflict → retry → reject if insufficient. Long-running transaction: projections lag (alert on the age of the oldest open transaction). Poison event in a projector: stall that projection only, and alert. Upcaster bug: caught by golden tests; if found later, fix the upcaster and rebuild the projections (events are untouched). Snapshot corruption: discard and replay.

10. Observability. Append conflicts/s per stream type, stream length distribution, snapshot age, projection lag (positions and seconds) per projection, projection reconciliation results (events counted vs applied), rebuild progress, upcaster invocations by version, the age of the oldest open DB transaction.

14. Decision (ADR-058–062 summary). The wallet is event-sourced on PostgreSQL with expected-version appends. Projections use transaction-id-safe checkpoints stored atomically with the read model, and are rebuildable blue/green. Snapshots every 1,000 events plus yearly period closing. Every event is versioned and upcast exactly on read. Orders and carts stay table-based with outbox events and CQRS read models.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
Level New requirement that forces the step L1 "Share an address change with delivery-service: notification, state transfer, or event sourcing?" (plain Java) L2 "The wallet must never go below zero, and every rupee must be explainable." (real PostgreSQL event store) L3 "Order tracking must never miss an event, and must be rebuildable." (real PostgreSQL projections under concurrency) L4 "Wallets with years of history must load fast, and old events must keep working as the format changes." (real PostgreSQL)

How the code in this chapter was verified

L1 is plain Java. L2–L4 are JDBC programs run against a real PostgreSQL 16 (PostgreSQL JDBC driver 42.7.4, Java 21), and every output below is copied from a run. Concurrency makes exact counts vary between runs, but not the invariants. The Spring versions after L2 and L3 are one-to-one translations of the verified SQL and logic into the four-layer structure. They weren't compiled here (no Maven Central access) and are marked VERIFY.

docs.title: L1 — Concept: three ways to share a change (plain Java) B2
docs.text:
// EventStylesL1.java — run with: java EventStylesL1.java
// The same fact — "the customer changed the delivery address of an order" — shared three ways:
// event notification, event-carried state transfer, and event sourcing.
import java.util.*;

public class EventStylesL1 {

    record Address(String line, String pincode) { }

    /** order-service: the owner of the data. It can be down. */
    static final class OrderService {
        final Map<String, Address> addresses = new HashMap<>();
        boolean up = true; int reads = 0;
        Address getAddress(String orderId) {
            if (!up) throw new IllegalStateException("order-service unavailable");
            reads++; return addresses.get(orderId);
        }
    }

    // 1. Event notification: "something changed, ask me"
    record AddressChanged(String orderId) { }
    // 2. Event-carried state transfer: "here is the new state"
    record AddressChangedWithState(String orderId, Address newAddress) { }
    // 3. Event sourcing: the events ARE the state
    record AddressSet(String orderId, Address address, int version) { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        OrderService orders = new OrderService();
        List<String> changes = new ArrayList<>();
        List<AddressSet> log = new ArrayList<>();
        Random rnd = new Random(1);
        for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
            String id = "ord-" + rnd.nextInt(2_000);
            Address a = new Address("Flat " + i, "5600" + (10 + rnd.nextInt(90)));
            orders.addresses.put(id, a);
            changes.add(id);
            int v = (int) log.stream().filter(e -> e.orderId().equals(id)).count() + 1;
            log.add(new AddressSet(id, a, v));
        }
        orders.up = false;                               // order-service is down while delivery-service consumes

        // delivery-service consuming style 1
        int failed = 0; Map<String, Address> local1 = new HashMap<>();
        for (String id : changes) {
            try { local1.put(id, orders.getAddress(id)); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { failed++; }
        }
        System.out.println("1. Event notification (AddressChanged{orderId}), order-service down:");
        System.out.printf("   %,d events → %,d callbacks needed, %,d failed; delivery-service knows %,d addresses%n", changes.size(), changes.size(), failed, local1.size());
        orders.up = true; orders.reads = 0;
        for (String id : changes) local1.put(id, orders.getAddress(id));
        System.out.printf("   with order-service up: %,d synchronous reads back into the producer (coupling + load)%n", orders.reads);

        // style 2
        Map<String, Address> local2 = new HashMap<>();
        orders.up = false;
        for (int i = 0; i < changes.size(); i++) local2.put(changes.get(i), log.get(i).address());
        System.out.println("2. Event-carried state transfer (AddressChangedWithState{orderId, address}), order-service down:");
        System.out.printf("   0 callbacks; delivery-service's local copy has %,d addresses, identical to the source: %s%n",
                local2.size(), local2.equals(orders.addresses));

        // style 3
        Map<String, Address> state = new HashMap<>();
        for (AddressSet e : log) state.put(e.orderId(), e.address());          // current state = fold(events)
        String sample = log.get(0).orderId();
        List<AddressSet> history = log.stream().filter(e -> e.orderId().equals(sample)).toList();
        System.out.println("3. Event sourcing (AddressSet events are the record of truth):");
        System.out.printf("   state rebuilt from %,d events equals the current table: %s%n", log.size(), state.equals(orders.addresses));
        System.out.printf("   %s history: %d versions, first %s, current %s — the other two styles only know 'current'%n",
                sample, history.size(), history.get(0).address().pincode(), history.get(history.size() - 1).address().pincode());
    }
}

Actual output from running it:

1. Event notification (AddressChanged{orderId}), order-service down:
   10,000 events → 10,000 callbacks needed, 10,000 failed; delivery-service knows 0 addresses
   with order-service up: 10,000 synchronous reads back into the producer (coupling + load)
2. Event-carried state transfer (AddressChangedWithState{orderId, address}), order-service down:
   0 callbacks; delivery-service's local copy has 1,994 addresses, identical to the source: true
3. Event sourcing (AddressSet events are the record of truth):
   state rebuilt from 10,000 events equals the current table: true
   ord-985 history: 5 versions, first 560038, current 560049 — the other two styles only know 'current'

What L1 shows: notifications couple the consumer to the producer's availability and load (10,000 failed callbacks). State transfer lets the consumer work alone, with an identical copy. Event sourcing gives the same current state and keeps the history the other two throw away.

docs.title: L2 — An event store with optimistic concurrency (real PostgreSQL) B3
docs.text:
Requirement: the store-credit wallet must never be overdrawn, even with concurrent checkouts and refunds, and every balance must be explainable.

// EventStoreL2.java — run with: java -Duser.timezone=UTC -cp postgresql-42.7.4.jar EventStoreL2.java   (PostgreSQL on :5551)
// An event-sourced store-credit wallet on PostgreSQL. State = fold(events). Writes append events with an
// EXPECTED VERSION (optimistic concurrency); PRIMARY KEY (stream_id, version) rejects a concurrent append.
import java.sql.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

public class EventStoreL2 {

    // ---------- events (the source of truth) ----------
    sealed interface WalletEvent permits Opened, Credited, Debited { }
    record Opened(String customerId) implements WalletEvent { }
    record Credited(long paise, String reason) implements WalletEvent { }
    record Debited(long paise, String orderId) implements WalletEvent { }

    // ---------- the aggregate: rebuilt from events, decides new events ----------
    static final class Wallet {
        long balance; int version; boolean open;
        void apply(WalletEvent e) {
            switch (e) {
                case Opened o -> open = true;
                case Credited c -> balance += c.paise();
                case Debited d -> balance -= d.paise();
            }
            version++;
        }
        /** Business rule lives here, against state rebuilt from events. */
        List<WalletEvent> debit(long paise, String orderId) {
            if (!open) throw new IllegalStateException("wallet not open");
            if (paise > balance) throw new InsufficientFunds();
            return List.of(new Debited(paise, orderId));
        }
    }
    static final class InsufficientFunds extends RuntimeException { }
    static final class ConcurrencyConflict extends RuntimeException { }

    // ---------- the event store ----------
    static final class EventStore {
        final String url = "jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5551/eventstore";
        final boolean checkVersion;
        EventStore(boolean checkVersion) { this.checkVersion = checkVersion; }
        Connection conn() throws SQLException { return DriverManager.getConnection(url, "postgres", ""); }

        void init() throws SQLException {
            try (Connection c = conn(); Statement s = c.createStatement()) {
                s.execute("drop table if exists events");
                s.execute(checkVersion
                    ? """
                      create table events (
                        global_position bigserial,
                        stream_id text not null,
                        version int not null,
                        type text not null,
                        payload jsonb not null,
                        recorded_at timestamptz not null default now(),
                        primary key (stream_id, version))"""
                    : """
                      create table events (
                        global_position bigserial primary key,
                        stream_id text not null,
                        version int not null,
                        type text not null,
                        payload jsonb not null,
                        recorded_at timestamptz not null default now())""");
            }
        }

        Wallet load(Connection c, String stream) throws SQLException {
            Wallet w = new Wallet();
            try (var ps = c.prepareStatement("select type, payload->>'paise', payload->>'id' from events where stream_id = ? order by version")) {
                ps.setString(1, stream);
                try (var rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                    while (rs.next()) w.apply(switch (rs.getString(1)) {
                        case "Opened" -> new Opened(rs.getString(3));
                        case "Credited" -> new Credited(Long.parseLong(rs.getString(2)), "");
                        default -> new Debited(Long.parseLong(rs.getString(2)), rs.getString(3));
                    });
                }
            }
            return w;
        }

        /** Append events after expectedVersion. With the version check, a concurrent append makes this fail. */
        void append(Connection c, String stream, int expectedVersion, List<WalletEvent> events) throws SQLException {
            c.setAutoCommit(false);
            try (var ps = c.prepareStatement("insert into events(stream_id, version, type, payload) values (?, ?, ?, ?::jsonb)")) {
                int v = expectedVersion;
                for (WalletEvent e : events) {
                    ps.setString(1, stream); ps.setInt(2, ++v); ps.setString(3, e.getClass().getSimpleName());
                    ps.setString(4, switch (e) {
                        case Opened o -> "{\"id\":\"" + o.customerId() + "\"}";
                        case Credited cr -> "{\"paise\":" + cr.paise() + "}";
                        case Debited d -> "{\"paise\":" + d.paise() + ",\"id\":\"" + d.orderId() + "\"}";
                    });
                    ps.executeUpdate();
                }
                c.commit();
            } catch (SQLException ex) {
                c.rollback();
                if ("23505".equals(ex.getSQLState())) throw new ConcurrencyConflict();   // unique_violation on (stream_id, version)
                throw ex;
            } finally { c.setAutoCommit(true); }
        }
    }

    static Map<String, Object> run(boolean checkVersion) throws Exception {
        EventStore store = new EventStore(checkVersion);
        store.init();
        String stream = "wallet-cust-42";
        try (Connection c = store.conn()) {
            store.append(c, stream, 0, List.of(new Opened("cust-42"), new Credited(10_000, "refund ord-900")));
        }
        AtomicInteger ok = new AtomicInteger(), rejected = new AtomicInteger(), conflicts = new AtomicInteger();
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
        List<Future<?>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int t = 0; t < 16; t++) {
            int tt = t;
            fs.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                try (Connection c = store.conn()) {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
                        String order = "ord-" + tt + "-" + i;
                        while (true) {                                            // load → decide → append, retry on conflict
                            Wallet w = store.load(c, stream);
                            List<WalletEvent> decided;
                            try { decided = w.debit(100, order); } catch (InsufficientFunds e) { rejected.incrementAndGet(); break; }
                            try { store.append(c, stream, w.version, decided); ok.incrementAndGet(); break; }
                            catch (ConcurrencyConflict e) { conflicts.incrementAndGet(); }
                        }
                    }
                }
                return null;
            }));
        }
        for (Future<?> f : fs) f.get();
        pool.shutdown();
        Map<String, Object> out = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        try (Connection c = store.conn()) {
            Wallet w = store.load(c, stream);
            out.put("debits accepted", ok.get());
            out.put("rejected (insufficient funds)", rejected.get());
            out.put("version conflicts retried", conflicts.get());
            out.put("final balance (paise)", w.balance);
            try (var rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("select count(*) - count(distinct version) from events where stream_id = '" + stream + "'")) {
                rs.next(); out.put("events sharing a version", rs.getLong(1));
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("Wallet credited 10,000 paise; 16 threads each try 20 debits of 100 paise (32,000 requested)");
        System.out.println("no expected-version check: " + run(false));
        System.out.println("expected-version check   : " + run(true));

        // time travel: the balance as it was after any event, from the same log
        try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5551/eventstore", "postgres", "");
             var rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("""
                 select version, type, balance from (
                   select version, type, sum(case type when 'Credited' then (payload->>'paise')::bigint
                                                       when 'Debited' then -(payload->>'paise')::bigint else 0 end)
                                   over (order by version) as balance
                     from events where stream_id = 'wallet-cust-42') running
                  where version in (1, 2, 3, 52, 101, 102) order by version""")) {
            System.out.println("Audit / time travel from the same events (running balance at selected versions):");
            while (rs.next()) System.out.printf("   v%-4d %-9s balance %,d%n", rs.getInt(1), rs.getString(2), rs.getLong(3));
        }
    }
}

Actual output from running it:

Wallet credited 10,000 paise; 16 threads each try 20 debits of 100 paise (32,000 requested)
no expected-version check: {debits accepted=111, rejected (insufficient funds)=209, version conflicts retried=0, final balance (paise)=-1100, events sharing a version=56}
expected-version check   : {debits accepted=100, rejected (insufficient funds)=220, version conflicts retried=649, final balance (paise)=0, events sharing a version=0}
Audit / time travel from the same events (running balance at selected versions):
   v1    Opened    balance 0
   v2    Credited  balance 10,000
   v3    Debited   balance 9,900
   v52   Debited   balance 5,000
   v101  Debited   balance 100
   v102  Debited   balance 0
  • Without the version check, threads that loaded the same state each decided "enough balance" and all appended. That's 111 debits against ₹100, a final balance of −₹11.00, and 56 events sharing a version number.
  • With primary key (stream_id, version), the database rejected every append made on a stale decision. After 649 reload-and-retry cycles, exactly 100 debits went through, and the balance ended at ₹0.00.
  • The running balance at any version comes straight from the log with a window function: audit and time travel for free.
