package com.grocery.wallet.repository;

import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.dao.DuplicateKeyException;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Repository
public class WalletEventStore {

    public record StoredEvent(String streamId, int version, String type, int schemaVersion, String payloadJson, String metadataJson) { }

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;

    public WalletEventStore(JdbcClient jdbc) { this.jdbc = jdbc; }

    public List<StoredEvent> read(String streamId, int afterVersion) {
        return jdbc.sql("""
                select stream_id, version, type, schema_version, payload::text, metadata::text
                  from events where stream_id = :s and version > :v order by version""")
            .param("s", streamId).param("v", afterVersion)
            .query(StoredEvent.class).list();
    }

    /** Throws WalletConcurrencyException when another writer appended first (unique (stream_id, version)). */
    @Transactional
    public void append(String streamId, int expectedVersion, List<StoredEvent> events) {
        int v = expectedVersion;
        try {
            for (StoredEvent e : events) {
                jdbc.sql("""
                        insert into events(stream_id, version, type, schema_version, payload, metadata)
                        values (:s, :v, :t, :sv, :p::jsonb, :m::jsonb)""")
                    .param("s", streamId).param("v", ++v).param("t", e.type()).param("sv", e.schemaVersion())
                    .param("p", e.payloadJson()).param("m", e.metadataJson())
                    .update();
            }
        } catch (DuplicateKeyException conflict) {
            throw new WalletConcurrencyException(streamId, expectedVersion);
        }
    }
}

package com.grocery.wallet.service;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class WalletCommandService {

    private final WalletEventStore store;
    private final WalletSnapshots snapshots;
    private final EventCodec codec;                 // serialize + upcast (L4)

    public WalletCommandService(WalletEventStore store, WalletSnapshots snapshots, EventCodec codec) {
        this.store = store; this.snapshots = snapshots; this.codec = codec;
    }

    public DebitResult debit(DebitWallet cmd) {
        for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= 5; attempt++) {
            Wallet w = snapshots.latest(cmd.walletId()).orElseGet(Wallet::empty);
            store.read(cmd.walletId(), w.version()).forEach(e -> w.apply(codec.decode(e)));
            if (w.alreadyProcessed(cmd.commandId())) return DebitResult.duplicate(w.version());   // idempotent retry
            var decided = w.debit(cmd.amountPaise(), cmd.orderId(), cmd.commandId());          // throws InsufficientFunds
            try {
                store.append(cmd.walletId(), w.version(), codec.encode(decided, cmd.metadata()));
                return DebitResult.ok(w.version() + decided.size());
            } catch (WalletConcurrencyException conflict) {
                // someone else appended; loop reloads and re-decides against the new state
            }
        }
        throw new WalletBusyException(cmd.walletId());
    }
}

docs.title: L3 — Projections that don't skip events, and rebuilds (real PostgreSQL) B3 B4
docs.text:
Requirement: order tracking read models are built from events while 8 writers append concurrently. They must end up exact, and they must be rebuildable.

// ProjectionL3.java — run with: java -Duser.timezone=UTC -cp postgresql-42.7.4.jar ProjectionL3.java   (PostgreSQL on :5551)
// CQRS read models built by projectors that tail the event store WHILE writers are appending.
// A bigserial position is assigned at INSERT time but becomes visible at COMMIT time, so positions can
// appear out of order. A projector that checkpoints "max position seen" silently skips late committers.
import java.sql.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

public class ProjectionL3 {

    static Connection conn() throws SQLException { return DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5551/eventstore", "postgres", ""); }

    static void exec(Connection c, String sql) throws SQLException { try (Statement s = c.createStatement()) { s.execute(sql); } }

    /** One projector pass: read a batch after the checkpoint, apply it to the read model, store the checkpoint — one txn. */
    static int projectOnce(Connection c, String model, boolean safe) throws SQLException {
        c.setAutoCommit(false);
        try {
            long cpTx = 0, cpPos = 0;
            try (var rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("select tx_id::text::bigint, position from checkpoints where projection = '" + model + "' for update")) {
                rs.next(); cpTx = rs.getLong(1); cpPos = rs.getLong(2);
            }
            String sql = safe
                ? """
                  select stream_id, version, global_position, tx_id::text::bigint from events
                   where (tx_id, global_position) > (?::text::xid8, ?)
                     and tx_id < pg_snapshot_xmin(pg_current_snapshot())      -- only transactions that can no longer commit "behind" us
                   order by tx_id, global_position limit 500"""
                : """
                  select stream_id, version, global_position, tx_id::text::bigint from events
                   where global_position > ?
                   order by global_position limit 500""";
            int n = 0; long lastTx = cpTx, lastPos = cpPos;
            try (var ps = c.prepareStatement(sql)) {
                if (safe) { ps.setLong(1, cpTx); ps.setLong(2, cpPos); } else ps.setLong(1, cpPos);
                try (var rs = ps.executeQuery();
                     var up = c.prepareStatement("insert into " + model + "(order_id, last_version, events_applied) values (?, ?, 1) " +
                             "on conflict (order_id) do update set last_version = greatest(" + model + ".last_version, excluded.last_version), " +
                             "events_applied = " + model + ".events_applied + 1")) {
                    while (rs.next()) {
                        up.setString(1, rs.getString(1)); up.setInt(2, rs.getInt(2)); up.executeUpdate();
                        lastPos = rs.getLong(3); lastTx = rs.getLong(4); n++;
                    }
                }
            }
            try (var ps = c.prepareStatement("update checkpoints set tx_id = ?::text::xid8, position = ? where projection = ?")) {
                ps.setLong(1, lastTx); ps.setLong(2, lastPos); ps.setString(3, model); ps.executeUpdate();
            }
            c.commit();
            return n;
        } catch (SQLException e) { c.rollback(); throw e; }
        finally { c.setAutoCommit(true); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (Connection c = conn()) {
            exec(c, "drop table if exists events, checkpoints, order_status_naive, order_status_safe");
            exec(c, """
                create table events (
                  global_position bigserial,
                  tx_id xid8 not null default pg_current_xact_id(),
                  stream_id text not null,
                  version int not null,
                  type text not null,
                  payload jsonb not null default '{}',
                  primary key (stream_id, version))""");
            exec(c, "create index on events (global_position)");
            exec(c, "create index on events (tx_id, global_position)");
            exec(c, "create table checkpoints (projection text primary key, tx_id xid8 not null, position bigint not null)");
            exec(c, "insert into checkpoints values ('order_status_naive', '0', 0), ('order_status_safe', '0', 0)");
            for (String m : List.of("order_status_naive", "order_status_safe"))
                exec(c, "create table " + m + " (order_id text primary key, last_version int not null, events_applied int not null)");
        }
        int writers = 8, perWriter = 1_500;
        AtomicBoolean writing = new AtomicBoolean(true);
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(writers + 2);
        List<Future<?>> ws = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int w = 0; w < writers; w++) {
            int ww = w;
            ws.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                Random rnd = new Random(ww);
                Map<String, Integer> versions = new HashMap<>();
                try (Connection c = conn()) {
                    c.setAutoCommit(false);
                    for (int i = 0; i < perWriter; i++) {
                        String stream = "ord-" + ww + "-" + rnd.nextInt(200);
                        int v = versions.merge(stream, 1, Integer::sum);
                        try (var ps = c.prepareStatement("insert into events(stream_id, version, type) values (?, ?, 'OrderStatusChanged')")) {
                            ps.setString(1, stream); ps.setInt(2, v); ps.executeUpdate();
                        }
                        Thread.sleep(rnd.nextInt(4));                               // position taken; commit comes a bit later
                        c.commit();
                    }
                }
                return null;
            }));
        }
        AtomicInteger passes = new AtomicInteger();
        List<Future<?>> ps = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String model : List.of("order_status_naive", "order_status_safe")) {
            boolean safe = model.endsWith("safe");
            ps.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                try (Connection c = conn()) {
                    while (true) {
                        int n = projectOnce(c, model, safe);
                        passes.incrementAndGet();
                        if (n == 0) { if (!writing.get() && projectOnce(c, model, safe) == 0) break; Thread.sleep(5); }
                    }
                }
                return null;
            }));
        }
        for (Future<?> f : ws) f.get();
        writing.set(false);
        for (Future<?> f : ps) f.get();
        pool.shutdown();

        try (Connection c = conn()) {
            long total;
            try (var rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("select count(*) from events")) { rs.next(); total = rs.getLong(1); }
            System.out.printf("%d writers appended %,d events to %,d order streams while two projectors tailed the store%n",
                    writers, total, writers * 200);
            for (String model : List.of("order_status_naive", "order_status_safe")) {
                try (var rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("""
                        select coalesce(sum(m.events_applied), 0),
                               count(*) filter (where m.last_version is distinct from e.max_version)
                          from (select stream_id, max(version) max_version from events group by stream_id) e
                          left join %s m on m.order_id = e.stream_id""".formatted(model))) {
                    rs.next();
                    System.out.printf("   %-20s events applied %,6d of %,d   missed %,5d   orders with a wrong current version %,4d%n",
                            model, rs.getLong(1), total, total - rs.getLong(1), rs.getLong(2));
                }
            }
            // rebuild: a read model is disposable — drop it and replay from position 0
            exec(c, "truncate order_status_naive");
            exec(c, "update checkpoints set tx_id = '0', position = 0 where projection = 'order_status_naive'");
            long t0 = System.nanoTime();
            while (projectOnce(c, "order_status_naive", true) > 0) { }
            long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000;
            try (var rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("select sum(events_applied) from order_status_naive")) {
                rs.next(); System.out.printf("   rebuild of the broken read model from the log: %,d events re-applied in %d ms → correct again%n", rs.getLong(1), ms);
            }
        }
        System.exit(0);
    }
}

Actual output from running it:

8 writers appended 12,000 events to 1,600 order streams while two projectors tailed the store
   order_status_naive   events applied  9,046 of 12,000   missed 2,954   orders with a wrong current version  417
   order_status_safe    events applied 12,000 of 12,000   missed     0   orders with a wrong current version    0
   rebuild of the broken read model from the log: 12,000 events re-applied in 549 ms → correct again
  • The naive projector missed 2,954 of 12,000 events, and 417 orders show a stale current version. No errors, no warnings. Each writer's transaction took its global_position at insert and committed a few milliseconds later, so the projector moved its checkpoint past positions that became visible afterwards.
  • The xid-safe projector reads only events from transactions older than the oldest still-running one (tx_id < pg_snapshot_xmin(...)), in (tx_id, position) order. It missed 0.
  • The broken read model was repaired by a rebuild: truncate, reset the checkpoint, replay all 12,000 events in 549 ms. That's why read models must be derived-only and rebuildable.

package com.grocery.orders.tracking;

import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.scheduling.annotation.Scheduled;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Component
public class OrderTrackingProjector {

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;
    private final ProjectorLeadership leadership;            // one active instance per projection (Ch 12)

    public OrderTrackingProjector(JdbcClient jdbc, ProjectorLeadership leadership) { this.jdbc = jdbc; this.leadership = leadership; }

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 200)
    @Transactional
    public void project() {
        if (!leadership.isLeader()) return;
        var cp = jdbc.sql("select tx_id::text as tx, position from checkpoints where projection = 'order_tracking' for update")
                     .query((rs, i) -> new long[]{Long.parseLong(rs.getString("tx")), rs.getLong("position")}).single();
        var batch = jdbc.sql("""
                select stream_id, version, type, payload::text, global_position, tx_id::text as tx
                  from events
                 where (tx_id, global_position) > (:tx::text::xid8, :pos)
                   and tx_id < pg_snapshot_xmin(pg_current_snapshot())
                 order by tx_id, global_position
                 limit 500""")
            .param("tx", cp[0]).param("pos", cp[1])
            .query(EventRow.class).list();
        for (EventRow e : batch) apply(e);                    // upserts with "where last_version < :v"
        if (!batch.isEmpty()) {
            EventRow last = batch.get(batch.size() - 1);
            jdbc.sql("update checkpoints set tx_id = :tx::text::xid8, position = :pos where projection = 'order_tracking'")
                .param("tx", Long.parseLong(last.tx())).param("pos", last.globalPosition()).update();
        }
    }

    private void apply(EventRow e) { /* status, timestamps, rider info per event type */ }
}

docs.title: L4 — Snapshots and upcasting (real PostgreSQL) B3 B4
docs.text:
Requirement: B2B wallets with years of history must load within the p99 budget, and 2019-era events that stored rupees as decimals must still be read correctly by code that uses paise.

// SnapshotUpcastL4.java — run with: java -Duser.timezone=UTC -cp postgresql-42.7.4.jar SnapshotUpcastL4.java   (PostgreSQL on :5551)
// A. Loading a long-lived aggregate: full replay vs snapshot + tail.
// B. Upcasting: v1 events stored amounts in rupees as JSON decimals; v2 uses integer paise. Old events are never
//    rewritten — an upcaster converts them on read. Doing the conversion with double arithmetic loses paise.
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.sql.*;
import java.util.*;

public class SnapshotUpcastL4 {

    static Connection conn() throws SQLException { return DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5551/eventstore", "postgres", ""); }

    record Loaded(long balance, int version, int eventsRead) { }

    /** Fold events of a wallet stream starting after `fromVersion` onto (balance, version). */
    static Loaded fold(Connection c, String stream, long balance, int fromVersion) throws SQLException {
        int v = fromVersion, n = 0;
        try (var ps = c.prepareStatement("select version, type, (payload->>'paise')::bigint from wallet_events where stream_id = ? and version > ? order by version")) {
            ps.setString(1, stream); ps.setInt(2, fromVersion);
            ps.setFetchSize(5_000);
            c.setAutoCommit(false);                                    // fetch size needs a transaction in pgjdbc
            try (var rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                while (rs.next()) { balance += rs.getString(2).equals("Credited") ? rs.getLong(3) : -rs.getLong(3); v = rs.getInt(1); n++; }
            }
            c.commit(); c.setAutoCommit(true);
        }
        return new Loaded(balance, v, n);
    }

    static Loaded loadWithSnapshot(Connection c, String stream) throws SQLException {
        long bal = 0; int ver = 0;
        try (var ps = c.prepareStatement("select balance, version from wallet_snapshots where stream_id = ? order by version desc limit 1")) {
            ps.setString(1, stream);
            try (var rs = ps.executeQuery()) { if (rs.next()) { bal = rs.getLong(1); ver = rs.getInt(2); } }
        }
        return fold(c, stream, bal, ver);
    }

    /** Upcaster: turn any stored version of a Credited event into the current shape (paise as long). */
    static long creditedPaise(int schemaVersion, String rawAmount, boolean useDouble) {
        return switch (schemaVersion) {
            case 1 -> useDouble
                    ? (long) (Double.parseDouble(rawAmount) * 100)                     // ❌ 19.99 * 100 = 1998.9999… → 1998
                    : new BigDecimal(rawAmount).movePointRight(2).longValueExact();    // ✅ exact decimal → 1999
            case 2 -> Long.parseLong(rawAmount);
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown Credited schema v" + schemaVersion);
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (Connection c = conn(); Statement s = c.createStatement()) {
            s.execute("drop table if exists wallet_events, wallet_snapshots, legacy_events");
            s.execute("create table wallet_events (stream_id text, version int, type text, payload jsonb, primary key (stream_id, version))");
            s.execute("create table wallet_snapshots (stream_id text, version int, balance bigint, primary key (stream_id, version))");
            // a busy B2B customer's wallet: 200,000 events over two years
            s.execute("""
                insert into wallet_events
                select 'wallet-b2b-7', g, case when g % 3 = 0 then 'Debited' else 'Credited' end,
                       jsonb_build_object('paise', 100 + g % 900)
                  from generate_series(1, 200000) g""");
            // snapshot every 1,000 events (a projector or the command side writes these; they are disposable)
            s.execute("""
                insert into wallet_snapshots
                select 'wallet-b2b-7', v, sum(case when type = 'Credited' then (payload->>'paise')::bigint else -(payload->>'paise')::bigint end)
                         over (order by version)
                  from (select version as v, version, type, payload from wallet_events where stream_id = 'wallet-b2b-7') x
                """);
            s.execute("delete from wallet_snapshots where version % 1000 <> 0");
            s.execute("insert into wallet_events select 'wallet-b2b-7', 200000 + g, 'Credited', jsonb_build_object('paise', 500) from generate_series(1, 437) g");
            s.execute("analyze");
        }
        System.out.println("A. Load a wallet with 200,437 events (snapshots every 1,000 events)");
        try (Connection c = conn()) {
            for (int warm = 0; warm < 2; warm++) { fold(c, "wallet-b2b-7", 0, 0); loadWithSnapshot(c, "wallet-b2b-7"); }
            long t0 = System.nanoTime(); Loaded full = fold(c, "wallet-b2b-7", 0, 0); long tFull = System.nanoTime() - t0;
            t0 = System.nanoTime(); Loaded snap = loadWithSnapshot(c, "wallet-b2b-7"); long tSnap = System.nanoTime() - t0;
            System.out.printf("   full replay     : read %,7d events, balance %,d at v%d in %6.1f ms%n", full.eventsRead(), full.balance(), full.version(), tFull / 1e6);
            System.out.printf("   snapshot + tail : read %,7d events, balance %,d at v%d in %6.1f ms%n", snap.eventsRead(), snap.balance(), snap.version(), tSnap / 1e6);
            System.out.println("   same state: " + (full.balance() == snap.balance() && full.version() == snap.version()));
        }

        System.out.println("B. Upcasting 2019-era Credited events (v1: rupees as decimals) to v2 (paise)");
        try (Connection c = conn(); Statement s = c.createStatement()) {
            s.execute("create table legacy_events (id serial, schema_version int, payload jsonb)");
            s.execute("""
                insert into legacy_events(schema_version, payload)
                select 1, jsonb_build_object('amount', ((10 + g % 5000) / 100.0)::numeric(12,2)) from generate_series(1, 100000) g""");
            s.execute("insert into legacy_events(schema_version, payload) select 2, jsonb_build_object('paise', 10 + g % 5000) from generate_series(1, 100000) g");
            long exactSum = 0, doubleSum = 0, wrong = 0;
            try (var rs = s.executeQuery("select schema_version, coalesce(payload->>'amount', payload->>'paise') from legacy_events")) {
                while (rs.next()) {
                    long ok = creditedPaise(rs.getInt(1), rs.getString(2), false), bad = creditedPaise(rs.getInt(1), rs.getString(2), true);
                    exactSum += ok; doubleSum += bad; if (ok != bad) wrong++;
                }
            }
            System.out.printf("   200,000 events (100,000 v1 + 100,000 v2): BigDecimal upcaster total ₹%,.2f, double upcaster total ₹%,.2f%n", exactSum / 100.0, doubleSum / 100.0);
            System.out.printf("   events where the double upcaster lost a paisa: %,d  (e.g. \"%s\" → %d paise)%n", wrong, "19.99", creditedPaise(1, "19.99", true));
        }
    }
}

Actual output from running it:

A. Load a wallet with 200,437 events (snapshots every 1,000 events)
   full replay     : read 200,437 events, balance 36,962,034 at v200437 in  179.8 ms
   snapshot + tail : read     437 events, balance 36,962,034 at v200437 in    3.4 ms
   same state: true
B. Upcasting 2019-era Credited events (v1: rupees as decimals) to v2 (paise)
   200,000 events (100,000 v1 + 100,000 v2): BigDecimal upcaster total ₹5,019,000.00, double upcaster total ₹5,018,942.60
   events where the double upcaster lost a paisa: 5,740  (e.g. "19.99" → 1998 paise)
  • Snapshots: the same state from 437 events instead of 200,437, 3.4 ms vs 179.8 ms. The snapshot is a cache: it's verified here by comparing it against a full replay, and it can be discarded at any time.
  • Upcasting: events are never rewritten. The upcaster converts v1 (amount in rupees) to v2 (paise) on read. Doing it with double arithmetic lost a paisa on 5,740 of 100,000 legacy events, ₹57.40 in total, with no exception. Upcasters are data migrations that run forever: exact types, golden tests against real historical samples, and no clever rounding.

docs.title: What changed from L1 to L4
docs.text: Concern L1 L2 L3 L4 Role of events Notification vs state vs source of truth Source of truth (wallet) Feed for read models Long-lived, evolving Concurrency — Expected version: overdraft −₹11 → ₹0 Writers commit out of position order — Correctness risk Callback coupling Lost updates Skipped events (2,954 → 0) Lossy upcasting (₹57.40) Recovery — Retry on conflict (649) Rebuild read model (549 ms) Discard snapshot → replay Performance — Contention on hot streams Projection lag bound by the oldest open transaction Snapshot 3.4 ms vs 179.8 ms

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Detection signal Blast radius Mitigation Projector skips late-committing events Nightly reconciliation: events counted vs applied per projection Stale read models, silently (L3: 2,954 missed) xid-safe checkpoints or a commit-ordered log; reconciliation job Lost updates on aggregates Invariant violations (negative balances) Money errors (L2: −₹11) Expected-version appends enforced by a unique key Hot stream contention Append conflict rate for one stream Latency, retries, timeouts Smaller aggregates; commutative commands; period closing Long-running transactions Age of the oldest open transaction xid-safe projections stop advancing (lag) Statement/idle timeouts; alert; no long batch transactions on the store DB Poison event in a projection Projection stalled with repeated errors That read model only Per-projection error handling; skip-and-park with alert; fix and resume Lossy or buggy upcaster Golden tests; reconciliation of sums Wrong derived state everywhere (L4: ₹57.40) Exact types; tests on production samples; rebuild after fix Unbounded stream growth Stream length p99, load time Slow commands Snapshots (L4: 3.4 ms), period closing Rebuild takes too long Rebuild ETA vs SLO Can't fix read models quickly Parallel rebuild by stream hash; blue/green Side effects re-run on replay Duplicate emails after a rebuild Customer-visible Reactors separate from projectors; dedup by event id PII in events Data scan, DPDP requests Compliance PII out of events; crypto-shredding

docs.title: 6.2 Observability
docs.text:
• Per projection: lag in positions and seconds, events/s applied, errors, last checkpoint time, and a completeness check (count and sum per stream type vs the store, run periodically).
  • Event store: appends/s, conflicts/s by stream type, stream length histogram, snapshot hit rate and age, DB size growth.
  • Commands: load time (events read per load), decide/append latency, and retries per command.
  • Upcasters: invocations by type and version (shows how much legacy data is still read), and failures.
  • Metadata on every event (correlation id, causation id, user, HLC) makes "why is this balance ₹0?" a query, not an investigation.

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Append-only enforcement: application roles get INSERT and SELECT only on events. Corrections are compensating events, never updates.
  • Event metadata records who issued the command (user or service identity), and it's part of the audit trail.
  • PII: keep references in events and details in mutable stores. Encrypt unavoidable PII with per-subject keys (crypto-shredding), and propagate erasure to read models, search indexes, caches, backups and the warehouse (Ch 36).
  • Read models may aggregate data from many streams: apply authorization at the query API, not in projections.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance & tuning knobs
docs.text: Knob Default here Effect Snapshot interval 1,000 events Load time vs snapshot writes Projector batch size / poll interval 500 / 200 ms Lag vs DB load Parallel projection Partition by hash(stream_id) Rebuild speed; per-stream order kept Period closing Yearly for wallets Bounded streams, faster rebuilds Event payload size Keep < 4 KB; store blobs elsewhere Store size, replay speed idle_in_transaction_session_timeout 30 s on the store DB Keeps xmin advancing for projectors Index (tx_id, global_position) Required Projector query cost

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• Storage grows forever with the events (~44 GB/year for the wallet). Archive closed periods to cheaper storage, and keep read models small.
  • Every read model is another copy of data plus a projector to run and monitor. Add read models for real query needs, not speculatively.
  • The engineering cost is the main cost: versioning discipline, upcaster tests, rebuild tooling and reconciliation. Budget for it before choosing event sourcing.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Checkpointing projections by "max position seen" on a database sequence.

-- ❌ before: skips events whose transactions commit after a later position (L3: 2,954 missed)
select * from events where global_position > :checkpoint order by global_position limit 500;

-- ✅ after: only read transactions older than the oldest in-flight one, in (tx_id, position) order
select * from events
 where (tx_id, global_position) > (:cp_tx, :cp_pos)
   and tx_id < pg_snapshot_xmin(pg_current_snapshot())
 order by tx_id, global_position limit 500;

2. Appending without an expected version. Symptom: Two commands decide against the same state, and both append (L2: overdraft −₹11). Fix: primary key (stream_id, version) and expected-version appends, with reload-and-retry.

3. Event-sourcing everything. Symptom: Carts with 40,000 events, and upcasters for data nobody reads (§1.1). Fix: Event-source only where history is the requirement. Everywhere else, use tables + outbox + read models.

4. Publishing internal domain events as the public contract. Symptom: A refactor of the aggregate breaks five consumers. Fix: Map to versioned integration events in the outbox (Ch 13/14).

5. Upcasters with floating-point or lossy logic.

// ❌ before: 19.99 * 100 = 1998.9999… → 1998 paise (L4: 5,740 events, ₹57.40 lost)
long paise = (long) (Double.parseDouble(rupees) * 100);

// ✅ after: exact decimal arithmetic; throws if the input can't be represented exactly
long paise = new BigDecimal(rupees).movePointRight(2).longValueExact();

6. Side effects inside projectors. Symptom: A rebuild re-sends 3 months of SMS. Fix: Projectors only update read models. Reactors perform side effects, with dedup, and don't run on rebuilds.

7. Read models treated as a source of truth. Symptom: Services write corrections into a read model, and a rebuild wipes them. Fix: Read models are derived-only. Corrections are commands that produce events.

8. Rewriting stored events to "fix" them. Symptom: Audit trail broken, other consumers' projections diverge. Fix: Compensating events, and upcasters for format changes.

9. Querying across aggregates by replaying streams on request. Symptom: "All wallets with a balance > ₹500" replays millions of events per request. Fix: A projection built for that query.

10. No snapshot or period strategy for long-lived aggregates. Symptom: Command latency grows every month. Fix: Snapshots (L4: 180 → 3.4 ms), and period closing for accounting-style streams.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What is event sourcing, in one paragraph?

30-second answer: Instead of storing an entity's current state and overwriting it, you store every change as an immutable event (Credited ₹500, Debited ₹320). The current state is computed by replaying the events in order. You get a full audit trail, time travel and the ability to build new views from history. You pay with complexity in versioning, projections and concurrency.

Deep answer: L2 computed the wallet's balance at any version from the same log. The event store enforces per-stream ordering and optimistic concurrency. Reads usually come from projections, not replays.

Trade-offs I'd call out: History and audit vs complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. Where is it a good fit? → Ledgers, wallets, bookings. 2. Where isn't it? → Carts, profiles, CRUD.

Red flags: "Event sourcing means using Kafka."

Q2 [B1] ⭐ What is CQRS?

30-second answer: Command Query Responsibility Segregation separates the model that handles writes (commands, validated against an aggregate) from the models that serve reads (read models or projections shaped for each query). Read models are updated asynchronously from the write side's changes or events.

Deep answer: It doesn't require event sourcing or separate databases. A projector filling a second table is CQRS. Benefits: fast, simple queries and independent scaling. Costs: eventual consistency and more moving parts. Read models can be rebuilt (L3: 12,000 events in 549 ms).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Query performance vs staleness and complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. How does a user see their own change? → Return state from the command, or wait for a min version. 2. Is CQS the same thing? → CQS is the method-level principle, CQRS the architectural one.

Red flags: Using CQRS for a simple CRUD screen.

Q3 [B1] Event notification vs event-carried state transfer?

30-second answer: A notification says "X changed" with an id, and consumers call back for details. State transfer includes the new data, so consumers keep a local copy and don't call back. Notifications create runtime coupling and load on the producer. State transfer creates data duplication and larger events.

Deep answer: L1 with the producer down: 10,000 notification callbacks failed, while the state-transfer consumer had an identical copy. Use notifications for sensitive or large data (fetch with authorization), and state transfer for data consumers need to operate independently.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Coupling vs duplication.

Follow-ups: 1. What about ordering? → State transfer needs versions so stale events don't overwrite newer copies. 2. Size limits? → Keep events small; link to blobs.

Red flags: "Events should only contain ids" as a universal rule.

Q4 [B1] What's a projection (read model)?

30-second answer: A view of data built by processing events, stored in a form that makes a particular query fast (order tracking, a store dashboard). It's derived data: you can delete it and rebuild it from the events at any time.

Deep answer: Projectors read events in order, apply them idempotently, and store a checkpoint with the read model update in the same transaction. The checkpoint must be safe under concurrent writers (L3).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed of reads vs lag and storage.

Follow-ups: 1. What if the projection has a bug? → Fix it and rebuild. 2. Can a projection write to another service? → It shouldn't. Side effects belong in reactors.

Red flags: Treating a read model as a source of truth.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do you handle concurrent writes to the same aggregate in an event store?

30-second answer: Optimistic concurrency. Load the stream (version N), decide, and append with "expected version N". The store rejects the append if the stream is no longer at N. The caller reloads, re-decides against the new state (which may now reject the command) and retries.

Deep answer: In PostgreSQL, primary key (stream_id, version) makes a concurrent append fail with a unique violation. L2: without it, 111 debits against ₹100 (overdraft); with it, exactly 100, after 649 retries. High conflict rates signal an aggregate that's too big or too hot.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Retries under contention vs locks.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not pessimistic locking? → It blocks, and it doesn't fit a distributed or async flow. 2. How do you make retries safe? → A command id for idempotency.

Red flags: Appending without any version check.

Q6 [B2] ⭐ Why can a projector miss events, and how do you prevent it?

30-second answer: If the global position comes from a database sequence, it's assigned at insert, but the row becomes visible at commit. Transactions commit out of order, so a projector that checkpoints "the highest position seen" can move past a position that commits later and never read it. Prevent it by reading only up to what can't change anymore (PostgreSQL: transaction ids below the snapshot's xmin), or by using a commit-ordered log.

Deep answer: L3 with 8 writers: the naive projector missed 2,954 of 12,000 events and left 417 orders stale, silently. The xid-safe projector missed 0. Alternatives: serialize appends, CDC from the WAL (commit order), or a purpose-built store (EventStoreDB, Kafka offsets). Add a completeness reconciliation job either way.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Lag bound by the longest transaction vs correctness.

Follow-ups: 1. What stalls the xid approach? → A long-running or idle-in-transaction session. Set timeouts. 2. Does Kafka have this problem? → Offsets are assigned in log order, so no, but the outbox relay feeding it can (Ch 13).

Red flags: Not knowing about the gap problem.

Q7 [B2] How do you make projections idempotent?

30-second answer: Store the checkpoint in the same transaction as the read model update, so a crash either applies both or neither. Make each apply an upsert keyed by entity with a version guard (where last_version < :v), so replays and duplicates are no-ops. Keep side effects out of projections.

Deep answer: For projections in other stores (OpenSearch, Redis) you can't share a transaction: use versioned writes (external version in OpenSearch) and store the checkpoint there too, or accept at-least-once with idempotent writes.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Simplicity vs cross-store atomicity.

Follow-ups: 1. What about counters (sum per day)? → Keep the last applied position per counter, or recompute from base events. 2. Parallel projection? → Partition by stream hash, which keeps order per stream.

Red flags: Checkpoint committed separately from the read model.

Q8 [B2] When do you need snapshots?

30-second answer: When aggregates have long streams, so replaying them on every command costs too much. Store state every N events and load the snapshot plus the tail. Snapshots are caches: versioned, disposable, and rebuilt by replay.

Deep answer: L4: 200,437 events loaded in 179.8 ms by replay vs 3.4 ms from snapshot + 437 events, with the same state verified. Often a better fix is modelling: close periods (yearly wallet streams) or split aggregates.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Load latency vs snapshot maintenance.

Follow-ups: 1. What if the aggregate's class changes? → Bump the snapshot version and discard old snapshots. 2. Sync or async snapshots? → Async, off the command path.

Red flags: Snapshots treated as the source of truth.

Q9 [B2] Domain events vs integration events?

30-second answer: Domain events are internal to a bounded context: fine-grained and free to change. Integration events are the context's public contract: stable, versioned, designed for consumers. Map domain events to integration events (in the outbox) rather than exposing your event store.

Deep answer: This protects consumers from internal refactors and lets you shape payloads (state transfer), strip PII, and version independently (Ch 14 §2.10).

Trade-offs I'd call out: A mapping layer vs coupling.

Follow-ups: 1. Can consumers read the event store directly? → They shouldn't. It couples them to your storage and schema. 2. What about one-to-many mappings? → Common. Aggregate several domain events into one integration event.

Red flags: "Our Kafka topics are our event store."

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ How do you evolve event schemas in an event-sourced system?

30-second answer: Never rewrite history. Make additive changes where possible, version every event, and convert old versions on read with upcasters (pure, exact, deterministic functions, chained v1 → v2 → v3). Use a new event type for semantic changes, and copy-and-transform migrations only as a last resort.

Deep answer: L4: a double-based upcaster turned "19.99" rupees into 1,998 paise and lost ₹57.40 across 5,740 events with no error. The BigDecimal version was exact. Test upcasters with golden samples from production, and monitor how often legacy versions are still read.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Keeping old formats forever vs migration risk.

Follow-ups: 1. Where do upcasters run? → In the event deserialization path, before the aggregate or projector sees the event. 2. Can you delete old upcasters? → Only after migrating or archiving all events of that version.

Red flags: "We'll just update the old events."

Q11 [B3] ⭐ How do you rebuild a read model without downtime?

30-second answer: Blue/green projections. Build order_tracking_v2 alongside v1 from position 0, in parallel by stream hash if needed. When v2 has caught up with the live position, switch queries to v2 (a feature flag or view swap), then retire v1.

Deep answer: L3's rebuild took 549 ms for 12 K events. For 120 M events, partitioned workers make it about 25 minutes (§4). Reconcile v2 against the store before switching. Side-effecting reactors must not run during rebuilds.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Temporary double storage vs zero downtime.

Follow-ups: 1. What if events keep arriving? → v2 catches up to live and then tails normally. 2. How do you verify v2? → Counts/sums per stream type, plus sampled comparisons with v1.

Red flags: Truncating the live read model in production.

Q12 [B3] How do you give users read-your-writes with CQRS?

30-second answer: The command returns the new version (or global position), and the query waits until the read model has reached it, with a timeout. Or the command returns the resulting state directly. Or the UI reads the user's own entity from the write model for a short window.

Deep answer: It's the same idea as Ch 10's LSN tokens. Read models store last_version per entity, and the query API checks it. Across many read models, track per-projection positions.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Latency (waiting) vs staleness.

Follow-ups: 1. What if the projection is far behind? → Time out and fall back to the write model or show "updating". 2. Is this needed everywhere? → No. Only for flows where users immediately look at what they changed.

Red flags: Accepting "the user sees old data" without a plan.

Q13 [B3] How does event sourcing interact with sagas and process managers?

30-second answer: Aggregates emit events. Process managers subscribe to events, keep their own state per correlation id, and issue commands to other aggregates or services, which is how cross-aggregate workflows run. They must be idempotent and must not re-run side effects when projections are rebuilt.

Deep answer: Example: PaymentCaptured + StockReserved → ConfirmOrder. The process manager's state can itself be event-sourced. Commands carry ids for idempotency, and timeouts are scheduled events. It's the event-driven form of Ch 13's orchestrator.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Decoupled flows vs visibility (use tracing and correlation ids).

Follow-ups: 1. Where's the saga state? → In the process manager's own store. 2. How do you replay safely? → Skip command dispatch during replays, or dedup commands by id.

Red flags: Process managers that resend commands on every replay.

Q14 [B3] What are the hard parts of running event sourcing in production?

30-second answer: Projection correctness (gaps, idempotency) and lag, rebuild time as history grows, schema evolution forever, hot streams and contention, PII erasure in an immutable log, and team skills. Each needs tooling: safe checkpoints, reconciliation, blue/green rebuilds, upcaster tests, snapshots or period closing, and crypto-shredding.

Deep answer: Evidence from this chapter: 2,954 missed events with a naive checkpoint (L3), ₹57.40 lost by a lossy upcaster (L4), 649 conflicts on one hot wallet (L2). Monitoring must include the age of the oldest open transaction on PostgreSQL-based stores.

Trade-offs I'd call out: The value of history vs the operational burden.

Follow-ups: 1. What's the first thing you'd build? → A reconciliation job comparing projections with the store. 2. Would you use a framework? → Axon or EventStoreDB can help, but understand the fundamentals first.

Red flags: "Event sourcing is simpler than CRUD."

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Should the grocery platform event-source orders?

30-second answer: Probably not. The business needs the current order state and a timeline, which tables + outbox events + a CQRS timeline read model provide. Event-source where history is the product: the wallet ledger (audit, disputes) and slot bookings. Keep orders in tables with state transitions guarded by versions (Ch 12).

Deep answer: Event-sourcing orders would add upcasting, projections and rebuild costs for little benefit. The order timeline can be a projection of integration events. Revisit if regulations require full order history as the system of record, or if many analytic models need exact historical order states.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Uniform architecture vs fit-for-purpose.

Follow-ups: 1. What about the order timeline? → A read model from events, with HLC ordering. 2. Could you migrate later? → Yes: start writing events via the outbox now, and they become history.

Red flags: "Everything should be event-sourced for consistency."

Q16 [B4] How do you handle GDPR/DPDP erasure with event sourcing?

30-second answer: Keep personal data out of events (reference ids, details in a mutable store). Where it must be in events, encrypt it with a per-person key and delete the key to erase (crypto-shredding). Then propagate erasure to read models, caches, search, backups and the warehouse, and record the erasure itself.

Deep answer: Projections must handle undecryptable fields. Compacted Kafka topics need tombstones. Legal retention for financial records (tax) may override erasure for specific fields, so define retention per field with legal. Test erasure end to end.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Immutability and audit vs the right to erasure.

Follow-ups: 1. Is deleting events acceptable? → Sometimes, as a last resort via copy-and-transform with an audit record. 2. Where are the keys stored? → A KMS/vault, per subject, with access audit.

Red flags: Ignoring erasure because "events are immutable".

Q17 [B4] PostgreSQL vs EventStoreDB vs Kafka as the event store?

30-second answer: PostgreSQL: familiar, transactional with outbox and read models, but you must solve global ordering for projections (xid approach) and scale it yourself. EventStoreDB/KurrentDB: purpose-built (per-stream expected versions, commit-ordered $all, subscriptions), but another system to run. Kafka: a great commit-ordered log for integration and replay, but no per-stream expected-version append, and per-entity stream reads are expensive, so it's a poor source of truth for aggregates.

Deep answer: For a team with PostgreSQL skills and a few event-sourced aggregates, PostgreSQL + the patterns in L2–L4 is pragmatic. With many event-sourced services, a dedicated store reduces custom tooling. Kafka complements both as the integration backbone.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Familiarity vs purpose-built features.

Follow-ups: 1. Can Kafka do optimistic concurrency? → Only per partition, with a single writer or transactional hacks. Not per stream. 2. How do you scale PostgreSQL-based stores? → Partition events by time or stream hash, and archive closed periods.

Red flags: "Kafka is an event store, so use it for aggregates."

Q18 [B4] Design the order tracking read model for 10x growth.

30-second answer: Feed it from Kafka order events, keyed by order, into a tracking store partitioned like the orders (Ch 11) or into a key-value store. Projectors run in parallel per Kafka partition, with idempotent version-guarded upserts. Reads by order id and customer id use a secondary read model. Rebuild via replay from Kafka retention or a compacted snapshot topic, blue/green.

Deep answer: Watch rebuild time (history × rate), lag SLOs (p99 < 2 s), hot orders (none, really) and hot customers (B2B). Serve read-your-writes via min-version checks, and reconcile against the order DB nightly.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Store choice (PostgreSQL shards vs Cassandra/DynamoDB) vs query flexibility.

Follow-ups: 1. How long must Kafka retain for rebuilds? → As long as a full rebuild needs, or snapshot to a compacted topic. 2. How do you backfill new fields? → Rebuild v2 with the new projection code.

Red flags: No rebuild plan.

Q19 [B4] A projection has shown wrong balances for 2 hours. What do you do?

30-second answer: Contain it: flag the view as degraded, and serve critical reads from the write model if possible. Find the cause (a projector bug, a skipped range, an upcaster bug, a poison event) by reconciling against the store. Fix the code, rebuild blue/green, verify with reconciliation, switch, and postmortem. Events were never wrong, so no data is lost.

Deep answer: If an upcaster was the cause, check every projection and consumer that used it. If events were skipped because of checkpoint logic, fix it (xid-safe, L3) and add a completeness check alert. Communicate the financial impact if customers acted on wrong balances.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed of fix vs thoroughness.

Follow-ups: 1. Why is this less scary with ES? → The truth is intact, and read models can be regenerated. 2. What alert would have caught it sooner? → Periodic count/sum reconciliation.

Red flags: Patching the read model by hand.

Q20 [B4] What would make you reject event sourcing in a design review?

30-second answer: No requirement that needs history (audit, temporal queries, many future read models). Mostly CRUD with cross-aggregate invariants. A team without ES experience and no time to build tooling (projections, upcasting, rebuilds, reconciliation). Heavy PII without an erasure strategy. Or aggregates that would become very long or hot streams without natural boundaries.

Deep answer: Offer alternatives: tables + outbox events + CQRS read models, a history table via CDC, or temporal tables. They deliver most of the benefits at a fraction of the cost. Approve ES for well-bounded, history-centric aggregates with an operational plan.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Architectural ambition vs delivery risk.

Follow-ups: 1. What's a middle ground? → Event-source one aggregate as a pilot, with the tooling built properly. 2. How do you measure success? → Audit queries answered, dispute resolution time, projection correctness.

Red flags: Choosing ES because it's fashionable.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Events play three roles: notification (with coupling), state transfer (with duplication), and source of truth (with history). L1 measured the difference.
  2. CQRS separates writes from purpose-built reads. Read models are derived, disposable and rebuildable (549 ms for 12 K events).
  3. Event sourcing: state = fold(events). You get audit and time travel, and pay in versioning, projections and concurrency.
  4. Expected-version appends protect invariants (L2: overdraft −₹11 without them, ₹0 with them).
  5. Projection checkpoints must be safe under concurrent commits: naive positions missed 2,954 of 12,000 events, and xid-safe ones missed 0.
  6. Projections are idempotent: the checkpoint is updated in the same transaction, upserts are version-guarded, and there are no side effects.
  7. Snapshots and period closing bound load time (179.8 ms → 3.4 ms).
  8. Never rewrite events. Version them and upcast exactly (a double upcaster lost ₹57.40).
  9. Keep PII out of events, or crypto-shred it.
  10. Use event sourcing where history is the business, and CRUD + outbox + read models elsewhere.

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Choose Other services need the fact only Event notification (small payload) Other services need the data and autonomy Event-carried state transfer (versioned) Full audit / time travel of an aggregate Event sourcing with expected-version appends Fast, varied queries CQRS read models, rebuildable Projector on a PostgreSQL event store xid-safe checkpoint + atomic checkpoint update Long streams Snapshots + period closing Format change Additive → upcaster → new event type PII References, or per-subject encryption keys

docs.title: 16. Microservices Architecture ⭐
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B2 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 09, Ch 13, Ch 14, Ch 15 · What you will build: The decomposition of the grocery platform into 26 services, and the machinery that keeps it from becoming a distributed monolith.

  • L1 quantifies what synchronous call chains do to availability and tail latency.
  • L2 runs architecture fitness functions over the service graph: synchronous cycles, chain depth, shared databases and fan-in, before and after redrawing boundaries.
  • L3 is a modular monolith whose boundaries are enforced by the Java compiler (JPMS). Reaching into another module's internals, an undeclared dependency and a cycle are all compile errors, shown verbatim.
  • L4 uses real HTTP on localhost for three things: service discovery with heartbeats vs a static list while an instance dies, API composition with a latency budget, and a strangler-fig migration with shadow diffing and a canary.

Every program was run, and outputs are verbatim. · Reading time: 110 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: 14 services, one deploy train
docs.text:
Two years after "moving to microservices", the grocery platform had 14 services, and every release still went out together on Thursday night. What had happened:

  • Three services shared the orders database. Order, fulfilment and invoicing all read and wrote the same tables. Adding a column needed three teams in one meeting, and a slow invoicing query locked rows that checkout needed.
  • Synchronous cycles. Order called payment to capture, and payment called order back to fetch the amount. Fulfilment and order called each other. When payment slowed down, order threads piled up, fulfilment's calls to order timed out, and checkout failed.
  • A checkout needed 10 services to be up at the same time. At 99.9 % each, that's roughly 99.0 % for checkout, or about 7 hours of failed checkouts a month, even though every service met its own SLO.
  • The order-details page called order, payment and tracking one after another. Tracking had occasional 2-second stalls, which became the page's p99.

The architecture had the costs of microservices (network calls, partial failures, distributed data) without the benefit (independent deployability). It was a distributed monolith.

The fix wasn't "more microservices". It was better boundaries:

  • One database per service. Facts flow as events (Ch 14), not as shared tables or callbacks.
  • Synchronous calls only where the caller needs an answer now, with no cycles, a shallow depth and timeouts (Ch 18).
  • Pages that call several services do it in parallel, with a latency budget and partial results.
  • New capabilities start in a modular monolith with enforced module boundaries. They're extracted into services only when there's a reason (a team, scaling, a different release cadence).
  • Legacy paths are replaced piece by piece with a strangler fig: a routing facade, shadow traffic and canaries.

The thesis of this chapter

Microservices are a way to let teams change and deploy parts of a system independently. Everything else follows from that: boundaries along business capabilities, a database per service, asynchronous facts, few and shallow synchronous calls. If services can't be deployed independently, or a request needs ten of them to be up, you've built a distributed monolith, and a modular monolith would have served you better.

docs.title: 1.2 Where this lives in the grocery platform
docs.text:
The 26 services and their bounded contexts are listed in Ch 00 §3.3. This chapter explains why they're split that way and what rules keep them independent:

Rule Example Check Split by business capability / bounded context pricing-service owns prices and GST rates; catalog doesn't Ownership in the service catalog One database per service invoice-service has invoice_db and builds what it needs from events Fitness function: no shared DB (L2) Facts as events, commands as calls order.order.placed.v1 → fulfilment, invoicing, notifications Async edges in the service graph No synchronous cycles; depth ≤ 4 Checkout calls cart, pricing, inventory, payment, order in parallel Fitness function (L2) Pages compose in parallel with budgets Order details: order + payment required, tracking optional p99 SLO (L4 B) Start modular, extract when justified New subscription capability starts as a module in order-service JPMS/Modulith boundary checks (L3) Replace legacy with a strangler fig Order history moved off the legacy PHP admin behind the gateway Shadow diff = 0 before cutover (L4 C)

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text: Band After this chapter you can… B2 Explain what microservices are for, decompose by business capability, and state the database-per-service rule and its consequences B3 Design service discovery, externalized configuration and API composition; detect distributed-monolith smells with fitness functions B4 Choose between a modular monolith and microservices, plan a strangler-fig migration, and align service boundaries with team topology (Conway's law)

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: one big kitchen vs a food court B2
docs.text:
• A big restaurant kitchen (a monolith) has one head chef, one menu and one set of equipment. Coordination is easy (shout across the room), and changing the menu is one decision. But every new dish means the whole kitchen retrains, and a fire at the grill stops everything.
  • A food court (microservices) is independent stalls, each with its own staff, menu, suppliers and hours. The dosa stall can change its recipe without asking the pizza stall. But a combo meal needs several stalls to coordinate, the customer walks between counters, and if the drinks stall is closed, the combo is incomplete.
  • A food court where every stall shares one fridge and must ask the next stall for every ingredient is the distributed monolith. You get all the walking and none of the independence.
  • A big kitchen with clearly separated stations, each with its own shelf and a rule that nobody takes from another station's shelf, is the modular monolith. It keeps the easy coordination and most of the independence, and it can become a food court later, station by station.

docs.title: 2.2 What microservices are, and what they're for ⭐ B2
docs.text:
A microservice is an independently deployable unit that owns a business capability and its data, and communicates through well-defined APIs and events. The defining property is independent deployability: a team can change, test and release its service without coordinating a release with other teams.

Benefit Only if… Team autonomy and parallel delivery Boundaries match teams (Conway's law), contracts are versioned Independent scaling Services have different load shapes (search vs invoicing) Fault isolation Calls have timeouts and fallbacks, and dependencies are few (Ch 18) Technology fit The platform can support more than one stack (usually: don't) Smaller codebases Boundaries are stable and cohesive Cost Consequence Network calls instead of method calls Latency, partial failure, retries, serialization Distributed data No joins or transactions across services: sagas (Ch 13), events (Ch 14), CQRS (Ch 15) Operations N deployments, dashboards, on-calls, CVEs, pipelines (Ch 24, 26) Testing Contracts, environments, end-to-end cost (Ch 29) Availability math Every synchronous dependency multiplies in (L1)

L1 puts numbers on the last line:

  • Availability multiplies: 5 synchronous services in series at 99.9 % each gives 99.50 % (216 min/month of failures). 12 gives 98.81 %.
  • Latency adds up when calls are sequential: 8 calls go from p50 20 ms to 178 ms.
  • Parallel calls take the maximum instead, but the tail still grows: 26 parallel calls give 23 % of page loads that hit at least one dependency's p99.

docs.title: 2.3 Decomposition: business capabilities and bounded contexts ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
By business capability: what the business does. Examples: catalog management, pricing, promotions, ordering, fulfilment, delivery dispatch, payments, settlements, invoicing, customer support.

By bounded context (DDD, Ch 33): where a model and its language are consistent.

  • "Product" in the catalog has descriptions and images.
  • In pricing, it has MRP, selling price and GST slab.
  • In inventory, it's a SKU with stock per dark store.
  • In fulfilment, it's a pick location and weight.

These are four models of one real-world thing, in four contexts. Forcing one shared Product model across them is how the monolith got coupled.

Heuristics for boundaries:

Heuristic Good sign Bad sign Change together → belong together A feature touches one service Every feature touches 3 services Data ownership Each table has one writer Several services write the same table Transactions Invariants are enforced inside one service Invariants need cross-service transactions Language Terms mean one thing inside the service "Order" means three things Team One team owns it end to end Several teams commit to it weekly Chattiness A few coarse calls per use case Dozens of fine-grained calls

Granularity: start coarser than you think. Splitting a service later is easier than merging services that share nothing but pain. The grocery platform's 26 services map to about 8 teams (Ch 37). A team owning 3–4 cohesive services is normal. A service per entity (address-service, gst-rate-service) isn't.

docs.title: 2.4 Database per service ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
Each service owns its data. Other services access it only through the owner's API or events. They never read or write its tables.

  • Why: schema changes stay local, the owner enforces invariants, the owner chooses the right storage (Ch 06), and a noisy neighbour can't lock your rows.
  • "Private tables on a shared server" is an acceptable start: separate schemas and users on one PostgreSQL cluster, as long as grants enforce the separation. It's the shared tables that are the problem.
  • Consequences, and their patterns:
    • Cross-service queries → API composition (§2.8) or a CQRS read model built from events (Ch 15).
    • Cross-service transactions → sagas + outbox (Ch 13).
    • Reference data (pincodes, GST rates) → owned by one service, replicated to others via event-carried state transfer (Ch 15), and cached with versions.
    • Reporting → CDC into the warehouse (Ch 21), never live joins across service databases.

L2's "before" graph had two shared databases (orders_db used by order, fulfilment and invoice; catalog_db used by catalog and pricing), and the fitness check failed on them.

docs.title: 2.5 Communication styles ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
Style Use for Watch out for Synchronous request/response (REST, gRPC; Ch 04, 17) Queries and commands where the caller needs the answer now (price, stock check, payment result) Availability multiplication, cascading latency, cycles Asynchronous events (Ch 14) Facts others react to (order placed, price changed) Eventual consistency, duplicates, ordering Asynchronous commands / jobs (queues) Work for one owner, later (send SMS, generate invoice) Retries, DLQs

Rules the platform follows:

  1. No synchronous cycles. A calls B, and B calls A is a single deployable unit in disguise, and a deadlock/cascade risk. L2 found two cycles in the "before" graph (order ↔ payment ↔ fulfilment, catalog ↔ inventory).
  2. Shallow synchronous depth: gateway → aggregator → leaf (≤ 4 hops). The "before" graph had a 6-hop chain (gateway → checkout → order → invoice → pricing → catalog → inventory).
  3. Invert dependencies with events. Instead of payment calling order back, payment publishes payment.payment.captured.v1, and the order saga reacts.
  4. Every call has a timeout, and retries only on idempotent operations with backoff (Ch 18).
  5. Keep the synchronous blast radius small: L2's "after" graph cut the services a checkout needs synchronously from 10 to 6.

docs.title: 2.6 Service discovery and load balancing ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Instances come and go (autoscaling, deploys, crashes), so callers need the current, healthy set.

Approach How Examples Platform DNS + L4/L7 LB A stable name resolves to a virtual IP or load balancer; the platform tracks health Kubernetes Services, cloud LBs Client-side discovery The client asks a registry for instances and balances itself Eureka + Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, Consul Service mesh A sidecar or ambient proxy does discovery, retries, mTLS and outlier detection Istio, Linkerd, Cilium

Whatever the mechanism, three behaviours matter:

  • Dead instances are removed quickly: health checks, heartbeats with a TTL, readiness probes (Ch 26).
  • Callers retry on another instance for idempotent requests.
  • Clients don't cache instance lists forever.

L4 A made 3,000 calls to three catalog instances, and one crashed after call 500:

  • A static instance list failed 833 calls (every third call went to the dead instance).
  • A registry with a 300 ms heartbeat TTL plus one retry failed 0.

On Kubernetes, the Service/Endpoints mechanism does the registry part. Readiness probes must fail before an instance stops accepting traffic (graceful shutdown), or the same failures appear during every deploy.

docs.title: 2.7 Externalized configuration B3
docs.text:
• Configuration (URLs, timeouts, feature flags, limits) lives outside the artifact, so one build runs in every environment (12-factor).
  • Sources: environment variables and ConfigMaps (Kubernetes), Spring Cloud Config, Consul/etcd (Ch 12), and a secrets manager for credentials (Vault, cloud KMS; Ch 23).
  • Dynamic config and flags (rate limits, kill switches) are versioned and audited, with safe defaults when the config store is unreachable, and validated before rollout. A config push is a deployment.
  • Avoid a "config service" that every request depends on synchronously. Load it at startup and on change (watch), then serve from memory.

docs.title: 2.8 API composition and the gateway ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Many screens need data from several services. Options:

  • Client-side composition (the app calls several APIs): chatty over mobile networks, and it exposes internal APIs.
  • API composition in a gateway or BFF (backend-for-frontend): one call from the app, and the BFF calls services in parallel, with a latency budget and partial results for optional parts.
  • A CQRS read model (Ch 15) when the combined view is requested often or needs filtering/sorting across services. It's pre-joined by events.

L4 B, 500 order-details page loads (order 20 ms, payment 30 ms, tracking 25 ms, but 3 % of tracking calls take 2 s):

Strategy p50 p99 Partial pages Sequential 79 ms 2,054 ms 0 Parallel 31 ms 2,002 ms 0 Parallel + 250 ms budget for the optional part 31 ms 251 ms 10 (tracking shown as "updating…")

Parallelism fixes the median. Budgets and optional parts fix the tail. Decide per field whether it's required (fail the page) or optional (degrade gracefully). That's a product decision.

docs.title: 2.9 The distributed monolith: smells and fitness functions ⭐ B3 B4
docs.text:
Smell Symptom Measure (L2) Lock-step deploys "Release train"; services versioned together Deploys per service per week; % releases touching > 1 service Shared database Schema changes need cross-team meetings Tables with > 1 writer; shared databases Synchronous cycles Cascading failures, deadlock-like stalls synchronous cycles Deep call chains Latency and availability multiply longest sync chain, services a checkout needs Chatty interfaces Hundreds of calls per page Calls per request (tracing, Ch 24) Shared domain library One "common-model" jar in every service Dependency analysis Hub service Everyone calls one service synchronously highest sync fan-in

Architecture fitness functions (Ford, Parsons & Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures) turn these into CI checks over a machine-readable catalog of services, dependencies and databases (Backstage catalog, OpenAPI/AsyncAPI specs, tracing data). L2 shows the "before" graph FAIL (2 cycles, 6-hop chain, 2 shared databases, 10 synchronous dependencies for checkout) and the "after" graph PASS (no cycles, 2 hops, no shared databases, 6 dependencies).

docs.title: 2.10 The modular monolith ⭐ B3 B4
docs.text:
One deployable unit made of modules with enforced boundaries: each module owns its data (its own schema and tables), exposes a small API, and communicates with others through that API or in-process events.

Monolith (big ball of mud) Modular monolith Microservices Deploy One unit One unit Independent Boundaries Conventions, eroded Enforced (compiler/JPMS, ArchUnit, Spring Modulith) Network Calls between parts Method calls anywhere Method calls to published APIs, events Network calls Transactions across parts Easy Possible, but discouraged across modules Sagas Operational cost Low Low High Extraction later Hard A module becomes a service —

L3 enforces the boundaries with the Java Platform Module System. Each module exports only its api package. grocery.order requires grocery.catalog and grocery.shared, but not grocery.inventory, and it reaches inventory only by publishing OrderPlaced. Then three violations are attempted, and the compiler rejects each one:

  • Importing com.grocery.catalog.internal.ProductRepository → package com.grocery.catalog.internal is not visible.
  • Using inventory without declaring it → package com.grocery.inventory.api is not visible.
  • Adding requires grocery.order to catalog → cyclic dependence involving grocery.catalog.

In Spring Boot, Spring Modulith gives the same idea with packages instead of JPMS modules: ApplicationModules.of(App.class).verify() fails the build on illegal dependencies. It also offers @ApplicationModuleListener for transactional in-process events with an event publication registry (outbox semantics), and documentation of the module graph.

When to extract a module into a service: a different team owns it and needs its own release cadence, its load or scaling profile differs sharply, it needs different technology or isolation (PCI scope for payments), or failure isolation justifies the network hop. "It feels big" isn't on the list.

docs.title: 2.11 Migrating: the strangler fig ⭐ B4
docs.text:
Martin Fowler's strangler fig replaces a legacy system gradually, not in a big-bang rewrite:

  1. Put a facade in front (the API gateway or a routing proxy). All traffic flows through it.
  2. Pick a slice: one capability, and ideally one that's read-heavy first (order history), not the most entangled.
  3. Build the new service, and feed it data via CDC or events from the legacy DB (Ch 13).
  4. Shadow: the facade sends real requests to both. The legacy answers, and the responses are diffed. L4 C: 468 mismatches in 2,000 requests, all for large baskets, a rounding bug found before any user saw it.
  5. Canary: after the fix, route a small share (L4: 214 of 2,000) to the new service while still diffing (0 mismatches). Then ramp up.
  6. Cut over and retire the legacy path. Delete the dead code and tables.
  7. Repeat with the next slice. Writes are harder: move the write path only after reads are stable, and use CDC in the reverse direction during the transition if the legacy still needs the data.

Anti-corruption layer (ACL): translate the legacy's model to the new context's model at the boundary, so legacy concepts don't leak into the new service.

docs.title: 2.12 Microservices and teams ⭐ B4
docs.text:
• Conway's law: systems mirror the communication structure of the organizations that build them. The inverse Conway manoeuvre designs teams to get the architecture you want.
  • Team Topologies (Skelton & Pais): stream-aligned teams own services end to end. A platform team provides paved roads (CI/CD, observability, the service template). Enabling teams coach, and complicated-subsystem teams own things like search ranking.
  • Cognitive load is the real limit. If one team owns 9 services and 4 of them page at night, the boundaries (or the team count) are wrong.
  • A service template ("golden path") is how 26 services stay consistent: the four-layer structure, logging, tracing, health, config, security, the outbox/inbox library and the CI pipeline, generated from one template (Ch 37).

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Service Boundaries for the Grocery Platform
docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers Principal engineer / all team leads, SRE, Security Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-063 Decompose by bounded context (26 services, 8 teams); ADR-064 Database per service; ADR-065 Synchronous-call rules and fitness functions; ADR-066 Modular monolith first for new capabilities; ADR-067 Strangler fig for legacy admin

1. Context & Problem. 14 services deployed together weekly. Three services shared orders_db, there were synchronous cycles, checkout depended on 10 services, and page p99s were dominated by optional data (§1.1).

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: any service deployable alone on any day; checkout available ≥ 99.9 %; order-details page p99 ≤ 300 ms; clear ownership of every table and API; a repeatable way to add capabilities and retire legacy.
  • Non-goals: polyglot stacks (Java/Spring for all backend services); splitting services below team granularity.

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement NFR-1 0 synchronous cycles; synchronous depth ≤ 4; checkout synchronous dependencies ≤ 6 (CI fitness function) NFR-2 0 tables with more than one writing service (DB grant audit in CI) NFR-3 ≥ 90 % of releases touch exactly one service NFR-4 Every synchronous call has a timeout; optional data has a budget and a fallback NFR-5 Dead instances are removed from rotation in ≤ 5 s; deploys cause 0 failed requests (graceful shutdown) NFR-6 Legacy endpoints are migrated only after a shadow diff of 0 mismatches over ≥ 7 days of traffic

4. Capacity & latency estimates.

Item Calculation Result Checkout availability 6 synchronous services × 99.95 % (tier-1 SLO) ≈ 99.70 % → need retries/fallbacks on idempotent reads to reach 99.9 % Order-details p99 max(order, payment) p99 ≈ 80 ms + BFF overhead; tracking budget 250 ms ≤ 300 ms Service count vs teams 26 services / 8 teams ~3 per team (OK) Deploy frequency target 26 services × 3/week ~80 deploys/week, needs a paved-road pipeline (Ch 26)

5. Proposed design.

  1. Boundaries: 26 services as in Ch 00 §3.3, grouped under 8 stream-aligned teams, with a platform team for gateway, discovery, observability and the service template.
  2. Data: a database (or at least a schema with exclusive grants) per service. Reference data is replicated via events. Reporting goes through CDC to the warehouse.
  3. Communication: events for facts (outbox, Ch 13). Synchronous calls only where an answer is needed now; no cycles, depth ≤ 4, timeouts everywhere. Payment → order callbacks are replaced by payment.payment.captured.v1.
  4. Discovery: Kubernetes Services, readiness probes, graceful shutdown (preStop + drain), client retries for idempotent calls on another instance.
  5. Composition: a mobile BFF and a web BFF with parallel calls, per-field required/optional classification, budgets, partial responses.
  6. Fitness functions in CI: service catalog + OpenAPI/AsyncAPI → cycle, depth, fan-in and shared-DB checks (L2). Spring Modulith verify() inside each service with modules.
  7. New capabilities start as modules. Extraction criteria are an ADR per extraction.
  8. Legacy admin is migrated by strangler fig through the gateway: shadow → canary → cutover, slice by slice.

7. Alternatives considered.

Option Pros Cons Verdict Stay with the current 14 services No migration Distributed monolith costs stay Rejected Bounded-context services + rules + fitness functions Autonomy, isolation, measurable More services to operate Chosen Consolidate into one modular monolith Simplest ops, local transactions 8 teams on one deploy pipeline; scaling of search/tracking differs Rejected for the whole platform; used within services Finer-grained services (per entity) Small codebases Chattiness, cycles, cognitive load Rejected Service mesh now Uniform retries/mTLS Operational complexity Deferred; revisit with the mTLS requirement (Ch 23)

8. Failure modes. A dependency is down: required → fail fast with a clear error, optional → degrade. An instance dies: removed by readiness/endpoints, and idempotent calls retry. Config store down: serve the last known config. Legacy and new disagree during migration: shadow diff blocks the cutover.

10. Observability. A service dependency graph from tracing (actual vs declared), calls per request, synchronous depth per endpoint, deploys per service, % multi-service releases, error budget per service, partial-response rate per BFF field.

14. Decision (ADR-063–067 summary). The platform is 26 bounded-context services owned by 8 teams, each with its own data. Facts flow as events. Synchronous calls follow no-cycle/shallow/timeout rules enforced by fitness functions in CI. New capabilities start as enforced modules. Legacy is replaced by strangler fig with shadow diffing.
