docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Platform Calling Conventions
docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers Platform team / all service owners, SRE Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-068 Sync/async decision rules; ADR-069 gRPC for internal high-QPS calls, REST at the edge; ADR-070 Deadlines and timeouts; ADR-071 Retry placement; ADR-072 Mesh scope (mTLS, outlier detection)

1. Context & Problem. A 4 s slowdown in promotions cascaded into a checkout outage through missing timeouts, shared pools, layered retries (27x load) and work continuing after users gave up (§1.1).

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: a slow dependency degrades only the features that need it; no orphan work after deadlines; bounded retry amplification; schema changes never break a peer during rollout; uniform mTLS.
  • Non-goals: replacing Kafka events with RPC; a mesh-managed L7 policy for every route on day one.

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement NFR-1 Every outbound call has connect and response timeouts ≤ the remaining deadline (checked by a client library + lint) NFR-2 Deadlines propagate on all synchronous calls (grpc-timeout / X-Request-Timeout-Ms) NFR-3 Retries only at the gateway/mesh layer for idempotent calls, retry budget ≤ 10 % NFR-4 Each dependency has its own connection pool and concurrency limit (bulkhead) NFR-5 Breaking API/proto changes are blocked in CI (buf breaking, OpenAPI diff, contract tests) NFR-6 All service-to-service traffic uses mTLS with workload identity

4. Capacity & latency estimates.

Item Calculation Result Checkout → pricing concurrency 420 req/s × p99 80 ms ~34 in flight → pool 50, limit 100 During degradation without timeout 420 × 4 s 1,680 in flight → exhaustion (L2 A) With a 300 ms timeout 420 × 0.3 s ≤ 126 in flight, bounded Payload savings with protobuf 706 → 271 bytes per order (L3) × ~2 K internal calls/s ~0.9 MB/s less on internal links Mesh overhead (sidecar) ~0.5–1 ms p50 per hop, ~50–100 MB per proxy Measure; consider ambient for L4 mTLS

5. Proposed design.

  1. A client library (in the service template) wraps RestClient/gRPC stubs. It reads the incoming deadline, computes the remaining budget, applies per-dependency timeouts (config), attaches deadline headers, enforces a per-dependency concurrency limit, and exposes metrics. Direct use of raw clients fails a lint rule.
  2. gRPC for internal synchronous calls with more than 100 req/s (pricing, inventory, cart). REST for everything else and at the edge. The .proto files live in a shared schema repo with buf breaking in CI.
  3. Retries: the gateway retries idempotent GETs once on another instance, and the mesh does not retry (it's disabled, to avoid double retries). Payment calls use idempotency keys and are retried only by the saga (Ch 13).
  4. Fallbacks are declared per call: required (fail fast) or optional (default value + flag).
  5. Mesh (phase 1): Istio ambient for mTLS and L4 telemetry. Waypoints only for namespaces needing L7 traffic shifting (canaries). Outlier detection on.

7. Alternatives considered.

Option Pros Cons Verdict REST everywhere One stack, simple Larger payloads; custom deadline headers; weaker contracts Kept for the edge and low-QPS internal calls gRPC for hot internal paths Contracts, deadlines, performance Browser/gateway translation; binary debugging Chosen Retries in every client Simple locally Multiplicative load (L2 C: 27x) Rejected Sidecar mesh Mature L7 features Per-pod cost, proxy restarts Rejected for phase 1 Ambient mesh mTLS without sidecars; L7 opt-in Newer; feature parity varies by version Chosen for phase 1 (with a fallback to sidecars if a gap blocks us)

8. Failure modes. Dependency slow: timeout → fallback/error in ≤ budget, no pool exhaustion. Deadline already spent: the hop rejects immediately. Retry storm: prevented by single-layer retries + budget + breaker. Proto change breaking a consumer: blocked in CI. Mesh control plane down: existing config keeps working; new workloads are affected.

10. Observability. Per dependency: latency histograms, timeouts, fallbacks served, in-flight concurrency, pool waits. Deadline-exceeded counts per hop (where the time went). Retries per request and retry-budget usage. Mesh golden metrics and mTLS coverage.

14. Decision (ADR-068–072 summary). Use events for facts, sync calls only when an answer is needed now. gRPC for hot internal paths, REST at the edge. Every call goes through the platform client with deadline propagation, per-dependency timeouts, bulkheads and declared fallbacks. Retries at one layer with budgets. An ambient mesh provides mTLS, outlier detection and telemetry, and doesn't retry.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
Level New requirement that forces the step L1 "Why does a slow dependency need more threads, and do virtual threads fix it?" (real threads) L2 "A slow dependency must not take down unrelated endpoints, waste work, or be retried to death." (real HTTP) L3 "REST or gRPC, and which schema changes are safe?" (real protoc) L4 "Make it the default in every Spring service, and decide what the mesh owns."

How the code in this chapter was verified

L1 and L2 are Java 21 programs using real threads and real HTTP servers and clients on localhost (JDK HttpServer/HttpClient). L3 uses the real protoc 28.3 to encode and decode protobuf. The Spring, gRPC-Java and Istio code in L4 wasn't compiled or applied here (no Maven Central or Kubernetes in this environment) and is marked VERIFY. It implements exactly the behaviours measured in L2.

docs.title: L1 — Concept: Little's law with real threads B2
docs.text:
// ConcurrencyL1.java — run with: java ConcurrencyL1.java
// Little's law for synchronous calls: in-flight requests = arrival rate × latency. When a dependency slows down,
// the caller needs proportionally more concurrency — or it queues. Measured with real threads.
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class ConcurrencyL1 {

    static double runMs(ExecutorService pool, int tasks, long blockMs) throws Exception {
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        List<Future<?>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) fs.add(pool.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(blockMs); return null; }));   // "waiting on pricing-service"
        for (var f : fs) f.get();
        pool.shutdown();
        return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("A. Little's law: threads busy waiting = requests/s × dependency latency");
        for (long latencyMs : new long[]{50, 200, 1_000, 5_000})
            System.out.printf("   400 req/s × %,5d ms → %,5d requests in flight%n", latencyMs, 400 * latencyMs / 1000);

        System.out.println("B. 4,000 calls that each wait 500 ms on a dependency (real threads)");
        System.out.printf("   fixed pool of 200 platform threads : %,7.0f ms%n", runMs(Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200), 4_000, 500));
        System.out.printf("   virtual thread per task            : %,7.0f ms%n", runMs(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), 4_000, 500));
        System.out.println("   → virtual threads remove the thread-pool ceiling, but NOT the dependency's own limits:");
        System.out.println("     4,000 concurrent calls now reach pricing-service at once, so bound them (semaphore/bulkhead, Ch 18)");
    }
}

Actual output from running it:

A. Little's law: threads busy waiting = requests/s × dependency latency
   400 req/s ×    50 ms →    20 requests in flight
   400 req/s ×   200 ms →    80 requests in flight
   400 req/s × 1,000 ms →   400 requests in flight
   400 req/s × 5,000 ms → 2,000 requests in flight
B. 4,000 calls that each wait 500 ms on a dependency (real threads)
   fixed pool of 200 platform threads :  10,144 ms
   virtual thread per task            :     551 ms
   → virtual threads remove the thread-pool ceiling, but NOT the dependency's own limits:
     4,000 concurrent calls now reach pricing-service at once, so bound them (semaphore/bulkhead, Ch 18)

What L1 shows: concurrency needed = rate × latency, so a dependency's slowdown is multiplied into the caller's resource usage. Virtual threads make waiting cheap (10.1 s → 0.55 s for the same work), which makes it easier to flood a struggling dependency. So bound concurrency per dependency.

docs.title: L2 — Timeouts, deadlines and retry placement over real HTTP B3
docs.text:
// CallsL2.java — run with: java CallsL2.java
// Real HTTP on localhost (JDK HttpServer + HttpClient):
//   A. a slow dependency without timeouts exhausts the caller's thread pool and takes down an UNRELATED endpoint
//   B. per-hop timeouts vs a propagated deadline: work that continues after the user has already given up
//   C. retries at every layer multiply load on a failing leaf
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpExchange;
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;
import java.net.*;
import java.net.http.*;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

public class CallsL2 {

    static final HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_1_1)
            .connectTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)).executor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()).build();

    interface Handler { String handle(HttpExchange ex) throws Exception; }

    static HttpServer server(int port, ExecutorService pool, Handler h) throws Exception {
        HttpServer s = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("127.0.0.1", port), 1000);
        s.createContext("/", ex -> {
            int code = 200; String body;
            try { body = h.handle(ex); } catch (Exception e) { code = 503; body = e.getClass().getSimpleName(); }
            byte[] b = body.getBytes();
            try { ex.sendResponseHeaders(code, b.length); ex.getResponseBody().write(b); } catch (Exception ignored) { }
            ex.close();
        });
        s.setExecutor(pool); s.start(); return s;
    }

    static HttpResponse<String> call(String url, Duration timeout, Map<String, String> headers) throws Exception {
        var b = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(url));
        if (timeout != null) b.timeout(timeout);
        headers.forEach(b::header);
        return client.send(b.build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
    }

    // ---------------- A ----------------
    static void experimentA(boolean withTimeout) throws Exception {
        HttpServer pricing = server(19002, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), ex -> { Thread.sleep(5_000); return "price"; });  // degraded
        HttpServer checkout = server(19001, Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20), ex -> {                  // the caller: 20 worker threads
            if (ex.getRequestURI().getPath().startsWith("/cart")) return "cart ok";                   // local work only
            try {
                return call("http://127.0.0.1:19002/price", withTimeout ? Duration.ofMillis(300) : null, Map.of()).body();
            } catch (HttpTimeoutException e) { return "price unavailable (cached MRP shown)"; }       // fallback
        });
        int n = 1_000; long[] cartLat = new long[n / 2]; AtomicInteger cartOk = new AtomicInteger(), priceOk = new AtomicInteger();
        ExecutorService load = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); List<Future<?>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            int ii = i; boolean cart = i % 2 == 0;
            fs.add(load.submit(() -> {
                long t0 = System.nanoTime();
                try {
                    var r = call("http://127.0.0.1:19001/" + (cart ? "cart" : "price"), Duration.ofSeconds(2), Map.of());   // the app gives up after 2 s
                    if (r.statusCode() == 200) (cart ? cartOk : priceOk).incrementAndGet();
                } catch (Exception ignored) { }
                if (cart) cartLat[ii / 2] = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000;
                return null;
            }));
            Thread.sleep(10);                                                                          // 100 requests/s for 10 s
        }
        for (var f : fs) f.get();
        Arrays.sort(cartLat);
        System.out.printf("   %-26s /cart ok %3d/500 (p99 %5d ms)   /price ok %3d/500%n", withTimeout ? "300 ms timeout + fallback" : "no timeout",
                cartOk.get(), cartLat[cartLat.length * 99 / 100], priceOk.get());
        checkout.stop(0); pricing.stop(0);
    }

    // ---------------- B ----------------
    static void experimentB(boolean propagate) throws Exception {
        AtomicLong orphanMs = new AtomicLong(); AtomicInteger orphanRequests = new AtomicInteger(), abandoned = new AtomicInteger();
        ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> userGaveUpAt = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        Random rnd = new Random(4);
        HttpServer promo = server(19013, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), ex -> {
            String id = ex.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("X-Request-Id");
            long work; synchronized (rnd) { work = rnd.nextDouble() < 0.3 ? 1_500 : 60; }              // 30 % slow coupon evaluation
            long deadline = propagate ? Long.parseLong(ex.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("X-Deadline-Epoch-Ms")) : Long.MAX_VALUE;
            long end = System.currentTimeMillis() + work;
            while (System.currentTimeMillis() < end) {                                                // work in slices; check the deadline
                if (System.currentTimeMillis() > deadline) { abandoned.incrementAndGet(); throw new TimeoutException(); }
                Thread.sleep(10);
            }
            Long gaveUp = userGaveUpAt.get(id);
            if (gaveUp != null) { orphanRequests.incrementAndGet(); orphanMs.addAndGet(System.currentTimeMillis() - gaveUp); }
            return "discount 5%";
        });
        Handler hop = ex -> {                                                                          // checkout → pricing → promotion
            String id = ex.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("X-Request-Id");
            String next = ex.getLocalAddress().getPort() == 19011 ? "http://127.0.0.1:19012/" : "http://127.0.0.1:19013/";
            Map<String, String> h = new HashMap<>(Map.of("X-Request-Id", id));
            Duration timeout = Duration.ofSeconds(1);                                                  // each hop's own fixed timeout
            if (propagate) {
                String dl = ex.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("X-Deadline-Epoch-Ms");
                long remaining = Long.parseLong(dl) - System.currentTimeMillis() - 20;                // keep 20 ms for our own reply
                if (remaining <= 0) throw new TimeoutException();                                      // don't even start
                h.put("X-Deadline-Epoch-Ms", dl); timeout = Duration.ofMillis(remaining);
            }
            Thread.sleep(15);                                                                          // own work
            return call(next, timeout, h).body();
        };
        HttpServer checkout = server(19011, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), hop);
        HttpServer pricing = server(19012, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), hop);
        int n = 300, ok = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            String id = "req-" + i; long budget = 500;                                                 // the app waits 500 ms, then shows a fallback
            Map<String, String> h = new HashMap<>(Map.of("X-Request-Id", id));
            if (propagate) h.put("X-Deadline-Epoch-Ms", Long.toString(System.currentTimeMillis() + budget));
            try { if (call("http://127.0.0.1:19011/", Duration.ofMillis(budget), h).statusCode() == 200) ok++; }
            catch (HttpTimeoutException e) { userGaveUpAt.put(id, System.currentTimeMillis()); }
        }
        Thread.sleep(2_000);                                                                          // let orphans finish
        System.out.printf("   %-30s answered %3d/%d   work finished AFTER the user gave up: %3d requests, %,6d ms   abandoned early: %d%n",
                propagate ? "propagated deadline" : "fixed 1 s timeout per hop", ok, n, orphanRequests.get(), orphanMs.get(), abandoned.get());
        checkout.stop(0); pricing.stop(0); promo.stop(0);
    }

    // ---------------- C ----------------
    static void experimentC(int attemptsPerLayer) throws Exception {
        AtomicInteger leafCalls = new AtomicInteger();
        HttpServer leaf = server(19023, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), ex -> { leafCalls.incrementAndGet(); throw new IllegalStateException("down"); });
        Handler retrying = ex -> {
            String next = ex.getLocalAddress().getPort() == 19021 ? "http://127.0.0.1:19022/" : "http://127.0.0.1:19023/";
            int attempts = attemptsPerLayer;                                                           // retries at THIS layer
            for (int a = 1; a <= attempts; a++) {
                var r = call(next, Duration.ofSeconds(1), Map.of());
                if (r.statusCode() == 200) return r.body();
            }
            throw new IllegalStateException("gave up");
        };
        HttpServer l1 = server(19021, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), retrying);
        HttpServer l2 = server(19022, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), retrying);
        int edgeAttempts = 3;
        for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) for (int a = 0; a < edgeAttempts; a++) if (call("http://127.0.0.1:19021/", Duration.ofSeconds(5), Map.of()).statusCode() == 200) break;
        System.out.printf("   %-44s leaf received %,5d calls for 100 user requests (%.0fx)%n",
                attemptsPerLayer == 3 ? "3 attempts at the edge AND at each of 2 layers" : "3 attempts at the edge only", leafCalls.get(), leafCalls.get() / 100.0);
        l1.stop(0); l2.stop(0); leaf.stop(0);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.setProperty("sun.net.httpserver.nodelay", "true");
        System.out.println("A. checkout-service (20 worker threads) serves /cart (local) and /price (calls pricing); pricing now takes 5 s");
        experimentA(false);
        experimentA(true);
        System.out.println("B. app (500 ms budget) → checkout → pricing → promotion; 30 % of promotion calls take 1.5 s");
        experimentB(false);
        experimentB(true);
        System.out.println("C. edge → layer-1 → layer-2 → leaf, leaf is down");
        experimentC(3);
        experimentC(1);
        System.exit(0);
    }
}

Actual output from running it:

A. checkout-service (20 worker threads) serves /cart (local) and /price (calls pricing); pricing now takes 5 s
   no timeout                 /cart ok  20/500 (p99  2002 ms)   /price ok   0/500
   300 ms timeout + fallback  /cart ok 500/500 (p99     6 ms)   /price ok 500/500
B. app (500 ms budget) → checkout → pricing → promotion; 30 % of promotion calls take 1.5 s
   fixed 1 s timeout per hop      answered 214/300   work finished AFTER the user gave up:  86 requests, 89,157 ms   abandoned early: 0
   propagated deadline            answered 215/300   work finished AFTER the user gave up:   0 requests,      0 ms   abandoned early: 86
C. edge → layer-1 → layer-2 → leaf, leaf is down
   3 attempts at the edge AND at each of 2 layers leaf received 2,700 calls for 100 user requests (27x)
   3 attempts at the edge only                  leaf received   300 calls for 100 user requests (3x)
  • A. With no timeout, /cart, which never calls pricing, succeeded 20 times out of 500: every worker thread was stuck waiting on pricing. A 300 ms timeout with a cached-price fallback kept both endpoints at 500/500, with /cart p99 at 6 ms.
  • B. Fixed per-hop timeouts left promotion-service finishing 86 requests nobody was waiting for, 89 seconds of CPU and DB time. A propagated deadline made promotion abandon those 86 as soon as the deadline passed. The users got the same answers.
  • C. Three attempts at each of three layers turned 100 user requests into 2,700 calls on a failing leaf. Retrying at the edge only: 300.

What changed from L1 to L4

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Detection signal Blast radius Mitigation Missing timeout on a slow dependency Thread/connection pool saturation, rising in-flight count Unrelated endpoints on the same pool (L2 A: /cart 20/500) Timeouts from budgets, bulkheads per dependency, fallbacks Orphan work after callers give up Callee busy while callers time out; deadline-exceeded at the edge Wasted capacity during overload (L2 B: 89 s) Deadline propagation, cancel on deadline/disconnect Retry amplification Leaf QPS ≫ edge QPS during incidents Overloaded dependency can't recover (L2 C: 27x) One retry layer, budgets, breakers, jitter Double retries (app + mesh) Retries per request > 1 layer Same as above Decide an owner: mesh retries off or app retries off Silent schema breakage Default/empty values appearing, no errors Wrong data propagated (L3: empty total) buf breaking, reserved numbers, contract tests Connection churn High TLS handshake rate, port exhaustion Latency, CPU Pooling, keep-alive, HTTP/2 Mesh misconfiguration Sudden 503s/mTLS errors after a policy change Whole namespace Staged rollout of mesh config, istioctl analyze DNS caching of dead endpoints Errors to one IP after a scale-down 1/N of calls Platform VIPs, short JVM DNS TTL, outlier detection

docs.title: 6.2 Observability
docs.text:
• Per dependency, per caller: request rate, errors by type (timeout, 5xx, connection), latency histogram, in-flight concurrency, pool waits, fallbacks served. Name metrics by dependency so the dashboard answers "who is slowing me down?".
  • Deadline accounting: log or trace the remaining budget at each hop. A trace showing remaining=12ms at pricing tells you where the time went.
  • Retries: attempts per request, retry-budget usage, and retries by status code.
  • Mesh: golden signals per service pair, mTLS coverage (% of traffic encrypted), ejections by outlier detection.
  • Contracts: counts of unknown fields seen (protobuf) and deserialization errors (JSON). Both are early warnings of version skew.

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• mTLS between services with workload identities (mesh or library), plus authorization per caller and endpoint: pricing accepts calls from checkout and the BFFs, not from notification-service.
  • Propagate the end-user identity as a token (a JWT, or an exchanged token with narrowed scopes), never as a trusted X-User-Id header that any caller can set.
  • Deadline and retry headers are inputs too: cap them (a client can't ask for a 10-minute budget) and validate them.
  • Webhooks from external parties: verify signatures, check timestamps against replay, and use allowlists (Ch 23).

docs.title: 6.4 Performance & tuning knobs
docs.text: Knob Default here Effect Connect timeout 300 ms Fail fast on dead hosts Per-call timeout min(remaining − margin, dependency cap) Bounded waiting Deadline margin per hop 10–20 ms Time to answer your own caller Pool size per dependency Little's law × 1.5 Enough concurrency without flooding Concurrency limit (bulkhead) 2–3 × normal in-flight Protects the caller and the callee Retry attempts / budget 1 retry at the gateway / ≤ 10 % Transient fault tolerance without storms Protocol gRPC for hot internal paths Payload size (L3: 2.6x smaller), deadlines HTTP/2 multiplexing On for gRPC Fewer connections

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• Serialization is CPU. At tens of thousands of internal calls per second, JSON → protobuf is a measurable CPU and bandwidth saving (L3: 706 → 271 bytes per order).
  • Cross-AZ calls cost money per GB. Prefer zone-local routing for chatty paths (locality-aware load balancing in the mesh).
  • Sidecar meshes add CPU/memory per pod, which is significant at hundreds of pods. Ambient reduces it for L4-only needs.
  • Orphan work and retry storms are pure waste. Deadlines and single-layer retries directly reduce the capacity needed for peak events.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. No timeout (library defaults).

// ❌ before: waits as long as pricing takes; holds a thread and a connection the whole time (L2 A)
RestClient.create("http://pricing-service").get().uri("/prices/{sku}", sku).retrieve().body(Price.class);

// ✅ after: per-dependency client with connect + call timeouts derived from the remaining deadline, and a fallback
try { return pricingClient.get().uri("/prices/{sku}", sku).retrieve().body(Price.class); }
catch (ResourceAccessException timeout) { return Price.mrpOnly(catalogCache.mrp(sku)); }

2. Timeouts longer than the caller's deadline. Symptom: The callee keeps working after the user is gone (L2 B: 89 s of orphan work). Fix: Propagate deadlines, and set timeout = min(remaining − margin, cap).

3. Retries at every layer. Symptom: 27x load on the failing dependency (L2 C). Fix: One retry layer, retry budgets, and only idempotent operations.

4. Shared thread or connection pools across dependencies. Symptom: One slow dependency blocks unrelated features. Fix: Bulkheads: a pool and concurrency limit per dependency.

5. Synchronous call for something that's really an event. Symptom: order-service calls notification, invoice and loyalty in the checkout path. Fix: Publish order.order.placed.v1 and let them react (Ch 14).

6. Changing a protobuf field's type or reusing its number.

// ❌ before: same number, new type → readers silently see no value (L3)
string total_paise = 4;

// ✅ after: keep the old field, reserve it when retired, add a new number
reserved 4;
reserved "total_paise";
Money total = 8;

7. Trusting identity headers from callers. Symptom: Any service can impersonate any user with X-User-Id. Fix: Signed tokens and mTLS identity.

8. A mesh and the application both retrying and timing out differently. Symptom: Confusing behaviour, double retries, timeouts that never fire. Fix: Document which layer owns what (§2.9), and set the mesh timeout as an upper ceiling only.

9. Assuming virtual threads remove the need for limits. Symptom: Thousands of concurrent calls flood a dependency (L1). Fix: Semaphores and bulkheads per dependency.

10. Chatty fine-grained APIs. Symptom: 40 calls to render a cart. Fix: Coarse-grained endpoints (batch GetPrices(skus[])), composition at a BFF (Ch 16).

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ When do you call another service synchronously vs asynchronously?

30-second answer: Synchronously when the caller needs the answer to continue right now (a price, a stock check, a payment result). Asynchronously when the work can happen later or is a fact others react to (order placed → invoice, notification). Synchronous calls couple availability and latency, and asynchronous calls add eventual consistency.

Deep answer: Every synchronous dependency multiplies unavailability (Ch 16) and consumes caller resources while waiting (Little's law, L1). Use events for facts and queues for deferred jobs. Keep synchronous paths short, with timeouts and fallbacks.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Immediacy vs coupling.

Follow-ups: 1. Example of the wrong choice? → Checkout calling notification synchronously. 2. Can a user flow be async? → Yes: 202 Accepted + status updates.

Red flags: "Always use events" or "always use REST".

Q2 [B1] ⭐ Why must every remote call have a timeout?

30-second answer: Without one, a slow dependency holds the caller's threads and connections indefinitely. The caller then runs out of capacity and fails even for requests that don't need that dependency, which is a cascade.

Deep answer: L2 A: with pricing slowed to 5 s and no timeout, a /cart endpoint that never calls pricing succeeded only 20/500 times. With a 300 ms timeout and a fallback, 500/500. Set timeouts from budgets and the dependency's latency distribution.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Too short gives false failures, too long gives cascades.

Follow-ups: 1. Connect vs read timeout? → Setup time vs waiting for data. 2. What value? → Roughly the dependency's p99.9 + margin, capped by the remaining deadline.

Red flags: "The default is fine."

Q3 [B1] REST or gRPC?

30-second answer: REST/JSON for external and browser-facing APIs, and wherever simplicity, caching and tooling matter. gRPC/protobuf for internal high-volume calls, polyglot services and streaming, where typed contracts, compact payloads and built-in deadlines help.

Deep answer: L3 with the real protoc: the same order is 706 bytes as JSON vs 271 as protobuf. gRPC needs HTTP/2, a gateway or gRPC-Web for browsers, and binary-aware tooling.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Performance and contracts vs universality and debuggability.

Follow-ups: 1. Can you expose gRPC externally? → Via a transcoding gateway (JSON ↔ gRPC). 2. What about GraphQL? → A client-driven query layer, often in BFFs.

Red flags: "gRPC is always faster, so use it everywhere."

Q4 [B1] What is a service mesh?

30-second answer: An infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication (mTLS, load balancing, retries/timeouts, traffic shifting, telemetry) via proxies (sidecars or node-level/ambient), configured centrally instead of in each service's code.

Deep answer: It gives uniform security and telemetry and safe canaries. It costs a control plane to operate, proxy latency and resources, and configuration complexity. Business logic (fallbacks, deadlines) stays in the app.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Consistency vs operational overhead.

Follow-ups: 1. Examples? → Istio, Linkerd, Cilium service mesh. 2. Do you need one? → Not with a few services. It becomes valuable with many teams and a zero-trust requirement.

Red flags: "The mesh makes services resilient automatically."

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do you choose timeout values?

30-second answer: Start from the user-facing budget and split it across the call graph. Parallel calls share a slice, and sequential calls add up. Each call's timeout is min(remaining deadline − margin, dependency cap), where the cap is about the dependency's p99.9 plus headroom. Review with real latency histograms.

Deep answer: Checkout's 1.2 s: parallel pricing/inventory/cart at 300 ms, payment 600 ms, order 200 ms. Include pool-acquire time. Timeouts longer than the caller's deadline are useless (L2 B), and timeouts below the normal p99 create errors.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Completeness vs responsiveness.

Follow-ups: 1. Adaptive timeouts? → Some systems adjust from observed latency; keep hard caps. 2. What happens after a timeout? → Fallback, error, or a retry within the budget.

Red flags: "30 seconds everywhere."

Q6 [B2] ⭐ What is deadline propagation?

30-second answer: Passing the remaining time budget along with each request, so every hop limits its own work and downstream timeouts to what's left, and refuses to start work that can't finish. gRPC carries it in grpc-timeout. For HTTP, use a remaining-milliseconds header.

Deep answer: L2 B: with fixed per-hop timeouts, promotion-service did 89 s of work for 86 requests whose users had already given up. With a propagated deadline, it abandoned them and wasted nothing. Prefer relative budgets to avoid clock skew (Ch 12). Apply them to DB statement timeouts too.

Trade-offs I'd call out: A little plumbing vs wasted capacity during overload.

Follow-ups: 1. Absolute or relative? → Relative per hop; absolute only with well-synced clocks. 2. Does it help the user? → Mostly the system: freed capacity during incidents.

Red flags: Never having heard of cancellation downstream.

Q7 [B2] Which protobuf changes are safe?

30-second answer: Adding fields with new numbers, renaming fields (names aren't on the wire), and removing fields if their numbers and names are reserved. Unsafe: changing a field's type or number, reusing numbers, and changing semantics.

Deep answer: L3: an old reader decoding v2 kept the new field as unknown (7) and ignored the rename. A new reader decoding v1 saw the new field absent. Changing int64 to string under number 4 produced no error and an empty value, which is silent data loss. Enforce with buf breaking.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Flexibility vs contract discipline.

Follow-ups: 1. What about enums? → Add values; handle unknown values in code (proto3 keeps them as unrecognized numbers). 2. JSON equivalents? → Additive changes + tolerant readers.

Red flags: "Protobuf is backward compatible, so any change is fine."

Q8 [B2] How should Spring services call other services?

30-second answer: Use RestClient (or HTTP interfaces on top of it) for synchronous REST, with a client per dependency that has its own connection pool, connect and response timeouts, a deadline-propagating interceptor, a concurrency limit, and metrics. Use generated gRPC stubs with withDeadlineAfter for gRPC. Avoid raw clients with default settings.

Deep answer: HTTP interfaces (@HttpExchange) give typed, declarative clients. With virtual threads, blocking clients are efficient, but you still need limits (L1). Put all of this in the platform template so every service gets it by default.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Standardization vs flexibility.

Follow-ups: 1. WebClient? → For reactive stacks or streaming. 2. Feign? → Fine in existing code; HTTP interfaces for new code.

Red flags: new RestTemplate() per request.

Q9 [B2] Why can retries make an outage worse?

30-second answer: Retries add load exactly when the dependency is struggling, and when several layers each retry, the load multiplies (3 attempts × 3 layers = 27x). The dependency can't recover, and latency grows for everyone.

Deep answer: L2 C measured 2,700 leaf calls for 100 user requests with retries at every layer, vs 300 with retries at the edge only. Use one retry layer, budgets (retries ≤ x % of traffic), backoff with jitter, circuit breakers, Retry-After, and only idempotent operations.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Masking transient faults vs amplifying overload.

Follow-ups: 1. Which layer should retry? → The closest to the user (edge/BFF) or the mesh, not both. 2. What's a retry budget? → A cap on the ratio of retries to requests.

Red flags: "Retry 3 times everywhere."

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ Design the calling conventions for a 26-service platform.

30-second answer: Rules for sync vs async. REST at the edge, gRPC internally for hot paths. A platform client library that propagates deadlines, applies per-dependency timeouts, bulkheads and metrics, and declares fallbacks. Retries at one layer with budgets. Contract checks in CI. mTLS via the mesh.

Deep answer: The evidence behind each rule: L2 A (timeouts/bulkheads), L2 B (deadlines), L2 C (retry placement), L3 (contracts). Enforce with lint rules (no raw clients), fitness functions (Ch 16), and dashboards per dependency. Document which layer owns retries, timeouts and mTLS.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Library consistency vs service autonomy.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you roll out the library? → In the template plus automated upgrades. 2. Exceptions? → Streaming and external APIs, with documented deviations.

Red flags: Leaving each team to choose.

Q11 [B3] How do you prevent a slow optional dependency from hurting critical flows?

30-second answer: Give it a short timeout within a budget, a fallback (cached or default value plus a flag to the UI), its own pool and concurrency limit (bulkhead), and a circuit breaker to stop calling it while it's failing. Ideally, make it asynchronous or precomputed.

Deep answer: §1.1's promotions: a 150 ms budget, fallback to "no coupon" with a banner, and a breaker that opens on sustained timeouts. L2 A showed pool isolation keeping /cart at 500/500. Also consider precomputing promotions into pricing via events.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Feature completeness vs availability.

Follow-ups: 1. Who decides it's optional? → Product, per field. 2. How do you know fallbacks are working? → A metric of fallbacks served.

Red flags: Treating every dependency as required.

Q12 [B3] How do you evolve an internal API without coordinated deploys?

30-second answer: Make only backward- and forward-compatible changes (additive fields, tolerant readers, no type or number changes), deploy the server first when adding capabilities, and keep old fields until all clients have migrated. Breaking changes get a new version served in parallel. Enforce with CI checks and consumer-driven contract tests.

Deep answer: L3 showed both safe changes (rename, add) and a silent break (type change). Track client versions via telemetry (user agent or metadata) before removing anything. Use expand/contract for semantics changes (Ch 28).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Temporary duplication vs coordination cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Who owns the proto repo? → Service owners, with platform-provided linting. 2. How long do you keep old versions? → Until telemetry shows zero use, plus a grace period.

Red flags: "We deploy all services together to change APIs."

Q13 [B3] What does a service mesh give you, and what should stay in the app?

30-second answer: The mesh gives mTLS and workload identity, uniform telemetry, load balancing with outlier detection, and traffic shifting (canary/mirroring), plus optionally retries and timeouts. The app keeps deadlines (it knows the business budget), fallbacks, idempotency and business-level retries. Pick one owner per concern.

Deep answer: Double retries (mesh + app) recreate L2 C's amplification, and mesh timeouts longer than app deadlines are useless. Configure the mesh as the security and telemetry layer plus an outer ceiling. Ambient mode reduces per-pod cost when only L4 features are needed.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Central control vs app knowledge.

Follow-ups: 1. Sidecar or ambient? → Ambient for mTLS at lower cost; sidecars or waypoints where rich L7 is needed. 2. Linkerd vs Istio? → Linkerd is simpler and lighter; Istio is richer and heavier.

Red flags: Turning on mesh retries without checking app retries.

Q14 [B3] Virtual threads: what do they change for service-to-service calls?

30-second answer: Blocking calls become cheap. Waiting doesn't consume a platform thread, so simple synchronous code scales to many concurrent calls (L1: 4,000 waiting calls in 0.55 s vs 10.1 s on 200 platform threads). They don't make dependencies faster or bigger, so you still need timeouts, concurrency limits and deadlines.

Deep answer: Watch pinning (synchronized blocks holding carrier threads, largely addressed in JDK 24+), ThreadLocal-heavy libraries, and connection pools becoming the new bottleneck. Structured concurrency helps with parallel calls and cancellation.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Simpler code vs the risk of flooding dependencies.

Follow-ups: 1. Do you still need reactive? → Mostly for streaming/backpressure-heavy workloads. 2. How do you bound concurrency? → A semaphore per dependency.

Red flags: "Virtual threads mean no more capacity planning."

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ A dependency's latency spiked and your whole platform went down. Postmortem and fixes?

30-second answer: The chain: no timeouts → pool exhaustion in callers → unrelated endpoints failing → retries at every layer amplifying load on the slow dependency → orphan work continuing after users left. Fixes: timeouts from budgets, bulkheads, deadline propagation, single-layer retries with budgets, circuit breakers, fallbacks for optional features, and dashboards per dependency.

Deep answer: L2 reproduces each link: 20/500 → 500/500 with timeouts, 89 s orphan work → 0 with deadlines, 27x → 3x with retry placement. Action items get owners, and the platform client makes the fixes the default. Game days inject latency to verify.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Engineering time vs repeated outages.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you verify fixes? → Latency injection in staging and controlled production game days. 2. What's the first thing to add? → Timeouts and bulkheads on the dependency that failed.

Red flags: "Scale up the slow service" as the only action.

Q16 [B4] Should the grocery platform adopt a service mesh?

30-second answer: Yes, for mTLS and telemetry across 26 services owned by 8 teams, in ambient or lightweight mode first. Keep retries and deadlines in the app/gateway, and add L7 features (canaries, mirroring) per namespace when needed. Measure latency and resource overhead before and after.

Deep answer: The alternative is library-based mTLS and telemetry in the service template, which is fine for a single-stack (Java) platform, but certificate rotation and policy enforcement are harder. Decide with requirements: zero-trust compliance, polyglot services, traffic-shifting needs, and ops capacity.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Platform complexity vs uniform security.

Follow-ups: 1. Rollout plan? → Permissive mTLS → strict per namespace, telemetry first, then L7 policies. 2. Exit plan? → Keep app-level timeouts and deadlines regardless.

Red flags: Adopting a mesh to fix resilience problems caused by missing timeouts.

Q17 [B4] How do you set end-to-end latency SLOs across service calls?

30-second answer: Define the SLO at the user journey (checkout p99 ≤ 1.5 s), decompose it into a budget per hop (parallel slices, sequential sums, margins), set dependency SLOs and timeouts from those budgets, and monitor with traces that show where each request's time went. Revisit the budgets when the graph changes.

Deep answer: Fan-out makes tails worse (Ch 16 L1), so budget optional calls separately. Use deadline propagation so budgets are enforced at runtime, not just in documents. Error budgets per journey drive priorities.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Tight budgets vs feature richness.

Follow-ups: 1. What if one team can't meet its budget? → Cache, precompute, make it optional, or renegotiate. 2. How do you detect budget drift? → A per-hop latency share from tracing.

Red flags: Per-service SLOs with no journey view.

Q18 [B4] When would you use async request-reply instead of a synchronous call?

30-second answer: When the operation takes long or has unpredictable latency (PDF invoices, bulk price updates, KYC checks), when the callee has limited capacity and should pull work at its own pace, or when the caller shouldn't hold resources while waiting. Respond with 202 Accepted + a status resource (or a correlation id and a reply topic), and notify on completion.

Deep answer: You need correlation ids, idempotency, timeouts on the whole operation, and a place to show progress. It converts latency into eventual completion and naturally applies backpressure (Ch 14).

Trade-offs I'd call out: UX complexity vs resilience.

Follow-ups: 1. Polling or push? → Push (webhook/WebSocket) when available, polling as a fallback. 2. How do you cancel? → A cancel command keyed by the correlation id.

Red flags: Synchronous 60-second calls.

Q19 [B4] How do you handle calls to external providers (Razorpay, SMS vendors)?

30-second answer: Isolate them behind an adapter service with its own timeouts, bulkheads and circuit breakers. Use idempotency keys and treat timeouts as unknown outcomes (Ch 13). Run async queues for non-interactive sends, reconcile with the provider's reports, verify webhook signatures, and keep multiple vendors with failover where possible (SMS).

Deep answer: Provider SLAs and rate limits shape timeouts and concurrency. Honour 429/Retry-After. Track per-vendor success rates and latency. Watch data residency and PII for payment data (Ch 36).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Vendor redundancy vs complexity and cost.

Follow-ups: 1. SMS vendor down? → Fail over to a second vendor. Dedup by message id. 2. Webhook arrives before the API response? → Handle both orders idempotently.

Red flags: Retrying payment captures without keys.

Q20 [B4] How do you make good calling behaviour the default for every team?

30-second answer: Build it into the golden path: a platform client library (timeouts, deadlines, bulkheads, metrics, fallback API), service templates that wire it in, lint and fitness checks that forbid raw clients and missing timeouts, contract checks in CI, mesh policies for mTLS and outlier detection, and dashboards per dependency that come for free.

Deep answer: Measure adoption (the % of calls through the platform client), run game days with latency injection, and make the easy path the safe path. Share incident learnings (like §1.1) as reasons, not rules.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Platform investment vs repeated incidents.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you handle exceptions? → ADRs with explicit compensating controls. 2. What gets checked in CI? → No new RestTemplate() or raw HttpClient without timeouts, and proto/OpenAPI breaking changes.

Red flags: Relying on a wiki page.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Sync when an answer is needed now, async for facts and deferrable work. Every sync dependency costs availability and capacity.
  2. Little's law: in-flight requests = rate × latency. Slow dependencies consume caller resources (L1: 10.1 s vs 0.55 s).
  3. Every call gets a timeout from the budget, and optional data gets a fallback (L2 A: 20/500 → 500/500).
  4. Propagate deadlines, and don't start work that can't finish (L2 B: 89 s of orphan work → 0).
  5. Retry at one layer, with budgets, for idempotent operations only (L2 C: 27x → 3x).
  6. Bulkheads: a pool and a concurrency limit per dependency, virtual threads or not.
  7. REST at the edge, gRPC for hot internal paths (L3: 706 → 271 bytes, built-in deadlines).
  8. Schema evolution: add and rename are safe; type or number changes break silently (L3). Check in CI.
  9. A mesh owns mTLS, telemetry and outlier detection. The app owns deadlines, fallbacks and idempotency. One retry owner.
  10. Make it the default via a platform client library and a template.

docs.text: Situation Choose Need an answer now Sync call with timeout from budget Fact for others Event (Ch 14) Long-running work Async request-reply / 202 + status Hot internal path, many calls gRPC with deadlines External/browser API REST/JSON (+ OpenAPI) Optional data Short budget + fallback + breaker Transient errors One retry layer with jitter and budget mTLS for all traffic Mesh (ambient/sidecar) or library

docs.title: 18. Resilience Patterns ⭐
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B2 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 16, Ch 17 · What you will build: The resilience toolkit of every grocery-platform service, with numbers for why each piece exists.

  • L1 simulates 1,000 clients retrying after a failure against a server that pays to reject. Immediate, fixed and plain exponential retries never recover (congestion collapse). Exponential backoff with jitter recovers in 290–540 ms.
  • L2 runs a circuit breaker against a real HTTP dependency that fails slowly for 6 s: 296 → 55 calls reach the broken service, and caller p50 goes from 802 ms to 0 ms, at the price of a slower recovery. It also covers a bug found while building the breaker.
  • L3 compares five rate-limiting algorithms on the same bursty traffic. A fixed window lets 175 requests through in one second against a limit of 100. It also covers a leaky-bucket shaper, and a shared token bucket in real Redis (Lua) vs per-pod limiters (133 vs 240 req/s against a 100 req/s limit).
  • L4 offers a real HTTP service twice its capacity. An unbounded queue collapses goodput to 4 req/s, and bounded-queue or deadline-aware shedding keeps 390–400 req/s.

Resilience4j configuration for Spring Boot is included (VERIFY: the library couldn't be downloaded here, so the patterns are implemented and measured directly). · Reading time: 110 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: the outage that lasted longer than its cause
docs.text:
At 7:02 pm on a Saturday, inventory-service's database failed over (Ch 10). The failover took 25 seconds. The checkout outage that followed lasted 41 minutes.

  • Every checkout pod retried inventory calls immediately, three times, at every layer. When the new primary came up, it received roughly 30 times its normal load in the first second, and its connection pool saturated. Many requests now timed out, and those timeouts triggered more retries. The database was up, but the system couldn't get back to working.
  • Inventory's request queue was unbounded. Requests waited 8–20 seconds in the queue, long after the app (3 s budget) had given up. Inventory spent almost all its capacity finishing work nobody was waiting for, so goodput stayed near zero while CPU showed 100 %.
  • No circuit breaker: every checkout thread kept calling inventory and waiting for the timeout, so checkout itself ran out of threads (Ch 17).
  • No fallback: browsing the catalog also called inventory (to show "only 3 left"), so browsing failed too, although it didn't need live stock.
  • The fix that worked, at 7:43 pm: someone scaled checkout down to zero for two minutes. The load vanished, inventory drained its queue, and everything recovered. The system was metastable: the trigger was over, but the overload sustained itself.

This chapter's patterns are exactly what was missing:

  • Retries with exponential backoff and jitter, at one layer, with a budget.
  • Load shedding: bounded queues, deadline-aware dropping and fast 503s, so capacity goes to requests that can still succeed.
  • Circuit breakers, so callers stop hammering a failing dependency and fail fast.
  • Bulkheads, so one dependency can't consume every thread.
  • Fallbacks and graceful degradation: show "in stock" from cache instead of failing the catalog page.
  • Rate limits to protect shared dependencies from any single caller.

The thesis of this chapter

Failures are normal. Outages are what happens when the system's reaction to a failure makes it worse: retries, queues and waiting amplify a small problem into a self-sustaining one. Resilience patterns cap that amplification. Bound every wait, every queue, every retry and every caller's share, and decide in advance what the user sees when a dependency is gone.

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text: Band After this chapter you can… B2 Configure timeouts, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and fallbacks, and explain why retries can cause outages B3 Implement and tune circuit breakers, bulkheads and rate limiters (token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window), and configure Resilience4j B4 Design load shedding and admission control, prevent metastable failures, plan graceful degradation, and run resilience game days

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: a dark store on sale day B2
docs.text:
• Timeouts: a picker who can't find an item in 2 minutes moves on instead of blocking the order forever.
  • Retries with jitter: when the billing system reboots, 20 riders shouldn't all tap "retry" at the same second. Each waits a random few seconds, so the counter isn't mobbed.
  • Circuit breaker: after the third time the freezer door jams, the supervisor puts a sign on it, "freezer out, use the backup". Nobody walks over to try again every minute. After 10 minutes someone checks it once.
  • Bulkhead: 2 of the 8 pickers handle only frozen goods, so a freezer problem can't pull all 8 pickers into it.
  • Rate limiting: each B2B customer can place at most 50 orders a minute, so one bulk buyer can't starve everyone else.
  • Load shedding: when the queue at the packing station is longer than packers can clear before the 10-minute delivery promise expires, the store stops accepting new slots rather than accepting orders it will deliver late.
  • Graceful degradation: if the scale for weighing produce breaks, sell produce by the piece rather than stopping produce sales.

docs.title: 2.2 The amplification problem ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
A dependency fails or slows, and then the system's reactions multiply the load:

  • Retries: every failed call becomes 2–3 calls. At every layer, that's 27x (Ch 17 L2 C).
  • Queues: requests pile up and wait longer than callers do, so the server works on requests nobody wants (L4).
  • Waiting callers: threads and connections are held (Little's law, Ch 17 L1), and callers fail too.
  • Rejection isn't free: accepting, parsing and rejecting still costs capacity. An overloaded server can end up serving fewer requests than its capacity.

When those loops keep the system overloaded after the trigger has gone, it's a metastable failure (Bronson et al., 2021). L1 models it: once the server spends capacity rejecting retries, synchronized retry schedules never get all 1,000 clients served in 100 simulated seconds.

docs.title: 2.3 Timeouts (recap) B2
docs.text: Ch 17 covers timeouts in depth: from budgets, with deadlines propagated. In resilience terms, a timeout is what turns a slow failure into a fast failure that the other patterns (fallback, breaker) can act on. Without timeouts, none of the rest works.

docs.title: 2.4 Retries with exponential backoff and jitter ⭐ B2
docs.text:
When to retry: transient failures (connection reset, a 503 from one instance, a lock timeout), idempotent operations (or with idempotency keys, Ch 20), and while the deadline still allows it.

How:

  • Exponential backoff: wait base × 2^attempt, capped.
  • Jitter spreads retries out in time, so clients that failed together don't retry together:
    • Full jitter: wait random(0, backoff).
    • Equal jitter: wait backoff/2 + random(0, backoff/2).
  • Bounded attempts (2–3) and a retry budget (e.g. retries ≤ 10 % of requests per client). Beyond that, fail.
  • Honour Retry-After / 429. Don't retry non-retryable errors (400, 401, 404, validation).

L1 simulated 1,000 clients failing together against a server that spends 0.25 of a slot to reject a call:

Retry schedule All served after Total calls Immediate retry Never (100 s) 10,000,000 Fixed 100 ms Never 1,000,000 Exponential, no jitter Never 56,000 Exponential + full jitter 540 ms 4,327 Exponential + equal jitter 290 ms 4,059

Plain exponential backoff still fails here: the clients back off together and arrive together again, every time above the server's capacity. Jitter is what breaks the synchronization. And retries at one layer only (Ch 17): the gateway or the first caller, not every hop.

docs.title: 2.5 Circuit breaker ⭐ B3
docs.text:
A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and tracks their outcomes:

  • CLOSED: calls flow. Outcomes are recorded in a sliding window (count-based: the last N calls; time-based: the last N seconds).
  • OPEN: when the failure rate (or slow-call rate) exceeds a threshold, after a minimum number of calls, calls fail fast without touching the dependency, and the fallback runs.
  • HALF_OPEN: after a wait, a few probe calls are allowed. If they succeed the breaker closes, and if not it reopens.

L2 ran against a real HTTP pricing service that failed slowly (800 ms, then 500) from 2 s to 8 s, with callers at 50 req/s:

Calls reaching the failing service Caller p50 during the outage First live price after recovery at 8.0 s Timeout + fallback, no breaker 296 802 ms 8.0 s Breaker (window 20, ≥ 50 % failures, open 2 s, 3 probes) 55 0 ms (fail fast) 10.7 s

What this shows:

  • The breaker protects the dependency (5x fewer calls while it's down, which helps it recover) and the caller (no threads waiting 800 ms).
  • The cost is recovery latency: the probe at 7.8 s hit the last moments of the outage and reopened the breaker for another 2 s. Tune waitDurationInOpenState against how fast the dependency typically recovers, and consider exponential open durations with a cap.
  • Record slow calls as failures too (slowCallDurationThreshold). A dependency that answers in 5 s is failing from the caller's point of view.
  • Scope breakers correctly: per dependency and, where it matters, per endpoint or instance. One breaker for "Razorpay" would open for UPI when only cards are failing.

A bug worth knowing: the first version of L2's breaker recorded the results of calls that were still in flight when it opened. Each late failure reopened the breaker and reset its timer, so it logged 40 "OPEN" transitions and stayed open far longer than configured. Late results from calls admitted before a state change must not drive the state machine. Resilience4j handles this, but hand-rolled breakers often don't.

docs.title: 2.6 Bulkheads ⭐ B3
docs.text:
A bulkhead limits the resources one dependency or workload can use, so failures stay in their compartment:

  • Semaphore bulkhead: at most N concurrent calls to a dependency. Callers beyond N fail fast (or wait briefly). With virtual threads this is the natural form (Ch 17 L1).
  • Thread-pool bulkhead: a dedicated pool per dependency, which isolates blocking calls in platform-thread stacks.
  • Connection-pool per dependency: Ch 17's /cart failure (20/500) came from shared threads, and a per-dependency pool plus limit isolates it.
  • At the infrastructure level: separate deployments or node pools for critical vs batch workloads, and separate database pools for OLTP vs reports. Cells (Ch 34) are bulkheads at the architecture level.

Size bulkheads with Little's law (normal rate × p99 latency × 1.5–2). Too small rejects normal traffic, and too large doesn't protect anything.

docs.title: 2.7 Rate limiting ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Rate limiting caps how much a client or caller may send, protecting shared capacity and enforcing fairness or quotas. L3 compares algorithms on the same traffic (~83 req/s steady plus a 150-request burst straddling a window edge, limit 100 req/s):

Algorithm Allowed Max allowed in any 1 s span Notes Fixed window 283 175 Burst at a window edge gets ~2x the limit Sliding window log 266 100 Exact; memory per request Sliding window counter 266 100 Weighted estimate of two windows; O(1) memory Token bucket (100/s, burst 100) 349 183 Allows bursts up to the bucket size by design Token bucket (100/s, burst 20) 269 103 Small burst ≈ smooth rate Leaky bucket (queue) 300 accepted, 100 rejected Output exactly 100/s Shapes: adds up to 499 ms delay instead of rejecting

Choosing:

  • Token bucket is the usual choice for APIs: average rate + allowed burst, and cheap.
  • Sliding window counter for strict "N per window" quotas.
  • Leaky bucket when the downstream needs a smooth rate (SMS vendor limits) and waiting is acceptable (async jobs).
  • Avoid fixed windows for protection (the boundary burst).

Distributed limits:

  • A limit on a shared dependency must be global. L3 C ran 4 pods, each offered 60 req/s against a 100 req/s total limit:
    • Per-pod limiters let 240 req/s through. Each pod is under its own 100 req/s.
    • A shared token bucket in Redis (one atomic Lua script) held the total to 133 req/s over 3 s (the initial 100-token burst + 100/s), split evenly across the pods.
  • Options: a central store (Redis + Lua, Ch 09/39), approximate local limits = global/N with periodic rebalancing, or the gateway doing it. Decide what happens when the limiter store is down: fail open for protection limits, fail closed for paid quotas.
  • Respond with 429 Too Many Requests + Retry-After, and include the limit headers (RateLimit-*). Clients must back off (§2.4).

docs.title: 2.8 Load shedding and admission control ⭐ B3 B4
docs.text:
When offered load exceeds capacity, something must be rejected. The question is whether it's rejected early and cheaply, or served late and uselessly. L4 offered a real HTTP service (capacity ~400 req/s) 800 req/s for 8 s, with clients timing out at 500 ms:

Server policy Goodput Shed (503) Timed out p99 of successes Work done for clients that had left Unbounded queue 4 req/s 0 6,369 500 ms 3,409 requests Bounded queue (40) + fast 503 390 req/s 3,278 0 141 ms 0 Drop if waited > 250 ms 400 req/s 3,203 0 275 ms 0

What the numbers mean:

  • The unbounded queue collapses. Every request waits longer than the client, so the server spends all its capacity on responses nobody reads, and goodput drops to ~1 % of capacity. That's §1.1's inventory service.
  • Bounding the queue, or dropping requests that already waited too long, keeps goodput at capacity. The rejected clients get a fast, honest 503 they can retry later with backoff, instead of a slow timeout.

Techniques:

  • Bounded queues and concurrency limits: reject when full.
  • Deadline-aware dropping: skip requests whose caller's deadline has passed or is about to (Ch 17 deadlines). CoDel-style: drop when queueing delay stays above a target.
  • LIFO under overload: serve the newest requests (their clients are still waiting). Used by some RPC stacks.
  • Adaptive concurrency limits (TCP-like AIMD, Netflix concurrency-limits, Envoy adaptive concurrency): lower the limit when latency rises.
  • Priority shedding: shed analytics and prefetch before checkout. Tag requests with a criticality class (Google's "criticality").
  • Shed at the edge, where it's cheapest: the gateway rate limits and rejects before work enters the system.

docs.title: 2.9 Fallbacks and graceful degradation ⭐ B2 B3
docs.text:
A fallback is what you do instead. Its quality ranges from good to bad:

Fallback Example Risk Cached/stale data Last known stock badge, price cache with TTL Staleness: show "as of" where it matters Default/simplified behaviour Price without coupon; generic recommendations Business impact must be accepted Alternative provider Second SMS vendor; another payment method Cost, consistency Queue for later Accept the order, confirm by SMS when payment settles UX and state complexity Fail fast with a clear message "Payments are slow right now, try UPI" Honest, often the best for money ❌ Silently wrong data Default price 0, or "in stock" for checkout Never for correctness-critical paths

Graceful degradation plan:

  • Each feature is classified as critical (checkout, payment, order status) or degradable (recommendations, reviews, ETA precision, coupons).
  • Kill switches / feature flags turn degradable features off under load (brownout), and it's tested regularly.
  • Rule: fallbacks must never be riskier than failures. A fallback path used once a year is untested code, so exercise fallbacks in game days.

docs.title: 2.10 Putting the patterns together (and in what order) ⭐ B3
docs.text:
The order of wrapping matters. Resilience4j's default aspect order is:

Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( RateLimiter ( TimeLimiter ( Bulkhead ( call ) ) ) ) )

  • The bulkhead is innermost: it limits the concurrency of actual calls.
  • The time limiter bounds each attempt.
  • The circuit breaker sees each attempt's outcome (including timeouts) and fails fast when open.
  • Retry is outermost: it retries attempts, and when the breaker is open, the retry gets CallNotPermittedException immediately. Configure it not to retry that exception, or you're retrying against an open breaker.
  • The fallback is applied at the outermost level, after retries are exhausted.

docs.title: 2.11 Testing resilience: chaos and game days B4
docs.text:
• Fault injection: latency, errors, dropped connections (mesh fault injection, Toxiproxy, Chaos Mesh, AWS FIS), process kills, and DB failovers (Ch 10 lab).
  • Hypothesis-driven experiments: "if inventory adds 2 s latency, checkout success stays ≥ 99 % and catalog pages show cached badges". Measure against SLOs, and keep the blast radius small with a quick abort.
  • Game days with the on-call team, including the runbooks (§1.1's "scale checkout to zero" should be a documented, tested lever, not a lucky guess).
  • Load tests beyond capacity verify shedding. Many systems are only tested up to their capacity, never past it.

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Platform Resilience Standard
docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers SRE + platform team / all service owners Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-073 Retry policy (one layer, jitter, budget); ADR-074 Breakers and bulkheads per dependency; ADR-075 Load shedding at every service ingress; ADR-076 Rate limits (gateway + shared-dependency limits in Redis); ADR-077 Degradation catalogue and brownout flags

1. Context & Problem. A 25-second database failover became a 41-minute outage through retry storms, unbounded queues, missing breakers and no fallbacks (§1.1).

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: recovery within 60 s of a dependency recovering; goodput ≥ 90 % of capacity under 2x overload; degradable features degrade instead of failing critical flows; no single client can exceed its share of a shared dependency.
  • Non-goals: eliminating dependency failures (Ch 27 covers redundancy); exactly-once semantics (Ch 13).

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement NFR-1 Retries: max 1 at the gateway (idempotent), clients use exponential backoff with full jitter, retry budget ≤ 10 % NFR-2 Every outbound dependency has a timeout, a breaker (failure + slow-call thresholds) and a bulkhead NFR-3 Every service ingress has bounded concurrency/queues and drops requests past their deadline NFR-4 Under 2x offered load in a load test, goodput ≥ 90 % of capacity and p99 of successes ≤ 2x normal NFR-5 Each feature is classified critical/degradable, and degradable features have a tested fallback and a brownout flag NFR-6 Shared dependencies with limits (vendor APIs, legacy ERP) are protected by a global limiter

4. Capacity & latency estimates.

Item Calculation Result Inventory reserve capacity 12 pods × ~40 req/s ~480 req/s Sale-day peak 420 req/s + retries Retries must stay ≤ 10 % → ≤ 462 req/s Bulkhead (checkout → inventory) 420 req/s × p99 80 ms × 1.8 ~60 concurrent Queue bound at inventory ingress Capacity × acceptable wait (100 ms) ~48 requests Breaker window 50 req/s per pod → 20-call window ≈ 0.4 s of traffic Reacts within ~1 s

5. Proposed design.

  1. Resilience4j in the service template with per-dependency instances configured from application.yml: timeouts from the deadline (Ch 17), breakers (count window 20–50, failure rate 50 %, slow-call 1 s/50 %, open 5 s with a cap, 3 probes), semaphore bulkheads, and no retries except where explicitly allowed.
  2. Ingress shedding: Tomcat/Jetty thread and queue limits aligned with the service's concurrency, a filter that drops requests whose deadline has passed or that waited > 250 ms, and 503 + Retry-After responses.
  3. Gateway: token-bucket rate limits per API key and per customer (Redis), priority classes (checkout > browse > prefetch), and a single retry for idempotent GETs with jitter.
  4. Shared-dependency limiters: a Redis Lua token bucket per vendor (SMS, Razorpay settlement APIs, ERP).
  5. Degradation catalogue: every degradable feature has an owner, a fallback, a flag and a quarterly game-day test.

7. Alternatives considered.

Option Pros Cons Verdict Resilience4j in apps Fine-grained, business-aware fallbacks Per-service config to maintain Chosen (template defaults) Mesh-only resilience No code No fallbacks; double retries with app code Mesh for outlier detection + mTLS only (Ch 17) Hystrix Familiar In maintenance mode Rejected Adaptive concurrency limits Self-tuning Harder to reason about Phase 2 for the busiest services

8. Failure modes. A breaker opens on a healthy dependency (bad thresholds): alert on breaker state and tune with data. Fallback bugs: covered by game days. The limiter store (Redis) is down: fail open for protection limits and log. Shedding too aggressively: alert on the 503 rate vs capacity, and tune the queue bounds.

10. Observability. Per dependency: calls, failures, slow calls, breaker state and transitions, bulkhead saturation, fallbacks served. Per service: queue depth, requests shed (by reason), goodput vs capacity, retries and the retry budget. Brownout flags in use. Game-day outcomes.

14. Decision (ADR-073–077 summary). Retries at one layer with jitter and budgets. Breakers, bulkheads and deadline-bounded timeouts per dependency. Bounded, deadline-aware queues at every ingress. Global limiters for shared dependencies. A tested degradation catalogue with brownout flags. Resilience4j via the service template.
