                    if (aApplied == 0) { long v = claim(a, 7); retried = fencedWrite(a, v + 1, 7, "fence = ?") == 1; }   // A retries with a new lease
                }
                System.out.printf("scripted pause, fencing token %-17s: A's stale write %s, B's write %s%s → value %d after 2 increments%n",
                        claimAtRead ? "claimed at read" : "checked on write", aApplied == 1 ? "accepted" : "rejected",
                        bApplied == 1 ? "accepted" : "rejected", retried ? ", A retried with token 7" : "", read(a));
            }
        }

        // A lock without a TTL and a holder that crashes
        try (Redis a = new Redis(); Redis b = new Redis()) {
            a.cmd("DEL", "lock:settlement");
            a.cmd("SET", "lock:settlement", "worker-a", "NX");                       // no TTL
            a.close();                                                                 // worker-a crashes while holding it
            long t0 = System.nanoTime(); boolean got = false;
            while (System.nanoTime() - t0 < 3_000_000_000L) { if (b.cmd("SET", "lock:settlement", "worker-b", "NX") != null) { got = true; break; } Thread.sleep(10); }
            System.out.printf("SET NX without TTL, holder crashed: worker-b acquired within 3 s: %s; key TTL: %s (held forever)%n", got, b.cmd("PTTL", "lock:settlement"));
        }
    }
}
java -Duser.timezone=UTC -cp pgjdbc.jar LocksL4.java
8 workers × 150 increments (expected 1,200); lock TTL 100 ms; 3 % of critical sections pause 150 ms
   scheme                                   final   lost 2 holders  foreign  rejected     time
                                            value          at once  unlocks & retried         
   no lock                                    152  1,048         0        0         0 1,540 ms
   Redis TTL lock, DEL release                510    690      1172      307         0 2,749 ms
   Redis TTL lock, owner-checked release      776    424       851        0         0 4,429 ms
   + fencing token checked on write         1,200      0       833        0        36 5,200 ms
   + fencing token claimed at read          1,200      0       857        0        42 6,386 ms
   PostgreSQL advisory xact lock            1,200      0         0        0         0 7,223 ms
   no lock, optimistic CAS + retry          1,200      0         0        0       769 1,804 ms
scripted pause, fencing token checked on write : A's stale write accepted, B's write accepted → value 1 after 2 increments
scripted pause, fencing token claimed at read  : A's stale write rejected, B's write accepted, A retried with token 7 → value 2 after 2 increments
SET NX without TTL, holder crashed: worker-b acquired within 3 s: false; key TTL: -1 (held forever)

Reading it:

  • No lock: 1,048 of 1,200 increments lost, as a baseline.
  • Redis TTL lock with plain DEL release:
    • The paused holder's lock expires and another worker takes it.
    • When the first wakes, it writes a stale value and deletes the new holder's lock (307 foreign unlocks), which cascades into more overlap.
    • 690 increments lost.
  • Owner-checked release (Lua compare-and-delete) stops the foreign unlocks but not the overlap. Pauses still create two holders at once, and 424 increments were lost. A TTL lock is an efficiency lock.
  • Fencing tokens:
    • Both variants lost 0 in the random run. The resource rejected 36–42 stale operations, which then retried under a new lease.
    • The scripted interleaving shows the difference. With the token checked only on the write, A's stale write is accepted because no newer token had written yet, so the value is 1 after 2 increments. With the token claimed at read, A is rejected and retries, and the value is 2.
  • PostgreSQL advisory transaction lock:
    • 0 lost and no overlaps, because the lock lives in the same database as the data and has no TTL. A paused holder simply keeps it.
    • The cost is liveness: it was the slowest option (7.2 s), since each pause stalls everyone. Set session and statement timeouts.
  • No lock, optimistic CAS: update … where value = :read, retried on conflict. 0 lost, and the fastest correct option (1.8 s). 769 retries is the cost under this contention. When the resource can do a conditional write, the lock is unnecessary.
  • A lock without a TTL whose holder crashes is held forever (PTTL -1). TTLs are required for liveness, and fencing is required for safety.

Spring shapes (VERIFY: libraries not downloadable here)

// Idempotent endpoint: claim + effect in one transaction (platform module from ADR-083)
@PostMapping("/payments")
@Idempotent(scope = "customer", retention = "P7D")
public ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse> pay(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key, @Valid @RequestBody PaymentRequest req) { … }

// Idempotent consumer with an inbox row in the listener's transaction
@KafkaListener(topics = "order.order.placed.v1", groupId = "loyalty")
@Transactional
public void on(OrderPlaced e) {
    if (inbox.markProcessed("loyalty", e.eventId())) loyalty.award(e.customerId(), e.points());
}

// Efficiency lock for a scheduled job (ShedLock), with an idempotent body
@Scheduled(cron = "0 5 0 * * *")
@SchedulerLock(name = "daily-sales-report", lockAtMostFor = "PT30M", lockAtLeastFor = "PT1M")
public void dailySalesReport() { … }

// UUIDv7 primary key (Hibernate 6.5+/7; check the style name in your version)
@Id @UuidGenerator(style = UuidGenerator.Style.VERSION_7) private UUID id;

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Symptom Cause Mitigation Double charge / double order Ledger has two charges for one order Retry without a key, check-then-act, key generated per HTTP attempt Atomic claim (L1), client persists the key per logical operation Lost effect Points/stock missing, no error anywhere Dedup marker in a different store than the effect (L2) Inbox in the same transaction Stuck IN_PROGRESS records 409s for a key that never completes Crash after an external call, before recording the result Recovery points + reconciler; timeout → resume or fail False 422s Legit retries rejected Fingerprint includes volatile fields (timestamps, header order) Canonical fingerprint of business fields; contract tests Idempotency table bloat Slow claims, huge table No retention Daily partitions, drop by age Duplicate IDs Unique violations, or worse, silent overwrites in stores without constraints Shared Snowflake worker id, clock step back (L3) Leased worker ids, clock guards, unique constraints Slow inserts, WAL growth Write latency rises as tables grow Random UUIDv4 PKs (L3) UUIDv7 / identity; migrate hot tables Two lock holders Double settlement, corrupted aggregate TTL lock + pause (L4) Fencing claimed at read, DB-held locks, CAS Lock never released Job stops running No TTL + holder crash (L4) TTL / session-bound locks; alert on lock age Foreign unlock Cascading overlaps DEL without an owner check (L4) Compare-and-delete in Lua

docs.title: 6.2 Observability
docs.text:
• Idempotency: replay rate per endpoint (a sudden rise means client or network trouble), 422 and 409 rates, IN_PROGRESS age histogram, records per day.
  • Consumers: duplicates skipped per consumer (inbox hits). A rise signals rebalances or producer retries.
  • Payments with unknown outcome: count and age, and reconciler resolutions.
  • Locks: acquisition wait, hold time vs TTL (alert when hold time approaches the TTL), fencing rejections (each is a would-be incident), lock age for TTL-less locks.
  • IDs: Snowflake clock-rollback waits, sequence exhaustion waits, worker-id lease renewals and losses.
  • Database: WAL rate and index bloat for tables keyed by random UUIDs.

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Scope keys per principal: (customer_id, key). Otherwise one customer's key could replay another customer's stored response (an information leak).
  • Stored responses may contain PII or payment data. Encrypt or minimise them, apply retention, and exclude them from logs.
  • Public identifiers: non-enumerable references (random or v7 plus authorization checks). Sequential IDs in URLs invite IDOR scraping and reveal business volume.
  • UUIDv7 and Snowflake leak the creation time. Usually fine for orders, but not for everything (for example, account IDs that reveal signup dates).
  • Lock keys in shared Redis need a namespace and ACLs. Anyone who can DEL your lock can break mutual exclusion.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance & tuning knobs
docs.text: Knob Guidance Idempotency claim One insert … on conflict on a PK index: sub-ms. Keep the record in the same DB as the effect Concurrent duplicates Same-DB claim: the second waits on the index lock (bounded by the first transaction). Keep transactions short Inbox inserts Composite PK (consumer, event_id); batch consumers can insert many at once (insert … select unnest(?) on conflict do nothing returning) Primary key type UUIDv7 (16 B) or bigint (8 B). Every FK and secondary index repeats it Snowflake bit split 41/10/12 default; fewer worker bits if you have fewer pods, more sequence bits for bursty generators Lock TTL ≫ p99.9 critical-section time; renew for long jobs; fencing regardless Advisory locks pg_try_advisory_xact_lock for non-blocking; lock_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout for liveness

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• Idempotency records and inbox rows are cheap compared with the cost of support tickets, refunds and chargebacks for duplicate charges. One Diwali evening's 1,900 double charges also cost gateway fees twice.
  • UUIDv4 → v7 migration of an existing table is expensive (every FK changes). Adopt v7 for new tables and migrate only the hottest ones.
  • Consensus-backed locking (etcd) is an operational dependency. Most "we need a distributed lock" cases are solved more cheaply by the database already holding the data.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Check-then-act idempotency (L1: 77 double charges per 100 double-clicks).

// ❌ before
if (redis.get("idem:" + key) == null) { charge(req); redis.set("idem:" + key, "done"); }
// ✅ after: claim with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the effect
tx.execute(s -> {
    if (jdbc.update("insert into idempotency_record(scope, key, fingerprint, status) values (?,?,?,'IN_PROGRESS') on conflict do nothing",
                    customerId, key, fp) == 0) return replayOrReject(customerId, key, fp);
    var charge = charges.create(req);
    records.complete(customerId, key, 201, charge);
    return charge;
});

2. A new idempotency key per HTTP attempt.

// ❌ before: the key is generated inside the retry loop, so every retry is a "new" payment
retry(3) { api.pay(req, idempotencyKey = UUID.randomUUID()) }
// ✅ after: one key per checkout attempt, persisted with the pending payment, reused on every retry and app restart
val key = pendingPayments.getOrCreateKey(checkoutId)
retry(3) { api.pay(req, idempotencyKey = key) }

3. Replaying a response for a different request. Without a fingerprint, a client bug that reuses a key for a new amount gets the old response, and the customer is told a different amount was paid. Store a fingerprint and return 422 (L1).

4. Dedup marker in a different store than the effect (L2: 159 points lost).

// ❌ before
if (redis.setIfAbsent("processed:" + e.id(), "1")) loyalty.award(e);        // crash in between = lost
// ✅ after
@Transactional void on(OrderPlaced e) { if (inbox.insertIfAbsent("loyalty", e.id())) loyalty.award(e); }

5. Relying on "exactly-once" middleware for external effects. Kafka EOS covers Kafka-to-Kafka. The moment you write to a database or call an API, you need the inbox or offset-in-DB pattern.

6. Random UUIDv4 primary keys on large, write-heavy tables (L3: 2.3x slower inserts, 2.2x WAL).

-- ❌ before
create table orders (id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(), …);
-- ✅ after (PostgreSQL 18: default uuidv7(); on 16/17 generate v7 in the application)
create table orders (id uuid primary key, …);   -- value from the ids library (UUIDv7)

7. Snowflake worker ids from hostnames or config files.

// ❌ before: two pods can hash to the same id; a copied config reuses one (L3: 20 % duplicates)
long workerId = Math.abs(hostname.hashCode()) % 1024;
// ✅ after: leased, exclusive, renewed; stop issuing if the lease is lost
long workerId = workerIdLease.acquire("snowflake/workers", Duration.ofSeconds(30));   // etcd lease or DB row

8. Ignoring clock rollback in time-based generators (L3: 10,000 duplicates for a 5 ms step). Wait out small rollbacks, refuse large ones, and never issue below the last timestamp.

9. Releasing a lock with a plain DEL (L4: 307 foreign unlocks).

// ❌ before
redis.delete("lock:store-17");
// ✅ after: only the owner can release
redis.execute(RELEASE_IF_OWNER, List.of("lock:store-17"), ownerId);

10. Using a TTL lock for correctness (L4: 424 lost updates with a "correct" Redis lock).

// ❌ before: the settlement write trusts that we still hold the lock
if (lock.tryLock("settle:17", 30, SECONDS)) { var s = compute(); settlements.save(s); }
// ✅ after: fencing token claimed at the resource, write conditional on it
long token = lease.token();
long balance = jdbc.queryForObject("update store_settlement set fence = ? where store_id = 17 and fence < ? returning balance", Long.class, token, token);
jdbc.update("update store_settlement set balance = ? where store_id = 17 and fence = ?", compute(balance), token);   // 0 rows → stale, abort

11. A distributed lock where a conditional write suffices (L4: CAS was the fastest correct option).

-- ❌ before: acquire lock, read stock, check, write, release
-- ✅ after: one statement, no lock
update stock set available = available - :qty, version = version + 1
 where store_id = :store and sku = :sku and available >= :qty;

12. Short random public codes without a uniqueness check (L3: 30-bit codes collide after ~41K). Always add a unique constraint and retry on conflict.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What does idempotent mean, and why does it matter in distributed systems?

30-second answer: An operation is idempotent if doing it several times has the same effect as doing it once. It matters because networks lose responses: a client that times out can't tell whether the server processed the request, so it retries. If the operation isn't idempotent, the retry duplicates the effect (a second charge, a second order).

Deep answer: Some operations are naturally idempotent (PUT a full resource, DELETE, "set status to PAID"). Others need help: an idempotency key for API calls, an inbox table for message consumers, or a conditional update. L1: a naive payment API created 1,657 charges for 1,000 orders when 30 % of responses were lost.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Extra storage and a lookup per request vs correctness.

Follow-ups: 1. Is GET idempotent? → Yes, and safe (no effect). 2. Is DELETE idempotent if the second call returns 404? → Yes: idempotency is about state, not the response code.

Red flags: "We don't retry, so we don't need it." (Clients, proxies and SDKs retry anyway.)

Q2 [B1] ⭐ What is an idempotency key?

30-second answer: A unique value the client generates for one logical operation and sends with every attempt, usually in an Idempotency-Key header. The server remembers the keys it has processed and, for a repeat, returns the stored result instead of doing the work again.

Deep answer: The key must be per logical operation (one checkout attempt), persisted by the client across retries and restarts, and scoped per customer on the server. The server stores a fingerprint of the request to reject reuse with different data (422), and keeps records for a retention window longer than any retry.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Server storage and retention vs safe retries.

Follow-ups: 1. Who generates it? → The client, before the first attempt. 2. How long is it kept? → Days (24 h–7 d), longer than any retry path.

Red flags: "The server generates the key when it receives the request."

Q3 [B1] What are the options for generating unique IDs?

30-second answer: - Database sequences: simple, small, ordered, but need the database. - UUIDv4: random, no coordination, but 16 bytes and unordered. - UUIDv7 / ULID: time-ordered UUIDs, no coordination. - Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs: time + worker id + sequence, ordered and small, but need unique worker ids.

Deep answer: L3 on 4M rows: UUIDv4 took 25.3 s and 1.5 GB of WAL, UUIDv7 10.8 s and 0.7 GB, a sequence 11.2 s. Keep public order references separate from primary keys.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Coordination vs size vs ordering vs guessability.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not auto-increment everywhere? → It doesn't work across shards/regions without coordination, and it's enumerable. 2. What's in a UUIDv7? → A 48-bit ms timestamp, version bits, and random/counter bits.

Red flags: "UUIDs never collide, so use them for everything, including short codes."

Q4 [B1] What is a distributed lock?

30-second answer: A lock shared by processes on different machines, so only one of them does something at a time, for example running tonight's settlement for a store. It's usually implemented with a shared store (Redis SET NX with an expiry, etcd, ZooKeeper, or the database).

Deep answer: Unlike an in-process lock, the holder can crash or pause, so locks need an expiry (a lease). But an expiry means a paused holder can lose the lock without knowing it. So for correctness, the resource must also check a fencing token. L4: a Redis lock with a TTL still lost 424 of 1,200 updates under pauses.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Liveness (TTL) vs safety (fencing).

Follow-ups: 1. What happens without a TTL? → A crashed holder blocks everyone forever (L4: PTTL −1). 2. Is Redis good enough? → For efficiency, yes; for correctness, only with fencing at the resource.

Red flags: "It works like synchronized across servers."

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ Implement idempotency for POST /payments. Walk me through the table and the flow.

30-second answer: - The table: idempotency_record(scope, key, fingerprint, status, status_code, response, created_at) with PK (scope, key). - The flow: in one transaction, insert … on conflict do nothing. If inserted, create the charge and store the response, then commit. If not, compare the fingerprint (422 if different) and replay the stored status and body. - Retention: daily partitions dropped after 7 days.

Deep answer: - The unique constraint closes the race that check-then-act leaves open (L1: 77 → 0 double charges). - A concurrent duplicate blocks on the index until the first commits, then replays the response. - For the external gateway call, split into phases: record INITIATED, call the gateway with a deterministic key, then record the result, with a reconciler for stuck records.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Same-DB atomicity vs a shared idempotency service (not atomic with effects).

Follow-ups: 1. What status do you return while the first is in progress? → Same-DB: the duplicate waits; otherwise 409 + Retry-After. 2. What goes into the fingerprint? → Canonical business fields (amount, currency, order id), not timestamps.

Red flags: Redis GET then SET around the charge.

Q6 [B2] ⭐ How do you make a Kafka consumer idempotent?

30-second answer: Record the event id in an inbox table in the same database transaction as the effect: insert into inbox(consumer, event_id) on conflict do nothing, and apply the effect only if the row was inserted. Commit offsets after the transaction. Redeliveries and producer duplicates then become no-ops.

Deep answer: - Alternatives: naturally idempotent effects (conditional state transitions, upserts), or storing the partition offsets in the same transaction and seeking on startup. - L2: naive over-awarded 38,642 points, and a Redis dedup marker lost 159 (crash between the marker and the DB write). The inbox was exact. - Inbox retention must exceed the redelivery/replay horizon.

Trade-offs I'd call out: One insert per message vs correctness; partitioned retention.

Follow-ups: 1. Does enable.idempotence solve it? → No: it deduplicates producer retries at the broker only. 2. And Kafka transactions? → Exactly-once within Kafka, not into your database.

Red flags: "Kafka guarantees exactly-once, so we don't need dedup."

Q7 [B2] Why are random UUIDs bad primary keys in PostgreSQL or MySQL, and what do you use instead?

30-second answer: B-tree indexes stay efficient when new keys go to the right edge. Random UUIDs insert everywhere in the index. Once it's bigger than memory, inserts read random pages, cause page splits, and write full-page images to WAL after every checkpoint. L3: 2.3x slower inserts and 2.2x WAL vs UUIDv7. Use UUIDv7 (or a bigint identity/Snowflake).

Deep answer: - In MySQL InnoDB, the primary key is the clustered index, so random keys fragment the table itself, and every secondary index carries the 16-byte PK. - PostgreSQL 18 has uuidv7(). On 16/17 or with JPA, generate v7 in the application. - L3's nuance: concurrent writers of ordered keys give ~61 % leaf density vs 90 % with one writer, so the index is bigger even though inserts are faster.

Trade-offs I'd call out: v7 leaks creation time; bigint is smaller but needs coordination.

Follow-ups: 1. Would you migrate an existing v4 table? → Only hot ones; the FK churn is expensive. 2. What about ULID? → Same idea; prefer v7 for native UUID columns.

Red flags: "The database doesn't care about key order."

Q8 [B2] ⭐ How do you implement a lock in Redis correctly?

30-second answer: Acquire with SET lock:<name> <unique-owner-id> NX PX <ttl>. Release with a Lua script that deletes only if the value is still your owner id. Set the TTL well above the critical section's worst case, and renew it for long jobs.

Deep answer: - Plain DEL can delete another holder's lock after yours expired (L4: 307 foreign unlocks, 690 lost updates). - Even correct release doesn't prevent two holders when a holder pauses past the TTL (L4: 424 lost). So use it for efficiency, and for correctness add a fencing token (atomic INCR on acquire) that the resource checks. - Redlock adds a majority of independent nodes but still has no fencing.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Simplicity vs correctness under pauses.

Follow-ups: 1. Why a unique owner id? → To release only your own lock. 2. What does Redisson's watchdog add? → Automatic renewal while the process is alive, which doesn't help during a pause.

Red flags: SETNX followed by a separate EXPIRE (a crash between them leaves a lock with no TTL).

Q9 [B2] How do you generate customer-facing order numbers?

30-second answer: Separate from the primary key. A readable format such as BLR17-250925-7KQ4M (store, date, random base32), with a unique constraint and a retry on conflict. Optionally add a check digit if it's typed by hand. Never use sequential numbers that reveal volume or allow guessing.

Deep answer: Size the random part with the birthday bound: first collision after about √(π/2·N). L3: 30 random bits collided after ~41K codes. Per store per day, 25 bits collides around 7K orders, which is fine with a retry. Authorization still protects access; the code isn't a secret.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Length vs collision rate vs readability.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not show the UUID? → Unreadable over the phone. 2. Why not a global sequence? → A bottleneck, and it leaks business volume.

Red flags: "6 random characters will never collide."

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ The payment call goes to an external gateway. How do you keep it idempotent end to end?

30-second answer: Split it into recoverable phases:

  1. Claim the key and create payment(INITIATED), then commit.
  2. Call the gateway with a deterministic idempotency key (the payment_id).
  3. Record the result and the response, then commit.

A retry resumes from the recorded phase. A reconciler resolves payments stuck in INITIATED by querying the gateway. Every hop must be idempotent under the same logical key.

Deep answer: - If the gateway lacks idempotency support, query by merchant reference before retrying, and never retry blindly. - Webhooks from the gateway are at-least-once too, so use an inbox keyed by the gateway's event id. - The client sees "pending" for unknown outcomes and polls with the same key. - Ch 45 builds the full payment system.

Trade-offs I'd call out: More states and a reconciler vs never double-charging.

Follow-ups: 1. What if the gateway succeeded but our commit failed? → The retry resends with the same key; the gateway returns the original result. 2. How long do you keep INITIATED? → Reconcile after minutes; alert if unresolved.

Red flags: Calling the gateway inside a DB transaction and hoping.

Q11 [B3] ⭐ What is a fencing token, and why isn't a lock with a TTL enough?

30-second answer: A number that increases with every lock grant, sent with every operation on the protected resource. The resource rejects operations carrying a token older than the newest it has seen. It's needed because a holder can pause (GC, VM steal) beyond its TTL without knowing. Another process gets the lock, and the paused one wakes up and writes anyway.

Deep answer: - L4: a correct Redis TTL lock lost 424 of 1,200 updates under 150 ms pauses with a 100 ms TTL, and fencing lost 0. - Subtlety: for read-modify-write, checking the token only on the write is insufficient. The scripted interleaving had the old holder write after the new holder read but before it wrote, and it was accepted. - Claim the resource with the token before reading (set fence = :t where fence < :t), then write where fence = :t. - etcd revisions and ZooKeeper zxids make natural tokens (Ch 12).

Trade-offs I'd call out: The resource must participate; not every resource can (e.g. an email provider).

Follow-ups: 1. What if the resource can't check tokens? → Make the operation idempotent, or accept rare duplicates. 2. Where does the token come from in Redis? → INCR in the same Lua script as SET NX.

Red flags: "Set the TTL longer than any GC pause."

Q12 [B3] How would you assign Snowflake worker ids in Kubernetes?

30-second answer: Take a lease on a worker id from a coordination store: an etcd lease on workers/<id>, or a DB row claimed with for update skip locked plus a heartbeat. Renew it while running, and stop generating if the lease is lost. StatefulSet ordinals work for fixed-size sets. Never derive ids from hostnames.

Deep answer: - L3: two pods sharing a worker id collided on 20 % of ids. - Include a guard for clock rollback: wait for small steps, refuse large ones (L3: 10,000 duplicates unguarded for a 5 ms step). - Persist the last timestamp if a restart can be faster than a clock correction. - With 10 worker bits, you have 1,024 ids to recycle, so a released id must not be reused within the clock-skew window.

Trade-offs I'd call out: A coordination dependency at startup vs uniqueness.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not UUIDv7 instead? → Fine if 16 bytes is acceptable; Snowflake wins on size for huge event tables. 2. Multi-region? → Region bits in the worker id space.

Red flags: "Random worker id, collisions are unlikely."

Q13 [B3] Two requests with the same idempotency key arrive at the same time. What happens in your design?

30-second answer: Both try insert … on conflict do nothing on the unique key. PostgreSQL lets one insert, and the other blocks on the index entry until the first transaction commits or rolls back. On commit, the second sees the conflict and replays the stored response. On rollback, the second's insert succeeds and it processes the request.

Deep answer: - That's the behaviour L1 relied on: 100 double-clicks, 0 double charges. - If the claim and the effect are in separate transactions (external calls), the second sees IN_PROGRESS and gets 409 + Retry-After, or waits with a bounded poll. - The first transaction must be short, or duplicates hold connections while waiting.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Blocking wait (simple) vs immediate 409 (client retries).

Follow-ups: 1. What about MySQL? → INSERT IGNORE or a unique-key conflict with similar locking; test the isolation level. 2. With Redis instead? → SET NX is atomic, but not with the DB effect.

Red flags: "Duplicates can't arrive concurrently."

Q14 [B3] Kafka offers idempotent producers and exactly-once semantics. Why do you still need an inbox?

30-second answer: The idempotent producer (PID + sequence numbers) removes duplicates caused by the producer's own retries to a broker. Kafka transactions make consume → process → produce atomic within Kafka. Neither covers side effects in your database or other systems, application-level double publishes, or reprocessing after an offset reset. The consumer's effect must be idempotent on its own.

Deep answer: For a consumer that writes to PostgreSQL, the options are an inbox row or the offset stored in the same transaction. L2: exact with the inbox, lost or over-awarded otherwise. Outbox (Ch 13) on the producer side plus inbox on the consumer side is the standard pairing.

Trade-offs I'd call out: EOS has throughput and complexity costs and covers only part of the path.

Follow-ups: 1. When is Kafka EOS enough? → Pure stream processing (Kafka Streams) with state in Kafka. 2. What event id do you dedup on? → A producer-assigned id in the envelope, not the offset (offsets change on replay to a new topic).

Red flags: "enable.idempotence=true makes consumers exactly-once."

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ When do you actually need a distributed lock? What would you use instead?

30-second answer: Rarely for correctness. First try:

  • atomic conditional updates (where available >= :n, where version = ?);
  • unique constraints;
  • for update skip locked work queues in the database that owns the data;
  • single-writer partitioning (a Kafka partition per key);
  • leader election with fencing for singleton jobs.

Use a TTL lock (Redis, ShedLock) only as an efficiency optimisation, where an occasional duplicate is harmless.

Deep answer: - L4 ranked the options: CAS was the fastest correct option (1.8 s, 0 lost), fencing and the advisory lock were correct but slower, and TTL locks lost updates. - The database holding the data is usually the right coordinator, because it's where the invariant lives. - For cross-database singletons, use an etcd lease with fencing tokens stored in the target DB (Ch 12 lab).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Locks serialise, and serialisation limits throughput and adds failure modes.

Follow-ups: 1. How would you run a nightly job exactly once across pods? → Leader election + fencing + an idempotent job keyed by date. 2. What about Redlock? → I wouldn't use it for correctness: no fencing, and timing assumptions.

Red flags: "Wrap it in a distributed lock" as the first answer.

Q16 [B4] ⭐ Design the platform standard for idempotency across 26 services.

30-second answer: - Public APIs: every non-idempotent public operation accepts an Idempotency-Key scoped per principal. - Service side: a platform library claims the key in the service's own database in the same transaction as the effect, fingerprints requests, replays responses, and returns 422/409. - Consumers: every consumer with side effects uses an inbox. - External calls: carry deterministic downstream keys, with reconcilers. - Proof: chaos tests (lost responses, duplicates, crashes) in CI.

Deep answer (§4): - NFR: 0 duplicate charges under 30 % lost responses and 10 % double submits (L1), and exact counts under crash + redelivery (L2). - Retention via daily partitions. - Metrics: replays, 422s, stuck IN_PROGRESS records, inbox hits. - The gateway only forwards the header and retries idempotent calls. It doesn't store records, because it can't be atomic with effects.

Trade-offs I'd call out: A shared library couples services to its versioning vs every team reinventing it (badly).

Follow-ups: 1. How do you prove compliance? → Contract tests + a chaos suite per service + ArchUnit rules. 2. Internal service-to-service calls? → Same keys, propagated from the originating request.

Red flags: A central "idempotency service" called over the network before every effect.

Q17 [B4] How would you choose the primary-key strategy for the grocery platform?

30-second answer: - UUIDv7 by default for entities that cross service boundaries: no coordination, index-friendly, safe to generate in the app and offline. - bigint identity for tables private to one database, where size matters. - Snowflake for very high-volume event and tracking ids where 8 bytes counts, with leased worker ids. - Public references kept separate.

Deep answer: - L3 numbers drive it: v4 costs 2.3x inserts and 2.2x WAL at scale. - Watch concurrent-writer density (~61 %) and the timestamp leakage of v7/Snowflake. - For sharded tables (Ch 11), the key must carry or derive the shard (customer_id), so ordering is per shard. - Hibernate/JPA: generator style v7 (VERIFY for the version); avoid GenerationType.AUTO surprises.

Trade-offs I'd call out: 16 vs 8 bytes across every FK and index vs coordination.

Follow-ups: 1. Will v7's timestamp prefix create a hot shard? → With range sharding on the id, yes. Hash-shard on the tenant/customer instead. 2. Offline-created carts? → v7 generated on the device, validated server-side.

Red flags: One scheme for everything, chosen by habit.

Q18 [B4] Explain the Redlock debate and your position.

30-second answer: Redlock acquires a lock on a majority of N independent Redis nodes with a TTL. Kleppmann argued it's unsafe for correctness: there's no fencing token, and safety depends on bounded process pauses, network delays and clock drift, which real systems violate. Antirez argued the assumptions are reasonable and timing checks mitigate them. My position: use Redlock or any TTL lock only for efficiency. For correctness, use a consensus system with fencing tokens checked by the resource, or let the database enforce the invariant.

Deep answer: L4 demonstrated the core issue with a single Redis node: a pause past the TTL produces two holders even with correct release, and that's independent of how many nodes grant the lease. Fencing needs the resource's cooperation; etcd revisions or an INCR counter provide the tokens.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Operational simplicity of Redis vs a correctness guarantee.

Follow-ups: 1. Does a majority help with pauses? → No, the pause is in the client. 2. How do you get a token from Redis? → INCR in the acquire script.

Red flags: Picking sides by popularity without the pause argument.

Q19 [B4] ⭐ A customer reports a double charge. How do you investigate and what do you change?

30-second answer: - Find the duplicate: two charges for one order in the ledger (group by order_id having count > 1). Check whether they share an idempotency key: - Different keys → the client generated a key per attempt, or the app reinstalled. - Same key → a server-side race or split transactions. - No key → a path without idempotency. - Check the gateway side for duplicates under different merchant references. - Refund, then fix the root cause, then add a chaos test that reproduces it.

Deep answer: - Correlate traces for both requests: timing (a concurrent double-click vs a retry), which pod, response codes. - The Diwali case was check-then-act in Redis (L1 reproduced it: 77/100 concurrent duplicates). - The fix: an atomic claim, the key persisted on the client, and the key passed to the gateway. - Add monitoring for duplicate charges per order as a canary metric, and run a reconciliation job that flags them before customers do.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed of refund vs completeness of the investigation (do both).

Follow-ups: 1. How do you find all affected customers? → A ledger query plus gateway settlement reports. 2. How do you prevent a regression? → The chaos test in CI with lost responses and double submits.

Red flags: "It was a one-off network glitch."

Q20 [B4] How do idempotency, IDs and locks relate to 'exactly-once' in your architecture?

30-second answer: Exactly-once delivery is impossible across unreliable networks. The architecture achieves exactly-once effects by combining:

  • at-least-once delivery (retries, redelivery);
  • stable identifiers for every logical operation and message (idempotency keys, event ids);
  • deduplication or conditional writes enforced by the system of record, atomically with the effect (idempotency records, inbox, CAS, fencing).

Locks are a special case: mutual exclusion is only as good as the resource's ability to reject stale holders.

Deep answer: The chapter's labs show each piece: L1 keys (0 duplicates), L2 the inbox (exact), L3 the IDs that name operations without coordination, and L4 fencing/CAS (0 lost). Together with the outbox (Ch 13) and sagas, they form the platform's reliability contract: every hop idempotent under a stable key, and every invariant enforced where the data lives.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Storage, latency and design effort vs duplicated money and stock.

Follow-ups: 1. Where does the stable key originate? → At the edge (the client) for commands; at the producer for events. 2. What breaks the chain? → A hop that isn't idempotent or generates a new key.

Red flags: "Our message broker gives us exactly-once, so we're done."

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Every request and message may arrive 0, 1 or many times. Exactly-once effects come from at-least-once delivery plus idempotency.
  2. Idempotency keys are per logical operation, generated and persisted by the client, and reused on every retry.
  3. Claim the key atomically with the effect (unique constraint, same transaction). Check-then-act still double-charged 77 of 100 concurrent duplicates (L1).
  4. Fingerprint requests: key reuse with different data returns 422, not a replay.
  5. External effects need phases, deterministic downstream keys and reconciliation. An unknown outcome isn't a failure.
  6. Consumers use an inbox in the same transaction. A dedup marker in another store loses effects (L2: −159) and naive consumers duplicate them (+38,642).
  7. IDs: UUIDv7 by default, bigint identity locally, Snowflake with leased worker ids and clock guards. UUIDv4 cost 2.3x inserts and 2.2x WAL (L3).
  8. Short random codes collide early (√N): add a unique constraint and a retry.
  9. TTL locks are efficiency locks. For correctness, use fencing tokens claimed at the resource, or a database-held lock (L4: 424 lost vs 0).
  10. The best lock is often none: conditional writes, constraints, single-writer partitioning (L4: CAS was the fastest correct option).

docs.text: Situation Choice Public POST that moves money/stock Idempotency key, claimed in the same transaction as the effect Call to an external API Phased state machine + downstream idempotency key + reconciler Message consumer with DB side effects Inbox (consumer, event_id) in the same transaction New table PK, cross-service entity UUIDv7 PK private to one database bigint generated always as identity Very high-volume event ids Snowflake with leased worker ids Customer-visible order number Separate readable code + unique constraint + retry Avoid duplicate work (reports, cache warmers) Redis/ShedLock TTL lock + idempotent job Protect an invariant Conditional update / constraint; if needed, lease + fencing claimed at the resource

docs.title: 21. Data at Scale
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B2 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 05, Ch 06, Ch 07, Ch 13, Ch 14 · What you will build: Where the grocery platform's big data lives, and how it moves: blobs in object storage, static bytes through a CDN, analytics off the OLTP path in a columnar lake, and batch and streaming pipelines that stay correct through crashes and late data. Four labs on real tools: SeaweedFS (S3 API), JDK HTTP servers, PostgreSQL 16, DuckDB 1.1 and Parquet.

  • L1: object storage over the S3 API with hand-written SigV4. Presigned upload/download, expiry and tampering (403), multipart upload with a single part retried, and content-addressed dedup.
  • L2: a pull-through CDN node. Normalising the cache key raised the hit ratio from 57 % to 97.5 % (origin egress 953 → 23 MB). Request coalescing cut 400 origin requests to 1. Purge or versioned URLs removed 93 stale price responses, and stale-if-error served 50 of 50 requests during an origin outage.
  • L3: OLTP vs OLAP on 10M order lines. An ELT step turned 754 MB of CSV into 58 MB of Parquet. DuckDB answered most analytical queries 3.5–4x faster than PostgreSQL on 2 vCPUs, with identical results, while PostgreSQL won the point lookup (0.9 ms vs 11 ms). Precomputing the local date during ELT made one query 7x faster.
  • L4: batch and stream. A restartable chunked batch job was off by ₹5.4 crore when its checkpoint was committed separately from its output, and exact otherwise. For streaming windows over out-of-order events, processing-time windows were 30 % exact, a 5 s watermark 43 %, and a 5 s watermark with 30 min allowed lateness 100 %.

· Reading time: 110 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: the Monday morning report
docs.text:
At 9:30 on the Monday after the Diwali weekend, checkout p99 jumped from 300 ms to 4 s. The cause was a BI dashboard: the finance team's weekly GMV report ran fifty count(distinct order_id) … group by week queries against the orders primary. Each one scanned 10 million rows (L3: 5.4 s on PostgreSQL), and together they took the buffer cache and the CPUs away from checkout.

The review found four more problems:

  • Product images were served by catalog-service itself. They were stored as bytea rows and streamed through the JVM, so 40 % of the service's CPU and most of its egress went to bytes that never change.
  • The CDN had been added the previous month, but its hit ratio was 55 %. Marketing push notifications appended utm_source, utm_campaign and fbclid to image URLs, and the CDN used the full URL as the cache key. L2: 57.4 % → 97.5 % once the key was normalised.
  • A price cut went live at 00:00, but some customers saw the old price until 00:05, because product JSON was cached for 5 minutes and there was no purge. L2 reproduces it at a smaller scale: 93 of 138 responses stale with a TTL alone, and 0 with purge or versioned URLs.
  • The dark-store demand board undercounted evening orders by up to 30 %. It counted orders by the minute they arrived at the stream processor, not the minute they were placed, and riders' phones in basements delivered events minutes late. L4: processing-time windows were exact for 29.8 % of store-minutes.

The fixes:

  • Analytics moved off the OLTP path: CDC and nightly ELT into a Parquet lake, queried by a columnar engine.
  • Blobs moved to object storage with presigned uploads.
  • The CDN got normalised keys and coalescing, plus versioned URLs for static assets, purge for prices, and stale-if-error.
  • The demand board moved to event-time windows with a watermark and allowed lateness.

The thesis of this chapter

Different data has different physics. Transactions want rows, indexes and locks. Analytics want columns, compression and full scans. Blobs want cheap, durable, flat namespaces. Static bytes want to live near users. Scaling the data layer is mostly about putting each kind of data in the store built for it, and moving it between stores with pipelines that are replayable, idempotent and honest about time.

docs.title: 1.2 Where this lives in the grocery platform
docs.text: Data Store / path Why Product images, invoices (PDF), proof-of-delivery photos, exports Object storage (S3 API), private buckets, presigned URLs Cheap, durable (11 nines on S3), no app servers in the byte path Images, JS/CSS, app bundles CDN, versioned URLs, immutable Hit ratio > 95 %, origin offload Product/price JSON for anonymous browse CDN, short TTL, purge on change, stale-if-error Burst absorption, resilience Orders, payments, inventory (OLTP) PostgreSQL per service (Ch 05) Transactions, point reads/writes Order lines, events, clickstream for analytics Lakehouse: Parquet/Iceberg on object storage, partitioned by date Columnar scans, cheap storage, many engines BI dashboards, finance reports Warehouse / lakehouse SQL engine (Trino, BigQuery, Snowflake, DuckDB for small data) Never on OLTP primaries Daily settlement, invoices, loyalty reconciliation Batch (Spring Batch), restartable, idempotent Correct, auditable, cheap Demand board, surge, fraud signals Streaming (Kafka Streams / Flink) with event time Seconds-fresh, and correct despite late events

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text: Band After this chapter you can… B2 Use object storage with presigned URLs and multipart uploads, set CDN cache headers, and explain OLTP vs OLAP and row vs column storage B3 Design cache keys, invalidation and coalescing for a CDN; build an ELT pipeline into a partitioned lake; write restartable batch jobs; use event-time windows with watermarks B4 Choose warehouse vs lake vs lakehouse, lambda vs kappa, and batch vs streaming for a use case, and define the platform's data architecture

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition B2
docs.text:
• Object storage is the warehouse's back room of labelled boxes. You don't open a box to change one item. You replace the whole box (immutable objects). Boxes are addressed by label (key), anyone with a signed slip (presigned URL) can pick one up, and it's vast and cheap.
  • A CDN is a set of small shops near every neighbourhood, stocking copies of the most popular items from the central warehouse (the origin). The trick is labelling: if "Atta 5 kg" and "Atta 5 kg (from the Diwali leaflet)" are shelved separately, the shop keeps running back to the warehouse (the cache key).
  • OLTP vs OLAP is the billing counter vs the monthly stock-take:
    • The counter needs one customer's cart, fast (rows, indexes).
    • The stock-take needs a total per category across every shelf (columns, scans). Doing the stock-take at the billing counter during rush hour is the Monday morning incident.
  • Batch vs stream is counting the day's takings after closing vs a live tally:
    • The live tally is fast but must handle receipts that arrive late (event time and watermarks).
    • The after-closing count is exact, but only if you can restart it without counting a drawer twice (checkpoints).

docs.title: 2.2 Blob and object storage ⭐ B2
docs.text:
Block storage (EBS) File storage (EFS/NFS) Object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob, MinIO, SeaweedFS, Ceph RGW) Unit Block on a volume File in a hierarchy Immutable object in a flat bucket, key + metadata Access Mounted by one host Mounted by many HTTP API (S3 is the de facto standard) Scale TBs per volume Large Effectively unlimited objects and bytes Durability Replicated in a zone Regional 11 nines (S3 Standard), erasure-coded across zones Use Databases Shared config, legacy apps Media, backups, logs, data lakes

The rules the grocery platform follows:

  • Don't put blobs in the OLTP database. It bloats backups, replication and the buffer cache. Store the object key and metadata in the DB and the bytes in object storage.
  • Don't proxy bytes through app servers. Use presigned URLs: the service authorises the action and signs a URL scoped to one method, one key and a short expiry, and the client talks directly to storage.
    • L1: the presigned PUT and GET succeeded (200).
    • The same URL with the key changed (rider-78) got 403, because the signature covers the path.
    • An expired URL got 403, and an unsigned GET of a private object got 403.
  • Multipart upload for large objects (S3 recommends it above ~100 MB; parts are 5 MB–5 GB, up to 10,000 of them):
    • Parts upload in parallel, and a failed part is retried alone. L1 sent 44 MB for a 40 MB object with one failure, where a single PUT would have resent all 40.
    • Clean up incomplete uploads with a lifecycle rule, or they're billed forever.
  • Keys:
    • Design for listing (products/<sku>/…, exports/<date>/…) and for lifecycle rules by prefix.
    • Content-addressed keys (blobs/sha256/<hash>) give deduplication and immutability for free (L1: 3 uploads, 1 object).
    • Old advice about random prefixes for throughput is obsolete on S3: each prefix scales to thousands of requests per second automatically.
  • Consistency: S3 has been strongly consistent for reads after writes and for lists since December 2020. Many S3-compatible stores are too, but check yours.
  • Lifecycle and storage classes: transition old invoices to infrequent-access or archive tiers, expire temporary uploads, version buckets that hold critical data, and use Object Lock (WORM) for compliance (Ch 36).
  • ETags of multipart objects aren't content MD5s (L1: …-10). Verify integrity with your own checksum or the newer checksum headers.

docs.title: 2.3 CDN fundamentals ⭐ B2
docs.text:
A CDN is a network of edge caches (points of presence) that serve content close to users and shield the origin.

Pull vs push:

Pull (origin pull) Push How The edge fetches from the origin on a miss and caches per the headers You upload content to the CDN's storage ahead of time Good for Most web content, APIs, images Large, predictable releases (app bundles, videos) Risk The first request per edge is a miss; herds on expiry You manage what's there

Cache headers the origin controls:

  • Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable for versioned assets.
  • max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30, stale-if-error=86400 for semi-dynamic JSON.
  • s-maxage sets the shared-cache TTL separately from browsers.
  • private / no-store for personalised responses.
  • Vary for content negotiation (keep it minimal; Vary: User-Agent destroys hit ratios).

Cache keys: by default, the full URL plus some headers. Normalise them:

  • drop tracking params (utm_*, fbclid, gclid);
  • sort query params;
  • lower-case where safe;
  • bucket device classes instead of varying on the raw User-Agent.

L2: 20,000 image requests with 40 % carrying tracking params. A full-URL key gave 57.4 % hits and 406 MB of origin egress; a normalised key gave 97.5 % and 23 MB.

Request coalescing (collapsed forwarding): when many requests for the same key miss at once, send one to the origin and make the rest wait for it. L2: 400 → 1 origin requests when a hot product expired. Most CDNs do this per POP, and origin shield / tiered caching extends it across POPs.

docs.title: 2.4 Invalidation ⭐ B3
docs.text:
There are three strategies, and you usually combine them:

Strategy How Staleness Cost TTL only Wait for max-age Up to the TTL (L2: 93 of 138 stale over 2 s) Free Purge / invalidate API call per URL, prefix or surrogate key/tag when the data changes Propagation time across POPs (seconds to minutes) API limits; purge storms Versioned URLs The URL contains a content hash or version (/v/p39/sku-7, app.3f9a1c.js); pages link to the new URL None: a new URL is a new object Needs the referencing page to change
  • Static assets: versioned + immutable, never purged.
  • Prices and stock on public pages: short TTL + surrogate-key purge (tag every response with sku-7, purge the tag on change) + stale-if-error.
  • Personalised data (cart, addresses): not cached at the CDN.

Stale-if-error turns the CDN into a resilience layer. L2: origin down for 5 s, and the strict TTL returned 50 errors while stale-if-error served 50 of 50.

docs.title: 2.5 OLTP vs OLAP ⭐ B2
docs.text:
OLTP OLAP Queries Many small reads/writes by key Few large scans and aggregations Storage Row-oriented pages + B-tree indexes Columnar, compressed, often sorted/partitioned Execution Tuple at a time, index lookups Vectorised, SIMD, parallel scans Concurrency Thousands of short transactions Tens of long queries Freshness Now Minutes to a day behind (CDC/ELT) Examples PostgreSQL, MySQL BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, ClickHouse, Druid, Pinot, DuckDB, Trino over Parquet/Iceberg

L3 on the same 10M order lines, 2 vCPUs, identical answers verified by hash:

Query PostgreSQL 16 DuckDB on Parquet One order's lines by primary key 0.9 ms 11 ms Revenue by city × category, last 30 days 650 ms 164 ms Top 10 SKUs in Bengaluru, quarter 628 ms 180 ms Weekly distinct orders + GMV 5,449 ms 3,331 ms; 463 ms with dt precomputed in ELT One day's GMV 17 ms (index range) 4 ms (reads 1 of 90 partition files)

Why:

  • Columnar storage reads only the needed columns. Q3 needed 3 of 11 columns, 22 MB of 57 MB, while PostgreSQL reads whole rows.
  • Compression: 754 MB of CSV, 1.4 GB in PostgreSQL with indexes, and 58 MB as zstd Parquet.
  • Vectorised execution processes batches of values per operator call.
  • Partition pruning skips files whose partition value doesn't match, and min/max statistics skip row groups within files.

And the lesson from Q4: model for the query. Computing the local date once during the transform (instead of time-zone math on every row, every query) was worth 7x.

docs.title: 2.6 Warehouse, lake, lakehouse ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Data warehouse Data lake Lakehouse Storage Managed, proprietary columnar Files (Parquet/ORC/JSON) on object storage Open table format (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi) over Parquet on object storage Schema Schema-on-write, strongly modelled Schema-on-read, often messy ("swamp") Schema-on-write with evolution; ACID commits; time travel Engines The warehouse's own Anything that reads files Many engines (Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB, Snowflake, BigQuery) on the same tables Updates/deletes Yes Rewrite files by hand Yes (merge-on-read / copy-on-write), essential for GDPR/DPDP deletes Cost Compute + storage coupled (less so now) Cheapest storage Cheap storage + choice of compute

Table formats add a metadata layer (manifests, snapshots) over immutable Parquet files. That gives atomic commits (a new snapshot pointer), concurrent writers, schema and partition evolution, time travel ("revenue as of last Tuesday's snapshot") and efficient deletes. L3's hive-style dt= directories are the pre-table-format version of partitioning. They work, but renames aren't atomic and every reader must list directories.

The grocery platform: Iceberg tables on object storage, written by CDC (Debezium → Kafka → Flink/Spark sink) and nightly ELT, and queried by Trino for BI and by Spark for ML features. A star schema (fact order_line, dimensions store, sku, customer, date) in the "gold" layer.

docs.title: 2.7 ETL vs ELT B3
docs.text:
• ETL: Extract → Transform (in a separate engine) → Load the cleaned result. Classic warehousing, where transformations happen before the warehouse.
  • ELT: Extract → Load raw data into the lake/warehouse → Transform inside it with SQL (dbt). Raw data is kept, so transforms can be re-run when logic changes.

Medallion layers:

  • bronze: raw, append-only, as received;
  • silver: cleaned, deduplicated, conformed;
  • gold: business aggregates and marts.

L3's pipeline is ELT in miniature: extract with COPY (754 MB CSV, 9.2 s), then load and transform in DuckDB into partitioned Parquet with a derived local-date column (58 MB, 7.0 s).

Extraction options:

  • Batch COPY/snapshot: simple, but loads the source; use a replica.
  • Incremental by updated_at: misses deletes and needs indexes.
  • CDC from the WAL (Debezium, Ch 13): complete, low latency, captures deletes. The platform standard.

docs.title: 2.8 Batch processing ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Batch jobs process a bounded dataset: nightly settlement, invoice generation, loyalty expiry, reconciliation, ML feature backfills. Spring Batch's model:

  • Job → Steps. A step is either chunk-oriented (ItemReader → ItemProcessor → ItemWriter with a commit interval) or a tasklet.
  • A JobRepository stores execution state and the ExecutionContext (the checkpoint, e.g. the last key read). A failed job restarts from the last committed chunk.
  • Skip/retry policies handle bad records, and partitioning or remote chunking scale out.

The correctness rule, from L4 Part A: the checkpoint and the chunk's output must commit atomically, or the output must be idempotent.

Restart strategy Result after one crash Output committed, crash before the checkpoint Chunk 60 re-processed, 200 (day, store) rows wrong, ₹5.37 crore overcounted Checkpoint in the same transaction as the output Exact Recompute and overwrite the output partition in one transaction Exact, simplest. Re-read everything (20M rows for 10M), still fastest here

In lakehouse terms, overwrite means "INSERT OVERWRITE partition dt=…" or an Iceberg replacePartitions commit. Recomputing a day and atomically replacing it is the most robust batch pattern.

docs.title: 2.9 Stream processing ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Streaming processes an unbounded log continuously: Kafka Streams (a library inside your service), Apache Flink (a cluster), Spark Structured Streaming. The core concepts:

  • Event time vs processing time:
    • Event time is when it happened on the rider's phone.
    • Processing time is when the processor saw it.
    • They differ by seconds to minutes (L4: 10 % of events more than 5 s late, 2 % more than 2 min).
  • Windows:
    • tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping: orders per minute);
    • hopping/sliding (overlapping: 5-min demand every minute);
    • session (gap-based: a customer's browsing session).
  • Watermark: the processor's assertion that no events older than t are still expected. Commonly max event time seen − bounded delay. A window's result is emitted when the watermark passes its end.
  • Allowed lateness: keep window state after firing, and emit updated results for late events up to a limit. Downstream must accept upserts.
  • State and checkpoints: window state lives in a local store (RocksDB), checkpointed together with input offsets (Flink snapshots, Kafka Streams changelog topics), which gives exactly-once state semantics.

L4 Part B: orders per store per minute over 1.08M out-of-order events, compared with the batch ground truth:

Strategy Windows exact Dropped Result delay p50 Updates per window Processing-time windows 29.8 % 0 (misassigned) immediate 0 Event time, watermark 5 s, drop late 43.0 % 60,625 5.1 s 0 Event time, watermark 60 s, drop late 74.3 % 21,343 60.1 s 0 Event time, watermark 5 s + 30 min lateness 100 % 0 5.1 s 0.84

The trade-off is between latency, completeness and cost (state kept, updates emitted). A longer watermark buys completeness with latency. Allowed lateness buys completeness with state and downstream updates. The demand board takes the last row: fast first results, corrected as stragglers arrive.

docs.title: 2.10 Lambda vs Kappa ⭐ B4
docs.text:
• Lambda runs a batch layer (complete, recomputed from the master dataset) and a speed layer (streaming, approximate, recent), merged at query time.
    • It's robust: batch corrects the stream.
    • But it has two codebases for the same logic that drift apart.
  • Kappa has one streaming codebase. Reprocessing means replaying the log (Kafka with long retention or tiered storage, or the lake's bronze layer) through a new version of the job, into a new output, and then switching readers over.
    • It needs a replayable log and a job that can catch up fast. L4's toy job replayed the evening at ~4.5M events/s on one core; real jobs with state and I/O are much slower, so plan catch-up capacity.

In practice, 2026: most platforms run kappa-style streaming for fresh metrics, plus a lakehouse whose tables are the durable history and can be recomputed by batch (a "lakehouse lambda"). Unified engines (Flink, Spark) share code between batch and streaming, which removes the classic lambda drift. The grocery platform:

  • Streaming: the demand board, surge, fraud and live ETAs (Flink/Kafka Streams).
  • Batch: finance, settlement and ML training (Spark/Spring Batch on Iceberg).
  • Where both exist, the batch figure is the source of truth, and the streaming figure is labelled provisional.

docs.title: 2.11 Choosing batch or stream B4
docs.text: Question Batch Stream How fresh must the answer be? Hours/day is fine Seconds/minutes Must it be exact and auditable? Yes (money) Provisional, corrected later, is acceptable Does it need the whole dataset (joins across days, dedup over all history)? Natural Hard (state size) Does the action happen in the moment (surge, fraud block)? Too late Required Operational cost Cheap, scheduled Always-on, state, checkpoints, on-call

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Grocery Data Platform v1
docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers Data platform team / catalog, orders, finance, SRE, security Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-088 Object storage + presigned URLs for all blobs; ADR-089 CDN key normalisation, versioned assets, surrogate-key purge, stale-if-error; ADR-090 No analytics on OLTP primaries; Iceberg lakehouse via CDC; ADR-091 Batch outputs idempotent (partition overwrite) or checkpointed atomically; ADR-092 Streaming in event time with watermarks and allowed lateness; batch is the source of truth for money

1. Context & Problem. The Monday incident (§1.1): BI on the OLTP primary, blobs in PostgreSQL behind the JVM, a 55 % CDN hit ratio, stale prices, and processing-time demand counts.

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: no analytical load on OLTP primaries; a CDN hit ratio > 95 % for media; price changes visible within 10 s; demand metrics exact within the lateness bound; finance numbers reproducible from raw data.
  • Non-goals: real-time finance (T+1 is fine); a self-built CDN.

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement FR-1 Uploads go directly to object storage with presigned URLs (≤ 5 min expiry, one key, content type fixed) FR-2 Every static asset URL is content-versioned; product/price JSON is tagged with surrogate keys and purged on change FR-3 BI and finance query only the lakehouse; OLTP read access for analysts is revoked NFR-1 Media hit ratio ≥ 95 %; origin egress ≤ 10 % of edge egress NFR-2 Lakehouse freshness: silver ≤ 15 min behind OLTP (CDC); gold daily by 03:00 NFR-3 Batch jobs restartable with exact results (tested with injected crashes) NFR-4 Demand board first result ≤ 10 s after the minute ends; exact after 30 min

4. Capacity estimates.

Item Calculation Result Media 400K SKUs × 6 images × 3 sizes × 150 KB ~1.1 TB, plus PoD photos 60K/day × 300 KB ≈ 18 GB/day CDN egress 10M app sessions/day × 40 images × 60 KB ~24 TB/day at the edge; ≤ 1.2 TB/day at the origin with a 95 % hit ratio Order lines 1.2M orders/day × 5 lines 6M rows/day, ~35 MB/day as Parquet (L3: 58 MB per 10M rows) 3 years of order lines 6.6B rows ~40 GB Parquet, trivial for a lakehouse; would be ~900 GB in PostgreSQL Stream state 900 stores × 31 open minutes (30 min lateness) × a few counters Kilobytes per store: tiny

5. Proposed design.

  1. Object storage: private buckets per data class (media, documents, exports), SSE-KMS encryption, lifecycle rules (temp uploads 1 day, incomplete multipart 7 days, invoices → IA after 90 days), versioning on documents, Object Lock for tax invoices.
  2. CDN:
    • Cache policy per path: /img/* gets a normalised key and 1 year immutable. /api/catalog/* gets 60 s + SWR 30 s + SIE 24 h + surrogate keys.
    • Origin shield. catalog-service purges by SKU tag on price or stock-status change.
  3. Lakehouse:
    • Debezium CDC → Kafka → a Flink sink writes bronze Iceberg tables. Flink/Spark jobs build silver (dedup by event id, Ch 20) and gold (star schema) tables.
    • Partitioned by local date. Trino for BI, with DuckDB allowed for local analysis of extracts.
  4. Batch: Spring Batch jobs for settlement and invoices, with chunk checkpoints in the job's own DB transaction. Spark jobs for gold tables use partition overwrite.
  5. Streaming: Kafka Streams for the demand board (per-store tumbling 1-min windows, grace 30 min, suppress-until-final for the finance-facing view), and Flink for surge and fraud.

7. Alternatives considered.

Option Pros Cons Verdict Read replica for BI Quick Still row storage (L3), replica lag and conflicts, no history Stop-gap only Lakehouse (Iceberg + Trino) Open, cheap storage, many engines, deletes and time travel More moving parts Chosen Managed warehouse (BigQuery/Snowflake) Least ops Cost at scale, lock-in Acceptable alternative; Iceberg keeps the option open Lambda with separate batch/speed code Robust Two codebases Replaced by unified engines + batch truth Processing-time streaming Simple Wrong under late data (L4: 30 % exact) Rejected

8. Failure modes.

  • CDC lag → the silver freshness SLO alerts, and dashboards show "data as of".
  • Purge API failure → retry with backoff, and the TTL bounds staleness.
  • Presigned URL leak → short expiry, one key, and authorisation at signing.
  • Stream job restart → restored from the checkpoint; the lateness bound covers the downtime or a reprocess runs.

10. Observability.

  • CDN: hit ratio by path, origin egress, purge latency.
  • Object storage: 4xx/5xx rates, incomplete multipart bytes.
  • Lake: freshness per table, file counts and small-file compaction backlog.
  • Batch: duration, rows, restarts.
  • Stream: watermark lag, late-event and dropped counts, updates emitted, checkpoint duration.

14. Decision (ADR-088–092 summary). Blobs in object storage behind presigned URLs. A CDN with normalised keys, versioned assets and stale-if-error. Analytics only on an Iceberg lakehouse fed by CDC. Batch that is idempotent or atomically checkpointed. Streaming in event time with watermarks and allowed lateness, and batch as the source of truth for money.

docs.text:
Level New requirement that forces the step L1 "Get media and documents out of the database and off our servers." (S3 API on SeaweedFS, SigV4, presigned URLs, multipart) L2 "Make the CDN actually offload the origin and stay correct on price changes." (edge cache: keys, coalescing, invalidation, stale-if-error) L3 "Stop running BI on the orders primary." (ELT to Parquet, PostgreSQL vs DuckDB on 10M rows) L4 "Nightly jobs must survive crashes; the demand board must be right despite late events." (restartable batch on PostgreSQL, event-time windows)

All four levels ran on a 2 vCPU container, with the tools downloaded from their GitHub releases:

  • SeaweedFS 3.80 (S3 API on :8333)
  • DuckDB 1.1.3 CLI
  • PostgreSQL 16 (:5543, shared_buffers = 1GB)
  • Java 21 with the pgjdbc driver

The outputs below are verbatim. Lab files are in labs/ch21-data-at-scale/.

docs.title: L1 — Object storage over the S3 API, presigned URLs, multipart B2
docs.text:
Requirement: "Store product images, invoices and proof-of-delivery photos outside the database, and let the apps upload and download without our servers carrying the bytes."

The program speaks the S3 REST API directly, with AWS Signature V4 written out (canonical request → string to sign → derived key → HMAC). SDKs hide this, and seeing it once explains why presigned URLs are safe: the signature covers the method, path, expiry and signed headers.

ObjectStoreL1.java
// ObjectStoreL1.java — run with: java ObjectStoreL1.java     (needs an S3-compatible endpoint; the lab uses SeaweedFS 3.80 on :8333)
// Product images and invoices in object storage, using the plain S3 REST API with AWS Signature V4 written out by hand:
// bucket + PUT/GET/HEAD, range reads, prefix listing, presigned upload/download URLs (direct from the app, bypassing our servers),
// expiry and tampering, multipart upload with a failed part retried alone, and content-addressed keys for deduplication.
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.URLEncoder;
import java.net.http.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.time.*;
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.regex.*;
import javax.crypto.Mac;
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec;

public class ObjectStoreL1 {
    static final String ENDPOINT = "http://127.0.0.1:8333", HOST = "127.0.0.1:8333", REGION = "us-east-1";
    static final String ACCESS = "AKIDGROCERY", SECRET = "grocery-secret-key";
    static final HttpClient HTTP = HttpClient.newBuilder().version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_1_1).build();
    static final DateTimeFormatter AMZ = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyyMMdd'T'HHmmss'Z'").withZone(ZoneOffset.UTC);

    // ---------------- Signature V4 ----------------
    static String hex(byte[] b) { return HexFormat.of().formatHex(b); }
    static byte[] sha256(byte[] b) throws Exception { return MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(b); }
    static byte[] hmac(byte[] key, String data) throws Exception {
        Mac m = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256"); m.init(new SecretKeySpec(key, "HmacSHA256")); return m.doFinal(data.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    }
    static String enc(String s, boolean keepSlash) {
        String e = URLEncoder.encode(s, StandardCharsets.UTF_8).replace("+", "%20").replace("*", "%2A").replace("%7E", "~");
        return keepSlash ? e.replace("%2F", "/") : e;
    }
    static String canonicalQuery(Map<String, String> q) {
        var sb = new StringJoiner("&");
        new TreeMap<>(q).forEach((k, v) -> sb.add(enc(k, false) + "=" + enc(v, false)));
        return sb.toString();
    }
    static String signature(String method, String path, Map<String, String> query, Map<String, String> headers, String payloadHash, Instant t) throws Exception {
        String date = AMZ.format(t).substring(0, 8), scope = date + "/" + REGION + "/s3/aws4_request";
        var sorted = new TreeMap<String, String>(); headers.forEach((k, v) -> sorted.put(k.toLowerCase(), v.trim()));
        var ch = new StringBuilder(); sorted.forEach((k, v) -> ch.append(k).append(':').append(v).append('\n'));
        String signed = String.join(";", sorted.keySet());
        String canonical = method + "\n" + enc(path, true) + "\n" + canonicalQuery(query) + "\n" + ch + "\n" + signed + "\n" + payloadHash;
        String toSign = "AWS4-HMAC-SHA256\n" + AMZ.format(t) + "\n" + scope + "\n" + hex(sha256(canonical.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)));
        byte[] k = hmac(("AWS4" + SECRET).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8), date);
        k = hmac(k, REGION); k = hmac(k, "s3"); k = hmac(k, "aws4_request");
        return hex(hmac(k, toSign));
    }

    /** A signed request with the Authorization header (what an SDK does for server-side calls). */
    static HttpResponse<byte[]> s3(String method, String path, Map<String, String> query, byte[] body, Map<String, String> extra) throws Exception {
        Instant t = Instant.now();
        String payloadHash = body == null ? hex(sha256(new byte[0])) : hex(sha256(body));
        var headers = new LinkedHashMap<String, String>();
        headers.put("host", HOST); headers.put("x-amz-date", AMZ.format(t)); headers.put("x-amz-content-sha256", payloadHash);
        headers.putAll(extra);
        String sig = signature(method, path, query, headers, payloadHash, t);
        String date = AMZ.format(t).substring(0, 8);
        var signedNames = new TreeSet<String>(); headers.keySet().forEach(h -> signedNames.add(h.toLowerCase()));
        String auth = "AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 Credential=" + ACCESS + "/" + date + "/" + REGION + "/s3/aws4_request, SignedHeaders="
                + String.join(";", signedNames) + ", Signature=" + sig;
        String qs = query.isEmpty() ? "" : "?" + canonicalQuery(query);
        var b = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(ENDPOINT + enc(path, true) + qs)).header("Authorization", auth);
        headers.forEach((k, v) -> { if (!k.equals("host")) b.header(k, v); });
        b.method(method, body == null ? HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.noBody() : HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofByteArray(body));
        return HTTP.send(b.build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofByteArray());
    }
    static HttpResponse<byte[]> s3(String method, String path) throws Exception { return s3(method, path, Map.of(), null, Map.of()); }

    /** A presigned URL: the signature travels in the query string; anyone holding the URL may do exactly this operation until it expires. */
    static String presign(String method, String path, Duration expiresIn, Instant t) throws Exception {
        String date = AMZ.format(t).substring(0, 8);
        var q = new TreeMap<String, String>();
        q.put("X-Amz-Algorithm", "AWS4-HMAC-SHA256");
        q.put("X-Amz-Credential", ACCESS + "/" + date + "/" + REGION + "/s3/aws4_request");
        q.put("X-Amz-Date", AMZ.format(t));
        q.put("X-Amz-Expires", String.valueOf(expiresIn.toSeconds()));
        q.put("X-Amz-SignedHeaders", "host");
        String sig = signature(method, path, q, Map.of("host", HOST), "UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD", t);
        return ENDPOINT + enc(path, true) + "?" + canonicalQuery(q) + "&X-Amz-Signature=" + sig;
    }

    static int plain(String method, String url, byte[] body) throws Exception {
        var b = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(url)).method(method, body == null ? HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.noBody() : HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofByteArray(body));
        return HTTP.send(b.build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.discarding()).statusCode();
    }

    static String xml(byte[] body, String tag) { Matcher m = Pattern.compile("<" + tag + ">(.*?)</" + tag + ">").matcher(new String(body)); return m.find() ? m.group(1) : null; }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String bucket = "/catalog-media";
        s3("PUT", bucket);                                                                         // create bucket (idempotent here)
        Random rnd = new Random(1);

        System.out.println("A. Basic object operations (SeaweedFS S3 API, SigV4 signed)");
        byte[] img = new byte[480_000]; rnd.nextBytes(img);
        var put = s3("PUT", bucket + "/products/sku-1001/main.jpg", Map.of(), img, Map.of("content-type", "image/jpeg", "cache-control", "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"));
        System.out.printf("   PUT products/sku-1001/main.jpg (%,d B)  → %d, ETag %s%n", img.length, put.statusCode(), put.headers().firstValue("etag").orElse("?"));
        var head = s3("HEAD", bucket + "/products/sku-1001/main.jpg");
        System.out.printf("   HEAD                                  → %d, Content-Length %s, Content-Type %s%n", head.statusCode(),
                head.headers().firstValue("content-length").orElse("?"), head.headers().firstValue("content-type").orElse("?"));
        var range = s3("GET", bucket + "/products/sku-1001/main.jpg", Map.of(), null, Map.of("range", "bytes=0-1023"));
        System.out.printf("   GET Range bytes=0-1023                → %d, %,d bytes (thumbnail header / resumable download)%n", range.statusCode(), range.body().length);
        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) s3("PUT", bucket + "/products/sku-1002/img-" + i + ".jpg", Map.of(), new byte[1000 * i], Map.of());
        var list = s3("GET", bucket, Map.of("list-type", "2", "prefix", "products/sku-1002/"), null, Map.of());
        System.out.printf("   LIST prefix products/sku-1002/        → %d, %s keys%n", list.statusCode(), xml(list.body(), "KeyCount"));

        System.out.println("B. Presigned URLs: the app uploads straight to storage; our servers only sign");
        Instant now = Instant.now();
        String upUrl = presign("PUT", bucket + "/uploads/rider-77/proof-of-delivery.jpg", Duration.ofMinutes(5), now);
        System.out.printf("   presigned PUT, valid 5 min            → %d%n", plain("PUT", upUrl, img));
        String getUrl = presign("GET", bucket + "/uploads/rider-77/proof-of-delivery.jpg", Duration.ofMinutes(5), now);
        System.out.printf("   presigned GET                         → %d%n", plain("GET", getUrl, null));
        String tampered = getUrl.replace("rider-77", "rider-78");
        System.out.printf("   same URL, key changed to rider-78     → %d (signature covers the path)%n", plain("GET", tampered, null));
        String expired = presign("GET", bucket + "/uploads/rider-77/proof-of-delivery.jpg", Duration.ofSeconds(60), now.minus(Duration.ofMinutes(10)));
        System.out.printf("   URL signed 10 min ago, valid 60 s     → %d (expired)%n", plain("GET", expired, null));
        System.out.printf("   unsigned GET of a private object      → %d%n", plain("GET", ENDPOINT + bucket + "/uploads/rider-77/proof-of-delivery.jpg", null));

        System.out.println("C. Multipart upload: 40 MB invoice archive in 8 MB parts, part 3 fails once and is retried alone");
        byte[] big = new byte[40 * 1024 * 1024]; rnd.nextBytes(big);
        String key = bucket + "/exports/2026-09-25/invoices.tar";
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        String uploadId = xml(s3("POST", key, Map.of("uploads", ""), null, Map.of()).body(), "UploadId");
        var etags = new ArrayList<String>(); long sent = 0; int partSize = 8 * 1024 * 1024; boolean failedOnce = false;
        for (int part = 1; part <= 5; part++) {
            byte[] chunk = Arrays.copyOfRange(big, (part - 1) * partSize, part * partSize);
            if (part == 3 && !failedOnce) { failedOnce = true; sent += chunk.length / 2; System.out.println("   part 3: (simulated) connection reset after 4 MB → only part 3 is sent again"); }
            var r = s3("PUT", key, Map.of("partNumber", String.valueOf(part), "uploadId", uploadId), chunk, Map.of());
            etags.add(r.headers().firstValue("etag").orElseThrow()); sent += chunk.length;
        }
        var cx = new StringBuilder("<CompleteMultipartUpload>");
        for (int i = 0; i < etags.size(); i++) cx.append("<Part><PartNumber>").append(i + 1).append("</PartNumber><ETag>").append(etags.get(i)).append("</ETag></Part>");
        cx.append("</CompleteMultipartUpload>");
        var done = s3("POST", key, Map.of("uploadId", uploadId), cx.toString().getBytes(), Map.of());
        long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000;
        var check = s3("GET", key);
        System.out.printf("   complete → %d in %,d ms; bytes sent %,d MB for a %,d MB object (a failed single PUT resends all 40 MB)%n",
                done.statusCode(), ms, sent >> 20, big.length >> 20);
        System.out.printf("   multipart ETag %s: not the MD5 of the object; verify with your own checksum%n", xml(done.body(), "ETag").replace(""", "\""));
        System.out.printf("   downloaded object identical: %s%n", Arrays.equals(sha256(check.body()), sha256(big)));

        System.out.println("D. Content-addressed keys: the same image uploaded by 3 sellers is stored once");
        byte[] sellerImg = new byte[300_000]; rnd.nextBytes(sellerImg);
        int stored = 0;
        s3("DELETE", bucket + "/blobs/sha256/" + hex(sha256(sellerImg)));                        // clean start for re-runs
        for (String seller : List.of("seller-a", "seller-b", "seller-c")) {
            String cas = bucket + "/blobs/sha256/" + hex(sha256(sellerImg));
            if (s3("HEAD", cas).statusCode() == 404) { s3("PUT", cas, Map.of(), sellerImg, Map.of()); stored++; }
            // the catalog row stores (seller, sku) → blob key; the blob key never changes, so it can be cached forever
        }
        System.out.printf("   uploads 3, objects stored %d, key blobs/sha256/%s…%n", stored, hex(sha256(sellerImg)).substring(0, 16));
    }
}
java ObjectStoreL1.java (SeaweedFS: weed server -s3 -s3.config=s3.json)
A. Basic object operations (SeaweedFS S3 API, SigV4 signed)
   PUT products/sku-1001/main.jpg (480,000 B)  → 200, ETag "929df4cadcea3fdff1ba15cacfdb132b"
   HEAD                                  → 200, Content-Length 480000, Content-Type image/jpeg
   GET Range bytes=0-1023                → 206, 1,024 bytes (thumbnail header / resumable download)
   LIST prefix products/sku-1002/        → 200, 3 keys
B. Presigned URLs: the app uploads straight to storage; our servers only sign
   presigned PUT, valid 5 min            → 200
   presigned GET                         → 200
   same URL, key changed to rider-78     → 403 (signature covers the path)
   URL signed 10 min ago, valid 60 s     → 403 (expired)
   unsigned GET of a private object      → 403
