    static float[] concepts(String spec, Random noise, double sigma) {
        float[] x = new float[DIMS.length];
        for (String part : spec.split(" ")) {
            if (part.isBlank()) continue;
            String[] kv = part.split(":"); int d = Arrays.asList(DIMS).indexOf(kv[0]);
            x[d] += kv.length > 1 ? Float.parseFloat(kv[1]) : 1f;
        }
        double norm = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < x.length; i++) { if (noise != null) x[i] += (float) (noise.nextGaussian() * sigma); norm += x[i] * x[i]; }
        if (norm == 0) return x;
        for (int i = 0; i < x.length; i++) x[i] /= (float) Math.sqrt(norm);
        return x;
    }
    static float[] embedQuery(String q) {
        String spec = Catalog.tokenize(q).stream().map(t -> QUERY_LEXICON.getOrDefault(t, "")).collect(Collectors.joining(" "));
        return concepts(spec, null, 0);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // ---------- Part A ----------
        int n = 100_000, dim = 64;
        float[][] data = clustered(n, dim, 200, 11), queries = clustered(200, dim, 200, 99);
        System.out.printf("A. %,d vectors × %d dims (200 clusters), 200 queries, top-10 by cosine%n", n, dim);
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        int[][] truth = new int[queries.length][];
        for (int i = 0; i < queries.length; i++) truth[i] = exactTopK(data, queries[i], 10);
        double bruteMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6 / queries.length;
        System.out.printf("   brute force (exact)          : recall 1.000, %6.2f ms/query%n", bruteMs);
        for (boolean heur : List.of(false, true)) {
            t0 = System.nanoTime();
            Hnsw h = new Hnsw(data, 16, 100, heur);
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) h.insert(i);
            long buildMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000;
            long edges = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) for (int c : h.counts[i]) edges += c;
            System.out.printf("   HNSW, %s neighbour selection (M=16, efConstruction=100): build %,d ms, %,d links (~%,d KB on top of %,d KB of vectors)%n",
                    heur ? "heuristic" : "simple   ", buildMs, edges, edges * 4 / 1024, (long) n * dim * 4 / 1024);
            for (int ef : new int[]{10, 20, 40, 80, 160}) {
                double recall = 0; long s = System.nanoTime();
                for (int r = 0; r < 3; r++) for (int i = 0; i < queries.length; i++) {
                    int[] got = h.search(queries[i], 10, ef);
                    if (r == 0) { Set<Integer> tset = Arrays.stream(truth[i]).boxed().collect(Collectors.toSet()); recall += Arrays.stream(got).filter(tset::contains).count() / 10.0; }
                }
                double ms = (System.nanoTime() - s) / 1e6 / (3 * queries.length);
                System.out.printf("      efSearch=%-4d : recall@10 %.3f, %6.3f ms/query (%.0fx faster than brute force)%n", ef, recall / queries.length, ms, bruteMs / ms);
            }
        }

        // ---------- Part B ----------
        List<Catalog.Product> docs = Catalog.products(20_000);
        var bm25 = new SearchL1.Index(new SearchL1.Analyzer("final", true, true, true, true, 2, true), docs);
        Random noise = new Random(3);
        float[][] pv = new float[docs.size()][];
        for (int i = 0; i < docs.size(); i++) pv[i] = concepts(TYPE_CONCEPTS.get(docs.get(i).type()), noise, 0.05);

        List<Catalog.Judged> intents = List.of(
            new Catalog.Judged("healthy breakfast", Set.of("oats", "poha", "banana"), null),
            new Catalog.Judged("something for chai", Set.of("tea", "biscuit", "milk", "sugar", "namkeen"), null),
            new Catalog.Judged("party snacks", Set.of("chips", "namkeen", "cola"), null),
            new Catalog.Judged("cleaning supplies", Set.of("detergent", "dishwash"), null),
            new Catalog.Judged("dal tadka ingredients", Set.of("toor-dal", "moong-dal", "chana-dal", "cumin", "turmeric", "ghee", "onion", "tomato"), null),
            new Catalog.Judged("high protein veg", Set.of("paneer", "toor-dal", "moong-dal", "chana-dal", "curd"), null),
            new Catalog.Judged("breakfast", Set.of("cornflakes", "oats", "poha", "bread", "eggs", "milk", "butter", "banana"), null),
            new Catalog.Judged("bath essentials", Set.of("soap", "shampoo"), null));

        System.out.println("B. Lexical vs vector vs hybrid (RRF, k = 60, top 100 from each) — toy concept embeddings, see header");
        System.out.printf("   %-36s %18s %18s%n", "retriever", "20 lexical queries", "8 intent queries");
        for (String mode : List.of("BM25 (L1 final analyzer)", "vector (concept embedding)", "hybrid: RRF(BM25, vector)", "hybrid: weighted RRF (vector ×0.5)")) {
            double[] sums = new double[2]; int set = 0;
            for (List<Catalog.Judged> qs : List.of(Catalog.QUERIES, intents)) {
                for (var q : qs) {
                    List<Integer> lex = bm25.score(q.query()).entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.<Integer, Double>comparingByValue().reversed().thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey()))
                            .limit(100).map(Map.Entry::getKey).toList();
                    float[] qv = embedQuery(q.query());
                    boolean emptyQ = true; for (float x : qv) if (x != 0) emptyQ = false;
                    List<Integer> vec = emptyQ ? List.of() : Arrays.stream(exactTopK(pv, qv, 100)).boxed()
                            .sorted(Comparator.comparingDouble((Integer i) -> -Hnsw.dot(pv[i], qv)).thenComparing(i -> i)).toList();
                    List<Integer> ranked;
                    if (mode.startsWith("BM25")) ranked = lex;
                    else if (mode.startsWith("vector")) ranked = vec;
                    else {
                        Map<Integer, Double> rrf = new HashMap<>();
                        for (int i = 0; i < lex.size(); i++) rrf.merge(lex.get(i), 1.0 / (60 + i + 1), Double::sum);
                        double w = mode.contains("weighted") ? 0.5 : 1.0;
                        for (int i = 0; i < vec.size(); i++) rrf.merge(vec.get(i), w / (60 + i + 1), Double::sum);
                        ranked = rrf.entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.<Integer, Double>comparingByValue().reversed().thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey()))
                                .map(Map.Entry::getKey).toList();
                    }
                    sums[set] += Catalog.ndcg(q, ranked.stream().limit(10).map(docs::get).toList(), docs, 10);
                }
                sums[set] /= qs.size(); set++;
            }
            System.out.printf("   %-36s %18.3f %18.3f%n", mode, sums[0], sums[1]);
        }
    }
}

   retriever                            20 lexical queries   8 intent queries
   BM25 (L1 final analyzer)                          1.000              0.542
   vector (concept embedding)                        0.289              0.740
   hybrid: RRF(BM25, vector)                         0.903              0.769
   hybrid: weighted RRF (vector ×0.5)                1.000              0.797

Reading it:

  • ANN trade-off:
    • With the simple "keep the M closest" neighbour lists, recall plateaus: 0.945 at efSearch 160, where the graph clusters and search gets stuck.
    • The paper's heuristic keeps a neighbour only if it's closer to the node than to already-kept neighbours, so links point in diverse directions. That reaches 0.991 at efSearch 40 (34x faster than brute force) and 1.000 at 80, for 50 % more build time.
    • Use mature libraries (Lucene HNSW, FAISS, hnswlib, pgvector), and still measure recall on your data and filters.
  • Hybrid:
    • BM25 is perfect on the lexical set and weak on intents (0.542). Vectors are the reverse (0.289 vs 0.740).
    • Plain RRF helps intents (0.769) but dilutes exact queries (0.903). Down-weighting the vector list keeps exact queries at 1.000 and lifts intents to 0.797, better than either retriever alone.
    • The weight was tuned on the same queries it reports. In production, tune on a held-out set and confirm online with interleaving.

Spring shapes (VERIFY: OpenSearch client and Spring Data not downloadable here)

// search-service: query with analyzer-aware multi_match, synonyms at search time, function score, filters
SearchResponse<ProductDoc> r = client.search(s -> s.index("products-" + city)
    .query(q -> q.functionScore(fs -> fs
        .query(inner -> inner.bool(b -> b
            .must(m -> m.multiMatch(mm -> mm.query(userQuery).fields("name^2", "aliases^1.5", "type^3", "brand", "category")
                    .fuzziness("AUTO:5,8").analyzer("grocery_search")))
            .filter(f -> f.term(t -> t.field("available_stores").value(storeId)))))
        .functions(fn -> fn.fieldValueFactor(fv -> fv.field("popularity").modifier(FieldValueFactorModifier.Log1p).factor(0.1)))
        .boostMode(FunctionBoostMode.Multiply)))
    .aggregations("category", a -> a.terms(t -> t.field("category")))
    .size(20), ProductDoc.class);

// indexer: Kafka keyed by productId → bulk with external versioning (older versions rejected)
@KafkaListener(topics = "catalog.product.changed.v1", groupId = "search-indexer", batch = "true")
void index(List<ProductChanged> events) throws IOException {
    var bulk = new BulkRequest.Builder();
    for (var e : events) bulk.operations(op -> op.index(i -> i.index("products-" + e.city()).id(e.productId())
            .version(e.version()).versionType(VersionType.External).document(ProductDoc.from(e))));
    client.bulk(bulk.build());
}

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Symptom Cause Mitigation Zero results for common intents High zero-result rate, lost orders No transliteration/synonyms, vocabulary mismatch Analyzer stages (L1), aliases (L3), weekly zero-result review Relevance regression after a config change CTR drops, complaints Untested synonym/boost/fuzzy change (L1: fuzzy broke "chai") Judged-query CI, staged rollout, config in Git Out-of-stock at the top Low add-to-cart Ranking ignores availability Stock filter/demotion at query time (L1 C) Index lag Old prices/stock in results Indexer synchronous per request, bulk too small, refresh too frequent Pipelining, bulk sizing (L3: 22 s → 0.8 s), refresh interval Stale documents Index disagrees with DB permanently Out-of-order updates (L3: 26 regressions), lost deletes Key-partitioned stream, external versions, tombstones, periodic reconciliation Reindex outage Empty results during rebuild In-place rebuild Build new index + alias swap (L3: 0 errors) Hot shard / GC pauses p99 spikes during sales Large shards, deep pagination, expensive aggregations Shard sizing (10–50 GB), search_after instead of deep from, circuit breakers ANN recall collapse with filters Few or wrong results for filtered vector queries Pre-filtering breaks HNSW graph connectivity Engine's filtered-ANN mode; fall back to exact search for highly selective filters Query-of-death Cluster CPU saturates Leading wildcards, huge OR expansions, regexes Query validation, disallow leading wildcards, limits on expansion

docs.title: 6.2 Observability
docs.text:
• Quality: zero-result rate (by script/language, by city), CTR@k, add-to-cart per search, reformulation rate, nDCG on the judged set per deploy, top zero-result queries (a daily report).
  • Latency: p50/p99 for search and autocomplete; engine-side took-time vs service-side total (network, re-ranking, inventory lookups).
  • Indexing: end-to-end lag (commit → searchable), bulk rejections, version conflicts (a proxy for out-of-order events), document count vs source count (reconciliation).
  • Engine health: heap, GC, segment count, merge throttling, query cache hit rates, shard balance.

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Treat queries as untrusted input. Build queries with the client's typed API, never by concatenating a query DSL string. Disallow scripting and leading wildcards, and cap query length and expansions.
  • Document-level security: customers must never see unpublished products, other sellers' drafts or restricted items (age-restricted, region-restricted). Use filters applied server-side, not client-provided ones.
  • Don't index PII into product search. Back-office search over customers/orders is a separate, access-controlled index with audit logging (Ch 23, Ch 36).
  • Logs: search queries can contain personal data (names, phone numbers typed into the box). Redact before storing query logs, and set retention.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance & tuning knobs
docs.text: Knob Guidance Shard size 10–50 GB per shard; shards × replicas sized to QPS and data Refresh interval 1 s default; raise during bulk loads (or -1), lower only if the product needs it Bulk size 5–15 MB per request; pipeline several in flight (L3) Fuzziness AUTO:5,8 style; prefix_length 1–2; max expansions ≤ 50 Result window Avoid deep from; use search_after or scroll/PIT for exports Filters Put exact constraints in filter context (cached, not scored) Re-ranking Re-rank only the top 100–1,000 with expensive features/models HNSW M 16–32, efConstruction 100–200, efSearch tuned to recall target (L4); quantise for memory Autocomplete Client debounce 100–150 ms, prefix cache, a dedicated lightweight index

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• Search clusters are memory-hungry (heap + OS page cache for segments), and vector fields multiply that. Quantisation and dimension choice (384 vs 1,536) are cost decisions.
  • Replicas cost the same as primaries. Scale replicas for QPS and primaries for data size.
  • The cheapest relevance gains in this chapter came from data: aliases, synonyms, a type field. They cost merchandising hours, not machines.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. LIKE '%term%' as product search.

-- ❌ before: sequential scan, no ranking, no typos, no transliteration
select * from product where name ilike '%' || :q || '%' limit 20;
-- ✅ after (small scale): trigram + full-text with ranking; (large scale) a search engine
select id, name from product where doc @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', :q)
order by ts_rank(doc, websearch_to_tsquery('english', :q)) desc limit 20;

2. Different analyzers at index and query time by accident. If the index lowercases and transliterates but the query path doesn't (or the reverse), matches silently vanish. Define analyzers once, in the index settings, and test them with the _analyze API in CI.

3. Unbounded fuzziness (L1: "chai" → "chakki").

// ❌ before
{ "match": { "name": { "query": "chai patti", "fuzziness": 2 } } }
// ✅ after: no edits for short terms, first chars exact, fuzzy matches score lower than exact ones
{ "bool": { "should": [
    { "match": { "name": { "query": "chai patti", "boost": 2 } } },
    { "match": { "name": { "query": "chai patti", "fuzziness": "AUTO:5,8", "prefix_length": 1 } } } ] } }

4. Synonyms edited in production without tests. One bad rule ("oil ↔ ghee") reshapes thousands of queries. Keep synonyms in Git, run judged-query CI, and deploy with search-time synonym sets that can be reloaded and rolled back.

5. Ranking by text score alone. Out-of-stock and unpopular items float to the top (L1: 11 of 60 top-3 slots out of stock). Combine text relevance with availability and popularity in a function score, or re-rank.

6. Dual writes from the service to the index.

// ❌ before
productRepo.save(p); searchClient.index(p);        // either can fail; the index drifts forever
// ✅ after: outbox in the same transaction, indexer consumes it (Ch 13)
tx.execute(s -> { productRepo.save(p); outbox.add(ProductChanged.of(p)); return null; });

7. Parallel indexers without per-key ordering (L3: 26 regressions, 3 stale).

// ❌ before: workers grab any batch
executor.submit(() -> index(batch));
// ✅ after: partition by product id (Kafka key) and/or send external versions so older writes are rejected
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("catalog.product.changed.v1", productId, event));

8. Synchronous indexing, one request per change (L3: 22 s lag). Batch and pipeline. Let the engine's queue and bulk API absorb bursts.

9. Reindexing in place. Deleting and rebuilding the live index shows customers empty results. Build alongside, validate, swap the alias (L3).

10. Vector-only search.

❌ "atta 5kg" → vector search → rice, poha, oats (all "staple grains")      (L4: 0.289 on lexical queries)
✅ hybrid: BM25 for exact tokens + vectors for intent, fused with weighted RRF   (L4: 1.000 lexical, 0.797 intent)

11. Trusting relevance numbers from a tiny, self-written judged set. L1 hit 1.000. Real evaluation needs hundreds of sampled queries, independent judges, and online confirmation.

12. Deep pagination with from/size. from=10000 makes every shard collect 10,020 hits. Use search_after with a point-in-time for exports, and cap UI pagination.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What is an inverted index?

30-second answer: A map from each term to the list of documents that contain it (a postings list), often with term frequencies and positions. To search, you look up each query term's postings and combine them, instead of scanning every document. It's how search engines answer queries over millions of documents in milliseconds.

Deep answer: - Engines like Lucene store a sorted term dictionary and compressed postings in immutable segments, which get merged in the background. - L1's from-scratch index answered queries 194x faster than scanning 20,000 products. - Positions allow phrase queries, and doc values (columnar) support sorting and facets.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Fast reads vs index build/update cost and near-real-time visibility.

Follow-ups: 1. Why are segments immutable? → Simple concurrency and caching; updates are delete + add. 2. What is a refresh? → Making new segments searchable (default 1 s).

Red flags: "It's a B-tree on the text column."

Q2 [B1] ⭐ What is an analyzer, and why does it matter?

30-second answer: The pipeline that turns text into index terms: normalise characters, split into tokens, then filter (lowercase, stem, synonyms, remove stop words, transliterate). The same analysis must happen to documents at index time and to queries at search time, or they won't match. It's the biggest single lever on search quality.

Deep answer: L1 measured it: lowercase-and-split scored nDCG 0.367. Adding units, stemming, Devanagari transliteration, Hinglish phonetic normalisation, synonyms and guarded fuzziness reached 0.950, and a type field reached 1.000, on the same data and the same BM25.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Aggressive normalisation improves recall but can hurt precision (over-stemming, over-fuzzing).

Follow-ups: 1. Index-time vs query-time synonyms? → Query-time can change without reindexing. 2. How do you debug one? → The _analyze API / printing the tokens.

Red flags: "The engine handles language automatically."

Q3 [B1] What is BM25?

30-second answer: The standard relevance-scoring function in search engines. It scores a document higher when:

  • query terms are rare in the collection (IDF);
  • they appear more often in the document, with diminishing returns (tf saturation, k1);
  • the matching field is shorter (length normalisation, b).

Per-field boosts weight matches in the name above the description.

Deep answer: Defaults are k1 ≈ 1.2 and b ≈ 0.75. BM25F combines fields. L1 implements it in about 20 lines with name ×2 and a type field ×3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Purely lexical: no understanding of meaning (hence vectors, §2.12).

Follow-ups: 1. Why saturate tf? → Keyword stuffing shouldn't win. 2. What does IDF do for "fresh" vs "paneer"? → "fresh" is common and weighs less.

Red flags: "It counts how many times the word appears."

Q4 [B1] What are facets?

30-second answer: Counts of results per attribute value for the current query, such as "Masala 1,022, Snacks 240" or brand and price bands. They're shown as filters so customers can narrow down. They're computed from columnar doc values in the engine, or with GROUP BY in SQL.

Deep answer: L1, L2 and L3 compute facets for "masala". Facet counts respect the current filters, except the facet being selected, so multi-select works. Engines may approximate totals (L3: an estimated 1,000 vs 1,262).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Many facets with high cardinality cost latency and memory.

Follow-ups: 1. Filter vs query? → Filters don't score and can be cached. 2. How do you do price bands? → Range aggregations.

Red flags: Computing facets by fetching all results into the service.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How would you support Hindi, Hinglish and typos in grocery search?

30-second answer: - Normalise to a common form at both index and query time: Unicode normalisation, Devanagari→Latin transliteration, and a phonetic normaliser for Hinglish spellings (aa→a, oo→u, collapse double letters). - Add cross-language synonyms (milk↔doodh) keyed on the normalised forms, plus index-time aliases per product type. - Use guarded fuzziness (≥ 5 characters, penalised) for typos. - Measure each step on judged queries.

Deep answer: - L1: आटा, aata and Atta all become ata. nDCG went 0.457 → 0.607 with transliteration + phonetic, then 0.900 with synonyms. - Naive fuzzy mapped "chai" to "chakki". - L3 shows aliases taking a stock engine from 0.779 to 0.979. - For more languages, use ICU transforms / IndicNLP, and a multilingual embedding model in hybrid search.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Normalisation collisions (different words mapping to the same form) vs recall.

Follow-ups: 1. Where do aliases come from? → Query logs, merchandisers, click data. 2. What about regional scripts? → The same approach per script; transliterate to Latin or index both forms.

Red flags: "Turn on fuzziness 2."

Q6 [B2] ⭐ How do you keep a search index in sync with the database?

30-second answer: Treat the index as a derived read model. The service writes the entity and an outbox row in one transaction. CDC or a relay publishes events to Kafka keyed by product id. An indexer consumes them and sends bulk upserts/deletes to the engine, preserving per-product order (or using external versions so older writes are rejected). A periodic reconciliation compares counts and checksums, and full rebuilds go to a new index behind an alias.

Deep answer: - L3 measured it: pipelined bulk indexing kept commit→searchable at ~0.8 s, where waiting per task gave 22 s. - Unordered parallel indexers overwrote newer data 26 times, and key partitioning gave 0. - Deletes need tombstones. - Denormalised fields (a brand rename) need fan-out reindex jobs.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Seconds of staleness vs coupling the write path to the engine.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not update the index in the request? → Dual-write drift and coupling (Ch 13). 2. How do you backfill? → Snapshot + stream from the snapshot's position.

Red flags: "We reindex everything nightly" for price/stock.

Q7 [B2] When is PostgreSQL full-text search enough?

30-second answer: For small-to-medium catalogs, internal/admin tools, and when you want transactional consistency and one fewer system:

  • tsvector + GIN with websearch_to_tsquery and ts_rank;
  • pg_trgm for substring and typo tolerance;
  • GROUPING SETS for facets.

Move to an engine when you need custom analyzers (transliteration), sophisticated relevance tuning, high QPS isolated from OLTP, or vector/hybrid at scale.

Deep answer: L2 on 200K listings: trigram GIN halved substring search, full-text stemmed "tomatos" correctly, and word_similarity found "Shampoo" for "shampo". But Devanagari produced no lexemes, and Hinglish found nothing.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Simplicity and consistency vs capability and isolation.

Follow-ups: 1. What about pgvector? → Fine for vectors at moderate scale; the same OLTP-isolation question applies. 2. Can you add custom dictionaries? → Yes (ispell/synonym dictionaries), with limits.

Red flags: "Postgres can't do search."

Q8 [B2] How do you implement autocomplete?

30-second answer: Options:

  • an edge n-gram field (prefixes indexed ahead of time);
  • a completion suggester (in-memory FST with weights);
  • prefix queries;
  • suggesting popular past queries.

Combine with typo tolerance for longer prefixes, filter by availability, and rank by popularity. On the client, debounce (100–150 ms) and cancel superseded requests. Cache hot prefixes. Target < 50 ms.

Deep answer: L2 shows to_tsquery('sham:*') and trigram similarity. Meilisearch does prefix search by default (L3). A query-log-based suggester needs moderation (no offensive or personal suggestions).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Index size (n-grams) vs query cost (prefix scans).

Follow-ups: 1. Why suggest queries, not products? → They generalise better and lead to a full results page. 2. How do you handle the first character? → Require 2+ characters, or serve cached top suggestions.

Red flags: A full search per keystroke with no debounce.

Q9 [B2] How do you combine text relevance with business signals?

30-second answer: Retrieve candidates by text relevance, then adjust. A function score multiplies BM25 by functions of popularity, recency or margin, and availability becomes a filter or a strong demotion. Or re-rank the top N with a learning-to-rank model trained on clicks and purchases. Keep filters for hard constraints (the store's assortment), and scores for preferences.

Deep answer: L1: score × (1 + 0.1·ln(1+popularity)) × (inStock ? 1 : 0.3) removed out-of-stock items from the top 3 (11 → 0 of 60) with nDCG 1.000 → 0.992. Log-scaling stops popular items from swamping relevance. Measure with online metrics (add-to-cart), not just nDCG.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Business boosts can bury the most relevant item. Cap their weight.

Follow-ups: 1. What about sponsored products? → A separate, labelled slot, not mixed into relevance. 2. Personalisation? → A re-ranking feature, with privacy controls.

Red flags: Sorting purely by margin.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ How do you evaluate and improve search relevance systematically?

30-second answer: - Offline: a judged query set sampled from logs (head, torso, tail, zero-result), graded judgments, and metrics (nDCG@10, precision@k, zero-result rate) run in CI on every change. - Online: CTR, add-to-cart from search, reformulation rate, with A/B tests or interleaving. - Loop: a weekly review of zero-result and low-CTR queries feeds synonyms, aliases, analyzer changes and training data.

Deep answer: - Every table in this chapter is an offline evaluation: L1's stages, L3's configurations, L4's retrievers. - Beware overfitting: L1's 1.000 on 20 self-written queries. - Click data has position bias: use interleaving, or correct with propensity models.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Judgment cost vs confidence; offline metrics vs business outcomes.

Follow-ups: 1. How many queries? → Hundreds to thousands, stratified by traffic. 2. What is interleaving? → Merging two rankings into one list and attributing clicks to each; needs less traffic than A/B.

Red flags: "It looks good to me" as the evaluation.

Q11 [B3] ⭐ Explain how HNSW works and how you tune it.

30-second answer: A multi-layer proximity graph. Upper layers are sparse, long-range links, and layer 0 has all nodes. A search greedily walks from the top entry point down, then does a best-first search with a candidate list of size efSearch on layer 0. Parameters:

  • M (links per node): memory and recall;
  • efConstruction: graph quality and build time;
  • efSearch: recall vs latency per query.

Deep answer: - L4 from scratch on 100K × 64: simple neighbour selection plateaued at 0.945 recall. - The paper's diversity heuristic reached 0.991 at efSearch 40 (34x faster than brute force) and 1.000 at 80. - Tune efSearch per recall SLO on your own data, including filtered queries. - Memory is vectors plus ~4 B × links. Quantise for large collections.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Memory and build time vs query speed; recall is probabilistic.

Follow-ups: 1. IVF-PQ vs HNSW? → IVF-PQ is memory-efficient on disk/GPU; HNSW has the best recall/latency in RAM. 2. Deletes in HNSW? → Tombstones plus periodic rebuilds.

Red flags: "Vector search is exact."

Q12 [B3] Two indexers update the same product out of order. What happens and how do you prevent it?

30-second answer: The engine applies the later-arriving write, even if it carries older data, so the index shows a stale price until the next update, which may never come. Prevent it by:

  • preserving per-key order (Kafka key = product id, one consumer per partition);
  • making writes version-aware (external versioning rejects lower versions);
  • reconciling periodically against the source.

Deep answer: L3: two indexers with alternating chunks applied 26 older versions over newer ones and left 3 of 20 hot products stale. Partitioning by product id fixed both. It's the same race as the fencing problem in Ch 20: the resource must reject stale writes, or ordering must be guaranteed.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Partitioning limits parallelism per hot key; versioning needs a monotonic version from the source.

Follow-ups: 1. Where does the version come from? → A row version / LSN from the source DB. 2. What about deletes? → Versioned tombstones.

Red flags: "Last write wins is fine."

Q13 [B3] How do you reindex a live index with new analyzers without downtime?

30-second answer: 1. Create products_v2 with the new settings, bulk-load from a snapshot, and record the stream position at the start. 2. Replay changes from that position until caught up (or dual-index both versions from the stream). 3. Validate counts, judged-query nDCG and shadow traffic. 4. Atomically swap the alias (or Meilisearch's swap-indexes). 5. Keep v1 for rollback.

Deep answer: L3 rebuilt and swapped in ~5 s while 4 clients searched: 6,604 queries, 0 empty, 0 errors. For large indexes: raise the refresh interval and turn replicas off during the load, then restore. Throttle to protect live search.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Double capacity during the rebuild.

Follow-ups: 1. What if validation fails? → Discard v2; the alias never moved. 2. How do you avoid missing updates? → Stream position captured before the snapshot.

Red flags: Deleting and recreating the live index.

Q14 [B3] ⭐ Should product search results reflect real-time stock at the customer's dark store? How?

30-second answer: Yes: showing unavailable items first loses orders. But don't reindex product documents on every stock change across hundreds of stores. Options:

  • index per-store availability as a compact field (a store-id list or bitset) updated from inventory events;
  • apply availability at query time from a fast inventory read model (Redis) as a filter or a re-rank on the top N candidates.

Hybrid: a coarse "available somewhere in the city" in the index, precise per-store at query time.

Deep answer: L1 showed ranking with stock demotion (11 → 0 out-of-stock in the top 3). Stock changes are high-frequency, so keep them out of heavy documents. The checkout re-validates availability anyway (Ch 46).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Index churn vs query-time lookup latency.

Follow-ups: 1. Filter or demote? → Filter for "unavailable forever here", demote for "temporarily out". 2. Latency budget for the stock lookup? → Under ~10 ms for 200 candidates via batched Redis.

Red flags: Reindexing a 2 KB document per stock tick per store.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design product search for a grocery platform with 400K SKUs in 12 cities.

30-second answer: - Engine: OpenSearch, an index alias per city (assortment), ~5M docs, 3 primaries × 2 replicas. - Analyzer: transliteration + Hinglish phonetics + units + light stemming, plus an aliases field and a type field. Query-time synonyms as reviewed config. - Ranking: a multi_match with field boosts, a function score for popularity, and per-store stock applied at query time. - Sync: outbox → Kafka keyed by product id → a bulk indexer with external versions. - Relevance CI on judged queries; hybrid vectors in phase 2. - Targets: p99 < 150 ms, lag < 5 s.

Deep answer (§4): Capacity: ~350 QPS average, 1,400 peak, 7,000 autocomplete QPS. Failure modes: lag alerts, a degraded mode with cached popular results, judged-query gating of config. Each design choice ties to a lab: analyzers (L1), sync and ordering (L3), hybrid (L4).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Operating a search cluster vs SaaS (data residency and cost at this scale).

Follow-ups: 1. Why per-city indexes? → Assortment and relevance differ; smaller shards. 2. How do you launch a new city? → A new index from a template, bulk load, alias.

Red flags: No mention of relevance measurement.

Q16 [B4] ⭐ Lexical, vector or hybrid: how do you decide, and how do you fuse results?

30-second answer: Lexical (BM25) wins on exact tokens: brands, sizes, SKUs, rare words. Vectors win on intent and paraphrase. Most product search needs both. Run both retrievers and fuse with reciprocal rank fusion (k ≈ 60), weighted by retriever, or normalise scores and blend. Optionally re-rank the fused top 100 with a cross-encoder or LTR model. Decide weights on held-out judged queries and confirm online.

Deep answer: L4 (toy embeddings): BM25 scored 1.000 lexical / 0.542 intent, vectors 0.289 / 0.740, plain RRF 0.903 / 0.769, and weighted RRF 1.000 / 0.797. Hybrid costs two retrievals plus vector infrastructure, so gate it by query type if latency matters (a classifier routes intent-like queries).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Latency and cost vs coverage of intent queries.

Follow-ups: 1. Why RRF over score blending? → Scores aren't comparable across retrievers; ranks are. 2. Which embedding model? → A multilingual sentence model, fine-tuned on query–product click pairs.

Red flags: Replacing BM25 with vectors wholesale.

Q17 [B4] Search latency p99 doubles during a flash sale. How do you investigate and fix it?

30-second answer: Split the latency into engine took-time vs service time (re-ranking, stock lookups, network).

  • Engine side: check hot shards (uneven routing), GC and heap, query cache hit rate, merge storms from heavy indexing (price updates), and expensive queries (deep pagination, big aggregations, fuzzy expansions).
  • Short term: add replicas, raise the refresh interval, throttle indexing, cache popular queries.
  • Longer term: shard sizing, separate autocomplete nodes, query guardrails.

Deep answer: Sale starts cause both query spikes and update spikes (price changes). Indexing and search compete for CPU and IO. Batching and pipelining indexing (L3), coalescing updates per product, and scheduling bulk price changes before the sale all help. Use adaptive replica selection and circuit breakers on aggregations.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Freshness vs query latency during peaks.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you pre-warm? → Replay popular queries after deploys and scale-ups. 2. Could you pre-compute results for the top queries? → Yes: cache with short TTLs keyed by (query, store).

Red flags: "Add more nodes" without looking at shard balance or indexing load.

Q18 [B4] How do you handle multi-tenant search for 2,000 sellers' back-office catalogs?

30-second answer: Choose by tenant size and isolation needs:

  • a shared index with a mandatory seller_id filter (applied server-side, with routing by seller_id to limit shard fan-out);
  • index-per-large-tenant for the biggest sellers;
  • never trusting client filters.

Add document-level security, quotas per tenant, and separate indexes from customer-facing search.

Deep answer: - Routing by seller_id keeps each seller's docs on one shard, so queries hit one shard. - Watch mapping explosion if tenants have custom attributes: use a fixed schema with a flexible attributes field. - Reindexing a tenant is easier with index-per-tenant.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Isolation and noisy-neighbour control vs cluster overhead (too many small indexes).

Follow-ups: 1. What if a tenant's data must stay in-country? → A per-region cluster (Ch 36). 2. How many indexes are too many? → Thousands of small shards hurt the cluster; group small tenants.

Red flags: Filtering by tenant in the frontend.

Q19 [B4] How would you build 'did you mean' and synonyms from data rather than by hand?

30-second answer: - Mine query logs: reformulations within a session ("aata" → "atta" followed by a click), queries with the same clicked products (co-click graphs), and edit-distance neighbours with click evidence. - Propose candidates to merchandisers for review, with evidence. - Evaluate on judged queries before deploying. - Embeddings trained on query–product clicks can suggest cross-lingual equivalents.

Deep answer: - Guard against harmful expansions (L1's fuzzy "chai" → "chakki"): require click evidence and category consistency. - Synonyms should be directional in some cases ("cooking oil" → sunflower/mustard, not the reverse). - Keep them as versioned config with CI and rollback.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Automation speed vs precision; human review cost.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you measure a synonym's impact? → Judged queries plus an online zero-result/CTR delta. 2. How often? → A weekly cycle.

Red flags: Auto-deploying mined synonyms without review.

Q20 [B4] What would you put in a search platform's 'definition of done' for any relevance change?

30-second answer: 1. The change is expressed as config/code in Git. 2. It's tested with the analyzer (_analyze snapshots for key terms). 3. It passes judged-query CI (no nDCG drop > 0.01, and no new zero-result queries). 4. It's shadow- or interleaving-tested online for high-traffic changes. 5. It has a monitored rollout with auto-rollback on CTR/zero-result regressions. 6. It's documented with before/after examples.

Deep answer: L1's fuzzy regression ("chai" → "chakki") is the canonical example of a plausible change that CI would have caught and eyeballing wouldn't. The same gate applies to synonyms, boosts, embedding models and fusion weights (L4).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Process overhead vs protecting a revenue-critical feature.

Follow-ups: 1. Who owns judgments? → The search team, with merchandising and periodic external judging. 2. How do you keep the set fresh? → Monthly sampling from logs; retire stale queries.

Red flags: "We'll know from complaints."

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Search = inverted index + analysis + ranking. The index makes it fast (L1: 194x); analysis and ranking make it right.
  2. Measure relevance with judged queries (nDCG@10, zero-result rate) on every change. Eyeballing misses regressions.
  3. For Indian grocery: transliterate, normalise Hinglish phonetics, normalise units, and add cross-language synonyms (L1: 0.367 → 0.900).
  4. Fuzziness needs guard rails (L1: "chai" → "chakki"). Prefer spell correction from logs.
  5. Query understanding (type intent, attributes) fixes what text scoring can't ("potato" vs potato chips).
  6. Business ranking: stock and popularity via a function score or re-ranking (L1: out-of-stock in the top 3, 11 → 0).
  7. PostgreSQL FTS + trigram suits admin and small catalogs, but has no transliteration and shares load with OLTP (L2).
  8. Index sync: outbox → keyed stream → pipelined bulk indexer, per-key order or external versions (L3: 22 s → 0.8 s lag; 26 → 0 regressions).
  9. Reindex by building alongside and swapping an alias (L3: 0 errors).
  10. Vectors add intent; hybrid keeps exactness. HNSW recall depends on details (L4: 0.945 vs 0.991), and weighted RRF beat either retriever alone.

docs.title: 23. Security Architecture ⭐
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B2 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 04, Ch 08, Ch 16, Ch 17, Ch 20 · What you will build: The security backbone of the grocery platform — how customers, riders and staff prove who they are, what they're allowed to do, and how their data is protected. All four labs run real crypto and a real KMS.

  • L1: JWT validation. A naive validator accepted 7 of 9 forged or invalid tokens (alg:none, algorithm confusion, a key embedded in the header, an expired token, wrong audience). A hardened validator accepted only the one valid token. Plus JWKS key rotation and refresh-token reuse detection: a stolen refresh token bought an attacker 43,200 minutes vs 15.
  • L2: login. A control-conformance harness over real HTTP shows the hardened OTP endpoint locking after 5 wrong codes (vs unlimited) and the OAuth flow enforcing PKCE, registered redirect URIs, and single-use codes where the naive one issued tokens to every malformed request.
  • L3: authorization. The same 12 requests through RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC. RBAC alone allowed the IDOR read, a cross-store edit, an over-limit refund and a no-purpose PII read; ABAC and ReBAC denied them. A vulnerable handler that checks the role but not the object leaks other customers' orders.
  • L4: encryption. Envelope encryption with OpenBao (a real KMS): AES-256-GCM per record, DEKs wrapped by a KEK that never leaves the KMS. Tamper detection, KEK rotation that rewraps kilobytes not terabytes, crypto-shredding for "delete my data", and DEK caching that was 115x cheaper than a KMS call per record.

· Reading time: 120 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: five ways in
docs.text:
A security review of the grocery platform, a month before a funding round's due diligence, found five issues that each map to a control in this chapter:

  1. The refunds tool trusted the JWT's header. An engineer's hand-rolled validator read the alg field from the token and used it, so a token with alg: none (no signature) and role: admin was accepted. L1 reproduces this and four more forgeries a naive validator waves through.
  2. The OTP login had no attempt limit. A six-digit code with unlimited guesses is not a secret. L2 shows the difference between unlimited attempts and a lockout after five.
  3. A customer could read another customer's order by changing the ID in the URL (/orders/o-99). The handler checked that the caller was logged in, not that the order was theirs — the classic IDOR (OWASP API #1, Broken Object Level Authorization). L3 shows a role-only check leaking it, and an object-level check stopping it.
  4. Store managers could refund any amount, in any store. Roles said "manager can refund"; they couldn't say "up to ₹5,000, in your own store". L3 contrasts RBAC with attribute- and relationship-based models.
  5. Customer addresses and phone numbers were stored in plaintext, and "delete my account" left copies in backups for 35 days. L4 builds envelope encryption and crypto-shredding.

None of these needed a sophisticated attacker. They're the routine failures that the OWASP API Top 10, the OAuth 2.0 Security BCP and basic key management exist to prevent.

The thesis of this chapter

Security is not a feature you add; it's a set of defaults that fail closed at every layer. Authentication proves who; authorization decides what, and must be checked on every object, not just at the door. Secrets and keys live in a KMS, never in code or config. Data is encrypted so that losing the storage doesn't mean losing the data. And every one of these is testable — the labs here are the kind of conformance checks that belong in CI, because "we think it's secure" is not evidence.

A note on this chapter: it teaches how to build the defenses. Every lab hardens a control and verifies bad inputs are refused. It does not provide attack tooling.

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text: Band After this chapter you can… B2 Explain authN vs authZ, validate JWTs safely, describe OAuth2/OIDC and OTP flows, and use RBAC B3 Implement PKCE and refresh-token rotation, choose RBAC/ABAC/ReBAC, prevent the OWASP API Top 10, and apply envelope encryption B4 Design zero-trust service auth, KMS-backed key management with rotation and shredding, and a defense-in-depth architecture with a threat model

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition B2
docs.text:
• Authentication is the ID check at the door; authorization is what your wristband lets you into. Being inside the building (logged in) doesn't mean you may enter the cash room (an admin action) or open someone else's locker (another customer's order). The IDOR bug is a guard who checks you have a wristband but never which locker is yours.
  • A JWT is a tamper-evident wristband. It carries claims (who, what role, until when) and a signature. Trusting the writing on the band about how to check the signature ("this band says to verify it with no ink at all") is the alg-confusion class of bugs.
  • A KMS is the hotel's key-cutting machine that never leaves the back office. You send it a locked box (a wrapped data key) and it hands back the contents, but the master die never comes out front. Destroy a guest's die and every box cut from it is permanently locked — that's crypto-shredding.
  • Zero trust is "show your badge at every door", not "you're past reception, so wander freely". On a network, being inside the perimeter grants nothing; each service still proves its identity (mTLS) and checks permissions.

docs.title: 2.2 Authentication vs authorization ⭐ B2
docs.text:
Authentication (authN) Authorization (authZ) Question Who are you? What may you do? Proof Password, OTP, passkey, certificate Roles, attributes, relationships, policy Where At the edge / IdP, once per session On every request and every object Failure Impersonation Privilege escalation, data exposure (IDOR)

The commonest security bug is conflating them: authenticating a request and treating that as authorization. L3's IDOR control shows a handler that authenticates fine and leaks every customer's orders because it never checks the object.

docs.title: 2.3 Sessions, tokens and JWTs ⭐ B2
docs.text:
• Opaque session tokens: a random ID; the server looks up state. Easy to revoke (delete the row), needs a lookup, and is stateful.
  • JWTs (self-contained): signed claims the resource server validates without a lookup. Scales statelessly, but is hard to revoke before expiry, so keep them short-lived and pair them with a revocation list for logout.

A JWT is base64url(header).base64url(claims).signature. Validation must:

  1. Fix the algorithm from your key config, never from the token's header. Accepting alg: none or letting the token pick RS256 vs HS256 is the alg-confusion vulnerability.
  2. Resolve the key by kid against a trusted JWKS — never a key embedded in the header (jwk/jku/x5u) or fetched from a token-supplied URL.
  3. Verify the signature.
  4. Check registered claims: iss, aud, exp, nbf (with small clock skew), and reject absurd lifetimes.
  5. Check revocation (jti against a denylist) for logout/compromise.

L1's naive validator skips 1–2 and 4–5, and accepts:

Token presented to the payment API Naive Hardened Valid token ACCEPTED ACCEPTED alg: none, no signature, role admin ACCEPTED rejected (unsigned) HS256 signed with our RSA public key as the secret ACCEPTED rejected (alg mismatch) Attacker's key embedded in the header (jwk) ACCEPTED rejected (key in header) Payload edited to role admin, old signature rejected rejected (bad signature) Expired two hours ago ACCEPTED rejected (expired) Valid, but audience is rider-app ACCEPTED rejected (aud) Valid, but jti revoked at logout ACCEPTED rejected (revoked) Valid signature, 30-day lifetime ACCEPTED rejected (lifetime)

Seven of nine bad tokens accepted. Use a vetted library (Nimbus, java-jwt, jose4j) configured with a fixed algorithm and a JWKS, not a hand-rolled parser.

Algorithm choice (L1 D, measured):

Algorithm Sign Verify Token size Use RS256 (RSA-2048) 1,193 µs 47 µs 582 B Asymmetric; many verifiers, few signers (the common default) ES256 (P-256) 208 µs 762 µs 326 B Smaller tokens, cheaper signing; verify-heavy HS256 (shared secret) 7 µs 4 µs 283 B Symmetric; only when signer and verifier are the same trust domain

Asymmetric (RS256/ES256) lets resource servers verify with a public key without holding a signing secret. That's why the "HS256 with the public key as the secret" attack matters: if the verifier accepts HS256, an attacker signs with the well-known public key.

docs.title: 2.4 OTP and passwords ⭐ B2
docs.text:
The grocery app uses phone OTP. The controls (L2 A):

  • Attempt limit per code (lock after ~5), so a 6-digit code (1,000,000 values) can't be guessed. Naive: unlimited; hardened: 5.
  • Send limit per phone (e.g. 3 per 10 minutes) to stop SMS-bombing and cost abuse.
  • Store codes hashed (salted) with a short expiry (5 minutes), single-use.
  • Constant-time comparison of the hash.
  • Don't leak whether the phone is registered (uniform responses).

For passwords (staff, some flows): Argon2id (or scrypt/bcrypt), never fast hashes or encryption; per-user salt; a pepper in the KMS; check against breached-password lists; and rate-limit plus lockout with care not to enable denial of service.

MFA: TOTP or, preferably, passkeys / WebAuthn (phishing-resistant, hardware-backed). SMS OTP is a usability floor, not strong MFA (SIM-swap risk).

docs.title: 2.5 OAuth 2.0 and OIDC ⭐ B3
docs.text:
• OAuth 2.0 is authorization delegation (an app gets a token to call an API on the user's behalf). OIDC adds authentication on top (an id_token proving who logged in).
  • Roles: resource owner (the user), client (the app), authorization server (issues tokens), resource server (the API).
  • Flows:
    • Authorization Code + PKCE — for web and mobile apps, the only recommended interactive flow now.
    • Client Credentials — service-to-service (no user).
    • Device Code — TVs, CLIs.
    • Implicit and Resource Owner Password — deprecated; don't use them.
  • PKCE (RFC 7636): the app generates a random code_verifier, sends its SHA-256 hash (code_challenge) with the authorization request, and presents the verifier when exchanging the code. An intercepted code is useless without the verifier. S256 only — never plain.

L2 B verifies the OAuth controls on a real HTTP server:

Request presented to /token Naive server Hardened (Security BCP) Correct verifier, registered redirect token issued token issued Wrong PKCE verifier token issued reject (PKCE) No verifier at all token issued reject (PKCE) Attacker-controlled redirect_uri token issued reject (redirect not registered) Same code exchanged a second time — reject (replay) First token after that replay — revoked

The BCP rules L2 enforces: exact-match registered redirect URIs (no wildcards), PKCE for all clients, single-use codes (and on replay, revoke tokens already issued from that code), the state parameter for CSRF, and short-lived codes.

docs.title: 2.6 Token lifecycle and rotation ⭐ B3
docs.text:
• Access tokens: short-lived (5–15 min). A leaked one expires quickly.
  • Refresh tokens: longer-lived, rotating. Each use issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If an old (already-used) refresh token appears again, that's reuse detection: someone has a stolen copy, so revoke the whole token family and force re-login.

L1 C models a refresh token stolen from a phone backup:

  • Long-lived reusable refresh token: the attacker kept access for 43,200 minutes (the full 30 days), unnoticed.

  • Rotation + reuse detection: the attacker got 15 minutes (one access token); the customer's next refresh presented the now-used token, reuse was detected, and the family was revoked.

  • Key rotation (JWKS): publish the new signing key alongside the old, sign with the new one, keep verifying both until older tokens expire, then retire the old key. L1 B: during the overlap both tokens validate; after retirement, the old kid is rejected. Never rotate by deleting the current key.

docs.title: 2.7 Zero trust and service-to-service auth ⭐ B4
docs.text:
Zero trust: no implicit trust from network location. Every request is authenticated and authorized, inside the perimeter as much as outside.

  • Service identity: each workload gets a cryptographic identity (SPIFFE/SPIRE issues SVIDs), used for mTLS. The service mesh (Ch 17) can enforce mTLS and identity-based policy transparently.
  • Short-lived credentials: certificates and tokens minted per workload, rotated automatically (minutes to hours), so a leaked credential is briefly useful.
  • Authorization between services: the calling service's identity plus the end-user context (a propagated token or a signed request) decide access. "payment-service may call ledger-service's POST /postings" is policy, not firewall.
  • Least privilege and segmentation: default-deny network policy, per-service DB users with minimal grants, and dynamic DB credentials from the KMS (short TTL) instead of a shared password.

docs.title: 2.8 Authorization models: RBAC, ABAC, ReBAC ⭐ B3
docs.text:
L3 runs the same 12 grocery requests through all three:

Model Decides by Good at Weak at RBAC The subject's roles → permissions Simple, auditable, coarse-grained org roles Can't express "own", "same store", "≤ limit", "with purpose" (role explosion if you try) ABAC Attributes of subject/resource/action/env, via policy Fine-grained conditions, context (time, amount, purpose) Policies get complex; hard to answer "who can access X?" ReBAC Relationships in a graph (Zanzibar) "Manager of the store that owns this order", inherited/nested access, sharing Needs the graph and a check service; conditions still need ABAC

L3's result table:

  • RBAC alone allowed: the IDOR read (customer → another's order), the cross-store update, the ₹8,000 over-limit refund, the Bengaluru manager reading a Mumbai order, and the PII read with no ticket. Roles simply can't say no to these.
  • ABAC denied all of them via ownership, store scope, a ₹5,000 refund limit, city scope, and an "open ticket" purpose check.
  • ReBAC answered order reads from the graph: owner, delivering rider, and manager via store→city inheritance — without the order row carrying storeId/city; the edges carry it.

In practice, platforms layer them: RBAC for coarse org roles, ABAC conditions for limits and context, and ReBAC (an authorization service like OpenFGA/SpiceDB, or a policy engine like OPA/Cedar) for object- and relationship-level checks. The decision is centralized (policy) but enforced locally (each service checks before acting).

docs.title: 2.9 The OWASP API Security Top 10, on this platform B3
docs.text:
# Risk Grocery example Defense API1 Broken Object Level Authorization (IDOR) /orders/{id} returns any order Object-level check on every fetch (L3) API2 Broken Authentication alg:none, no OTP limit Hardened JWT + OTP (L1, L2) API3 Broken Object Property Level Auth Client sets role/price in the body (mass assignment) Allow-list writable fields; never trust client-set authority fields API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption Unbounded page size, no rate limit Limits, quotas, pagination caps (Ch 18) API5 Broken Function Level Authorization Customer calls an admin endpoint Deny by default; check function permission API6 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows Bots draining flash-sale stock Bot defense, per-user flow limits API7 SSRF "image URL" fetched by the server hits internal metadata Allow-list egress, no raw URLs (Ch 21 lesson) API8 Security Misconfiguration Debug endpoints, permissive CORS Hardened baselines, config review API9 Improper Inventory Management Forgotten /v1 with no auth API catalog, retire old versions API10 Unsafe Consumption of 3rd-party APIs Trusting a gateway callback blindly Verify signatures/idempotency (Ch 20)

Injection (SQLi, command injection) sits under secure coding: parameterized queries always (Ch 05), never string-built SQL or shell.

docs.title: 2.10 Secrets management ⭐ B3
docs.text:
• Never in code or Git, never in plain env vars or images. Use a secrets manager (Vault/OpenBao, cloud KMS/Secrets Manager).
  • Dynamic secrets: the KMS mints short-lived DB credentials per service on demand and revokes them on TTL, so there's no shared, long-lived DB password to leak.
  • Rotation: automated, with overlap (like JWKS).
  • Access: authenticated by workload identity, least-privilege policies, and every read audited.
  • Detection: secret-scanning in CI and on commits; treat any committed secret as compromised and rotate it.

docs.title: 2.11 Encryption ⭐ B3
docs.text:
• In transit: TLS 1.3, HSTS, modern ciphers; mTLS internally (§2.7). Terminate at the edge, re-encrypt internally.
  • At rest: full-disk/volume encryption is table stakes but only protects against stolen disks. Application-level encryption protects specific fields (PII, payment data) against a compromised database or backup.
  • Envelope encryption (L4) is the standard pattern:
    1. Generate a data encryption key (DEK) per record (or per tenant/batch).
    2. Encrypt the field with the DEK using authenticated encryption (AES-256-GCM) — a unique IV per encryption, and a tag that detects tampering.
    3. Wrap (encrypt) the DEK with a key-encryption key (KEK) that lives in the KMS and never leaves it.
    4. Store ciphertext + wrapped DEK + KEK version. To read, ask the KMS to unwrap the DEK.

L4 with OpenBao's transit engine:

  • A 60-byte address → 76-byte ciphertext + a 12-byte IV + an 89-byte wrapped DEK; the row holds no plaintext and no key material.
  • Tampering: flipping one ciphertext bit makes GCM decryption throw AEADBadTagException — the record is rejected, not silently corrupted.
  • KEK rotation: rotate the KEK in the KMS; old rows still decrypt (the KMS keeps old versions), and you rewrap only the small DEKs (kilobytes), never the data (terabytes). The ciphertext is byte-for-byte unchanged.
  • Cost: a KMS call per record was 1.72 ms/field; reusing one wrapped DEK across records (each with its own IV) was 0.015 ms/field, 115x cheaper. Cache/derive DEKs per tenant or batch; never cache the KEK.

docs.title: 2.12 Crypto-shredding and the right to erasure ⭐ B4
docs.text:
"Delete all my data" (DPDP/GDPR, Ch 36) is hard because data spreads into backups, replicas, logs and the lake. Crypto-shredding: encrypt a customer's data under a per-customer key; to erase, destroy the key. Every copy, everywhere, becomes permanently unrecoverable ciphertext.

L4 D: after destroying the customer's KEK in the KMS, unwrapping the DEK fails, so the data is gone "everywhere it was copied", without hunting down every backup. Caveats: it only works if the customer's data was only ever encrypted under that key (no plaintext copies escaped), and you still delete what you can directly; shredding covers the long tail (backups, archives).

docs.title: 2.13 Defense in depth and threat modeling B4
docs.text:
No single control is trusted. Layers: edge (WAF, TLS, rate limits), gateway (authN, coarse authZ), service (fine authZ, input validation), data (encryption, least-privilege access), and monitoring (audit logs, anomaly detection).

Threat modeling (STRIDE) per feature: Spoofing → strong authN; Tampering → signatures, GCM, integrity; Repudiation → audit logs; Information disclosure → encryption, authZ; Denial of service → rate limits (Ch 18); Elevation of privilege → least privilege, authZ checks. Do it at design time, keep a risk register, and re-test with the conformance harnesses these labs illustrate.

docs.title: 3.1 Component view
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    APP[Customer / rider app] -->|TLS 1.3| EDGE[Edge: WAF, rate limit, TLS]
    EDGE --> GW[API gateway: validate JWT, coarse authZ]
    GW -->|mTLS + propagated user context| SVC[Service: fine-grained authZ per object]
    SVC --> PDP[Authorization service: ABAC/ReBAC policy]
    SVC --> DB[(DB: envelope-encrypted PII)]
    SVC --> KMS[KMS / OpenBao: KEKs, dynamic DB creds]
    APP -->|Auth Code + PKCE, OTP| AS[Authorization server / IdP]
    AS --> JWKS[JWKS: signing keys, rotated]
    GW --> JWKS
    SVC --> AUDIT[(Audit log: who did what to which object)]

docs.title: 3.2 Sequence: happy path, mobile login with OAuth Code + PKCE
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App
    participant AS as Authorization server
    participant API as Resource server
    App->>App: generate code_verifier, code_challenge = S256(verifier)
    App->>AS: OTP login, then /authorize with challenge, registered redirect
    AS-->>App: redirect with one-time code
    App->>AS: /token with code + code_verifier
    AS->>AS: verify code unused, redirect matches, S256(verifier) = challenge
    AS-->>App: short-lived access token + rotating refresh token
    App->>API: request with access token
    API->>API: validate JWT (fixed alg, JWKS kid, iss/aud/exp), authZ on the object
    API-->>App: data

docs.title: 3.3 Sequence: failure path, refresh-token reuse detected
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Attacker
    participant Owner
    participant AS as Authorization server
    Attacker->>AS: refresh with stolen token RT1
    AS-->>Attacker: new access token + RT2, RT1 marked used
    Owner->>AS: refresh with RT1 (the copy the owner still has)
    AS->>AS: RT1 already used → reuse detected
    AS-->>Owner: revoke the whole token family, force re-login
    Note over AS: attacker RT2 revoked too, window was one access-token lifetime

docs.title: 3.4 State: envelope-encrypted record through KEK rotation and shredding
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Sealed: DEK encrypts field (AES-GCM), KEK wraps DEK (v1)
    Sealed --> Rotated: KEK rotated to v2, DEK rewrapped (ciphertext unchanged)
    Rotated --> Readable: KMS unwraps DEK on demand
    Sealed --> Readable
    Readable --> Shredded: per-customer KEK destroyed
    Shredded --> [*]: ciphertext unrecoverable everywhere, backups included

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Grocery Platform Security Architecture
docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers Security team / platform, payments, SRE, legal (DPDP) Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-098 OAuth2 Code+PKCE + OIDC, short access tokens, rotating refresh with reuse detection; ADR-099 JWT validation library with fixed alg + JWKS (no hand-rolled parsers); ADR-100 AuthZ = RBAC + ABAC conditions + ReBAC via a central policy service, enforced per object; ADR-101 Zero-trust service auth (mTLS/SPIFFE, dynamic DB creds); ADR-102 Envelope encryption for PII with per-tenant keys and crypto-shredding

1. Context & Problem. The review (§1.1): a token-header-trusting validator, an unlimited-attempt OTP, IDOR, role-only refund authority, and plaintext PII with no real erasure.

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: no token forgery accepted; brute-force-resistant login; object- and context-level authorization; secrets and keys in a KMS; encrypted PII with erasure; zero-trust internal calls; everything testable in CI.
  • Non-goals: building our own IdP or crypto primitives; SMS OTP as strong MFA (it's a floor).

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement FR-1 JWTs validated with a vetted library: fixed algorithm, JWKS by kid, iss/aud/exp/nbf, revocation on logout FR-2 OTP: ≤ 5 attempts/code, ≤ 3 sends/phone/10 min, hashed + expiring codes; app uses Code+PKCE (S256), registered redirects, single-use codes FR-3 Access tokens ≤ 15 min; refresh tokens rotate with reuse detection FR-4 Every object access checks the subject's relation to that object (no IDOR); refunds/edits enforce store scope and amount limits FR-5 PII fields encrypted with envelope encryption; per-customer keys enable crypto-shredding NFR-1 Internal calls use mTLS with workload identity; DB credentials are dynamic and short-lived NFR-2 Conformance tests (token forgeries, OTP limits, IDOR, PKCE) run in CI and block merge on regression NFR-3 All authN/authZ decisions and PII access are audit-logged

4. Estimates & choices.

Item Choice Rationale Token signing RS256 (or ES256 for size) Public-key verification at every resource server (L1 D) Access token TTL 15 min Balances revocation lag and refresh load KEK KMS, non-exportable, per-tenant for PII Rotation + shredding (L4) DEK Per record, cached per tenant/batch 115x cheaper than per-record KMS calls (L4 E) AuthZ engine OPA/Cedar for ABAC + OpenFGA/SpiceDB for ReBAC Central policy, local enforcement

5. Proposed design.

  1. AuthN: an authorization server (or managed IdP) issues OIDC tokens via Code+PKCE for apps and Client Credentials for services. A gateway validates JWTs (fixed alg, cached JWKS) and passes verified user context downstream.
  2. AuthZ: a shared library calls the policy service for each protected action, always with the object identity. RBAC for roles, ABAC conditions (store, amount, purpose), ReBAC for ownership/hierarchy. Default deny.
  3. Service auth: the mesh enforces mTLS with SPIFFE identities; services get dynamic DB creds from the KMS.
  4. Data: an encryption library seals PII fields (AES-256-GCM + KMS-wrapped DEKs, per-tenant KEKs). Erasure destroys the tenant key.
  5. Assurance: the conformance harnesses (L1–L3 style) run in CI; secret-scanning on commits; periodic pen tests and threat models per feature.

7. Alternatives considered.

Option Pros Cons Verdict Opaque sessions everywhere Easy revocation Central lookup, stateful at scale Used for browser sessions; JWTs for APIs Hand-rolled JWT validation No dependency Alg-confusion and claim bugs (L1) Rejected RBAC only Simple Can't express own/scope/limit (L3) Rejected as sole model Encrypt only the disk Simple No protection from a compromised DB/backup Insufficient for PII Per-record KMS calls Simplest 115x cost, KMS bottleneck (L4) Cache DEKs per tenant

8. Failure modes. Signing key compromise → rotate via JWKS, revoke families. KMS outage → cached DEKs keep reads working; fail closed on new writes. Policy service down → cached decisions with short TTL, fail closed for sensitive actions. Stolen refresh token → reuse detection (L1 C).

10. Observability. AuthN success/failure by reason, OTP lockouts, token validation failures by cause (a spike in "alg mismatch" is an attack), authZ denials by policy, PII access logs, KMS operations, mTLS handshake failures.

14. Decision (ADR-098–102). Standard OAuth2/OIDC with PKCE and rotating refresh; library-based JWT validation; layered RBAC/ABAC/ReBAC enforced per object; zero-trust service auth; envelope encryption with per-tenant keys and crypto-shredding; conformance tests in CI.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
Level New requirement that forces the step L1 "Our refunds tool accepted a forged admin token." (JWT validation, rotation, refresh reuse detection) L2 "Logins can be brute-forced and the app's OAuth flow issues tokens to anyone." (OTP + OAuth/PKCE control conformance) L3 "A customer read another customer's order, and managers refund anything." (RBAC vs ABAC vs ReBAC, IDOR) L4 "PII is in plaintext and we can't really delete it." (envelope encryption, rotation, crypto-shredding with a real KMS)

All labs are defensive: each hardens a control and asserts that bad inputs are refused. Machine: 2 vCPU container, Java 21, and OpenBao 2.1 (an open-source Vault, from its GitHub release) as the KMS for L4. Outputs are verbatim; lab files are in labs/ch23-security/.

docs.title: L1 — JWT validation, key rotation and refresh-token reuse detection B2
docs.text:
Requirement: "A hand-rolled validator accepted a forged admin token. Show what a safe validator checks."

The program builds JWTs with the JDK's own crypto (RS256/ES256/HS256), then runs a battery of good and forged tokens through a naive validator (trusts the header) and a hardened one (fixed algorithm per kid, JWKS, all registered claims, denylist). It also rotates keys through a JWKS and models refresh-token rotation.

TokensL1.java
// TokensL1.java — run with: java TokensL1.java      (JDK 17+, no dependencies)
// JWTs built from the JDK's own crypto: issue RS256/ES256/HS256 tokens, then validate a battery of good and forged tokens
// with a NAIVE validator (trusts the header) and a HARDENED one (allow-listed alg per kid, iss/aud/exp/nbf, denylist).
// Also: key rotation through a JWKS with two keys, refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, and sign/verify cost.
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.*;
import java.security.interfaces.*;
import java.security.spec.*;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.regex.*;
import javax.crypto.Mac;
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec;

public class TokensL1 {
    static final Base64.Encoder B64 = Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding();
    static final Base64.Decoder D64 = Base64.getUrlDecoder();
    static String b64(String s) { return B64.encodeToString(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)); }
    static String unb64(String s) { return new String(D64.decode(s), StandardCharsets.UTF_8); }

    /** Tiny flat-JSON reader: "key":"string" | "key":number | "key":true/false. Enough for JWT headers and claims. */
    static Map<String, String> json(String j) {
        Map<String, String> m = new HashMap<>();
        Matcher x = Pattern.compile("\"(\\w+)\"\\s*:\\s*(\"((?:[^\"\\\\]|\\\\.)*)\"|[-\\w.]+|\\{[^}]*\\})").matcher(j);
        while (x.find()) m.put(x.group(1), x.group(3) != null ? x.group(3) : x.group(2));
        return m;
    }

    // ---------------- signing ----------------
    static byte[] sign(String alg, Key key, byte[] data) throws Exception {
        switch (alg) {
            case "RS256" -> { Signature s = Signature.getInstance("SHA256withRSA"); s.initSign((PrivateKey) key); s.update(data); return s.sign(); }
            case "ES256" -> { Signature s = Signature.getInstance("SHA256withECDSAinP1363Format"); s.initSign((PrivateKey) key); s.update(data); return s.sign(); }
            case "HS256" -> { Mac m = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256"); m.init(key instanceof SecretKeySpec k ? k : new SecretKeySpec(key.getEncoded(), "HmacSHA256")); return m.doFinal(data); }
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(alg);
        }
    }
    static boolean verify(String alg, Key key, byte[] data, byte[] sig) throws Exception {
        switch (alg) {
            case "RS256" -> { Signature s = Signature.getInstance("SHA256withRSA"); s.initVerify((PublicKey) key); s.update(data); return s.verify(sig); }
            case "ES256" -> { Signature s = Signature.getInstance("SHA256withECDSAinP1363Format"); s.initVerify((PublicKey) key); s.update(data); return s.verify(sig); }
            case "HS256" -> { return MessageDigest.isEqual(sign("HS256", key, data), sig); }                 // constant-time compare
            default -> { return false; }
        }
    }
    static String jwt(String headerJson, String claimsJson, String alg, Key key) throws Exception {
        String si = b64(headerJson) + "." + b64(claimsJson);
        return si + "." + (key == null ? "" : B64.encodeToString(sign(alg, key, si.getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII))));
    }
    static String claims(String sub, String aud, long iat, long exp, String role, String jti) {
        return "{\"iss\":\"https://auth.grocery.example\",\"sub\":\"" + sub + "\",\"aud\":\"" + aud + "\",\"iat\":" + iat + ",\"nbf\":" + iat
                + ",\"exp\":" + exp + ",\"role\":\"" + role + "\",\"jti\":\"" + jti + "\"}";
    }

    // ---------------- validators ----------------
    record Result(boolean ok, String why) {}

    /** What many hand-rolled validators do: believe the header, check nothing else. */
    static Result naive(String token, PublicKey configuredKey) {
        try {
            String[] p = token.split("\\.", -1);
            var h = json(unb64(p[0]));
            byte[] si = (p[0] + "." + p[1]).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII);
            String alg = h.get("alg");
            if ("none".equalsIgnoreCase(alg)) return new Result(true, "alg none");
            Key key = configuredKey;
            if (h.containsKey("jwk")) {                                                         // "the token tells us its key"
                var jwk = json(h.get("jwk"));
                key = KeyFactory.getInstance("RSA").generatePublic(new RSAPublicKeySpec(
                        new java.math.BigInteger(1, D64.decode(jwk.get("n"))), new java.math.BigInteger(1, D64.decode(jwk.get("e")))));
            }
            if (alg.equals("HS256")) key = new SecretKeySpec(pem(configuredKey).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII), "HmacSHA256");
            return new Result(verify(alg, key, si, D64.decode(p[2])), "signature");
        } catch (Exception e) { return new Result(false, e.getClass().getSimpleName()); }
    }

    record TrustedKey(String alg, Key key, boolean retired) {}

    /** Hardened: kid must be known, alg fixed by our key config (never by the token), all registered claims checked, denylist. */
    static Result hardened(String token, Map<String, TrustedKey> jwks, String expectedAud, Set<String> revokedJti, long now) {
        try {
            String[] p = token.split("\\.", -1);
            if (p.length != 3 || p[2].isEmpty()) return new Result(false, "unsigned");
            var h = json(unb64(p[0]));
            if (h.containsKey("jwk") || h.containsKey("jku") || h.containsKey("x5u")) return new Result(false, "key in header");
            TrustedKey k = jwks.get(h.get("kid"));
            if (k == null || k.retired()) return new Result(false, "unknown/retired kid");
            if (!k.alg().equals(h.get("alg"))) return new Result(false, "alg mismatch");
            if (!verify(k.alg(), k.key(), (p[0] + "." + p[1]).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII), D64.decode(p[2]))) return new Result(false, "bad signature");
            var c = json(unb64(p[1]));
            long skew = 30;
            if (!"https://auth.grocery.example".equals(c.get("iss"))) return new Result(false, "iss");
            if (!expectedAud.equals(c.get("aud"))) return new Result(false, "aud");
            if (Long.parseLong(c.get("exp")) + skew < now) return new Result(false, "expired");
            if (Long.parseLong(c.get("nbf")) - skew > now) return new Result(false, "not yet valid");
            if (Long.parseLong(c.get("exp")) - Long.parseLong(c.get("iat")) > 3600) return new Result(false, "lifetime too long");
            if (revokedJti.contains(c.get("jti"))) return new Result(false, "revoked");
            return new Result(true, "valid");
        } catch (Exception e) { return new Result(false, e.getClass().getSimpleName()); }
    }

    static String pem(PublicKey k) { return "-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----\n" + Base64.getMimeEncoder(64, "\n".getBytes()).encodeToString(k.getEncoded()) + "\n-----END PUBLIC KEY-----\n"; }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        long now = Instant.now().getEpochSecond();
        KeyPairGenerator rsa = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("RSA"); rsa.initialize(2048);
        KeyPair k1 = rsa.generateKeyPair(), k2 = rsa.generateKeyPair(), attacker = rsa.generateKeyPair();
        Map<String, TrustedKey> jwks = new HashMap<>(Map.of("k1", new TrustedKey("RS256", k1.getPublic(), false)));
        Set<String> revoked = new HashSet<>(Set.of("jti-logged-out"));
        String H1 = "{\"alg\":\"RS256\",\"typ\":\"JWT\",\"kid\":\"k1\"}";

        Map<String, String> cases = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        cases.put("valid token (payment API audience)", jwt(H1, claims("cust-42", "payment-api", now, now + 900, "customer", "j1"), "RS256", k1.getPrivate()));
        cases.put("alg:none, no signature", jwt("{\"alg\":\"none\",\"kid\":\"k1\"}", claims("cust-42", "payment-api", now, now + 900, "admin", "j2"), "none", null));
        cases.put("HS256 signed with our PUBLIC key as secret", jwt("{\"alg\":\"HS256\",\"kid\":\"k1\"}", claims("cust-42", "payment-api", now, now + 900, "admin", "j3"), "HS256",
                new SecretKeySpec(pem(k1.getPublic()).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII), "HmacSHA256")));
        var ap = (RSAPublicKey) attacker.getPublic();
        cases.put("attacker key embedded in header (jwk)", jwt("{\"alg\":\"RS256\",\"kid\":\"k1\",\"jwk\":{\"kty\":\"RSA\",\"n\":\"" + B64.encodeToString(ap.getModulus().toByteArray())
                + "\",\"e\":\"" + B64.encodeToString(ap.getPublicExponent().toByteArray()) + "\"}}", claims("cust-42", "payment-api", now, now + 900, "admin", "j4"), "RS256", attacker.getPrivate()));
        String good = cases.get("valid token (payment API audience)");
        String[] gp = good.split("\\.");
        cases.put("payload edited (role→admin), old signature", gp[0] + "." + b64(claims("cust-42", "payment-api", now, now + 900, "admin", "j1")) + "." + gp[2]);
        cases.put("expired 2 hours ago", jwt(H1, claims("cust-42", "payment-api", now - 8100, now - 7200, "customer", "j5"), "RS256", k1.getPrivate()));
        cases.put("valid, but audience rider-app", jwt(H1, claims("rider-7", "rider-app", now, now + 900, "rider", "j6"), "RS256", k1.getPrivate()));
        cases.put("valid, but jti revoked at logout", jwt(H1, claims("cust-42", "payment-api", now, now + 900, "customer", "jti-logged-out"), "RS256", k1.getPrivate()));
        cases.put("valid signature, 30-day lifetime", jwt(H1, claims("cust-42", "payment-api", now, now + 30 * 86400, "customer", "j7"), "RS256", k1.getPrivate()));

        System.out.println("A. Validating tokens presented to payment-api");
        System.out.printf("   %-46s %-16s %-26s%n", "token", "naive validator", "hardened validator");
        for (var e : cases.entrySet()) {
            Result n = naive(e.getValue(), k1.getPublic()), h = hardened(e.getValue(), jwks, "payment-api", revoked, now);
            System.out.printf("   %-46s %-16s %-26s%n", e.getKey(), n.ok() ? "ACCEPTED" : "rejected", (h.ok() ? "ACCEPTED" : "rejected") + " (" + h.why() + ")");
        }

        System.out.println("B. Key rotation through the JWKS (kid k1 → k2)");
        String oldTok = jwt(H1, claims("cust-9", "payment-api", now, now + 900, "customer", "r1"), "RS256", k1.getPrivate());
        jwks.put("k2", new TrustedKey("RS256", k2.getPublic(), false));                         // 1. publish k2 first
        String newTok = jwt("{\"alg\":\"RS256\",\"typ\":\"JWT\",\"kid\":\"k2\"}", claims("cust-9", "payment-api", now, now + 900, "customer", "r2"), "RS256", k2.getPrivate());
        System.out.printf("   overlap (JWKS has k1+k2): old-key token %s, new-key token %s%n",
                hardened(oldTok, jwks, "payment-api", revoked, now).ok() ? "valid" : "rejected", hardened(newTok, jwks, "payment-api", revoked, now).ok() ? "valid" : "rejected");
        jwks.put("k1", new TrustedKey("RS256", k1.getPublic(), true));                           // 3. retire k1 after max token lifetime
        System.out.printf("   after k1 retired (> max token lifetime later): old-key token %s, new-key token %s%n",
                hardened(oldTok, jwks, "payment-api", revoked, now).why(), hardened(newTok, jwks, "payment-api", revoked, now).why());

        System.out.println("C. A refresh token is stolen from a phone backup; the attacker and the customer both use it (30-day refresh, 15-min access)");
        for (boolean rotation : List.of(false, true)) {
            Map<String, String> family = new HashMap<>(); Set<String> used = new HashSet<>(); Set<String> revokedFamilies = new HashSet<>();
            String stolen = "rt-1"; family.put(stolen, "fam-A");
            int attackerMinutes = 0; String attackerRt = stolen, customerRt = stolen; boolean customerForcedLogin = false;
            for (int minute = 0; minute < 30 * 24 * 60; minute += 15) {                           // both refresh every 15 minutes
                for (int who = 1; who >= 0; who--) {                                     // the attacker refreshes first
                    String rt = who == 0 ? customerRt : attackerRt;
                    String fam = family.get(rt);
                    boolean ok = fam != null && !revokedFamilies.contains(fam);
                    if (ok && rotation && used.contains(rt)) { revokedFamilies.add(fam); ok = false; }   // reuse detected → kill the whole family
                    if (ok) {
                        String next = rt;
                        if (rotation) { used.add(rt); next = "rt-" + UUID.randomUUID(); family.put(next, fam); }
