Reading it:

  • Critical path is the lever: the slow trace's path is bff → pricing → fx-rates. Optimizing catalog or inventory (off the path) changes nothing; only the nested fx-rates call does.
  • Aggregate across 10,000 traces localizes p99: pricing/fx-rates is on the critical path ~68% of the time and carries the whole tail (the 30% of calls hitting the slow currency service). Per-service metrics can't see this; the trace tree can.
  • Sampling: head-based at 1% kept only 6 of 554 slow traces — cheap but blind to the tail. Tail-based kept all 554 (plus a 1% baseline) at the cost of buffering every trace until it completes. Keep all error/slow traces however you sample.

docs.title: L4 — SLOs, error budgets and burn-rate alerting B4
docs.text:
Requirement: "The old alert paged 40 times a month and got muted. Page only when the SLO is genuinely threatened."

The program generates 30 days of minute-by-minute checkout traffic (diurnal load, a tiny baseline error rate, and three injected incidents), computes the SLO and error budget, then runs three alerting strategies over the identical stream and counts pages, false pages, missed incidents and time-to-detect.

SloL4.java
// SloL4.java — run with: java SloL4.java      (JDK 17+, no dependencies)
// SLIs, SLOs, error budgets and alerting. A 30-day minute-by-minute stream of good/bad requests for checkout, with a
// steady low error rate plus three injected incidents. We compute the SLO/error budget, then compare three alerting
// strategies on the SAME stream: a naive threshold, a single long-window burn rate, and Google SRE's multi-window
// multi-burn-rate. We count pages, false pages, missed incidents and time-to-detect.
import java.util.*;

public class SloL4 {
    static final int DAYS = 30, MIN = DAYS * 24 * 60;             // one data point per minute
    static final double SLO = 0.999;                              // 99.9% success → 0.1% error budget
    static final double BUDGET = 1 - SLO;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Random r = new Random(24);
        int[] total = new int[MIN], bad = new int[MIN];
        // background traffic: ~50 rpm off-peak to ~600 rpm at lunch/dinner; baseline error ~0.02% (well under budget)
        boolean[] incident = new boolean[MIN];
        // three incidents: a short total outage, a slow partial-error burn, a brief blip
        int[][] incidents = {{8 * 24 * 60 + 13 * 60, 20, 90},      // day 8, 13:00, 20 min, 90% errors (sharp)
                             {15 * 24 * 60 + 2 * 60, 6 * 60, 4},    // day 15, 02:00, 6 h, 4% errors (slow burn, low rate)
                             {22 * 24 * 60 + 20 * 60, 3, 60}};      // day 22, 20:00, 3 min, 60% errors (blip)
        for (int m = 0; m < MIN; m++) {
            int hour = (m / 60) % 24;
            double rpm = 50 + 550 * Math.max(0, Math.sin((hour - 6) / 24.0 * Math.PI * 2)) + r.nextGaussian() * 20;
            int t = Math.max(1, (int) rpm);
            double errRate = 0.0002;
            for (int[] inc : incidents) if (m >= inc[0] && m < inc[0] + inc[1]) { errRate = inc[2] / 100.0; incident[m] = true; }
            int b = 0; for (int i = 0; i < t; i++) if (r.nextDouble() < errRate) b++;
            total[m] = t; bad[m] = b;
        }

        long totalReq = 0, totalBad = 0; for (int m = 0; m < MIN; m++) { totalReq += total[m]; totalBad += bad[m]; }
        double observedErr = (double) totalBad / totalReq;
        System.out.printf("Checkout SLO: %.1f%% success over 30 days. Requests %,d, failures %,d, error rate %.4f%%%n", SLO * 100, totalReq, totalBad, observedErr * 100);
        double budgetReq = totalReq * BUDGET;
        System.out.printf("Error budget: %.4f%% = %,.0f failed requests allowed in 30 days; used %,d (%.0f%% of budget)%n",
                BUDGET * 100, budgetReq, totalBad, 100 * totalBad / budgetReq);

        // ---- burn rate over a trailing window: (errors/requests in window) / BUDGET ----
        // A burn rate of 1 exactly exhausts the 30-day budget in 30 days; 14.4 exhausts it in ~2 days.
        java.util.function.BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Double> burn = (endExclusive, windowMin) -> {
            long tr = 0, br = 0; for (int m = Math.max(0, endExclusive - windowMin); m < endExclusive; m++) { tr += total[m]; br += bad[m]; }
            if (tr == 0) return 0.0; return ((double) br / tr) / BUDGET;
        };

        System.out.println("\nComparing alert strategies on the same 30 days (an alert 'fires' when its condition holds; we page on a rising edge):");
        System.out.printf("   %-42s %7s %8s %10s %14s%n", "strategy", "pages", "false", "missed", "median detect");
        // strategy 1: naive — page whenever the last 5 min error rate > 1% (a fixed threshold)
        evaluate("naive threshold: 5-min err > 1%", total, bad, incident, m -> burn.apply(m, 5) * BUDGET > 0.01);
        // strategy 2: single long window burn rate > 1 over 1 hour
        evaluate("single window: 1-hour burn > 1", total, bad, incident, m -> burn.apply(m, 60) > 1.0);
        // strategy 3: Google SRE multi-window multi-burn-rate (page tier)
        //   fast: 14.4x over 1h AND 5m ; slow: 6x over 6h AND 30m  (the short window confirms it's still happening)
        evaluate("multi-window multi-burn (SRE page)", total, bad, incident, m ->
                (burn.apply(m, 60) > 14.4 && burn.apply(m, 5) > 14.4) || (burn.apply(m, 360) > 6 && burn.apply(m, 30) > 6));

        System.out.println("\n   incidents to catch: day 8 (20 min, 90% — sharp), day 15 (6 h, 4% — slow burn), day 22 (3 min, 60% — blip)");
        System.out.println("   → naive fixed threshold: its pages don't map to budget (a 1% rate is a crisis at 600 rpm, noise at 50 rpm), so it both over- and under-pages;");
        System.out.println("     single long window: it flaps — the condition dips and re-crosses during an incident, so one incident becomes many pages (alert fatigue);");
        System.out.println("     multi-window multi-burn: fewest pages, zero false pages, ~2-min detect. The short window confirms the incident is still live before paging,");
        System.out.println("     and the burn-rate framing means every page corresponds to real error-budget burn (see the per-incident budget below).");

        // budget-burn view of each incident
        System.out.println("\n   How much budget each incident burned (page only when it matters):");
        String[] names = {"day 8 sharp outage", "day 15 slow burn", "day 22 blip"};
        for (int i = 0; i < incidents.length; i++) {
            long tr = 0, br = 0; for (int m = incidents[i][0]; m < incidents[i][0] + incidents[i][1]; m++) { tr += total[m]; br += bad[m]; }
            System.out.printf("     %-20s burned %,6d failed reqs = %5.1f%% of the 30-day budget%n", names[i], br, 100 * br / budgetReq);
        }
    }

    interface Cond { boolean firing(int minute); }
    static void evaluate(String name, int[] total, int[] bad, boolean[] incident, Cond cond) {
        int pages = 0, falsePages = 0; boolean prev = false;
        Set<Integer> incidentsCaught = new HashSet<>();
        List<Integer> detectDelays = new ArrayList<>();
        // map each minute to its incident id (or -1)
        int[] incId = incidentId(incident);
        Map<Integer, Integer> firstFire = new HashMap<>();
        for (int m = 0; m < total.length; m++) {
            boolean f = cond.firing(m);
            if (f && !prev) {                                                     // rising edge = one page
                pages++;
                int id = incId[m];
                if (id >= 0) { incidentsCaught.add(id); firstFire.putIfAbsent(id, m); }
                else falsePages++;
            }
            prev = f;
        }
        // time to detect: first fire minus incident start
        int[][] starts = incidentStarts(incident);
        for (int[] st : starts) {
            int id = st[1];
            if (firstFire.containsKey(id)) detectDelays.add(firstFire.get(id) - st[0]);
        }
        int totalIncidents = starts.length;
        long missed = totalIncidents - incidentsCaught.size();
        String detect = detectDelays.isEmpty() ? "n/a" : median(detectDelays) + " min";
        System.out.printf("   %-42s %7d %8d %10d %14s%n", name, pages, falsePages, missed, detect);
    }

    static int[] incidentId(boolean[] incident) {
        int[] id = new int[incident.length]; Arrays.fill(id, -1); int cur = -1; boolean prev = false;
        for (int m = 0; m < incident.length; m++) { if (incident[m] && !prev) cur++; id[m] = incident[m] ? cur : -1; prev = incident[m]; }
        return id;
    }
    static int[][] incidentStarts(boolean[] incident) {
        List<int[]> starts = new ArrayList<>(); int cur = -1; boolean prev = false;
        for (int m = 0; m < incident.length; m++) { if (incident[m] && !prev) { cur++; starts.add(new int[]{m, cur}); } prev = incident[m]; }
        return starts.toArray(new int[0][]);
    }
    static int median(List<Integer> xs) { var s = xs.stream().sorted().toList(); return s.get(s.size() / 2); }
}
java SloL4.java
Checkout SLO: 99.9% success over 30 days. Requests 9,661,153, failures 13,517, error rate 0.1399%
Error budget: 0.1000% = 9,661 failed requests allowed in 30 days; used 13,517 (140% of budget)

Comparing alert strategies on the same 30 days (an alert 'fires' when its condition holds; we page on a rising edge):
   strategy                                     pages    false     missed  median detect
   naive threshold: 5-min err > 1%                  5        1          0          1 min
   single window: 1-hour burn > 1                  20       17          0          1 min
   multi-window multi-burn (SRE page)               4        0          0          2 min

   incidents to catch: day 8 (20 min, 90% — sharp), day 15 (6 h, 4% — slow burn), day 22 (3 min, 60% — blip)
   → naive fixed threshold: its pages don't map to budget (a 1% rate is a crisis at 600 rpm, noise at 50 rpm), so it both over- and under-pages;
     single long window: it flaps — the condition dips and re-crosses during an incident, so one incident becomes many pages (alert fatigue);
     multi-window multi-burn: fewest pages, zero false pages, ~2-min detect. The short window confirms the incident is still live before paging,
     and the burn-rate framing means every page corresponds to real error-budget burn (see the per-incident budget below).

   How much budget each incident burned (page only when it matters):
     day 8 sharp outage   burned 10,501 failed reqs = 108.7% of the 30-day budget
     day 15 slow burn     burned  1,046 failed reqs =  10.8% of the 30-day budget
     day 22 blip          burned     99 failed reqs =   1.0% of the 30-day budget

Reading it:

  • Error budget makes the month legible: 99.9% allows 9,661 failed requests; one sharp 20-minute outage burned 108% of the whole month's budget on its own, while the 3-minute blip burned 1%.
  • The strategies diverge sharply on the same data:
    • Naive threshold ("5-min error > 1%") pages don't map to budget (1% is a crisis at peak, noise off-peak), and it raised a false page.
    • Single long window ("1-hour burn > 1") flapped into 17 false pages — the condition dips and re-crosses during an incident, so one incident becomes many pages. This is how alerts get muted.
    • Multi-window multi-burn (Google SRE) paged 4 times, 0 false, ~2-min detect: the short window confirms the incident is still live before paging, and every page maps to real budget burn.
  • The lesson is the whole point of SLOs: alert on how fast you're burning the budget, over multiple windows, so a page always means "a human must act now."

Spring/Micrometer shapes (VERIFY: libraries not downloadable here)

// Micrometer: a timer with SLO-aligned histogram buckets, exported to Prometheus
Timer.builder("http.server.requests").tag("route", route)
     .serviceLevelObjectives(Duration.ofMillis(100), Duration.ofMillis(200), Duration.ofMillis(300))
     .publishPercentileHistogram().register(registry);

// OpenTelemetry manual span with context propagation (auto-agent covers HTTP/DB)
Span span = tracer.spanBuilder("pricing.getPrice").startSpan();
try (Scope s = span.makeCurrent()) { span.setAttribute("sku", sku); return pricing.price(sku); }
finally { span.end(); }

// Logback JSON with trace_id from MDC (populated by the OTel/Micrometer context)
// logback-spring.xml: <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder"/>  → {"trace_id":"…","level":"…",…}
A multi-window burn-rate alert (Prometheus rule, SRE style)
- alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn
  expr: |
    (slo:checkout_error:ratio_rate1h  > (14.4 * 0.001)
     and slo:checkout_error:ratio_rate5m  > (14.4 * 0.001))
  for: 2m
  labels: { severity: page }
  annotations: { runbook: "https://runbooks/checkout-error-budget" }

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Symptom Cause Mitigation Blind to the tail "All green" while users suffer Charting averages (§1.1, L2) Percentile metrics, histograms with SLO-aligned buckets Can't correlate Hours lost reconstructing one request No trace id on logs (L1) Propagate traceparent, log trace_id on every line Alert fatigue On-call mutes the pager Threshold/flapping alerts (L4: 17 false pages) Multi-window burn-rate, actionable pages only Missed slow burn SLO blown before anyone notices No burn-rate alert on long windows Slow-burn tier (6× over 6h) Cardinality explosion Prometheus OOM, huge bill Unbounded metric labels (L1: 18,530 series) Bound label values; drop risky labels at ingest Wrong service blamed Fix doesn't help Optimizing off the critical path (L3) Trace critical-path analysis Lost slow traces Can't debug the tail Head sampling only (L3: 6/554) Tail sampling; keep all errors Exporter down, looks healthy Silent gap No "absence of data" alert Alert on up==0 / stale series PII in logs Compliance breach Logging raw request bodies Redaction filter (Ch 23), retention Clock skew across services Negative span durations, wrong ordering Unsynchronized clocks NTP; rely on span parent/child, not wall-clock (Ch 12)

docs.title: 6.2 Observability of the observability stack
docs.text:
• Meta-metrics: scrape success (up), ingestion rate, active series count (cardinality trend), dropped spans/logs, Collector queue depth, alert volume and the page-to-real-incident ratio.
  • SLOs on the pipeline itself: "95% of traces for errors are retained," "metrics freshness < 30 s."
  • Cost dashboards: series per team, log GB per service, trace storage — with owners, so cost has an owner.

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Telemetry carries sensitive data. Redact PII/secrets from logs (Ch 23), don't put customer identifiers in metric labels, and scrub span attributes (no tokens, no full addresses).
  • Access control on dashboards and log/trace search: production logs can contain personal data; scope by team and audit access (Ch 36).
  • Integrity: protect the audit-relevant logs (append-only/WORM) separately from debug telemetry.
  • The pipeline is an attack surface: an open /metrics or trace endpoint leaks internals; require auth/network policy on scrape and ingest.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance & tuning knobs
docs.text: Knob Guidance Scrape interval 15–30 s typical; 1 s only for short-lived debugging (L2 used 1 s) Histogram buckets Cluster around SLO thresholds; use native/exponential histograms where available Metric cardinality Hard limits per metric; relabel-drop high-cardinality labels Log level & sampling Errors always; sample INFO by trace (L1); dynamic level per service Trace sampling Head baseline (1–10%) + tail keep-all-errors; cap Collector memory Retention Metrics: months (downsampled); logs: 7–30 days; traces: days Cardinality of traces Limit span attributes; don't attach large payloads

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• Logs are usually the biggest bill, then traces, then metrics — but metrics blow up fastest via cardinality (L1). Control each: sample logs by trace, tail-sample traces, and bound metric labels.
  • Downsample and tier: raw metrics for weeks, downsampled for a year; hot log storage for days, archived after.
  • Observability commonly runs 5–15% of infra spend; the cost of not having it is the §1.1 incident measured in lost conversion and long MTTR.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Charting and alerting on averages.

# ❌ before: the mean hides the tail (L2: avg 74 ms, p99 1,545 ms)
rate(http_request_duration_ms_sum[5m]) / rate(http_request_duration_ms_count[5m])
# ✅ after: percentiles from the histogram
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_ms_bucket[5m])))

2. Logs with no correlation id (L1). Generate a trace id at the edge, propagate it, and log it on every line (MDC). Without it, cross-service debugging is guesswork.

3. Free-text logs. log.info("processed order " + id + " for " + user) can't be filtered or aggregated by field. Log structured key/values.

4. High-cardinality metric labels (L1: 18,530 series).

// ❌ before: user_id / order_id / trace_id as a label — one series each
Counter.builder("orders").tag("user_id", userId).tag("order_id", orderId).register(registry);
// ✅ after: bounded labels only; identifiers go to logs/traces
Counter.builder("orders").tag("route", route).tag("status", status).register(registry);

5. Threshold alerts on raw rates (L4: false pages, flapping). Alert on multi-window burn rate against an SLO.

6. Paging on causes, not symptoms. "CPU > 80%" pages at 3am for a healthy batch job. Page on user-facing SLO burn; make CPU a dashboard and a ticket.

7. Buckets that miss the SLO (L2: +25% at p99). Put histogram buckets around your target latency, or use native histograms.

8. Head sampling only, then trying to debug the tail (L3: 6/554 slow traces kept). Tail-sample and always keep error traces.

9. Optimizing off the critical path (L3). Trace first; speeding up a service that isn't on the critical path is wasted work.

10. Alerts with no runbook and no action. If a page doesn't tell the on-call what to do, it trains them to ignore pages. Every alert links a runbook or is deleted.

11. Dashboards nobody reads. A 60-panel wall is not observability. Start each dashboard with "what's burning and where," then drill down.

12. Not propagating context through async code. Spans and trace ids vanish across thread pools and message queues unless you propagate context (Ch 19: ScopedValue, context-wrapping executors; OTel context in Kafka headers).

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ Metrics, logs and traces — what's each for?

30-second answer: Metrics are cheap numeric time series (rates, gauges, latency histograms) for "is it broken and how much," and drive dashboards and alerts. Logs are detailed structured events for "what exactly happened." Traces follow one request across services for "where did the time or error go." You need all three, sharing a trace id so you can pivot between them.

Deep answer: Metrics have bounded cardinality and are cheap; logs and traces carry high-cardinality detail. An exemplar links a metric bucket to a trace; logs carry the trace id. L1–L3 build each and show where each shines.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Cost and cardinality rise from metrics → traces → logs; sample the expensive ones.

Follow-ups: 1. Which is cheapest? → Metrics (constant per series). 2. Where do identifiers go? → Logs/traces, never metric labels.

Red flags: "Logs are enough for everything."

Q2 [B1] ⭐ Why percentiles instead of averages?

30-second answer: Averages hide the tail. If most requests are fast but 1% take seconds, the average looks fine while some users have a terrible experience — and those are often the ones who abandon. p99/p99.9 show what the worst-served users actually get. L2: a 74 ms average alongside a 1,545 ms p99.

Deep answer: You also can't average percentiles across instances; you aggregate histograms and compute the quantile over the sum. Use p50 for typical, p99/p99.9 for the tail that drives SLOs.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Percentiles need histograms (more series) than a single mean.

Follow-ups: 1. Can you average two servers' p99s? → No; aggregate the buckets. 2. Which percentile for an SLO? → The one that reflects user pain, often p99.

Red flags: "Our average latency is 50 ms, so we're fast."

Q3 [B1] What is a correlation/trace id and why does it matter?

30-second answer: A unique id generated when a request enters the system and propagated to every service it touches, logged on every line and attached to every span. It lets you retrieve everything about one request across all services with a single query. Without it, you can't reconstruct a request's path.

Deep answer: L1: with a trace id, one filter returns a failed request's ordered journey across five services; without it, those lines are anonymous among ~25,000. Propagate via W3C traceparent; put it in the logging MDC.

Trade-offs I'd call out: You must propagate it through async code and message queues, or the chain breaks.

Follow-ups: 1. Where is it generated? → At the edge/gateway. 2. Standard format? → W3C Trace Context (traceparent).

Red flags: Correlating by timestamp and user.

Q4 [B1] What are RED and USE?

30-second answer: RED for services: Rate, Errors, Duration — the health of request handling. USE for resources: Utilization, Saturation, Errors — for CPU, memory, pools, disks. RED tells you the service is unhealthy; USE tells you which resource is the cause. Google's four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors, saturation (RED + saturation).

Deep answer: L2 computes RED from counters and a histogram. USE applies to thread pools and connection pools (Ch 19). Instrument both so you can go from symptom (RED) to cause (USE).

Trade-offs I'd call out: USE needs resource-level metrics that vary by runtime/host.

Follow-ups: 1. What's saturation? → How full a resource is (queue depth, wait time). 2. Which do you alert on? → Symptoms (RED/SLO), not raw USE.

Red flags: Only watching CPU.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How does a Prometheus histogram work, and why are tail quantiles approximate?

30-second answer: A histogram counts observations into cumulative buckets (le), plus _sum and _count. histogram_quantile(q, …) finds the bucket containing the q-th observation and interpolates linearly within it. Accuracy depends on bucket width: where buckets are wide (usually the tail), the estimate is coarse.

Deep answer: L2 (real Prometheus): p50/p95 within a few percent, p99 +25%, p99.9 +36%, because the tail lands in the wide 1000–2500 ms bucket. Put buckets around your SLO threshold; you can't recover accuracy the buckets didn't capture. Native histograms (exponential auto-buckets) largely fix this.

Trade-offs I'd call out: More buckets = more series (cost) but better tail accuracy.

Follow-ups: 1. Histogram vs summary? → Histograms aggregate across instances; summaries don't. 2. Where do you put buckets? → Around each SLO threshold.

Red flags: "Just read p99 off the default buckets."

Q6 [B2] ⭐ How do you keep logs useful and affordable at scale?

30-second answer: Structure them (JSON/logfmt) so they're queryable by field; put a trace id on every line; sample by trace (keep a request's lines together) not by line; keep all errors; redact PII; and set retention by class. L1: sampling 1% of INFO traces cut volume to 3% while keeping every error.

Deep answer: Dynamic log levels per service, structured schemas, and centralized search (Loki/ES). Logs are the costliest signal, so they get the most aggressive sampling — but never on the error path.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Sampling loses some detail on non-error requests; keep enough for baselines.

Follow-ups: 1. Sample by line or trace? → Trace, so requests stay whole. 2. What never gets sampled? → Errors and audit logs.

Red flags: Logging full request/response bodies at INFO.

Q7 [B2] What is cardinality and why is it dangerous?

30-second answer: Cardinality is the number of distinct label-value combinations, and each is a separate time series. Unbounded labels (user id, order id, URL) create millions of series, which OOMs the metrics store and inflates cost. L1: (service, level, user_id) → ~18,530 series vs 10 for (service, level). Keep identifiers in logs and traces, not metric labels.

Deep answer: Guardrails: bound label value sets, drop risky labels at scrape/ingest, and review new metrics. Monitor active series as a first-class meta-metric.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Fewer labels = less slice-and-dice in metrics; compensate with traces/logs.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not label by endpoint with path params? → /orders/{id} templated is fine; raw /orders/123 is not. 2. What breaks first? → Metrics store memory and query latency.

Red flags: "Add a label for the customer so we can filter."

Q8 [B2] What is an SLI, SLO, SLA and error budget?

30-second answer: SLI is the measured ratio of good events (e.g. checkout success). SLO is the target (99.9% over 30 days). SLA is a contractual SLO with penalties, usually looser. The error budget is 1 − SLO — the allowed failure. It's the shared currency: within budget you ship features; burning it fast, you stop and stabilize.

Deep answer: L4: 99.9% over 30 days = 9,661 failed requests allowed; one incident burned 108% of it. Choose SLIs users feel; don't aim for 100% (infinitely costly, no room to ship).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Tighter SLO = higher cost and less feature velocity.

Follow-ups: 1. Where does the budget "reset"? → Rolling window (e.g. 30 days). 2. Who owns the budget decision? → Product + SRE together.

Red flags: "Our SLO is 100%."

Q9 [B2] Head vs tail sampling for traces?

30-second answer: Head sampling decides at the start (on the trace id, a fixed probability) — cheap, no buffering, and the decision propagates — but it drops most slow and error traces. Tail sampling decides after the trace completes, so it can keep all errors and slow traces plus a baseline, at the cost of buffering every trace in the Collector until it finishes.

Deep answer: L3: head at 1% kept 6 of 554 slow traces; tail kept all 554. Production often combines: head baseline + tail keep-all-errors. Always keep error traces.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Tail sampling needs Collector memory and can back-pressure.

Follow-ups: 1. How does head sampling propagate? → The sampled flag rides in traceparent. 2. What do you always keep? → Errors and slow traces.

Red flags: "1% head sampling is enough to debug latency."

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ Design multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting for a 99.9% checkout SLO.

30-second answer: Burn rate = (error ratio in a window) / error budget. Page when a fast and a slow signal agree:

  • fast: 14.4× over 1 h and 14.4× over 5 min;
  • slow: 6× over 6 h and 6× over 30 min.

Lower rates over long windows become tickets. The short window in each pair confirms the incident is still active, avoiding pages for spikes that already resolved.

Deep answer: L4 on 30 days: naive threshold raised a false page and doesn't map to budget; a single window flapped into 17 false pages; multi-window paged 4 times, 0 false, ~2-min detect. 14.4× burns a 30-day budget in ~2 days, 6× in ~5 days. Generate the rules from SLO definitions (Sloth/Pyrra).

Trade-offs I'd call out: More windows = more rules; detection speed vs false pages is tunable via the burn factors.

Follow-ups: 1. Why the AND of two windows? → The short one prevents alerting on a spike that's already over. 2. What about low-traffic services? → Longer windows or request-count guards to avoid noise.

Red flags: A single fixed error-rate threshold.

Q11 [B3] ⭐ How do you use tracing to find why p99 latency is high?

30-second answer: Take slow traces and compute the critical path — the chain of spans that determines end-to-end time. Optimize only what's on it. Then aggregate many slow traces to see which service or operation is on the critical path most often at the tail. That names the p99 driver, which per-service metrics can't reveal.

Deep answer: L3: the slow trace's critical path is bff → pricing → fx-rates; catalog and inventory are off it, so speeding them up does nothing. Across 10,000 traces, fx-rates is on the critical path 68% of the time and carries the tail. Fix: cache/timeout the fx call.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Needs traces retained for slow requests (tail sampling).

Follow-ups: 1. Why not just look at each service's p99? → A service can be fine on average but on the critical path only sometimes. 2. What obscures the critical path? → Missing async context propagation.

Red flags: Optimizing the service with the highest average latency regardless of the path.

Q12 [B3] How do you choose SLIs and SLOs for a new service?

30-second answer: Pick SLIs the user actually experiences — success ratio and latency of key journeys (checkout success, product-page < 300 ms) — not internal proxies like CPU. Set SLOs from what keeps users happy and the business healthy, with headroom to ship (not 100%). Define "good" precisely (which status codes, which latency threshold, measured where).

Deep answer: Measure at the point closest to the user (the edge/gateway) for the user's view, and per-service for ownership. Start loose, tighten with data. L4's checkout SLO of 99.9% gives a 0.1% budget that a single bad incident can exhaust — which is the signal to invest in that path's reliability.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Edge measurement includes the network; service measurement misses it. Track both.

Follow-ups: 1. Latency or availability SLI? → Often both, as separate SLOs. 2. What window? → 28–30 days rolling is common.

Red flags: SLOs on CPU or on 100%.

Q13 [B3] How do you propagate trace context across services and async boundaries?

30-second answer: Use W3C Trace Context: the traceparent header carries the trace id, parent span id and sampled flag over HTTP/gRPC, and trace headers ride in message metadata (Kafka headers). Within a process, the OTel context flows on the current thread; across thread pools and reactive pipelines you must explicitly propagate it (context-wrapping executors, ScopedValue, Ch 19), or spans detach.

Deep answer: Auto-instrumentation (OTel Java agent) handles most framework boundaries. The gaps are custom thread pools, batching, and message consumers — instrument those to extract/inject context. A broken chain shows as orphan spans or missing trace ids in logs.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Manual propagation is error-prone; prefer the agent and helper executors.

Follow-ups: 1. Kafka? → Inject/extract trace headers on produce/consume. 2. What breaks it? → new Thread(...) without context propagation.

Red flags: Trace ids that reset at every service.

Q14 [B3] What makes an alert good, and how do you fight alert fatigue?

30-second answer: A good alert is a symptom that needs a human now, is tied to an SLO/user impact, has a runbook, and fires rarely and precisely. Fight fatigue by: alerting on burn rate not thresholds (L4), grouping and inhibiting related alerts, deleting alerts with no action, alerting on missing data, and reviewing every incident's alerts afterward (what over/under-paged).

Deep answer: L4 shows a single-window rule flapping into 17 false pages — the fatigue generator. The page-to-incident ratio is a meta-metric: if most pages aren't real incidents, the alerting is broken.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Fewer, better alerts risk missing rare cases; cover those with slow-burn tiers and tickets.

Follow-ups: 1. Page vs ticket? → Page = act now; ticket = look this week. 2. How do you catch a slow burn? → 6×/6h tier.

Red flags: Hundreds of alerts, most muted.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design the observability strategy for the grocery platform.

30-second answer: - Instrument once with OpenTelemetry + Micrometer; export metrics (Prometheus/Mimir), logs (Loki), traces (Tempo) to Grafana. - Metrics: RED per service, USE per resource, SLO-aligned histogram buckets, controlled cardinality. - Logs: structured JSON with trace id, trace-based sampling, PII redaction. - Traces: context propagation, tail sampling keeping all errors. - SLOs per critical journey with multi-window burn-rate pages; everything else is a ticket. - Exemplars connect metrics → traces → logs.

Deep answer (§4): Standardize dashboards (RED+USE+SLO templates), meta-monitor cardinality and cost, and gate new metrics for cardinality. The design's job is to answer unknown-unknowns during an incident, which is why the three signals must be correlated by trace id.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Vendor APM (turnkey, lock-in/cost) vs OTel + CNCF (portable, more ops).

Follow-ups: 1. Build or buy? → OTel instrumentation keeps the backend swappable. 2. First thing to add to a legacy system? → Trace ids on logs and percentile latency.

Red flags: Averages, threshold alerts, no correlation.

Q16 [B4] ⭐ How do you control observability cost without going blind?

30-second answer: - Metrics: bound cardinality (the main cost driver), drop risky labels at ingest, downsample old data. - Logs (usually the biggest bill): structure, sample by trace, keep errors, short retention, archive. - Traces: tail-sample keeping errors/slow, cap attributes. - Ownership: per-team cost dashboards so cost has an owner, and review new high-cardinality metrics.

Deep answer: L1 shows cardinality's leverage (18,530 vs 10 series). Tier storage: hot for days, downsampled/archived after. Target observability at a fixed fraction of infra spend and manage to it, rather than letting it grow unbounded.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Aggressive sampling/retention loses some forensic depth; keep errors and baselines.

Follow-ups: 1. What's usually the biggest line? → Logs, then traces. 2. What blows up fastest? → Metric cardinality.

Red flags: No cardinality limits, infinite retention.

Q17 [B4] Walk through debugging the §1.1 incident (conversion down, dashboards green) with your stack.

30-second answer: 1. SLO burn shows the checkout latency SLO burning even though the average is fine. 2. Percentile dashboard shows p99 spiking (the average hid it). 3. Exemplar on the slow bucket links to a slow trace. 4. Trace shows the critical path through pricing → fx-rates. 5. Logs for that trace id confirm timeouts to the currency service. 6. Mitigate: cache/timeout fx; the burn stops; write a runbook and an alert.

Deep answer: Each step maps to a lab: L4 (burn/SLO), L2 (percentiles/exemplar), L3 (critical path), L1 (correlated logs). The point is the pivot between signals via the trace id — that's observability, not monitoring.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Requires the tail trace to have been sampled (keep-all-errors/slow).

Follow-ups: 1. What if the trace wasn't sampled? → Reproduce with a forced-sample header; add tail sampling. 2. Root cause vs mitigation? → Mitigate first (stop budget burn), then fix fx.

Red flags: Staring at averages during an incident.

Q18 [B4] How do you make a system observable for unknown-unknowns, not just pre-built dashboards?

30-second answer: High-cardinality, correlated, queryable telemetry: wide structured events (many attributes per log/span), a trace id linking all signals, and tools that let you slice by arbitrary dimensions after the fact. Monitoring answers pre-set questions; observability lets you ask new ones during a novel incident. The enabler is that identifiers and context live in logs/traces (high cardinality) while metrics stay bounded for cheap alerting.

Deep answer: This is the "observability 2.0 / wide events" idea: emit rich events you can group and filter arbitrarily, rather than only pre-aggregated metrics. Keep exemplars so a metric anomaly leads to concrete traces. The §1.1 incident was an unknown-unknown (a nested fx call) found only because traces existed.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Wide events cost storage; sample and tier.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not just more dashboards? → You can't dashboard a problem you didn't foresee. 2. What enables ad-hoc slicing? → High-cardinality event stores (traces/logs), not metrics.

Red flags: "We have a dashboard for everything."

Q19 [B4] What's your rollout plan to add observability to a legacy Java service?

30-second answer: 1. Add the OTel Java agent (auto-instruments HTTP/DB/messaging) — traces and basic metrics with no code change. 2. Put the trace id in logs (MDC) and switch logs to structured JSON. 3. Add RED metrics via Micrometer with SLO-aligned histograms. 4. Define one SLO for the key journey and a burn-rate alert. 5. Add exemplars and a standard dashboard. 6. Iterate: custom spans for business steps, tail sampling, cardinality review.

Deep answer: The agent gives the fastest value; structured logs + trace id give correlation; the SLO + burn-rate alert replaces the noisy threshold. Each step is independently shippable and low-risk.

Trade-offs I'd call out: The agent adds a little overhead and needs config; measure.

Follow-ups: 1. Overhead of the agent? → Usually a few percent; benchmark. 2. First metric? → Request rate/errors/latency histogram.

Red flags: A big-bang rewrite to add telemetry.

Q20 [B4] How does observability relate to reliability and the on-call experience?

30-second answer: Observability is what makes reliability operable: SLOs define the target, error budgets govern risk, burn-rate alerts turn budget threats into (rare, actionable) pages, and correlated signals make MTTR short. A good stack means the on-call is paged only when a human must act, opens one dashboard to see what's burning, and pivots via a trace id to the cause — instead of drowning in noise (L4) or staring at averages (L2).

Deep answer: It closes the loop with Ch 18 (resilience) and Ch 27 (DR): you can't run error budgets or fast incident response without observability. The health of the on-call rotation (pages per week, page-to-incident ratio, MTTR) is itself a metric of the observability system's quality.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Investment in tooling and discipline vs incident cost and burnout.

Follow-ups: 1. What's a healthy page rate? → Low enough that every page is taken seriously. 2. How do you measure MTTR improvement? → Time from alert to mitigation across incidents.

Red flags: Treating observability as "nice to have."

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Monitoring answers known questions; observability lets you ask new ones — via correlated logs, metrics and traces sharing a trace id.
  2. Percentiles, never averages for user-facing latency (L2: 74 ms avg hid a 1,545 ms p99).
  3. Structured logs with a correlation id on every line; sample by trace, keep errors (L1: 3% volume, 100% of errors).
  4. RED for services, USE for resources; histograms with buckets around your SLO threshold (L2: p99 +25% otherwise).
  5. Cardinality is the cost/outage risk — identifiers go in logs/traces, not metric labels (L1: 18,530 vs 10 series).
  6. Traces find the critical path; fix what's on it, not what looks slow (L3: fx-rates, not catalog).
  7. Sample traces tail-first for the interesting ones (L3: head 1% kept 6/554 slow; tail kept all).
  8. SLIs/SLOs/error budgets are the reliability contract and the ship/stop signal (L4).
  9. Alert on multi-window burn rate, not thresholds (L4: 4 pages/0 false vs 17 false).
  10. Every page is actionable with a runbook; review alerts after every incident.

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Choice "Is it broken, how much, trends" Metrics (RED/USE), cheap, low cardinality "What happened to this request" Structured logs with trace id "Where did time/errors go across services" Traces, critical-path analysis Latency reporting Percentiles from histograms, SLO-aligned buckets Request identifiers Logs/traces, never metric labels Trace volume control Head baseline + tail keep-all-errors Reliability target SLO + error budget per journey Paging Multi-window multi-burn-rate; actionable only Instrumentation OpenTelemetry + Micrometer, export anywhere

docs.title: 25. Performance Engineering
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B2 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 09, Ch 19, Ch 24 · What you will build: How the grocery platform's services are made fast and kept fast — measuring tails, profiling hotspots, choosing a GC, and planning capacity. Labs use real JFR recordings and real JVM garbage collectors on JDK 21 and 25.

  • L1: tail latency. At fan-out 100, ~99% of requests hit at least one slow backend — a backend's rare tail becomes the request's norm. On a real queue, wait time went 1× → 159× from 50% to 99% utilization (the knee). And coordinated omission hid a 500 ms freeze (naive p999 0 ms, corrected 460 ms).
  • L2: garbage collection, same workload across collectors. Parallel's worst pause was 118 ms, G1's 55–69 ms; generational ZGC on JDK 25 kept the request tail at max 7.5 ms / p999 3.4 ms while allocating the most (92 GB).
  • L3: profiling. A real JFR recording located a planted hotspot: 97% of allocation was byte[] from string-building, and the hot CPU frames rolled up to one method. The profile-guided fix ran 175× faster with an identical checksum.
  • L4: capacity. A real contended service scaled to ~10,000 req/s then plateaued; a Universal Scalability Law fit (α≈0.05) predicted the peak (~11,000 req/s at ~69 concurrent) from a handful of load points, and Little's law sized the pool.

· Reading time: 120 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: the p99 that wouldn't budge
docs.text:
The product-page team spent a sprint optimizing the catalog service — caching, query tuning, faster serialization — and the page's p99 barely moved. The performance review found four separate misunderstandings, each a section of this chapter:

  1. They optimized the wrong service. A trace (Ch 24) showed the slow path ran through pricing, not catalog; catalog was never on the critical path. And because the page fanned out to ~20 services, the tail compounded: at that fan-out, most requests hit someone's slow tail (L1). Cutting catalog's median did nothing for the page's p99.
  2. A GC pause was half the tail. The service ran the Parallel collector with a 4 GB heap; its stop-the-world pauses reached 118 ms (L2), landing squarely in the p99. Nobody had looked at GC logs.
  3. Nobody had profiled. When they finally took a JFR recording, one method — building a cache key by string concatenation in a loop — accounted for almost all the allocation and most of the CPU (L3). A ten-minute fix gave a 175× speedup on that method.
  4. The capacity plan was a guess. "It handles 10k rps" came from a load test that ran at fixed concurrency (so it couldn't overload the service) and measured latency wrong (coordinated omission, L1). The real knee was lower, and the service was already running past 80% utilization at peak — on the steep part of the queueing curve (L1 C).

The rebuild was disciplined: measure the tail, trace to the critical path, profile before optimizing, read GC logs, and plan capacity with a model rather than a vibe.

The thesis of this chapter

Performance work is measurement first, always. You cannot optimize what you haven't profiled, and intuition about where time goes is usually wrong (L3). Measure tails, not averages (Ch 24), because at scale the tail is what users feel and what fan-out amplifies (L1). Know your queueing curve — latency turns a corner near 100% utilization, so plan to run well below it. And treat the GC and the JVM as tunable parts of the system, not a black box.

docs.title: 1.2 Where this lives in the grocery platform
docs.text: Concern Approach Notes Latency SLOs p99/p99.9 per journey (Ch 24) The tail is the target, not the mean Tail reduction Hedged requests, timeouts, fewer serial hops, caching Ch 17, Ch 18; L1 GC Generational ZGC (JDK 21+/25) for latency-sensitive services; G1 default elsewhere L2 Profiling Continuous JFR + async-profiler; flame graphs L3; low overhead, always on JVM in containers Correct CPU/memory limits, MaxRAMPercentage, availableProcessors awareness §2.8 Load testing Gatling/k6, open model, measured from scheduled time L1 D, L4 Capacity planning Little's law + USL from load-test points; run at ~60–70% of peak L4, L1 C

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text: Band After this chapter you can… B2 Explain why tails dominate and compound, read a queueing curve, and profile a JVM with JFR B3 Choose and tune a GC, avoid coordinated omission in load tests, and use Little's law for sizing B4 Diagnose latency systematically, fit the USL to plan capacity, and run the JVM correctly in containers

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition B2
docs.text:
• The tail is the product. If a page needs 20 services and each is fast 99% of the time, the page is fast only 0.99²⁰ ≈ 82% of the time — nearly one in five requests hits someone's bad moment. Speeding up the common case doesn't help; you must cut the tail. (L1)
  • A busy queue is a traffic jam. At 50% utilization there's slack; at 95% a small burst backs everything up. Latency doesn't rise gently to a wall — it curves sharply near 100%. Running "efficiently" at 90% is running on the cliff edge. (L1 C)
  • Profiling is turning on the lights. Optimizing by intuition is fixing what you think is slow; a profiler shows what is. It's routinely a surprise — a logging call, a string concat, a needless copy. (L3)
  • The GC is a background tax. Most of the time it's invisible; occasionally it stops the world for a pause that lands in your p99. Which collector you pick decides how big that pause is. (L2)

docs.title: 2.2 Tail latency and why it compounds ⭐ B2
docs.text:
From Dean & Barroso's The Tail at Scale: in a system that fans out to many components and waits for all of them, the slowest component sets the latency. If each backend is slow (say > p95) 5% of the time, then across N backends the chance that at least one is slow is 1 − 0.95ᴺ. L1:

Fan-out N P[≥1 slow backend] Request p50 Request p99 1 5% 10 ms 270 ms 5 23% 17 ms 303 ms 20 64% 174 ms 310 ms 100 99% 283 ms 316 ms

At fan-out 100 the request's median (283 ms) is near the single backend's p99 — the rare tail has become the norm. Consequences:

  • Reduce fan-out where possible (fewer, coarser calls; Ch 16).
  • Cut the tail, not the mean: timeouts, hedged/backup requests (Ch 17), and fixing the specific slow dependency (Ch 24 L3).
  • L1 B: a single-copy hedge issued only when the first call passes p95 cut fan-out-20 p99 from 310 ms to 126 ms for 5% extra load — a good trade because it's capped.

docs.title: 2.3 Queueing theory, practically ⭐ B2
docs.text:
A server is a queue. The key result (M/M/1): mean time waiting in the queue is S · ρ / (1 − ρ), where S is service time and ρ is utilization. As ρ → 1, wait → ∞. L1 C, measured on a simulated queue and matching the formula:

Utilization Measured wait vs 50% 50% 5.0 ms 1× 80% 19.4 ms 4× 90% 47.4 ms 9× 95% 107 ms 21× 99% 798 ms 159×

The lessons:

  • There's a knee around 70–80% utilization. Below it, latency is stable; above it, small load changes cause big latency jumps.
  • Plan to run at ~60–70%, so a traffic spike or a lost instance (which raises everyone else's utilization) doesn't push you over the knee.
  • Variability makes it worse: bursty arrivals or variable service times (a fat tail) push the knee lower. Little's law (L = λW, Ch 9) ties it together: in-flight work = arrival rate × time in system.

docs.title: 2.4 Profiling: JFR and async-profiler ⭐ B2
docs.text:
Don't optimize without a profile. The tools:

  • JDK Flight Recorder (JFR): built into the JVM, ~1% overhead, always-on-capable. Records execution samples (CPU), allocation, locks, GC, I/O, and more, into a .jfr file you analyze with jfr print, JMC, or IntelliJ.
  • async-profiler: a low-overhead sampling profiler that avoids the "safepoint bias" of older profilers and produces flame graphs for CPU, allocation, locks and cache misses.

L3 recorded a real JFR profile of a workload with a planted hotspot and analyzed it with jfr print:

  • CPU (execution samples): the hot self-time frames were Integer.getChars and ArraysSupport.mismatch, both rolling up to one method (3,139 of 3,159 samples). The profiler named the method to fix.
  • Allocation samples: 97% were byte[] — the signature of building strings by concatenation in a loop.
  • The profile-guided fix (a StringBuilder plus a precomputed map instead of an O(n²) concat and a linear scan) ran 175× faster (90,020/s → 15.8M/s) with an identical checksum — same behavior, vastly less work.

Read a profile as: self time (where the CPU actually is) vs total time (inclusive), the top allocation sites (allocation pressure drives GC, §2.5), and lock contention (Ch 19). Flame graph width = time; look for wide frames you didn't expect.

docs.title: 2.5 Garbage collection ⭐ B3
docs.text:
The JVM's collectors trade throughput, pause time and footprint:

Collector Pause behavior Best for Notes Serial Stop-the-world, single-threaded Tiny heaps, single-core, CLIs Simple Parallel STW, multi-threaded; highest throughput, longest pauses Batch jobs where throughput > latency L2: 118 ms max pause G1 (default) Mostly-concurrent, target pause (~200 ms default), region-based General-purpose services L2: 55–69 ms max pause ZGC Concurrent, sub-millisecond pauses, scales to TB heaps Latency-sensitive services L2: request max 7.5 ms; generational since JDK 21, default in 25 Shenandoah Concurrent, low pause (OpenJDK/Red Hat) Same niche as ZGC Alternative to ZGC

L2 ran the same allocation-heavy workload (1 GB heap, ~15 s, churning a 300 MB live set) under each collector and measured both GC pauses and the resulting request latency tail:

JDK / GC Requests Allocated STW total STW max req p99 req p999 req max JDK 21 Parallel 67,510 70.8 GB 4,099 ms 118.4 ms 0.37 ms 13.8 ms 118.9 ms JDK 21 G1 72,817 76.4 GB 3,817 ms 54.8 ms 0.54 ms 17.6 ms 55.9 ms JDK 21 ZGC 70,240 73.7 GB sub-ms* sub-ms* 0.52 ms 14.3 ms 36.3 ms JDK 25 G1 65,493 68.7 GB 4,817 ms 68.8 ms 0.39 ms 22.3 ms 89.0 ms JDK 25 ZGC (gen) 87,764 92.0 GB sub-ms* sub-ms* 0.54 ms 3.4 ms 7.5 ms

* ZGC's stop-the-world pauses are concurrent and sub-millisecond, so they don't appear as "Pause … ms" in the GC log; their effect is the request tail.

Reading it: Parallel gives the classic "few but long" pauses (118 ms); G1 trades those for "more but shorter"; generational ZGC on JDK 25 both did the most work (92 GB allocated, most requests) and had the shortest tail (max 7.5 ms). For a latency-SLO service, that tail is the headline. For a nightly batch job, Parallel's throughput may win.

Allocation is the real lever: GC work is proportional to allocation rate and live-set size. The cheapest GC tuning is allocating less (L3's fix), and the second is sizing the heap so the collector isn't constantly busy.

docs.title: 2.6 GC tuning knobs B3
docs.text:
• Pick the collector for the goal: ZGC/Shenandoah for latency, G1 for general, Parallel for throughput/batch.
  • Heap size (-Xms = -Xmx to avoid resizing): big enough that GC isn't constant, not so big that a pause (on STW collectors) is huge or the container OOMs.
  • G1: -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis (a target, not a guarantee); watch for humongous allocations and mixed-GC behavior.
  • Observe, don't guess: -Xlog:gc* (unified logging), JFR GC events, and pause/allocation-rate dashboards (Ch 24). Tune against measured pauses and allocation, never by copying flags from a blog.
  • Beware full GCs (a fallback when concurrent collection can't keep up): they're long STW pauses and signal the heap is too small or allocation too high.

docs.title: 2.7 JIT and warm-up B3
docs.text:
The JVM interprets bytecode first, then the JIT (C1 then C2) compiles hot methods to native code, so the first requests are much slower than steady state. Implications:

  • Warm up before measuring (every lab here warms up first) — a benchmark of cold code measures the interpreter.
  • Production warm-up: send synthetic traffic before a new instance takes real load, or the first users after a deploy hit slow code (and a scale-up during a spike serves the spike on cold JITs).
  • JMH for microbenchmarks (it handles warm-up, dead-code elimination and fork isolation) — hand-rolled micro-timing is usually wrong.
  • AOT / CRaC / GraalVM native image reduce warm-up for fast-start use cases (serverless), trading peak throughput or build complexity. Project Leyden is bringing more AOT to mainstream JDKs.

docs.title: 2.8 The JVM in containers ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Containers changed JVM defaults, and getting this wrong is a common performance bug:

  • CPU: the JVM sizes GC threads, ForkJoinPool.commonPool and availableProcessors() from the container's CPU quota. A wrong or unset limit gives too few or too many threads. CPU limits (throttling) can cause latency spikes when the container is throttled mid-request; many teams set CPU requests but not hard limits for latency-sensitive services.
  • Memory: use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage (e.g. 75%) rather than a fixed -Xmx, so the heap tracks the container's memory limit. Leave headroom for non-heap memory (metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, code cache) — the container limit must cover all JVM memory, or the kernel OOM-kills the process (exit 137), which looks like a crash, not a GC problem.
  • Modern JDKs are container-aware (since 8u191/10+), but verify: check availableProcessors() and Runtime.maxMemory() inside the container.

docs.title: 2.9 Load testing done right ⭐ B3
docs.text:
• Open vs closed model:
    • Closed (fixed number of virtual users looping): in-flight is capped at N, so the test cannot overload the service — throughput just plateaus (L4). Good for finding a per-concurrency operating point.
    • Open (fixed arrival rate, independent of responses): this is how real traffic behaves and the only way to see the overload cliff.
  • Coordinated omission: the classic load-test bug. If the tool sends the next request only after the previous responds, then when the server stalls the tool stops sending — and never records the requests that would have been slow. L1 D: a 500 ms freeze showed as p999 = 0 ms naively, and 460 ms when measured from the scheduled send time. Fixes: measure latency from intended start time (wrk2, Gatling, k6 do this correctly), or use an open model.
  • Tools: Gatling and k6 (open model, scripting), wrk2 (coordinated-omission-corrected), JMeter. Test against production-like data and dependencies; a load test against a warm cache and empty tables measures nothing.
  • What to measure: throughput, latency percentiles (p50/p99/p99.9), error rate, and resource USE (Ch 24) — and find the knee, not just one number.

docs.title: 2.10 Capacity planning and the USL ⭐ B4
docs.text:
• Little's law (Ch 9): L = λ · W. To serve λ requests/s at W seconds each, you have L in flight — which sizes thread pools and connection pools. L4: 2,000 rps × 1.1 ms ≈ 2 in flight, so a pool of ~4 with headroom (not hundreds).
  • Amdahl's law: a serial fraction α caps speedup at 1/α no matter how many cores.
  • Universal Scalability Law (USL): X(N) = N·X₁ / (1 + α(N−1) + βN(N−1)), adds a coherency term β (crosstalk between workers). Because of β, throughput doesn't just plateau — it can retrograde (fall) as concurrency rises.

L4 fit the USL to a real contended service's measured throughput curve:

  • Measured: scaled to ~10,000 req/s by N=16, then flat/slightly falling to N=256.
  • Fit: α ≈ 0.048 (the serialized critical section), β ≈ 0.0002 (coherency), predicting a peak of ~11,000 req/s at ~69 concurrent, beyond which throughput retrogrades.
  • The value: fit the model from a handful of load points and predict the peak, instead of testing to destruction — and it tells you why (contention vs coherency), pointing at the fix (shrink the serial section, Ch 19/20).

Capacity plan: measure the per-instance peak, run at ~60–70% of it (queueing knee, L1 C), size instances for peak traffic plus headroom for a lost instance and a spike, and re-measure as the workload changes.

docs.title: 2.11 A performance investigation method B4
docs.text:
1. Start from the SLO/symptom (Ch 24): which journey, which percentile, how bad.
  2. Trace to the critical path (Ch 24 L3): which service/span dominates the tail. Don't optimize off the critical path (§1.1).
  3. Profile that service (JFR/async-profiler, L3): find the hot method or allocation site by evidence.
  4. Check the platform: GC pauses (L2), CPU throttling, lock contention (Ch 19), connection-pool waits (Ch 19).
  5. Fix the biggest thing, then re-measure. One change at a time; performance is full of surprises.
  6. Guard it: a load test in CI (open model, percentiles) and a latency SLO so regressions page.

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Performance Engineering Practice
docs.text:
Field Value Author / Reviewers Performance guild / service teams, SRE Status Approved Related ADRs ADR-108 Generational ZGC for latency-sensitive services, G1 default elsewhere; ADR-109 Continuous JFR in production; ADR-110 Load tests are open-model, percentile-based, in CI; ADR-111 JVM container defaults (MaxRAMPercentage, CPU awareness); ADR-112 Capacity plans from USL + Little's law, run at ≤ 70% of peak

1. Context & Problem. The §1.1 review: optimizing off the critical path, an unread 118 ms GC pause in the p99, never profiling, and a capacity number from a flawed load test.

2. Goals / Non-Goals.

  • Goals: latency SLOs met at the tail; evidence-based optimization (profile first); GC pauses out of the p99 for latency services; capacity planned with a model; regressions caught in CI.
  • Non-goals: micro-optimizing cold paths; chasing 100% CPU efficiency at the cost of the latency knee.

3. Requirements.

ID Requirement NFR-1 Latency services run a low-pause GC; no GC pause > 10 ms in the p99 (JFR-checked) NFR-2 Continuous JFR in production (~1% overhead); profiles retrievable per incident NFR-3 Load tests are open-model, report p50/p99/p99.9, and run in CI with a regression budget NFR-4 JVMs use MaxRAMPercentage and correct CPU awareness in containers; no OOM-kills from misconfigured limits NFR-5 Capacity plans state per-instance peak (from load tests / USL) and target ≤ 70% utilization with headroom for a lost node

4. Estimates.

Item Method Result Product-page in-flight Little's law: 300 rps × 150 ms p99 ~45 in flight DB pool (catalog) 400 qps × 5 ms ~2 busy → pool 10 Per-instance peak (pricing) USL fit from load test (L4) ~11k rps; run to ~7k GC choice (pricing) Latency SLO 300 ms p99 Generational ZGC

5. Proposed design.

  1. GC: generational ZGC for product-page, pricing, checkout, search; G1 for batch/settlement; heaps sized with MaxRAMPercentage=75, -Xlog:gc* to the observability pipeline.
  2. Profiling: JFR always on with a profile settings template; async-profiler on demand for flame graphs; profiles attached to incident tickets.
  3. Load testing: k6/Gatling open-model scenarios per journey, against a production-like environment, in CI with percentile budgets; wrk2-style coordinated-omission correction.
  4. Capacity: a quarterly capacity model per service (USL fit + Little's law), instances sized for peak × headroom, autoscaling targets set below the queueing knee.
  5. Method: the §2.11 runbook — SLO → trace → profile → platform → fix → guard.

7. Alternatives considered.

Option Pros Cons Verdict G1 everywhere One collector Pauses in the p99 for latency services (L2) ZGC for latency services Optimize by intuition Fast to start Usually wrong (L3) Profile first Closed-model load tests only Simple Can't see the overload cliff; coordinated omission (L1 D, L4) Open model Fixed -Xmx in containers Explicit Drifts from limits, OOM-kills MaxRAMPercentage Guess capacity No work The §1.1 outage USL + Little's law

8. Failure modes. GC pause regression → JFR alert. CPU throttling → container metrics + no hard limits on latency services. Coordinated omission → open-model tooling. Warm-up misses → pre-warm on deploy/scale-up.

10. Observability (Ch 24). Latency percentiles per journey, GC pause and allocation-rate metrics, JFR on demand, CPU throttling, pool saturation, and load-test results tracked over time.

14. Decision (ADR-108–112). Low-pause GC for latency services, continuous profiling, open-model percentile load tests in CI, correct JVM container settings, and model-based capacity planning at ≤ 70% utilization.
