docs.title: L3 — Are the doc's numbers consistent with its own assumptions? B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "The capacity section says 500 orders/s and 2 TB. Before we size the cluster, check those against the doc's stated assumptions."

Every derived figure is recomputed from the doc's assumptions with the Ch 02 method and compared with the claim; anything off by more than 2x is flagged.

EstimateL3.java
// EstimateL3.java — run with: java EstimateL3.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// INTERNAL CONSISTENCY OF A DESIGN DOC'S NUMBERS. Design docs state assumptions (DAU, orders per user, payload size,
// retention) in one section and derived figures (peak QPS, storage, bandwidth) in another — often written on different
// days, sometimes by different people. Reviewers rarely recompute them. This check derives every figure from the stated
// assumptions (the back-of-envelope method of Ch 02) and compares it with what the doc claims, flagging anything off by
// more than 2x. An order-of-magnitude error in a capacity claim becomes a wrong instance count, a wrong DB, a wrong budget.
import java.util.*;

public class EstimateL3 {
    record Check(String metric, double claimed, double derived, String unit, String formula) {
        double ratio() { return claimed / derived; }
        boolean ok() { return ratio() >= 0.5 && ratio() <= 2.0; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // ---- assumptions as written in the doc's "Scale assumptions" section ----
        double dau = 2_000_000;             // daily active users
        double ordersPerDauPerDay = 0.5;    // half of DAU place an order each day
        double peakFactor = 5;              // festival peak vs daily average
        double orderBytes = 4 * 1024;       // stored order row + items + audit, bytes
        double retentionYears = 3;
        double readsPerOrder = 40;          // order-status polls, history views, support lookups per order lifetime
        double eventBytes = 1.5 * 1024;     // OrderPlaced event on Kafka
        double replicationFactor = 3;

        // ---- figures the doc CLAIMS in its "Capacity" section ----
        Map<String, Double> claimed = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        claimed.put("peak order writes/s", 500.0);
        claimed.put("order storage (3 yr, 1 copy)", 2.0);       // TB
        claimed.put("peak order reads/s", 2_300.0);
        claimed.put("Kafka ingest (3 replicas)/day", 4.2);      // GB/day
        claimed.put("avg order writes/s", 11.6);

        // ---- derive from assumptions ----
        double ordersPerDay = dau * ordersPerDauPerDay;
        double avgWps = ordersPerDay / 86_400;
        double peakWps = avgWps * peakFactor;
        double storageTB = ordersPerDay * 365 * retentionYears * orderBytes / 1e12;
        double peakRps = peakWps * readsPerOrder;
        double kafkaGBday = ordersPerDay * eventBytes * replicationFactor / 1e9;

        List<Check> checks = List.of(
            new Check("avg order writes/s", claimed.get("avg order writes/s"), avgWps, "/s", "2M DAU × 0.5 ÷ 86,400"),
            new Check("peak order writes/s", claimed.get("peak order writes/s"), peakWps, "/s", "avg × peak factor 5"),
            new Check("peak order reads/s", claimed.get("peak order reads/s"), peakRps, "/s", "peak writes × 40 reads/order"),
            new Check("order storage (3 yr, 1 copy)", claimed.get("order storage (3 yr, 1 copy)"), storageTB, " TB", "1M/day × 365 × 3 × 4 KiB"),
            new Check("Kafka ingest (3 replicas)/day", claimed.get("Kafka ingest (3 replicas)/day"), kafkaGBday, " GB", "1M/day × 1.5 KiB × 3")
        );

        System.out.println("Recomputing a design doc's capacity figures from its own stated assumptions (flag if off by >2x).\n");
        System.out.printf("   Assumptions: %,.0f DAU, %.1f orders/DAU/day, peak ×%.0f, %.0f KiB/order, %.0f yr retention, %.0f reads/order%n%n",
                dau, ordersPerDauPerDay, peakFactor, orderBytes / 1024, retentionYears, readsPerOrder);
        System.out.printf("   %-30s %10s %10s %7s   %s%n", "figure", "claimed", "derived", "ratio", "derivation");
        int bad = 0;
        for (Check c : checks) {
            System.out.printf("   %-30s %10s %10s %6.1fx   %-30s %s%n", c.metric(), fmt(c.claimed(), c.unit()), fmt(c.derived(), c.unit()),
                    c.ratio(), c.formula(), c.ok() ? "✓" : "✗ INCONSISTENT");
            if (!c.ok()) bad++;
        }
        System.out.printf("%n   → %d of %d figures disagree with the doc's own assumptions by more than 2x.%n", bad, checks.size());
        System.out.println("     The peak write rate is overstated ~9x — yet the peak READ figure matches the CORRECT derivation, which proves");
        System.out.println("     the author had the right number (58/s) when computing reads and the 500 is an isolated slip on one line. Storage");
        System.out.println("     is understated ~2.2x and the doc shows no working, so nobody can tell which assumption it silently changed.");
        System.out.println("     Each mistake changes a decision: 500 writes/s suggests sharding, 58 fits one PostgreSQL");
        System.out.println("     primary with room to spare. Put derivations in an estimation appendix, generated from the assumptions, so the");
        System.out.println("     numbers in the doc cannot drift apart — and so a reviewer can challenge an ASSUMPTION rather than a result.");
    }

    static String fmt(double v, String unit) {
        return (v >= 100 ? String.format("%,.0f", v) : String.format("%.1f", v)) + unit;
    }
}
java EstimateL3.java
Recomputing a design doc's capacity figures from its own stated assumptions (flag if off by >2x).

   Assumptions: 2,000,000 DAU, 0.5 orders/DAU/day, peak ×5, 4 KiB/order, 3 yr retention, 40 reads/order

   figure                            claimed    derived   ratio   derivation
   avg order writes/s                 11.6/s     11.6/s    1.0x   2M DAU × 0.5 ÷ 86,400          ✓
   peak order writes/s                 500/s     57.9/s    8.6x   avg × peak factor 5            ✗ INCONSISTENT
   peak order reads/s                2,300/s    2,315/s    1.0x   peak writes × 40 reads/order   ✓
   order storage (3 yr, 1 copy)       2.0 TB     4.5 TB    0.4x   1M/day × 365 × 3 × 4 KiB       ✗ INCONSISTENT
   Kafka ingest (3 replicas)/day      4.2 GB     4.6 GB    0.9x   1M/day × 1.5 KiB × 3           ✓

   → 2 of 5 figures disagree with the doc's own assumptions by more than 2x.
     The peak write rate is overstated ~9x — yet the peak READ figure matches the CORRECT derivation, which proves
     the author had the right number (58/s) when computing reads and the 500 is an isolated slip on one line. Storage
     is understated ~2.2x and the doc shows no working, so nobody can tell which assumption it silently changed.
     Each mistake changes a decision: 500 writes/s suggests sharding, 58 fits one PostgreSQL
     primary with room to spare. Put derivations in an estimation appendix, generated from the assumptions, so the
     numbers in the doc cannot drift apart — and so a reviewer can challenge an ASSUMPTION rather than a result.

Reading it:

  • Peak writes: 500/s claimed vs 58/s derived (8.6x over). The peak reads figure (2,300/s) matches the correct derivation (58 × 40 = 2,315), so the author clearly had the right write rate when computing reads — the 500 is an isolated slip that nobody recomputed.
  • Storage: 2.0 TB claimed vs 4.5 TB derived (2.2x under), with no working shown — so a reviewer can't even tell which assumption was silently changed.
  • Both errors change decisions: 500 writes/s pushes toward sharding (Ch 11); 58/s is comfortable on one PostgreSQL primary. An understated storage figure under-provisions disks and backups.
  • The fix is structural, not "be more careful": put assumptions in one place and generate the derived numbers, so reviewers argue about assumptions and the figures can't drift.

docs.title: L4 — Detecting drift between the doc and the code B4
docs.text:
Requirement: "The container diagram was approved six months ago. What has changed since?"

The lab parses a real (small) Java source tree — Feign clients for sync calls, Kafka send/@KafkaListener for async, WebClient.create for external hosts — recovers the actual dependency graph, and diffs it against the relationships drawn in the design doc.

src/checkout/CheckoutService.java (one of the scanned files)
package in.grocery.checkout;
@FeignClient(name = "catalog", url = "${services.catalog}")
interface CatalogClient { Price price(String sku); }
@FeignClient(name = "promotions", url = "${services.promotions}")      // not in the documented model
interface PromotionsClient { Discount best(String cartId); }
class CheckoutService {
  @Autowired KafkaTemplate<String, OrderPlaced> kafka;
  void place(Order o) { kafka.send("order-events", o.id(), new OrderPlaced(o)); }
}
DriftL4.java
// DriftL4.java — run with: java DriftL4.java src documented_model.txt   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// DOCUMENTATION DRIFT DETECTION. A design doc's container diagram is true on the day it's approved and starts rotting the
// next day. Here we recover the ACTUAL architecture from the source code — Feign clients (sync calls), Kafka producers and
// listeners (async), and outbound WebClients to external hosts — and diff it against the relationships the doc DRAWS.
//   UNDOCUMENTED  = in the code, not in the doc   (the diagram is lying by omission — often the dangerous dependency)
//   STALE         = in the doc, not in the code   (the diagram shows something that no longer exists)
// Real tools do this from runtime data (service-mesh telemetry, distributed traces) or bytecode; here we parse source so
// the mechanism is visible. Run it in CI and a design doc can't quietly diverge from the system it describes.
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.regex.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class DriftL4 {
    static final Pattern FEIGN    = Pattern.compile("@FeignClient\\(name\\s*=\\s*\"([\\w-]+)\"");
    static final Pattern PRODUCE  = Pattern.compile("\\.send\\(\"([\\w-]+)\"");
    static final Pattern CONSUME  = Pattern.compile("@KafkaListener\\(topics\\s*=\\s*\"([\\w-]+)\"");
    static final Pattern EXTERNAL = Pattern.compile("WebClient\\.create\\(\"https?://([\\w.-]+)");
    static final Map<String,String> KNOWN_HOSTS = Map.of("api.razorpay.com", "ext:razorpay", "sms.gateway.example", "ext:sms");

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Path src = Path.of(args[0]);
        Set<String> actual = new TreeSet<>();
        Map<String,String> evidence = new HashMap<>();
        try (Stream<Path> files = Files.walk(src)) {
            for (Path f : files.filter(p -> p.toString().endsWith(".java")).toList()) {
                String service = src.relativize(f).getName(0).toString();     // top-level dir = service
                List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(f);
                for (int i = 0; i < lines.size(); i++) {
                    String l = lines.get(i), where = src.relativize(f) + ":" + (i + 1);
                    if (l.trim().startsWith("//")) continue;                  // ignore commented-out code
                    Matcher m;
                    if ((m = FEIGN.matcher(l)).find())    add(actual, evidence, service + " -> " + m.group(1), where);
                    if ((m = PRODUCE.matcher(l)).find())  add(actual, evidence, service + " -> topic:" + m.group(1), where);
                    if ((m = CONSUME.matcher(l)).find())  add(actual, evidence, "topic:" + m.group(1) + " -> " + service, where);
                    if ((m = EXTERNAL.matcher(l)).find()) add(actual, evidence, service + " -> " + KNOWN_HOSTS.getOrDefault(m.group(1), "ext:" + m.group(1)), where);
                }
            }
        }
        Set<String> documented = Files.readAllLines(Path.of(args[1])).stream()
                .map(String::trim).filter(l -> !l.isEmpty() && !l.startsWith("#")).collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new));

        System.out.println("Architecture drift: dependencies recovered from source code vs relationships drawn in the design doc.\n");
        System.out.println("   Recovered from code (" + actual.size() + "):");
        for (String a : actual) System.out.printf("      %-36s  (%s)%n", a, evidence.get(a));
        System.out.println("   Documented in the design doc (" + documented.size() + "): " + documented + "\n");

        Set<String> undocumented = new TreeSet<>(actual); undocumented.removeAll(documented);
        Set<String> stale = new TreeSet<>(documented); stale.removeAll(actual);
        Set<String> agree = new TreeSet<>(actual); agree.retainAll(documented);
        for (String u : undocumented) System.out.printf("   ✗ UNDOCUMENTED  %-36s found at %s%n", u, evidence.get(u));
        for (String s : stale)        System.out.printf("   ✗ STALE         %-36s drawn in the doc, absent from the code%n", s);
        System.out.printf("%n   → %d of %d documented relationships still hold; %d real dependencies are missing from the diagram; %d drawn%n",
                agree.size(), documented.size(), undocumented.size(), stale.size());
        System.out.println("     relationship(s) no longer exist. The undocumented ones matter most: checkout's synchronous call to promotions is now on the");
        System.out.println("     checkout critical path (a latency and availability dependency no reviewer approved), and promotions itself calls");
        System.out.println("     catalog. The stale dispatch → checkout arrow was removed from the code in June but still shapes how people reason");
        System.out.println("     about failure blast radius. Generate the container diagram from recovered dependencies (or fail CI on drift) and");
        System.out.println("     the design doc stays a description of the system rather than of its past.");
    }
    static void add(Set<String> s, Map<String,String> ev, String edge, String where) { s.add(edge); ev.putIfAbsent(edge, where); }
}
java DriftL4.java src documented_model.txt
Architecture drift: dependencies recovered from source code vs relationships drawn in the design doc.

   Recovered from code (8):
      catalog -> topic:price-changes        (catalog/CatalogService.java:4)
      checkout -> catalog                   (checkout/CheckoutService.java:2)
      checkout -> ext:razorpay              (checkout/PaymentAdapter.java:3)
      checkout -> promotions                (checkout/CheckoutService.java:4)
      checkout -> topic:order-events        (checkout/CheckoutService.java:8)
      dispatch -> ext:sms                   (dispatch/DispatchListener.java:4)
      promotions -> catalog                 (promotions/PromotionsService.java:2)
      topic:order-events -> dispatch        (dispatch/DispatchListener.java:3)
   Documented in the design doc (6): [checkout -> catalog, checkout -> ext:razorpay, checkout -> topic:order-events, dispatch -> checkout, dispatch -> ext:sms, topic:order-events -> dispatch]

   ✗ UNDOCUMENTED  catalog -> topic:price-changes       found at catalog/CatalogService.java:4
   ✗ UNDOCUMENTED  checkout -> promotions               found at checkout/CheckoutService.java:4
   ✗ UNDOCUMENTED  promotions -> catalog                found at promotions/PromotionsService.java:2
   ✗ STALE         dispatch -> checkout                 drawn in the doc, absent from the code

   → 5 of 6 documented relationships still hold; 3 real dependencies are missing from the diagram; 1 drawn
     relationship(s) no longer exist. The undocumented ones matter most: checkout's synchronous call to promotions is now on the
     checkout critical path (a latency and availability dependency no reviewer approved), and promotions itself calls
     catalog. The stale dispatch → checkout arrow was removed from the code in June but still shapes how people reason
     about failure blast radius. Generate the container diagram from recovered dependencies (or fail CI on drift) and
     the design doc stays a description of the system rather than of its past.

Reading it:

  • 8 real dependencies were recovered with file-and-line evidence; 5 of the 6 documented relationships still hold.
  • 3 are undocumented. The important one is checkout → promotions: a synchronous call added to the checkout critical path that no design review saw. Its latency now sits inside the checkout p99 budget (Ch 31 L3), and a promotions outage now becomes a checkout outage unless someone adds a timeout and fallback (Ch 18). Promotions itself calls catalog, deepening the chain.
  • 1 is stale: dispatch → checkout was removed from the code (the scanner ignores the comment mentioning it) but is still on the diagram, where it misleads anyone reasoning about blast radius.
  • In production, combine sources: code scanning (intent, including rare paths), distributed traces / service-mesh telemetry (reality, including config-driven calls — Ch 24), and infrastructure inventories. Report drift on every PR and weekly per domain; better still, generate the container view from the recovered graph.

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes of architecture documentation
docs.text: Failure Symptom Mitigation Buried decision Key trade-off never discussed in review (§1.1) "Key decisions" section with alternatives up front Adjective requirements Nothing to check the design against Every NFR has a number; lint (L1) Wrong altitude Reviewers comment on naming, miss architecture Layered doc; detail in appendices (§2.2) Inconsistent numbers Wrong capacity plan, wrong DB choice Assumptions → derivations, recomputed (L3) Contradicting diagrams Slides, doc, wiki disagree One model, generated views (L2) Stale docs Diagram shows removed deps, misses new ones Drift detection vs code/traces (L4) Review theatre Many invitees, no substantive comments, no outcome Named asks, async window, recorded outcome (§2.6) Doc as bureaucracy Template filled mechanically, no thinking Drop sections with a reason; short docs; reviewers ask the §2.6 checklist questions

docs.title: 6.2 Observability of the documentation
docs.text:
• Track doc lint findings, drift counts and "last verified" age per domain; a rising drift count is architecture erosion made visible.
  • Runtime-recovered dependency graphs (from traces, Ch 24) are the most honest drift source — they include dependencies that exist only via configuration or reflection.
  • Measure review health: time from "In review" to outcome, number of substantive comments, percentage of reviews with a recorded outcome.

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Design docs often contain threat models, trust boundaries, and secrets-handling details. Keep sensitive sections in access-controlled repos or appendices; never paste real credentials, internal hostnames or customer data into examples (Ch 23).
  • The Security & privacy section is required: trust boundaries on the container diagram, data classification per store, authn/authz per interface.
  • Security reviewers should get a specific ask (§2.6), not a generic invite.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance of the process
docs.text:
• Lint and estimation checks run in seconds — make them PR checks so authors get feedback before reviewers do.
  • Time-box reviews (3–5 days); unresolved items become open questions with owners rather than blocking indefinitely.
  • Reuse: link standard sections (e.g., the platform's standard observability setup) rather than rewriting them in every doc.

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text: • A design doc costs a few days of an engineer's time; §1.1's missed durability decision cost a customer-facing incident, a redesign and a migration. The return on a well-reviewed design is highest for one-way-door decisions — scale the effort to the reversibility (Ch 31).

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. The buried decision

The expensive-to-reverse choice sits on page 23 between an ER diagram and a status-code table (§1.1). Put key decisions in their own section, with alternatives.

2. Adjectives as requirements

"Fast", "scalable", "highly available" give reviewers nothing to check. Every NFR gets a number (L1).

3. The novel

A 28-page doc that nobody reads fully. Keep it to what reviewers must decide on; move detail to appendices.

4. The slide deck instead of a doc

Slides hide gaps behind a presenter's voice and don't survive the meeting. Write prose; use slides only to summarize a written doc.

5. Unlabeled boxes and arrows

An arrow without direction, verb and protocol means different things to every reader. Use C4 notation rules (§2.4).

6. Mixed abstraction levels

Classes on a container diagram, infrastructure on a context diagram. One level per diagram.

7. Hand-maintained duplicate diagrams

Context, container, slides and wiki drawn separately will disagree. Generate views from one model (L2).

8. Numbers with no working

Reviewers can't challenge them and errors propagate into capacity plans. Assumptions first, derivations shown (L3).

9. Review by meeting

Reading the doc together in a meeting reaches few people and produces shallow feedback. Async first, meeting for disagreements.

10. No review outcome

"We discussed it" isn't a decision. Record approved / changes / rejected in the doc.

11. Treating the design doc as living documentation

Nobody updates a 10-page design doc for years. Keep the model, ADRs and generated docs true; mark the design doc point-in-time.

12. No open questions

A doc with no unknowns is either trivial or hiding them. List what you don't know, with owners.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What goes into a good design document?

30-second answer: A summary; the problem with evidence; goals and non-goals; measurable requirements (NFRs with numbers) and constraints; scale assumptions with derived figures; the proposed design at the right level (context and container diagrams, key flows, data ownership); the key decisions with alternatives considered; trade-offs, risks and failure modes; security; observability; rollout and rollback; cost; and open questions. It leads with what the reader must decide on.

Deep answer: §2.3 is the full template. L1 lints for the mechanical failures — missing sections, adjective requirements, one-option "alternatives", thin rollouts — so human reviewers can focus on whether the design is right.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Completeness vs brevity — drop sections that don't apply, with a one-line reason.

Follow-ups: 1. Most-skipped section that matters? → Alternatives considered, and non-goals. 2. How long should it be? → As short as possible; typically 4–10 pages plus appendices.

Red flags: Describing a design doc as an API spec or class diagram collection.

Q2 [B1] ⭐ What is the C4 model?

30-second answer: A way to draw software architecture at four levels of zoom: System Context (your system, its users and external systems), Container (the deployable units and how they talk), Component (the building blocks inside one container), and Code. Each diagram stays at one level, and every element and arrow is labeled with name, type/technology and purpose. Most designs need Levels 1 and 2 plus a few sequence diagrams.

Deep answer: L2 generates both levels from one model, which keeps them consistent; §3.1 and §3.2 are its output. The value is less in the shapes than in the rules: labeled, directional arrows with protocols; one abstraction level per diagram.

Trade-offs I'd call out: C4 is deliberately simple; it doesn't replace deployment or sequence views, it complements them.

Follow-ups: 1. Which level for executives? → Context. 2. What's a "container" in C4? → A deployable/runnable unit, not a Docker container specifically.

Red flags: Boxes and arrows with no labels.

Q3 [B1] Why write non-goals?

30-second answer: They draw the boundary of the design. They stop reviewers from spending comments on things you're deliberately not doing, stop scope creep during implementation, and make trade-offs explicit — "we are not replacing the payment provider" tells everyone the design must work with the existing one.

Deep answer: Non-goals are also where you record things that are desirable but deferred, which is useful later: the next design can pick them up. L1 treats a missing non-goals section as a finding.

Trade-offs I'd call out: None really; they cost a few lines and save many comments.

Follow-ups: 1. Non-goal vs out of scope? → Same idea; non-goal emphasizes it's deliberate. 2. Can a non-goal become a goal later? → Yes, in a new design.

Red flags: No boundary, leading to endless scope discussions in review.

Q4 [B1] What makes a requirement 'measurable'?

30-second answer: It has a number and a condition you can test: "checkout p99 < 300 ms at 800 req/s", "99.95% monthly availability for POST /checkout", "RPO 0 for orders". "Fast", "reliable" and "scalable" aren't requirements because no design can be checked against them.

Deep answer: Use the quality-attribute scenario form from Ch 31: stimulus, environment, response, measure. If you don't know the number yet, list it as an open question rather than writing an adjective. L1 flags adjectives without numbers.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Early numbers may be estimates; state them as such and revisit.

Follow-ups: 1. Why p99 rather than average? → Tail latency is what users and timeouts feel. 2. Where do numbers come from? → Current metrics, product targets, estimation.

Red flags: "The system must be highly available."

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do you run a design review that produces useful feedback?

30-second answer: Lint first so reviewers don't waste time on missing sections. Name reviewers and give each a specific ask. Run it asynchronously with a deadline for written comments, and point people at the open decisions. Hold a meeting only for disagreements the comments surfaced. Resolve every substantive comment explicitly, and end with a recorded outcome: approved, approved with changes, another round, or rejected.

Deep answer: §1.1's review failed on every point — broad invite, no asks, a meeting, naming comments, no discussion of the durability decision. The §2.6 reviewer checklist (source of truth, failure modes, hardest-to-change part, rollback) directs attention to what matters.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Async reviews take days; for urgent two-way-door changes, a short sync review is fine.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you get people to actually read it? → Specific asks, short docs, deadlines; or Amazon-style silent reading at the start of the meeting. 2. What if a reviewer blocks on preference? → Ask for the reason tied to requirements; otherwise record and move on.

Red flags: "We presented it in the architecture meeting and nobody objected."

Q6 [B2] ⭐ Why generate diagrams from a model instead of drawing them?

30-second answer: Hand-drawn diagrams drift: context, container, slides and wiki get edited separately and start contradicting each other and the system. With one model, every view is generated, so they can't disagree, renames happen once, and the model can be validated and queried — which container has no owner, which element is orphaned, which arrows lack a protocol.

Deep answer: L2 builds a 13-element model, generates both C4 levels, and validation finds three problems no picture reveals by itself. Structurizr DSL is the production tool; rendering in CI keeps the docs site current.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Less layout freedom than a drawing tool; a small learning curve.

Follow-ups: 1. Minimum step if you can't adopt a modeling tool? → Diagrams as text (Mermaid/PlantUML) in the repo. 2. What can you validate on a model? → Ownership, orphans, labels, illegal dependencies.

Red flags: Architecture diagrams that exist only as PNGs in a slide deck.

Q7 [B2] How do you make sure the numbers in a design doc are right?

30-second answer: Separate assumptions from derived figures, show the working for each derivation, and ideally generate the derived figures from the assumptions with a small script. Then reviewers argue about assumptions (which is productive) and the derived numbers can't drift apart.

Deep answer: L3 recomputes a doc's capacity section: peak writes overstated 8.6x and storage understated 2.2x. The first changes the architecture: 500 writes/s suggests sharding, while 58 fits one PostgreSQL primary. The reads matched the correct derivation, which revealed the 500 as an isolated slip.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Precision theater — round honestly and give ranges when uncertain.

Follow-ups: 1. What's the most useful review comment on numbers? → Challenging an assumption. 2. Where do derivations live? → An estimation appendix, or a script in the repo.

Red flags: Capacity numbers with no stated assumptions.

Q8 [B2] Design doc vs ADR vs RFC — when do you use each?

30-second answer: A design doc describes how to build something non-trivial and gets feedback on its decisions before building. An ADR records one significant decision and its reasoning — design docs link ADRs for their key decisions. An RFC proposes a cross-cutting change affecting many teams (a new standard, platform or technology), open to broad comment with a named decider.

Deep answer: They form a hierarchy: RFCs set direction, design docs apply it to a specific system, ADRs capture each decision durably. Design docs are point-in-time; ADRs and the architecture model are the living record (Ch 31).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Too many formats create confusion; define them clearly in one standard.

Follow-ups: 1. Which one survives longest? → ADRs. 2. What precedes a design doc? → Often a one-pager to decide whether to invest.

Red flags: Using a design doc as a permanent record that's never updated.

Q9 [B2] What should a design doc say about failure modes?

30-second answer: For each dependency and each stateful component: what happens when it's slow, down, or returns wrong data; what the user sees; how the system detects it; and how it recovers. Also where the source of truth for each piece of data lives and its durability (RPO/RTO). It should name single points of failure and the mitigations.

Deep answer: §1.1's failure was precisely a missing failure-mode discussion — slot bookings held in Redis with asynchronous persistence meant a failover lost customer promises. A simple table (dependency × failure × effect × mitigation) forces the conversation. Link resilience patterns from Ch 18.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Exhaustive FMEA is heavy; focus on critical-path dependencies and stateful stores.

Follow-ups: 1. The single most important question? → Where is the source of truth and how durable is it? 2. How do you verify the claims later? → Chaos experiments (Ch 27).

Red flags: A design with no failure section, only the happy path.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ How do you keep architecture documentation from rotting?

30-second answer: Keep docs next to code and change them in the same PR; generate what can be generated (API references, schema docs, diagrams from the model); detect drift automatically by recovering the actual architecture from code or traces and diffing it against the documented model; make rules executable as fitness functions; and treat design docs as point-in-time, keeping the living truth in the model and ADRs.

Deep answer: L4 recovers 8 dependencies from source and finds 3 undocumented (including a synchronous checkout → promotions call on the critical path) and 1 stale. Trace-based discovery (Ch 24) is even more honest because it captures config-driven and reflective calls.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Drift checks need maintenance (new client libraries, new patterns); start with the critical-path dependencies.

Follow-ups: 1. Why are undocumented dependencies dangerous? → Nobody reviewed their latency/availability impact. 2. Code scanning vs traces? → Code shows intent incl. rare paths; traces show reality incl. config-driven calls.

Red flags: "We update the wiki quarterly."

Q11 [B3] ⭐ How do you pitch the same architecture to executives and to engineers?

30-second answer: Same facts, different altitude. Executives: business problem, options framed as business trade-offs (time, cost, risk, scalability limits), one context diagram, the ask. Engineers: requirements with numbers, container-level design, key decisions and alternatives, failure modes, contracts, rollout. Layer the document so both can stop reading at the right point.

Deep answer: Translate technical options into outcomes: "ship in 6 weeks with a limit at 3x today's load, or 12 weeks without it." Evidence (before/after metrics) persuades both audiences. §2.2 and §2.10.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Oversimplifying for executives can hide real risk; always state the top risk plainly.

Follow-ups: 1. What's the one diagram for executives? → System context. 2. How do you present risk? → Probability, impact, mitigation, and what it costs to reduce.

Red flags: Showing a container diagram with 30 boxes to a CFO.

Q12 [B3] What level of detail belongs in a design doc vs in code review?

30-second answer: The design doc covers decisions that are expensive to change and that cross boundaries: service boundaries, data ownership and durability, integration styles, contracts between teams, consistency model, failure behavior, rollout. Code review covers what's cheap to change: internal class structure, naming, algorithms within a component, most API field details.

Deep answer: §1.1's doc inverted this — pages of API and class detail, two paragraphs of architecture. Contract-level API design (resources, idempotency, pagination, versioning) does belong in the doc because it crosses team boundaries; field-level detail usually doesn't.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Some internal details are architecturally significant (e.g., a concurrency model); include them when they affect NFRs.

Follow-ups: 1. Is the data model in scope? → Ownership and key entities yes; every column no. 2. How do you tell what's significant? → Would it be expensive to change after launch?

Red flags: Design docs full of getters and setters.

Q13 [B3] How do you handle a design review where a senior reviewer strongly disagrees?

30-second answer: Make the disagreement concrete: is it a fact (the design violates a requirement) or a preference? Facts get evidence — a model, a spike, a benchmark. Preferences get weighed against the requirements; if they don't change an outcome, record them and move on. For genuine trade-off disagreements, use a decision matrix with sensitivity (Ch 31) and escalate priority conflicts to the owner of the priority.

Deep answer: Record the dissent in the doc or ADR — it's valuable when the decision is revisited. Don't let a design review turn into a status contest; the §2.6 rule "separate facts from preferences" is the tool.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Time spent resolving vs moving on; for two-way doors, pick one and set a trigger.

Follow-ups: 1. What if they're right and you're past the deadline? → Correct it; a wrong one-way door costs more than a delay. 2. How do you avoid it next time? → Involve them earlier (advice process).

Red flags: Approving to avoid conflict, or overriding without addressing the argument.

Q14 [B3] What belongs in the rollout section of a design doc?

30-second answer: The phases (shadow, canary percentages, full), the feature flags, any data migration and its order (expand/contract), the guardrail metrics that gate each phase, the rollback trigger and procedure — including what happens to data written by the new version if you roll back — and who is on point.

Deep answer: L1 flags a rollout shorter than a sentence. A good rollout connects to Ch 26 (canary, blue-green) and Ch 28 (expand/contract): data written by the new version must remain readable by the old one until the rollback window closes.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Slower rollouts reduce blast radius but delay value and prolong dual-running.

Follow-ups: 1. The most-forgotten rollback issue? → Data written in the new format. 2. What gates a canary step? → SLO metrics vs the baseline.

Red flags: "Deploy it."

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ How would you set up architecture documentation for a 200-engineer organization?

30-second answer: A small set of formats with clear purposes: one-pagers, design docs (one template), ADRs, RFCs for cross-cutting change. Everything as code in the owning repos. A C4 model per domain as the single source of diagrams, rendered in CI into a docs portal. Automated checks: doc lint, estimation consistency, model validation, drift against code and traces. Async reviews with named asks and recorded outcomes. Living truth in model + ADRs + generated docs; design docs point-in-time.

Deep answer: That's the §4 standard. The leverage is automation and defaults: the template and checks raise the floor without a central reviewer; the drift report surfaces erosion to owning teams; a portal (Backstage-style) makes it discoverable.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Some process overhead; keep formats few and checks fast, or teams route around them.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you make docs discoverable? → A portal indexing repos, with ownership metadata. 2. How do you measure success? → Review outcomes recorded, drift trend, incidents traced to undiscussed decisions.

Red flags: A central wiki with 3,000 unowned pages.

Q16 [B4] How do you recover the real architecture of a system you just inherited?

30-second answer: Combine sources: distributed traces and service-mesh telemetry for runtime dependencies; code scanning for clients, topics and datastores; infrastructure-as-code and cloud inventories for deployed resources; database grants for who touches which data. Merge them into a model, diff against whatever documentation exists, and interview owners about the differences — the undocumented dependencies are where the surprises live.

Deep answer: L4 shows code scanning; traces add config-driven and reflective calls; IaC shows what's deployed but unused. The result becomes the C4 model going forward (L2) and the baseline for drift detection.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Traces only see exercised paths (rare batch jobs may be missing); code shows possibilities that may be dead.

Follow-ups: 1. Why combine sources? → Each has blind spots. 2. What do you produce first? → A container-level model with owners.

Red flags: Trusting the existing diagram.

Q17 [B4] What are the trade-offs between written design docs and design-by-whiteboard?

30-second answer: Whiteboarding is fast, collaborative and great for exploring options, but its reasoning evaporates, it reaches only the people present, and gaps get filled charitably by the room. Written docs are slower but force precision, scale review to everyone affected, and leave a record. The best practice combines them: explore on a whiteboard, then write the decision down.

Deep answer: Amazon's six-page narrative culture exists because prose exposes muddled thinking that slides and whiteboards hide. But over-documenting two-way doors wastes time — scale to reversibility (Ch 31).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed and collaboration vs precision and durability.

Follow-ups: 1. When is a whiteboard enough? → Two-way doors within one team. 2. How do you capture a whiteboard session? → Photo plus an ADR or doc section.

Red flags: Either extreme — no writing at all, or a doc for every change.

Q18 [B4] How do you use documentation to reduce operational risk after launch?

30-second answer: The design doc's failure-mode and observability sections become runbooks, alerts and dashboards; SLOs defined in the doc become monitored; the container model tells on-call what depends on what (blast radius); drift detection flags new unreviewed dependencies; and postmortems feed back into ADRs and the model. Documentation is part of the operational system, not separate from it.

Deep answer: The L4 finding — an undocumented synchronous call on the checkout critical path — is exactly the kind of thing that turns a promotions-service blip into a checkout outage. Surfacing it before the incident lets the owning team add a timeout and fallback (Ch 18).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Keeping runbooks current is work; generate what you can and test runbooks in game days.

Follow-ups: 1. What does on-call need most? → Dependencies, SLOs, failure behavior, runbook steps. 2. How do you test runbooks? → Game days (Ch 27).

Red flags: Runbooks that were never exercised.

Q19 [B4] How do you write a design doc when requirements are still uncertain?

30-second answer: State the uncertainty explicitly: give ranges for assumptions, list open questions with owners and dates, design for the range (not a single point), identify which decisions are one-way doors and defer them if possible, and choose options that keep flexibility. Where the uncertainty is quantitative, show how the design behaves across the range (Ch 31 L4).

Deep answer: Uncertainty isn't a reason to skip the doc — it's a reason to write down what you'd need to know and which parts of the design depend on it. Phase the rollout to learn: build the reversible parts first, measure, then decide the irreversible parts.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Designing for a wide range costs more; design for the likely range with a clear trigger for the rest.

Follow-ups: 1. What's a decision trigger? → An observable condition that reopens a decision. 2. How do you avoid analysis paralysis? → Time-box and phase.

Red flags: Writing false precision to look confident.

Q20 [B4] What distinguishes a principal engineer's design doc from a senior engineer's?

30-second answer: Scope and emphasis. A senior's doc designs a system well. A principal's doc frames the problem in business terms, sets measurable goals others can check, presents the few decisions that matter as decisions with alternatives and quantified trade-offs, anticipates cross-team and organizational impact, designs the rollout and the reversibility, states uncertainty honestly, and is readable by executives and implementers alike. It's also short.

Deep answer: It reflects the practices of this chapter and Ch 31: numbers over adjectives, sensitivity over certainty, models over drawings, and review designed to surface the decisions that are expensive to change.

Trade-offs I'd call out: More upfront thinking time; far less rework.

Follow-ups: 1. What would you cut from a typical doc? → Implementation detail better reviewed in code. 2. What would you add? → Alternatives, failure modes, revisit triggers.

Red flags: Length as a proxy for rigor.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. A design doc is a tool for feedback on expensive decisions before they're made — not a record of effort (§1.1).
  2. Lead with the summary, problem, goals and measurable requirements; put the key decisions where reviewers can't miss them (§2.2, §2.3).
  3. Use the template (§2.3) and drop sections only with a reason. Lint the mechanical failures before humans review (L1).
  4. Draw with C4: labeled, directional arrows; one abstraction level per diagram; mostly Levels 1–2 (§2.4).
  5. Generate diagrams from one model so they can't contradict each other, and validate the model (L2).
  6. Numbers come with assumptions and working so reviewers can check and challenge them (L3).
  7. Reviews are async-first, with named asks and a recorded outcome (§2.6).
  8. Keep architecture documentation true with docs-as-code, generation, fitness functions and drift detection (L4).

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: Situation Artifact / practice Should we invest in this at all? One-pager Building something non-trivial or cross-team Design doc (§2.3 template) One significant decision ADR (Ch 31) Change affecting many teams / a new standard RFC with a named decider Documenting an existing system arc42 + C4 model Diagrams for a design C4 L1 + L2, sequence diagrams for key flows, generated from a model Capacity figures Assumptions → derivations, recomputable (L3) Keeping docs true Docs-as-code, generated references, drift detection (L4), fitness functions Getting a good review Lint first, named asks, async window, recorded outcome

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (B2) Take a design doc from your work (or §1.1's description) and rewrite its first page using the template's Summary, Context, Goals, Non-goals and Requirements. Run L1 on before and after.
  2. (B2) Draw the C4 context and container diagrams for your current system. Label every arrow with verb and protocol. What did you discover?
  3. (B3) Extend L2 with a deployment view: map containers to Kubernetes namespaces and nodes. Add a validation that every container has a deployment.
  4. (B3) Extend L3 to read assumptions and claims from a YAML block in a real Markdown doc, so it can run as a CI check.
  5. (B4) Extend L4 to consume a dependency list exported from distributed traces (a CSV of caller → callee) in addition to code. Which dependencies appear only in traces, and why?

docs.title: 33. Domain-Driven Design
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B2 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 13, Ch 15, Ch 16, Ch 31 · What you will build: How to draw boundaries that match the business — strategic DDD (subdomains, bounded contexts, context maps, ubiquitous language) and tactical DDD (aggregates, entities, value objects, domain events, repositories) — applied to the grocery platform, with four runnable labs that measure what good and bad boundaries do.

  • L1: rich aggregate vs anemic model. The same 9 operations — a UI bug, bulk abuse, an admin tool, an oversized coupon, a second code path, a client retry — left the anemic Order invalid after 8 of 9 (ending CANCELLED with a negative quantity and a total of −₹4,999.01 against a real subtotal of ₹1,455); the aggregate stayed valid after all 9, treating the retried cancel as an idempotent no-op.
  • L2: aggregate size vs contention. 20,000 stock reservations, 16 in flight: one store-wide aggregate took 16.0x the ideal time and wasted 93.7% of work on version conflicts; per-SKU aggregates 3.2x; per-SKU with the 5 hot SKUs split into stock buckets 1.1x.
  • L3: anti-corruption layer. 12 legacy ERP rows: the naive mapping put a wrong product into the Catalog for 9 of 12 (unnormalized units, ₹78.85 → ₹78.84, a discontinued item on sale, a blank tax code treated as exempt); the ACL produced 0 wrong products — 8 translated, 4 quarantined with reasons.
  • L4: finding bounded contexts. Splitting by nouns made 78.9% of weekly work cross boundaries. Modularity clustering independently found Catalog and Fulfilment contexts — and challenged the domain experts' draft in two concrete places.

· Reading time: 130 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: twenty-six services and one ball of mud
docs.text:
When the grocery platform moved to microservices, the team drew the service boundaries in an afternoon: one service per database table that "felt important." Product service. Price service. Stock service. Cart service. Order service. Customer service. Address service. Coupon service. Twenty-six in all.

Eighteen months later, the symptoms were unmistakable:

  1. Every feature touched five services. Adding "buy 2, get 1 free" required changes to Coupon, Price, Cart, Order and Product services, five pull requests across four teams, and a release train to deploy them in the right order.
  2. The word "product" meant four different things. To the catalog team it was a description with images; to pricing, a price book entry; to inventory, a stock-keeping unit in a specific dark store; to fulfilment, a physical item with a weight and a temperature class. The shared Product table had 63 columns, 40 of them nullable, and every team was afraid to change it.
  3. Business rules lived nowhere in particular. The rule "an order can't be modified after it's packed" was enforced in the Order service, re-implemented (differently) in the admin tool, and forgotten in the customer-support tool — which is how a support agent added items to an order already on a rider's bike (L1).
  4. One service became a global lock. Stock was modeled as a single "store inventory" document per dark store, so during a flash sale every reservation in the store queued behind every other (L2).
  5. The legacy ERP's model leaked everywhere. Its unit codes, status codes and rupee-as-float prices appeared in every service that touched products, each with its own conversion bugs (L3).

The team had microservices, but not boundaries. They'd split the system by nouns, not by the business capabilities, language and consistency rules that actually belong together. The re-architecture started not with technology but with a two-day event-storming workshop and a question: where does each word mean one thing?

The thesis of this chapter

Domain-Driven Design is a way to make software boundaries follow the business. Strategically, you find the places where the language and rules of the business are consistent — bounded contexts — and draw your module, service and team boundaries there, with explicit relationships (a context map) between them. Tactically, inside a context you model the business in code: aggregates that own their invariants, value objects that make illegal values unrepresentable, and domain events that tell other contexts what happened. The payoff is changes that stay local, rules that can't be bypassed, and services that don't need to be deployed together.

docs.title: 1.2 Where this lives in the grocery platform
docs.text: DDD concept Grocery platform Lab Core subdomain Slot & dark-store fulfilment, flash-sale inventory §2.2 Supporting subdomains Catalog, promotions, ordering §2.2 Generic subdomains Payments (Razorpay), SMS, GST invoicing rules, identity §2.2 Bounded contexts Catalog, Ordering, Inventory, Fulfilment, Billing L4 Context map Ordering → Inventory (customer/supplier), Catalog ← ERP (ACL), Billing → Razorpay (conformist) §3.1, L3 Aggregates Order, Cart, SkuStock (per dark store), DeliverySlot L1, L2 Value objects Money (paise), Quantity + Unit, Pincode, GSTIN, DeliveryLocation L1, L3 Domain events OrderPlaced, StockReserved, SlotBooked, OrderDispatched §2.9

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end you will be able to:

  • Distinguish core, supporting and generic subdomains and invest accordingly.
  • Find bounded contexts using ubiquitous language, invariants and usage data (L4), and draw a context map.
  • Choose context-integration patterns — ACL, open host service, published language, customer/supplier, conformist, shared kernel — and build an ACL (L3).
  • Design aggregates that enforce invariants (L1) and are sized for concurrency (L2).
  • Use value objects, domain events, repositories and domain services correctly.
  • Map bounded contexts to services and teams — and know when not to.

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: model the business, not the database B2
docs.text:
Most enterprise code starts from the database: tables become classes, classes get getters and setters, and "services" manipulate them. It works for CRUD — and falls apart when the business rules get interesting, because the rules end up scattered across every place that writes data (L1).

DDD, introduced by Eric Evans in 2003, flips the starting point: start from how domain experts talk about and run the business. What are the things that matter? What rules must always hold? What happens, in what order? Where does the same word mean different things? The code should read like the business — order.place(), slot.book(order), stock.reserve(qty) — and the boundaries should sit where the business itself has seams.

DDD has two halves that are often confused:

  • Strategic DDD — the big picture: subdomains, bounded contexts, context maps, ubiquitous language. This is where the architectural value is, and it applies whether you build a monolith or microservices.
  • Tactical DDD — the patterns inside one context: aggregates, entities, value objects, domain events, repositories, domain services, factories. Valuable where the domain is complex; overkill for CRUD.

A common failure is adopting the tactical patterns (lots of classes called ...Aggregate and ...Repository) without the strategic work — which gives you the ceremony without the boundaries.

docs.title: 2.2 Subdomains: core, supporting, generic ⭐ B2
docs.text:
A domain is the business area the software serves (grocery quick-commerce). It decomposes into subdomains, which are problem-space areas — they exist whether or not you write software:

  • Core subdomain — what differentiates the business and wins customers. For the grocery platform: getting the right items to the customer within the promised slot from a dark store — slot capacity, dark-store inventory under flash-sale load, dispatch. This is where you put your best engineers, build custom software, and apply rich DDD.
  • Supporting subdomain — necessary and business-specific, but not a differentiator: catalog management, promotions, ordering workflow. Build it, but more simply; don't gold-plate.
  • Generic subdomain — solved problems every business has: payments, SMS, identity, GST invoice formatting, email. Buy or use off-the-shelf (Razorpay, a notification provider, an identity provider), and integrate through an anti-corruption layer or a conformist relationship.

The classification is an investment decision (Ch 31): the §1.1 platform spent months building its own coupon engine (supporting) and its own OTP delivery (generic) while its slot allocation (core) was a spreadsheet-driven batch job.

docs.title: 2.3 Ubiquitous language ⭐ B2
docs.text:
Ubiquitous language is a shared vocabulary between domain experts and developers, used everywhere — in conversations, documents, and the code itself (class names, method names, event names). If the dark-store manager says "we short-pick an item when the shelf is empty," the code has a ShortPick event, not ItemStatusUpdate(status=4).

Why it matters:

  • Translation is where bugs hide. Every time a developer maps "what the business said" to "what the code calls it," meaning is lost.
  • It exposes boundaries. When the same word means different things to different groups — "product," "order," "customer," "address" — that's a signal of different bounded contexts, each with its own model (§2.4).
  • It makes code reviewable by the business. if (order.isPacked()) throw new OrderAlreadyPacked() can be checked with an operations manager; if (o.st >= 4) cannot.

The language is bounded: it's ubiquitous within a context, not across the enterprise. Trying to create one enterprise-wide canonical model with one definition of "Product" is how you get §1.1's 63-column table.

docs.title: 2.4 Bounded contexts ⭐ B3
docs.text:
A bounded context is a boundary within which a particular model and its language are consistent. Inside it, "Product" means exactly one thing; outside, it may mean something else entirely.

Context What "Product" means there Model Catalog A listing: name, description, images, category, attributes ProductListing Pricing A price book entry: MRP, selling price, effective dates PriceBookEntry Inventory Stock of one SKU in one dark store: on-hand, reserved SkuStock Fulfilment A physical item: weight, temperature class, bin location PickItem

They share an identifier (the SKU code) but not a model. Each context evolves its model independently.

How to find bounded contexts (combine several signals):

  • Language — where does the meaning of a key term change?
  • Invariants — which data must be consistent together, immediately? That data belongs in one context (and usually one aggregate).
  • Business capabilities and processes — "fulfil an order" vs "manage the catalog."
  • Change patterns — what changes together in practice? (Change coupling from git history is good evidence.)
  • Usage patterns — which entities do use cases touch together? (L4 builds this from event-storming output.)
  • Team ownership — Conway's Law (Ch 37): a context owned by one team stays coherent; one owned by three teams fractures.

L4 shows that usage data is a useful challenge to a human draft but not a substitute for it: modularity clustering independently found the Catalog and Fulfilment contexts, and pulled Address into Fulfilment (the busy use cases need a delivery location, not the customer's address book — a real modeling insight). It also proposed a grouping, {Cart, Coupon, StockLevel}, that follows call patterns rather than any invariant or language.

Bounded context ≠ microservice. A context is a model boundary. It can be one service, several services (if it's big), or a module inside a modular monolith. What it should almost never be is split across teams or shared by several contexts' code.

docs.title: 2.5 Context maps and integration patterns ⭐ B3
docs.text:
A context map shows the bounded contexts and the relationships between them — both technical (how they integrate) and organizational (who has power over whose model). The standard relationship patterns:

Pattern Meaning Grocery example Partnership Two teams succeed or fail together; coordinate changes closely Ordering + Fulfilment during the slot-booking rebuild Shared kernel Two contexts share a small, jointly-owned piece of model/code A shared Money/Sku value-object library — keep it tiny Customer/Supplier Downstream (customer) needs influence upstream (supplier) priorities Ordering (customer) ← Inventory (supplier) Conformist Downstream adopts upstream's model as-is, with no influence Billing conforms to Razorpay's payment model Anti-corruption layer (ACL) Downstream translates upstream's model into its own, protecting it Catalog ← legacy ERP (L3) Open host service (OHS) Upstream offers a well-defined protocol/API for many consumers Catalog's public product API Published language A documented shared exchange format Versioned OrderPlaced event schema in the registry (Ch 28) Separate ways No integration; duplicate instead Marketing's own product copy for campaigns

The anti-corruption layer deserves emphasis because it's the most common pattern in brownfield systems (L3). The legacy ERP's concepts — GM/GMS/LTR unit codes, status S1..S9, rupees as floats, sometimes-blank tax codes — must not leak into the Catalog's model. The ACL translates into the Catalog's language (Unit, Money, Availability), uses exact arithmetic, and quarantines what it can't translate faithfully. In L3 the naive mapping put a wrong product into the domain for 9 of 12 rows; the ACL for none.

docs.title: 2.6 Entities and value objects ⭐ B2
docs.text:
• An entity has an identity that persists through change: an Order is the same order whether it's draft or delivered. Equality is by ID.
  • A value object is defined entirely by its attributes, is immutable, and has no identity: Money(2850 paise, INR), Quantity(500, ML), Pincode("560034"), DeliveryLocation(lat, lng, landmark). Two Money(2850) are interchangeable. Equality is by value.

Value objects are the most underused, highest-return tactical pattern:

  • They make illegal values unrepresentable. A Pincode constructor that validates six digits means no code anywhere can hold an invalid pincode. A Money that stores paise as a long means no floating-point rounding bugs (L3's ₹78.85 → ₹78.84).
  • They carry behavior. money.add(other) checks currency; quantity.convertTo(Unit.G); slotWindow.overlaps(other).
  • They're trivially thread-safe and easy to test.

In Java, record types are ideal value objects:

Value objects as Java records
public record Money(long paise) {
    public Money { if (paise < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative money"); }
    public static Money ofRupees(String r) { return new Money(new BigDecimal(r).movePointRight(2).setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_UP).longValueExact()); }
    public Money plus(Money o) { return new Money(Math.addExact(paise, o.paise)); }
    public Money times(int qty) { return new Money(Math.multiplyExact(paise, qty)); }
}
public record Pincode(String value) {
    public Pincode { if (!value.matches("[1-9][0-9]{5}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid pincode " + value); }
}

docs.title: 2.7 Aggregates: consistency boundaries ⭐ B3
docs.text:
An aggregate is a cluster of entities and value objects treated as one unit for data changes, with one entity as the aggregate root — the only object outside code may hold a reference to. The aggregate's job is to protect its invariants: rules that must be true after every transaction.

For the Order aggregate (root Order, containing OrderLine entities and Money/Quantity values):

  • total = Σ(line qty × unit price) − discount — derived, never stored independently;
  • quantities are positive and ≤ 10 per SKU;
  • discount ∈ [0, subtotal];
  • items can only be added while DRAFT;
  • only a PLACED order can be cancelled (and cancelling a CANCELLED order is an idempotent no-op).

The rules of aggregate design (Vaughn Vernon's formulation):

  1. Protect true invariants inside the aggregate boundary. All changes go through the root's intention-revealing methods (addItem, applyCoupon, place), which refuse invalid transitions. No public setters. L1: the anemic Order became invalid after 8 of 9 operations; the aggregate after none.
  2. Design small aggregates. An aggregate is loaded, locked and saved as a unit, so it is also the unit of concurrency (L2). A store-wide StoreInventory aggregate serializes every reservation — 16x slower than ideal with 94% of work wasted on conflicts. A per-SKU SkuStock aggregate matches the actual invariant (stock ≥ 0 per SKU) and runs 5x faster; splitting the hottest SKUs' stock into buckets gets within 10% of ideal.
  3. Reference other aggregates by identity. An Order holds a CustomerId, not a Customer object. This keeps aggregates small and makes their transactional boundaries explicit.
  4. Update other aggregates with eventual consistency. One transaction modifies one aggregate. If placing an order must reserve stock, the Order aggregate emits OrderPlaced and the Inventory context reacts — or a saga coordinates (Ch 13). Rules spanning aggregates are therefore eventually consistent; if the business truly needs them to be immediately consistent, that's a sign they belong in one aggregate (and you pay the concurrency cost).

docs.title: 2.8 Repositories, factories, domain services, application services B3
docs.text:
• Repository — a collection-like interface for loading and saving aggregates (not tables): orders.byId(id), orders.save(order). One repository per aggregate root. The domain defines the interface; infrastructure implements it (JPA, JDBC) — the dependency direction L2 of Ch 31 enforces.
  • Factory — encapsulates complex creation so an aggregate is born valid: Order.startFor(customerId, cart, pricingSnapshot).
  • Domain service — domain logic that doesn't naturally belong to one entity, typically involving several aggregates or an external policy: SlotAllocationService.bestSlotFor(order, darkStore). Stateless, named in the ubiquitous language.
  • Application service — orchestrates a use case: load aggregates via repositories, call domain methods, save, publish events, handle transactions and authorization. It contains no business rules. If an application service has if statements about business policy, the logic is leaking out of the domain.
Application service: orchestration only (VERIFY: Spring wiring)
@Service
class PlaceOrderHandler {
    private final Orders orders; private final Carts carts; private final PricingSnapshotPort pricing;
    @Transactional
    public OrderId handle(PlaceOrder cmd) {
        Cart cart = carts.byId(cmd.cartId()).orElseThrow();
        Order order = Order.startFor(cmd.customerId(), cart, pricing.snapshotFor(cart));   // factory
        order.place();                                                                      // invariants enforced here
        orders.save(order);                  // saves aggregate + its OrderPlaced event to the outbox atomically (Ch 15)
        return order.id();
    }
}

docs.title: 2.9 Domain events B3
docs.text:
A domain event records something that happened in the domain that domain experts care about, named in the past tense in the ubiquitous language: OrderPlaced, StockReserved, SlotBooked, ItemShortPicked, OrderDispatched.

  • Within a context, events decouple side effects from the aggregate that caused them.
  • Across contexts, events are the primary integration mechanism: Ordering publishes OrderPlaced; Inventory, Fulfilment and Billing react. This implements "one aggregate per transaction, eventual consistency between aggregates" (§2.7 rule 4).
  • Reliably: save the event in the same transaction as the aggregate (the transactional outbox, Ch 15) and publish it asynchronously — otherwise you can commit the order and lose the event.
  • Internal vs integration events: events inside a context can carry rich domain objects; events crossing contexts form a published language — versioned, schema-registered, minimal, and stable (Ch 28).

Event storming (Alberto Brandolini) is the workshop technique that discovers events, commands, aggregates, policies and boundaries together with domain experts: everyone writes domain events on orange stickies along a timeline, then adds commands, actors, aggregates, policies and hotspots. Boundaries appear where the language changes and where flows hand off. L4's use-case/entity data is the kind of output an event-storming session produces.

docs.title: 2.10 From bounded contexts to services and teams B4
docs.text:
Bounded contexts are the best starting point for service boundaries (Ch 16), but the mapping isn't mechanical:

  • Start with a modular monolith where contexts are modules with enforced boundaries (fitness functions, Ch 31 L2). Extract a context into a service when it has a real driver: independent scaling, independent release cadence, a different team, a different availability requirement.
  • One context → one team (a team may own several small contexts). Never split one context across teams — its model will fracture.
  • Don't split a context by technical layer (a "product-read-service" and a "product-write-service" owned by different teams) unless you're deliberately applying CQRS inside one team's context.
  • Microservices smaller than a context are fine when there's a reason (a scaling hotspot), but they share the context's language and ideally its team.
  • Data ownership follows the context. Each context owns its data; others get it through APIs, events or read models — never by querying its tables (the §1.1 shared 63-column Product table is the anti-pattern).

docs.title: 2.11 When DDD is overkill B4
docs.text:
DDD's tactical patterns carry real cost: more classes, more mapping, eventual consistency between aggregates, and a learning curve. They pay off when the domain has complex, evolving rules and concurrent actors. They don't pay off for:

  • CRUD — a settings screen, a reference-data admin page. Use simple data-centric code (transaction script, active record).
  • Generic subdomains — you'll integrate a product, not model the domain.
  • Reporting/analytics — read models and SQL, not aggregates.

Strategic DDD — finding contexts, speaking the business's language, drawing a context map, protecting boundaries with ACLs — is almost always worth it, even in a system that uses no tactical patterns at all.

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Grocery Domain Re-architecture
docs.text:
Design Document (excerpt) — Bounded Contexts & Domain Model v1.0

Status: Accepted · Authors: Principal engineers + domain leads (ops, catalog, finance) · Reviewers: All tech leads

Field Value Context 26 entity-shaped services; typical feature touches 5 services and 4 teams; a shared 63-column Product table; business rules duplicated across Order service, admin tool and support tool; store-wide inventory document serializes flash-sale reservations; ERP concepts leak into every product consumer. Decision Re-draw boundaries around five bounded contexts (Catalog, Pricing & Promotions, Ordering, Inventory, Fulfilment) plus Billing, found by event storming and checked against usage data (L4). Each context owns its model and data, one team per context. Rich aggregates where rules are complex; ACL in front of the ERP; integration by published events via outbox. Related ADRs ADR-190 Five bounded contexts + context map; ADR-191 Aggregates own invariants, no public setters (L1); ADR-192 Per-SKU SkuStock aggregate, hot-SKU stock buckets (L2); ADR-193 ACL for ERP item master with quarantine (L3); ADR-194 Money/Quantity/Pincode value-object kernel (shared kernel, versioned); ADR-195 Cross-context integration via versioned events + outbox; ADR-196 Contexts as modules first, extract to services on demand

Requirements.

  • R1 — Local change. A typical feature touches one context (target: ≥ 80% of features, measured by PRs per feature).
  • R2 — Rules in one place. Every business invariant is enforced inside an aggregate or value object; no code path can bypass it (L1).
  • R3 — Flash-sale throughput. Stock reservations sustain ≥ 90% of ideal throughput under Zipf-skewed load (L2).
  • R4 — Clean ingestion. No ERP concept appears outside the Catalog ACL; untranslatable rows are quarantined with reasons (L3).
  • R5 — Independent deploys. Contexts integrate only through published APIs and versioned events.

Decisions in detail.

  1. Contexts (ADR-190). Catalog, Pricing & Promotions, Ordering, Inventory, Fulfilment, Billing. Address is modeled per context: Customer's address book in Ordering; a DeliveryLocation value object copied onto the order for Fulfilment (a finding from L4).
  2. Aggregates (ADR-191). Order, Cart, SkuStock(darkStore, sku), DeliverySlot, PriceBookEntry. One aggregate per transaction; cross-aggregate rules via events or sagas.
  3. Hot SKUs (ADR-192). For the top-N SKUs by volume, stock split into buckets with background rebalancing (L2 design C).
  4. ERP ACL (ADR-193). Unit, status and tax-code translation tables; exact decimal money; plausibility checks; quarantine queue owned by catalog ops (L3).
  5. Shared kernel (ADR-194). A tiny versioned library: Money, Quantity, Unit, Pincode, SkuCode. Anything bigger is not shared.
  6. Integration (ADR-195). OrderPlaced, StockReserved, SlotBooked, OrderDispatched as a published language in the schema registry.
  7. Modules first (ADR-196). Ordering and Catalog start as modules in one deployable; Inventory and Fulfilment are separate services (independent scaling for flash sales).

Consequences. Eventual consistency between Ordering and Inventory (a reservation may fail after the order is placed → compensating cancel, Ch 13). More code for value objects and translation. In return: features land in one context, rules can't be bypassed, and flash-sale throughput stops collapsing on a single aggregate.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
What's real here

All four labs are self-contained JDK 21 programs with deterministic output. L1 implements a real aggregate and an anemic model side by side. L2 is a discrete simulation of optimistic concurrency on different aggregate boundaries (the same conflict rule a @Version column enforces). L3 parses a real legacy feed file through a naive mapper and an ACL. L4 builds an entity-affinity graph from use cases and compares decompositions, including Louvain-style modularity clustering. JPA/Spring snippets are marked VERIFY.

docs.title: L1 — Rich aggregate vs anemic model B2
docs.text:
Requirement: "A support agent added items to an order already on a rider's bike. Make that — and every rule like it — impossible, whichever code path calls us."

The same Order is implemented as an anemic data bag and as an aggregate root. Nine realistic operations — a UI bug, bulk abuse, an admin tool writing the total, an oversized coupon, a second code path, and a client retry — are replayed against both, checking five business rules after each.

AggregateL1.java
// AggregateL1.java — run with: java AggregateL1.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// ANEMIC MODEL vs RICH AGGREGATE. The same Order is implemented twice:
//   ANEMIC — a data bag with public setters; business rules live (or don't) in whichever service happens to touch it.
//   RICH   — an AGGREGATE ROOT that owns its invariants: state changes only through intention-revealing methods
//            (addItem, applyCoupon, place, cancel) that refuse to produce an invalid Order.
// We replay the same 8 operations — the kinds of calls real callers make: a bug, a race, a second code path — against both,
// and count how many leave the Order in a state that violates a business rule.
import java.util.*;

public class AggregateL1 {
    // ---------------- ANEMIC ----------------
    static class AnemicOrder {
        public String status = "DRAFT";
        public List<long[]> lines = new ArrayList<>();       // {skuHash, qty, unitPaise}
        public long totalPaise = 0;
        public long discountPaise = 0;
    }
    // ---------------- RICH AGGREGATE ----------------
    static final class Order {
        enum Status { DRAFT, PLACED, CANCELLED }
        record Line(String sku, int qty, long unitPaise) {}
        private Status status = Status.DRAFT;
        private final Map<String, Line> lines = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        private long discountPaise = 0;
        static final int MAX_QTY_PER_SKU = 10;

        void addItem(String sku, int qty, long unitPaise) {
            requireDraft("add items");
            if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("quantity must be positive");
            if (unitPaise <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("price must be positive");
            int newQty = qty + (lines.containsKey(sku) ? lines.get(sku).qty() : 0);
            if (newQty > MAX_QTY_PER_SKU) throw new IllegalStateException("max " + MAX_QTY_PER_SKU + " per SKU");
            lines.put(sku, new Line(sku, newQty, unitPaise));
        }
        void applyCoupon(long discount) {
            requireDraft("apply coupons");
            if (discount < 0 || discount > subtotal()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("discount must be within 0..subtotal");
            discountPaise = discount;
        }
        void place() {
            requireDraft("place");
            if (lines.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("cannot place an empty order");
            status = Status.PLACED;
        }
        void cancel() {
            if (status == Status.CANCELLED) return;                          // idempotent: a retried cancel is a no-op (Ch 20)
            if (status != Status.PLACED) throw new IllegalStateException("only a placed order can be cancelled");
            status = Status.CANCELLED;
        }
        long subtotal() { return lines.values().stream().mapToLong(l -> l.qty() * l.unitPaise()).sum(); }
        long total() { return subtotal() - discountPaise; }                 // DERIVED — can never disagree with lines
        private void requireDraft(String what) { if (status != Status.DRAFT) throw new IllegalStateException("cannot " + what + " when " + status); }
    }

    // business rules both models are supposed to honour — checked after every operation
    static List<String> violations(String status, List<long[]> lines, long total, long discount) {
        List<String> v = new ArrayList<>();
        long subtotal = lines.stream().mapToLong(l -> l[1] * l[2]).sum();
        if (total != subtotal - discount) v.add("total != subtotal - discount");
        if (lines.stream().anyMatch(l -> l[1] <= 0)) v.add("non-positive quantity");
        if (lines.stream().anyMatch(l -> l[1] > 10)) v.add("qty > 10 per SKU");
        if (discount < 0 || discount > subtotal) v.add("discount outside 0..subtotal");
        if (status.equals("PLACED") && lines.isEmpty()) v.add("placed with no items");
        return v;
    }

    interface Op { String name(); void anemic(AnemicOrder o); void rich(Order o); }
    static Op op(String name, java.util.function.Consumer<AnemicOrder> a, java.util.function.Consumer<Order> r) {
        return new Op() { public String name() { return name; } public void anemic(AnemicOrder o) { a.accept(o); } public void rich(Order o) { r.accept(o); } };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Op> ops = List.of(
            op("add 2 x milk @ ₹60",                o -> { o.lines.add(new long[]{1, 2, 6000}); o.totalPaise += 12000; },
                                                    o -> o.addItem("milk", 2, 6000)),
            op("add -1 x bread (UI bug)",           o -> { o.lines.add(new long[]{2, -1, 4000}); o.totalPaise += -4000; },
                                                    o -> o.addItem("bread", -1, 4000)),
            op("add 15 x rice (bulk abuse)",        o -> { o.lines.add(new long[]{3, 15, 9000}); o.totalPaise += 135000; },
                                                    o -> o.addItem("rice", 15, 9000)),
            op("admin tool sets total directly",    o -> o.totalPaise = 99,
                                                    o -> { /* no setter exists: the total is derived */ }),
            op("coupon larger than subtotal",       o -> { o.discountPaise = 500000; o.totalPaise -= 500000; },
                                                    o -> o.applyCoupon(500000)),
            op("place the order",                   o -> o.status = "PLACED",
                                                    Order::place),
            op("add item AFTER placing (2nd path)", o -> o.lines.add(new long[]{4, 1, 2500}),     // forgot to update total too
                                                    o -> o.addItem("eggs", 1, 2500)),
            op("cancel the order",                  o -> o.status = "CANCELLED",
                                                    Order::cancel),
            op("cancel again (client retry)",       o -> o.status = "CANCELLED",
                                                    Order::cancel)
        );

        AnemicOrder a = new AnemicOrder(); Order r = new Order();
        int anemicBad = 0, richBad = 0;
        System.out.println("Replaying the same 9 operations against an ANEMIC Order and a RICH aggregate.\n");
        System.out.printf("   %-36s | %-40s | %s%n", "operation", "anemic: rules broken after this op", "rich aggregate");
        Set<String> seen = new LinkedHashSet<>();
        for (Op o : ops) {
            o.anemic(a);
            List<String> va = violations(a.status, a.lines, a.totalPaise, a.discountPaise);
            String richResult;
            try { o.rich(r); richResult = "accepted"; }
            catch (RuntimeException e) { richResult = "REJECTED: " + e.getMessage(); }
            List<long[]> rl = new ArrayList<>();
            for (var l : r.lines.values()) rl.add(new long[]{0, l.qty(), l.unitPaise()});
            List<String> vr = violations(r.status.name(), rl, r.total(), r.discountPaise);
            if (!va.isEmpty()) anemicBad++;
            if (!vr.isEmpty()) richBad++;
            List<String> fresh = new ArrayList<>(va); fresh.removeAll(seen); seen.addAll(va);
            String anemicCol = va.isEmpty() ? "valid" : va.size() + " broken" + (fresh.isEmpty() ? " (carried over)" : " (+" + String.join(", +", fresh) + ")");
            System.out.printf("   %-36s | %-40s | %s%n", o.name(), anemicCol, richResult + (vr.isEmpty() ? "" : "  → INVALID " + vr));
        }
        System.out.printf("%n   Operations that left the order violating a business rule:  anemic %d/9   rich %d/9%n", anemicBad, richBad);
        System.out.printf("   Final anemic order: status=%s, %d line(s), total ₹%.2f (true subtotal ₹%.2f)%n", a.status, a.lines.size(),
                a.totalPaise / 100.0, a.lines.stream().mapToLong(l -> l[1] * l[2]).sum() / 100.0);
