     31 pods  0.85 × optimum           72.1 L       95.8 L                 6.9 L
     37 pods  optimum (expected)       70.6 L       92.0 L                 3.1 L
     44 pods  1.2 × optimum            70.6 L       89.5 L                 2.7 L
     92 pods  p90 of demand            94.3 L      103.0 L                35.7 L

   → against a known curve the rule is crisp: commit up to the level the fleet sits at or above for the break-even share
     of hours (60% at a 40% discount) and buy the rest on demand. Committing to the p90 or the peak is the expensive
     mistake — most of those pods idle while being paid for, which shows up as the worst expected cost and by far the
     largest regret. Under uncertainty two things matter. The cost curve is FLAT around the optimum (0.85x to 1.2x are
     within a few percent), so precision matters less than avoiding the tails. And the right hedge follows the SKEW:
     here demand is more likely to grow than shrink, so committing a little above the expected-demand optimum does as
     well on average and better in the bad tail. In practice: commit to the floor you're confident of, ratchet up each
     quarter as growth materialises (commitments are easier to add than to exit), and put only interruptible work
     (batch, async consumers) on spot/preemptible capacity — never the checkout path.

Reading it:

  • The break-even rule works exactly: the optimum (37 pods) is where the marginal pod is busy 62% of hours — just above the 60% break-even (10.80 / 18). It saves 23% versus all on-demand.
  • Committing to the p90 is the expensive mistake: worse expected cost than everything else, and ₹35.7 L of p95 regret. Committing to the peak would be far worse still.
  • Under uncertainty the curve is flat between 0.85x and 1.2x of the optimum (expected cost within ~2%), so avoiding the tails matters more than precision.
  • The hedge follows the skew. Demand here is more likely to grow than shrink (the triangle's mean is above its mode), so 1.2x the expected-demand optimum ties on expected cost and has the lowest p95 regret. For a shrinking-market risk you'd hedge the other way.

docs.title: L4 — Storage and data transfer: measure, then rank B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "Should we switch our event log to a binary format to save money? And what about cross-zone traffic?"

Part 1 measures four encodings of 50,000 real-shaped order events with java.util.zip. Parts 2 and 3 apply the measured compression ratio to three real data streams — order events, application logs (volume from L1's usage data) and app clickstream — and price three years of retention and monthly cross-zone transfer.

StorageL4.java
// StorageL4.java — run with: java StorageL4.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// STORAGE AND DATA-TRANSFER COSTS — the lines on the bill nobody designed. Part 1 MEASURES real encodings of 50,000 order
// events (JSON, gzip'd JSON, a compact binary encoding, gzip'd binary) with java.util.zip; Part 2 extrapolates to the
// platform's event volume and prices three years of retention under different lifecycle policies; Part 3 prices a chatty
// cross-zone call pattern. ALL PRICES ARE ILLUSTRATIVE assumptions (₹ per GB-month / per GB), not current vendor rates.
import java.io.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.zip.*;

public class StorageL4 {
    static final String[] TYPES = {"OrderPlaced", "StockReserved", "PaymentCaptured", "OrderPacked", "OrderDelivered"};
    static final String[] CITIES = {"pune", "delhi", "bengaluru", "mumbai", "chennai", "hyderabad", "kolkata", "jaipur"};

    record Event(String type, String orderId, String customerId, String city, long tsMillis, long totalPaise, int items, String[] skus) {}

    static List<Event> events(int n) {
        Random r = new Random(3); List<Event> l = new ArrayList<>(); long ts = 1_780_000_000_000L;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            int items = 1 + r.nextInt(12); String[] skus = new String[items];
            for (int k = 0; k < items; k++) skus[k] = "SKU" + (100000 + r.nextInt(3000));
            ts += r.nextInt(400);
            l.add(new Event(TYPES[i % 5], "ORD" + (50_000_000 + i / 5), "CUST" + (1_000_000 + r.nextInt(2_000_000)),
                    CITIES[r.nextInt(CITIES.length)], ts, 5000 + r.nextInt(400_000), items, skus));
        }
        return l;
    }
    static byte[] json(List<Event> es) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (Event e : es) {
            sb.append("{\"eventType\":\"").append(e.type()).append("\",\"orderId\":\"").append(e.orderId())
              .append("\",\"customerId\":\"").append(e.customerId()).append("\",\"city\":\"").append(e.city())
              .append("\",\"occurredAt\":").append(e.tsMillis()).append(",\"totalPaise\":").append(e.totalPaise())
              .append(",\"itemCount\":").append(e.items()).append(",\"skus\":[");
            for (int k = 0; k < e.skus().length; k++) sb.append(k > 0 ? "," : "").append('"').append(e.skus()[k]).append('"');
            sb.append("]}\n");
        }
        return sb.toString().getBytes();
    }
    static byte[] binary(List<Event> es) throws IOException {     // schema'd binary: enums as bytes, ids/numbers as varints
        ByteArrayOutputStream bo = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); DataOutputStream o = new DataOutputStream(bo);
        for (Event e : es) {
            o.writeByte(Arrays.asList(TYPES).indexOf(e.type())); varint(o, Long.parseLong(e.orderId().substring(3)));
            varint(o, Long.parseLong(e.customerId().substring(4))); o.writeByte(Arrays.asList(CITIES).indexOf(e.city()));
            varint(o, e.tsMillis()); varint(o, e.totalPaise()); o.writeByte(e.items());
            for (String s : e.skus()) varint(o, Long.parseLong(s.substring(3)));
        }
        return bo.toByteArray();
    }
    static void varint(DataOutputStream o, long v) throws IOException { while ((v & ~0x7FL) != 0) { o.writeByte((int) ((v & 0x7F) | 0x80)); v >>>= 7; } o.writeByte((int) v); }
    static byte[] gzip(byte[] in) throws IOException { ByteArrayOutputStream bo = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        try (GZIPOutputStream g = new GZIPOutputStream(bo) { { def.setLevel(6); } }) { g.write(in); } return bo.toByteArray(); }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int N = 50_000; List<Event> es = events(N);
        byte[] j = json(es), jg = gzip(j), b = binary(es), bg = gzip(b);
        System.out.printf("Part 1 — measured encodings of %,d real-shaped order events (java.util.zip, level 6):%n%n", N);
        System.out.printf("   %-26s %12s %12s %10s%n", "encoding", "total", "bytes/event", "vs JSON");
        Object[][] enc = {{"JSON", j}, {"JSON + gzip", jg}, {"compact binary (varints)", b}, {"compact binary + gzip", bg}};
        for (Object[] e : enc) { byte[] x = (byte[]) e[1];
            System.out.printf("   %-26s %,10.0f KB %12.1f %9.1fx%n", e[0], x.length / 1024.0, (double) x.length / N, (double) j.length / x.length); }

        // Part 2 — three data streams, three years of retention. Order events use the measured sizes; logs and clickstream
        // use the measured JSON→gzip ratio as a proxy compression ratio (an assumption: logs typically compress 5–10x).
        double gzRatio = (double) j.length / jg.length;
        double[] rawGbPerDay = { 1_000_000 * 5.0 * j.length / N / 1e9,     // order events: ~1M orders × 5 events, measured bytes
                                 36_300 / 30.0,                              // application logs: 36,300 GB/month (L1 usage data)
                                 2_000_000.0 * 300 * 400 / 1e9 };            // clickstream: 2M DAU × 300 events × ~400 B
        String[] stream = {"order events", "application logs", "app clickstream"};
        double HOT = 8.0, STD = 1.9, IA = 1.0, ARCH = 0.08;                 // ₹/GB-month, illustrative
        int months = 36;
        System.out.printf("%n Part 2 — three data streams kept for 3 years. Illustrative ₹/GB-month: hot (DB / search cluster) %.1f,%n", HOT);
        System.out.printf("   object standard %.1f, infrequent %.1f, archive %.2f. Compression ratio applied: %.1fx (measured above).%n%n", STD, IA, ARCH, gzRatio);
        System.out.printf("   %-17s %10s %20s %22s %24s%n", "stream", "raw GB/day", "all hot, raw", "object store, gzip", "gzip + lifecycle tiers");
        double worstAll = 0, bestAll = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
            double g = rawGbPerDay[i];
            double hotRaw = tiered(g, months, new double[]{HOT}, new int[]{9999});
            double stdGz = tiered(g / gzRatio, months, new double[]{STD}, new int[]{9999});
            double life = tiered(g / gzRatio, months, new double[]{STD, IA, ARCH}, new int[]{1, 11, 9999});
            worstAll += hotRaw; bestAll += life;
            System.out.printf("   %-17s %10.1f %18s %20s %22s%n", stream[i], g, rupees(hotRaw), rupees(stdGz), rupees(life));
        }
        System.out.printf("   %-17s %10s %18s %20s %22s%n", "all three", "", rupees(worstAll), "", rupees(bestAll));

        // Part 3 — cross-zone transfer for the same streams (3 zones; default placement vs zone-aware)
        double XAZ = 1.6;   // ₹ per GB crossing a zone boundary (both directions billed), illustrative
        System.out.printf("%n Part 3 — cross-zone transfer per month (3 zones, ₹%.1f per GB that crosses a zone, illustrative):%n", XAZ);
        System.out.printf("   %-17s %24s %28s%n", "stream", "default (2/3 cross zones)", "zone-aware (~5% spill-over)");
        double monthDefault = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
            double gbMonth = rawGbPerDay[i] / gzRatio * 30 * 3;            // produced + replicated ×2 + consumed, compressed
            double def = gbMonth * (2.0 / 3.0) * XAZ, za = gbMonth * 0.05 * XAZ; monthDefault += def;
            System.out.printf("   %-17s %24s %28s%n", stream[i], rupees(def), rupees(za));
        }
        double bill = 22_800_000;
        System.out.printf("%n   For scale: the monthly cloud bill in L1 is %s. Worst-case storage for all three streams averages %s/month over%n",
                rupees(bill), rupees(worstAll / months));
        System.out.printf("   the 3 years; default cross-zone transfer is %s/month.%n", rupees(monthDefault));

        System.out.println("\n   → the measurement is real: gzip shrinks these JSON events ~6x and a schema'd binary encoding + gzip ~9x (Protobuf/Avro in");
        System.out.println("     practice, Ch 28). But proportionality decides where effort goes. Order events — the data engineers worry about — are");
        System.out.println("     a rounding error at any policy. Logs and clickstream are 100–1,000x bigger, and for them the retention policy, not the");
        System.out.println("     encoding, is the lever: 'keep everything hot, uncompressed' versus 'compress and tier' is the difference between a");
        System.out.println("     real line on the bill and a negligible one. Cross-zone transfer is small at this platform's scale; it becomes a");
        System.out.println("     top-five line for data-heavy systems (media, ML features, analytics replication), where zone-aware routing and");
        System.out.println("     follower-fetching consumers matter. FinOps rule: rank the streams by size first, then optimise the big ones.");
    }

    // cost of a growing dataset over `months`: each month's data ages through tiers; ageLimit[i] = months spent in tier i
    static String rupees(double v) { return v >= 1e7 ? String.format("₹%.2f Cr", v / 1e7) : v >= 1e5 ? String.format("₹%.1f L", v / 1e5) : String.format("₹%,.0f", v); }
    static double tiered(double gbPerDay, int months, double[] price, int[] ageLimit) {
        double gbPerMonth = gbPerDay * 30, cost = 0;
        for (int m = 0; m < months; m++)                   // for each billing month
            for (int born = 0; born <= m; born++) {        // each monthly cohort still stored
                int age = m - born, tier = 0, acc = 0;
                while (tier < ageLimit.length - 1 && age >= acc + ageLimit[tier]) { acc += ageLimit[tier]; tier++; }
                cost += gbPerMonth * price[tier];
            }
        return cost;
    }
}
java StorageL4.java
Part 1 — measured encodings of 50,000 real-shaped order events (java.util.zip, level 6):

   encoding                          total  bytes/event    vs JSON
   JSON                           11,981 KB        245.4       1.0x
   JSON + gzip                     1,912 KB         39.2       6.3x
   compact binary (varints)        1,900 KB         38.9       6.3x
   compact binary + gzip           1,332 KB         27.3       9.0x

 Part 2 — three data streams kept for 3 years. Illustrative ₹/GB-month: hot (DB / search cluster) 8.0,
   object standard 1.9, infrequent 1.0, archive 0.08. Compression ratio applied: 6.3x (measured above).

   stream            raw GB/day         all hot, raw     object store, gzip   gzip + lifecycle tiers
   order events             1.2             ₹2.0 L               ₹7,433                 ₹2,481
   application logs      1210.0          ₹19.34 Cr              ₹73.3 L                ₹24.5 L
   app clickstream        240.0           ₹3.84 Cr              ₹14.5 L                 ₹4.9 L
   all three                             ₹23.20 Cr                                     ₹29.3 L

 Part 3 — cross-zone transfer per month (3 zones, ₹1.6 per GB that crosses a zone, illustrative):
   stream            default (2/3 cross zones)  zone-aware (~5% spill-over)
   order events                           ₹19                           ₹1
   application logs                   ₹18,538                       ₹1,390
   app clickstream                     ₹3,677                         ₹276

   For scale: the monthly cloud bill in L1 is ₹2.28 Cr. Worst-case storage for all three streams averages ₹64.4 L/month over
   the 3 years; default cross-zone transfer is ₹22,233/month.

   → the measurement is real: gzip shrinks these JSON events ~6x and a schema'd binary encoding + gzip ~9x (Protobuf/Avro in
     practice, Ch 28). But proportionality decides where effort goes. Order events — the data engineers worry about — are
     a rounding error at any policy. Logs and clickstream are 100–1,000x bigger, and for them the retention policy, not the
     encoding, is the lever: 'keep everything hot, uncompressed' versus 'compress and tier' is the difference between a
     real line on the bill and a negligible one. Cross-zone transfer is small at this platform's scale; it becomes a
     top-five line for data-heavy systems (media, ML features, analytics replication), where zone-aware routing and
     follower-fetching consumers matter. FinOps rule: rank the streams by size first, then optimise the big ones.

Reading it:

  • Encoding (measured): JSON 245 bytes/event; gzip 6.3x smaller; compact binary 6.3x; binary + gzip 9.0x. Real, and worth doing for high-volume streams.
  • Proportionality decides everything else. The order events engineers debate cost ₹2 L over three years even kept hot and raw — a rounding error. Application logs (~1,000x the volume) and clickstream (~200x) are where the money is: ₹23.2 crore hot and raw vs ₹29.3 lakh compressed and tiered (illustrative prices). Retention policy is the lever, not encoding.
  • Cross-zone transfer is small at this scale (~₹22k/month) and zone-aware routing cuts it ~13x. It becomes a major line only for data-heavy systems — check the size before investing.
  • The FinOps rule the lab demonstrates: rank the streams by size first, then optimise the big ones.

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Symptom Mitigation Unowned spend Shared/untagged lines grow with no one accountable Tag policy at provisioning; driver-based allocation (L1) Paying for peak all year Single-digit average utilisation Autoscaling + calendar pre-scale (L2) Under-provisioning to save money Overload during sales, the most valuable hours Pre-scale known events; target utilisation below the queueing knee Committing to the peak Idle reserved capacity, already paid Commit to the confident floor; ratchet quarterly (L3) Runaway logs/metrics Observability cost growing faster than traffic Log levels, sampling, cardinality limits, retention (L4) Cut the wrong thing Removing an expensive service that drives revenue Cost with value: experiments, unit margin (L1) Surprise invoice Misconfiguration found a month later Daily anomaly detection per team Non-prod sprawl Staging costs rival production Off-hours shutdown, ephemeral environments, smaller shapes

docs.title: 6.2 Observability of cost
docs.text:
• A cost panel on every service dashboard: daily cost, cost per request/order, trend — next to latency and errors (Ch 24).
  • Anomaly alerts on per-team and per-service cost deviations, with the top driver (resource, SKU) in the alert.
  • Utilisation dashboards: requested vs used CPU/memory per workload (the gap is waste), commitment utilisation and coverage.
  • Observability is itself a cost: sample traces, cap metric cardinality, and set per-team log budgets.

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Cost anomalies are also security signals: cryptomining on a compromised account shows up as a compute spike first.
  • Enforce budgets and quotas per account/project so a leaked credential or a runaway loop can't create unbounded spend.
  • Deleting "unused" resources needs care: confirm ownership and check for backups and compliance retention before removal (Ch 36).

docs.title: 6.4 Performance trade-offs
docs.text:
• Target utilisation trades cost against tail latency (Ch 31 L3); set it per service by latency sensitivity.
  • Cheaper storage tiers are slower (archive retrieval takes hours) — match tier to access pattern, not just price.
  • Spot interruptions add retries and tail latency; keep them off user-facing critical paths.
  • Compression costs CPU; for hot paths, measure CPU vs bytes saved (usually a good trade for storage and transfer, not always for latency-critical RPC).

docs.title: 6.5 Cost of FinOps itself
docs.text: • Tagging, allocation pipelines and a small FinOps team cost money and attention. Keep effort proportionate (§2.10): at ₹0.76 of cloud per ₹650 order, the priority is removing waste and bad incentives — not squeezing every rupee at the expense of delivery.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Treating the bill as finance's problem

Engineers make the spending decisions every day. Without visibility and ownership, cost grows by default (§1.1).

2. Reporting cost by cloud product

"EC2 ₹X, RDS ₹Y" answers nobody's question. Report by team, service and unit of business value (L1).

3. Even-split shared costs

Charges teams for others' usage and removes the incentive to reduce your own. Allocate by drivers (L1).

4. Cutting by size instead of value

The biggest line may be the best investment (L1: 8.5x return). Pair cost with measured value.

5. Sizing the fleet for the festival, all year

4% of provisioned capacity actually needed (L2). Autoscale and pre-scale.

6. Relying on reactive autoscaling for known spikes

A step faster than the control loop overloads the first minutes of a sale (L2). Pre-scale from the calendar.

7. Committing to the peak (or p90)

Idle, prepaid capacity; in L3 committing to the p90 was worse than no commitment. Commit to the confident floor.

8. Infinite retention by default

"Keep everything hot, just in case" turns logs into the fastest-growing line (L4: ₹23.2 crore vs ₹29.3 lakh). Retention per data class.

9. Optimising the small stuff

Compressing order events that cost ₹2 lakh over three years while logs cost crores. Rank first (L4).

10. Spot instances on the critical path

Interruptions become customer-facing errors. Spot is for interruptible, retry-safe work.

11. Finding problems on the invoice

A month is far too slow. Daily anomaly detection per team.

12. Cost cutting that erodes reliability

Removing headroom, replicas or DR to hit a number — until the outage costs more than the savings. Cost is one quality among several.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What is FinOps?

30-second answer: The practice of managing cloud cost as a shared responsibility between engineering, finance and product: make spend visible and owned (inform), reduce waste and buy capacity smartly (optimise), and keep it that way with budgets, anomaly alerts and cost in design reviews (operate). The goal is maximum business value per rupee, not the lowest bill.

Deep answer: In the cloud every engineer makes spending decisions daily — replica counts, log levels, retention — so cost is an architecture quality that needs owners and metrics like cost per order (L1).

Trade-offs I'd call out: FinOps effort itself costs time; keep it proportionate to where money goes.

Follow-ups: 1. The three phases? → Inform, optimise, operate. 2. Who owns cost? → The teams that build and run the services, supported by a small central function.

Red flags: "FinOps means cutting costs."

Q2 [B1] ⭐ What is unit economics and why does it matter?

30-second answer: Expressing cost per unit of business value — per order, per active customer, per tenant — instead of as a total. It shows whether growth is efficient: a bill that doubles with cost per order flat is healthy; cost per order rising means efficiency is getting worse. It also makes costs comparable to revenue and margin per unit.

Deep answer: L1 turns a ₹2.28 crore bill into ₹0.76 per order (0.12% of order value) and per-service cost per order, which makes value questions answerable.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Allocation choices affect the numbers; be consistent and transparent.

Follow-ups: 1. Best unit for a marketplace? → Cost per order, plus per active customer. 2. For SaaS? → Cost per tenant (Ch 30).

Red flags: Tracking only the total bill.

Q3 [B1] On-demand vs reserved/committed vs spot?

30-second answer: On-demand: pay as you go, most flexible, most expensive. Commitments (reserved instances, savings plans): commit to capacity or spend for 1–3 years for a big discount, paid whether used or not. Spot/preemptible: deep discount on spare capacity that can be reclaimed at short notice — only for interruptible work.

Deep answer: Commit to the floor of your demand, run the variable part on demand (with autoscaling), and put batch and async consumers on spot (L3).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Discount vs flexibility and interruption risk.

Follow-ups: 1. What should never run on spot? → The checkout path and stateful primaries. 2. Why not commit to everything? → Unused commitments are paid anyway.

Red flags: Buying reserved capacity for the peak.

Q4 [B1] Why do tags matter so much in cloud cost management?

30-second answer: Tags (owner, service, environment, cost centre) are how spend is attributed to teams and services. Untagged resources have no owner, so nobody reviews or turns them off — they're where forgotten load-test instances, orphaned volumes and unattached IPs accumulate. Enforce tags at provisioning, not after the fact.

Deep answer: L1's untagged line was 4.5% of the bill, entirely orphaned resources. Policy as code (Terraform checks, admission controllers) rejects untagged resources before they exist.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Enforcement adds friction; automate tags from IaC modules.

Follow-ups: 1. What about shared resources? → Tag as shared and allocate by drivers. 2. How do you clean up existing untagged spend? → Report daily, find owners, set a deadline, then remove.

Red flags: Tagging as a quarterly clean-up exercise.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do you allocate shared costs like Kafka, observability and networking?

30-second answer: By usage drivers that reflect who causes the cost: Kafka by bytes produced (or partitions), observability by log/metric/trace volume, NAT and egress by gigabytes out, cluster overhead by resource requests or requests served, non-prod proportional to production footprint. An even split is simple but shifts cost to low-usage teams and removes incentives.

Deep answer: L1: driver-based allocation moved up to ₹3.7 L/month between teams versus an even split. Publish the method so teams can see and influence their drivers.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Driver data must be collected and trusted; perfect precision isn't needed.

Follow-ups: 1. Showback or chargeback? → Showback first. 2. What if a driver is unavailable? → Use a proxy (share of direct spend) and improve later.

Red flags: "We split shared costs equally."

Q6 [B2] ⭐ How do you rightsize a service?

30-second answer: Compare what's provisioned with what's used: CPU/memory requests vs actual usage, replica counts vs demand over time, instance shape vs workload profile. Set a target utilisation that respects latency (often 50–70% for latency-sensitive services), autoscale to it, pre-scale for known events, and fix shape mismatches (memory-heavy on compute-optimised). Re-check after every major release.

Deep answer: L2: a fleet sized for the festival peak all year used 4% of what it provisioned; autoscaling + pre-scale cost 7% with zero overload.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Lower headroom saves money and raises latency risk (Ch 31 L3).

Follow-ups: 1. Kubernetes-specific waste? → Requests set far above usage. 2. Why not 90% utilisation? → The queueing cliff.

Red flags: Rightsizing by averages without looking at peaks.

Q7 [B2] Why isn't reactive autoscaling enough for a flash sale?

30-second answer: Autoscalers react to observed metrics with a lag — metric window, decision, scheduling, image pull, JVM warm-up — often several minutes. A sale that multiplies traffic 5x in seconds overloads the fleet before new capacity arrives. Known events should be pre-scaled from a calendar; unknown spikes need warm pools, fast-starting images and load shedding.

Deep answer: L2: reactive autoscaling was overloaded for the first 5 minutes of the sale; adding a scheduled floor from 30 minutes before removed it for a few extra pod-hours.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Pre-scaling costs a little extra; overload during the most valuable minutes costs far more.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you shorten the lag? → Smaller images, faster startup (CDS, native images), warm pools. 2. What if the event isn't on the calendar? → Load shedding and queueing (Ch 18).

Red flags: "The HPA will handle Diwali."

Q8 [B2] How do you reduce observability cost without going blind?

30-second answer: Log at INFO in production with DEBUG switchable per service; sample traces (head or tail-based, keeping errors and slow requests); control metric cardinality (no user IDs as labels); set retention by value — hot for days, archive for compliance; convert high-volume logs to metrics where you only need counts; and give teams per-service log budgets with alerts.

Deep answer: L4: application logs were ~1,000x the volume of order events, and the retention policy was the dominant lever (₹19.3 crore hot and raw vs ₹24.5 lakh compressed and tiered over 3 years, illustrative).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Less data means occasionally missing a detail; keep errors and slow traces at full fidelity.

Follow-ups: 1. Tail-based sampling? → Decide after the trace completes, keep interesting ones. 2. Cardinality risk? → Metric series explode cost and query time.

Red flags: DEBUG logs retained forever in the search cluster.

Q9 [B2] How do storage tiers and lifecycle policies work?

30-second answer: Data gets less valuable to access quickly as it ages, so you move it through cheaper tiers: hot database/SSD → object storage standard → infrequent access → archive, with lifecycle rules doing the moves automatically. Each colder tier is cheaper per GB but slower or more expensive to read. Retention policies delete data you no longer need.

Deep answer: L4: compression plus lifecycle tiering took three-year storage for logs and clickstream from ₹23.2 crore (hot, raw) to ₹29.3 lakh (illustrative). Choose tiers by access pattern; archive retrieval can take hours.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Retrieval fees and latency on cold data; compliance requirements on retention.

Follow-ups: 1. Where do GST invoices go? → Archive with mandated retention (Ch 36). 2. Analytics data? → Columnar (Parquet) in a lakehouse.

Red flags: No retention policy ("keep forever").

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ How much capacity should you commit to for a year?

30-second answer: Commit to the floor, not the peak: a marginal committed unit pays off only if it would be busy in at least (commit price ÷ on-demand price) of the hours — 60% at a 40% discount. Against a forecast, sweep the commitment level and pick the minimum-cost point; under uncertainty, check expected cost and regret across plausible futures, and ratchet up quarterly as the floor rises.

Deep answer: L3: optimum 37 pods (busy 62% of hours), −23% vs all on-demand; committing to the p90 was worse than no commitment and had the largest regret. The curve was flat between 0.85x and 1.2x of the optimum; demand skewed toward growth made the upper end slightly better in the tail.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Deeper discounts for longer terms vs flexibility to change architecture or provider.

Follow-ups: 1. Savings plan vs reserved instance? → Plans commit to spend and flex across instance types. 2. Who buys them? → Central FinOps, pooled across teams.

Red flags: Committing to cover the festival fleet.

Q11 [B3] ⭐ A service is the most expensive line on the bill. Do you cut it?

30-second answer: Not without its value. Measure what it contributes — an A/B test, attributed revenue, cost avoided, or its role in reliability — and compare with its fully allocated cost. If value clearly exceeds cost, optimise it (cheaper model, caching, rightsizing) rather than cut it. If it doesn't, challenge it.

Deep answer: L1: recommendations looked like a cut candidate but its measured uplift returned ~8.5x its cost (illustrative). Unit economics per service is what makes the comparison possible.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Value is sometimes hard to measure; use experiments where possible and proxies otherwise.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you measure value for infrastructure services? → Cost avoided, incidents prevented, developer time saved. 2. What if value is uncertain? → Time-boxed experiment with a kill criterion.

Red flags: Cutting by size alone.

Q12 [B3] Which architecture decisions most affect cost?

30-second answer: Service granularity (each service has an HA and operational floor); statefulness and startup time (determine how well you can autoscale); synchronous vs asynchronous processing (async flattens peaks); data placement, retention and replication (storage and transfer); tenancy model (pooling amortises, silos multiply); cells (duplicate infrastructure); serverless vs containers (different cost curves); and code efficiency in hot paths.

Deep answer: These set the cost curve; FinOps optimisations move along it. Put estimated monthly cost and its biggest lever in every design doc (Ch 32).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Most cost-saving choices trade against isolation, latency or delivery speed.

Follow-ups: 1. Cost of 26 microservices? → An HA floor of ~78 pods before traffic. 2. Cheapest scaling lever? → Efficient code in the hottest path.

Red flags: Treating cost as something to fix after launch.

Q13 [B3] How do you detect cost problems before the invoice?

30-second answer: Daily cost data (billing export) joined with tags and usage drivers, per team and per service; anomaly detection on day-over-day and forecast deviations with the top driver named; budgets with alerts at 50/80/100%; and per-service cost panels so engineers see changes right after deploys.

Deep answer: §3.3's scenario — a DEBUG log level left on — is caught within a day as an 11x observability anomaly for one team, instead of a month later. Cost spikes can also signal security incidents (cryptomining).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Noisy alerts get ignored; tune thresholds and group by owner.

Follow-ups: 1. Who receives the alert? → The owning team, not only finance. 2. Hard limits? → Quotas and budgets per account for runaway protection.

Red flags: Monthly invoice review as the only control.

Q14 [B3] How do you control non-production environment costs?

30-second answer: Shut them down outside working hours, use smaller instance shapes and fewer replicas, create ephemeral per-PR environments that are destroyed automatically, share heavy dependencies where isolation isn't needed, use spot for CI, and give non-prod its own budget and anomaly alerts.

Deep answer: L1's illustrative dev/staging line (₹11.5 L/month) exceeded several production services. Off-hours shutdown alone removes ~65% of an always-on environment's hours.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Less fidelity to production; keep one production-like staging for release validation.

Follow-ups: 1. Ephemeral environments' main risk? → Orphans if teardown fails — enforce TTLs. 2. Load tests? → Scheduled, time-boxed, auto-destroyed.

Red flags: Five always-on full copies of production.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design a FinOps operating model for a 200-engineer organisation.

30-second answer: Engineers own their services' cost; a small central FinOps function owns tooling, commitments and policy. Every resource tagged at provisioning (policy as code); shared costs allocated by drivers; cost per order and per service on every team dashboard; budgets and daily anomaly alerts per team; commitments purchased centrally against the confident floor and reviewed quarterly; retention and tiering defaults per data class; cost sections in design docs; and a monthly review of unit economics with product and finance.

Deep answer: That's the §4 standard. The labs back each part: allocation and value (L1), capacity (L2), commitments (L3), data (L4).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Process overhead vs accountability; automate as much as possible.

Follow-ups: 1. First 90 days? → Tagging and allocation, then the top five waste items. 2. How do you measure success? → Cost per order trend, untagged %, commitment utilisation.

Red flags: A central team that "owns cost" for everyone.

Q16 [B4] How do cost and reliability trade off, and how do you decide?

30-second answer: Reliability costs money — headroom, replicas, multi-zone, DR regions, cells — and cutting it saves money until an outage costs more. Decide by pricing both sides: expected outage cost (probability × duration × cost per minute, Ch 34 L3) against the reliability spend, tiered by the business criticality of each service.

Deep answer: Checkout gets headroom and pre-scaling (L2) because its peak minutes are the most valuable; a reporting service can run hot and single-zone. Express it as SLO tiers with cost per tier, and review with the business (Ch 31).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Probabilistic benefits vs certain costs; use Monte Carlo and sensitivity.

Follow-ups: 1. Cost per outage minute? → Peak GMV per minute plus refunds and churn. 2. Where would you cut first? → Non-prod and low-tier services, not the checkout path.

Red flags: Across-the-board cost cuts that remove headroom from critical paths.

Q17 [B4] How would you reduce cost by 30% without harming the product?

30-second answer: Rank spend by owner and driver, then attack structural waste first: autoscale and pre-scale instead of static peak fleets; commit to the confident floor; enforce retention and tiering on logs and clickstream; shut down idle and non-prod capacity; remove orphans; fix requests-vs-usage gaps; move interruptible work to spot. Only then look at code efficiency and architecture changes, and pair every cut with its value and reliability impact.

Deep answer: L2 (static peak → autoscale: large compute savings), L3 (commitment sizing: ~23% on committed workload), L4 (retention: order-of-magnitude on logs) typically deliver more than 30% combined in a platform like §1.1's, without touching features.

Trade-offs I'd call out: One-time savings vs recurring discipline — add guardrails so waste doesn't return.

Follow-ups: 1. What wouldn't you cut? → Reliability of the revenue path. 2. How do you keep savings? → Policies, budgets, anomaly alerts.

Red flags: Starting with a rewrite for efficiency.

Q18 [B4] How do you forecast cloud cost for a new product or region?

30-second answer: Build a driver-based model: business volume forecasts (orders, users, events) → resource drivers (requests, storage, transfer) → cost via unit prices and your current cost per unit, including fixed floors (HA, non-prod, observability). Express demand as ranges and run it as a Monte Carlo to get expected cost and a p90; revisit monthly against actuals.

Deep answer: Same method as Ch 31 L4 and L3 here: uncertainty and skew change decisions (commitments, architecture). For a new region add fixed costs that don't scale with volume (a full stack, cross-region replication).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Model precision vs effort; the drivers matter more than decimal places.

Follow-ups: 1. Biggest forecasting error? → Ignoring fixed floors and non-prod. 2. How do you validate? → Compare cost per unit with existing regions.

Red flags: Forecasting from last month's bill × growth rate.

Q19 [B4] How do you make engineers care about cost without slowing them down?

30-second answer: Visibility and good defaults, not gates. Show cost next to latency on their dashboards; make cost per order a team metric; put cheap-by-default choices in the paved road (autoscaling templates, finite retention, INFO logging, right-sized base images); alert them quickly on anomalies; and celebrate savings. Reserve reviews for large commitments and one-way-door decisions.

Deep answer: Most waste in §1.1 came from defaults and ratchets nobody noticed. Changing the defaults (platform templates, policy as code) removes it without asking anyone to remember anything.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Too much cost pressure slows delivery; keep effort proportionate (§2.10).

Follow-ups: 1. Chargeback? → Only where teams really own budgets. 2. Gamification? → Can work, but tie to value, not just savings.

Red flags: Approval tickets for every instance.

Q20 [B4] What distinguishes a principal engineer's view of cost?

30-second answer: They treat cost as a design quality with explicit trade-offs, express it in business units, connect it to value, and focus on structural levers rather than one-off cuts. They know which architecture choices set the cost curve, quantify decisions under uncertainty (commitments, serverless vs containers), design guardrails so savings persist, and keep effort proportionate to where the money actually goes.

Deep answer: L1–L4 in one sentence: allocate to owners and units, match capacity to demand, commit to the floor, and put data in the tier its access pattern deserves — then automate the defaults.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Cost vs reliability vs speed; say explicitly which one you're prioritising and why.

Follow-ups: 1. First question about a new design's cost? → What's the cost per unit and what drives it. 2. When is cost not the priority? → Pre-product-market-fit, where speed matters most.

Red flags: "We'll optimise cost later."

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Cost is an architecture quality with owners, budgets and trade-offs — not a finance afterthought (§2.1).
  2. Allocate every rupee — direct, shared by usage drivers, untagged driven to zero — and express it per order, per customer, per tenant (L1).
  3. Judge spend by value, not size: the biggest line may be the best investment (L1).
  4. Autoscale the daily curve, pre-scale known events, keep target utilisation below the queueing knee (L2).
  5. Commit to the confident floor, never the peak; the curve is flat near the optimum, so avoid the tails and ratchet quarterly (L3).
  6. Retention and tiering beat encoding for big streams; rank data by size before optimising (L4).
  7. Design for cost: service granularity, startup time, async processing, tenancy and cells set the cost curve (§2.8).
  8. Run FinOps continuously: inform, optimise, operate — with anomaly alerts, policy as code and cost in design docs (§2.9).
  9. Be proportionate: remove waste and bad incentives; don't trade delivery speed or reliability for pennies (§2.10).

docs.text: Question Answer How do we see where money goes? Tags + driver-based allocation → cost per service and per order Is this expensive service worth it? Compare allocated cost with measured value (A/B, margin) How big should the fleet be? Autoscale to a target utilisation; pre-scale known events How much to commit? Up to where the marginal unit is busy ≥ commit/on-demand ratio of hours; ratchet Spot? Only interruptible, retry-safe work Logs and clickstream? Finite retention, compression, lifecycle tiers, sampling Cross-zone costs? Check size first; zone-aware routing where it matters How do we avoid surprises? docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (B2) Add a cost-centre column to L1's bill and produce showback per team (a team owns several services). Which team's number changes most between allocation methods?
  2. (B2) In L2, change the target utilisation to 45% and 75%. How do cost and degraded minutes change? Where would you set it for checkout vs a batch service?
  3. (B3) Extend L3 with a 3-year commitment at 60% off. When does it beat the 1-year option under the same demand uncertainty?
  4. (B3) In L4, add Parquet-like columnar encoding (group each field across events before compressing). How much smaller than row-wise binary + gzip is it?
  5. (B4) Build a cost model for launching the platform in a new region: fixed floors, variable costs per order, cross-region replication. What's the break-even order volume?

docs.title: 36. Compliance, Governance & Data Residency
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B2 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 21, Ch 23, Ch 27, Ch 30 · What you will build: How regulation shapes architecture — privacy by design under India's DPDP Act (and GDPR for comparison), payment-data localisation and card tokenisation, statutory retention, audit evidence, and data governance — turned into engineering mechanisms you can test. Four runnable labs with real cryptography and hashing.

  • L1: the right to erasure. A customer's data lived in 6 stores plus a legally retained GST invoice. Deleting from the primary left 5 copies readable (including the backup, with a sensitive shopping-basket inference); deleting "everywhere we remembered" left 2 (backup, warehouse); crypto-shredding (per-customer AES-256-GCM key destroyed) left 0, kept the invoice under a separate legal-retention key, and left the other customer intact.
  • L2: finding PII in logs. On 20,000 log lines with planted synthetic identifiers, format-only regexes had 1.9% precision for Aadhaar-format numbers and 0.9% for card numbers; checksums (Verhoeff, Luhn + issuer prefix) raised that to 16.4% and 97.8%; key-aware scanning reached 100% with no loss of recall — and redaction left 0 planted values and destroyed 0 order ids.
  • L3: residency as policy-as-code. 10 data flows checked against 5 rules: 5 blocked, including a Singapore DR replica holding payment data, card numbers in logs shipped to a vendor, and clickstream reused for ad targeting without consent. A full orders-DB replica may only go to Mumbai or Hyderabad.
  • L4: tamper-evident audit log. 103,500 hash-chained events (~25k/s). The chain alone caught edits, deletes and reorders but not a delete-and-recompute; external write-once anchors caught that — neither caught deletion of the 3,500 entries written since the last anchor.

· Reading time: 120 min + code

Not legal advice

This chapter explains how engineers turn regulatory obligations into architecture. Laws and regulators' directions change, and their application depends on facts. Statements about specific laws reflect the author's understanding as of mid-2026 and are marked where status may have changed — confirm every obligation with your legal and compliance teams before relying on it.

docs.title: 1.1 A story: the audit that found what the architecture diagram didn't show
docs.text:
In its fourth year, the grocery platform prepared for three things at once: a payment-partner audit, its first formal privacy review under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, and due diligence from an investor. The architecture diagrams looked clean. The auditors didn't look at diagrams; they looked at data.

What they found:

  1. The DR region was in Singapore. Chosen years earlier for latency and price, it held a full replica of the orders database — including payment transaction data that the platform's payment-data policy (and RBI's 2018 direction) required to be stored only in India (L3).
  2. Card numbers were in the logs. A payment-adapter debug statement had logged request payloads for two weeks during an incident, and those logs had been shipped to a third-party observability vendor abroad (L2, L3).
  3. "Delete my account" didn't. The erasure feature deleted the customer row. Their name, phone, address and order history remained in the read model, the support search index, caches, nightly backups and the analytics warehouse — for years (L1).
  4. Nobody could prove who issued refunds. The refund audit table sat in the same database the operations team administered; several entries had been edited, and there was no way to show which (L4).
  5. Nobody knew where personal data was. There was no inventory of which stores held which categories of personal data, for what purpose, for how long, or who could access it.

None of this was malice; each was an ordinary engineering choice made without the compliance constraint in view. The remediation took two quarters — moving the DR region, purging and re-shipping logs, retrofitting encryption for erasure, rebuilding the audit trail — and it would have cost a fraction of that if the constraints had been architecture requirements from the start.

The thesis of this chapter

Compliance obligations are non-functional requirements with legal consequences. Treat them like latency or availability: identify them early, turn each into a concrete engineering mechanism (a key hierarchy, a residency policy, a retention rule, a tamper-evident log, a scanner), make those mechanisms testable and automated, and keep the evidence continuously rather than assembling it for an audit. The recurring architectural moves are few: know your data (inventory and classification), minimise it, encrypt it with keys you can destroy, control where it goes, retain it exactly as long as required, and prove what happened.

docs.title: 1.2 Where this lives in the grocery platform
docs.text: Obligation (source) Engineering mechanism Lab Erasure when the purpose is served / on request (DPDP; GDPR Art. 17) Per-customer keys, crypto-shredding, erasure log L1 Security safeguards; data minimisation (DPDP; PCI DSS) PII discovery + redaction in logs; structured logging allow-lists L2 Payment data stored only in India (RBI 2018 direction) Residency policy-as-code; in-country DR L3 No storage of card numbers by merchants (RBI card-on-file tokenisation) Network tokens; PCI vault boundary L3, §2.5 Purpose limitation and consent (DPDP) Purpose tags on data flows; consent records L3, §2.3 Statutory retention (GST records) Retention schedule + legal-retention keys + WORM L1, L3 Accountability, forensics (DPDP; CERT-In log retention; audits) Hash-chained, externally anchored audit log L4

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end you will be able to:

  • Translate regulatory obligations into architecture requirements and mechanisms.
  • Design erasure that actually erases, including backups and derived stores, while honouring legal retention (L1).
  • Discover and prevent personal data in the wrong places (L2).
  • Enforce data residency and transfer rules as policy-as-code over the architecture (L3).
  • Build tamper-evident audit trails and know their limits (L4).
  • Set up data governance — classification, ownership, retention, access reviews, evidence — that scales.

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: compliance as non-functional requirements B2
docs.text:
Laws rarely say "use AES-256" or "put the DR region in Hyderabad". They state outcomes: protect personal data with reasonable safeguards; process it only for the purpose it was collected; erase it when that purpose is served; keep tax records for a period; store payment data in the country; report breaches promptly. The architect's job is the translation:

Legal outcome Engineering requirement Mechanism "Erase when no longer needed" Every copy of a customer's data can be made unrecoverable within N days Crypto-shredding (L1) "Reasonable security safeguards" No plaintext personal data outside approved stores Encryption, access control, PII scanning (L2) "Store only in India" No replica, backup or export of class X outside Indian regions Residency policy in CI (L3) "Be able to show what happened" Tamper-evident record of privileged actions Hash chain + external anchors (L4)

Two principles run through everything:

  • Privacy by design and by default — build the protection in (minimise, encrypt, restrict) rather than bolting it on; the default configuration should be the compliant one.
  • Evidence, continuously — an obligation you can't demonstrate is, for an auditor or regulator, an obligation you didn't meet. Automate the evidence (scanner reports, policy results, verification runs) as part of normal operations.

docs.title: 2.2 The regulatory landscape for an Indian platform ⭐ B2
docs.text:
A summary for engineers — confirm specifics with counsel:

  • Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act). India's general personal-data law. Key concepts: Data Principal (the individual), Data Fiduciary (who decides purpose and means — the platform), Data Processor (acts on the fiduciary's behalf — vendors). Processing on consent (free, specific, informed, unconditional, unambiguous, by clear affirmative action, withdrawable as easily as given) or for specified legitimate uses. Obligations include notice, purpose limitation, accuracy, reasonable security safeguards, breach notification to the Data Protection Board and affected individuals, erasure once the purpose is served (unless retention is required by law), grievance redressal, and additional duties for Significant Data Fiduciaries (e.g., a Data Protection Officer, DPIAs, audits). Children's data needs verifiable parental consent and bars tracking/behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children. Cross-border transfer is permitted except to countries the government restricts by notification. Penalties are substantial (up to ₹250 crore for a failure to take reasonable security safeguards, per the Act's schedule). The DPDP Rules, 2025 were notified in November 2025 with obligations phasing in over roughly 18 months — verify current commencement dates and the Rules' specifics, e.g. breach-reporting timelines, with counsel.
  • RBI payment-data localisation (2018 direction on storage of payment system data, with 2019 FAQs). Payment system operators must store the entire payment data in systems only in India; processing abroad is permitted if the data is deleted abroad and brought back within a short window (one business day/24 hours per the FAQs). It applies to payment system operators and flows through to their partners via contracts — so merchants' architectures are shaped by it.
  • RBI card-on-file tokenisation (effective October 2022). Merchants and payment aggregators (other than card networks and issuers) may not store customers' actual card data; they use network/issuer tokens (retaining only limited data such as the last four digits for reference).
  • PCI DSS (v4.x). The card industry's security standard for any system that stores, processes or transmits card data. The main architectural lever is scope reduction: hosted payment pages, tokenisation, and keeping card data inside a small, isolated vault.
  • GST record retention. Under the CGST Act (s.36), books and records — including invoices — must be kept for 72 months from the due date of the annual return for the year (longer if under appeal/investigation).
  • CERT-In directions (April 2022). Report specified cyber incidents to CERT-In within 6 hours of noticing them; maintain ICT system logs for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction; synchronise clocks to specified NTP sources. Verify the current directions and applicability.
  • GDPR (for EU residents' data, e.g., an EU-based seller or customer) — similar principles with notable differences: six lawful bases, 72-hour breach notification to the supervisory authority, transfer mechanisms (adequacy, standard contractual clauses), fines up to 4% of global turnover.
  • Assurance frameworks — ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2 — aren't laws, but partners and enterprise customers require them; they're the governance scaffolding that evidence hangs on.

The architectural consequences cluster into five themes: where data is stored and flows (residency), how long it's kept and how it's erased (retention/erasure), what is collected and for what (minimisation/purpose), how it's protected (security safeguards), and what can be proven (audit/evidence).

docs.title: 2.3 Data inventory, classification and purpose ⭐ B2
docs.text:
Every compliance mechanism depends on knowing what data you have, where it lives, why you have it, and how long you need it — the §1.1 platform knew none of these.

  • Classify data into a small number of classes with handling rules. For the grocery platform: public (catalog), internal (operational metrics), personal (name, phone, address, order history), sensitive/special (inferences from baskets — health, pregnancy, religion; children's data), payment (transaction data subject to localisation), card (PAN — never outside the vault), legal-record (GST invoices).
  • Inventory (a data catalog / record of processing): for each store — which classes it holds, owner, purpose(s), legal basis, retention, location, who can access it, which processors receive it.
  • Tag at the source: schema annotations (@Personal, @Sensitive), column tags in the catalog, and purpose tags on data flows (L3) so tooling can enforce rules automatically.
  • Discover what escaped: scan logs, exports, object storage and warehouses for identifiers that shouldn't be there (L2). Discovery is how you find the gaps between the inventory and reality.

Purpose limitation and consent: record why each piece of personal data is processed, and check new uses against it. L3's clickstream flow (F4) reused personal data for ad targeting — a purpose the customer never agreed to — and was blocked; the aggregated, anonymised version (F5) passed. Consent should be recorded as data (who, what purpose, when, which notice version, withdrawn when) and checked at use, not just collected at sign-up.

docs.title: 2.4 Minimisation, pseudonymisation and encryption ⭐ B3
docs.text:
The cheapest data to protect is data you don't have.

  • Minimise collection: don't ask for a date of birth to deliver groceries.
  • Minimise propagation: pass IDs, not personal data, in events and to downstream systems; give each context only the fields it needs (Ch 33: Fulfilment gets a DeliveryLocation, not the customer profile).
  • Pseudonymise for analytics: replace direct identifiers with keyed tokens (HMAC with a secret key), so analysts work without names and phone numbers. Pseudonymised data is still personal data under most laws (re-identification is possible with the key); anonymised aggregate data generally is not — but true anonymisation is harder than it looks (small groups, rare combinations).
  • Encrypt at rest and in transit as a baseline (Ch 23); field-level encryption with per-subject or per-tenant keys for personal fields enables crypto-shredding (L1) and limits who can read them even with database access.
  • Structured logging with allow-lists: log known-safe fields by name; never log whole request/response bodies. This is the upstream fix for L2's findings.

docs.title: 2.5 Payment data: tokenisation and the PCI boundary B3
docs.text:
Card data is the most regulated data most platforms touch, and the best strategy is to not touch it:

  • Hosted payment pages / SDKs from the payment aggregator collect card details directly, so card numbers never reach your servers.
  • Network/issuer tokens replace stored card numbers for repeat payments (as RBI's card-on-file rules require of merchants).
  • If any component must handle card data, isolate it in a small vault (its own network segment, accounts, keys and admins) and keep everything else out of PCI scope. L3's rule R2 blocks any flow carrying raw card numbers; L2 finds them where they leaked.

Payment transaction data (amounts, parties, timestamps, references — not just card numbers) is what localisation rules address: store it in India, and design DR, analytics and vendor flows accordingly (L3). Foreign legs of processing (a card network abroad) are acceptable only when transient.

docs.title: 2.6 Data residency and cross-border transfer ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Residency constraints turn into concrete architecture:

  • DR and replication: a full replica of a store containing localised data must stay in-country — for the grocery platform, a Mumbai primary with a Hyderabad DR region rather than Singapore (L3: the only allowed regions). This also matters for cells (Ch 34) and multi-region designs (Ch 27).
  • Backups and snapshots are copies — they follow the same residency rules as the primary.
  • Vendors (processors): observability, support desks, email/SMS, analytics, fraud tools. Each is a data flow with a destination, data classes and purpose. Send them the minimum (pseudonymised IDs, no card data), under a data-processing agreement, encrypted.
  • Regional isolation for tenants/markets: per-region clusters or cells for data that must stay in a jurisdiction (Ch 30).
  • Policy-as-code: encode the rules and evaluate every flow in the architecture manifest in CI (L3). Architects and reviewers then argue about the rules once, and every design is checked against them automatically.

docs.title: 2.7 Retention and the right to erasure ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Retention cuts both ways: keep data no longer than the purpose requires, and keep some records at least as long as the law requires.

  • Retention schedule: per data class — debug logs 14 days; application logs 30–90 days hot then deleted (or longer only where required, e.g. security logs per CERT-In's 180-day direction); order history for the customer relationship plus a defined period; GST invoices 72+ months; marketing data until consent is withdrawn. Enforce with TTLs, lifecycle rules (Ch 35) and scheduled deletion jobs.
  • Erasure is hard because data spreads (L1): the primary, CQRS read models, search indexes, caches, message logs (Kafka retention, compacted topics), backups, warehouses, vendor copies. Deleting from the primary left 5 readable copies; chasing copies still missed the immutable backup and the warehouse.
  • Crypto-shredding makes erasure a single, provable action: encrypt personal fields with a per-customer key everywhere they're written (including backups and exports), and destroy the key. L1: 0 readable copies afterwards, other customers untouched. Pre-conditions: personal data is never written in plaintext anywhere (logs, exports, caches), keys live in a KMS with deletion controls, and derived stores (search, warehouse) index encrypted fields or pseudonymous IDs rather than plaintext.
  • Legal retention alongside erasure: data the law requires you to keep (GST invoices) is encrypted under a separate legal-retention key with only the fields the law needs; it's retained, access-restricted, and deleted when the retention period ends.
  • Erasure log: record that an erasure happened (request, subject ID, keys destroyed, what was retained and why, when) — without the personal data — as evidence.
  • Backups: rotate within a bounded period, so even without crypto-shredding the data ages out; with crypto-shredding it's unreadable immediately.
  • Legal holds (litigation, investigations) override deletion for specific subjects; the retention system must support suspending deletion with an audit trail.

docs.title: 2.8 Audit trails and evidence ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Accountability obligations and forensics need a reliable record of who did what to which object, when — especially privileged actions: viewing personal data in support tools, issuing refunds, changing roles, exporting data, changing configuration.

What makes an audit trail trustworthy (L4):

  1. Completeness: emitted from the application for every sensitive action, including by service accounts; include actor, action, target, time (synchronised clocks), source, and a correlation ID.
  2. Tamper evidence: a hash chain detects edits, deletions and reorders — but an insider who controls the whole store can delete an entry and recompute every later hash (L4 case 4).
  3. External anchoring: periodically write the chain head to a write-once store outside the insider's control (object storage with Object Lock/WORM in a separate account, or a public timestamping service). That defeats rewrites; the remaining gap is entries since the last anchor (L4 case 5) — shrink it by anchoring frequently or streaming each entry to the external store.
  4. Separation of duties: the people who administer the application can't administer the audit store.
  5. Retention and access: keep audit logs as long as required; restrict and audit access to them.
  6. Verification as a job: verify the chain and anchors continuously and alert on failure — evidence you never check isn't evidence.

Beyond audit logs, compliance evidence includes access-review records, policy-check results (L3), scanner reports (L2), key-destruction records (L1), change approvals and DR test results. Automate collection so an audit is a report, not a project.

docs.title: 2.9 Breach readiness B4
docs.text:
Breach notification obligations have short clocks (CERT-In: 6 hours for reportable incidents; DPDP: prompt notification to the Board and affected individuals, with details specified in the Rules; GDPR: 72 hours). You can't meet them without preparation:

  • Know which data is where (inventory) so you can scope impact in hours, not weeks.
  • Keep logs and audit trails sufficient to reconstruct access (and retained per CERT-In where applicable).
  • A runbook with legal, security, communications and engineering roles, and pre-drafted notices.
  • Encryption and minimisation reduce impact: a stolen backup of crypto-shredded or field-encrypted data exposes far less.
  • Practise it (tabletop exercises), like DR drills (Ch 27).

docs.title: 2.10 Data governance at scale B4
docs.text:
Governance is how an organisation keeps these mechanisms working as teams and systems multiply:

  • Ownership: every data store has an owning team and a data steward; every class has handling rules.
  • Catalog + lineage: where data came from and where it flows (lineage from pipelines/CDC), so an erasure or a residency rule can be traced through derived datasets.
  • Policy-as-code everywhere it can be: residency and transfer rules (L3), required encryption and tags at provisioning, retention defaults, allowed log fields — checked in CI and at deploy.
  • Access governance: least privilege, just-in-time elevated access for production data with approval and audit, periodic access reviews.
  • Privacy reviews / DPIAs for new features that process personal data in new ways — part of the design-doc process (Ch 32).
  • Metrics: % of stores classified, % of flows passing policy, PII findings in logs per week (L2), erasure SLA, audit-verification status (L4).
  • Proportionality: as with cost (Ch 35), concentrate effort where the risk is — payment data, children's data, sensitive inferences — rather than equal ceremony for every table.

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Grocery Compliance Architecture
docs.text:
Design Document (excerpt) — Privacy, Residency & Audit Architecture v1.0

Status: Accepted · Authors: Security architecture + Data platform · Reviewers: Legal, Compliance, DPO, SRE, all tech leads

Field Value Context Payment-partner audit, DPDP readiness review and investor due diligence found: payment data replicated to a Singapore DR region; card numbers in logs shipped abroad; erasure that deleted only the primary row; an editable refund audit table; no data inventory. Decision Treat compliance obligations as NFRs with automated mechanisms and continuous evidence: data classification and catalog; field-level encryption with per-customer keys and crypto-shredding; in-country DR; residency and transfer policy-as-code; PII scanning and structured-logging allow-lists; card data only in a tokenised vault; hash-chained audit log with external WORM anchors. Related ADRs ADR-220 Data classes + catalog + owners; ADR-221 Per-customer and legal-retention keys, crypto-shredding for erasure (L1); ADR-222 Structured logging allow-lists + PII scanner on logs and exports (L2); ADR-223 Residency and transfer rules as code, evaluated on every manifest change (L3); ADR-224 DR moved to Hyderabad; no localised data abroad; ADR-225 Card data only via aggregator hosted pages and network tokens; ADR-226 Audit log: hash chain + 1-minute external anchors in a separate account (L4); ADR-227 Retention schedule per data class, enforced by TTL/lifecycle

Requirements.

  • R1 — Erasure. A verified erasure request makes the customer's personal data unrecoverable in every store, including backups and the warehouse, within 30 days; legally retained records are kept under a separate key with minimum fields.
  • R2 — No stray PII. Zero card numbers and zero unapproved personal identifiers in logs and exports; findings alert the owning team within 1 hour.
  • R3 — Residency. Payment data and full replicas of localised stores exist only in Indian regions; every data flow passes the policy check before deploy.
  • R4 — Purpose. Every flow of personal data carries a purpose that matches consent or a documented legitimate use.
  • R5 — Audit integrity. Privileged actions are recorded in a tamper-evident log; verification runs hourly; the unanchored window is ≤ 1 minute.
  • R6 — Evidence. Policy results, scanner reports, key destructions and audit verifications are retained and reportable on demand.

Decisions in detail.

  1. Classification (ADR-220). Seven classes (§2.3); schema annotations generate catalog entries; every store has an owner and retention.
  2. Keys (ADR-221). Envelope encryption: per-customer data keys wrapped by a KMS key; personal fields encrypted in the service before any write; search indexes store pseudonymous tokens.
  3. Logs (ADR-222). Logging library only emits allow-listed fields; scanner runs on the log pipeline and on exports, key-aware (L2).
  4. Residency (ADR-223/224). Manifest of data flows in the repo; rules in code; CI blocks violations (L3). DR region Hyderabad.
  5. Payments (ADR-225). Aggregator hosted checkout and network tokens; the platform never receives card numbers.
  6. Audit (ADR-226). Chain head anchored every minute to an Object-Lock bucket in a security-owned account; hourly verification (L4).
  7. Retention (ADR-227). Debug logs 14 d; app logs 90 d; security logs 180 d in India; GST invoices 72 months+; marketing data until consent withdrawn.

Consequences. Encryption adds latency and complexity (key management, re-encryption on rotation, search over pseudonymous tokens); a second Indian region costs more than Singapore; engineers lose free-form logging. In return: erasure is provable, residency is enforced by construction, audit evidence is trustworthy, and audits become reports.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
What's real here

All four labs are JDK 21 programs using the JDK's real cryptography (javax.crypto AES-256-GCM in L1, SHA-256 in L4) and real checksum algorithms (Verhoeff, Luhn) in L2. All identifiers are synthetic: Aadhaar-format numbers are randomly generated with a valid checksum, card numbers are the card networks' public test numbers, and names, phones and emails are invented. L3's rules are an illustrative engineering encoding of obligations, not legal advice. Output is deterministic except timings in L4.

docs.title: L1 — The right to erasure, across every copy B2
docs.text:
Requirement: "A customer asked us to delete their data. Prove it's gone — from everywhere — while keeping the GST invoice the law requires."

Two customers' data is written to six stores (orders DB, read model, support search, cache, nightly backup, warehouse) plus a GST invoice archive. Three erasure strategies are applied to one customer, and every store is scanned for anything still readable. Encryption uses the JDK's real AES-256-GCM; the "KMS" is an in-memory key map.

ErasureL1.java
// ErasureL1.java — run with: java ErasureL1.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// THE RIGHT TO ERASURE vs WHERE DATA ACTUALLY LIVES. A customer asks the platform to delete their personal data (DPDP Act
// 2023 / GDPR Art. 17). Their data is not in one table: it's in the orders DB, a CQRS read model, the support search index,
// a cache, last night's backup, and the analytics warehouse. Three strategies:
//   A) delete from the primary database only             (what most first implementations do)
//   B) delete from every store we remembered              (but backups are immutable and the warehouse is someone else's)
//   C) CRYPTO-SHREDDING: personal fields are encrypted with a per-customer key (AES-256-GCM) at write time, in EVERY copy;
//      erasure destroys the key. Records the law requires us to KEEP (GST invoices, ~6 years) are encrypted under a separate
//      per-customer "legal-retention" key with only the minimum fields, and are kept.
// After each strategy we scan every store for the customer's personal data in readable form.
import javax.crypto.*;
import javax.crypto.spec.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.SecureRandom;
import java.util.*;

public class ErasureL1 {
    static final SecureRandom RNG = new SecureRandom();
    // ---- a toy KMS: key id -> key. Destroying a key is irreversible. ----
    static final Map<String, SecretKey> KMS = new HashMap<>();
    static SecretKey key(String id) {
        return KMS.computeIfAbsent(id, k -> { try { KeyGenerator g = KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES"); g.init(256); return g.generateKey(); }
                                                catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } });
    }
    static String enc(String keyId, String plain) throws Exception {
        byte[] iv = new byte[12]; RNG.nextBytes(iv);
        Cipher c = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding"); c.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key(keyId), new GCMParameterSpec(128, iv));
        return "enc:" + keyId + ":" + Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(iv) + ":" + Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(c.doFinal(plain.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)));
    }
    static String dec(String v) {
        if (!v.startsWith("enc:")) return v;
        String[] p = v.split(":"); SecretKey k = KMS.get(p[1]);
        if (k == null) return null;                                                  // key destroyed → unrecoverable
        try { Cipher c = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding"); c.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, k, new GCMParameterSpec(128, Base64.getDecoder().decode(p[2])));
              return new String(c.doFinal(Base64.getDecoder().decode(p[3])), StandardCharsets.UTF_8); }
        catch (Exception e) { return null; }
    }

    // ---- the six places a customer's data lives ----
    static final List<String> STORES = List.of("orders DB", "read model", "support search", "cache", "nightly backup", "warehouse");
    static Map<String, List<Map<String, String>>> world;

    static void populate(boolean encrypt, String... customers) throws Exception {
        world = new LinkedHashMap<>(); STORES.forEach(s -> world.put(s, new ArrayList<>()));
        for (String cust : customers) {
            String name = cust.equals("C-1001") ? "Priya Sharma" : "Arjun Mehta", phone = cust.equals("C-1001") ? "+91 98450 11223" : "+91 99000 44556";
            String addr = cust.equals("C-1001") ? "12 MG Road, Pune 411001" : "7 Park St, Kolkata 700016";
            String pk = "pii-" + cust, lk = "legal-" + cust;
            for (String store : STORES) {
                Map<String, String> r = new LinkedHashMap<>();
                r.put("customer", cust); r.put("store", store);
                r.put("name", encrypt ? enc(pk, name) : name);
                r.put("phone", encrypt ? enc(pk, phone) : phone);
                r.put("address", encrypt ? enc(pk, addr) : addr);
                r.put("basket", encrypt ? enc(pk, "milk, eggs, baby formula, pregnancy test") : "milk, eggs, baby formula, pregnancy test"); // sensitive inference
                world.get(store).add(r);
            }
            // the GST invoice: legally required to be retained — minimum fields, separate legal-retention key
            Map<String, String> inv = new LinkedHashMap<>();
            inv.put("customer", cust); inv.put("store", "GST invoice archive"); inv.put("invoiceNo", "INV-" + cust.substring(2));
            inv.put("name", encrypt ? enc(lk, name) : name); inv.put("address", encrypt ? enc(lk, addr) : addr); inv.put("taxablePaise", "129900");
            world.computeIfAbsent("GST invoice archive", k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(inv);
        }
    }

    // scan: which stores still expose the customer's personal data in readable form?
    static List<String> exposure(String cust) {
        List<String> exposed = new ArrayList<>();
        for (var e : world.entrySet())
            for (Map<String, String> r : e.getValue())
                if (cust.equals(r.get("customer"))) {
                    String nm = r.containsKey("name") ? dec(r.get("name")) : null;
                    if (nm != null) exposed.add(e.getKey() + (r.containsKey("basket") && dec(r.get("basket")) != null ? " (incl. basket)" : ""));
                }
        return exposed;
    }
    static void deleteFrom(String cust, List<String> stores) { for (String s : stores) world.get(s).removeIf(r -> cust.equals(r.get("customer"))); }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String cust = "C-1001", other = "C-2002";
        System.out.println("Customer C-1001 asks us to erase their personal data. It lives in 6 stores (+ a GST invoice we must retain).\n");

        populate(false, cust, other);
        deleteFrom(cust, List.of("orders DB"));
        report("A) delete from the orders DB only", cust, other);

        populate(false, cust, other);
        deleteFrom(cust, List.of("orders DB", "read model", "support search", "cache"));  // backup is immutable; warehouse owned by another team
        report("B) delete from every store we remembered", cust, other);

        populate(true, cust, other);
        KMS.remove("pii-" + cust);                              // crypto-shred: destroy the personal-data key (KMS schedule-deletion)
        deleteFrom(cust, List.of("orders DB", "read model", "support search", "cache")); // tidy up live stores; not required for erasure
        report("C) crypto-shredding (per-customer key destroyed)", cust, other);

        // what the erasure log records — proof of erasure WITHOUT the personal data
        System.out.println("   Erasure log entry (kept as evidence):");
        System.out.println("        {\"request\":\"ER-2026-0931\",\"subject\":\"C-1001\",\"keyDestroyed\":\"pii-C-1001\",\"retainedUnderLaw\":[\"GST invoice INV-1001 (legal-C-1001)\"],");
        System.out.println("         \"completedAt\":\"2026-09-29T07:12:03Z\",\"stores\":6}");

        System.out.println("\n   → deleting from the primary leaves the customer readable in 5 other places — including the backup, which also keeps");
        System.out.println("     a sensitive INFERENCE (the basket) that was never a 'field' anyone thought to erase. Chasing every copy misses the");
        System.out.println("     immutable backup and the warehouse another team owns. Crypto-shredding makes erasure a single, provable action:");
        System.out.println("     every copy — backups included — was written as ciphertext under the customer's key, so destroying the key erases");
        System.out.println("     them all at once, while other customers are untouched. The GST invoice survives because the law requires it,");
        System.out.println("     under a separate purpose key with only the fields the law needs. Crypto-shredding only works if personal data is");
        System.out.println("     NEVER written in plaintext anywhere (logs, exports, caches) — enforce that at write time.");
    }

    static void report(String label, String cust, String other) {
        List<String> ex = new ArrayList<>(exposure(cust));
        boolean invoice = ex.remove("GST invoice archive");
        System.out.printf("   %-50s NOT erased (still readable): %d %s%n", label, ex.size(), ex);
        System.out.printf("   %-50s retained under legal obligation: %s%n", "", invoice ? "GST invoice (name + address only)" : "none");
        System.out.printf("   %-50s other customer C-2002 still intact: %s%n%n", "", exposure(other).size() == 7 ? "yes (7/7)" : "NO (" + exposure(other).size() + "/7)");
    }
}
java ErasureL1.java
Customer C-1001 asks us to erase their personal data. It lives in 6 stores (+ a GST invoice we must retain).

   A) delete from the orders DB only                  NOT erased (still readable): 5 [read model (incl. basket), support search (incl. basket), cache (incl. basket), nightly backup (incl. basket), warehouse (incl. basket)]
                                                      retained under legal obligation: GST invoice (name + address only)
                                                      other customer C-2002 still intact: yes (7/7)

   B) delete from every store we remembered           NOT erased (still readable): 2 [nightly backup (incl. basket), warehouse (incl. basket)]
                                                      retained under legal obligation: GST invoice (name + address only)
                                                      other customer C-2002 still intact: yes (7/7)

   C) crypto-shredding (per-customer key destroyed)   NOT erased (still readable): 0 []
                                                      retained under legal obligation: GST invoice (name + address only)
                                                      other customer C-2002 still intact: yes (7/7)

   Erasure log entry (kept as evidence):
        {"request":"ER-2026-0931","subject":"C-1001","keyDestroyed":"pii-C-1001","retainedUnderLaw":["GST invoice INV-1001 (legal-C-1001)"],
         "completedAt":"2026-09-29T07:12:03Z","stores":6}

   → deleting from the primary leaves the customer readable in 5 other places — including the backup, which also keeps
     a sensitive INFERENCE (the basket) that was never a 'field' anyone thought to erase. Chasing every copy misses the
     immutable backup and the warehouse another team owns. Crypto-shredding makes erasure a single, provable action:
     every copy — backups included — was written as ciphertext under the customer's key, so destroying the key erases
     them all at once, while other customers are untouched. The GST invoice survives because the law requires it,
     under a separate purpose key with only the fields the law needs. Crypto-shredding only works if personal data is
     NEVER written in plaintext anywhere (logs, exports, caches) — enforce that at write time.

Reading it:
