   strategy                                                        done after   effort spent  workarounds services done by 4 / 8 / 12
   A) central migration team, 2 parallel streams                     31.0 spr       58.0 spr            0             0 /  2 /  5
   B) platform migrates libraries first, teams own their services    11.0 spr       58.0 spr            0             0 / 18 / 26
   C) teams start immediately, libraries not ready (workarounds)     10.4 spr       76.4 spr            9             3 / 18 / 26
   D) B + automated codemods (−40% service effort)                    8.6 spr       36.8 spr            0             0 / 25 / 26
   (1 sprint = 2 weeks. Effort per service from services.csv; penalties/savings are stated assumptions.)

   → a central team is the bottleneck: 58 sprints of work through 2 streams takes 31 sprints (~14 months), and the teams
     who own the services learn nothing about their new stack. Team ownership parallelises across 8 teams and finishes
     in 11 sprints. Starting every team immediately, before the shared libraries are migrated, finishes at about the
     same time (10.4 vs 11.0 sprints) — parallelism hides the wait — but burns 32% more effort on workarounds that must
     later be removed: a false economy. Codemods cut both time and effort. The architect's job is the plan and the
     enablers: sequence dependencies, fund the platform work first, supply recipes, track progress with a fitness
     function (L3's scanner: % of services on Boot 3), and let each team own its migration.

Reading it:

  • A) Central team: 58 sprints of work through 2 streams takes 31 sprints (~14 months) — only 5 services are done after 12 sprints. This is the §1.1 migration squad.
  • B) Platform-first, team-owned: the same 58 sprints of effort, spread across 8 teams after the libraries are ready — done in 11 sprints.
  • C) Everyone starts immediately: finishes at about the same time (10.4 sprints) because parallelism hides the wait, but spends 76.4 sprints of effort — 32% more — and leaves 9 workarounds to unpick. A calendar-only view would call this the winner.
  • D) B + codemods: 8.6 sprints and 36.8 sprints of effort — 25 of 26 services done by sprint 8. Automating the mechanical changes is the biggest single lever.
  • The architect's contribution is the plan and the enablers, not the typing: sequencing, funding the platform work first, recipes, and a tracking fitness function.

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Symptom Mitigation Teams split by layer Every feature needs several teams (L1) Stream-aligned teams by change flow (L2) Teams aligned to nouns, not flow Contexts on paper, coordination in practice (L1) Measure change coupling; realign Overloaded teams Slow changes, painful on-call, quality drops Cognitive-load limits; platform takes shared capabilities Template drift Old services miss every improvement (L3) Versioned libraries, automated upgrade PRs, scorecards Ticket-ops platform Queues and workarounds (§3.3) Self-service with guardrails; platform as product Central migration squad Migration never finishes (L4) Platform-first enablers, team ownership, codemods Architecture review bottleneck Teams bypass architects Advice process, principles, guardrails Reorg without architecture New seams where the old ones were Inverse Conway: design teams and architecture together

docs.title: 6.2 Observability of the organisation
docs.text:
• DORA metrics per team from CI/CD and incident data.
  • Coordination: multi-team features and cross-team PR reviews per quarter (L1/L2 method on real ticket and git data).
  • Paved-road adoption: scanner scorecards per service and team (L3), trend over time.
  • Migration progress: a fitness function per programme (% migrated), with the tail listed by owner (L4).
  • Surveys: cognitive load, on-call health, platform satisfaction — quarterly and anonymous.

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• The paved road is the most effective security control at scale: SBOMs, vulnerability scanning, secure defaults and patched base images reach every service automatically — or don't reach drifted ones (L3).
  • Ownership in the catalog is a security requirement: every service has someone who receives its vulnerability alerts and on-call pages.
  • Migrations are often security-driven (end-of-support frameworks); track them like vulnerabilities, with deadlines.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance and flow
docs.text:
• Team size and ownership affect delivery speed more than most technical choices: every extra team on a feature adds hand-off latency (L1's model assumes 4 days; measure your own).
  • Collaboration mode is expensive; time-box it and move to X-as-a-service once the interface is clear.
  • Platform APIs need SLOs like any product — a slow or flaky platform taxes every team.

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• A platform team costs headcount; it pays back through fewer hand-offs, faster service creation, fewer incidents from drift, and migrations that finish (L4's 31 → 8.6 sprints).
  • Reorganisations have real costs (context switching, lost knowledge, morale); do them deliberately, rarely, and with evidence.
  • Allocate a standing share of capacity to platform and debt work (§2.8), or it loses every prioritisation battle.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Ignoring Conway's law

Drawing a target architecture without changing team boundaries; the org chart rewrites it (§1.1, L1).

2. Teams by technical layer

Frontend team, backend team, database team: every feature crosses all of them.

3. Aligning teams to nouns rather than flow

Contexts that look right on paper but don't match how work actually changes (L1). Measure change coupling.

4. One team owning too much

Minimising hand-offs by piling services onto one team trades coordination cost for cognitive overload (L2's degenerate case).

5. Architects as gatekeepers

Central review of everything becomes a bottleneck and gets bypassed. Guardrails, principles and advice.

6. Standards as wiki pages

What isn't the default doesn't happen consistently (§1.1). Paved roads and automated checks.

7. Templates without upgrades

A template is a one-time copy; the fleet drifts from it (L3). Versioned libraries and automated PRs.

8. Ticket-ops platform teams

A platform that provisions by ticket is a queue, not a product. Self-service with guardrails.

9. The two-person migration squad

Central teams can't migrate a fleet in reasonable time, and owners learn nothing (L4).

10. Starting everyone before the enablers are ready

Looks faster, finishes about the same, costs a third more effort in workarounds (L4).

11. Measuring individuals

DORA and flow metrics are for finding system constraints, not ranking people.

12. Reorganising without evidence

Frequent, intuition-driven reorgs destroy ownership. Use change data and cognitive-load limits, then keep teams stable.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What is Conway's law?

30-second answer: Organisations design systems that mirror their communication structures. If teams are organised by technical layer, the system grows layer-shaped seams and every feature crosses teams; if teams own business capabilities end to end, the system tends toward capability-shaped services. The "inverse Conway manoeuvre" uses this deliberately: design the teams you need for the architecture you want.

Deep answer: L1 measures it: the same services and features need very different coordination depending only on ownership — 91% of features were multi-team when organised by layer.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Reorganising is costly; align gradually and with evidence.

Follow-ups: 1. What's the inverse Conway manoeuvre? → Shape teams to match the target architecture. 2. Can architecture change without team changes? → Usually it drifts back.

Red flags: Treating the org chart as irrelevant to architecture.

Q2 [B1] ⭐ What are the four team types in Team Topologies?

30-second answer: Stream-aligned teams own a slice of the value stream end to end (the default); platform teams provide internal self-service capabilities that reduce stream teams' cognitive load; enabling teams coach other teams to adopt new capabilities and then step away; complicated-subsystem teams own parts needing deep specialist knowledge.

Deep answer: The grocery platform has seven stream-aligned teams, a platform team (template, CI, observability, messaging, identity, notification), an enabling team for migrations, and a routing-optimisation subsystem team (§3.1).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Too many platform/enabling teams create dependencies; keep most teams stream-aligned.

Follow-ups: 1. The three interaction modes? → Collaboration, X-as-a-service, facilitating. 2. Which is the default type? → Stream-aligned.

Red flags: A "platform team" that is really a ticket queue.

Q3 [B1] What is a paved road (golden path)?

30-second answer: A supported, well-maintained default way to build and run services — a template, shared libraries, CI pipelines, infrastructure modules and docs — that makes the standard-compliant choice the easiest choice. Teams can leave it with good reason, but most don't need to.

Deep answer: L3: services from the current template passed all 8 checks; older-template and hand-rolled services drifted badly. The road must be kept current across the fleet, not just offered to new services.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Standardisation vs team autonomy; keep escape hatches.

Follow-ups: 1. What goes in it? → Template, starter library, CI, observability, catalog entry. 2. How do you keep old services on it? → Versioned libraries and automated upgrade PRs.

Red flags: Standards that exist only as documents.

Q4 [B1] What are the DORA metrics?

30-second answer: Four measures of software delivery performance: deployment frequency, lead time for changes (commit to production), change failure rate, and time to restore service after a failure. Together they capture throughput and stability, and they improve with good team boundaries, automation and platform quality.

Deep answer: Use them per team to find constraints — e.g., long lead times from cross-team hand-offs (L1) or manual release steps — not to rank people.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Easy to game if tied to rewards; pair with qualitative measures.

Follow-ups: 1. What moves lead time most? → Hand-offs and manual steps. 2. What else would you measure? → Coordination, adoption, cognitive load.

Red flags: Using DORA to compare individual engineers.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do you decide team boundaries?

30-second answer: Start from how change flows: which services change together (feature and git data), which bounded contexts exist, and which capabilities are shared. Group services so most features need one team, within cognitive-load limits (a few services per team, balanced change and on-call load). Move shared capabilities to a platform team as self-service. Validate with domain language and skills, then keep teams stable.

Deep answer: L2: within limits, change-based grouping cut hand-offs from 500 (contexts on paper) to 240 and multi-team features from 86% to 43%. Some groupings were accidental coupling (messaging used by many flows) better handled by a platform service.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Optimising coordination vs team size, skills and stability.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not one big team? → Cognitive load and communication overhead. 2. How often revisit? → Quarterly analysis; change teams rarely.

Red flags: Boundaries drawn from the org chart or from nouns.

Q6 [B2] ⭐ What is team cognitive load and why does it matter for architecture?

30-second answer: The total mental effort a team needs to understand, change and operate what it owns — domains, services, technologies, on-call. When it exceeds capacity, changes slow, quality drops and on-call becomes unsustainable. Architecture should be split so each team's share fits; platforms exist to remove undifferentiated load (infrastructure, observability, messaging).

Deep answer: L2 encodes cognitive load as limits (2–4 services, change load ≤ 1.5x average); without them the optimiser collapses everything into one team. Measure it with surveys and ownership counts.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Smaller scopes mean more teams and more interfaces.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you reduce it? → Platform services, simpler architecture, fewer technologies. 2. Signals of overload? → Slow changes, burnout, incident rate.

Red flags: Assigning services to teams by headcount alone.

Q7 [B2] How do you keep 100 services consistent without central control?

30-second answer: Put the standard into defaults and automation: a service template, shared versioned libraries (logging, tracing, security, outbox), a CI pipeline, infrastructure modules, and a conformance scanner that produces scorecards. Automate upgrades with Renovate/OpenRewrite. Publish principles and a tech radar for decisions the paved road doesn't cover.

Deep answer: L3 shows why the automation matters: without it, services created at different times drift apart (v1 28%, v2 60%, current 100%).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Shared libraries create coupling; version them and avoid business logic in them.

Follow-ups: 1. Library vs template? → Libraries upgrade; templates copy once. 2. Hand-rolled services? → Scorecards and help to converge.

Red flags: "We have a standards page."

Q8 [B2] What makes a platform team successful?

30-second answer: Treating the platform as a product for internal users: understand stream teams' needs, provide self-service capabilities with clear APIs and SLOs, measure adoption and satisfaction, keep it the thinnest viable platform, and maintain it (upgrades, deprecations). It should reduce cognitive load, not add gates.

Deep answer: §3.3 shows the failure: ticket-based provisioning becomes a queue and teams work around it, adding coupling. Self-service by pull request with policy checks fixes that.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Building platform features vs letting teams choose their own tools.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you measure it? → Adoption, time to production-ready service, satisfaction. 2. What shouldn't it own? → Business logic.

Red flags: A platform nobody chose to use.

Q9 [B2] How do architects govern without becoming a bottleneck?

30-second answer: Replace review gates with principles, guardrails (fitness functions, policy-as-code, scanners), paved roads, and the advice process — teams decide after seeking advice, and record ADRs. Reserve light review for one-way doors. Architects facilitate a guild and spend time embedded with teams.

Deep answer: This scales decisions across many teams while keeping them coherent (Ch 31 §2.8).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Less central control; requires trust and good defaults.

Follow-ups: 1. What still needs review? → New datastores, trust boundaries, cross-context contracts, big migrations. 2. How do you know it's working? → Fitness-function pass rates, fewer escalations.

Red flags: Every change waits for an architecture board.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ How would you lead a Spring Boot 2 → 3 migration across 100 services?

30-second answer: Make the case (support dates, CVEs), map dependencies, fund the enablers first (shared libraries migrated, OpenRewrite recipes, a reference migration by one team), then let each team own its services with an enabling team available. Track a fitness function (% of services on Boot 3) on a dashboard, announce an end date for the old path, and plan the long tail.

Deep answer: L4: a central squad would take ~14 months for 26 services; team-owned with libraries first 11 sprints; starting everyone before libraries were ready finished about the same but cost 32% more effort; codemods brought it to 8.6 sprints with 37% less effort.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Upfront platform investment delays the visible start but reduces total effort.

Follow-ups: 1. What about teams that won't prioritise it? → Deadline, capacity allocation, escalation with data. 2. How do you avoid a long tail? → Track the tail by owner; help the last teams directly.

Red flags: "Assign two engineers to migrate everything."

Q11 [B3] ⭐ Your target architecture keeps drifting. How do you diagnose and fix it?

30-second answer: Check the socio-technical causes first: do team boundaries match the architecture's boundaries (Conway)? Are standards defaults or documents? Are rules enforced by guardrails? Measure coordination (multi-team features), drift (fitness functions, dependency drift), and adoption. Then fix structurally: realign teams to change flow, strengthen the paved road, add guardrails.

Deep answer: L1 shows drift's typical cause — contexts split across layer-based teams. Ch 32 L4 detects dependency drift; L3 here detects configuration drift.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Enforcement vs autonomy; start with visibility, then defaults, then enforcement.

Follow-ups: 1. First metric to collect? → Multi-team features per quarter. 2. What if teams disagree with the target? → Revisit it — they may be right.

Red flags: More architecture reviews as the only response.

Q12 [B3] When should two teams collaborate closely, and when should they interact as a service?

30-second answer: Collaborate (high-bandwidth, joint work) when discovering something new with an unclear interface — a new capability, a redesign across a boundary — and time-box it. Once the interface is clear, move to X-as-a-service: one team provides a stable API, the other consumes it with minimal coordination.

Deep answer: L1's busiest pairs (e.g., the ordering and pricing-promo teams sharing 110 features a year) suggest either a missing team boundary change or a missing service interface; L2 addresses the first, API design the second.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Collaboration is fast for discovery but expensive to sustain.

Follow-ups: 1. Sign a collaboration should end? → The interface stopped changing. 2. Sign it should become one team? → Collaboration never ends.

Red flags: Permanent "collaboration" between the same two teams.

Q13 [B3] How do you handle ownership transfers during a reorganisation?

30-second answer: Treat each service transfer as a migration: a handover checklist (runbooks, alerts, dashboards, known issues, secrets, on-call shadowing), a period of joint on-call, updated catalog ownership, and a scorecard check (L3) so the receiving team knows what it inherits. Transfer fewer, larger chunks rather than scattering services.

Deep answer: Reorgs fail when ownership is transferred on paper only; incidents during handover are common. The service lifecycle (§3.4) includes an explicit "transferred" state.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed of reorganisation vs operational risk.

Follow-ups: 1. What's the riskiest part? → Undocumented operational knowledge. 2. How long is joint on-call? → Until the new team handles incidents alone.

Red flags: Changing the owner field and calling it done.

Q14 [B3] How do you prioritise platform and tech-debt work against features?

30-second answer: Give it a standing capacity allocation (often 15–25%) rather than competing item by item, and back specific large investments with data: incidents caused, lead-time impact, security exposure, migration deadlines. Frame debt as risk and cost in business terms, and show results.

Deep answer: L4's comparison (31 vs 8.6 sprints) is the kind of evidence that funds enablers; L3's scorecards show where drift carries risk.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Features now vs speed and safety later.

Follow-ups: 1. What if leadership refuses? → Quantify risk; start with the highest-leverage item. 2. How do you show value? → DORA and incident trends.

Red flags: "We'll do it when things calm down."

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design the engineering organisation for a 150-engineer grocery platform.

30-second answer: 15–18 stream-aligned teams of 6–9 grouped around value streams (checkout, orders and payments, catalog and discovery, store operations, inventory, delivery, customer), boundaries validated with change data and cognitive-load limits; a platform group (developer platform, data platform, messaging/identity/notification as services); one or two enabling teams; complicated-subsystem teams for routing and search ranking. Govern with principles, paved roads, guardrails and an advice process; measure DORA, coordination and adoption.

Deep answer: §4 is the 8-team version; L1–L4 provide the evidence and mechanisms (ownership analysis, team optimisation, paved-road scanning, migration planning).

Trade-offs I'd call out: More teams mean more interfaces; keep interaction modes explicit.

Follow-ups: 1. Where does architecture sit? → Principal engineers embedded across value streams plus a small guild. 2. How many platform engineers? → Enough to keep stream teams' load down — often 15–25% of engineering.

Red flags: A central architecture department that designs for everyone.

Q16 [B4] How do you write and drive a multi-year technical strategy?

30-second answer: Diagnose honestly with data (coordination costs, drift, reliability, DORA), choose a few guiding policies, and define coherent actions with owners, sequencing and measures. Write it down, socialise it before publishing, tie it to business goals, allocate capacity, and review it at least yearly as evidence changes.

Deep answer: Rumelt's kernel (diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions) works well for engineering strategy. The labs show the sort of diagnosis that makes strategy concrete.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Specific enough to guide decisions, flexible enough to adapt.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you get buy-in? → Involve teams in the diagnosis. 2. How do you know it's working? → The chosen measures move.

Red flags: A strategy that's a list of technologies.

Q17 [B4] How do you lead without authority across teams that don't report to you?

30-second answer: Earn influence through evidence, writing, and making others successful: bring data that reframes problems, write clear proposals, build consensus before meetings, sponsor and mentor, stay close to the code, choose battles (one-way doors), and disagree-and-commit once decisions are made. Align your work with leaders' goals so they want your help.

Deep answer: Every lab in this chapter is a tool for that kind of influence: L1/L2 turn "our org slows us down" into numbers; L3 turns "standards drift" into a scorecard; L4 turns "we need more time" into a plan.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed of deciding alone vs durability of decisions others own.

Follow-ups: 1. What if a team refuses a necessary change? → Understand why, adjust, then escalate with data if needed. 2. How do you scale yourself? → Write, delegate, and grow other leaders.

Red flags: "I'm the architect, so they must follow."

Q18 [B4] Centralised platform vs team autonomy — where do you draw the line?

30-second answer: Centralise what's undifferentiated and where consistency matters (build and deploy, observability, security baselines, identity, messaging, data governance); leave to teams what's specific to their domain (domain models, service design within principles, feature technology choices within the radar). Make the central parts self-service and optional-but-attractive, with guardrails only for true non-negotiables.

Deep answer: The paved road with escape hatches is the balance; L3's scorecards make deviation visible without forbidding it.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Consistency and leverage vs local optimisation and innovation.

Follow-ups: 1. When is a guardrail justified? → Security, compliance, reliability non-negotiables. 2. What if a team needs something the platform lacks? → Build it and consider contributing it back.

Red flags: Mandating tools that don't fit teams' problems.

Q19 [B4] How would you evaluate whether a reorganisation worked?

30-second answer: Define measures before it: multi-team features and hand-offs (L1/L2 method on real data), DORA metrics per team, incident and on-call load, cognitive-load survey results, and golden-path adoption. Compare over two to three quarters, accounting for the dip during transition, and check qualitative signals from teams.

Deep answer: Reorgs are experiments with a hypothesis ("aligning to change flow will halve cross-team features"); treat them that way and be ready to adjust.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Short-term disruption vs long-term flow.

Follow-ups: 1. How long before judging? → At least two quarters. 2. What if metrics worsen? → Look for missing platform capabilities or wrong boundaries.

Red flags: Declaring success on the day of the announcement.

Q20 [B4] What distinguishes a principal engineer's impact from a senior engineer's?

30-second answer: Scope and leverage. A senior engineer delivers excellent systems within a team. A principal engineer shapes how many teams build systems: team boundaries aligned to change, platforms that make good choices easy, governance that scales, migrations that finish, and a strategy that connects technology to business outcomes. Their output is measured in other teams' results.

Deep answer: The move from "I design" to "I design the conditions under which others design well" is the core shift; this chapter's labs are the evidence-gathering tools of that role.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Less direct coding vs broader impact — stay close enough to the code to keep judgement sharp.

Follow-ups: 1. How do you measure your impact? → Changes in org-level measures and in others' growth. 2. Biggest risk in the role? → Losing touch with the code and the teams.

Red flags: Impact described only as "I designed X."

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Architecture at scale is socio-technical: team boundaries, defaults and incentives shape the system (§2.1).
  2. Conway's law is a force: align teams to how change actually flows, not to layers or nouns (L1).
  3. Use Team Topologies' vocabulary: stream-aligned, platform, enabling and complicated-subsystem teams; collaboration, X-as-a-service and facilitating modes; cognitive load as the constraint (§2.3).
  4. Derive boundaries from change data within load limits — and treat the result as evidence for human judgement (L2).
  5. Run the paved road as a product and keep the fleet on it: versioned libraries, automated upgrades, scorecards (L3).
  6. Govern with principles, guardrails and advice, reserving review for one-way doors (§2.6).
  7. Lead migrations with a plan and enablers: platform first, team ownership, codemods, a tracking fitness function (L4).
  8. Measure flow and adoption, not individuals (§2.9).
  9. Lead through evidence, writing and others' success (§2.10).

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: Situation Approach Features constantly cross teams Measure change coupling; realign teams to flow (L1, L2) A capability everyone needs Platform team, X-as-a-service Teams need to adopt something new Enabling team, facilitating mode Deep specialist component Complicated-subsystem team Services configured inconsistently Paved road + versioned libraries + scanner + auto-upgrade PRs (L3) Fleet-wide upgrade Platform-first enablers, team ownership, codemods, tracking (L4) Architecture review queue Principles + guardrails + advice process Is the reorg working? DORA, hand-offs per feature, surveys over 2–3 quarters

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (B3) Export six months of your team's tickets or PRs with the services each touched. Run L1's analysis on them: what share of changes needs more than one team?
  2. (B3) In L2, change the limits to 3–5 services per team and 6 teams. How do hand-offs and max load change? Where would you draw the line?
  3. (B3) Add two checks to L3's scanner — "uses the standard base image digest" and "has a runbook link in catalog-info" — and compute per-team scorecards.
  4. (B4) In L4, give the platform team two parallel streams and add a "reference migration" task that must finish before other teams start. Does it change the finish date? The effort?
  5. (B4) Write a one-page technical strategy for your organisation using diagnosis / guiding policies / coherent actions, with one measure per action.

docs.title: 38. Case Study: URL Shortener & SMS Short Links
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 02, Ch 07, Ch 11, Ch 20 · What you will build: The grocery platform's short-link service, gro.cr. It carries every order-tracking, slot-reminder and refund SMS, plus marketing campaigns. This is the classic first interview case study, done properly: requirements, estimation, code generation, the redirect path, caching under campaign spikes, click analytics, abuse prevention and expiry. Four runnable labs, one with a real HTTP server on PostgreSQL.

  • L1: minting codes. Over 2 million codes, 6-character truncated MD5 hashes produced 40 collisions (the birthday bound predicts 35). A plain counter gives 5-character codes, but 100% of their neighbours are other customers' live links. A counter passed through a keyed Feistel permutation is unique by construction, needs no lookup, and neighbour guesses hit 0.00%.
  • L2: a real shortener. JDK HttpServer and PostgreSQL. A retried create returned the same code. http, a grocery.in@evil.example userinfo trick and a look-alike domain were all refused. An expired link returned 410 and an unknown one 404. Under 50,000 Zipf-distributed redirects the cache absorbed 85%. 716 of the database reads were concurrent misses on the same cold code, a small thundering herd.
  • L3: the read path. An LRU cache holding 1% of links served 58.5% of 10 million clicks; 10x the memory reached only 77.7%. A 20-million-SMS campaign put 27,184 req/s on one Redis shard, 49x its peers. A 1-second near-cache on each node cut that to 570.
  • L4: counting clicks. On PostgreSQL with durable commits, a per-click UPDATE on one hot campaign row ran at ~2,300 clicks/s with a ~67 ms p99. Micro-batching made the redirect's cost a 0.01 ms memory increment and used 20x fewer statements. Merged HyperLogLog sketches counted 663,668 unique devices within +0.41% in 16 KB each; adding per-node counts overstated them by 294%.

· Reading time: 100 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: the link that took down checkout
docs.text:
The grocery platform's first short-link service was a weekend project: a links table with an auto-increment id, base62-encoded, and a controller that looked it up and returned a 301. It worked for a year. Then four things happened in one Diwali week:

  1. Enumeration. A security researcher noticed that gro.cr/6laZE and gro.cr/6laZF were both order-tracking links — for different customers. Each tracking page showed the delivery address and the rider's phone number. Sequential codes had turned every SMS into a key to its neighbours.
  2. The campaign spike. Marketing sent 20 million SMS with one offer link at 7 pm. Every click hit the same row, the same Redis key, the same shard. The redirect service's connection pool — shared with the order-tracking API — was exhausted, and customers opening "where is my order?" links saw errors.
  3. Analytics lied. The dashboard showed 40% fewer clicks than the SMS gateway's delivery count suggested. The 301 redirects were cached by browsers: repeat clicks never reached the server. At the same time WhatsApp's link-preview crawler inflated the "clicks" on shared links.
  4. Phishing. Anyone with an internal API token could shorten any URL. A compromised partner account created gro.cr/kyc pointing at a look-alike login page, and the platform's own trusted domain delivered it.

The rebuilt service, which this chapter designs, treats a short link as what it is: a tiny, public, security-sensitive, read-heavy key-value lookup with spiky traffic and analytics on the side.

The thesis of this chapter

A URL shortener looks trivial — a map from code to URL — which is why interviewers love it: all the difficulty is in the details that production adds. Code generation is a trade-off between coordination, collisions, length and guessability (L1). Writes must be idempotent and validated, because retries are normal and a trusted domain is a phishing tool (L2). The read path is a caching problem with a hot-key twist: skewed popularity makes a small cache effective, but a campaign concentrates load on one key that sharding cannot spread (L3). Analytics must never slow the redirect: count asynchronously, and use sketches for unique counts (L4). Get those four right and the "simple" service survives Diwali.

docs.title: 1.2 Where this lives in the grocery platform
docs.text:
Producer of links Volume Lifetime Notes Notification service — order tracking, OTP-free deep links, slot reminders, refunds ~2M/day 30 days Personal: the page behind must still authenticate Marketing — campaign links, one per campaign or per recipient 1–20M per campaign 90 days Personalised links for attribution; UTM parameters Support — links in chat and email ~50k/day 90 days Partners/vendors — store pages, offers Low Until revoked Allow-listed destinations only

The service sits behind the SMS pipeline (Ch 40) and in front of the web and app landing pages. India's SMS rules make it part of compliance too: links in commercial and transactional SMS must be on the sender's registered, whitelisted URLs in the DLT system (TRAI, from late 2024 — VERIFY current rules), so a controlled first-party shortener is effectively mandatory.

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end you will be able to:

  • Run the interview framework on a classic problem: requirements, estimation, API, data model, high-level design, deep dives.
  • Choose a code-generation scheme and justify it with collision, coordination, length and privacy numbers (L1).
  • Build the write path: idempotent creation, destination validation, custom aliases, expiry (L2).
  • Design the read path: 301 vs 302, caching layers, hot keys and campaign spikes (L2, L3).
  • Design click analytics that never slows a redirect, including unique counts (L4).
  • Handle abuse, privacy and lifecycle: phishing, enumeration, bots, deletion and data retention.

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: a coat-check counter B1
docs.text:
A short link is a coat-check ticket. You hand over a long URL (the coat) and get a small ticket (the code). Anyone holding the ticket can collect the coat. So:

  • Tickets must be unique. Two coats on one ticket is a disaster.
  • Tickets should be short. They go into 160-character SMS.
  • Tickets should not be guessable if the coats are personal. Ticket 41 shouldn't tell you that ticket 42 exists.
  • The counter must be fast at returning coats, because far more people collect than deposit.
  • Old coats are eventually cleared out, and a cleared ticket must say "gone", not hand out someone else's coat.

docs.title: 2.2 Requirements B1
docs.text:
Functional

  • Create a short link for a long URL, with owner, optional custom alias and optional expiry; bulk-create for campaigns.
  • Redirect GET /{code} to the long URL.
  • Expire and revoke links; report abuse.
  • Click analytics per link and campaign: total clicks, unique visitors, by time, device and region.

Non-functional

  • Redirect latency: p99 under 20 ms server-side; the redirect is on the path of every SMS tap.
  • Availability: 99.95% for redirects, since a broken tracking link becomes a support call. Creation can be less available, because notification sends can retry.
  • Scale: see §2.3; spikes from campaigns matter more than averages.
  • Security: destinations limited to allow-listed domains; codes not enumerable; no personal data in codes or URLs.
  • Durability: a link must not disappear or change destination before it expires.

Out of scope (say so in an interview): link-in-bio pages, QR design, a public consumer shortener.

docs.title: 2.3 Estimation B1
docs.text:
Using Ch 02's method:

Quantity Estimate Transactional links 2M/day ≈ 23 creates/s average Personalised campaign 20M links in 1 hour ≈ 5,600 creates/s (bulk API) Redirects, normal ~3 clicks per tracking link ≈ 6M/day ≈ 70/s average, a few thousand/s at evening peak Redirects, campaign 20M SMS × 12% click-through, decaying over ~10 min → ~30,000/s peak on one code (L3) Row size code 7 B + URL ~150 B + owner, timestamps, hash ≈ ~300 B with index overhead Live rows 2M × 30 d + ~8M/day campaign × 90 d ≈ ~780M rows ≈ 230 GB — bounded by expiry Code space 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion; at 2M/day that lasts thousands of years (L1)

Three conclusions shape the design. Reads dominate and are spiky, so the read path is cache-first and must survive hot keys. Storage is modest because links expire, so a single well-run relational database (partitioned) is enough — no need to reach for a wide-column store by reflex. Bulk creation needs a batch API and cheap code minting.

docs.title: 2.4 API B2
docs.text:
POST /api/links                       Idempotency-Key: 7f3c...   (or natural key: owner + url)
{ "url": "https://track.grocery.in/orders/ORD-88213?t=f3a9", "owner": "notification-svc", "ttlDays": 30 }
→ 201 { "code": "jFF7XOx", "short": "https://gro.cr/jFF7XOx", "expiresAt": "..." }
→ 200 same body with "existing": true    (retry)
→ 422 { "error": "destination host 'grocery-in.example' is not on the allow-list" }

POST /api/links:batch                 up to 10,000 items → 202 + job id, results file (campaigns)
PUT  /api/aliases/diwali              custom alias → 409 if taken or reserved
DELETE /api/links/{code}              revoke → subsequent GET returns 410
GET  /{code}                          → 302 Location: ... | 404 | 410
GET  /api/links/{code}/stats          clicks, uniques, by hour/device/region (from the analytics store)

The redirect endpoint is public and unauthenticated. The management API is internal, authenticated per service (Ch 23), and rate-limited per owner (Ch 39).

docs.title: 2.5 Generating codes ⭐ B2
docs.text:
L1 compares four schemes over 2 million codes:

Scheme Length Collisions Uniqueness check per insert Guessable neighbours A) Hash of URL, truncated to 6 base62 6 40 (birthday bound ≈ 35) Yes (must detect and retry) No B) Random 7 base62, check-and-retry 7 0 (after retry) Yes, every insert No C) Counter → base62 5 0 No 100% D) Counter → keyed permutation → base62 7 0 No 0.00%
  • Hash truncation is attractive because it needs no coordination and dedupes identical URLs for free. But collisions grow with n²/2N — 40 in 2M codes, millions per year at scale — so you still need check-and-retry. And "same URL → same code" is wrong across owners anyway (different expiry, analytics, revocation).
  • Random codes are simple and unguessable, and collisions stay rare while the space is sparse (0.00006% full in L1). The cost is a uniqueness check on every insert — a unique index and a retry loop. That's fine for most systems.
  • Counters are perfect for the database: unique, short, no lookup. They are a privacy failure for personal links (§1.1).
  • Counter + permutation keeps the counter's properties and removes the ordering. A Feistel network with secret round keys is a bijection on the 62^7 space; cycle-walking keeps outputs inside it. Two consecutive counter values map to unrelated-looking codes (jFF7XOx, jstj0mT, pt1IVd8…).

Getting counter values without a bottleneck: each node reserves a block (L2: one nextval on a sequence per 1,000 codes — 11 round-trips for 10,003 codes). Alternatives are a Snowflake-style id (Ch 20), whose 64 bits are too long for 7 characters, or ranges leased from ZooKeeper/etcd. Blocks waste unused values when a node restarts — irrelevant in a 3.5-trillion space.

A permutation hides order, not existence

Codes from a 3.5-trillion space with a few hundred million live links are sparse, so random guessing rarely hits. But "rarely" isn't "never" at millions of guesses. Rate-limit 404s per client (Ch 39), and never let a short code alone unlock personal data: the tracking page behind it still requires a signed token or login.

docs.title: 2.6 The write path B2
docs.text:
1. Authenticate the calling service; check its quota.
  2. Validate the destination (L2): parse it with a real URL parser, require https, reject user-info (https://grocery.in@evil.example points at evil.example), and require an allow-listed host — exact match, not "contains grocery". Optionally scan with a safe-browsing service for partner links.
  3. Idempotency: the notification service retries on timeouts. Either honour an Idempotency-Key header or use a natural key — L2 uses a unique (owner, sha256(url)) constraint with insert … on conflict do nothing, then reads the existing code. A retry returns 200 with the same code, never a second link.
  4. Mint the code (§2.5) or reserve a custom alias (checked against a reserved-word list: api, admin, login, brand names, profanity).
  5. Store with owner, created/expiry timestamps and campaign id.
  6. Warm the cache for campaign links created ahead of a send (L3).

docs.title: 2.7 The read path: 301 vs 302 ⭐ B2
docs.text:
Status Meaning Browser caching Use 301 Moved Permanently Destination will never change Browsers and proxies may cache indefinitely Rarely: you lose analytics and the ability to revoke 302 Found / 307 Temporary Destination may change Not cached unless headers say so Default: every click reaches you, revocation works 308 Permanent (method-preserving) As 301 for non-GET Cached Not for short links 404 / 410 Unknown / gone for good 410 may be cached Unknown code / expired or revoked

L2 returns 302 with Cache-Control: private, max-age=0. The §1.1 analytics gap came from 301s: browsers served repeat clicks from cache. The trade-off is explicit: 302 means you serve every click, so the read path must be cheap.

The read path, in order:

  1. Edge/CDN (optional) for campaign codes, with short TTLs and the redirect logic in an edge function.
  2. In-process near-cache on every redirect node — seconds of TTL, the hot-key defence (L3).
  3. Distributed cache (Redis) — minutes to hours of TTL, holding the working set.
  4. Database — the source of truth, reached on cold misses. Coalesce concurrent misses per key: L2 saw 716 duplicate reads when many requests missed the same cold, popular code at once (Ch 07).
  5. Negative caching for unknown codes, briefly, so enumeration attempts don't reach the database.

docs.title: 2.8 Caching under skew and hot keys ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Link popularity is heavily skewed. L3 models it as Zipf (s = 1.0 — measure your own) and replays 10 million clicks over 1 million links:

LRU size % of links Hit ratio Memory 1,000 0.1% 40.3% 0.2 MB 10,000 1% 58.5% 2 MB 100,000 10% 77.7% 20 MB 250,000 25% 85.5% 50 MB

The curve flattens: the head is cheap to cache, the long tail always reaches the database. Size the cache for the head and the database for the tail.

A campaign is a different shape: one key takes most of the traffic. Sharding spreads keys, not load, so every click on the offer code lands on one Redis shard — 27,184 req/s, 49x its peers in L3's 20M-SMS blast. That is still within one shard's capacity (~27% of ~100k simple GETs/s — VERIFY), but the load scales with the size of the blast, not the cluster: a ~74M-SMS festival campaign would saturate it, and adding shards changes nothing. Defences:

  • Near-cache on each node: at most one lookup per node per TTL. With a 1-second TTL on 20 nodes, the hot shard sees 570 req/s.
  • Pre-warm scheduled campaigns on every node before the send.
  • Edge caching of the redirect with a short TTL for campaign codes.
  • Bulkheads: a separate connection pool and deployment for the redirect path, so a spike can't starve order tracking (§1.1) (Ch 18).

docs.title: 2.9 Data model and storage B3
docs.text:
create table links (
  code        char(7)      primary key,
  long_url    text         not null,
  owner       text         not null,
  url_hash    bytea        not null,          -- sha256(long_url), for idempotent create
  campaign_id text,
  created_at  timestamptz  not null default now(),
  expires_at  timestamptz,
  revoked_at  timestamptz,
  unique (owner, url_hash)
) partition by range (expires_at);            -- expiry = drop a partition, not a mass DELETE

The access pattern is pure key-value (lookup by code), and the live set is ~230 GB. A partitioned PostgreSQL with a read replica or two, fronted by caches, meets it comfortably. Partitioning by expiry month turns expiry into DROP PARTITION rather than billions of deletes. Put permanent (no-expiry) links in their own partition.

When would you choose DynamoDB or Cassandra instead? When the live set reaches many terabytes, you need multi-region active-active writes, or you want native per-item TTL. The key-value access pattern ports easily. In an interview, name the trigger rather than picking by reflex (Ch 06).

Sharding, if needed, is by hash of code (Ch 11). Because codes come from a permutation, they are already uniformly distributed.

docs.title: 2.10 Click analytics ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Marketing wants clicks, unique visitors, time series and breakdowns — in near real time. The iron rule: the redirect must not wait for analytics.

L4 measured three ways to count 40,000 clicks against PostgreSQL with durable commits:

Strategy Clicks/s p99 cost on the redirect DB statements UPDATE per click, spread over 1,000 links ~12,000 ~11 ms 40,000 UPDATE per click, one hot campaign link ~2,300 ~67 ms 40,000 Buffer + 1 s micro-batch upsert paced 10,000 0.01 ms ~2,000

A synchronous counter update puts a row lock on the redirect path. It degrades exactly when a campaign makes one link hot, because every commit on that row queues behind the previous one. In production:

  • The redirect node emits a click event (code, timestamp, hashed device id, user agent, coarse region) to a local buffer, then to Kafka (Ch 14).
  • A stream aggregator (Flink/Kafka Streams) produces per-minute counts per link and campaign into an analytics store (ClickHouse, Druid or Pinot), and the raw events land in the lake for ad-hoc analysis.
  • Unique visitors use HyperLogLog: unique counts don't add across nodes or time windows (L4: adding 20 per-node counts overstated uniques by 294%), but HLL sketches merge. L4's 16 KB sketches came within +0.41% (standard error 0.81% at p = 14). Redis PFADD/PFMERGE and ClickHouse uniqHLL12 implement the same idea.
  • Bot filtering: link-preview crawlers (WhatsApp, Slack, iMessage), security scanners and prefetchers fetch links without a human. Identify them by user agent and behaviour (HEAD requests, no JS beacon) and count them separately. Don't block them — previews help click-through.

Counts are seconds behind real time; say so on the dashboard. For money-related attribution (affiliate payouts), reconcile from raw events, not from the real-time counters.

docs.title: 2.11 Abuse, privacy and lifecycle B3
docs.text:
• Phishing and open redirects: allow-listed destination hosts, parsed properly (L2); no public creation; partner links scanned and reviewed; an abuse-report endpoint and a kill switch that revokes a code everywhere, including caches (publish invalidation events).
  • Enumeration: permuted codes (L1), rate limits on 404s, negative caching, and nothing sensitive behind a code alone.
  • Personal data: never put phone numbers, names or order details in the long URL's query string in clear. Use opaque tokens resolved server-side. Click events store a salted hash of the device id, with retention limits and erasure support (Ch 36).
  • Expiry: 410 after expiry. Don't recycle codes for at least the retention period of any system that might still hold them (SMS archives, screenshots). With a 3.5-trillion space there is no reason to recycle at all.
  • Revocation: a revoked_at column plus a cache-invalidation event; near-caches' short TTLs bound the staleness.

docs.title: 2.12 Multi-region and availability B4
docs.text:
• Reads are replicated to every serving region; a region can serve redirects from its cache and replica even if the primary is down. Stale reads are acceptable for links created seconds ago, except for the creator's own immediate test click. Handle that with read-your-writes, by routing the first lookup of a fresh code to the primary, or by writing through the cache on create (Ch 10).
  • Writes go to one primary region, with the second region as warm standby (Ch 27). Because counter blocks are reserved, the standby's minting just continues from the sequence after failover, without collisions.
  • Degraded mode: if the database is unavailable, redirects continue from caches for the working set; creation fails fast and callers retry (notifications can send without a link as a last resort).
  • SLOs: redirect availability and latency per region; creation success rate; analytics freshness (Ch 24).

docs.title: 2.13 Interview framing B4
docs.text: In a 45-minute interview, spend roughly: 5 min requirements, 5 min estimation, 5 min API and data model, 10 min high-level design, 15 min on two deep dives, and 5 min on failure modes and evolution. The strongest deep dives are code generation (show the trade-off table, not one scheme) and hot keys / analytics (show you know the redirect path must stay cheap). Staff-level signals: bounded storage via expiry, abuse and privacy as first-class requirements, choosing PostgreSQL or a KV store with a stated trigger, and bulkheads between campaign spikes and transactional links.

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: gro.cr Short-Link Service
docs.text:
Design Document (excerpt) — Short-Link Service v2

Status: Accepted · Authors: Messaging platform team · Reviewers: Security, SRE, Marketing tech

Field Value Context v1 used sequential codes (enumerable), 301 redirects (lost analytics), one shared pool (campaign spike broke order tracking), synchronous counters, and unrestricted destinations (phishing). TRAI DLT requires whitelisted URLs in SMS. Decision 7-char codes from block-allocated counters through a keyed Feistel permutation; 302 redirects; allow-listed https destinations; idempotent create; near-cache + Redis + partitioned PostgreSQL; clicks via Kafka to a stream aggregator with HLL uniques; separate redirect deployment. Related ADRs ADR-240 Code scheme: counter blocks + permutation (L1); ADR-241 302 + no-store for redirects; ADR-242 Destination allow-list and idempotent create (L2); ADR-243 Three-tier read path with 1 s near-cache and campaign pre-warm (L3); ADR-244 Async click pipeline, HLL for uniques (L4); ADR-245 PostgreSQL partitioned by expiry month; KV store when live set exceeds ~2 TB or multi-region writes needed; ADR-246 No code recycling; 410 after expiry

Requirements.

  • R1 Redirect p99 < 20 ms server-side, 99.95% availability per region.
  • R2 Survive a 100M-SMS campaign on a single code without affecting transactional links.
  • R3 No destination outside the allow-list; no enumerable codes; nothing personal in codes or URLs.
  • R4 Create is idempotent; bulk create 20M links in under an hour.
  • R5 Click counts within 1 minute; unique visitors within 2%.

Decisions in detail.

  1. Codes (ADR-240). Blocks of 1,000 from a sequence; 4-round Feistel over 62^7 with keys in the secrets manager; custom aliases from a separate namespace with a reserved list.
  2. Redirects (ADR-241). 302 with Cache-Control: private, max-age=0; 410 for expired/revoked; 404 negative-cached for 60 s.
  3. Write path (ADR-242). URL parsed with the platform's URL library; https, no user-info, exact host match; unique (owner, url_hash).
  4. Read path (ADR-243). Caffeine near-cache 1 s TTL (10k entries); Redis TTL 24 h; miss coalescing per code; campaign codes pre-warmed 10 min before send.
  5. Analytics (ADR-244). Click events to Kafka link-clicks keyed by code; Flink per-minute aggregates + HLL (p = 14) per link/day; bots flagged by UA list.
  6. Storage (ADR-245). Monthly partitions by expires_at; permanent links in a never partition; two read replicas.

Consequences. 302 means every click is served, so the read path's cost is the design's centre. Counts lag by seconds. Codes are 7 characters, not 5. In exchange: private links, working analytics, isolation from campaigns, and bounded storage.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
What's real here

All four labs are JDK 21. L2 and L4 run against a real PostgreSQL 16 (L2 also runs a real JDK HttpServer and HttpClient over TCP); L1 and L3 are deterministic simulations with a fixed seed. Timings in L2 and L4 vary by machine; the shapes don't. The Zipf popularity, click-through rate, Redis capacity and decay constant in L3 are stated assumptions.

L2 and L4 need PostgreSQL 16 on port 5581 with a database shop and the JDBC driver jar (postgresql-42.7.4.jar) in the lab folder; the lab README has a one-command Docker alternative. Run every lab with -Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8; JDBC labs also need -Duser.timezone=UTC.

docs.title: L1 — Four ways to mint a short code B2
docs.text:
Requirement: "Every order-tracking SMS carries a link. Codes must be short, unique, cheap to mint — and must not let one customer find another's order."

Two million codes are minted four ways. The permutation is a 4-round Feistel network on 42 bits with cycle-walking to stay within 62^7 — a bijection, so uniqueness is guaranteed without storing or checking anything.

CodeGenL1.java
// CodeGenL1.java — run with: java CodeGenL1.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// FOUR WAYS TO MINT A SHORT CODE. The grocery platform sends ~2 million SMS a day with a link (order tracking, slot reminders,
// "your refund is processed"). Each link needs a short, unique code: gro.cr/aZ3kP9q. We mint 2,000,000 codes four ways
// and measure what matters: collisions, extra database round-trips, length, and whether an attacker can ENUMERATE other
// customers' links by guessing neighbouring codes (tracking links carry an order id and an address on the page behind them).
//   A) hash the long URL (MD5) and keep the first 6 base62 chars     — no coordination, but collisions
//   B) random 7-char base62, check-and-retry on collision            — needs a uniqueness check per insert
//   C) global counter → base62                                       — unique and short, but sequential (guessable)
//   D) counter → Feistel permutation over 62^7 → base62              — unique, no check needed, not sequential
import java.math.BigInteger;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.util.*;

public class CodeGenL1 {
    static final String ALPHABET = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz";
    static final long SPACE7 = pow(62, 7);                       // 3,521,614,606,208

    static long pow(long b, int e) { long r = 1; for (int i = 0; i < e; i++) r *= b; return r; }
    static String base62(long v, int width) {
        char[] c = new char[width];
        for (int i = width - 1; i >= 0; i--) { c[i] = ALPHABET.charAt((int) (v % 62)); v /= 62; }
        return v == 0 ? new String(c) : null;
    }
    static String base62(long v) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); do { sb.append(ALPHABET.charAt((int) (v % 62))); v /= 62; } while (v > 0); return sb.reverse().toString(); }

    // --- D: a 4-round Feistel network on two halves, with cycle-walking so the result stays inside [0, 62^7) ---
    static final long HALF = 1L << 21;                           // 2^42 > 62^7, so split 42 bits into 2 × 21
    static final long[] KEYS = {0x5DEECE66DL, 0x2545F491L, 0x9E3779B9L, 0x7F4A7C15L};  // secret round keys
    static long round(long x, long k) { long h = (x * 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15L) ^ k; h ^= h >>> 29; h *= 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9L; h ^= h >>> 32; return h & (HALF - 1); }
    static long feistel(long v) {
        long l = v >>> 21, r = v & (HALF - 1);
        for (long k : KEYS) { long t = l ^ round(r, k); l = r; r = t; }
        return (l << 21) | r;
    }
    static long permute(long v) { long x = feistel(v); while (x >= SPACE7) x = feistel(x); return x; }   // cycle-walk

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int n = 2_000_000; Random rnd = new Random(38);
        System.out.printf("Minting %,d short codes. 62^6 = %,d   62^7 = %,d%n%n", n, pow(62, 6), SPACE7);
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %6s %12s %14s %18s%n", "strategy", "length", "collisions", "extra lookups", "neighbour guess hits");

        // A) hash-truncate
        MessageDigest md5 = MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5"); Set<String> a = new HashSet<>(); int aColl = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            String url = "https://grocery.in/orders/ORD-" + (10_000_000 + i) + "/track?t=" + Long.toHexString(rnd.nextLong());
            byte[] h = md5.digest(url.getBytes());
            String code = base62(new BigInteger(1, h).mod(BigInteger.valueOf(pow(62, 6))).longValue(), 6);
            if (!a.add(code)) aColl++;
        }
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %6d %,12d %,14d %18s%n", "A) MD5(url) truncated to 6 base62 chars", 6, aColl, 0, "~0% (random)");

        // B) random + retry
        Set<String> b = new HashSet<>(); int bRetry = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { String c; do { c = base62(Math.floorMod(rnd.nextLong(), SPACE7), 7); if (b.contains(c)) bRetry++; } while (!b.add(c)); }
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %6d %,12d %,14d %18s%n", "B) random 7 chars, check-and-retry", 7, 0, n + bRetry, "~0% (random)");

        // C) counter
        long start = 100_000_000L; Set<String> c = new HashSet<>(); int cHits = 0;
        for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) c.add(base62(start + i));
        List<String> cList = new ArrayList<>(c);
        for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) { String s = cList.get(rnd.nextInt(cList.size())); if (c.contains(base62(decode(s) + 1))) cHits++; }
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %6d %,12d %,14d %17.1f%%%n", "C) counter → base62", base62(start + n).length(), 0, 0, 100.0 * cHits / 10_000);

        // D) counter → permutation
        Set<Long> dSet = new HashSet<>(); List<String> dList = new ArrayList<>(); Set<String> dCodes = new HashSet<>();
        for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) { long p = permute(start + i); dSet.add(p); String s = base62(p, 7); dList.add(s); dCodes.add(s); }
        int dHits = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) { String s = dList.get(rnd.nextInt(dList.size())); String nb = base62(decode(s) + 1, 7); if (nb != null && dCodes.contains(nb)) dHits++; }
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %6d %,12d %,14d %17.2f%%%n", "D) counter → Feistel permutation → base62", 7, n - dSet.size(), 0, 100.0 * dHits / 10_000);

        System.out.println("\n   First five codes minted by C and D (consecutive counter values):");
        StringBuilder sc = new StringBuilder(), sd = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { sc.append(base62(start + i)).append(' '); sd.append(dList.get(i)).append(' '); }
        System.out.println("        C: " + sc.toString().trim()); System.out.println("        D: " + sd.toString().trim());

        // birthday check on A
        double expectedA = (double) n * (n - 1) / 2 / pow(62, 6);
        System.out.printf("%n   Birthday estimate for A: n²/2N = %,.0f expected colliding pairs (measured %,d).%n", expectedA, aColl);
        System.out.printf("   Random 7-char space is %.5f%% full after %,d codes, so B needed %,d retries — but still one lookup per insert.%n", 100.0 * n / SPACE7, n, bRetry);
        System.out.printf("   At 2M links/day, 62^7 lasts %,.0f years for C/D; 62^6 would last %,.0f years.%n", SPACE7 / 2e6 / 365, pow(62, 6) / 2e6 / 365);

        System.out.println("\n   → hashing needs no coordination but collides (and two customers' different URLs can't share a code), so it");
        System.out.println("     still needs a check-and-retry — at which point it is B with extra steps. B is simple and unguessable but");
        System.out.println("     costs a uniqueness check on every insert (a unique index and a retry loop). C is perfect for the database and");
        System.out.println("     terrible for privacy: every tracking link's neighbour is another customer's order. D keeps C's properties —");
        System.out.println("     unique by construction, no lookup, one short range per node — and a keyed permutation makes neighbours useless.");
        System.out.println("     A permutation hides ORDER, not existence: codes are still 7 chars from a 3.5-trillion space, so pair it with");
        System.out.println("     rate limiting (Ch 39) and never put secrets behind a short link alone.");
    }
    static long decode(String s) { long v = 0; for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) v = v * 62 + ALPHABET.indexOf(ch); return v; }
}
java -Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8 CodeGenL1.java
Minting 2,000,000 short codes. 62^6 = 56,800,235,584   62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208

   strategy                                     length   collisions  extra lookups neighbour guess hits
   A) MD5(url) truncated to 6 base62 chars           6           40              0       ~0% (random)
   B) random 7 chars, check-and-retry                7            0      2,000,000       ~0% (random)
   C) counter → base62                               5            0              0             100.0%
   D) counter → Feistel permutation → base62         7            0              0              0.00%

   First five codes minted by C and D (consecutive counter values):
        C: 6laZE 6laZF 6laZG 6laZH 6laZI
        D: jFF7XOx jstj0mT pt1IVd8 d5RctH9 JNOJwOr

   Birthday estimate for A: n²/2N = 35 expected colliding pairs (measured 40).
   Random 7-char space is 0.00006% full after 2,000,000 codes, so B needed 0 retries — but still one lookup per insert.
   At 2M links/day, 62^7 lasts 4,824 years for C/D; 62^6 would last 78 years.

   → hashing needs no coordination but collides (and two customers' different URLs can't share a code), so it
     still needs a check-and-retry — at which point it is B with extra steps. B is simple and unguessable but
     costs a uniqueness check on every insert (a unique index and a retry loop). C is perfect for the database and
     terrible for privacy: every tracking link's neighbour is another customer's order. D keeps C's properties —
     unique by construction, no lookup, one short range per node — and a keyed permutation makes neighbours useless.
     A permutation hides ORDER, not existence: codes are still 7 chars from a 3.5-trillion space, so pair it with
     rate limiting (Ch 39) and never put secrets behind a short link alone.

Reading it:

  • A) Hash truncation produced 40 collisions in 2M codes, right where the birthday estimate n²/2N = 35 says it should. At a year's volume the collisions number in the tens of thousands, so hashing still needs a check-and-retry.
  • B) Random codes needed 0 retries, because the 7-character space is only 0.00006% full, but it still paid 2,000,000 uniqueness lookups.
  • C) Counter codes are 5 characters and need nothing, but 100% of sampled neighbours were other live links: 6laZE 6laZF 6laZG….
  • D) Counter + permutation: 0 collisions, 0 lookups, 0.00% neighbour hits: jFF7XOx jstj0mT pt1IVd8…. The cost is two extra characters.

docs.title: L2 — A real shortener on PostgreSQL B2
docs.text:
Requirement: "Services create links, customers follow them. Retries must not duplicate links; nothing may point outside our domains; expired links must say so."

A JDK HttpServer on virtual threads serves POST /api/links and GET /{code} from PostgreSQL. Codes come from a sequence in blocks of 1,000 per node, passed through L1's permutation. A load phase then sends 50,000 Zipf-distributed redirects over 10,000 links from 200 concurrent clients.

ShortenerL2.java
// ShortenerL2.java — run with (PostgreSQL 16 on :5581, db "shop"):
//   java -cp postgresql-42.7.4.jar -Dsun.net.httpserver.nodelay=true ShortenerL2.java
// A REAL SHORTENER: JDK HttpServer + PostgreSQL. Create links with POST /api/links, follow them with GET /{code}.
// What makes it production-shaped rather than a toy:
//   • codes come from a database SEQUENCE handed out in BLOCKS of 1,000 per node (one round-trip per 1,000 links), then a
//     keyed permutation (L1 strategy D) — unique by construction, not guessable
//   • create is IDEMPOTENT per (owner, url): the notification service retries on timeouts, and must not mint a second code
//   • destinations are VALIDATED: https only, host on an allow-list — a public shortener on our domain is a phishing kit,
//     and India's DLT rules for SMS require that links in templates resolve to registered domains
//   • expired links return 410 Gone, unknown ones 404; redirects are 302 (not 301) so every click reaches us (analytics)
//   • a small read-through cache in front of the database for the redirect path
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;
import java.net.*;
import java.net.http.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.sql.*;
import java.time.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;
import java.util.regex.*;

public class ShortenerL2 {
    static final String DB = "jdbc:postgresql://127.0.0.1:5581/shop?user=claude";
    static final Set<String> ALLOWED_HOSTS = Set.of("grocery.in", "track.grocery.in", "pay.grocery.in", "offers.grocery.in");
    static final AtomicLong dbReads = new AtomicLong();

    // ---- code minting: block-allocated sequence + permutation (see CodeGenL1 strategy D) ----
    static final String ALPHABET = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz";
    static final long SPACE7 = 3_521_614_606_208L, HALF = 1L << 21;
    static final long[] KEYS = {0x5DEECE66DL, 0x2545F491L, 0x9E3779B9L, 0x7F4A7C15L};
    static long round(long x, long k) { long h = (x * 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15L) ^ k; h ^= h >>> 29; h *= 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9L; h ^= h >>> 32; return h & (HALF - 1); }
    static long feistel(long v) { long l = v >>> 21, r = v & (HALF - 1); for (long k : KEYS) { long t = l ^ round(r, k); l = r; r = t; } return (l << 21) | r; }
    static String code(long counter) { long x = feistel(counter); while (x >= SPACE7) x = feistel(x); char[] c = new char[7]; for (int i = 6; i >= 0; i--) { c[i] = ALPHABET.charAt((int) (x % 62)); x /= 62; } return new String(c); }

    static long blockNext = 0, blockEnd = 0; static int blocksFetched = 0;
    static synchronized long nextCounter(Connection c) throws SQLException {
        if (blockNext == blockEnd) {
            try (ResultSet rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("select nextval('link_block_seq')")) { rs.next(); blockNext = rs.getLong(1) * 1000; blockEnd = blockNext + 1000; blocksFetched++; }
        }
        return blockNext++;
    }

    // ---- validation ----
    static String validate(String url) {
        URI u;
        try { u = new URI(url); } catch (URISyntaxException e) { return "not a valid URL"; }
        if (!"https".equals(u.getScheme())) return "only https destinations are allowed";
        if (u.getRawUserInfo() != null) return "credentials in URL are not allowed";
        if (u.getHost() == null || !ALLOWED_HOSTS.contains(u.getHost().toLowerCase())) return "destination host '" + u.getHost() + "' is not on the allow-list";
        if (url.length() > 2048) return "URL too long";
        return null;
    }

    // ---- read-through cache (bounded LRU) ----
    record Link(String url, Instant expires) {}
    static final Map<String, Link> cache = Collections.synchronizedMap(new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) {
        protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<String, Link> e) { return size() > 5_000; } });

    static BlockingQueue<Connection> pool = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>();

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        for (int i = 0; i < 16; i++) pool.add(DriverManager.getConnection(DB));
        try (Statement s = pool.peek().createStatement()) {
            s.execute("drop table if exists links"); s.execute("drop sequence if exists link_block_seq");
            s.execute("create sequence link_block_seq start 100000");
            s.execute("""
                create table links(code char(7) primary key, long_url text not null, owner text not null,
                  url_hash bytea not null, created_at timestamptz not null default now(), expires_at timestamptz,
                  unique(owner, url_hash))""");
        }
        HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("127.0.0.1", 0), 512);
        server.setExecutor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor());
        server.createContext("/api/links", ex -> {
            String body = new String(ex.getRequestBody().readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            String url = field(body, "url"), owner = field(body, "owner"), ttl = field(body, "ttlDays");
            String err = url == null ? "url is required" : validate(url);
            if (err != null) { send(ex, 422, "{\"error\":\"" + err + "\"}"); return; }
            Connection c = take();
            try {
                byte[] hash = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(url.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
                String code = code(nextCounter(c));
                try (PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("insert into links(code,long_url,owner,url_hash,expires_at) values (?,?,?,?,?) on conflict (owner,url_hash) do nothing")) {
                    ps.setString(1, code); ps.setString(2, url); ps.setString(3, owner); ps.setBytes(4, hash);
                    ps.setObject(5, ttl == null ? null : OffsetDateTime.now(ZoneOffset.UTC).plusDays(Long.parseLong(ttl)));
                    if (ps.executeUpdate() == 1) { send(ex, 201, "{\"code\":\"" + code + "\",\"short\":\"https://gro.cr/" + code + "\"}"); return; }
                }
                try (PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("select code from links where owner=? and url_hash=?")) {   // idempotent replay
                    ps.setString(1, owner); ps.setBytes(2, hash); ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery(); rs.next();
                    send(ex, 200, "{\"code\":\"" + rs.getString(1) + "\",\"short\":\"https://gro.cr/" + rs.getString(1) + "\",\"existing\":true}");
                }
            } catch (Exception e) { send(ex, 500, "{\"error\":\"" + e.getMessage() + "\"}"); } finally { pool.add(c); }
        });
        server.createContext("/", ex -> {
            String code = ex.getRequestURI().getPath().substring(1);
            if (!code.matches("[0-9A-Za-z]{7}")) { send(ex, 404, ""); return; }
            Link l = cache.get(code);
            if (l == null) {
                Connection c = take();
                try (PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("select long_url, expires_at from links where code=?")) {
                    dbReads.incrementAndGet(); ps.setString(1, code); ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery();
                    if (!rs.next()) { send(ex, 404, ""); return; }
                    Timestamp t = rs.getTimestamp(2); l = new Link(rs.getString(1), t == null ? null : t.toInstant()); cache.put(code, l);
                } catch (SQLException e) { send(ex, 500, ""); return; } finally { pool.add(c); }
            }
            if (l.expires() != null && l.expires().isBefore(Instant.now())) { send(ex, 410, ""); return; }
            ex.getResponseHeaders().add("Location", l.url()); ex.getResponseHeaders().add("Cache-Control", "private, max-age=0");
            ex.sendResponseHeaders(302, -1); ex.close();
        });
        server.start();
        String base = "http://127.0.0.1:" + server.getAddress().getPort();
        HttpClient http = HttpClient.newBuilder().version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_1_1).followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NEVER)
                .executor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()).build();

        System.out.println("Shortener on " + base + " (PostgreSQL 16, JDK HttpServer on virtual threads)\n");
        System.out.println("   Creating links:");
        String track = post(http, base, "{\"url\":\"https://track.grocery.in/orders/ORD-88213?t=f3a9\",\"owner\":\"notification-svc\",\"ttlDays\":\"30\"}");
        post(http, base, "{\"url\":\"https://track.grocery.in/orders/ORD-88213?t=f3a9\",\"owner\":\"notification-svc\",\"ttlDays\":\"30\"}");
        post(http, base, "{\"url\":\"https://offers.grocery.in/diwali?utm_source=sms\",\"owner\":\"marketing\"}");
        post(http, base, "{\"url\":\"http://track.grocery.in/orders/ORD-1\",\"owner\":\"notification-svc\"}");
        post(http, base, "{\"url\":\"https://grocery.in@evil.example/login\",\"owner\":\"marketing\"}");
        post(http, base, "{\"url\":\"https://grocery-in.example/kyc-update\",\"owner\":\"marketing\"}");
        try (Statement s = pool.peek().createStatement()) {   // an expired reminder link, created 31 days ago with a 30-day TTL
            s.execute("insert into links values ('Zz0exp1','https://grocery.in/slots/remind','notification-svc','\\x00'::bytea, now()-interval '31 days', now()-interval '1 day')");
        }
        String trackCode = field(track, "code");
        System.out.println("\n   Following links:");
        for (String c : List.of(trackCode, "Zz0exp1", "aaaaaaa", "../etc")) {
            HttpResponse<Void> r = http.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(base + "/" + c)).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.discarding());
            System.out.printf("        GET /%-8s → %d %s%n", c, r.statusCode(), r.headers().firstValue("Location").map(x -> "Location: " + x).orElse(""));
        }

        // ---- load: 10,000 links, then 50,000 redirects with a skewed (Zipf-like) popularity, 200 concurrent clients ----
        List<String> codes = new ArrayList<>();
        try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(DB); PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("insert into links(code,long_url,owner,url_hash) values (?,?,?,?)")) {
            c.setAutoCommit(false);
            for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
                String code = code(nextCounter(c)); String url = "https://track.grocery.in/orders/ORD-" + (200_000 + i);
                ps.setString(1, code); ps.setString(2, url); ps.setString(3, "bulk"); ps.setBytes(4, MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(url.getBytes())); ps.addBatch(); codes.add(code);
            }
            ps.executeBatch(); c.commit();
        }
        double[] cdf = new double[codes.size()]; double sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < cdf.length; i++) { sum += 1.0 / (i + 1); cdf[i] = sum; }
        Random rnd = new Random(38); int total = 50_000; String[] picks = new String[total];
        for (int i = 0; i < total; i++) { double x = rnd.nextDouble() * sum; int idx = Arrays.binarySearch(cdf, x); picks[i] = codes.get(idx < 0 ? -idx - 1 : idx); }
        cache.clear(); dbReads.set(0);
        long[] lat = new long[total]; AtomicInteger ok = new AtomicInteger(); Semaphore conc = new Semaphore(200);
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < total; i++) {
                final int k = i; conc.acquire();
                exec.submit(() -> {
                    try { long s = System.nanoTime();
                        HttpResponse<Void> r = http.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(base + "/" + picks[k])).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.discarding());
                        lat[k] = System.nanoTime() - s; if (r.statusCode() == 302) ok.incrementAndGet();
                    } catch (Exception e) { lat[k] = Long.MAX_VALUE; } finally { conc.release(); }
                });
            }
        }
        double secs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9; Arrays.sort(lat);
        long distinct = Arrays.stream(picks).distinct().count();
        System.out.printf("%n   Load: %,d redirects over 10,000 links (Zipf popularity, %,d distinct links hit), 200 concurrent clients%n", total, distinct);
        System.out.printf("        302s: %,d   throughput: %,.0f redirects/s   p50 %.2f ms   p99 %.2f ms   (timings vary by machine)%n",
                ok.get(), total / secs, lat[total / 2] / 1e6, lat[(int) (total * 0.99)] / 1e6);
        System.out.printf("        database reads: %,d for %,d redirects — the cache absorbed %.1f%%%n", dbReads.get(), total, 100.0 * (total - dbReads.get()) / total);
        System.out.printf("        but only %,d distinct links were requested: %,d reads were CONCURRENT misses for a code another request was%n", distinct, dbReads.get() - distinct);
        System.out.println("        already loading — a small thundering herd on cold, popular links (fix: coalesce misses per key, Ch 7)");
        System.out.printf("        counter values used: %,d via %d sequence round-trips (blocks of 1,000)%n", codes.size() + 3, blocksFetched);

        System.out.println("\n   → the retry returned the SAME code (200, existing) instead of minting a second link; http, a userinfo trick");
        System.out.println("     that really points at evil.example, and a look-alike domain were all refused before anything was stored.");
        System.out.println("     Expired links say 410 (gone for good), unknown ones 404. Redirects are 302 with no browser caching, so every");
        System.out.println("     click reaches us — the price of analytics is that we must serve every one, which is why the cache matters.");
        server.stop(0); System.exit(0);
    }

    static Connection take() { try { return pool.take(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } }
    static String field(String json, String k) { Matcher m = Pattern.compile("\"" + k + "\"\\s*:\\s*\"([^\"]*)\"").matcher(json); return m.find() ? m.group(1) : null; }
    static void send(com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpExchange ex, int status, String body) throws java.io.IOException {
        byte[] b = body.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8); ex.getResponseHeaders().add("Content-Type", "application/json");
        ex.sendResponseHeaders(status, b.length == 0 ? -1 : b.length); if (b.length > 0) ex.getResponseBody().write(b); ex.close();
    }
    static String post(HttpClient http, String base, String json) throws Exception {
        HttpResponse<String> r = http.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(base + "/api/links")).header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(json)).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
        System.out.printf("        POST %-58s → %d %s%n", field(json, "url"), r.statusCode(), r.body());
        return r.body();
    }
}

Reading it:

  • The retry returned 200 … "existing":true with the same code jFF7XOx. The unique (owner, url_hash) constraint makes a concurrent double-create impossible, not just unlikely.
  • Validation refused http://, the user-info trick (grocery.in@evil.example really points at evil.example) and the look-alike host, all before anything was stored.
