docs.title: L3 — The read path: cache sizing and the campaign spike B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "How much cache do we need, and what happens at 7 pm when marketing sends 20 million SMS with one link?"

Part 1 replays 10 million Zipf-distributed clicks through a real LRU cache at five sizes. Part 2 simulates the campaign second by second against 20 redirect nodes and a 6-shard Redis cluster, with and without a 1-second near-cache.

ReadPathL3.java
// ReadPathL3.java — run with: java ReadPathL3.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// THE READ PATH AT SCALE: how big a cache, and what happens when marketing sends 20 million SMS at 7 pm.
// Part 1 replays 10,000,000 clicks over 1,000,000 links with a skewed popularity (Zipf, s = 1.0 — an assumption; measure
// your own) through a real LRU cache (LinkedHashMap in access order) of several sizes and reports the hit ratio, the
// database reads that remain, and the cache's memory at ~200 bytes per entry.
// Part 2 simulates a campaign spike second by second: 20M SMS with one offer link, clicks decaying over 10 minutes on top
// of normal traffic, served by 20 redirect nodes in front of a 6-shard Redis cluster. Every request for the offer code
// hashes to ONE shard. We compare shard load without and with a 1-second in-process near-cache on each node.
import java.util.*;

public class ReadPathL3 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int links = 1_000_000, clicks = 10_000_000; Random rnd = new Random(38);
        double[] cdf = new double[links]; double sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < links; i++) { sum += 1.0 / (i + 1); cdf[i] = sum; }
        int[] perm = new int[links]; for (int i = 0; i < links; i++) perm[i] = i;
        for (int i = links - 1; i > 0; i--) { int j = rnd.nextInt(i + 1); int t = perm[i]; perm[i] = perm[j]; perm[j] = t; }
        int[] stream = new int[clicks];
        for (int i = 0; i < clicks; i++) { int idx = Arrays.binarySearch(cdf, rnd.nextDouble() * sum); stream[i] = perm[idx < 0 ? -idx - 1 : idx]; }
        long distinct = Arrays.stream(stream).distinct().count();

        System.out.printf("Part 1 — %,d clicks over %,d links (Zipf s=1.0); %,d distinct links clicked at least once.%n%n", clicks, links, distinct);
        System.out.printf("   %-18s %12s %11s %20s %18s%n", "LRU cache size", "% of links", "hit ratio", "DB reads remaining", "cache memory");
        for (int size : new int[]{1_000, 10_000, 50_000, 100_000, 250_000}) {
            LinkedHashMap<Integer, Boolean> lru = new LinkedHashMap<>(size * 2, 0.75f, true) {
                protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<Integer, Boolean> e) { return size() > size; } };
            long hits = 0;
            for (int k : stream) { if (lru.get(k) != null) hits++; else lru.put(k, Boolean.TRUE); }
            System.out.printf("   %,18d %11.1f%% %10.1f%% %,20d %15.0f MB%n", size, 100.0 * size / links, 100.0 * hits / clicks, clicks - hits, size * 200 / 1e6);
        }

        // ---------------- Part 2: the campaign spike ----------------
        int nodes = 20, shards = 6, seconds = 600; double baseRps = 3_000;           // normal redirect traffic
        double totalCampaignClicks = 20_000_000 * 0.12;                              // 12% click-through (assumption)
        double tau = 90;                                                              // clicks decay with a 90 s time constant
        int hotShard = 2;
        long[][] shardLoad = new long[2][shards]; long[] peakHot = new long[2]; long[] peakOther = new long[2]; long peakRps = 0;
        for (int s = 0; s < seconds; s++) {
            double campaign = totalCampaignClicks / tau * Math.exp(-s / tau);
            long hot = Math.round(campaign), normal = Math.round(baseRps * (0.9 + 0.2 * rnd.nextDouble()));
            peakRps = Math.max(peakRps, hot + normal);
            for (int mode = 0; mode < 2; mode++) {
                long[] load = new long[shards];
                for (int k = 0; k < shards; k++) load[k] = normal / shards;              // background spread evenly (misses of L1)
                load[hotShard] += mode == 0 ? hot : Math.min(hot, nodes);               // near-cache: ≤ 1 miss per node per second
                for (int k = 0; k < shards; k++) shardLoad[mode][k] += load[k];
                peakHot[mode] = Math.max(peakHot[mode], load[hotShard]);
                long other = 0; for (int k = 0; k < shards; k++) if (k != hotShard) other = Math.max(other, load[k]);
                peakOther[mode] = Math.max(peakOther[mode], other);
            }
        }
        System.out.printf("%nPart 2 — campaign: 20M SMS × 12%% click-through = %,.0f clicks on ONE code, decaying over 10 min; peak %,d redirects/s.%n",
                totalCampaignClicks, peakRps);
        System.out.println("   Redis cluster: 6 shards. A single Redis shard comfortably serves ~100k simple GETs/s (VERIFY on your hardware).\n");
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %22s %20s %16s%n", "", "peak on HOT shard /s", "peak other shard /s", "hot / other");
        String[] label = {"no near-cache (every click → Redis)", "1 s near-cache on each of 20 nodes"};
        for (int m = 0; m < 2; m++)
            System.out.printf("   %-44s %,22d %,20d %15.0fx%n", label[m], peakHot[m], peakOther[m], (double) peakHot[m] / peakOther[m]);

        double saturatingBlast = 20_000_000.0 * 100_000 / peakHot[0];
        System.out.printf("%n   At this blast the hot shard runs at ~%.0f%% of one shard's capacity — fine today. But its load scales with the%n", 100.0 * peakHot[0] / 100_000);
        System.out.printf("   SIZE OF THE BLAST, not the cluster: a ~%,.0fM-SMS festival campaign saturates it, and adding shards changes nothing.%n", saturatingBlast / 1e6);
        System.out.println("\n   → the cache curve flattens fast: 1% of links as cache serves 58% of clicks, 10x more memory only gets to 78%,");
        System.out.println("     and the long tail of cold links always reaches the database — size the database for the tail, the cache for");
        System.out.println("     the head. The campaign is a different problem: sharding spreads KEYS, not load, so every click on the offer");
        System.out.println("     code lands on one shard at ~49x its peers' load. A near-cache of even one second on each node caps it at one");
        System.out.println("     lookup per node per second; for a scheduled campaign, pre-warm the code on every node before the blast.");
    }
}

Reading it:

  • Diminishing returns: 0.1% of links as cache already serves 40%; 1% serves 58.5%; 25x more (25%) reaches only 85.5%. About 763k distinct links were clicked at least once, and that tail always reaches the database.
  • The campaign pushes 27,184 req/s onto the shard holding the offer code, 49x the other shards. That is fine at this size (~27% of one shard) but scales with the blast: ~74M SMS would saturate it, whatever the shard count.
  • A 1-second near-cache caps the hot shard at one lookup per node per second: 570 req/s, the same as its peers.

docs.title: L4 — Counting clicks without hurting redirects B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "Marketing wants clicks and unique visitors per link, live — without slowing a single redirect."

Part 1 counts 40,000 clicks against PostgreSQL with durable commits, using 32 concurrent writers, three ways. Part 2 counts unique devices across 20 nodes exactly and with a HyperLogLog implemented in the lab.

AnalyticsL4.java
// AnalyticsL4.java — run with (PostgreSQL 16 on :5581, db "shop"):
//   java -cp postgresql-42.7.4.jar AnalyticsL4.java
// COUNTING CLICKS WITHOUT HURTING REDIRECTS. Marketing wants clicks and UNIQUE visitors per link, per campaign, in near
// real time. Part 1 measures three ways to count 40,000 clicks against real PostgreSQL with 32 concurrent writers:
//   A) UPDATE the link's counter on every click — clicks spread over 1,000 links
//   B) the same, but every click is on ONE campaign link (a single hot row)
//   C) append clicks to an in-memory buffer; a flusher aggregates per code and upserts once a second (micro-batching)
// Part 2 counts unique visitors: exact (a HashSet of device ids) vs a HyperLogLog sketch implemented below (p = 14,
// 16,384 registers), including MERGING the sketches of 20 redirect nodes — something exact sets can't do cheaply.
import java.sql.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport;

public class AnalyticsL4 {
    static final String DB = "jdbc:postgresql://127.0.0.1:5581/shop?user=claude";

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(DB); Statement s = c.createStatement()) {
            s.execute("drop table if exists link_stats"); s.execute("create table link_stats(code text primary key, clicks bigint not null)");
            s.execute("insert into link_stats select 'L' || g, 0 from generate_series(0, 999) g");
        }
        int clicks = 40_000, writers = 32;
        System.out.printf("Part 1 — %,d clicks, %d concurrent writers, PostgreSQL 16 with durable commits (fsync on)%n%n", clicks, writers);
        System.out.printf("   %-52s %10s %22s %14s %10s%n", "strategy", "clicks/s", "p99 cost on redirect", "DB statements", "counted");
        run("A) UPDATE per click, spread over 1,000 links", clicks, writers, false);
        run("B) UPDATE per click, ONE hot campaign link", clicks, writers, true);
        batched(clicks, writers);

        // ---------------- Part 2: unique visitors ----------------
        int nodes = 20, events = 3_000_000; Random rnd = new Random(38);
        long[] devicePool = new long[900_000]; for (int i = 0; i < devicePool.length; i++) devicePool[i] = rnd.nextLong();
        Set<Long> exact = new HashSet<>(); HLL[] perNode = new HLL[nodes]; for (int i = 0; i < nodes; i++) perNode[i] = new HLL(14);
        for (int i = 0; i < events; i++) {
            long dev = devicePool[(int) Math.min(devicePool.length - 1, Math.abs(rnd.nextGaussian()) * 300_000)];   // repeat visitors
            exact.add(dev); perNode[rnd.nextInt(nodes)].add(dev);                                                   // any node may serve a click
        }
        HLL merged = new HLL(14); for (HLL h : perNode) merged.merge(h);
        long sumOfNodes = 0; for (HLL h : perNode) sumOfNodes += Math.round(h.estimate());
        long est = Math.round(merged.estimate());
        System.out.printf("%nPart 2 — %,d clicks from repeat visitors across %d redirect nodes%n%n", events, nodes);
        System.out.printf("   %-46s %,14d %20s%n", "exact unique devices (HashSet)", exact.size(), "~" + (exact.size() * 56L / 1_000_000) + " MB of set entries");
        System.out.printf("   %-46s %,14d %20s   error %+.2f%%%n", "HyperLogLog, 20 node sketches merged", est, "16 KB per sketch", 100.0 * (est - exact.size()) / exact.size());
        System.out.printf("   %-46s %,14d %20s   error %+.0f%%%n", "adding the 20 per-node unique counts instead", sumOfNodes, "", 100.0 * (sumOfNodes - exact.size()) / exact.size());
        System.out.printf("   HLL standard error at p=14: 1.04/√16384 = %.2f%%%n", 104.0 / Math.sqrt(16384));

        System.out.println("\n   → counting with a synchronous UPDATE puts a row lock on the redirect's critical path; it is tolerable when");
        System.out.println("     clicks spread out and collapses onto one lock exactly when a campaign makes one link hot (several times slower,");
        System.out.println("     with a far worse p99). Micro-batching makes the redirect's cost a memory increment and turns 40,000 increments into one upsert");
        System.out.println("     per link per second (20x fewer statements) — take clicks off the redirect path (in production: a");
        System.out.println("     Kafka topic + stream aggregation, Ch 14), accepting counts that are a second or so behind. Unique visitors");
        System.out.println("     don't add up across nodes or days; HyperLogLog sketches do merge, in kilobytes, within about 1%.");
        System.exit(0);
    }

    static void run(String label, int clicks, int writers, boolean hot) throws Exception {
        try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(DB)) { c.createStatement().execute("update link_stats set clicks = 0"); }
        AtomicInteger next = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicLong stmts = new AtomicLong(); long[] lat = new long[clicks];
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        try (var exec = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(writers)) {
            for (int w = 0; w < writers; w++) exec.submit(() -> {
                try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(DB); PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("update link_stats set clicks = clicks + 1 where code = ?")) {
                    int i;
                    while ((i = next.getAndIncrement()) < clicks) { long s0 = System.nanoTime(); ps.setString(1, hot ? "L7" : "L" + (i * 7919 % 1000)); ps.executeUpdate(); lat[i] = System.nanoTime() - s0; stmts.incrementAndGet(); }
                } catch (SQLException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }
                return null;
            });
        }
        double secs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9;
        Arrays.sort(lat);
        System.out.printf("   %-52s %,10.0f %19.2f ms %,14d %,10d%n", label, clicks / secs, lat[(int) (clicks * 0.99)] / 1e6, stmts.get(), total());
    }

    static void batched(int clicks, int writers) throws Exception {
        try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(DB)) { c.createStatement().execute("update link_stats set clicks = 0"); }
        ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> buffer = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); AtomicLong stmts = new AtomicLong();
        Connection fc = DriverManager.getConnection(DB);
        Runnable flush = () -> {
            try {
                Map<String, Long> snap = new TreeMap<>();
                for (String k : buffer.keySet()) { long v = buffer.get(k).sumThenReset(); if (v > 0) snap.put(k, v); }
                if (snap.isEmpty()) return;
                try (PreparedStatement ps = fc.prepareStatement("insert into link_stats values (?, ?) on conflict (code) do update set clicks = link_stats.clicks + excluded.clicks")) {
                    for (var e : snap.entrySet()) { ps.setString(1, e.getKey()); ps.setLong(2, e.getValue()); ps.addBatch(); }
                    ps.executeBatch(); stmts.addAndGet(snap.size());
                }
            } catch (SQLException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }
        };
        ScheduledExecutorService flusher = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor();
        flusher.scheduleAtFixedRate(flush, 1, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        // clicks arrive at a steady 10,000/s for 4 s (as they would from redirect traffic), so the flusher runs several times
        AtomicInteger next = new AtomicInteger(); long[] lat = new long[clicks]; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); double pace = 10_000;
        try (var exec = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(writers)) {
            for (int w = 0; w < writers; w++) exec.submit(() -> {
                int i;
                while ((i = next.getAndIncrement()) < clicks) {
                    long due = t0 + (long) (i / pace * 1e9); long wait = due - System.nanoTime();
                    if (wait > 0) LockSupport.parkNanos(wait);
                    long s0 = System.nanoTime();
                    String code = i % 2 == 0 ? "L7" : "L" + (i * 7919 % 1000);           // half the clicks on the hot link
                    buffer.computeIfAbsent(code, k -> new LongAdder()).increment();
                    lat[i] = System.nanoTime() - s0;
                }
            });
        }
        double secs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9;
        flusher.shutdown(); flusher.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); flush.run();   // final flush on shutdown
        Arrays.sort(lat);
        System.out.printf("   %-52s %,10.0f %19.4f ms %,14d %,10d%n", "C) buffer + 1 s micro-batch upsert (half on hot link)", clicks / secs, lat[(int) (clicks * 0.99)] / 1e6, stmts.get(), total());
        System.out.println("      (C is paced at 10,000 clicks/s — its limit is the redirect traffic, not the counter)");
        fc.close();
    }

    static long total() throws SQLException {
        try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(DB); ResultSet rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("select sum(clicks) from link_stats")) { rs.next(); return rs.getLong(1); }
    }

    // ---------------- HyperLogLog ----------------
    static final class HLL {
        final int p, m; final byte[] reg;
        HLL(int p) { this.p = p; this.m = 1 << p; this.reg = new byte[m]; }
        static long mix(long z) { z = (z ^ (z >>> 33)) * 0xff51afd7ed558ccdL; z = (z ^ (z >>> 33)) * 0xc4ceb9fe1a85ec53L; return z ^ (z >>> 33); }
        void add(long item) {
            long h = mix(item); int idx = (int) (h >>> (64 - p)); long w = h << p;
            byte rho = (byte) (w == 0 ? 64 - p + 1 : Long.numberOfLeadingZeros(w) + 1);
            if (rho > reg[idx]) reg[idx] = rho;
        }
        void merge(HLL o) { for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) if (o.reg[i] > reg[i]) reg[i] = o.reg[i]; }
        double estimate() {
            double sum = 0; int zeros = 0;
            for (byte r : reg) { sum += Math.pow(2, -r); if (r == 0) zeros++; }
            double alpha = 0.7213 / (1 + 1.079 / m), e = alpha * m * m / sum;
            return (e <= 2.5 * m && zeros > 0) ? m * Math.log((double) m / zeros) : e;   // small-range correction
        }
    }
}
java -cp postgresql-42.7.4.jar -Duser.timezone=UTC AnalyticsL4.java
Part 1 — 40,000 clicks, 32 concurrent writers, PostgreSQL 16 with durable commits (fsync on)

   strategy                                               clicks/s   p99 cost on redirect  DB statements    counted
   A) UPDATE per click, spread over 1,000 links             12,253               11.33 ms         40,000     40,000
   B) UPDATE per click, ONE hot campaign link                2,263               67.22 ms         40,000     40,000
   C) buffer + 1 s micro-batch upsert (half on hot link)     10,000              0.0100 ms          2,029     40,000
      (C is paced at 10,000 clicks/s — its limit is the redirect traffic, not the counter)

Part 2 — 3,000,000 clicks from repeat visitors across 20 redirect nodes

   exact unique devices (HashSet)                        663,668 ~37 MB of set entries
   HyperLogLog, 20 node sketches merged                  666,410     16 KB per sketch   error +0.41%
   adding the 20 per-node unique counts instead        2,613,952                        error +294%
   HLL standard error at p=14: 1.04/√16384 = 0.81%

   → counting with a synchronous UPDATE puts a row lock on the redirect's critical path; it is tolerable when
     clicks spread out and collapses onto one lock exactly when a campaign makes one link hot (several times slower,
     with a far worse p99). Micro-batching makes the redirect's cost a memory increment and turns 40,000 increments into one upsert
     per link per second (20x fewer statements) — take clicks off the redirect path (in production: a
     Kafka topic + stream aggregation, Ch 14), accepting counts that are a second or so behind. Unique visitors
     don't add up across nodes or days; HyperLogLog sketches do merge, in kilobytes, within about 1%.

Reading it:

  • Spread-out updates manage ~12,000/s with an ~11 ms p99, already a cost on every redirect. On one hot row throughput drops to ~2,300/s and p99 to ~67 ms: each commit on the row waits for the previous one to flush.
  • Micro-batching makes the redirect's cost a 0.01 ms memory increment and writes ~2,000 upserts (one per link per flush) instead of 40,000. All 40,000 clicks were counted, including the final flush on shutdown.
  • Unique visitors: merged HLL sketches estimated 666,410 against an exact 663,668 (+0.41%, inside the 0.81% standard error) in 16 KB per sketch. Adding per-node unique counts gave 2.6 million (+294%), because the same device clicks through many nodes.
  • In production the buffer is a Kafka topic and the flusher a stream job. The principle is the same: counts are a second behind, and the redirect never waits.

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Symptom Mitigation Sequential codes Neighbouring links enumerable (L1) Keyed permutation; no personal data behind code alone 301 redirects Missing clicks; can't revoke 302/307 with no-store Campaign hot key One shard/row saturated; shared pool exhausted (L3) Near-cache, pre-warm, edge, bulkheads Cold-miss stampede Duplicate DB reads (L2: 716) Per-key miss coalescing Synchronous counters Redirect latency tied to row locks (L4) Async events + aggregation Unrestricted destinations Phishing on the trusted domain Allow-list, parser-based validation, abuse kill switch Mass expiry deletes Vacuum storms, replica lag Partition by expiry, drop partitions Bot traffic Inflated clicks UA/behaviour filtering, separate counts

docs.title: 6.2 Observability
docs.text:
• RED metrics on the redirect path, per region and per status (302/404/410), plus cache hit ratio per tier.
  • Hot-key detection: top codes per node per minute (count-min sketch), alerting when one code exceeds a share of traffic.
  • 404 rate per client as an enumeration signal.
  • Analytics lag: event time vs aggregation time.
  • Creation: idempotent replays (200s), validation rejections by reason — a spike in rejections may be an attack or a misconfigured campaign.

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Destination allow-list managed as code, reviewed changes, audit log (Ch 36).
  • Management API: mTLS/service identity, per-owner quotas.
  • Permutation keys rotate only for new codes (old codes stay valid — the mapping is only used at mint time).
  • Tracking pages behind links require a signed token bound to the order and expiry.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance
docs.text:
• The redirect handler does no allocation-heavy work: a near-cache lookup, a header, an async enqueue. It's a good fit for virtual threads or a non-blocking server (Ch 19).
  • Keep responses tiny: no body on 302, keep-alive, HTTP/2 at the edge.
  • Bulk creation: batch inserts (L2 inserted 10,000 in one batch), pre-reserved counter blocks, async results.

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• Storage is small and bounded by expiry; the main costs are the redirect fleet and the analytics pipeline.
  • Edge caching of campaign codes is the cheapest capacity for spikes.
  • Keep raw click events for a limited period (e.g., 90 days) and aggregates longer (Ch 35).

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Auto-increment ids as public codes

Every link reveals its neighbours (L1). Permute, or use random codes.

2. Hash truncation without collision handling

Birthday collisions arrive far sooner than intuition says — 40 in 2 million at 6 characters (L1).

3. Deduplicating identical URLs across owners

Different owners need different expiry, analytics and revocation. Dedupe per owner, if at all.

4. 301 by default

Browser caching hides clicks and makes revocation impossible for those who've clicked before.

5. Validating destinations with string matching

contains("grocery.in") accepts grocery.in.evil.example and grocery.in@evil.example. Parse, then compare hosts exactly (L2).

6. Public or unauthenticated link creation

Your trusted domain becomes a phishing service.

7. Counting clicks synchronously

A row lock on the redirect path, worst exactly during campaigns (L4).

8. Summing unique counts

Uniques don't add across nodes, days or links (L4: +294%). Use mergeable sketches.

9. Expecting sharding to fix a hot key

Sharding spreads keys, not load. One code lives on one shard (L3).

10. One pool for campaigns and transactional links

A campaign spike starves order tracking (§1.1). Bulkhead them.

11. Deleting expired rows one by one

Billions of deletes cause vacuum and replication pain. Partition by expiry.

12. Recycling codes

Old SMS and screenshots still point at them; a recycled code sends someone else's customer to a new destination.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ Design a URL shortener — what are the core components?

30-second answer: A write API that validates the long URL, mints a unique short code and stores code → URL. A redirect endpoint that looks up the code, through caches, and returns a 302 to the long URL. A database as the source of truth, a cache for the hot working set, and an asynchronous pipeline for click analytics. Plus expiry, abuse controls and monitoring.

Deep answer: Reads dominate (clicks ≫ creates) and are spiky, so the redirect path is cache-first and must survive hot keys (L3). Code generation is the interesting write-side choice (L1).

Trade-offs I'd call out: 302 vs 301 (analytics vs caching); random vs counter codes (lookups vs guessability).

Follow-ups: 1. How long should codes be? → 7 base62 chars ≈ 3.5 trillion. 2. Which status code? → 302/307 by default.

Red flags: Jumping to a NoSQL database without estimating anything.

Q2 [B1] ⭐ 301 or 302 — which would you use and why?

30-second answer: 302 (or 307) by default. A 301 says the redirect is permanent, so browsers and proxies may cache it — repeat clicks never reach you, analytics undercount, and you can't revoke or change the destination for anyone who has the cached redirect. A 302 means every click reaches the service, so the read path has to be cheap and well-cached.

Deep answer: L2 returns 302 with Cache-Control: private, max-age=0. A 301 can be right for truly permanent vanity links where analytics don't matter.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Server load vs control and measurement.

Follow-ups: 1. What about 308? → Permanent and method-preserving; same caching issue. 2. And for expired links? → 410 Gone.

Red flags: "301, because it's faster" without mentioning analytics or revocation.

Q3 [B1] How many characters does a short code need?

30-second answer: Work it out from the number of codes you'll ever mint and the alphabet. Base62 gives 62^6 ≈ 56.8 billion and 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion. At 2M links/day, 7 characters lasts thousands of years; 6 would last about 78 years but random schemes would collide much sooner. For random codes you also want the space sparse enough that guesses rarely hit a live code.

Deep answer: L1 computes both: 62^7 lasts 4,824 years at 2M/day. A counter needs only 5 characters today — which is exactly why it's guessable.

Trade-offs I'd call out: SMS characters vs sparsity and privacy.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not base64? → + and / are awkward in URLs; base62 is URL-safe. 2. Case-insensitive codes? → Base36 needs more characters.

Red flags: Picking a length without arithmetic.

Q4 [B1] How do you estimate the load for a shortener?

30-second answer: Creates per day from the business (2M transactional links/day ≈ 23/s, plus bulk campaigns up to ~5,600/s), clicks per link (~3) for average redirects, and the campaign spike for peak (20M SMS × 12% click-through, decaying over ~10 minutes ≈ 30k/s on one code). Storage = live rows × row size, bounded by expiry: ~780M rows × ~300 B ≈ 230 GB.

Deep answer: The conclusion drives the design: reads are spiky and concentrated, storage is modest, bulk creation needs a batch API (§2.3).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Designing for average vs peak; peaks dominate here.

Follow-ups: 1. What if links never expired? → Storage grows ~1 TB/year; partition and archive. 2. What dominates cost? → The redirect fleet and analytics.

Red flags: Using averages only.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ Compare ways to generate short codes.

30-second answer: Hash-and-truncate needs no coordination but collides (birthday bound) and still needs check-and-retry. Random codes are unguessable but need a uniqueness check per insert. A counter is unique and short with no lookup but is enumerable. A counter through a keyed permutation keeps the counter's uniqueness and no-lookup property while hiding the order.

Deep answer: L1 over 2M codes: hash-truncate 40 collisions (35 predicted); random 0 retries but 2M lookups; counter 100% neighbour hits; permutation 0 collisions, 0 lookups, 0.00% neighbour hits.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Coordination (counter blocks) vs per-insert checks vs privacy.

Follow-ups: 1. How do nodes get counter values? → Reserve blocks from a sequence or a coordination service. 2. What if a node crashes mid-block? → Unused values are lost — harmless.

Red flags: "MD5 the URL and take 6 characters" with no collision plan.

Q6 [B2] How do you make link creation idempotent?

30-second answer: Either an Idempotency-Key header stored with the result, or a natural key: a unique constraint on (owner, hash(url)). Insert with on conflict do nothing; if nothing was inserted, read and return the existing code with 200. Retries then never mint a second link.

Deep answer: L2: the notification service's retry returned the same code jFF7XOx with existing: true. Note that a counter value was still consumed — harmless.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Natural key dedupes legitimately repeated creates too — usually desired per owner.

Follow-ups: 1. Different TTL on retry? → Treat as the same link; or include TTL in the key if semantics differ. 2. Across owners? → Different links.

Red flags: Checking existence with a SELECT then INSERT without a unique constraint (race).

Q7 [B2] How do you stop the shortener being used for phishing?

30-second answer: No public creation; authenticated services with quotas; destinations restricted to allow-listed hosts, validated by parsing the URL (https only, no user-info, exact host match), not string matching; safe-browsing scans for partner links; an abuse report endpoint and a kill switch that revokes a code and invalidates caches.

Deep answer: L2 rejected http://, https://grocery.in@evil.example/login (really evil.example) and grocery-in.example. DLT rules for SMS in India also require whitelisted URLs.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Flexibility for marketing vs safety; manage the allow-list as code with review.

Follow-ups: 1. Redirect chains? → Don't allow destinations that are themselves shorteners. 2. How fast can you revoke? → Cache TTLs plus invalidation events bound it to seconds.

Red flags: url.contains("grocery.in").

Q8 [B2] ⭐ How would you cache redirects?

30-second answer: Three tiers: a short-TTL in-process near-cache on each redirect node, a distributed cache (Redis) for the working set, and the database for cold misses — with per-key miss coalescing and brief negative caching of unknown codes. Popularity is skewed, so a small cache captures most traffic; the tail always reaches the database.

Deep answer: L3: 1% of links as cache served 58.5% of clicks, 10% only 77.7%. L2 saw 716 duplicate DB reads from concurrent misses on the same cold code — coalescing fixes that.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Near-cache staleness vs hot-key protection.

Follow-ups: 1. Revocation with near-caches? → Short TTL plus invalidation events. 2. Cache warming? → Pre-warm campaign codes before sends.

Red flags: Only a Redis cache, with no plan for hot keys.

Q9 [B2] SQL or NoSQL for the links table?

30-second answer: Estimate first. With expiry the live set is ~230 GB of pure key-value lookups, which partitioned PostgreSQL with read replicas and caches serves comfortably, and it gives unique constraints for idempotency. Move to DynamoDB/Cassandra if the live set grows to many terabytes, if you need multi-region active-active writes, or if you want native per-item TTL at huge scale.

Deep answer: Partition by expiry month so expiry is dropping partitions (Ch 06).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Operational familiarity and constraints vs horizontal write scaling.

Follow-ups: 1. Shard key? → Hash of code; permuted codes are already uniform. 2. How do you delete expired links? → Drop partitions.

Red flags: "NoSQL because it's a key-value problem" with no numbers.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ A campaign sends 20M SMS with one link. What breaks and how do you design for it?

30-second answer: All clicks hit one key: one Redis shard, one DB row if you count synchronously, and possibly a shared connection pool. Sharding doesn't help because it spreads keys, not load. Defend with a near-cache on every node (at most one lookup per node per TTL), pre-warming, edge caching for campaign codes, async click counting, and a separate deployment/pool for redirects so transactional links are unaffected.

Deep answer: L3: 27,184 req/s on one shard, 49x its peers, reduced to 570 with a 1 s near-cache on 20 nodes. At ~74M SMS that shard would saturate. L4: a synchronous hot-row counter ran at ~2,300 clicks/s with a ~67 ms p99.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Near-cache staleness (1 s) vs load.

Follow-ups: 1. What if the campaign is unannounced? → Hot-key detection promotes codes to the near-cache automatically. 2. Per-recipient links instead? → Spreads load, costs 20M creates — use the bulk API.

Red flags: "Add more Redis shards."

Q11 [B3] ⭐ How do you build click analytics without slowing redirects?

30-second answer: The redirect only emits an event (buffered, async) to Kafka. A stream processor aggregates per link and time bucket into an analytics store, and raw events go to the lake. Unique visitors use HyperLogLog sketches, which merge across nodes and windows. Bots and link-preview crawlers are flagged and counted separately.

Deep answer: L4: micro-batching cut the redirect's cost to a 0.01 ms memory increment and statements 20x; HLL merged across 20 nodes was within +0.41%, while summing per-node uniques overstated by 294%.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Seconds of lag; possible loss of buffered events on a crash (acceptable for analytics, not billing).

Follow-ups: 1. Exactly-once counts? → Idempotent event ids and transactional sinks, if money depends on it. 2. Real-time dashboard? → Per-minute aggregates, clearly labelled as lagging.

Red flags: UPDATE clicks = clicks + 1 in the redirect handler.

Q12 [B3] How do you handle expiry and deletion at scale?

30-second answer: Store expires_at, return 410 after it (checked on read, so expiry is exact without a sweeper), and partition by expiry month so purging is DROP PARTITION after a retention period. Revocation sets revoked_at and publishes a cache invalidation. Never recycle codes.

Deep answer: L2 returned 410 for a link past its TTL. Mass deletes would cause vacuum and replication lag.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Keeping expired rows for a grace period (support queries, "this link expired" pages) vs storage.

Follow-ups: 1. Can users extend expiry? → Yes, if the row still exists; moves partitions. 2. Erasure requests? → Delete the link and the hashed-device click events per policy.

Red flags: A nightly DELETE WHERE expires_at < now() over billions of rows.

Q13 [B3] How do you prevent enumeration of short links?

30-second answer: Non-sequential codes (random, or a keyed permutation of a counter), a sparse code space, rate limits and alerts on 404s per client, negative caching so probes don't reach the database, and — most important — nothing sensitive reachable by the code alone: the page behind it requires a signed token or login.

Deep answer: L1: counter codes had 100% neighbour hits, permuted codes 0.00%. With ~780M live codes in 3.5T, a random guess hits ~0.02% of the time — which is why rate limits still matter.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Longer codes vs SMS length.

Follow-ups: 1. Is the permutation secret important? → Yes; with the keys, codes can be inverted to counters. 2. What about custom aliases? → Public by nature; never for personal links.

Red flags: "Nobody will guess them."

Q14 [B3] How do you support a bulk campaign of 20M personalised links?

30-second answer: A batch API that accepts large files or streams, returns a job id, and writes results asynchronously. Pre-reserve large counter blocks, mint codes in memory, and insert with batched statements or COPY into the right expiry partition. Warm caches only for the likely-hot subset. Throttle so transactional creates keep their SLO.

Deep answer: At ~5,600 inserts/s for an hour, PostgreSQL batching is comfortable; L2 inserted 10,000 in one batch.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Personalised attribution vs 20M rows and a larger cache footprint.

Follow-ups: 1. Alternative? → One campaign link plus a signed recipient parameter. 2. Partial failures? → Idempotent per-item keys; resumable jobs.

Red flags: 20M synchronous single-row API calls.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design the short-link service for a national-scale grocery platform, end to end.

30-second answer: Internal-only creation with allow-listed destinations and idempotent create; 7-char codes from counter blocks through a keyed permutation; 302 redirects; a separate redirect deployment with near-cache, Redis and replicas; PostgreSQL partitioned by expiry; click events to Kafka, stream-aggregated with HLL uniques; hot-key detection, pre-warming and edge caching for campaigns; abuse kill switch; SLOs per region.

Deep answer: §4 and the labs: L1 for codes, L2 for the write/read contract, L3 for capacity and hot keys, L4 for analytics.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Postgres vs KV store trigger; 302 cost; count lag.

Follow-ups: 1. Multi-region? → Replicated reads everywhere, single write region, block allocation survives failover. 2. Biggest risk? → Abuse of the trusted domain.

Red flags: A design without abuse, privacy or campaign considerations.

Q16 [B4] How do you make redirects survive a database or region outage?

30-second answer: Redirects are read-only and cacheable: serve from near-cache and Redis for the working set, from local replicas for misses, and fail creation fast while the primary is down. Replicate to a second region with its own caches; route users by DNS or anycast. Tolerate stale reads except read-your-writes for a creator's first click.

Deep answer: Degraded mode keeps the vast majority of clicks working because the head of the popularity curve is cached (L3).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Long cache TTLs improve survival but slow revocation.

Follow-ups: 1. Fresh links during failover? → May 404 until replicated; creation retries. 2. How do you test it? → Game days that kill the primary (Ch 27).

Red flags: No distinction between the read and write availability requirements.

Q17 [B4] Build vs buy: would you use a SaaS shortener?

30-second answer: For marketing-only links a SaaS (Bitly-style) can be fine. For transactional links carrying order tracking, you want a first-party domain, control over destinations and data (DLT whitelisting, privacy, residency), latency and availability you control, and no per-click fees at millions of clicks per day. Many companies run both: first-party for transactional, SaaS for some marketing.

Deep answer: The core is small; the value is in integration (notifications, analytics, abuse) — a strong case for building it on the paved road (Ch 37).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Build and run cost vs control and compliance.

Follow-ups: 1. What would change your mind? → No platform team; low volume. 2. Data residency? → A SaaS may store click data abroad (Ch 36).

Red flags: Ignoring compliance for SMS links.

Q18 [B4] How would you evolve the code scheme without breaking existing links?

30-second answer: Codes are forever: existing codes stay resolvable by lookup regardless of how they were minted. A new scheme (longer codes, new permutation keys, a prefix for a new namespace) applies only to new codes. Keep the namespaces disjoint (e.g., by length or a leading character) so new codes never collide with old ones.

Deep answer: Because the permutation is used only at mint time, rotating keys changes future codes but must guarantee disjointness — for example by using a fresh counter range per key version.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Simplicity vs future flexibility; reserve a version bit early.

Follow-ups: 1. Moving from 7 to 8 characters? → Disjoint by length; nothing to migrate. 2. Migrating from sequential v1 codes? → Keep them resolvable; expire them naturally.

Red flags: Re-minting codes for existing links.

Q19 [B4] What are the privacy obligations for click analytics?

30-second answer: Click events contain personal data (IP, device id, possibly linked to a customer via the personalised link). Minimise: coarse region, salted hashed device ids, no raw IPs beyond short security retention; state the purpose; set retention (raw 90 days, aggregates longer); support erasure; keep data in-region; and never put personal identifiers in URLs.

Deep answer: HLL sketches store no identifiers — a privacy win as well as a size win (Ch 36).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Attribution precision vs minimisation.

Follow-ups: 1. Per-recipient links? → Personal data by design; treat accordingly. 2. Third-party pixels on landing pages? → Consent required.

Red flags: Logging full URLs with phone numbers in query strings.

Q20 [B4] What would you monitor to know the service is healthy, and what would page you?

30-second answer: Page on redirect SLO burn (availability and p99 per region), a sudden rise in 5xx or 404s, cache hit ratio collapse, and hot-key saturation. Ticket-level alerts on creation errors, analytics lag, validation rejection spikes and abuse reports. Dashboards for top codes, per-client 404 rates and campaign traffic.

Deep answer: Hot-key detection (count-min sketch of codes) both alerts and promotes codes into the near-cache (Ch 24).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Paging on symptoms (SLO burn) rather than causes.

Follow-ups: 1. What's your SLI? → Fraction of redirects returning 3xx/410/404 correctly within 20 ms. 2. Campaign readiness? → Pre-send checklist: pre-warm, capacity, allow-list.

Red flags: Only CPU and memory alerts.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Estimate first: reads dominate and spike; expiry bounds storage (~230 GB live) (§2.3).
  2. Code generation is a trade-off: hashes collide, random codes need lookups, counters leak order; counter blocks + keyed permutation get the best of each (L1).
  3. Creation is idempotent and validated: natural-key upserts; parse URLs, allow-list hosts (L2).
  4. 302 by default: every click reaches you, so the read path must be cheap (§2.7).
  5. Cache the head, size the DB for the tail; coalesce misses (L2, L3).
  6. Hot keys defeat sharding: near-cache, pre-warm, edge, bulkheads (L3).
  7. Analytics off the redirect path; HLL for uniques (L4).
  8. Abuse and privacy are requirements, not afterthoughts (§2.11).

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: Question Default answer Code length 7 base62 (3.5T) Code scheme Counter blocks + keyed permutation; random + unique index is also fine Redirect status 302/307, no-store; 410 for expired Store Partitioned PostgreSQL + replicas; KV store past a stated trigger Cache Near-cache (seconds) + Redis + miss coalescing + negative caching Campaigns Pre-warm, near-cache, edge, separate pool Analytics Kafka → stream aggregation → OLAP; HLL uniques; bots flagged Abuse Internal creation only, allow-list, kill switch, 404 rate limits

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (B2) In L1, change the code length for strategy A to 7 characters and re-run. How many collisions now? At what number of codes would you expect the first collision?
  2. (B2) Add custom aliases to L2 with a reserved-word list and a 409 on conflict.
  3. (B3) Add per-key miss coalescing (a ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<Link>>) to L2 and show database reads fall to the number of distinct links.
  4. (B3) In L3, change the Zipf exponent to 0.8 and 1.2. How does the cache size needed for 80% hit ratio change?
  5. (B4) Extend L4 with per-hour HLL sketches and compute daily uniques by merging 24 of them; compare with an exact count.

docs.title: 39. Case Study: Distributed Rate Limiter
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B2 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 08, Ch 18 (rate-limiting algorithms), Ch 23 · What you will build: The grocery platform's rate-limiting service. It sets per-customer limits at the gateway, enforces partner API contracts, protects OTP against SMS-pumping fraud, and paces calls to outbound vendors. Ch 18 compared the algorithms on one client. This chapter designs the system: millions of keys, many gateway nodes, two regions, adversaries, and the limiter's own failures.

  • L1: state per key (real Redis). An exact sliding-window log for 100,000 users took 987 bytes per key, ~9.9 GB at 10M keys. GCRA took 90 bytes, one integer, and made exactly the token bucket's decisions (0 of 2.2M differ). On bursty traffic the sliding-window counter disagreed with the exact log on 4.3% of decisions and let a key reach 108 requests in a true 60-second window against a limit of 60.
  • L2: one global limit from 8 nodes (real Redis Lua). A partner with a 1,000 req/s contract sent 900 req/s, skewed onto one node. Local per-node limits rejected 4,093 in-contract requests. A central GCRA rejected 0, at 1 Redis call per request. Adaptive token leasing rejected 0 with 0.17 calls per request, and still held the cap at 2,000 req/s offered.
  • L3: OTP SMS pumping. Per-IP limits sent 47,175 attack SMS and locked out 57.5% of real users, who share carrier CGNAT addresses. Per-phone limits blocked no real users but let 59,199 attack SMS through. Per-destination-range budgets plus attestation cut the attack to 79 SMS (₹356 instead of ₹266,396), with 3 real users affected.
  • L4: regions and failures. A static 500/500 split between regions refused 99,370 in-contract requests when the partner's traffic moved. Rebalancing every 10 s refused 914. A central limiter admitted 1,468/s against a 1,000 contract during a partition. With the limiter's Redis down for 2 minutes, failing open sent 2,059 attack SMS (₹9,265), failing closed refused 3,955 real logins, and a local fallback allowed 30 attack SMS and refused 16 real logins.

· Reading time: 100 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: the limiter that locked out Jio
docs.text:
The grocery platform had rate limiting from day one: a Redis token bucket at the gateway (Ch 08), keyed by IP address, 10 OTP requests per hour. Then, in one month:

  1. Real customers were locked out. On a Sunday morning, thousands of customers on one mobile carrier couldn't log in. Carrier-grade NAT puts thousands of phones behind one public IP, and the per-IP OTP limit treated them as one abusive client.
  2. An SMS-pumping attack cost ₹18 lakh in a weekend. Fraudsters triggered OTPs to international number ranges where they shared the termination fees. They used thousands of residential-proxy IPs and never sent more than two OTPs to any number. No per-IP or per-phone limit fired.
  3. A logistics partner was throttled inside its contract. Its 1,000 req/s limit was enforced as 125 req/s on each of 8 gateway nodes, and the partner's traffic arrived mostly on one node. The partner escalated; the account manager doubled the limit to make the complaints stop.
  4. The limiter took down login. Redis for rate limits had a failover. The gateway was configured to fail closed, so for 90 seconds nobody could request an OTP.
  5. The SMS vendor throttled us. The vendor's contract was 500 SMS/s. During a campaign, notification workers across three services collectively sent 1,200/s, and the vendor dropped messages — including OTPs.

Each of these is a system design failure of the limiter, not an algorithm choice. The rebuilt limiter, designed here, starts from what each limit protects, who it limits, where it's enforced, and what happens when it breaks.

The thesis of this chapter

A rate limiter is several different controls sharing one mechanism: abuse prevention (fraud, scraping, credential stuffing), fairness (one customer can't starve others), contracts (partner quotas), and protection of our capacity and of vendors'. Each needs the right key (L3), the right accuracy and state size (L1), the right enforcement topology for many nodes and regions (L2, L4), and an explicit failure mode (L4). The algorithm — token bucket, GCRA, sliding window — is the easy part.

docs.title: 1.2 Where this lives in the grocery platform
docs.text: Limit Protects Key Typical rule On limiter failure Customer API Fairness, capacity User id (fallback: device, IP) 20 req/s, burst 40 Fail open, local fallback Search/catalog scraping Data, capacity Device + IP + ASN Adaptive Fail open OTP send Fraud (SMS cost), abuse Phone, destination range, device, IP (loose) 3/10 min per phone; range budgets Local fallback, never fully open Login verify Credential stuffing Phone + device; global failure ratio 5 failed / 15 min Fail closed per phone Partner API Contract API key 1,000 req/s global Fail open (paid customer) Vendor egress (SMS, Razorpay, ERP) Vendor contract Vendor account 500 SMS/s Queue and shape (leaky bucket)

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end you will be able to:

  • Specify limits by what they protect, choosing keys that attackers can't cheaply rotate and customers don't share (L3).
  • Choose the state representation for millions of keys: GCRA, token bucket, sliding counter or log (L1).
  • Enforce a global limit across many nodes: central store, local splits, or token leasing (L2).
  • Span regions and decide failure behaviour per limit (L4).
  • Design the limiter service: rule configuration, headers, observability, and the tiers where limits apply.

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: turnstiles with different jobs B2
docs.text: A stadium has turnstiles at each gate (per-node limits), a total capacity (a global limit), a rule of four tickets per buyer (per-customer quota), and guards watching for touts buying hundreds of tickets through many friends (abuse detection). They all "limit rate", but they answer different questions and fail differently. A turnstile jam at one gate shouldn't close the stadium; a broken ticket scanner shouldn't let the touts in free.

docs.title: 2.2 Requirements B2
docs.text:
Functional

  • Evaluate a request against one or more rules (key, algorithm, rate, burst, window) and return allow/deny plus remaining quota and retry-after.
  • Rules configured per route, per client class, per partner, without redeploying.
  • Support rate limits (per second/minute), quotas (per day/month) and budgets (per destination range per hour).
  • Shadow mode: evaluate new rules and log what they would do, without enforcing.

Non-functional

  • Latency: under 1 ms p99 added at the gateway, and never a network round-trip per request on hot paths if avoidable (L2).
  • Scale: 150k req/s at the gateway at sale peaks; 10M+ active keys.
  • Accuracy: contracts within a few percent; fraud budgets as hard caps.
  • Availability: the limiter must never be the reason the platform is down; failure behaviour is explicit per rule (L4).
  • Multi-region: two regions, active-active.

docs.title: 2.3 Estimation B2
docs.text:
Quantity Estimate Gateway requests at peak 150k req/s; 1–3 rules evaluated each → up to ~450k rule checks/s Active keys ~5M customers/day + devices + IPs + partners + phones ≈ 10M keys State with GCRA 10M × ~90 B ≈ 0.9 GB (L1) — a small Redis cluster State with exact logs 10M × ~1 KB ≈ ~10 GB, and write amplification per request Central store load 450k Lua calls/s — several Redis shards, ~20–40 µs each on localhost (L2), 0.5–1 ms across AZs OTP sends ~120k/hour normal; attack traffic of the same order (L3)

The estimates point at the design. GCRA state is small, so storage is not the problem. One store call per rule per request is expensive at 450k/s and across AZs, so hot-path limits should be local or leased (L2), and exact central checks reserved for low-volume, high-value rules like OTP.

docs.title: 2.4 Choosing the key: who are you actually limiting? ⭐ B3
docs.text:
The key decides who shares a bucket. L3 shows how badly the obvious key can fail:

Policy Attack SMS Attack cost Real users blocked Per IP, 10/hour 47,175 ₹212,288 57.5% Per phone, 3/10 min and 5/hour 59,199 ₹266,396 0% Per phone + per IP 60/hour + per device 5/hour 59,199 ₹266,396 48.1% Per phone + per destination-range budget + attestation → challenge 79 ₹356 3 users
  • IP addresses are shared and cheap. Carrier CGNAT puts hundreds or thousands of real customers behind one IPv4 address. Residential-proxy networks give attackers thousands of addresses. Per-IP limits hurt customers more than attackers. Use them loosely, and per ASN or subnet for clearly abusive networks.
  • Device fingerprints are cheap to rotate unless backed by attestation (Play Integrity, App Attest).
  • Phone numbers are the right key against repeated OTPs to one number, but a pump spreads across thousands of numbers.
  • Key on what the attacker must concentrate. An SMS pump earns only from certain destination ranges. Budget those ranges, with limits learned from normal traffic, and the attack has nowhere to hide. Expect the attacker to adapt: add a per-country and a global international budget, and alert on anomalies.
  • Spend friction on risk. Attestation failures and unusual ranges get a challenge, not a block, so the few real users there still get through.

For authenticated APIs, the user id is the natural key: stable, not shared, and costly to multiply. Limit anonymous endpoints (OTP, search, catalog) with layered keys, and treat the limit as a fraud control with costs on both sides.

docs.title: 2.5 State: GCRA, token bucket, windows ⭐ B3
docs.text:
With millions of keys, per-key state size and write cost matter as much as behaviour. L1 measured real Redis memory:

Representation Bytes per key 10M keys Sliding-window log (sorted set, 30 timestamps) 987 9.87 GB Sliding-window counter (two counters) 149 1.49 GB Token bucket (hash of tokens + timestamp) 123 1.23 GB GCRA (one "theoretical arrival time") 90 0.90 GB

GCRA (Generic Cell Rate Algorithm, from ATM networks) stores one number per key: the theoretical arrival time (TAT) of the next request if the client sent at exactly the allowed rate. With emission interval T = 1/rate and burst tolerance τ:

new_tat = max(tat, now) + T
if new_tat - now > τ + T  → deny   (retry after new_tat - T - τ - now)
else                       → allow, tat = new_tat

It is mathematically a token bucket (L1: 0 of 2.2M decisions differ), with one integer of state and a natural retry-after. It is what redis-cell and several gateways implement.

Sliding-window counters are approximate. The weighted two-window estimate assumes the previous window's requests were evenly spread. Ch 18's single-burst test hid the error; L1's bursty traffic exposed it: 4.3% of decisions differed from the exact log (73,704 extra allows, 22,468 extra denials), and a key reached 108 in a true 60-second span against a limit of 60. That's better than the fixed window's 120, but not a hard cap. Use them where "roughly N per window" is enough.

Exact logs are the only hard "at most N in any window". Use them where that matters and volume is low — OTP sends per phone — with short TTLs.

docs.title: 2.6 Enforcing a global limit across many nodes ⭐ B3
docs.text:
L2 enforced one partner's 1,000 req/s contract from 8 gateway nodes, with the partner sending 900 req/s skewed 60% onto node 0:

Strategy In-contract requests rejected Redis calls per request Over the limit (2,000 req/s offered) Local only (limit ÷ 8 per node) 4,093 0 Capped only because load was even Central GCRA in Redis 0 1.00 Capped at ~1,010/s Token leasing (adaptive) 0 0.17 Capped; 0.39 calls/request
  • Local splits are free but wrong whenever load is uneven — sticky connections, one partner data centre, uneven load-balancing — and nodes come and go with autoscaling, changing N.
  • Central checks are exact and simple (one atomic Lua script — Ch 18 L3), but add a network round-trip and a store call to every request: fine for thousands of req/s, costly at 450k rule checks/s across AZs.
  • Token leasing: a node takes a small batch of tokens from the central GCRA and spends them locally. L2 needed three refinements before leasing matched the central limiter: size leases to each node's recent rate (~50 ms of its traffic), give unused tokens back when a lease expires, and cache denials until tokens are due. Fixed large leases stranded tokens on quiet nodes and rejected in-contract traffic. Over the limit, leases shrink because tokens are scarce, so the call rate rises (0.39 per request).
  • Other options: approximate local limits with periodic count synchronisation (gossip), or a sticky routing of each key to one limiter node (consistent hashing), which moves the hot-key problem to that node.

A practical tiering: local limiters for coarse protection (per-node concurrency, load shedding — Ch 18), leased or central GCRA for customer and partner limits, and central exact checks for low-volume fraud controls.

docs.title: 2.7 Multi-region limits B4
docs.text:
A global contract served from two regions needs either a global store or a split. L4:

Design In-contract requests rejected Max admitted in 1 s (contract 1,000) Cross-region calls Static split 500/500 99,370 944 0 Static split from history 800/200 167,179 945 0 Rebalance every 10 s by demand 914 1,000 0 Central limiter in one region 0 1,468 during a partition (fail open) 308,377

Traffic between regions moves — failovers, DNS changes, a partner's own routing — so a static split refuses in-contract traffic exactly when it moves. Rebalancing shares by recent demand keeps both properties, with only periodic, asynchronous exchange of counts between regions. A single central limiter is exact until the regions partition, and then it must either over-admit or fail. Most platforms accept approximate global limits (a few percent) for contracts, and keep hard fraud budgets per region with conservative shares.

docs.title: 2.8 When the limiter fails ⭐ B4
docs.text:
The limiter's store will fail. Decide the behaviour per rule, in advance. L4 took the OTP limiter's Redis down for 2 minutes during an attack:

Behaviour Attack SMS in 2 min Real OTPs refused Fail open 2,059 (₹9,265) 0 Fail closed 0 3,955 — nobody can log in Local fallback (1/8 of each budget per node, 3x headroom) 30 (₹135) 16
  • Fail open where the limit protects fairness or capacity and other layers (load shedding) still protect the system: customer API limits, partner quotas.
  • Fail closed only where the downside of allowing is worse than an outage, and scope it narrowly (per phone after failed logins, not "all OTPs").
  • Local fallback for fraud controls: each node enforces a conservative share of the budget from its last known configuration. The 16 refused logins in L4 come from an assumed 0.4% of retries landing on a node whose local per-phone limit is stricter — an assumption to measure.
  • Protect the limiter: timeouts of a few milliseconds on limiter calls, a circuit breaker around the store, and an alert on fallback mode.

docs.title: 2.9 Responding: headers, retry-after and clients B2
docs.text:
• 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After, and the RateLimit-Policy / RateLimit headers (IETF draft — VERIFY the current field names) so clients can pace themselves.
  • Don't reveal fraud-control internals: an OTP budget denial can look like "Please try again later" with a challenge, not "range budget exceeded".
  • Clients back off with jitter (Ch 18); partners get documented limits and a dashboard of their usage.
  • Shape instead of reject for outbound vendor limits: queue SMS and pace them at the vendor's TPS with a leaky bucket, prioritising OTPs over marketing (Ch 40).

docs.title: 2.10 Rules, configuration and rollout B3
docs.text:
• Rules as data: {match: route/client class, key: [phone], algorithm: gcra, rate: 3/600s, burst: 3, onFailure: localFallback, mode: enforce|shadow}.
  • Stored in a config service, versioned, reviewed; pushed to gateways and cached locally, so a config store outage doesn't stop limiting.
  • Shadow mode first: log would-be denials for a week, check false positives against known-good traffic, then enforce.
  • Budgets learned from baselines (L3's range budgets ≈ 3x normal hourly volume), recomputed daily, with manual overrides for campaigns.
  • Per-tenant/plan limits for B2B (Ch 30).

docs.title: 2.11 Where limits live B3
docs.text: Tier Limits Why there Edge/CDN/WAF Volumetric per IP/ASN, bot scores Cheapest place to drop floods API gateway Per user, per API key, per route class Knows identity, before work starts Service Business rules (OTP per phone, orders per minute per B2B account), concurrency limits Knows domain context Egress Vendor TPS Protects vendor contracts Data tier Connection pools, statement timeouts Last line of defence

docs.title: 2.12 Interview framing B4
docs.text: Spend five minutes on what the limits protect and who they key on. Most candidates jump to "Redis token bucket", so that alone is a strong signal. Then cover the algorithm and state size (GCRA), the distributed enforcement options with their trade-offs (central, local, leasing), multi-region, and failure modes per rule. Staff-level signals: CGNAT and residential proxies, SMS pumping, shadow mode, and fail-open vs fail-closed as a per-rule decision.

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Platform Rate-Limiting Service
docs.text:
Design Document (excerpt) — Rate Limiting v2

Status: Accepted · Authors: Edge platform team · Reviewers: Security/fraud, SRE, Partner engineering

Field Value Context v1 limited OTPs per IP (locked out CGNAT customers), missed an SMS-pumping attack, enforced partner contracts as per-node splits, failed closed on a Redis failover, and didn't pace vendor egress. Decision Rules as versioned data with shadow mode; GCRA state in regional Redis; leased tokens for high-volume limits, exact central checks for fraud controls; destination-range budgets and attestation for OTP; demand-based cross-region rebalancing for contracts; per-rule failure mode with local fallback; egress shaping for vendors. Related ADRs ADR-250 GCRA as the default algorithm, exact log only for OTP-per-phone (L1); ADR-251 Adaptive token leasing at the gateway (L2); ADR-252 OTP keys: phone + destination-range budgets + attestation/challenge; IP limits loose and ASN-based (L3); ADR-253 Cross-region share rebalancing every 10 s (L4); ADR-254 Failure mode declared per rule; local fallback for fraud budgets (L4); ADR-255 Shadow mode mandatory before enforcement; ADR-256 Vendor egress via leaky-bucket shaper with OTP priority

Requirements.

  • R1 Added latency under 1 ms p99 at the gateway at 150k req/s.
  • R2 Partner contracts enforced within 2% globally; no in-contract rejections when traffic moves between regions.
  • R3 SMS-pumping cost under ₹5,000/day at attack volumes seen so far; real-user OTP denial under 0.05%.
  • R4 No platform outage caused by the limiter's store; failure mode per rule.
  • R5 Vendor TPS never exceeded.

Decisions in detail.

  1. State (ADR-250). GCRA with TAT in microseconds, PX expiry of burst + 1 s; OTP-per-phone as a sorted set with 1 h TTL.
  2. Enforcement (ADR-251). Leases of ~50 ms of each node's rate (1–50 tokens), 100 ms expiry, give-back on expiry, denial caching.
  3. OTP (ADR-252). Range budgets = 3x the 28-day hourly baseline per range, a per-country and a global international budget; attestation failure → challenge.
  4. Regions (ADR-253). Each region publishes per-key demand every 10 s; shares recomputed proportionally.
  5. Failure (ADR-254). Limiter calls time out at 5 ms; breaker; fallback shares = budget ÷ nodes × 3; alert.
  6. Rollout (ADR-255). Every new rule spends ≥7 days in shadow with a false-positive review.

Consequences. More moving parts than a single Redis token bucket: rule configuration, leasing logic and fallback shares to test. Contracts are approximate by a few percent. Fraud budgets need tuning and on-call attention during campaigns. In return: no locked-out carriers, attack cost bounded, partners served within contract, and a limiter that can't take the platform down.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
What's real here

All four labs are JDK 21. L1 and L2 run against a real Redis 7: L1 measures memory with INFO, and L2 executes the GCRA and lease scripts in Lua with a simulated clock passed in, so the decisions are reproducible. L3 and L4 are deterministic simulations with a fixed seed. Traffic mixes, attack parameters, SMS prices, attestation pass rates and the L4 fallback's 0.4% refusal rate are stated assumptions.

L1 and L2 need a Redis 7 on port 6390: redis-server --port 6390 --save '' --appendonly no. Run every lab with -Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8.

docs.title: L1 — State per key, and how accurate it is B2
docs.text:
Requirement: "We'll hold limiter state for 10 million keys. Which representation, how much memory, and how wrong is each?"

Part 1 writes 100,000 keys of each representation into a real Redis (pipelined) and measures used_memory. Part 2 replays 2.2 million bursty decisions through the exact log, the sliding counter, the fixed window, a token bucket and GCRA, all in exact integer arithmetic.

LimiterStateL1.java
// LimiterStateL1.java — run with (Redis 7 on :6390):  java LimiterStateL1.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// WHAT A RATE LIMITER COSTS PER KEY, AND HOW ACCURATE IT IS. Ch 18 compared algorithms on one client. A platform limiter
// holds state for MILLIONS of keys (every user, device, IP, phone number, API key), so state size and accuracy per key
// decide the design. Part 1 stores 100,000 keys of each representation in a REAL Redis (pipelined) and measures memory
// with INFO: a sliding-window LOG (sorted set of timestamps), a sliding-window COUNTER (two fixed-window counters),
// a TOKEN BUCKET (hash of tokens + timestamp) and GCRA (one "theoretical arrival time" per key). Each key models a user
// halfway through a 60-requests-per-minute limit (30 requests in the window).
// Part 2 replays bursty traffic for 20,000 keys through exact and approximate algorithms in memory and measures how often
// the approximations decide differently, and the worst overshoot in any true 60-second window.
import java.io.*;
import java.net.Socket;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.*;

public class LimiterStateL1 {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int keys = 100_000;
        System.out.printf("Part 1 — %,d keys per representation in real Redis (limit 60/min, 30 requests in the current window)%n%n", keys);
        System.out.printf("   %-40s %14s %18s%n", "representation", "bytes per key", "10M keys would need");
        try (Redis r = new Redis("127.0.0.1", 6390)) {
            long now = 1_790_000_000_000L; Random rnd = new Random(39);
            String[] names = {"sliding log (ZSET of 30 timestamps)", "sliding counter (2 window counters)", "token bucket (HASH tokens + ts)", "GCRA (one TAT integer)"};
            for (int kind = 0; kind < 4; kind++) {
                r.cmd("FLUSHALL"); long before = usedMemory(r);
                List<String[]> batch = new ArrayList<>();
                for (int k = 0; k < keys; k++) {
                    String key = "rl:" + kind + ":user:" + (9_000_000 + k);
                    switch (kind) {
                        case 0 -> { String[] c = new String[2 + 60]; c[0] = "ZADD"; c[1] = key;
                                    for (int i = 0; i < 30; i++) { long ts = now - rnd.nextInt(60_000); c[2 + 2 * i] = Long.toString(ts); c[3 + 2 * i] = ts + "-" + i; }
                                    batch.add(c); }
                        case 1 -> { long w = now / 60_000; batch.add(new String[]{"SET", key + ":" + w, "18"}); batch.add(new String[]{"SET", key + ":" + (w - 1), "41"}); }
                        case 2 -> batch.add(new String[]{"HSET", key, "t", "30.000", "ts", Long.toString(now)});
                        default -> batch.add(new String[]{"SET", key, Long.toString(now + 30_000)});
                    }
                    if (batch.size() >= 1000) { r.pipeline(batch); batch.clear(); }
                }
                r.pipeline(batch);
                long bytes = usedMemory(r) - before; double perKey = (double) bytes / keys;
                System.out.printf("   %-40s %,14.0f %15.2f GB%n", names[kind], perKey, perKey * 10_000_000 / 1e9);
            }
            r.cmd("FLUSHALL");
        }

        // ---------------- Part 2: accuracy ----------------
        int nKeys = 20_000, limit = 60; long windowMs = 60_000, horizon = 10 * 60_000; Random rnd = new Random(7);
        long decisions = 0, cntFalseAllow = 0, cntFalseDeny = 0, diffCounter = 0, diffGcra = 0, worstLog = 0, worstCounter = 0, worstFixed = 0, diffFixed = 0, worstG = 0;
        for (int k = 0; k < nKeys; k++) {
            // a user: quiet background plus 0–3 bursts (app retries, pull-to-refresh storms, scripts)
            List<Long> t = new ArrayList<>();
            double rate = 0.2 + rnd.nextDouble() * 0.8;                                   // requests per second baseline... per 10 s
            for (long ms = 0; ms < horizon; ms += (long) (-Math.log(1 - rnd.nextDouble()) * 10_000 / rate)) t.add(ms);
            int bursts = rnd.nextInt(4);
            for (int b = 0; b < bursts; b++) { long at = (long) (rnd.nextDouble() * horizon); int n = 20 + rnd.nextInt(60); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) t.add(at + i * (50 + rnd.nextInt(400))); }
            Collections.sort(t);
            Deque<Long> log = new ArrayDeque<>(); long curW = -1, cur = 0, prev = 0; long fW = -1, fCount = 0;
            long emission = windowMs / limit;                                             // 1,000 ms per request
            long tat = 0;                                                                 // GCRA state: one integer
            long milliTokens = limit * 1000L, lastTs = 0;                                 // token bucket in exact integer milli-tokens
            List<Long> allowedLog = new ArrayList<>(), allowedCounter = new ArrayList<>(), allowedFixed = new ArrayList<>(), allowedG = new ArrayList<>();
            for (long ts : t) {
                if (ts >= horizon) continue; decisions++;
                // exact sliding log
                while (!log.isEmpty() && log.peekFirst() <= ts - windowMs) log.pollFirst();
                boolean aLog = log.size() < limit; if (aLog) { log.addLast(ts); allowedLog.add(ts); }
                // sliding window counter (Cloudflare-style weighted previous window)
                long w = ts / windowMs; if (w != curW) { prev = (w == curW + 1) ? cur : 0; cur = 0; curW = w; }
                double est = prev * (1 - (double) (ts % windowMs) / windowMs) + cur;
                boolean aCnt = est < limit; if (aCnt) { cur++; allowedCounter.add(ts); }
                // fixed window
                long fw = ts / windowMs; if (fw != fW) { fW = fw; fCount = 0; }
                boolean aFix = fCount < limit; if (aFix) { fCount++; allowedFixed.add(ts); }
                // token bucket and GCRA (same parameters: 1 per second, burst 60) — should agree exactly
                milliTokens = Math.min(limit * 1000L, milliTokens + (ts - lastTs) * 1000 / emission); lastTs = ts;
                boolean aTb = milliTokens >= 1000; if (aTb) milliTokens -= 1000;
                long newTat = Math.max(tat, ts) + emission; boolean aG = newTat - ts <= windowMs; if (aG) { tat = newTat; allowedG.add(ts); }
                if (aCnt && !aLog) cntFalseAllow++; if (!aCnt && aLog) cntFalseDeny++;
                if (aCnt != aLog) diffCounter++; if (aFix != aLog) diffFixed++; if (aG != aTb) diffGcra++;
            }
            worstLog = Math.max(worstLog, maxInWindow(allowedLog, windowMs));
            worstCounter = Math.max(worstCounter, maxInWindow(allowedCounter, windowMs));
            worstFixed = Math.max(worstFixed, maxInWindow(allowedFixed, windowMs));
            worstG = Math.max(worstG, maxInWindow(allowedG, windowMs));
        }
        System.out.printf("%nPart 2 — %,d decisions for %,d bursty keys over 10 minutes, limit %d per 60 s%n%n", decisions, nKeys, limit);
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %22s %28s%n", "algorithm", "decisions ≠ exact log", "max allowed in any 60 s");
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %22s %28d%n", "sliding window log (exact reference)", "—", worstLog);
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %21.3f%% %28d%n", "sliding window counter (weighted)", 100.0 * diffCounter / decisions, worstCounter);
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %21.3f%% %28d%n", "fixed window", 100.0 * diffFixed / decisions, worstFixed);
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %22s %28d%n", "GCRA / token bucket (1/s, burst 60)", "(a rate, not a window)", worstG);
        System.out.printf("   sliding counter errors: %,d extra allows, %,d extra denials (it assumes the previous window was evenly spread)%n", cntFalseAllow, cntFalseDeny);
        System.out.printf("   GCRA vs token bucket (1/s, burst 60): %,d of %,d decisions differ.%n", diffGcra, decisions);

        System.out.println("\n   → at platform scale the limiter is a memory problem first: the exact log stores every request (~1 KB per");
        System.out.println("     key here, ~10 GB for 10M keys); GCRA stores one integer and makes exactly the token bucket's decisions.");
        System.out.println("     The sliding-window counter is cheap but only approximate, and its error depends on the traffic's SHAPE:");
        System.out.println("     it assumes last window's requests were evenly spread, so a burst at the end of one window lets a key through");
        System.out.println("     well above the limit within a true 60 s span — better than the fixed window's double, but not a hard cap.");
        System.out.println("     Use GCRA/token bucket for rates, and an exact log only where 'at most N per window' must hold (OTP per phone).");
    }

    static long maxInWindow(List<Long> ts, long w) { int j = 0; long best = 0; for (int i = 0; i < ts.size(); i++) { while (ts.get(i) - ts.get(j) >= w) j++; best = Math.max(best, i - j + 1); } return best; }
    static long usedMemory(Redis r) throws IOException {
        String info = (String) r.cmd("INFO", "memory");
        for (String l : info.split("\r\n")) if (l.startsWith("used_memory:")) return Long.parseLong(l.substring(12));
        throw new IOException("no used_memory");
    }

    /** Minimal RESP client (from Ch 18) plus pipelining. */
    static final class Redis implements Closeable {
        final Socket s; final OutputStream out; final BufferedInputStream in;
        Redis(String host, int port) throws IOException { s = new Socket(host, port); out = new BufferedOutputStream(s.getOutputStream(), 1 << 16); in = new BufferedInputStream(s.getInputStream(), 1 << 16); }
        void write(String... parts) throws IOException {
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("*").append(parts.length).append("\r\n");
            for (String p : parts) { byte[] b = p.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8); sb.append('$').append(b.length).append("\r\n").append(p).append("\r\n"); }
            out.write(sb.toString().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        }
        Object cmd(String... parts) throws IOException { write(parts); out.flush(); return read(); }
        void pipeline(List<String[]> cmds) throws IOException { for (String[] c : cmds) write(c); out.flush(); for (int i = 0; i < cmds.size(); i++) read(); }
        Object read() throws IOException {
            int type = in.read(); String line = line();
            return switch (type) {
                case '+' -> line; case ':' -> Long.parseLong(line);
                case '$' -> { int n = Integer.parseInt(line); if (n < 0) yield null; byte[] b = in.readNBytes(n); line(); yield new String(b, StandardCharsets.UTF_8); }
                case '*' -> { int n = Integer.parseInt(line); List<Object> l = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) l.add(read()); yield l; }
                case '-' -> throw new IOException("redis error: " + line);
                default -> throw new IOException("unexpected reply type " + (char) type);
            };
        }
        String line() throws IOException { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); int c; while ((c = in.read()) != '\r') sb.append((char) c); in.read(); return sb.toString(); }
        public void close() throws IOException { s.close(); }
    }
}
