  • The rules are perfect here because the lab knows which patterns it injected. Real reconciliation needs review of what the rules auto-clear.

docs.title: L4 — Whose failure is it? B4
docs.text:
Requirement: "Keep payment success high through gateway incidents and bank outages, without making things worse."

Two hours of simulated UPI traffic through two gateways and 8 issuer banks, with a gateway incident and a bank outage.

RoutingL4.java
// RoutingL4.java — run with: java RoutingL4.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// WHOSE FAILURE IS IT? Payment success depends on the gateway (PSP) AND on the customer's bank. Two hours of UPI
// checkouts (~40/s, fixed seed) across two PSPs and 8 issuer banks. Normally 93% succeed (the rest are customer-side:
// wrong PIN, insufficient balance). Two incidents:
//   PSP incident     minutes 20–50: PSP-A's UPI switch degrades, 40% success for every bank through PSP-A
//   BANK incident    minutes 70–90: issuer Bank-3 (20% of customers) is down, 5% success through ANY PSP
// A customer whose payment fails retries once 60% of the time. Four routing policies:
//   S1 everything through PSP-A (the cheaper contract)
//   S2 PSP-level health: if PSP-A's success over the last 5 min falls below 80%, send ALL traffic to PSP-B
//   S3 health per (PSP, bank): move only the traffic that is failing; if a bank fails on BOTH PSPs, it's the bank —
//      don't reroute, tell the customer ("Bank-3 UPI is down — pay by card or another UPI account")
//   S4 S3 + a failed attempt is retried once on the other PSP automatically if the failure looks PSP-side
import java.util.*;

public class RoutingL4 {
    static final double[] BANK_SHARE = {0.22, 0.18, 0.20, 0.12, 0.10, 0.08, 0.06, 0.04};

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("UPI checkouts ~40/s for 2 h; PSP-A degraded minutes 20–50; Bank-3 (20% of customers) down minutes 70–90.\n");
        System.out.printf("   %-58s %9s %12s %13s %15s %13s%n", "routing policy", "overall", "during PSP", "during BANK", "routing flips", "customers");
        System.out.printf("   %-58s %9s %12s %13s %15s %13s%n", "", "success", "incident", "incident", "", "nudged");
        String[] names = {"S1) everything via PSP-A", "S2) PSP-level health, fail over all traffic", "S3) health per (PSP, bank); bank-side → nudge customer",
                "S4) S3 + auto-retry on the other PSP for PSP-side failures"};
        for (int p = 0; p < 4; p++) run(p, names[p]);
        System.out.println("\n   → a gateway-level health check can't tell a gateway problem from a bank problem: when Bank-3 went down, S2 saw");
        System.out.println("     PSP-A's success fall and moved everyone to PSP-B, which failed Bank-3 just the same — churn without benefit.");
        System.out.println("     Measuring success per (gateway, bank) shows where the failure is: move only the traffic a healthy gateway can");
        System.out.println("     carry, and when every gateway fails for one bank, no routing helps — the only rescue is steering the customer to");
        System.out.println("     another bank or method. An automatic retry on a second gateway rescues gateway-side failures within the same");
        System.out.println("     checkout, but only with an idempotent order so the customer can't be charged twice. (S3/S4 flip often because an");
        System.out.println("     avoided path gets no traffic, so its window empties and it looks healthy again — real routers keep a small");
        System.out.println("     probe share on avoided paths, as in Ch 40's vendor routing.)");
    }

    static void run(int policy, String name) {
        Random r = new Random(45); int seconds = 7200; double rate = 40;
        long ok = 0, total = 0, okPsp = 0, totPsp = 0, okBank = 0, totBank = 0, flips = 0, nudged = 0;
        // health windows: success counts per (psp, bank) and per psp over the last 300 s, bucketed per 10 s
        int buckets = 30; long[][][] att = new long[2][9][buckets], suc = new long[2][9][buckets];
        int allTo = 0; boolean[][] avoid = new boolean[2][8];
        for (int t = 0; t < seconds; t++) {
            int b = (t / 10) % buckets;
            if (t % 10 == 0) for (int ps = 0; ps < 2; ps++) for (int k = 0; k < 9; k++) { att[ps][k][b] = 0; suc[ps][k][b] = 0; }
            if (t % 30 == 0 && t > 300) {                                                    // re-evaluate routing every 30 s
                if (policy == 1) { int want = rateOf(att[0][8], suc[0][8]) < 0.80 ? 1 : 0; if (want != allTo) { flips++; allTo = want; } }
                if (policy >= 2) for (int k = 0; k < 8; k++) for (int ps = 0; ps < 2; ps++) {
                    boolean bad = rateOf(att[ps][k], suc[ps][k]) < 0.80; if (bad != avoid[ps][k]) { flips++; avoid[ps][k] = bad; } }
            }
            int n = poisson(r, rate);
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                int bank = pickBank(r); boolean inPsp = t >= 1200 && t < 3000, inBank = t >= 4200 && t < 5400;
                total++; if (inPsp) totPsp++; if (inBank) totBank++;
                int psp = policy == 0 ? 0 : policy == 1 ? allTo : (avoid[0][bank] && !avoid[1][bank] ? 1 : 0);
                boolean bankDown = policy >= 2 && avoid[0][bank] && avoid[1][bank];
                if (bankDown && r.nextDouble() < 0.6) { nudged++; ok++; if (inPsp) okPsp++; if (inBank) okBank++; continue; }   // pays by card / other account
                boolean s = attempt(r, t, psp, bank, att, suc, b);
                if (!s && policy == 3 && pspSide(t, psp)) s = attempt(r, t, 1 - psp, bank, att, suc, b);                         // automatic second gateway
                if (!s && r.nextDouble() < 0.6) s = attempt(r, t, psp, bank, att, suc, b);                                        // customer retries once
                if (s) { ok++; if (inPsp) okPsp++; if (inBank) okBank++; }
            }
        }
        System.out.printf("   %-58s %8.1f%% %11.1f%% %12.1f%% %,15d %,13d%n", name, 100.0 * ok / total, 100.0 * okPsp / totPsp, 100.0 * okBank / totBank, flips, nudged);
    }
    static boolean pspSide(int t, int psp) { return psp == 0 && t >= 1200 && t < 3000; }   // failure codes say "gateway" (PSP-side) in this window
    static boolean attempt(Random r, int t, int psp, int bank, long[][][] att, long[][][] suc, int b) {
        double p = 0.93;
        if (psp == 0 && t >= 1200 && t < 3000) p = 0.40;
        if (bank == 2 && t >= 4200 && t < 5400) p = 0.05;
        boolean s = r.nextDouble() < p;
        att[psp][bank][b]++; att[psp][8][b]++; if (s) { suc[psp][bank][b]++; suc[psp][8][b]++; }
        return s;
    }
    static double rateOf(long[] a, long[] s) { long x = 0, y = 0; for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { x += a[i]; y += s[i]; } return x < 30 ? 1 : (double) y / x; }
    static int pickBank(Random r) { double x = r.nextDouble(), c = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { c += BANK_SHARE[i]; if (x < c) return i; } return 7; }
    static int poisson(Random r, double l) { double L = Math.exp(-l), p = 1; int k = 0; do { k++; p *= r.nextDouble(); } while (p > L); return k - 1; }
}
java -Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8 RoutingL4.java
UPI checkouts ~40/s for 2 h; PSP-A degraded minutes 20–50; Bank-3 (20% of customers) down minutes 70–90.

   routing policy                                               overall   during PSP   during BANK   routing flips     customers
                                                                success     incident      incident                        nudged
   S1) everything via PSP-A                                       83.2%        54.4%         79.1%               0             0
   S2) PSP-level health, fail over all traffic                    92.4%        91.3%         78.7%              20             0
   S3) health per (PSP, bank); bank-side → nudge customer         94.2%        91.6%         88.7%             106         5,852
   S4) S3 + auto-retry on the other PSP for PSP-side failures     95.5%        96.9%         88.7%             106         5,834

   → a gateway-level health check can't tell a gateway problem from a bank problem: when Bank-3 went down, S2 saw
     PSP-A's success fall and moved everyone to PSP-B, which failed Bank-3 just the same — churn without benefit.
     Measuring success per (gateway, bank) shows where the failure is: move only the traffic a healthy gateway can
     carry, and when every gateway fails for one bank, no routing helps — the only rescue is steering the customer to
     another bank or method. An automatic retry on a second gateway rescues gateway-side failures within the same
     checkout, but only with an idempotent order so the customer can't be charged twice. (S3/S4 flip often because an
     avoided path gets no traffic, so its window empties and it looks healthy again — real routers keep a small
     probe share on avoided paths, as in Ch 40's vendor routing.)

Reading it:

  • S1 has no defence: 54% success during the gateway incident.
  • S2 handles the gateway incident (91%) but not the bank outage (78.7%). It even moved all traffic to PSP-B during the bank outage, which fails Bank-3 just the same.
  • S3 sees that Bank-3 fails on both gateways and steers those customers to another method. Success during the bank outage rises to 88.7% (5,852 customers steered).
  • S4 adds one automatic retry on the other gateway for gateway-side errors: 96.9% during the gateway incident.
  • The high flip counts show the missing probe traffic; see exercise 4.

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Symptom Mitigation Mutable balances Drift, lost updates (L1) Journal + locked balance projection Hot ledger accounts Retry storms or lock waits (L1) Sub-accounts, async aggregation for internal accounts Trusting the client Unpaid fulfilment (L2) Server-side verification only Duplicate/out-of-order webhooks Double fulfilment, paid marked failed (L2) Guarded transitions, event dedupe Lost webhooks Charged, not fulfilled (L2) Status poller, reconciliation Settlement differences Unexplained gaps (L3) Line matching with rules, three-way Bank outage misread as gateway outage Useless failover (L4) Health per (gateway, bank), customer steering Retry on another gateway after a debit Double charge Auto-retry only for pre-debit gateway errors Float money Paise errors Integer minor units

docs.title: 6.2 Observability
docs.text:
• Payment success rate by method, gateway, bank; error-code classes.
  • Time from gateway decision to our CAPTURED (webhook lag); poller resolutions per hour (should be small).
  • Non-terminal payments by age; unfulfilled captures; refunds pending.
  • Ledger invariants (daily job) and reconciliation exceptions by category and value.
  • Alerts: success-rate drops per segment, webhook signature failures, reconciliation breaks above thresholds.

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• No card data; tokenisation; hosted checkout (Ch 23).
  • Webhook authentication; secrets in a vault; mTLS to gateways where supported.
  • Four-eyes approval for manual refunds and payout changes; audit logs (Ch 36).
  • Fraud controls on promos, refunds and wallet top-ups (Ch 39).

docs.title: 6.4 Performance
docs.text:
• Payment creation is a few inserts and one gateway call; keep it off shared pools (Ch 18 bulkheads).
  • Ledger writes are small; partition by month; index by account and reference.
  • Reconciliation as a batch job over files; streaming ingestion of settlement data when available.

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• Gateway fees (MDR) dominate: route by cost among healthy options, and verify fees in reconciliation (L3 found overcharges).
  • Failed payments cost conversions; per-bank routing and customer steering recover revenue (L4).
  • Chargebacks and fraud losses are costs to track per method.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Marking paid on the app's say-so

Clients can be modified (L2: 35 unpaid fulfilments).

2. Fulfilling on every capture message

Duplicates ship twice (L2: 1,621).

3. Last-write-wins statuses

A stale failure overwrites a capture.

4. Waiting forever for a webhook

Some never arrive; poll and reconcile.

5. Balance columns updated in application code

Lost updates create and destroy money (L1).

6. SERIALIZABLE on hot accounts without a plan

Retry storms (L1: 58,764 retries).

7. Floating-point money

Rounding errors compound; use paise.

8. Reconciling totals

A matching total can hide offsetting errors (L3).

9. Reconciliation reports nobody reads

Noise from timing and rounding buries real problems.

10. Failing over gateways for bank outages

No routing fixes an issuer outage (L4).

11. Retrying a payment on another gateway after a possible debit

Double charges.

12. Storing card numbers

PCI scope, regulatory breach — tokenise.

docs.title: Beginner B2
docs.text:
Q1 [B2] ⭐ Design a payment system for an e-commerce app — the main components?

30-second answer: A payment service with a state machine per payment (created → captured → refunded), integrating one or more gateways via hosted checkout; a webhook receiver that verifies and dedupes events; a status poller for unknown outcomes; a double-entry ledger; an outbox to notify checkout and fulfilment; daily reconciliation against settlement files; and security controls (tokenisation, signatures, audit).

Deep answer: §3.1; L1–L4 cover ledger, flow, reconciliation and routing.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed of confirmation vs certainty; single vs multiple gateways.

Follow-ups: 1. Who decides an order is paid? → A verified gateway event or status check, never the client. 2. Where is card data stored? → Nowhere in our systems.

Red flags: "The app calls /markPaid after success."

Q2 [B2] ⭐ How do you prevent double charges?

30-second answer: Idempotency at every hop: an idempotency key per checkout attempt on our API; our payment id as the gateway order's receipt so the gateway dedupes order creation; one gateway order per checkout, reused on retries; payment attempts only through the gateway's checkout for that order; and refunds for any duplicate captures found by reconciliation.

Deep answer: §2.6 table; Ch 20 for the key store.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Key lifetime vs storage.

Follow-ups: 1. Customer pays twice via two UPI apps? → Second capture detected, auto-refund. 2. Retry after timeout? → Same key, same order.

Red flags: Creating a new gateway order on every retry.

Q3 [B2] What is double-entry bookkeeping, and why use it in software?

30-second answer: Every movement of money is recorded as an entry with legs that sum to zero — a debit somewhere and a credit somewhere else. The ledger is append-only; balances are derived. It makes errors detectable (entries that don't balance), gives a full audit trail, and lets you reconstruct any balance at any time.

Deep answer: L1: the journal designs kept every entry balanced and every balance exact; a mutable balance created ₹34,011.55 from nothing.

Trade-offs I'd call out: More rows vs auditability.

Follow-ups: 1. Correcting a mistake? → A reversing entry. 2. Balance queries? → Cached balance projections.

Red flags: UPDATE statements on historical money records.

Q4 [B2] Why not trust the payment success callback from the app?

30-second answer: The app runs on a device you don't control; responses can be forged or replayed, and network issues mean it may never arrive. Use it only to trigger a server-side status check; the gateway's signed webhook or status API is the truth.

Deep answer: L2: trusting it shipped 35 unpaid orders and duplicated fulfilments.

Trade-offs I'd call out: A second of extra latency for certainty.

Follow-ups: 1. Signed client payloads? → Verify with the gateway anyway. 2. UX while waiting? → "Confirming payment…" with polling.

Red flags: Fulfilment triggered by a client request.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do you handle webhooks correctly?

30-second answer: Verify the signature, store the event id with a unique constraint and process in the same transaction as the state change, apply only allowed transitions (guarded UPDATE), treat events as at-least-once and unordered, respond 200 quickly (queue heavy work), and never rely on webhooks alone — poll non-terminal payments.

Deep answer: L2: guarded transitions + dedupe removed duplicates and wrong statuses; polling fixed 87 lost webhooks.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Synchronous processing vs queueing webhook bodies first.

Follow-ups: 1. Out-of-order failure after capture? → CAPTURED is terminal for failures. 2. Signature secret rotation? → Accept two during rotation.

Red flags: Last-write-wins status updates.

Q6 [B2] ⭐ A payment's outcome is unknown after a timeout. What do you do?

30-second answer: Don't guess and don't blindly retry. Record it as pending, query the gateway's status by our reference (with backoff), and apply the result through the same guarded transition. If still unknown after the window, mark it NEEDS_ATTENTION and let reconciliation resolve it; show the customer "payment processing".

Deep answer: Ch 13 unknown outcomes; L2's poller.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Customer wait vs certainty.

Follow-ups: 1. Gateway status API down? → Retry later; don't create a new order. 2. Customer pays again meanwhile? → Detect and refund the duplicate.

Red flags: "Retry the charge."

Q7 [B2] How do refunds work?

30-second answer: A refund is its own idempotent object with a state machine, created against a captured payment, checked under a lock so total refunds never exceed the capture, sent to the gateway with our refund id, confirmed by webhook or polling, recorded as ledger entries, and reconciled in the settlement file (negative rows).

Deep answer: §2.7; L3 found 12 refunds issued manually in the gateway dashboard and unknown to the ledger.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Instant refunds to wallet vs to source.

Follow-ups: 1. Partial refunds? → Track refunded amount per payment. 2. Refund to a closed card? → The gateway/bank handles it; reconcile outcome.

Red flags: Refunds as UPDATEs to the payment's amount.

Q8 [B2] How do you represent money in code and databases?

30-second answer: Integer minor units (paise) with an explicit currency, or a decimal type with fixed scale in the database; never binary floating point. Define rounding rules (banker's rounding or as contracts specify) for fees and taxes, and apply them once, in one place.

Deep answer: L3's 200 one-paisa differences are what rounding disagreements look like.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Integers vs decimals for multi-currency.

Follow-ups: 1. Java? → long paise or BigDecimal with scale 2. 2. Tax computation? → Per line, rounded per rule.

Red flags: double amount.

Q9 [B2] Why and how do you reconcile with the gateway?

30-second answer: Because messages get lost, duplicated or wrong, and the gateway and banks make mistakes too. Match each settlement row to the ledger by reference, with rules for timing, rounding and expected fees, and produce a categorised exception queue with rupee impact; do three-way matching with bank statements.

Deep answer: L3: totals explained nothing; exact matching gave 500 false alarms; rules left 232 real exceptions, including 40 customers charged with no order.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Auto-clear rules vs hidden problems.

Follow-ups: 1. Frequency? → Daily plus intraday for high volume. 2. Who owns exceptions? → Finance ops with engineering for systemic causes.

Red flags: "The totals matched."

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ How do you keep a ledger correct under concurrency?

30-second answer: Append-only balanced entries; a balance row per account updated in the same transaction under a row lock (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) with checks (non-negative); serializable isolation only where contention is low; hot internal accounts split into sub-accounts or aggregated asynchronously; nightly invariant checks.

Deep answer: L1: read-then-write left 116 of 200 wallets wrong; row locks exact at ~4,100 ops/s; SERIALIZABLE exact but 58,764 retries and 712 ops/s.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Lock contention on hot accounts vs complexity of sharding them.

Follow-ups: 1. Deadlocks? → Lock accounts in a consistent order. 2. Scale beyond one database? → Shard by account with a transfer saga.

Red flags: Balances computed in application memory.

Q11 [B3] How do you route payments across multiple gateways?

30-second answer: Track success rates and error classes per (gateway, method, issuer bank) over a short window; route each payment to the cheapest healthy option; keep a probe share on degraded paths; when every gateway fails for a bank, steer the customer to another method; auto-retry on a second gateway only for pre-debit gateway errors, with idempotent orders.

Deep answer: L4: gateway-level failover did nothing for a bank outage (78.7%); per-(gateway, bank) with steering 88.7%; auto-retry lifted the gateway incident to 96.9%.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Cost-based routing vs success; contract minimums.

Follow-ups: 1. Tokenised cards across gateways? → Network tokens are portable; gateway tokens aren't. 2. UPI intent? → The customer's app chooses the bank; route the PSP.

Red flags: Failover on overall success rate.

Q12 [B3] How does fulfilment learn about payments reliably?

30-second answer: The payment service writes an outbox event in the same transaction as the transition to CAPTURED; a relay publishes it; checkout and fulfilment consume idempotently by payment id. Fulfilment never polls or listens to webhooks directly.

Deep answer: Ch 13 outbox; L2's fulfilment row is written in the transition transaction.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Seconds of latency vs consistency.

Follow-ups: 1. Payment captured after order expired? → Refund automatically or honour the order. 2. Inventory reserved? → Released on expiry (Ch 46).

Red flags: Dual writes to database and Kafka.

Q13 [B3] What are the PCI DSS implications, and how do you minimise them?

30-second answer: Handling card numbers puts your systems in PCI DSS scope (the strictest levels if you store or process them). Minimise scope by using the gateway's hosted checkout/SDK so cards go directly to the gateway, store only tokens (network or gateway tokens, as RBI requires), and never log payment payloads.

Deep answer: Ch 23, Ch 36.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Checkout UX control vs compliance burden.

Follow-ups: 1. Saved cards? → Tokens with consent. 2. Logs? → Scrub; test that PAN patterns never appear.

Red flags: A card table in your database.

Q14 [B3] How do you handle a festival sale with 10x payments?

30-second answer: Pre-scale the payment service and webhook receivers, confirm gateway capacity and rate limits, spread traffic across gateways by health, queue webhook processing with backpressure, keep the ledger and state machine transactions small, watch success rates per bank and method in real time, and have customer-facing fallbacks (other methods, COD) and runbooks.

Deep answer: L4's routing plus Ch 18 bulkheads.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Aggressive retries vs gateway overload.

Follow-ups: 1. Gateway rate limit hit? → Shape requests; route elsewhere. 2. Webhook storm? → Accept quickly, process from a queue.

Red flags: Discovering gateway limits during the sale.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design the payments platform for a national grocery marketplace end to end.

30-second answer: Payment service with guarded state machines for payments and refunds; multi-gateway router with health per (gateway, method, bank); hosted checkout and tokenisation; verified, deduped webhooks plus status polling; double-entry ledger with locked projections; outbox to checkout and fulfilment; wallet as ledger accounts; daily three-way reconciliation with an exception queue; vendor payouts; audit, approvals and fraud controls; observability by segment.

Deep answer: §4 and L1–L4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Build vs buy of orchestration; single vs multiple gateways.

Follow-ups: 1. What would you build first? → State machine, ledger, reconciliation. 2. Biggest risk? → Unreconciled money and double fulfilment.

Red flags: No reconciliation.

Q16 [B4] How would you scale the ledger beyond one database?

30-second answer: Shard by account (customer wallets), keep each entry's legs within a shard where possible, and use a saga with a clearing account for cross-shard transfers; aggregate hot internal accounts from per-shard sub-accounts; keep a global, append-only event stream for reporting and reconciliation; verify invariants per shard and globally.

Deep answer: Purpose-built ledgers (e.g., TigerBeetle) optimise for exactly this workload.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Cross-shard transfers become eventual.

Follow-ups: 1. Consistency for balances? → Per shard strict, global eventual. 2. Audits? → Replay the event stream.

Red flags: Distributed transactions across shards for every payment.

Q17 [B4] Build vs buy for payments?

30-second answer: Buy gateways (and possibly a payment orchestration layer) for method coverage, compliance and bank connectivity. Build the parts that encode your business and your correctness: the state machine around your orders, the ledger, reconciliation, routing policy and customer steering — they differ by business and are where losses hide.

Deep answer: Orchestration vendors offer routing, but you still own reconciliation and the ledger.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Vendor lock-in vs time to market.

Follow-ups: 1. Open-source ledgers? → Consider for the core. 2. When to add a second gateway? → When outages or success rates cost more than integration.

Red flags: No ownership of reconciliation.

Q18 [B4] How do you design for regulatory change (tokenisation, data localisation, e-mandates)?

30-second answer: Isolate gateway- and regulation-specific logic in adapters, keep sensitive data out of your systems (tokens only), store payment data in-region, make consent and mandate flows explicit states, and track regulatory deadlines as architecture work with owners.

Deep answer: Ch 36 — policy as code and residency checks.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Flexibility vs speed.

Follow-ups: 1. Recurring payments? → UPI Autopay/e-mandates with pre-debit notifications (VERIFY current rules). 2. Data residency audits? → Evidence from infrastructure policy.

Red flags: Regulation handled as last-minute patches.

Q19 [B4] How do you test a payment system?

30-second answer: A gateway simulator (like L2's) with fault injection — duplicates, reordering, drops, timeouts, tampered callbacks — plus property tests on the ledger (every entry balances, balances equal sums), concurrency tests (L1), reconciliation tests with synthetic discrepancies (L3), gateway sandbox tests, and production canaries with small real payments.

Deep answer: Ch 29.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Simulator fidelity vs real gateway behaviour.

Follow-ups: 1. Invariants to monitor in production? → Captures without fulfilment/refund after 1 hour. 2. Chaos? → Block webhooks for an hour in staging.

Red flags: Only happy-path sandbox tests.

Q20 [B4] What metrics tell you the payment system is healthy?

30-second answer: Success rate by method, gateway and bank (excluding customer-side failures); time to confirmed status; captures not fulfilled or refunded after N minutes (should be ~0); duplicate captures; reconciliation exceptions by category and value; ledger invariant violations (must be 0); refund turnaround; fees vs expected; chargeback and fraud rates.

Deep answer: §6.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Business vs technical metrics — watch both.

Follow-ups: 1. Page on what? → Success-rate drops per segment, invariant violations. 2. Weekly review? → Exceptions trends with finance.

Red flags: Only API latency and error rate.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Double-entry, append-only ledger with locked balance projections; integer paise (L1).
  2. Guarded state machine; the client's success is a hint, never the truth (L2).
  3. Webhooks are at-least-once, unordered, lossy: dedupe, guard, and poll (L2).
  4. Reconciliation finds the bugs: line matching with rules, three-way, exception queue with rupee impact (L3).
  5. Route by (gateway, bank), steer customers on bank outages, retry only pre-debit (L4).
  6. Idempotency at every hop, tokenisation, audit.

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Choice Money records Entries + legs, sum to zero, never updated Balances Balance row per account under FOR UPDATE, CHECK constraints Payment status Guarded UPDATEs, terminal states, outbox on CAPTURED Webhooks Signature, event-id dedupe, fast ack Unknown outcomes Status polling, NEEDS_ATTENTION, reconciliation Reconciliation Daily, line-level, rules, three-way Routing Health per (gateway, method, bank), probes, steering Cards Hosted checkout, tokens only

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (B2) In L1, add a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint to design A and observe what happens instead of silent drift.
  2. (B3) In L2, make 10% of webhooks arrive before the payment row exists (race with creation). Handle it.
  3. (B3) In L3, add a new discrepancy type (settlement in the wrong currency) and see whether any rule wrongly auto-clears it.
  4. (B4) In L4, add a 5% probe share on avoided paths and measure flips and recovery time.
  5. (B4) Design the vendor payout job: inputs, ledger entries, idempotency, failure handling and reconciliation.

docs.title: 46. Case Study: Grocery Checkout & Inventory Reservation
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B2 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 02 (hot-SKU estimate), Ch 05, Ch 13 (checkout saga), Ch 18, Ch 45 · What you will build: The grocery checkout: cart → price and promo validation → stock reservation in the customer's dark store → payment → order confirmation, with reservations that expire, dark-store stock that doesn't match the shelf, and 8 pm flash sales. Earlier chapters deferred the hard parts here: the national single-SKU deal on one hot row (Ch 02, Ch 05), bucketing and a Redis front-gate, and "checkout re-validates availability" (Ch 22).

  • L1: the ₹1 onion deal (real PostgreSQL + Redis). 5,000 units, 20,000 attempts, 64 workers.
    • One row with an atomic conditional UPDATE sold out in 6.1 s (~820/s, p99 254 ms). SELECT FOR UPDATE was slower.
    • 16 buckets sold out 4.7x faster (1.29 s). Without a sold-out flag, though, the losers probed every bucket: 245,489 DB transactions.
    • A Redis front-gate kept the database to 5,000 transactions, yet sold out no faster.
    • All four designs oversold 0.
  • L2: how long to hold stock. A flash sale of 10,000 boxes for 25,000 customers.
    • A 30-minute hold left 1,621 boxes unsold while 10,897 customers were told "sold out".
    • A 3-minute hold sold everything but charged 460 slow payers for boxes already gone.
    • Holding 3 minutes and extending to 15 once payment starts sold 9,993 with 123 late captures.
  • L3: phantom stock. Recorded stock overstated the shelf by 1,619 units in one day.
    • Selling to recorded stock left 3.91% of orders with a missing item.
    • A flat 2-unit buffer cut that to 1.23% but hid 2,160 real units.
    • A per-SKU buffer learned from pick failures, plus correcting the record on a failed pick, reached 0.40%, hiding 1,509 units.
  • L4: the 8 pm crowd, end to end (real HTTP + PostgreSQL). 8,000 customers arrived in 2 s for 2,000 boxes.
    • With no admission control, 7,575 got no answer in 25 s, and 1,838 buyers never heard that they'd bought.
    • A fast-503 limit answered everyone, but only 31% of buyers were among the first 2,000 to arrive.
    • A virtual waiting room answered everyone, and 92% of buyers were among the first 2,000.

· Reading time: 110 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: Diwali at 8 pm
docs.text:
Marketing announced "₹1 onions, 5,000 kg, 8 pm tonight" across India. The checkout team had load-tested for 3x normal traffic. At 8:00:00:

  1. One row became the whole company's bottleneck. Every checkout with onions tried to decrement the same stock row. Checkouts for customers who didn't even want onions slowed down, because the connection pool was full of transactions queued on that row.
  2. Timeouts turned into retries. Apps timed out after 3 seconds and retried; the retries joined the same queue. The service was busy completing checkouts for people who had already given up and tapped again.
  3. "Sold out" while carts held stock. The first 5,000 checkouts reserved onions for 30 minutes. Thousands abandoned, but their reservations kept the onions off sale until 8:30, long after the crowd had left.
  4. Charged for nothing. Customers whose UPI app took a long time paid after their reservation had expired and the onions had gone to someone else.
  5. Missing items at the door. For fresh produce, recorded stock overstated the shelf. Pickers couldn't find items that checkout had happily sold; customers got partial orders and refunds.
  6. Unfair. Who got the deal depended on retry timing, not on who came first. Social media noticed.

This chapter designs the checkout that survives 8 pm: fast and correct stock reservation under contention, reservations with sensible lifetimes, honesty about physical stock, and admission control that is fair.

The thesis of this chapter

Checkout is where scarce physical stock meets unbounded demand, and every design choice decides who gets what. Contention on hot items is solved by spreading the lock (buckets), keeping losers away from the database (a gate) and never holding locks across round trips (L1). Reservations are leases with a business-chosen lifetime; extend on evidence of intent, and handle late payments explicitly (L2). Recorded stock is an estimate of the shelf; buffer where it's wrong and correct it from the picker's feedback (L3). And under a crowd, admission control decides both whether the system survives and whether it's fair (L4).

docs.title: 1.2 Where this lives in the grocery platform
docs.text:
Step Service Notes Cart Cart service Per customer; prices shown are indicative Validate Pricing, promotions, serviceability Final prices, coupon budgets, slot availability Reserve Inventory service (per dark store) Leases on stock units; TTL Pay Payment service (Ch 45) Idempotent, webhook-driven Confirm Order service Outbox events → fulfilment, notifications (Ch 40) Pick & pack Dark-store app Reports missing items → inventory corrections

The checkout is a saga (Ch 13): reserve → pay → confirm, with compensations (release the reservation, refund) on failure or expiry.

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end you will be able to:

  • Reserve stock correctly under extreme contention and choose between single rows, buckets, gates and queues (L1).
  • Design reservation lifetimes and the late-payment path (L2).
  • Handle inventory inaccuracy with learned buffers and feedback from picking (L3).
  • Protect checkout with admission control and a fair waiting room (L4).
  • Assemble the checkout saga with idempotency, price and promo consistency, and failure handling.

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: a counter with a limited batch of sweets B2
docs.text: A sweet shop has 5,000 boxes of a special. If everyone crowds one counter, the queue is the counter. Open 16 counters with a share of boxes each and the crowd moves faster, but "sold out" means asking every counter. Put a guard at the door with a clicker who stops letting people in after 5,000, and the counters never see the crowd. Give each buyer a few minutes to pay before the box goes back. And remember that the shop's ledger may say 5,000 while a few boxes were dropped in the back.

docs.title: 2.2 Requirements B2
docs.text:
Functional

  • Checkout validates prices, promotions and delivery slot; reserves every line item in the customer's dark store; takes payment; confirms the order.
  • Partial availability: offer to proceed without unavailable items or suggest substitutes.
  • Reservations expire; abandoned checkouts release stock.
  • Flash sales with per-customer limits and fair access.

Non-functional

  • Never oversell a reserved item beyond recorded stock; minimise shortfalls at picking.
  • Latency: checkout p99 < 1 s in normal load; graceful and fair under flash crowds.
  • Throughput: ~850 checkouts/s at normal peak (Ch 02); flash sales far above that on a few SKUs.
  • Availability: a hot SKU must not take down checkout for everything else.

docs.title: 2.3 Estimation B2
docs.text:
Quantity Estimate Checkouts at evening peak ~850/s nationally, spread over ~300 dark stores Per store per SKU Usually a few per second — row locks are fine National flash deal ~250/s+ on one SKU if stock is national (Ch 02) Single-row lock throughput ~800 reservations/s with a short transaction on the sandbox (L1); lower with longer transactions Reservations outstanding Checkouts/s × TTL: 850/s × 10 min ≈ 500k leases

The ordinary case is easy because stock is per store. The flash sale is hard because it concentrates demand on one row and brings a crowd far above normal load.

docs.title: 2.4 Reserving stock under contention ⭐ B3
docs.text:
L1 ran 20,000 attempts at 5,000 units from 64 workers against real PostgreSQL:

Design Sold out in Reservations/s p99 Oversold DB transactions One row, atomic conditional UPDATE 6.08 s 822 254 ms 0 20,000 One row, SELECT FOR UPDATE then UPDATE 6.89 s 726 299 ms 0 20,000 16 buckets 1.29 s 3,864 107 ms 0 245,489 Redis front-gate + DB write 5.90 s 848 250 ms 0 5,000
  • Atomic conditional update (UPDATE … SET qty = qty − 1 WHERE qty > 0) is correct and minimal: the check and the write are one statement. Holding a row lock across round trips (SELECT … FOR UPDATE, then UPDATE) lengthens the queue.
  • Buckets split stock into N rows; each reservation picks one (randomly or by customer hash) and falls back to others when it's empty. Lock throughput scales with N. The cost: deciding "sold out" means checking every bucket. Cache a sold-out flag (or a total counter) once all buckets reach zero, or losers keep probing, as L1's 245k transactions show. Rebalance buckets near the end so no bucket strands stock.
  • A Redis gate (Lua decrement-if-positive) answers winners and losers in microseconds and keeps losers away from the database. It is a second copy of the count: seed it from the database, and reconcile it, because a crash between gate and database leaks stock. It doesn't speed up the winners, who still queue on the database row — combine it with buckets.
  • Queued reservations: put reservation requests on a partitioned queue and have a single consumer per SKU apply them in order. That's throughput without lock contention, with asynchronous answers.
  • Keep the reservation transaction tiny: no payment calls, no remote calls, only the stock decrement and the reservation insert (Ch 05).

docs.title: 2.5 Reservations as leases ⭐ B3
docs.text:
A reservation is a lease: stock held for a customer until an expiry time. Model it explicitly:

create table reservations (
  id bigserial primary key, store_id int, sku text, qty int, checkout_id text,
  status text check (status in ('HELD','CONFIRMED','RELEASED','EXPIRED')),
  expires_at timestamptz not null, created_at timestamptz default now());
  • Expiry: a sweeper returns expired HELD quantities to stock (in the same transaction as the status change), plus lazy checks at confirmation.
  • Confirmation: payment captured → reservation CONFIRMED (idempotently, Ch 45).
  • Late capture: payment arrives after expiry. If stock is still available, re-reserve and confirm. Otherwise auto-refund and tell the customer; never silently oversell.

L2 simulated a flash sale with 60% payers (median 90 s, 5% over 10 minutes) and 40% abandoners:

Policy Sold (of 10,000) Turned away while stock sat in abandoned carts Late captures refunded Unsold at end Hold 30 min 8,379 10,897 0 1,621 Hold 10 min 9,830 8,100 202 170 Hold 3 min 10,000 7,417 460 0 3 min, extend to 15 when payment starts 9,993 7,964 123 7

The TTL is a business trade between stranded stock and disappointed slow payers. Extending on evidence of intent (the customer entered the payment flow) gets most of both. Normal days tolerate longer holds; flash sales need short ones.

docs.title: 2.6 Physical stock vs recorded stock ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Recorded stock is an estimate of what's on the shelf. Fresh produce, damage, misplacement and wastage make it wrong in one direction: phantom units. L3 simulated a day in a dark store:

Policy Orders with a missing item Units on the shelf hidden by the buffer Items sold Sell to recorded stock 3.91% 0 160,720 Hide the last 2 units of every SKU 1.23% 2,160 158,680 Per-SKU buffer from last week's pick failures 0.50% 1,509 159,267 + correct the record when a pick fails 0.40% 1,509 159,267
  • Learn buffers per SKU from pick failures and cycle counts: large for fresh produce, near zero for packaged goods.
  • Close the loop: when a picker reports an item missing, correct recorded stock immediately (and trigger a cycle count), so the next checkout doesn't sell the same phantom unit.
  • Buffers cost sales. The right level is a business trade between refunds and support contacts on one side, and hidden stock on the other.
  • Offer substitutions at checkout for low-confidence items ("if unavailable, replace with a similar item?").

docs.title: 2.7 Admission control and the waiting room ⭐ B4
docs.text:
A flash crowd far exceeds checkout capacity. L4 sent 8,000 customers in 2 seconds at a real checkout service with 10 database connections:

Design Bought Told "sold out" No answer in 25 s Answer p99 Buyers among the first 2,000 to arrive No admission control 162 (+1,838 who never heard back) 263 7,575 24.8 s 43% 40 in flight, fast 503 + Retry-After 2,000 6,000 0 9.5 s 31% Virtual waiting room, 300/s FIFO 2,000 6,000 0 9.9 s 92%
  • No admission control: requests queue for connections inside the service, clients time out and retry, and the service does work for people who have already given up. 1,838 customers bought a box and never learned it.
  • Load shedding (a concurrency limit with a fast 503) saves the service (Ch 18), but the winners are whoever's retry lands at the right moment.
  • A waiting room hands out tickets in arrival order and admits them at a rate the backend can sustain. The database sees a steady load, every customer has a position, and first come is first served. Real waiting rooms add a pre-queue before the sale starts (randomised order among early arrivals), per-customer limits, and bot protection (Ch 39).
  • Idempotent checkout: a customer's retry must return their existing order, not "sold out".

docs.title: 2.8 Prices, promotions and coupon budgets B3
docs.text:
• The cart shows indicative prices; checkout recomputes with the current price list and promotions and shows changes before payment.
  • Coupon budgets ("first 10,000 orders get ₹100 off") are another hot counter: use the same techniques (atomic decrement, buckets, gates) and reserve the budget with the order, releasing it on expiry.
  • Snapshot the final price, tax and promo per line into the order (immutable) for invoices (Ch 36) and refunds (Ch 45).

docs.title: 2.9 The checkout saga B3
docs.text:
1. POST /checkout with an idempotency key → validate cart, prices, promos, slot.
  2. Reserve all lines in one transaction per store (or all-or-nothing with compensation). Partial availability → ask the customer.
  3. Create the payment (Ch 45) with the checkout id as reference.
  4. On payment captured (event) → confirm reservations and create the order (outbox → fulfilment, notifications).
  5. On failure, abandonment or expiry → release reservations; late capture → re-reserve or refund.
  6. Everything keyed by checkout id; every step idempotent; stuck sagas surface as NEEDS_ATTENTION (Ch 13).

docs.title: 2.10 Interview framing B4
docs.text: Draw the saga first. Then go deep on stock reservation under contention with the options table, and on the reservation lease (TTL trade-off, late captures). Staff-level signals: phantom inventory and feedback from picking, admission control and fairness, idempotent retries returning the original outcome, and keeping payment calls out of database transactions.

docs.title: 3.4 State: a reservation's lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Held: stock decremented, expiry set
    Held --> Held: payment started, expiry extended
    Held --> Confirmed: payment captured before expiry
    Held --> Released: customer cancelled or payment failed
    Held --> Expired: expiry passed, stock returned
    Expired --> Confirmed: late capture and stock re-reserved
    Expired --> Refunded: late capture, no stock
    Confirmed --> Picked: picker scanned item
    Confirmed --> Short: picker reports missing, record corrected
    Picked --> [*]
    Short --> [*]
    Released --> [*]
    Refunded --> [*]

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Checkout & Inventory v2
docs.text:
Design Document (excerpt) — Checkout & Inventory v2

Status: Accepted · Authors: Checkout and Inventory teams · Reviewers: Payments, Dark-store ops, Marketing, SRE

Field Value Context Diwali flash sale: one hot row saturated the pool; timeouts and retries amplified load; 30-minute holds stranded stock; late payments charged for sold-out items; phantom stock caused missing items; outcomes were unfair. Decision Atomic conditional updates with stock buckets for hot SKUs and a Redis gate for flash sales; reservation leases with short TTL extended on payment start and an explicit late-capture path; per-SKU buffers learned from picking plus immediate corrections; waiting room with FIFO admission for flash sales; idempotent checkout. Related ADRs ADR-320 Reservation = one small transaction: conditional UPDATE + INSERT; no remote calls inside (L1); ADR-321 Hot SKUs: 16 buckets, sold-out flag, Redis gate seeded from DB and reconciled every minute (L1); ADR-322 TTL 3 min, extend to 15 min on payment start; late capture → re-reserve or auto-refund (L2); ADR-323 Per-SKU buffers from 7-day pick failures; picker "missing" corrects stock and opens a cycle count (L3); ADR-324 Flash sales behind a waiting room admitting at 70% of measured checkout capacity, FIFO with randomised pre-queue (L4); ADR-325 Checkout idempotency key returns the original outcome

Requirements.

  • R1 Zero oversell against recorded stock; missing-item orders < 0.5%.
  • R2 Flash sales never degrade checkout for other items (bulkheads).
  • R3 Every customer in a flash sale gets an answer within 30 s; buyers ≥ 90% in arrival order.
  • R4 Late captures refunded automatically within 5 minutes.
  • R5 Stranded stock (held by abandoned checkouts) < 5% of flash-sale stock at any time.

Decisions in detail.

  1. Stock model (ADR-320/321). stock(store, sku, bucket, qty CHECK qty >= 0); buckets = 1 normally, 16 for configured hot SKUs.
  2. Leases (ADR-322). Reservation rows with expires_at; sweeper every 10 s; payment-started events extend.
  3. Accuracy (ADR-323). Buffer = ceil(1.5 × daily average misses) per SKU per store; nightly recompute.
  4. Waiting room (ADR-324). Edge-hosted queue; tokens signed; admission rate adjusted from checkout latency.
  5. Idempotency (ADR-325). Keys stored with outcome for 24 h (Ch 20).

Consequences. More moving parts for flash sales (gate, buckets, waiting room); buffers hide some sellable stock; short TTLs require the late-capture path. In return: sales that finish in seconds without collateral damage, fewer missing items, and outcomes customers can see are fair.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
What's real here

All four labs are JDK 21. L1 and L4 run against a real PostgreSQL 16 with durable commits. L1 also uses a real Redis 7 for the gate, and L4 runs a real HTTP checkout service with real HTTP clients. L2 and L3 are deterministic simulations; customer behaviour, payment times and shrinkage rates are stated assumptions. Timings vary by machine.

L1 needs PostgreSQL 16 on port 5581 (database shop) and Redis 7 on port 6390; L4 needs PostgreSQL. Both need postgresql-42.7.4.jar and -Duser.timezone=UTC. Run every lab with -Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8.

docs.title: L1 — The ₹1 onion deal B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "5,000 units of one SKU, a national crowd. Never oversell, sell out fast, and don't let the rest of the platform feel it."

Four reservation designs against real PostgreSQL, with Redis as the gate in D. 64 workers make 20,000 attempts.

HotSkuL1.java
// HotSkuL1.java — run with (PostgreSQL 16 on :5581 db "shop", Redis 7 on :6390):
//   java -cp postgresql-42.7.4.jar -Duser.timezone=UTC HotSkuL1.java
// THE NATIONAL ₹1 ONION DEAL. 5,000 units, one SKU, and 64 concurrent checkout workers hammering it (Ch 02 flagged this
// as the case where one row approaches its lock limit). Each reservation must also be recorded durably. Four designs:
//   A) ONE ROW, atomic:   UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty > 0, + INSERT reservation, one txn
//   B) ONE ROW, locked:   SELECT … FOR UPDATE, check, UPDATE, INSERT — the lock is held across two round trips
//   C) 16 BUCKETS:        stock split across 16 rows; a worker tries a random bucket, then the others if it's empty
//   D) REDIS FRONT-GATE:  a Lua DECR-if-positive in Redis admits or rejects instantly; admitted requests then write
//                         the reservation to PostgreSQL (the database never sees the rejected ones)
// 20,000 attempts in total (4x the stock). Measured: time to sell out, reservations/s while stock lasts, p99 latency,
// OVERSOLD units (must be 0) and how many database transactions were attempted.
import java.io.*;
import java.net.Socket;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.sql.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

public class HotSkuL1 {
    static final String DB = "jdbc:postgresql://127.0.0.1:5581/shop?user=claude";
    static final int STOCK = 5_000, ATTEMPTS = 20_000, WORKERS = 64, BUCKETS = 16;
    static final String GATE = "local v = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0') if v > 0 then redis.call('DECR', KEYS[1]) return 1 end return 0";

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.printf("One SKU, %,d units, %,d reservation attempts from %d concurrent workers (PostgreSQL 16, durable commits).%n%n", STOCK, ATTEMPTS, WORKERS);
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %10s %14s %11s %10s %14s %16s%n", "design", "sold", "sold out in", "reserv./s", "p99", "oversold", "DB transactions");
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %10s %14s %11s %10s %14s %16s%n", "", "", "", "", "", "", "attempted");
        String[] names = {"A) one row, atomic conditional UPDATE", "B) one row, SELECT FOR UPDATE then UPDATE", "C) 16 buckets, random then fallback", "D) Redis Lua front-gate + DB write"};
        for (int d = 0; d < 4; d++) run(d, names[d]);
        System.out.println("\n   → one row is correct and simple, and every buyer queues on its lock: ~800 reservations/s here, with a p99 over");
        System.out.println("     a quarter of a second. Holding the lock across two round trips (FOR UPDATE, then UPDATE) is slower still.");
        System.out.println("     Sixteen buckets spread the lock and sold out about 4x faster — but once stock ran out, every attempt probed all");
        System.out.println("     16 buckets before saying 'sold out', twelve times the database transactions of A. Cache a sold-out flag.");
        System.out.println("     The Redis front-gate kept the 15,000 losers away from the database entirely (5,000 transactions), yet sold out");
        System.out.println("     no faster: the winners still queue on the one row behind it. Combine them — gate plus buckets — for the");
        System.out.println("     biggest deals, and remember the gate is a second copy of the stock count that must be seeded and reconciled.");
    }

    static void run(int design, String name) throws Exception {
        try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(DB); Statement s = c.createStatement()) {
            s.execute("drop table if exists reservations"); s.execute("drop table if exists stock");
            s.execute("create table stock(sku text, bucket int, qty int not null check (qty >= 0), primary key (sku, bucket))");
            s.execute("create table reservations(id bigserial primary key, sku text, bucket int, customer int, created_at timestamptz default now())");
            if (design == 2) s.execute("insert into stock select 'ONION-1KG', g, " + (STOCK / BUCKETS) + " + case when g < " + (STOCK % BUCKETS) + " then 1 else 0 end from generate_series(0," + (BUCKETS - 1) + ") g");
            else s.execute("insert into stock values ('ONION-1KG', 0, " + STOCK + ")");
        }
        String sha;
        try (Redis r = new Redis()) { r.cmd("SET", "gate:ONION-1KG", String.valueOf(STOCK)); sha = (String) r.cmd("SCRIPT", "LOAD", GATE); }
        AtomicInteger next = new AtomicInteger(), sold = new AtomicInteger(); long[] lat = new long[ATTEMPTS]; AtomicLong soldOutAt = new AtomicLong();
        AtomicInteger dbTx = new AtomicInteger(); DB_TX.set(dbTx);
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        try (var pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(WORKERS)) {
            for (int w = 0; w < WORKERS; w++) pool.submit(() -> {
                try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(DB); Redis r = new Redis()) {
                    Random rnd = new Random(Thread.currentThread().threadId());
                    int i;
                    while ((i = next.getAndIncrement()) < ATTEMPTS) {
                        long s = System.nanoTime(); boolean ok = switch (design) {
                            case 0 -> atomic(c, 0, i); case 1 -> locked(c, i); case 2 -> buckets(c, rnd, i);
                            default -> ((Long) r.cmd("EVALSHA", sha, "1", "gate:ONION-1KG")) == 1 && atomic(c, 0, i);
                        };
                        lat[i] = System.nanoTime() - s;
                        if (ok) { if (sold.incrementAndGet() == STOCK) soldOutAt.set(System.nanoTime() - t0); }
                    }
                }
                return null;
            });
        }
        int left; try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(DB)) { left = remaining(c); }
        int reservations; try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(DB); ResultSet rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("select count(*) from reservations")) { rs.next(); reservations = rs.getInt(1); }
        Arrays.sort(lat); double out = soldOutAt.get() / 1e9;
        System.out.printf("   %-44s %,10d %12.2f s %,11.0f %7.1f ms %,14d %,16d%n", name, reservations, out, STOCK / out, lat[(int) (ATTEMPTS * 0.99)] / 1e6,
                Math.max(0, reservations - STOCK), dbTx.get());
    }

    static int remaining(Connection c) throws SQLException { try (ResultSet rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("select coalesce(sum(qty),0) from stock")) { rs.next(); return rs.getInt(1); } }
    static final java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference<AtomicInteger> DB_TX = new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference<>();
    static boolean atomic(Connection c, int bucket, int customer) throws SQLException {
        DB_TX.get().incrementAndGet(); c.setAutoCommit(false);
        try (PreparedStatement u = c.prepareStatement("update stock set qty = qty - 1 where sku = 'ONION-1KG' and bucket = ? and qty > 0")) {
            u.setInt(1, bucket);
            if (u.executeUpdate() == 0) { c.rollback(); return false; }
            try (PreparedStatement ins = c.prepareStatement("insert into reservations(sku, bucket, customer) values ('ONION-1KG', ?, ?)")) { ins.setInt(1, bucket); ins.setInt(2, customer); ins.executeUpdate(); }
            c.commit(); return true;
        } catch (SQLException e) { c.rollback(); throw e; } finally { c.setAutoCommit(true); }
    }
    static boolean locked(Connection c, int customer) throws SQLException {
        DB_TX.get().incrementAndGet(); c.setAutoCommit(false);
        try {
            int qty; try (ResultSet rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("select qty from stock where sku = 'ONION-1KG' and bucket = 0 for update")) { rs.next(); qty = rs.getInt(1); }
            if (qty <= 0) { c.rollback(); return false; }
            c.createStatement().executeUpdate("update stock set qty = qty - 1 where sku = 'ONION-1KG' and bucket = 0");
            try (PreparedStatement ins = c.prepareStatement("insert into reservations(sku, bucket, customer) values ('ONION-1KG', 0, ?)")) { ins.setInt(1, customer); ins.executeUpdate(); }
            c.commit(); return true;
        } catch (SQLException e) { c.rollback(); throw e; } finally { c.setAutoCommit(true); }
    }
    static boolean buckets(Connection c, Random rnd, int customer) throws SQLException {
        int start = rnd.nextInt(BUCKETS);
        for (int k = 0; k < BUCKETS; k++) if (atomic(c, (start + k) % BUCKETS, customer)) return true;   // all buckets empty → truly sold out
        return false;
    }

    static final class Redis implements Closeable {
        final Socket s; final OutputStream out; final InputStream in;
        Redis() throws IOException { s = new Socket("127.0.0.1", 6390); s.setTcpNoDelay(true); out = new BufferedOutputStream(s.getOutputStream()); in = new BufferedInputStream(s.getInputStream()); }
        Object cmd(String... parts) throws IOException {
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("*").append(parts.length).append("\r\n");
            for (String p : parts) { byte[] b = p.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8); sb.append('$').append(b.length).append("\r\n").append(p).append("\r\n"); }
            out.write(sb.toString().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)); out.flush(); return read();
        }
        Object read() throws IOException {
            int type = in.read(); String line = line();
            return switch (type) {
                case '+' -> line; case ':' -> Long.parseLong(line);
                case '$' -> { int n = Integer.parseInt(line); if (n < 0) yield null; byte[] b = in.readNBytes(n); line(); yield new String(b, StandardCharsets.UTF_8); }
                case '-' -> throw new IOException(line);
                default -> throw new IOException("unexpected " + (char) type);
            };
        }
        String line() throws IOException { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); int c; while ((c = in.read()) != '\r') sb.append((char) c); in.read(); return sb.toString(); }
        public void close() throws IOException { s.close(); }
    }
}

                                                                                                                       attempted

   B) one row, SELECT FOR UPDATE then UPDATE         5,000         6.89 s         726   299.2 ms              0           20,000
   C) 16 buckets, random then fallback               5,000         1.29 s       3,864   107.3 ms              0          245,489
   D) Redis Lua front-gate + DB write                5,000         5.90 s         848   249.7 ms              0            5,000

   → one row is correct and simple, and every buyer queues on its lock: ~800 reservations/s here, with a p99 over
     a quarter of a second. Holding the lock across two round trips (FOR UPDATE, then UPDATE) is slower still.
     Sixteen buckets spread the lock and sold out about 4x faster — but once stock ran out, every attempt probed all
     16 buckets before saying 'sold out', twelve times the database transactions of A. Cache a sold-out flag.
     The Redis front-gate kept the 15,000 losers away from the database entirely (5,000 transactions), yet sold out
     no faster: the winners still queue on the one row behind it. Combine them — gate plus buckets — for the
     biggest deals, and remember the gate is a second copy of the stock count that must be seeded and reconciled.

Reading it:

  • A: ~820 reservations/s on one row, with a quarter-second p99 for everyone in the queue. B holds the lock across two round trips and is slower still.
  • C: 16 buckets sold out 4.7x faster. Once stock was gone, though, each of the remaining ~15,000 attempts tried all 16 buckets: 245,489 transactions to say "sold out". Exercise 1 adds the flag.
  • D: the gate answered the 15,000 losers without the database (5,000 transactions in total), but the winners still queued on one row. Exercise 2 combines gate and buckets.
  • Oversold: 0 everywhere. The designs differ in speed and in how much work the database does, not in correctness.

docs.title: L2 — How long to hold stock B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "Hold stock long enough for real payers, short enough that abandoned carts don't starve everyone else."

An event-driven simulation of a one-hour flash sale: 10,000 boxes, 25,000 customers, realistic payment times and abandonment.

ReservationTtlL2.java
// ReservationTtlL2.java — run with: java ReservationTtlL2.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// HOW LONG DO YOU HOLD STOCK FOR SOMEONE WHO MIGHT PAY? A one-hour flash sale: 10,000 mango boxes, 25,000 customers
// arriving (fixed seed). Checkout reserves one box. 60% of customers go on to pay — median 90 s (switching to the UPI app,
// entering the PIN), 5% take over 10 minutes (retries, bank OTP delays); 40% abandon and never pay. A reservation that
// expires returns its box to stock. A payment that completes after the reservation expired is a LATE CAPTURE: the box
// may already be someone else's, so the customer is charged for nothing and must be refunded (or the order oversold).
//   T30  reservation TTL 30 minutes          T10  TTL 10 minutes          T3  TTL 3 minutes
//   T3+  TTL 3 minutes, extended to 15 minutes the moment the customer actually starts paying (enters the gateway)
// Measured: boxes sold, customers told "sold out" while boxes were sitting in abandoned reservations, late captures
// that had to be refunded, and boxes left unsold at the end.
import java.util.*;

public class ReservationTtlL2 {
    record Customer(double arrive, boolean pays, double payStart, double payDone) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Random r = new Random(46); List<Customer> cs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 25_000; i++) {
            double arrive = r.nextDouble() * 3600; boolean pays = r.nextDouble() < 0.6;
            double start = arrive + 10 + r.nextDouble() * 40;                                    // time to reach the gateway
            double dur = r.nextDouble() < 0.05 ? 600 + r.nextDouble() * 600 : Math.exp(Math.log(90) + 0.6 * r.nextGaussian());
            cs.add(new Customer(arrive, pays, start, start + dur));
        }
        cs.sort(Comparator.comparingDouble(Customer::arrive));
        System.out.println("Flash sale: 10,000 boxes, 25,000 customers over 1 hour; 60% pay (median 90 s, 5% > 10 min), 40% abandon.\n");
        System.out.printf("   %-52s %8s %22s %16s %14s%n", "reservation policy", "sold", "turned away while stock", "late captures", "unsold at end");
        System.out.printf("   %-52s %8s %22s %16s %14s%n", "", "", "sat in abandoned carts", "refunded", "");
        String[][] ps = {{"T30) hold 30 minutes", "1800", "0"}, {"T10) hold 10 minutes", "600", "0"}, {"T3) hold 3 minutes", "180", "0"},
                {"T3+) hold 3 minutes, extend to 15 when paying starts", "180", "900"}};
        for (String[] p : ps) run(cs, p[0], Double.parseDouble(p[1]), Double.parseDouble(p[2]));
        System.out.println("\n   → a long hold protects slow payers and starves everyone else: boxes sit in carts that will never pay while");
        System.out.println("     real buyers are told 'sold out'. A short hold recycles abandoned stock fast, but the slow payers' reservations");
        System.out.println("     expire under them — they get charged for a box that's gone, and must be refunded. Holding briefly and");
        System.out.println("     extending only when there's evidence of intent (the customer actually entered the payment flow) gets most of");
        System.out.println("     both. The TTL is a business policy with a measurable cost on each side; make the expiry and the late-capture");
        System.out.println("     path (auto-refund, or honour it if stock allows) explicit states, not accidents.");
    }

    static void run(List<Customer> cs, String name, double ttl, double extendTo) {
        int stock = 10_000, sold = 0, turnedAwayStranded = 0, lateRefunded = 0;
        // events: reservation expiries and payment completions
        PriorityQueue<double[]> ev = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingDouble(a -> a[0]));   // [time, type(0 expire,1 pay), idx]
        double[] expiresAt = new double[cs.size()]; boolean[] active = new boolean[cs.size()]; int abandonedHeld = 0;
        int ci = 0;
        while (ci < cs.size() || !ev.isEmpty()) {
            double nextArrive = ci < cs.size() ? cs.get(ci).arrive() : Double.MAX_VALUE;
            if (!ev.isEmpty() && ev.peek()[0] <= nextArrive) {
                double[] e = ev.poll(); int idx = (int) e[2]; Customer c = cs.get(idx);
                if (e[1] == 0) {                                                         // expiry check
                    if (active[idx] && expiresAt[idx] <= e[0] + 1e-9) { active[idx] = false; stock++; if (!c.pays()) abandonedHeld--; }
                } else if (e[1] == 2) {                                                  // payment started: extend
                    if (active[idx] && extendTo > 0) { expiresAt[idx] = Math.max(expiresAt[idx], e[0] + extendTo); ev.add(new double[]{expiresAt[idx], 0, idx}); }
                } else {                                                                 // payment completed
                    if (active[idx]) { active[idx] = false; sold++; }
                    else if (stock > 0) { stock--; sold++; }                             // late, but a box happens to be free: honour it
                    else lateRefunded++;
                }
                continue;
            }
            Customer c = cs.get(ci); int idx = ci++;
            if (stock == 0) { if (abandonedHeld > 0) turnedAwayStranded++; continue; }
            stock--; active[idx] = true; expiresAt[idx] = c.arrive() + ttl; ev.add(new double[]{expiresAt[idx], 0, idx});
            if (c.pays()) { ev.add(new double[]{c.payStart(), 2, idx}); ev.add(new double[]{c.payDone(), 1, idx}); } else abandonedHeld++;
        }
        System.out.printf("   %-52s %,8d %,22d %,16d %,14d%n", name, sold, turnedAwayStranded, lateRefunded, stock);
    }
}

                                                                 sat in abandoned carts         refunded               
   T30) hold 30 minutes                                    8,379                 10,897                0          1,621
   T10) hold 10 minutes                                    9,830                  8,100              202            170
