Reading it:

  • 30 minutes: 1,621 boxes unsold at the end. They sat in abandoned carts until after the crowd left, while 10,897 customers were told "sold out".
  • 3 minutes: everything sold, but 460 slow payers were charged for boxes their reservation no longer held.
  • 3 minutes + extend when paying starts: 9,993 sold and 123 late captures. The extension targets the people who are actually paying. The remaining late captures are the 5% whose payments take longer than 15 minutes.

docs.title: L3 — Phantom stock B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "Customers shouldn't find items missing at the door because our records were optimistic — and we shouldn't hide half the shelf to avoid it."

One simulated day in a dark store: 2,000 SKUs, 30,000 orders, shrinkage concentrated in fresh produce, and four stock policies.

PhantomStockL3.java
// PhantomStockL3.java — run with: java PhantomStockL3.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// THE SYSTEM SAYS 3, THE SHELF HAS 1. A dark store's recorded stock drifts from what's physically on the shelf: damaged
// produce, misplaced items, unrecorded wastage, theft. Checkout reserves against RECORDED stock; the picker finds out the
// truth. One simulated day (fixed seed) in a dark store with 2,000 SKUs (25% fresh produce with large discrepancies,
// the rest packaged with small ones) and 30,000 orders of ~6 items. Four policies:
//   P1 sell down to recorded stock (no buffer)
//   P2 hide the last 2 units of every SKU (a global safety buffer)
//   P3 per-SKU buffer learned from last week's pick failures (fresh produce gets a bigger one)
//   P4 P3 + when a picker reports an item missing, recorded stock is corrected to the shelf count at once
// Measured: orders that reached the customer with an item missing, units physically on the shelf at close that the buffer
// never offered (sales lost to caution), and items sold.
import java.util.*;

public class PhantomStockL3 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int skus = 2_000; Random r = new Random(47);
        int[] recorded = new int[skus]; double[] lambda = new double[skus]; double[] demand = new double[skus]; boolean[] fresh = new boolean[skus];
        for (int i = 0; i < skus; i++) {
            fresh[i] = r.nextDouble() < 0.25; recorded[i] = 5 + r.nextInt(56);
            lambda[i] = fresh[i] ? 2.5 : 0.25;                                             // expected missing units per day
            demand[i] = 1.0 / Math.pow(i + 1, 0.6);
        }
        double sum = Arrays.stream(demand).sum(); double[] cdf = new double[skus]; double c = 0; for (int i = 0; i < skus; i++) { c += demand[i] / sum; cdf[i] = c; }
        List<int[]> orders = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int o = 0; o < 30_000; o++) { int n = 3 + r.nextInt(7); int[] items = new int[n]; for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) { int idx = Arrays.binarySearch(cdf, r.nextDouble()); items[k] = idx < 0 ? Math.min(skus - 1, -idx - 1) : idx; } orders.add(items); }
        // today's discrepancies (shrinkage) and last week's observed pick failures (to learn buffers)
        int[] shrink = new int[skus], lastWeekMisses = new int[skus];
        for (int i = 0; i < skus; i++) { shrink[i] = poisson(r, lambda[i]); for (int d = 0; d < 7; d++) lastWeekMisses[i] += poisson(r, lambda[i]); }
        // restock: recorded stock should cover a day's demand for most SKUs
        for (int i = 0; i < skus; i++) recorded[i] = Math.max(recorded[i], (int) Math.ceil(30_000 * 6 * demand[i] / sum * 0.9));

        System.out.printf("Dark store: %,d SKUs (25%% fresh), %,d orders; recorded stock overstates the shelf by %,d units in total.%n%n", skus, orders.size(), Arrays.stream(shrink).sum());
        System.out.printf("   %-58s %14s %16s %16s%n", "policy", "orders with a", "units on shelf,", "items sold");
        System.out.printf("   %-58s %14s %16s %16s%n", "", "missing item", "hidden by buffer", "");
        String[] names = {"P1) sell down to recorded stock", "P2) hide the last 2 units of every SKU", "P3) per-SKU buffer from last week's pick failures",
                "P4) P3 + correct recorded stock when a pick fails"};
        for (int p = 0; p < 4; p++) {
            int[] rec = recorded.clone(), shelf = new int[skus]; for (int i = 0; i < skus; i++) shelf[i] = Math.max(0, recorded[i] - shrink[i]);
            int[] buffer = new int[skus];
            for (int i = 0; i < skus; i++) buffer[i] = p == 0 ? 0 : p == 1 ? 2 : (int) Math.ceil(lastWeekMisses[i] / 7.0 * 1.5);
            int missingOrders = 0, lostSales = 0, sold = 0;
            for (int[] o : orders) {
                boolean missing = false;
                for (int it : o) {
                    if (rec[it] - buffer[it] <= 0) continue;                                      // shown out of stock
                    rec[it]--;                                                                   // reserved against recorded stock
                    if (shelf[it] > 0) { shelf[it]--; sold++; }
                    else { missing = true; if (p == 3) rec[it] = 0; }                             // picker can't find it; P4 fixes the record
                }
                if (missing) missingOrders++;
            }
            for (int i = 0; i < skus; i++) if (rec[i] - buffer[i] <= 0) lostSales += Math.max(0, shelf[i]);   // on the shelf, never offered
            System.out.printf("   %-58s %13.2f%% %,16d %,16d%n", names[p], 100.0 * missingOrders / orders.size(), lostSales, sold);
        }
        System.out.println("\n   → selling to recorded stock turns every discrepancy into a disappointed customer at the door — refunds, missing");
        System.out.println("     items and support calls (3.9% of orders here). A flat buffer hides stock that is really there and still misses");
        System.out.println("     the fresh produce that drifts most. A buffer learned per SKU from pick failures puts the caution where the errors");
        System.out.println("     are, and fixing the record the moment a picker finds a gap stops the same phantom unit being sold again. Inventory");
        System.out.println("     accuracy is a data-quality loop between the picker's handheld and the checkout — not a property of the database.");
        System.out.println("     Buffers do cost sales (compare items sold): the right buffer is a business trade between refunds and lost sales.");
    }
    static int poisson(Random r, double l) { double L = Math.exp(-l), p = 1; int k = 0; do { k++; p *= r.nextDouble(); } while (p > L); return k - 1; }
}
java -Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8 PhantomStockL3.java
Dark store: 2,000 SKUs (25% fresh), 30,000 orders; recorded stock overstates the shelf by 1,619 units in total.

   policy                                                      orders with a  units on shelf,       items sold
                                                                missing item hidden by buffer                 
   P1) sell down to recorded stock                                     3.91%                0          160,720
   P2) hide the last 2 units of every SKU                              1.23%            2,160          158,680
   P3) per-SKU buffer from last week's pick failures                   0.50%            1,509          159,267
   P4) P3 + correct recorded stock when a pick fails                   0.40%            1,509          159,267

   → selling to recorded stock turns every discrepancy into a disappointed customer at the door — refunds, missing
     items and support calls (3.9% of orders here). A flat buffer hides stock that is really there and still misses
     the fresh produce that drifts most. A buffer learned per SKU from pick failures puts the caution where the errors
     are, and fixing the record the moment a picker finds a gap stops the same phantom unit being sold again. Inventory
     accuracy is a data-quality loop between the picker's handheld and the checkout — not a property of the database.
     Buffers do cost sales (compare items sold): the right buffer is a business trade between refunds and lost sales.

Reading it:

  • Recorded stock sells every phantom unit: 3.91% of orders arrive with something missing.
  • A flat buffer cuts that to 1.23%, but hides 2,160 real units and still under-protects fresh produce.
  • A learned per-SKU buffer does better on both counts: 0.50%, with 1,509 hidden units.
  • Correcting the record on a failed pick stops repeat failures: 0.40%.
  • Every buffer costs sales (compare "items sold" with P1); the level is a business decision.

docs.title: L4 — The 8 pm crowd, end to end B4
docs.text:
Requirement: "8,000 people tap 'Buy' within two seconds for 2,000 boxes. Everyone gets an answer quickly, the service survives, and the first to arrive are the first served."

A real checkout service (JDK HttpServer, 10 PostgreSQL connections, ~20 ms of DB work per checkout) and 8,000 real HTTP clients that time out at 3 s and retry. Three admission strategies.

WaitingRoomL4.java
// WaitingRoomL4.java — run with (PostgreSQL 16 on :5581, db "shop"):
//   java -cp postgresql-42.7.4.jar -Duser.timezone=UTC -Dsun.net.httpserver.nodelay=true WaitingRoomL4.java
// THE 8 PM FLASH SALE, END TO END. A real checkout service (JDK HttpServer on virtual threads) with a 10-connection
// PostgreSQL pool: a checkout does ~20 ms of database work (price, promo, address checks), reserves stock (8 buckets)
// and inserts the order in one transaction, then calls the payment service (15 ms, simulated). A repeated request from
// a customer who already bought returns the earlier result. 2,000 boxes; 8,000 customers arrive within 2 seconds. Clients time out after 3 s
// and retry (with jitter) until they get an answer or 25 s pass. Three ways to face the crowd:
//   W1 no admission control: every request waits for a database connection
//   W2 concurrency limit: at most 40 checkouts in flight; the rest get 503 + Retry-After immediately
//   W3 virtual waiting room: customers join a queue and get a ticket; tickets are admitted at 300/s in arrival order;
//      the app polls its position every 1.5–2.5 s and checks out when admitted
// Measured: customers who got a definite answer (bought, or told "sold out"), p50/p99 time to that answer, requests the
// server absorbed, and FAIRNESS — of the 2,000 who bought, how many were among the first 2,000 to arrive.
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;
import java.net.*;
import java.net.http.*;
import java.sql.*;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

public class WaitingRoomL4 {
    static final String DB = "jdbc:postgresql://127.0.0.1:5581/shop?user=claude";
    static final int STOCK = 2_000, CUSTOMERS = 8_000, BUCKETS = 8;
    static final BlockingQueue<Connection> pool = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>();
    static final AtomicLong ticketSeq = new AtomicLong(), admittedUpTo = new AtomicLong(), requests = new AtomicLong();
    static final Semaphore inFlight = new Semaphore(40);
    static volatile boolean soldOut; static int design;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) pool.add(DriverManager.getConnection(DB));
        HttpServer srv = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("127.0.0.1", 0), 8192); srv.setExecutor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor());
        srv.createContext("/join", ex -> { requests.incrementAndGet(); byte[] b = String.valueOf(ticketSeq.incrementAndGet()).getBytes(); ex.sendResponseHeaders(200, b.length); ex.getResponseBody().write(b); ex.close(); });
        srv.createContext("/status", ex -> { requests.incrementAndGet(); long t = Long.parseLong(ex.getRequestURI().getQuery().substring(7));
            byte[] b = (soldOut ? "soldout" : t <= admittedUpTo.get() ? "admitted" : "wait " + (t - admittedUpTo.get())).getBytes(); ex.sendResponseHeaders(200, b.length); ex.getResponseBody().write(b); ex.close(); });
        srv.createContext("/checkout", ex -> {
            requests.incrementAndGet(); int code;
            if (design == 1 && !inFlight.tryAcquire()) { ex.getResponseHeaders().add("Retry-After", "1"); ex.sendResponseHeaders(503, -1); ex.close(); return; }
            try { int cust = Integer.parseInt(ex.getRequestURI().getQuery().substring(9)); code = alreadyBought(cust) ? 200 : soldOut ? 409 : checkout(cust); }
            catch (Exception e) { code = 500; } finally { if (design == 1) inFlight.release(); }
            ex.sendResponseHeaders(code, -1); ex.close();
        });
        srv.start();
        String base = "http://127.0.0.1:" + srv.getAddress().getPort();
        System.out.printf("Checkout service (10 DB connections, ~20 ms DB work per checkout), %,d boxes, %,d customers arriving within 2 s;%nclients time out at 3 s and retry.%n%n", STOCK, CUSTOMERS);
        System.out.printf("   %-46s %10s %12s %12s %12s %14s %14s%n", "design", "bought", "told sold", "no answer", "answer p50", "answer p99", "fair (bought");
        System.out.printf("   %-46s %10s %12s %12s %12s %14s %14s%n", "", "", "out", "in 25 s", "", "", "& first 2,000)");
        String[] names = {"W1) no admission control", "W2) 40 in flight, fast 503 + Retry-After", "W3) virtual waiting room, admit 300/s FIFO"};
        for (design = 0; design < 3; design++) run(base, names[design]);
        System.out.println("\n   → without admission control the crowd queues inside the service for database connections: requests time out,");
        System.out.println("     clients retry, and the retries join the same queue — work is done for people who have already given up, and");
        System.out.println("     who gets a box is decided by retry luck. Shedding with a fast 503 protects the database, but the order in which");
        System.out.println("     people are served is still random. A waiting room turns the crowd into an ordered queue in front of the");
        System.out.println("     service: the database sees a steady, safe rate, every customer gets an answer and a position, and the first");
        System.out.println("     to arrive are the first to buy. For a flash sale, fairness is part of correctness.");
        System.exit(0);
    }

    static boolean alreadyBought(int customer) throws Exception {                        // idempotent retry: return the earlier result
        Connection c = pool.poll(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS); if (c == null) return false;
        try (PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("select 1 from orders where customer = ?")) { ps.setInt(1, customer); try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) { return rs.next(); } }
        finally { pool.add(c); }
    }
    static int checkout(int customer) throws Exception {
        Connection c = pool.poll(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS); if (c == null) return 503;
        boolean ok = false;
        try {
            c.setAutoCommit(false); int start = customer % BUCKETS;
            try (Statement w = c.createStatement()) { w.execute("select pg_sleep(0.02)"); }       // price, promo, address checks: ~20 ms of DB work
            for (int k = 0; k < BUCKETS && !ok; k++) try (PreparedStatement u = c.prepareStatement("update stock set qty = qty - 1 where bucket = ? and qty > 0")) { u.setInt(1, (start + k) % BUCKETS); ok = u.executeUpdate() == 1; }
            if (ok) try (PreparedStatement ins = c.prepareStatement("insert into orders(customer) values (?) on conflict do nothing")) { ins.setInt(1, customer); if (ins.executeUpdate() == 0) { c.rollback(); return 200; } }   // already bought
            c.commit();
        } finally { c.setAutoCommit(true); pool.add(c); }
        if (!ok) { soldOut = true; return 409; }
        Thread.sleep(15);                                                                 // create the payment order (outside the transaction)
        return 200;
    }

    static void run(String base, String name) throws Exception {
        try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(DB); Statement s = c.createStatement()) {
            s.execute("drop table if exists orders"); s.execute("drop table if exists stock");
            s.execute("create table stock(bucket int primary key, qty int not null check (qty >= 0))");
            s.execute("insert into stock select g, " + (STOCK / BUCKETS) + " from generate_series(0," + (BUCKETS - 1) + ") g");
            s.execute("create table orders(customer int primary key, created_at timestamptz default now())");
        }
        soldOut = false; ticketSeq.set(0); admittedUpTo.set(0); requests.set(0);
        ScheduledExecutorService admitter = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor();
        if (design == 2) admitter.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> admittedUpTo.addAndGet(30), 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        HttpClient http = HttpClient.newBuilder().version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_1_1).executor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()).build();
        long[] answeredAt = new long[CUSTOMERS]; int[] outcome = new int[CUSTOMERS]; long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        Random r = new Random(48); long[] arriveAt = new long[CUSTOMERS];
        for (int i = 0; i < CUSTOMERS; i++) arriveAt[i] = (long) (r.nextDouble() * 2_000_000_000L);
        Integer[] byArrival = new Integer[CUSTOMERS]; for (int i = 0; i < CUSTOMERS; i++) byArrival[i] = i; Arrays.sort(byArrival, Comparator.comparingLong(i -> arriveAt[i]));
        int[] arrivalRank = new int[CUSTOMERS]; for (int k = 0; k < CUSTOMERS; k++) arrivalRank[byArrival[k]] = k;
        try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < CUSTOMERS; i++) {
                final int id = i;
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    long wait = t0 + arriveAt[id] - System.nanoTime(); if (wait > 0) Thread.sleep(wait / 1_000_000, (int) (wait % 1_000_000));
                    long start = System.nanoTime(), deadline = start + 25_000_000_000L; Random jr = new Random(id);
                    if (design == 2) {
                        long ticket = Long.parseLong(http.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(base + "/join")).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());
                        while (System.nanoTime() < deadline) {
                            String st = http.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(base + "/status?ticket=" + ticket)).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body();
                            if (st.equals("soldout")) { outcome[id] = 409; answeredAt[id] = System.nanoTime() - start; return null; }
                            if (st.equals("admitted")) break;
                            Thread.sleep(1500 + jr.nextInt(1000));                 // poll interval the waiting room asks for
                        }
                    }
                    while (System.nanoTime() < deadline) {
                        try {
                            int code = http.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(base + "/checkout?customer=" + id)).timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3)).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.discarding()).statusCode();
                            if (code == 200 || code == 409) { outcome[id] = code; answeredAt[id] = System.nanoTime() - start; return null; }
                            Thread.sleep(1000 + jr.nextInt(1000));                           // 503: Retry-After, with jitter
                        } catch (HttpTimeoutException e) { Thread.sleep(200 + jr.nextInt(300)); }   // gave up waiting; try again
                    }
                    return null;
                });
            }
        }
        admitter.shutdownNow();
        int bought = 0, sold409 = 0, none = 0, fair = 0; List<Long> t = new ArrayList<>();
        int dbOrders; try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(DB); ResultSet rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("select count(*) from orders")) { rs.next(); dbOrders = rs.getInt(1); }
        Set<Integer> buyers = new HashSet<>(); try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(DB); ResultSet rs = c.createStatement().executeQuery("select customer from orders")) { while (rs.next()) buyers.add(rs.getInt(1)); }
        for (int i = 0; i < CUSTOMERS; i++) {
            if (outcome[i] == 200) bought++; else if (outcome[i] == 409) sold409++; else none++;
            if (outcome[i] != 0) t.add(answeredAt[i]);
        }
        for (int b : buyers) if (arrivalRank[b] < STOCK) fair++;
        Collections.sort(t);
        System.out.printf("   %-46s %,10d %,12d %,12d %9.2f s %11.2f s %13.1f%%%n", name, bought, sold409, none, t.get(t.size() / 2) / 1e9, t.get((int) (t.size() * 0.99)) / 1e9,
                100.0 * fair / Math.max(1, dbOrders));
        if (dbOrders != bought) System.out.printf("        (%,d orders in the database — %,d buyers never heard back: their request timed out after the box was theirs)%n", dbOrders, dbOrders - bought);
    }
}
java -cp postgresql-42.7.4.jar -Duser.timezone=UTC -Dsun.net.httpserver.nodelay=true WaitingRoomL4.java
Checkout service (10 DB connections, ~20 ms DB work per checkout), 2,000 boxes, 8,000 customers arriving within 2 s;
clients time out at 3 s and retry.

   design                                             bought    told sold    no answer   answer p50     answer p99   fair (bought
                                                                      out      in 25 s                             & first 2,000)
   W1) no admission control                              162          263        7,575     22.48 s       24.76 s          43.4%
        (2,000 orders in the database — 1,838 buyers never heard back: their request timed out after the box was theirs)
   W2) 40 in flight, fast 503 + Retry-After            2,000        6,000            0      7.72 s        9.47 s          31.2%
   W3) virtual waiting room, admit 300/s FIFO          2,000        6,000            0      7.93 s        9.91 s          91.7%

   → without admission control the crowd queues inside the service for database connections: requests time out,
     clients retry, and the retries join the same queue — work is done for people who have already given up, and
     who gets a box is decided by retry luck. Shedding with a fast 503 protects the database, but the order in which
     people are served is still random. A waiting room turns the crowd into an ordered queue in front of the
     service: the database sees a steady, safe rate, every customer gets an answer and a position, and the first
     to arrive are the first to buy. For a flash sale, fairness is part of correctness.

Reading it:

  • W1: the database sold all 2,000 boxes, but only 162 customers heard so. 1,838 buyers timed out after their box was already theirs, and 7,575 customers got no answer within 25 s. This is the retry storm: requests queued inside the service for connections, clients gave up and retried, and the retries joined the queue.
  • W2: the concurrency limit sheds quickly and everyone gets an answer in under 10 s. But who wins depends on retry timing: only 31% of buyers were among the first 2,000 arrivals.
  • W3: the waiting room answers everyone in a similar time, and 92% of buyers were among the first 2,000. The database saw a steady 300 checkouts/s.
  • Idempotent checkout matters here too. The first version of this lab returned "sold out" to customers whose earlier, timed-out request had already bought them a box. The fix returns the existing order.

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Symptom Mitigation Hot row Pool exhaustion, collateral latency (L1) Buckets, gate, bulkheads per SKU class Locks across round trips Longer queues (L1) Conditional UPDATE, tiny transactions Probing empty buckets DB flooded after sell-out (L1) Sold-out flag Gate/DB drift Leaked or oversold stock Seed from DB, reconcile, gate never authoritative Long holds Stranded stock (L2) Short TTL + extension on intent Late captures Charged, no item (L2) Re-reserve or auto-refund Phantom stock Missing items (L3) Learned buffers, picker feedback Flash crowd Timeouts, retry storms, unfairness (L4) Waiting room, idempotent retries

docs.title: 6.2 Observability
docs.text:
• Reservation latency and lock waits per SKU; top contended rows.
  • Held vs confirmed vs expired reservations; stranded stock; late captures.
  • Pick shortfalls per SKU/store; buffer effectiveness.
  • Waiting-room queue length, admission rate, time to answer, abandonment.

docs.title: 6.3 Security
docs.text:
• Bot protection and per-customer limits on flash deals (Ch 39).
  • Signed waiting-room tokens bound to customer and sale.
  • Server-side price and promo computation only.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance
docs.text:
• Reservation transaction: two statements, no remote calls.
  • Separate connection pools (bulkheads) for flash-sale SKUs.
  • Pre-warm and pre-scale before announced sales; load test with the real crowd shape.

docs.title: 6.5 Cost
docs.text:
• Flash-sale infrastructure (gate, waiting room) is used a few hours a month: edge-hosted and serverless options fit.
  • Buffers trade hidden stock for fewer refunds and support calls; measure both in rupees (Ch 35).

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Read-check-write stock updates

Race conditions oversell; use a conditional UPDATE.

2. Payment calls inside the reservation transaction

Locks held for seconds.

3. One row for a national deal

~800/s and a 250 ms p99 for everyone (L1).

4. Buckets without a sold-out flag

Losers probe every bucket forever (L1).

5. Treating the Redis gate as the truth

It drifts; the database decides.

6. Long reservation holds in flash sales

Stock stranded in abandoned carts (L2).

7. No late-capture path

Customers charged for items that are gone (L2).

8. Believing recorded stock

Phantom units become missing items (L3).

9. Ignoring picker feedback

The same phantom unit is sold again and again.

10. No admission control

Retry storms; buyers who never learn they bought (L4).

11. Non-idempotent checkout retries

"Sold out" shown to a customer who already bought.

12. Unfair access

Retry luck decides winners (L4) — customers notice.

docs.title: Beginner B2
docs.text:
Q1 [B2] ⭐ How do you prevent overselling stock?

30-second answer: Make the check and the decrement one atomic operation — UPDATE stock SET qty = qty − 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty > 0 — and treat zero rows updated as "not available", with a CHECK (qty >= 0) as a safety net. Record the reservation in the same transaction. Never read, check in code, then write.

Deep answer: L1: all four designs oversold 0; they differed in throughput and database load.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Row-lock contention on hot items.

Follow-ups: 1. Multiple items? → One transaction per store, lock rows in a consistent order. 2. Across stores? → Separate reservations, saga.

Red flags: if (stock > 0) stock-- in application code.

Q2 [B2] ⭐ What is a stock reservation and why does it expire?

30-second answer: A lease: stock set aside for a checkout until payment completes or the lease expires. It prevents selling the same unit twice while the customer pays, and expiry returns stock from abandoned checkouts. The TTL is a business choice between stranded stock and slow payers.

Deep answer: L2: 30-minute holds left 1,621 boxes unsold; 3-minute holds refunded 460 late payers.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Normal days vs flash sales need different TTLs.

Follow-ups: 1. Extend? → On evidence of intent (payment started). 2. Late payments? → Re-reserve or refund.

Red flags: Reservations that never expire.

Q3 [B2] What is the checkout flow?

30-second answer: Validate cart, prices, promos and slot; reserve stock; create payment; on capture confirm reservations and create the order; on failure or expiry release reservations; everything idempotent under a checkout id; implemented as a saga with an outbox.

Deep answer: §2.9; Ch 13.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Reserve before or after payment? Before, so customers don't pay for unavailable items.

Follow-ups: 1. Partial availability? → Ask the customer. 2. Price change mid-checkout? → Show and confirm.

Red flags: A distributed transaction across inventory and payment gateway.

Q4 [B2] Why is a flash sale harder than normal peak traffic?

30-second answer: Normal load is spread across stores and SKUs; a flash sale concentrates demand on one SKU (one hot row) and brings a crowd far above capacity within seconds. That causes lock contention, pool exhaustion, timeouts and retry storms — and fairness becomes visible to customers.

Deep answer: L1 and L4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Engineering effort for a few hours a month.

Follow-ups: 1. Estimation? → Ch 02: ~250/s on one row nationally. 2. First mitigation? → Bulkhead the flash SKU.

Red flags: "Autoscaling will handle it."

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do you handle a single SKU with thousands of reservations per second?

30-second answer: Split its stock into buckets (N rows) so locks spread; cache a sold-out flag; put a Redis decrement-if-positive gate in front to reject losers without touching the database; or queue reservations per SKU to a single consumer. Keep the reservation transaction tiny and isolate the SKU's traffic.

Deep answer: L1: one row ~820/s; 16 buckets ~3,860/s but 245k DB transactions without a sold-out flag; gate kept the DB to 5,000 transactions.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Complexity; stranded stock in buckets; gate drift.

Follow-ups: 1. Bucket count? → From target rate / per-row rate. 2. End of sale? → Rebalance buckets.

Red flags: Just adding database replicas (writes don't scale that way).

Q6 [B2] SELECT FOR UPDATE or a conditional UPDATE?

30-second answer: A conditional UPDATE does the check and write in one statement and holds the lock only for that statement's duration inside a short transaction. SELECT FOR UPDATE holds the lock across at least two round trips. Use FOR UPDATE only when the decision needs data you can't express in the UPDATE.

Deep answer: L1: FOR UPDATE ~13% slower and higher p99 on the hot row.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Expressiveness vs lock time.

Follow-ups: 1. Optimistic locking? → Retry storms on hot rows. 2. SKIP LOCKED? → For work queues, not stock.

Red flags: Long transactions with user think-time.

Q7 [B2] How do you release stock from abandoned checkouts?

30-second answer: Reservations carry expires_at; a sweeper periodically marks expired HELD reservations EXPIRED and returns their quantity in the same transaction; confirmation checks expiry too. Payment events extend active leases when the customer starts paying.

Deep answer: L2's policies.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Sweeper frequency vs precision.

Follow-ups: 1. Redis TTL keys instead? → Expiry notifications aren't reliable; keep the DB authoritative. 2. Sweeper crashes? → Idempotent, restartable.

Red flags: Relying on the client to release.

Q8 [B2] How do you keep prices and promotions consistent through checkout?

30-second answer: Recompute prices and promos server-side at checkout, show changes before payment, reserve coupon budgets like stock, and snapshot final line prices, taxes and discounts into the order for invoices and refunds.

Deep answer: §2.8.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Honour cart prices briefly vs always current prices.

Follow-ups: 1. Coupon exhaustion race? → Atomic decrement of the budget. 2. Price drop after payment? → Policy decision.

Red flags: Trusting prices from the client.

Q9 [B2] What's phantom inventory and how do you deal with it?

30-second answer: Recorded stock that isn't physically on the shelf (damage, wastage, misplacement, theft). Checkout sells it; pickers can't find it. Mitigate with per-SKU buffers learned from pick failures, immediate record correction when a pick fails, cycle counts, and substitution options.

Deep answer: L3: 3.91% of orders had a missing item selling to recorded stock; learned buffers + corrections 0.40%.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Buffers hide sellable stock.

Follow-ups: 1. Fresh produce? → Larger buffers, weight-based items. 2. Measure accuracy? → Cycle-count variance per SKU.

Red flags: Treating the database as the shelf.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ Design admission control for a flash sale.

30-second answer: A waiting room in front of checkout: customers get signed tickets in arrival order (with a randomised pre-queue for those who arrive before start), are admitted at a rate the backend sustains (adjusted from latency), poll with server-suggested intervals, and check out idempotently when admitted. Add per-customer limits and bot protection.

Deep answer: L4: no control left 7,575 of 8,000 without an answer; fast 503 answered all but only 31% of buyers were early arrivals; the waiting room 92%.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Waiting-room latency vs fairness and stability.

Follow-ups: 1. Where to host it? → Edge/CDN workers. 2. Estimating wait? → Position ÷ admission rate.

Red flags: Relying on autoscaling for a 100x spike.

Q11 [B3] A payment completes after its reservation expired. What happens?

30-second answer: The checkout saga handles it explicitly: try to re-reserve the items; if available, confirm the order; if not, refund automatically and notify the customer. Never confirm without stock, and never ignore the payment.

Deep answer: L2: late captures ranged from 0 (30-minute holds) to 460 (3-minute holds); extending on payment start cut them to 123.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Holding longer vs refunding more.

Follow-ups: 1. Partial availability? → Confirm available items, refund the rest. 2. Communication? → Immediate, with refund timeline.

Red flags: Oversell to avoid the refund.

Q12 [B3] How do you keep a hot SKU from slowing down every other checkout?

30-second answer: Bulkheads: separate connection pools or even a separate service path for flash SKUs, admission control in front of them, timeouts shorter than the pool wait, and a gate that rejects losers without touching the database. Normal SKUs keep their own capacity.

Deep answer: §1.1's failure was shared pool exhaustion (Ch 18).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Idle reserved capacity.

Follow-ups: 1. Which SKUs? → Configured by merchandising for sales, detected automatically otherwise. 2. Database-level? → Separate schema or instance for flash inventory.

Red flags: One pool for everything.

Q13 [B3] How would you use Redis in inventory, safely?

30-second answer: As a front-gate or cache, not the source of truth: seed counts from the database, decrement atomically with Lua, write winners durably to the database, reconcile gate and database periodically (and after crashes), and fall back to database-only if Redis is unavailable.

Deep answer: L1: the gate kept 15,000 losers off the database.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed vs a second copy of truth.

Follow-ups: 1. Gate says yes, DB says no? → Reject; the DB wins. 2. Gate says no, DB has stock? → Reconciliation returns it.

Red flags: Redis as the only stock record.

Q14 [B3] How do you make checkout retries safe?

30-second answer: An idempotency key per checkout attempt stored with its outcome: retries return the original result (order created, or failure reason) rather than re-running reservation or payment; downstream calls carry the checkout id; consumers dedupe by it.

Deep answer: L4: without idempotent results, a timed-out buyer who retried could be told "sold out" for a box they'd bought.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Key retention vs storage.

Follow-ups: 1. Concurrent duplicates? → Unique key insert first; second waits or returns in-progress. 2. Changed cart with same key? → Reject: key bound to request hash.

Red flags: Deduping by timestamps.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design checkout and inventory reservation for a 300-store quick-commerce platform end to end.

30-second answer: Inventory per dark store with atomic conditional updates; buckets and a Redis gate for hot SKUs; reservation leases with short TTLs extended on payment start; a checkout saga with idempotency, outbox and explicit late-capture handling; per-SKU buffers and picker feedback; waiting rooms and bulkheads for flash sales; observability on contention, leases, shortfalls and fairness.

Deep answer: §4 and L1–L4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Simplicity for normal days vs machinery for sales.

Follow-ups: 1. Multi-region? → Stores are regional; inventory stays in-region. 2. Biggest risk? → Flash sales and phantom stock.

Red flags: Global inventory row for all stores.

Q16 [B4] How do you estimate and load-test a flash sale?

30-second answer: Estimate peak arrivals from audience × click-through × time window, per SKU and per store; compute required reservation rate vs per-row capacity; load-test with the real crowd shape (a spike in seconds, retries with timeouts), not a ramp; verify admission, bulkheads and fairness; rehearse the runbook.

Deep answer: L4 shows why ramps lie: the failure is the spike plus retries.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Test cost vs incident cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Client retry behaviour? → Include it in the load model. 2. Kill switch? → Pause admission.

Red flags: Testing at 3x steady load.

Q17 [B4] Reserve inventory at add-to-cart or at checkout?

30-second answer: At checkout for most grocery flows: add-to-cart reservations strand stock for browsing customers. Exceptions: extremely scarce items where a short cart hold improves experience. In both cases, use leases with short TTLs and show availability honestly.

Deep answer: L2's stranded-stock numbers grow with hold time.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Disappointment at checkout vs stranded stock.

Follow-ups: 1. Show "only 2 left"? → From recorded stock minus buffer. 2. Slot capacity? → Same lease pattern.

Red flags: Holding stock for every cart.

Q18 [B4] How do inventory accuracy and the checkout connect organisationally?

30-second answer: Accuracy is a joint data loop: dark-store ops (counts, wastage recording, picker scans) feed inventory; checkout consumes it with buffers. Define shared metrics (pick shortfall rate, cycle-count variance), give ops tools to correct stock quickly, and make buffer policy a joint business decision.

Deep answer: L3's picker feedback reduced missing-item orders by a further 20%.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Ops effort vs customer experience.

Follow-ups: 1. Incentives? → Reward accurate counts, not just speed. 2. Automation? → Computer vision shelf counts.

Red flags: Treating inventory as purely an engineering table.

Q19 [B4] How do you make flash sales fair?

30-second answer: A waiting room with arrival-order admission (randomised among pre-start arrivals), per-customer limits, bot and multi-account detection, signed tickets, and transparent positions; no advantage from faster retries. Measure fairness (buyers' arrival ranks) and publish rules.

Deep answer: L4: 92% vs 31% of buyers among the first arrivals.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Friction for customers vs fairness.

Follow-ups: 1. Bots? → Device attestation, limits (Ch 39). 2. Lottery instead? → Fairer for very scarce items.

Red flags: First-to-retry wins.

Q20 [B4] What metrics prove checkout is healthy?

30-second answer: Checkout success rate and latency; reservation lock waits per SKU; held/expired/confirmed ratios; stranded stock and late captures; missing-item rate at picking; oversell (must be 0); waiting-room time-to-answer and fairness during sales; conversion from cart to order.

Deep answer: §6.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Technical vs customer outcome metrics — both.

Follow-ups: 1. Page on? → Oversell > 0, checkout success drop, lock waits. 2. Post-sale review? → Fairness and stranded stock.

Red flags: Only API latency.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Atomic conditional updates in tiny transactions; never hold locks across round trips (L1).
  2. Hot SKUs: buckets + sold-out flag + Redis gate; the database stays authoritative (L1).
  3. Reservations are leases: short TTL, extend on intent, explicit late-capture path (L2).
  4. Recorded stock is an estimate: learned buffers and picker feedback (L3).
  5. Flash crowds need a waiting room for survival and fairness; retries must be idempotent (L4).

docs.title: Decision cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Choice Normal reservations Conditional UPDATE + INSERT per store Hot SKU 16+ buckets, sold-out flag, Redis gate Reservation TTL 3 min in sales, extend to 15 on payment start; longer on normal days Late capture Re-reserve or auto-refund Inventory accuracy Per-SKU buffers, picker corrections, cycle counts Flash crowd Waiting room FIFO + bulkheads + idempotent checkout

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (B2) In L1, add a sold-out flag to design C. How many DB transactions remain?
  2. (B3) In L1, combine the Redis gate with 16 buckets. Does sell-out time improve?
  3. (B3) In L2, add a per-customer limit of 2 boxes and a 20% share of customers who re-try after abandonment.
  4. (B3) In L3, vary the buffer multiplier (0.5–3.0) and plot missing-item orders against hidden units.
  5. (B4) In L4, make the admission rate adaptive (increase while p95 < 500 ms). What rate does it settle at?

docs.title: 47. Case Study: Delivery Dispatch & Live Tracking
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B2 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 03 (SSE tracking), Ch 06 (Redis GEO), Ch 14 (rider location topic), Ch 41 (presence from location) · What you will build: Everything between "order packed" and "delivered": geofenced serviceability, rider GPS ingestion, the live rider index, dispatch (which rider takes which order), ETAs and live tracking on the customer's screen. This is the "design Uber/Swiggy dispatch" interview question for a quick-commerce platform. Earlier chapters deferred all of it here: polygon serviceability (Ch 01), telemetry ingestion (Ch 03, Ch 14), H3/geohash indexing and dispatch algorithms (Ch 06).

  • L1: geo indexes (real Redis for riders). Serviceability over 400 store polygons and 200,000 customer locations:
    • Testing every polygon took 1,457 ms (136.7 polygon tests per lookup).
    • A 500 m grid index took 78 ms (1.9 tests per lookup), with the same answers.
    • For the nearest 5 of 20,000 riders, brute force took 780 µs p50, a 1 km grid 11 µs, and Redis GEOSEARCH 468 µs including the network round trip.
  • L2: GPS ingestion (real Redis). 250,000 pings from 50,000 riders, 3% delivered late:
    • Two commands per ping reached ~12,800 pings/s and left 480 riders at an older position.
    • An ordering-safe Lua script per ping gave 0 stale riders.
    • Pipelining reached ~94,500 pings/s.
    • A movement filter for the live index cut Redis writes from 250,000 to 145,061.
  • L3: dispatch. 6 dark stores × 10 riders at evening peak:
    • FIFO to riders standing at the store delivered 40% within the 20-minute promise.
    • Also assigning riders on their way back raised that to 53%.
    • Batching two orders to nearby customers raised it to 61%.
    • Both together reached 69%, with the average falling from 24.8 to 18.0 minutes.
  • L4: ETAs. Across 6,677 evaluated deliveries:
    • A city-wide speed was off by 4.6 min on average, and 49% arrived after the promise.
    • Zone × hour speeds and learned door times per building brought that to 2.4 min and 28%.
    • Re-estimating halfway from the rider's actual pace brought it to 1.2 min and 11.5%.

· Reading time: 110 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: the rider who was "2 minutes away" for 20 minutes
docs.text:
The first delivery system was simple: customers served by pincode, the nearest idle rider at the store assigned when an order was packed, rider positions written to a table every 4 seconds, and an ETA of distance ÷ 18 km/h. At scale:

  1. Serviceability was wrong at the edges. Pincodes don't match 3 km delivery radii. Customers across a lake or a highway were accepted and then waited 40 minutes; customers just inside the radius but in the "wrong" pincode were turned away.
  2. The position table melted. 50,000 riders × 1 ping every 4 s is 12,500 writes/s. Updates queued; "live" positions were a minute old, and dispatch sent riders who had already left.
  3. Positions jumped backwards. Phones buffer pings in tunnels and send them later; a late ping overwrote a newer position, and the customer's map showed the rider reversing.
  4. Riders waited while orders waited. At 8 pm, orders queued for riders at the store while riders were two minutes away on their way back. Dispatch only considered riders standing at the store.
  5. The ETA lied most at the worst time. "Arriving in 2 minutes" in the evening jam, and in the gated complex whose security desk takes five minutes. Support calls peaked exactly when the ETA was least honest.

Delivery is where the product's promise ("in 20 minutes") is kept or broken. This chapter designs the geo, streaming, optimisation and estimation systems behind it.

The thesis of this chapter

Delivery is a real-time, geo-indexed control loop: positions stream in, an index answers "who is near", an optimiser decides "who goes where", and an estimator tells the customer "when". Geo questions are answered by a coarse index plus an exact check (L1). Telemetry is a high-volume stream that must be order-safe and thinned before it hits the live index (L2). Dispatch is an optimisation over the next few minutes — predicted availability and batching beat nearest-idle-rider (L3). ETAs come from learned speeds, learned last-100-metre times and live progress, and promises are sized from the error distribution (L4).

docs.title: 1.2 Where this lives in the grocery platform
docs.text: Concern Data Freshness Store Serviceability Store delivery polygons Hours In-memory grid/H3 index per city Rider positions Raw GPS pings Seconds Kafka delivery.rider.location.v1 → Redis GEO (live), time-series store (history) Rider state Idle, to-store, at-store, delivering, offline Seconds Redis hash + dispatch service memory Dispatch Packed and soon-packed orders, rider predictions Every ~10–30 s Dispatch service per store cluster ETA Speeds per zone × hour, door times per building, live progress Model daily, estimate per update Model store + request-time computation Tracking Rider position and ETA for the customer ~2–5 s SSE stream (Ch 03)

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end you will be able to:

  • Index geo data for serviceability polygons and nearest-rider queries (L1).
  • Ingest rider telemetry at scale, order-safely, and keep the live index lean (L2).
  • Design dispatch: assignment, predicted availability, batching, and fairness to riders (L3).
  • Estimate and communicate ETAs honestly (L4).
  • Serve live tracking, handle privacy and operate the loop.

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: an air-traffic controller for scooters B2
docs.text: A controller has a radar (positions), a map of airspace (zones), a queue of planes wanting to land (orders), and runways (riders). They don't assign the nearest runway to each plane the moment it appears; they plan a few minutes ahead, pair things efficiently, and tell each plane an honest arrival time, updated as conditions change. Dispatch works the same way, with the radar fed by 50,000 phones.

docs.title: 2.2 Requirements B2
docs.text:
Functional

  • Decide if an address is serviceable and by which store (polygon zones, with overrides for rain, events and store load).
  • Track rider positions and states; show the customer the rider on a map with an ETA.
  • Assign packed orders to riders, with batching; reassign on problems.
  • Rider app: offers, navigation, proof of delivery, earnings.

Non-functional

  • Serviceability lookup < 5 ms; nearest riders < 10 ms.
  • Ingest ~12,500 pings/s (peaks ~20k), live positions < 5 s old.
  • Dispatch decisions within seconds of an order being packed (or predicted to be packed).
  • ETA error small enough that promises hold ≥ 90% of the time.

docs.title: 2.3 Estimation B2
docs.text:
Quantity Estimate Riders online at peak ~50,000 Ping rate 1 per 4 s → 12,500/s; ~200 bytes each → ~2.5 MB/s raw, ×RF3 in Kafka (Ch 14 exercise) Live index 50k riders × ~100 B = ~5 MB in Redis GEO — trivial size, high write rate History ~1 billion pings/day; days in the hot time-series store, months in the lake Dispatch ~1.5M orders/day; peak ~50/s nationally, ~0.5/min per store at the busiest (L3's setting) Tracking streams ~150k concurrent customers watching

The data is small; the rates and freshness are the challenge.

docs.title: 2.4 Geo indexing ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Every geo question is answered in two steps: a coarse index to find a few candidates near the point, then an exact check on those candidates.

Question Coarse index Exact check Which store's polygon contains this address? Grid/geohash/H3 cells → polygons overlapping each cell Point-in-polygon (ray casting) Nearest available riders Grid cells or Redis GEO (geohash in a sorted set) Distance, then road distance/ETA for the top few Riders inside a zone Cells covering the zone Point-in-polygon

L1 measured both:

Query Method Cost Correct Serviceability (400 polygons, 200k lookups) Brute force 1,457 ms, 136.7 polygon tests/lookup ✓ 500 m grid index 78 ms, 1.9 tests/lookup ✓ identical Nearest 5 of 20k riders Brute force 780 µs p50 ✓ 1 km grid, expanding rings 11 µs p50 ✓ identical Redis GEOSEARCH 468 µs p50, incl. network ✓ (near-ties can swap: haversine vs flat distance)
  • Geohash encodes lat/lon into a string prefix: nearby points usually share prefixes, but neighbours across cell boundaries don't. Always search neighbouring cells too.
  • H3 (Uber's hexagonal grid) and S2 (Google's) give uniform cells and hierarchical resolutions. H3 hexagons have equidistant neighbours, which is useful for zone-level aggregates such as demand, supply and surge.
  • Serviceability as data: store polygons are edited by ops, versioned, and compiled into a per-city index (cell → candidate stores) that every service loads in memory. Dynamic overrides (rain, store overload) shrink polygons or change priorities in real time.
  • Straight line is only a filter. Final ranking needs road distance or ETA (L4), especially across rivers, railway lines and one-way systems.

docs.title: 2.5 Telemetry ingestion ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Rider apps send positions over HTTP/2 or MQTT to a gateway, which writes them to Kafka keyed by rider id (per-rider order within a partition). Consumers then feed:

  • the live index (Redis GEO + last-seen hash) for dispatch and presence (Ch 41),
  • the tracking fan-out for customers watching their order,
  • the history store (time-series or lake) for ETAs, disputes and payouts.

L2 replayed 250,000 pings with 3% delivered late into a real Redis:

Ingester Throughput Redis commands Riders left at an older position GEOADD + HSET per ping, no ordering check 12,781 pings/s 500,000 480 Lua per ping, drops older pings 20,865 250,000 0 Lua, pipelined in batches of 200 94,526 250,000 0 + write only if moved > 20 m or 15 s passed 162,832 145,061 0
  • Order safety: phones buffer and resend. Compare timestamps atomically (Lua, or a conditional update), or late pings move riders backwards.
  • Batching: one round trip per ping caps throughput; batch per consumer poll.
  • Thinning: the live index needs news, not every ping. Stationary riders at the store send nothing new. Raw pings still go to history.
  • GPS noise: snap to roads, drop impossible jumps (speed > 80 km/h), and smooth positions for display.
  • Battery and data: adaptive ping rates (faster while delivering, slower while idle) are the biggest lever of all.

docs.title: 2.6 Dispatch ⭐ B4
docs.text:
Dispatch assigns orders to riders to minimise delivery time (and keep promises) at a given fleet size. L3 simulated the evening peak:

Policy Avg p90 Within 20 min Riding min/order FIFO to riders standing at the store 24.8 min 39.3 min 40.0% 20.0 + assign riders on their way back 21.6 min 33.3 min 53.2% 20.0 + batch 2 orders to nearby customers 19.0 min 26.3 min 61.3% 17.5 Both 18.0 min 24.6 min 69.1% 17.8
  • Predicted availability: include riders who will reach the store before the order is packed. Dispatch plans on when things will be ready, from packing ETAs and rider ETAs, not on current state.
  • Batching: two orders to neighbouring doors turn one return trip into two deliveries. Cap the detour and the second customer's extra wait.
  • Assignment algorithms: greedy (fast, myopic) → batched optimisation every N seconds (bipartite matching / Hungarian algorithm or min-cost flow over orders × riders, with costs from ETAs and penalties for promise risk) → rolling-horizon optimisation with predicted orders.
  • Constraints: rider shift ends, vehicle capacity, cold-chain items, rider acceptance (offers can be declined; handle timeouts and re-offers), fairness of earnings across riders.
  • Rebalancing: move idle riders between nearby stores when demand is uneven (H3 cell demand forecasts).

docs.title: 2.7 ETAs ⭐ B3
docs.text:
L4 evaluated four estimators on 6,677 held-out deliveries (promise = estimate + 2 min):

ETA method Mean error p90 error Arrived after the promise Straight line × 1.4 at 18 km/h + 2 min 4.6 min 10.5 min 49.0% Speed per (zone, hour) + 2 min 3.2 min 7.4 min 40.0% + door time per building 2.4 min 5.2 min 27.7% + re-estimate halfway from actual pace 1.2 min 2.7 min 11.5%
  • Ride time from learned speeds by zone and hour (or a routing engine with live traffic such as OSRM/GraphHopper, or a maps API), corrected by models trained on your riders' actual trips.
  • The last 100 metres — gated complexes, lifts, security desks — often dominate the error, and only your own delivery history per building knows them.
  • Live updates: once the rider is moving, their actual pace beats any prior. Update the ETA every few pings, and never let it count up suspiciously without explanation.
  • Promises use the error distribution: promise the p80–p90, not the mean. The checkout promise ("20 min") also depends on packing time and rider availability, so it must come from the same models.

docs.title: 2.8 Live tracking B3
docs.text:
• Customers watching an order subscribe via SSE (Ch 03). The tracking service consumes the rider location topic filtered by active deliveries and pushes a smoothed position + ETA every ~3–5 s.
  • Privacy: show the rider's position only during an active delivery, approximate the rider's position before pickup, and never show the customer's address to anyone but the assigned rider. Retain raw tracks for a limited time (Ch 36).
  • Degradation: if updates stop (tunnel, dead battery), show "last updated 1 min ago" and extrapolate along the route, rather than freezing silently.

docs.title: 2.9 Rider state and presence B3
docs.text:
• States: OFFLINE → IDLE_AT_STORE → ASSIGNED → PICKED_UP → DELIVERING → RETURNING → IDLE_AT_STORE. Transitions come from app actions and geofences (entered store radius, reached customer).
  • Presence is derived from the location stream with grace periods (Ch 41 L3).
  • Stuck-state detection: "delivering" for 60 minutes triggers support outreach.

docs.title: 2.10 Interview framing B4
docs.text: Draw the loop: rider app → gateway → Kafka → live index / tracking / history; order events → dispatch → offers → rider app; ETA service used by checkout, dispatch and tracking. Then go deep on geo indexing (two-step), telemetry (order, batching, thinning), and dispatch (predicted availability, batching, matching). Staff-level signals: ETAs from learned door times and live progress, promises from error distributions, privacy of positions, and planning on predictions.

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Delivery Platform v2
docs.text:
Design Document (excerpt) — Delivery Platform v2

Status: Accepted · Authors: Delivery platform team · Reviewers: Dark-store ops, Rider experience, Checkout, SRE, Legal

Field Value Context Pincode serviceability mismatched delivery radii; a position table couldn't take 12.5k writes/s; late pings moved riders backwards; dispatch ignored returning riders; ETAs were wrong in jams and at gated complexes. Decision Polygon serviceability compiled into grid/H3 indexes; telemetry through Kafka into an order-safe, batched, thinned Redis live index; dispatch with predicted availability, batching and periodic matching; ETAs from zone × hour speeds, building door times and live pace; SSE tracking with privacy rules. Related ADRs ADR-330 Serviceability polygons, versioned, compiled to 500 m grid / H3 res 8 per city (L1); ADR-331 Telemetry: Kafka keyed by rider, Lua timestamp-guarded updates, batches of 200, movement thinning for the live index (L2); ADR-332 Dispatch every 15 s per store cluster: min-cost matching over packed + soon-packed orders and present + returning riders, max 2-order batches within 1 km (L3); ADR-333 ETA = learned ride + learned door time, live re-estimation; promise at p85 (L4); ADR-334 Tracking via SSE only during active deliveries; raw tracks retained 30 days

Requirements.

  • R1 Serviceability decision < 5 ms; zone edits live within 5 minutes.
  • R2 Live positions < 5 s old for 99% of active riders; 0 backwards moves from late pings.
  • R3 ≥ 85% of orders delivered within the promise at peak.
  • R4 ETA shown to customers late by > 3 min for < 10% of deliveries.
  • R5 Rider positions visible to customers only during their active delivery.

Decisions in detail.

  1. Geo (ADR-330). Cells → candidate stores in memory in every checkout pod; overrides applied at request time.
  2. Telemetry (ADR-331). 48 partitions; consumers batch 200 or 50 ms; idle riders ping every 15 s, delivering riders every 4 s.
  3. Dispatch (ADR-332). Costs = predicted delivery time + promise-breach penalty + batch detour; Hungarian algorithm per cluster; offers expire in 20 s.
  4. ETA (ADR-333). Daily training on the last 8 weeks; door time per building with shrinkage to the neighbourhood mean for sparse buildings.
  5. Tracking (ADR-334). Smoothed positions; "last updated" when stale.

Consequences. More models to train and monitor; dispatch complexity; building-level data to maintain. In return: honest promises, faster deliveries at the same fleet size, and a live index that stays fresh at peak.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
What's real here

All four labs are JDK 21. L1 (nearest riders) and L2 run against a real Redis 7, with real GEOADD/GEOSEARCH and Lua. L1's serviceability part, L3 and L4 are deterministic simulations with fixed seeds over a synthetic city. Traffic, door times, packing times and rider speeds are stated assumptions. Timings vary by machine.

L1 and L2 need Redis 7 on port 6390. Run every lab with -Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8.

docs.title: L1 — Geo indexes B2
docs.text:
Requirement: "Decide serviceability from polygons and find nearby riders in microseconds — with exactly the same answers as checking everything."

A synthetic Bengaluru-sized city with 400 store polygons and 20,000 riders. The riders are also loaded into a real Redis GEO set.

GeoL1.java
// GeoL1.java — run with (Redis 7 on :6390):  java GeoL1.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// THE TWO GEO QUESTIONS EVERY ORDER ASKS. Bengaluru-sized synthetic city (fixed seed):
//   1) SERVICEABILITY — "which dark store's delivery zone contains this customer?" 400 stores, each with an irregular
//      polygon (12–20 vertices) — the move from pincodes to geofences that Ch 01 deferred here. 200,000 lookups:
//        brute force ray-casting against every polygon  vs  a grid index (500 m cells → candidate polygons)
//   2) NEAREST RIDERS — "the 5 closest available riders to this store": 20,000 riders.
//        brute force distance to every rider (in memory)  vs  a geohash-style grid (in memory)  vs  REAL Redis GEOSEARCH
// Correctness is checked against brute force for every query.
import java.io.*;
import java.net.Socket;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.*;

public class GeoL1 {
    static final double LAT0 = 12.85, LON0 = 77.45, SPAN = 0.30;                // ~33 km square
    static final double M_PER_DEG_LAT = 111_320, M_PER_DEG_LON = 111_320 * Math.cos(Math.toRadians(12.97));

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Random r = new Random(47);
        // ---------- 1) serviceability polygons ----------
        List<double[][]> polys = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int s = 0; s < 400; s++) {
            double cx = LAT0 + 0.02 + r.nextDouble() * (SPAN - 0.04), cy = LON0 + 0.02 + r.nextDouble() * (SPAN - 0.04); int n = 12 + r.nextInt(9);
            double[][] p = new double[n][2];
            for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) { double a = 2 * Math.PI * k / n, rad = (1_200 + r.nextDouble() * 1_400) / M_PER_DEG_LAT; p[k][0] = cx + rad * Math.cos(a); p[k][1] = cy + rad * Math.sin(a) * M_PER_DEG_LAT / M_PER_DEG_LON; }
            polys.add(p);
        }
        double cell = 500 / M_PER_DEG_LAT; int gridN = (int) Math.ceil(SPAN / cell) + 1;
        List<List<Integer>> grid = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < gridN * gridN; i++) grid.add(new ArrayList<>());
        for (int s = 0; s < polys.size(); s++) {                                     // register each polygon in the cells its bounding box covers
            double[][] p = polys.get(s); double minA = 99, maxA = -99, minB = 999, maxB = -999;
            for (double[] v : p) { minA = Math.min(minA, v[0]); maxA = Math.max(maxA, v[0]); minB = Math.min(minB, v[1]); maxB = Math.max(maxB, v[1]); }
            for (int a = cellOf(minA, LAT0, cell); a <= cellOf(maxA, LAT0, cell); a++) for (int b = cellOf(minB, LON0, cell); b <= cellOf(maxB, LON0, cell); b++)
                if (a >= 0 && b >= 0 && a < gridN && b < gridN) grid.get(a * gridN + b).add(s);
        }
        double[][] pts = new double[200_000][2]; for (double[] q : pts) { q[0] = LAT0 + r.nextDouble() * SPAN; q[1] = LON0 + r.nextDouble() * SPAN; }
        long t0 = System.nanoTime(); int[] brute = new int[pts.length]; long tests = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < pts.length; i++) { brute[i] = -1; for (int s = 0; s < polys.size(); s++) { tests++; if (inside(polys.get(s), pts[i])) { brute[i] = s; break; } } }
        double bruteMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6;
        t0 = System.nanoTime(); int mismatch = 0, served = 0; long gTests = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < pts.length; i++) {
            int found = -1; int a = cellOf(pts[i][0], LAT0, cell), b = cellOf(pts[i][1], LON0, cell);
            for (int s : grid.get(a * gridN + b)) { gTests++; if (inside(polys.get(s), pts[i])) { found = s; break; } }
            if (found != -1) served++;
            if ((found == -1) != (brute[i] == -1) || (found != -1 && !inside(polys.get(brute[i]), pts[i]))) mismatch++;
        }
        double gridMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6;
        System.out.printf("1) Serviceability: 400 store polygons, 200,000 customer locations (%.0f%% inside some zone).%n%n", 100.0 * served / pts.length);
        System.out.printf("   %-46s %12s %22s %12s%n", "method", "total time", "polygon tests / lookup", "wrong");
        System.out.printf("   %-46s %9.0f ms %22.1f %,12d%n", "brute force: test every polygon", bruteMs, (double) tests / pts.length, 0);
        System.out.printf("   %-46s %9.0f ms %22.1f %,12d%n", "grid index (500 m cells → candidate polygons)", gridMs, (double) gTests / pts.length, mismatch);

        // ---------- 2) nearest riders ----------
        int riders = 20_000; double[][] rp = new double[riders][2];
        for (double[] q : rp) { q[0] = LAT0 + r.nextDouble() * SPAN; q[1] = LON0 + r.nextDouble() * SPAN; }
        double rc = 1_000 / M_PER_DEG_LAT; int rn = (int) Math.ceil(SPAN / rc) + 1; List<List<Integer>> rg = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < rn * rn; i++) rg.add(new ArrayList<>());
        for (int i = 0; i < riders; i++) rg.get(cellOf(rp[i][0], LAT0, rc) * rn + cellOf(rp[i][1], LON0, rc)).add(i);
        try (Redis red = new Redis()) {
            red.cmd("DEL", "riders:blr"); List<String[]> batch = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int i = 0; i < riders; i++) { batch.add(new String[]{"GEOADD", "riders:blr", String.valueOf(rp[i][1]), String.valueOf(rp[i][0]), "r" + i}); if (batch.size() == 1000) { red.pipeline(batch); batch.clear(); } }
            red.pipeline(batch);
            int queries = 5_000; double[][] qs = new double[queries][2]; for (double[] q : qs) { q[0] = LAT0 + 0.03 + r.nextDouble() * (SPAN - 0.06); q[1] = LON0 + 0.03 + r.nextDouble() * (SPAN - 0.06); }
            long[] tb = new long[queries], tg = new long[queries], tr = new long[queries]; int gridWrong = 0, redisWrong = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < queries; i++) {
                long s = System.nanoTime(); List<Integer> b = bruteK(rp, qs[i], 5); tb[i] = System.nanoTime() - s;
                s = System.nanoTime(); List<Integer> g = gridK(rp, rg, rn, rc, qs[i], 5); tg[i] = System.nanoTime() - s;
                s = System.nanoTime(); List<?> res = (List<?>) red.cmd("GEOSEARCH", "riders:blr", "FROMLONLAT", String.valueOf(qs[i][1]), String.valueOf(qs[i][0]), "BYRADIUS", "3", "km", "ASC", "COUNT", "5"); tr[i] = System.nanoTime() - s;
                if (!new HashSet<>(g).equals(new HashSet<>(b))) gridWrong++;
                Set<Integer> rs = new HashSet<>(); for (Object o : res) rs.add(Integer.parseInt(((String) o).substring(1)));
                if (!rs.equals(new HashSet<>(b))) redisWrong++;
            }
            Arrays.sort(tb); Arrays.sort(tg); Arrays.sort(tr);
            System.out.printf("%n2) Nearest 5 riders to a point, %,d riders, %,d queries.%n%n", riders, queries);
            System.out.printf("   %-46s %12s %12s %30s%n", "method", "p50", "p99", "different from exact top-5");
            System.out.printf("   %-46s %9.1f µs %9.1f µs %30d%n", "brute force over every rider", tb[queries / 2] / 1e3, tb[queries * 99 / 100] / 1e3, 0);
            System.out.printf("   %-46s %9.1f µs %9.1f µs %30d%n", "grid index (1 km cells, expanding rings)", tg[queries / 2] / 1e3, tg[queries * 99 / 100] / 1e3, gridWrong);
            System.out.printf("   %-46s %9.1f µs %9.1f µs %30d%n", "Redis GEOSEARCH (network round trip incl.)", tr[queries / 2] / 1e3, tr[queries * 99 / 100] / 1e3, redisWrong);
            red.cmd("DEL", "riders:blr");
        }
        System.out.println("   (Redis uses haversine distance and 52-bit geohash-rounded positions; this lab uses a flat approximation, so riders at");
        System.out.println("    almost equal distance — the 5th and 6th — occasionally swap. Pick one distance function for ranking.)");
        System.out.println("\n   → both questions are 'find the few candidates near here, then do the exact check': a grid (or geohash, S2, H3)");
        System.out.println("     index turns 'test all 400 polygons' into ~1–3 tests, and 'measure 20,000 riders' into a few cells, with");
        System.out.println("     identical answers. Redis GEO is the same idea behind a network round trip, shared by every dispatcher. Straight-line");
        System.out.println("     distance is only the candidate filter: the final choice needs road distance and ETA (L4), and 'available' needs");
        System.out.println("     fresh positions (L2).");
    }

    static int cellOf(double v, double origin, double cell) { return (int) Math.floor((v - origin) / cell); }
    static boolean inside(double[][] poly, double[] p) {                               // ray casting
        boolean in = false;
        for (int i = 0, j = poly.length - 1; i < poly.length; j = i++)
            if ((poly[i][1] > p[1]) != (poly[j][1] > p[1]) && p[0] < (poly[j][0] - poly[i][0]) * (p[1] - poly[i][1]) / (poly[j][1] - poly[i][1]) + poly[i][0]) in = !in;
        return in;
    }
    static double dist(double[] a, double[] b) { double dx = (a[0] - b[0]) * M_PER_DEG_LAT, dy = (a[1] - b[1]) * M_PER_DEG_LON; return Math.sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy); }
    static List<Integer> bruteK(double[][] rp, double[] q, int k) {
        PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) -> Double.compare(dist(rp[y], q), dist(rp[x], q)));
        for (int i = 0; i < rp.length; i++) { pq.add(i); if (pq.size() > k) pq.poll(); }
        return new ArrayList<>(pq);
    }
    static List<Integer> gridK(double[][] rp, List<List<Integer>> g, int n, double cell, double[] q, int k) {
        int a = cellOf(q[0], LAT0, cell), b = cellOf(q[1], LON0, cell);
        PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) -> Double.compare(dist(rp[y], q), dist(rp[x], q)));
        for (int ring = 0; ring < n; ring++) {
            for (int i = a - ring; i <= a + ring; i++) for (int j = b - ring; j <= b + ring; j++) {
                if (Math.max(Math.abs(i - a), Math.abs(j - b)) != ring || i < 0 || j < 0 || i >= n || j >= n) continue;
                for (int id : g.get(i * n + j)) { pq.add(id); if (pq.size() > k) pq.poll(); }
            }
            if (pq.size() == k && dist(rp[pq.peek()], q) <= ring * cell * M_PER_DEG_LAT) break;   // kth best is closer than any unvisited ring
        }
        return new ArrayList<>(pq);
    }

    static final class Redis implements Closeable {
        final Socket s; final OutputStream out; final InputStream in;
        Redis() throws IOException { s = new Socket("127.0.0.1", 6390); s.setTcpNoDelay(true); out = new BufferedOutputStream(s.getOutputStream(), 1 << 16); in = new BufferedInputStream(s.getInputStream(), 1 << 16); }
        void write(String... parts) throws IOException { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("*").append(parts.length).append("\r\n"); for (String p : parts) { byte[] b = p.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8); sb.append('$').append(b.length).append("\r\n").append(p).append("\r\n"); } out.write(sb.toString().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)); }
        Object cmd(String... parts) throws IOException { write(parts); out.flush(); return read(); }
        void pipeline(List<String[]> cmds) throws IOException { for (String[] c : cmds) write(c); out.flush(); for (int i = 0; i < cmds.size(); i++) read(); }
        Object read() throws IOException {
            int type = in.read(); String line = line();
            return switch (type) {
                case '+' -> line; case ':' -> Long.parseLong(line);
                case '$' -> { int n = Integer.parseInt(line); if (n < 0) yield null; byte[] b = in.readNBytes(n); line(); yield new String(b, StandardCharsets.UTF_8); }
                case '*' -> { int n = Integer.parseInt(line); List<Object> l = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) l.add(read()); yield l; }
                case '-' -> throw new IOException(line);
                default -> throw new IOException("unexpected " + (char) type);
            };
        }
        String line() throws IOException { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); int c; while ((c = in.read()) != '\r') sb.append((char) c); in.read(); return sb.toString(); }
        public void close() throws IOException { s.close(); }
    }
}

2) Nearest 5 riders to a point, 20,000 riders, 5,000 queries.

   brute force over every rider                       780.1 µs    2538.9 µs                              0

    almost equal distance — the 5th and 6th — occasionally swap. Pick one distance function for ranking.)

     identical answers. Redis GEO is the same idea behind a network round trip, shared by every dispatcher. Straight-line
