   Grocery orders (this handbook)         347 / 360              13.9k / 14.4k          19.7 TB / 19.4 TB        same: distributed storage
   Chat messages                          92.6k / 80.0k          138.9k / 160.0k        1.3 PB / 1.1 PB          same: shard/partition writes, cache tier, distributed storage, stream ingest
   Rider GPS pings (writes)               15.0k / 16.0k          3.0k / 3.2k            15.1 TB / 11.5 TB        same: shard/partition writes, distributed storage
   Product reviews                        2 / 2                  1.9k / 1.6k            329 GB / 360 GB          same: single primary + replicas
   Notification sends                     4.2k / 3.6k            417 / 360              7.9 TB / 6.5 TB          same: single primary + replicas
   Photo uploads (social app)             3.1k / 2.7k            156.3k / 135.0k        739.1 PB / 729.0 PB      same: cache tier, distributed storage
   Ad click events                        130.2k / 200.0k        6.5k / 10.0k           615.9 TB / 1.1 PB        same: shard/partition writes, distributed storage, stream ingest
   worst ratio estimate vs exact: 1.8x; design decisions unchanged in 8 of 8 prompts

   → interviewers don't grade arithmetic; they grade whether the numbers drive the design. But rounding error
     compounds: rounding five inputs to 1-or-5 multiplies small errors into a 7x miss and flips decisions for
     prompts near a threshold. Keeping ONE significant figure per input is still easy mental math and keeps the
     estimate close enough that the architecture it implies rarely changes. When a result lands near a threshold,
     say so out loud and design for the higher side.

Reading it:

  • Coarse rounding compounds across five inputs into a 7× miss. It flipped the decision for GPS pings: shard or not. It flipped photos: whether writes need sharding. It flipped ad clicks: whether ingest needs a stream.
  • One significant figure is still head-arithmetic, and it never changed a decision here.

docs.title: L2 — Robust choice or close call? B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "Defend each choice under 'why not X?' — and know which ones are genuinely close."

Three decision matrices, perturbed 100,000 times.

TradeoffL2.java
// TradeoffL2.java — run with: java TradeoffL2.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// DEFENDING A CHOICE UNDER QUESTIONING. Interviewers push: "why not X?" A weighted decision matrix makes the reasoning
// explicit — but is the winner robust, or an artefact of the weights you picked? Three decisions from this handbook,
// with criteria weights and 1–5 scores as a candidate might state them (ILLUSTRATIVE judgements, not benchmarks).
// For each: the base-case winner, then 100,000 perturbations (every weight ±40%, every score ±1 with 30% chance):
// how often each option wins, and which single criterion, if its weight doubled, would change the winner.
import java.util.*;

public class TradeoffL2 {
    record Decision(String name, String[] criteria, double[] weights, String[] options, int[][] scores) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Decision> ds = List.of(
            new Decision("Cart store (read-your-writes, 5M active carts, sale spikes)",
                new String[]{"read-your-writes", "write throughput", "ops burden", "team familiarity", "cost"}, new double[]{5, 4, 3, 2, 2},
                new String[]{"PostgreSQL (partitioned)", "Redis + PG snapshot", "Managed KV (DynamoDB-like)", "Cassandra"},
                new int[][]{{5, 3, 4, 5, 4}, {4, 5, 3, 4, 3}, {4, 5, 5, 3, 3}, {3, 5, 2, 2, 3}}),
            new Decision("Event backbone (order events, replay, 20 consumers)",
                new String[]{"replay/retention", "throughput", "ordering per key", "ops burden", "ecosystem"}, new double[]{5, 3, 4, 3, 3},
                new String[]{"Kafka", "RabbitMQ", "SQS/SNS", "Pulsar"},
                new int[][]{{5, 5, 5, 2, 5}, {2, 3, 3, 4, 4}, {1, 4, 2, 5, 3}, {5, 5, 5, 2, 3}}),
            new Decision("Product search (250k SKUs, typo tolerance, facets)",
                new String[]{"relevance features", "latency at 10k qps", "ops burden", "consistency with catalog", "cost"}, new double[]{5, 4, 3, 2, 2},
                new String[]{"OpenSearch", "PostgreSQL full-text", "Managed search SaaS"},
                new int[][]{{5, 4, 2, 3, 3}, {2, 3, 5, 5, 5}, {5, 5, 5, 3, 2}}));
        Random r = new Random(57);
        for (Decision d : ds) {
            int n = d.options().length; double[] base = score(d, d.weights(), d.scores());
            int bw = argmax(base); double second = -1; for (int o = 0; o < n; o++) if (o != bw) second = Math.max(second, base[o]);
            System.out.printf("%s%n", d.name());
            for (int o = 0; o < n; o++) System.out.printf("   %-30s base score %5.1f%s%n", d.options()[o], base[o], o == bw ? "   ← base-case winner" : "");
            int[] wins = new int[n];
            for (int k = 0; k < 100_000; k++) {
                double[] w = d.weights().clone(); for (int i = 0; i < w.length; i++) w[i] *= 0.6 + 0.8 * r.nextDouble();
                int[][] s = new int[n][]; for (int o = 0; o < n; o++) { s[o] = d.scores()[o].clone(); for (int i = 0; i < s[o].length; i++) if (r.nextDouble() < 0.3) s[o][i] = Math.max(1, Math.min(5, s[o][i] + (r.nextBoolean() ? 1 : -1))); }
                wins[argmax(score(d, w, s))]++; }
            System.out.print("   wins under perturbation: "); for (int o = 0; o < n; o++) System.out.printf("%s %.0f%%   ", d.options()[o].split(" ")[0], wins[o] / 1000.0); System.out.println();
            List<String> flips = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int i = 0; i < d.criteria().length; i++) { double[] w = d.weights().clone(); w[i] *= 2; int win = argmax(score(d, w, d.scores())); if (win != bw) flips.add("'" + d.criteria()[i] + "' → " + d.options()[win]); }
            System.out.printf("   margin over runner-up: %s; doubling one weight flips it: %s%n%n", base[bw] - second < 1e-9 ? "TIE" : String.format("%.1f points", base[bw] - second), flips.isEmpty() ? "no" : String.join("; ", flips));
        }
        System.out.println("   → a matrix doesn't make the decision; it makes your reasoning inspectable. The useful output is not the");
        System.out.println("     winner but its robustness: a choice that wins under most reasonable weightings can be defended calmly;");
        System.out.println("     a tie or narrow margin should be presented as a close call, naming what would flip it ('if write throughput");
        System.out.println("     or ops burden mattered more, I'd take the managed KV'). And when the matrix disagrees with the choice you");
        System.out.println("     made (search here), say which criterion it is missing — that is the conversation senior interviews reward.");
    }
    static double[] score(Decision d, double[] w, int[][] s) { double[] out = new double[s.length]; for (int o = 0; o < s.length; o++) for (int i = 0; i < w.length; i++) out[o] += w[i] * s[o][i]; return out; }
    static int argmax(double[] a) { int b = 0; for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) if (a[i] > a[b]) b = i; return b; }
}
java TradeoffL2.java
Cart store (read-your-writes, 5M active carts, sale spikes)
   PostgreSQL (partitioned)       base score  67.0   ← base-case winner
   Redis + PG snapshot            base score  63.0
   Managed KV (DynamoDB-like)     base score  67.0
   Cassandra                      base score  51.0
   wins under perturbation: PostgreSQL 45%   Redis 12%   Managed 43%   Cassandra 0%   
   margin over runner-up: TIE; doubling one weight flips it: 'write throughput' → Managed KV (DynamoDB-like); 'ops burden' → Managed KV (DynamoDB-like)

Event backbone (order events, replay, 20 consumers)
   Kafka                          base score  81.0   ← base-case winner
   RabbitMQ                       base score  55.0
   SQS/SNS                        base score  49.0
   Pulsar                         base score  75.0
   wins under perturbation: Kafka 87%   RabbitMQ 0%   SQS/SNS 0%   Pulsar 13%   
   margin over runner-up: 6.0 points; doubling one weight flips it: no

Product search (250k SKUs, typo tolerance, facets)
   OpenSearch                     base score  59.0
   PostgreSQL full-text           base score  57.0
   Managed search SaaS            base score  70.0   ← base-case winner
   wins under perturbation: OpenSearch 3%   PostgreSQL 2%   Managed 95%   
   margin over runner-up: 11.0 points; doubling one weight flips it: no

   → a matrix doesn't make the decision; it makes your reasoning inspectable. The useful output is not the
     winner but its robustness: a choice that wins under most reasonable weightings can be defended calmly;
     a tie or narrow margin should be presented as a close call, naming what would flip it ('if write throughput
     or ops burden mattered more, I'd take the managed KV'). And when the matrix disagrees with the choice you
     made (search here), say which criterion it is missing — that is the conversation senior interviews reward.

Reading it:

  • Kafka and managed search win under most reasonable weightings. Defend them calmly.
  • The cart store is a tie. Present it as a close call and name what flips it.
  • Search: the matrix picks SaaS. The handbook chose self-run OpenSearch, which is a prompt to name the criterion the matrix is missing (control, cost at scale, residency).

docs.title: L3 — The value of the first questions B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "Design the system the interviewer means, not the one in your head."

Every plausible reading of "design a notification system", and the design each needs.

ClarifyL3.java
// ClarifyL3.java — run with: java ClarifyL3.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// WHY THE FIRST FIVE MINUTES ARE QUESTIONS. Prompt: "Design a notification system." Five things the prompt doesn't
// say, each with plausible answers (every combination is a requirement set an interviewer might have in mind):
//   scale: 1k/s | 50k/s | 1M/s burst        latency: seconds OK | < 500 ms (OTP)       guarantee: best effort | at-least-once
//   channels: push only | SMS+push+email     user prefs/quiet hours: no | yes
// A rule set (from Ch 40 and Parts I–II) maps each requirement set to the architecture it needs: queue type, priority
// lanes, provider failover, dedup store, preference service, rate limiting. We then compare:
//   Q0 skip the questions: design for the "typical" set (50k/s, seconds, at-least-once, all channels, prefs)
//   Q1..Q2 ask the most INFORMATIVE questions first (greatest reduction in uncertainty about the architecture), then
//      assume typical values for the rest
//   Q5 ask all five
// Measured: share of requirement sets for which the resulting design is right (not over-built, not missing a need).
import java.util.*;

public class ClarifyL3 {
    static final String[][] DIMS = {{"1k/s", "50k/s", "1M/s burst"}, {"seconds OK", "<500 ms"}, {"best effort", "at-least-once"}, {"push only", "SMS+push+email"}, {"no prefs", "prefs + quiet hours"}};
    static final String[] NAMES = {"scale", "latency", "guarantee", "channels", "preferences"};
    static final int[] TYPICAL = {1, 0, 1, 1, 1};

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<int[]> sets = new ArrayList<>(); enumerate(new int[5], 0, sets);
        System.out.printf("%d plausible requirement sets for \"design a notification system\"; each implies an architecture.%n%n", sets.size());
        // information gain of each question (entropy of the architecture over sets)
        Map<String, Integer> archCount = new HashMap<>(); for (int[] s : sets) archCount.merge(arch(s), 1, Integer::sum);
        double h0 = entropy(archCount.values(), sets.size());
        System.out.printf("   distinct architectures implied: %d (uncertainty %.2f bits)%n", archCount.size(), h0);
        Integer[] order = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}; double[] gain = new double[5];
        for (int d = 0; d < 5; d++) { double h = 0; for (int v = 0; v < DIMS[d].length; v++) { Map<String, Integer> c = new HashMap<>(); int n = 0; for (int[] s : sets) if (s[d] == v) { c.merge(arch(s), 1, Integer::sum); n++; } h += (double) n / sets.size() * entropy(c.values(), n); } gain[d] = h0 - h; }
        Arrays.sort(order, (a, b) -> Double.compare(gain[b], gain[a]));
        System.out.print("   information gain per question: "); for (int d : order) System.out.printf("%s %.2f bits   ", NAMES[d], gain[d]); System.out.println("\n");
        System.out.printf("   %-52s %22s %14s %14s%n", "strategy", "design right for", "over-built", "missing a need");
        for (int k : new int[]{0, 1, 2, 5}) {
            int right = 0, over = 0, under = 0;
            for (int[] s : sets) { int[] assumed = TYPICAL.clone(); for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) assumed[order[i]] = s[order[i]];
                Set<String> need = parts(s), built = parts(assumed);
                if (need.equals(built)) right++; else { if (!built.containsAll(need)) under++; else over++; } }
            String name = k == 0 ? "Q0) no questions: assume the typical set" : k == 5 ? "Q5) ask all five" : "Q" + k + ") ask the " + k + " most informative question" + (k > 1 ? "s" : "") + " (" + String.join(", ", Arrays.stream(order).limit(k).map(d -> NAMES[d]).toList()) + ")";
            System.out.printf("   %-62s %13d of %d %14d %14d%n", name, right, sets.size(), over, under);
        }
        System.out.println("\n   → an unclarified prompt is 48 different systems here. Designing for a 'typical' reading fits one of them; it");
        System.out.println("     is over-built for some (Kafka and provider failover for push-only at 1k/s) and, worse, MISSING something");
        System.out.println("     essential for 40 (usually the OTP priority lane, because 'seconds are fine' was assumed). Scale splits the");
        System.out.println("     space most, so ask it first; latency is next because its wrong default does damage rather than waste. After");
        System.out.println("     two questions nothing essential is missing, and the rest can be stated as assumptions ('I'll assume at-least-");
        System.out.println("     once and multi-channel — tell me if not'), which costs seconds and fixes the over-building.");
    }
    static void enumerate(int[] cur, int d, List<int[]> out) { if (d == 5) { out.add(cur.clone()); return; } for (int v = 0; v < DIMS[d].length; v++) { cur[d] = v; enumerate(cur, d + 1, out); } }
    static Set<String> parts(int[] s) {
        Set<String> p = new TreeSet<>();
        p.add(s[0] == 0 ? "single DB-backed queue" : s[0] == 1 ? "Kafka, partitioned workers" : "Kafka + autoscaled workers + provider rate limiting");
        if (s[1] == 1) p.add("priority lane for OTP/transactional");
        if (s[2] == 1) p.add("idempotency/dedup store + retries");
        if (s[3] == 1) p.add("per-channel adapters + provider failover");
        if (s[4] == 1) p.add("preference service + scheduler for quiet hours");
        if (s[0] == 2 && s[2] == 1) p.add("outbox + DLQ");
        return p;
    }
    static String arch(int[] s) { return String.join("|", parts(s)); }
    static double entropy(Collection<Integer> counts, int n) { double h = 0; for (int c : counts) { double p = (double) c / n; h -= p * Math.log(p) / Math.log(2); } return h; }
}
java ClarifyL3.java
48 plausible requirement sets for "design a notification system"; each implies an architecture.

   distinct architectures implied: 48 (uncertainty 5.58 bits)
   information gain per question: scale 1.58 bits   latency 1.00 bits   guarantee 1.00 bits   channels 1.00 bits   preferences 1.00 bits   

   strategy                                                   design right for     over-built missing a need
   Q0) no questions: assume the typical set                                   1 of 48              7             40
   Q1) ask the 1 most informative question (scale)                            3 of 48             21             24
   Q2) ask the 2 most informative questions (scale, latency)                  6 of 48             42              0
   Q5) ask all five                                                          48 of 48              0              0

   → an unclarified prompt is 48 different systems here. Designing for a 'typical' reading fits one of them; it
     is over-built for some (Kafka and provider failover for push-only at 1k/s) and, worse, MISSING something
     essential for 40 (usually the OTP priority lane, because 'seconds are fine' was assumed). Scale splits the
     space most, so ask it first; latency is next because its wrong default does damage rather than waste. After
     two questions nothing essential is missing, and the rest can be stated as assumptions ('I'll assume at-least-
     once and multi-channel — tell me if not'), which costs seconds and fixes the over-building.

Reading it:

  • Without questions, the design misses an essential component in 40 of 48 readings.
  • Asking scale, then latency removes every "missing" case.
  • Stating the remaining assumptions aloud removes the over-building.

docs.title: L4 — What the rubric rewards B4
docs.text:
Requirement: "Know which behaviours move the score, at your level."

Three illustrative transcripts scored against senior and staff rubrics.

RubricL4.java
// RubricL4.java — run with: java RubricL4.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// HOW A 45-MINUTE DESIGN INTERVIEW IS SCORED. A rubric of 8 signals (the ones this chapter's framework is built to
// produce), each needing specific evidence, weighted by level, plus time discipline. Three ILLUSTRATIVE transcripts of
// "design a grocery checkout" (written for this lab — timelines of what the candidate did, minute by minute) are
// scored for a senior (B3) and a staff (B4) bar. The point is to see which behaviours move the score.
import java.util.*;

public class RubricL4 {
    record Event(int minute, String signal, int quality) {}                                        // quality 1 weak – 3 strong
    static final String[] SIGNALS = {"requirements", "estimation", "api+data model", "high-level design", "deep dive", "trade-offs", "failure handling", "operability/cost"};
    static final double[] W_SENIOR = {1.0, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 1.2, 1.2, 0.6}, W_STAFF = {1.2, 0.8, 0.8, 1.0, 1.4, 1.6, 1.5, 1.2};

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, List<Event>> t = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        t.put("A — draws boxes fast", List.of(ev(1, "high-level design", 2), ev(12, "api+data model", 1), ev(18, "deep dive", 1), ev(35, "high-level design", 2), ev(43, "trade-offs", 1)));
        t.put("B — solid senior", List.of(ev(1, "requirements", 3), ev(5, "estimation", 2), ev(8, "api+data model", 2), ev(12, "high-level design", 3), ev(18, "deep dive", 3),
                ev(30, "failure handling", 2), ev(36, "trade-offs", 2), ev(42, "operability/cost", 1)));
        t.put("C — staff signals", List.of(ev(1, "requirements", 3), ev(4, "estimation", 3), ev(7, "api+data model", 2), ev(10, "high-level design", 3), ev(14, "deep dive", 3),
                ev(24, "failure handling", 3), ev(30, "trade-offs", 3), ev(36, "operability/cost", 3), ev(40, "trade-offs", 3)));
        System.out.printf("   %-24s %-10s %-10s  %-40s %s%n", "transcript (illustrative)", "senior", "staff", "missing or weak signals", "time discipline");
        System.out.printf("   %-24s %-10s %-10s%n", "", "(bar 70%)", "(bar 85%)");
        for (var e : t.entrySet()) {
            int[] best = new int[SIGNALS.length]; for (Event x : e.getValue()) { int i = Arrays.asList(SIGNALS).indexOf(x.signal()); best[i] = Math.max(best[i], x.quality()); }
            double s = score(best, W_SENIOR), st = score(best, W_STAFF);
            List<String> weak = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < SIGNALS.length; i++) if (best[i] < 2) weak.add(SIGNALS[i] + (best[i] == 0 ? " (absent)" : " (weak)"));
            int firstDesign = e.getValue().stream().filter(x -> x.signal().equals("high-level design")).mapToInt(Event::minute).min().orElse(99);
            int deep = e.getValue().stream().filter(x -> x.signal().equals("deep dive")).mapToInt(Event::minute).min().orElse(99);
            String time = firstDesign < 5 && best[0] == 0 ? "designed before asking" : deep > 25 ? "deep dive started late" : "on plan";
            System.out.printf("   %-24s %4.0f%% %-5s %4.0f%% %-5s  %-40s %s%n", e.getKey(), s, s >= 70 ? "hire" : "no", st, st >= 85 ? "hire" : "no", weak.isEmpty() ? "—" : String.join(", ", weak.subList(0, Math.min(3, weak.size()))) + (weak.size() > 3 ? " +" + (weak.size() - 3) : ""), time);
        }
        System.out.println("\n   bars (illustrative): senior ≥ 70%, staff ≥ 85%. The two rubrics also weigh the same evidence differently:");
        System.out.println("   staff puts more weight on trade-offs, failure handling and operability, less on API detail.");
        System.out.println("\n   → the fast box-drawer loses on everything the boxes don't show: no requirements, no numbers, no failure");
        System.out.println("     story. The solid senior clears the senior bar and not the staff one — the gap is exactly trade-offs argued");
        System.out.println("     under pressure, failure handling as a first-class part of the design, and cost/operability. Nothing in the");
        System.out.println("     staff transcript is exotic; it is the same framework, with every phase done deliberately and on time.");
    }
    static Event ev(int m, String s, int q) { return new Event(m, s, q); }
    static double score(int[] best, double[] w) { double s = 0, max = 0; for (int i = 0; i < best.length; i++) { s += w[i] * best[i]; max += w[i] * 3; } return 100 * s / max; }
}
java RubricL4.java
   transcript (illustrative) senior     staff       missing or weak signals                  time discipline
                            (bar 70%)  (bar 85%) 
   A — draws boxes fast       24% no      20% no     requirements (absent), estimation (absent), api+data model (weak) +4 designed before asking
   B — solid senior           79% hire    75% no     operability/cost (weak)                  on plan
   C — staff signals          96% hire    97% hire   —                                        on plan

   bars (illustrative): senior ≥ 70%, staff ≥ 85%. The two rubrics also weigh the same evidence differently:
   staff puts more weight on trade-offs, failure handling and operability, less on API detail.

   → the fast box-drawer loses on everything the boxes don't show: no requirements, no numbers, no failure
     story. The solid senior clears the senior bar and not the staff one — the gap is exactly trade-offs argued
     under pressure, failure handling as a first-class part of the design, and cost/operability. Nothing in the
     staff transcript is exotic; it is the same framework, with every phase done deliberately and on time.

Reading it:

  • Speed without requirements, numbers or failures scores poorly at any level.
  • The senior-to-staff gap is trade-offs, failure handling and operability done as first-class work. The transcripts and bars are illustrative.

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Symptom Fix Designing before asking Wrong system (L3) Two questions first, then assumptions Coarse estimates Wrong decisions (L1) One significant figure, name the thresholds No numbers at all "Hand-wavy" feedback 4–6 numbers on the board Over-engineering "Didn't fit the scale" Add components only when a number demands it Shallow everywhere "No depth" One real deep dive with code-level detail Losing the clock No failure discussion (L4) Timebox out loud Defending everything equally "Rigid" Robust vs close-call trade-offs (L2) Ignoring hints "Didn't listen" Treat questions as steering

docs.title: 6.2 Preparation plan
docs.text:
• Weeks 1–2: the foundations and core chapters on your path (Ch 00 paths).
  • Weeks 3–4: one case study a day, timed at 45 minutes on paper, before reading the chapter.
  • Weeks 5–6: mock interviews (Ch 60) with the rubric (L4), recorded and reviewed.

docs.title: 6.3 Whiteboard and virtual hygiene
docs.text:
• Layout: requirements top-left, numbers top-right, diagram in the centre, decisions and failure tables below.
  • Virtual: pre-agree on a tool (Excalidraw, a doc). Share early, and narrate what you draw.

docs.title: 6.4 Pacing
docs.text:
• Glance at the clock at minutes 5, 14, 20, 35 and 41. If you're behind, say what you'll skip.
  • If the interviewer dives early, follow them, and return to the skipped steps briefly at the end.

docs.title: 6.5 Mindset
docs.text:
• The interviewer wants you to succeed. Treat it as a design review with a colleague.
  • Say "I don't know" plus how you would find out. It beats bluffing.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Drawing in the first minute

Designing an unspecified system (L3).

2. Asking twenty questions

Ask the few that split the space, then state assumptions.

3. Arithmetic theatre

Precision without decisions.

4. Coarse rounding near thresholds

Flipped architectures (L1).

5. Buzzword architecture

Kafka, Kubernetes and microservices with no requirement behind them.

6. Never going deep

Senior interviews are won in the deep dive.

7. Ignoring failure handling

The staff signal.

8. 'Industry standard' as a justification

Name requirements and costs (L2).

9. Arguing with the interviewer

Probes are invitations, not attacks.

10. Monologuing

Check in at step boundaries.

11. Recreating your employer's system verbatim

Fit the design to the stated requirements.

12. Running out of time silently

Say what you would cover next.

docs.title: Beginner B2
docs.text:
Q1 [B2] ⭐ How do you structure a 45-minute system design interview?

30-second answer: Clarify (5 min), estimate (3), API and data model (6), high-level design (6), deep dive (15), failures and scaling (6), wrap-up (4) — timeboxed out loud, with requirements and numbers on the board and check-ins at each transition.

Deep answer: §2.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Following the interviewer's lead vs the plan.

Follow-ups: 1. 60 minutes? → Longer deep dive or evolution. 2. Interviewer jumps ahead? → Follow, backfill later.

Red flags: No structure.

Q2 [B2] ⭐ Which questions do you ask first?

30-second answer: The ones that change the architecture most: scale (orders of magnitude) and latency/consistency needs, plus the core use cases; then state assumptions for the rest and invite correction.

Deep answer: L3: no questions fit 1 of 48 readings; asking scale and latency left nothing essential missing.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Time vs certainty.

Follow-ups: 1. Interviewer says "you decide"? → State assumptions and why. 2. Non-functional list? → Availability, retention, regions.

Red flags: Starting to draw immediately.

Q3 [B2] How precise do estimates need to be?

30-second answer: Precise enough not to change decisions: one significant figure per input, standard shortcuts (a day ≈ 10⁵ s), and explicit thresholds; flag results near a threshold.

Deep answer: L1: 1-sig-fig stayed within 1.8× and preserved all 8 decisions; coarser rounding flipped 3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed vs accuracy.

Follow-ups: 1. Which numbers? → Peak writes, reads, storage, bandwidth. 2. Forgot a number? → Estimate from first principles.

Red flags: Skipping estimation entirely.

Q4 [B2] How do you choose what to deep dive on?

30-second answer: Where scarcity, money, concurrency or extreme scale meet — the part most likely to break or be wrong — or what the interviewer steers to; propose it and confirm.

Deep answer: §2.6 table.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Your strength vs their interest.

Follow-ups: 1. Two candidates? → Pick the riskier. 2. Out of depth? → Reason from principles aloud.

Red flags: Deep diving on the load balancer.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do you justify a technology choice?

30-second answer: Tie it to requirements and numbers, state its costs, and name the condition under which you'd choose the alternative: "Kafka because we need replay and per-key ordering at 50k/s; it costs operational complexity; for 1k/s without replay, a database queue would do."

Deep answer: L2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Familiarity bias.

Follow-ups: 1. Close call? → Say so. 2. Interviewer disagrees? → Explore their criterion.

Red flags: "Industry standard."

Q6 [B2] What if you realise mid-interview that you went wrong?

30-second answer: Say so explicitly, explain what changed your mind, and adjust — noticing and correcting is a positive signal; hiding it is not.

Deep answer: §3.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Time spent reworking.

Follow-ups: 1. Late in the interview? → Describe the fix verbally. 2. Interviewer hinted? → Thank and incorporate.

Red flags: Doubling down.

Q7 [B2] How much of the design should be on the board?

30-second answer: Requirements, key numbers, a clear diagram with the critical path and sync/async edges, the data model's keys, and a short failure table — the interviewer's write-up follows the board.

Deep answer: §6.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Drawing time vs talking.

Follow-ups: 1. Virtual? → Shared doc or Excalidraw. 2. Messy board? → Redraw the final version.

Red flags: Everything in speech only.

Q8 [B2] How do you handle a domain you don't know?

30-second answer: Use the framework — requirements and numbers are domain-independent; ask domain questions as requirements; map to known patterns (booking, feed, ledger, matching); be explicit about assumptions.

Deep answer: §2.10.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Asking vs assuming.

Follow-ups: 1. Specialised terms? → Ask for definitions. 2. Regulation? → Flag and move on.

Red flags: Freezing.

Q9 [B2] How do you avoid over-engineering?

30-second answer: Start with the simplest design that meets the requirements and add each component only when a requirement or number demands it, saying which; mention the evolution path for 10× instead of building it now.

Deep answer: §2.5; Ch 56 §2.11.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Showing breadth vs fit.

Follow-ups: 1. Interviewer asks for scale? → Show the 10× step. 2. Microservices? → Justify by teams/load.

Red flags: Twelve services for 300 req/s.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ What distinguishes a senior answer from a mid-level one?

30-second answer: Completeness and correctness under realistic constraints: explicit requirements and numbers, a coherent design, one deep dive with code-level precision (atomic operations, state machines), named trade-offs, and failure handling on the critical path.

Deep answer: L4: the solid senior transcript scored 79%.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Depth vs breadth.

Follow-ups: 1. What pushes to staff? → Q15. 2. Weakest area usually? → Operability.

Red flags: A generic design.

Q11 [B3] How do you discuss failures without running out of time?

30-second answer: A compact failure table for the critical path — component, failure, detection, user impact, recovery — plus money/inventory specifics (unknown outcomes, idempotency, sagas); 5–6 minutes.

Deep answer: §2.7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Breadth vs depth.

Follow-ups: 1. Region outage? → DR summary. 2. Poison messages? → DLQ.

Red flags: "We'll add retries."

Q12 [B3] How do you present data model choices?

30-second answer: From access patterns: list the queries and writes, pick keys/partitioning for them, choose the store per pattern with a reason, and note consistency needs (transactions for money/stock).

Deep answer: §2.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Polyglot complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. Hot partition? → Key design. 2. Joins? → Denormalise or read models.

Red flags: Choosing NoSQL "for scale" by default.

Q13 [B3] How do you use the interviewer's hints?

30-second answer: Treat every question as steering: acknowledge, answer briefly, and adjust the plan — a question about X usually means they want depth on X or think you missed it.

Deep answer: §6.1.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Your plan vs their signal.

Follow-ups: 1. Silent interviewer? → Check in more often. 2. Conflicting hints? → Ask what matters most.

Red flags: Ignoring questions.

Q14 [B3] How should you prepare in the last two weeks?

30-second answer: Timed practice of 8–10 core prompts on paper before reading solutions, mock interviews scored against a rubric, a personal list of thresholds and shortcuts, and 2–3 stories of real systems you can deep dive on.

Deep answer: §6.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Breadth of prompts vs depth.

Follow-ups: 1. Recording yourself? → Yes, review pacing. 2. Which prompts? → The §2.6 table.

Red flags: Reading only.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ What distinguishes a staff/principal answer?

30-second answer: Driving ambiguity (scoping, phasing), trade-offs argued with flip conditions, failure handling and operability as first-class design (blast radius, SLOs, cost), organisational awareness (teams, migration), and knowing what not to build.

Deep answer: L4: same framework, every phase deliberate — 97% vs the senior's 75% on the staff rubric.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Depth vs leadership signals.

Follow-ups: 1. Example of phasing? → Monolith → extracted cores. 2. Cost talk? → Unit cost per order.

Red flags: Just a bigger diagram.

Q16 [B4] How do you run a 'design your past system' interview?

30-second answer: Context and constraints, the key decisions with alternatives considered, what went wrong and how you found out, metrics of impact, and what you would change now — owning mistakes and showing learning.

Deep answer: §2.10.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Confidentiality vs detail.

Follow-ups: 1. Your role vs team's? → Be precise. 2. Numbers? → Approximate but real.

Red flags: Taking credit for everything.

Q17 [B4] How do you handle an interviewer who challenges a correct choice?

30-second answer: Engage with their criterion — ask what they're weighing, restate your reasoning with the requirement it serves, concede where their point changes the balance, and state the flip condition; it's a test of reasoning, not of stubbornness or capitulation.

Deep answer: L2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Holding vs updating.

Follow-ups: 1. They're wrong? → Explain politely with evidence. 2. They're right? → Update visibly.

Red flags: Folding immediately or arguing.

Q18 [B4] How do you bring cost and operations into a design interview?

30-second answer: A sentence per major component on cost drivers (egress, storage, compute at peak), unit cost (per order/request), the operability plan (SLOs, dashboards, on-call), and where you'd accept degraded behaviour to save money.

Deep answer: Ch 35.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Time budget.

Follow-ups: 1. Managed vs self-hosted? → Team capacity. 2. Biggest cost lever? → Usually data and egress.

Red flags: Never mentioning cost.

Q19 [B4] How do you show organisational thinking?

30-second answer: Mention team boundaries aligned with services (Conway), migration strategies (strangler, dual writes), rollout plans (flags, canaries), and governance (ADRs, SLO ownership) where they affect the design.

Deep answer: Ch 37.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Relevance to the prompt.

Follow-ups: 1. Team of 5 vs 50? → Different architecture. 2. Legacy constraints? → Migration path.

Red flags: Ignoring who builds it.

Q20 [B4] What are the most common reasons strong engineers fail design interviews?

30-second answer: Designing their own past system instead of the prompt, skipping requirements and numbers, no deep dive, defending choices by authority, and running out of time before failures — all fixable with the framework and timed practice.

Deep answer: §1.1, L3, L4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Experience vs presentation.

Follow-ups: 1. Fastest fix? → Timed mocks. 2. Feedback? → Ask recruiters for specifics.

Red flags: "I know this stuff, I don't need to practise."

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Clarify first. Scale and latency split the space. State the rest as assumptions (L3).
  2. Estimate to one significant figure. Name the thresholds (L1).
  3. Trade-offs: know robust from close calls, and the flip conditions (L2).
  4. Win in the deep dive and failures. That's where the rubric weights are (L4).
  5. Timebox out loud and keep the board as the record.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Minute Step Must-have output 0–5 Clarify Requirements, non-goals, assumptions 5–8 Estimate Peak writes/reads, storage, bandwidth 8–14 API + data Signatures with idempotency, keys and stores 14–20 High-level Diagram, critical path, sync/async 20–35 Deep dive Atomic ops, state machines, numbers 35–41 Failures Table: failure, detection, impact, recovery 41–45 Wrap-up Trade-offs, 10× plan, cost/ops

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (B2) Run L1 with your own assumptions for "design Instagram". Which decisions are near thresholds?
  2. (B3) Build a decision matrix for "SQL or NoSQL for orders" in L2. Is your choice robust?
  3. (B3) Enumerate the requirement space for "design a rate limiter" in L3's style. Which question comes first?
  4. (B4) Record a 45-minute mock, then score it with L4's rubric: which signals were missing?
  5. (B4) Write the one-page plan (§4) for three case studies from memory.

docs.title: 58. Level Expectations: From Engineer to Principal
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 57 (the interview framework)

What you will learn: what interviewers and promotion committees expect at each level, in behaviour rather than job titles. The four levels map to this handbook's bands:

Band Role Typical experience B1 Engineer 0–3 years B2 Senior engineer 3–7 years B3 Staff / lead 7–12 years B4 Principal / architect 12+ years

Titles vary by company (VERIFY each company's ladder). The behaviours are remarkably consistent.

The one lab answers a single question, "handle the payment gateway's webhooks", at all four levels, against real PostgreSQL. 5,000 payments with 13,475 deliveries, including duplicates, reordering, 178 lost events, two nodes and a restart:

Level What it adds Effects applied twice Status went backwards Final status wrong Money effects missing B1 In-memory dedup 830 747 755 104 B2 Database dedup in the same transaction 0 747 755 104 B3 + the domain's forward-only state machine 0 0 82 82 B4 + reconciliation with the gateway 0 0 0 0

Each level is correct under one more kind of reality.

· Reading time: 70 min + code

docs.title: 1.1 A story: the promotion packet that said "senior" for the third year
docs.text:
Priya had fifteen years of experience and a strong track record. Her staff-promotion packet listed the systems she built: the payment integration, the search migration, the notification platform. The committee's feedback was the same for the third year: "Excellent senior engineer. Staff impact not demonstrated."

Her manager eventually translated it:

  • Her packet described what she built.
  • A staff packet describes which problems she found that nobody had assigned, which decisions she drove across teams, what she chose not to build, and how the organisation's systems got better because of her (standards, reviews, mentoring, incident follow-through).

The same distinction appears in interviews. A senior candidate designs the system correctly. A staff candidate reframes the problem, argues the trade-offs, anticipates the failure modes that the organisation will actually hit, and makes the design operable and evolvable.

Level is not years, and it is not how many technologies you can name. It is the scope and ambiguity you can handle, and the kinds of failure you design for without being asked.

The thesis of this chapter

Levels differ less in what you know than in what you anticipate and how far your influence reaches:

  • B1 makes it work.
  • B2 makes it work under concurrency and load.
  • B3 makes it correct under the domain's real failure modes, and owns the trade-offs.
  • B4 makes it correct under loss and change, across teams and years: reconciliation, evolution, operability, organisation.

The lab shows the ladder on one problem.

docs.title: 1.2 The levels in one table
docs.text: Dimension B1 Engineer B2 Senior B3 Staff B4 Principal Scope A task or feature A service or feature end to end A system or domain across teams Multiple domains, platform, company direction Ambiguity Clear specs Some ambiguity, asks good questions Defines the problem; finds unassigned problems Sets direction where none exists Design depth Correct happy path Concurrency, scale, API/data design Domain failure modes, consistency, trade-offs argued Loss, evolution, economics, organisational fit Failure thinking Handles errors Retries, timeouts, idempotency State machines, sagas, degradation, SLOs Reconciliation, blast radius, DR, correlated failure Operability Logs Metrics, alerts SLOs, runbooks, on-call quality Reliability strategy, cost per unit, platform standards Influence Own work Own team, code reviews Several teams, design reviews, mentoring seniors Org-wide standards, strategy, hiring bar Time horizon Days–weeks Weeks–quarter Quarters–year Years In an interview Solves the prompt with guidance Solves it independently, one good deep dive Drives it, trade-offs with flip conditions, failures first-class Reframes it, phases it, ties it to cost, org and evolution

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end you will be able to:

  • Describe each level's expectations in observable behaviours.
  • Calibrate your own answers to the level you're interviewing for (the lab).
  • Recognise down-levelling signals and fix them.
  • Build evidence of staff/principal impact for interviews and promotions.

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: four drivers on the same road B1
docs.text:
• A learner drives safely on a clear road.
  • An experienced driver handles traffic and bad weather.
  • A professional driver knows the route's hazards (the blind curve, the flooding underpass) and plans around them.
  • A fleet manager ensures a hundred drivers are safe for years: routes, maintenance, training, incident reviews, cost.

Same road, different scope of what they anticipate and own.

docs.title: 2.2 B1: Engineer B1
docs.text:
• Expectation: implements well-defined components correctly, with tests, and asks for help appropriately.
  • In a design interview (rare at this level): produces a reasonable single-service design, knows basic storage and caching, and handles the happy path.
  • In the lab: an in-memory dedup set works in a demo, and silently double-credits once there are two nodes or a restart.
  • Growth edge: think about what happens when there are two of everything, and when things restart.

docs.title: 2.3 B2: Senior engineer ⭐ B2
docs.text:
• Expectation: owns a service or feature end to end, independently. It is correct under concurrency and load, well designed at the API and data level, and tested and monitored.
  • In a design interview:
    • clarifies requirements;
    • estimates;
    • gives a clean API and data model;
    • produces a coherent high-level design;
    • delivers one solid deep dive with atomic operations and idempotency;
    • names trade-offs.
  • In the lab: dedup in the database, in the same transaction as the effect, makes duplicates harmless. It still trusts arrival order and delivery.
  • Growth edge: model the domain's state machine and its real-world failure modes, and own decisions beyond your service.

docs.title: 2.4 B3: Staff engineer ⭐ B3
docs.text:
• Expectation: owns a system or domain across teams. Defines problems as well as solving them. Makes and documents the decisions others build on (ADRs, design docs). Raises the bar for other seniors.
  • In a design interview:
    • drives the whole session;
    • chooses the deep dive where the risk is;
    • argues trade-offs with flip conditions;
    • treats failure handling (state machines, sagas, degradation, SLOs) as part of the design;
    • discusses operability and cost unprompted.
  • In the lab: encodes the domain rule that a payment's status only moves forward, so reordered events can't corrupt it. Side effects go to an outbox. The remaining gap is loss.
  • Growth edge: assume every channel lies eventually, and design the correction loop. Think in years and organisations.

docs.title: 2.5 B4: Principal / architect ⭐ B4
docs.text:
• Expectation: sets technical direction across domains. Designs for loss, change and scale over years. Aligns architecture with organisation and economics. Shapes standards, the hiring bar and culture.
  • In a design interview:
    • reframes the prompt (what's the business goal? what's the smallest thing that works?);
    • phases the design (now, next year, at 10×);
    • designs the correction loops (reconciliation, audits);
    • quantifies reliability and cost;
    • addresses migration and team structure;
    • knows what not to build.
  • In the lab: accepts that at-least-once channels can still lose messages, and closes the loop with reconciliation against the source of truth. Every invariant reaches zero.
  • Growth edge: none that is technical. It is judgement, communication, and multiplying others.

docs.title: 2.6 The same prompt at four levels ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Prompt B1 B2 B3 B4 URL shortener Hash → DB row ID generation, cache, 301 vs 302 Hot keys, abuse, analytics pipeline, custom domains Multi-region, cost per redirect, abuse economics, product phasing Rate limiter Counter in memory Token bucket in Redis, atomic Lua Distributed accuracy vs cost, fail-open/closed per route, tenant fairness Platform policy, SLO impact, abuse strategy, org-wide adoption Checkout Insert order, decrement stock Conditional update, idempotency keys Saga with unknown outcomes, hot SKUs, degradation Reconciliation, cells, SLO composition, sale-day strategy Chat WebSocket + DB Fan-out, ordering per conversation Presence, offline delivery, exactly-once display, moderation Multi-region, privacy/compliance, cost of fan-out, product evolution Feed Query on read Fan-out on write vs read Ranking pipeline, freshness, celebrity problem Experimentation platform, ML infra, cost per impression

Every column to the right includes the one to its left. Senior answers aren't wrong at staff level; they're incomplete.

docs.title: 2.7 Down-levelling signals B3
docs.text: Signal Reads as Fix Waits for the interviewer to drive B1/B2 Propose the plan and the deep dive Components without numbers B2 Estimate, and let the numbers choose "We'll add retries" B2 Idempotency, unknown outcomes, sagas No state machine for stateful entities B2 Draw the states and allowed transitions Trade-offs stated as preferences B2 Requirement → choice → cost → flip condition Failure handling only when asked B2/B3 A failure table before the interviewer asks No operability or cost B3 SLOs, dashboards, unit cost Over-engineering for stated scale Any Phase it: now vs at 10× Past-system storytelling without the prompt Any Design what was asked

docs.title: 2.8 Evidence for staff/principal B4
docs.text:
Interviews and promotion committees look for evidence of scope, told as situation → your judgement → others' actions → measurable outcome:

  • Problems you found: "Nobody owned reconciliation. I discovered a 0.3% silent drift and drove the fix across three teams."
  • Decisions you drove: "I wrote the ADR choosing the outbox over dual writes, and it became the standard for 20 services."
  • What you stopped: "I argued against a rewrite, and proposed a strangler migration that finished in two quarters."
  • Multiplication: design reviews, a mentoring programme, guardrails in CI, paved roads.
  • Outcomes with numbers: incidents down, latency p99 down, cost per order down, lead time down.

Ch 61 turns these into interview stories.

docs.title: 2.9 Calibrating your preparation B2
docs.text: Target Prioritise B2 (senior) Foundations (Ch 02–09), core distributed systems (Ch 10–20), 8–10 case studies, timed practice B3 (staff) Plus production (Ch 21–30), decisions and docs (Ch 31–32), failure-first deep dives, trade-off drills (Ch 57 L2) B4 (principal) Plus architecture leadership (Ch 33–37), the capstone (Ch 56), evolution and economics narratives, past-system deep dives

docs.title: 2.10 Levels differ by company B4
docs.text:
• Titles don't map one-to-one across companies (a "senior" at one can be "staff" at another). Ask the recruiter for the ladder and the expectations for the loop (VERIFY per company).
  • Some loops weight coding more at senior and design more at staff. Principal loops often add a past-system deep dive and a written exercise.
  • Down-levelling offers are common. Understand the rubric gap they cite, and use this chapter's table to close it.

docs.title: 3.1 The level ladder as expanding scope
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    B1[B1 Engineer - correct happy path, a task] --> B2[B2 Senior - correct under concurrency and load, a service]
    B2 --> B3[B3 Staff - correct under the domain's failure modes, a system across teams]
    B3 --> B4[B4 Principal - correct under loss and change, a platform over years]
    B1 -. influence: own work .-> B1
    B2 -. influence: team .-> B2
    B3 -. influence: several teams .-> B3
    B4 -. influence: organisation .-> B4

docs.title: 3.2 Sequence: a staff-level exchange
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant I as Interviewer
    participant C as Staff candidate
    I->>C: design webhook handling for payments
    C->>I: at-least-once, can arrive out of order or be lost - is the gateway the source of truth
    I-->>C: yes, it has a list API
    C->>I: dedup in the same transaction as the effect
    C->>I: payment state machine, forward-only transitions
    C->>I: outbox for receipts, reconciliation job against the list API
    C->>I: metrics - lag, dedup rate, reconciliation drift, alert if drift above 0.01 percent
    I->>C: what if reconciliation finds thousands of mismatches
    C->>I: stop auto-repair, page, it is a systemic bug not noise

docs.title: 3.3 Sequence: down-levelled answer and the recovery
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant I as Interviewer
    participant C as Candidate
    I->>C: design webhook handling for payments
    C->>I: keep a set of seen event ids in memory
    I->>C: what happens with two instances
    C->>I: move dedup to a database table with a unique key
    I->>C: what if CAPTURED arrives before AUTHORIZED
    C->>I: guard transitions - status only moves forward
    I->>C: what if an event never arrives
    C->>I: reconcile daily against the gateway list API
    Note over I,C: each fix was prompted - reads senior, not staff

docs.title: 3.4 State: the payment's forward-only lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Authorized
    Authorized --> Captured: capture event
    Captured --> Refunded: refund event
    Authorized --> Voided: void event
    Captured --> Captured: late AUTHORIZED ignored
    Refunded --> Refunded: late CAPTURED ignored
    Voided --> [*]
    Refunded --> [*]

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Level Rubric
docs.text:
Design Document (excerpt) — Engineering Level Rubric for System Design (illustrative)

Status: Illustrative template · Use: calibrating interview feedback and promotion packets. Adapt it to your company's ladder (VERIFY).

Field Value Context Interviewers disagreed on levels. Feedback said "strong" without evidence. Packets listed projects, not impact. Decision Score eight dimensions on observable behaviour. Each level has anchor examples. Level = the lowest level that all "must-have" dimensions meet. Related Ch 57 L4 rubric; Ch 61 story format; the level table in §1.2.

Requirements.

  • R1: Every score cites evidence (a quote, a board artefact, a decision).
  • R2: Levels are consistent across interviewers (calibration sessions quarterly).
  • R3: Down-level decisions name the missing dimension.
  • R4: Promotion packets map evidence to dimensions.
  • R5: The rubric is published to candidates at a high level.

Decisions in detail.

  1. Must-haves for B3: drives ambiguity; failure handling unprompted; trade-offs with flip conditions.
  2. Must-haves for B4: also phasing/evolution, economics, organisational impact.
  3. Anchors: the §2.6 table serves as calibration examples.

Consequences. Longer feedback writing, in return for fairer, more consistent levelling.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
What's real here

  • One program implements all four levels against a real PostgreSQL: real transactions, unique constraints, guarded updates and an outbox.
  • It uses two concurrent consumer threads, one of which "restarts" by losing its memory.
  • The gateway's truth, the duplicates, the reordering and the losses are generated with a fixed seed.
  • The duplicate count for B1 varies slightly between runs, because thread interleaving differs.

The program:

WebhookLevelsL.java
// WebhookLevelsL.java — run with (PostgreSQL on :5581, db shop):
//   java -Duser.timezone=UTC -cp /tmp/eslab/postgresql-42.7.4.jar WebhookLevelsL.java   (JDK 21)
// ONE QUESTION, FOUR LEVELS OF ANSWER: "Handle the payment gateway's webhooks." 5,000 payments; the gateway sends
// status events (AUTHORIZED → CAPTURED, 20% later REFUNDED) at least once: 25% are duplicated, 15% arrive out of order
// (a later status before an earlier one), and 2% are never delivered at all. Two consumer nodes process concurrently;
// node 1 restarts halfway. Each accepted "CAPTURED" triggers a side effect (credit the order + send a receipt), each
// "REFUNDED" a reverse effect. Four implementations, each the natural answer at one level (REAL PostgreSQL):
//   B1 in-memory "seen" set per node; apply the event's status to the payment row
//   B2 dedup in the database: INSERT event_id (primary key) in the SAME transaction as the effect
//   B3 B2 + ordering: a status only moves forward along AUTHORIZED < CAPTURED < REFUNDED (guarded UPDATE); effects
//      go to an outbox in the same transaction
//   B4 B3 + reconciliation: after the stream, compare with the gateway's "list payments" API and repair drift
// Measured against the gateway's truth: receipts/credits applied twice, payments whose stored status went BACKWARDS,
// payments whose final status is wrong, and money effects missing.
import java.sql.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

public class WebhookLevelsL {
    static final String URL = "jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5581/shop?user=claude";
    static final String[] ST = {"AUTHORIZED", "CAPTURED", "REFUNDED"};
    record Ev(String id, int payment, int status) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Random r = new Random(58); int P = 5000; int[] truth = new int[P]; List<Ev> stream = new ArrayList<>(); Set<String> lost = new HashSet<>();
        for (int p = 0; p < P; p++) { int last = r.nextDouble() < 0.2 ? 2 : 1; truth[p] = last; List<Ev> evs = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int s = 0; s <= last; s++) evs.add(new Ev("evt-" + p + "-" + s, p, s));
            if (r.nextDouble() < 0.15 && evs.size() > 1) { int i = r.nextInt(evs.size() - 1); Collections.swap(evs, i, i + 1); }      // out of order
            for (Ev e : evs) { if (r.nextDouble() < 0.02) { lost.add(e.id()); continue; } stream.add(e); if (r.nextDouble() < 0.25) stream.add(e); } }   // lost / duplicated
        // interleave per payment roughly in time, preserve per-payment order of the list above
        List<Ev> ordered = new ArrayList<>(); Map<Integer, Deque<Ev>> per = new HashMap<>(); for (Ev e : stream) per.computeIfAbsent(e.payment(), k -> new ArrayDeque<>()).add(e);
        List<Integer> keys = new ArrayList<>(per.keySet()); while (!keys.isEmpty()) { int k = r.nextInt(keys.size()); Ev e = per.get(keys.get(k)).poll(); ordered.add(e); if (per.get(keys.get(k)).isEmpty()) { keys.set(k, keys.get(keys.size() - 1)); keys.remove(keys.size() - 1); } }
        System.out.printf("5,000 payments, %,d webhook deliveries (25%% duplicated, 15%% of payments out of order, %d events never delivered); 2 nodes, one restart.%n%n", ordered.size(), lost.size());
        System.out.printf("   %-58s %14s %16s %14s %14s%n", "answer", "effects applied", "status went", "final status", "money effects");
        System.out.printf("   %-58s %14s %16s %14s %14s%n", "", "twice", "backwards", "wrong", "missing");
        String[] names = {"B1) in-memory seen-set per node, apply status", "B2) dedup by event id in the same DB transaction", "B3) B2 + forward-only status + outbox", "B4) B3 + reconciliation with the gateway's list API"};
        for (int lvl = 1; lvl <= 4; lvl++) run(lvl, names[lvl - 1], ordered, truth);
        System.out.println("\n   → every answer 'handles webhooks'; they differ in which failure modes they have thought about. B1 works in a demo");
        System.out.println("     and double-credits in production (two nodes, restarts). B2 makes duplicates harmless but trusts arrival order.");
        System.out.println("     B3 encodes the domain's state machine, so late events can't move a payment backwards. B4 accepts that an");
        System.out.println("     at-least-once channel can still lose messages and closes the loop with reconciliation. That progression —");
        System.out.println("     correct once, correct under concurrency, correct under reordering, correct under loss — is what the levels mean.");
    }

    static void run(int lvl, String name, List<Ev> events, int[] truth) throws Exception {
        try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(URL); Statement s = c.createStatement()) {
            s.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS pay, processed_event, effect, outbox");
            s.execute("CREATE TABLE pay (id int PRIMARY KEY, status int NOT NULL DEFAULT -1, regressions int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)");
            s.execute("CREATE TABLE processed_event (event_id text PRIMARY KEY)");
            s.execute("CREATE TABLE effect (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, payment int, kind text)");
            s.execute("CREATE TABLE outbox (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, payment int, kind text)");
            s.execute("INSERT INTO pay (id) SELECT g FROM generate_series(0," + (truth.length - 1) + ") g");
        }
        AtomicInteger next = new AtomicInteger(); int half = events.size() / 2;
        ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2); List<Future<?>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int node = 0; node < 2; node++) { final int nd = node; fs.add(ex.submit(() -> {
            Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>(); boolean restarted = false;
            try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(URL)) { c.setAutoCommit(false); int i;
                while ((i = next.getAndIncrement()) < events.size()) {
                    if (nd == 1 && !restarted && i > half) { seen.clear(); restarted = true; }        // node 1 restarts: memory gone
                    Ev e = events.get(i);
                    if (lvl == 1) { if (!seen.add(e.id())) continue; apply(c, lvl, e); c.commit(); continue; }
                    try (PreparedStatement p = c.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO processed_event VALUES (?) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING")) { p.setString(1, e.id()); if (p.executeUpdate() == 0) { c.rollback(); continue; } }
                    apply(c, lvl, e); c.commit();
                }
            }
            return null; })); }
        for (Future<?> f : fs) f.get(); ex.shutdown();
        if (lvl == 4) try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(URL)) {                        // reconciliation: gateway list API = truth
            c.setAutoCommit(false);
            for (int p = 0; p < truth.length; p++) { int cur; try (Statement s = c.createStatement(); ResultSet rs = s.executeQuery("SELECT status FROM pay WHERE id = " + p)) { rs.next(); cur = rs.getInt(1); }
                for (int st = cur + 1; st <= truth[p]; st++) apply(c, 3, new Ev("recon-" + p + "-" + st, p, st)); }
            c.commit();
        }
        long twice, back, wrong, missing;
        try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(URL); Statement s = c.createStatement()) {
            String tbl = lvl >= 3 ? "outbox" : "effect";
            twice = one(s, "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT payment, kind FROM " + tbl + " GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING count(*) > 1) x");
            back = one(s, "SELECT count(*) FROM pay WHERE regressions > 0");
            StringBuilder vals = new StringBuilder(); for (int p = 0; p < truth.length; p++) vals.append(p == 0 ? "" : ",").append("(").append(p).append(",").append(truth[p]).append(")");
            wrong = one(s, "SELECT count(*) FROM pay JOIN (VALUES " + vals + ") t(id, st) USING (id) WHERE pay.status <> t.st");
            long expected = 0; for (int t : truth) expected += t >= 1 ? (t == 2 ? 2 : 1) : 0;
            missing = expected - one(s, "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT payment, kind FROM " + tbl + ") x");
        }
        System.out.printf("   %-58s %,14d %,16d %,14d %,14d%n", name, twice, back, wrong, missing);
    }
    static long one(Statement s, String q) throws SQLException { try (ResultSet rs = s.executeQuery(q)) { rs.next(); return rs.getLong(1); } }

    static void apply(Connection c, int lvl, Ev e) throws SQLException {
        String effTable = lvl >= 3 ? "outbox" : "effect";
        if (lvl >= 3) {                                                                                // forward-only transition
            try (PreparedStatement p = c.prepareStatement("UPDATE pay SET status = ? WHERE id = ? AND status < ?")) { p.setInt(1, e.status()); p.setInt(2, e.payment()); p.setInt(3, e.status()); if (p.executeUpdate() == 0) return; }
        } else {
            int cur; try (PreparedStatement p = c.prepareStatement("SELECT status FROM pay WHERE id = ? FOR UPDATE")) { p.setInt(1, e.payment()); try (ResultSet rs = p.executeQuery()) { rs.next(); cur = rs.getInt(1); } }
            try (PreparedStatement p = c.prepareStatement("UPDATE pay SET status = ?, regressions = regressions + ? WHERE id = ?")) { p.setInt(1, e.status()); p.setInt(2, e.status() < cur ? 1 : 0); p.setInt(3, e.payment()); p.executeUpdate(); }
        }
        if (e.status() >= 1) try (PreparedStatement p = c.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO " + effTable + " (payment, kind) VALUES (?, ?)")) { p.setInt(1, e.payment()); p.setString(2, e.status() == 1 ? "CREDIT+RECEIPT" : "REFUND"); p.executeUpdate(); }
        if (lvl >= 3 && e.status() == 2) {                                                             // refund after a skipped capture: capture effect also owed
            try (PreparedStatement p = c.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO outbox (payment, kind) SELECT ?, 'CREDIT+RECEIPT' WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM outbox WHERE payment = ? AND kind = 'CREDIT+RECEIPT')")) { p.setInt(1, e.payment()); p.setInt(2, e.payment()); p.executeUpdate(); }
        }
    }
}
java -Duser.timezone=UTC -cp postgresql-42.7.4.jar WebhookLevelsL.java
5,000 payments, 13,475 webhook deliveries (25% duplicated, 15% of payments out of order, 178 events never delivered); 2 nodes, one restart.

   B2) dedup by event id in the same DB transaction                        0              747            755            104

   B4) B3 + reconciliation with the gateway's list API                     0                0              0              0

   → every answer 'handles webhooks'; they differ in which failure modes they have thought about. B1 works in a demo

docs.title: L1 — The B1 answer: in-memory dedup B1
docs.text:
Requirement: "Don't process a webhook twice."

Reading it:

  • It works on one node until it restarts. With two nodes, and one restarting, 830 effects were applied twice.
  • It also overwrites status in arrival order, so 747 payments moved backwards at some point.
  • The 2% lost events leave 104 money effects missing.

docs.title: L2 — The B2 answer: dedup in the same transaction B2
docs.text:
Requirement: "Duplicates must be harmless across nodes and restarts."

Reading it:

  • The event-id primary key, inserted in the same transaction as the effect, makes every duplicate a no-op: 0 double effects.
  • Ordering and loss are untouched. The status still goes backwards, and final statuses are still wrong for 755 payments.

docs.title: L3 — The B3 answer: the domain's state machine B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "A late event must never move a payment backwards."

Reading it:

  • The guarded UPDATE (WHERE status < new) encodes AUTHORIZED < CAPTURED < REFUNDED: 0 regressions.
  • Effects go to an outbox in the same transaction.
  • A refund implies the capture happened, so its credit is owed. The domain knowledge recovers some losses.
  • 82 payments remain wrong. Their final event never arrived.

docs.title: L4 — The B4 answer: reconciliation B4
docs.text:
Requirement: "Our records must match the gateway's, even when messages are lost."

Reading it:

  • Comparing against the gateway's list API and repairing through the same forward-only path brings every invariant to 0.
  • In production, add metrics on drift. A sudden jump in drift is a systemic bug, not noise, so page and stop auto-repair (Ch 45).

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Symptom Fix Answering at the wrong level Down-levelled offer Match §1.2 behaviours to the target Depth without breadth "Narrow" Operability, cost, evolution Breadth without depth "Hand-wavy" One code-level deep dive Prompted fixes only "Needed guidance" Anticipate failure modes (§3.3) Project lists "Impact unclear" Evidence format (§2.8)

docs.title: 6.2 Signals interviewers write down
docs.text:
• "Asked about ordering before I did." (B3)
  • "Proposed reconciliation unprompted." (B4)
  • "Needed hints to handle duplicates." (B1/B2)
  • "Great design, but no discussion of operations or cost." (B2/B3 boundary)

docs.title: 6.3 Ethics and honesty
docs.text:
• Describe your real role: "I led", "I contributed", "the team did". Inflation is detectable and disqualifying.
  • It's fine to say "I haven't operated X, but here's how I'd reason about it."

docs.title: 6.4 Pacing by level
docs.text:
• B2: most time in the deep dive, briefly on failures.
  • B3/B4: a shorter high-level design, with more on failures, trade-offs, evolution and operations.

docs.title: 6.5 After a down-level
docs.text: • Ask for the rubric gap. Map it to §2.7. Build evidence at work, then re-interview in 6–12 months.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Equating years with level

Scope and anticipation decide it.

2. Naming technologies as depth

Depth is failure modes and invariants.

3. Solving only the happy path

That's B1 (lab row 1).

4. Dedup in memory

Two nodes and a restart break it (L1).

5. Trusting message order

Regressions (L2).

6. Trusting delivery

Loss (L3 → L4).

7. Waiting for the interviewer to find the holes

That's senior at best (§3.3).

8. Staff answers without operability

Incomplete.

9. Principal answers without phasing

Unrealistic.

10. Promotion packets as project lists

No evidence of scope.

11. Inflating your role

Integrity risk.

12. Assuming ladders are identical across companies

Calibrate per loop.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What's expected of a junior engineer in system design?

30-second answer: A reasonable single-service design that works on the happy path, basic knowledge of databases, caching and APIs, clear communication, and willingness to take hints; growing toward concurrency and failure thinking.

Deep answer: §2.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Breadth vs depth at the start of a career.

Follow-ups: 1. How to grow? → Ask "what if there are two of these?" 2. Best habit? → Write down requirements.

Red flags: Buzzwords without basics.

Q2 [B1] What's the single biggest jump from junior to senior?

30-second answer: Designing for concurrency and repetition — two instances, retries, restarts — with atomic operations and idempotency, instead of assuming one clean run.

Deep answer: The lab's B1 → B2 row: 830 double effects → 0.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Complexity vs correctness.

Follow-ups: 1. Where to learn? → Ch 13, 20. 2. Example? → Unique constraint in the same transaction.

Red flags: In-memory dedup.

Q3 [B1] How do levels differ in how they ask questions?

30-second answer: Juniors ask clarifying questions about the spec; seniors ask about scale and constraints; staff ask about failure modes and hidden requirements; principals ask about the business goal and whether to build at all.

Deep answer: §1.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: None.

Follow-ups: 1. Example staff question? → "Can events be lost?" 2. Principal? → "What's the smallest version that proves value?"

Red flags: No questions.

Q4 [B1] Does a senior need to know every technology?

30-second answer: No — they need to know categories, trade-offs and failure modes deeply enough to choose and justify, and to learn specifics quickly.

Deep answer: §2.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Depth in a few vs shallow in many.

Follow-ups: 1. What must be deep? → Databases, concurrency, messaging. 2. Unknown tech in interview? → Reason from principles.

Red flags: Name-dropping.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ What makes an answer senior-level?

30-second answer: Independent, complete, correct under concurrency and load: requirements and numbers, clean API/data model, coherent design, one deep dive with atomic operations and idempotency, trade-offs named, basic failure handling.

Deep answer: §2.3; Ch 57 L4 transcript B.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Time allocation.

Follow-ups: 1. Most common gap? → Operability. 2. Deep dive choice? → Where money/scarcity is.

Red flags: Needing the interviewer to drive.

Q6 [B2] How do you demonstrate ownership in a design interview?

30-second answer: Drive the agenda, propose the deep dive, state assumptions, commit to decisions, and talk about how you'd operate and evolve the system — as if you'll be on call for it.

Deep answer: §2.4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Driving vs listening.

Follow-ups: 1. Interviewer redirects? → Follow. 2. On-call mention? → Alerts, runbooks.

Red flags: "It depends" without deciding.

Q7 [B2] What are common down-levelling signals?

30-second answer: Waiting to be driven, no numbers, "we'll add retries", no state machines, preferences instead of trade-offs, failures only when asked, no operability/cost, over-engineering.

Deep answer: §2.7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: None.

Follow-ups: 1. Fastest fix? → Failure table unprompted. 2. Practice? → Mocks with rubric.

Red flags: Unaware of these.

Q8 [B2] How does failure thinking change with level?

30-second answer: B1 handles errors; B2 adds retries, timeouts, idempotency; B3 models domain failure modes (reordering, sagas, degradation, SLOs); B4 designs correction loops for loss and drift (reconciliation, audits) and bounds blast radius.

Deep answer: The lab, row by row.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Cost of each loop.

Follow-ups: 1. Example of B4 loop? → Daily reconciliation. 2. Blast radius? → Cells.

Red flags: Only retries.

Q9 [B2] How do you prepare differently for senior vs staff loops?

30-second answer: Senior: breadth of core patterns and case studies, timed practice. Staff: add failure-first deep dives, trade-off drills with flip conditions, operability/cost narratives, and past-system stories showing cross-team impact.

Deep answer: §2.9.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Study time.

Follow-ups: 1. Principal? → Evolution and economics. 2. Behavioural? → Ch 61.

Red flags: Same preparation for both.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ What distinguishes staff from senior in a design interview?

30-second answer: Staff candidates find the real problem and its failure modes before being asked — ordering, loss, contention, degradation — argue trade-offs with flip conditions, and treat operability and cost as part of the design; seniors produce a correct design when the problem is defined.

Deep answer: §2.4, §3.2 vs §3.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Depth vs scope.

Follow-ups: 1. Evidence? → Unprompted failure table. 2. Communication? → Structured, concise.

Red flags: Only a bigger diagram.

Q11 [B3] How do you show cross-team influence in an interview?

30-second answer: In past-system discussions: problems you found, decisions you drove (ADRs), standards you set, people you mentored, outcomes with numbers — told as situation, your judgement, others' actions, results.

Deep answer: §2.8.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Credit vs honesty.

Follow-ups: 1. Conflict? → Ch 61. 2. Failure story? → What you learned.

Red flags: "We" for everything or "I" for everything.

Q12 [B3] How should a staff candidate handle a simple prompt?

30-second answer: Solve it cleanly and quickly, then show judgement: realistic failure modes, operability, evolution at 10×, and what you would not build — without over-engineering the base design.

Deep answer: §2.6 table.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Showing depth vs over-building.

Follow-ups: 1. URL shortener at staff? → Abuse, hot keys, analytics, cost. 2. Time? → Keep base design short.

Red flags: Twelve services for a shortener.

Q13 [B3] What is 'anticipation', and how do you practise it?

30-second answer: Naming the failure modes and requirements before they're raised. Practise with a checklist per component — duplicates, reordering, loss, contention, partial failure, overload, bad input, operator error — and apply it in every mock.

Deep answer: Lab rows map to checklist items.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Time budget.

Follow-ups: 1. Too many to cover? → Critical path first. 2. Show it? → A failure table.

Red flags: Reactive fixes only.

Q14 [B3] How do you present a design decision at staff level?

30-second answer: Context, options considered, the decision, its costs, the conditions that would change it, and how it will be validated — the ADR format, spoken.

Deep answer: Ch 31, Ch 57 L2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Brevity vs completeness.

Follow-ups: 1. Reversibility? → Say whether it's a one-way door. 2. Evidence? → Numbers or experiments.

Red flags: "Because it's best practice."

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ What distinguishes principal from staff?

30-second answer: Horizon and scope: designing for years of change and loss (reconciliation, migrations, evolution), across domains and organisations, with economics and people in the design; reframing problems and choosing what not to build.

Deep answer: §2.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Abstraction vs concreteness — principals still go deep when needed.

Follow-ups: 1. Example reframe? → "Do we need real-time here?" 2. Economics? → Cost per unit.

Red flags: Only abstractions.

Q16 [B4] How does a principal approach an interview prompt differently?

30-second answer: Starts with the goal and constraints, proposes a phased plan (smallest valuable version, next, at scale), designs the correction and observability loops, quantifies SLOs and cost, and addresses migration and team structure — then dives deep where risk is highest.

Deep answer: §2.6 table rightmost column.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Time for depth.

Follow-ups: 1. Phasing example? → Monolith first. 2. Deep dive still needed? → Yes.

Red flags: Never going below boxes.

Q17 [B4] What evidence convinces a promotion committee of staff/principal impact?

30-second answer: Problems you identified unassigned, decisions others built on, standards adopted across teams, measurable organisational outcomes (incidents, latency, cost, lead time), and people you grew — with peer testimony.

Deep answer: §2.8.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Visibility vs work.

Follow-ups: 1. Quiet contributors? → Write design docs, ADRs. 2. Metrics? → Before/after.

Red flags: Lists of shipped features.

Q18 [B4] How should interview loops calibrate levels fairly?

30-second answer: Published rubrics with behavioural anchors, evidence-based feedback, calibration sessions, level decided by must-have dimensions, and structured debriefs that separate signal from impression.

Deep answer: §4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Process overhead.

Follow-ups: 1. Bias? → Structured questions, diverse panels. 2. Disagreement? → Evidence wins.

Red flags: "Culture fit" as a level signal.

Q19 [B4] How do principals stay technically credible?

30-second answer: They still read code and designs, go deep on the riskiest parts, prototype, participate in incidents, and measure outcomes — breadth built on regular depth.

Deep answer: Ch 37.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Time across many teams.

Follow-ups: 1. Hands-on time? → A deliberate slice. 2. Signals? → Accurate intuition.

Red flags: Architecture astronaut.

Q20 [B4] If you're down-levelled, what should you do?

30-second answer: Ask for the rubric gap, map it to behaviours (§2.7), build evidence at work (lead a cross-team design, drive a reliability loop), practise the missing signals in mocks, and re-interview after 6–12 months.

Deep answer: §6.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Accept offer vs wait.

Follow-ups: 1. Negotiation? → Level vs compensation. 2. Internal promotion? → Evidence packet.

Red flags: Blaming the interviewer.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Levels are scope and anticipation, not years.
  2. B1 works; B2 works under concurrency; B3 works under domain failure modes; B4 works under loss and change (the lab).
  3. Down-levelling signals are behavioural and fixable (§2.7).
  4. Staff/principal evidence is problems found, decisions driven, standards set and outcomes measured.
  5. Calibrate preparation to the target level.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Level Must show in a design interview B1 Clean happy-path design, basics B2 Requirements, numbers, API/data, a deep dive with atomicity and idempotency B3 Unprompted failure modes, state machines, trade-offs with flip conditions, SLOs, operability B4 Reframing, phasing, reconciliation and correction loops, economics, organisation

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (B1) Add a third consumer node to the lab. How do B1's duplicates change?
  2. (B2) Implement a "VOIDED" status in the lab's state machine.
  3. (B3) Add metrics to the B3 answer: dedup rate, regressions prevented, outbox lag.
  4. (B4) Design an alert for reconciliation drift, and decide what should pause auto-repair.
  5. (B4) Rewrite one of your project descriptions in the §2.8 evidence format.
