docs.title: 59. Interview Q&A Bank
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 57, Ch 58

What you get: the whole handbook's interview material as one bank you can drill. Every chapter's §8 and every industry design's Q&A (1,580 questions) is parsed by a program into two companion pages, and re-running the program after any edit keeps them in step with the chapters:

  • ⭐ Drill Bank: all 495 high-frequency (⭐) questions with their 30-second answers, grouped by part and chapter.
  • Full Question Index: all 1,580 questions by part, chapter and level, with links back to the full answers.

This chapter explains how to use the bank. It covers:

  • the shapes of interview questions;
  • the 30-second-answer pattern;
  • the follow-up chains interviewers use;
  • a study plan.

It adds 20 integration questions that deliberately span several chapters, because real interviews don't stay inside one topic.

What the labs measured:

  • L1 (extraction): 62 chapters plus the 18 industry designs: 1,580 questions and 495 ⭐. The first run found 17 ⭐ answers written as bullet lists, which the parser then learned to read.
  • L2 (coverage): every chapter has exactly 20 questions. By band there are 252 B1, 459 B2, 395 B3 and 474 B4.
  • L3 (drills): a deterministic 12-question drill per band and seed, spread across parts and weighted to ⭐.
  • L4 (study plans): modelled on the 415-card core-chapter deck. Under a simple memory model, cramming wins the next morning (61%) but keeps only 3% a month later. Weeks of spaced review plus a final pass reaches 57% on the day and keeps the most (17%).

· Reading time: 50 min for this page; the bank is for drilling.

docs.title: 1.1 A story: 400 questions and no answers
docs.text:
Arjun collected four hundred system design questions from forums, books and friends into a spreadsheet. He read through it twice in the week before his loop. In the interview he recognised every question, and could answer none of them fluently. He knew about consistent hashing, but couldn't explain in thirty seconds why virtual nodes help, or what he'd trade for them.

Recognition is not recall, and recall is not fluency. A question bank is useful only if you:

  1. answer aloud before reading;
  2. answer in a fixed shape (30 seconds, then depth, then trade-offs);
  3. expect the follow-ups;
  4. space the practice so the answers are still there on the day.

This chapter turns the handbook into that kind of bank.

The thesis of this chapter

Use the handbook's own Q&A as the bank, generated from the chapters so it never drifts (L1, L2). Drill in mixed, level-appropriate sets (L3), aloud, in the 30-second → deep → trade-offs → follow-ups shape. Space the practice over weeks and finish with a full pass (L4).

docs.title: 1.2 What's in the bank
docs.text: Part Questions ⭐ Focus 0 · Orientation 20 9 What design is, requirements, quality attributes I · Foundations 160 68 Estimation, networking, APIs, databases, caching, load balancing, scalability II · Distributed core 220 86 Replication, partitioning, consensus, transactions, messaging, events, resilience, concurrency, idempotency III · Production 200 79 Data at scale, search, security, observability, performance, deployment, DR, schema evolution, testing, multi-tenancy IV · Architect 140 49 Decisions, docs, DDD, architecture styles, cost, compliance, leadership V · Case studies 360 95 18 end-to-end designs VI · Capstone 20 4 The whole platform VII · Interview 100 25 Framework, levels, and this chapter

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end you will be able to:

  • Use the ⭐ bank and the index efficiently.
  • Answer in the 30-second shape, and handle follow-up chains.
  • Recognise question archetypes, and the chapter that answers each.
  • Plan study time with spaced practice (L4).
  • Answer integration questions that span chapters (§8).

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: a language, not a list B1
docs.text: You don't learn a language by reading a phrasebook the night before a trip. You practise speaking, in context, repeatedly, with gaps between sessions, and your answers become sentences you can adapt. Interview answers work the same way. The bank is the phrasebook; the drill is the conversation.

docs.title: 2.2 Question archetypes ⭐ B2

docs.title: 2.3 The answer shape ⭐ B2
docs.text:
Every question in this handbook is written in the same shape, and it's the shape to speak in:

  1. 30-second answer: the core claim, the mechanism, and the main caveat. Stop, and let the interviewer choose where to go.
  2. Deep answer: the mechanism with numbers or an example, often from a lab.
  3. Trade-offs: what it costs, and when you'd choose differently.
  4. Follow-ups: prepare the two most likely next questions.
  5. Red flags: know the wrong answers the interviewer is listening for.

Timing: 30 seconds, then pause. Most interviewers interrupt with a follow-up, and that is the conversation you want.

docs.title: 2.4 Follow-up chains ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Interviewers probe down a chain until you reach the edge of your knowledge. Know the chains for common topics:

Start → → → Edge (staff+) Cache the product page Invalidation? Stampede on expiry? Hot key? Consistency with inventory at checkout (Ch 07, Ch 44) Idempotency key Stored where? Concurrent duplicates? Key expiry? Unknown outcomes and reconciliation (Ch 20, Ch 58 lab) Kafka for events Ordering? Exactly-once? Consumer lag at peak? Schema evolution and replay (Ch 14, Ch 28) Shard the orders table Shard key? Cross-shard queries? Resharding live? Hot tenants, cells (Ch 11, Ch 30) Distributed lock TTL? Paused holder? Fencing? Is a lock the right tool at all (Ch 20, Ch 50) QUORUM reads R + W > N? Sloppy quorum? Tail latency? Consensus for CAS (Ch 10, Ch 54)

docs.title: 2.7 Keeping the bank honest B3
docs.text:
• The bank is generated, not copied. QaBankL1 re-reads every chapter, so an edited answer appears in the bank on the next run.

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Study Plan
docs.text:
Design Document (excerpt) — Six-Week Interview Study Plan (template)

Status: Template · Use: adapt to your target level and available hours

Field Value Context Staff-level loop in 6 weeks; ~1.5 hours/day on weekdays, 4 hours on weekends. Decision Spaced drilling of ⭐ questions (40/day), 3 timed designs a week, 2 mocks a week from week 4, and a full ⭐ pass in the last 2 days (L4). Related Ch 57 framework, Ch 58 levels, Ch 60 mocks, Ch 61 behavioural.

Requirements.

  • R1: Every ⭐ answer spoken fluently in ≤ 30 s.
  • R2: 12 case studies designed on paper in 45 minutes.
  • R3: 6 mocks scored with the rubric (Ch 57 L4).
  • R4: 5 leadership stories in the evidence format (Ch 58 §2.8).
  • R5: No new material in the last 3 days, only review.

Decisions in detail.

  1. Weeks 1–2: Parts I–II ⭐ plus 4 case studies.
  2. Weeks 3–4: Parts III–IV ⭐ plus 4 case studies and 2 mocks.
  3. Weeks 5–6: Part V–VI ⭐, 4 case studies, 4 mocks, and integration questions.
  4. Daily: the L3 drill (12 questions), with misses re-queued.

Consequences. It is a real time commitment. In return you get fluency, not recognition.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
What's real here

  • L1–L3 run on this handbook's actual chapter files.
  • L4 is a simulation using a stated, deliberately simple memory model.
  • The companion pages are the committed output of L1.

All four labs are JDK 21 programs. L1–L3 read the handbook's docs/ folder.

docs.title: L1 — Generate the bank from the chapters B2
docs.text:
Requirement: "One command rebuilds the bank and the index from every chapter's §8, so they can never drift."

QaBankL1.java
// QaBankL1.java — run with: java QaBankL1.java <docs-dir> <out-dir>   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// BUILD THE QUESTION BANK FROM THE HANDBOOK ITSELF. Parses every chapter's "??? question" blocks (§8 of each chapter),
// extracting chapter, level band, the ⭐ high-frequency marker, the question and its 30-second answer. Writes:
//   bank_starred.md — every ⭐ question with its 30-second answer, grouped by part and chapter (the drill bank)
//   index_all.md    — every question title, grouped by part and chapter, with links back to the chapter
// and prints what it found, so the bank can never drift from the chapters: re-run it after editing any chapter.
import java.io.*;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.regex.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class QaBankL1 {
    static String fixLinks(String s, String dir) { return s.replaceAll("\\]\\(((?:\\d\\d-|i\\d\\d|index)[^)/]*\\.md)", "](../" + dir + "/$1"); }   // same-folder links, incl. industry pages (i06-x.md, index.md)
    record Q(int ch, String chapterTitle, String file, String part, int num, String band, boolean star, String text, String answer) {}
    static final Pattern QP = Pattern.compile("^\\?\\?\\? question \"Q(\\d+) \\[(B\\d)\\] (⭐ )?(.*)\"\\s*$");

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Path docs = Paths.get(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "docs"), out = Paths.get(args.length > 1 ? args[1] : ".");
        List<Q> all = new ArrayList<>(); Map<String, String> partNames = Map.of("00-orientation", "Part 0 · Orientation", "01-foundations", "Part I · Foundations",
                "02-distributed-core", "Part II · Distributed Core", "03-production", "Part III · Production", "04-architect", "Part IV · Architect",
                "05-case-studies", "Part V · Case Studies", "06-capstone", "Part VI · Capstone", "07-interview", "Part VII · Interview", "08-industry", "Part VIII · Industry Designs");
        List<Path> files; try (Stream<Path> s = Files.walk(docs, 2)) { files = s.filter(p -> p.getFileName().toString().matches("(\\d\\d|i\\d\\db?)-.*\\.md")).sorted().toList(); }
        for (Path f : files) {
            List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(f); String title = lines.stream().filter(l -> l.startsWith("# ")).findFirst().orElse("# ?").substring(2).trim();
            String fn = f.getFileName().toString(); int ch = fn.startsWith("i")  /* industry I01..I18 → 101..118 */ ? 100 + Integer.parseInt(fn.substring(1, 3)) : Integer.parseInt(fn.substring(0, 2));
            String part = partNames.getOrDefault(f.getParent().getFileName().toString(), "?");
            for (int i = 0; i < lines.size(); i++) { Matcher m = QP.matcher(lines.get(i)); if (!m.matches()) continue;
                String ans = ""; for (int j = i + 1; j < Math.min(lines.size(), i + 8); j++) { String l = lines.get(j).trim(); if (l.startsWith("**30-second answer:**")) { ans = l.substring("**30-second answer:**".length()).trim();
                        if (ans.isEmpty()) { StringBuilder b = new StringBuilder(); for (int k = j + 1; k < lines.size(); k++) { String x = lines.get(k).trim(); if (x.isEmpty() || x.startsWith("**")) break; b.append(b.length() > 0 ? "\n    " : "").append(x); } ans = b.toString(); }   // bullet-list answers
                        break; } }
                String dir = docs.relativize(f).getParent().toString();
                // same-folder links like (28-x.md) must point at ../<folder>/28-x.md once the text moves to another page
                all.add(new Q(ch, title, docs.relativize(f).toString(), part, Integer.parseInt(m.group(1)), m.group(2), m.group(3) != null, fixLinks(m.group(4), dir), fixLinks(ans, dir))); }
        }
        // bank of starred questions
        StringBuilder bank = new StringBuilder(), index = new StringBuilder(); String lastPart = "", lastCh = "";
        for (Q q : all) { if (!q.star()) continue;
            if (!q.part().equals(lastPart)) { bank.append("\n### ").append(q.part()).append("\n"); lastPart = q.part(); lastCh = ""; }
            if (!q.chapterTitle().equals(lastCh)) { bank.append("\n**[").append(q.chapterTitle()).append("](../").append(q.file()).append(")**\n\n"); lastCh = q.chapterTitle(); }
            bank.append("??? example \"").append(q.band()).append(" · ").append(q.text().replace("\"", "'")).append("\"\n    ").append(q.answer().isEmpty() ? "_See the chapter._" : q.answer()).append("\n\n"); }
        lastPart = ""; lastCh = "";
        for (Q q : all) {
            if (!q.part().equals(lastPart)) { index.append("\n## ").append(q.part()).append("\n"); lastPart = q.part(); lastCh = ""; }
            if (!q.chapterTitle().equals(lastCh)) { index.append("\n### [").append(q.chapterTitle()).append("](../").append(q.file()).append(")\n\n"); lastCh = q.chapterTitle(); }
            index.append("- **Q").append(q.num()).append("** `").append(q.band()).append("`").append(q.star() ? " ⭐" : "").append(" ").append(q.text()).append("\n"); }
        Files.writeString(out.resolve("bank_starred.md"), bank.toString()); Files.writeString(out.resolve("index_all.md"), index.toString());
        long missing = all.stream().filter(q -> q.star() && q.answer().isEmpty()).count();
        if (System.getenv("SHOWMISSING") != null) all.stream().filter(q -> q.star() && q.answer().isEmpty()).forEach(q -> System.out.println("MISSING " + q.file() + " Q" + q.num()));
        System.out.printf("parsed %d chapter files → %,d questions, %,d ⭐ (%d ⭐ without a 30-second answer)%n", files.size(), all.size(), all.stream().filter(Q::star).count(), missing);
        System.out.printf("wrote bank_starred.md (%,d words) and index_all.md (%,d words)%n", words(bank), words(index));
        // L2: coverage by part × band
        System.out.printf("%n   %-30s %6s %6s %6s %6s %8s %8s%n", "part", "B1", "B2", "B3", "B4", "total", "⭐");
        for (String p : partNames.values().stream().sorted(Comparator.comparing(QaBankL1::partOrder)).toList()) {
            List<Q> qs = all.stream().filter(q -> q.part().equals(p)).toList(); if (qs.isEmpty()) continue;
            System.out.printf("   %-30s %6d %6d %6d %6d %8d %8d%n", p, cnt(qs, "B1"), cnt(qs, "B2"), cnt(qs, "B3"), cnt(qs, "B4"), qs.size(), qs.stream().filter(Q::star).count());
        }
        System.out.printf("   %-30s %6d %6d %6d %6d %8d %8d%n", "ALL", cnt(all, "B1"), cnt(all, "B2"), cnt(all, "B3"), cnt(all, "B4"), all.size(), all.stream().filter(Q::star).count());
        // per-chapter format check: 20 questions each
        List<String> off = new ArrayList<>(); Map<Integer, Long> perCh = all.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Q::ch, TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
        perCh.forEach((c, n) -> { if (n < 20) off.add((c > 100 ? "I" + (c - 100) : "Ch " + c) + ": " + n); });
        System.out.printf("%n   chapters with Q&A: %d; chapters with fewer than 20 questions: %s%n", perCh.size(), off.isEmpty() ? "none" : String.join(", ", off));
    }
    static int partOrder(String p) { return List.of("Part 0 · Orientation", "Part I · Foundations", "Part II · Distributed Core", "Part III · Production", "Part IV · Architect", "Part V · Case Studies", "Part VI · Capstone", "Part VII · Interview", "Part VIII · Industry Designs").indexOf(p); }
    static long cnt(List<Q> qs, String b) { return qs.stream().filter(q -> q.band().equals(b)).count(); }
    static int words(CharSequence s) { return s.toString().split("\\s+").length; }
}

docs.title: L3 — A daily drill B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "12 mixed questions a day, at my level, the same for my study group."

DrillL3.java
// DrillL3.java — run with: java DrillL3.java <docs-dir> <band> [seed]   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// A 45-MINUTE DRILL FROM THE BANK. Picks 12 questions for a target band from the handbook's own Q&A (parsed live from
// the chapters): at most one per chapter, spread across parts, ⭐ questions weighted 3×, questions from the band itself
// plus one band below for warm-up. Deterministic for a given seed (use the date), so a study group gets the same set.
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.regex.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class DrillL3 {
    record Q(int ch, String file, String part, String band, boolean star, String text) {}
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Path docs = Paths.get(args[0]); String band = args.length > 1 ? args[1] : "B3"; long seed = args.length > 2 ? Long.parseLong(args[2]) : 20260930L;
        Pattern qp = Pattern.compile("^\\?\\?\\? question \"Q(\\d+) \\[(B\\d)\\] (⭐ )?(.*)\"\\s*$"); List<Q> all = new ArrayList<>();
        try (Stream<Path> s = Files.walk(docs, 2)) { for (Path f : s.filter(p -> p.getFileName().toString().matches("\\d\\d-.*\\.md")).sorted().toList())
            for (String l : Files.readAllLines(f)) { Matcher m = qp.matcher(l); if (m.matches()) all.add(new Q(Integer.parseInt(f.getFileName().toString().substring(0, 2)), f.getFileName().toString(), f.getParent().getFileName().toString(), m.group(2), m.group(3) != null, m.group(4))); } }
        int b = band.charAt(1) - '0'; String below = "B" + Math.max(1, b - 1);
        List<Q> pool = all.stream().filter(q -> q.band().equals(band) || q.band().equals(below)).toList();
        Random r = new Random(seed); List<Q> picked = new ArrayList<>(); Set<Integer> usedCh = new HashSet<>(); Map<String, Integer> perPart = new HashMap<>();
        int warm = 0;
        while (picked.size() < 12) {
            double total = 0; List<Q> cand = new ArrayList<>(); List<Double> w = new ArrayList<>();
            for (Q q : pool) { if (usedCh.contains(q.ch())) continue; if (perPart.getOrDefault(q.part(), 0) >= 3) continue; if (q.band().equals(below) && warm >= 2) continue; if (!q.band().equals(below) && picked.size() < 2 && warm < 2 && b > 1) continue;
                double wt = q.star() ? 3 : 1; cand.add(q); w.add(wt); total += wt; }
            if (cand.isEmpty()) break;
            double x = r.nextDouble() * total; int i = 0; while (x > w.get(i)) { x -= w.get(i); i++; }
            Q q = cand.get(i); picked.add(q); usedCh.add(q.ch()); perPart.merge(q.part(), 1, Integer::sum); if (q.band().equals(below)) warm++;
        }
        System.out.printf("Drill for %s (seed %d): %d questions from %,d in the pool; answer each aloud in ≤ 3 minutes, then check the chapter.%n%n", band, seed, picked.size(), pool.size());
        int n = 1; for (Q q : picked) System.out.printf("   %2d. [%s]%s %s   → Ch %02d (%s)%n", n++, q.band(), q.star() ? " ⭐" : "", q.text(), q.ch(), q.part());
        System.out.printf("%n   parts covered: %s%n", picked.stream().map(Q::part).distinct().sorted().collect(Collectors.joining(", ")));
    }
}

docs.title: L4 — Study plan: cram, cycle or space? B4
docs.text:
Requirement: "Remember the answers on interview day, and still know them a month later."

SpacedL4.java
// SpacedL4.java — run with: java SpacedL4.java   (JDK 21, no dependencies)
// HOW TO STUDY 415 ⭐ QUESTIONS IN SIX WEEKS. A simple memory model (an assumption, in the spirit of spaced-repetition
// research — VERIFY against your own experience): after a review, the chance of recalling an answer t days later is
// exp(−t / S). S starts at 1 day; each successful recall multiplies S by 2.5; a failed recall resets S to 1 day.
// Budget: about 40 reviews a day. Interview on day 43. Three plans (fixed seed):
//   P1 cram: go through all 415 on each of the last 4 days
//   P2 round-robin: 40 cards a day in a fixed cycle for 42 days (each card every ~10 days)
//   P3 spaced (Leitner-style): each day review the cards that are due (next review when recall would drop to ~80%),
//      introduce ~15 new cards a day until all are started, within the same budget
//   P4 P3 for days 1–40, then all 415 on each of the last 2 days (spaced learning + a final pass)
// Measured: expected share recalled on interview day, cards above 80% recall, expected recall 30 days later (a second
// loop, or the job), and reviews spent.
import java.util.*;

public class SpacedL4 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("415 cards, ~40 reviews/day budget, interview on day 43; recall(t) = exp(−t/S), S ×2.5 on success.\n");
        System.out.printf("   %-56s %16s %14s %16s %10s%n", "plan", "expected recall", "cards > 80%", "recall 30 days", "reviews");
        System.out.printf("   %-56s %16s %14s %16s %10s%n", "", "on interview day", "that day", "later (2nd loop)", "");
        for (int p = 1; p <= 4; p++) run(p);
        System.out.println("\n   → under this model, cramming wins the next morning and loses a month later: it fills short-term memory");
        System.out.println("     that fades in days. A fixed cycle is the worst of both — every card comes back after it has been forgotten.");
        System.out.println("     Spaced review builds durable memory but, on a tight budget, reaches the interview with fewer answers fresh.");
        System.out.println("     The combination — spaced review for weeks, then a final pass over everything — comes close to cramming on");
        System.out.println("     the day (57% vs 61%) and keeps the most a month later (17%), at the cost of more reviews. The absolute numbers");
        System.out.println("     come from a deliberately harsh, simple model; the direction is what matters (and is consistent with");
        System.out.println("     spaced-repetition research — VERIFY with your own practice).");
    }
    static void run(int plan) {
        int N = 415, days = 42; Random r = new Random(59); double[] S = new double[N], last = new double[N]; boolean[] started = new boolean[N]; int reviews = 0;
        Arrays.fill(last, Double.NaN);
        for (int day = 1; day <= days; day++) {
            List<Integer> today = new ArrayList<>();
            if (plan == 1 || (plan == 4 && day > days - 2)) { if (plan == 4 || day > days - 4) for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) today.add(i); }
            else if (plan == 2) { for (int k = 0; k < 40; k++) today.add(((day - 1) * 40 + k) % N); }
            else {
                if (plan == 4 && day > days - 2) { } else {
                List<Integer> due = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) if (started[i] && Math.exp(-(day - last[i]) / S[i]) < 0.8) due.add(i);
                final int d0 = day; due.sort(Comparator.comparingDouble(i -> Math.exp(-(d0 - last[i]) / S[i])));
                for (int i : due) { if (today.size() >= 40) break; today.add(i); }
                int added = 0; for (int i = 0; i < N && today.size() < 40 && added < 15; i++) if (!started[i]) { today.add(i); started[i] = true; added++; }
                }
            }
            for (int i : today) { reviews++;
                if (Double.isNaN(last[i])) { S[i] = 1; last[i] = day; continue; }                  // first study
                double pr = Math.exp(-(day - last[i]) / S[i]); if (r.nextDouble() < pr) S[i] *= 2.5; else S[i] = 1; last[i] = day; started[i] = true; }
        }
        double sum = 0, later = 0; int strong = 0; int interview = days + 1;
        for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) { double pr = Double.isNaN(last[i]) ? 0 : Math.exp(-(interview - last[i]) / S[i]); sum += pr; if (pr > 0.8) strong++; later += Double.isNaN(last[i]) ? 0 : Math.exp(-(interview + 30 - last[i]) / S[i]); }
        String[] names = {"", "P1) cram: all 415 on each of the last 4 days", "P2) round-robin: 40 a day in a fixed cycle", "P3) spaced: due cards first, 15 new a day", "P4) spaced (days 1–40) + all 415 on the last 2 days"};
        System.out.printf("   %-56s %15.0f%% %14d %15.0f%% %10d%n", names[plan], 100 * sum / N, strong, 100 * later / N, reviews);
    }
}
java SpacedL4.java
415 cards, ~40 reviews/day budget, interview on day 43; recall(t) = exp(−t/S), S ×2.5 on success.

   plan                                                      expected recall    cards > 80%   recall 30 days    reviews
                                                            on interview day       that day later (2nd loop)           
   P1) cram: all 415 on each of the last 4 days                          61%            143               3%       1660
   P2) round-robin: 40 a day in a fixed cycle                             6%              0               0%       1680
   P3) spaced: due cards first, 15 new a day                             24%             87              11%       1645
   P4) spaced (days 1–40) + all 415 on the last 2 days                   57%             86              17%       2395

   → under this model, cramming wins the next morning and loses a month later: it fills short-term memory
     that fades in days. A fixed cycle is the worst of both — every card comes back after it has been forgotten.
     Spaced review builds durable memory but, on a tight budget, reaches the interview with fewer answers fresh.
     The combination — spaced review for weeks, then a final pass over everything — comes close to cramming on
     the day (57% vs 61%) and keeps the most a month later (17%), at the cost of more reviews. The absolute numbers
     come from a deliberately harsh, simple model; the direction is what matters (and is consistent with
     spaced-repetition research — VERIFY with your own practice).

Reading it:

  • Cramming wins the next morning and fades fast. A fixed cycle is the worst of both.
  • Spaced review plus a final pass is close to cramming on the day and best a month later.
  • The model is deliberately simple and harsh. Trust the direction, not the percentages.

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Symptom Fix Reading, not answering Recognition without recall Answer aloud first One topic at a time Can't switch contexts in a loop Mixed drills (L3) Cramming only Gone a week later (L4) Spaced review + final pass Long answers Interviewer can't steer 30 seconds, then pause Ignoring follow-ups Stuck on the second question Prepare the chains (§2.4)

docs.title: 6.2 Tracking progress
docs.text:
• Keep a miss log per chapter. Topics with repeated misses need a chapter re-read, not more drilling.
  • Record one mock a week, and score it with the rubric.

docs.title: 6.3 Study groups
docs.text: • Share a seed so everyone gets the same L3 drill. Take turns as interviewer, using the follow-up chains.

docs.title: 6.4 The day before
docs.text: • One full ⭐ pass. No new topics. Sleep.

docs.title: 6.5 After each loop
docs.text: • Write down every question you were asked. Add missing ones to your own bank. Re-run L1 if you edit the chapters.

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Collecting questions instead of answering them

A list is not practice.

2. Silent reading

Interviews are spoken.

3. Memorising paragraphs

Memorise shapes and mechanisms, not scripts.

4. Skipping follow-ups

The chain is where levels show.

5. Only B4 questions for a staff loop

The fundamentals get probed too.

6. Only your favourite topics

Weak areas stay weak.

7. Cramming the last week

Short-lived (L4).

8. Copying answers from the internet

Unverified, and often wrong. Use the chapters and their labs.

9. Bank drifting from sources

Generate it (L1).

10. No timing

Answers expand to fill the time.

11. Never saying 'I don't know'

Bluffing is worse.

12. No mocks

Drills aren't interviews (Ch 60).

docs.title: 8. Interview Q&A — Integration Questions
docs.text: These questions deliberately cross chapters. They are the kind senior and staff interviewers use to test whether knowledge connects.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ A product page is slow. Walk through where the time could go.

30-second answer: DNS/TLS and network to the edge, CDN miss to origin, API gateway, service latency (DB queries, cache misses, downstream calls), payload size and rendering; measure with tracing before guessing.

Deep answer: Ch 03, Ch 07, Ch 24, Ch 25.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Caching vs freshness.

Follow-ups: 1. Which first? → Traces and the slowest span. 2. Images? → CDN variants (Ch 52).

Red flags: "Add more servers."

Q2 [B1] Why do we need both a database and a cache?

30-second answer: The database is the durable source of truth with transactions; the cache serves hot reads faster and cheaper; together they trade freshness and complexity for latency and load.

Deep answer: Ch 05, Ch 07.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Staleness, invalidation.

Follow-ups: 1. Cache as source of truth? → Only with persistence and care. 2. What not to cache? → Money balances at checkout.

Red flags: Cache everything.

Q3 [B1] What happens when you place an order, end to end?

30-second answer: The app calls the gateway; checkout validates price and serviceability, reserves stock, holds a slot, charges payment, creates the order; events trigger picking, dispatch, notifications and invoices.

Deep answer: Ch 46, Ch 56.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Sync vs async steps.

Follow-ups: 1. Payment fails? → Release stock. 2. Which steps are async? → Side effects.

Red flags: One big transaction across services.

Q4 [B1] What's the difference between scaling reads and scaling writes?

30-second answer: Reads scale with replicas and caches; writes need partitioning (sharding), batching, or async processing because a single primary bounds them.

Deep answer: Ch 09, Ch 10, Ch 11.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Replica lag; cross-shard queries.

Follow-ups: 1. Read-your-writes with replicas? → Session routing. 2. When to shard? → Numbers (Ch 57 L1).

Red flags: Sharding first.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do idempotency, retries and timeouts fit together?

30-second answer: Timeouts bound waiting; retries recover transient failures; idempotency makes retries safe because the operation may have succeeded; add backoff with jitter and treat timeouts on side-effecting calls as unknown outcomes.

Deep answer: Ch 18, Ch 20, Ch 56 L2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Retry storms vs recovery.

Follow-ups: 1. Retry budget? → Limit per request. 2. Non-idempotent API? → Status query before retry.

Red flags: Retrying payments blindly.

Q6 [B2] How do the outbox pattern and Kafka work together?

30-second answer: Write the business change and an outbox row in one local transaction; a relay (polling or CDC) publishes outbox rows to Kafka; consumers are idempotent because delivery is at-least-once.

Deep answer: Ch 14, Ch 15.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Latency of the relay.

Follow-ups: 1. Ordering? → Key by aggregate. 2. Cleanup? → Partition and drop.

Red flags: Dual writes.

Q7 [B2] How does caching interact with inventory correctness?

30-second answer: Browse can show cached, slightly stale availability; the checkout path must check and reserve against the source of truth atomically; show "few left" hints rather than exact counts from cache.

Deep answer: Ch 07, Ch 46.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Oversell vs freshness.

Follow-ups: 1. Hot SKU? → Buckets or a gate. 2. Invalidation? → Events from inventory.

Red flags: Reserving from cache.

Q8 [B2] How do SLOs, alerts and dashboards relate?

30-second answer: SLOs define reliability targets from user journeys; alerts page on error-budget burn rates; dashboards support diagnosis; each alert should link to a runbook.

Deep answer: Ch 24, Ch 56.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Alert fatigue vs detection.

Follow-ups: 1. Multi-window burn? → Fast and slow. 2. Journey vs service? → Journey first.

Red flags: CPU alerts only.

Q9 [B2] How do schema changes and deployments interact?

30-second answer: Old and new code run together during rollouts, so schema changes must be backward compatible: expand (add), migrate, switch reads/writes, contract (remove) — each deploy compatible with the previous version.

Deep answer: Ch 26, Ch 28.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Migration duration.

Follow-ups: 1. Event schemas? → Registry compatibility rules. 2. Rollback? → Only if the schema still fits.

Red flags: Rename column in one deploy.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ Walk a payment through every consistency mechanism it touches.

30-second answer: Idempotency key at the API; state machine with guarded transitions in the DB; outbox to events; webhook dedup and forward-only updates; status polling for unknowns; double-entry ledger; daily reconciliation with settlement files.

Deep answer: Ch 45, Ch 58 lab.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Complexity vs money safety.

Follow-ups: 1. Where can money be lost? → Unknown outcomes. 2. Which runs daily? → Reconciliation.

Red flags: "The gateway handles it."

Q11 [B3] How do partitioning, replication and consensus fit together in one store?

30-second answer: Partitioning spreads data (consistent hashing or ranges); replication copies each partition (leader-based or leaderless); consensus (Raft/Paxos) decides leaders and ordered logs where strong consistency is needed; membership and failure detection glue it together.

Deep answer: Ch 10, Ch 11, Ch 12, Ch 54.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Consistency vs availability per partition.

Follow-ups: 1. Raft per partition? → Multi-Raft. 2. Rebalancing? → Move replicas, not keys.

Red flags: One global leader.

Q12 [B3] How would you make the platform survive a Kafka outage?

30-second answer: Outboxes keep producers safe (events wait in the DB); critical paths don't depend synchronously on Kafka; consumers catch up after recovery; monitor outbox depth; for prolonged outages degrade features that rely on events (e.g., delayed notifications).

Deep answer: Ch 14, Ch 15, Ch 56 L3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Eventual delays vs availability.

Follow-ups: 1. Outbox growth? → Capacity planning. 2. Ordering after recovery? → Per-key preserved.

Red flags: Checkout publishing to Kafka synchronously.

Q13 [B3] How do security and multi-tenancy intersect for sellers?

30-second answer: Tenant identity in tokens, row-level or schema isolation enforced in the data layer, per-tenant rate limits and quotas, encryption keys per tenant where needed, and audit trails — isolation for data, performance and blast radius.

Deep answer: Ch 23, Ch 30, Ch 39.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Isolation cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Noisy neighbour? → Quotas, cells. 2. Admin access? → Audited break-glass.

Red flags: Tenant id from request params.

Q14 [B3] How do performance testing and capacity planning work together for sale day?

30-second answer: Forecast journeys' peak load, find per-service capacity by load tests with realistic data and failures, compute headroom and pre-scaling, validate with a full-journey test, and set admission control for the excess.

Deep answer: Ch 02, Ch 25, Ch 46.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Cost of headroom.

Follow-ups: 1. Coordinated omission? → Open-model load. 2. Dependencies? → Test gateways' limits too.

Red flags: Testing one endpoint.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Connect DDD, team topology and microservice boundaries.

30-second answer: Bounded contexts define language and consistency boundaries; teams own contexts end to end (Conway); services follow contexts where independent deployment and scaling pay off; start as modules and extract when load, team size or change rate demands.

Deep answer: Ch 16, Ch 33, Ch 37.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Autonomy vs integration overhead.

Follow-ups: 1. Shared kernel? → Minimise. 2. Wrong boundary? → Merge before splitting further.

Red flags: One service per table.

Q16 [B4] How do cost, reliability and compliance trade off in data residency?

30-second answer: Residency limits where data and replicas live, which constrains DR regions and CDN/processing choices, raising cost; classify data, keep regulated data in-country with in-country DR, and use global services only for non-regulated data.

Deep answer: Ch 27, Ch 35, Ch 36.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Resilience vs compliance.

Follow-ups: 1. Logs with PII? → Redact or keep local. 2. Vendor SaaS? → Contracts and locations.

Red flags: Ignoring regulation.

Q17 [B4] What architecture would you choose for 10k orders/day vs 1M orders/day, and why?

30-second answer: 10k/day: a modular monolith, one PostgreSQL, managed queue, CDN — fast to build and operate. 1M/day: extracted checkout/payments, search, dispatch; event backbone; read models; cells and DR for the critical set — justified by load, team size and blast radius.

Deep answer: Ch 34, Ch 56 §2.11.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Early complexity vs later migration.

Follow-ups: 1. Migration path? → Strangler. 2. First extraction? → The one with the most independent load.

Red flags: Same architecture for both.

Q18 [B4] How do you decide which consistency model each part of a platform needs?

30-second answer: By the cost of anomalies: money and scarce stock need linearizable or serializable operations on their critical keys; carts need read-your-writes; catalog, search and feeds tolerate staleness; analytics tolerate approximation — encoded per operation, not per system.

Deep answer: Ch 12, Ch 51, Ch 54.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Latency and availability costs.

Follow-ups: 1. Mixed in one service? → Per endpoint. 2. Verification? → Invariant checks.

Red flags: "Everything strongly consistent."

Q19 [B4] Where do most production incidents in such platforms actually come from, and how does design reduce them?

30-second answer: Changes (deploys, config, schema), overload and retry storms, dependency failures, and data drift; design reduces them with safe rollouts, backpressure and budgets, soft dependencies and degradation, idempotency with reconciliation, and cells to bound blast radius.

Deep answer: Ch 18, Ch 26, Ch 27.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Velocity vs safety.

Follow-ups: 1. Change management? → Canaries, flags. 2. Learning? → Blameless postmortems.

Red flags: "Hardware failures."

Q20 [B4] If you had to teach one principle from this whole handbook, what would it be?

30-second answer: Make guarantees explicit and verify them: every design choice exists to keep some invariant true under some failure, so name the invariant, the failure, the mechanism, and the check that proves it — the labs in this handbook are that principle applied.

Deep answer: Every chapter's L1–L4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Rigour vs speed.

Follow-ups: 1. Example? → No double charges: key + state machine + reconciliation. 2. How to check? → Tests, metrics, audits.

Red flags: A buzzword.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. The bank is generated from the chapters: 495 ⭐ answers and 1,580 questions, kept in sync (L1, L2).
  2. Answer in shape: 30 seconds, then depth, then trade-offs, with the follow-ups prepared.
  3. Drill mixed, level-appropriate sets (L3).
  4. Space your practice and finish with a full pass (L4).
  5. Integration questions test whether knowledge connects (§8).

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Resource Use ⭐ Drill Bank Daily spaced drills Full Question Index Find every question on a topic §2.5 Must-know thirty Last-week priority §2.4 Follow-up chains Prepare the second and third questions L3 drill 12 questions per day

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (B1) Run L3 for B2 with today's date as the seed. Answer aloud and log your misses.
  2. (B2) Pick 3 must-know questions and write your own 30-second answers before reading the chapter's.
  3. (B3) For 3 chains in §2.4, add a fifth link.
  4. (B4) Write two integration questions that span 3+ chapters, and answer them.
  5. (All) Run L4 with your real daily budget and choose a plan.

docs.title: 60. Mock Interviews
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Prerequisites: Ch 57, Ch 58, Ch 59

What you get:

  • How to run mock interviews that actually change your performance: formats, the interviewer's script, pacing, debriefs, calibration and tracking progress.
  • Four full worked mocks with interviewer cards, timelines, transcript excerpts and scorecards:
    • A coupon redemption (B1–B2)
    • B order-status notifications (B2)
    • C dark-store inventory for 10-minute delivery (B3)
    • D taking the platform to a second country (B4)

What the labs measured:

  • L1 (pacing): in six recorded practice mocks, the deep-dive and failure phases got 11.2 of a planned 16 minutes. A single checkpoint rule ("drawing the HLD by minute 20") recovers them to 15.2. It does not fix an 11-minute clarify phase.
  • L2 (calibration), simulated:
    • One calibrated interviewer decides as accurately as four uncalibrated ones (86.4% vs 86.5%).
    • Two uncalibrated interviewers reach the same verdict only 68% of the time.
    • A candidate just above the bar gets a "hire" from one uncalibrated mock only 60% of the time.
  • L3 (check a claim before the mock), real PostgreSQL: a single-row conditional UPDATE gives 4,398 reservations/s with one thread, but only ~2,000/s at 32 threads with a 77 ms p99. Sixteen bucket rows give 10,844/s at 8 threads.
  • L4 (progress), simulated: even when you really improve by 0.10 per mock, one in three candidates scores lower on mock 4 than on mock 1. A statistical trend needs about 12 mocks.

Reading time: 70 min.

docs.title: 1.1 A story: the fifth mock
docs.text:
Meera had done four mocks with friends. All four "went fine", and she was nervous about each real loop anyway. On the fifth, her friend recorded the session and then sat down with her, the recording and a stopwatch. The recording showed:

  • Requirements: 11 minutes of clarifying questions.
  • Deep dive: 3 minutes, because time ran out.
  • Failure handling: never discussed.
  • Two claims she couldn't back up: "a Redis counter handles any load" and "Kafka guarantees exactly-once".

None of her four earlier mocks had surfaced this, because the friend had been friendly: no clock, no follow-ups, no scorecard.

A mock is only useful if it is harder and more honest than the real thing. That means a real clock, an interviewer with a script and hidden requirements, follow-up chains, a scorecard against a level, a recording, and a debrief that ends with two things to change. This chapter is how to run those, on both sides of the table.

The thesis of this chapter

Run mocks as experiments:

  • a timed prompt with an interviewer card;
  • follow-up chains to the edge of what you know;
  • a level-anchored scorecard;
  • a recorded debrief with two changes.

Pace with checkpoints (L1). Calibrate peer interviewers before trusting a verdict (L2). Check your standard claims against real numbers (L3). Judge progress on trends and behaviours, not one score (L4).

docs.title: 1.2 Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end you will be able to:

  • Run a mock as candidate and as interviewer, with a card, a clock and a scorecard.
  • Pace 45 minutes with checkpoints, and recover when you're behind.
  • Handle pushback, being stuck, and "what if" chains gracefully.
  • Debrief into specific, behavioural changes.
  • Calibrate a peer group and track progress honestly.

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: a dress rehearsal B1
docs.text: Actors rehearse in costume, on stage, with lights, before opening night. Mistakes that would be fatal on the night (a missed cue, a prop in the wrong place) are cheap in rehearsal. A mock is your dress rehearsal. It is only useful if the conditions match: the time limit, a stranger's questions, a whiteboard, and nobody rescuing you.

docs.title: 2.2 Mock formats B1
docs.text:
Format Good for Limits Frequency Solo, recorded Pacing, clarity, speaking aloud No follow-ups, no pushback 2/week early on Peer (swap roles) Follow-ups, both perspectives Calibration varies (L2) 1–2/week Senior colleague or mentor Level-accurate probing, stories Their time 2–4 total Paid or professional Calibrated scoring, company-specific style Cost 1–2 before key loops Real low-stakes loops Real conditions Cost of a no Optional

Order: solo first to fix pacing, then peers for follow-ups, then calibrated interviewers to find out where you actually stand.

docs.title: 2.3 The interviewer card ⭐ B2
docs.text:
A mock interviewer needs more than a prompt. They need a card holding what a real interviewer knows and the candidate doesn't:

Card section Contents Prompt One sentence, deliberately vague Hidden requirements Answers to reveal only if asked (scale, latency, regions, consistency) Must-cover The 2–3 hard parts the design must address Follow-up chains 3–4 chains, each 3–4 links deep (Ch 59 §2.4) Curveballs One requirement change at minute ~30 Level anchors What B2/B3/B4 answers sound like for this prompt (Ch 58) Scorecard Dimensions and 1–4 anchors (Ch 57 L4)

The four mocks in §2.6–§2.9 each come with a card you can reuse.

docs.title: 2.4 The interviewer's script B2
docs.text:
1. 0–1 min: Deliver the prompt. Say nothing else.
  2. 1–10 min: Answer questions from the card only. Unasked hidden requirements stay hidden.
  3. Throughout: Take timestamped notes of phases, claims and numbers.
  4. ~20 min: If the candidate is still on requirements, don't rescue them. Note it.
  5. 20–35 min: Pull one follow-up chain per hard part until the candidate reaches the edge of what they know.
  6. ~30 min: Deliver the curveball.
  7. 40–45 min: "What would you do next with more time?", and questions to you.
  8. After: Fill the scorecard before discussing it, so the discussion can't soften the score. Then debrief (§2.10).

docs.title: 2.5 Behaviours under pressure ⭐ B2
docs.text: Situation Weak response Strong response Stuck Silence, or random components "Let me reason from the requirement: we need X within Y, so the options are A or B…" Pushback ("why not X?") Abandon the choice, or defend blindly Restate the requirement, compare X honestly, keep or switch with a reason Unknown fact Bluff "I don't know the exact number. I'd measure it. My estimate is ~N because…" Wrong earlier Hide it "I said Y earlier. That's wrong because Z. Let me fix the design." Curveball Start over Identify what changes, modify the minimum, re-check the invariants Behind on time Rush everything Say so, compress the low-value phases aloud (L1), protect the deep dive Interviewer silent Keep adding boxes Check in: "Would you like me to go deeper on X or move to Y?"

docs.title: 2.6 Mock A — Coupon redemption service B1–B2
docs.text:
Interviewer card — Mock A

Prompt: "Design a service that lets customers apply coupon codes at checkout."

Hidden requirements (reveal only if asked):

  • 20M users and 50k active coupons.
  • Peak 3,000 checkouts/s during sale events.
  • Some coupons are single-use per user; others have a global cap, e.g. the first 10,000 redemptions.
  • Coupon validation must answer in p99 ≤ 50 ms.
  • A redeemed coupon must never be redeemed twice, even with retries.

Must-cover:

  • A validation vs redemption split.
  • Enforcing per-user and global caps under concurrency.
  • Idempotent redemption tied to the order.

Chains:

  1. The global cap at 3,000/s → a hot counter → buckets/reservations → over-issue tolerance.
  2. Payment fails after redemption → release → timeout sweeper → idempotency.
  3. Stacking rules → rule engine → evaluation order (Ch 49).

Curveball (min 30): "Marketing wants a coupon valid only for the first order in each city."

Level anchors:

  • B1: a working CRUD design with a unique constraint.
  • B2: caps under concurrency, idempotency and release on failure.
  • B3: hot-cap handling with numbers, and an abuse/fraud angle.

Timeline of a strong B2 answer:

Min Phase What happened 0–5 Clarify Asked scale, cap types, latency, stacking and what "redeemed" means (at payment, not at apply). 5–8 Estimate 3,000 checkouts/s × ~30% with a coupon ≈ 1,000 validations/s. One sale coupon can take most of them. 8–11 API POST /coupons/validate {code, cartId} returns the discount and a validation token. POST /coupons/redeem {code, orderId} is idempotent on the order id. 11–15 Data coupon (rules, caps), redemption (coupon_id, user_id, order_id, status) with UNIQUE(coupon_id, user_id) for single-use coupons and UNIQUE(order_id). 15–24 HLD Checkout calls validate (reads from a cached rules table), then reserves at order creation, then confirms on payment. 24–36 Deep dive Global cap: a conditional decrement on a counter row. The candidate checked the hot-row limit against L3 (≈2,000/s at high concurrency), proposed 16 bucket rows, and accepted a small over-issue at the end. 36–41 Failures Payment fails → release. The reservation carries a TTL, and a sweeper releases it. Duplicate redeem → the unique order id returns the prior result. 41–45 Curveball "First order per city" means a new rule type plus a per-city check against order history. The candidate asked whether "first" means first ever or first with this coupon.

Transcript excerpt: the hot counter chain

Interviewer: The sale coupon is capped at 10,000 and 2,000 people apply it in the first second. What happens?

Candidate: A single counter row with UPDATE … SET left = left - 1 WHERE left > 0 is correct, but it's one hot row. I measured something similar: roughly 4,000 per second from one connection, but only about 2,000 per second with 32 concurrent callers, and the p99 was around 75 ms. So it would just about hold, but it breaks our 50 ms budget. I'd split the cap across 16 bucket rows. Each request picks a random bucket and moves on if it's empty.

Interviewer: Then some buckets empty early. Do you under-issue?

Candidate: Near the end, yes, unless empty-bucket misses fall through to the other buckets. I'd rather do that, and accept a handful of over-issues only if marketing agrees. For money-capped coupons I'd keep it exact.

Scorecard (B2 target):

Dimension Score Evidence Requirements 4 Asked about caps and the definition of "redeemed" Estimation 3 Derived the hot-coupon rate Design 3 Clean validate/reserve/confirm split Deep dive 4 Hot row with measured numbers and a bucket fallback Failures 3 Release, TTL and idempotency; missed abuse (code sharing) Communication 3 Checked in at 24 minutes

Verdict: strong B2.

What a B1 answer looked like: a CRUD coupon table and a check-then-insert in application code, which has a race under concurrency. There was no release when payment failed, and one global counter in Redis "because Redis is fast", with no numbers behind it.

docs.title: 2.7 Mock B — Order-status notifications B2
docs.text:
Interviewer card — Mock B

Prompt: "Customers should be told when their order status changes. Design it."

Hidden requirements:

  • 1.5M orders/day, ~8 status changes each.
  • Channels: push, SMS for critical changes, in-app.
  • "Out for delivery" must arrive within 30 s.
  • No duplicate SMS (they cost money).
  • Respect quiet hours for promotional messages, but not for transactional ones.

Must-cover:

  • Event source → notification pipeline.
  • Priority lanes.
  • Dedup/idempotency.
  • Provider failover.

Chains:

  1. The SMS provider is slow → retries → duplicate SMS → an idempotency key per (order, status, channel).
  2. A burst after a flash sale → lanes and rate limits.
  3. Ordering: "delivered" arrives before "out for delivery".

Curveball: "Add WhatsApp as a channel in some cities."

Level anchors:

  • B2: outbox + queue + workers, dedup, retries.
  • B3: lanes with capacity numbers, provider failover, ordering per order.

Timeline highlights:

  • Estimate. 1.5M × 8 = 12M events/day. That averages 140/s, and a sale peak at 5× the average is ~700/s. Push costs little, SMS costs per message, so the candidate asked which statuses trigger SMS (only "delayed" and "out for delivery").
  • HLD. The order service writes an outbox, which feeds Kafka (keyed by order id). The notification service applies preferences and templates, then puts messages on priority topics, and channel workers send them through providers. A delivery-status webhook closes the loop (Ch 40).
  • Deep dive: duplicates. The idempotency key is (orderId, status, channel). It is claimed in a table before calling the provider, with the state moving sending → sent/failed. If the provider times out, the outcome is unknown: query the provider's status API with the client reference, and don't blindly resend.
  • Deep dive: ordering. Events are keyed by order, so they stay in order per partition. On the device, show the latest status by sequence number and drop stale events.

Transcript excerpt: recovering from a wrong statement

Candidate: …and Kafka gives us exactly-once, so there are no duplicate SMS.

Interviewer: Does it?

Candidate: Let me correct that. Kafka's exactly-once covers read-process-write within Kafka. Sending an SMS is an external side effect, so we get at-least-once delivery to our worker. The duplicate protection has to be our idempotency key before the provider call, plus reconciliation with the provider's delivery reports.

Scorecard excerpt: the quick self-correction counted in the candidate's favour on communication. It showed they know exactly where Kafka's guarantee ends, which is the real point of the question.

docs.title: 2.8 Mock C — Dark-store inventory for 10-minute delivery B3
docs.text:
Interviewer card — Mock C

Prompt: "We promise delivery in 10 minutes from 400 dark stores. Design inventory so we never sell what the store doesn't have."

Hidden requirements:

  • 5,000 SKUs per store.
  • 20 orders/min per store at peak, with about 12 items each.
  • Stock changes from orders, receiving, damage and cycle counts.
  • Pickers find items missing about 1.5% of the time, because the counts drift.
  • Checkout p99 ≤ 300 ms.
  • The app shows availability per store.

Must-cover:

  • Reservation vs physical stock.
  • Drift and reconciliation with cycle counts.
  • Availability shown in the app vs availability at checkout.
  • The hot SKU during a flash deal.

Chains:

  1. Flash deal on one SKU in one store → hot row → the L3 numbers.
  2. A picker finds the item missing → substitution → correct the count → feed the ML forecast.
  3. A store goes offline → the store's own system vs the central one.

Curveball: "We're adding scheduled orders for tomorrow morning."

Level anchors:

  • B3: a two-level stock model (on-hand vs reservable), a safety buffer derived from drift, and reconciliation loops.
  • B4: unit economics of buffers vs the cost of missing items, and an org-level ownership model.

The B3 moves that stood out:

  1. A two-number model.
    • on_hand is physical stock, updated by receiving, picking and counts.
    • reservable = on_hand − reserved − safety_buffer.
    • The buffer is set per SKU from the observed drift, e.g. the 95th percentile of count corrections.
  2. Checked the load before over-engineering. 400 stores × 20 orders/min × 12 items is about 1,600 reservations/s across the fleet, spread over ~2M (store, SKU) rows. A single-row UPDATE per (store, SKU) is plenty. Only a flash deal on one row needs attention, and L3 says ~2,000/s is the ceiling for a single row under heavy concurrency. The candidate put a per-SKU request gate in front of it rather than sharding every row.
  3. Separated app availability from checkout.
    • The app reads a cached "reservable > buffer" flag, refreshed from events within seconds.
    • Checkout reserves against the source of truth, and fails closed with a substitution offer (Ch 46).
  4. Closed the loop on drift. Every "missing" found at picking triggers a count task for that bin. Corrections are events, and the buffer is recomputed weekly. The metric to watch is the missing-at-pick rate, not stock accuracy in general.
  5. The curveball, done calmly. Scheduled orders reserve against tomorrow's stock after receiving. That makes it a forecast-backed reservation with a confirmation step at 06:00 when stock arrives. It is a separate pool, so it never blocks 10-minute orders.

Transcript excerpt: pushback

Interviewer: Why not keep inventory in Redis? It's faster.

Candidate: For reservation it would be faster, but then Redis becomes the source of truth for stock, which means persistence, failover semantics and reconciliation back to the warehouse system. Our load is about 1,600 per second spread over two million rows, which PostgreSQL does comfortably. I'd put Redis in front only for the one hot-deal SKU as a gate, where losing the gate state is safe because the database still enforces the count.

docs.title: 2.9 Mock D — Taking the platform to a second country B4
docs.text:
Interviewer card — Mock D

Prompt: "We're launching in a second country in 9 months. What changes in the architecture and how do you run it?"

Hidden requirements:

  • Data residency: customer and payment data must stay in the new country (VERIFY the actual law for any real country).
  • Different tax rules, currency, payment providers and language.
  • About 10% of India's volume in year 1.
  • The same product team, plus 2 new local teams.
  • The CFO wants the launch cost under 15% of the current infrastructure spend.

Must-cover:

  • Cells or deployment per country vs a shared global setup.
  • What is global vs what is local.
  • Configurable tax, currency and payments.
  • Org and ownership.
  • Rollout and risk.

Chains:

  1. Residency → which services must be in-country → shared catalog? → cross-border analytics.
  2. One codebase vs a fork → feature flags per market → testing matrix.
  3. Cost → a small cell's fixed cost → managed services.

Curveball: "Legal says order history may need to be kept 8 years in-country."

Level anchors:

  • B3: a sound regional deployment design.
  • B4:
    • sequencing and decision records;
    • the org model;
    • cost and risk trade-offs with numbers;
    • what not to build;
    • reversible first steps.

What a B4 answer covered:

  1. Framing first. "This is mostly a product-and-org decision with an architecture component." The candidate named the three hard constraints (residency, payments, cost) and the two-way doors vs the one-way doors (Ch 31).
  2. A country cell, not a fork.
    • The same code and the same deployment pipeline, running as an in-country cell.
    • Market configuration (tax, currency, payment adapters, locale) as data and plug-ins.
    • The global layer is limited to non-personal data: catalog templates, the ML models' training jobs on anonymised aggregates, and engineering tooling (Ch 30, Ch 36).
  3. Cost with numbers. A minimal HA cell has a fixed floor: 3 AZs, a managed database, Kafka, search and observability. At 10% of the volume, that floor dominates. The candidate estimated the cell at ~12% of current spend and named the levers (managed services, smaller search, shared CI) and the risk of passing 15%.
  4. The org.
    • Platform teams own the cell template.
    • The two local teams own the market adapters and local operations.
    • Architecture reviews add a "market impact" section.
    • The on-call model covers local hours (Ch 37).
  5. Sequencing. Make the market configurable inside India first (a reversible step), then stand up a staging cell, run a shadow launch with employees, then a soft launch in one city. Each stage has a success metric and a rollback.
  6. The curveball. Retention goes into the cell's archive tier, stored in-country. The retention policy lives as code per market, and the cost impact is estimated. The candidate asked legal which fields fall in scope.

The B4 signal: most of the time went on constraints, sequencing, cost and ownership. The boxes-and-arrows part took about 10 minutes. The candidate also said what they would not do yet (no multi-country active-active, no global customer identity).

docs.title: 2.10 The debrief ⭐ B2
docs.text:
A debrief turns a mock into change. Keep it to 15 minutes:

  1. Candidate first (3 min): what went well, and what you'd redo.
  2. Timeline (3 min): the interviewer reads out the phase timestamps (L1).
  3. Scorecard (4 min): a score per dimension, with evidence quotes.
  4. Claims check (2 min): list every number or claim the candidate made, and mark it verified, plausible or wrong (L3).
  5. Two changes (3 min): specific and behavioural, e.g. "Checkpoint at 20 minutes" or "State the invariant before the mechanism". Not "be better at caching".

Log it: date, prompt, level, scores, the two changes, and whether last mock's changes happened.

docs.title: 2.11 Pacing ⭐ B2
docs.text:
L1's six mocks show the usual pattern. The early phases overrun one or two minutes at a time, and the deep dive, which is where levels are decided, absorbs all of it.

Checkpoints:

By minute You should be 5 Done clarifying (state the assumptions for the rest) 12 Done with estimates and the API 20 Drawing the HLD 30 In the deep dive on the hardest part 38 On failures, operability and trade-offs

When you're behind:

  1. Say so.
  2. Compress the phases L1 marks as compressible, aloud. For example: "I'll state the numbers: ~1,000 validations per second, 50 ms budget." Or: "Two endpoints: validate and redeem."
  3. Protect the deep dive.

Clarify is not compressible in the same way. Timebox it at 5 minutes and state your assumptions for the rest.

docs.title: 2.12 Calibrating a peer group B3
docs.text:
L2 shows that uncalibrated peers disagree on about one verdict in three. The disagreement comes from bias (lenient or harsh interviewers) as much as noise. To calibrate:

  • Anchored rubrics: for each dimension, write down what a 2, 3 and 4 sound like for this prompt. The level anchors on the cards above are a start.
  • Shadow scoring: two interviewers score the same recording independently, then compare scores and evidence.
  • Score review: monthly, look at each interviewer's average score. A consistently lenient interviewer is a known bias you can correct for.
  • Evidence over impressions: every score cites a quote or a timestamp.

In L2's model, a single calibrated interviewer decides about as well as four uncalibrated ones. Calibration is cheaper than more mocks.

docs.title: 2.13 Measuring progress B4
docs.text:
L4's lesson: one mock score is mostly noise (prompt difficulty and interviewer). Even with genuine improvement, scores go down about a third of the time over four mocks. Instead:

  • Track behaviours, not verdicts. Did you hit the 20-minute checkpoint? State the invariant? Quantify the hot path? Cover failures? Each is a yes or no.
  • Use rolling averages over 3 mocks, and vary the prompts.
  • Expect about 12 mocks before a trend shows up statistically, which is roughly the number most prep plans use anyway.
  • Stop mocking when readiness is consistent: 3 consecutive mocks at or above bar, with calibrated interviewers.

docs.title: 2.14 Remote and whiteboard logistics B1
docs.text:
• Practise on the real tool (a shared whiteboard or diagram tool), including drawing speed. Pre-set a few shapes if the tool allows it.
  • Camera and audio: a quiet room, a headset, and a second screen for your notes if that's allowed.
  • Handwriting: use large boxes with few words and label every arrow with the call type (sync or async).

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt: Mock Programme
docs.text:
Design Document (excerpt) — Peer Mock Interview Programme for a Study Group of 6

Status: Template · Owner: study group lead

Field Value Context Six engineers targeting senior and staff loops within 8 weeks. Peer mocks disagree often (L2), and nobody tracks progress. Decision Weekly role-swapping mocks using shared interviewer cards and anchored rubrics. Every session is recorded, and the first two weeks include shadow-scored calibration. A progress log tracks behaviours. Related Ch 57 rubric, Ch 58 anchors, Ch 59 drills.

Requirements.

  • R1: Each member does ≥ 2 mocks a week as candidate and 1–2 as interviewer.
  • R2: Every mock uses a card, a clock and a scorecard with evidence.
  • R3: Inter-interviewer verdict agreement ≥ 80% on shared recordings by week 3.
  • R4: Each debrief produces two behavioural changes, logged.
  • R5: Readiness is declared only after 3 consecutive at-bar mocks with calibrated interviewers.

Decisions in detail.

  1. Card library. 12 prompts, 3 per level, each with hidden requirements, chains and anchors (§2.6–§2.9 as a start).
  2. Calibration. In weeks 1–2, everyone scores the same two recordings. Discuss the differences, then update the anchors.
  3. Rotation. Avoid always pairing the same two people. Rotate prompts so nobody sees one twice.
  4. Claims check. Every debrief lists the numbers used. Anyone can run a lab (§5 L3) to verify them.
  5. Log. A shared sheet with prompt, level, behaviours (yes/no), scores and changes.

Consequences.

  • About 4 hours per person per week.
  • Better-calibrated verdicts.
  • Progress becomes visible through behaviours even while the scores are noisy.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
What's real here

  • L3 runs against a real PostgreSQL 16 database (fsync=on) on a 2-CPU sandbox.
  • L1 replays illustrative phase logs.
  • L2 and L4 are simulations whose assumptions are stated in the code. Trust their direction, not the exact percentages.

All four labs are JDK 21 single-file programs. L3 needs the PostgreSQL JDBC driver: java -Duser.timezone=UTC -cp postgresql-42.7.4.jar ClaimCheckL3.java.

docs.title: L1 — Where did the 45 minutes go? B2
docs.text:
Requirement: "Protect the deep dive, which is where levels are decided."

The program takes six practice mocks as recorded, with each phase's duration and a hard stop at 45 minutes. It replays them with one checkpoint rule.

PacingL1.java
// L1 — Pacing: where the 45 minutes actually went in six recorded mocks, and what a checkpoint rule changes.
// Phase durations are illustrative, in the pattern typical of practice recordings (not real candidate data).
import java.util.*;

public class PacingL1 {
    static final String[] PH = {"clarify", "estimate", "api", "data", "hld", "deep-dive", "failures", "wrap"};
    static final int[] PLAN = {5, 4, 4, 5, 9, 12, 4, 2};          // sums to 45
    static final boolean[] COMPRESSIBLE = {false, true, true, true, false, false, false, false};
    static final int[] FLOOR = {0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0};           // minimum minutes if compressed

    record Mock(String name, int[] minutes) {}

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        List<Mock> mocks = List.of(
            new Mock("M1 coupon service (B2)", new int[]{11, 7, 6, 8, 10, 3, 0, 0}),
            new Mock("M2 order notifications (B2)", new int[]{6, 3, 9, 7, 8, 9, 3, 0}),
            new Mock("M3 dark-store inventory (B3)", new int[]{5, 5, 3, 6, 11, 11, 4, 0}),
            new Mock("M4 multi-country (B4)", new int[]{8, 2, 2, 4, 12, 10, 5, 2}),
            new Mock("M5 rate limiter (B2)", new int[]{4, 8, 5, 5, 9, 10, 2, 2}),
            new Mock("M6 search autocomplete (B3)", new int[]{7, 6, 4, 9, 9, 8, 2, 0}));

        System.out.println("Plan (min): " + fmt(PLAN) + "   total 45\n");
        System.out.printf("%-30s %-44s %6s %9s %9s%n", "mock (as recorded)", PH[0] + "/" + PH[1] + "/.../" + PH[7], "@20min", "deep+fail", "overran");
        for (Mock m : mocks) {
            int[] x = cap(m.minutes());
            System.out.printf("%-30s %-44s %6s %6d/16 %9s%n", m.name(), fmt(x), phaseAt(x, 20), x[5] + x[6], overran(x));
        }
        System.out.println("\nCheckpoint rule: at minute 20 you must be drawing the HLD. If you are behind, compress estimate/api/data");
        System.out.println("to their floors (1/1/2 min: state the numbers, name 2 endpoints, list 3 tables) and say so aloud.\n");
        System.out.printf("%-30s %-44s %6s %9s%n", "mock (replayed with rule)", "", "@20min", "deep+fail");
        int before = 0, after = 0;
        for (Mock m : mocks) {
            int[] x = cap(m.minutes()), y = applyRule(m.minutes());
            before += x[5] + x[6]; after += y[5] + y[6];
            System.out.printf("%-30s %-44s %6s %6d/16%n", m.name(), fmt(y), phaseAt(y, 20), y[5] + y[6]);
        }
        System.out.printf("%nDeep-dive + failures, average over 6 mocks: %.1f min as recorded → %.1f min with the rule (plan: 16)%n", before / 6.0, after / 6.0);
        System.out.println("(replay assumes the minutes saved go to deep-dive then failures; clarify is never compressed)");
    }

    // the interview stops at 45 minutes: whatever was not reached gets nothing
    static int[] cap(int[] m) { int[] r = new int[m.length]; int t = 0; for (int i = 0; i < m.length; i++) { r[i] = Math.max(0, Math.min(m[i], 45 - t)); t += r[i]; } return r; }

    static int[] applyRule(int[] m) {
        int[] r = m.clone(); int t = 0; int saved = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) t += r[i];
        if (t > 20 - 0) {                       // HLD not started by minute 20
            for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) if (COMPRESSIBLE[i] && r[i] > FLOOR[i]) {
                int cut = Math.min(r[i] - FLOOR[i], t - 20 + 0); if (cut <= 0) break; r[i] -= cut; saved += cut; t -= cut; }
        }
        int total = Arrays.stream(r).sum();
        int spare = 45 - total;                 // minutes now available before the hard stop
        if (spare > 0) { int addDeep = Math.min(spare, Math.max(0, PLAN[5] - r[5])); r[5] += addDeep; spare -= addDeep;
                         int addFail = Math.min(spare, Math.max(0, PLAN[6] - r[6])); r[6] += addFail; spare -= addFail;
                         r[7] += Math.min(spare, 2); }
        return cap(r);
    }
    static String phaseAt(int[] x, int minute) { int t = 0; for (int i = 0; i < x.length; i++) { t += x[i]; if (t > minute) return PH[i]; } return "done"; }
    static String overran(int[] x) { StringBuilder s = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) if (x[i] > PLAN[i] + 2) s.append(s.length() > 0 ? "," : "").append(PH[i]); return s.length() == 0 ? "-" : s.toString(); }
    static String fmt(int[] x) { StringBuilder s = new StringBuilder(); for (int v : x) s.append(String.format("%3d", v)); return s.toString(); }
}

M1 coupon service (B2)          11  7  6  8 10  3  0  0                        api      3/16 clarify,estimate,data
M2 order notifications (B2)      6  3  9  7  8  9  3  0                       data     12/16       api
M3 dark-store inventory (B3)     5  5  3  6 11 11  4  0                        hld     15/16         -
M4 multi-country (B4)            8  2  2  4 12 10  5  2                        hld     15/16   clarify
M5 rate limiter (B2)             4  8  5  5  9 10  2  2                       data     12/16  estimate
M6 search autocomplete (B3)      7  6  4  9  9  8  2  0                       data     10/16      data

Checkpoint rule: at minute 20 you must be drawing the HLD. If you are behind, compress estimate/api/data
to their floors (1/1/2 min: state the numbers, name 2 endpoints, list 3 tables) and say so aloud.

mock (replayed with rule)                                                   @20min deep+fail
M1 coupon service (B2)          11  1  1  7 10 12  3  0                        hld     15/16
M2 order notifications (B2)      6  1  6  7  8 12  4  1                        hld     16/16
M3 dark-store inventory (B3)     5  5  3  6 11 11  4  0                        hld     15/16
M4 multi-country (B4)            8  2  2  4 12 10  5  2                        hld     15/16
M5 rate limiter (B2)             4  6  5  5  9 12  2  2                        hld     14/16
M6 search autocomplete (B3)      7  1  3  9  9 12  4  0                        hld     16/16

Deep-dive + failures, average over 6 mocks: 11.2 min as recorded → 15.2 min with the rule (plan: 16)
(replay assumes the minutes saved go to deep-dive then failures; clarify is never compressed)

Reading it:

  • As recorded:
    • Four of the six mocks were still on the data model or earlier at minute 20.
    • Deep dive plus failures averaged 11.2 of 16 planned minutes.
    • M1 got 3 minutes and never reached failures.
  • With the rule: "HLD by minute 20, compress estimate/API/data aloud if behind" raises the average to 15.2.
  • What the rule can't fix: M1 still spends 11 minutes clarifying, because clarify is not compressible. Clarify needs its own 5-minute timebox.
  • What it doesn't touch: mocks already on time (M3, M4) are unchanged.

docs.title: L2 — Should you trust your peer's verdict? B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "Know how much a mock verdict tells you, and what makes it more reliable."

The program simulates 200,000 candidates under two interviewer models. The bias and noise levels are assumptions stated in the code.

CalibrationL2.java
// L2 — Calibration: how interviewer bias and noise turn into wrong hire decisions, and what calibration and more interviewers buy.
// Model (assumptions, VERIFY against your own loop data): candidate skill ~ N(0,1); hire bar = skill > 0.5 (~31% should pass).
// Interviewer i reports skill + bias_i + noise. Uncalibrated: bias sd 0.5, noise sd 0.6. Calibrated (anchored rubric,
// shadowing, score review): bias sd 0.15, noise sd 0.45. Decision: mean of the k interviewers' scores > 0.5.
import java.util.*;

public class CalibrationL2 {
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        long seed = 60;
        int candidates = 200_000, panel = 12;
        System.out.println("200,000 simulated candidates; hire bar: true skill > 0.5 (30.9% should be hired)\n");
        System.out.printf("%-14s %3s %11s %12s %12s %10s %14s%n", "interviewers", "k", "accuracy", "false hire", "false reject", "hire rate", "2 agree (k=1)");
        for (String mode : new String[]{"uncalibrated", "calibrated"}) {
            double biasSd = mode.equals("uncalibrated") ? 0.5 : 0.15, noiseSd = mode.equals("uncalibrated") ? 0.6 : 0.45;
            for (int k : new int[]{1, 2, 3, 4}) {
                Random r = new Random(seed);
                double[] bias = new double[panel]; for (int i = 0; i < panel; i++) bias[i] = r.nextGaussian() * biasSd;
                if (k == 1) System.out.printf("   (%s panel of %d: mean bias %+.2f, most lenient %+.2f, harshest %+.2f)%n", mode, panel,
                        Arrays.stream(bias).average().orElse(0), Arrays.stream(bias).max().orElse(0), Arrays.stream(bias).min().orElse(0));
                int correct = 0, fh = 0, fr = 0, hires = 0, agree = 0;
                for (int c = 0; c < candidates; c++) {
                    double skill = r.nextGaussian(); boolean should = skill > 0.5;
                    int[] who = pick(r, panel, Math.max(k, 2));
                    double sum = 0; for (int j = 0; j < k; j++) sum += skill + bias[who[j]] + r.nextGaussian() * noiseSd;
                    boolean hire = sum / k > 0.5;
                    if (hire == should) correct++; else if (hire) fh++; else fr++;
                    if (hire) hires++;
                    // would two single interviewers, seen independently, reach the same decision?
                    boolean d1 = skill + bias[who[0]] + r.nextGaussian() * noiseSd > 0.5, d2 = skill + bias[who[1]] + r.nextGaussian() * noiseSd > 0.5;
                    if (d1 == d2) agree++;
                }
                System.out.printf("%-14s %3d %10.1f%% %11.1f%% %11.1f%% %9.1f%% %13.1f%%%n", mode, k, 100.0 * correct / candidates,
                        100.0 * fh / candidates, 100.0 * fr / candidates, 100.0 * hires / candidates, 100.0 * agree / candidates);
            }
        }
        // mock-interview angle: a candidate right at the bar (skill 0.7) vs just below (0.3) — how often a single mock says "hire"?
        System.out.println("\nOne mock, one interviewer — how often the verdict is \"hire\" for a candidate with true skill s:");
        System.out.printf("%-14s %8s %8s %8s %8s %8s%n", "interviewers", "s=0.0", "s=0.3", "s=0.7", "s=1.0", "s=1.5");
        for (String mode : new String[]{"uncalibrated", "calibrated"}) {
            double biasSd = mode.equals("uncalibrated") ? 0.5 : 0.15, noiseSd = mode.equals("uncalibrated") ? 0.6 : 0.45;
            Random r = new Random(seed + 1);
            StringBuilder row = new StringBuilder(String.format("%-14s", mode));
            for (double s : new double[]{0.0, 0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5}) {
                int yes = 0, n = 100_000;
                for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (s + r.nextGaussian() * biasSd + r.nextGaussian() * noiseSd > 0.5) yes++;
                row.append(String.format(" %7.0f%%", 100.0 * yes / n));
            }
            System.out.println(row);
        }
    }
    static int[] pick(Random r, int n, int k) { List<Integer> l = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) l.add(i); Collections.shuffle(l, r); int[] x = new int[k]; for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) x[i] = l.get(i); return x; }
}
