docs.title: I01b. Amazon-Style Marketplace — How the Whole System Works
docs.text:
What this page adds

I01 focuses on four hard problems with runnable labs. This page is the system walkthrough, with no code. It follows one order from search to doorstep and the seller's payout, and explains each subsystem:

  • catalog, search, recommendations, pricing and the buy box, cart, checkout and payments;
  • the order pipeline, fulfilment centres, transportation and delivery, returns;
  • the seller side and advertising;
  • the algorithms behind them;
  • the data platform and warehouse;
  • the tech stack, with what has been publicly described kept separate from a reference choice.

Sources and honesty

Everything attributed to Amazon comes from public sources:

  • papers such as Dynamo (2007) and item-to-item collaborative filtering (2003);
  • AWS blog posts, the AWS Builders' Library, re:Invent talks and news coverage.

These are marked VERIFY. Internal details are not public, so where this page says "a system like this would…" it is describing a reference design, not Amazon's implementation.

docs.title: 1. The Business in Numbers (orders of magnitude)
docs.text:
Quantity Order of magnitude (VERIFY current figures) Products (catalog entries) Hundreds of millions Sellers Millions, with the majority of units sold by third-party sellers (VERIFY share) Customers Hundreds of millions Fulfilment and delivery sites Hundreds of fulfilment centres, plus sortation centres and delivery stations worldwide Peak events Prime Day and holiday peaks, with AWS publishing per-service peak metrics for the retail business in yearly blog posts (VERIFY)

What this scale implies:

  • Everything is sharded by customer, product or seller.
  • Everything is owned by a small team behind an API.
  • Everything is measured.

docs.title: 2. The Architecture in Layers
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Clients
        WEB[Web]
        MOB[Mobile apps]
        VOICE[Voice and devices]
        SELLER[Seller Central]
    end
    subgraph Edge
        CDN[CDN - images, static, cached fragments]
        LB[Load balancers and front-end fleets - cells, shuffle sharded]
    end
    subgraph Experience[Page composition]
        AGG[Page aggregators - detail, search, cart, checkout]
    end
    subgraph Domains[Domain services - hundreds, each team-owned]
        CAT[Catalog]
        SRCH[Search and ranking]
        REC[Recommendations]
        OFF[Offers, pricing, buy box]
        PROM[Delivery promise]
        CART[Cart]
        CHK[Checkout]
        PAY[Payments and fraud]
        ORD[Order pipeline - workflows]
        FC[Fulfilment - warehouse systems]
        TRN[Transportation and last mile]
        RET[Returns]
        ADS[Advertising]
        REV[Reviews]
        SELL[Seller services - listings, inventory, settlement]
    end
    subgraph Data
        STREAM[Event streams]
        LAKE[Data lake on object storage]
        DW[Warehouse and query engines]
        MLP[ML platform]
    end
    Clients --> Edge --> Experience --> Domains
    Domains --> STREAM --> LAKE --> DW
    LAKE --> MLP --> Domains

Organising principles (publicly described; VERIFY):

  • Service-oriented from early on. Teams own services end to end, including on-call. They communicate only through APIs, with no shared databases.
  • Small teams, often described as "two-pizza teams".
  • Cells, shuffle sharding and constant-work designs for blast-radius control. Deployments roll out in waves, region by region and cell by cell (AWS Builders' Library).
  • Correction of Errors (COE) documents after incidents, a blameless postmortem culture with root-cause analysis (VERIFY).

docs.title: 3.1 Search
docs.text:
1. Request: a customer types "running shoes men". The request reaches a front-end fleet in their region, routed to a cell.
  2. Query understanding:
    • spelling correction;
    • tokenisation and normalisation;
    • category and attribute prediction (department = shoes, gender = men, activity = running);
    • brand detection;
    • synonyms;
    • intent classification: navigational ("nike air zoom") vs exploratory ("gift for runner").
  3. Candidate retrieval:
    • lexical retrieval over an inverted index of product text (titles, bullets, attributes, backend keywords sellers provide);
    • semantic retrieval with neural embeddings (query and product encoded into the same vector space; approximate nearest-neighbour search) to catch products that don't share words with the query. Amazon published semantic product search work (VERIFY: "Semantic Product Search", KDD 2019);
    • filters: availability in the customer's region, and deliverability to the customer's address.

  4. Ranking: a learning-to-rank model scores candidates. Features:

    • text relevance, and behavioural signals (clicks, add-to-carts, purchases for this query);
    • price, delivery speed, reviews and ratings, availability, seller quality;
    • personalisation.

    It is trained on historical searches with purchase and engagement labels. Ranking is multi-objective: relevance, conversion, customer experience signals. 5. Blending: sponsored products (from the ads auction, §3.12) and widgets are blended into the results with limits. 6. Rendering: the page aggregator combines results with prices and delivery promises (from the offer and promise services), then renders. The whole flow has a latency budget of a few hundred ms.

docs.title: 3.2 Product detail page
docs.text:
When the customer clicks a product, the detail page aggregator calls tens of services in parallel with deadlines:

  • catalog (title, images, attributes, variations);
  • offer listing and buy box (the winning offer);
  • price and deals;
  • delivery promise for the customer's address;
  • stock status;
  • reviews summary;
  • Q&A;
  • recommendations ("frequently bought together", "customers also viewed");
  • ads;
  • the customer's own state (bought before, in cart).

Critical widgets (price, buy box, availability, Add to Cart) must render. Optional widgets degrade (see I01 §2.6).

docs.title: 3.3 Catalog — one product, many sellers
docs.text:
• Identity: each product has an identifier (ASIN). Sellers either match their offer to an existing ASIN (using UPC/EAN/ISBN or matching) or create one.
  • Contributions: many sellers and vendors contribute data about the same product, which conflicts (different titles, wrong weights).
    • An arbitration process picks the displayed value per attribute, using contributor trust, consistency checks and ML-based quality models.
    • Duplicate detection merges accidental duplicates.
  • Product types and schemas: attributes are defined per product type (shoes have size and width; TVs have screen size). Listings are validated against the schema.
  • Variations: parent–child relationships (size and colour) group variants on one page.
  • Storage: a versioned, attribute-level store, with change events feeding search indexing, the detail page and the data lake.

docs.title: 3.4 Offers, pricing and the buy box
docs.text:
• An offer = seller + ASIN + condition + price + shipping + fulfilment channel (seller-fulfilled or platform-fulfilled) + quantity.
  • Pricing:
    • sellers set prices, often through automated repricers;
    • the platform's own retail pricing uses automated competitive pricing (monitoring prices elsewhere, cost, demand elasticity; VERIFY specifics);
    • fair-pricing policies block unusually high prices (VERIFY policy details).
  • The buy box: one offer wins the default Add to Cart position. The factors publicly described to sellers include landed price, fulfilment method and delivery speed, seller performance metrics and stock (VERIFY; the exact formula is not public). I01 L2 shows how to maintain it consistently under repricing.

docs.title: 3.5 Cart
docs.text:
• Always writable: the cart is the original use case of the Dynamo paper's highly available key-value design (VERIFY; today's implementation isn't public).
  • Contents: item references and quantities, not prices, which are re-read at checkout.
  • Merge semantics: see I01 L1.
  • "Saved for later" is a separate list.
  • Guest carts are merged into the account at sign-in.

docs.title: 3.6 Checkout
docs.text:
1. Address and delivery options. The promise service computes delivery dates per shipping speed from inventory positions, carrier cut-offs and capacity (§3.9).
  2. Payment selection: cards (tokenised), wallets, gift balances, instalments and local methods per country.
  3. Order total:
    • item prices re-validated;
    • promotions and coupons applied (a rules engine; Ch 49);
    • tax computed per jurisdiction by a tax engine using product tax codes and the ship-to address.

  4. Place order:

    • a risk check (fraud score);
    • payment authorisation;
    • order creation with the promise and fulfilment plan attached;
    • confirmation to the customer.

    Payment is usually captured later, when items ship (common e-commerce practice; VERIFY per market).

docs.title: 3.7 Payments and fraud
docs.text:
• Payments:
    • an authorisation at order time, and capture at shipment (partial captures for split shipments);
    • refunds on returns;
    • card data kept out of most systems through tokenisation (PCI DSS scope reduction; Ch 45).

  • Fraud detection: real-time models score each order, using:

    • account age and history, device and network signals;
    • address risk, payment instrument risk, velocity;
    • graph links between accounts.

    The actions are: accept, hold for review, step-up verification, or cancel. Amazon offers related capability as an AWS service, Amazon Fraud Detector (VERIFY that it is still offered), which reflects the kind of models used. - Seller-side risk: new-seller verification, suspicious listing detection, counterfeit reports and brand registry protections (VERIFY programme names).

docs.title: 3.8 The order pipeline
docs.text:
• A long-running workflow: placed → payment authorised → released to fulfilment → picked → packed → shipped (capture) → delivered → return window → closed.
  • Each shipment is its own sub-workflow. Cancellation is possible until release to the fulfilment centre.
  • Orchestrated by workflow engines with durable state and timers. The public analogue is AWS Step Functions and the Simple Workflow Service (SWF), whose paradigm came from internal use (VERIFY) (Ch 13, Ch 50).
  • Events from every step go to tracking pages, notifications, analytics and finance.

docs.title: 3.9 Inventory placement and the promise
docs.text:
• Demand forecasting per product, per region, per day, as probabilistic (quantile) forecasts. Amazon researchers published deep-learning forecasting methods such as DeepAR and multi-horizon quantile recurrent forecasters (MQ-RNN) (VERIFY papers and use).

  • Buying and placement:

    • how much to buy, from forecasts, lead times and cost of stock-outs vs holding;
    • where to place it (which fulfilment centres), so most customers are near stock.

    I01 L3 shows placement dominates the promise. - Inbound: - vendors ship to the platform, and sellers using the platform's fulfilment (FBA) send inbound shipments; - the system chooses the destination FCs, and inventory is distributed later between FCs as needed. - The promise: for a customer and item, find FCs with available stock, pick and ship cut-off times, carrier transit time and capacity. The fastest feasible option is shown as "Arrives Tuesday".

docs.title: 3.10 Inside a fulfilment centre
docs.text:
1. Receive: inbound units are scanned and checked.
  2. Stow: units are placed into any available bin, not a fixed location per product. This is random ("chaotic") stow, widely described (VERIFY).
    • It maximises space use and spreads popular items so many pickers can reach them.
    • The system records exactly which bin holds what.
  3. Pick:
    • Traditional FCs: pickers follow optimised pick paths through aisles.
    • Robotic FCs: drive units carry shelving pods to picker stations (from the Kiva Systems acquisition in 2012, now Amazon Robotics; VERIFY current systems). Pick lists are batched by wave and by the chosen shipping cut-off.
  4. Pack: the system recommends a box size from item dimensions (cartonisation, a 3D bin-packing heuristic), or uses automated packaging.
  5. Label and sort: a label is applied, and the parcel is sorted to the right outbound lane: carrier and destination sortation centre.
  6. Throughput control: the warehouse management system balances work across stations. Labour planning uses forecasts of units per hour.

docs.title: 3.11 Transportation and last mile
docs.text:
• Middle mile: trucks and planes move parcels from FCs to sortation centres and delivery stations. Linehaul schedules are optimised against volume forecasts.
  • Last mile:
    • parcels are sorted by route at delivery stations;
    • route planning solves a vehicle routing problem with time windows (VRP-TW), with stop sequences, road network travel times and driver hours;
    • drivers include in-house partners and crowd-sourced drivers (VERIFY programmes).
  • Tracking: scan events and driver app GPS update tracking. Delivery photo proof and OTPs are used for high-value items.
  • Alternatives: lockers and pickup points.

docs.title: 3.12 Advertising
docs.text:
• Sponsored products: advertisers bid on keywords or targets. For each search, eligible ads go through an auction:

    • the ranking combines bid × predicted click-through rate × relevance;
    • pricing is a second-price-like auction (VERIFY the current auction design).

    Budget pacing spreads spend across the day (Ch 49 L3 for pacing concepts). - Measurement: attribution of purchases to ad clicks, and advertiser reporting from the data platform.

docs.title: 3.13 Reviews
docs.text:
• Collection: reviews and ratings, with "Verified Purchase" badges.
  • Abuse detection: ML models, graph analysis of reviewer–seller relationships, and bulk suppression (VERIFY).
  • Aggregated rating: a weighted model rather than a simple average. Amazon has said its star ratings use ML weighting by factors such as recency and verification (VERIFY).

docs.title: 3.14 Returns
docs.text:
• The return request is checked against policy.
  • Options: drop-off, pickup, or refund at drop-off for some items.
  • Grading: returned items are graded and routed to restock, sell as used or open-box, return to the seller, liquidate, or dispose.
  • Money and fraud: refunds via payments, and return-abuse detection.

docs.title: 3.15 The seller's side
docs.text:
• Onboarding: identity and business verification, tax information and bank account.
  • Listing: matching or creating ASINs, and bulk upload through APIs.
  • Inventory: seller-fulfilled or platform-fulfilled.
  • Orders: notifications and SLAs for seller-fulfilled orders, and performance metrics (late shipment, cancellation, defect rates).
  • Settlement:
    • a per-seller ledger: sales, less fees (referral, fulfilment, storage, ads), refunds and chargebacks;
    • held until the return window, then disbursed on a schedule, with statements;
    • double-entry accounting as in Ch 45 and I03.

docs.title: 4. Algorithms Catalog
docs.text: Problem Algorithm (typical) Where Similar products ("customers who bought") Item-to-item collaborative filtering (publicly described, 2003): compute similarity between items from co-purchases, offline; online, look up similar items for what the customer bought or viewed Recommendations Personalised ranking Learning-to-rank (gradient-boosted trees, neural rankers) on engagement and purchase labels Search, feeds Semantic matching Two-tower neural embeddings + approximate nearest neighbour (HNSW/IVF) Search retrieval Query understanding Classifiers for category, attributes and intent; spell correction; synonyms Search Demand forecasting Probabilistic deep-learning forecasters (quantiles) Buying, placement, labour Inventory placement Optimisation: minimise expected shipping cost and missed promises under capacity Supply chain Buy box Scoring on landed price, delivery, seller performance (formula not public) Offers Pricing Competitive price monitoring, elasticity models, rules Retail pricing Fulfilment plan Search over FC combinations, minimising cost under the promise Order release (I01 L3) Pick paths Heuristic TSP within zones, batching and wave planning Fulfilment centres Box selection 3D bin packing heuristics Packing Route planning Vehicle routing with time windows (heuristics + local search) Last mile Fraud Gradient-boosted models, graph features, rules Checkout, sellers, reviews Ads auction Bid × predicted CTR × relevance ranking; pacing controllers Advertising Review ranking Helpfulness models, abuse detection Reviews Availability of the site Cells, shuffle sharding, constant work Infrastructure (I01 L4)

docs.title: 4.1 Item-to-item collaborative filtering
docs.text:
A closer look at the algorithm from the published 2003 paper (VERIFY: Linden, Smith and York, IEEE Internet Computing):

  1. Offline, build an item–item table. For each item A, look at customers who bought A. For each other item B those customers bought, compute a similarity between A and B, e.g. the cosine similarity of their customer-purchase vectors. Keep the top N similar items per item.
  2. Online, for a customer: take the items they bought, rated or viewed, and collect each one's similar items. Sum the similarity scores, remove items already bought, and rank.
  3. Why it scales:
    • the expensive part is offline, and grows with items and co-purchase pairs, not with customers × items;
    • online, it is a few table lookups.
  4. What it teaches: precompute the heavy relationship offline, serve it cheaply online, and personalise by combining precomputed pieces. Modern systems add deep learning, sequence models and real-time signals on the same principle.

docs.title: 4A.1 From a seller's new listing to a searchable product
docs.text:
1. Submission: the seller submits a listing (via portal, feed file or API), which is validated against the product type schema.
  2. Matching:
    • an identifier match (UPC/EAN/ISBN) links it to an existing product;
    • otherwise ML matching compares titles, attributes and images to detect duplicates;
    • if no match is found, a new product is created.
  3. Content arbitration chooses the displayed attribute values. Image and content quality checks run, and prohibited or restricted products are screened by rules and classifiers.
  4. Change events: the resulting catalog change events trigger:
    • search document rebuild and partial index update;
    • embedding refresh (batch);
    • detail-page cache invalidation;
    • lake ingestion.
  5. Offer events: when the seller's offer (price, quantity) is created, events update the buy box (I01 L2) and the availability used for search filtering.

docs.title: 4A.2 The recommendation pipeline in a modern form
docs.text:
1. Offline:
    • item-to-item similarity tables (the 2003 approach) and embedding models trained on sequences of views and purchases;
    • candidate tables per item and per customer segment.
  2. Nearline: recent customer activity (last views, cart adds) is kept in a fast profile store and updated from streams within seconds.
  3. Online:
    • gather candidates from several sources;
    • rank with a model using customer, item and context features;
    • apply business rules (availability, deliverability, diversity, no already-purchased consumables unless re-buy is likely).
  4. Placement: widget selection per page, with experiments on each widget's contribution.

docs.title: 4A.3 How the promise stays true
docs.text:
• Promise inputs: inventory positions (by FC), open capacity (by FC and shift), carrier cut-offs, and transit time distributions by lane.
  • Using history: the service uses historical delivery performance by lane and day to pick a date it can meet with high probability. It is a quantile decision, not an average: a promise must be kept most of the time.
  • When capacity tightens (peak season), promises lengthen automatically instead of being broken.
  • After ordering: the order stores the promise it was sold with. Downstream systems prioritise orders at risk of missing it.

docs.title: 4A.4 A peak-day request path
docs.text:
1. Front end: a request hits a cell's front-end fleet, and page aggregators fan out with deadlines.
  2. Degradation: under load, optional widgets are dropped first, and shedding protects checkout (Ch 18).
  3. Orders: they flow into the pipeline, where queues absorb bursts. Fulfilment release is paced by FC capacity.
  4. Monitoring: operations dashboards watch per-cell error rates, order rates and payment success. Deployments pause during peak windows.

docs.title: 5.1 What flows in
docs.text:
• Event streams from every service: page views, searches, clicks, add-to-carts, orders, shipments, FC scans, delivery scans, ad impressions and clicks, payments, reviews.
  • Change data from operational databases.
  • External data: carrier data and competitor prices.

docs.title: 5.2 How it is organised (reference design, informed by public AWS material)
docs.text:

Public milestones:

  • AWS publicly described Amazon's consumer business migrating off Oracle databases to AWS services, including DynamoDB, Aurora and Redshift, completed in 2019 (VERIFY: AWS News Blog, "Migration Complete — Amazon's Consumer Business Just Turned off its Final Oracle Database").
  • AWS has also described an internal consumer-business data lake on S3 with a catalog and self-service access (VERIFY name and details).

docs.title: 5.3 Modelling
docs.text:
• Data ownership follows service ownership (data-mesh style). Each team publishes curated datasets with schemas and SLAs, and a central catalog makes them discoverable.
  • Star schemas for business reporting:
    • facts: orders, order items, shipments, page views, ad events, returns;
    • dimensions: product (ASIN), customer (pseudonymised for analytics), seller, marketplace, date, fulfilment centre.
  • Metrics: conversion by page and search, delivery promise accuracy, cost per unit shipped, ad return on spend, seller performance, forecast accuracy.
  • Experimentation:
    • an A/B testing platform assigns customers to treatments;
    • metrics are computed from the lake;
    • a change is launched only on measured customer impact. Amazon is publicly known for heavy experimentation (VERIFY its internal platform names).

docs.title: 7. Reliability and Operations
docs.text:
• Cells and shuffle sharding limit how many customers one failure touches (I01 L4).
  • Timeouts, retries with jitter, and load shedding everywhere (AWS Builders' Library articles; Ch 18).
  • Peak readiness: load tests beyond forecast peaks, game days, pre-scaling, and change freezes near peak events (VERIFY practices).
  • Operational reviews: weekly metric reviews per team, and COE postmortems with action items.
  • Degradation: optional widgets turn off, heavy features pause, and core buying stays up.

docs.title: I02. Flipkart-Style Sale-Day E-Commerce
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Sector: E-commerce (India, festive sales) · Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Builds on: Ch 02, Ch 45, Ch 46, Ch 49, I01

What you get: the design of an Indian e-commerce platform for its biggest days: a multi-day festive sale with midnight deal unlocks. It covers what is specific to India:

  • cash on delivery and parcels returned undelivered;
  • pincode serviceability;
  • bank offers and no-cost EMI;
  • slow networks and low-end phones;
  • vernacular shoppers;
  • reseller rings on limited deals;
  • the operating model of a sale: readiness, war rooms and change freezes.

The waiting room and hot-SKU reservation are in Ch 46, and payment routing is in Ch 45. This chapter builds on them rather than repeating them.

What the labs measured:

  • L1 (deal unlock): with a million phones whose clocks are wrong, polling the origin every 2 s costs 102M requests and gets only 37% of shoppers within 1 s of the unlock. Trusting the phone clock is worse: 17.5% tap early and 12% are late by more than 5 s. Syncing from the server's clock gets 96.6%, and a millisecond re-sync at T−10 s gets 100%.
  • L2 (COD policy, illustrative economics): turning off COD loses a third of orders, and is the worst policy once new-customer value counts. OTP confirmation for medium-risk orders cuts parcels returned undelivered (RTO) by half and gives the best result on both measures.
  • L3 (page weight, real compression): a 40-product listing is 65 KB of full JSON and 1.5 KB trimmed and gzipped. On 2G that is 8.0 s vs 2.9 s on a new connection, and 5.9 s vs 0.8 s on a reused one. Connection setup dominates once payloads are small.
  • L4 (reseller rings): per-account and exact-address limits let a 400-account ring take 800 and 778 deal units. A normalised tower/flat/pincode key cuts that to 24, the theoretical minimum of 2 per drop point, while blocking 82 genuine buyers against an unavoidable floor of 82 (same household or the drop point itself). Fuzzy text similarity is worse on both counts.

Reading time: 80 min.

What this chapter is, and isn't

  • This is a design in the style of a large Indian e-commerce platform during festive sales, based on public talks, engineering blogs and news coverage.
  • It is not a description of Flipkart's internal systems.
  • Business numbers (COD share, RTO rates, costs, network profiles) are illustrative.
  • Regulatory statements are marked VERIFY.

docs.title: 1.1 A story: midnight, and the phone that thought it was 11:58
docs.text:
The sale's headline deal, a phone at ₹9,999 with 5,000 units, unlocks at 12:00:00.

  • The early taps. At 11:59:58 the origin receives 40,000 "Buy" requests from phones whose clocks run fast. They are rejected, the apps retry, and the retries land at 12:00:00, exactly when the real demand arrives.
  • The late shoppers. Some shoppers' phones run slow. Their Buy button appears at 12:00:40, after the units have gone.
  • The complaints. Social media fills with "the sale was rigged".
  • The ring. A reseller ring with 400 accounts ships 800 units to a dozen flats, with each address typed a different way.
  • The returns. Three days later, 18% of the cash-on-delivery orders in some regions come back undelivered, and the reverse shipping eats the margin.

None of this is a database problem. It is time, trust, networks and money, and in India each of these has its own shape.

The thesis of this chapter

An Indian sale day is won before it starts and at the edges.

  • Synchronise clients to server time instead of polling (L1).
  • Price the risk of cash on delivery instead of banning it (L2).
  • Design for 2G and cold connections (L3).
  • Enforce deal limits on the real delivery address (L4).
  • Behind all of that: the capacity, waiting room and reservation machinery of Ch 46.

docs.title: 1.2 What's specific to India
docs.text: Factor Effect on design Where Cash on delivery is still widely used, especially outside metros (VERIFY current share) Parcels returned undelivered (RTO), cash reconciliation, risk scoring §2.5, L2 ~19,000+ pincodes with very different courier coverage (VERIFY count) Serviceability, promise by pincode Ch 01 Slow and variable mobile networks; entry-level Android phones Payload budgets, fewer connections, lite apps §2.6, L3 Many languages Vernacular UI and search, transliteration §2.7 UPI, cards, EMI, bank offers Payment mix, offer eligibility at checkout §2.8, Ch 45 Festive season concentration A large share of annual sales in a few days §2.9 Consumer-protection and e-commerce rules Display of seller details, country of origin, flash-sale rules (VERIFY current rules) §6.5

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end you will be able to:

  • Design a sale-day architecture and readiness plan.
  • Synchronise millions of clients to a deal unlock fairly.
  • Decide COD eligibility with risk and economics, not blanket rules.
  • Budget payloads and connections for slow networks.
  • Enforce purchase limits against reseller rings without blocking households.

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: a festival market that opens at midnight B1
docs.text: Imagine a market where every shop opens at the stroke of midnight and the best items go in seconds. Some shoppers' watches are wrong. Some came on slow buses. Some pay in cash at their door and change their minds. And a few professional buyers send twenty cousins to queue for the same item. A good market organiser fixes all of these before midnight: one clock everyone trusts, a door that admits people in order, clear rules on cash, and limits per household, not per person.

docs.title: 2.2 Requirements and estimates B1
docs.text:
Type Requirement Functional Deal pages with countdowns; sale-only prices and bank offers; limited-quantity deals with per-customer limits; cart; checkout with UPI, cards, EMI, wallets and COD; order tracking; returns. Scale (assumptions) 100M app opens on day 1; at peak minutes, ~1M concurrent shoppers on the deal page; ~10–20× normal checkout rate (VERIFY with your own history). Latency Deal page usable within 3 s on a slow 3G connection; Buy button enabled within ±1 s of unlock for ≥ 99% of shoppers. Fairness First to tap is first served (within network variance); per-customer limits enforced on the delivery household. Correctness No overselling deal units (Ch 46); the bank offer shown is the one applied.

Estimation (Ch 02): 1M shoppers tapping Buy within ~2 seconds of unlock gives ~500k requests/s for a few seconds at the origin (L1: ~580–680k in the peak second). That is why the tap must be admitted through a waiting room and reserved against sharded stock (Ch 46), and why nothing else may hit the origin at that second (L1).

docs.title: 2.3 Architecture overview ⭐ B2
docs.text: Component Role on sale day Edge / CDN Static assets, deal pages, and the edge-cached time endpoint (L1) Deal service Deal definitions, unlock times, quantity pools, per-customer limits Time service Millisecond server time served from the edge Waiting room and admission Fair entry to checkout at a sustainable rate (Ch 46) Inventory reservation Bucketed deal stock, holds with a TTL (Ch 46) Pricing and offers engine Sale prices, bank instant discounts, EMI plans, coupons (Ch 49) Checkout and payments UPI, cards, EMI, wallets, COD; gateway routing (Ch 45) Risk and abuse Reseller detection (L4), COD risk (L2), payment fraud Serviceability and promise Pincode coverage, delivery dates (Ch 01, I01 L3) Order and logistics Manifests, courier allocation, returns, cash reconciliation Notifications Sale reminders, order updates, with priority lanes (Ch 40)

docs.title: 2.4 Unlocking a deal on a million phones ⭐ B2
docs.text:
• Polling the origin to ask "is it live?" is the worst option (L1): 102M requests in five minutes, and still only 37% of shoppers ready within a second, because of the poll interval.
  • The phone's own clock is wrong for a meaningful minority (L1's assumption: 30% are off by more than a second). So 17.5% tap early (rejected, then retried at the worst moment), and 12% are more than 5 s late. That is the "rigged sale" complaint.
  • Sync from the server once.
    • On page load, compute offset = serverTime − localTime, using the response's Date header or a time field, and correct for half the round trip.
    • The Date header has one-second resolution, which gives 96.6% within ±1 s.
  • Re-sync at T−10 s from an edge-cached, millisecond-precision time endpoint (measure the round trip, use its midpoint). That gives 100% within ±1 s.
  • Also:
    • Pre-fetch the deal page and assets before unlock.
    • Enable the button locally.
    • The server still checks the time authoritatively on the Buy request, and rejects early taps without penalising them.
  • The unavoidable part is the Buy spike itself (~0.6M requests/s in the peak second). It goes to the waiting room, not straight to checkout.

docs.title: 2.5 Cash on delivery and RTO ⭐ B3
docs.text:
• COD lets the customer pay at the door. It widens reach (new customers, customers without cards, low trust), but adds:
    • RTO: the parcel is refused or undeliverable and travels back, so you pay both shipping legs and make no sale.
    • Cash handling and reconciliation (Ch 45 §2.7).
  • The risk model scores each order's chance of RTO. Illustrative features: pincode tier, whether the customer is new, their past RTO history, order value, and time to delivery. Actions by score:
    • Low risk: COD offered normally.
    • Medium risk: COD with confirmation, by OTP/IVR before dispatch, or a small partial prepayment.
    • High risk: prepaid only.
  • L2 findings (illustrative economics):
    • Blocking COD entirely keeps only 68% of orders and is worst once the future value of new customers counts.
    • Aggressive blocking (P3, P4) raises this order's profit but gives up future value.
    • The best policy blocks only very high risk and confirms the middle band (P5): best on both measures.
  • Operations matter too: a promise that slips raises refusals, and delivery attempt scheduling and customer calls reduce RTO. Measure RTO by pincode, courier and seller.

docs.title: 2.6 Slow networks and entry-level phones B2
docs.text:
• Budget the payload per screen. L3's list view: 65 KB of full JSON shrinks to 1.5 KB when trimmed to the rendered fields and gzipped.
  • On 2G the connection costs more than the bytes.
    • A new HTTPS connection costs 3 round trips of DNS, TCP and TLS, which is 2.1 s at 700 ms RTT.
    • Reusing connections, limiting the number of origins, and HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 multiplexing matter as much as compression.
    • Trimmed + gzip took 2.9 s on a new connection and 0.8 s on a reused one.
  • Images dominate real pages: list thumbnails in modern formats at the rendered size, lazy loading, and low-quality placeholders.
  • Lite apps and PWAs for low-end phones and slow networks. Flipkart publicly launched a PWA, Flipkart Lite, in 2015 (VERIFY details).
  • Offline-tolerant cart and retries with idempotency keys, because connections drop mid-checkout.

docs.title: 2.7 Vernacular shoppers B2
docs.text:
• UI localisation for many Indian languages, with content from the catalog in multiple languages.
  • Search:
    • handle transliteration ("mobail" / "मोबाइल" → mobile), mixed-script queries and voice input;
    • query understanding maps them to the same catalog (Ch 22, Ch 42);
    • measure search success per language.
  • Keep font and layout budgets in mind for complex scripts on low-end phones.

docs.title: 2.8 Bank offers, EMI and the price at checkout B3
docs.text:
• Sale prices often come with bank instant discounts (e.g. 10% off with specific cards, up to a cap) and no-cost EMI. In no-cost EMI, the interest is funded as a discount (VERIFY accounting and disclosure rules).
  • Eligibility is only known at payment time, from the card BIN or UPI app, bank, EMI tenure and cap usage. So the checkout must:
    • show the estimated offer early;
    • recompute exactly when the instrument is chosen;
    • reserve the bank's offer budget atomically (per-bank daily caps are the budget-pacing problem of Ch 49);
    • release it on payment failure.
  • Price integrity: the order stores the price, each discount line and who funds it (seller, platform, bank) for settlement and invoicing (GST).

docs.title: 2.9 Reseller rings and purchase limits ⭐ B3
docs.text:
• Limited deals ("2 per customer") attract rings: many accounts, cards and phones, but few real delivery points.
  • L4:
    • Per-account limits give the ring everything, 800 units.
    • Exact-address matching gives it 778, because the ring types each address differently.
    • Normalising to tower + flat + pincode gives it exactly 24, which is 2 per drop point, the minimum possible.
    • It blocks 82 genuine buyers, exactly the unavoidable cases: 79 second buyers in the same household, and 3 who live in the drop-point flats.
  • Fuzzy text similarity is worse: "Flat 1102" and "Flat 1103" look 80% similar, so it merged neighbours (2,034 blocked) and still let 202 units through. Parse structure first; use fuzzy matching only on leftovers.
  • Combine signals: device, payment instrument, phone number, address, and graph links between accounts. Enforce at checkout (reservation) and again before dispatch.
  • Communicate household limits clearly so genuine families understand.

docs.title: 2.10 Readiness: running a sale like a launch B4
docs.text:
When Activity T−8 weeks Capacity plan from forecasts; dependency limits (banks, gateways, couriers, SMS) T−6 weeks Full-journey load tests at 1.5× forecast; chaos drills on critical paths T−4 weeks Degradation switches built and tested (recommendations, reviews, search suggestions) T−2 weeks Change freeze on critical services; on-call rosters; war room plan T−1 day Pre-scale; warm caches; verify time sync, waiting room and deal configs Sale War room with journey dashboards; decision owners; comms templates T+1 week Retrospective: forecast vs actuals, incidents, RTO, abuse

The pattern is constant preparation over heroics: known limits, rehearsed switches, one decision owner per journey (Ch 27, Ch 37).

docs.title: 2.11 Dependencies you don't own B4
docs.text:
• Payment gateways and banks, UPI apps, SMS/OTP providers, couriers are each rate-limited and can fail on sale day.
  • Agree peak volumes in advance. Route across providers (Ch 45 L4). Degrade gracefully, e.g. allow the order with a delayed OTP, or queue confirmations.
  • Watch a per-dependency success rate on the war-room dashboard, with pre-agreed switch-over thresholds.

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt
docs.text:
Design Document (excerpt) — COD Eligibility Service

Field Value Context RTO on COD orders varies by region, customer and value. The current rule turns off COD above ₹5,000 everywhere, which loses genuine orders and misses risky low-value ones. Decision Score every COD-eligible order for RTO risk. Offer plain COD below 12%, COD with OTP/IVR confirmation from 12% to 40%, and prepaid only above 40%. Review thresholds monthly per region. Related ADRs ADR-I02-1 time sync for deal unlocks; ADR-I02-2 household-level deal limits; ADR-I02-3 payload budgets per screen

Requirements.

  • R1: The decision is made in ≤ 30 ms at checkout, and falls back to "COD with confirmation" if the model is unavailable.
  • R2: The RTO rate on COD orders is reduced without losing more than 5% of COD orders.
  • R3: The decision and its reasons are logged for customer support and fairness audits.
  • R4: Thresholds are configurable per region and category, with a shadow mode for changes.
  • R5: No protected attributes are used as features (VERIFY applicable rules).

Decisions in detail.

  1. Three bands, not a binary. L2 shows confirmation beats blocking for the middle band.
  2. Future value included in evaluation: blocking new customers costs more than this order's margin (L2).
  3. Shadow mode for two weeks before any threshold change.
  4. Fail open to confirmation, not to plain COD or blocking.

Consequences. Confirmation adds a step for some customers. The model needs monitoring for drift, especially at sale time, when the customer mix changes.

docs.title: 5. Hands-On Code — Level Ladder
docs.text:
What's real here

  • L3 measures real serialised and gzip-compressed payloads.
  • L4 runs real address parsing and matching on synthetic Indian addresses.
  • L1 and L2 are simulations whose assumptions are stated in the code.
  • The economics and network profiles are illustrative.

docs.title: L1 — A fair deal unlock on a million phones B2
docs.text:
Requirement: "Every shopper sees the Buy button within a second of 12:00:00, without flooding the origin."

DealUnlockL1.java
// L1 — "Deal unlocks at 12:00:00". A million phones must start the deal at the same moment, but phone clocks are
// wrong (some by minutes). Compare four client strategies: how much load hits the origin before and at unlock, and how
// many shoppers are ready within 1 s of the true unlock. Clock-skew distribution is an assumption (VERIFY with your
// own client telemetry).
import java.util.*;

public class DealUnlockL1 {
    static final int USERS = 1_000_000, WINDOW = 300;            // users waiting on the deal page in the last 5 minutes

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        Random r = new Random(1202);
        double[] skew = new double[USERS], rtt = new double[USERS], arrive = new double[USERS];
        for (int i = 0; i < USERS; i++) {
            double u = r.nextDouble();                                   // phone clock minus true time, seconds
            skew[i] = u < 0.70 ? r.nextGaussian() * 0.4 : u < 0.92 ? r.nextGaussian() * 15 : r.nextGaussian() * 120;
            rtt[i] = 0.05 + Math.abs(r.nextGaussian()) * (r.nextDouble() < 0.2 ? 0.8 : 0.15);   // 20% on slow networks
            arrive[i] = -WINDOW * Math.sqrt(r.nextDouble());            // more arrivals close to unlock
        }
        System.out.printf("%,d shoppers on the deal page during the last %d s; phone clocks: 70%% within ~1 s, 22%% off by ~15 s, 8%% by ~2 min%n%n", USERS, WINDOW);
        System.out.printf("%-48s %14s %14s %12s %14s %12s%n", "strategy", "origin reqs", "peak origin/s", "early taps", "within ±1 s", "late > 5 s");
        for (int s = 1; s <= 4; s++) run(s, skew, rtt, arrive, r);
        System.out.println("\norigin reqs / peak: requests reaching the origin from arrival until 10 s after unlock (edge-cached polls excluded)");
        System.out.println("early taps: 'Buy' requests sent before the true unlock (rejected, and often retried)");
        System.out.println("within ±1 s: shoppers whose app shows the Buy button within 1 s of the true unlock (early or late)");
    }

    static void run(int s, double[] skew, double[] rtt, double[] arrive, Random r) {
        long origin = 0, early = 0, ready = 0, late = 0; long[] perSec = new long[WINDOW + 20];
        for (int i = 0; i < USERS; i++) {
            double t0 = arrive[i], start;                                // true time the app enables Buy
            switch (s) {
                case 1 -> {                                              // poll the origin every 2 s until it says "live"
                    double first = t0 + r.nextDouble() * 2; int polls = 0; double t = first;
                    while (t < 0) { add(perSec, t); polls++; t += 2; }
                    add(perSec, t); polls++; origin += polls; start = t + rtt[i];
                }
                case 2 -> start = -skew[i];                              // local timer on the phone's own clock
                case 3 -> {                                              // one origin call on page load: offset = server Date − local clock
                    add(perSec, t0); origin++;
                    // the Date header is truncated to whole seconds (up to 1 s behind) and the one-way delay is unknown (±RTT/2)
                    start = r.nextDouble() + (r.nextDouble() - 0.5) * rtt[i];
                }
                default -> {                                             // S3, then at T−10 s re-sync from an edge-cached, ms-precision time endpoint
                    add(perSec, t0); origin++;
                    start = (r.nextDouble() - 0.5) * rtt[i] * 0.5;       // RTT measured, so only asymmetry error remains
                }
            }
            // the shopper taps Buy ~0.3–1.5 s after the button appears; that tap always goes to the origin
            double tap = start + 0.3 + r.nextDouble() * 1.2;
            add(perSec, tap); origin++;
            if (tap < 0) early++;
            if (Math.abs(start) <= 1) ready++;
            if (start > 5) late++;
        }
        long peak = Arrays.stream(perSec).max().getAsLong();
        String[] names = {"", "S1 poll the origin every 2 s", "S2 timer on the phone's clock", "S3 offset from server Date on page load", "S4 S3 + ms-precision re-sync at T−10 s"};
        System.out.printf("%-48s %,14d %,14d %11.1f%% %13.1f%% %11.1f%%%n", names[s], origin, peak, 100.0 * early / USERS, 100.0 * ready / USERS, 100.0 * late / USERS);
    }
    static void add(long[] perSec, double t) { int idx = (int) Math.floor(t) + WINDOW; if (idx >= 0 && idx < perSec.length) perSec[idx]++; }
}

strategy                                            origin reqs  peak origin/s   early taps    within ±1 s   late > 5 s
S1 poll the origin every 2 s                        101,959,847        870,823         0.0%          37.3%         0.0%
S2 timer on the phone's clock                         1,000,000        375,953        17.5%          70.4%        12.0%

origin reqs / peak: requests reaching the origin from arrival until 10 s after unlock (edge-cached polls excluded)
early taps: 'Buy' requests sent before the true unlock (rejected, and often retried)
within ±1 s: shoppers whose app shows the Buy button within 1 s of the true unlock (early or late)

Reading it:

  • S1, polling the origin, costs 102M requests in five minutes, and still only 37% of shoppers are ready within a second. The 2-second poll interval spreads them out.
  • S2, the phone's clock: only one request each, but 17.5% tap early, get rejected and retry into the peak, and 12% are more than 5 s late. With this skew distribution (an assumption), that is the "rigged sale" complaint.
  • S3, an offset from the server Date on page load, reaches 96.6% within ±1 s. The rest is the header's one-second resolution plus network asymmetry.
  • S4 adds a millisecond re-sync at T−10 s and reaches 100%.
  • The Buy taps themselves always peak at ~0.6M/s in one second. That is the demand, and it goes to the waiting room (Ch 46). The peak differs between S3 and S4 only because of how the taps fall into one-second buckets.

docs.title: L2 — Who gets cash on delivery? B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "Cut returned undelivered parcels (RTO) without losing the customers COD brings in."

CodPolicyL2.java
// L2 — Cash on delivery (COD) and "return to origin" (RTO): the customer refuses the parcel at the door and it
// travels back. Which orders should be offered COD? Compare policies on 300,000 simulated orders with a risk model.
// All rates, costs and behaviours are ILLUSTRATIVE assumptions (VERIFY against your own data before using the numbers).
import java.util.*;

public class CodPolicyL2 {
    record Order(double value, double margin, double pRto, boolean wouldPrepay, double pAbandonIfNoCod, double pAcceptOtp, boolean newCust) {}

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        Random r = new Random(1203); List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 300_000; i++) {
            double tier = r.nextDouble();                                            // city tier: metro / tier-2 / tier-3+
            boolean newCust = r.nextDouble() < 0.35, pastRto = !newCust && r.nextDouble() < 0.08;
            double value = Math.exp(6.3 + r.nextGaussian() * 0.8);                   // ₹ (median ~₹545)
            double base = tier < 0.4 ? 0.06 : tier < 0.75 ? 0.12 : 0.20;              // RTO rate for COD by tier (assumption)
            double p = base * (newCust ? 1.5 : 1.0) * (pastRto ? 3.0 : 1.0) * (value > 2000 ? 1.3 : 1.0);
            p = Math.min(0.85, p * Math.exp(r.nextGaussian() * 0.35));               // unobserved noise
            boolean prepay = r.nextDouble() < (tier < 0.4 ? 0.55 : tier < 0.75 ? 0.35 : 0.20);   // would pay online anyway
            orders.add(new Order(value, 0.18 * value, p, prepay, tier < 0.4 ? 0.35 : 0.60, 0.85, newCust));
        }
        double shipFwd = 45, shipRev = 40, codFee = 15;                               // ₹ per parcel (assumption)
        System.out.println("300,000 orders; contribution margin 18%; forward shipping ₹45, return ₹40, COD handling ₹15;");
        System.out.println("a successfully delivered NEW customer is worth ₹" + (int) LTV + " of future margin (all illustrative)\n");
        System.out.printf("%-46s %11s %11s %13s %13s %15s%n", "policy", "orders kept", "RTO parcels", "this order ₹L", "₹ per order", "incl. future ₹L");
        // the model's score is the true risk plus estimation error (a real model is not perfect)
        double[] score = orders.stream().mapToDouble(o -> Math.min(0.95, o.pRto() * Math.exp(r.nextGaussian() * 0.30))).toArray();
        policy("P1 COD for everyone", orders, score, 1.01, 1.01, shipFwd, shipRev, codFee, r);
        policy("P2 no COD at all", orders, score, -1, -1, shipFwd, shipRev, codFee, r);
        policy("P3 block COD if risk > 25%", orders, score, 0.25, 0.25, shipFwd, shipRev, codFee, r);
        policy("P4 block > 25%, OTP-confirm COD at 12–25%", orders, score, 0.12, 0.25, shipFwd, shipRev, codFee, r);
        policy("P5 block > 40%, OTP-confirm COD at 12–40%", orders, score, 0.12, 0.40, shipFwd, shipRev, codFee, r);
        System.out.println("\nOTP-confirm: the customer confirms by OTP/IVR before dispatch; assumed to cut RTO risk by 40% and lose 15% of those orders.");
    }

    // risk < confirmAt: plain COD offered; confirmAt ≤ risk < blockAt: COD with OTP confirmation; risk ≥ blockAt: prepaid only
    static final double LTV = 250;
    static void policy(String name, List<Order> os, double[] score, double confirmAt, double blockAt, double fwd, double rev, double fee, Random r) {
        Random rr = new Random(99); long kept = 0, rto = 0; double profit = 0, future = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < os.size(); i++) {
            Order o = os.get(i); double s = score[i];
            if (o.wouldPrepay()) { kept++; profit += o.margin() - fwd; if (o.newCust()) future += LTV; continue; }       // prepaid orders: no RTO modelled
            if (s >= blockAt) {                                                            // COD refused: some pay online, others leave
                if (rr.nextDouble() < o.pAbandonIfNoCod()) continue;
                kept++; profit += o.margin() - fwd; if (o.newCust()) future += LTV; continue;
            }
            double p = o.pRto();
            if (s >= confirmAt) { if (rr.nextDouble() > o.pAcceptOtp()) continue; p *= 0.6; }
            kept++;
            if (rr.nextDouble() < p) { rto++; profit -= fwd + rev; }                       // lost both legs, no sale
            else { profit += o.margin() - fwd - fee; if (o.newCust()) future += LTV; }
        }
        System.out.printf("%-46s %,11d %,11d %13.1f %13.1f %15.1f%n", name, kept, rto, profit / 1e5, profit / os.size(), (profit + future) / 1e5);
    }
}

300,000 orders; contribution margin 18%; forward shipping ₹45, return ₹40, COD handling ₹15;
a successfully delivered NEW customer is worth ₹250 of future margin (all illustrative)

policy                                         orders kept RTO parcels this order ₹L   ₹ per order incl. future ₹L
P1 COD for everyone                                300,000      32,290         189.0          63.0           417.7
P2 no COD at all                                   203,982           0         183.5          61.2           361.5
P3 block COD if risk > 25%                         275,533      18,364         194.8          64.9           410.3
P4 block > 25%, OTP-confirm COD at 12–25%          265,392      12,453         196.5          65.5           408.6
P5 block > 40%, OTP-confirm COD at 12–40%          277,199      16,337         198.1          66.0           419.8

OTP-confirm: the customer confirms by OTP/IVR before dispatch; assumed to cut RTO risk by 40% and lose 15% of those orders.

Reading it (all economics are illustrative):

  • No COD at all (P2) keeps only 68% of orders. It ends slightly below COD-for-everyone on this order's profit, and is clearly the worst once new-customer value counts (₹361.5L vs ₹417.7L).
  • Blocking above 25% (P3, P4) raises this order's profit but gives up future value.
  • Blocking only above 40% and confirming the 12–40% band (P5) is best on both measures: ₹198.1L now and ₹419.8L with future value. It also halves RTO parcels (32,290 → 16,337).
  • The lesson is the method, not the thresholds: evaluate COD policy on both horizons, and prefer confirmation to blocking for the middle band. The first version of this lab assumed a 12% margin and ₹55 shipping. There, no COD policy was profitable at all, because the margin on a median order barely covered shipping. That is a reminder that the conclusion depends on unit economics you must take from your own data.

docs.text:
Requirement: "The deal list loads in under 3 s on a congested 3G connection."

PayloadL3.java
// L3 — The sale page on a slow phone network. Build a real product-listing response (40 products), measure its REAL
// size as full JSON, trimmed JSON (only fields the list view renders) and gzip-compressed, then estimate load time on
// 2G/3G/4G profiles with TCP slow start (initial window 10 segments). Network profiles are assumptions (VERIFY).
import java.io.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.zip.*;

public class PayloadL3 {
    public static void main(String[] a) throws Exception {
        Random r = new Random(1204);
        String full = listing(r, true), trim = listing(new Random(1204), false);
        byte[] fullB = full.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8), trimB = trim.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        byte[] fullGz = gzip(fullB, 6), trimGz = gzip(trimB, 6), trimGz9 = gzip(trimB, 9);
        String[] names = {"full JSON", "full JSON + gzip", "trimmed JSON", "trimmed + gzip", "trimmed + gzip -9"};
        int[] sizes = {fullB.length, fullGz.length, trimB.length, trimGz.length, trimGz9.length};
        // name, downlink kbit/s, RTT ms (illustrative profiles)
        Object[][] nets = {{"2G/EDGE", 100, 700}, {"3G congested", 400, 350}, {"4G busy (sale evening)", 3000, 120}, {"4G good", 15000, 50}};
        System.out.printf("40-product listing response, sizes measured; times = new HTTPS connection + transfer with slow start%n%n");
        System.out.printf("%-20s %10s", "payload", "bytes");
        for (Object[] n : nets) System.out.printf(" %22s", n[0]);
        System.out.println();
        for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
            System.out.printf("%-20s %,10d", names[i], sizes[i]);
            for (Object[] n : nets) System.out.printf(" %20.2f s", seconds(sizes[i], (int) n[1], (int) n[2], true));
            System.out.println();
        }
        System.out.printf("%nsame, on an already-open connection (no DNS/TCP/TLS setup, window already grown):%n");
        for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
            System.out.printf("%-20s %,10d", names[i], sizes[i]);
            for (Object[] n : nets) System.out.printf(" %20.2f s", seconds(sizes[i], (int) n[1], (int) n[2], false));
            System.out.println();
        }
        System.out.println("\nfull: 17 fields per product incl. description, specs, 6 image URLs, offers, seller; trimmed: id, title, price, mrp, rating, 1 image");
    }

    // setup: DNS 1 RTT + TCP 1 RTT + TLS 1.3 1 RTT, then request 1 RTT; transfer in slow-start rounds (10 × 1460 B, doubling)
    // until the bandwidth-delay product is reached, then at link rate
    static double seconds(int bytes, int kbps, int rttMs, boolean cold) {
        double rtt = rttMs / 1000.0, bw = kbps * 1000 / 8.0, t = cold ? 3 * rtt : 0; double sent = 0, window = cold ? 14600 : Math.max(14600, bw * rtt);
        t += rtt / 2;                                                    // request reaches the server
        while (sent < bytes) {
            double burst = Math.min(window, bytes - sent);
            t += Math.max(burst / bw, 0) + (sent + burst < bytes ? Math.max(0, rtt - burst / bw) : rtt / 2);
            sent += burst; window = Math.min(window * 2, Math.max(bw * rtt, 14600));
        }
        return t;
    }
    static byte[] gzip(byte[] in, int level) throws IOException {
        ByteArrayOutputStream bo = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        try (GZIPOutputStream g = new GZIPOutputStream(bo) {{ def.setLevel(level); }}) { g.write(in); }
        return bo.toByteArray();
    }
    // product copy varies per product (a repeated sentence would compress unrealistically well)
    static final String[] WORDS = ("powerful fast octa core processor smooth display amoled bright sunlight battery lasts all day charging watt turbo camera portrait night mode " +
        "sensor lens ultra wide selfie video stabilisation gaming cooling chamber storage expandable memory slot dual sim network band support sleek design slim body " +
        "glass back matte finish fingerprint unlock face secure stereo speakers dolby audio headphone jack software updates security patches years durable splash resistant " +
        "premium value best in segment students professionals everyday use travel streaming social media multitasking apps").split(" ");
    static String prose(Random r, int n) { StringBuilder b = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (i > 0) b.append(i % 12 == 0 ? ". " : " "); b.append(WORDS[r.nextInt(WORDS.length)]); } return b.append('.').toString(); }
    static String listing(Random r, boolean full) {
        String[] brands = {"Redmi", "Samsung", "realme", "POCO", "Moto", "iQOO", "OnePlus", "vivo"}, colors = {"Black", "Blue", "Green", "Silver", "Purple"};
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("{\"page\":1,\"items\":[");
        for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) {
            String brand = brands[r.nextInt(brands.length)]; int mrp = 9999 + r.nextInt(30) * 1000, price = (int) (mrp * (0.6 + r.nextDouble() * 0.3));
            if (i > 0) sb.append(',');
            sb.append("{\"id\":\"MOB").append(100000 + r.nextInt(900000)).append("\",\"title\":\"").append(brand).append(" ").append(r.nextInt(90) + 10)
              .append(" 5G (").append(colors[r.nextInt(5)]).append(", ").append(4 << r.nextInt(3)).append("GB RAM, ").append(64 << r.nextInt(3)).append("GB)\",")
              .append("\"price\":").append(price).append(",\"mrp\":").append(mrp).append(",\"rating\":").append(3.5 + r.nextInt(15) / 10.0)
              .append(",\"img\":\"https://img.example.in/p/").append(Long.toHexString(r.nextLong())).append("_312x312.webp\"");
            if (full) {
                sb.append(",\"ratingCount\":").append(r.nextInt(90000)).append(",\"reviewCount\":").append(r.nextInt(9000))
                  .append(",\"description\":\"").append(prose(r, 60 + r.nextInt(60))).append("\"")
                  .append(",\"specs\":{\"display\":\"6.7 inch FHD+\",\"battery\":\"").append(5000 + r.nextInt(3) * 500).append(" mAh\",\"camera\":\"50MP + 2MP\",\"processor\":\"Octa-core\",\"warranty\":\"1 year\"}")
                  .append(",\"images\":[");
                for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) sb.append(k > 0 ? "," : "").append("\"https://img.example.in/p/").append(Long.toHexString(r.nextLong())).append("_832x832.jpeg\"");
                sb.append("],\"offers\":[\"10% instant discount on select bank cards\",\"No-cost EMI from ₹").append(price / 12).append("/month\",\"Exchange offer up to ₹").append(r.nextInt(15) * 1000).append(" off\"]")
                  .append(",\"seller\":{\"id\":\"S").append(r.nextInt(99999)).append("\",\"name\":\"RetailNet ").append(r.nextInt(99)).append("\",\"rating\":4.").append(r.nextInt(9)).append("}")
                  .append(",\"deliveryPromise\":\"Delivery by tomorrow\",\"returnPolicy\":\"7 days replacement\",\"trackingTags\":[\"sale\",\"bbd\",\"slot").append(r.nextInt(9)).append("\"]");
            } else {
                for (int k = 0; k < 18; k++) r.nextInt(99999);   // keep the random stream aligned with the full listing where it matters little
            }
            sb.append('}');
        }
        return sb.append("]}").toString();
    }
}
