Reading it:

  • Real sizes:
    • full JSON is 65 KB;
    • gzip alone reduces it to 13.9 KB;
    • trimming to the six fields the list renders reduces it to 6.7 KB;
    • trimming plus gzip gives 1.5 KB. Maximum gzip level adds almost nothing.
  • On 2G with a new connection, full JSON takes 8.0 s and trimmed + gzip 2.9 s. Of that 2.9 s, about 2.1 s is DNS + TCP + TLS setup, three 700 ms round trips.
  • On an already-open connection the same payload takes 0.8 s. Once payloads are small, connections matter more than bytes: reuse connections, keep few origins, and pre-connect.
  • The requirement:
    • congested 3G, new connection: 1.43 s for trimmed + gzip, which meets it;
    • full JSON on 3G: 2.76 s, which barely meets it;
    • full JSON on 2G misses badly.
  • Images are not included. Budget them separately: thumbnails at the rendered size, in modern formats, lazy-loaded.
  • The network profiles and the slow-start model are simplifications (VERIFY with real-user measurements).

docs.title: L4 — Reseller rings vs purchase limits B3
docs.text:
Requirement: "2 units per customer means per household. Don't block neighbours or families."

ResellerL4.java
// L4 — Reseller rings on deal day. The deal allows 2 units per customer; a ring uses 400 accounts that ship to 12 real
// drop points, each address written many different ways. Genuine buyers include neighbours in the same apartment
// complexes. Compare per-account, exact-address, normalised-address and fuzzy (token-similarity) limits: how many deal
// units reach the ring, and how many genuine buyers are wrongly blocked. Addresses are synthetic, in Indian formats.
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class ResellerL4 {
    record Order(String account, String address, String pincode, boolean ring, int dropOrHome) {}

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        Random r = new Random(1205);
        String[] soc = {"Prestige Lakeside Habitat", "Sobha Dream Acres", "Brigade Metropolis", "Purva Riviera", "Salarpuria Greenage", "Mantri Espana"};
        String[] roads = {"Varthur Road", "Whitefield Main Road", "Sarjapur Road", "Outer Ring Road", "Hosur Road", "Bannerghatta Road"};
        String[] pins = {"560087", "560066", "560035", "560103", "560068", "560076"};
        List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();
        // 12 ring drop points: real flats/shops in the same complexes genuine customers live in
        int[][] drops = new int[12][3]; for (int d = 0; d < 12; d++) drops[d] = new int[]{r.nextInt(6), 1 + r.nextInt(12), (1 + r.nextInt(25)) * 100 + 1 + r.nextInt(8)};
        for (int acc = 0; acc < 400; acc++) {
            int[] d = drops[acc % 12];
            orders.add(new Order("R" + acc, variant(r, soc[d[0]], roads[d[0]], d[1], d[2], true), pins[d[0]], true, acc % 12));
        }
        // 20,000 genuine buyers at their own homes; 1,500 live in the same six complexes (12 towers × 25 floors × 8 flats each)
        for (int g = 0; g < 20_000; g++) {
            int c = r.nextInt(6); int tower = 1 + r.nextInt(12), flat = (1 + r.nextInt(25)) * 100 + 1 + r.nextInt(8);
            boolean inComplex = g < 1_500;
            String addr = inComplex ? variant(r, soc[c], roads[c], tower, flat, false)
                                    : (100 + r.nextInt(900)) + ", " + (1 + r.nextInt(20)) + "th Cross, " + (1 + r.nextInt(12)) + "th Main, Sector " + (1 + r.nextInt(7)) + ", HSR Layout";
            orders.add(new Order("G" + g, addr, inComplex ? pins[c] : "5601" + (10 + r.nextInt(80)), false, inComplex ? c * 1_000_000 + tower * 10_000 + flat : 100_000_000 + g));
        }
        Collections.shuffle(orders, r);
        Map<Integer, Long> homes = orders.stream().filter(o -> !o.ring()).collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::dropOrHome, Collectors.counting()));
        long sameHome = homes.values().stream().filter(v -> v > 1).mapToLong(v -> v - 1).sum();
        long nearDrop = orders.stream().filter(o -> !o.ring() && Arrays.stream(drops).anyMatch(d -> d[0] * 1_000_000 + d[1] * 10_000 + d[2] == o.dropOrHome())).count();
        System.out.println("deal limit: 2 units per customer; ring = 400 accounts × 2 units → 12 drop points; 20,000 genuine buyers (1,500 in the same 6 complexes)\n");
        System.out.printf("%-44s %16s %24s %12s%n", "limit keyed on", "units to ring", "genuine buyers blocked", "keys");
        run("account", orders, o -> o.account());
        run("exact address string", orders, o -> o.address() + "|" + o.pincode());
        run("normalised address (tower, flat, pincode)", orders, ResellerL4::normKey);
        run("fuzzy: normalised + token similarity ≥ 0.8", orders, null);
        System.out.printf("%nfloor on 'genuine blocked' for any address-based limit: %d buyers share a flat with an earlier genuine buyer (same household),%n", sameHome);
        System.out.printf("and %d genuine buyers live in a flat the ring uses as a drop point%n", nearDrop);
        System.out.println("\nexamples of one drop point as the ring typed it:");
        orders.stream().filter(o -> o.ring() && o.dropOrHome() == 0).limit(5).forEach(o -> System.out.println("  " + o.address() + " — " + o.pincode()));
    }

    interface Key { String of(Order o); }
    static void run(String name, List<Order> orders, Key key) {
        Map<String, Integer> used = new HashMap<>(); List<String[]> fuzzyKeys = new ArrayList<>(); List<Integer> fuzzyUsed = new ArrayList<>();
        int ringUnits = 0, blocked = 0;
        for (Order o : orders) {
            int allowed;
            if (key != null) { String k = key.of(o); int u = used.getOrDefault(k, 0); allowed = Math.max(0, 2 - u); used.put(k, u + allowed); }
            else {                                                         // fuzzy: compare with earlier keys in the same pincode
                String[] me = {o.pincode(), normText(o.address())}; int hit = -1;
                for (int i = 0; i < fuzzyKeys.size(); i++) if (fuzzyKeys.get(i)[0].equals(me[0]) && sim(fuzzyKeys.get(i)[1], me[1]) >= 0.8) { hit = i; break; }
                if (hit < 0) { fuzzyKeys.add(me); fuzzyUsed.add(0); hit = fuzzyKeys.size() - 1; }
                allowed = Math.max(0, 2 - fuzzyUsed.get(hit)); fuzzyUsed.set(hit, fuzzyUsed.get(hit) + allowed);
            }
            if (o.ring()) ringUnits += allowed; else if (allowed < 2) blocked++;
        }
        long keys = key != null ? used.size() : fuzzyKeys.size();
        System.out.printf("%-44s %16d %24d %,12d%n", name, ringUnits, blocked, keys);
    }

    // normalise: lowercase, expand common abbreviations, pull out tower/block and flat numbers
    static String normText(String s) {
        s = s.toLowerCase().replaceAll("[.,#/\\-]", " ")
             .replaceAll("\\b(flt|flat no|flat|apt|apartment|no)\\b", " flat ").replaceAll("\\b(twr|tower|block|blk|wing)\\b", " tower ")
             .replaceAll("\\b(rd)\\b", " road ").replaceAll("\\b(opp|opposite|near|nr|behind)\\b.*", " ").replaceAll("\\s+", " ").trim();
        return s;
    }
    static String normKey(Order o) {
        String s = normText(o.address());
        String tw = find(s, "\\btower (\\d+)", "\\bt(\\d+)\\b");
        String fl = find(s, "\\bflat (\\d{3,4})\\b", "\\b(?:tower |t)\\d+ (\\d{3,4})\\b", "(?:^| )(\\d{3,4})(?= |$)");
        return tw == null || fl == null ? s + "|" + o.pincode() : tw + "|" + fl + "|" + o.pincode();   // unparsed: fall back to the full text
    }
    static String find(String s, String... patterns) {
        for (String p : patterns) { java.util.regex.Matcher m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile(p).matcher(s); if (m.find()) return m.group(1); }
        return null;
    }
    static double sim(String a, String b) {                              // Jaccard similarity of word sets
        Set<String> x = new HashSet<>(Arrays.asList(a.split(" "))), y = new HashSet<>(Arrays.asList(b.split(" ")));
        Set<String> i = new HashSet<>(x); i.retainAll(y); Set<String> u = new HashSet<>(x); u.addAll(y);
        return u.isEmpty() ? 0 : (double) i.size() / u.size();
    }

    // one real address, written the way different people (or a ring deliberately) would write it
    static String variant(Random r, String soc, String road, int tower, int flat, boolean evasive) {
        int unit = flat;                                                  // floor × 100 + flat on the floor, e.g. 1203
        String[] towerForms = {"Tower " + tower, "T" + tower, "Block " + tower, "Twr-" + tower, "Wing " + tower};
        String[] flatForms = {"Flat " + unit, "Flat No. " + unit, "#" + unit, unit + "", "Apt " + unit, "Flt " + unit};
        String tf = towerForms[r.nextInt(evasive ? 5 : 2)], ff = flatForms[r.nextInt(evasive ? 6 : 2)];
        String socName = evasive && r.nextBoolean() ? soc.replace(" ", "").toUpperCase() : soc;
        String rd = r.nextBoolean() ? road : road.replace("Road", "Rd");
        String landmark = evasive && r.nextDouble() < 0.5 ? ", near " + (r.nextBoolean() ? "Decathlon" : "Forum Mall") : "";
        String name = evasive && r.nextDouble() < 0.4 ? "C/o " + (char) ('A' + r.nextInt(26)) + ". Kumar, " : "";
        return r.nextBoolean() ? name + ff + ", " + tf + ", " + socName + ", " + rd + landmark
                               : name + tf + "-" + unit + ", " + socName + ", " + rd + landmark;
    }
}
java ResellerL4.java
deal limit: 2 units per customer; ring = 400 accounts × 2 units → 12 drop points; 20,000 genuine buyers (1,500 in the same 6 complexes)

limit keyed on                                  units to ring   genuine buyers blocked         keys
account                                                   800                        0       20,400
exact address string                                      778                        7       20,382
normalised address (tower, flat, pincode)                  24                       82       19,930
fuzzy: normalised + token similarity ≥ 0.8                202                     2034       18,067

floor on 'genuine blocked' for any address-based limit: 79 buyers share a flat with an earlier genuine buyer (same household),
and 3 genuine buyers live in a flat the ring uses as a drop point

examples of one drop point as the ring typed it:
  C/o P. Kumar, Twr-6-1102, Purva Riviera, Outer Ring Rd — 560103
  Tower 6-1102, Purva Riviera, Outer Ring Road, near Decathlon — 560103
  Flat No. 1102, T6, Purva Riviera, Outer Ring Rd, near Forum Mall — 560103
  Flt 1102, Twr-6, Purva Riviera, Outer Ring Rd, near Forum Mall — 560103
  Wing 6-1102, Purva Riviera, Outer Ring Rd, near Forum Mall — 560103

Reading it:

  • Per-account limits give the ring all 800 units. Exact address strings give it 778, because the ring typed each drop point differently: "Twr-6-1102", "Flat No. 1102, T6", "Wing 6-1102", plus C/o names and landmarks.
  • A normalised tower + flat + pincode key gives the ring 24 units, exactly 2 per drop point, which is the minimum possible. It blocks 82 genuine buyers, and all of them are unavoidable: 79 second buyers in the same household, and 3 who live in the drop-point flats. The first version of the parser missed the "T6" form, which left the tower unknown and merged flats across towers (388 wrongly blocked). The fix was to parse more forms and fall back to the full text when parsing fails.
  • Fuzzy word similarity is worse on both counts: 202 units to the ring and 2,034 genuine buyers blocked. "Flat 1102, Tower 6" and "Flat 1103, Tower 6" share most words, so neighbours merge, while landmark and C/o noise splits the ring's own variants. Parse structure first, and use fuzzy matching only on what can't be parsed.

docs.title: 6.1 Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Effect Mitigation Client clock skew Early and late taps, "rigged" complaints Server-time sync + re-sync (L1) Buy spike Checkout overload Waiting room, bucketed reservation (Ch 46) Gateway or bank degraded Payment failures Routing and health-based switching (Ch 45) OTP/SMS provider throttled Logins and COD confirmations fail Multiple providers, WhatsApp/IVR fallback, queueing Reseller ring Genuine customers miss deals Household keys (L4), device and payment graph RTO surge Margin loss Risk bands (L2), promise accuracy

docs.title: 6.2 Observability
docs.text:
The war-room dashboards show:

  • journey success rates: browse, add to cart, checkout, payment by method and bank;
  • waiting-room depth and admission rate;
  • deal units remaining;
  • time-sync error from clients (reported by the app);
  • payload sizes by screen;
  • RTO and COD confirmation rates by region;
  • limit hits and abuse blocks.

docs.title: 6.3 Security and abuse
docs.text:
• Bot traffic on deal pages is handled by device attestation, behavioural checks and rate limits (Ch 39).
  • Account takeover spikes around sales need step-up authentication.
  • Promo and bank-offer abuse is handled by per-instrument caps.

docs.title: 6.4 Performance and cost
docs.text:
• Pre-scaling and reserved capacity for the sale window (Ch 35).
  • Payload budgets (L3) reduce CDN egress as well as latency.
  • RTO is a logistics cost line to track per region (L2).

docs.title: 6.5 Compliance
docs.text:
• E-commerce rules on seller information display, country of origin, grievance officers, and restrictions on certain flash-sale practices (VERIFY the current Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules and amendments).
  • Invoicing with GST per seller.
  • Payment data rules (RBI tokenisation for cards; VERIFY) (Ch 36).

docs.title: 7. Anti-Patterns & Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Polling the origin for deal status

It costs 100M requests for nothing (L1).

2. Trusting the phone's clock

Early and late taps (L1).

3. Rejecting early taps with a penalty

It punishes clock skew, not cheating.

4. Turning off COD to cut RTO

It loses a third of orders (L2).

5. Judging COD policy on this order's profit only

It ignores new-customer value (L2).

6. Shipping full product JSON to list views

Payload bloat (L3).

7. Many origins per screen on 2G

Connection setup dominates (L3).

8. Per-account deal limits

Rings win (L4).

9. Fuzzy address matching as the main key

It blocks neighbours (L4).

10. Estimating bank offers without reserving the budget

Caps are overspent.

11. Changes during the sale

Freeze critical services.

12. Unagreed peak volumes with banks, SMS providers and couriers

Dependencies fail first.

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What makes a big Indian sale day different from a normal day?

30-second answer: Traffic spikes of an order of magnitude or more concentrated at deal unlocks, limited-quantity deals, heavy COD and slow networks outside metros, bank offers and EMI at checkout, and dependencies (banks, SMS, couriers) that also peak.

Deep answer: §1.2, §2.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Headroom cost vs lost sales.

Follow-ups: 1. Which component breaks first? → Often a dependency. 2. How to prepare? → §2.10.

Red flags: "Autoscaling handles it."

Q2 [B1] How would you show a countdown that ends at the same moment for everyone?

30-second answer: Send the unlock time and server time with the page, compute the phone's clock offset, re-sync precisely shortly before unlock, and let the server check the time again on the Buy request.

Deep answer: §2.4, L1: 96.6% → 100% within ±1 s.

Trade-offs I'd call out: One extra request vs fairness.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not the phone clock? → 17.5% early taps. 2. Why not poll? → 102M requests.

Red flags: Polling every second.

Q3 [B1] What is RTO and why does it matter?

30-second answer: Return to origin — the parcel isn't delivered (refused or unreachable) and comes back; you pay shipping both ways and make no sale, so it's a major cost for COD orders.

Deep answer: §2.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Reach vs cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Main drivers? → Customer intent, delays, address quality. 2. Measure? → By pincode, courier, seller.

Red flags: Ignoring reverse logistics.

Q4 [B1] How would you keep the app usable on 2G?

30-second answer: Send only what the screen renders, compress, reuse connections and limit origins, right-size images, cache aggressively, and consider a lite app or PWA.

Deep answer: L3: 65 KB → 1.5 KB; 8.0 s → 0.8 s with reuse.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Two API shapes to maintain.

Follow-ups: 1. Images? → Modern formats, lazy load. 2. Offline? → Cached cart, idempotent retries.

Red flags: Same payload for list and detail.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ Design the deal-unlock flow for a million concurrent shoppers.

30-second answer: Deal pages and assets from the CDN before unlock; server-time sync on load and a millisecond re-sync from an edge time endpoint at T−10 s; local enable at unlock; Buy goes to a waiting room that admits to checkout at a sustainable rate; the server rechecks time and per-customer limits; bucketed stock reservation.

Deep answer: §2.4, L1; Ch 46.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Waiting-room latency vs overload.

Follow-ups: 1. Peak origin RPS? → ~0.6M/s in L1's peak second. 2. Early taps? → Reject softly, no penalty.

Red flags: Everything to origin at once.

Q6 [B2] How do you decide whether to offer COD on an order?

30-second answer: Score RTO risk from features like region, customer history and value; offer plain COD at low risk, COD with OTP/IVR confirmation in the middle, prepaid-only at high risk; evaluate policies on this order's margin and on new-customer value.

Deep answer: L2: P5 best on both measures; no-COD worst with future value.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Friction vs RTO.

Follow-ups: 1. Model down? → Fall back to confirmation. 2. Fairness? → No protected attributes; audits.

Red flags: Blanket COD ban.

Q7 [B2] How are bank offers applied correctly at checkout?

30-second answer: Show an estimate early, recompute when the payment instrument is known (card BIN, bank, EMI tenure), reserve the offer budget atomically against daily caps, release on failure, and store each discount line with its funder for settlement and invoicing.

Deep answer: §2.8; Ch 49.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Checkout step vs accuracy.

Follow-ups: 1. Cap exhausted mid-checkout? → Show before paying. 2. Refunds? → Reverse the discount lines.

Red flags: Discount computed after payment.

Q8 [B2] How do you support shoppers in many languages?

30-second answer: Localised UI and catalog content, search that handles transliteration, mixed scripts and voice mapping to the same catalog, and success metrics per language.

Deep answer: §2.7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Content translation cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Seller content? → Machine translation with review. 2. Fonts? → Size budgets.

Red flags: English-only search.

Q9 [B2] How would you prepare external dependencies for a sale?

30-second answer: Agree peak volumes with banks, gateways, SMS providers and couriers; route across providers; build fallbacks (IVR/WhatsApp OTP, delayed confirmations); watch per-dependency success on the war-room dashboard with switch thresholds.

Deep answer: §2.11.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Multi-provider cost.

Follow-ups: 1. OTP provider throttles? → Switch, queue. 2. Courier capacity? → Allocation limits.

Red flags: Discovering limits on the day.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ A deal says '2 per customer'. How do you stop reseller rings without blocking families?

30-second answer: Enforce limits on the delivery household, not the account: normalise addresses into structured keys (tower, flat, pincode) and combine with device, payment and phone signals; use fuzzy matching only for unparsed leftovers; explain household limits to customers.

Deep answer: L4: ring units 800 → 24 (minimum); genuine blocks 82 = unavoidable floor; fuzzy blocked 2,034.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Households with multiple buyers.

Follow-ups: 1. Rings with many addresses? → Payment/device graph. 2. Enforcement point? → Checkout and before dispatch.

Red flags: Per-account limits.

Q11 [B3] Why does trusting the phone clock produce complaints even when servers are fine?

30-second answer: A minority of phones are seconds to minutes off: fast ones tap early and get rejected, slow ones see the button after stock is gone; to users the sale looks rigged. Server-time sync removes almost all of it.

Deep answer: L1: 17.5% early, 12% late > 5 s on phone clocks.

Trade-offs I'd call out: None meaningful.

Follow-ups: 1. Detect skew? → Report offset in telemetry. 2. Airplane-mode users? → Sync on reconnect.

Red flags: "Our servers were fast."

Q12 [B3] On a slow network, what matters more: payload size or connections?

30-second answer: Both, but once payloads are trimmed and compressed, connection setup dominates — a new HTTPS connection costs several round trips (2+ s on 2G); reuse connections, reduce origins, use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, and pre-connect before the user needs it.

Deep answer: L3: trimmed + gzip 2.9 s cold vs 0.8 s warm on 2G.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Consolidating origins vs isolation.

Follow-ups: 1. TLS 1.3 / 0-RTT? → Fewer round trips (VERIFY replay risks). 2. Images? → Separate budget.

Red flags: Only minifying JSON.

Q13 [B3] How do you reduce RTO beyond blocking COD?

30-second answer: Confirmation for medium-risk orders, accurate promises (late deliveries get refused), better addresses (validation, geocoding), delivery attempt scheduling and customer calls, incentives to prepay, and courier/pincode performance management.

Deep answer: §2.5, L2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Friction vs conversion.

Follow-ups: 1. Attribution? → RTO reason codes. 2. Seller-driven RTO? → Seller scorecards.

Red flags: COD ban as the only lever.

Q14 [B3] What does your sale-day war room look at?

30-second answer: Journey success rates, waiting-room depth and admission, deal inventory, payment success by method, bank and gateway, dependency health, error budgets, and abuse/limit hits — with a named decision owner per journey and pre-agreed switches.

Deep answer: §2.10, §6.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Too many dashboards.

Follow-ups: 1. First switch to flip? → Non-critical widgets. 2. Comms? → Templates.

Red flags: Host metrics only.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Plan the engineering readiness for a festive sale.

30-second answer: Forecast journeys and dependency peaks, capacity plan with headroom, full-journey load and chaos tests, degradation switches, change freeze, pre-scaling and cache warming, war room with owners and comms, then a retrospective feeding next year's forecast.

Deep answer: §2.10 timeline.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Freeze vs feature pressure.

Follow-ups: 1. Load test realism? → Real journeys, real data. 2. Budget? → Reserved capacity.

Red flags: Plan starts a week before.

Q16 [B4] How would you evaluate a proposal to stop offering COD nationally?

30-second answer: Model the whole economics: orders lost (not every COD customer prepays), RTO saved, and the lifetime value of new customers who only start with COD; compare with targeted risk bands; pilot by region with shadow scoring before any national change.

Deep answer: L2: no-COD keeps 68% of orders and is worst with future value.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Short-term margin vs growth.

Follow-ups: 1. Regional rollout? → Yes, by tier. 2. Prepay incentives? → Test them.

Red flags: Decision on RTO alone.

Q17 [B4] How do you make limited deals perceived as fair?

30-second answer: Synchronised unlocks, first-come order via a waiting room, household limits against rings, clear communication (position in queue, sold-out quickly), post-sale transparency on units, and no penalties for honest early taps.

Deep answer: L1, L4; Ch 46.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Lottery vs first-come.

Follow-ups: 1. Lottery instead? → Fairer on slow networks. 2. Bots? → Attestation, behaviour.

Red flags: Silent failures.

Q18 [B4] How would you architect for entry-level phones and slow networks across the whole platform?

30-second answer: Per-screen payload and request budgets enforced in CI, BFFs shaping responses per client, image pipeline with device-aware variants, connection reuse and few origins, offline-tolerant flows with idempotency, and a lite client; measure real-user performance by network type.

Deep answer: §2.6, L3; Ch 34 BFF.

Trade-offs I'd call out: More client variants to maintain.

Follow-ups: 1. Budget enforcement? → Fail builds over budget. 2. RUM? → By network class.

Red flags: Testing only on office Wi-Fi.

Q19 [B4] What regulatory and trust constraints shape Indian e-commerce design?

30-second answer: Consumer-protection e-commerce rules on disclosures and certain flash-sale practices, grievance redressal, GST invoicing per seller, RBI rules for card data and payment aggregators, and personal-data protection — all to be checked against current text (VERIFY).

Deep answer: §6.5; Ch 36.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed vs compliance review.

Follow-ups: 1. Card tokenisation? → Network tokens. 2. Seller data? → Display requirements.

Red flags: Ignoring rules until audit.

Q20 [B4] Compare the design priorities of an Indian sale-day platform with a global marketplace.

30-second answer: Both need cells, reservation and resilience; the Indian sale adds extreme synchronised spikes, COD/RTO economics, slow-network design, household-level limits, bank-offer complexity and vernacular reach — so edge, client and risk design matter as much as back-end scale.

Deep answer: I01 vs this chapter.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Where to invest first.

Follow-ups: 1. Shared platform? → Yes, market-specific edges. 2. Biggest risk? → Dependencies on the day.

Red flags: Copying a global design unchanged.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Sync clients to server time and re-sync before unlock. Never poll the origin (L1).
  2. Price COD risk with bands and confirmation, and count new-customer value (L2).
  3. Budget payloads and connections for 2G. Setup round trips dominate small payloads (L3).
  4. Enforce limits on structured household keys, not accounts or fuzzy text (L4).
  5. Sale days are won by readiness: capacity, dependencies, switches, freeze, war room.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Problem Pattern Deal unlock Server-time offset + millisecond re-sync; authoritative server check Buy spike Waiting room + bucketed reservation (Ch 46) COD risk Risk bands: COD, COD + OTP, prepaid only Slow networks Trim + compress, reuse connections, few origins, lite client Resellers Normalised tower/flat/pincode key + device/payment graph Bank offers Recompute at instrument choice, reserve cap budget

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. (B1) Estimate origin requests if 1M shoppers poll every 5 s for 10 minutes.
  2. (B2) Add a "partial prepayment of ₹99" option to L2. Where does it beat OTP confirmation?
  3. (B3) Add a 5 KB thumbnail per product to L3 and recompute the 2G times.
  4. (B3) Extend L4 so the ring also rotates phone numbers and cards. Which signal catches it?
  5. (B4) Write the war-room runbook for "UPI success rate drops by 20% at 12:01".

docs.title: I02b. Flipkart-Style E-Commerce — How the Whole System Works
docs.text:
What this page adds

I02 focuses on four sale-day problems with labs. This page is the system walkthrough, with no code. It follows a customer and a seller through an Indian e-commerce platform:

  • the app and edge, catalog and seller onboarding, vernacular search and discovery, recommendations and ads;
  • pricing, offers and loyalty, cart and checkout, payments including UPI, EMI and COD;
  • fraud and abuse, and the order pipeline;
  • the logistics network: warehouses, hubs, pincode serviceability, last mile, COD cash, and returns;
  • customer support;
  • the algorithms, the data platform and warehouse, and the tech stack.

Sources and honesty

Statements about Flipkart come from public sources: its engineering blog, conference talks, case studies published by technology vendors, and news. They are marked VERIFY. Internal details are not public, so "a system like this would…" describes a reference design.

docs.title: 1. What Makes Indian E-Commerce Different

docs.title: 3. The Customer Journey, Step by Step
3.1 Opening the app
docs.text:
1. App launch: a single home page API call returns a personalised layout.
    • Widgets such as banners, deals and "recently viewed" are chosen by a content/widget platform that marketing configures for sales without code deployments.
    • Personalisation ranks the widgets.
  2. Caching:
    • Static assets and images come from the CDN in sizes appropriate to the device.
    • Personalised parts are fetched separately from cacheable parts, so most bytes are cacheable at the edge.
  3. Device constraints: for low-end devices and slow networks, the app or PWA downloads less (fewer widgets, lower-resolution images). Flipkart publicly launched a PWA, Flipkart Lite, in 2015 (VERIFY).

docs.title: 3.2 Searching in Hindi, Hinglish or by voice
docs.text:
1. The query can be typed in English, Hindi script, Latin-script Hindi ("mobail cover") or spoken.
  2. Speech: voice input goes through speech recognition to text. Flipkart has publicly discussed vernacular voice search (VERIFY details).
  3. Query understanding:
    • transliteration and normalisation to a common representation;
    • spell correction trained on Indian spelling patterns;
    • vernacular-to-English mapping for catalog terms;
    • category and attribute prediction (e.g. "under 15000" becomes a price filter).
  4. Retrieval:
    • lexical matches from an inverted index;
    • semantic retrieval with multilingual embeddings;
    • filtered by serviceability to the user's pincode.
  5. Ranking: learning-to-rank on relevance, conversion history, price competitiveness, delivery speed, ratings and seller quality. Sponsored listings are blended through the ads auction.

docs.title: 3.3 The product page
docs.text:
• Components:
    • catalog content (possibly translated);
    • the chosen seller's offer (a buy-box-like selection among sellers, similar to I01);
    • price with sale discount;
    • bank offers and EMI options (estimated);
    • exchange offers;
    • delivery date for the user's pincode;
    • COD availability;
    • ratings and reviews;
    • questions and answers;
    • recommendations.
  • Pincode check: the serviceability service answers from precomputed tables:
    • pincode × seller or warehouse × product size/weight class × payment type;
    • result: can we deliver, by when, and is COD allowed.

docs.title: 3.4 Cart and checkout
docs.text:
1. Cart: the cart stores items and quantities. It can be merged across devices at login.
  2. Checkout:
    • address selection, with address quality checks: pincode validation, geocoding, and prompts for missing landmarks;
    • serviceability re-check.
  3. Price computation:
    • sale price;
    • coupon;
    • bank offer once the payment instrument is known;
    • coins or loyalty redemption;
    • delivery fee rules;
    • taxes (GST per item and seller).
  4. Payment options: UPI (intent or collect), cards (tokenised), net banking, EMI (card EMI, cardless EMI or pay later), wallets and gift cards, and COD if the risk score allows (I02 L2).
  5. Order placement:
    • reservation of stock from the chosen warehouse or seller;
    • payment authorisation (or COD confirmation flow);
    • order created with the promise, the fulfilment plan and price breakdown lines (who funds each discount: seller, platform or bank).

docs.title: 3.5 Payments
docs.text:
• Routing: a payments orchestrator routes each transaction to a gateway or processor by method, bank and live success rates (Ch 45 L4).
  • UPI flows: intent (opens a UPI app) or collect (request in the UPI app), with status polling and callbacks; see I03 for the bank side.
  • EMI and pay later: eligibility checks with lenders. The platform may partner with lenders for credit products (VERIFY).
  • Refunds go to the source instrument or wallet. Reconciliation against gateway and bank settlement files, as in Ch 45.

docs.title: 3.6 Order management and fulfilment choice
docs.text:
• The order management system (OMS) splits the order into shipments by seller, warehouse and size class. Each shipment is a state machine: created → packed → dispatched → in transit → out for delivery → delivered or RTO.
  • Fulfilment models:
    • platform warehouses hold seller inventory (a fulfilment-by-platform model; Flipkart's "Flipkart Assured" signals quality and fast delivery, VERIFY);
    • seller-fulfilled items are picked up from the seller.
  • Cancellation is allowed until dispatch. Payment is authorised or captured according to the method.

docs.title: 3.7 Warehouses and the logistics network
docs.text:
1. Warehouses (fulfilment centres): inbound from sellers, stow, pick, pack.
    • Large-appliance warehouses are separate from small-item ones.
    • Sortation is automated at big sites (VERIFY specific automation).
  2. Network: fulfilment centre → mother hubs (large sortation) → delivery hubs near pincode clusters → delivery agents. This is a hub-and-spoke network run by the in-house logistics arm (Ekart; VERIFY current structure) plus third-party couriers.
  3. Line-haul: truck schedules between hubs, planned from volume forecasts. Sale periods add temporary hubs and vehicles.
  4. Last mile:
    • shipments assigned to delivery agents by area;
    • route optimisation (VRP with time windows and capacity);
    • agent app with navigation, proof of delivery (OTP, photo);
    • COD cash collection and UPI-at-door.
  5. COD cash: agents deposit cash at hubs. Cash is reconciled per shipment and remitted. Mismatches are investigated (Ch 45 §2.7).
  6. Failed deliveries: re-attempt scheduling, customer calls. If it still fails, RTO back to the warehouse or seller.

docs.title: 3.8 Returns
docs.text:
• Return request: reason captured; policy checked (return, replacement, or not returnable).
  • Reverse pickup: scheduled, with doorstep quality checks for some categories (e.g. matching IMEI for phones).
  • Refund: issued on pickup or on receipt, depending on the customer's trust tier.
  • Returned item: graded at the warehouse, then restocked, returned to the seller, or refurbished.

docs.title: 3.9 Customer support
docs.text:
• Self-service first: order tracking, cancellation, returns and refund status.
  • Chat: a chatbot with intent classification, handing off to agents with full order context.
  • Voice support in multiple languages.
  • Operations: support tickets link to orders and shipments. Common issues are auto-resolved by rules, e.g. refunding automatically when a shipment is marked lost.

docs.title: 4. The Seller Journey
docs.text:
1. Onboarding: GST and PAN verification, bank account verification, and address and pickup location (VERIFY required documents).
  2. Listing:
    • match to an existing catalog product, or create a new listing with attributes per category;
    • quality checks on images and content, with ML models detecting prohibited items, counterfeit indicators and poor images.
  3. Inventory and pricing: sellers manage stock and prices through the portal or APIs. Pricing recommendations suggest competitive prices.
  4. Orders: notifications with dispatch SLAs, labels and manifests, and pickup scheduling.

  5. Settlement:

    • the platform collects payments;
    • it deducts commission, fees (fixed, shipping, collection) and taxes (TCS under GST, VERIFY);
    • it settles to the seller on a schedule, with detailed statements.

    This needs a per-seller ledger. 6. Performance: metrics (cancellation, late dispatch, returns) affect visibility and eligibility for programmes. 7. Ads: sellers buy sponsored placements with bids and budgets.

docs.title: 5. Algorithms Catalog
docs.text: Problem Algorithm (typical) Where Query understanding (vernacular) Transliteration models, spell correction, multilingual classifiers for category and attributes Search Retrieval Inverted index + multilingual embeddings with ANN (HNSW) Search Ranking Learning-to-rank (gradient-boosted trees → neural rankers) Search, browse Recommendations Item-to-item co-view/co-purchase; embedding-based candidate generation (two-tower) + ranking; session-based sequence models Home, product pages Home page layout Widget ranking (contextual bandits or learned ranking) Home Pricing Elasticity and competitive price models; sale pricing rules Pricing Bank offer budgets Budget pacing controllers (Ch 49) Offers Demand forecasting Hierarchical time-series forecasting (category → product, national → region), with sale uplift features Inventory, capacity Serviceability Precomputed lookup tables from courier coverage and SLAs Promise COD risk Gradient-boosted classifiers on customer, pincode and order features Checkout (I02 L2) Address intelligence Address parsing, normalisation and geocoding; clustering to delivery hubs Logistics, abuse (I02 L4) Fraud and abuse Graph features across devices, payments and addresses; anomaly detection Risk Hub routing Network flow / shortest path with capacities Middle mile Last-mile routing VRP with time windows (heuristics, local search) Delivery agents Warehouse slotting and picking Velocity-based slotting, batch picking, route heuristics Warehouses Deal unlocks Client time sync (I02 L1) Sale events Support Intent classification, automated resolution rules Customer support

docs.title: 5A.1 How the search index is built and kept fresh
docs.text:
1. Source events: catalog changes (new listing, attribute edit), offer changes (price, stock, seller) and serviceability changes all emit events.
  2. Document assembly: an indexing pipeline joins these into a search document per product. It holds:
    • title and attributes;
    • vernacular and transliterated variants;
    • category path;
    • best price and discount;
    • rating;
    • seller-quality score;
    • availability by region (bitmaps or lists of serviceable warehouse clusters).

  3. Two update paths:

    • real-time partial updates for price and stock, within seconds, so sold-out items don't rank;
    • periodic full rebuilds (e.g. nightly) for text and embedding changes.

    Blue-green index aliases switch rebuilt indexes in without downtime (Ch 22). 4. Embeddings: product embeddings are recomputed in batch by the ML platform and pushed to the vector index. Query embeddings are computed online. 5. Serving: search nodes shard the index by product and replicate each shard. A query fans out to shards, merges top-K, then re-ranks with the heavier model on the top few hundred (Ch 42 for autocomplete).

docs.title: 5A.2 How recommendations are produced
docs.text:
1. Candidate generation. Several cheap sources each propose hundreds of items:
    • co-view and co-buy item-to-item tables (precomputed daily);
    • embedding nearest neighbours of recently viewed items;
    • trending in the user's city;
    • category affinity;
    • "continue where you left off".
  2. Ranking: one model scores all candidates with user features, item features, context (time, device, language, sale day) and cross features, trained on clicks and purchases.
  3. Re-ranking: business rules and diversity, such as:
    • not five similar phones in a row;
    • boosting in-stock items that are fast to deliver to this pincode;
    • removing out-of-stock or non-serviceable items;
    • frequency caps for sponsored items.
  4. Serving:
    • precomputed recommendations for the home page are stored per user in a key-value store, so reading them is a single lookup;
    • real-time signals (the last few views in this session) re-rank at request time;
    • everything degrades to popular-in-category if the model service is slow.
  5. Measurement: A/B tests on conversion and revenue per session, and guardrails on page latency.

docs.title: 5A.3 How serviceability and the promise are computed
docs.text:
• Inputs:
    • courier and own-logistics coverage per pincode;
    • hub mappings;
    • transit time matrices (origin hub → destination hub, hub → pincode);
    • cut-off times;
    • capacity per hub per day;
    • product constraints (weight, size, hazardous items, high value);
    • payment constraints (COD limits per pincode).

  • Precompute: a batch job builds a table:

    origin warehouse cluster × destination pincode × product class → {serviceable, promise days, COD allowed, courier options}

    It is loaded into a low-latency key-value store and refreshed several times a day, plus immediately on disruptions (hub closure, floods). - At request time: find warehouses holding stock for the product, look up each (warehouse, pincode, class), and choose the fastest serviceable option with capacity. The result is the "Delivery by Tuesday" and COD flag. - Feedback: actual delivery times feed back into transit-time estimates, so promises reflect reality. Promise accuracy is tracked per pincode and hub.

docs.title: 5A.4 Inside a warehouse (WMS)
docs.text:
1. Inbound: receive against the seller's advance shipping notice, with quality checks per category.
  2. Put-away and slotting: fast-moving items go to locations close to packing. Slotting is recomputed by sales velocity before sales.
  3. Order release in waves: orders are grouped by dispatch cut-off and destination hub.
  4. Picking:
    • batch picking: one picker collects items for many orders, then they are sorted to orders (put-wall);
    • pick paths are optimised per zone.
  5. Packing: box recommendation by item dimensions; invoice and label printing.
  6. Sortation: sorted by destination hub into bags or cages, then manifested per truck.
  7. Sale preparation: pre-packing of hot deal items before the sale (packed and labelled once the order arrives), and extra shifts.

docs.title: 5A.5 A sale-day request, end to end
docs.text:
1. Before the unlock: the user opens the deal page from the CDN, and the app syncs to server time (I02 L1).
  2. Buy: the tap goes through the gateway (bot checks, rate limits) into the waiting room, which admits the user at checkout's sustainable rate (Ch 46).
  3. Checkout:
    • the deal quantity is reserved from bucketed stock;
    • the household limit is checked (I02 L4);
    • the price is computed with bank offers, the offer budget reserved, the payment authorised, and the order created.
  4. Events: order events flow to OMS, the warehouse release queue, notifications, and the real-time sale dashboard via stream processing.
  5. Fulfilment: pre-packed items ship within hours. Logistics hubs run extended shifts, and customers see live tracking from scan events.

docs.title: 5A.6 Loyalty coins and membership
docs.text:
• Coins are earned on orders and credited after the return window. They are redeemable on later orders and partner offers, and expire.
  • Accounting: a ledger per customer, where earning, redemption, expiry and reversal on return are all entries (Ch 45 patterns). Coin liability is tracked by finance.
  • Membership tiers unlock benefits (early sale access, free delivery). Tier eligibility is computed from spend or coins over a window.

docs.title: 6.1 Public milestones (VERIFY)
docs.text:
• Flipkart has publicly described an in-house data platform built on the Hadoop ecosystem for batch processing and reporting, plus streaming pipelines, in engineering blog posts.
  • Flipkart announced a strategic partnership with Google Cloud (2021), which included cloud infrastructure (VERIFY scope).

docs.title: 6.3 Data model highlights
docs.text:
• Facts:
    • sessions and events (views, searches, clicks);
    • cart events, orders and order items;
    • shipments with every logistics scan;
    • deliveries, RTOs and returns;
    • payments and refunds;
    • ad impressions and clicks;
    • seller settlements.
  • Dimensions: customer (pseudonymised), product and category tree, seller, pincode (with city tier, state, hub), warehouse, courier, payment method and bank, date and time (with sale-event flags).
  • Key derived metrics:
    • conversion funnel by channel and language;
    • search success rate by language;
    • promise accuracy by pincode;
    • RTO rate by pincode, courier and payment type;
    • COD share;
    • bank offer spend vs budget;
    • seller performance;
    • cost per shipment.
  • Real-time sale dashboards (seconds-level) come from stream processing, not the batch warehouse.

docs.text: Layer Publicly reported for Flipkart (VERIFY each) Reference choice Services Java-based microservices widely reported Java 21 / Spring Boot, gRPC Front end Native Android/iOS; React-based web and PWA (Flipkart Lite) Kotlin/Swift or Flutter; React/Next.js PWA Key-value and caching Aerospike reported in vendor case studies Aerospike or Redis for sessions and carts Relational MySQL widely reported MySQL/PostgreSQL, sharded (Vitess/Citus) Wide-column / big tables HBase reported in the Hadoop-based platform HBase/Cassandra, or cloud equivalents Search Solr/Elasticsearch-family engines reported OpenSearch/Elasticsearch + vector search Messaging Kafka widely used Kafka Data platform Hadoop ecosystem; Google Cloud partnership (2021) Iceberg/Hudi + Spark + Trino/BigQuery Infrastructure Private cloud plus public cloud Kubernetes, Terraform, Argo CD Observability — OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana, ELK/OpenSearch

docs.title: 8. Reliability and Sale Operations
docs.text:
• Readiness: capacity planning, load tests at a multiple of forecast, dependency agreements, and freeze windows (I02 §2.10).
  • Isolation: sale-specific services (deal pages, waiting rooms) scaled and isolated from the everyday catalog, with feature switches to degrade non-critical widgets.
  • Logistics surge: temporary hubs, additional delivery agents, extended hours, and serviceability tightened when capacity is exceeded.
  • War room: journey dashboards, per-bank payment success, logistics backlog by hub, RTO early indicators.

docs.title: 9. Interview Angles
docs.text:
• B2: customer journey and services.
  • B3: serviceability, COD risk, vernacular search, logistics hubs.
  • B4: data platform, sale readiness, algorithms across the funnel.

The 20 interview questions for this design are in I02 §8.

docs.title: I03. Core Banking & UPI Payments
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Sector: Banking (India) · Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Builds on: Ch 05, Ch 13, Ch 20, Ch 36, Ch 45

What you get: the design of a bank's core ledger and its UPI switch integration. It covers:

  • accounts, balances and holds;
  • the general ledger and end-of-day processing in a 24×7 world;
  • hot merchant accounts;
  • UPI's multi-party flow and what to do when a response never arrives;
  • interest accrual to the paisa;
  • finding mule accounts in the payment graph.

Ch 45 covers a merchant's payment system (gateways, webhooks, ledger, reconciliation). This chapter is the bank's side of the same money.

What the labs measured:

  • L1 (hot account, real PostgreSQL): a single balance row handles 1,585 txn/s with p50 6.7 ms. An append-only journal with a 200 ms roll-up handles 5,687/s, and 16 sub-accounts 3,932/s. In a refund storm (30% debits) the gap narrows to 1,741 vs ~2,450/s, because debits must serialise. The balance invariant held in every run.
  • L2 (UPI timeouts):
    • Reversing immediately on a timeout paid 60,381 people twice.
    • Treating the payment as successful left 49,494 payers short for over 24 h.
    • Status checks with backoff, plus reversal at the next settlement cycle for anything still unknown, left 0 short for over 24 h and 0 paid twice.
  • L3 (interest, BigDecimal):
    • Rounding daily interest to the paisa looks harmless in total (+₹306 on ₹95 crore). It still changes 977,265 of 1,000,000 accounts by up to ₹0.45.
    • Truncating underpays by ₹4.38 lakh, and dividing by 365 in a leap year overpays by ₹26 lakh.
  • L4 (mule accounts):
    • Fan-in or pass-through rules alone have 2% and 0.5% precision. Combining them in the same 2-hour window reaches 98.5% precision.
    • Following the money to accounts fed by ≥ 2 flagged mules finds 23 of 24 collectors: 90 of 104 bad accounts at 96.8% precision.

Reading time: 85 min.

Regulatory content

Banking is heavily regulated. Statements about RBI or NPCI rules are summaries and are marked VERIFY: turnaround times and compensation, UPI limits, KYC, data localisation, reporting. Check the current circulars and your bank's compliance function before building on them. Numbers in the labs are illustrative.

docs.title: 1.1 A story: the timeout that paid twice
docs.text:
At 2:10 pm a beneficiary bank's UPI systems slow down. The remitter bank has already debited its customers' accounts, sent the credit requests through the UPI switch, and is now receiving timeouts.

  • The first fix. An engineer adds a rule: on timeout, reverse the debit. Customers get their money back immediately, and complaints stop.
  • The morning after. The settlement file shows that more than half of those "failed" payments were in fact credited to the beneficiary. The bank has paid tens of thousands of payments twice, and must now recover money from customers who believe they did nothing wrong.
  • Rolling it back. The rule is reversed to treat timeouts as successful. At the next incident, customers whose payments really failed wait a day or more for their money. Some go past the regulator's turnaround time, and the bank owes compensation (VERIFY: RBI's TAT framework for failed transactions).

Both rules were simple, and both were wrong. The correct answer is a state machine with status checks, settlement-driven resolution and a deadline. Banking is full of these: money that must never be created or lost, even when the systems holding it disagree.

The thesis of this chapter

A bank is a ledger with deadlines.

  • Every rupee is in exactly one account at every moment (double entry).
  • Every state change is recorded and never overwritten.
  • Hot accounts are fed by an append-only journal (L1).
  • Unknown outcomes are resolved by status and settlement, not guesses (L2).
  • Arithmetic follows the product terms to the paisa (L3).
  • The payment graph is watched for money that moves like fraud (L4).

docs.title: 1.2 Core banking in one picture
docs.text: Concept Meaning Customer (CIF) The customer information file, linked to KYC Account Savings, current, loan, fixed deposit; a product defines its rules (interest, limits, fees) Ledger balance The sum of posted entries Available balance Ledger balance − holds (liens) + any overdraft limit Hold / lien Money reserved for a pending debit (a card authorisation, a UPI debit awaiting the outcome, a court order) Posting A balanced set of entries (debits = credits) with a value date General ledger (GL) Bank-level accounts (e.g. "UPI settlement receivable", "interest expense") that customer postings roll into EOD / BOD End- and beginning-of-day processing: interest accrual, charges, standing instructions, statements, GL balancing

docs.title: 1.3 Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end you will be able to:

  • Model accounts, holds and double-entry postings with value dates.
  • Scale hot accounts without breaking the no-overdraft rule.
  • Handle UPI timeouts with a state machine that meets turnaround times.
  • Compute interest and fees exactly as the product terms say.
  • Detect mule accounts using time-windowed, graph-aware features.

docs.title: 2.1 Intuition: a very careful notebook B1
docs.text: A bank's core system is a notebook where every line moves money from one page to another, the two sides always add up, and nobody ever erases a line: mistakes are fixed with new lines. The balance on each page is just the sum of its lines. Everything else (apps, UPI, cards, branches) is a way of asking the notebook to add lines, and every one of them must be answered "yes, written" or "no, not written". "Maybe" must never be the final answer.

docs.title: 2.2 Requirements B1
docs.text: Type Requirement Functional Open accounts (with KYC); deposits, withdrawals and transfers (IMPS, NEFT, RTGS, UPI); holds; interest and fees; statements; loans and EMIs; standing instructions; disputes. Scale (assumptions) 50M accounts; UPI peak of a few thousand transactions/s for a large bank, much more for the switch as a whole (VERIFY current NPCI volumes); a few merchant accounts receiving hundreds of credits per second. Correctness Double entry always balanced; no overdraft beyond the limit; exactly-once posting per request; interest exactly per product terms. Availability UPI and cards 24×7, with no EOD downtime for payments. Deadlines Failed-transaction reversals within regulator TATs, with compensation otherwise (VERIFY). Compliance KYC/AML, transaction monitoring, payment data stored in India (VERIFY RBI storage directive), audit trails.

docs.title: 2.3 Postings, holds and balances ⭐ B2
docs.text:
• A posting is a set of entries that sum to zero:
    • a debit to the customer's account;
    • a credit to the UPI settlement GL;
    • and for fees, lines to the fee income GL and a GST GL.
  • Entries are immutable. A correction is a reversing posting that references the original.
  • Holds separate intent from movement. A UPI debit or card authorisation first places a hold, which reduces available balance. The hold is then either converted to a posting or released. Holds have expiry times and reasons.
  • Idempotency. Every posting carries the upstream reference (for UPI, the transaction's reference id) with a unique constraint, so a retried request returns the original result (Ch 20).
  • Value date vs posting date: interest is computed on value-dated balances. A back-dated correction changes interest, which needs recomputation.

docs.title: 2.4 Hot accounts ⭐ B3
docs.text:
• A large merchant's or aggregator's settlement account can receive hundreds or thousands of credits per second. Updating one balance row serialises all of them on one row lock (L1: 1,585 txn/s, p50 6.7 ms with 16 clients).
  • Credits are safe to decouple: adding money can never break the no-overdraft rule.
    • Append-only journal: each credit is an insert, and a roll-up folds committed rows into the balance every few hundred ms. L1: 5,687/s.
    • Sub-accounts: credits are spread across N balance rows. L1: 3,932/s.
  • Debits must see the whole balance. They take a per-account lock and check the effective balance: rolled-up balance plus unrolled journal rows, or the sum of the sub-accounts. In a refund storm, debits dominate and all designs converge (L1: ~2,450/s at 30% debits).
  • The sequence-gap trap:
    • Rolling up "everything below sequence N" skips rows whose transactions haven't committed yet, because sequences are assigned before commit.
    • L1 marks rows as rolled instead, which only sees committed rows.
    • Alternatives: roll up rows older than the longest possible transaction, or use the database's commit-order facilities (VERIFY for your database).
  • The display balance for a hot account may lag by the roll-up interval. The debit check never does.

docs.title: 2.5 UPI: four parties and one truth ⭐ B2
docs.text:
The parties (P2M example):

  • the payer's app (payer PSP);
  • the UPI switch (NPCI);
  • the payer's bank (remitter), which debits;
  • the beneficiary's bank, which credits;
  • plus the merchant's PSP or aggregator.

The simplified flow (VERIFY against the current NPCI specifications):

  1. Collect or intent, then PIN on the payer's device.
  2. Debit request to the remitter bank, which debits and responds.
  3. Credit request to the beneficiary bank, which credits and responds.
  4. Final status to both PSPs.
  5. Net settlement between banks happens in cycles, with settlement files.

Where it breaks: any hop can time out after doing its work. The most dangerous case is the one this chapter's story is about: the remitter has debited but doesn't know whether the beneficiary credited.

The design rule: no participant guesses. Each has:

  • a state machine;
  • a status-check operation keyed by the transaction reference;
  • a reconciliation against settlement files;
  • a deadline: reversal within the regulator's TAT, or compensation (VERIFY).

docs.title: 2.6 Resolving unknown outcomes ⭐ B3
docs.text:
Policy What L2 showed R1 reverse immediately 60,381 paid twice: the beneficiary had credited, and the payer was refunded too. Recovery is painful and customer-hostile. R2 treat as success, fix later 49,494 payers short for more than 24 h, all failed payments waiting for the T+1 batch. R3 status checks with backoff, then decide Most resolved within minutes. Those still unknown after the checks (the beneficiary's status API was down during its 3.5 h incident) fall to T+1: 19,530 short for more than 24 h. R4 R3, plus reverse at the next settlement cycle 0 paid twice, 0 short for more than 24 h, no manual cases. 22,593 were short for more than 1 h: those waiting for the settlement cycle after a long incident.

Engineering details:

  • Hold the debit as PENDING (not reversed, not final).
  • Schedule status checks at growing intervals (Ch 18) and budget their load: R3/R4 made 705k calls, concentrated at incident recovery. Add jitter.
  • Consume settlement and reconciliation files as the source of truth.
  • Track every PENDING against the TAT deadline, with alerts well before it.

docs.title: 2.7 Interest, fees and the paisa B3
docs.text:
• Product terms define the arithmetic: rate, day-count convention (actual/365, actual/actual, 30/360), accrual frequency, rounding and credit frequency (VERIFY RBI rules for savings interest).
  • L3 on a million accounts:
    • Daily rounding looks harmless in aggregate: +₹306 on ₹95 crore. But it changes 977k accounts by up to ₹0.45, so no account matches the product terms.
    • Truncation systematically underpays: −₹4.38 lakh a quarter, a conduct risk.
    • The wrong day count in a leap year overpays ₹26 lakh.
  • The rules:
    • accrue at high precision (a decimal type, never floating point);
    • round once at posting, as the terms specify;
    • store the accrual basis for audit;
    • test against published examples.
  • EOD at 24×7: accrual runs against a consistent snapshot of value-dated balances. It must not freeze payments, so use snapshot reads or an accrual journal fed by postings (Ch 21).

docs.title: 2.8 Mule accounts and transaction monitoring B3
docs.text:
• Mule accounts receive fraud proceeds from many victims and forward them within minutes to collector accounts before cash-out.

  • Legitimate accounts look similar on any single feature:

    Feature Also seen in Many payers Shops Fast pass-through Salary followed by rent Many payers, then one payment Group collections paid to a vendor

  • L4 on synthetic data:

    • Single-feature rules flag thousands of accounts, at 0.5–2% precision.
    • Requiring fan-in, pass-through, few receivers and a meaningful amount in the same 2-hour window, excluding payments to registered merchants, reaches 98.5% precision and finds 67 of 80 mules.
    • Following the money (accounts fed by ≥ 2 flagged mules) finds 23 of 24 collectors.
  • In production:
    • features are computed in streaming windows (Ch 21, Ch 51);
    • graph features are refreshed frequently;
    • a model is trained on labelled cases;
    • actions are graded: monitor, then a credit hold, then a debit freeze, subject to legal process (VERIFY);
    • suspicious transaction reporting follows regulatory requirements (VERIFY).
  • Real-time controls at payment time: device binding, new-device cooling limits, per-transaction and daily limits, and beneficiary risk (VERIFY current UPI limits).

docs.title: 2.9 24×7 banking and the end of "end of day" B4
docs.text:
• Traditional core banking systems ran EOD batches that paused transactions. Instant payments made that unacceptable.
  • Approaches:
    • Separate the payment ledger (always on) from batch processes that read snapshots.
    • Business date vs calendar date: transactions after the cut-over belong to the next business date.
    • Accrual and charges as streaming jobs over postings.
    • Stand-in processing during core maintenance: a shadow ledger authorises within limits, and postings are replayed later (VERIFY applicability per product and regulator).
  • Modernising a legacy core is a strangler migration (Ch 16):
    • a payments hub in front of the old core;
    • new products on a new ledger;
    • accounts migrated in cohorts, with dual-run reconciliation.

docs.title: 2.10 Resilience, residency and regulators B4
docs.text: Concern Design Data localisation Payment system data stored in India (VERIFY the RBI directive and FAQs) (Ch 36) DR Near-zero RPO for the ledger (synchronous replication within a region, async to the DR site); tested DR drills; regulator expectations for recovery times (VERIFY) (Ch 27) Audit Immutable postings, maker-checker for manual entries, privileged access logging Change management Controlled releases outside peak hours; regulator reporting of outages where required (VERIFY) Third parties Outsourcing and cloud guidelines for regulated entities (VERIFY)

docs.text:
sequenceDiagram

docs.title: 3.3 Sequence: credit timeout resolved by status and settlement
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant N as UPI switch
    participant R as Remitter bank
    participant B as Beneficiary bank
    participant S as Settlement files
    N->>R: debit request U777
    R-->>N: debit success
    N->>B: credit request U777
    B--xN: timeout - bank degraded
    N-->>R: status deemed or pending
    R->>R: mark U777 PENDING, customer told payment is processing
    R->>N: status check at 30 seconds, 2 and 5 minutes
    N-->>R: still unknown

docs.title: 3.4 State: a remitter-side UPI debit
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Initiated
    Initiated --> Held: risk ok, hold placed
    Held --> Debited: posting written
    Held --> Declined: insufficient funds or limits
    Debited --> Success: credit confirmed
    Debited --> Pending: credit response lost
    Pending --> Success: status check or settlement says credited
    Pending --> Reversed: status check or settlement says not credited
    Pending --> Escalated: near TAT deadline and still unknown
    Escalated --> Reversed
    Escalated --> Success
    Success --> [*]
    Reversed --> [*]
    Declined --> [*]

docs.title: 4. Design Document Excerpt
docs.text:
Design Document (excerpt) — Pending-Outcome Resolution for UPI Debits

Field Value Context Credit-leg timeouts during beneficiary-bank incidents leave debited payments unknown. The current auto-reverse rule caused double payments, and the previous "treat as success" rule caused TAT breaches. Decision A PENDING state with scheduled status checks (30 s to 2 h, jittered). Resolution from status responses or settlement files, whichever arrives first. Unknowns are reversed at the next settlement cycle, never later than the TAT deadline minus a safety margin. Related ADRs ADR-I03-1 append-only journal for hot accounts; ADR-I03-2 decimal accrual with single rounding; ADR-I03-3 mule scoring with graph features

Requirements.

  • R1: No customer is refunded for a payment that was credited (no double payment from our side).
  • R2: Every failed payment is reversed within the TAT (VERIFY current TAT), and at P99 within the same business day.
  • R3: Status checks never exceed an agreed rate towards the switch, even after an incident.
  • R4: Customers see the PENDING status and an expected resolution time.
  • R5: Every PENDING has an audit trail: checks, responses, the settlement record and the final action.

Decisions in detail.

  1. Settlement files are the source of truth. Status checks shorten the wait.
  2. Reversal is itself idempotent on the transaction reference, and can race with a late credit confirmation. The state machine guards it: only PENDING can move to REVERSED.
  3. Status-check load is spread with jitter and capped by a token bucket (Ch 39).
  4. TAT dashboards show the oldest PENDING per beneficiary bank.

Consequences. Some customers wait hours after long incidents (L2: 22,593 more than 1 h). Messaging and expectation-setting are part of the design.
