Key decisions:

Decision Choice Why Products as configuration A product configurator with versioned product definitions (coverages, rules, rate tables) interpreted by the rating, underwriting and policy engines New products without code changes; old versions preserved for in-force policies Policy data model Bitemporal: effective dates (when a change applies in the contract) and recorded dates (when we learned it) Back-dated endorsements, audits, "what did we know when" Claims Workflow engine with human tasks, SLAs and rules Long-running, multi-party processes (Ch 50) Buy vs build Many insurers buy a core suite (policy/billing/claims) and build digital channels, rating services, fraud and data around it Mature domain, regulatory features; differentiation is at the edges Integration APIs for partners, events internally, file exchanges where industry partners require them Real-world mix

docs.title: 4. How It Works — Journeys End to End
4.1 Journey 1: buying motor insurance on an aggregator
docs.text:
1. Quote request: the customer enters their vehicle registration number on an aggregator site, which calls the insurer's quote API.
  2. Enrichment:
    • the insurer fetches vehicle details (make, model, variant, fuel, registration date) from a vehicle registry integration (VERIFY data-access arrangements);
    • checks previous insurance and claims history through industry data where available (VERIFY);
    • looks up the insured declared value (IDV) from depreciation schedules.

  3. Rating (§6.1): base premium from rate tables by vehicle class, zone and age, then adjustments:

    • No Claim Bonus carried from the previous policy (VERIFY current NCB slabs);
    • add-ons (zero depreciation, engine protection, roadside assistance);
    • voluntary deductible;
    • the insurer's pricing model loading or discount within filed ranges;
    • taxes (GST).

    Third-party premium is set by the regulator (VERIFY). 4. Response: the quote returns within hundreds of milliseconds with a quote ID valid for a short time. Aggregators may show 20 insurers side by side. 5. Purchase: the customer selects and pays. - KYC is mandatory for all policies now (VERIFY), done with CKYC lookup or e-KYC. - Break-in cases (expired policy) need a self-inspection: the customer records a guided video or photos of the car in the app. An image model checks for damage and fraud (§6.5), and a human reviews exceptions. 6. Issuance: - underwriting rules pass; - the policy is created in PAS; - the premium is recorded in billing; - commission is accrued for the aggregator; - the policy document is generated (schedule plus wordings) and emailed instantly. 7. Downstream: the policy is reported to industry and regulatory repositories as required (VERIFY), and becomes a reinsurance cession if a treaty covers it.

docs.title: 4.2 Journey 2: buying a family health policy in the app
docs.text:
1. Proposal: the customer adds members (ages, pre-existing conditions, lifestyle questions).

  2. Underwriting rules:

    • accept at standard rates (young, no conditions);
    • accept with loading or a waiting period for declared conditions;
    • refer to medical underwriting (tele-medical interview or medical tests at partner labs);
    • decline outside appetite.

    A score (§6.3) orders referrals by risk. 3. Pricing: premium by age band per member, sum insured, zone (city tier), deductibles, add-ons. The family floater discount is applied. 4. Payment and mandate: annual payment, or instalments via NACH/UPI AutoPay mandates. 5. Issuance: the policy with waiting periods recorded per member and condition. A health card is issued (digital) for cashless use. 6. Free-look period: the customer can cancel within a set number of days for a refund minus proportionate costs (VERIFY the current period and rules). The PAS supports this as a special cancellation.

docs.title: 4.3 Journey 3: a cashless hospital claim
docs.text:
1. Admission and pre-auth request: the patient is admitted to a network hospital. The hospital's insurance desk sends a pre-authorisation request with the diagnosis, planned treatment, estimated cost and doctor notes. It arrives via the insurer's TPA portal/API or the National Health Claims Exchange (NHCX, FHIR-based; VERIFY adoption) (I04 §4.4).
  2. Coverage checks (automated first):
    • policy in force;
    • member covered;
    • waiting periods passed for this condition;
    • sum insured available (after previous claims);
    • sub-limits (room rent caps, disease-specific limits);
    • exclusions;
    • hospital in network with an agreed package tariff.
  3. Medical adjudication:
    • rules auto-approve standard packages (e.g. cataract surgery at the agreed tariff);
    • otherwise a medical officer reviews: are the treatment and length of stay appropriate for the diagnosis?
    • queries go back to the hospital as tasks.
  4. Approval: within the regulatory timeline for pre-auth decisions (VERIFY). An approved amount is issued, with enhancements if the stay extends.
  5. Discharge:
    • the hospital submits the final bill with itemisation and discharge summary;
    • bill audit (§6.7) checks items against the tariff, flags non-payables (consumables excluded by policy) and applies co-pay and deductibles;
    • final approval is issued, again within timelines (VERIFY);
    • the patient pays the non-payables and leaves.
  6. Settlement: the insurer pays the hospital via bank transfer in batches, reconciled per claim.
  7. Accounting: the claim updates the sum insured utilisation, the no-claim bonus status for renewal, reserves (§6.8) and reinsurance recoveries.

docs.title: 4.4 Journey 4: a motor accident claim
docs.text:
1. FNOL (first notice of loss): in the app, the customer records the accident location, photos and description, and chooses a garage.
  2. Triage:
    • small, simple claims with clear photos go to AI-assisted assessment: damage detection and estimate by part (§6.5), within a threshold;
    • larger or suspicious claims get a surveyor (licensed, per regulation; VERIFY thresholds for mandatory surveys);
    • third-party injury claims follow legal processes (motor accident claims tribunals) and are handled separately, with long durations.
  3. Survey:
    • the surveyor inspects, virtually or in person, and records findings in the surveyor app;
    • the garage submits a repair estimate;
    • the system compares the estimate to part price catalogues and labour norms;
    • depreciation is applied per part material, unless a zero-depreciation add-on applies.
  4. Approval: the repair is authorised. After repair, a re-inspection (photos) is done. The insurer pays the garage directly (cashless garage), or reimburses the customer.
  5. Fraud checks throughout (§6.6): inconsistent photos, previously claimed damage (image similarity against past claims), staged accident patterns, linked parties.
  6. Recovery:
    • salvage for total losses (the vehicle is sold via auction);
    • subrogation against a third party's insurer where applicable.

docs.title: 4.5 Journey 5: a life insurance death claim
docs.text:
1. Intimation: the nominee intimates the claim via the app, branch or call centre, with the death certificate, policy details, and their own KYC and bank details.
  2. Validation: policy in force at the date of death, no lapse, and nominee identity verified.
  3. Early claims (e.g. within the first few years) may be investigated for non-disclosure, within legal limits on contestability (VERIFY Section 45 of the Insurance Act as amended).
  4. Decision and payment: payment to the nominee's verified account within regulatory timelines, with interest for delays where required (VERIFY). Reinsurance recovery for amounts above retention.

docs.title: 4.6 Journey 6: renewal and lapse
docs.text:
1. Reminders: renewal notices go out before expiry by email, SMS and app. For motor and health, the renewal premium is recalculated (age band change, NCB, claims experience, rate revisions).
  2. Auto-renewal: where a mandate exists, the premium is debited after the pre-debit notification (VERIFY rules).
  3. Grace periods: during the grace period, cover continuity rules apply per product (VERIFY).
    • Health: continuity preserves waiting-period credit.
    • Life: unpaid premiums lead to lapse after the grace period. Revival is possible within a window, with arrears plus interest and possibly fresh underwriting.
  4. Lapse prediction (§6.9) triggers targeted outreach before due dates.

docs.title: 5.1 Product configurator
docs.text:
• A product definition includes:
    • coverages and benefits;
    • options and add-ons;
    • eligibility rules;
    • rating factors and rate tables;
    • underwriting rules;
    • policy wording templates;
    • claims rules (waiting periods, sub-limits, exclusions, co-pays);
    • commission rules;
    • regulatory identifiers.
  • Versioned with effective dates. A policy is always administered under the product version it was sold on, or renewed into, per rules.
  • Output: a machine-readable product model interpreted by the rating engine, the underwriting engine, PAS and claims. One definition, many consumers, which avoids inconsistencies between quoting and claims.
  • Testing: every product version has test cases (premium examples filed with the regulator, claims examples) run automatically before release.

docs.title: 5.2 Rating engine
docs.text:
• Stateless and fast. Input: risk data + product version. Output: premium breakdown (per coverage, loadings, discounts, taxes).
  • Rate tables are loaded in memory. Pricing models (§6.1) are served as tables or model artefacts.
  • Aggregator traffic: very high quote volumes with low conversion. Cache quotes by risk signature (vehicle variant + zone + age + NCB + add-ons) for minutes. Rate-limit per partner.
  • Explainability: every quote stores its factor contributions, for disputes and regulatory review.

docs.title: 5.3 Policy administration with bitemporal data
docs.text:
• Policy versions: each change (endorsement) creates a new version with an effective date range (when the change applies in the contract) and a transaction time (when it was recorded).
  • Back-dated changes (e.g. a vehicle change effective last week) produce premium adjustments computed pro-rata for the affected period.
  • Queries:
    • "what cover applied on the accident date?" uses effective time;
    • "what did we know when we approved that claim?" uses transaction time.
  • Documents: endorsement schedules generated per version.
  • Cancellations: pro-rata or short-period scales per rules. Refund computation and payment.

docs.title: 5.4 Billing and collections
docs.text:
• Payment modes: single premium, instalments (monthly or quarterly), mandates (NACH, UPI AutoPay; VERIFY limits and pre-debit rules), card, net banking.
  • Premium allocation: premium receivable accounts per policy; unallocated receipts handled by rules.
  • Dunning: failed debits → retry → notify → grace period → lapse or cancellation per product.
  • Integration with finance: premium income recognition, GST, commission payable.

docs.title: 5.5 Claims management
docs.text:
• A claim is a case with a workflow:
    1. intake (FNOL);
    2. coverage verification;
    3. triage (complexity, fraud score, value);
    4. assignment (automation, adjuster, surveyor, medical officer);
    5. investigation;
    6. assessment;
    7. approval (authority limits by role and amount);
    8. payment;
    9. recovery (reinsurance, salvage, subrogation);
    10. closure, and reopen if needed.
  • Human tasks with SLAs. Authority matrices (who can approve how much). Maker-checker for payments above thresholds.
  • Reserves per claim: an initial reserve at intimation (by triage model), updated as information arrives. These case reserves feed actuarial reserving.
  • Straight-through processing (STP): simple claims (low value, clear coverage, low fraud score) auto-approve and pay within minutes, e.g. small OPD health claims or windshield replacement.
  • Communication: status updates to customers and hospitals, and document requests as tasks visible in the app.

docs.title: 5.6 Reinsurance
docs.text:
• Treaties:
    • quota share: a fixed percentage of every policy ceded;
    • surplus: amounts above the retention ceded, per policy;
    • excess of loss: the reinsurer pays losses above a threshold per event or per risk;
    • catastrophe covers.
  • Cessions: computed per policy (at issuance and endorsement), with cession premiums.
  • Recoveries: computed per claim or per event (catastrophes aggregate many claims).
  • Bordereaux (listings) are sent to reinsurers periodically. Reinsurance accounting is reconciled.
  • Facultative reinsurance for individual large risks outside treaties (a workflow with reinsurer quotes).

docs.title: 5.7 Fraud management
docs.text:
• Scoring at key points: policy issuance (application fraud), claim intimation, and before payment.
  • Rules:
    • claims soon after inception;
    • high-value claims just below approval thresholds;
    • repeated claimants;
    • hospitals or garages with outlier patterns.
  • Models: supervised (from past confirmed fraud) plus anomaly detection.
  • Network analysis (§6.6): links between claimants, garages, hospitals, doctors, phones, bank accounts and addresses reveal rings.
  • SIU case management: investigation tasks, evidence, outcomes that feed back as labels.
  • Industry sharing: fraud repositories and claims history databases shared across insurers, where regulated (VERIFY).

docs.title: 6.1 Pricing with generalised linear models
docs.text:
• Frequency × severity:

    • model claim frequency (claims per policy-year) with a Poisson GLM (log link);
    • model claim severity (cost per claim) with a Gamma GLM (log link);
    • pure premium = frequency × severity.

    With log links, factors multiply: premium = base × factor(age) × factor(zone) × factor(vehicle)… - Tweedie GLMs model pure premium directly. - Credibility and smoothing: sparse cells are smoothed, e.g. a rare vehicle model gets credibility-weighted factors between its own experience and its group's. - Gradient-boosted models capture interactions but must be explainable and filed. Many insurers use GBMs to find interactions, then encode them in GLM-style tables for filing and transparency (VERIFY local product filing rules). - Final premium: pure premium + expense loadings + profit margin + commissions + taxes, within approved rate ranges.

docs.title: 6.2 Rules engines
docs.text:
• Underwriting, eligibility and claims coverage rules are expressed declaratively: "if age > 55 and sum insured > 50 lakh then refer".
  • Engines: the Rete algorithm (e.g. Drools) evaluates many rules efficiently by sharing conditions and incrementally matching facts. Decision tables are for business users.
  • Governance: versioned rule sets tied to product versions, test suites, and audit of which rules fired for each decision.

docs.title: 6.3 Underwriting scoring
docs.text:
• A risk score from applicant data (age, BMI, declared conditions, occupation, income-to-cover ratio), external data (bureau-based signals where permitted; VERIFY), and medical test results.
  • Decisions: thresholds map the score to bands (accept, loading, referral, decline), with rules as guard rails.
  • Accelerated underwriting: lower-risk applicants skip medical tests. The model must control mortality/morbidity slippage, monitored against actual claims experience.
  • Fairness: exclude prohibited factors; monitor outcomes across groups (VERIFY applicable rules).

docs.title: 6.4 Telematics (usage-based motor insurance)
docs.text:
• Data: trips from a phone app or device: distance, time of day, speeding relative to road limits, harsh braking and acceleration, phone use while driving.
  • Driving score: event rates per 100 km weighted by severity and exposure. Premium discounts are tied to the score (VERIFY regulatory framework for pay-as-you-drive products).
  • Pipeline: sensor streams → trip segmentation → map matching (I05 §6.5) → event detection → aggregation per policy period.

docs.title: 6.5 Image-based damage assessment
docs.text:
• Guided capture ensures angles and coverage. Photo metadata checks: time, location, device consistency.
  • Computer vision models:
    • part detection (bumper, door, headlamp);
    • damage detection and classification (scratch, dent, crack);
    • severity → repair vs replace decisions.
  • Estimate: parts price catalogue + labour norms + paint → estimated cost. The confidence decides auto-approve or survey.
  • Fraud:
    • perceptual hashing against past claim photos (reused images; I07 §6.8);
    • edited image detection;
    • odometer and plate consistency.

docs.title: 6.6 Fraud networks
docs.text:
• Graph: nodes = policyholders, claims, vehicles, garages, hospitals, doctors, phones, emails, bank accounts, addresses; edges = relationships.
  • Detection:
    • connected components and community detection find rings;
    • centrality finds hubs (a garage linked to many suspicious claims);
    • graph features (degree, shared attributes) feed supervised models.
  • Entity resolution first: the same person with different spellings or phones (I04 §6.1 patterns).

docs.title: 6.7 Claims triage and bill auditing
docs.text:
• Triage model: predicts complexity, expected cost and fraud risk at intimation. It routes to STP, a junior or senior adjuster, or the SIU, and sets the initial reserve.
  • Health bill audit:
    • map bill items to standard codes;
    • compare with the package tariff and reasonable-cost benchmarks for the diagnosis and city;
    • flag non-payable consumables per regulatory lists (VERIFY), duplicate charges, and room-rent proportionate deductions.
  • Length-of-stay benchmarks per diagnosis flag outliers for medical review.

docs.title: 6.8 Reserving (IBNR) with the chain-ladder method
docs.text:
• The problem: at any date, some claims have happened but aren't reported yet (IBNR), and reported claims will still develop. Reserves must cover the ultimate cost.
  • Chain ladder:
    • arrange paid (or incurred) claims in a triangle: rows = accident period, columns = development period;
    • compute age-to-age development factors as the ratio of cumulative claims between consecutive development periods, weighted across accident periods;
    • multiply the latest diagonal by the remaining factors to project ultimate claims per accident period;
    • IBNR = ultimate − reported.
  • Variants: Bornhuetter–Ferguson (blending expected loss ratio for immature periods), Mack's method for uncertainty, stochastic bootstraps.
  • Systems role: the data platform produces clean triangles by product, line and period, reconciled with finance. Actuaries run and sign off models.

docs.title: 6.9 Lapse and renewal prediction
docs.text:
• Model: classifier on payment history, tenure, channel, premium change at renewal, engagement and claims experience.
  • Use: targeted reminders, agent follow-ups, offering instalments. Measured by uplift experiments.

docs.title: 7.1 Operational stores
docs.text: Data Store (reference) Notes Product definitions, rules, rate tables Versioned configuration store (Git-backed + database) Released as artefacts Policies (bitemporal) PostgreSQL / core suite database Versions with effective and transaction time Claims and workflows Workflow engine store + PostgreSQL Tasks, SLAs, audit Billing and ledgers Relational with double-entry Ch 45 Documents Object storage + DMS metadata Encrypted; retention per regulation Quotes KV with TTL + warehouse copy for analytics High volume, low conversion Fraud graph Graph database or graph tables in the warehouse Updated daily and on events

docs.title: 7.2 Warehouse and actuarial data
docs.text:
• CDC/events from PAS, billing, claims and reinsurance → lakehouse → warehouse.
  • Core subject areas:
    • policy/exposure: earned exposure per policy per period;
    • premium: written and earned;
    • claims: transactions, payments, reserves by date;
    • reinsurance: ceded premium, recoveries;
    • commissions;
    • customer.
  • Actuarial marts: exposure and claims per accident period and development period (triangles), per product and line. Experience studies (loss ratios by factor, mortality and morbidity experience vs expected).
  • Finance and regulatory reporting: premium, claims, reserves, solvency calculations, and regulatory returns in prescribed formats (VERIFY IRDAI reporting and Ind AS 117 / IFRS 17 adoption status).
  • IFRS 17-style accounting (if adopted) needs grouping of contracts, cash flow projections and a contractual service margin, a significant data and calculation engine in its own right (VERIFY).

docs.title: 7.3 ML platform
docs.text:
• Models: pricing support, underwriting scores, lapse, claims triage, fraud, image damage, bill audit anomalies, catastrophe exposure analysis.
  • Governance:
    • model risk management (validation, documentation);
    • explainability for decisions affecting customers;
    • monitoring for drift (e.g. inflation changes severity);
    • human override paths.

docs.title: 7.4 Data flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    PAS[Policy admin] --> K[Kafka and CDC]
    BILL[Billing] --> K
    CLM[Claims] --> K
    RI[Reinsurance] --> K
    K --> LAKE[Lakehouse]
    LAKE --> DW[Warehouse - premium, claims, exposure]
    DW --> ACT[Actuarial marts - triangles, experience]
    DW --> FIN[Finance and regulatory reporting]
    LAKE --> FEAT[Features]
    FEAT --> MODELS[Pricing, underwriting, fraud, triage models]
    MODELS --> SVC[Rating, underwriting, claims services]
    ACT --> RES[Reserving by actuaries]
    RES --> FIN

docs.title: 8. Tech Stack (reference choice)
docs.text: Layer Choice Notes Core policy/billing/claims Commercial suite (e.g. Guidewire, Duck Creek, or Indian vendors) or built on Java/Spring Many insurers buy; digital layers are built Rating and underwriting Java/Kotlin services; Drools for rules; model serving Fast, explainable Workflows Camunda/Temporal (BPMN for human tasks) Claims and underwriting referrals APIs Spring Boot, API gateway with partner management Aggregator scale Databases PostgreSQL; Redis for quote cache Proven Documents Object storage + DMS; templating for policy documents Long retention Messaging Kafka + Debezium CDC Events to data platform Lakehouse/warehouse Iceberg + Spark + Trino, or a cloud warehouse (in-country per rules) Actuarial marts BI Superset/Power BI Finance and ops dashboards ML Python (scikit-learn, XGBoost, PyTorch for images), MLflow Model governance Graph Neo4j or graph features in the warehouse Fraud rings Mobile Native or cross-platform app with guided photo/video capture Self-inspection, FNOL Platform Kubernetes, Terraform, Argo CD Standard

docs.title: 9. Security, Privacy & Compliance
docs.text:
• Health data: strict access by role and claim assignment, and audit (I04 §10 patterns). Consent for data use. DPDP Act obligations (VERIFY).
  • KYC/AML: KYC for all policies, sanctions and PEP screening, suspicious transaction reporting for large premiums or refunds (VERIFY).
  • Policyholder protection:
    • free-look;
    • claim decision and payment timelines;
    • grievance redressal with escalation to the Bima Bharosa system and ombudsman;
    • disclosure of rejection reasons (VERIFY current rules).
  • Distribution compliance: commission and expense limits, disclosure by intermediaries, aggregator rules (VERIFY).
  • Industry platforms: Bima Sugam, an IRDAI-backed insurance marketplace platform in development, and insurance repositories for e-policies (VERIFY current status).
  • Cybersecurity: IRDAI information and cyber security guidelines (VERIFY).

docs.title: 10. Reliability & Operations
docs.text:
• Channel availability: quote and buy APIs are horizontally scaled and stateless. Aggregator traffic is rate-limited per partner. Rating is cached.
  • Cashless approvals must work 24×7. The TPA and medical officer workflow needs on-call coverage. System outages delay patient discharges.
  • Catastrophe mode: after floods or cyclones, activate simplified claims processes:
    • self-survey with photos;
    • relaxed documentation per regulator advisories (VERIFY);
    • surge surveyor allocation;
    • dedicated dashboards;
    • reserve estimates per event for reinsurance notification.
  • Month-end and year-end: closing processes (earned premium, reserves, reinsurance accounting) run as scheduled pipelines with reconciliation checks.
  • Data quality: exposure and claims data errors directly distort pricing and reserves. Build validation rules into pipelines and reconcile with finance.

docs.title: 11. Key Trade-offs
docs.text: Decision Chosen Accepted cost Core systems Buy a suite, build the edges Vendor constraints; integration work Product definition Configuration-driven, versioned Configurator complexity Policy data Bitemporal Harder queries and storage Claims Workflows with STP for simple cases Model risk in auto-approvals Pricing GLM tables (with ML insights) Less flexible than pure ML Fraud Rules + models + graphs + SIU Investigation cost; false positives Reserving Actuarial models on clean triangles Data engineering effort

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What are the core systems of an insurance company?

30-second answer: Product configuration and rating, distribution channels, underwriting, policy administration (issuance, endorsements, renewals), billing and collections, claims management, fraud, reinsurance, actuarial and finance, customer service, and a data platform for reporting and pricing.

Deep answer: §1.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Buy a suite vs build.

Follow-ups: 1. Most complex? → Claims. 2. Most changed? → Products and pricing.

Red flags: "It's just a CRUD app for policies."

Q2 [B1] How is a motor insurance premium calculated?

30-second answer: From vehicle details (class, age, value), zone, the insured declared value, no-claim bonus, add-ons and deductibles through rate tables and model-based loadings, plus the regulated third-party premium and taxes.

Deep answer: §4.1, §6.1 (VERIFY current rules).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed vs enrichment lookups.

Follow-ups: 1. NCB? → Discount for claim-free years. 2. Aggregators? → Cached quotes.

Red flags: Hard-coded premiums in code.

Q3 [B1] What happens in a cashless hospital claim?

30-second answer: The hospital requests pre-authorisation; the insurer checks policy coverage, waiting periods, limits and network tariffs; a medical officer reviews if needed; an approved amount is issued; at discharge the final bill is audited; the insurer pays the hospital and the patient pays non-payables.

Deep answer: §4.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed vs checks.

Follow-ups: 1. Timelines? → Regulatory limits. 2. Enhancements? → For longer stays.

Red flags: Only reimbursement claims.

Q4 [B1] What is an endorsement?

30-second answer: A mid-term change to a policy — adding a member, changing a vehicle or address — creating a new policy version with an effective date and, often, a pro-rata premium adjustment.

Deep answer: §5.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Versioning complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. Back-dated? → Bitemporal data. 2. Documents? → Endorsement schedule.

Red flags: Overwriting the policy row.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ Why use a bitemporal data model for policies?

30-second answer: Changes can apply from a past or future date (effective time) and are recorded at a different time (transaction time); claims need "what cover applied on the loss date" and audits need "what did we know when we decided" — both require keeping both timelines.

Deep answer: §5.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Query and storage complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. Example? → Back-dated vehicle change. 2. Implementation? → Valid-from/to plus recorded-at columns.

Red flags: Only the latest state.

Q6 [B2] How do you launch new insurance products quickly?

30-second answer: A product configurator with versioned definitions (coverages, rules, rate tables, wordings, claims rules) consumed by rating, underwriting, policy and claims engines, with automated test cases per version — code changes only for genuinely new behaviour.

Deep answer: §5.1.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Configurator complexity vs speed.

Follow-ups: 1. Old policies? → Stay on their version. 2. Regulatory approval? → Before release (VERIFY).

Red flags: Product logic scattered in code.

Q7 [B2] How would you handle aggregator quote traffic?

30-second answer: Stateless, horizontally scaled rating with in-memory tables, caching by risk signature, per-partner rate limits and quotas, fast external lookups with fallbacks, short quote retention, and monitoring conversion per partner.

Deep answer: §5.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Cache freshness vs cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Registry outage? → Manual details path. 2. Price changes? → Cache invalidation by version.

Red flags: Full underwriting per quote.

Q8 [B2] How do claims workflows work?

30-second answer: A case moves through intake, coverage checks, triage, assignment, investigation, assessment, authority-based approval, payment and recovery, with human tasks, SLAs, reserves updated along the way, and straight-through processing for simple low-risk claims.

Deep answer: §5.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Automation vs control.

Follow-ups: 1. Authority limits? → Matrix by role/amount. 2. Reopen? → Allowed with audit.

Red flags: Email-driven claims.

Q9 [B2] What is reinsurance and how does the system support it?

30-second answer: Insurers transfer part of their risk to reinsurers via treaties (quota share, surplus, excess of loss, catastrophe) or facultative deals; the system computes cessions per policy, recoveries per claim or event, and produces bordereaux and reinsurance accounting.

Deep answer: §5.6.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Accuracy vs batch timing.

Follow-ups: 1. Catastrophe? → Event aggregation. 2. Retention? → Per treaty.

Red flags: Spreadsheet reinsurance.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ How would you price motor insurance with data?

30-second answer: Frequency (Poisson GLM) × severity (Gamma GLM) with log links giving multiplicative factors, credibility smoothing for sparse cells, ML to discover interactions then encoded in explainable tables, plus expense and profit loadings, within filed ranges — and monitor actual vs expected.

Deep answer: §6.1.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Accuracy vs explainability and filing.

Follow-ups: 1. Telematics? → Behaviour-based factors. 2. Inflation? → Severity trends.

Red flags: One flat rate per vehicle class.

Q11 [B3] ⭐ How do you detect insurance fraud rings?

30-second answer: Entity resolution across people, vehicles, providers, phones, bank accounts and addresses; build a graph; find communities and hubs; combine graph features with rules and supervised models; route high scores to the SIU; feed outcomes back as labels.

Deep answer: §5.7, §6.6.

Trade-offs I'd call out: False positives delay honest claims.

Follow-ups: 1. Garages? → Outlier patterns. 2. Photos? → Perceptual hashing.

Red flags: Only per-claim rules.

Q12 [B3] How would AI-assisted motor claims work safely?

30-second answer: Guided photo capture, metadata checks, part and damage detection models producing a repair estimate from parts catalogues and labour norms, confidence thresholds for auto-approval of small claims, surveys for the rest, and image-reuse and editing detection — with human override and monitoring.

Deep answer: §4.4, §6.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed vs leakage.

Follow-ups: 1. Thresholds? → By value and confidence. 2. Drift? → New car models.

Red flags: Fully automated high-value claims.

Q13 [B3] How do you compute IBNR reserves, and what does the data platform provide?

30-second answer: Actuaries use development triangles (accident vs development period) and methods like chain ladder or Bornhuetter–Ferguson to project ultimate claims; IBNR is ultimate minus reported; the data platform must produce clean, reconciled triangles per product and period.

Deep answer: §6.8, §7.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Method choice vs data maturity.

Follow-ups: 1. Uncertainty? → Mack, bootstrap. 2. Reconciliation? → With finance.

Red flags: Reserves from current open claims only.

Q14 [B3] How do you audit hospital bills automatically?

30-second answer: Map items to standard codes, compare against package tariffs and cost benchmarks by diagnosis and city, apply policy rules (room-rent limits, co-pays, non-payables lists), flag duplicates and length-of-stay outliers, and route exceptions to medical officers.

Deep answer: §6.7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Automation vs disputes with hospitals.

Follow-ups: 1. Standards? → Coding and exchange formats. 2. Timelines? → Regulatory limits.

Red flags: Manual review of every bill.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design a digital insurer's platform end to end.

30-second answer: Channel APIs for app, agents and aggregators; product configurator driving rating, underwriting, policy and claims engines; bitemporal policy administration; billing with mandates; claims workflows with STP, fraud scoring and SIU; reinsurance; Kafka to a lakehouse with actuarial marts, finance and regulatory reporting; ML for pricing, underwriting, triage, fraud and images.

Deep answer: §3–§7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Buy core vs build.

Follow-ups: 1. Biggest risk? → Data quality for pricing and reserves. 2. Differentiation? → Claims experience.

Red flags: No actuarial data design.

Q16 [B4] Buy an insurance core suite or build?

30-second answer: Buy the heavily regulated, mature core when a suite fits; build the differentiating edges; insist on APIs, events and data access to avoid lock-in.

Deep answer: Evaluate product fit, regulatory features, total cost, vendor lock-in, configurability, APIs and data access; many insurers buy policy/billing/claims cores and build channels, rating services, fraud, data and customer experience around them.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed vs control.

Follow-ups: 1. Migration? → Product by product. 2. Customisation? → Configure, don't fork.

Red flags: Building everything from scratch.

Q17 [B4] How would you migrate millions of in-force policies from a legacy system?

30-second answer: Map product versions and rules carefully, migrate by product or cohort with parallel runs comparing premiums, renewals and claims calculations, reconcile financials, keep legacy read-only for history, and plan cut-over around renewal cycles.

Deep answer: Ch 28, Ch 16.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Parallel run cost vs risk.

Follow-ups: 1. Life policies? → Decades of history. 2. Validation? → Automated comparisons.

Red flags: Big-bang migration.

Q18 [B4] How do you prepare systems for a catastrophe event?

30-second answer: Catastrophe mode with simplified self-survey flows, surge assignment of surveyors, event tagging of claims, per-event reserves and reinsurance notifications, capacity for claim intake and document uploads, and dashboards for regulators and management.

Deep answer: §10.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed vs fraud risk.

Follow-ups: 1. Exposure analysis? → Geocoded policies. 2. Communication? → Proactive outreach.

Red flags: Business as usual.

Q19 [B4] How do regulations shape insurance systems in India?

30-second answer: Product approvals and filed rates constrain pricing; policyholder protection sets free-look, claim and grievance timelines; KYC for all policies; distribution and commission rules; data protection; solvency and reporting (and accounting standards) requirements — so rules and timelines must be configurable and auditable (VERIFY current texts).

Deep answer: §9.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Agility vs compliance.

Follow-ups: 1. Timelines as SLAs? → Workflow timers. 2. Audit? → Decision logs.

Red flags: Compliance as an afterthought.

Q20 [B4] What makes insurance data platforms harder than typical analytics platforms?

30-second answer: Long-lived contracts with bitemporal history, earned vs written measures, development over years, reconciliation with finance, actuarial triangles, regulatory formats, and model governance — errors directly change prices, reserves and solvency.

Deep answer: §7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Rigor vs speed of insight.

Follow-ups: 1. Earned premium? → Exposure over time. 2. Restatements? → Versioned data.

Red flags: Treating it like clickstream analytics.

docs.title: 13. Summary
docs.text:
1. An insurer prices risk, administers contracts for years, pays claims and holds reserves. Each is a distinct system with its own correctness needs.
  2. Configuration-driven products and a bitemporal policy model make changes safe over long lifetimes.
  3. Claims are workflows: straight-through for simple cases, human expertise for the rest, fraud scoring and network analysis throughout.
  4. Algorithms: GLM pricing, rules engines, underwriting scores, telematics, computer vision for damage, fraud graphs, bill audits, chain-ladder reserving.
  5. The data platform serves pricing, reserving, finance and regulators. Data quality errors cost money directly.

docs.title: I10. Travel & Railway Ticketing
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Sector: Travel and transport · Format: system design walkthrough (no code) · Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Builds on: Ch 46 (reservation, waiting room), Ch 48 (capacity booking), Ch 45, Ch 39

What you get: two booking systems.

1. A national railway reservation system in the IRCTC style:

  • the train inventory model (seats by segment along a route, quotas, classes);
  • berth allocation, waitlists and RAC;
  • charting, cancellations and refunds;
  • the Tatkal rush, when a large share of the day's demand arrives in the first minutes after the window opens;
  • bots and agents, payments at peak.

2. An online travel agency (OTA) for flights and buses:

  • flight search across airlines through GDS and NDC connections;
  • fare caching and the look-to-book problem;
  • booking and ticketing, schedule changes;
  • bus aggregator inventory.

Also covered:

  • the algorithms: segment inventory with bitsets, berth allocation, waitlist confirmation prediction, fare caching and invalidation, admission control, bot detection, dynamic fares, demand forecasting;
  • the data platform and tech stack.

Reading time: 85 min.

Sources and honesty

  • Indian Railways' reservation system (PRS) is built and run by CRIS, and ticketing on the web is through IRCTC. Their internal designs are not fully public.
  • Rules such as quota types, Tatkal opening times, advance reservation period, charting times, refund rules and ID requirements change over time and are summarised with VERIFY.
  • GDS, NDC and airline rules are industry standards and practices, also marked VERIFY where specific.
  • This is a reference design.

docs.title: 1.1 Why train ticketing is special
docs.text:
A flight is one hop: 180 seats from A to B. A long-distance train is one vehicle serving many journeys. A berth from Delhi to Mumbai via 20 stations can be sold to one passenger for Delhi → Kota and another for Kota → Mumbai. The system must:

  • track each berth's occupancy per segment of the route;
  • apply quotas: general, Tatkal, ladies, senior citizen, and pooled quotas for intermediate stations (VERIFY current quota names and rules);
  • sell waitlisted tickets that may confirm later when others cancel;
  • handle RAC (a shared berth, with a seat guaranteed);
  • produce a final chart before departure;
  • survive demand spikes where far more people want seats than exist, all within minutes.

docs.title: 1.2 Main systems
docs.text: System What it does Train master and schedules Trains, routes, stops, coach compositions, running days, fares Inventory service Seat/berth availability per train, date, class, quota and segment Booking engine Allocates berths or waitlist positions atomically; creates the PNR Waitlist and RAC manager Promotes waitlisted passengers on cancellations; final charting Availability service Fast, cached answers to "how many seats?" across trains and dates Fare engine Base fares by class and distance, dynamic fares where applicable, charges, taxes Payments Gateways, UPI, cards, wallets; reconciliation; refunds User accounts Registration, verification, saved passengers, agent accounts Admission and anti-bot Waiting room, CAPTCHA, rate limits, bot detection at Tatkal time Cancellation and refunds Rules by time before departure and ticket status Notifications PNR status updates, chart prepared, platform info OTA flights and buses Search, fare caching, supplier connections (GDS, NDC, bus operators), booking, ticketing Data platform Demand analytics, forecasting, fraud, reporting

docs.title: 1.3 Scale for this design (assumptions; VERIFY real figures)
docs.text:
Quantity Value Trains per day ~13,000 passenger trains (VERIFY) Reserved tickets per day ~1.5M (web + counters + apps; VERIFY) Registered users Hundreds of millions Tatkal window Opens daily at a fixed time for AC classes and a later time for non-AC (VERIFY times) Peak booking attempts Tens of thousands per second in the first minute; far more availability checks and page loads Availability queries per day Hundreds of millions (users compare trains and dates)

Estimation — the Tatkal minute:

  • Suppose 200k Tatkal berths go on sale at opening, and 2M users are ready to book, each checking availability several times and submitting once or twice.
  • In the first 2 minutes, the booking engine faces ~20k booking submissions/s plus 100k+ availability checks/s.
  • Most berths on popular trains sell out in seconds.
  • The design goal isn't to satisfy everyone, because demand is 10× supply. It is to stay up, be fair (first valid request wins), never double-sell, and tell losers quickly.

docs.title: 2.1 Functional (railways)
docs.text:
1. Search trains between stations for a date, with availability per class and quota.
  2. Book up to a maximum number of passengers per ticket (VERIFY limits), with berth preferences, senior citizen and child rules, and ID details where required.
  3. Allocate confirmed berths, RAC or waitlist positions.
  4. Tatkal booking with its own quota, opening time, charges and refund rules (VERIFY).
  5. Cancel, fully or partially, with refunds by rules.
  6. Waitlist promotion as cancellations happen. Final chart before departure, with a second chart for last-minute vacancies (VERIFY charting times).
  7. PNR status enquiries; notifications.
  8. Agents with separate limits and timing restrictions (VERIFY agent rules during Tatkal).

docs.title: 2.2 Functional (OTA)
docs.text:
1. Search flights (one-way, return, multi-city) across airlines. Show fares, fare families and baggage rules.
  2. Price-check and book, then issue the ticket. Handle schedule changes and cancellations.
  3. Search and book buses from many operators with seat maps.

docs.title: 2.3 Non-functional
docs.text: Attribute Target Correctness Never allocate the same berth-segment twice; waitlist order strictly by booking time per quota rules Fairness First-come first-served among valid requests; bots and scripted agents excluded Availability Stay up through the Tatkal minute; degrade search before booking Latency Booking confirmation (allocation) in seconds; search in < 1 s Payments No ticket without payment; no payment without a ticket or a timely refund Audit Every booking, cancellation and chart change recorded

Key decisions:

Decision Choice Why Partitioning Inventory and booking partitioned by (train, journey date); each partition owned by one booking worker All bookings for one train-date must be serialised to avoid double allocation; different trains are independent (Ch 11) Inventory representation Per berth, a bitset over route segments; per quota, pools of berths Fast overlap checks and allocation (§6.1) Availability A cache updated from inventory changes; search never reads the booking engine directly Protect the booking path Payment and allocation order Allocate (hold) first, then pay, confirm on payment success; release on failure or timeout Avoid taking money for nothing; bounded holds (Ch 46) Tatkal defence Waiting room + bot defence + per-user limits + fair queueing into partitions Demand ≫ supply

docs.title: 4. How It Works — Journeys End to End
4.1 Journey 1: searching for a train
docs.text:
1. Search: the user enters "New Delhi → Mumbai Central, 15 Nov".
    • The train search service finds trains serving both stations in the right order on that day, from the timetable graph (§6.6).
    • Results are cached per (from, to, date), because schedules change rarely.
  2. Availability per class and quota comes from the availability cache, not the booking engine. Each entry is the count of berths free for that segment, or the waitlist number: "AVAILABLE-0042", "RAC 12", "WL 35".
  3. Freshness:
    • the cache is updated from inventory change events within seconds;
    • in rush periods, entries may be marked "availability may change quickly";
    • the booking engine is the truth.
  4. Fare: the fare engine computes the fare per class: base fare by distance slab and class, reservation charge, superfast charge, GST for AC classes (VERIFY components). Dynamic fares apply on some premium trains (§6.7).

docs.title: 4.2 Journey 2: a regular booking
docs.text:
1. Submit: the user selects a train and class, adds passengers (name, age, gender, berth preference, ID where needed) and submits.
  2. Admission: the gateway checks the session, the per-user booking limits (tickets per month per verified user; VERIFY limits) and CAPTCHA if the risk score is high. The request is routed to the booking worker owning (train, date).
  3. Allocation (§6.1, §6.2), inside the worker, serially for that train-date:
    • find berths in the right quota pool free for every segment from boarding to destination;
    • honour preferences where possible (lower berths for seniors and women with children per rules; VERIFY);
    • keep the group together if possible;
    • if not enough confirmed berths remain: allocate RAC (sharing a side-lower berth) if available, else a waitlist number in the quota's waitlist;
    • hold the allocation for a short payment window.
  4. Payment: the user pays via the gateway (UPI, cards, net banking, wallets).
    • On success, the allocation becomes booked. A PNR is created with passengers, berths/status, fare and payment reference, and the e-ticket is sent.
    • On failure or timeout, the hold is released and the availability cache updated.
  5. Unclear payment status: if the gateway reports success after the hold expired (late callback), the system must either allocate if still possible or auto-refund within a defined time. It must never keep money without a ticket (Ch 45, I03).

docs.title: 4.3 Journey 3: the Tatkal minute
docs.text:
It is 09:59:30 and 2 million users are logged in with passengers pre-filled ("master list").

  1. Before opening:
    • static pages and scripts are served from the CDN;
    • users are admitted to a waiting room at login or near opening, so login and session creation don't all happen at 10:00;
    • a server-synchronised countdown (the same idea as I02 L1) prevents early submissions.
  2. At opening:
    • submissions go through anti-bot checks (§6.5) and per-user and per-IP limits;
    • the admission controller passes requests to booking partitions at the rate each partition can process;
    • requests for the same train-date queue in arrival order (FIFO) at that partition.
  3. Allocation: each partition's worker processes its queue serially: allocate or waitlist, hold, return.
    • Most popular trains fill in seconds. Later requests get waitlist numbers, or "not available" once the waitlist quota is exhausted (VERIFY waitlist limits).
  4. Payment peak: thousands of payments per second hit gateways. Payment orchestration spreads the load across gateways, with health checks (Ch 45 L4).
    • Holds are long enough to complete payment under peak load (a few minutes).
    • Expired holds go back into the pool, and are re-offered to queued requests in order, not to whoever refreshes fastest.
  5. Communication: users see their queue position and a quick answer ("waitlisted WL 42", "not available").
    • The availability cache is updated continuously.
    • The search tier may be degraded (cached results only) to protect booking.
  6. Aftermath: the booking data feeds fraud analysis. Accounts with bot-like patterns are flagged and cancelled per rules (VERIFY).

docs.title: 4.4 Journey 4: a cancellation and the waitlist moves
docs.text:
1. Cancellation: a confirmed passenger cancels one day before departure. The refund is computed by rules (flat charges by class, percentage deductions by time before departure, special Tatkal rules; VERIFY).
  2. Release: the inventory worker for that train-date releases the berth-segment.

  3. Promotion: the waitlist manager promotes in order:

    • the first RAC passenger(s) move to the confirmed berth (fitting segments);
    • the first waitlisted passenger moves to RAC.

    This is per quota, with pooled-quota rules for intermediate stations (VERIFY). 4. Notification: promoted passengers are notified by SMS or app, and the PNR status updates. 5. Charting: - First chart: a set time before departure, the final allocation is frozen and waitlisted passengers who didn't confirm are cancelled with an automatic refund (for e-tickets; VERIFY). - Second chart: remaining vacancies are released for current booking until close to departure (VERIFY timings).

docs.title: 4.5 Journey 5: booking a flight on an OTA
docs.text:
1. Search: the user searches "BLR → DEL, 20 Dec, 1 adult".
    • Cache first: the flight search service checks its fare cache for recent results for this route-date (§6.8).
    • If the cache is fresh enough, results return in < 1 s. Otherwise it queries suppliers:
      • GDS (Amadeus, Sabre, Travelport) for full-service and some low-cost carriers;
      • NDC APIs directly from airlines for richer offers (fare families, ancillaries);
      • low-cost carrier direct APIs.
    • Results are merged, deduplicated and sorted, and cached.
  2. Look-to-book: hundreds of searches per booking are normal. Supplier calls are expensive and rate-limited, which is why caching matters. Stale cache means price changes at booking, so price-check before payment.
  3. Offer selection and price check: the user picks a flight and fare family. The OTA re-prices with the supplier. If the fare changed, the user is told before paying.
  4. Booking:
    • create a PNR with the airline or GDS (passengers, contact, segments);
    • take payment;
    • issue the ticket (e-ticket number) through the GDS or airline;
    • if ticketing fails after payment, retry, then auto-refund with a clear message.
  5. Post-booking: web check-in links, seat selection and ancillaries. Schedule changes pushed by airlines (queues in the GDS, or NDC notifications) are processed, and customers informed and offered options.
  6. Settlement: with airlines through industry settlement systems (BSP for IATA agents) or direct arrangements; OTA commission or markup accounting (VERIFY).

docs.title: 4.6 Journey 6: booking a bus seat
docs.text:
1. Search: the user searches "Bengaluru → Chennai, tonight". Bus inventory comes from operators' reservation systems through APIs, or from operators using the aggregator's inventory software.
  2. Seat map: a seat layout (sleeper/seater, lower/upper) shows availability, from the operator in real time or with short caching.
  3. Booking: a seat block (hold) with the operator for a few minutes, then payment, then confirmation. Timeouts release the block.
  4. Journey day: boarding point details, live bus tracking (GPS from the operator; Ch 47), and cancellation per the operator's policy.

docs.title: 5.1 The train inventory model
docs.text:
• Route segments: a train's route is a sequence of stops S0, S1, …, Sn. A journey from Si to Sj occupies segments i … j−1.
  • Berths: each coach has berths (lower, middle, upper, side lower, side upper per class layout).
    • Each berth's occupancy is a bitset of length n: bit k set means the berth is occupied on segment k.
    • A journey fits a berth if the AND of the berth's bitset and the journey mask is zero (§6.1).
  • Quotas: berths are assigned to quota pools (general, Tatkal, ladies, senior/lower berth, defence, pooled quotas for intermediate stations; VERIFY names and rules).
    • Pools can have remote locations and roadside station quotas, so intermediate stations get fair shares.
    • Quotas may be released to other pools at defined times (e.g. unused quota released to general before charting; VERIFY).
  • Waitlists: per quota per train-date, ordered by booking time. RAC: side lower berths are shared by two passengers until a berth frees up.
  • State size: a train with 22 coaches × 72 berths ≈ 1,600 berths × a bitset of ~30 segments is tiny. All inventory for one train-date fits in memory in the booking worker, which is why a single-threaded worker per partition is fast.

docs.title: 5.2 Booking engine partitions
docs.text:
• One owner per (train, date):

    • the worker loads the inventory into memory;
    • it processes booking and cancellation commands serially from its queue;
    • it writes each result to a durable log (and the database) before acknowledging.

    This is the single-writer model of Ch 55: no locks, no double allocation, and deterministic replay after a crash. - Partition count: there are a lot of trains × dates (advance reservation period of ~60 days or more; VERIFY), but most are cold. Active hot partitions are few. Partitions are assigned to workers by consistent hashing, and moved on failure. - Throughput per partition: thousands of commands per second in memory. During Tatkal, a popular train-date partition is the hot spot. The admission controller queues requests for it rather than letting them retry and pile up.

docs.title: 5.3 Availability cache
docs.text:
• Per (train, date, class, quota, from, to): there are too many combinations to precompute every pair for long routes, so the cache stores per-segment free counts per quota and computes the minimum over the journey's segments on request. It also caches recent answers for popular pairs.
  • Updates: from inventory events (booking, cancellation, quota release), pushed to cache nodes within seconds.
  • During peaks: the cache may lag the truth. The booking result is final, and the UI communicates it clearly.

docs.title: 5.4 Waitlist, RAC and charting
docs.text:
• Promotion runs inside the train-date partition, after each cancellation. It re-checks segment fit for each waitlisted passenger in order.
    • A long-distance cancellation may confirm several short-distance waitlisted passengers.
    • A short one may confirm nobody.
  • Charting:
    • a scheduled command to each partition at the charting time;
    • it freezes allocations, generates the reservation chart (for coaches and the ticket examiner's handheld device), cancels unconfirmed waitlisted e-tickets with refunds, and publishes vacant berths for current booking.
  • Handheld devices for ticket examiners can update berth occupancy on board (no-shows, on-board allocation of vacant berths to RAC passengers), synchronised when connectivity allows (VERIFY deployment).

docs.title: 5.5 Payments and refunds at peak
docs.text:
• Idempotent payment callbacks keyed by booking reference.
  • Hold timers in the booking partition. A late payment success after hold expiry → try to re-allocate. If that's impossible, auto-refund within a defined time.
  • Refund engine: rules by ticket status, class, time before departure and Tatkal status (VERIFY). Refunds go to the source instrument. Reconciliation and customer notification.

docs.title: 5.6 OTA: supplier connectivity
docs.text:
• GDS: a global distribution system aggregates many airlines' schedules, availability and fares. It is accessed through APIs (historically cryptic terminal commands). There is a cost per transaction and per segment booked (VERIFY commercial models).
  • NDC: IATA's New Distribution Capability, XML/JSON APIs direct from airlines, with richer content (bundles, ancillaries, personalised offers).
  • Low-cost carrier APIs: direct connections.
  • Normalisation: all responses map to an internal offer model (segments, fares, rules, baggage, refundability). Supplier-specific quirks are isolated in connectors.
  • Resilience: timeouts per supplier; partial results are fine ("some airlines didn't respond"). Circuit breakers (Ch 18).

docs.title: 6.1 Segment inventory with bitsets
docs.text:
• Journey mask: for journey (i, j), the mask has bits i … j−1 set.
  • Fit check: a berth b fits if occupancy[b] AND mask == 0. Book it by occupancy[b] |= mask. Cancel by clearing the mask bits (only this booking's).
  • Free count per segment for availability: count berths with bit k clear per quota, maintained incrementally.
  • Performance: a few thousand berths × one AND each is microseconds per request, in memory.

docs.title: 6.2 Berth allocation heuristics
docs.text:
Goals, in order:

  1. Satisfy the journey.
  2. Honour preferences and priority rules (seniors, women, children; VERIFY).
  3. Keep a group in the same coach or bay.
  4. Minimise fragmentation, so the remaining capacity stays useful for future journeys.

Fragmentation example: a berth free for segments 0–10 is valuable. Using it for a 4–6 journey leaves two short holes (0–4 and 6–10) that fewer future journeys can use.

Best-fit heuristic: among fitting berths, prefer the one where the booked segments touch existing occupancy (the berth is already occupied just before or after). That fills gaps rather than creating new ones, like best-fit in memory allocation.

Quota and pool rules: allocate from the journey's quota pool first, then from designated overflow pools per rules (VERIFY).

Evaluation: simulate booking streams to compare heuristics on seats sold and berth-km utilisation. Railways' actual algorithms are not public (VERIFY).

docs.title: 6.3 Waitlist promotion
docs.text:
• The ordered list per quota: for each waitlisted passenger in order, try to fit their journey into the released capacity. A "head-of-line" rule decides whether a later passenger can confirm when the first can't (e.g. because their segments don't fit), per rules (VERIFY).
  • RAC passengers are promoted to confirmed berths when a full berth frees for their segment, and waitlisted passengers move into vacated RAC places.

docs.title: 6.4 Waitlist confirmation prediction
docs.text:
• The question: "WL 42 on train X, travel in 10 days, 3AC — will it confirm?"
  • Features: train, class, quota, waitlist number, days to departure, day of week, season and festivals, historical cancellation curves for this train and class, current booking pace.
  • Model: historical data on waitlist movement → a probability of confirmation by charting. A gradient-boosted classifier or survival-style models of cancellations.
  • Several travel apps offer such predictions (VERIFY).
  • Use: helps users decide whether to book the waitlisted ticket or choose another train. Suggest alternatives.

docs.title: 6.5 Anti-bot and fairness
docs.text:
• Signals:
    • request timing too fast for humans (forms filled in milliseconds);
    • scripted browser fingerprints, headless browsers;
    • many accounts per device/IP/payment instrument;
    • known automation tools;
    • CAPTCHA solving patterns.
  • Controls:
    • CAPTCHAs (with accessibility options);
    • device attestation in the mobile app;
    • per-user and per-instrument limits;
    • restrictions on agents during the opening minutes (VERIFY);
    • server-side queueing, so speed of retries doesn't help;
    • after-the-fact cancellation of tickets from detected bot accounts.
  • Fairness principle: FIFO at the partition among admitted requests. The admission controller never lets fast retries jump the queue (Ch 46).

docs.title: 6.6 Train search across a timetable
docs.text:
• Direct trains: index trains by station, and for each station pair check the stop order.
  • Connections (optional): a time-dependent graph (stations and departure events). Earliest-arrival search with CSA (Connection Scan Algorithm) or RAPTOR, with a minimum transfer time. Journey planners use these to find two-train options when direct ones are full.

docs.title: 6.7 Dynamic fares
docs.text:
• Flexi fares on some premium trains: the fare increases in steps as a percentage of berths are sold, up to a cap (VERIFY the current scheme and trains covered).
  • Implementation: the fare engine reads sold percentage per train-date-class from inventory and applies the step function. The quoted fare is held with the booking.
  • Airline pricing in OTAs: fares come from airlines' revenue management (booking classes opened and closed by demand forecasts). The OTA shows them; it doesn't set them.

docs.title: 6.8 Fare cache for flights
docs.text:
• Keys: (origin, destination, date, passenger mix, cabin), plus result sets from suppliers.
  • TTL by volatility: short for near-term departures, whose fares change fast, and longer for far-future dates.
  • Refresh: popular routes are pre-fetched in the background from search logs. Refresh on booking attempts that show price changes.
  • Measure: price-change rate at price-check (the cache's "lie rate") vs supplier cost. Tune TTLs per route and date band (Ch 07).

docs.title: 6.9 Demand forecasting
docs.text:
• For railways: demand per train, class and date from historical bookings and waitlists, holidays and festivals, and events. It is used for special trains, extra coaches, and quota allocation decisions.
  • For OTAs: search volume forecasts for capacity planning, and pre-fetching fare caches for trending routes.

docs.title: 7.1 Operational stores
docs.text: Data Store (reference) Notes Train master, routes, schedules Relational + cached Versioned by timetable period Inventory per train-date In memory in the booking worker + durable log + relational snapshot Single writer per partition PNRs and passengers Relational, partitioned by journey date Retained per rules; PII protected Availability cache Distributed in-memory cache Rebuilt from inventory Users and sessions Relational + Redis Limits and verification Payments Relational ledger Idempotent callbacks OTA fare cache Redis/KV with TTL Large, volatile OTA bookings Relational Supplier references (PNR, ticket numbers)

docs.title: 7.2 Warehouse and analytics
docs.text:
• Events (search, availability views, booking attempts, allocations, payments, cancellations, chart outcomes) → Kafka → lakehouse → warehouse.
  • Analyses:
    • demand vs supply per route and date;
    • waitlist movement curves;
    • cancellation rates;
    • Tatkal success rates and bot detection outcomes;
    • payment success by gateway;
    • OTA look-to-book, cache hit and lie rates, supplier performance.
  • Uses: extra coaches and special trains, quota tuning, fraud models, waitlist prediction, OTA pricing and markup analysis.

docs.title: 7.3 Data flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    BOOK[Booking partitions] -->|events| K[Kafka]
    PAY[Payments] --> K
    SRCH[Search and availability logs] --> K
    K --> AVL[Availability cache updates]
    K --> LAKE[Lakehouse]
    LAKE --> DW[Warehouse]
    DW --> FC[Demand forecasting]
    DW --> WLM[Waitlist prediction model]
    DW --> BOT[Bot and fraud models]
    FC --> OPS[Special trains, extra coaches, quotas]
    WLM --> APP[Apps - confirmation probability]
    BOT --> EDGE[Edge defences]

docs.title: 8. Tech Stack (reference choice)
docs.text: Layer Choice Notes Edge CDN, WAF, bot management, waiting room Tatkal defence APIs Java/Spring Boot or Go services behind a gateway Session and limits Booking engine Java (single-writer workers, in-memory inventory, journal via Kafka or Chronicle/Aeron-style logs) Deterministic replay Databases PostgreSQL/Oracle for PNRs and masters (legacy systems often Oracle; VERIFY), partitioned by date Durability Caching Redis/Hazelcast for availability Fast reads Messaging Kafka Inventory events, analytics Payments Payment orchestration over multiple gateways Peak resilience OTA connectors Java/Go connectors for GDS (SOAP/REST), NDC (XML/JSON), bus operators Normalised offer model Search (OTA) Fare cache in Redis; background refreshers Look-to-book Analytics Iceberg/Spark/Trino or a warehouse Forecasting and reports ML Python models, served as APIs Waitlist prediction, bots Platform Kubernetes for stateless services; dedicated nodes for booking workers Predictable latency

docs.title: 9. Security, Fairness & Compliance
docs.text:
• Identity: verified accounts (mobile/email, possibly Aadhaar-based verification for higher booking limits; VERIFY current rules). ID proof is required during travel.
  • Agents: registered agents with separate rules and timing restrictions (VERIFY).
  • Payment security: tokenised cards and gateway compliance (Ch 45).
  • Privacy: passenger data (names, ages, IDs) protected, with limited retention (DPDP Act; VERIFY).
  • Fairness and transparency: published rules for quotas, refunds and waitlists, consistent enforcement, and anti-bot measures explained at a high level without revealing detection details.

docs.title: 10. Reliability & Operations
docs.text:
• Tatkal readiness:
    • daily pre-scaling before the opening times;
    • waiting room configured;
    • search degraded mode ready;
    • payment gateways notified of peak;
    • dashboards per partition (queue depth, processing time), per gateway (success rate), and for bot blocks.
  • Partition failover: each booking worker has a standby replaying the same log. Failover within seconds, while queued requests wait, not fail.

  • Graceful degradation: order of shedding:

    1. recommendations and non-essential APIs;
    2. live availability refresh (serve cached);
    3. search for far-future dates.

    Protect booking and payment callbacks. - Charting jobs are scheduled per train and must finish on time. Monitor late charts. - OTA: supplier outages are handled by partial results. GDS connectivity failover. Airline disruption events (weather) cause mass schedule changes, processed from queues with customer communication at scale.

docs.title: 11. Key Trade-offs
docs.text: Decision Chosen Accepted cost Inventory ownership Single writer per train-date Hot partitions during Tatkal must queue Allocation Heuristic best-fit per segment Not globally optimal Availability Cached, eventually consistent Users may see seats that are gone Hold then pay Bounded holds Seats locked briefly by users who don't pay Anti-bot Layered controls + FIFO Some friction for genuine users OTA caching TTL by volatility + price check Price changes at booking

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What makes train ticketing harder than flight ticketing?

30-second answer: A train serves many overlapping journeys along its route, so each berth's occupancy must be tracked per segment; plus quotas, RAC, waitlists that confirm on cancellations, charting, and demand spikes like Tatkal.

Deep answer: §1.1, §5.1.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Utilisation vs complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. Data structure? → Bitset per berth. 2. Waitlist? → Ordered per quota.

Red flags: Treating a train like a flight with 1,600 seats.

Q2 [B1] What happens when you book a train ticket?

30-second answer: Search and availability from a cache; submit passengers; the booking engine for that train-date allocates berths (or RAC/waitlist) and holds them; you pay; on success a PNR is created and the e-ticket sent; on failure the hold is released.

Deep answer: §4.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Hold time vs availability.

Follow-ups: 1. Payment late? → Re-allocate or refund. 2. Preferences? → Heuristics.

Red flags: Taking payment before checking inventory.

Q3 [B1] What is a PNR?

30-second answer: The passenger name record — a booking reference holding the train, date, class, passengers, their berth or waitlist status, fare and payment details; used to check status and on board.

Deep answer: §4.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: —

Follow-ups: 1. Partial cancellation? → Per passenger. 2. Status changes? → Notifications.

Red flags: —

Q4 [B1] Why cache availability separately from bookings?

30-second answer: Availability is queried far more often than bookings are made; serving it from a cache updated by inventory events protects the booking engine, at the cost of occasionally showing seats that were just sold.

Deep answer: §5.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Freshness vs protection.

Follow-ups: 1. Update lag? → Seconds. 2. UI? → Booking result is final.

Red flags: Search queries hitting the booking engine.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do you represent and allocate berths along a route?

30-second answer: Each berth has a bitset over route segments; a journey is a mask of its segments; a berth fits if AND is zero; book by OR, cancel by clearing; choose among fitting berths with best-fit heuristics that reduce fragmentation and honour preferences and quotas.

Deep answer: §6.1, §6.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Heuristic vs optimal allocation.

Follow-ups: 1. Fragmentation? → Touch existing occupancy. 2. Groups? → Same bay preference.

Red flags: One boolean per seat for the whole trip.

Q6 [B2] How do waitlist and RAC promotions work?

30-second answer: On cancellation, the released berth-segments are offered to RAC passengers first (moving them to full berths), then waitlisted passengers move into RAC or confirmed places in order, per quota and segment fit, and passengers are notified; at charting unconfirmed e-tickets are cancelled with refunds.

Deep answer: §4.4, §6.3 (VERIFY rules).

Trade-offs I'd call out: Strict order vs utilisation.

Follow-ups: 1. Short segments? → May confirm several. 2. Charting? → Freeze and publish vacancies.

Red flags: Random promotion.

Q7 [B2] How do you prevent double booking of a berth?

30-second answer: Partition inventory by train and date with a single writer processing commands serially in memory, journaling each allocation before acknowledging; different train-dates proceed in parallel.

Deep answer: §5.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Hot partitions.

Follow-ups: 1. Crash? → Replay journal. 2. Throughput? → Thousands/s per partition.

Red flags: Row locks across a shared seat table during Tatkal.

Q8 [B2] How does an OTA search flights across airlines quickly?

30-second answer: Check a fare cache keyed by route, date and passengers with TTLs based on volatility; on miss, query GDS, NDC and low-cost carrier APIs in parallel with timeouts, normalise into one offer model, merge, sort and cache — then price-check before booking.

Deep answer: §4.5, §6.8.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Staleness vs supplier cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Look-to-book? → Hundreds to one. 2. Partial results? → Acceptable.

Red flags: Querying every airline live on every search.

Q9 [B2] What happens if payment succeeds but the ticket isn't issued?

30-second answer: Retry issuance or allocation with idempotent keys; if still impossible (hold expired, seats gone, ticketing failed), auto-refund within a defined time and notify the user — never keep money without a ticket.

Deep answer: §4.2, §5.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Retry window vs refund speed.

Follow-ups: 1. Late callback? → Reconciliation. 2. Customer view? → Clear status.

Red flags: Manual refunds only.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ Design the system for the Tatkal minute.

30-second answer: Pre-scale; CDN for static content; a waiting room and server-synced countdown; anti-bot and per-user limits; an admission controller routing requests FIFO into single-writer train-date partitions; short holds with payment spread across gateways; cached availability and degraded search; fast "not available" answers; post-hoc bot cancellations.

Deep answer: §4.3, §6.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Fairness vs friction.

Follow-ups: 1. Retry storms? → Server-side queues. 2. Expired holds? → Re-offered in order.

Red flags: "Add more servers."

Q11 [B3] How would you predict waitlist confirmation?

30-second answer: Train a model on historical waitlist movement with features like train, class, quota, WL number, days to departure, seasonality and current booking pace; output a probability by charting; show it with alternatives.

Deep answer: §6.4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Calibration vs overconfidence.

Follow-ups: 1. Festivals? → Special features. 2. Evaluation? → Calibration curves.

Red flags: Heuristic "WL < 20 confirms".

Q12 [B3] How do you detect bots in ticket booking?

30-second answer: Timing and behaviour signals, browser fingerprints and headless detection, device attestation in apps, account/device/payment clustering, CAPTCHA patterns — combined into risk scores that trigger challenges, limits, blocks and later cancellations — with server-side FIFO so speed can't win.

Deep answer: §6.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: False positives on real users.

Follow-ups: 1. Agents? → Time restrictions. 2. Accessibility? → Alternative CAPTCHAs.

Red flags: CAPTCHA only.

Q13 [B3] How would you design the OTA's booking and ticketing flow?

30-second answer: Price-check, create a PNR with the supplier, take payment, issue the ticket, and handle failures with retries and refunds; process airline schedule changes from queues or notifications; reconcile with airline settlement and supplier invoices.

Deep answer: §4.5, §5.6.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Holding PNRs vs cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Fare changed? → Inform before payment. 2. Supplier down? → Circuit breaker.

Red flags: Payment after ticketing without hold.

Q14 [B3] How do dynamic fares on trains work in the system?

30-second answer: The fare engine reads sold percentage per train-date-class from inventory and applies the scheme's step function up to a cap; the quoted fare is fixed with the booking; rules are configurable per train (VERIFY scheme details).

Deep answer: §6.7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Revenue vs public acceptance.

Follow-ups: 1. Consistency? → Price with hold. 2. Refunds? → Rules.

Red flags: Fare computed after payment.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design a national railway reservation system.

30-second answer: Timetable and train master; in-memory inventory per train-date with segment bitsets and quotas, owned by single-writer partitions with journals and standbys; booking with holds and payment orchestration; waitlist, RAC and charting jobs; cached availability; cancellation and refund rules; admission control and anti-bot for Tatkal; Kafka to a warehouse for forecasting, waitlist prediction and fraud.

Deep answer: §3–§7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Heuristics vs optimal allocation.

Follow-ups: 1. Counters and web? → Same engine. 2. Scale? → Partition by train-date.

Red flags: Central seat table with locks.

Q16 [B4] How would you evaluate a new berth allocation algorithm safely?

30-second answer: Replay historical booking streams through a simulator with the current and new heuristics, compare berth-km utilisation, confirmed tickets and preference satisfaction, test edge cases (groups, quotas), then pilot on a few trains with monitoring before rollout.

Deep answer: §6.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Simulation fidelity.

Follow-ups: 1. Metrics? → Seats sold, fragmentation. 2. Fairness? → Rules intact.

Red flags: Deploying to all trains at once.

Q17 [B4] How would you modernise a legacy reservation system?

30-second answer: Put APIs and an event stream around the legacy core, move read paths (search, availability, PNR status) out first, then migrate booking partitions train by train with dual-run comparison of allocations, keeping the journal as the reconciliation point.

Deep answer: Ch 16, Ch 28.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Parallel run cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Counters? → Same APIs. 2. Risk? → Charting correctness.

Red flags: Big-bang rewrite.

Q18 [B4] How do you balance fairness and efficiency in scarce inventory systems?

30-second answer: Define fairness (FIFO among admitted, limits per person), enforce it server-side (queues, not races), defend against bots, keep quotas and published rules, measure outcomes (success rates by segment of users), and accept that efficiency optimisations must not undermine perceived fairness.

Deep answer: §6.5; Ch 46.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Lottery vs FIFO.

Follow-ups: 1. Lottery? → Fairer across networks. 2. Transparency? → Published rules.

Red flags: Fastest client wins.

Q19 [B4] What does the look-to-book ratio mean for OTA architecture?

30-second answer: Searches vastly outnumber bookings and suppliers charge or throttle per call, so the architecture centres on caching, pre-fetching and cost-aware supplier routing, with price checks to manage staleness — measured by cache hit rate, lie rate and supplier cost per booking.

Deep answer: §4.5, §6.8.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Freshness vs cost.

Follow-ups: 1. TTL tuning? → By route and date. 2. NDC? → Richer but more calls.

Red flags: Live search everywhere.

Q20 [B4] Compare railway reservation with an e-commerce flash sale.

30-second answer: Both face demand far above supply, need fair admission, holds and payment orchestration; railways add segment-based inventory, quotas, waitlists that confirm later, charting deadlines and regulatory rules — so inventory logic is richer, while admission and payment patterns are shared.

Deep answer: Ch 46, I02.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Shared platform patterns.

Follow-ups: 1. Shared components? → Waiting room, payments. 2. Different? → Segments, waitlist.

Red flags: Identical designs.

docs.title: 13. Summary
docs.text:
1. Train inventory is per berth per route segment. Bitsets make fit checks and allocations trivial in memory.
  2. Single-writer partitions per train-date guarantee no double booking and simple recovery. Cached availability protects them.
  3. Waitlists, RAC and charting are rule-driven processes inside the partition. Predictions help users decide.
  4. The Tatkal minute is won with admission control, anti-bot measures, FIFO queues, bounded holds and payment orchestration.
  5. OTAs live on caching and supplier normalisation because of the look-to-book ratio. Price checks and reliable ticketing protect customers.
