Key decisions:

Decision Choice Why Shipment state Event-sourced: every scan is an immutable event; the current state and timeline are projections Custody chain, disputes, analytics (Ch 15) Facility systems Edge nodes at hubs with local databases and sort plans; sync to central Hubs must keep sorting when the WAN is down Mobile apps Offline-first with local queues and idempotent event IDs Poor connectivity in the field Tracking Separate read models (per AWB timeline, per shipper views) with caches Read-heavy, public-facing Planning Batch optimisation (nightly/weekly) producing plans consumed by operations Complex solvers off the real-time path

docs.title: 4. How It Works — A Parcel's Journey
docs.text: Follow AWB 123456789: a ₹1,299 COD order from a D2C brand's warehouse in Bhiwandi (Maharashtra) to a customer in Jorhat (Assam).

docs.title: 4.1 Booking
docs.text:
1. API call: the brand's order system (or its shipping aggregator) calls Create Shipment: consignee name, phone, address, pincode, weight 0.8 kg, dimensions, COD ₹1,299, service "surface express".
  2. Serviceability: is pincode 785001 served for COD on this service? What is the TAT from the origin cluster? The answer comes from a precomputed TAT matrix (§5.2).

  3. Address intelligence (§6.1):

    • parse the free-text address;
    • geocode it to coordinates;
    • validate that the pincode matches the location;
    • assign the delivery centre and a delivery zone/beat.

    If the address is poor quality (no landmark, pincode mismatch), flag it for early correction via the consignee (a WhatsApp/SMS link). 4. Routing: the booking service assigns the AWB, computes the planned route (origin hub → Mumbai sort hub → Kolkata gateway → Guwahati hub → Jorhat delivery centre), and generates the label with barcode, AWB and sort codes. 5. Response: the shipment is created with a promised date and returned to the brand. The event SHIPMENT_CREATED is recorded.

docs.title: 4.2 Pickup and first mile
docs.text:
1. Pickup planning: pickup requests are grouped by client location and time window, and assigned to pickup vehicles by area (a VRP with pickup windows; Ch 47).
  2. At the warehouse: the pickup executive scans each parcel's AWB in the app. The handover manifest is signed digitally by both parties, and the scans become PICKED_UP events.
    • Parcels expected but not handed over are flagged. Parcels scanned but not booked are rejected, or booked on the spot.
  3. To the first hub: the pickup vehicle returns to the origin hub, and the parcels are inbound-scanned.

docs.title: 4.3 Hub sortation
docs.text:
1. Induction: parcels are inducted onto an automated sorter (cross-belt or shoe sorter; VERIFY equipment types).
  2. Scan tunnel: it reads barcodes, captures dimensions and weight (DWS: dimensioning, weighing, scanning) and takes images.
  3. Chute decision: the sorter controller looks up the AWB's next destination in the sort plan (§6.3), e.g. "bag for Kolkata gateway", and sends the parcel to the corresponding chute within milliseconds.
  4. Bagging: at the chute, parcels are bagged. A bag gets its own barcode, and the bag–parcel mapping is recorded (BAGGED).
  5. Manifest: bags are loaded onto an outbound trip's vehicle and scanned (BAG_LOADED). The trip manifest lists bags and parcels.
  6. Exceptions:
    • unreadable labels → manual scan station;
    • damaged parcels → photo and exception flow;
    • weight discrepancy (declared 0.8 kg, measured 1.6 kg) → the billing weight is updated with evidence images (§6.7);
    • misrouted parcels → re-sort.

docs.title: 4.4 Line-haul
docs.text:
1. Trip plan: a trip Mumbai hub → Kolkata gateway, departing 22:00, is planned from the trip plan (§6.4). The vehicle and driver are assigned, with GPS tracking via a device or driver app.
  2. Compliance: the e-way bill is generated for the consignment where required (GST rules on goods value and movement; VERIFY thresholds and consolidated e-way bill processes). Toll crossings via FASTag can serve as tracking signals (VERIFY data availability).
  3. In transit: trip events are recorded: departed, checkpoints, delays, arrival. The ETA to the next hub is predicted continuously (§6.5).
  4. Arrival: bags are unloaded and scanned. Missing bags against the manifest trigger an exception.
  5. Onward legs: Kolkata gateway → Guwahati hub (by road), then Guwahati → Jorhat. Each hub repeats inbound, sort (to the next hub or delivery centre) and outbound.

docs.title: 4.5 Last mile
docs.text:
1. At the delivery centre:
    • the bag is opened and parcels inbound-scanned (AT_DELIVERY_CENTRE);
    • the beat planning assigns parcels to riders by zone, with sequencing (route optimisation);
    • riders scan parcels into their bag (OUT_FOR_DELIVERY);
    • the consignee gets an SMS/WhatsApp: "Out for delivery today, ₹1,299 to be paid".
  2. Delivery:
    • the rider navigates and calls the customer (masked number) if needed;
    • collects COD in cash or via UPI QR (dynamic QR for the exact amount, confirming payment in the app);
    • captures OTP or signature (DELIVERED).
  3. Failed attempt:
    • the rider records a reason (customer unavailable, refused, address not found, asked to reschedule);
    • an NDR event goes to the NDR workflow (§4.6);
    • the parcel returns to the delivery centre.
  4. End of day:
    • the rider reconciles cash at the delivery centre: cash handed over plus UPI collected = COD due for delivered parcels;
    • discrepancies are recorded against the rider;
    • the delivery centre deposits cash to the bank. Deposits are reconciled (§5.6).

docs.title: 4.6 NDR and RTO
docs.text:
1. Notify: the shipper is notified of the NDR (API webhook and panel). The consignee is contacted by automated IVR or WhatsApp to confirm intent and preferred time, or to correct the address.
  2. Instructions: from the shipper or consignee, e.g. reattempt tomorrow, reattempt with an updated address, or return.
  3. Retry: re-attempts up to a limit (e.g. 3; per shipper contract).
  4. RTO: after the limit, or if the customer refuses, the parcel is marked RTO and travels back through the network to the origin (RTO_IN_TRANSIT … RTO_DELIVERED). The shipper receives it back and is charged RTO fees.
  5. Measurement: the RTO rate by pincode, shipper, payment type and reason feeds shippers' COD risk models (I02 L2).

docs.title: 4.7 COD remittance and billing
docs.text:
1. Remittance: COD collected for delivered parcels is remitted to the shipper on an agreed schedule (e.g. T+2 after delivery), net of shipping charges if agreed. The remittance report lists every AWB with amounts.
  2. Billing: shipping charges are based on chargeable weight, the greater of actual and volumetric weight (L × B × H / divisor; VERIFY divisors per service), zone (origin–destination distance class), COD fee, and RTO charges.
  3. Weight disputes: the shipper may dispute a weight change. Evidence (DWS images, measurements) supports resolution.

docs.title: 5.1 Shipment event store
docs.text:
• Every action is an event: created, picked_up, hub_in(hub), sorted(chute), bagged(bag), loaded(trip), trip_departed, trip_arrived, hub_out, out_for_delivery(rider), delivery_attempted(reason), delivered(pod), rto_initiated, and so on.
  • Each event carries:
    • the AWB (or bag/trip ID, with bag events expanding to their parcels);
    • location (facility or GPS);
    • the actor (user/device);
    • device timestamp and server receipt time;
    • a unique event ID generated on the device, which makes offline retries idempotent.
  • Storage: an append-only event log, partitioned by AWB (Kafka + a store like Cassandra, or partitioned PostgreSQL for recent data). Projections:
    • current status per AWB;
    • timeline for tracking;
    • location of every bag and trip;
    • facility inventory (what's physically in the hub now);
    • exception queues.
  • Out-of-order events: device clocks and offline sync deliver events late. Projections order events by device timestamp, with sanity rules (can't be delivered before being out for delivery), and flag inconsistencies.

docs.title: 5.2 Serviceability and TAT matrix
docs.text:
• Serviceability: per pincode, which services (surface, express, air), COD allowed and the COD amount limit, reverse pickup allowed, heavy parcels, and ODA (out-of-delivery-area) surcharges.

  • TAT: for each (origin cluster, destination pincode, service), the promised days. Computed from:

    • the network route;
    • trip schedules and cut-off times;
    • historical performance: the P90 transit of the lane, not the average.

    It is updated weekly or when the network changes. - Serving: a precomputed table in a low-latency key-value store, answering millions of API checks per day in milliseconds.

docs.title: 5.3 Hub edge systems
docs.text:
• Why: a large hub runs 24×7 with sorters, scanners and hundreds of staff. A WAN outage must not stop sorting.
  • Edge node:
    • a local database with the sort plan, expected inbound (manifests), and parcels currently in the hub;
    • local services for scanning apps and sorter controllers;
    • an event outbox that syncs to central when connected.
  • Sort plan distribution: a new sort plan version is pushed from central before shift start and activated at a set time. The sorter controller keeps the active version in memory.

docs.title: 5.4 Line-haul TMS
docs.text:
• Trips: planned (from the trip plan) and ad hoc (extra capacity). Each trip has a vehicle (own, leased or market vehicle), driver, route, schedule, capacity, and seal numbers for security.
  • Vehicle tracking: GPS from devices or driver apps, geofences for hubs, and alerts for delays, route deviations and long stops.
  • Loading: bags and pallets are assigned to trips by destination and cut-off. Load planning (§6.6) maximises fill while respecting unloading order.
  • Cost: per trip, fuel, tolls and driver payments; cost per kg per lane is a key metric.

docs.title: 5.5 Last mile
docs.text:
Covered in Ch 47: rider assignment, route sequencing and live tracking. Parcel-specific additions:

  • Beat planning: delivery centres divide their area into beats. Parcels are assigned by geocoded location, and each rider's sequence is optimised.
  • Delivery windows: customer-selected slots for some shippers.
  • POD capture: OTP, signature or photo, with geotag validation (the delivery location is near the address geocode; mismatches are flagged for fake-delivery checks).

docs.title: 5.6 COD reconciliation
docs.text:
• The chain: rider → delivery centre → bank deposit → central account → remittance to shipper.
  • Ledgers: per rider (cash due, submitted), per delivery centre (cash on hand, deposited), per shipper (COD collected, remitted), and UPI collections reconciled with payment gateway settlements.
  • Controls:
    • daily reconciliation;
    • cash limits per rider and per delivery centre (security);
    • aging of unremitted amounts;
    • dispute handling (Ch 45 patterns).

docs.title: 5.7 Tracking and notifications
docs.text:
• Read models:
    • per AWB, the latest status, the timeline of customer-friendly events, and the expected delivery date;
    • updated from events within seconds, and cached at the edge for public tracking pages.
  • Webhooks to shippers on status changes, with retries and signatures, so shippers stop polling (Ch 40).
  • Consignee notifications: shipped, out for delivery, delivered, attempted (with NDR options).

docs.title: 6.1 Address parsing and geocoding
docs.text:
• Indian addresses: free text, mixed languages and scripts, landmarks ("near Hanuman temple"), missing or wrong pincodes, local area names that don't appear on maps.
  • Pipeline:
    1. Normalisation: case, abbreviations, transliteration.
    2. Parsing into components (house, building, street, locality, landmark, city, pincode) with a sequence labelling model trained on labelled addresses.
    3. Geocoding: match locality and landmark names against a gazetteer, and historical delivery coordinates. The best source is where riders actually delivered to similar addresses before.
    4. Confidence scoring.
    5. Pincode validation: does the geocode fall in the pincode polygon?
  • Clustering: delivered GPS points for the same normalised address are clustered to learn exact locations over time.
  • Uses: delivery centre assignment, beat planning, fake-delivery checks, address-quality nudges to consignees, and reseller detection for shippers (I02 L4).

docs.title: 6.2 Network design (facility location)
docs.text:
• The question: where should hubs and delivery centres be, and which pincodes should each serve, to minimise transport and facility costs while meeting TATs?
  • Model: a mixed-integer linear program:
    • binary variables for opening facilities;
    • assignment variables for pincode → delivery centre → hub;
    • flow variables on lanes;
    • capacity constraints;
    • TAT constraints;
    • objective: fixed costs + variable handling costs + transport costs.
  • Scale: solved with commercial or open solvers, with decomposition and heuristics for large instances. Run for strategic planning (quarterly), with scenarios for demand growth.

docs.title: 6.3 Sort plans
docs.text:
• The input: for each hub, destinations (next hubs or delivery centres) mapped to chutes on the sorter. There are more destinations than chutes, so some chutes combine destinations ("mixed bags" sorted again downstream).

  • The optimisation:

    • assign high-volume destinations to dedicated chutes;
    • group low-volume destinations whose next hop is the same;
    • balance chute load so no chute overflows;
    • respect physical constraints (chute positions near their outbound docks).

    Solved by a greedy heuristic plus local search, or by integer programming, per shift pattern and volume forecast. - Versioning: plans are versioned, pushed to the edge, and activated at shift boundaries.

docs.title: 6.4 Trip planning (middle mile)
docs.text:
• The problem: given forecast volume between hub pairs and time windows (hub cut-offs, arrival needed for downstream connections), choose the vehicles and routes (direct, or multi-stop milk runs) to minimise cost while meeting TATs.
  • Model: a vehicle routing / service network design problem. Heuristics construct routes, and local search improves them. Capacity by weight and volume.
  • Daily adjustments: dynamic dispatch: if actual volume exceeds plan, add vehicles; if lower, consolidate trips.

docs.title: 6.5 ETA and delay prediction
docs.text:
• Shipment ETA: predict delivery date and time from the current location, the remaining route, trip schedules, historical lane performance, hub backlogs, weather and festivals. A gradient-boosted model or a survival model per remaining leg.
  • Trip ETA: GPS progress, road network travel times (I05 §6.3), driver stops.
  • At-risk shipments (likely to miss the promise) are flagged in the control tower for intervention: prioritise them in sorting, or move them to a faster service.

docs.title: 6.6 Load planning (3D bin packing)
docs.text:
• The problem: pack bags, cartons or pallets into a truck, maximising volume and weight utilisation.
  • Constraints:
    • weight distribution;
    • stackability and fragility;
    • unloading order (last stop's cargo loaded first, i.e. last in, first out by stop).
  • Methods: heuristics (layer-building, extreme-point placement, first-fit decreasing by volume), with visual loading plans for staff.
  • Measure: fill rate per trip, a key cost lever.

docs.title: 6.7 Weight discrepancy detection
docs.text:
• Compare declared weight and dimensions with DWS measurements at first hub scan. Chargeable weight is max(actual, volumetric).
  • Flag discrepancies above tolerance. Use evidence images and measurement confidence.
  • Pattern detection: shippers who consistently under-declare. SKU-level learned weights ("this product ID usually weighs 1.4 kg") help predict and pre-empt disputes.

docs.title: 6.8 Carrier allocation (for shipping aggregators)
docs.text:
• Aggregators (platforms like Shiprocket that route shipments across many carriers) choose a carrier per shipment:
    • score each carrier by price, predicted TAT, delivery success rate and RTO rate for the destination pincode, COD remittance speed, and pickup reliability at the origin;
    • optimise the shipper's objective (cost vs speed vs success).
  • Learning: multi-armed bandit exploration keeps estimates fresh per lane.

docs.title: 6.9 Lost and stuck shipment detection
docs.text:
• Expected next event per shipment state (e.g. after hub_out for trip X, expect trip_arrived at Y by time T).
  • Missing events beyond a threshold → an exception.
  • Facility reconciliation: expected inbound (from manifests) vs actual scans; parcels in the hub inventory not scanned for N hours.
  • Searches: trigger hub searches (with last-known locations). Unresolved cases become lost claims.

docs.title: 6.10 Supply chain planning for shippers
docs.text:
• Demand forecasting: hierarchical forecasts by SKU, location and week, with promotions and seasonality. Probabilistic outputs (quantiles).
  • Inventory optimisation:
    • safety stock per SKU per location = z × σ(demand during lead time), where z comes from the target service level;
    • multi-echelon optimisation (central warehouse + regional warehouses) places stock where it minimises total cost for a service level;
    • reorder points and quantities (EOQ with constraints) (I04 §6.8 uses the same logic for hospital supplies).
  • Allocation of stock across marketplaces and warehouses by forecast demand. Replenishment plans feed purchase orders and inbound logistics.

docs.title: 7.1 Operational stores
docs.text: Data Store (reference) Notes Shipments (booking data) PostgreSQL, partitioned by date Client references, addresses (PII) Events Kafka + Cassandra/ScyllaDB (by AWB) or partitioned PostgreSQL Append-only, idempotent IDs Tracking read models Redis/KV + CDN caching Public reads Serviceability/TAT KV store with precomputed tables Millisecond lookups Hub edge DBs PostgreSQL/SQLite on edge servers Offline operation Trips and vehicles PostgreSQL + time-series store for GPS TMS COD ledgers PostgreSQL with double-entry Daily reconciliation Address knowledge Search index (OpenSearch) + geospatial DB (PostGIS) Gazetteer, historical coordinates

docs.title: 7.2 Lakehouse and analytics
docs.text:
• Events and CDC → Kafka → lakehouse (Iceberg/Hudi) → warehouse marts.
  • Facts: shipments, events, attempts, trips, facility throughput per hour, rider productivity, COD collections, costs per lane.
  • Dimensions: client, pincode (with geography, tier), facility, lane, vehicle, rider, service, date.
  • Key metrics:
    • on-time delivery by lane and client;
    • first-attempt delivery rate;
    • RTO rate;
    • cost per shipment (first mile, hub, line-haul, last mile);
    • hub throughput and sorter utilisation;
    • trip fill rate;
    • COD remittance timeliness;
    • weight dispute rate;
    • lost shipment rate.
  • Control tower dashboards come from near-real-time aggregates (Flink + ClickHouse/Druid): backlogs per hub, delayed trips, at-risk shipments.

docs.title: 7.3 Data flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    APPS[Scanner, rider, pickup apps - offline first] --> SYNC[Sync services]
    EDGE[Hub edge nodes] --> SYNC
    GPS[Vehicle GPS] --> K
    SYNC --> K[Kafka - events by AWB]
    K --> PROJ[Projections - status, timeline, facility inventory]
    PROJ --> TRACK[Tracking APIs and webhooks]
    K --> FL[Flink - backlogs, at-risk shipments]
    FL --> CT[Control tower - ClickHouse or Druid]
    K --> LAKE[Lakehouse]
    LAKE --> DW[Warehouse marts]
    DW --> PLAN[Network, sort and trip planning]
    DW --> ML[ETA, address, weight, fraud models]
    ML --> SVC[Booking, serviceability, control tower]

docs.title: 8. Tech Stack (reference choice)
docs.text: Layer Choice Notes APIs and services Java/Spring Boot or Go microservices Client APIs at scale Mobile apps Native Android (rugged scanners run Android), offline-first local DB and sync Field reliability Edge at hubs Small Kubernetes (k3s) or VM clusters with PostgreSQL Local autonomy Sorter integration Industrial controller interfaces (PLC via vendor middleware) Millisecond decisions Events Kafka; Cassandra/ScyllaDB for event history High write, ordered per AWB Databases PostgreSQL (+ PostGIS), Redis Operational data Search OpenSearch for addresses and shipments Operations search Streaming Flink Control tower aggregates Real-time OLAP ClickHouse or Druid Dashboards Lakehouse Iceberg/Hudi + Spark + Trino Analytics and ML Optimisation OR-Tools, commercial MILP solvers, custom heuristics Network, sort and trip plans ML Python, feature store, MLflow ETA, address, weights Maps Commercial map APIs + own geocoding data Indian address coverage Platform Kubernetes, Terraform Central services

docs.title: 9. Security, Privacy & Compliance
docs.text:
• Consignee data: names, phones and addresses are PII. They are masked on labels where possible (phone masked, calls via proxy), restricted in apps, retained per policy, and subject to the DPDP Act (VERIFY).
  • Cash handling: limits, secure deposits, audits.
  • Custody and theft: seal numbers on trips, CCTV at hubs, scan-based custody, and investigation workflows for lost high-value parcels.
  • Regulatory:
    • GST e-way bills for goods movement above thresholds (VERIFY);
    • dangerous goods restrictions for air (lithium batteries; VERIFY IATA/DGCA rules);
    • labour and vehicle regulations.
  • Client integrations: API keys and OAuth, webhook signatures, rate limits.

docs.title: 10. Reliability & Operations
docs.text:
• Offline-first everywhere: scanners and apps store events locally and sync. Hubs run on edge nodes. Central outages delay tracking, not operations.
  • Peak readiness (festive sales, I02):
    • volume forecasts per lane;
    • temporary hubs and extra trips;
    • extra riders;
    • sort plans for peak;
    • pre-alerts from shippers (expected volumes);
    • capacity caps per shipper to protect the network.
  • Control tower watches backlogs per hub and shift, delayed trips, at-risk shipments and NDR rates, with playbooks (divert trips, add shifts, move volume to air).
  • Data quality: scans with wrong facility codes or clock errors corrupt projections. Validation rules at capture, plus reconciliation.
  • Weather and disruption: floods and strikes reroute lanes; update the TAT matrix and shipper communication.

docs.title: 11. Key Trade-offs
docs.text: Decision Chosen Accepted cost Shipment state Event-sourced Projection complexity; out-of-order handling Facilities Edge autonomy Sync conflicts and version management TAT promises P90-based by lane Conservative promises vs competitors Sort plans Batch-optimised per shift Less adaptive to sudden volume shifts Tracking Read models + webhooks Eventual consistency (seconds) Planning Heuristics + MILP offline Not globally optimal in real time

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ Walk through a parcel's journey in an express network.

30-second answer: Booking via API (AWB, label, promised date) → pickup scan → first hub inbound → sortation into bags by next destination → line-haul trips between hubs → destination delivery centre → rider out for delivery → delivered with OTP and COD, or failed attempt → NDR → reattempt or RTO; every step is a scan event.

Deep answer: §4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Consolidation vs speed.

Follow-ups: 1. Why hubs? → Consolidation. 2. Tracking? → Events.

Red flags: Point-to-point vans for every parcel.

Q2 [B1] What is volumetric weight and why does it matter?

30-second answer: Light but bulky parcels take space, so carriers charge the greater of actual weight and volumetric weight (length × breadth × height ÷ a divisor), which affects shipper costs and requires measurement to resolve disputes.

Deep answer: §4.7, §6.7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Measurement cost vs revenue.

Follow-ups: 1. Measurement? → DWS scanners. 2. Disputes? → Evidence images.

Red flags: Trusting declared weight.

Q3 [B1] What happens when delivery fails?

30-second answer: The rider records a reason; an NDR is raised to the shipper and customer; instructions (reattempt, new address, return) are collected; the parcel is re-attempted up to a limit or returned to origin (RTO).

Deep answer: §4.6.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Reattempt cost vs conversion.

Follow-ups: 1. Fake attempts? → GPS and call logs. 2. RTO rate? → Key metric.

Red flags: Silent returns.

Q4 [B1] How does parcel tracking work at scale?

30-second answer: Every scan is an event; projections maintain the latest status and a customer-friendly timeline per AWB in a cache; tracking pages read those; shippers receive webhooks instead of polling.

Deep answer: §5.1, §5.7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Freshness vs cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Offline scans? → Late events. 2. Public pages? → CDN caching.

Red flags: Querying all scans per page view.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ Why model shipments as event streams?

30-second answer: Every physical action is a fact with a time, place and actor; an append-only log gives a complete custody chain for disputes and analytics, supports offline devices with idempotent events, and lets different projections (status, timeline, facility inventory) serve different needs.

Deep answer: §5.1; Ch 15.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Out-of-order handling.

Follow-ups: 1. Bag events? → Expand to parcels. 2. Corrections? → New events.

Red flags: Updating a status column only.

Q6 [B2] How do you compute and serve delivery promises (TAT)?

30-second answer: Per origin cluster, destination pincode and service, compute days from the route, trip schedules and cut-offs, calibrated to the lane's historical P90 transit; precompute into a key-value table for millisecond lookups; update with network changes and disruptions.

Deep answer: §5.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Conservative vs competitive promises.

Follow-ups: 1. Festive peaks? → Adjust. 2. Floods? → Lane updates.

Red flags: Average transit times.

Q7 [B2] How do hubs keep working when the network is down?

30-second answer: Edge nodes at each hub hold sort plans, manifests and hub inventory locally, serve scanners and sorter controllers, and queue events in an outbox that syncs to central when connectivity returns.

Deep answer: §5.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Edge operations cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Sort plan updates? → Versioned push. 2. Conflicts? → Idempotent events.

Red flags: Central calls per scan.

Q8 [B2] How does COD money flow and get reconciled?

30-second answer: Riders collect cash or UPI, reconcile with the delivery centre daily, the delivery centre deposits to the bank, collections are reconciled with bank and gateway data, and remittances go to shippers per AWB on schedule — each step tracked in ledgers with limits and aging.

Deep answer: §5.6.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Remittance speed vs float.

Follow-ups: 1. Rider shortfall? → Ledger and recovery. 2. UPI? → Gateway settlement.

Red flags: Spreadsheet reconciliation.

Q9 [B2] How would you handle messy Indian addresses?

30-second answer: Normalise and parse with a trained sequence model, geocode using a gazetteer and historical delivery coordinates, validate pincode against location, score confidence, and nudge consignees to correct low-confidence addresses before dispatch.

Deep answer: §6.1.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Model accuracy vs coverage.

Follow-ups: 1. Landmarks? → Gazetteer. 2. Learning? → Delivered GPS clusters.

Red flags: Relying only on pincode.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ How do you design a hub's sort plan?

30-second answer: Map destinations to chutes: dedicated chutes for high-volume destinations, grouped chutes for low-volume ones sharing a next hop, balanced chute loads, physical constraints near outbound docks — optimised per shift from forecasts, versioned and pushed to the edge for activation at shift change.

Deep answer: §6.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Mixed bags need resorting downstream.

Follow-ups: 1. Volume shifts? → Mid-shift overrides. 2. Chute overflow? → Balancing.

Red flags: Static sort plans for years.

Q11 [B3] How would you detect lost or stuck shipments?

30-second answer: Define the expected next event per state with time windows, flag shipments missing them, reconcile manifests vs inbound scans per facility and trip, age hub inventory without scans, trigger searches with last-known locations, and escalate to lost claims.

Deep answer: §6.9.

Trade-offs I'd call out: False alarms vs losses.

Follow-ups: 1. Bag-level loss? → Many parcels. 2. Theft? → Seals, CCTV.

Red flags: Customer complaints as the detection mechanism.

Q12 [B3] How do you plan middle-mile trips?

30-second answer: From lane volume forecasts and hub time windows, solve a vehicle routing/service network design problem with capacity by weight and volume, using heuristics and local search; adjust daily by adding or consolidating trips based on actual volumes; measure fill rate and on-time performance.

Deep answer: §6.4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Cost vs TAT.

Follow-ups: 1. Milk runs? → Multi-stop. 2. Market vehicles? → Spot capacity.

Red flags: One truck per lane regardless of volume.

Q13 [B3] How would a shipping aggregator choose carriers per shipment?

30-second answer: Score each carrier on price, predicted TAT, delivery success and RTO rates for the destination pincode, remittance speed and pickup reliability at origin; optimise the shipper's objective, with bandit exploration to keep lane estimates fresh.

Deep answer: §6.8.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Cost vs success.

Follow-ups: 1. Cold lanes? → Priors by region. 2. Carrier outages? → Remove quickly.

Red flags: Cheapest carrier always.

Q14 [B3] How do you predict and prevent missed delivery promises?

30-second answer: Predict ETA per remaining leg from lane history, trip progress, hub backlogs, weather and festivals; flag at-risk shipments in the control tower; intervene by prioritising sorting, switching to faster lanes or proactive customer communication.

Deep answer: §6.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Intervention cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Model? → Gradient boosting/survival. 2. Metrics? → On-time rate.

Red flags: Discovering delays when customers complain.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design an express logistics platform end to end.

30-second answer: Client APIs for booking with serviceability, TAT and address intelligence; offline-first field apps and hub edge nodes producing idempotent scan events; an event store with projections for tracking, facility inventory and exceptions; TMS for trips and e-way bills; last-mile dispatch; NDR/RTO and COD workflows; planning (network, sort, trips, forecasts) offline; a control tower from streaming aggregates; a lakehouse for analytics and ML.

Deep answer: §3–§7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Edge autonomy vs central control.

Follow-ups: 1. Peak? → Forecast-driven capacity. 2. Biggest risk? → Data quality of scans.

Red flags: A CRUD app with a status column.

Q16 [B4] How would you decide where to build new hubs?

30-second answer: A facility location MILP with open/assign/flow variables, capacities and TAT constraints, minimising fixed plus variable costs across demand scenarios; validate with simulation, real estate constraints and phased rollout.

Deep answer: §6.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Model fidelity vs solve time.

Follow-ups: 1. Growth uncertainty? → Scenarios. 2. Automation? → Hub type choice.

Red flags: Opening hubs where competitors are.

Q17 [B4] How do you prepare the network for a festive sale?

30-second answer: Volume forecasts per lane from shippers' pre-alerts and history, temporary hubs, peak sort plans, extra trips and riders, shipper capacity caps, TAT adjustments, control-tower playbooks and daily reviews during the peak.

Deep answer: §10.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Idle capacity after peak.

Follow-ups: 1. Caps? → Protect the network. 2. Air? → For premium lanes.

Red flags: Business as usual planning.

Q18 [B4] How would you build supply chain planning for a D2C brand?

30-second answer: Hierarchical probabilistic demand forecasts by SKU and location, safety stock from service levels and lead-time variability, multi-echelon placement across warehouses, replenishment plans into purchase orders and inbound logistics, and allocation across marketplaces — measured by fill rate, inventory turns and stock-outs.

Deep answer: §6.10.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Service level vs working capital.

Follow-ups: 1. Promotions? → Uplift features. 2. New SKUs? → Similar-item priors.

Red flags: Reordering on gut feel.

Q19 [B4] What makes logistics data platforms tricky?

30-second answer: Events come from offline devices with unreliable clocks, physical-world errors (wrong scans, missing scans), bag and trip hierarchies, and long-running shipments — so validation, reconciliation, idempotency and careful projections matter as much as scale.

Deep answer: §5.1, §7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Strict validation vs operational friction.

Follow-ups: 1. Clock skew? → Server receipt times plus sanity rules. 2. Hierarchies? → Bag expansion.

Red flags: Trusting device timestamps blindly.

Q20 [B4] Compare a 3PL network with a marketplace's captive logistics.

30-second answer: A 3PL serves many shippers with varied data quality, contracts and SLAs, so APIs, serviceability, billing and disputes are central; a captive network (like a marketplace's own) integrates tightly with order and inventory systems and can optimise end to end — both share hubs, sort plans, trips, last mile and event tracking.

Deep answer: I01, I02b vs this chapter.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Flexibility vs integration.

Follow-ups: 1. Aggregators? → Carrier choice layer. 2. Shared tech? → Events, planning.

Red flags: Identical designs.

docs.title: 13. Summary
docs.text:
1. A parcel's life is a chain of custody events. An event store with projections gives tracking, facility inventory and exceptions.
  2. Hubs are autonomous at the edge, running sort plans that are optimised offline and pushed per shift. Apps are offline-first.
  3. Planning drives cost: network design (MILP), sort plans, trip plans, load planning. Prediction drives service: TAT, ETA, at-risk shipments.
  4. India-specific depth: address intelligence, COD cash chains, NDR/RTO workflows, e-way bills.
  5. The data platform turns scans into control-tower visibility and ML. Supply chain planning extends the same data to shippers' inventory.

docs.title: I13. Online Exams & Live Classes
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Sector: Education (EdTech and national testing) · Format: system design walkthrough (no code) · Reader bands: B1 → B4 · Builds on: I06 (streaming), Ch 41 (chat), Ch 51 (top-K), Ch 59 L4 (spaced repetition)

What you get: two connected systems.

1. A large EdTech platform:

  • live classes where one teacher teaches up to 100,000 students with chat, polls, doubts and a shared whiteboard;
  • recorded lectures, courses and subscriptions;
  • test series with timers, autosave, instant results and all-India ranks;
  • adaptive practice and doubt solving from a photo of a question;
  • parent reports.

2. A national high-stakes computer-based test (CBT) in the style of large entrance exams:

  • question paper security;
  • exam centres with local servers;
  • response capture;
  • normalisation across multiple shifts (percentiles);
  • results for over a million candidates;
  • remote proctoring for online exams.

Also covered:

  • the algorithms: item response theory, computerised adaptive testing, knowledge tracing, paper assembly under a blueprint, percentile normalisation, collusion detection, proctoring anomaly detection, leaderboards at scale, live-class fan-out and aggregation;
  • the data platform (learning analytics) and tech stack.

Reading time: 85 min.

Sources and honesty

  • National testing agencies publish their normalisation methodology (e.g. percentile scores for multi-shift exams). Summaries here are marked VERIFY.
  • Details of exam centre operations and security are only partly public.
  • EdTech companies' internal systems aren't public.
  • This is a reference design. Children's data needs special care under the DPDP Act (VERIFY rules).

docs.title: 1.1 Two very different load shapes
docs.text: Live class Mock test at 10 am Sunday National CBT Concurrency 100k students in one class; thousands of classes a day 500k students start one test at once ~1M candidates over several shifts at centres Hard part Low latency to 100k, interaction at scale Everyone starts, saves and submits at the same time Security, fairness, zero data loss, normalisation Failure impact Poor experience Anger, lost trust Legal challenges, re-exams

docs.title: 1.2 Main systems
docs.text: System What it does Identity and profiles Students (often minors), parents, teachers, roles Catalogue and enrolment Courses, batches, schedules, subscriptions, payments Live class platform Teacher broadcast, student viewing, chat, polls, doubts, whiteboard, recordings Content and VOD Lecture recordings, notes, PDFs; streaming (I06) Question bank Questions with metadata (topic, difficulty, IRT parameters), versions, media Test engine Test assembly, delivery, timers, autosave, submission, evaluation, results, ranks Adaptive learning Learner model, practice recommendations, spaced revision Doubt solving Photo → OCR → search similar solved questions → human tutor fallback Proctoring Webcam/mic monitoring, browser lockdown, anomaly flags, review CBT centre system Local servers, secure paper delivery, candidate verification, response sync Results and normalisation Scores, percentiles, ranks, answer key challenges Notifications and parent reports Class reminders, test results, progress Data platform Learning analytics, content quality, ML

docs.title: 1.3 Scale for this design (assumptions)
docs.text:
Quantity Value Registered learners 30M; 3M daily active Live classes per day 5,000; largest class 100k concurrent Chat messages in a big class Up to 5k/s at peak moments All-India mock test 500k concurrent candidates, 3 hours, 90 questions Answer saves in a mock Each candidate saves ~2 times per minute → ~17k saves/s average, higher bursts Test submissions 500k within the last 5 minutes (auto-submit at time end) National CBT ~1M+ candidates across ~10 shifts at ~500 centres (VERIFY actual numbers)

Estimation highlights:

  • Live class video: 100k viewers × 1 Mbps = 100 Gbps from the CDN. That is fine for CDNs, but only if the class is delivered as a stream (HLS/LL-HLS) to most viewers. It cannot be done by making 100k WebRTC connections to an SFU cluster (§5.1).
  • Test start: 500k candidates fetching the paper at 10:00:00 is a flash crowd.
    • Pre-download encrypted papers before the start.
    • Release the decryption key at the start time, one small request each, or served by a signed time-based key.
  • Test end: 500k submissions in a few minutes, i.e. ~2–5k/s. Answers are already autosaved, so "submit" is just a marker, and evaluation is asynchronous.

docs.title: 2.1 EdTech functional
docs.text:
1. Browse courses and batches; enrol; pay (subscriptions, EMIs, UPI).
  2. Join live classes with ~2–5 s latency (interactive enough for polls and doubts); ask questions in chat; answer polls; raise hand (selected students go on stage).
  3. Watch recordings shortly after class; download notes.
  4. Take tests (practice, chapter tests, all-India mock tests) with timers, section rules, question palette, mark-for-review, autosave; get results, solutions and analysis; see all-India rank and percentile.
  5. Adaptive practice: personalised question sets; revision reminders.
  6. Doubt solving: photo of a question → instant solution if similar exists → tutor chat otherwise.
  7. Parent dashboards; teacher dashboards for class engagement.

docs.title: 2.2 National CBT functional
docs.text:
1. Registration, fee payment, admit cards with centre and shift.
  2. Secure delivery of question papers to centres. Candidate verification (biometrics/photo; VERIFY).
  3. A reliable exam in centres with local servers, whatever the internet or power conditions.
  4. Response capture with audit, and upload to central.
  5. Provisional answer keys, challenges, final keys, scoring, normalisation across shifts, results, ranks.
  6. Online (remote-proctored) variants for some exams, with proctoring.

docs.title: 2.3 Non-functional
docs.text: Attribute Target Live latency 2–5 s glass-to-glass for mass viewers; < 500 ms for on-stage participants Test durability No answer ever lost once the candidate sees "saved" Timer integrity Server-authoritative timing; client clock manipulation can't add time Security Papers unseen before start; no tampering with responses; audit everything Fairness Equal conditions across shifts; normalisation methodology applied consistently Availability Test windows are fixed-time events; plan for zero downtime during them Privacy Minors' data protected; proctoring recordings with consent and limited retention

docs.title: 3. High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Clients
        STU[Student app and web]
        TEA[Teacher studio]
        PAR[Parent app]
        CENTRE[Exam centre nodes]
    end
    subgraph Edge
        CDN[CDN - video, papers, static]

    end
    subgraph Live[Live class platform]
        SFU[SFU - teacher and on-stage students]

    end
    subgraph Learn[Learning platform]
        CAT[Courses, batches, enrolment]
        QB[Question bank]

    subgraph Data
        K[Kafka]

    TEA --> SFU --> MIX --> CDN --> STU

Key decisions:

Decision Choice Why Live delivery Hybrid: WebRTC/SFU for the teacher and on-stage students; LL-HLS/CMAF via CDN for the mass audience WebRTC to 100k viewers is costly and hard to scale; streaming scales cheaply with 2–5 s latency Chat at scale Sampled/aggregated fan-out, not every message to everyone 5k msgs/s × 100k viewers is impossible and unreadable Test delivery Pre-download encrypted paper; key release at start; autosave each answer; submit is a marker Removes start and end spikes, protects against disconnects Timing Server-authoritative start and end; client shows a countdown synced to server time Prevents clock tampering (I02 L1) Evaluation Asynchronous, idempotent, per candidate Handles 500k submissions calmly CBT centres Local server per centre with encrypted papers and local response storage, synced centrally Survive internet loss; security

docs.title: 4. How It Works — Journeys End to End
4.1 Journey 1: a live physics class for 60,000 students
docs.text:
1. Before class:
    • enrolled students get a reminder 15 minutes before;
    • the class page loads from the CDN;
    • the app fetches a join token (entitlement check: is the student in this batch or subscription?).
  2. Teacher goes live:
    • the teacher's studio app sends camera, screen/tablet and audio over WebRTC to an SFU;
    • a composer mixes the teacher video and slides/whiteboard into one layout, or keeps them as separate tracks;
    • it encodes an ABR ladder and packages LL-HLS (CMAF chunks);
    • the CDN serves 60,000 students. Latency is ~2–5 s, while mobile viewers on 3G get lower renditions (I06 §6.3).
  3. Whiteboard:
    • strokes are sent as vector events (not video) over WebSockets, and rendered on devices;
    • this is crisp at any resolution and needs little bandwidth;
    • it is synced with the video timeline via timestamps.
  4. Chat (§5.2):
    • students send messages to the chat service through WebSocket gateways;
    • messages are moderated (profanity filters, rate limits per student);
    • the service samples what to fan out: every student sees a manageable stream (e.g. 5 messages/s), with teacher and moderator messages and "top questions" pinned;
    • all messages are stored for the teacher and moderators to see and search.
  5. Doubts: students can mark a message as a doubt. Similar doubts are clustered (text similarity), and moderators surface the top clusters to the teacher.
  6. Polls: the teacher launches a poll ("What is the SI unit of force?").
    • 60,000 answers arrive in 20 seconds (~3k/s);
    • aggregated in memory per option, and the running result is broadcast every second;
    • individual answers are stored for analytics and student reports.
  7. Hand raise: the teacher invites a student on stage. That student joins the SFU with WebRTC for sub-second interaction, and their video is composed into the stream for everyone else.
  8. After class: the recording (the composed stream, or tracks plus whiteboard events for interactive playback) is packaged as VOD within minutes. Attendance, watch time, poll accuracy and doubts go to analytics.

docs.title: 4.2 Journey 2: an all-India mock test at 10 am Sunday
docs.text:
1. Before the test:
    • the test is assembled from the question bank according to a blueprint: sections, topics, difficulty distribution, marks scheme (§6.3);
    • variants may be created (shuffled order, different question sets of equal difficulty) to reduce copying;
    • from 9:30, registered students' apps pre-download the encrypted test package from the CDN: questions, images, instructions. Downloads spread over 30 minutes.
  2. Start:
    • at 10:00:00 (server time), the app requests the decryption key and a start token. The server records the start time for that candidate;
    • late joiners get the time remaining for their window, per test rules;
    • key requests are small, and served by a scaled, cached key service.
  3. During the test:
    • each answer change is autosaved: (candidate, test, question, answer, client sequence, client time) goes to the autosave service. It is written to a durable store and acknowledged, showing "saved";
    • if offline, answers queue locally and sync when the connection returns, with sequence numbers resolving order (§6.8);
    • the timer shows a countdown synced to server time. The server's recorded start plus duration defines the end, regardless of the client clock.
  4. End:
    • at the end time the app auto-submits: a small "submitted" marker plus any unsynced answers. The server rejects answers timestamped after the end (with tolerance for network delay, per rules);
    • candidates who lost connectivity have their last synced answers evaluated. Their buffered answers are accepted if their sequence and time prove they were answered before the end (policy).
  5. Evaluation:
    • asynchronous workers score each candidate per the marks scheme (+4/−1, partial marks for multi-correct; VERIFY exam patterns), idempotently;
    • within minutes, results: score, section scores, time analysis, accuracy by topic.
  6. Ranks:
    • all-India rank and percentile among 500k candidates come from a score distribution (§6.6);
    • ranks become final after a cut-off time, when late submissions and re-evaluations are done.

docs.title: 4.3 Journey 3: a national CBT at an exam centre
docs.text:
1. Weeks before:
    • the question papers for each shift are set by experts, reviewed and stored encrypted;
    • centres are prepared: networked computers, a local server, power backup, CCTV, and a biometric or photo verification set-up (VERIFY specific procedures).
  2. Day before or morning of:
    • the encrypted paper for the shift is downloaded to the local server;
    • the decryption key is released only shortly before the exam starts, through a secure channel. Keys may be split among officials (VERIFY procedures).
  3. Candidate entry: verified by admit card, photo and biometrics. Each is assigned a computer, which boots into a locked-down exam client (no other apps, no internet).
  4. During the exam:
    • each candidate's responses are saved to the local server continuously, with a local audit log (every click with a timestamp);
    • the local server replicates to a second local disk or server (VERIFY);
    • if a computer fails, the candidate moves to a spare, and the session resumes from the server with remaining time preserved.
  5. After the shift:
    • response files are encrypted and signed, then uploaded to central over the network (or physically transported if needed);
    • central verifies checksums and signatures, and reconciles counts: candidates present vs response files.
  6. Keys and scoring:
    • provisional answer keys and candidates' response sheets are published;
    • candidates can challenge keys, for a fee, within a window;
    • experts review; final keys are published;
    • scoring runs.
  7. Normalisation: multiple shifts had different papers, so raw scores are converted to percentile scores within each shift (§6.5). Merit lists are formed from the normalised scores per the methodology (VERIFY the agency's published rules, including tie-breaking).
  8. Results: published for a million candidates on one day, via a CDN-cached results site with candidate login. Expect traffic spikes of tens of thousands of requests per second (pre-generated result documents).

docs.title: 4.4 Journey 4: remote-proctored online exam
docs.text:
1. Setup: the candidate installs a lockdown browser or app. It checks the environment: a single screen, no virtual machines, no screen sharing or remote desktop tools.
  2. Identity: face photo matched to the registration photo, and ID document capture.
  3. Room scan: a 360° camera sweep of the room.
  4. During the exam:
    • AI proctoring analyses webcam and microphone streams at the edge or server (§6.7): face absent, multiple faces, gaze away repeatedly, voices, mobile phone detected, tab switching attempts;
    • events are flagged with timestamps and short clips;
    • live proctors monitor many candidates (e.g. 1:20) with AI flags prioritised, and can message or terminate.
  5. Review: flags are reviewed after the exam, and decisions are recorded with evidence. Recordings are retained for a limited period per policy and consent (VERIFY).

docs.title: 4.5 Journey 5: adaptive practice and doubts
docs.text:
1. Adaptive practice: a student opens "Practice: Kinematics".
    • The learner model estimates mastery per concept (§6.2).
    • The recommender picks questions near the student's ability, "just hard enough", mixing weak concepts and spaced revision of earlier ones (Ch 59 L4 principle).
    • Each answer updates mastery immediately.
  2. Doubt solving: the student photographs a question from a textbook.
    • OCR handles printed text and math notation (math OCR to LaTeX).
    • Math-aware text embeddings are used for semantic search over millions of solved questions.
    • If a near-duplicate exists with high confidence, the student sees the solution video and steps instantly.
    • Otherwise the doubt goes to a tutor queue (chat), with subject routing and SLA.

docs.title: 5.1 Live class delivery at scale
docs.text:
• Why hybrid:
    • WebRTC via SFUs gives sub-second latency but needs server resources per viewer and complex scaling;
    • LL-HLS via CDN gives 2–5 s latency and scales to millions at low cost;
    • classes need low latency only for the teacher and a few on-stage students.
  • Small classes (up to a few hundred) can be all-WebRTC for full interactivity. Big classes use the hybrid.
  • Synchronising interaction with video delay:
    • a poll the teacher launches at time T arrives at viewers' screens with the video at T + 3 s;
    • send poll events with a video timestamp, so clients show the poll when their playback reaches that moment;
    • the same applies to whiteboard events.
  • Teacher-side reliability: the teacher's upload is the single point of failure. Use a backup encoder path, an internet quality check before class, and fallback to audio + whiteboard if the video uplink degrades.

docs.title: 5.2 Chat and interaction at 100k
docs.text:
• Ingest: WebSocket gateways (sharded by connection) → chat service partitioned by class → storage (append-only per class).
  • Fan-out:
    • never broadcast every message to every viewer;
    • the class room service selects a stream per interval: teacher and moderator messages always; a sample of student messages (rate-limited per interval); "highlighted" doubts;
    • the selected stream is broadcast via gateways, one message per interval per connection batch.
  • Reactions and poll votes are aggregated as counts per interval (I06 §6.8).
  • Moderation: profanity and spam filters, per-user rate limits, slow mode, bans.
  • Doubt clustering: embed doubt messages, cluster them online (incremental clustering), and show the teacher a ranked list of clusters with counts.

docs.title: 5.3 Question bank
docs.text:
• Each question has:
    • text (with LaTeX), images, options, correct answers;
    • solution (text/video);
    • topic tags (syllabus hierarchy);
    • difficulty labels;
    • IRT parameters (§6.1);
    • exposure counts;
    • version history;
    • review status (created → reviewed → approved → retired).
  • Search and assembly: index by topic, difficulty, type and exposure, for assembly and practice.
  • Quality loop: item statistics from tests (difficulty, discrimination, distractor analysis) flag bad questions: ambiguous, wrong key, or too easy or hard.

docs.title: 5.4 Test engine and autosave
docs.text:
• Test definitions: sections, timers (overall and per section), navigation rules, marking schemes, question pools or fixed papers, variants.
  • Delivery package: encrypted per test (and per variant), downloadable in advance. The key is released at start. Optional per-candidate watermarking of content deters leaks.
  • Autosave store:
    • writes keyed by (test, candidate, question) with the highest sequence number wins;
    • partitioned by candidate;
    • a durable, replicated key-value store (e.g. Cassandra/ScyllaDB/DynamoDB-style) handles high write rates;
    • acknowledgements only after a durable write.
  • Submission: a marker plus a final flush. Evaluation is triggered via an event.
  • Evaluation: idempotent per candidate. Recomputable if the answer key changes (§4.3 step 6), so keep responses separately from scores.

docs.title: 5.5 Results, ranks and analytics
docs.text:
• Per-candidate results: score, section-wise breakdown, time spent per question, accuracy by topic, comparison to toppers and averages.
  • Ranks: computed from the score distribution after the test window closes (§6.6), and published once stable.
  • Teacher and parent reports: batch performance, weak topics, attendance, engagement.

docs.title: 5.6 CBT centre system
docs.text:
• Local server:
    • receives the encrypted paper;
    • holds decryption keys only at exam time;
    • serves the exam client to all terminals;
    • stores responses with an audit trail;
    • replicates locally;
    • uploads signed response packages after the shift.
  • Exam client: locked-down OS image, no internet, timer from the local server, and seamless resume on terminal failure.
  • Monitoring: central dashboards show centre readiness (downloads done, clocks synced, terminals up), candidates present, and upload status after shifts. CCTV and observers are part of the process (VERIFY).

docs.title: 6.1 Item response theory (IRT)
docs.text:
• The model: the probability that a student with ability θ answers item i correctly. In the 3-parameter logistic (3PL) model:

    P(correct | θ) = c_i + (1 − c_i) / (1 + e^(−a_i(θ − b_i)))

    where: - b_i is difficulty; - a_i is discrimination (how sharply the item separates abilities); - c_i is the guessing floor (e.g. ~0.25 for four options). - Calibration: estimate item parameters from many students' responses by maximum likelihood (EM / marginal maximum likelihood) or Bayesian methods. - Ability estimation: estimate θ for each student from their responses. - Uses: scores comparable across different question sets; question quality checks; adaptive testing; better practice recommendations.

docs.title: 6.2 Knowledge tracing
docs.text:
• Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT): per concept, a hidden "mastered or not" state, with parameters for:

    • initial knowledge;
    • learning rate (probability of learning after each attempt);
    • slip (wrong answer despite mastery);
    • guess (right answer without mastery).

    After each answer, update P(mastered) by Bayes' rule. - Deep knowledge tracing: sequence models over the student's full interaction history predict the next answer's correctness across concepts. - Uses: mastery bars in the app; choosing the next question; deciding when to revise (spaced repetition, with intervals growing as mastery holds).

docs.title: 6.3 Test assembly under a blueprint
docs.text:
• Constraints:
    • number of questions per topic and section;
    • difficulty distribution (e.g. 30% easy, 50% medium, 20% hard, or a target test information curve with IRT);
    • question types;
    • no overlapping or duplicate concepts;
    • exposure limits (don't reuse recent questions);
    • variants with equal difficulty.

  • Methods:

    • integer programming (select binary x_i for each question to satisfy constraints and hit target information);
    • or greedy heuristics with repair.

    Parallel forms (variants) are generated so their test characteristic curves match.

docs.title: 6.4 Computerised adaptive testing (CAT)
docs.text:
• Loop:
    1. Start with a medium item.
    2. After each answer, update θ.
    3. Choose the next item with maximum information at the current θ, subject to content constraints and exposure control (randomisation among top items).
    4. Stop when the standard error is small enough, or after a maximum number of items.
  • Benefits: shorter tests with equal precision. Used in some standardised exams (VERIFY which).

docs.title: 6.5 Percentile normalisation across shifts
docs.text:
• The problem: a multi-shift exam uses different papers per shift. One shift may be harder, so raw scores aren't comparable.
  • Percentile method (as published by some national agencies; VERIFY details):
    • within each shift, a candidate's percentile score = 100 × (number of candidates in that shift with raw score ≤ the candidate's score) / (total candidates in the shift);
    • computed to several decimal places;
    • merit is based on percentile scores, with tie-breaking rules;
    • the assumption is that ability distributions are similar across shifts, so candidates are randomly allocated to shifts.
  • Alternatives: equipercentile equating, and IRT-based equating using common (anchor) items, which is more robust if shift populations differ.
  • Systems view:
    • sort each shift's scores;
    • compute the cumulative distribution;
    • map each candidate's score;
    • publish with full precision and audit;
    • make it reproducible from stored responses and final keys.

docs.title: 6.6 Ranking half a million candidates
docs.text:
• Scores are discrete (e.g. −90 to 360), so ranks come from a count histogram: rank(score) = 1 + number of candidates with a higher score. This is O(number of distinct scores) and trivially fast, even for millions.
  • Live leaderboard during a test window:
    • maintain counts per score bucket in a sharded counter store (Ch 51);
    • a candidate's provisional rank = the sum of counts above their score;
    • top-100 lists from a sorted set.
  • Ties: break by time taken, accuracy, or sectional scores per test rules.

docs.title: 6.7 Proctoring anomaly detection
docs.text:
• Signals:
    • face detection (none, multiple);
    • face match drift (a different person);
    • head pose and gaze away (away for longer than N seconds, repeatedly);
    • object detection (phone, book);
    • audio (speech detection, multiple voices);
    • screen events (focus loss, attempts to open apps).
  • Scoring: a weighted sum of events over time windows with decay; thresholds for a live proctor alert vs a post-exam review.
  • Fairness: tune for lighting and skin tone variations, network conditions and disabilities. Always have human review before penalties.

docs.title: 6.8 Autosave ordering
docs.text:
• Per question, the client increments a sequence number for each change. The server stores the answer with the highest sequence (last write by sequence, not by arrival order).
  • Offline queue replay sends changes in order. The server ignores stale ones.
  • The end-time rule: changes with client sequence after the recorded end, or arriving after end + grace, are rejected (policy).
  • Evidence: the audit log stores every change for disputes.

docs.title: 6.9 Collusion and cheating detection
docs.text:
• Answer similarity: pairs of candidates with unusually many identical wrong answers (shared wrong answers are much stronger evidence than shared right ones).
    • Statistical indices compare to the expected overlap given their abilities.
    • Compute within centres, labs, or IP subnets to limit pair counts.
  • Timing patterns: answers entered at identical times across candidates, or extremely fast correct answers on hard items (possible leak).
  • Score jumps: sudden large improvements vs history (EdTech mock tests).
  • Outcome: flags → review → action per rules. Evidence only, never automatic penalties for high-stakes exams.

docs.title: 7.1 Operational stores
docs.text: Data Store (reference) Notes Users, enrolments, payments PostgreSQL Minors: guardian consent records Live class state (rooms, participants) In-memory + Redis Ephemeral Chat and doubts Append-only per class (Kafka + Cassandra) Searchable for moderators Question bank PostgreSQL + object storage (images, videos) + OpenSearch Versioned Test packages Object storage + CDN (encrypted) Keys in KMS Autosaved answers Distributed KV (Cassandra/ScyllaDB/DynamoDB) partitioned by candidate High write rates Results and ranks PostgreSQL + cached result pages Read spikes Proctoring media Object storage with short retention Access-controlled CBT centre data Local server DB + signed packages centrally Chain of custody

docs.title: 7.2 Learning analytics
docs.text:
• Events (video watched, pauses and rewinds, attempts, answers with time taken, doubts, poll responses, test results) → Kafka → lakehouse → warehouse.
  • Models: IRT calibration jobs, knowledge tracing training, dropout/churn prediction, content quality analytics (which lecture segments cause rewinds), teacher effectiveness metrics (engagement, outcomes).
  • Dashboards: for teachers (batch), parents (child), content teams (question quality) and business (retention, conversion).

docs.title: 7.3 Data flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    APP[Student apps] --> RT[Realtime gateways]
    APP --> API[APIs - tests, practice, doubts]
    RT --> K[Kafka]
    API --> K
    K --> AGG[Stream aggregation - polls, chat sampling]
    K --> LAKE[Lakehouse]
    LAKE --> IRT[IRT calibration]
    LAKE --> KT[Knowledge tracing training]
    LAKE --> DW[Warehouse - reports]
    IRT --> QB[Question bank parameters]
    KT --> ADAPT[Adaptive practice service]
    DW --> DASH[Teacher, parent and business dashboards]

docs.title: 8. Tech Stack (reference choice)
docs.text: Layer Choice Notes Live media WebRTC SFU (LiveKit, mediasoup, Janus) + encoder/packager for LL-HLS; CDN Hybrid delivery Realtime WebSocket gateways (Go/Elixir/Node) + Redis pub/sub or NATS Chat, polls, whiteboard Services Java/Kotlin (Spring Boot) or Go Test engine, catalogue Autosave store Cassandra/ScyllaDB or DynamoDB Write-heavy, partitioned Databases PostgreSQL, Redis Core data Search OpenSearch with vector search Questions and doubts OCR and ML Math OCR models, embeddings (Python/PyTorch), model serving Doubts, proctoring Streaming Kafka, Flink Aggregations Lakehouse Iceberg + Spark + Trino Analytics Psychometrics IRT libraries (Python/R), custom calibration jobs Question calibration Apps Native Android (low-end friendly), web India's device mix CBT centres Hardened Linux images, local servers, signed packages Security

docs.title: 9. Security, Privacy & Compliance
docs.text:
• Children's data: verifiable parental consent, no tracking-based advertising to children, and limits on behavioural monitoring under the DPDP Act (VERIFY rules for children's data).
  • Exam integrity:
    • encrypted papers;
    • just-in-time keys;
    • access logs;
    • watermarking;
    • lockdown clients;
    • CCTV at centres;
    • chain-of-custody for response data;
    • penalties for leaks under applicable public examination laws (e.g. anti-cheating legislation for public exams; VERIFY).
  • Proctoring: transparent disclosure and consent, minimal data, short retention, human review, and accommodations for disabilities.
  • Payments and refunds: clear refund policies for courses (consumer protection; VERIFY), and EMI and loan disclosures when financing courses.

docs.title: 10. Reliability & Operations
docs.text:
• Fixed-time events:
    • mock tests and national exams are scheduled, so pre-scale and pre-download;
    • rehearse with load tests at full concurrency;
    • freeze changes on test days.
  • Graceful handling of disconnects: autosave and local queues, resume with remaining time, and server-authoritative timers.
  • Live classes:
    • pre-class teacher connectivity checks;
    • backup encoder paths;
    • a degraded mode (audio + whiteboard);
    • CDN capacity for the day's schedule.
  • Results day: pre-generate result pages; serve via CDN with login tokens; queue traffic if needed.
  • CBT centres: readiness dashboards, spare terminals, power backups, and contingency plans for centre failures (rescheduling candidates; VERIFY policies).

docs.title: 11. Key Trade-offs
docs.text: Decision Chosen Accepted cost Live delivery WebRTC for stage, LL-HLS for audience 2–5 s delay for most viewers Chat Sampled fan-out Not every message visible to everyone Test start Pre-download + key release Complexity; security of pre-positioned content Autosave Per-answer durable writes Higher write load Normalisation Percentiles within shifts (as mandated) Assumes comparable shift populations Adaptive learning IRT + knowledge tracing Calibration data needed Proctoring AI flags + human review Cost; privacy concerns

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ How would you stream a live class to 100,000 students?

30-second answer: The teacher sends video over WebRTC to an SFU; it's composed, encoded into an ABR ladder and packaged as low-latency HLS served by a CDN to the audience with 2–5 s latency; only on-stage students use WebRTC; whiteboard and polls travel as small events over WebSockets.

Deep answer: §4.1, §5.1.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Latency vs scale and cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not WebRTC for all? → Server cost per viewer. 2. Poll sync? → Video timestamps.

Red flags: One video call with 100k participants.

Q2 [B1] How do you make sure a student's answers aren't lost in an online test?

30-second answer: Autosave each answer change to a durable, replicated store with a sequence number; show "saved" only after acknowledgement; queue locally when offline and sync later; submission just marks the end.

Deep answer: §4.2, §5.4, §6.8.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Write load vs safety.

Follow-ups: 1. Conflicts? → Highest sequence wins. 2. Browser crash? → Resume from server.

Red flags: Save everything at submit.

Q3 [B1] Why should test timers be server-authoritative?

30-second answer: Client clocks can be wrong or manipulated; the server records each candidate's start and computes the end, while the client shows a countdown synced to server time; late answers are rejected per rules.

Deep answer: §4.2 step 3, §6.8.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Network delays need tolerance.

Follow-ups: 1. Late joiners? → Remaining time rules. 2. Disconnects? → Pause policies.

Red flags: Trusting the browser clock.

Q4 [B1] How is an all-India rank computed?

30-second answer: After the test window closes, count how many candidates scored higher using a histogram of scores (scores are discrete), apply tie-break rules, and compute percentiles; provisional ranks can update live from bucket counts.

Deep answer: §6.6.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Live vs final ranks.

Follow-ups: 1. Ties? → Rules. 2. Scale? → Histogram is tiny.

Red flags: Sorting all candidates on every request.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How do you handle 500,000 students starting a test at the same second?

30-second answer: Pre-download the encrypted paper from the CDN over the preceding 30 minutes, then release a small decryption key and start token at start time from a scaled key service; record server-side start times; late joiners get remaining time.

Deep answer: §4.2, §5.4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Security of pre-positioned papers.

Follow-ups: 1. Key leak? → Per-test keys, short window. 2. Images? → In the package.

Red flags: Everyone downloads the paper at 10:00.

Q6 [B2] How would you design chat for a class of 100k?

30-second answer: WebSocket gateways → chat service partitioned by class → append-only storage; moderation and rate limits; fan out only a sampled stream plus teacher and moderator messages and pinned doubts; aggregate reactions; cluster doubts for the teacher.

Deep answer: §5.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Completeness vs readability.

Follow-ups: 1. Spam? → Slow mode, bans. 2. Search? → Moderator tools.

Red flags: Broadcasting every message.

Q7 [B2] What is item response theory and why use it?

30-second answer: A model of the probability of a correct answer as a function of student ability and item parameters (difficulty, discrimination, guessing); it makes scores comparable across different question sets, reveals bad questions, and powers adaptive testing and practice.

Deep answer: §6.1.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Calibration data needs.

Follow-ups: 1. 3PL? → Adds guessing. 2. Calibration? → EM/MML.

Red flags: Difficulty as percent correct only.

Q8 [B2] How does doubt solving from a photo work?

30-second answer: Math-aware OCR turns the photo into text and LaTeX, an embedding model searches millions of solved questions for near-duplicates, high-confidence matches return solutions instantly, and others go to a tutor queue routed by subject.

Deep answer: §4.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: False matches vs speed.

Follow-ups: 1. Handwriting? → Harder OCR. 2. Confidence? → Thresholds.

Red flags: Keyword search only.

Q9 [B2] How do you assemble a fair test from a question bank?

30-second answer: Define a blueprint (topics, sections, difficulty or target information curve, question types, exposure limits) and select questions via integer programming or heuristics, generating equal-difficulty variants when needed.

Deep answer: §6.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Variety vs comparability.

Follow-ups: 1. Variants? → Matched curves. 2. Exposure? → Limits.

Red flags: Random selection.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ How do you normalise scores across multiple exam shifts?

30-second answer: Compute percentile scores within each shift — 100 × candidates with score ≤ yours ÷ total in shift — to high precision and rank on those, as some national agencies do (VERIFY); alternatives are equipercentile or IRT equating with anchor items; make it reproducible from stored responses and final keys.

Deep answer: §6.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Assumption of comparable shift populations.

Follow-ups: 1. Key challenges? → Rescore before normalising. 2. Ties? → Rules.

Red flags: Comparing raw scores across shifts.

Q11 [B3] How would you build adaptive practice?

30-second answer: Estimate mastery per concept with knowledge tracing (BKT or deep models) and ability with IRT; choose next questions near the learner's ability, mixing weak concepts and spaced revision; update after each answer; evaluate by learning gains, not engagement alone.

Deep answer: §6.2, §4.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Challenge vs frustration.

Follow-ups: 1. Cold start? → Diagnostic test. 2. Revision timing? → Spaced repetition.

Red flags: Random practice sets.

Q12 [B3] How do you detect collusion in online tests?

30-second answer: Compare answer patterns within centres, labs or networks, focusing on shared wrong answers relative to expected overlap given abilities; look at synchronised timing and implausibly fast correct answers on hard items; flag for human review with evidence.

Deep answer: §6.9.

Trade-offs I'd call out: False positives.

Follow-ups: 1. Pair explosion? → Limit to groups. 2. Leaks? → Timing plus score jumps.

Red flags: Auto-penalising similarity.

Q13 [B3] Design remote proctoring.

30-second answer: Lockdown client with environment checks, identity verification and room scan, on-device or server AI detecting absence, multiple faces, gaze, objects and voices, weighted scoring with live proctor alerts and post-exam review, consent and short retention, fairness tuning and human decisions.

Deep answer: §4.4, §6.7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Integrity vs privacy and fairness.

Follow-ups: 1. Bandwidth? → Edge inference, snapshots. 2. Accessibility? → Accommodations.

Red flags: Fully automated disqualification.

Q14 [B3] How do you keep polls and whiteboard in sync with a delayed video stream?

30-second answer: Timestamp interactive events with the video timeline (not wall clock) and have clients display them when playback reaches that timestamp; aggregate poll results server-side and broadcast periodically.

Deep answer: §5.1.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Slight delay for everyone.

Follow-ups: 1. On-stage students? → Real-time path. 2. Recording? → Replay events.

Red flags: Popping polls before the teacher is seen asking.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design a national computer-based test system.

30-second answer: Encrypted papers pre-positioned on hardened local centre servers with just-in-time key release, locked-down terminals, continuous local response saving with audit and replication, signed upload after shifts, provisional keys and challenges, scoring, percentile normalisation across shifts, and CDN-served results — with readiness monitoring and contingencies.

Deep answer: §4.3, §5.6, §6.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Centre infrastructure cost vs control.

Follow-ups: 1. Internet loss? → Local operation. 2. Terminal failure? → Resume.

Red flags: Exam served from a central website to centres.

Q16 [B4] How would you scale an EdTech platform for exam season?

30-second answer: Forecast concurrency for tests and classes, pre-scale APIs, autosave stores and realtime gateways, pre-position test packages and schedule CDN capacity, stagger non-essential jobs, and rehearse with full-concurrency load tests.

Deep answer: §10.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Idle cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Result day? → Pre-generated pages. 2. Live classes? → Schedule-aware capacity.

Red flags: Reactive autoscaling only.

Q17 [B4] What data platform would you build for learning analytics?

30-second answer: Events from classes, videos, practice and tests into Kafka and a lakehouse; IRT calibration and knowledge tracing training jobs feeding the question bank and adaptive service; warehouse marts for teacher, parent and business dashboards; content quality analytics; strict handling of minors' data.

Deep answer: §7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Insight vs privacy.

Follow-ups: 1. Consent? → Guardian records. 2. Model governance? → Validation.

Red flags: Using children's data for ads.

Q18 [B4] How would you evaluate whether adaptive learning actually works?

30-second answer: Randomised experiments comparing learning outcomes (post-test gains, exam results), not just engagement; control for prior ability; measure retention over time; watch for unintended effects like frustration or dropout.

Deep answer: §6.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Long feedback loops.

Follow-ups: 1. Proxy metrics? → Mastery predictions. 2. Ethics? → Fair access.

Red flags: Time spent as the success metric.

Q19 [B4] What are the security risks of online exams, and the countermeasures?

30-second answer: Paper leaks (encryption, JIT keys, access logs, watermarking), impersonation (identity checks, face match), device cheating (lockdown clients, proctoring), collusion (answer similarity analytics), tampering with responses (signed packages, audit logs), and insider risk (separation of duties).

Deep answer: §9, §6.7, §6.9.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Friction vs integrity.

Follow-ups: 1. Insiders? → Key splitting. 2. Evidence? → Audit trails.

Red flags: Security by obscurity.

Q20 [B4] Compare live classes with live sports streaming.

30-second answer: Both use ABR streaming via CDNs; classes need two-way interaction (polls, doubts, on-stage students) synced to a delayed stream, smaller audiences per stream but many concurrent streams, and teacher-side uplink reliability — sports needs extreme single-event scale, ads and rights.

Deep answer: I06 vs this chapter.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Interaction vs scale.

Follow-ups: 1. Shared tech? → Packaging, CDN. 2. Different? → WebRTC stage.

Red flags: Identical designs.

docs.title: 13. Summary
docs.text:
1. Live classes are hybrid: WebRTC for the teacher and on-stage students, LL-HLS via CDN for the audience. Chat is sampled; polls and whiteboard are events synced to video time.
  2. Online tests remove the start and end spikes with pre-downloaded encrypted papers, key release at start, per-answer autosave and asynchronous evaluation. Timers are server-authoritative.
  3. High-stakes CBTs rely on local centre servers, just-in-time keys, audit trails, signed uploads, answer key challenges and percentile normalisation across shifts.
  4. Psychometrics and ML (IRT, CAT, knowledge tracing, blueprint assembly) make tests fair and practice adaptive. Integrity uses collusion analytics and proctoring with human review.
  5. Children's privacy and exam integrity are design constraints, not add-ons.
