docs.title: I14. National Digital ID & Vaccination-Scale Registration
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Sector: government and public digital infrastructure. Format: a system design walkthrough with no code. Reader bands: B1 → B4.

Builds on:

  • I03 (UPI and national rails)
  • Ch 36 (compliance)
  • Ch 48 (slot booking)
  • Ch 39 (rate limiting)

This chapter covers two connected population-scale systems.

1. A national digital identity platform, in the style of India's Aadhaar:

  • enrolment of more than a billion residents, with demographic and biometric capture;
  • biometric de-duplication, so each person gets exactly one ID;
  • online authentication (fingerprint, iris, face, OTP) at hundreds of millions of requests a day;
  • eKYC with consent;
  • virtual IDs and tokenisation for privacy;
  • the ecosystem of registered agencies and devices.

2. A vaccination-scale registration and certificate platform, in the style of CoWIN:

  • registering hundreds of millions of people in weeks;
  • booking slots at centres, with flash crowds when new age groups open;
  • recording each dose at the centre, sometimes offline;
  • issuing digitally signed QR certificates that anyone can verify offline;
  • dashboards for supply and coverage.

Also covered: the algorithms (biometric matching and de-duplication at scale, liveness detection, identity token design, slot allocation under scarcity, bot defence, signature schemes for verifiable credentials), the data platform and the tech stack.

Reading time: 85 min.

Sources and honesty

  • The architecture of India's Aadhaar and CoWIN has been partly described in public documents, talks and regulations. Those details are marked "publicly described (VERIFY)".
  • The legal framework cited here is marked VERIFY: the Aadhaar Act and its regulations, Supreme Court judgments on its permitted uses, and the DPDP Act.
  • Everything else is a reference design for a population-scale identity and registration system. It is not a description of any government's actual implementation.

docs.title: 1.1 Why population-scale public systems are different
docs.text: Aspect Commercial platform National public platform Users Customers who chose you Everyone, including people with no smartphone, low literacy or worn fingerprints Failure Lost revenue A person denied rations, a pension or a vaccine Traffic Business peaks Policy-driven flash crowds ("registrations open at 4 pm for 18–44") Trust Brand Legal mandate, privacy, audit, courts Integration Your apps Thousands of banks, telcos and government departments Longevity Years Decades, for identities that last a lifetime

docs.title: 1.2 Main systems
docs.text:
Digital ID

System What it does Enrolment client Captures demographics, photo, 10 fingerprints and 2 irises at an enrolment centre, signed and encrypted on the device Enrolment server Receives packets, runs quality checks and manual review, then de-duplication against everyone already enrolled ABIS (automated biometric identification system) 1:N biometric search across more than a billion records ID generation Issues a random, non-meaningful 12-digit number with a checksum after de-dup passes Identity repository The master record, with a history of updates Authentication service 1:1 match of a given ID plus biometric or OTP, answered yes/no eKYC With resident consent, returns the demographics and photo to a regulated entity Virtual ID and tokens Revocable alias IDs and per-agency tokens, so the real number need not be shared or stored Ecosystem management Registered agencies, device certification, licence keys, audit Resident self-service Update address, lock biometrics, see auth history

Vaccination registration

System What it does Registration Mobile OTP login, beneficiaries linked to a phone (up to N per phone), ID document details Centre and session management Centres, vaccines, daily sessions with capacity, age groups, dose numbers Slot search and booking Search by pincode or district, book a slot, reschedule Vaccinator app Verify the beneficiary at the centre, record the dose (works offline) Certificate service Signed certificate with a QR code, available instantly Verification Anyone scans the QR and checks the signature offline Supply and dashboards Doses administered, coverage by region, wastage, adverse events (AEFI) Open APIs Third-party apps can show availability and download certificates

docs.title: 1.3 Scale (assumptions for this design, with public orders of magnitude marked VERIFY)
docs.text:
Quantity Value Identities ~1.3B+ (publicly reported order of magnitude, VERIFY) Biometric template gallery 1.3B × (10 fingers + 2 irises + face) Enrolments and updates Hundreds of thousands to over a million a day Authentication Tens of crores (hundreds of millions) of transactions a month, with daily peaks over 100M (VERIFY) Vaccine registrations Hundreds of millions within months; tens of millions on peak days Slot-search traffic at a new release Millions of requests per minute, heavy bot traffic Vaccinations recorded Peak days of tens of millions of doses (a peak above 20M a day was publicly reported, VERIFY) Certificates Billions of doses, each with a signed certificate

Estimation highlights

  • De-dup cost:
    • Comparing one new enrollee against 1.3B people with 10 fingers + 2 irises is ~1.3B × several comparisons each, per enrolment.
    • At 1M enrolments a day, that is on the order of 10^15 comparisons a day.
    • This is only feasible with fast template matchers (e.g. iris codes compared with bit operations), indexing/binning to prune candidates, and a massive parallel cluster.
    • Historically this was spread across multiple independent ABIS vendors (publicly described, VERIFY).
  • Authentication:
    • 100M auths a day averages ~1,200/s, with peaks of perhaps 5–10k/s.
    • Each is a 1:1 match: fetch this person's template and compare. That is cheap.
    • The hard parts are latency across the country, availability and security.
  • Vaccine slot booking:
    • A release of 1M slots with 50M people trying means slot demand far exceeds supply.
    • The design goal is to be fair and not crash. Serving everyone is impossible.

docs.title: 2.1 Functional: digital ID
docs.text:
1. Enrol a resident with demographic and biometric data, operator and verifier signatures, and supporting documents (or an "introducer" for people without documents, VERIFY).
  2. De-duplicate: never issue two IDs to one person, and flag suspected duplicates for manual adjudication.
  3. Generate a unique random ID. Deliver the ID letter and a digital copy.
  4. Authenticate: yes/no answers for an ID plus a biometric, OTP or demographic data, within a few seconds.
  5. eKYC: with consent (biometric or OTP), share limited attributes with regulated entities.
  6. Updates: address, mobile number, biometric refresh (for children, at mandatory ages, VERIFY).
  7. Privacy features:
    • a virtual ID that can be regenerated;
    • biometric locking;
    • an authentication history visible to the resident;
    • tokenised references for agencies (UID tokens), so agencies do not store the ID number.
  8. Ecosystem:
    • onboarding of authentication user agencies and KYC agencies;
    • certified capture devices (registered devices, which encrypt and sign on the device);
    • audits.

docs.title: 2.2 Functional: vaccination platform
docs.text:
1. Register with mobile OTP. Add beneficiaries using an ID document number, age and name.
  2. Browse centres, see availability by age group, vaccine and dose, and book or cancel.
  3. Walk-in registration at centres (the assisted mode).
  4. Vaccinator records the dose with batch number and time, captures AEFI, and schedules the next dose due date.
  5. Instant certificate by SMS link and download: verifiable and tamper-evident, with an international-travel format (ICAO/EU-compatible variants, VERIFY).
  6. Open APIs (public read-only availability, protected booking and certificate APIs).
  7. Dashboards: doses by region, age and vaccine, stock and wastage, and centre utilisation.

docs.title: 2.3 Non-functional
docs.text: Attribute Target Availability 99.9%+ for authentication (people wait at ration shops and bank counters), with graceful degradation Auth latency < 1–2 s end to end at the agency, even on rural networks De-dup accuracy Extremely low false match rate (no wrong merges) and low false non-match rate (duplicates caught) Inclusion Fallbacks for people whose biometrics fail (iris, face, OTP, exception handling) Privacy Data minimisation, purpose limitation, no central tracking of the purpose of authentication (VERIFY what is logged) Security End-to-end encryption from device to server, HSMs, signed packets, zero trust Fairness under scarcity No advantage for bots, spread demand, transparent rules Verifiability Certificates verifiable offline by anyone, forever Openness Open standards and APIs so the ecosystem can build on top ("digital public infrastructure")

docs.title: Key decisions
docs.text: Decision Choice Why ID number Random, non-meaningful, with a checksum No information leaks from the number itself, and it never needs re-issuing (publicly described, VERIFY) Minimal data Store only what is needed: demographics, photo, biometrics. No caste, religion or income (VERIFY) Privacy, and less to protect Authentication response Yes/no only (plus eKYC with consent), never raw biometrics Minimises exposure Biometric security Encrypted and signed at the capture device (registered devices) Stops replay and tampering between device and server De-dup Multiple independent ABIS vendors, with results combined Accuracy and no vendor lock-in (publicly described, VERIFY) Federated ecosystem Agencies connect via licensed gateways (ASAs), not directly Controlled access and accountability Vaccine slot search Heavily cached, read-only, open APIs, rate-limited Absorbs flash crowds and bots Certificates Digitally signed QR (verifiable credential), verifiable offline Trust without calling the server

docs.title: 4.1 Journey 1: enrolling a resident
docs.text:
1. At an enrolment centre, run by a registrar's agency with a certified operator:
    • the operator logs in with their own biometric;
    • the resident gives name, date of birth, gender, address, optional mobile and email, and supporting documents (or verification by an introducer/head of family where rules allow, VERIFY);
    • the kit captures a photo, 10 fingerprints and 2 irises, with quality checks at capture (retake a poor-quality finger; record exceptions for missing fingers or eyes).
  2. Packet creation:
    • demographics, biometrics and document scans are bundled into an enrolment packet;
    • the packet is encrypted with the ID authority's public key and signed by the operator and supervisor;
    • it is stored on the kit and uploaded when connected, with an enrolment ID receipt handed to the resident;
    • the kit may be offline for days in remote areas, so packets carry timestamps and signatures.
  3. At central ingest:
    • decrypt the packet in a secure zone;
    • validate the signatures, operator and device;
    • run quality and fraud checks (operator anomalies, duplicate packets);
    • run demographic de-dup as a quick filter.
  4. Biometric de-dup (1:N):
    • templates (fingerprint minutiae, iris codes, face embeddings) are extracted;
    • they are searched against the entire gallery by ABIS, possibly more than one vendor, whose results are fused (§6.1–6.3).
    • Outcomes:
      • unique → proceed;
      • clear duplicate → reject, and tell the resident they already have an ID;
      • ambiguous (possible match with low confidence) → manual adjudication, where trained experts compare images.
  5. ID generation:
    • generate a random 12-digit number, excluding certain patterns, with a Verhoeff checksum (publicly described, VERIFY);
    • write to the identity repository;
    • add templates to the ABIS galleries and the authentication template store;
    • send a letter by post and make an electronic download available.
  6. Timeline: days to weeks, since the heavy compute and manual adjudication are batch pipelines with queues.

docs.title: 4.2 Journey 2: fingerprint authentication at a ration shop
docs.text:
1. The fair-price shop operator enters the resident's ID (or scans the QR code on the card). The resident places a finger on a registered device (RD).
  2. The device:
    • captures the fingerprint;
    • checks liveness as supported;
    • builds the PID block (biometric data plus timestamp);
    • encrypts it with a session key, which is itself encrypted with the ID authority's public key;
    • signs it with the device's private key (certified device, with the key in secure hardware);
    • so the application software never sees raw biometrics.
  3. The shop's application (the AUA, e.g. the food department's system) builds the auth request (ID or VID/token, PID block, AUA code, licence key, transaction ID) and signs it with the AUA's key.
  4. The request goes through an ASA, a licensed network gateway with secure leased lines, to the ID authority's authentication service.
  5. The authentication service:
    • validates the AUA and ASA licences and signatures, the device certificate and the timestamp (preventing replay);
    • decrypts the PID in an HSM-backed secure environment;
    • looks up the templates for that ID (1:1);
    • matches them (fingerprint matcher, with thresholds tuned for 1:1);
    • responds Yes/No with an error code, signed. There is no personal data unless eKYC was requested.
  6. Logging:
    • the authority logs the transaction: which AUA, time, result, device, without the purpose of the transaction (publicly described, VERIFY);
    • the resident can see their authentication history.
  7. Failure paths:
    • retry with another finger, then an iris or face, then OTP to the registered mobile;
    • or a manual exception with officer approval.
    • Worn fingerprints (manual labourers, the elderly) are the classic inclusion issue, so the design must support fallbacks.
  8. Performance: a template lookup from a key-value store, plus a match in milliseconds. End-to-end latency is dominated by the network and device.

docs.title: 4.3 Journey 3: eKYC to open a bank account
docs.text:
1. The bank (a KUA, a KYC user agency) asks the customer for consent for eKYC.
  2. The customer authenticates by biometric or OTP. The request includes an eKYC flag and consent.
  3. On success, the authority returns signed and encrypted demographics and photo to the bank:
    • the bank verifies the signature;
    • the signed record is equivalent to a verified document, if permitted by regulation (VERIFY RBI/PMLA rules on Aadhaar eKYC eligibility).
  4. Privacy features:
    • the bank may receive a token instead of storing the ID number;
    • reference keys go into a vault with restricted access;
    • offline KYC options (a signed XML/QR the resident downloads and shares, without an online auth, VERIFY) avoid central logging altogether.

docs.title: 4.4 Journey 4: vaccine registration and the 4 pm flash crowd
docs.text:
1. Registration (days before):
    • enter a mobile number and receive an OTP (via an SMS gateway, with rate limits);
    • add up to N beneficiaries with an ID proof type and number, name, birth year and gender;
    • where an ID is used, optional demographic auth or de-dup on (ID type, number) ensures one registration per person.
  2. Release announced: "slots for 18–44 open at 4 pm". Millions wait with the page open, and bot scripts poll the APIs.
  3. At 4 pm, slot search:
    • search by district or pincode for a date range;
    • responses are cached per district and date with short TTLs (tens of seconds) at the CDN and in service caches;
    • the public API is rate-limited per IP and the available counts are approximate;
    • the protected booking API needs an OTP login token.
  4. Booking:
    • the user selects a session and slot and passes a CAPTCHA (bot defence);
    • the booking service atomically decrements capacity for (session, dose) using a conditional update: "if available ≥ 1, decrement and create the appointment" (Ch 48).
    • If a slot is gone, the user gets "fully booked" and the search refreshes.
    • Rules are enforced: one active appointment per beneficiary, correct age group, dose interval.
  5. Confirmation: an appointment slip goes out by SMS, and the centre's list is updated.

  6. What goes wrong without design:

    • the database melts from search traffic;
    • bots grab all slots in seconds;
    • users see stale "available" counts and fail repeatedly;
    • the OTP service is overwhelmed.

    Mitigations are covered in §5.6 and §6.6.

docs.title: 4.5 Journey 5: vaccination at the centre and the certificate
docs.text:
1. Verification: the beneficiary arrives. The vaccinator app (on a tablet or phone) searches the appointment by reference or mobile number and verifies the ID proof photo, or registers a walk-in on the spot.
  2. Record the dose:
    • vaccine name, batch number, dose number, vaccinator ID, centre and time;
    • the next dose due date is computed automatically.
    • If offline, the app stores records locally with signatures and syncs later. The certificate is then generated after sync.
  3. Certificate:
    • the certificate service creates a record: beneficiary name, birth year or age, gender, ID reference (masked), vaccine, dose, date, centre and certificate ID;
    • it digitally signs it (§6.7) with the programme's private key kept in an HSM;
    • it encodes the signed payload in a QR code, rendered as a PDF;
    • the beneficiary receives an SMS with a download link, also available via partner apps and digital document lockers (VERIFY).
  4. Verification anywhere:
    • a verifier app, at an airport, office or hotel, scans the QR code;
    • it checks the signature with the published public key, offline;
    • it displays the details. Tampering invalidates the signature.
    • This is a verifiable credential pattern (W3C VC-like; publicly described as based on an open-source credentialing platform, VERIFY).
  5. Post-vaccination: adverse events (AEFI) are reported and flow to surveillance. Second-dose reminders go out on the due date.

docs.title: 4.6 Journey 6: resident privacy controls
docs.text:
1. The resident logs in to self-service with an OTP.
  2. Biometric lock: the resident locks biometric authentication, so any biometric auth fails until they unlock it temporarily. This guards against fingerprint spoofing.
  3. Virtual ID: the resident generates a VID, a random 16-digit alias mapped to the ID, which can be revoked and regenerated. Agencies accept the VID instead of the ID number.
  4. Auth history: the resident sees which agency authenticated them and when, which helps detect misuse.

docs.title: 5.1 Enrolment pipeline
docs.text:
• Stages: ingest → decrypt → validate → quality → demographic de-dup → biometric de-dup → adjudication → ID generation → print/dispatch.
  • Each stage is a queue-driven worker pool with idempotency by enrolment ID, so it is re-runnable.
  • Backpressure: the ABIS has finite capacity, so the ingest queue absorbs bursts (enrolment drives).
  • Operator fraud detection: patterns such as many enrolments with the same biometrics under different names, or many exceptions (missing fingers) from one operator, lead to suspension.
  • Rejections and reasons are sent back to the resident via the enrolment ID status.

docs.title: 5.2 ABIS: 1:N search at population scale
docs.text:
• Gallery partitioning: billions of templates are split across many nodes. Each node holds a shard in memory for speed.
  • Search: a query template is broadcast to all shards, which compare in parallel. The top-k candidates by score go to a combiner.
  • Multi-modal fusion: fingerprint, iris and face scores are combined (score-level fusion) for final decisions (§6.3).
  • Multi-vendor: gallery subsets or full copies across vendors. Decisions compare or combine results, and disagreements go to manual adjudication (publicly described, VERIFY).
  • Throughput tuning: binning/indexing narrows candidates (e.g. fingerprint pattern classes, iris code prefilters), and hardware (SIMD/GPU) speeds up matching.

docs.title: 5.3 Authentication service
docs.text:
• Stateless front ends validate signatures, licences and replay (timestamp window plus transaction ID de-dup).
  • The template store is a key-value lookup from the ID (or its token) to the templates. It is replicated across data centres, and templates are encrypted at rest.
  • Matching engines run a 1:1 match per modality with configurable thresholds.
  • Active-active data centres: the authority publicly describes multiple DCs (VERIFY), and ASAs route to the nearest healthy DC.
  • Rate limits and quotas apply per AUA. Anomaly detection covers the pattern of failures per device or agency.
  • The response is signed (so an AUA can prove the result) and includes a response code for audit.

docs.title: 5.4 Token vault and virtual IDs
docs.text:
• VID: a random 16-digit alias that maps to the ID. A resident can have one active VID at a time. A new one revokes the old.
  • UID tokens: a per-AUA/KUA token derived from the ID, so different agencies cannot link records by a common identifier.
  • Reference key vault at agencies: they must store ID numbers only in an HSM-backed vault, referenced by a random reference key elsewhere in their systems (VERIFY the regulation).

docs.title: 5.5 Registered device ecosystem
docs.text:
• Certification: device models are certified, and each device has a key pair provisioned in secure hardware. Its certificate is signed by the manufacturer's CA, which is trusted by the authority.
  • Management server: device keys rotate, and compromised devices are revoked.
  • Result: biometrics are encrypted inside the device. Host applications never see or replay raw biometrics.

docs.title: 5.6 Vaccine platform under flash crowds
docs.text:
• Separate read and write paths:
    • search is served from pre-computed availability snapshots per district and date, refreshed every few seconds from the bookings DB;
    • snapshots are pushed to a cache and the CDN;
    • booking hits the primary with atomic operations.
  • Protect the core:
    • rate limits at the edge (IP, token);
    • a CAPTCHA on booking;
    • OTP throttles;
    • WAF bot signatures;
    • a cap on booking attempts per user per minute.
  • Spread demand:
    • publish release schedules by state;
    • release in batches;
    • allow centre-specific timings;
    • notification-based access (a queue or waiting room at release time, with random admission among those present at T0, which is fairer than "fastest click wins").
  • Consistency: the capacity counter in the DB is the source of truth. The cache may say "available" while the booking fails, so the UI explains this and refreshes.
  • Open APIs: the public read API lets ecosystem apps show availability. It is rate-limited, and some data is delayed to reduce bot advantage (VERIFY actual policies).

docs.title: 5.7 Certificate issuance and verification
docs.text:
• Signing service: stateless workers call an HSM with keys rotated per policy. Signatures are compact (ECDSA/EdDSA), so they fit in a QR code.
  • Key distribution: public keys are published with key IDs. Verifier apps embed them and update periodically.
  • Revocation: rare, for fraudulent records. The verifier can check a revocation list when online.
  • Formats: national format plus interoperable formats for travel (e.g. EU DCC-compatible or ICAO, VERIFY).
  • Corrections: for errors in name or date, re-issue with a new certificate ID. The old certificate is marked superseded.

docs.title: 6.1 Fingerprint matching
docs.text:
• Features: minutiae, meaning ridge endings and bifurcations, each with position and angle. A good fingerprint has ~40–100 minutiae.
  • Matching:
    • align two minutiae sets (rotation, translation, distortion);
    • count the corresponding minutiae within tolerance;
    • compute a similarity score.
    • Algorithms use local structures (minutia triplets, cylinder codes) for alignment-free matching.
  • Standards: ISO/IEC 19794-2 minutiae templates enable interoperability across vendors.
  • Quality: NFIQ-style quality scores at capture drive retakes, since poor quality means higher error rates.

docs.title: 6.2 Iris and face matching
docs.text:
• Iris (Daugman's method):
    • segment the iris;
    • normalise it to a rectangle (rubber-sheet model);
    • apply Gabor filters;
    • produce a ~2,048-bit iris code with a mask;
    • compare two codes by fractional Hamming distance, using XOR, AND masks and popcount;
    • a small distance means the same eye.
    • This is extremely fast (bit operations) and very discriminating, which makes it ideal for 1:N de-dup at a billion scale.
  • Face: deep CNN embeddings (e.g. 512-dim) compared by cosine similarity. These are used for 1:1 face auth and as an additional modality in fusion. Accuracy varies with lighting, age and pose, so thresholds need care.

docs.title: 6.3 De-duplication decision and fusion
docs.text:
• Per candidate, compute scores for each modality: 10 fingers, 2 irises, face.
  • Fusion:
    • normalise the scores (z-score or likelihood ratios);
    • combine them (sum, or a weighted/logistic model trained on known genuine and impostor pairs).
  • Thresholds:
    • above the high threshold → duplicate;
    • below the low threshold → unique;
    • in between → manual adjudication.
  • Error rates:
    • the False Match Rate (FMR) and False Non-Match Rate (FNMR) trade off;
    • at 1:N with N = 1B, even an FMR of 10^−10 per comparison gives ~0.1 false candidates per search, so thresholds must be extremely strict, with multi-modal fusion to keep FNMR low.
    • Public reports have cited very low de-dup error rates (VERIFY).
  • Special cases: twins (iris differs even for identical twins, while face may not), children (biometrics change, so updates are needed), and people with missing biometrics (use the available modalities with stricter manual checks).

docs.title: 6.4 Liveness detection (presentation attack detection)
docs.text:
• Attacks: silicone or gelatin fake fingers, printed irises, photos or videos of faces, masks, deepfakes.
  • Defences:
    • hardware (multispectral sensors, pulse detection, temperature);
    • software (texture analysis, distortion patterns for fingers; challenge-response for face such as blink, head turn, or passive CNN-based liveness);
    • device certification requiring a PAD level (VERIFY);
    • plus a biometric lock for residents.

docs.title: 6.5 ID number design
docs.text:
• Random generation: sample uniformly from the valid space, excluding patterns (e.g. not starting with 0 or 1, VERIFY), and check for no collision with issued IDs.
  • Verhoeff checksum: detects all single-digit errors and all adjacent transpositions, the typical typing errors. It is better than Luhn for transpositions.
  • Why random: no information leakage (no birth date or region encoded), no re-issue when details change, and hard to guess sequential IDs.

docs.title: 6.6 Fair slot allocation under scarcity
docs.text:
• Naive approach: first come, first served at 4 pm, which rewards bots and people with fast internet.
  • Better approaches:
    • Randomised lottery among those present: everyone who registers interest in a window gets a random position in a queue, then books in order. This is fair across connection speeds.
    • Rate-limited booking tokens: issue a booking token per user per window, and each booking needs a token plus a CAPTCHA.
    • Staggered releases by region or age, with published schedules to spread load.
    • Priority rules set by policy: health workers first, then the elderly, those with comorbidities, and so on.
    • Reservation holds: hold a slot briefly (e.g. 2 minutes) while the user confirms. Release it on timeout.
  • Capacity counters: an atomic decrement per session. For very hot sessions, partition capacity into buckets (as in inventory sharding in I02).

docs.title: 6.7 Verifiable credential signing
docs.text:
• Payload: canonical JSON (or CBOR) of the certificate fields.
  • Signature: ECDSA P-256 or Ed25519 over the canonical bytes, then embedded with a key ID.
  • Encoding: compress (e.g. zlib), then base45/base64, then the QR code. The EU DCC uses COSE, CBOR and base45 (publicly documented; the Indian format was publicly described as a signed VC in JSON-LD, VERIFY).
  • Verification: the verifier recomputes the canonical form and checks the signature with the public key. No network is needed.
  • Selective disclosure (advanced): future credentials may let the holder reveal only "vaccinated: yes" and not their name or age (BBS+ signatures, SD-JWT).

docs.title: 6.8 Bot and abuse detection
docs.text:
• Signals:
    • request rates per IP, token and device;
    • automation fingerprints (headless browsers, missing JS signals);
    • timing regularity;
    • many beneficiaries from one account;
    • OTP request bursts.
  • Response: step-up challenges (CAPTCHA), throttling, token revocation and temporary blocks, with monitoring for false positives.

docs.title: 7.1 Operational stores
docs.text: Data Store (reference) Notes Enrolment packets Encrypted object storage, retained per policy Evidence Identity repository Partitioned RDBMS/NoSQL with strict access, versioned records Master data Biometric templates In-memory ABIS galleries plus an encrypted template KV store for 1:1 Separated from demographics Raw biometric images Offline encrypted archive (for re-extraction with better algorithms) Tight access Auth logs Append-only store, time-partitioned, retained per regulation (VERIFY) Audit, resident history Token vault HSM-backed Mapping IDs to VIDs/tokens Vaccine registrations and appointments Sharded RDBMS (by state or district) Booking consistency Availability snapshots Redis/cache + CDN Read path Vaccination records Sharded RDBMS + event stream Source for certificates Certificates Object storage (PDF) + signed payload records Re-download

docs.title: 7.2 Analytics and dashboards
docs.text:
• Events: enrolments, auths (aggregated), registrations, bookings, doses, AEFI → streams → warehouse.
  • Public dashboards: doses by state, age, gender and vaccine per day, with near-real-time counters that update every few minutes.
  • Operational analytics:
    • centre utilisation and wastage;
    • stock forecasts (links to I12 cold chain, e.g. eVIN-style vaccine logistics, VERIFY);
    • auth failure rates by region and device (inclusion monitoring);
    • operator fraud patterns.
  • Privacy:
    • aggregates only for public use;
    • differential privacy or small-cell suppression for fine-grained stats;
    • strict separation of identity data from analytics (pseudonymous IDs).

docs.title: 7.3 Data flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    ENR[Enrolment packets] --> PIPE[Enrolment pipeline]
    PIPE --> CIDR[Identity repository]
    PIPE --> ABIS[ABIS galleries]
    AUTH[Auth transactions] --> LOG[Auth log store]
    BOOK[Bookings] --> VDB[Vaccine records DB]
    VAX[Vaccinations] --> VDB
    VDB --> CERT[Certificate service]
    LOG --> STREAM[Event streams]
    VDB --> STREAM
    PIPE --> STREAM
    STREAM --> DW[Warehouse - pseudonymised]
    DW --> PUB[Public dashboards - aggregates]
    DW --> OPS[Operations and fraud analytics]

docs.title: 8. Tech Stack
docs.text: Layer Publicly described (VERIFY) Reference choice Core platform (ID) Open-source, scale-out architecture: Java, Hadoop/HBase-era big data stack, MySQL, messaging queues, commodity hardware, multiple ABIS vendors (from public talks, VERIFY) Java/Go services, Kafka, Cassandra/HBase-like stores, K8s, HSMs Biometrics Commercial ABIS vendors; ISO template standards Multi-vendor ABIS, ISO/IEC 19794, NFIQ, PAD Crypto PKI, HSMs, signed and encrypted XML/JSON APIs HSM (FIPS 140-2/3), PKI, mTLS Vaccination platform Cloud-hosted, microservices; certificates on an open-source credentialing platform (VERIFY) Spring Boot/Go microservices, PostgreSQL sharded, Redis, CDN, WAF Signing Digitally signed QR certificates ECDSA/Ed25519 in an HSM, W3C VC, EU DCC compat Messaging SMS gateways for OTP Multi-provider SMS with failover Analytics Public dashboards Kafka → lakehouse (Iceberg/Spark/Trino) → BI Clients Enrolment kits, Android vaccinator app Android with offline storage, signed sync

docs.title: 9. Security, Privacy & Compliance
docs.text:
• Legal basis (VERIFY):
    • the Aadhaar Act, 2016 and its regulations;
    • Supreme Court judgments on privacy as a fundamental right (2017) and on Aadhaar (2018), which limit mandatory use of Aadhaar and private-sector authentication (VERIFY the current scope and amendments);
    • the DPDP Act, 2023 for personal data processing;
    • IT Act rules;
    • health data rules for vaccination records and the national digital health ecosystem.
  • Data minimisation: collect only the fields needed. No purpose logging of authentication, and store only what audit requires (VERIFY).
  • Security architecture:
    • end-to-end encryption from capture device to server;
    • HSMs for keys;
    • data centre security;
    • a tiered network (ASA leased lines);
    • separation of duties;
    • audits by independent agencies;
    • a security operations centre.
  • Resident controls: biometric lock, VID, auth history, and grievance redressal.
  • Inclusion safeguards: no denial of service for authentication failure where the law provides exceptions (VERIFY), fallback modes, and monitoring of failure rates by region.
  • Vaccination:
    • consent at vaccination;
    • health data protection;
    • no public exposure of individual records;
    • certificates showing minimal data (masked ID).

docs.title: 10. Reliability & Operations
docs.text:
• Authentication as critical infrastructure:
    • active-active data centres;
    • capacity for peak (month-start pension and ration distribution days);
    • graceful degradation (OTP-only if biometric matching is overloaded, policy-dependent).
  • Enrolment: queues absorb spikes, and batch ABIS processing capacity is planned against enrolment drives.
  • Vaccination launches:
    • load test for 10–50× the expected crowd;
    • cache everything readable;
    • freeze changes before release;
    • scale OTP gateways with multiple SMS providers;
    • war room;
    • public communication of status.
  • Offline-first field apps: enrolment kits and vaccinator apps store and forward with signatures, since rural connectivity is intermittent.
  • Observability:
    • auth success and failure by modality, region, device model and AUA;
    • ABIS queue depth;
    • booking success rates;
    • certificate generation lag.

docs.title: 11. Key Trade-offs
docs.text: Decision Chosen Accepted cost Biometric de-dup Multi-modal, multi-vendor, manual adjudication Enormous compute and cost; slower enrolment Auth response Yes/no only Agencies must use eKYC (with consent) for data Central auth vs offline Online auth, plus offline signed XML/QR options Connectivity dependence for online Tokens and VIDs Unlinkable identifiers per agency Complexity for agencies Slot booking Cached search, atomic booking, bot defences Stale availability; CAPTCHA friction Fairness Staggered releases and randomisation Less "instant" gratification Certificates Offline verifiable signatures Key management and rotation complexity Inclusion vs security Fallbacks (OTP, exceptions) Weaker assurance in fallback paths

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What is the difference between 1:1 authentication and 1:N identification?

30-second answer: 1:1 authentication compares a biometric against the templates of one claimed identity — "is this person who they say they are?" — and is cheap. 1:N identification searches the whole gallery — "is this person already enrolled?" — which at a billion people needs massive parallel matching, pruning and strict thresholds.

Deep answer: §4.1, §4.2, §5.2, §6.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Error rates scale with N.

Follow-ups: 1. Which is used where? → De-dup vs auth. 2. Why is 1:N harder? → False matches grow with N.

Red flags: Using 1:N for every authentication.

Q2 [B1] Why is the ID number random instead of encoding birth date or region?

30-second answer: A random number leaks nothing about the person, never changes when their details change, and can't be guessed sequentially; a Verhoeff checksum catches typing errors.

Deep answer: §6.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Not human-meaningful.

Follow-ups: 1. Verhoeff vs Luhn? → Transpositions. 2. Collisions? → Check at generation.

Red flags: Sequential IDs.

Q3 [B1] How does someone verify a vaccination certificate without calling a server?

30-second answer: The certificate data is digitally signed with the programme's private key and encoded in a QR; the verifier app has the public key, recomputes the canonical data and checks the signature offline; any tampering breaks the signature.

Deep answer: §4.5, §6.7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Key rotation and revocation.

Follow-ups: 1. Revocation? → Lists when online. 2. QR size? → Compact signatures, compression.

Red flags: A QR that's just a URL to a lookup page, with no signature.

Q4 [B1] What happens when a person's fingerprints don't match?

30-second answer: Retry with another finger, then iris or face, then OTP to the registered mobile, then a manual exception process — biometric failure (worn fingerprints, elderly) must never mean denial of essential services.

Deep answer: §4.2 step 7, §9.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Security vs inclusion.

Follow-ups: 1. Monitoring? → Failure rates by region. 2. Children? → Biometric updates.

Red flags: Biometric-only with no fallback.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How would you handle 50 million people trying to book 1 million vaccine slots at 4 pm?

30-second answer: Serve search from cached availability snapshots via CDN, protect booking with rate limits, CAPTCHA and OTP tokens, decrement capacity atomically per session, stagger releases, and consider a randomised waiting room so fast connections and bots don't win.

Deep answer: §4.4, §5.6, §6.6.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Staleness and friction vs stability and fairness.

Follow-ups: 1. Stale counts? → UI refresh, explain. 2. Hot sessions? → Bucketed counters.

Red flags: Letting search hit the primary DB.

Q6 [B2] How are biometrics protected between the fingerprint scanner and the server?

30-second answer: Certified registered devices encrypt the biometric inside the device with a session key wrapped by the authority's public key, sign it with the device's private key, and include a timestamp; the host application never sees raw biometrics and the server rejects replays.

Deep answer: §4.2, §5.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Device certification cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Compromised device? → Revoke certificate. 2. Replay? → Timestamp and transaction ID.

Red flags: Sending raw fingerprint images over HTTPS from an app.

Q7 [B2] Why use virtual IDs and per-agency tokens?

30-second answer: So agencies don't store or share the real ID number, and different agencies can't link their records through a common identifier; VIDs are revocable aliases, tokens are agency-specific derivations kept in vaults.

Deep answer: §4.6, §5.4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Integration complexity.

Follow-ups: 1. Rotation? → New VID revokes old. 2. Vault? → HSM-backed.

Red flags: One global identifier stored everywhere.

Q8 [B2] How does iris matching work, and why is it good for de-duplication?

30-second answer: The iris is normalised and encoded into a ~2,048-bit code; two codes are compared by masked fractional Hamming distance using XOR and popcount, which is extremely fast and highly discriminating, making billion-scale 1:N search feasible.

Deep answer: §6.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Capture requires cooperative subjects and good devices.

Follow-ups: 1. Twins? → Different irises. 2. Speed? → Bit operations, SIMD.

Red flags: Treating iris like face embeddings.

Q9 [B2] How do you design the vaccinator app for poor connectivity?

30-second answer: Offline-first: download the day's appointments, record doses locally with signatures and sequence numbers, sync when connected with idempotent uploads, and generate certificates after sync; walk-ins registered locally with later de-dup.

Deep answer: §4.5, §10.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Delayed certificates; duplicates.

Follow-ups: 1. Conflicts? → Server rules. 2. Device loss? → Encrypted storage.

Red flags: Online-only field apps.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ Design biometric de-duplication for a billion people.

30-second answer: Extract templates for fingers, irises and face; shard the gallery in memory across many nodes; broadcast each query, compare in parallel with pruning, fuse multi-modal scores, use strict high/low thresholds with manual adjudication in between, and run multiple vendors for accuracy and resilience — all as a queued batch pipeline.

Deep answer: §5.1, §5.2, §6.1–6.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Cost vs accuracy; enrolment latency.

Follow-ups: 1. FMR at scale? → Per-search false candidates. 2. Algorithm upgrades? → Re-extract from raw images.

Red flags: A database index on fingerprints.

Q11 [B3] How do you choose biometric thresholds?

30-second answer: From labelled genuine and impostor score distributions, plot FMR vs FNMR (DET curves) and choose operating points for the use: 1:N de-dup needs extremely low per-comparison FMR because N is huge; 1:1 auth balances inclusion (FNMR) with security; add a manual-review band.

Deep answer: §6.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Inclusion vs fraud.

Follow-ups: 1. Demographic differentials? → Test per group. 2. Drift? → Monitor.

Red flags: One threshold for everything.

Q12 [B3] How would you build the authentication service for 10k requests per second nationwide?

30-second answer: Stateless validators behind licensed gateways, signature and replay checks, HSM-backed decryption, a replicated template KV store keyed by ID or token, fast 1:1 matchers, active-active data centres, per-agency quotas, signed yes/no responses and append-only audit logs.

Deep answer: §5.3.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Latency vs security layers.

Follow-ups: 1. DC failure? → Gateway routing. 2. Hot keys? → None, per-person lookups.

Red flags: Returning biometric data in responses.

Q13 [B3] How do you make certificate signing keys safe and manageable?

30-second answer: Keep private keys in HSMs, sign via a stateless service with audit, publish public keys with key IDs, rotate keys on a schedule while old keys remain valid for verification, support revocation lists, and plan compromise response (re-issue under a new key).

Deep answer: §5.7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Verifier updates.

Follow-ups: 1. Formats? → Interop standards. 2. Offline verifiers? → Embedded keys.

Red flags: Keys in application config.

Q14 [B3] How would you prevent bots from grabbing all the vaccine slots?

30-second answer: OTP-authenticated booking, CAPTCHA at booking, rate limits per IP, token and device, automation fingerprinting, capped attempts, delayed public availability data, and a randomised waiting room at release time.

Deep answer: §6.6, §6.8.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Friction for real users.

Follow-ups: 1. False positives? → Step-up, not block. 2. Ecosystem apps? → Rate-limited open APIs.

Red flags: Relying on CAPTCHA alone.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design a national digital identity system from scratch.

30-second answer: Minimal data, random IDs, certified offline-capable enrolment with signed encrypted packets, multi-modal multi-vendor biometric de-dup with adjudication, a yes/no authentication service via licensed gateways and certified devices, eKYC with consent, VIDs and tokens for unlinkability, resident controls and audit logs, legal safeguards and inclusion fallbacks.

Deep answer: §2–§6, §9.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Utility vs privacy; inclusion vs assurance.

Follow-ups: 1. Surveillance risk? → No purpose logging, tokens. 2. Ecosystem? → Open APIs, licensing.

Red flags: A central database that every agency queries for full profiles.

Q16 [B4] What privacy risks does a national ID create, and how would you mitigate them?

30-second answer: Profiling by linking records across agencies, function creep, breaches and exclusion; mitigate with data minimisation, unlinkable per-agency tokens and VIDs, yes/no responses, no purpose logging, consent-based eKYC, offline verification options, strong legal limits, independent audits and resident visibility of use.

Deep answer: §5.4, §9.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Convenience for agencies.

Follow-ups: 1. Breach at an agency? → Vault rules. 2. Legal checks? → Courts, regulator.

Red flags: Security only, no governance.

Q17 [B4] How would you run a mass vaccination platform end to end?

30-second answer: Registration with OTP and ID de-dup, centre and session management, cached slot search and atomic booking, walk-in support, an offline-first vaccinator app, instant signed QR certificates, open APIs for the ecosystem, supply and coverage dashboards, and heavy launch operations (load tests, staggered releases, bot defence, multi-provider OTP).

Deep answer: §4.4, §4.5, §5.6, §5.7, §10.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed of launch vs robustness.

Follow-ups: 1. International travel? → Interop formats. 2. Corrections? → Re-issue.

Red flags: Same database for search, booking and analytics.

Q18 [B4] What is 'digital public infrastructure' and how does it change system design?

30-second answer: Shared, open, interoperable rails (identity, payments, data sharing, credentials) that private and public actors build on; design emphasises open APIs and standards, minimal centralisation, federated participants, consent, certification of ecosystem components and governance — the platform enables rather than owns every application.

Deep answer: §3, links to I03.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Control vs ecosystem growth.

Follow-ups: 1. Examples? → ID, UPI, credentials. 2. Risks? → Concentration.

Red flags: Building every app inside the platform.

Q19 [B4] How would you upgrade biometric algorithms for a billion enrolled people?

30-second answer: Keep raw images in an encrypted archive, re-extract templates with the new algorithm in batch, run both old and new matchers in parallel (shadow mode) and compare decisions, recalibrate thresholds on labelled data, switch gradually by vendor or modality, and keep rollback.

Deep answer: §5.2, §7.1.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Storage and compute cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Templates only? → Can't upgrade. 2. Vendor change? → ISO standards.

Red flags: Discarding raw images.

Q20 [B4] How do you balance inclusion and security in national authentication?

30-second answer: Measure failure rates by region, age, occupation and device; offer multiple modalities and OTP fallback; keep manual exception processes with audit; tune thresholds per use-case risk; improve devices and liveness; and never let authentication failure silently deny entitlements.

Deep answer: §4.2, §9, §10.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Fraud through fallbacks.

Follow-ups: 1. Risk-based auth? → Use-case thresholds. 2. Feedback loop? → Grievances.

Red flags: Treating the false rejection rate as the user's problem.

docs.title: 13. Summary
docs.text:
1. Population-scale public systems serve everyone, face policy-driven flash crowds and are bound by law, privacy and inclusion as much as by scale.
  2. Digital ID separates 1:N de-duplication (a massive batch biometric pipeline with fusion, multi-vendor matching and manual adjudication) from 1:1 authentication (a fast yes/no with device-level encryption, licensed gateways and audit).
  3. Privacy by design means random IDs, minimal data, yes/no responses, VIDs and per-agency tokens, consent-based eKYC and resident controls.
  4. Vaccination platforms survive flash crowds with cached search, atomic booking, bot defences and staggered releases, and build trust with offline-verifiable signed certificates.
  5. Algorithms: minutiae matching, iris codes with Hamming distance, face embeddings, score fusion and thresholds, liveness detection, Verhoeff checksums, fair allocation under scarcity, and verifiable credential signatures.

docs.title: I15. Multiplayer Gaming & Leaderboards
docs.text:
Chapter at a glance

Sector: gaming (mobile and PC online multiplayer, casual and competitive) · Format: system design walkthrough with no code · Reader bands: B1 → B4

Builds on: Ch 51 (top-K), Ch 44 (cache), Ch 41 (chat), I13 (live events)

What you get: a reference platform for a popular online multiplayer game. Think a battle-royale or team shooter on mobile, plus casual PvP (player-versus-player) games. The platform covers:

  • accounts and login;
  • matchmaking by skill and latency;
  • dedicated game servers allocated worldwide;
  • real-time netcode: authoritative server, client prediction, lag compensation and rollback;
  • parties, friends, voice and chat;
  • leaderboards: global, regional, friends and seasonal, for tens of millions of players;
  • progression, inventory and the in-game economy and store;
  • anti-cheat;
  • live ops, with events, seasons and remote config.

It also explains the algorithms (Elo/Glicko/TrueSkill ratings, the matchmaking queue, server tick and interest management, lag compensation, leaderboard ranking at scale, anti-cheat detection, loot and drop fairness) and the data platform and tech stack.

Reading time: 80 min.

Sources and honesty

  • Some netcode techniques have been described publicly in developer talks and blogs, including Valve's lag compensation, rollback in fighting games and Overwatch's GDC talks. These are marked "publicly described (VERIFY)".
  • India's rules on online gaming changed significantly in 2025. The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 addresses real-money games (VERIFY its current status and rules). This chapter designs a free-to-play game with in-app purchases, not real-money gaming.
  • Everything else is a reference design.

docs.title: 1.1 What makes games different
docs.text: Aspect Typical web app Real-time multiplayer game Latency 100s of ms is fine < 50–100 ms round trip matters. Jitter ruins play State Request/response Continuous shared simulation at 20–60 ticks per second Consistency Strong or eventual Server-authoritative world with client-side prediction Load shape Diurnal Diurnal plus launch days, season starts, events with 10× spikes Adversaries Fraudsters Cheaters with full control of their client Fun n/a Fair matches, short queues. Business metrics depend on them

docs.title: 1.2 Main systems
docs.text: System What it does Identity and accounts Login (guest, phone, social, platform accounts), profiles, linking, bans Social Friends, parties, clans, presence, chat, voice Matchmaking Queues players by mode, skill, region and party. Forms balanced matches Game server fleet Dedicated servers per match, allocated in many regions, autoscaled Game server (the simulation) Authoritative game loop, netcode, hit detection, match results Session/lobby service Match lifecycle, reconnects, spectators Progression and inventory XP, levels, battle pass, unlocked items, loadouts Economy and store Currencies, purchases, offers, receipts, refunds Leaderboards and ranks Seasonal ranked tiers, global and regional boards, friends boards Anti-cheat Client integrity, server validation, statistical detection, reports and bans Live ops Events, remote config, A/B tests, news, push Telemetry and analytics Match events, performance, retention, monetisation

docs.title: 1.3 Scale for this design (assumptions)
docs.text:
Quantity Value Registered players 100M; 20M daily active Peak concurrent users (CCU) 3M Players per match 100 (battle royale) or 10 (5v5) Concurrent matches ~30k–100k Match length 20–30 min (BR), 10 min (casual) Server tick rate 30 Hz (BR), 60 Hz (competitive shooter) Leaderboard 20M entries per season, updated after every match Telemetry events ~5M events/s at peak

Estimation highlights:

  • Game server capacity: one process runs one BR match of 100 players at 30 Hz, using about 1–2 cores.
    • 3M CCU in BR gives 30k matches, which is roughly 30k–60k cores worldwide at peak.
    • That fleet has to be elastic, and it is the biggest infrastructure cost.
  • Bandwidth per player: 30 snapshots/s × ~500 bytes (after delta compression) is ~15 KB/s, or 120 kbps down.
    • 3M players need ~360 Gbps of egress from game servers.
    • Egress from game servers is a real cost item.
  • Match results: 30k matches ending every ~25 minutes is ~20 results/s. Each result updates up to 100 players, so ~2k leaderboard updates/s on average and more at the top of the hour.
  • Matchmaking: 3M players cycling every ~25 minutes means ~2k players/s entering queues. Queues are per region and mode.

docs.title: 2.1 Functional
docs.text:
1. Accounts. Log in, link devices, keep progress across devices, and let parents set controls for minors.
  2. Social. Friends, invites, parties of up to 4, clans, text and voice chat, and presence ("in match").
  3. Matchmaking.
    • Queue for a mode, solo or as a party.
    • Get a fair match (similar skill) with low latency, within about 30–60 s.
    • Backfill disconnected slots in some modes.
  4. Gameplay.
    • Smooth movement and shooting that feels responsive.
    • Fair hit registration.
    • Reconnect after a disconnect.
    • Spectating, and replays for some modes.
  5. Results. A match summary, then XP, rank changes, rewards and leaderboard updates.
  6. Leaderboards. Global, country, friends and clan boards; seasonal and all-time; "my rank" and "players around me".
  7. Economy. Buy currency through app stores or payment gateways. Buy items, a battle pass and bundles. Receive gifts, promotions and refunds.
  8. Anti-cheat. Detect and ban cheats; let players report; handle appeals.
  9. Live ops. Timed events, new modes, config changes without an app update, and staged rollout of content.

docs.title: 2.2 Non-functional
docs.text: Attribute Target In-match latency Players matched to a server with < 60–80 ms RTT where possible Server tick stability Frame time below the tick budget (33 ms at 30 Hz) with headroom Matchmaking time P50 < 30 s, P95 < 90 s (relaxed at low population) Availability Login, matchmaking and store at 99.9%+. A single match can fail without a global impact Economy correctness No duplicate grants, no lost purchases, and an audit of every currency movement Leaderboard freshness Rank updated within seconds of match end Fairness Balanced matches, cheat-free play, transparent odds for random rewards (VERIFY local rules) Cost Game server fleet cost per CCU hour kept under budget

docs.title: 4. How It Works — Journeys End to End
4.1 Journey 1: from app open to match start
docs.text:
1. App open.
    • The client checks its version against remote config and downloads updated content (maps, skins) from the CDN in the background.
    • It logs in with a device ID, phone OTP or a platform account, and receives a session token.
    • Presence connects over a WebSocket.
  2. Home screen.
    • The profile, inventory, battle pass progress, events (from live ops) and store offers load.
    • Offers may be personalised through experiments.
  3. Party up.
    • Friends accept an invite and a party is formed in the social service.
    • The party leader chooses a mode and queues. The whole party enters matchmaking as one ticket with the members' ratings.
  4. Latency probing. The client pings a set of region endpoints (quality-of-service beacons) and reports RTTs to the matchmaker. Candidate regions are those under the latency threshold.
  5. Matchmaking (§6.2).
    • The ticket enters queues for eligible regions.
    • The matchmaker groups tickets into a balanced match: similar ratings, parties matched to parties where possible, and team balance by total rating.
    • The acceptable skill range widens as wait time grows.
  6. Allocation.
    • Once the match is formed, the allocator requests a ready game server in the chosen region from the fleet manager, which keeps a warm buffer.
    • The server gets the match config (map, mode, player IDs, teams) and one-time join tokens for each player.
  7. Connect.
    • Clients receive the server IP:port and a join token, and connect over UDP.
    • The server validates tokens, loads players' loadouts from progression (or from the match config) and starts the pre-game lobby, where players drop in.

docs.title: 4.2 Journey 2: inside a match — the game loop
docs.text:
1. Client input. Each client frame (60 fps), the client samples input (movement, aim, fire) and sends input commands to the server, tagged with a sequence number and client timestamp. Batches of inputs are sent 30–60 times per second.
  2. Client prediction.
    • The client applies its own inputs immediately to its local copy of its own character, so movement feels instant.
    • It keeps a history of inputs not yet acknowledged.
  3. Server tick. At 30 Hz the authoritative server:
    1. Collects inputs from all players.
    2. Simulates movement with the game's physics and validates it (speed limits, collisions, no walking through walls).
    3. Processes shots with lag compensation (§6.4).
    4. Applies damage, deaths and item pickups.
    5. Updates the storm/zone.
    6. Produces the new world state.
  4. Snapshots to clients.
    • The server sends each client a snapshot of relevant state: its own authoritative position and entities in its area of interest (§6.5).
    • Snapshots are delta-compressed against the last acknowledged snapshot.
  5. Reconciliation. When the client receives the authoritative state for its own character, it rewinds to that state and replays unacknowledged inputs. Small differences are smoothed; big ones snap (the player feels "rubber-banding").
  6. Other players' rendering. Clients render other players slightly in the past (e.g. 100 ms interpolation buffer) between two snapshots, for smooth movement despite packet jitter.
  7. Hit registration.
    • When a player fires, the client may show hit effects immediately (optimistic), but the server decides.
    • Lag compensation rewinds other players to where the shooter saw them.
  8. Events and telemetry. Kills, deaths, damage, item use and positions (sampled) are streamed to telemetry. Suspicious patterns are flagged for anti-cheat.

docs.title: 4.3 Journey 3: match end, rewards and leaderboards
docs.text:
1. Match ends.
    • The server computes results: placement, kills, damage, survival time, team outcome.
    • It sends a signed match result to the session service.
  2. Session service.
    • Validates the result: signature, known server, match ID not already processed (idempotency).
    • Publishes a MatchCompleted event.
  3. Consumers (asynchronous, each idempotent by match ID and player):
    • Ratings: update each player's skill rating (§6.1) and ranked points or tier.
    • Progression: XP, battle pass progress, mission completions.
    • Economy: rewards such as soft currency and loot drops, credited through the ledger.
    • Leaderboards: update seasonal scores (§6.6).
    • Anti-cheat: statistical checks on the performance (§6.7).
    • Analytics: the match record goes to the lakehouse.
  4. Client summary. The client shows XP gained, rank change and rewards, typically within 1–3 s via a push over the realtime gateway.
  5. Server teardown. The game server uploads a replay (if recorded), cleans up and returns to the fleet (or is recycled).

docs.title: 4.4 Journey 4: buying the battle pass
docs.text:
1. The player taps "Buy Battle Pass (950 gems)". They have 500 gems, so they buy a gem pack for ₹449 through the app store (Google Play/App Store billing) or a payment gateway on PC (UPI/cards; VERIFY store policies for India).
  2. The store completes payment and the client receives a receipt.
  3. The client sends the receipt to the economy service:
    • The service verifies it with the store's server API.
    • It checks the transaction ID has not been used before (idempotency, stopping replayed receipts).
    • It credits gems in the ledger: debit "store revenue clearing", credit "player gems wallet".

  4. The player buys the battle pass. The economy service atomically:

    • debits 950 gems from the wallet;
    • grants the battle pass entitlement in inventory.

    This happens in one transaction, or as a saga with compensation. 5. Refunds. Store notifications (refund or chargeback) arrive through webhooks. The service claws back currency, going negative if already spent (policy), and flags abuse. 6. Audit. Every currency movement is a ledger entry with a reason, which supports support-team investigations and finance reconciliation with store reports.

docs.title: 4.5 Journey 5: a cheater and the ban wave
docs.text:
1. A player uses an aimbot. It reads game memory, and the client-side anti-cheat module may detect known signatures or tampering.

  2. Server-side, statistical signals appear:

    • inhumanly fast target acquisition;
    • headshot rate far above the rating norm;
    • tracking through walls;
    • impossible reaction times.

    The anti-cheat model (§6.7) scores the player per match. 3. Player reports add evidence. A replay or kill-cam clip goes to a review queue. 4. Action. - High-confidence detection leads to the account being flagged. Bans are often held for a ban wave, so cheat makers don't learn which change caused detection. - Devices or hardware IDs may be banned for repeat offenders. - Affected matches may have rating changes rolled back for victims. 5. Appeals go through a support process with evidence.

docs.title: 4.6 Journey 6: a season launch
docs.text:
1. Weeks before. New content (map, skins, battle pass) is built and delivered via the CDN in a patch.
    • Pre-download is enabled days before, which spreads the bandwidth load.
  2. Launch hour.
    • Remote config flips the season at a scheduled time.
    • Ranked tiers soft-reset (§6.1) and new leaderboards open.
    • CCU spikes 2–3× as lapsed players return.
  3. Capacity. The fleet is pre-scaled with extra warm servers per region, and matchmakers scale.
    • The login service has queueing ("You are #12,340 in queue") to protect the backend if needed.
  4. Monitoring. Watch queue times, match start failures, crash rates on new content, store purchase success and economy anomalies (an exploit granting infinite currency).
    • Kill switches exist for features and store items.

docs.title: 5.1 Game server fleet management
docs.text:
• Fleet per region. Pools of VMs or bare-metal machines, each running several game server processes (containers).
    • States: Ready (warm, waiting), Allocated (match assigned), Shutdown.
  • Buffer autoscaling.
    • Keep a buffer of Ready servers (e.g. 10–20% or a fixed count) per region and mode.
    • Scale nodes up as the buffer depletes. Scale down by draining nodes without matches.
    • Never kill a node with active matches.
  • Hybrid capacity. Bare metal or reserved instances for baseline load, cloud VMs for peaks, and spot instances only for short matches or with graceful handling (VERIFY cost trade-offs).
  • Tooling. Kubernetes + Agones (open source), or managed services such as GameLift or PlayFab Multiplayer Servers (VERIFY product names and capabilities).
  • Health. Servers report tick timing and player count. The allocator avoids unhealthy nodes, and crashed matches notify the session service to compensate players (e.g. no rank loss).

docs.title: 5.2 Matchmaking service
docs.text:
• Tickets. (ticket ID, player IDs, mode, ratings, party size, region RTTs, preferences, created time).
  • Pools. Per (region, mode, maybe platform). Tickets can be in several regional pools until matched.
  • Match function. Runs every ~1 s over each pool and forms matches that meet the constraints (§6.2).
    • Frameworks: Open Match (open source) separates the match function from the infrastructure (VERIFY).
  • Backfill. Replace leavers in ongoing matches (casual modes).
  • Low-population handling. Widen skill ranges, merge regions, add bots for casual modes (commonly done in mobile BR games; VERIFY for any specific title).

docs.title: 5.3 Netcode and the authoritative server
docs.text:
• The server holds the truth. Clients send inputs, not state ("I pressed forward", not "I am at x,y"), so they can't teleport.
  • Validation. Movement speed, fire rate, ammo, cooldowns and line-of-sight are all checked on the server.
  • Reliability over UDP.
    • Unreliable channel for snapshots (latest wins).
    • Reliable-ordered channel for important events (chat, item purchases in-match).
    • ACK bitfields in packet headers.
  • Bandwidth control. Delta compression, quantisation (positions to cm precision, angles to 16 bits), interest management, and priority for nearby entities.
  • Tick budget. Profile the server loop. At 100 players, physics, hit detection and replication must fit inside 33 ms with headroom. Spatial partitioning speeds up queries.

docs.title: 5.4 Economy ledger
docs.text:
• Double-entry. Every movement has matching debit and credit entries, per currency: hard (purchased) gems and soft (earned) coins. Hard currency may need separate accounting of paid vs free portions, for revenue recognition and regulations (VERIFY).
  • Idempotency keys. Store transaction IDs, match IDs and grant IDs. Retries never double-grant.
  • Inventory. Entitlements such as skins and battle pass tiers are recorded with their source (purchase, reward, gift) and time.
  • Exploit containment.
    • Anomaly detection on currency velocity (an account earning 100× normal).
    • Per-account limits.
    • Rollback tooling.

docs.title: 5.5 Leaderboards
docs.text:
• Types:
    • global;
    • regional/country;
    • friends;
    • clan;
    • seasonal (reset each season) vs lifetime;
    • event-specific (time-boxed).
  • Operations:
    • update a score (after a match);
    • get the top N;
    • get "my rank";
    • get neighbours ("players around me");
    • get friends' ranks.
  • Implementation: see §6.6.

docs.title: 5.6 Social, presence and chat
docs.text:
• Presence. Heartbeats over WebSocket to a presence store (Redis with TTL). Friends subscribe to changes.
  • Parties. A small state machine (invite, join, leave, leader). Party state is kept on a party service shard and pushed to members.
  • Chat. Similar to Ch 41, with moderation, filters and reporting, plus stricter settings for minors.
  • Voice. In-match team voice is carried by the game server or a separate voice SFU (Vivox-style services; VERIFY). Features include push-to-talk and mute and report.

docs.title: 5.7 Live ops and remote config
docs.text:
• Config service. Versioned JSON configs (drop rates, event schedules, balance tweaks, store layout), targeted by segment (country, platform, app version, experiment arm).
    • Clients fetch at login and on push.
    • Config reaches game servers at match start.
  • Experiments. A/B tests for store offers, onboarding and matchmaking parameters, with guardrail metrics (retention, match quality).
  • Kill switches. For buggy items, exploits, or modes causing crashes.

docs.title: 6.1 Skill rating systems
docs.text:
• Elo.
    • Expected score E_A = 1 / (1 + 10^((R_B − R_A)/400)).
    • After a match, R_A ← R_A + K(S_A − E_A).
    • Simple, and designed for 1v1.
  • Glicko / Glicko-2.
    • Adds rating deviation (RD), the uncertainty. New or returning players have high RD, so their ratings move fast. RD shrinks with play and grows with inactivity.
    • Glicko-2 adds volatility.
  • TrueSkill (published by Microsoft Research).
    • Bayesian: each player has skill ~ N(μ, σ²).
    • Supports teams and multi-player free-for-all (placements in a battle royale).
    • Updates via factor graphs and message passing.
    • The displayed "conservative" skill is μ − 3σ.
    • TrueSkill 2 adds factors such as individual performance and quitting (publicly described; VERIFY).
  • Battle royale adaptation.
    • Treat placement as a ranking of teams, and update pairwise or with a TrueSkill-style multi-team update.
    • Kills may add a performance factor.
  • Visible rank vs hidden MMR.
    • Ranked tiers (Bronze → Diamond) are points-based for motivation, with win streak bonuses.
    • The hidden MMR is used for matchmaking.
    • At season start, soft-reset visible ranks (compress toward the mean) and raise the RD.

docs.title: 6.2 Matchmaking algorithm
docs.text:
• Goal: form matches that minimise a cost combining:
    • skill disparity (within and across teams);
    • latency (all players under the threshold to the chosen region);
    • wait time (a penalty that grows as players wait);
    • party composition (premades vs solos);
    • other constraints (platform, input device, language).
  • Typical approach:
    1. Sort the pool by rating. Candidate groups come from windows around each ticket.
    2. Each ticket's acceptable window expands over time, e.g. ±50 MMR at 0 s, ±150 at 30 s, ±300 at 60 s.
    3. Greedily form matches starting from the oldest tickets, which guards against starvation.
    4. For team balance, assign players to teams to minimise the difference in total (or mean) skill. This is a partitioning heuristic: sort by skill and alternate snake-draft (1-2-2-1), or run a small search.
  • Battle royale: 100 players is a large match, so skill matching is looser. Use broad skill brackets, fill by time, and region is critical.
  • Evaluation: measure predicted match quality (e.g. the TrueSkill draw probability) against actual outcomes, and queue times by skill band. Top players wait longest.

docs.title: 6.3 Client prediction and reconciliation
docs.text:
• Prediction. The client runs the same movement code locally on its inputs. The server's authoritative state arrives later with the last processed input sequence number.
  • Reconciliation.
    • Set the local state to the server state at sequence N.
    • Re-apply inputs N+1 onwards.
    • If the result differs from the displayed state by a small error, smooth over a few frames; otherwise snap.
  • Entity interpolation. Other players are rendered by interpolating between buffered snapshots at a render time slightly behind the latest (e.g. 2 snapshot intervals). This handles jitter; extrapolation is used only briefly on packet loss.

docs.title: 6.4 Lag compensation
docs.text:
• Problem: the shooter sees enemies where they were ~RTT/2 + interpolation delay ago. Without compensation, players have to aim ahead.
  • Server-side rewind (publicly described for Source engine games; VERIFY):
    1. The server keeps a history of each player's hitboxes for the last ~1 s.
    2. When a shot command arrives, it estimates the time the shooter saw (current time − shooter latency − interpolation delay).
    3. It rewinds other players' hitboxes to that time, performs the ray cast and restores them.
  • Trade-off: "shot behind cover". The victim reaches cover on their screen but still dies, because the shooter saw them earlier.
    • Cap the rewind (e.g. 200 ms) to limit the advantage of high-ping players.
  • Rollback netcode (fighting games, 1v1):
    • Clients simulate with predicted remote inputs.
    • When the actual inputs arrive, they roll back and re-simulate frames.
    • This needs deterministic simulation and fast re-simulation (GGPO-style; publicly described).

docs.title: 6.5 Interest management
docs.text:
• Problem: 100 players × 1000s of entities. Sending everything to everyone is too much bandwidth, and it leaks information to wallhacks.
  • Spatial partitioning. A grid or quadtree over the map. Each client receives entities in nearby cells, with priority by distance and relevance.
  • Visibility culling. Don't send enemies the client cannot possibly see (occlusion checks). This reduces what wallhack cheats can reveal.
  • Update frequency by priority. Nearby enemies every tick; distant vehicles every few ticks.

docs.title: 6.6 Leaderboard ranking at scale
docs.text:
• Redis sorted sets (ZADD/ZREVRANK/ZREVRANGE) handle the top-N and rank for millions of entries in O(log N).
    • One sorted set with 20M members is feasible on a large node (memory ~ a few GB). It is a hot key for writes, though.
  • Scaling beyond one node.
    • Shard by score ranges. Keep a small count index (how many players are in each shard or score bucket).
      • Rank = (players in higher buckets) + (rank within the bucket).
      • Updates move a player between buckets.
    • Or shard by player hash, with approximate global rank:
      • maintain a histogram of scores (bucket counts) globally, updated incrementally;
      • rank ≈ sum of counts above the player's score, plus an estimate within the bucket;
      • show exact ranks only for the top 10k (a separate exact sorted set) and percentiles for everyone else ("Top 3%").
  • Friends leaderboards. Fetch friends' scores directly (a small N) and sort per request. Cache per user for a short TTL.
  • Seasonal resets. Create a new board keyed by season ID. Archive the old one to storage.
  • Ties. Encode the tie-break in the score, e.g. score × 10^10 + (MAX_TS − achieved time), so earlier achievers rank higher.
  • Integrity. Only server-validated results update boards. Anti-cheat can remove entries.

docs.title: 6.7 Anti-cheat detection
docs.text:
• Layers:
    1. Prevention by design: server authority, input validation, interest management (don't send hidden enemies).
    2. Client integrity:
      • anti-tamper and obfuscation;
      • integrity checks;
      • detection of known cheat software signatures, debuggers, emulators and rooted devices (with care for false positives);
      • on PC, kernel-level anti-cheat is used by some titles (controversial; VERIFY).

    3. Server-side statistics: features per player per match:

      • headshot ratio;
      • reaction time (time from an enemy becoming visible to aim on target);
      • aim snap angles;
      • accuracy vs distance;
      • tracking through occluders;
      • kill/death ratio vs MMR expectations.

      Models (gradient-boosted trees, sequence models over aim trajectories) score deviation from human distributions. 4. Reports and review: weight reports by the reporter's accuracy history. - Response policy: confidence thresholds, delayed ban waves, shadow pools (cheaters matched with cheaters), hardware or device bans, and appeals.

docs.title: 6.8 Random rewards and drop fairness
docs.text:
• Loot drop tables with configured probabilities, served by the server (never computed on the client).
  • Pity systems: a guarantee within N attempts (a counter per player), or increasing probability after failures ("bad luck protection").
  • Disclosure: publish odds where required, and consider regulations on paid random items (loot boxes) by country (VERIFY).
  • Auditability: log RNG seeds and outcomes per grant for dispute resolution.

docs.title: 7.1 Operational stores
docs.text: Data Store (reference) Notes Accounts, profiles PostgreSQL/MySQL sharded, or DynamoDB-style Low latency lookup Presence, parties, sessions Redis TTLs Matchmaking pools In-memory in the matchmaker (+ Redis for coordination) Ephemeral Match results Kafka + Cassandra/ScyllaDB (by player, time) Match history Progression, inventory NoSQL document per player + event log Frequent writes Economy ledger PostgreSQL (sharded by player), append-only Strong correctness Leaderboards Redis sorted sets (+ histograms), snapshots to object storage Seasonal archives Replays Object storage + CDN Retention policy Config Versioned store + CDN Remote config

docs.title: 7.2 Telemetry and analytics
docs.text:
• Events: client performance (FPS, crashes, RTT), gameplay (kills, deaths, positions sampled), economy (purchases, grants, spends), social, and funnel steps.
    • These flow to Kafka and then to the lakehouse.
  • Game analytics:
    • weapon balance (win rates, time-to-kill by weapon);
    • heatmaps of deaths by map location;
    • match quality (stomps vs close games);
    • queue times;
    • server performance.
  • Business analytics: DAU/MAU, retention cohorts (D1/D7/D30), ARPDAU, conversion, and churn prediction for re-engagement offers.
  • ML: MMR models, the cheat detector, churn and LTV prediction, offer personalisation, toxicity detection in chat.

docs.title: 7.3 Data flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    CLI[Game clients] --> K[Kafka]
    GS[Game servers] --> K
    SVC[Platform services] --> K
    K --> STREAM[Stream processing - real-time dashboards, fraud]
    K --> LAKE[Lakehouse]
    LAKE --> DW[Warehouse - KPIs, balance, economy]
    LAKE --> ML[ML training - MMR, cheat, churn]
