docs.title: Key decisions
docs.text: Decision Choice Why Geography City → zones (hexagons, e.g. H3, or polygons) for supply, demand and serviceability Bounded optimisation and local signals Serviceability Precomputed per (restaurant, customer hexagon) and refreshed every minute with zone stress Fast feed and honest ETAs ETA Decomposed: dispatch wait, rider to restaurant, prep remaining, pickup wait, travel to customer, last mile; ML per component Explainable, updatable Dispatch Batch optimisation every few seconds per zone, timed to food readiness Riders don't wait, food doesn't wait Order state Event-sourced state machine with Kafka events Many consumers, audit Peak control Zone-level levers: radius shrink, surge fees, longer ETAs, hiding far restaurants, rider incentives Keeps promises at peak Location In-memory geo index for live riders plus Kafka for history Fast nearest-rider queries

docs.title: 4. How It Works — Journeys End to End
4.1 Journey 1: opening the app at 8:15 pm
docs.text:
1. Location. The app sends the customer's location (GPS or saved address). The server maps it to a hexagon (H3 resolution ~8–9) and to a delivery zone.

  2. Serviceability (§5.2). The serviceability service returns the restaurants that can deliver to this hexagon now. For each one it applies:

    • open (timings, holiday, and whether it is currently accepting orders);
    • distance or travel time within the restaurant's radius, which shrinks when the zone is stressed;
    • ETA estimate: precomputed restaurant-to-hexagon travel time plus current prep-time and dispatch-delay signals;
    • delivery fee: base by distance, surge by zone stress, waived for members or by offers.

    This is a lookup into precomputed tables refreshed every ~1 minute by stream jobs. 3. Feed assembly (§6.6). The feed service: - takes the serviceable set (~400 restaurants); - scores each one for this user with a ranking model (cuisine affinity, past orders, price band, rating, ETA, offers, freshness); - mixes in ads: sponsored slots labelled and auctioned (Ch 43); - builds widgets such as "Order again", "Top picks for you", "Under 30 mins" and offer carousels. 4. Response. The feed is returned in ~200 ms. Images come from the CDN. Impressions are logged. 5. Rain mode. If it's raining in this zone, the feed may: - show fewer far restaurants; - show higher fees and ETAs; - show a banner: "High demand due to rain, delivery may take longer".

docs.title: 4.2 Journey 2: placing an order
docs.text:
1. Menu. Sameer opens a biryani restaurant and adds Chicken Biryani (full) with extra raita. The menu service shows availability, which the restaurant can toggle out of stock in real time.
  2. Cart. The cart service prices the order (§5.4):
    • items and add-ons;
    • packaging charges;
    • delivery fee (distance and surge);
    • platform fee;
    • GST: restaurant services through e-commerce operators at 5%, with the platform collecting and paying under Section 9(5) (VERIFY);
    • offers (restaurant-funded "50% off up to ₹100", platform coupons, membership);
    • final total and ETA promise.
  3. Checkout.
    • Address confirmation; a pin drop helps the rider.
    • Payment by UPI: the payment intent is created with an idempotency key. On success the order is created in the PLACED state.
    • With COD, the order is created directly, with risk checks such as COD limits for new users or risky addresses.
  4. Order event. OrderPlaced is published to Kafka. Consumers react:
    • restaurant notification;
    • ETA service (initial prediction);
    • dispatch (pre-planning);
    • analytics.
  5. Customer screen. "Waiting for restaurant to accept" with the ETA.

docs.title: 4.3 Journey 3: restaurant acceptance and prep
docs.text:
1. Notification. The restaurant's partner app (a tablet at the counter) rings loudly with the order details.
  2. Acceptance.
    • The staff accept within ~1–3 minutes and the app suggests a prep time, e.g. 18 minutes, which they can adjust.
    • Auto-accept is available for reliable restaurants.
    • Timeout or rejection triggers an attempt to call the restaurant. If that fails, the order is cancelled with a full refund, and the restaurant is penalised in ranking or reliability scores.
  3. Prep-time prediction (§6.2).
    • The platform's model predicts the actual food-ready time from:
      • the restaurant's history;
      • the items;
      • current kitchen load (open orders at that restaurant);
      • time of day;
      • the staff's entered estimate.
    • Restaurants often under- or over-estimate, so the model corrects for it.
  4. Mark ready. The restaurant taps "Food ready" when packed. This signal is noisy (some mark ready early to look good), so models also use rider wait times to calibrate.
  5. Item out of stock. The restaurant marks an item unavailable. The customer gets a prompt to choose a substitute or accept a partial refund, with a timeout default.

docs.title: 4.4 Journey 4: dispatch and pickup
docs.text:
1. Timing. Dispatch wants the rider to arrive at the restaurant just as the food is ready:

    • if the rider is early, they wait, which wastes rider time and capacity;
    • if they are late, the food waits and gets cold, and the ETA is missed.

    Dispatch therefore plans an assignment around (predicted ready time − rider travel time). 2. Batch optimisation (§6.4). Every ~10–20 s in each zone, the dispatcher: - collects unassigned orders and available riders: idle riders, and riders finishing a delivery nearby ("chained"); - computes costs (travel time to restaurant, wait at restaurant, delay to the customer vs promise, rider fairness); - solves an assignment problem (Hungarian / min-cost matching, or heuristics); - considers batching: two orders from the same or nearby restaurants going in the same direction can share a rider if neither customer's ETA suffers too much. 3. Offer to the rider. - The rider app shows the order (restaurant, distance, estimated earnings) and the rider accepts. - Rejections or timeouts send the order back to the pool, with a higher priority. 4. Pickup. - The rider navigates to the restaurant and is geofenced on arrival ("arrived at restaurant"). - Food is handed over, the rider confirms the order ID and items, and the status becomes PICKED_UP. - Rider wait time at the restaurant is recorded. It is a key signal for prep-time models. 5. Delivery. - The rider navigates to the customer, and the live location streams to the customer's map (§5.6). - The ETA is recomputed continuously from remaining route time plus a last-mile estimate (building access, finding the flat, apartment security). - Contact uses masked phone calls or chat. - Delivered: confirmed by geofence plus the rider tap. High-value orders may require a delivery OTP. 6. After delivery. - Rating prompts go to the customer. - Rider earnings are updated. - The rider becomes available, often already pre-assigned to a next order nearby.

docs.title: 4.5 Journey 5: the rain spike at 8:30 pm
docs.text:
1. Detection.
    • Order rates in Bengaluru zones jump 60% in 10 minutes.
    • Rider supply drops, because some riders log off in heavy rain.
    • Travel times increase. Zone stress, measured as open orders per available rider, crosses thresholds.
  2. Automatic levers, per zone, in a graduated order (§6.5):
    1. ETA inflation: show honest, longer ETAs so promises aren't broken.
    2. Rain or surge fee: this funds rider incentives and tempers demand.
    3. Rider incentives: "Rain bonus ₹30/order for the next 2 hours" pushed to offline riders nearby.
    4. Serviceability radius shrink: restaurants far from customers are hidden.
    5. Batching more aggressively: two orders per rider where routes align.
    6. Throttle: pause orders from restaurants with long prep backlogs. In extreme cases, show "Not accepting orders in your area right now".
  3. Monitoring. Ops dashboards show zone stress, ETA breaches and rider supply. City ops can override the levers manually.
  4. Recovery. As the rain stops, the levers relax gradually (hysteresis) to avoid oscillation.

docs.title: 4.6 Journey 6: a missing item complaint
docs.text:
1. Complaint. Sameer reports "raita missing" in the app's help section, with a photo option.
  2. Self-serve resolution. A rule and risk engine decides:
    • instant refund for low-value items when the customer is trustworthy (low complaint history);
    • escalation to an agent when the risk is high (frequent complaints, high-value claims).
  3. Refund. Issued to the source (UPI or card) or as platform credits, depending on the customer's choice and policy.
  4. Attribution. The cost is attributed to the restaurant (packing error) or the rider (tampering), based on evidence and patterns. It affects the restaurant's settlement through deductions, per contract, or its quality score.
  5. Abuse detection (§6.8): repeat complainers, linked accounts and photo reuse are flagged.

docs.title: 4.7 Journey 7: quick commerce (10-minute groceries)
docs.text:
1. Dark stores. Small warehouses within ~2–3 km of customers hold ~5–8k SKUs. Each store serves a tight polygon.
  2. Order. The customer orders milk, bread and chips. Serviceability shows a "10 mins" ETA, available only if the store has stock and pickers and riders are available.
  3. Picking.
    • The order drops to the store's picking system.
    • The pick route is optimised by slotting, since fast movers sit near the packing station (§6.9).
    • Picking takes ~2 minutes and packing ~1 minute.
  4. Dispatch. Riders wait at the store, so assignment is instant. Delivery takes ~5–7 minutes over short distances.
  5. Inventory.
    • Real-time stock per store.
    • Demand forecasting per SKU per store per hour drives replenishment from the mother warehouse (I12).
    • Stock-outs hide items from the app immediately.

docs.title: 5.1 Geo model: zones and hexagons
docs.text:
• Hexagons: the H3 grid (open-sourced by Uber) at a resolution where each cell is about 0.1–0.7 km². It is used for:
    • demand and supply counts;
    • serviceability tables;
    • ETA features (travel time between hexes);
    • surge.
  • Zones: operational areas (polygons) made of hexes, each with its own rider fleet, ops team and lever settings.
  • Travel time matrix: hex-to-hex travel times by time of day, learned from rider GPS traces, plus live traffic adjustments.

docs.title: 5.2 Serviceability and zone state
docs.text:
• Inputs, refreshed every 30–60 s by stream jobs:
    • restaurant status (open, accepting, current prep backlog);
    • zone stress (orders per available rider, rider wait times, ETA breach rate);
    • rain flags and weather;
    • lever settings (radius, fees).

  • Precomputed table: per (restaurant, customer hexagon) it holds:

    • serviceable or not;
    • ETA band;
    • delivery fee;
    • distance.

    Restaurants × nearby hexes is a manageable size, e.g. 250k × ~300 hexes ≈ 75M entries, held in Redis or an in-memory KV keyed by hex. - Consistency: the cart re-checks serviceability and fees at checkout, so the customer always sees a fresh promise before paying.

docs.title: 5.3 Catalogue and menus
docs.text:
• Structure:
    • restaurant → menu categories → items;
    • items carry variants (half/full), add-on groups (min/max choices), dietary tags, images, prices and tax category;
    • availability windows (breakfast menu) and out-of-stock flags.
  • Updates: restaurants edit through the partner app or POS integrations (some POS systems push menus and stock). Changes are versioned. The cart validates against the current version.
  • Search index: dishes and restaurants are indexed with synonyms ("biriyani" = "biryani"), transliteration (Hindi or Kannada typed in English) and spell correction (Ch 42).

docs.title: 5.4 Cart and pricing
docs.text:
• Components:
    • item subtotal;
    • packaging;
    • delivery fee (distance-based, plus surge, minus member waiver);
    • small-cart fee;
    • platform fee;
    • GST (per tax rules);
    • discounts with funding attribution (restaurant-funded vs platform-funded);
    • tip (optional, passed fully to the rider).
  • Offer engine (Ch 49): eligibility rules, stacking rules, budget caps and per-user limits.
  • Price snapshot: the final breakdown is stored with the order for invoices, settlements and refunds.

docs.title: 5.5 Order management
docs.text:
• State machine:
    • PLACED → ACCEPTED → (RIDER_ASSIGNED) → FOOD_READY → PICKED_UP → DELIVERED;
    • with branches: REJECTED, CANCELLED_BY_CUSTOMER / RESTAURANT / PLATFORM, UNDELIVERED (customer not reachable), and so on.
  • Event-sourced: each transition is an event. Consumers include notifications, tracking, ETA, settlements, support and analytics.
  • Timers: acceptance timeout, food-ready overdue, rider-not-assigned alerts, delivery overdue. These are scheduled timers (Ch 50) that trigger escalations.
  • Idempotency: client retries, payment callbacks and rider app retries over flaky networks all carry idempotency keys and state-transition guards.

docs.title: 5.6 Location and tracking
docs.text:
• Ingest:
    • rider apps send GPS every ~4 s while on a trip, less often when idle;
    • batches are uploaded when the network is poor;
    • the server applies map matching (snap to road), filters outliers and detects spoofing (I05).
  • Live geo index: an in-memory index (H3 cells or a geohash) of available riders, queried by dispatch for "riders within X minutes of the restaurant".
  • Customer tracking:
    • the rider's position is pushed through the realtime gateway every few seconds;
    • the client animates smoothly between points;
    • for privacy, it is shown only during the active order.

docs.title: 5.7 Fleet, shifts and incentives
docs.text:
• Riders:
    • log in to slots or shifts (some platforms use slot booking for guaranteed earnings windows);
    • get zone assignments;
    • get incentive programmes (orders completed in the peak window, rain bonuses, weekly targets).
  • Earnings: base pay per order plus distance pay, wait-time pay, incentives and tips. Earnings are transparent in the app.
  • Supply planning:
    • forecast demand per zone per 30 minutes;
    • compute the required riders from expected orders × time per order ÷ batching factor;
    • recruit and incentivise to fill gaps.

docs.title: 5.8 Settlements
docs.text:
• Restaurants: order value minus commission, payment gateway fees, restaurant-funded discounts and penalties, minus TDS/TCS (VERIFY). Paid on a weekly cycle or faster (some platforms offer daily payouts).
  • Riders: daily or weekly payouts. COD cash collected by riders is reconciled against their earnings: deposit or deduction.
  • Ledger: double-entry, per order and per party, with reconciliation against payment gateway reports (I03).

docs.title: 6.1 ETA decomposition
docs.text:
• Total ETA = t_accept + t_dispatch + max(t_rider_to_restaurant, t_prep_remaining) + t_pickup + t_travel_to_customer + t_last_mile.
  • Each term has its own model with its own features. For example:
    • t_travel: the hex-to-hex travel time matrix, plus route distance, time of day, weather and live zone speed;
    • t_last_mile: learned per building or society from history (gated communities, high-rises);
    • t_prep: §6.2.
  • Prediction targets: a distribution, via quantile regression. The promise shown to the customer is a conservative quantile (e.g. P80), while dispatch planning uses the median.
  • Continuous updates: after each event (accept, rider assigned, picked up), recompute with the actual times known so far. Tell the customer if the ETA moves materially.
  • Public descriptions: DoorDash and Swiggy have published about ETA models using gradient boosting and deep learning, with multi-stage predictions (VERIFY).

docs.title: 6.2 Prep-time prediction
docs.text:
• Features:
    • restaurant;
    • number and type of items (biryani is quick to serve; pizza needs baking time);
    • open orders at the restaurant (kitchen load);
    • time of day and day of week;
    • the staff-entered prep estimate;
    • the restaurant's historical bias between entered and actual times.
  • Labels:
    • true food-ready time is not directly observed, because the "mark ready" tap is noisy;
    • use rider arrival and pickup times: if the rider waited, food was ready later than arrival; if the food waited, it was ready earlier, estimated from the "ready" tap or pickup time;
    • this is a censored-data problem, handled with survival-style or censored-regression techniques.
  • Use: time the rider assignment so arrival ≈ ready time (§6.4). Dynamic updates come from the restaurant's real-time load.

docs.title: 6.3 Dispatch cost function
docs.text:
For an assignment of rider r to order o, the cost combines:

  • rider travel time to the restaurant;
  • expected rider wait = max(0, ready_time − arrival_time). This wastes rider capacity;
  • expected food wait = max(0, arrival_time − ready_time). This cools the food and delays the customer;
  • customer delay vs promise: the penalty grows steeply after the promised time;
  • rider fairness: spread orders across riders, and avoid giving long trips to riders near the end of their shift;
  • chaining benefit: a rider finishing a nearby delivery is "available soon" at a known location.

docs.title: 6.4 Assignment and batching
docs.text:
• Batch matching:
    • every Δt (10–30 s) per zone, build a bipartite graph of orders × riders, including soon-available riders;
    • edge costs come from §6.3;
    • solve min-cost bipartite matching with the Hungarian algorithm (O(n³), fine for a few hundred) or auction algorithms and greedy heuristics at bigger sizes.
  • Delayed assignment:
    • don't assign immediately if food will take 20 minutes. Wait until the "latest good assign time" (ready time − travel time − buffer);
    • this keeps riders free for urgent orders. It is a rolling-horizon decision.
  • Batching (two or more orders per rider):
    • candidate pairs share the same or a nearby restaurant, have ready times within a few minutes, and have customers in a similar direction;
    • evaluate the insertion cost: the extra delay for each order compared with solo delivery, which must stay under thresholds and promises;
    • this is a vehicle-routing problem with pickup and delivery and time windows (VRPPDTW) for small sets, solved heuristically.
  • Rejections: riders can decline. Model the acceptance probability (distance, pay, rider history) in the cost, so likely-rejected offers aren't made.
  • Public descriptions: Swiggy and DoorDash have blogged about batch dispatch optimisation and assignment timing (VERIFY).

docs.title: 6.5 Surge and demand shaping
docs.text:
• Zone stress metric: for example, (open unassigned orders + expected orders next 15 minutes) ÷ (available riders + riders becoming free in 15 minutes), alongside ETA breach rates.
  • Levers, by escalating thresholds:
    1. ETA inflation.
    2. Surge fee (a capped step function).
    3. Rider incentives (push to nearby offline riders).
    4. Radius shrink.
    5. Restaurant throttling.
    6. Order pausing.
  • Control loop: a PID-like or rule-based controller with hysteresis, so levers don't flap. Experiment carefully, since surge affects both customer trust and rider earnings.
  • Rider repositioning: suggest that idle riders move to hexes with predicted demand, using heatmaps in the rider app.

docs.title: 6.6 Discovery ranking
docs.text:
• Candidates: serviceable restaurants, plus dish-level candidates for search.
  • Model: a multi-objective learning-to-rank model. It predicts P(click), P(order | click) and expected satisfaction (a good rating, no complaint). It is combined with ETA and price fit, plus diversity and freshness.
  • Features:
    • user cuisine affinity and embeddings;
    • restaurant quality (rating, complaint rate, acceptance rate);
    • ETA;
    • offers;
    • time-of-day fit (breakfast places in the morning);
    • repeat behaviour ("Order again").
  • Ads blending: sponsored candidates from an auction (bid × predicted CTR × quality), placed in fixed or labelled slots with relevance thresholds.
  • New restaurants: cold-start exploration slots.

docs.title: 6.7 Demand forecasting and supply planning
docs.text:
• Forecast orders per zone per 15–30 minutes for the next day and the next hour, using:
    • history and seasonality;
    • weather forecasts;
    • holidays and festivals;
    • events (cricket matches);
    • marketing campaigns.
  • Use: rider shift planning, incentive budgets, restaurant prep readiness alerts, and quick-commerce replenishment.

docs.title: 6.8 Fraud and abuse
docs.text:
• Customer refund abuse: frequent "missing item" claims, linked accounts (device, phone, address, payment instrument graph), photo reuse (perceptual hash). The response is a risk score that gates instant refunds.
  • COD fraud: fake orders and repeated refusals at the door. The response is COD limits per risk tier.
  • Rider fraud: GPS spoofing (mock locations, impossible jumps), marking delivered without delivering, collusion with customers on claims. Detect with sensor consistency and pattern models.
  • Restaurant fraud: fake orders to farm ratings or offers. Use graph analysis of customers, devices and restaurants.
  • Promo abuse: multiple accounts for new-user offers. Use device fingerprinting and account linking.

docs.title: 6.9 Quick-commerce algorithms
docs.text:
• Store slotting: place fast-moving SKUs near the packing station, grouped by co-purchase affinity, to minimise pick path length.
  • Pick routing: a short path through the store (a TSP heuristic on the aisle graph) and batch picking of multiple orders.
  • Replenishment: a forecast per SKU per store per hour, a safety stock for the service level, and constraints from mother warehouse truck schedules.
  • Serviceability promise: 10 minutes only if stock is available and the picker and rider queues are short. Otherwise show a longer promise or hide the store.

docs.title: 7.1 Operational stores
docs.text: Data Store (reference) Notes Users, addresses PostgreSQL/MySQL sharded Geocoded addresses Restaurants, menus PostgreSQL + search index + cache Versioned menus Serviceability tables Redis/in-memory KV by hex Refreshed every minute Orders Sharded RDBMS (by order ID) + event log in Kafka State machine Live rider locations In-memory geo index (Redis geo or custom) Ephemeral Location history Kafka → Cassandra/lakehouse Analytics, disputes Payments and ledger PostgreSQL, append-only Reconciliation Ratings and reviews PostgreSQL + aggregates Quality scores Quick-commerce inventory Per-store DB with real-time stock Reservations at checkout

docs.title: 7.2 Analytics and ML platform
docs.text:
• Events: feed impressions, clicks, carts, orders, state transitions, rider pings, ETAs predicted vs actual, support tickets.
  • Feature store (online and offline):
    • real-time features (restaurant open orders, zone stress, rider wait times in the last 15 minutes) computed by Flink;
    • batch features (restaurant historical prep times, user affinities) computed by Spark.
  • ML models: ETA components, prep time, ranking, ads CTR, surge forecasting, fraud, demand forecasting, rider acceptance probability.
  • Warehouse marts:
    • orders and GMV by city and zone;
    • delivery performance (ETA accuracy, delays by component);
    • rider utilisation and earnings;
    • restaurant performance;
    • unit economics (contribution margin per order).
  • Experimentation:
    • A/B tests on ranking and fees;
    • switchback experiments for dispatch and surge, where whole zones alternate treatments over time windows. This is needed because marketplace interventions interfere across users (publicly described by DoorDash; VERIFY).

docs.title: 7.3 Data flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    APPS[Customer, restaurant and rider apps] --> K[Kafka]
    OMS[Order events] --> K
    K --> FLINK[Flink - real-time features and zone state]
    FLINK --> FS[Online feature store]
    FLINK --> SERV[Serviceability tables]
    FS --> MODELS[ETA, dispatch, ranking models]
    K --> LAKE[Lakehouse]
    LAKE --> TRAIN[Model training]
    TRAIN --> MODELS
    LAKE --> DW[Warehouse - ops and unit economics]
    LAKE --> EXP[Experiments - A/B and switchback]

docs.title: 8. Tech Stack (reference choice)
docs.text: Layer Choice Notes Services Java/Kotlin (Spring Boot), Go for high-throughput location and dispatch Realtime WebSockets/MQTT gateways, push notifications Tracking, restaurant alerts Geo H3, OSRM/Valhalla or commercial routing, map matching Travel times Datastores PostgreSQL/MySQL, Redis, Cassandra/ScyllaDB, DynamoDB-like stores Search Elasticsearch/OpenSearch Dishes, restaurants Streaming Kafka, Flink Features, zone state ML Python, XGBoost/LightGBM, PyTorch/TensorFlow, feature store, model serving ETA, ranking Optimisation Custom Hungarian/auction solvers, OR-Tools for routing experiments Dispatch Lakehouse Spark, Iceberg/Delta/Hudi, Trino/Presto, Snowflake/BigQuery Analytics Publicly described (VERIFY) Swiggy: Java/Go microservices, Kafka, ML platform for ETA and assignment. Zomato: AWS, Go/Java/PHP history, real-time features with Flink. DoorDash: Kotlin microservices, Kafka, Flink, switchback testing From engineering blogs

docs.title: 9. Security, Privacy & Compliance
docs.text:
• Food safety: an FSSAI licence is required for listing restaurants, and displayed (VERIFY).
  • Tax: GST on restaurant services through e-commerce operators is collected and paid by the platform (Section 9(5), VERIFY). TCS/TDS on settlements. Invoices per order.

  • Gig workers:

    • the Code on Social Security includes gig and platform workers (VERIFY notification status);
    • state laws (e.g. Rajasthan's 2023 act, Karnataka's ordinance or act; VERIFY) may require registration, welfare fees and transparency on algorithms and payouts.

    Designs should support earnings transparency, grievance redressal and data on working hours. - Consumer protection: transparent fees (no drip pricing), clear cancellation and refund policies, grievance officers, and dark patterns guidelines (VERIFY). - Privacy: - masked phone numbers; - rider locations shown only during active orders; - customer addresses visible to riders only during delivery; - DPDP Act compliance. - Payments: PCI-DSS, tokenisation and RBI rules (VERIFY). - Rider safety: SOS button, insurance, and no penalties that encourage unsafe speeding. Avoid ETAs that pressure riders unrealistically, a point raised publicly about 10-minute delivery (VERIFY).

docs.title: 10. Reliability & Operations
docs.text:
• Peak readiness:
    • pre-scale for dinner and events;
    • load-test order placement;
    • protect the critical path (place order, restaurant notification, dispatch, tracking);
    • shed non-critical features (recommendation widgets) first.
  • Degraded modes:
    • if the ETA model fails, fall back to heuristic ETAs from zone averages;
    • if dispatch optimisation is slow, fall back to a greedy nearest-rider assignment;
    • if the restaurant app is offline, fall back to automated calls (IVR).
  • City ops centre: dashboards per zone (stress, breach rates, rider supply), manual levers and incident playbooks for rain, festivals and outages.
  • Observability:
    • order funnel conversion;
    • acceptance times;
    • rider assignment delay;
    • rider wait at restaurants;
    • ETA error by component;
    • complaint rates;
    • refund costs;
    • payment success.
  • Restaurant reliability: acceptance rate, cancellation rate, prep accuracy and complaint rate are fed back into ranking and onboarding.

docs.title: 11. Key Trade-offs
docs.text: Decision Chosen Accepted cost ETA promise Conservative quantile Some lost orders from longer ETAs Dispatch timing Delayed assignment until near food-ready Risk if prep predictions are wrong Batching When delay is within thresholds Some customers wait a bit longer Peak levers Graduated surge, radius shrink, throttle Lost demand, customer annoyance Refunds Instant for low-risk customers Some abuse losses Serviceability Precomputed every minute Slight staleness; re-check at checkout Experimentation Switchback for marketplace levers Slower, noisier results Quick commerce Dark stores near customers High fixed costs, limited assortment

docs.title: Beginner B1
docs.text:
Q1 [B1] ⭐ What are the steps of a food delivery order?

30-second answer: Order placed and paid, restaurant accepts with a prep time, a rider is assigned timed to food readiness, rider picks up, delivers with live tracking, and the order is rated and settled — each step is a state transition event consumed by notifications, tracking, ETA and settlements.

Deep answer: §4.2–4.4, §5.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Many failure branches.

Follow-ups: 1. Restaurant doesn't accept? → Timeout, refund. 2. Customer unreachable? → Undelivered flow.

Red flags: Synchronous calls across every party in one request.

Q2 [B1] How do you show which restaurants can deliver to me right now?

30-second answer: Map the customer location to a hexagon and look up a precomputed serviceability table per (restaurant, hex) refreshed every minute from restaurant status, distance, zone stress and fees; re-check at checkout.

Deep answer: §4.1, §5.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Freshness vs speed.

Follow-ups: 1. Rain? → Radius shrink. 2. Size? → Tens of millions of entries.

Red flags: Computing routes for 400 restaurants per feed load.

Q3 [B1] How is live rider tracking built?

30-second answer: The rider app sends GPS every few seconds; the server snaps to roads and filters noise, updates an in-memory geo index and streams positions to the customer through a realtime gateway; the client animates between points; ETA is recomputed as the rider moves.

Deep answer: §5.6.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Battery and data vs freshness.

Follow-ups: 1. Poor network? → Batched uploads. 2. Spoofing? → Detection.

Red flags: The customer app polling the database.

Q4 [B1] Why does the delivery fee change in the rain?

30-second answer: Demand rises and rider supply falls; a surge fee funds rider incentives and tempers demand so ETAs stay honest — part of graduated zone-level levers.

Deep answer: §4.5, §6.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Customer trust.

Follow-ups: 1. Caps? → Yes. 2. Riders benefit? → Incentives.

Red flags: Unbounded surge.

docs.title: Intermediate B2
docs.text:
Q5 [B2] ⭐ How would you predict delivery ETA?

30-second answer: Decompose it into acceptance, dispatch, max(rider-to-restaurant, prep remaining), pickup, travel to customer and last mile; model each with ML (quantile regression) using features like restaurant load, travel time matrices, weather and building history; promise a conservative quantile and update after each event.

Deep answer: §6.1.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Promise vs conversion.

Follow-ups: 1. Why decompose? → Explainable, updatable. 2. Last mile? → Building-level learning.

Red flags: Distance ÷ speed.

Q6 [B2] How do you predict restaurant prep time when 'food ready' taps are unreliable?

30-second answer: Use restaurant, items, kitchen load, time of day and staff estimate as features, and derive labels from rider arrival and pickup times treating them as censored observations (rider waited vs food waited); correct each restaurant's bias.

Deep answer: §6.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Label noise.

Follow-ups: 1. New restaurant? → Category priors. 2. Real-time load? → Open orders.

Red flags: Trusting the tap.

Q7 [B2] How do you price a cart?

30-second answer: Item and add-on prices, packaging, distance and surge delivery fee, platform fee, GST per rules, offers with eligibility and stacking rules and funding attribution, optional tip; store a price snapshot with the order for invoices and settlements.

Deep answer: §5.4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Transparency.

Follow-ups: 1. Who funds discounts? → Attribution. 2. Re-check? → At checkout.

Red flags: Recomputing prices at refund time.

Q8 [B2] What happens when a restaurant marks an item out of stock after ordering?

30-second answer: Notify the customer with substitution options or a partial refund with a timeout default, update the order and price snapshot, adjust the settlement, and track restaurant reliability.

Deep answer: §4.3 step 5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Customer friction.

Follow-ups: 1. Whole order fails? → Cancel and refund. 2. Prevent? → Real-time stock toggles.

Red flags: Silent removal.

Q9 [B2] How do you handle missing-item complaints without being exploited?

30-second answer: Self-serve refunds gated by a risk score built from complaint history, account linking graphs, order value and photo checks; instant for low-risk, agent review for high-risk; attribute costs to restaurant or rider by evidence.

Deep answer: §4.6, §6.8.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Good customers' experience vs loss.

Follow-ups: 1. Linked accounts? → Graph. 2. Photo reuse? → Hashing.

Red flags: Unconditional refunds.

docs.title: Senior B3
docs.text:
Q10 [B3] ⭐ Design dispatch for food delivery.

30-second answer: Per zone every 10–30 s, collect unassigned orders and available or soon-available riders, compute costs from travel, rider wait, food wait, promise delay, fairness and acceptance probability, delay assignment until near food-ready, solve min-cost matching, evaluate batching via insertion cost, offer to riders and re-pool on rejection; fall back to greedy under load.

Deep answer: §4.4, §6.3, §6.4.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Optimality vs latency.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not immediate? → Rider idle wait. 2. Batching rules? → Delay thresholds.

Red flags: Always nearest rider immediately.

Q11 [B3] How do you manage a demand spike when it rains?

30-second answer: Measure zone stress and apply graduated levers — honest ETAs, surge fees, rider incentives, radius shrink, more batching, restaurant throttling, pausing — with hysteresis and ops overrides; recover gradually.

Deep answer: §4.5, §6.5.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Lost orders vs broken promises.

Follow-ups: 1. Flapping? → Hysteresis. 2. Rider safety? → No speed pressure.

Red flags: Accepting every order and missing every ETA.

Q12 [B3] How do you test changes to dispatch or surge?

30-second answer: Marketplace interventions interfere across users, so use switchback experiments — alternate treatment and control by zone and time window — plus simulation on historical data before launch, with metrics on ETA accuracy, rider utilisation, cost and conversion.

Deep answer: §7.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Noisier results.

Follow-ups: 1. Why not user A/B? → Shared riders. 2. Simulation? → Replays.

Red flags: User-level A/B for dispatch.

Q13 [B3] How would you rank restaurants in the home feed?

30-second answer: Multi-objective learning-to-rank predicting click, order and satisfaction, combined with ETA, price fit, offers, quality and time-of-day fit, user embeddings and repeat behaviour, plus labelled ads from an auction, diversity and cold-start exploration.

Deep answer: §6.6.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Ads vs relevance.

Follow-ups: 1. Bad restaurants? → Quality demotion. 2. New ones? → Exploration.

Red flags: Ranking by commission or ad spend only.

Q14 [B3] How do you detect rider GPS spoofing?

30-second answer: Check for mock-location flags, impossible speeds and jumps, mismatch between GPS and network or sensor data, deliveries marked without approaching the customer, and patterns across riders; apply holds and reviews.

Deep answer: §6.8.

Trade-offs I'd call out: False positives in poor GPS areas.

Follow-ups: 1. Map matching? → Helps. 2. Penalties? → Review first.

Red flags: Trusting client location blindly.

docs.title: Architect B4
docs.text:
Q15 [B4] ⭐ Design a food delivery platform for 3 million orders a day.

30-second answer: Hex and zone geo model; precomputed serviceability; personalised feed and search; cart and pricing with offers; event-sourced order management; prep and ETA models; batch dispatch with delayed assignment and batching; live tracking; graduated peak levers; ledgers for settlements; Kafka, Flink features and a lakehouse with switchback experiments.

Deep answer: §3–§7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed vs utilisation vs cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Bottleneck? → Dispatch at peak. 2. Unit economics? → Batching, fees.

Red flags: No zone model.

Q16 [B4] How do you improve unit economics without hurting customers?

30-second answer: Increase rider utilisation through better prep prediction and delayed assignment, batching within delay thresholds, demand shaping, reducing refunds via quality and fraud controls, optimising offer spend with targeting and budgets, and measuring contribution margin per order by zone.

Deep answer: §6, §7.2.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Speed vs cost.

Follow-ups: 1. Fees? → Transparency. 2. Rider earnings? → Fairness.

Red flags: Cutting rider pay only.

Q17 [B4] What real-time data platform would you build?

30-second answer: Kafka for all app and order events, Flink for real-time features (restaurant load, zone stress, rider waits) into an online feature store and serviceability tables, a lakehouse for training and analytics, model serving for ETA, dispatch and ranking, and an experimentation platform supporting switchbacks.

Deep answer: §7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Cost of real-time.

Follow-ups: 1. Training–serving skew? → Same feature definitions. 2. Late events? → Watermarks.

Red flags: Only daily batch features.

Q18 [B4] How is quick commerce different from restaurant delivery?

30-second answer: The platform controls the supply node (dark store) — so prep becomes picking with slotting and pick routing, inventory and replenishment forecasting become core, riders wait at stores for instant assignment, distances are short, and the 10-minute promise depends on stock and queue checks.

Deep answer: §4.7, §6.9.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Fixed costs, limited assortment.

Follow-ups: 1. Stock accuracy? → Real-time reservations. 2. Safety? → Realistic ETAs.

Red flags: Reusing restaurant prep models.

Q19 [B4] How would you design for gig worker regulations and fairness?

30-second answer: Transparent earnings breakdowns, explainable assignment and incentive rules, grievance workflows, records of working hours and earnings for welfare contributions, safety features and insurance, no penalties that encourage unsafe driving, and auditability of algorithms where laws require (VERIFY).

Deep answer: §9, §5.7.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Flexibility vs obligations.

Follow-ups: 1. Data retention? → For audits. 2. Incentives? → Clear rules.

Red flags: Opaque deactivation.

Q20 [B4] Compare food delivery with ride-hailing.

30-second answer: Both match moving supply with demand in real time using geo indexes, ETAs and surge; food delivery adds a third party (restaurant) with uncertain prep time, perishable goods, batching across orders and timing assignments to readiness, while ride-hailing matches people directly with pickup immediacy and pooling constraints.

Deep answer: I05 vs this chapter.

Trade-offs I'd call out: Prep uncertainty.

Follow-ups: 1. Shared tech? → Geo, dispatch. 2. Unique? → Prep models.

Red flags: Treating restaurants as passengers.

docs.title: 13. Summary
docs.text:
1. Food delivery is a three-sided, real-time marketplace with perishable goods. Every decision balances customer speed, rider utilisation and restaurant efficiency.
  2. Hexagons and zones organise the city for serviceability, ETAs, surge and dispatch. Serviceability is precomputed and re-checked at checkout.
  3. ETA is decomposed into parts. Prep-time models learn from rider wait signals. Dispatch delays assignment until near food-ready and batches orders within delay limits.
  4. Peak handling uses graduated zone levers with hysteresis. Marketplace changes are tested with switchback experiments.
  5. Settlements, refunds and fraud need ledgers and risk scoring. Quick commerce adds dark-store picking, slotting and replenishment.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
About this glossary

This glossary has 189 core terms, each with a one-line definition and a link to the chapter that explains it in depth.

It is checked against the book. GlossaryGen (in labs/appendix-tools/) verifies that every term actually appears in the chapter it links to. Hyphens and spaces count as the same, and there are optional exact-match probes. On the first run, 15 of 159 terms failed:

  • some pointed to the wrong chapter (anycast is covered in Ch 08, not Ch 03; backpressure in Ch 19, not Ch 18);
  • some were phrased differently from the chapter ("outbox pattern" vs "outbox");
  • one described something the chapter doesn't cover. "Fan-out on write vs on read" was reworded to the fan-out Ch 43 actually discusses.

The current version passes: 189 terms, 0 problems.

Interview-specific terms are in Chs 57–61. For questions on a term, use the Full Question Index.

docs.title: 0–9
docs.text: 2PC (two-phase commit) Atomic commit protocol: a coordinator asks every participant to prepare, then tells all to commit or all to abort; blocks if the coordinator fails after prepare. → Ch 13 Distributed Transactions 3-2-1 rule Backup rule of thumb: 3 copies, on 2 different media, 1 off-site (or in another region/account). → Ch 27 Reliability & Disaster Recovery

docs.title: A
docs.text: ACID Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the guarantees of a database transaction. → Ch 05 Relational Databases Deep Dive ADR (architecture decision record) A short document recording one decision: context, options, decision, consequences, and when to revisit it. → Ch 31 Architecture Decision Making Aggregate A cluster of domain objects changed together inside one transaction, with one root that enforces its invariants. → Ch 33 Domain-Driven Design Anti-corruption layer A translation layer that stops another context's model leaking into yours. → Ch 33 Domain-Driven Design Anycast One IP address announced from many locations; the network routes each client to the nearest. → Ch 08 Load Balancing, Proxies & Gateways API gateway Edge component that routes, authenticates, rate-limits and shapes requests for backend services. → Ch 08 Load Balancing, Proxies & Gateways At-least-once delivery Every message is delivered one or more times; consumers must tolerate duplicates. → Ch 14 Messaging & Event Streaming At-most-once delivery Every message is delivered zero or one time; losses are possible, duplicates are not. → Ch 14 Messaging & Event Streaming Availability The fraction of time (or requests) a system serves correctly, often expressed in "nines". → Ch 01 What System Design Is Avro A binary serialization format with reader and writer schemas resolved at read time. → Ch 28 Schema & Data Evolution

docs.title: B
docs.text: Back-of-the-envelope estimate A quick order-of-magnitude calculation of load, storage or bandwidth to guide design choices. → Ch 02 Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation Backfill Populating a new column or store with historical data, usually in batches alongside live writes. → Ch 28 Schema & Data Evolution Backpressure Signalling upstream to slow down when a component cannot keep up, instead of queueing without bound. → Ch 19 Concurrency at Scale in Java Base62 Encoding numbers with 0–9, a–z and A–Z, used for short URL codes. → Ch 38 Case Study: URL Shortener & SMS Short Links BFF (backend for frontend) A backend tailored to one client type (app, web) that aggregates and shapes calls for it. → Ch 34 Modern Architecture Styles Blast radius How many users or systems one failure or bad change can affect. → Ch 27 Reliability & Disaster Recovery Bloom filter A compact probabilistic set: "definitely not present" or "probably present", with a tunable false-positive rate. → Ch 53 Case Study: Web Crawler (Competitor Price Monitoring) Blue-green deployment Running two production environments and switching traffic from the old (blue) to the new (green) at once. → Ch 26 Deployment & Infrastructure BM25 A standard relevance-scoring function based on term frequency, document frequency and document length. → Ch 22 Search Systems Bounded context A boundary within which a model and its language are consistent; the unit of ownership in DDD. → Ch 33 Domain-Driven Design Bulkhead Isolating resources (threads, connections, pools) per dependency so one failure cannot exhaust all. → Ch 18 Resilience Patterns

docs.title: C
docs.text: Cache stampede Many requests miss the same expired key at once and overload the source; prevented by locking, coalescing or early refresh. → Ch 07 Caching Cache-aside The application reads the cache, falls back to the database on a miss, and fills the cache itself. → Ch 07 Caching Calibration (interviewers) Aligning interviewers' scoring through anchored rubrics and shared review so verdicts are consistent. → Ch 60 Mock Interviews Canary release Sending a small share of traffic to a new version and widening only if its metrics stay healthy. → Ch 26 Deployment & Infrastructure CAP theorem During a network partition a distributed store must choose between consistency and availability. → Ch 12 Consistency, Time & Consensus CDC (change data capture) Streaming a database's committed changes (usually from its log) to other systems. → Ch 15 Event-Driven Architecture, CQRS & Event Sourcing CDN (content delivery network) Edge caches close to users that serve static and cacheable content. → Ch 52 Case Study: Object Storage & Media Pipeline Cell-based architecture Splitting a system into independent full copies (cells), each serving a subset of users, to bound blast radius. → Ch 34 Modern Architecture Styles Chaos engineering Deliberately injecting failures in controlled experiments to verify resilience. → Ch 27 Reliability & Disaster Recovery Choreography Services react to each other's events without a central coordinator. → Ch 34 Modern Architecture Styles Circuit breaker Stops calling a failing dependency for a while after errors exceed a threshold, then probes before resuming. → Ch 18 Resilience Patterns Clock skew The difference between clocks on different machines; why wall-clock timestamps cannot order distributed events safely. → Ch 12 Consistency, Time & Consensus Connection pool A bounded set of reused database connections; its size is a key capacity limit. → Ch 05 Relational Databases Deep Dive Consistent hashing Mapping keys and nodes onto a ring so adding or removing a node moves only a small share of keys. → Ch 11 Partitioning & Sharding Consumer group Kafka consumers sharing a group id divide a topic's partitions among themselves. → Ch 14 Messaging & Event Streaming Consumer lag How far a consumer is behind the latest message in a partition. → Ch 14 Messaging & Event Streaming Contract testing Verifying that a provider still satisfies the requests and responses its consumers depend on (e.g. Pact). → Ch 29 Testing Distributed Systems Coordinated omission A load-testing error where a stalled system also stalls request sending, hiding the real latency. → Ch 25 Performance Engineering Cost per order A unit-economics metric: infrastructure cost divided by orders served. → Ch 35 Cost Engineering & FinOps Count-Min Sketch A small probabilistic table that estimates item frequencies in a stream, never underestimating. → Ch 51 Case Study: Real-time Analytics & Top-K (Trending) CQRS Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate models for writes and for reads. → Ch 15 Event-Driven Architecture, CQRS & Event Sourcing CRDT A conflict-free replicated data type whose replicas can merge concurrent updates deterministically. → Ch 10 Replication Crypto-shredding Making data unreadable by deleting its encryption key, used for erasure in backups and logs. → Ch 36 Compliance, Governance & Data Residency

docs.title: D
docs.text: DAG (workflow) A directed acyclic graph of jobs where each runs after its dependencies succeed. → Ch 50 Case Study: Distributed Job Scheduler Dark store A delivery-only warehouse serving quick-commerce orders from a small area. → Ch 46 Case Study: Grocery Checkout & Inventory Reservation Data residency A requirement that certain data be stored (and sometimes processed) within a given country or region. → Ch 36 Compliance, Governance & Data Residency Dead-letter queue A queue that holds messages that repeatedly fail processing, for inspection and replay. → Ch 14 Messaging & Event Streaming Deterministic simulation testing Running a whole distributed system in a simulated, seeded environment so failures can be reproduced exactly. → Ch 29 Testing Distributed Systems Disagree and commit Arguing a position with evidence before a decision, then fully supporting the decision once made. → Ch 61 Behavioural & Leadership Distributed lock A lock shared across processes; safe only with leases and fencing tokens. → Ch 20 Idempotency, IDs & Distributed Locks Distributed monolith Services that must be deployed or changed together — the costs of microservices without the independence. → Ch 34 Modern Architecture Styles DLQ See dead-letter queue. → Ch 14 Messaging & Event Streaming DNS The Domain Name System, mapping names to addresses through a hierarchy of cached lookups. → Ch 03 Networking Essentials Domain event A record that something meaningful happened in the domain, named in the past tense. → Ch 33 Domain-Driven Design Double-entry ledger Recording every money movement as equal debits and credits so balances always reconcile. → Ch 45 Case Study: Payment System Durability Once acknowledged, data survives crashes and failures. → Ch 01 What System Design Is

docs.title: E
docs.text: Erasure coding Splitting data into k data and m parity shards so any k of k+m can rebuild it, at lower overhead than replication. → Ch 52 Case Study: Object Storage & Media Pipeline Error budget The allowed unreliability under an SLO (e.g. 0.1% of requests); spending it slows releases. → Ch 24 Observability Event sourcing Storing state as the sequence of events that produced it; current state is derived by replay. → Ch 15 Event-Driven Architecture, CQRS & Event Sourcing Event storming A workshop technique that maps a domain by laying out its events on a timeline. → Ch 33 Domain-Driven Design Eventual consistency Replicas converge to the same value if updates stop; reads may be stale meanwhile. → Ch 12 Consistency, Time & Consensus Exactly-once processing Each input affects the output once, achieved by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotency or transactions. → Ch 14 Messaging & Event Streaming Expand/contract Changing a schema in backward-compatible steps: add the new, migrate, switch, then remove the old. → Ch 28 Schema & Data Evolution

docs.title: F
docs.text: Failover Moving service from a failed component (e.g. a primary database) to a standby. → Ch 27 Reliability & Disaster Recovery Fan-out One request or event multiplied into many downstream calls or writes — a feed request into feature lookups, or a post into every follower's feed. → Ch 43 Case Study: Home Feed & Recommendations Feature flag A runtime switch that turns code paths on or off without redeploying. → Ch 26 Deployment & Infrastructure Fencing token A monotonically increasing number checked by the resource, so a stale lock holder's writes are rejected. → Ch 20 Idempotency, IDs & Distributed Locks Fitness function An automated check that an architectural property (dependency rules, latency, cost) still holds. → Ch 31 Architecture Decision Making Flip point The weighting or value at which a decision matrix would choose a different option. → Ch 31 Architecture Decision Making

docs.title: G
docs.text: Geohash Encoding latitude and longitude into a string whose shared prefixes mean nearby cells. → Ch 47 Case Study: Delivery Dispatch & Live Tracking Graceful degradation Keeping the core function working with reduced features when dependencies fail. → Ch 18 Resilience Patterns gRPC A high-performance RPC framework using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers. → Ch 04 API Design

docs.title: H
docs.text: Head-of-line blocking One slow item holding up everything behind it on a connection or queue. → Ch 03 Networking Essentials Heartbeat A periodic signal that a node is alive, used for failure detection. → Ch 12 Consistency, Time & Consensus Hedged request Sending a duplicate request after a delay and using whichever answer returns first, to cut tail latency. → Ch 25 Performance Engineering Hexagonal architecture Ports and adapters: domain logic at the centre, infrastructure plugged in through interfaces. → Ch 34 Modern Architecture Styles Hinted handoff A node temporarily stores writes for an unavailable replica and forwards them when it returns. → Ch 54 Case Study: Distributed Key-Value Store Hot key / hot partition A key or shard receiving a disproportionate share of traffic. → Ch 11 Partitioning & Sharding HyperLogLog A probabilistic structure that estimates the number of distinct items in a few kilobytes. → Ch 51 Case Study: Real-time Analytics & Top-K (Trending)

docs.title: I
docs.text: Idempotency key A client-supplied key that lets the server recognise retries and return the original result. → Ch 20 Idempotency, IDs & Distributed Locks Idempotent An operation that has the same effect whether applied once or many times. → Ch 20 Idempotency, IDs & Distributed Locks Interviewer card A mock interviewer's sheet: prompt, hidden requirements, follow-up chains, curveball, level anchors. → Ch 60 Mock Interviews Invariant A rule that must always hold, e.g. "stock never goes below zero". → Ch 33 Domain-Driven Design Inverted index A map from each term to the documents containing it; the core structure of full-text search. → Ch 22 Search Systems Isolation level How much concurrent transactions can see of each other (read committed, repeatable read, serializable). → Ch 05 Relational Databases Deep Dive

docs.title: J
docs.text: Jitter Randomness added to retry delays so clients don't retry in synchronized waves. → Ch 18 Resilience Patterns Journey SLO A reliability objective for an end-to-end user journey (e.g. checkout), composed from the services it touches. → Ch 56 Capstone: The Grocery Marketplace, End to End JWT JSON Web Token: a signed, self-contained token carrying claims about a subject. → Ch 23 Security Architecture

docs.title: K
docs.text: Kafka partition An ordered, append-only log within a topic; the unit of ordering and parallelism. → Ch 14 Messaging & Event Streaming

docs.title: L
docs.text: L4 / L7 load balancing Balancing on transport-level connections (L4) versus on application requests such as HTTP (L7). → Ch 08 Load Balancing, Proxies & Gateways Lamport clock A logical counter that orders events consistently with causality. → Ch 12 Consistency, Time & Consensus Latency The time to complete one operation, reported as percentiles (p50, p99). → Ch 01 What System Design Is Leader election Choosing one node to act as coordinator, typically through consensus or a lease. → Ch 12 Consistency, Time & Consensus Leader lease A time-limited leadership grant; a leader stops acting when its lease may have expired. → Ch 50 Case Study: Distributed Job Scheduler Leaky bucket A rate limiter that drains requests at a constant rate, smoothing bursts. → Ch 39 Case Study: Distributed Rate Limiter Lease A time-limited grant (e.g. a lock) that expires unless renewed. → Ch 20 Idempotency, IDs & Distributed Locks Level expectations (B1–B4) What an interviewer expects at engineer, senior, staff and principal level in scope, depth and judgement. → Ch 58 Level Expectations: From Engineer to Principal Linearizability Every operation appears to take effect instantly at one point between its start and end, in real-time order. → Ch 12 Consistency, Time & Consensus Little's Law Items in a system = arrival rate × time in system (L = λW). → Ch 31 Architecture Decision Making Load shedding Rejecting some requests early under overload so the rest succeed. → Ch 18 Resilience Patterns LSM tree A log-structured merge tree: writes go to memory and immutable sorted files that are merged in the background. → Ch 54 Case Study: Distributed Key-Value Store

docs.title: M
docs.text: Merkle tree A hash tree used to find differing ranges between replicas cheaply. → Ch 54 Case Study: Distributed Key-Value Store Microservices Independently deployable services organised around business capabilities. → Ch 16 Microservices Architecture Modular monolith One deployable with strictly enforced internal module boundaries. → Ch 34 Modern Architecture Styles mTLS Mutual TLS: both client and server authenticate with certificates. → Ch 23 Security Architecture Multi-tenancy One system serving many customers (tenants) with isolation of data and performance. → Ch 30 Multi-Tenancy & SaaS Architecture Multipart upload Uploading a large object in independently retried parts that are assembled at the end. → Ch 52 Case Study: Object Storage & Media Pipeline MVCC Multi-version concurrency control: readers see a snapshot while writers create new row versions. → Ch 05 Relational Databases Deep Dive

docs.title: N
docs.text: Noisy neighbor A tenant or workload consuming shared resources and degrading others. → Ch 30 Multi-Tenancy & SaaS Architecture

docs.title: O
docs.text: OAuth 2.0 A delegation protocol for obtaining access tokens; OpenID Connect adds identity on top. → Ch 23 Security Architecture Observability Understanding a system's internal state from its outputs: metrics, logs and traces. → Ch 24 Observability Optimistic locking Detecting conflicting updates with a version check at write time instead of locking upfront. → Ch 05 Relational Databases Deep Dive Orchestration A central coordinator tells services what to do and tracks the workflow. → Ch 34 Modern Architecture Styles Order book The list of resting buy and sell orders for an instrument, sorted by price and time. → Ch 55 Case Study: Order Matching Engine Outbox pattern Writing an event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change, then relaying it. → Ch 15 Event-Driven Architecture, CQRS & Event Sourcing

docs.title: P
docs.text: p99 / tail latency The latency under which 99% of requests complete; the slow tail users notice. → Ch 25 Performance Engineering PACELC Extends CAP: if Partitioned choose Availability or Consistency, Else choose Latency or Consistency. → Ch 12 Consistency, Time & Consensus Pagination (cursor / keyset) Returning results in pages using a position marker rather than an offset. → Ch 04 API Design Paved road The supported, easiest path for building services, adopted because it saves effort. → Ch 31 Architecture Decision Making Paxos A family of consensus protocols for agreeing on values despite failures. → Ch 12 Consistency, Time & Consensus PCI DSS The card-industry security standard; scope shrinks when card data never touches your systems. → Ch 36 Compliance, Governance & Data Residency PITR (point-in-time recovery) Restoring a database to any moment by replaying archived logs onto a base backup. → Ch 27 Reliability & Disaster Recovery Politeness (crawler) Limiting request rate per host so a crawler does not overload the sites it visits. → Ch 53 Case Study: Web Crawler (Competitor Price Monitoring) Polyglot persistence Using different datastores for different access patterns within one system. → Ch 06 NoSQL & Polyglot Persistence Postmortem (blameless) A written incident review focused on systemic causes and actions, not individual blame. → Ch 27 Reliability & Disaster Recovery Price-time priority Matching rule: best price first, and among equal prices, the earliest order first. → Ch 55 Case Study: Order Matching Engine Priority lane A separate queue and worker pool for urgent traffic so bulk work cannot delay it. → Ch 40 Case Study: Notification System Property-based testing Tests that check properties over many generated inputs, shrinking failures to minimal cases. → Ch 29 Testing Distributed Systems Protobuf Protocol Buffers: a binary format whose field numbers enable backward-compatible evolution. → Ch 28 Schema & Data Evolution

docs.title: Q
docs.text: Quorum The minimum number of replicas (R, W) that must respond; R + W > N gives overlapping reads and writes. → Ch 10 Replication

docs.title: R
docs.text: Raft A consensus algorithm based on an elected leader replicating a log to a majority. → Ch 12 Consistency, Time & Consensus Rate limiting Capping how many requests a client may make per time window. → Ch 39 Case Study: Distributed Rate Limiter Read model (materialized view) A query-optimised copy of data, kept up to date from events or changes, that serves reads in CQRS. → Ch 15 Event-Driven Architecture, CQRS & Event Sourcing Read replica A copy of the database that serves reads, usually asynchronously updated. → Ch 10 Replication Read-your-writes A guarantee that a user sees their own writes immediately. → Ch 10 Replication Reconciliation Comparing records between two systems (e.g. ledger vs settlement file) and resolving differences. → Ch 45 Case Study: Payment System Reed-Solomon The erasure code used in many storage systems. → Ch 52 Case Study: Object Storage & Media Pipeline Replication lag How far a replica is behind the primary; bounds stale reads and data loss on failover. → Ch 10 Replication Reservation (inventory) Temporarily holding stock for a checkout until payment succeeds or the hold expires. → Ch 46 Case Study: Grocery Checkout & Inventory Reservation Retry storm Retries from many clients amplifying load on an already failing service. → Ch 18 Resilience Patterns Rightsizing Matching instance sizes to actual utilisation. → Ch 35 Cost Engineering & FinOps Robots.txt A site's file stating which paths crawlers may fetch; honouring it is part of polite crawling. → Ch 53 Case Study: Web Crawler (Competitor Price Monitoring) Row-Level Security (RLS) Database-enforced filtering of rows by tenant or user. → Ch 30 Multi-Tenancy & SaaS Architecture RPO / RTO Recovery Point Objective (acceptable data loss) and Recovery Time Objective (acceptable downtime). → Ch 27 Reliability & Disaster Recovery Rubric The scoring dimensions and anchors interviewers use to rate a system design answer. → Ch 57 The System Design Interview Framework

docs.title: S
docs.text: Saga A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions instead of a distributed commit. → Ch 13 Distributed Transactions Saga compensation The undo step for a completed saga step, run when a later step fails. → Ch 56 Capstone: The Grocery Marketplace, End to End Schema registry A service storing message schemas and enforcing compatibility rules. → Ch 28 Schema & Data Evolution Serializable The strongest isolation level: the result equals some serial order of the transactions. → Ch 05 Relational Databases Deep Dive Service mesh A layer of sidecar proxies handling traffic, security and telemetry between services. → Ch 17 Inter-Service Communication Settlement The payment provider transferring collected funds to the merchant, usually in daily batches with a report. → Ch 45 Case Study: Payment System Sharding Splitting data across independent database nodes by a shard key. → Ch 11 Partitioning & Sharding Sidecar A helper process deployed next to each service instance (proxy, agent). → Ch 17 Inter-Service Communication Signed URL (presigned URL) A time-limited URL that lets a client upload or download an object directly from storage. → Ch 52 Case Study: Object Storage & Media Pipeline SLI / SLO / SLA Indicator (what you measure), objective (the target), agreement (the contractual promise). → Ch 24 Observability Sliding window (rate limiting) Counting requests over a rolling time window rather than fixed buckets, avoiding boundary bursts. → Ch 39 Case Study: Distributed Rate Limiter Sloppy quorum Accepting writes on any reachable nodes during failures, reconciled later. → Ch 54 Case Study: Distributed Key-Value Store Snowflake ID A 64-bit, roughly time-ordered ID built from a timestamp, a worker id and a sequence number. → Ch 20 Idempotency, IDs & Distributed Locks Spaced repetition Reviewing material at growing intervals, timed to just before it would be forgotten. → Ch 59 Interview Q&A Bank Split brain Two nodes both believing they are the primary and accepting conflicting writes. → Ch 27 Reliability & Disaster Recovery Spot instance Discounted spare cloud capacity that can be reclaimed at short notice. → Ch 35 Cost Engineering & FinOps SSTable Sorted String Table: an immutable sorted file of key-value pairs in an LSM tree. → Ch 54 Case Study: Distributed Key-Value Store STAR Situation, Task, Action, Result — the standard structure for behavioural answers (this handbook adds Learning). → Ch 61 Behavioural & Leadership Story bank A set of prepared, tagged career stories covering the competencies interviewers probe at your level. → Ch 61 Behavioural & Leadership Strangler fig Migrating gradually by routing features one by one from the old system to the new. → Ch 16 Microservices Architecture Structured concurrency Treating concurrent subtasks as one unit with a shared lifetime, cancellation and error handling. → Ch 19 Concurrency at Scale in Java

docs.title: T
docs.text: Throughput Operations completed per unit time. → Ch 01 What System Design Is Thundering herd Many waiting clients woken or retrying at once, overwhelming a resource. → Ch 07 Caching Token bucket A rate-limiting algorithm that refills tokens at a fixed rate and allows bursts up to bucket size. → Ch 39 Case Study: Distributed Rate Limiter Top-K / heavy hitters The most frequent items in a stream, often estimated with sketches. → Ch 51 Case Study: Real-time Analytics & Top-K (Trending) Tracing (distributed) Following a request across services as a tree of timed spans. → Ch 24 Observability Transactional outbox See outbox pattern. → Ch 15 Event-Driven Architecture, CQRS & Event Sourcing Trie A prefix tree; each path from the root spells a prefix, which makes prefix lookups fast for autocomplete. → Ch 42 Case Study: Search Autocomplete (Typeahead) TTL Time to live: how long a cached or stored item remains valid. → Ch 07 Caching Two-way door A reversible decision that can be made quickly; a one-way door deserves more care. → Ch 31 Architecture Decision Making

docs.title: U
docs.text: Ubiquitous language The shared vocabulary of a bounded context, used in both conversation and code. → Ch 33 Domain-Driven Design Unit economics Cost and value per business unit (per order, per user). → Ch 35 Cost Engineering & FinOps Universal Scalability Law A model of throughput under contention and coherence costs, explaining why adding nodes can reduce throughput. → Ch 25 Performance Engineering

docs.title: V
docs.text: Vector clock Per-node counters that detect whether events are causally ordered or concurrent. → Ch 12 Consistency, Time & Consensus Virtual node Many ring positions per physical node in consistent hashing, to even out load. → Ch 11 Partitioning & Sharding Virtual threads Lightweight JVM threads (Project Loom) that make blocking I/O cheap at high concurrency. → Ch 19 Concurrency at Scale in Java

docs.title: W
docs.text: WAL (write-ahead log) Logging changes durably before applying them, so a crash can be recovered by replay. → Ch 54 Case Study: Distributed Key-Value Store Watermark In stream processing, an estimate that no older event times are still expected. → Ch 21 Data at Scale Webhook An HTTP callback from a provider notifying your system of an event. → Ch 45 Case Study: Payment System Write-through / write-behind Caches that update the store synchronously on write, or asynchronously later. → Ch 07 Caching

docs.text: Zero-downtime deployment Releasing a new version without making the service unavailable. → Ch 26 Deployment & Infrastructure

docs.title: Lab Catalogue
docs.text:
About this catalogue

Every chapter from 01 to 61 solves one problem at four levels (L1–L4) in its §5. This page lists all 244 labs with their band, the programs they show, and what each needs to run.

How it's built. LabCatalog (in labs/appendix-tools/) generates this page from the chapters. It detects the "Needs" column from the code itself: JDBC URLs, Redis clients, HttpServer/HttpClient, Spring and Testcontainers imports, and child-JVM launches.

What that detection means. A lab marked "JDK only" runs with java File.java. A lab needing Spring or Testcontainers is a project-style example: it needs a build and, for Testcontainers, Docker.

Where the code lives.

  • Chapters 01–09: the labs appear only in the chapter text.
  • Chapters 10–61: each also has a labs/chNN-* folder with the runnable programs, their recorded outputs and a README.

Services used when recording:

  • PostgreSQL 16 on port 5581 (database shop);
  • Redis on port 6390;
  • JDK 21 on a 2-CPU sandbox.

Adjust the connection settings in each program for your machine.

Totals by requirement (a lab can need several): {HTTP (local)=33, JDK only=141, Kafka client=5, PostgreSQL=36, Redis=25, Spring=43, Testcontainers=14, child JVM=4}.

docs.title: Full Question Index
docs.text:
How to use this page

This page lists every interview question in the handbook, by part, chapter and level (B1–B4). ⭐ marks high-frequency questions. Follow a chapter link to the full answer in that chapter's §8.

Generated by QaBankL1 (Ch 59). For drilling, use the ⭐ Drill Bank.

docs.title: 01. What System Design Is ⭐
docs.text:
• Q1 B1 ⭐ What is system design, and how is HLD different from LLD?
  • Q2 B1 ⭐ What's the difference between functional and non-functional requirements? Give examples.
  • Q3 B1 What is scalability? Vertical vs horizontal?
  • Q4 B1 What's the difference between latency and throughput?
  • Q5 B2 ⭐ Walk me through how you approach a system design problem in 45 minutes.
  • Q6 B2 ⭐ Checkout synchronously calls 5 services, each 99.9 % available. What's checkout's availability, and how would you improve it?
  • Q7 B2 Give a grocery example where you'd choose strong consistency and one where you'd accept eventual consistency.
  • Q8 B2 ⭐ Why aren't microservices always better than a monolith?
  • Q9 B2 A product manager says 'the app must be fast.' How do you turn that into a requirement?
  • Q10 B3 ⭐ Our service meets its p99 SLO, but users say the app is slow. What's going on?
  • Q11 B3 Which quality attributes typically conflict, and how do you resolve the conflict in practice?
  • Q12 B3 Explain durability vs availability with an example where you have one but not the other.
  • Q13 B3 How do you design for operability?
  • Q14 B3 ⭐ A cached serviceability answer caused 1,900 undeliverable orders. Walk me through your fix.
  • Q15 B4 ⭐ A team proposes 26 microservices for an MVP with 8 engineers. What's your response in the design review?
  • Q16 B4 You're starting a new platform. How do you decide which NFRs matter most?
  • Q17 B4 How do you treat cost as an architectural attribute?
  • Q18 B4 ⭐ What are reversible vs irreversible decisions? Give examples, and how you handle each.
  • Q19 B4 How do you evaluate a design document you didn't write?
  • Q20 B4 Trace the evolution from monolith to SOA to microservices. What's next, and what did each era teach us?

docs.title: 02. Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation ⭐
docs.text:
• Q1 B1 ⭐ Why do back-of-the-envelope estimates in a system design interview at all?
  • Q2 B1 ⭐ Convert 10 million requests per day into requests per second, and give the peak.
  • Q3 B1 Which latency numbers should every engineer know, and why do they matter?
  • Q4 B1 Estimate storage for 1 million orders per day for one year.
  • Q5 B2 ⭐ How do you derive a peak factor instead of just picking one?
  • Q6 B2 ⭐ Use Little's Law to size a database connection pool.
  • Q7 B2 Why does the read/write ratio matter for design?
  • Q8 B2 Estimate bandwidth for the product listing API at peak and how to reduce it.
  • Q9 B2 How many servers do you need for 20 K req/s?
  • Q10 B3 ⭐ Walk me through a capacity estimate for checkout during a festival sale.
  • Q11 B3 ⭐ We have autoscaling. Why did the sale still fail in the first minutes?
  • Q12 B3 How do you manage the database connection budget across 26 services?
  • Q13 B3 How would an estimate reveal a hot key problem before production?
  • Q14 B3 Your estimate was 3× off in production. What went wrong and how do you catch it earlier?
  • Q15 B4 ⭐ How would you set up capacity planning as an ongoing process for a 26-service platform?
  • Q16 B4 How do you estimate the infrastructure cost of a new feature per order?
  • Q17 B4 ⭐ The business expects 10× growth in 2 years. What breaks first and how do you plan?
  • Q18 B4 How do you present capacity estimates and their uncertainty to executives?
  • Q19 B4 How do you estimate when there's no historical data (a new city launch or a new product)?
  • Q20 B4 Is N+1 or zone-failure headroom worth the cost? How do you decide?
